_childDocuments_.review: normally when i like a game i'll leave a review that just says "this game's badass" to help it with the algorithm. with souldiers i have to say "this game's badass, but" and then type a lot more words.souldiers is a troidlike where you play as a generic but unreasonably capable guy with no name, personality, or backstory on a vague quest from which he gets constantly sidetracked. you have a choice of three generic guys to play as, which is locked in from the start of the game: sword guy, bow guy, or staff guy. the whole trinity of guys is here. i have only played as the sword guy so far, who is pretty simple but fun if you like to play as a guy with a sword who runs and jumps around and swings a sword. maybe the other guys are miserable to play as and you'll hate the game if you play as them, i don't know. anyway, as you play, your chosen guy will level up, acquire new abilities and elemental powers, and progress along a skill tree (that is honestly pretty underwhelming, at least for sword guy). there are other guys (mostly generic, some not) on the same quest as your guy but they don't do a whole lot. it's mostly just your guy. some people probably won't like that your guy is so totally generic, but i love it.souldiers is a good game. i can say this confidently. the action is simple, but quick and satisfying. the art is great. the music is good. the boss fights are fun and diverse, and the game as a whole presented a solid, but not overwhelming, challenge on its hardest difficulty. the world is huge, there are tons of subweapons and accessories to find, sidequests to complete, things to backtrack to as you get new abilities, etc.one of the things that, to me, makes souldiers stand out within the genre is that it feels more like a zelda game than a troidlike. the game's world is comprised of a number of sprawling dungeons, broken up by mostly linear overworld segments. you'll get to a dungeon, get a new ability or two in the dungeon, and then navigate some more overworld and plot before getting to the next dungeon, until the end of the game.all this probably makes souldiers sound like a fairly normal and good video game, which it is. but.souldiers is, for better or for worse, the longest troidlike i have played; my first playthrough took around 23 hours, ending at around 90% total completion. i tried to be thorough (within reason) and did not spend a lot of time being lost, so you can assume that at least 20 of those hours were totally productive. most of this time will come from the dungeons, of which there are 6, and they are all 2-3 hours long depending on how much you explore and how lost you get (plus more time later if you choose to backtrack, as most of them have significant chunks that are inaccessible until you have abilities acquired after the dungeon). normally i do not fault games for being too long, but in the case of most of these dungeons, it is just too much. you will get you abilities pretty early into the dungeon, and then it's the same handful of enemies and gimmicks for the entire thing, and it becomes something of a drag even if it never actually becomes bad.souldiers looks great, but can be frustrating to visually parse when things get hectic. most enemies are small, have very short tells for their attacks, or both. you have to squint to see what an enemy is doing, and good luck even doing that if you have damage numbers on, which make it even harder to see. when enemies overlap with each other, or with you, it becomes almost impossible to see what they are doing. you can play around all of this, but it doesn't feel like you SHOULD have to.i mentioned earlier that there are tons of subweapons and accessories to find, and quests to complete. there are in fact too many. there are, i think, 20-something subweapons? there are a lot of them. pretty sure i didn't find them all, and i don't feel like counting them in any case. some are of course more useful than others, but none are particularly useful until fully upgraded, which requires a limited resource you'll pick up throughout the game. the main issue here is that switching between these quickly becomes overwhelming; without going into the pause menu (which i'll mention now is a very clunky menu that i never fully got used to), you can only switch between weapons linearly along a list, and that's not something you want to do 10 times to find the weapon you want during combat; you're just going to have to stop and menu. accessories have the same issues; while there is a good degree of thought and choice that goes into picking them, you'll frequently want to swap them, and menuing this feels way less comfortable than it needs to be.most of the aforementioned sidequests involve going to a previously visited area and finding a miniboss, which exists in the form of a souped-up normal enemy enemy. the problem is you are not told where exactly the enemy is; sometimes there are obvious locations for them but in some cases, especially in the dungeons, i did not even want to bother combing these giant areas for an underwhelming reward. the sidequests that aren't doing this are usually unremarkable as well.lastly, and i'm pretty sure this is the main reason why the game's reviews are (at time of writing) mixed overall, the game can be buggy, and it used to be way buggier. a few times the game would start bugging out (sometimes significantly) during area transitions, and i had to restart the game to fix it. most significantly, though, there is a significant portion of map (which was fortunately optional) that i was entirely unable to access because a platforming element that i had to activate simply would not work. this persisted through restarting the game, and i'm not sure anything short of a new save (if that) would fix it. there are reports of gamebreaking bugs in this game, and i'm not sure if they were patched, and this game hasn't received any updates in quite some time so i wouldn't expect any remaining bugs to be fixed.i realize i've said a lot more bad about this game than good but it's just easier for me to talk about why things are bad than why they are good. as i said at the start of this review, this game's badass, but. it has some issues. those issues may be just a nuisance, or they may ruin the game for you if not render it unplayable. this is the studio's first game, and i'm really hoping it's not their last, because if they learn from the mistakes they made with this game, i think they can put out a game where i can just leave a review that says "this game's badass" and not have to type out an essay.this game is in the november 2023 humble monthly. i got the game from there. if you got the game from there and you own it anyway, you might as well give it a try because you, like me, might really like it in spite of its issues. if you're buying the game outright, just be aware that you're probably not going to know if you actually like it or not before the refund period is up.

_childDocuments_.review: Souldiers is easily the most Overwhelmingly Positive.... Mixed review game I've ever played.  I don't know if people were upset at the initial launch of this game or something, but it's a real shame.  This is a fantastic game!  It's like a Final Fantasy, Secret of Mana style Metroidvania.  It's drop dead gorgeous. The combat is fantastic and deep. Boss Fights are deliciously challenging. The Music is top-tier. The pixel art is about as close to perfection as you can get. The game world is a joy to explore.  The Mechanics are spot on.  Just about every element of this game is finely crafted to near perfection.I really don't understand the hate for the game, it's already approaching Masterpiece territory for me alongside the likes of Hollowknight and Ori 2.  It's the Fantasy Metroidvania I have always wanted to play that didn't exist.  The resource management, combat, and platforming all mesh marvelously, and I find the game extremely enthralling to play. The world and dungeons are staggeringly large, and within the dungeons they have many varied sections almost like sub-biomes with unique mechanics, visual elements, and enemies to keep gameplay fresh and the dungeons big!If we are so spoiled by the likes of Hollow Knight that a Metroidvania like Souldiers is considered mediocre, I fear we will scare away devs and investors from creating new ones.  This game would have blown people's minds had it released on the SNES or PSX... This is not your typical retro indie Metroidvania.  It’s more akin to HollowKnight, a semi-open world, genre-pushing entry that goes far beyond the typical length, mechanics, and freedom of exploration that the classics and their spiritual successors offer.Souldiers is criminally underrated considering its quality and scope.  I hope it can crawl out of the 'mixed' reviews hole and build the cult following it would seemingly already have if launch had been better. It's a Metroidvania that deserves a better score and more success. We should reward this type of money, effort, and love in an Indie Game. It's a shame that it's poor review scores have crippled it's chances of reaching a wider audience.

_childDocuments_.review: What a shambles. Massive blanket nerfs across the entire game trivialise everything rather than just tweaking things. While some of the issues I had have been fixed with the patch (see below), most of the things that made the game frustrating or I consider iffy design choices haven't been changed at all. I've left things in their original places to retain some semblance of the original review, but highlighted improvements.There are a lot of systems in Souldiers which are great in principle but meh in execution.I’ve written a lot about the negatives of the game, but it’s because I believe the design issues are very specific and thus diving into them in more detail than “combat = bad/unfair” is warranted.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of effort was put into the absolutely beautiful pixel graphics, and as far as I can see, not a lot of effort was put inot anything else. Level design varies with some aboslutely bland parts where you are just moving from left to right, killing enemies on the way, to some down right unnecessarily large dungeons which can take you hours to complete. At the start of the game you choose a class to which you are locked for the rest of the game, that's absolutely fine. Many games have you choose a class that you have to stick with. The problem with this game is that it hides all skills/talents for your class untill you've reached the necessary level. That means that from the start of your adventure you have no idea what kind of skills your class has access to. Also, you have a limited amount of skill points to distribute, basically forcing you to not spend anything if you want to specialize in any way. This is further compounded by the fact that you have to level quite a bit to unlock anything. This brings me to the combat which just gives you the impression that it wasn't tested enough to see whether it is actually fun or not. Combat generally feels same-y though in some cases you are just left baffled with some of the decisions made by the developers(more than once you get a powerup in a dungeon which heals the monsters in that area). The game offers you sub-weapons that you can use in combat and to solve puzzles. But all subweapons share the same "ammunition" which has a low drop rate and you're often left with no ammo to do anything. This becomes extra frustrating when you need one of your sub-weapons to solve a puzzle but you're out of ammo, forcing you to backtrack to a shop to buy more. I was also experiencing severe lagg whenever interacting with the save points, so much so that the game would basically freeze for a second or two before resuming. Also the loading times are unreasonably long for a game that is only about 800MB. Both of these problems could be on my end though. This game has the "Metroidvania" tag, it's not a Metroidvania. It is a platform action game that has a level design that is remniscient of other Metroidvania-games. Some people are saying that this is a hard game, it's not. This is an immensy frustrating game. I cannot in any capacity recommend this game. It you want a modern metroidvania, play Hollow Knight, Vigil The Longest Night or Ender Lillies. If you want a hard metroidvania, play La Mulana or its sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: 2024 Playthrough with all the latest patches and content changes.  Warrior Difficulty - Full Completion on Caster.I don't recommend this game to anyone that wants to play a fun game.From the very beginning, this seems like an innocent and cute looking metroidvania.  You get plunged in with a choice between 3 classes that you don't really get a clue as to how they will play and start with very little in the way of abilities or attacks like most metroidvanias.  From the start, you can feel that the controls are a little clunky.  Long input delays lead to the game feeling unresponsive even at the start, which is very baffling as it had to be an active developer decision to make the game play clunky.Most of the level design is okay, with simple puzzles, secret areas, and most of the time at least a decent handful of save points to stop you from feeling too frustrated at running out of resources between sections, since about 1/5 of the way through the game you have a town you can teleport to from any save point to rebuy potions and upgrade.For the most part, the boss design is okay and challenging (perhaps a bit frustrating on the higher difficulties, but still nothing egregiously bad).What really takes the game down is some very deliberate design decisions that feel designed to annoy the player.  At one point I think I had to fight 3 bosses back to back with no point to refresh resources and no sign that this was going to happen.  A lot of the puzzles rely on walljumping, which is possibly one of the worst coded mechanics in this game, just failing to register that you are in fact attached to the wall you are jumping from in 1 in 6 attempts.  There is a quest in the game that literally just makes you fight an overwhelming amount of non-boss creatures for 30 actual minutes with no break and no progress saves.I don't think I would ever play a game made by these devs again.  Games are played for enjoyment with a sprinkling of challenge mixed in.  I sure as heck am not playing games because I want to explore your purposefully designed tedium and baked in annoyances.Can you beat this game?  Yes.  Will you feel fulfilled once you are done?  Probably not.  This one is truly just a skip, you won't have missed anything if you choose to play any of the dozens of other highly rated metroidvanias out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, I don't hate the game.I think this game has a ton of potential, It's pretty, and handles semi-okay.The difficulty is there (albeit I am playing on Warrior/Hard) Feels about right for boss fights, regular enemies are just getting boring... My biggest complaints about this game would be...1. I'm playing a Mage, when do I start to feel like a mage? cause so far, there's nothing interesting about mage. Magic burst is by far the most depressing mage "strong attack" I've ever seen. Sure its damage is -okay- by the games standards, but the skill itself is so boring.2. Why is the pacing for this game so slow? Did I miss something? Like, its been giving me all these "upgrade" ore but I still don't have a spot to use them (at the time of this review i've only just entered the forest with a bunch of dog archers)(update, got to town and can now use them... much to my expectation, not enough to do anything with...) The Exp is slow, and the skill/mastery tree requires obscene amounts of levels to do anything with.3. Chests feel completely unrewarding... Like there hasn't been a time yet where I ran off to find a chest and be like "Omg this was completely worth it" its more like "Well.. Im not a completionist, if I die, I'll be skipping this chest..."4. Please add a means of ledge grabbing by holding a button or something, the amount of times I've taken pointless damage because my character just has to grab a ledge half a foot above him is honestly frustrating.5. Level ups feel near worthless.  The game itself is starting to feel very much like a mobile game in terms of aspects, with out the cash shop or gacha though.Seriously the game has potential, but for me, I can't recommend it in it's current state. Yes I do plan to finish it. and just pray it gets "fun" at a later point..

_childDocuments_.review: First the good: - Art is very pretty although that is often times tarnished by either missing soundeffects (bombs are completely silent, same as some waterfalls) or unfathomably loud ones (talking crowd in the middle of the hub city is incredibly loud even tho sound is completely turned off)Second the bad:- very bad class balance: The scout is quite nicely balanced although fighting any flying enemy is awful. The Archer and Mage are unplayable unless you're some sort of masochist. The Mage has ,on paper, the highest dmg-rating of the three yet deals the least amount of dmg (2 dmg per light attack vs 6 of the scout). The Archer only has 3 arrows to shoot, which you have to manually aim yourself, before using his bow as a boomerang to collect them.Every class comes with a skilltree with skills that are unlocked at lvls 5,8,12,18,20,30,35 and 40. You cannot see which skill is what until you unlock it, every skill except the middle one costs 3 skillpoints to unlock while only getting 1 per level and the available selection of skills really leaves much to be desired. - combat is clunky and dmg is quite unbalanced: Besides the dmg discrepancy mentioned above, the enemies deal a lot of it in mostly quick succession without any windup as a tell. Every class has a shield that can be used to block incoming hits, which is a nice idea although not very useful when it breaks after blocking even the lightest of slaps. Another defensive mechanism of every class is a dodge roll, is has a roughly 2-3s cooldown and can be used to dodge enemy attacks, which again is rendered completely useless either because enemies perform multiple hit combos or because the range of the dodge is too small and you're getting hit by the aoe. Also the cooldown of the dodge does take a lot longer than the enemies take to attack, leaving you naked most of the time with your only option to just run away after hitting once or maybe twice.- enemy design worse than Fromsoft's teleporting dogs: The general enemy design is very frustrating. Flying enemies fly up into the sky without any possibility to reach them as soon as you jump close to them, archers dodge back either while shooting at you or while you're swinging at them, enemies that teleport behind you to backstab or hold up a shield while activly following you while trying to get behind them. Fighting any enemy always feels like they move a lot more freely than you do, unhindered by attack or dodge animations or cooldowns. And if that is not enough, usually you get to fight 2-3 at the same time which often results in you getting combo'ed to death because i-frames are a luxury not included.Bosses feel the same as enemies do but with a lot more health. Fights feel too long and dragged out with infuriating mechanics, questionable hitboxes and unskippable introductions that you have to sit through every time you try again. - generally questionable choices: While playing the game you come across a large amount of very weird design choices. Menus are navigated by using the d-pad and LB and RB although the game is played with analog sticks, subweapons and potions are also switched by using the d-pad which often leads to you drinking a potion while sifting through your 7 different subweapons because you cannot unselect which weapon to use, same for potions with the nice caveat that you can only hold 3 of every potion (including healing potions) with none of them giving you any worthwhile bonus while taking a fairly long time to drink. Another fun choice is that you lose everything that you've collected/gained (exp, gold, items, map discovery) when you die since you last saved, which is only possible at special points that are quite rare between sections. In addition, traversing the different regions also isn't fun. Very narrow jumps, offscreen attacks, blind jumps, nearly invisible booby traps, dark rooms etc. all don't make it enjoyable to run around the too big and too winding dungeons with a map that almost doesn't help because everything looks the same on it.All in all the game feels as if it still needs a good couple of months in development and about twice as many ppl to playtest it to iron out all the bugs and kinks and completely random design choices to make it an enjoyable game.EDIT: After putting in a couple more hours to sate my curiosity to see wether it gets better with more levels or not, the answer is no.I discovered even more stupid crap that nobody wants to find in their game which are:-slow moving escort mechanics which include (timed) platforming and the escortee turning back if you leave their proximity-multi boss-fights that include multiple status effects (because fighting two bosses alone in this insane game isn't unfun enough)-flying bosses that you cannot attack atleast 70% of the whole fight-even longer safepoint-less sections than before-buggy teleporters that force you to reload your safe in order to use them (it happens a lot)Skip this one. It's absolutely not worth your money, time and sanity.

_childDocuments_.review: Souldiers is one of those games that was really appealing in the demo but completely fell apart in the full release.The largest issue, at least for me, is that the devs don't really seem to have any idea how to tune difficulty. Before the patch, the difficulty felt very artificial - pump up the enemy's health and damage while keeping the player's very low, which creates a very boring form of difficulty where enemies are fairly simple to deal with but you're doing so repeatedly over a long period of time which results in heavily punished mistakes that send you back to a checkpoint.Post patch, most of the enemy health and damage values were tweaked which only further revealed that the combat in this game is extremely hollow. Enemies simply are not engaging or fun to fight, leveling up is hilariously pointless, and the tension driven by the game's frustrating health and damage pools is replaced mostly by moment to moment encounters feeling like tedium.For anyone interested in the other metroidvania elements of exploration, treasure finding, etc, most of that is about as mediocre as it gets. Treasures are often just more currency, consumables, or bits to fill up your meters. Sometimes you may find an equippable item, they're often trash, very rarely you'll find this game's version of a heart container piece. Exploration generally amounts to a very obvious "come back with X power up to reach Y box" and nothing more, rather than leading to any new pathways or anything interesting.At least the art is good.TLDR: Souldiers is a game that was designed to succeed or fail completely based on its combat, how good the characters feel to play, and how fun the enemies are to fight. It failed at all of these things, and nothing else here is worth spending your time on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start with this one. For full fairness I DONT REALLY CARE FOR METROIDVANIAS for reasons we wont really get into. This game is BEAUTIFUL to look at and watch play out on screen. The combat is juicy just enough to keep me playing and experimenting. This game is also HUGE. After about the 5 hour mark, we looked in the log book and I think we saw like 8% of the monsters that are in this game which I loved. I am a SUCKER for monster design.We also got to the desert biome and we explored the temple for a good hour and a half to then check the map and only 10% of the temple was explored HOT DAMNMy main draw backs though is I wish there was more character progression to compliment along side all this exploration. There are 3 character classes you can start with which do feel like really shake up how you go through the game. Thats cool but I wish there was more ways to shape the feel or execution of how I played the characters THROUGH the story. You can pick things like a trinket that may give you some stats or a talent from the talent tree which is also slow and doesn't have to many options.  You can tell since there wasnt many talents they just made it so you get to unlock them SUPER slow. You need like 3 level ups to get one talent pick, then I think they also get more expensive ? Ill say the lack of character development is the real negative on this over all really fun game.I still recommend but just dont expect Diablo like customization for instance. You arent getting loot drops and things like that really but if you know that going into it, you are probably in for a awesome time. It had a real SNES vibe to it and the charm always felt really great.

_childDocuments_.review: Underrated. From what I've read, during launch the game had multiple bugs and balancing issues. Currently the game only contains some minor bugs that do not significantly affect the gameplay. The only bug still present that is a little bit bothersome is the map bug, moving the map in the direction you want can be a shore. I played it on the highest difficulty and I don't think there are any balancing problems, the combat is fast and satisfying, the enemies are diverse and have unique movements, the exploration is satisfactory, the final bosses represent a challenge that is satisfying to overcome, forcing you to use the various resources of the game (block, parry, elements, items). The story is good (not great) with some good characters, more tragic endings might have helped the plot. The combat and the exploration are the strong points of this game, a must play if you like a challenging combat and metrodivanias. I also loved some of the little details of this game, such as how the soldier hits the shield with the sword each time a new challenger appears or the game initial screen after you finish it.If a sequel comes out, I will definitely have a look at it.

_childDocuments_.review: The current overall average review score for Souldiers (as of the time of this writing, 64%) is criminally low. If you like the trailers for this game and you like action metroidvanias and JRPG style fantasy worlds, I think you're going to love this game. I just started playing this game in March of 2023, so I have the benefit of whatever patches were released following the game's initial launch. Maybe it was worse at some point, but I think Souldiers is a fantastic game and I hope to see its review scores crawl upward. - This game is poorly marketed as a Soulslike. That makes no sense to me. Yes there are save / heal points that respawn the enemies. Yes there is an active dodge. That doesn't make this game a soulslike.To better judge if you'd like the game, I wouldn't compare it to souls games, I'd compare it to action RPGs like Secret of Mana, plus metroidvanias like Metroid Dread and Hollow Knight.It has a very traditional JRPG style story with beautiful top-of-its-class pixel art and music, like Seiken Densetsu 3 for SNES (Trials of Mana). If that combo sounds fun, this game is what you want.The journey is long and epic, the locations are huge -- this is probably the biggest sidescrolling action RPG I've ever played. Buckle in for an epic adventure. These are not snack-sized dungeons. - On Warrior difficulty (the 2nd highest of 4 difficulty options), the game was very difficult, and I might say unforgivingly difficult at times. The game is unapologetic in giving you razor thin dodge windows, or enemy attack telegraph animations. Even the platforming can demand precision. This can sometimes be at odds against the fact that your character ability animations may take a little time to wind-up. In the game's toughest moments, you have to memorize enemy patterns, think ahead, AND be precise, in addition to knowing the correct strategy. It's a lot to ask of the player IMO. Games which demand precision also usually have extremely responsive controls, but like I said, even your basic attacks have some windup time.I ended up playing a lot of the game mashing the jump and attack buttons together because if you're standing on the ground when you attack, you can't move left and right. It's a bit silly, and strikes me as a design planning oversight and prototyping mistake.It is likely the lower difficulties are more generous in terms of combat in that you'll be able to survive taking more hits. But I would doubt that the actual combat mechanics are any easier in terms of whether or not you take or deal damage in any single instance. As a result, playing on a low difficulty is probably the right call unless you're a glutton for punishment like I am. I might've enjoyed the game more on the default difficulty.Based on other reviews I've read, and my own experience, picking the Caster class can also make your early game (maybe first 25%) experience more of a slog. I ended the game feeling like my Caster was extremely powerful, and I imagined that the other characters wouldn't be able to nuke enemies so rapidly as I was able to. But the start of the game is rough. You have few abilities, less health, very limited attack range, and punishingly low mana. You have to be SCRAPPY early game as a Caster. I might've had more fun as the Scout with less of a rags-to-riches feel in terms of game combat balance. - Exploration is not perfect. About 10% of the exploration secrets can be tedious. There are some progressive exploration elements, like when you learn to air-dash, double-jump, unlock bombs, sand platforms and water bubbles. However a lot of the secrets are just ... walls that you can walk through. There's no visual cue for these, and the game's purchasable maps don't always reveal unexplored space. There are also bombable surfaces with no clue that they're bombable, and again they don't show on the map. So basically if you want to 100% Souldiers, you'll either need a playthrough guide, or you'll have to bomb and walk into every surface manually. I recommend just not worrying about the secrets instead. Testing if you can arbitrarily move through literally every wall is not fun exploration IMO. - The story is a bit all over the place. The game does a lot of adding new questions and problems to the story without resolving most of them. It's great for building a universe that they may want to expand upon, but it can leave the conclusion of the story feeling unsatisfying. Given the low review scores, I'm concerned that they really shot themselves in the foot. If Souldiers doesn't sell well enough, this grand world they built will never conclude any of the major plot points introduced by the game which remain unresolved.Considering the beautiful cutscenes the game starts you with, the lack of payoffs to the plot's initial premise really stand out to me as a narrative mistake.There's a ton of fun characters, and you get to know each of them better, but the fundamental plot just barely moves by the end of the game. IMO they should've focused on making one great game with one great story to completion, and leave in minor hooks to build the big MCU-style meta-narrative that it seems like they're going for.Anyway, if you made it through this long ramble, thanks for reading.This is a really great game, and for what it is, it's huge and is really the very best you'll find in the genre in terms of art (with the exception of standard particle-style VFX which feel very out-of-place with the game's art style), action, exploration, and narrative, despite the flaws I mentioned. The flaws I pointed out are minor in the grand scheme. This game is a must-play for anyone who wishes there were more sidescroller RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? The pixel art is definitly master class.Your army got lost in a strange place, and you seem to be the only capable fighter to explore the underground surroundings. Your comrades are soon either dead, lost or trapped, and you free them or take their belongings from their dead corpses. The story becomes marginal after the introduction, so your long stretches of gameplay will not be interrupted very often. It is fun to meet the ninja Sinka or to free the shopkeeper from spiders, though. You can choose to play either a scout (swordfighter), archer or wizard, which have different weapons and stats. Switching them is not possible during the game, only a complete restart allows you to play a different class. Your character has not only hitpoints and stamina, but also skills. When you level up after killing enough enemies (which fully heals you), you receive Mastery Relics that allow you to learn skills (like counterattack or spinning slice and many more) for your character. The skill tree is different for the three classes, and you advance it... very slowly. The maps are large. Maybe a bit too large for my taste. Either you love large levels full of hard-hitting enemies and savepoints far apart, or you won't enjoy this game. You can play for hours and still have a 25% map reveal... The automap is good, but since it allows you only to scroll and not to zoom, you may get lost even when using the automap. Ok, maybe not get lost, but you need to scroll around like crazy to find a place where you might be able to continue. And when you select your next fast travel location, you cannot scroll at all... so you won't always be sure where you end up until you know all locations by heart. And I hate being stuck in a large level and have no idea where to continue. It has of course happened to me before in Metroidvanias, but I can't remember being frequently lost in such large levels and searching for a new opening or skill/item to continue. You jump, fight, dodge, pull rocks and levers or throw bombs, avoid traps and fight various monsters. Monsters respawn when you revisit a place later. They generally carry either coins or (very few) health points. Get hit once by a (lowly) monster and you lose a bunch of hitpoints. Try to hit flying enemies and you will begin to hate them. Some stationary enemies appear to be within easy reach of your sword when you jump, but you still cannot hit them, your sword just doesn't harm them. You cannot attack while ledge hanging, nor do you release the ledge when hitting the attack button. Bosses are deadly, but they are bosses so that's ok. I love to avoid a boss for 3 minutes to be able to attack him once and reduce 1% of his life (or miss him). Not lying. I also love to see the bossfight introduction over and over, because it seems unskippable. There are shops around the levels to turn your coins into potions or vials. You fight with a main weapon, and you can use a second weapon (bomb) which is upgradeable. Find emeralds to permanetly enhance your hero.Choose between 3 difficulty levels to adapt the combat to your skill level. It is still hard on easy, not that I played that. The game is saved when you activate a checkpoint (Dragon Sword). Dying brings you to the last savepoint without penalty (except losing everything you gained since the last save and all mobs respawning...), or you can use a feather to continue were you died. When you drown (you can't swim), you are revived at the same spot immediately. Checkpoints also serve as portals for fast travel. Sometimes it feels these checkpoints are a bit far away when you want to quit... and just don't find a (new) checkpoint to save. An automap shows your sourroundings, an encyclopedia writes down everything about characters, enemies or the tutorial. Like in any good Metroidvania, backtravelling is required to access parts of the gameworld (mostly just items) which have not been accessible before. Gamepad works fine.Fantastic looking Metroidvania with some annoying quirks for the average player - too large maps, too powerful mobs, too long cooldowns for some abilities.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game on recommendation from my brother. We both like a challenge, and this game was providing an enjoyable experience - it was challenging, it was satisfying, and the obstacles and bosses could be played very cleanly once you knew how they worked. There were minor bugs and some more responsive movement (crouching) would have been a nice QoL change. But in general, I play a lot of games and I can genuinely say I was having the most fun in a game this year.Que patch 1.1.1. Despite the fact that there were 3 difficulty levels for this exact reason, the usual crowd could not get over the percieved slight to their gamer ego that was Warrior (hard mode). Negative whiny reviews started pouring in and the devs caved. Oh boy they caved.Over night the game became a joke. You do effectively quadruple damage as compared to before. There are save points every 2 minutes (that heal you to full, so health management is out of the window since you can get hit half a dozen times every fight and just facetank) - yes they added extra savepoints in every concievable place. Enemies have half health, even the bosses, to the point where you don't get to see all phases because you accidentially skip them. Resources regenerate faster, secondary weapons cost less, yadda yadda. This is on HARD mode. Yes, it was not enough to make easy easier. They broke every challenge in every difficulty setting.They broke a trap at one point in the game where you could not teleport out of a level for a bit. Can't have that, somebody might be upset. They broke a time puzzle where you had to activate things in order because uuuh, having to try more than 3 times leads to consoooomer dissatisfacion I guess?I was making my way through the game on Warrior(hard) at my pace, progressing from checkpoint to checkpoint, dying quite a bit, figuring out how to get from A to B and how to approach fights. I'm older, I'm slow and not even a good player, but I was having fun. After the patch I walked straight through an entire zone in first try. Just to give you a sense what kind of change they went for. I watched the cutscene and uninstalled the game.If you want mind numbingly easy, play on freaking easy, my god, or petition the devs to add a very easy setting. It's there for a reason. Don't ruin an entire game for people who like to have to try more than once.Devs, at least add the original Warrior difficulty as a setting -.-

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend the game at this time. While fun and full of potential, the annoyance of the game stuttering and causing eaten inputs because of delay due to critical hits or elemental weakness hits and the hurt boxes on a lot of attacks being extremely disjointed causing you to take damage you should be avoiding based on what your eyeballs are seeing is too much. There are also enemies that will attack you from way off screen. Long before you've seen them or long after you'd think they lost interest. Hey, at least the art and music are FANTASTIC. SFX, however, will eventually destroy your ears when they stack on top of each other. I'm looking at you stacked enemies.Post June 23rd update: My review is pretty much the same. They fixed nothing that made the game bad and just did a blanket nerf to the game's difficulty (Which was fine where it was in my opinion. Not every game is meant to be easy and they had lower difficulty settings). The update notes even mention fixing the elemental and critical hit delay but it didn't change at all. I haven't noticed any black screens yet but I don't know if I'll make it back to the area where they were most common.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally published in Murphy's Multiverse:Whether it was intentional or not, the latest Metroidvania from 6-man team Retro Forge, Souldiers, has a strong JRPG essence that permeates it. Despite being a self-described Souls-like Metroidvania, nearly everything about is begging to be presented in turn-based combat. Its aesthetic harkens back to the old-school JRPG games from the 90s. Its sense of high-fantasy adventure echoes that of Dragon Quest and the original Final Fantasy. And you might as well as slap JRPG veteran Nobu Uematsu’s name on Souldier’s music. All this isn’t to say that Souldiers is better off as a completely different game. It’s to recognize how much of a love-letter Souldiers is to adventure stories of yore. You play as one of three unnamed soldiers who, along with the rest of their battalion, are suddenly transported into the afterlife by mysterious Valkyries. With the help of the surviving soldiers, your goal is to find out why you were transported into this unknown land between life and death in the first place and how to get back to your homeland. All this while traversing different biomes, solving puzzles, and fighting all kinds of creatures. There are three soldiers to choose from. A scout, archer, and caster. Like any RPG, each soldier has their own set of attainable skills and comes with their own pros and cons. For example, the caster has low health but has a mid-ranged basic attack that homes in on enemies. The archer, on the other hand, has a full-ranged arrow attack that needs to be refilled when the arrows run out. For better or worse, whichever character you pick will drastically alter your experience. Despite the game’s attempts to give each character equal footing, the punishing scenarios you are likely to find yourself in makes the experience feel unbalanced. You’re likely to run out of defensive and mobility options in a second when you run into a section where multiple enemies with unique attacks come at you at the same time. In the case of the caster, it’s a frequent scenario. That sense of imbalance and difficulty make up the game’s Souls-like elements. Like any game of the same vein, the mechanics are designed to keep players constantly on their feet. You run out of stamina blocking and parrying. Anytime you use a save point respawns enemies in the area.  But unlike most of the good Souls-likes, Souldiers’ progression system doesn’t feel rewarding. It takes a long while for your character to amass a good number of skills as some enemies just don’t drop enough experience points. On top of that, the currency items are scarce and basic healing items too expensive. Souls-likes are hard by design but they’re also very rewarding. You want to be rewarded with cool items for overcoming a tough fight or a tricky platforming section. Souldiers’ doesn’t quite feel satisfying or gratifying in its moment-to-moment gameplay. Its difficulty oftentimes feels questionable, with no engaging reason behind it other than to make a game hard.This gets in the way of the fun as it takes a while for Souldiers’ best systems to open up. You spend the first couple of hours with only basic skills and little maneuverability. The platforming starts off as generic and uninspired. It isn’t until you invest roughly 10 hours and get to the third biome that the combat and platforming elements get fun. Combined with its conservative sense of progression, players will really have to commit to get the most out of Souldiers.Despite these issues, Souldiers offers a depth of engagement with the most prominent being its combat system. There’s a lot to experiment with in Souldiers. One of the early skills acquired by the caster is the ability to automatically create a reflection anytime to you dodge. This reflection can be detonated, damaging all enemies nearby which add a layer of strategy to all your encounters. As the story progresses, you acquire the ability to imbue an element to your attacks which you can switch on a whim. Occasionally, these elemental attacks also serve platforming purposes. Like most RPGs, items and weapons can be upgraded at a price. Secondary weapons such as throwable bombs, axes, and spears can get a small damage buff. However, one missing component is the ability to sell items. In a game where it takes some time to save enough money, being able to sell useless items should be allowed. As a Metroidvania, Souldiers meets the usual requirements. Maps are vast and intricately connected and are sometimes gated by specific skills. Sadly, the exploration isn’t as intuitive or exciting as Hollow Knight as there’s some handholding on where to go to advance the story. Nonetheless, it fulfills its purpose.Solely through its beautifully rendered pixel art and the polished animation that gives it life, Souldiers bypasses all its flaws and manages to be a truly impressive piece of work. Pixelated colors of endless hues that pop on screen make up the detailed sprites of characters and landscapes. Every inch feels lively; even something as insignificant as the leaves in the background moves with the wind. Character stances look graceful and attack animations are brimming with style. Souldiers perfectly captures the visual essence of iconic anime-inspired 16-bit games.For all its problems, Souldiers has an ambition that is commendable. It successfully commits to being a decent Metroidvania with a steep Souls-like difficulty while paying homage to its JRPG influences. If you’re looking for a challenging game that rouses nostalgia, Souldiers can’t be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay I'm not one to ever write reviews for games but the mixed reception for this one is really baffling to me. The game is beautiful. Every sprite is artfully made with clear love and care. Animations are endearing and polished. Music is quite good albeit a bit forgettable at times, yet I still caught myself humming along to some tunes pretty often. Gameplay is what people seem to have most of a problem with... Game is definitely hard, but by no means unfair or glitchy from what I have experienced. The controls and their quirks can take a bit to get used to. However, much like every other modern 2D platformer, if you want to have smooth and clean movement, you need to put in time and effort into that. The game definitely allows for satisfying and smooth map traversal, but it is definitely dictated by skill. The spaces between save points can be long but all this does is encourage mindful and strategic gameplay. You can't just turn your brain off and hack-n-slash at everything until the next save. You will die several times getting between save points, and every single death, you will have learned something and become better for it. The monsters all pose a real threat in some way shape or form, and you WILL get hit a dumb slime sometimes, and that's just part of the game. You learn how to handle different combinations of mobs at the same time, and the game definitely eases you into learning each monsters attacks before throwing multiple mixes at you.Bosses are definitely the kind of encounters that you most likely won't beat on your 1st, 2nd, or even 5th attempt. They range from simple combat patterns to more complex and nuanced behaviors depending on your range, actions, timing, etc.. Every encounter feels meaningful and rewarding to best, and requires strategy, patience, and skill to overcome. I've been loving this game. Definitely a good timesink for completionists as well. Don't listen to the bad reviews. It's good.

THERE IS A PLATFORMING PUZZLE THAT IS IMPOSSIBLE FOR ME TO DO AS THE CHARACTER AUTO CLIMBS WHEN YOU NEED HIM TO HANG ONTO THE LEDGEbosses such to fight even though there is no penalty for death. platforming sectinos later in the game suuuuuuuuuuuuuck becuase the controls just don't work as you want them too. auto climbing when I don't want to, not auto climbing when I want to. etc etc etc etc. I wanted to finish the game. _childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I am halfway through the game, so this is an early review.I will start by saying this game, even with its flaws, is definitely worth a buy.At its current patch I have not encountered a single bug or performance hit in 20 hours of play.There is a lot that is well done here and if I had to score it, it would end up at around The art is absolutely incredible, there is no other way to put it. Characters have so many animations, everything you do is so tactile.Open your map and the character pulls the map from the backpack, drink potions, different skills and combos are animated differently, there is so much variety here.City folks are doing their daily routine fully animated, with variations on NPCs that fill it up.Dungeons are varied so it feels like you are really traversing this world.This one is a mixed bag for me, I do not really like old repetitive OSTs, so most of the music did not really do anything for me.The only one, so far, that I really loved was the Sewer one.General SFX are good, it is just the music itself that is a little lacking in my opinion.Nothing to write home about, there is some interesting world building and the concept surrounding the world .Characters motivations are good enough, they are usually tropes but not bad.There is also a different responses from NPCs as you progress through the story, which is always nice.Combat got me pleasantly surprised, there is a lot going on in terms of mechanical difficulty and variety.There is 3 classes, being your knight, archer and mage. They all play differently, with different skill trees and moveset.You have your standard dodge, block and parry, but you also have elemental affinities that need to be swapped on the fly, a counter dodge mechanic that gives you an extra dodge.The game throws different enemies with different elements and different attack patterns, so you need to manage positioning and elemental affinity quite quickly.I am playing on Master difficulty and it makes me have to pay attention to every single encounter, as you can die quite quickly.As the Archer you also have a refillable ammo meter, meaning you need to balance close range with medium range combat.Overall there is a lot of good things going on here, with the main negative being its tool weapons system, where you get different consumable weapons that recharge. Most of them are weak, which takes a little from the experience, and because the ammo for them is scarce, I end up saving them to stronger enemies and bosses, taking some of the spontaneity out of it.There are some good ideas and looping areas, but it loses track of what makes Metroidvania levels fun: exploration and mystery.The game is structured in such a way that levels end up being linear, you find an upgrade in a dungeon, then go back to the same dungeon to get more loot and more upgrades, and you then find the final boss.There is little sense of true exploration, back tracking and secrets.When you go back to a dungeon, it is usually a really small portion of it that actually uses these upgrades.The game does have quite a few of movement upgrades though, wall jumping, double jumping, air dashing and interaction between the elemental affinity and objects. I think this is the worst part of the game.Checkpoints can be sparse, which can mean you can lose 20 minutes of progress in an instant. This is compounded by the fact this game leans on RPG elements such as percentage based amulet drops from monsters, which you can lose if you die before saving with them and consumables.This causes unfortunate interactions with the save and checkpoint system, the save system works in a way that only player triggered saves are permanent, and checkpoints are temporary during that play session.This means that you might get a checkpoint before a boss, with no consumables, and if you quit out you will lose progress.This was very clear in a section where you fight 3 bosses in a row, with a save point after the first one.If you do not save, or do not purchase potions after the first fight, you will not be able to go back to buy more for the second two. As there is no way to know 2 more boss fights are coming, this is a point where players might get stuck.Tools are all over the place, with most of them being useless, the resource to upgrade them is also very common, making the fact that so many of them are unusable even more pronounced.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential it's unreal. However I cannot recommend it. The game begins like it could be a decent 8/10 game but after a certain time, it descends into the 5/10 depths.The art style is beautiful - one of the things that drew me to the game; that plus the setting and it being a metroidvania.I loved the soundtrack too.But! The story is incoherent - the story plots are strung together by random plot points that don't seem to explain anything prior; almost like several people wrote the narrative but each got a section without knowledge of the others. I know MV games don't NEED a decent story per se but still at the very least have something that is understandable.The game play very quickly becomes repetitive as the skill tree is pretty pointless as are the skills given through bosses. There is a parry system that would be great to be at the forefront of fighting but enemies are designed in such a way that there's no real need to even attempt to parry. The same applies with the skills. I will echo what others have said about the orb wheel too. Most games that include a wheel such as this will either slow the game down or pause it to allow the player to make the choice during chaotic situations. However, this game does no such thing and instead it's best to simply pause the game and manually select. The same applies to the items and secondary weapons.  The other frustrating thing that's also been mentioned is the fact I had to cycle through, in one direction mind, to get to my healing items and/or secondary weapons. Again, pause saves the day! On the topic of the secondary weapons, I found only a couple of them useful and there were FAR too many of them. I didn't even unlock them all! It was particularly frustrating that they tended to do reduced damage to certain enemies - it would have been nice if they had elemental traits much like the orbs did. The maps were far too large, I'm not sure how long  I averaged per map but the general consensus was they were all a slog to get through. The map designs were where I felt this game does not respect the player's time as it seems they were designed to simply prolong game play hours. And because of the fact the weapons you receive as a reward for said exploration were mediocre as mentioned above, the sense of reward fell flat. There was also several areas in certain maps where I had to circle round about 3 times to unlock everything - think it included the sand crystal and bubble, and I had to hit one, do a loop, then do the other, and do another loop.As a result of the slog fest that was to get through maps, I just did not want to go through the final collectathon to grab all the secrets. Most MVs I'm OK with backtracking to pick up missing items (though I'm certainly not a 100%-er) but this game, I dreaded the idea of going back.One last thing was the platforming. So many areas in the game required pixel perfect timing which I felt was a bit out of place in a game like this. Did I complete the game? Yes, but through sheer force of will and determination.Did I enjoy the game? Aspects of it, but majority no.Would I recommend this game? No, only if you are a die hard MV fan.Do I look forward to what the developer's do next? Yes, absolutely. As I stated at the start, there is an 8/10 game underneath all the mess. I think if the team learns from their mistakes, understanding that more doesn't mean better, and just improves what they did well, I really hope their next game is a big improvement and one that more people will enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be one of those unfortunate games that gets destroyed by a bad launch and from players who did not understand some of the core game mechanics. Don't get me wrong, there were countless game breaking bugs and the save system was terrible as the game had a lot fewer save spots. Instead of leaving their game in a frustrating state where players felt punished often by things that felt out of their control, the devs actually responded to their game, so I will address some of that initially.The bugs were initially REALLY frustrating from what I have heard and seen. Soft-locks, immune enemies, skills not working, volume issues. You name it, it was probably a bug. I am unsure as to why this happened, maybe they didn't test the game enough or they put in something last minute that broke everything. I agree that is definitely on the developers. However, the rest of the changes are mostly affected by the player-base not adapting to other play-styles or choosing really complex classes.They essentially downshifted the hp of the monsters from having the hard difficulty hp > normal hp and the normal difficulty hp > easy difficulty hp and made easy mode have monsters with almost half their hp. They also lowered the attack of most enemies by 5-15% damage. I decided to play on the warrior difficulty with the scout mainly because I was not experienced with the game and choose the easiest class that mainly did damage through auto attacks leaving the later classes for a more complex run if I wanted to do another run.  The combat was still challenging but nothing that wanted me to uninstall at all. I understand that archer and wizard were both buffed with some changes they deserved (all classes having the same BASE hp, increased stamina, healing, and lower mana costs), but I think that some of the mage and archer changes is really overblown with people going smorc/full autoattack with those classes when you are supposed to outkite enemies with your range and kill them with skills (especially wizard).I also think that if people are going for a more casual experience where they don't actually want full optimization, hard and normal difficulty are not the play. I EASILY first or second tried a lot of the final bosses in the game (albeit is was with the easiest class max everything). I think the difficulty players were having was WAY overblown for normal and easy pre-patch. A lot of the bosses have simple move sets that REACT to what you are doing and as a result you cannot go full smorc and you are expected to have a troubled time because it is a boss.One great example of this is the dark claw. Very simple boss that has a pet with two easily dodged and blocked laser attacks and the actual boss himself can dodge, attack, attack when ascending/descending levels (which he can only do if you are on a different vertical level), a move where he throws shruikans (used only 3-4 times entire fight and easily dodgable), and do a huge dash move he gets in phase two (used only 1-2 times really). Despite the overall simplicity since he mostly swipes, I would argue this is one of the harder bosses in the game unless you reach a mid game power spike from collecting all of the items. He shows almost no cues for his attacks vs dodge and can string combos together almost like a difficult AI in a fighting game. It took me a while to recognize what he is doing and how to punish him based off of his attacks based off my moveset. You fight a VERY similar boss in the end game and it took me one try only using one potion because I learned the fight. A lot of players get frustrated when they have to learn fights by not attacking when in reality that is how you get better at playing games.Now with that out of the way, I can talk about the actual game.This game's music and world building are amazing. You can definitely see the passion put into this game by the developers by that alone. It definitely feels like you are part of the world where you can interact and help characters in that world. I felt a little let down by the ending, but it did feel good that there might be a second game in the works for the future.Combat felt very fluid and intuitive once you know how the flashing system works. However, cycling between potions and items was very frustrating. This game suffers from the fact that it has a lot of items that are interesting and viable, but they get edged out by the really good items and the fact there are so many things to try. Instead of having 20+ items to cycle through and test. I would rather equip 5-6 at the save points so I can not feel overwelmed with the amount of choice. Potions feel extremely lacking in the early game, but later on they are just completely busted allowing you to heal for almost half health with 8 potions, not including regen vials or other healing items. It is unfortunate you have to do something similar to the grubs in hallowknight to get a necessary upgrade especially because you need to collect more and they are harder to find than grubs, but the reward pays off.Most of the trinkets were okay until the ones you get offered in the end game that are REALLY good and outclass most trinkets in the game. Buying trinkets is almost never worth which meant you felt very inflated if you did a lot of the quests as you usually end up with 90k+ gold in the end game waiting for something to purchase. The skill tree was okay. I would have liked to see costs/upgrades that happened at later levels instead of them being locked for viewing as I felt like I needed to hold points in case a good one comes up in a few levels. Otherwise the actual upgrades themselves were mostly benefitial and actually transformed combat. The mana skills are straight up broken and anyone who says otherwise is trolling. I'm talking 200+ dmg RANGED crits that occurred frequently (or guaranteed when you used some consumables) in the end game where most hp pools of regular enemies had 500 hp at most. Slinging together mana combos at mid/endgame felt amazing.Overall, the actual fights felt somewhat challenging on the warrior difficulty and really fun once you understood why you are using the skills/attacks in your kit which can take time and definitely cause player frustration. I can't really go into more detail unless I spoil more of the game than I already have.The only really big issue otherwise is the save system. I honestly do not understand it. There are checkpoints so you don't lose progress, but sometimes I would rather have a save before everyboss and NO checkpoints. This way I am not locked into some bosses and areas and I do not have to struggle to get through them with limited resources. Save locations are plenty with the patch so don't worry about losing anything important. Just know to save before you get off for the night because it will only take you to the saves.I think that the pyramid was a big problem as the enemies are difficult, but they don't have the large hp pools at launch which is understandably frustrating when you have to fight basically a boss every room. The other areas are not as difficult (unless MAYBE hell swamp which is an endgame area).Ending on a positive note, the puzzles were amazing. When a game makes you stop and think instead of trying to brute force a puzzle and it is NOT frustrating, it feels very rewarding when completed especially the platformers.Overall pros--Great environment-Great music-Fluid combat-GREAT Puzzles-Rewards completionists and people who want to learn the game-Challenging but not frustrating at medium and high difficultyOverall Cons--Saving is bad-Punishing to the casual gamer unless they take easy mode/class-Overabundance in item choice-The second area of the game is extremely challenging compared to power curve/other areasFinal review:Recommend to people looking for a more challenging experience that like metroidvanias. Not for the casual gamer (unless scout on easy mode).

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR version:This game is like entering your own birthday party and being fatally stabbed in the groin right at the door and having to walk 12 miles through broken glass while barefoot to get to a clinic that won't serve you because you need to be another 15 levels stronger.-----------------------------------I want to like this game, but it's challenging for all the wrong reasons.-The classes aren't balanced. Don't pick Ranger or mage in the for anything above easy difficulty. Their stats are terrible.- Enemies are meat shields with homing, unavoidedable, and overly aggressive attacks and will follow the player relentlessly into other enemies which will swarm the player and kill them.- The desert level... it's cancer. The design principles behind a specific scorpion boss are beyond lame. It's the ultimate cheese do to this game having not so good platforming and wall jumping and forcing the player to have to do that while the boss gets and unavoidable attack. - There is no practice, no prep for players with new scenarios or boss mechanics. It's bash your head into the wall until you figure it out. That's the dark souls part of this game. It's maddening and seems so off with the games graphics. Don't let the charm of this game fool you. It's BRUTAL and unfair to the player. Enemies have a league of attacks and evades in their tool belt (did I mention enemies input read?) while the player has 2 regular attacks, a flimsy block that goes on a long cooldown and a dodge that has a cooldown as well. I want to like the dodge, but enemies attack too frequently for you to spam it. You have to Sekiro this game and only dodge at the right moment. Otherwise you might be able to block the attack.. but most of the time you can't, so you eat dirt.The devs really need to look at the stat balancing and pacing in this game. The first dungeon is okay, but the 2nd dungeon is brutal. There's no ramp up. It's just hard out the gate and YOU CAN'T LEAVE IT UNTIL YOU BEAT IT.Don't play this game if you can't scream at the top of your lungs. Go play Elden Ring if you want a hard, but more enjoyable challenge.~~~~Edit with first content balance.The devs are listening to the players, but for me, the damage has been done. It's in a better state but I'm jaded from my first experience. I have 0 desire to 100% game which its tedious achievements and poor storytelling. The devs went for graphics and difficulty with this game. It's soul is a husk. The difficulty did make things exciting, but unrewarding. I don't know where the fun is in this game... and I've beat the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. I really did. The first dungeon was an enjoyable experience, but the game quickly took a nose dive in fun from there.First and foremost one of my biggest complaints is how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ linear it is, and have the gall to call itself a metroidvania. The only metroidvania aspect is simply that skills unlocked, like double jump, allow you to go back to previous areas and access previously unreachable locations. While this  like a typical metroidvania experience, the difference here is that you aren't going back to areas that unlock new areas that further progression, you simply can now access places that had unreachable chests for basic upgrade materials. These skills are used in  areas to simply complete those dungeons.You are forced to complete all the dungeons in the order the game decides, as the unlocks you get from them are required to progress in the next dungeon and so on and so on. It's as if you took a megaman game and put all the stages in an order that you cannot change, and the boss of each stage was weak to the weapon you unlocked in the previous stage. Linear as all hell.Now for the main complaint you see across most of the negative reviews. . I enjoy a challenge and like hard games, I played this game on its hardest difficulty setting. Despite what most reviews mention the game isn't hard. The game is It just masquerades as difficulty due to poor design, bad mechanics, cheap enemies, and a massive scaling of enemy HP and damage while you stagnate.The controls of the game are horrible and cause more frustration and death than anything else. Constantly getting stuck on a hanging ledge just to have one of 5 mobs on screen take potshots and nail you in the back for 2/3 of your hp in 1 hit. Iframes that last for WAY too short of a time for how much damage you take per hit, and how much is on screen trying to kill you at once.Enemies hit like trucks, have tons of cheap random "patterns", have abilities that do TONS of damage with zero wind up, none of their attacks can be interrupted leading to many many instances where you get your attack out earlier, but because they have shorter frame animations you tend to trade and they die while you lost 2/3 of your hp just to get sniped in the back instantly by one of the other mobs while still locked in your animation. Enemies can hit you from stages away with potential 1 hit kill skills that you can't react to, and when you can react to it your shield breaks in 1 or two hits......if it's even a skill that can be blocked. Your other option is a dodge that has an unbearably long cool down and is really only useful in 1v1 or 2v1 situations, and only if those mobs don't have tons of attacks that hit in rapid succession. And then top this whole pile off with tons of enemy ranged attacks that are homing with the accuracy of an aimbot.Wall jumping has to be the WORST mechanic in the game, it is so very unintuitive to how wall jumping works in pretty much any other game in existence. Usually you can jump to the wall, connect with it and then hold away and jump over and over. Not in Souldiers, no no you have to hold towards the jump WAIT UNTIL YOU LATCH ON then you jump, it slows down wall jumping and causes you to constantly just float down a wall 1 pixel away from actually grabbing it until you hit the ground to try it again. It's a horrible implementation and makes the game WAY more frustrating than it needs to be....but wait it gets better, they force you to use wall jump mechanics in boss fights. The same boss fights that typically kill you in 2 hits. So basically you aren't allowed to make mistakes, even when it's due to poor game mechanics and not you.None of this even touches the characters, how pathetic their HP pools are. How weak their attacks are compared to even basic enemy HP pools. The fact that dying and respawning at a checkpoint revives ALL MOBS, meaning if there was a strong mob inches away from the checkpoint, they respawn when you do, and typically get to attack you the millisecond you spawned back in. Alternate weapons are pretty much worthless, incredibly low ammo counts making them extremely niche and even when you use them, they hardly do that much damage. Upgrades are absurdly expensive and provide little to no benefit, your damage will go up by single digits while enemy HP pools jump up by 50+.The game seems to have had zero balance testing. I could honestly go on for like 15 more paragraphs of every stupid design choice, bug, unfair mechanic, poor control etc. but it's not worth it.The game looks great, and I really love the music. That's it. Do not buy this and if you do, wait for a massive sale. The game had so much potential and just went to crap due to seemingly no real testing.

_childDocuments_.review: The default class is serviceable, but the others feel very... not fair. It gets the graphics perfect, story, it should have been everything I wanted. _childDocuments_.review: I have yet to complete this game, but it is a definite recommend. Let me explain..At its core, the game is defined as a . Some items may reveal an enemy's health, give you stat bonuses, or provide a debuff to your attacker when you take damage.There's also a shop where you can buy maps to help you explore the realm, along with "reload" stations for potions and mana.There are  game modes  available job classes to choose from.The graphics are fun, stylish, and right up the alley of anyone looking for a classic, nostalgic GBA feel. The animations are smooth as  and a chefs kiss with the sprite style.RF did amazing in the graphics department, hitting that nostalgic itch with a modern twist!Will Savino did a fantastic job with the OST of Souldiers. Each song fits the situation where it's placed; whether it's a dialogue, an area, or a boss fight (Extreme Vigor is probably one of the best tracks in this game).The calming, yet adventurous feeling of plains/forests.The feeling of relief and exploration when you're in a new city.The high energy of an intense fight.Not once did it feel like a track . _childDocuments_.review: I played this on the release version and while I appreciated the huge potential of it, a very large amount of balancing and enemy design decisions ultimately made me frustrated and decide to wait for the June 23 patch. The issues I saw were mostly numbers issues with a few design ones, such as clunky save points and too few of them, potions so weak they felt worthless, and the Archer and Mage feeling awful to play compared to the Scout (a swordsman class) along with having tiny health pools.I can now happily fully recommend this game, they fixed basically every issue I had with it and I can now tell you that on Warrior difficulty (Hard), which was previously insanely annoying and difficult, the game is now genuinely fun and feels challenging in a fair way. Here are some of the changes I think are super important, especially if you played the release version and dropped it like I did:- Enemy and Boss HP is MASSIVELY decreased across the board. These HP pools do scale with difficulty but now, even on Hard, they feel fair and reasonable- Enemy, Boss, and Trap damage is significantly lower, even on Hard which increases the damage values- Traps are WAY less annoying, this was a big issue in the 3rd dungeon- Health drops appear far more common than before- Special weapons now cost less resources to use and the resource is easier to obtain from enemies- Special weapons no longer increase their costs once upgraded (that feature sucked)- Spells are more useful and cost WAY less mana- More save points are now present in stretches that were previously very long without any safety- Attacks that can be countered (blue spark) no longer require insanely precise timing- Frustrating enemy hitboxes have been fixed to be way more fair (a lot of the enemies in the 3rd dungeon had issues with this)- Drones that you have to follow (appears with the 3rd element you obtain) are way more lenient, faster, and no longer make me sigh when I see them- Some animations caused the game to act sluggish, such as saving or teleporting in the 3rd dungeon, but this seems to be far less present- Flying enemies no longer suck, they don't stay miles away from you in the air so all characters can deal with them more easily- Archer and Mage's health pools now match Scout so they are no longer insanely squishy (Previously at midgame Mage could die in 2 hits)- Scout has better air attacks to make flying enemies easier- Archer and Mage do more damage and are more functional (better Archer hitboxes and damage, better Mage tracking and damage)- Potions are now buffed to match their values once the first potion upgrade was obtained previously. This means Health Potions now restore 35 hp rather than 20 at the start of the game, which is a huge difference when the starting HP bar is close to 40- Strange bugs such as objects being intangible and unable to be interacted with are fixed, these were rare however- Better map clarity, particularly for the second dungeon- Second dungeon no longer prevents escape once enteredIf you like Metroidvania games now is definitely the time to pick this up. I myself will be doing multiple playthroughs now as the game is so much more fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this, but the game has some huge issues with balancing and QoL that can't be ignored. The first obvious red flag is saving...you have to interact with the save icon twice in order to save, and if you're used to games auto-saving when you run past them, you're probably not going to understand that the icon blinking and making a noise isn't actually doing anything, and can lose a ton of progress as a result.Another major issue is game balance. I played as an archer and was scratching my head at its gameplay: Having limited ammo and having to be temporarily defenseless is an odd design choice in what is supposed to be a fast-paced action game. Perhaps there's a little too much Dark Souls influence here, where indie devs have a tendency to not understand why that works for those games and not in something a little faster paced. The mastery relic system also needs a huge overhaul too: Why does it take five levels for my archer to start being viable in combat, while scouts can fight with no drawbacks? Enemies being spongy don't help with the pacing of combat either. Map design is also a major flaw: Too much emphasis on barely making jumps (and it is frequently not obvious what can be ledge grabbed and what can't,) and the ledge grab can mess with your timing, especially when trying to fight and platform at the same time.Let's give it another go in a couple of months and a couple of patches and maybe we'll have some magic on our hands.
