_childDocuments_.review: Overall I enjoyed the game, the dark bosses were fun, the story, characters, art and music is great.Mechanics, enemies and bosses were a bit of a let down, it felt artificially hard by poor mechanics and unreadable/unreachable enemies rather than just plain hard.Towards the end I had enough though. Before I fought the last boss I looked at my unfinished quests and decided I didn't care to go back into old dungeons guessing where things could be or grinding mobs for drops.Glad I bought it, it's a game where you can feel the devs put a lot into it which I'm happy to support.Spoilers below:Bad things that stuck out for me:Flying enemies almost ruined the game for me, they take too long to take down and are boring to fight, they spend the majority of time hovering outside of your max jump (even lategame) which would be okay if you could 2 shot them, but when you have to hit them 4-8 times (more lategame) why would I bother engaging.They also fly away from you sideways faster than you can catch at points (even when sprinting), you spend so long waiting for the small window to attack, I just felt like running past them.Also most of them have invincibility at points for some reason?I sighed when the 2nd to last boss would fly out of range the majority of the time, I'm just watching him float around whilst there's nothing I can do, I wouldn't care if he had another health bar as long as I could be doing something.The last boss is so boring, double jump attack once for a small amount of health, Before he swipes there's a long animation, and something like 8 swipes that never hit, have an eye that you can hit when this is happening.it's not fun that it felt like i'm spending more time dodging basic attacks with 0 attack windows, then actually hitting the boss.The race against the flying horse highlighted how clunky the ledge grabbing is. (ruins area)Sprinting puzzles were horrible as it didn't always register I wanted to sprint, especially the lava, some areas it was perfect and others it felt like the game wanted me to melt.Things to consider on next patch?:The noticeboard bosses should be marked specifically where they are on the map, I don't want to go all round the area they are trying to figure out where to find them.The mindflayer boss from that is bugged (has happened to other people too), I killed him and my game got stuck on the door opening scene, then I killed him again and he bugged where he couldn't move and I would get shocked when I went near him, the doors opened and I can't get the reward from the quest givers.Add another dragon statue in the town near the bug collector/forge, if i want to upgrade my weapon, I run so far into town and then back, I immediately thought why isn't there a closer port to what I want to do?Change the ground infestation mob to burrow attack once, it's never hitting it's 2nd ever, it's just long invincibility, it's an easy mob with high health with long windows where you can't attack it, you have to commit to killing it as it doesn't leave aggro.Change the late game flyer to be less invincible and not fly through walls/floors so much, again it was waiting for long periods for an opportunity to attack, I ran past them when I could.The experience of swapping accessories is horrible and slow, maybe make a forger NPC to make perfect versions past ++?.Endgame you have too much gold and get drops of + accessories, they just sit in my inventory because spending the time selling them for 50g+ each isn't worth it.Increase XP from dungeon bosses, I got to the last boss at level 38, no idea what the last skills even were and didn't care to grind for it.Thorns perk reduces damage instead? the 2nd level of it increases all resistance by 10%?I didn't see all the last parts of the skill tree so it might not make sense, but 50% returned melee damage doesn't seem worth it at all, especially when most time when you get hit it's a projectile.when you are doing 30-50 damage per strike, the odd returned 15 damage from an odd hit isn't worth it.The Pig NPC boss wants 20 gears in his quest, change it to 12. it's too grindey.At a high cost (5-10k?), have the mapper NPC upgrade your map when you buy his last piece to fully show where chests etc are.Do I want to explore all of the spider cavern or pyramid to try to find the final glowbug that I missed behind some random wall somewhere? no thanks.Reduce speed on flying enemies when the player is close to them and reduce time outside of attacking range and invincibility, the HP is fine if you can hit them, they already take too long to kill.Overall enemies should have better indication of attack and not hit you from far off the screen,The electric turret pinpoint shoots you from across the map that you can't even see, it need some windup animation and sound, there's plenty or others that need that too including main bosses.Same with the big mob in the lava dungeon, there's one I ran past (before the electrical gadget follow with platform jumping and sprinting back and forth) and his projectile came full speed from across the map direct towards me, he was so far away i'd have to run 20 seconds to get back to him. Increase text speed on the mirrors in the last dungeon. On the mirror boss that attacks you through the steam, it's so hard to tell compared to before, it needs to be more visible.I had a bug with this quest, when i accepted I ran past the giant chalice and jumped over the ledge and fought/killed the dark sword boss, I climbed up to the egg and decided I would go back down to save and finish the mirror quest before going ahead. I completed it expecting some reward or a big reason to with the map, it created 2 bridges leading to where i'd already been and didn't trigger the walk over the bridge completed quest as i'd already done it.Reduce ground dodge cooldown by half. jumping dodge would ruin jumping puzzles.Enable map markings, it would help with exploration, especially the pyramid, which deep pyramid doors connect to what and which don't I need to go in anymore.When an enemy recovers from being frozen, reset them with a small delay on any attack, I got hit a few times when they broke free with an immediate response that I couldn't dodge/block as there isn't an indication if someone coming.Let me attack upwards (I know if can strong attack) and block upwards.Add debuffs/resistance bars, 1 hit eats 50% of burning etc resistance, when 100% you get the debuff, an accessory lets you take 3/4 before the debuff hits, it being random if you are burned/paralysed is not fun.I felt that on the dark razor boss, I was full HP but didn't have any potions when I fought him so I had to beat him with barely getting hit, sometimes he would hit me once and give me bleeding and hit turret would paralyse me, other times nothing happens, the inconsistency is not fun.Also add a timer to them, it highlighted in the flying dungeon when I was hit with the paralysis debuff and just sat there until it wore off.Add a timer for vial usageParry now fills up your stamina bar rather than depletes and stuns the enemy for a brief time.it's actually a negative to parry, it's more difficult than plain blocking, you lose _childDocuments_.review: Amazing game with a bit of mix feelings over a few things.I'll start with the negative:Lore is all over the place. There are no hooks to any of the characters: The way everyone are introduced is treated like we're already halfway through season 2 broadcast, with drama that can't squeeze any emotions from the player thanks to no build-up whatsoever.Spending money on heals is just unnecessary and pointless, when you can simply grind a few coins when needed. Should've worked the same way as DS flasks instead of trying to be "different" but turned out annoying instead.There should've never been damage upgrade system in a game like this.Forced exploration in order to stay on par with enemies enormous health pools could be done better.For starters, all bosses as you can see have insane amount of hp, which would've been fine if they didn't keep doing the same s*** over and over again. You can literally break every fight into rinse / repeat situation.Don't even get me started on how you gotta pull a full combo with evasive maneuvers on every single enemy you meet, and they still won't die.Very few bosses keep the battle dynamic and create situations where you gotta think on your feet and adapt - the way a good boss fight should be.The art is amazing, and probably the reason you bought this game in the first place.The game is HUGE! There's so much to explore and find, that I have to tip my hat off to the devs. Amazing job there, especially with how dense they managed to make each area, with good levels design no less.I'm glad that there's a good ratio of platforming vs combat. (sometimes you gotta do both!)It's nice to have a break here and there from fighting, and focus instead at dodging lasers and spikes.Surprisingly there's some real replay value going for this game.NG+ is a thing (and harder), and you can always start a new playthrough with a different class.Even with all the cons, I still heavily recommend anyone to play this game.Just be mindful that warrior mode will kick your ass, and might even crush your soul a few times by losing progress since the last checkpoint.There's really nothing of this scale and passion in the 2D action adventure games.I'm positive that after investing this much in their game, the devs will listen to feedback and make the necessary changes to truly turn Souldiers into an indie GOTY.Well done. 👏

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, the game is obviously controversial, and considering all negative reviews I thought I'll make a positive one, since there's a lot of stuff to like.First things first - everyone seems to agree on that - the art is gorgeous. Now something somebody can disagree on, but I think bosses are cool and varied - their movesets are quite simple, but that allows you to try some complex stuff, some bosses have their gimmicks which are not always obvious. Their simplicity doesn't make them too easy though - you have to find counters to each move and execute them without too many mistakes. The levels are huge, and take a lot of time to explore. There are three heroes with very different play styles and they can do cool stuff(there are parries, which are hella satisfying to pull off). Some people say controls feel delayed, and for me it's not the case - overall feel of movement is very different from, let's say, Hollow Knight (which is THE G.O.A.T. metroidvania for me), but it's consistent and will feel natural after a while. The difference is - Hollow Knight compared to Souldiers had I feel like less wide arsenal of moves, but in the end that arsenal was much easier to use, which made stuff like Path of Pain and Colosseum of Fools very much doable after some practice, and each death felt like player's fault. In Souldiers I often found myself dying because I couldn't execute some vital thing  in the middle of a fight, because of complexity of fight systems (there's a lot of cooldown management, at least for archer class). This is not a bad thing necessary, since I think it elevates skill ceiling, which is good.Now for the most controversial thing - difficulty. Remember how Dark Souls and Hollow Knight are "tough but fair"? This is not it. I think they tried to balance it of course, but result is not so great. The amount of times that felt like "♥♥♥♥ you, buddy" from the game and level designers is about 2-4 per hour. Often game will demand to execute quite long sequences of quite complex stuff (e.g. escort mission where you must stay in certain radius of this robot thingy, while traversing complex level with hazards and enemies while trying to fignt off quite small heat-seeking indefinitely respawning enemies - often death feels like slap in the face, imagine Path of Pain with added respawning enemies, although level is not nearly as complex as PoP, but still requires timed and sometimes precise platforming). That is main flaw of the game I think - very often it feels like your death was unfair. Pair this with somewhat rare checkpoints, and you have a lot to rage about. So if you have short temper, give this one a pass - this will not be a good time for you, you will be boiling for a big part of playtime. Now, with that said, I recommend the game if you know you can handle this kind of difficulty. For it's art style, boss and creature design, different playable characters and quite competent and complex fighting system. Again, if you have short temper, skip this game, you will not be happy playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty damn solid; the platform and controls are responsive and fluid, the early-game battles teach you everything you need to know about the game, traps and hazards are simple enough to avoid, and leveling up feels rewarding.  What could go wrong?Oh.  So much.  After the first level, the game quickly gets tossed out of the 40th story and into the neighbor's rancid pool.  The difficulty cranks up to 'souls-like' style, and by this, I mean that this game adds to the already polluted and over-saturated game library of souls-vania games with cheap deaths and rage-inducing 'WTF' moments where you genuinely have no idea what killed you.  Granted, I am playing on the 'normal' difficulty, so I am fully ready to admit that as my own fault.  However, to me, it's almost as if a development team came in and finished the first level with all the love and care they could muster.  Then, a second team made up of bullied high-school kids came in and decided that life isn't and shouldn't be fair.  For anyone.Don't get me wrong, there's a TON going for this game.  For the first 3-4 hours, I was in love with it.  But like so many others here, once I hit the pyramid level, I started to see how quickly a game can fall apart.  I finished the pyramid and was glad to be done with it, but my desire to play further has almost been snuffed out.  I'm going to press on and see if it gets better, because curiosity is what drives me.Yes, I know.  I'm complaining about this game.  But you may see that my review is marked as recommended.  Why?  Because I firmly believe that I am very possibly missing something.  The art style, the controls, the music, a decent portion of the overall design, and a lot of everything I've seen so far have been very well crafted.  And so to you, dear reader, I say give it a chance.  Give Souldiers a fair chance.  This game deserves that much, at least.Summary -- PROS:- Quick, responsive, fluid controls- Battles that teach you as you go, 1st level is like a tutorial- Loads of items, gold, health pickups, and skill point system- Relics that grant different elements to your attacks, status effects, etc.- Appealing artwork, catchy music, and delightful graphics overall- Checkpoints that attempt to minimize time lost from dyingSummary -- CONS:- Difficulty ramps up way too quickly after first few hours, a lot of deaths feel cheap- Traps/Hazards deal a % of maximum health in damage, which leaves you feeling like level ups/powerups don't matter much- Later enemies can combo you literally to death, with some having no attacks with reasonable, telegraphed sequence(s)- Health Potions are useful at first, but quickly become like drops of water in a bucket.  Other, more effective healing items are extremely rare, and so you'll feel the need to hoard them.- Damage from enemies does not trigger an invincibility phase to enable the player to recover from a mistake, and some traps/hazards don't either.  This means that you can quite literally be bounced from one source of damage to another, very rapidly depleting your health bar.- The game (regarding mine, at least) will occasionally spaz out and forget that the controller is connected, resulting in complete immobility and an impending game over.TL;DR - The game is appealing on so many levels, but may frustrate a player with little patience and a lack of curiosity.  It will lure you in and pummel you mercilessly.  Don't give up!  Give this a shot, and see it through; I certainly plan to.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exactly what I look for when I want to play a metroidvania. The map design incorporates exploration really well so it isn't just a sprint through a linear area. The platforming is challenging without being impossible, with enemies making it more difficult at times. The controls handle really well with fluid movements letting you feel like you're covering ground quickly. I like the ledge grab mechanic as they incorporate it into vertical movement and let's you dodge around enemies and projectiles. I am currently playing the scout class so dealing with flying enemies is annoying when I run out of projectiles, but overall the enemies are unique and I have figured out how to combat each enemy. They can get difficult to deal with if there are a lot of enemies because you don't apply hitstun but the enemy does, so you can just get beat up by enemies if you get in a bad spot. The element system let's you deal bonus damage to specific enemies, I just wish there was an easier way to switch between them rather than hitting pause and navigating the menu (thankfully the menu pulls up fast, is quick to navigate and you can open it anytime). Edit: Turns out you use the right stick to select the element. I just didn't read the hint. For this being Retro Forge's FIRST GAME it is very clean and polished, and I haven't encountered any bugs or crashes. It is also much longer and more difficult than I expected going into this. I think it'll take me another 20-30 hours to finish my first playthrough if the areas are the same size or bigger, and I plan to do at least one more playthrough as the mage class. The gear and leveling system doesn't seem that integral to the overall game. I mainly find myself dodging/blocking enemy attacks and trying to get quick hits in between. Some bosses don't have the best tell for when they are going to attack and I am not a fan of highlighting the enemy if they're going to do an attack that can't be dodged/blocked. I might go back and format this better but rn I just want to play more. Think people are being knitpicky with the current rating.

_childDocuments_.review: Challenging game with beautiful pixel art! CON -I think my only gripe with it though is how the game punishes you so much. It could be that I'm not finding better items or grinding enough (probably just need to git gud), but the fact that if I can see an enemy ahead of me and I can't ambush them, or if I can try to hit them from afar I automatically miss while the enemy auto hits me is disheartening. It sucks to journey so far or even explore areas just to get trapped in a spot that I cannot leave because I don't have the right ability at the time. I got caught in an area where I could not double jump out and there was a spike maze where I cannot double jump out. Since I cannot escape, I had to kill the character, making me start over again. I think in the end it's just these type of challenges I'm not too use to, but I wish the game didn't punish the player so much. (At this point I have only tried the Archer class on Normal mode)PRO - Aside from all that complaining, this game is really fun and does make you think more about how to defend/evade your enemies! _childDocuments_.review: Graphics- Amazing, love the style, love all the work. Too many games these days don't put this much time into their art.Gameplay- Challenging, you will want to rip out your hair and smash your screen, but completion is hella rewarding. Haven't felt my reward receptors blast neurons like this in a long time.Story- It's alright, didn't really come for the story, but the art and styleMap Design- Like any other platformer style game, except it doesn't skip out on the extras, plenty of eye candy to go aroundControls- Keyboard and mouse was not my thing for this game, usually it's my go to for platformers, but I found myself succeeding much easier on a controllerOverall Comments-I have been on the look out for new challenging games that made me reminisce of older times. I finally found it, now I have no previous experience in the Dark Souls genre, nor metroidvania, but I've always enjoyed watching gameplay. So below you'll find my thoughts.I chose middle difficulty and the scout, and to my surprised I was humbled really early on. I kind of knew what to expect but boy is this game challenging. If you aren't a fan of dying at least 5-10 times before you clear a boss, then stay away, but if you love a challenge this is it. It will test you within the confines of the gameplay, you will not only fight, position, dodge, but you will need to look for openings, time your attacks, and maintain composure. If you think you can fight any mob like it is nothing trying to kill you, then you will fail, but learn from it and push on. You can also choose to just run, which I found myself doing a lot of, running and avoiding fights I could not take on allowed me to push deeper into other parts where I would not have lasted in combat. I did a good mix of two to get some exp, to find upgrades, and to gain map info. Final notes, watch where you tread, you might get stuck until you clear the whole area. This was a bummer, but with a little luck you'll get out. Fighting anything that flies with the scout made me want to gouge my eyes out on a few areas, but it's do-able, just a bit miserable. Oh and the market, and rain sounds are WAY TOO LOUD. I have to set ingame to 1 for all sounds and my mixer down. That needs to be addressed quickly as the noise can hurt ears.Remember you are not the main character of this game, and just as the name suggests you are a but a mere Souldier. Understand that you are just like any other souldier before you, many have failed, many continue to die. You are a souldier, and you can be a damn good one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot going for it. Mostly just incredible pixel art, which is consistently excellent. Possibly the best I've seen anywhere. The music is also decent. Never annoying, but not all that memorable. I've been playing as a mage and I'm switching my review to negative because there are just too many negatives for me to recommend this anymore.1 - Basic Attack. The mage's basic attack just feels constrained and unpleasant. "Ranged but only if it's close enough" was a crappy idea. Sometimes you can hit something that can't hit you, which is nice. But it doesn't so very much damage, and WAY too often, you're juuuuust out of range for the range attack to work, and then whatever you wanted to shoot at hits you at range instead. It just doesn't feel good to play.2 - Dodge teleport. It's on a cooldown, first off, which is not cool. I can't say how many times I needed to dodge twice and couldn't. Right now I'm on the Minotaur boss and it's effing tough because I'm just not mobile enough. Making the afterimage explode was a cool idea but I really, really hate that it was factored in to how much damage a mage is supposed to be able to do. It's a finicky ability and I wouldn't mind it as part of a much bigger skillset, but as a major attack? No, it sucks. And it sucks harder that once you use it twice you're out of mana and aren't allowed anymore.3 - weapon staff blast. It's okay. But again, it's not great. It doesn't feel awesome. It doesn't do anywhere near enough damage for it to feel cool that you used a 10 second timeout ability at short range. It's just part of the button mash combo for mage damage, and you have to take your eyes off the fight to see if it's ready again yet.4 - Why bother at all with a skill tree? I'm only like level 10 or so, and most of the abilities are still hidden, so I dunno if something cool is hidden in there. But so far, "better staff blast" and "better dodge teleport" and stuff is all I can see. Why even bother? Whose idea was it to have a skill tree that changes LITERALLY NOTHING about how you approach the game?At the end of the day, playing mage just doesn't feel good. They might as well call it 'acrobat' or something, except then they'd have to make him more mobile. Let you dodge twice, for example.I expect that they're gonna do a giant patch something that revamps a lot of stuff and pushes this game up to where it deserves to be, based on the art and animation. But how it is right now, I simply cannot recommend it. If you do get it, play as the warrior because everything feels like that's what they wanted and Mage and Archer are just half-assed afterthoughts.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and Brutal!Souldiers is immaculate in its daunting difficulty. More than anything, the art in this game stands out, featuring sprawling scenes of forests and dismal caves. Rather than just draw in the same trees that fade into the background, you might see a colony of ants migrating in the background or what resembles a cathedral in the middle of the forest. Mechanically, this game works just like any other metroidvania (nothing wrong with that) with some added customization. The main feature of Souldiers is its three distinct classes that offer a very different feel in play style; from puzzle solving to combat. I personally used my mage afterimages to make the torch puzzle in the cave easier, whereas an archer might just shoot the torches from across the room. The other notable feature is the element system, in which you can change your ability and weapon damage type on the fly. This isn't only used to counter enemy weaknesses and resistances, it affects the environment around you, sometimes in subtle ways. For example, destroying small trees and flowers will occasionally reward you with healing orbs. However, burning them with fire usually yields more. Its definitely more complex than it appears on the surface. The one area where I would caution gamers against is the difficulty. While a lot of people enjoy a difficult game, some of the difficulty spikes are a bit much. Boss fights in particular can be brutal with fast paced attacks that are not well telegraphed and deal a third of your HP. Expect to die on the first attempt. In fact, most enemies have fairly difficult to read attacks that deal gratuitous damage. This isn't so bad if you like a challenge, but where it gets painful is what occurs when you die. You go back to your last save in most cases, not your last save point. That means that if you collected some nice randomly dropped equipment, finished a puzzle, or did a series of complex platforming to get that last missing treasure chest and then die, you'll be doing some back tracking. Overall, I'd say this is a great game for any metroidvania fan who prefers Hollowknight to TImespinner.

_childDocuments_.review: Big fan of MetroidVania type games, played many different ones on Xbox/Switch and other consoles, finally started to look into getting some more and saw this one.Game looks awesome, the pixel design and music just hit the right level.Game is enjoyable and has some steep learning curves.I have only finished the first area (Spidercave) and progressed a little bit into the area after this.If you are a fan of Metroidvania type games I would recommend this, it definitely has room for improvement though.The game saves/replenishes your health/mana like Soulsborne type games, where enemies resurrect whenever you rest, however if you die, you lose all progress from when you last saved/rested which feels harsh. You can resurrect with a specific item but so far I have only found one of these.As far as the 3 classes go, Archer and Caster seem extremely underwhelming early on.Archer only has 3 arrows to fire and you then need to wait for them to recharge or throw your bow to hit enemies and recover them faster. The range of the bow is very short and timing your shots/throwing your bow to avoid getting hit is more of an annoyance than a good feature.Caster fires homing projectiles (these projectiles only fire when enemies are nearby) for low damage, a high damage attack can be down with a cooldown but its range is pitiful and you have to be very close to enemies resulting in a lot of waiting for opportunity to using it, or taking damage when using it.Scout is the main class and feels like the game was designed around this class primarily, it seems to be the most well rounded class with good damage/health and stamina. It also seems to be the easiest class to deal damage whilst also avoiding damage which makes the other classes redundant (for me) as I was hoping Archer/Caster had more to them. Caster needs additional range/damage. Archer needs either more arrows/faster recharge or less punishing move to regain them. So far Scout seems to be absolutely fine the way he is designed, the only improvement I could think of right now is to make it easier to hit airborne enemies but this so far is just a minor issue.Game is brand new though so some improvements will hopefully be made going forward. Check out some streams if you are unsure to get a better understanding before you buy.

name: Out of Line
detailed_description: Collect great memories with this artful game experience. Find and help new friends and yourself. Journey through this beautiful 2D puzzle platformer. Explore a unique and unfamiliar painted world with San.
about_the_game: Collect great memories with this artful game experience. Find and help new friends and yourself. Journey through this beautiful 2D puzzle platformer. Explore a unique and unfamiliar painted world with San.
short_description: A unique adventure game filled with beautiful puzzles all hand-drawn in an original 2D style . Out of Line follows the adventures of San in a quest to escape the Factory that was once home. Dive into a story set in a mysterious world that is revealed through multiple chapters.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yep, as long as you don't expect more than a linear puzzle-platformer.It is a day like any other: We slumber peacefully in a secluded corner of the factory, when a flying yellow cube wakes us up. We follow the cube and are thrown into a tube by a mechanical hand ... The yellow cube now turns into a spear, which we can call back to us at any time. Armed with the spear, we now run from left to right. Soon we see countless other workers who look exactly like us and have also taken the same path as us - but each on paths running parallel to us. We can wave at them, but not interact with them directly. This is how Out of Line begins - and as yet the story makes absolutely no sense.Out of Line is a (relatively simple) platform game with a focus on (not always so simple) different puzzles. We play the worker San, who tries to escape from a factory that has gone out of control. The game does completely without texts, the whole story is told purely visually. We have to recognize and correctly interpret various clues in the game environment in order to understand the deeper meaning and eventually grasp the entire story. The central mechanic revolves around San's spear. San doesn't consider this spear a weapon and usually doesn't use it to attack enemies directly. Instead, he uses his spear in different ways to avoid confrontations or to manipulate the world around him. The gameplay is similar to Limbo - we work our way from room to room in an unfamiliar dystopian world, always facing different challenges. Armed with the spear, which we can use as a ladder or a switch and call back to us at any time, we explore the colorful, but also deadly world. However, our demise is not tragic, we immediately reappear in the same room and can try again. Or think of a different approach.We face mechanical obstacles or chasms that we have to overcome. Again and again, however, we are also forced to avoid mechanical creatures that kill us immediately when they discover us. This creates a threatening, oppressive atmosphere. As the game progresses, we can indirectly cooperate with other workers to advance at certain points. For example, we move a platform for the colleague, who opens a door for us in return. We also meet another creature that is on the run and befriends us. With a little imagination and good powers of observation, we eventually understand what Out of Line is actually about - personally, I would have preferred some conversations or at least explanatory text anyway. San experiences a whimsical journey through a fantastic, mysterious world full of danger. Nerd Monkeys, who I previously only knew through the two Detective Case and Clown Bot adventures, have done a great job. If you like classic puzzle platform games in the style of Limbo, you can't go wrong with Out of Line.Puzzle-platformer with beautiful hand-drawn 2D graphics, smooth animations, an atmospheric soundtrack that matches the gameplay, and a variety of different puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Out of Line

_childDocuments_.review: Since Playdead’s 'Limbo', there has been a proliferation of puzzle platformers on the indie scene, including its spiritual successor – 'Inside' – a game many see as the pinnacle of the genre.  'Out of Line', clearly takes inspiration from these games, but has enough unique elements to make it stand out from the crowd.  The hand-painted art-style of the game is wonderful, reminiscent of Studio Ghibli films at times. The love and care that poured into the game by developer, Nerd Monkeys, is clear from the off – and it comes as no surprise that it’s already won awards, even before release. You play as San, a lone child trying to escape a dystopian world controlled by an ominous entity. Like ‘Inside’, the story is told through actions rather than words. And it is down the player to interpret it in their own way. It’s a game about identity, and rather than being ‘inside’ or part of something, you are on the periphery, and know very little about yourself, ‘Out of Line’ you could say.  Perhaps the most unique thing about the game is the spear wielding mechanics. Rather than use for combat, your golden spear allows you to create platforms, operate switches, and solve some rather imaginative puzzles.   Along your journey to escape the oppressive mechanical regime, you’ll encounter enemies, some will chase you, others try to grab you from above.  You’ll also meet other people and befriend strange creatures who aid you in your quest, one of which becomes central to the story, and provides many of the game’s most memorable puzzle sequences. ‘Out of Line’ is well paced, with new mechanics introduced regularly. Checkpoints are generous and progression is satisfying. And there’s very little hand-holding – it's all about self-discovery and testing the limits of your spear.  I particularly liked the incongruity between the beautiful painted natural world and the industrial evil plaguing the land - perhaps a metaphor for humankind’s ambition, and greed. From a creative and artistic perspective, I see ‘Out of Line’ as embracing the typical ideologies of Romanticism – a movement pre-occupied with escapism, individuality and admiration for nature.  But, that’s just my interpretation - I’m sure you’ll see things differently.

_childDocuments_.review: Out of Line is a hand drawn 2D puzzle platformer set in the confines of a regimented factory run by tyrannical machinery called Claws. The protagonist of the story is San, who is trying to escape from the factory.Avoiding the lethal glare of the claws and manipulating lifts, platforms and environmental hazards, San must engineer an escape aided by the use of his javelin. Once outside, San discovers a new world with new dangers, and encounters some allies to help him on his quest. The main tool that San uses is his javelin.An arc appears showing you where the javelin is going to land. It can be thrown into various materials and used as a jumping aid to reach higher ground. The javelin can be recalled at any time and travel back to you wherever you are.The javelin can also be thrown into the cogs of machinery to stop doors closing or mighty pillars from crushing you. Often, there are multiple cogs to sabotage, meaning you have to be quick with your recall and then throw again.The javelin can also be inserted into switches creating a handle for you to push or pull. Pushing or pulling can determine the movement of platforms.Pieces of rope can be tied to the javelin, which when fired, will create rope bridges for San to cross.Occasionally, there are levels with temporary javelins. These javelins are only affective for a small amount of time and then will explode. Once they disappear, they can be used again at their collection points. Usually, the temporary javelins have to be placed and then you can use your main javelin to perform tasks before the temporary one expires. During the game you will meet several characters who will aid you in your escape. You never control the other character but you do need to work together to complete tasks. Clearing their path of obstacles or pulling bridges across for them, for example, will allow them to repay the favor and clear your path too. The characters you meet often have different abilities to yourself so you need to take that into account when problem solving.For example, some of the enemies have been converted by The Claw to mindlessly work for them and attack intruders. One certain character has the ability to tame the enemy and make them work for San aiding him in puzzle solutions.You will only work with one character at a time but these moments are fleeting as most of the time you will be on your own.Sometimes you will need to advance but tread carefully under the noses of the Claw. They have a detection area which can change rapidly and if you are detected they will kill you immediately. During these stealth missions you will also have to perform other tasks whilst hiding away from their glare.There are also segments where light plays a part in keeping you safe. Enemies and allies are afraid of bright light due to the dark environments they frequent. San can push and pull lights if available creating a path for escape.Certain sections require you to run as fast as you can away from The Claw or other dangerous creatures. These include typical runner ingredients, performing puzzle elements whilst trying not to be caught.During your escape run you will find blue orbs strategically placed for you to collect. They don’t give you any special powers and are only here for achievements and an extra challenge. Once collected they are placed on to a tree at the end of the level.The game will take you between four and five hours to complete but may require subsequent playthroughs if you want to collect all the orbs. There is no chapter select after the game completes.Out of Line looks gorgeous with its hand drawn art and unusual backgrounds.It has a futuristic dystopian atmosphere depicting scenes of slavery and injustice within the factory. The music is quite ominous and threatening, heightening the feeling of danger and desperation whilst trying to flee your prisoners. The graphics enhance the gloomy and claustrophobic feel.The game isn’t generous with its explanations. Your origins are never discussed. There is no voice acting or text. You seem to look the same as everyone else but we can only assume why. Out of Line is a game relying on your interpretation. The only clues we receive are hand drawn paintings on walls depicting events and they’re very basic and just seem to mirror your abilities rather than offer any clear picture of what is happening. It’s not a narrative game with a defined story, but more of a puzzle game with a loose tale joining scenes together.Once we are out of the factory, environments look brighter and more detailed. A stark contrast to the depressing confinements of the factory. There are some nice-looking areas and I really liked the movement of the main character. He looks quite charming with his distinctive run. Even though there is no voice acting or text, his mannerisms can create emotion, and the game does this very well. Often, we see San expressing his feelings through body movements, and the soundtrack is an excellent accompaniment to this. They help to make the game more than just a run of the mill puzzle title.The puzzles are reasonably varied. San uses his javelin to perform a number of tasks. The aiming mechanic is functionable. Sometimes, I felt that the arc was difficult to control if you were trying to be precise. I think a mouse and keyboard would probably be easier but these moments are rare.The co-operative scenes were enjoyable. The characters you help are colorful and charismatic and add extra drama and interest into the game.  Story elements are revealed during these junctures and it is here that we see most of the poignant moments.The stealth sections are incredibly easy. I think I completed these on the first try on most occasions. The runner sections are also relatively painless and will only take you a few tries before you know the strategy and complete them.The main puzzle areas are much harder, but still not too difficult. I struggled twice with solutions during my playthrough but the rest was quite straight forward.The switch mechanics proved to be a little annoying, especially when there were timed puzzles. It’s not always obvious which way you have to pull the lever. Sometimes, nothing seems to happen and by the time you try again it is too late. This did cause a few moments of frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Out of Line. It is a lovingly crafted side-scrolling platformer in which you guide a small person through a series of environments. Along the way, he is assisted by a several characters who become an integral part of puzzle solutions. Your goal is to find 16 blue cubes and restore them to a central tree.The art is beautiful and the musical sound track is quite nice.  There is no dialog.  Although your character can (and probably will) die often, there are no violent death scenes and very little penalty for missing a jump. You have a spear which functions as a climbing tool, a lever, and a rope thrower. As you navigate the varied environments, the puzzle is to create a path forward using diverse mechanics. The platforming was fairly easy, with only a couple of sections that had tricky timing. The puzzles make sense and build on each other as you progress.  And, then there are the pesky mechanical claws scattered about, spewing death rays...All in all, a nice experience with one drawback. The game auto-saves to a single slot with no chapter select option. This means that achievement hunters will need to start from square one if any are missed on along the way. I ended up playing the first section three times before moving forward, as I kept forgetting about one of the cubes that is not obvious. The trick is to be sure you have explored all paths before moving on. While the game moves primarily from left to right, cubes may be in a level above, below, or to the right. For the most part, once an area is passed, there is no turning back.I recommend this to those who enjoy a peaceful platformer with a 'feel-good' ending. If you enjoyed games like Aspire: Ina's Tale and Inside, then you are quite likely be a fan of Out of Line.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so, here's the general outline regarding this game: If you like ambient Puzzle Platformers that follow the footsteps of the genre mainly set by Limbo, then you will love this game. If you are a bit indifferent to the genre, chances are, that feeling will remain the same and it's not going to be this game the one to change it.Out of Line, in spite of executing every idea it brings forward flawlessly, plays it very safe in general, so while in the one hand there might not be anything in particular that could be pointed out as a big negative aspect, in the other you've got a game comprised of ideas you've mostly seen before. The weight of both of these aspects is for each player to decide, but luckily, Out of Line has more to offer than a pure mechanics based experience.You play as a young protagonist that, much like the player, finds himself in an abstract and unfamiliar world, where there seems to be an infinite number of characters that look just like you. Unfortunately, all of you seem to be the target of several "claw-like" machines, which not only serve as the threat that sets the game in action, but they will also be the main and only threat you'll find across the game. While running from these machines, you will find and collect several floating cubes, the first one of which will transform into a spear that will serve as your main way of interacting with the world around you, mainly by throwing/recalling it. This provides the context from which the rest of the game will draw from, pitting you against several platforming and puzzle sections, which mainly use the spear in order to be surpassed, all the while, taking you into a journey across several beautifully hand-painted scenarios.The art in this game is one of the big stand-outs, and while several other games have a hand-painted look to them, Out of Line manages to make it into a style of its own. Not only do the visuals look charming, but the game also has some interesting concepts thrown in there for good measure. The bio-mechanical factory with pipes running all over it seems like the most obvious example, although an obligatory "introductory forest" section is to be expected.Sound wise, the game is also top notch, with a clear, sharp, and serene soundtrack, that while being comprised of mostly ambient pieces, it imbues them with a very personal feeling, preventing them from feeling like your typical generic ambient drone. If we come down to it, everything sound related has a lot of personality, not just the soundtrack, but also the sound effects and sound design. All of it sounds crisp, clean and interesting.Story wise, the game tackles some themes surrounding growth and growing older, although it leaves things a bit too vague in order to make any particular statement, with some elements, like the "Claw machines", being used just to serve as some kind of opposing threat, even though they don't tie as well with the remaining conceptual elements. Overall, don't go in expecting anything particularly deep or complex. The story mostly serves as context to keep the game going, and since the game is only about 2 and a half hours long, it serves its purpose.With all that said and going back to the beginning of this review, the small scope and budget of the game do show. Puzzles mostly consist of triggers and levers that require you to interact with them in the correct order, which don't offer the most engaging of experiences, even though they aren't poorly designed. Chase sequences are reduced to a matter of mostly keep walking forward, which no matter how intense the game makes them out to be, the disconnect between the player's actions and what the game actually portrays is inevitable. The distinction between background and foreground elements can be iffy at times, leading to avoidable deaths. Several animations seem to stutter as they move along, and while it is nothing game breaking, it's pretty much constant throughout the game. Mechanics are introduced only to be abandoned later on, never to be used again, and while they do get developed when it's their time to shine, it never feels like they reach their true potential.This leaves the game as a hard recommend to anyone that is not already biased towards Puzzle Platformers, but on the other side, anyone specifically familiar with this type of puzzle design will end up finding the puzzles a bit bland, while still being 100% serviceable for all intents and purposes. Even then, for any person that finds itself into this latter category, the overall aesthetic quality and personality that the game puts forward are enough to justify playing this solid, albeit familiar game. The experience is also rather small and compact and there never is a low moment per se, with all the achievements and in-game collectables being fairly enjoyable. And overall, I think that's what best describes Out of Line: enjoyable. If you think you'll like this game, then it is safe to assume that you'll spend an enjoyable afternoon beating it, and as such, it gets my recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the Next Fest demo and loved it enough to pick up the full game, but I feel slightly hoodwinked since that seemed to be a large concentrated bulk of the puzzles that are on offer here. There were elements in the demo that hinted at an interesting story, but after playing the full title I'm left with more questions that answers.What is the the importance of the tree? Why does it produce blue cubes? Why do the blue cubes fly back to it through out the game? Where do these claws come from? Who is the main guy? Why are we here? What did we wake up from?It sounds like I'm asking to be spoonfed, but I've played game that didn't have dialogue before and it was clear what was going on and why (Ato). The bizarre setup and occurrences in Out Of Line needed some explanation.That's many chase sequences but they just boil down to holding right. Very little is asked of you in terms of interaction to survive these.The artstyle looks great in stills but breakable branches and gears you can jam with your javelin don't really pop. The first puzzle section has what looks like a lower floor but it's a background platform, the sense of perspective poor. _childDocuments_.review: "Out of Line" is yet another of literally thousands of 2D retro platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.  In fairness, this Nintendo Switch ported handheld platformer is far from the worst on Steam, and doesn't even feature terrible pixel "art", there's no prizes for being fairly tall for a midget. This puzzle platformer features some handcrafted art and has puzzles that revolve around simplistic physics and other activities, as well as a somewhat whimsical story.  Such a concept might work if presented with extremely high quality 3D visuals and gameplay, but this is a Nintendo Switch game here on Steam. One important note is that even though this is an amateur project, it does seem to be sincerely and genuinely made.  I couldn't find any flipped assets, plagiarism or any other kind of insincere actions from the developer, but unfortunately genuine intentions alone are not enough to produce a brilliant PC gaming experience.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The 2D artwork here is middling at best, a hodge-podge of amateurish "My First Wacom Tablet" style drawings used instead professional looking game assets, and isn't of sufficient quality to make up for the other defects in the game. There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, left handed gamers or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.The game never really caught on with the millions of gamers on Steam, with a very low peak player count close to launch, and then just a handful of players launching this game every couple of days.  This is undoubtedly caused by factors such as those raised in this review.  It's always helpful with buying decisions to consider how popular and successful the product is, and unfortunately while this did accumulate a few participation trophy reviews, overall, people just aren't using it.So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?"Out of Line" has the greedy, cash grab price of around $8 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.  For comparison, the $8 asking price for this game could get you games like "Fallout: New Vegas", "Borderlands 2" or "Warhammer: Vermintide 2".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

_childDocuments_.review: It is hard to review a short game without spoiling the story but I will try. All I can say is that I liked the post-apocalypse world with esoteric elements. The story is told without words only by the beautiful hand drawn graphics of the game and all the paintings you see when playing. The graphic in this game creates a nice mysterious atmosphere. I think the story of this game is about growing older with time and changing ourselfs and world around us but it is just what I think and anyone can have their own idea what the story is really about because the world presented in the game also touches things like post-apocalypse and memories and hope and rebirth.This game is a good platform game with some puzzles and an interesting mechanic of spear throwing and using it to climb higher or to use our spear like a lever. It has some stealth sections and some sections where you have to run as fast as you can and some normal slower platforming sections mixed with some puzzles. All in all the gameplay is solid and fun and by mixing many things it does not get boring or repetitive. The game was too short. I 100% it in 3 hours without hurrying up and with a break in the middle of my game session so I think this game can be finished in 2 hours or less if you are fast. I also think puzzles were little too easy and not really challenging. I think that for the amount of fun and length this game has it should cost no more than 5$. _childDocuments_.review: Out of Line is a charming indie puzzle platformer whose world appears almost surreal due to its hand-drawn artwork.You play as San, an ambiguous being trying to escape from a factory, constantly stalked by corrupted machinery. The narrative is presented without dialogue, making it obscure, and the overall story is pieced together via context clues and murals seen in the game’s luscious backdrops. Unfortunately, the story is told solely using artwork, which makes it feel incomplete. After the game, I had a gist of the overarching narrative, but ended up with more questions than answers.Along your way, you encounter other amorphous characters that come to your aid. Out of Line does a fantastic job of synchronizing San’s actions with these characters in order to progress by activating a platform or avoiding the treacherous machinery. For a single player game, Out of Line unexpectedly juxtaposes the loneliness felt in a world desolated by robot claws and distorted gadgetry with its “cooperative play”.Out of Line differentiates itself from traditional puzzle platformers with the newly introduced spear mechanic. Instead of being used as a weapon, the spear can be hurled and utilized as a platform on walls and a key to power up devices. A minor disappointment is that there is no combat in this game, despite the fact that you wield this powerful tool. It cannot be thrown as a weapon and does no damage to enemies if you attempt to do so.Though the puzzles are quite easy, the game does a great job ramping up the player to increasingly challenging problems. The puzzles start off simple enough, asking you to create a single platform with the spear, and go as far as requiring you to correctly time spear throws and jumps. There are, of course, additional puzzle elements that include stopping gadgets from rotating with your spear, guiding friendly beetle-like creatures into powering machinery and redirecting pipes to let out steam. In addition, the puzzles are not repeated for the sake of artificially prolonging the game.For a 2-3 hour game, Out of Line is a fun straightforward puzzle platformer filled with relaxing scenery, innovative puzzles, gorgeous art design, and a vague but intriguing story. Other than to gather all collectibles for the trophy achievement, there is little to no replayability for this game. Priced at $12.99, this game is better purchased during a sale, especially for those that are on the fence. Though Out of Line does not break the mold of puzzle platformer games, it is a game worth checking out if you have a desire for a visual and sensory experience and a free evening.7.25/10

_childDocuments_.review: Out of Line is a great, beautiful and emotional platform adventure. _childDocuments_.review: It Beautiful, it's interesting, Fun and very easy. But it's extremely short. Completed the thing in under 3 hours. The story is never explained fully, and a lot of mechanics could have been flesh out to provide a fuller experience. Even at the sale price of 13$ it's not a good value. Don't expect any replayability. It is what it is, a visual, and sensory experience more than a game. The best parts are the collaboration with other NPC to solve puzzles. it makes this single player game like a friendship experience. It looks like a platformer but most of the time you just move on to the next screen to solve the next puzzle. It has a Machinarium vibe sometimes. I wish They had given us more to grab onto. Hard to put a thumbs down on this because it is really gorgeous and fun, but you should be aware that it's not a lot of value for the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Out of Line wasdesigned with a stylized approach. The mechanics of the game revolve around San’s spear, something the character sees as a tool that will help him navigate this strange world. We want players to learn through experimentation, constantly tinkering with puzzles until they find a logical solution. This design philosophy plays a thematic role in our game, as most individuals find their purpose through trial and error.

name: Saltsea Chronicles
detailed_description: Saltsea Chronicles is a new story-driven adventure game from the award-winning indie studio Die Gute Fabrik (Mutazione, Sportsfriends). Captain Maja’s misfit crew must heist their impounded ship and mount a rescue. Guide the crew across islands of a post-flood world known as ‘Saltsea’. Explore strange and wonderful communities, uncover a deep conspiracy, choose where to go and which crew members to investigate with, and chart a journey through twists and turns, difficulties and delights. A Post-Flood World Visit different island communities as you investigate the mystery at the heart of the game. Each built on pre-flood ruins – in beautiful and beguiling ways. As you explore you will uncover different pathways through a rich and varied series of islands. This flooded world, betrayed by the so-called Hoarders, barely remembers a time before the Flood. They rebuilt on the ruins of what came before, and new talents and technologies took the place of the old. Many surprises await! Choose Your Priorities In Saltsea Chronicles you guide the entire crew through the story. As well as investigating the mystery of your captain’s disappearance, you will uncover secrets, create and resolve tensions between the crew, and add to your number as you meet others who ask to join you. Each chapter, you pick which island to visit and who to send on the expedition. Your choices will unlock different content, develop relationships, and give you a chance to resolve (and create) tensions within the crew. With a lightning-fast navigation system, you’re free to hop around the islands as you explore. Choose between short and snappy observations, or dig deep into conversations with your crewmate or the locals, exploring the islands across different times of day. Uncover a Conspiracy Was your captain kidnapped? Or did she leave of her own free will? Keep track of the mystery in Murl’s Log and collect records of your encounters as stickers in the Almanac. Different playthroughs will take you to different islands, introduce different characters and have dramatic consequences for your crew. You can replay from any chapter and branch your save file to meet new crew members, explore different communities and trace alternative pathways through the rich and gripping story. Themes From an award-winning and diverse writersroom – with experience in Young Adult fiction, film, theatre, poetry and games – Saltsea Chronicles imagines a rich world where communities have rebuilt in the aftermath of disaster, creating a new society of connection, resilience and hope—but one still troubled by the universal questions of how to live together through conflict and change. This wide-reaching story game traces meaningful themes with humour, lightness of touch, and care. Features: Distinctive print-inspired art style: A unique art style inspired by risograph print techniques brings a storybook aesthetic to the fantasy-tinged world of Saltsea Chronicles , brought to life with beautiful bespoke animation. Try your hand at Spoils: Spoils is a trick-taking card game from the world of Saltsea Chronicles . Play cards with each local community, but watch out – some islands have their own house rules! An original soundtrack by Eli Rainsberry: IGF-nominated composer and sound artist Eli Rainsberry (No Longer Home, A Monster's Expedition) presents a musically hybrid score and soundscape guided by the spaces and characters of Saltsea Chronicles . Navigate the drama as well as the seas: Tensions between crew members are represented by Issues, small ‘relationships quests’ you can track, resolve, or, sometimes, just have to leave unsolved.

short_description: It begins with a kidnapped captain and a stolen ship. Where it leads next? That’s up to you… In this story-driven adventure game you will explore strange and wonderful communities, uncover a deep conspiracy, and chart a journey through twists and turns, difficulties and delights.

_childDocuments_.review: I insta-bought this game because I love Mutazione by the same devs so very much that I trusted them to deliver something excellent again, even if the description didn't sound too interesting to me. I was not disappointed. My attention span is at squirrel level at the moment, but the masterful world-building, characters and story of Saltsea managed to draw me in. It has strong Mutazione vibes and takes up some of the same themes again, but it's still very much its own thing. Again we get a well-written cast of lovable outsiders with enjoyable character growth; alternative communities emerging after tragic disaster; a maritime theme with lots of fantastical plants and animals; an overarching story that veers into the supernatural, a lot of minor and major personal "drama"; brilliant sound design, art and animation; no puzzles that could distract from the narrative and pull you out of immersion; and a story that goes much deeper than it first seemed. Unlike Mutazione though, you don't play a main character but instead switch between crew members that you often get to choose. No musical gardening (sadly). There are a lot of decisions to make that have actual consequences, though from what I've gathered they can't be right or wrong as such and only lead to different stories along the way. The world of Saltsea is more vast and complex. There's a huge amount of dialogue to be discovered in easily accessible chapter replays that you can branch out into different saves. The story is darker; warning for the sensitive that , but I think it was handled really well. The dialogues weren't 100% polished - there were many typos and a few inconsistencies, though pulling all of those strings together with all the possible variables from player choices must have been very challenging. It was obvious that a lot of thought has been put into the dialogues and story. I also found it rewarding to explore all the bits of lore and atmosphere around the maps, and to move my cursor over everything to discover all the little animations. It all made Saltsea feel like a familiar though strange place to me within a few hours, a vibrant place that I want to come back to, with characters that I still think about outside of the game. I laughed and cried with my crew, got literal goosebumps on a few occasions, and the ending took me by complete surprise - both with what happened and just leaving at that point. It took me a bit of staring at the ending screen to agree that it did make sense to end the game there, but OMG would I have loved to see it continue. My first playthrough took about 17 hours, including going back and forth through locations (which, thankfully, is quick and easy) to try and get ALL the interactive bits, and spending some time to take in scenes, re-read dialogues and ponder decisions. I already felt like checking out different outcomes while playing, and I think I'm going to go through chapters like episodes in a series. There's a pretty good log of what's been going on, you only need mouse clicks for navigation, there's even theme music with a (skippable) video at the end of each chapter and a sort of intro at the start, so it seems like a perfect interactive series to play an episode of while having dinner. * * * If you like chill and story-driven games, check out my curator . You're also welcome to join the .

_childDocuments_.review: I liked SALTSEA CHRONICLES, with some caveats.First, players should be aware that this is a narrative-heavy game with minimal gameplay; some choice of where to go next, but nothing in the form of puzzle-solving or action sequences. It does have a card game you can play at each location, which has no impact on outcomes, and is not a badly designed card game, but I wound up ignoring it after a few plays, because it was largely irrelevant to the game itself.The characters are well-imagined, diverse, and interesting, as are their interactions. Their dialogs (not fully voiced but with occasional one-word verbal interjections) are well written, and understandable in a colloquially English way, notwithstanding the developers' Danish origins. I am not actually a fan of the art style used to display the characters, which in some cases can be, to my eye, grotesque; but as a player of Mutazione (from the same developer -- which I also liked but didn't love), I expected that going in.The game is mostly about clicking on hotspots, and making dialog choices. The other major choice you make is that, each time you visit an island, one of the character ensemble will definitely explore the island, and you choose one person to companion them. Typically, only two other characters are available as companions, out of a larger crew -- which I totally understand as a development constraint. Writing dialog for two potential companion characters already expands your development scope, doing it for (say) six is a level of scope you probably don't want to bite off.I did play twice, because you cannot visit all islands on a single play-through, and I wanted to explore some of the others. The path you go does affect what other companions will join you on your journey, but does not materially affect the mainline story; you are still forced into chokepoint story beats, despite which islands you choose to visit. In particular, . So: Good writing, engaging characters, an entertaining setting, not a fan of the character art, would prefer more variability of outcome, but I do not regret the time I spent with the game, and can recommend it to players who like narrative games, and prefer a light experience over a challenging one.Oh: One other thing: The UI/UX design is excellent. I was never in any doubt as to where I could or should go next, or how to explore the game's features.
