_childDocuments_.review: [[Game Review]]This game is so much better than the first one. Basically any and all issues from the first game have been fixed. The game this time focuses much more on the action and story which were the major positive elements of the first game. Its signature style and bizarre, Japanese AF, humor is still very present and the combat feels way more action heavy, smooth, and satisfying with better animations and deeper mechanics. The empty and bland open world is replaced with a much more streamlined fast travel menu system.  The good but tedious mini-games have been replaced with NES style 8-bit mini-games. These are not throw away mini-games either. They feel like real authentic NES games. In addition to this you still have an assortment of combat side missions to complete which are your standard "Kill Everything Before The Timer Runs Out" style missions. Another interesting thing they added is this hilarious "help your fat cat lose weight" pet sim that you can play in between missions. The only negative aspects would be that a few of the mini-games you unlock towards the end are kind of bland and could have been cut. Also the last stage of the muscle training game was agonizing. But that's it, everything else is great!9/10[[Port Review]]As far as the port goes. Its still lacking basic features (graphics options, mouse and keyboard support) that most PC games have. However the 2nd game is much more stable than the first. Only had one crash the entire time I played.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: (Only reason I'm not recommending the game is because this game uses online-online DRM, which is a complete disgrace to this great game. DRM is a cancerous tumor and it's such a shame this game has it.)  No More Heroes 2: Desperate Struggle is a good hack 'n' slash game. As a sequel, well...It's good, but not the best in the world- I'll get into that soon. It's a fun game that improves on certain aspects of the original like the gameplay and soundtrack, but it does have its fair share of problems, especially this PC port. Let's get into the pros and cons.Pros:- Gameplay and combat's somewhat improved, it does not feel as simplistic as the original game- Killer soundtrack (It's Kill or Be Killed, No More Riot, Philistine, Charging Katana, and Sling Shot to name a few)- Good artstyle- Decent story- Cool boss fights (Skelter Helter. Margaret, Matt Helms, and Captain Vladimir)- Shinobu segments help change the game up- Nice and fun weapons (Rose Nasty and the Camellia)- Somewhat good set pieces- Collectables are not as annoying to search as the first game- 8-bit side missions are an interesting replacement for the original side missions, except for the scorpion one, just the same as the first game- Good voice acting- Death Match mode, which is just a boss rush mode on hard difficulty- at least you could replay the boss fights compared to the original game- Gym and Jeane's training missions are alright- In-game sword selection screen is a nice addition- Henry vs Mimmy boss fight was nice change of pace- Based on the great Nintendo Switch remasterCons:- Story is not as memorable as the first game- Getting knocked down very often is super annoying- Fat enemies can be a pain in the rear to deal, especially the ones with chainsaws- Ending is not as iconic or good as the original game's ending- Final boss is meh- Less replayability compared to No More Heroes 1- Removal of open world, which was alright in the original and could've been brought back and improved upon, but at least it made traveling to missions and side-jobs much quicker- Much shorter than No More Heroes 1- Suda 51 did not direct this- PC port is bare bones and a bit questionable, game froze on me before and it has weird screen artifacts and geometry, noticeable in the 8-bit parts of the game and save screen (must have something to do with the anti-aliasing). - Had to play it on windowed mode because it would not play on fullscreen (Why?)- 2 or 3 achievements are broken- Boss fights are not as memorable or iconic as the first game- Shinobu segments can be quite annoying (her floaty jumping controls and New Destroyman boss fight were really annoying)    Overall, even though No More Heroes 2: Desperate Struggle has its own problems, I still thinkit's a good game and sequel to No More Heroes. It still has good characters, story, and soundtrack like the original game. In regards to the PC port, well... It could've been much better and it's slightly disappointing considering how buggy it is, so I recommend buying on sale like I did. Other than that, I recommend this game if you want a fun hack 'n' slash action game or you're a fan of No More Heroes like I am.

_childDocuments_.review: Sequels are often treated with scrutiny as artists learn from their mistakes and iteratively improve. It's only fitting that No More Heroes 2 is in many ways superior to the prequel. True to its action movie aesthetic, the game has breakneck pacing as there are no longer ranking battle entry fees. The Assassination and Free Fight missions from NMH1 have also been streamlined into a series of Revenge Missions that are frustration-free and quick. Bosses are back and greater than ever with better variety to keep things fresh. There are fewer cheap instant-kill attacks, though the final boss has 2 particularly frustrating moves. Best of all is the introduction of the Ecstasy gauge, rewarding skilled players for landing blows without taking them in return. Once filled, Travis gets to live his inner samurai fantasy by rapidly cutting his enemies into ribbons.  Unfortunately, NMH2 has some rough spots. First, this is the same team that did the previous port, so there are crashing issues, screen-tearing at high frame rate, graphical pop-ups and freezing during menus. Achievements are broken as well, which is frankly unacceptable. In addition to the port issues, NMH2 makes the odd choice of nerfing evasive options. Perfect dodges are weaker, and dodges in general seem less responsive compared to its predecessor. These changes do not detract enough from the experience, as NMH2 is a good game. Unfortunately, I cannot in good faith recommend this version as the port is bad.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this game is so fun and fondly remembered because it's unafraid to take chances with experimental ideas, and its sense of humor is so completely irreverent of basically everything that it even makes sure to dismiss and parody its own self, every single chance it gets, and totally succeeds at it. It's a beautiful piece of art that is going to resonate best with some *very* specific audiences, namely those who have consumed a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of video games and anime, but the game is so uniquely unpredictable and wacky that I think basically anyone can get something out of it, assuming you at least played NMH 1 first (which is every bit as good/bad as this one). The vast majority of this game's weird ideas land, and even when they don't you still kinda appreciate them.  I can't think of a single other series that has actually left me feeling so rewarded for engaging with its version of grindy tedium, except maybe Yakuza. And there is absolutely some percentage of tedium here, which would be among my handful of complaints if it didn't suit Suda's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up universe so well. What few complaints I do have can basically all be explained as one avant-garde concept or janky forced mechanic that manifested alongside fifty one strokes of genius. And yes, some of the humor is dated, but we were all comparatively ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the 2000s, so it might be in your best interest to simply laugh off the most colorful jokes as products of an edgier era.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: The final score is a 6, which is hardly a strong recommendation, so it's best to consider this review a neutral one. Only play it if you're already a die-hard fan of the first game.Over the years, many have expressed that this game isn't as good as the first, and fails to match its tone. This makes some sense, considering Suda51 wasn't in the director's chair anymore. The surprising thing is, this game is actually so much like the first game that it's detrimental. It's the ultimate safe sequel, slightly improving on some aspects, but ditching the whole artistic integrity thing. The game starts off as a revenge story, with a Santa Destroy covered in snow, but then quickly becomes the first game all over again once the snow melts, and the revenge plot ends up feeling useless at best.The combat was improved somewhat, but still very simple. The biggest improvement is the boss fights, specifically the fact that the bosses can be attacked most of the time now, and no longer have moments of invulnerability. There's also a selection of four beam katanas this time around, with the standouts being a set of dual blades, and a very long sword that's slow to swing. These can be switched out on the fly once purchased. The cast of assassins is colorful, but lacking compared to the first game, especially the final boss. Everything that stood out about the first was streamlined for better or for worse, and so the open-world is gone, replaced by a menu. The side jobs are now 8-Bit styled minigames, and these range from weak to awful. Like in the prequel game, the best of the experience is found in the boss fights, so at least it's possible to get to them right away now, even though some of the soul was lost in the process.The mind-boggling thing about this game is that some of the boss fights still have useless level segments before the fights, and the basic enemies are still as uninteresting as ever, essentially serving as nothing more than pinatas. It gets particularly frustrating in two of the later levels where there are twenty to thirty minute-long segments where you need to fight wave after wave of the same enemies, and it doesn't help that there's no variety except in the size of them, which just means they take longer to mindlessly slice up. It can be argued all day that these moments have an "artistic purpose", but considering how thematically shallow this game already is, it's just annoying. Another saving grace of the game: the exceptional soundtrack by an ensemble of different artists. Ironically, this might be the one area where this game surpasses the first, which already had a phenomenal score by Masafumi Takada.The port itself is fine, seemingly based on the Switch version by Engine Software, which is faithful to the Wii original. Though, many have mentioned a problem with frequent crashes, so it might have problems with older operating systems.

_childDocuments_.review: So much like the first No more heroes people said that No more heroes 2 was worse in it's issues but I will admit that unlike No more heroes 1 where that seemed heavily over exaggerated, no more heroes 2 was a bit of a mess, now I don't mean in gameplay or visuals those are...actually fantastic bar a few annoying bosses but that's less to do with the port and more just the game in general but I'll get to that in a bit but rather the crashes, on the first where it was two time in the entire game, NH2 was rather frequent, at least 10 times and I beat NH2 in a shorter time at that, although do note that's because of how the world is now not due to a shorter game by any means dood.Ignoring the rather large issue the game plays totally fine much like the first game does, following our good assassin Otaku Travis Touchdown, he ends up back in town and back in the game but this time he's got 50 assassins to take down, you have your usual lightsaber and as before you can buy more, only this time you can switch them mid battle which is a really nice touch, combat is a mix of the same and yet different with the lightsabers working a little differently combo and use wise but also now you have meter so to speak, indicated by the tiger in the corner, this activates a special mode if you're doing good in a fight that lets you absolutely thrash the opponents at insane speeds and quite frankly is probably one of my favourite things ever to see in a game, a power up move based on skill that's just right out awesome! of course you also still have the slot machine that randomly gives you crazy power ups too if you're lucky dood.The world is now just a map rather than a whole town you can drive through, this is quite saddening to me to a degree as I did enjoy going through santa destroy but for budgets sake I don't mind entirely with the visual upgrade and although a quick travel option would have worked just as well if they did have the whole place, that and honestly it did make getting to places a lot faster and overall better and the places you fight all have their own unique areas and looks so that makes up for it too dood.Jobs are better/worse? I mean I liked being 3D to do the jobs in the first game and whats more it all worked, in NH2 they traded that off for 8-bit minigames 7 of them and the last minigame being the only 3D one of the worst minigame from the first game, especially considering you don't have the dash anymore, they are fun enough granted to a degree and certainly more fun concepts than mowing the lawn and such but honestly I'm just glad they aren't too hard and easy enough to earn money for stuff in this one, oh also no more paying for fights which helps there whoo dood!talking of mini games you also have the exercise place and the ideas behind them are fun but also they can be annoying enough that you kinda wish you didn't have to do them, especially on the harder ones, I'd much rather the old button mash and timing like it used to be but to each their own, I'm sure many people will find them easy and funny dood ^-^All in all they did a lot with NH2 a lot of good streamlining and focus on the fun aspects, okay a few bosses were...less than fun, not horrible but still annoying or overpowered enough to make you panic that you're going to lose, luckily that ends up not being the case due to certain mechanics but it would be nice to see less of the types of attacks I was up against, I hope that whenever NH3 comes to PC that it's more of the improvements I saw here and less if the ridiculous attacks in those particular fights, thank you for reading and hope you enjoy playing, hopefully with that patch they promised!...any day now...yeah dood XD

_childDocuments_.review: *RUN THE GAME IN WIN 7 COMPAT to fix CRASHING ISSUES*No More Heroes 2 continues 3 years after the story of the first game. Travis became the UAA's number 1 ranked assassin, and then walked away, the only one ever to do so, and became an myth and urban legend to the league of assassins.After Travis' best friend is killed, he decides to go on a revenge mission, rejoining the UAA for nothing other than revenge. What follows, is one mans suicide mission to avenge his fallen friend.Gameplay wise, NMH2 is more of the same, except, now one of the beam katanas you receive is dual wielded. The hud has received a re-work, and there is a new "ecstasy gauge", that allows you to attack faster, and continue your combo longer, the better you are performing. For the most part, the combat is still as satisfying as ever, so the actual in game stages and boss gameplay is still fine. You can also play as Shinobu, and Henry, at specific points, so the main gameplay loop does have variety this time around.The side content is where this game is def inferior to it's predecessor. While it's nice that they condensed Santa Destroy into a menu, thus passing a severely polarizing open world (You either enjoyed or hated the open world in 1 it seems, no in between) in doing so, they severely downgraded the jobs, and also the combat missions. Free Fights are gone, replaced instead with "Revenge Missions", which are basically the exact same gameplay as some of the assassin missions from the previous game, except with one big difference. You aren't rewarded money for these missions, and can only play them once per playthrough. The "Jobs" from the first game, have been severely downgraded as well, with all but one of them being presented as 8-bit style NES/Famicom styled mini-games. They are varied, but the monetary reward you earn from these jobs, is loathsomely pathetic compared to the first game.I think the director of this game was far too harsh on the open world from the first game, because actually grinding those jobs were fun and engaging, and even the earliest jobs could still net you a decent amount of money. Here, they are treated as nothing but filler for people that want to clear out Area 51.Since money is basically useless in this game, being mainly used firstly only in Ryan's Gym (which itself is worse than the gym mini games from the first game), and then secondly, Naomi's Lab for the two buyable katanas in the game, they compensated by making every single clothing item insanely expensive in this game. Essentially, if you want to unlock the cosmetics, you should get good at bug out perfect runs and that's it. NMH 1 does have an easy grinding assassination mission, Gamble Fight, however, the side jobs were actually fun and engaging in that game, and, because NG+ added new clothing items to buy, it made actually re-playing different jobs and assassin missions fun. I cannot suggest you actually care about the money system in this game, except for Ryan's Gym.Ryan's Gym is utilized the same way as the Thunder Ryu building from the first game. Here, you pay a fee for two mini games. "Stamina", and "Muscle". Both are presented like the side jobs, as 2D Retro NES/Famicom minigames.The Stamina minigame, like in the first game, is insanely easy. You use the bumpers and the stick and run on a treadmill, instead of using the sticks to perform squats. This increases your max health.The "Muscle" minigame, however, is the worst part of this game, bar none. Standing on the left of the screen, Travis has to punch and kick dumbells being thrown at him from Ryan, while also ducking under his "affection". The main issue with this mini game, is that, you fail it if you take too many hits, but rather than losing the mini game right away after too many hits, the game FORCES you to wait the entire time limit out. There is also no measure of how many hits is too much to fail. So basically, you have no way of knowing what the hit limit is on each level. I always make a save in the motel, and then attempt Muscle training first because, you have to repay the fee to try again, and it increases with every level. It starts out easy enough, but Level 7 is literally a 30 second gauntlet of projectile spam that costs way too much money to attempt every time. I have absolutely nothing good to say about the muscle mini game. It's just tedious and I hate the very concept of Ryan as a character purely.Those issues aside, the main gameplay, and the boss fights, are still as great as ever. There are def times in this game, where it can feel like filler (Rank fight number 4, literally has you kill 100+ goons, to START the gameplay level, then, you fight through basically 40+ more to start the bossfight, for example), however, all of the character designs, and their boss fights, are still enjoyable(with the exception of the final boss). During the standard gameplay levels before you initiate a boss fight, there are collectibles inside treasure chests just like the first game, however, instead of just being cards, these are actually furniture items, that Travis will display around his apartment as you collect them. This idea is insanely awesome in my opinion, and kinda makes me wish they had an apartment customization option, maybe with furniture or accessory store for the player to buy more items items to display. There are a lot of cutscenes in Travis' apartment, and it would be nice to be able to hide or change different items. As mentioned previously, there are segments where you play as Shinobu Jacobs, and Henry Cooldown. The Shinobu levels are fine, and Henry's segment is brief but he is crazy fun to play as. The only down side is these segments are extremely short lived.Overall, No More Heroes 2's main gameplay is still as fun as the first games, and the combat and dodging def feels no where near as stiff as the first games, but, almost all of the side content suffers. The clothing options are more varied, with you being able to buy shoes and gloves/wristbands, and the Jackets are more varied as well, not just being re-skins and re colors like the first games jackets, however, they are insanely expensive.The best side content in this game, in my opinion, is the Jeane mini games. At the start of the game, Jeane has gained weight due to Travis over feeding her. She starts at 25.9 pounds. She has a mood meter that is filled up to 5 icons, and there are 3 different types of food you can feed her. Basically, every time before you go fight the next ranked opponent, you can feed Jeane and then play with her, to get her to lose weight. Once she is lower than 11 pounds, you earn a single move for this trouble, but, the ability for Travis to interact with Jeane and have the player control it is def nice. In the first game, it was just an eye catcher.If you just want to experience the story, you can totally do that and still have immense fun with Desperate Struggle, as money is not required to progress the story, but, 100% completion is def not even anywhere CLOSE to being enjoyable, like it was in the first game. If the Original NMH is a 10/10, 2 is an 8/10 from me. The game does allow you to replay any boss fight you want during NG+, which is something I really wish the first game did (and it did on the PS3 version!), and the soundtrack as usual, is absolutely insane. I have not played a NG+ playthrough as of writing this game, but, if you bought the first game, you should grab the rest of them as well.tl;dr, base gameplay good, story good, music SEX, side content grindy and unfulfilling and boring.

_childDocuments_.review: No More Heroes 2 is a strange game. It makes many changes that would seem to make the title more appealing to most players. Gutting the open-world, making the mini-games mostly optional, increasing the amount of boss fights, and dialing up the game's crazy vulgarity were likely all attempts to make a bigger, better sequel that would be more consistent than what came before. However, nearly every change from the first game ultimately robs the series of what made it stand out in the first place. Rather than being an avant-garde action title that meditates on genre conventions, No More Heroes 2 ends up being a mostly average experience that doesn't really stick with you. This is a shame, because there are small moments where this sequel shows promise; it just never amounts to anything which matches No More Heroes 1

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, it's either a positive or negative review, I can't leave a "neutral" or "somewhat leaning towards no but I'd still recommend the experience".Compared to the original No More Heroes, 2 has a lot of problems. Combat is less enjoyable, the lock-on is horrible, and the big part of the No More Heroes series the bosses, aren't great. I didn't die to a single boss and for a majority of the time I was just bumrushing them, tanking their damage and dealing more damage than they could output. I never learned their patterns, I never got invested, it was just a button mash festival. The combat in general has been dumbed down, the Dark Step which in the first game was an extremely useful move that allowed extra hits onto an enemy or boss. It was difficult to learn at first but rewarding. In this game, it exists but I'm pretty sure no one knows how to perform it. Something as simple as the High and Low sign at the right side of the screen which allows you to determine what attack you should perform next so you can maximize your damage output is gone for some reason, but it's functionality isn't.Mini-games / Jobs are boring in my opinion and fundamentally pointless. You have 2 big things you should buy which would require a little bit of grinding, and the rest (gym training, Jeane) the bosses generally give you enough money to purchase. The most expensive training session I believe is 14k? Most T-Shirts in the game cost more than that (ofc that's assuming if you do the training session first try, which you probably aren't). The Camellia MK-3 (formerly the Tsubaki MK-3 which was a translation error) and Peony are the things that cost the most money, and afterwards money is somewhat pointless. Camellia gets outclassed by the Rose Nasty later into the game, and the Peony is actually different enough from the other 3 sets of Beam Katanas that I have to make a note for it: The Peony was the most enjoyable part of the game for me. It activated my ape brain, doing the equivalent of sniping enemies with a massive club.But that's besides the point: The jobs are boring, and in some cases (such as the gym training) are infuriating.The main line missions are generally grindy, and there isn't anything interesting / unique about them again, compared to the first game. No matter how much I disliked Darkstar's driving sequence, it at least offered a unique experience compared to spamming X and Y, then occasionally flicking down the right analog stick. There's an absurd amount of enemies, and during the Rank 4 Boss Stage, I had to kill enemies for a solid 10~ish minutes without doing anything else, then when the murder spree was finally over, I had to kill: more enemies, the same way.TL;DR: Play the First Game, if you played the First Game and you're deciding whether or not to play this game? You should be safe watching a playthrough. It's not a bad game, but it's not anything like No More Heroes 1. There are so many other things that I'd like to mention (such as the Health visuals changing, in 1 you got small little bonus hearts in your big heart, in this one it just looks visually the same but it's actually different) but it'd take forever. Peony is pretty funny though if someone just added the Peony to NMH 1, my ape brain would be satisfied for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: + great writing and voice acting+ gameplay has been refined over original+ killer soundtrack- cool bosses don't get much screentime- much shorter and much easier than first game- some technical issuesNo More Heroes does only a few things but does them really well: the punk sensibilities in its writing, humor, and art design; the bloody, frenetic combat; and some of the best bosses in gaming. No More Heroes 2 continues this trend, although with some caveats. A lot has been improved, a couple things have stayed the same, but in one key area (the bosses) I feel has stagnated a little bit.The writing is really nice but I felt like some of the progress was cheapened at times. I don't know how the game was advertised, but it initially leads you to believe there's 50 bosses ahead of you. Yet one boss takes out 25 of them, another boss another 10 of them, then some bosses are killed offscreen between bosses... there are more boss fights than the first game but it could have been written better. But, the writing still has that humor and charm about it, you can excuse this one bit of lazy writing because the rest is great.Gone is the overworld and replacing it is a list you select places from. In most games this would be an egregious downgrade but it's appreciated here. Rather than have a boring open world with nothing to do, it's quick and easy navigating the world. They could have improved the original game's open world but I don't fault them for instead doing it this way so they could focus on what really matters in a character action game: the combat.The gameplay is pretty much untouched from the original. You can now switch beam katanas at will, and some of the slot machine powerups are different, but mechanically it feels good. There's a couple things I don't like, like the sidestep dodge is next to impossible to pull off consistently now, and the camera control can be wonky at times, but it's still some of the most satisfying combat of the genre.Bosses this time around look really cool but that's about it. Their screentime is much shorter than the first game's bosses. Several bosses have very short introductions, some of them have no real introduction. The bosses don't feel memorable and instead feel rushed. The soundtrack accompanying the bosses does sound real good, though.Not only do bosses feel worse writing-wise, their fights also feel dumbed down. While most of them feel fun to play against, they also feel mechanically simple. Near the halfway point in the game, you could just rush bosses and tank hits and still be okay, when I felt like the original punished you for doing the same. Boss fights are shorter, easier, less memorable, basically a downgrade in every way.While the first No More Heroes had an abysmal PC port, it's a lot better here. I didn't experience any crashes or graphical issues, but it's still a very barebones port, with no graphic options, control options that don't save between launches, and again broken achievements. A couple of scenes are pre-rendered movies rather than ingame footage, you'll notice the quality drop dramatically to 480 lines. It's a shame but it's not a completely broken mess like the first game.I liked the game but it didn't have the same impact the first title had. If you want more No More Heroes, well, this is what we got, and I think it's worth a playthrough because the gameplay, music, writing is all still excellent. But it has dramatically worse boss encounters which I wouldn't argue with someone if they said they were the main reason to play the games. A lot of the fat from the original is cut and it seems like some of the bosses got caught in the crossfire.With max TDP at 5w, it can keep 60fps throughout. Sometimes onscreen effects like smoke might bring it down a hair to the 50s, but this happened once or twice in an entire playthrough.

Like working out, cooking, collecting anime figures, and doing part-time jobs. : Wait, what? So he's basically a part-time assassin?: Exactly! He needs to make money to pay for his beam katana maintenance and rent. Just like a real adult. Oh, and there's a lot of desperate simping too.: Desperate simping, you say?: Oh, yeah, he’s got a major thing for Sylvia Christel, the manipulative organizer of the assassins' ranks who loves to keep him on his toes.: Ah, desperate simping, every hero’s true struggle. So, what's the goal here?: Travis has to kill his way to the top of the assassins' ranks again, facing increasingly bizarre and dangerous enemies, each with their own unique style and backstory.: Bizarre enemies are tight. But are there any deeper themes?: Oh, definitely. It's about revenge, the price of violence, and the blurred line between reality and fiction. But mostly, it's about having a blast while kicking some serious butt. Oh, and did I mention the fanservice?: Fanservice, you say?: Yup! There are plenty of beeeeeewwwwwwbs (boobs), jiggle physics, and sultry characters that will have players, uh, .: Well, this sounds like a desperate struggle worth having. Because sometimes, being a desperate simp is just part of the job.****:So prepare for a journey that's as much about self-discovery as it is about extreme violence.  – where the struggle is real, the simping is desperate, and the fanservice is plentiful.

_childDocuments_.review: No More Heroes 2: Desperate Struggle to find something nice to say about this game.It's a slightly better port job I guess.The audio isn't wrecked like NMH 1, and skipping cutscenes doesn't crash the game any more. But thats bare minimum stuff. Still no keyboard support, still no graphics options or anything.Achievements are still bugged, the kill 510 enemies achievement is literally impossible since there's barely 300 enemies in the whole game.What about the game play? It sucks.The game never evolves beyond mindlessly mashing a four hit combo, then doing a dodge and doing it all over again. The hardest bosses are fought back to back when you play as Shinobu, since she taunts after every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ combo and basically begs the boss to slap her ♥♥♥♥. At time of writing I'm not sure I'll finish the game. The boss fights, while easy are much more fun than the endless hordes of copy pasted goons you fight constantly. Worst part is you'll spend most of combat waiting for the enemy to pick themselves up off the floor so you can keep hitting them.PRO TIP! Just alternate between mashing X and Y since Travis will never finish his combo the enemy will never get knocked down massively increasing your DPS.PRO TIP #2! Get a turbo controller so you don't get carpal tunnel.They did improve the mini games, but I find it hard to praise that either since you no longer need to farm money for each stage what's the point of even playing them?If I wanted to play a famicom game I'd download an emulator. NMH 2 does have a good story, Travis's character arc is genuinely interesting and the boss fight cut scenes are easily the best part. Suda51 is a master of creating and introducing absurd characters then making them feel unique even human without wasting a second of screen time. You can really feel his touch all over the game. Sadly many bosses were cut, much of the story is delivered through choppy exposition and on the whole it just feels like Suda wanted to give us more than he could.If the best parts of a game can be replicated by watching the cut scenes on Youtube, then why is it a game not a movie or show?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is tedious. It has the ingredients to be a successful sequel but I cannot help but feel Suda is taking the piss and basically making kak up as he goes. Like there is no deep story or anything, you play as a lunatic "Assassin" that just enjoys killing people. Except he tries unconvincingly to make excuses for it.  Storywise I do not know where Suda planned on taking the series, I dont think he was really invested in planning 1 for the game cause it comes off as stale.Gameplay-wise, the game is repetitive. You have to kill every enemy on the screen and half of them just have a massive health pool so its annoying, bear in mind the game could often just toss a ton of them per stage in the level. Half the bosses lacked a sense of challenge and do not leave a lasting impression. The best part of the game was the mid section when you can control characters aside from Travis. Another thing I will add is a lack of weapon diversity and incentive to try the wrestling moves. I felt the game would encourage me more to just spam sword slashes as punching or kicking to build up stun can give enemies and bosses opportunities to attack you.Something that bothered me was the lack of ability to explore the world compared to NMH1 with your bike. Its just something that made the 1st game very memorable to me.This game, like the NMH1 port, has buggy and broken achievements. The "Maybe you should see a doctor?" and "Minigame Masteroo" achievement counters are broken, due to a faulty counter. The "Desperate Massacre" achievement is also buggy due to a faulty counter. However I think there is a way to get it. I would like to mention within 30 minutes of playing the game during the 2nd boss stage( so after the tutorial boss) crashed on me. It tends to crash more when I go to the Gym or weapon shop. So be warned this is a iffy port, not as bad as the 1st game's port but still bad.Overall, the game is good but there are aspects about it that bother me. The story goes nowhere, the gameplay loses novelty quickly, some of the bosses are cool but are overwhelmingly gimmicky. 6/10 for me.  This 2nd game really put me off trying out the 3rd game when it gets a steam port.

started to make sense when i decided to focus on the Commodification aspect, a sort of texas chainsaw massacre 2 take where everything is louder and grosser and more colorful because now all the horror is being sold for mass entertainment. its pretty good, but i think it might work less as a capital s Statement (even compared to the original, which i can understand ppl finding a bit Passe in into pure abstraction (thru among other things, the removal of the hub world and lack of tactility to the 8 bit minigames), u could do a lot worse, and if the game lives or dies on the big setpieces with a slight (and ever increasing) Nightmarish Tint, it mostly works. the boss sequencing and general ramping of drama and tone in the runup to the finale is particularly striking, and makes the whole game feel more cohesive in hindsight,,,,alice is probably the best boss and best dramatic samurai movie moment in either of these, but even she wouldnt be as felt without the immediately preceding fights setting the stage so well. theres an almost Snyder Watchmen quality to this where im wondering if im underrating this because, as it engages with the original material as essentially pure pulp, it may understand it and its appeal better then i or anyone else who just wants to wax about it does. i think that might explain and add vibrancy to a lot of things. maybe not the _childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this review by saying I love this game to death, I have been a huge fan of the NMH series for many, many years and that NMH 2 is my favorite in the series. The music is top of the line and every song fits every single scenario its placed in perfectly. The gameplay has been improved from NMH 1 with more weapons choices, a more fluid combat system, and a better grasp of what makes the No More Heroes series so fun. The story, while it may not be everyone's cup of tea, does land more than it misses, specifically near the end with the fights after playing as Shinobu. The graphics have gotten a bump in quality since NMH 1 though this bump in quality doesn't shine in every place or cutscene.       However, this port on the PC isn't the proper way to play this game nowadays, it requires a controller which isn't inherently bad, NMH should be played with a controller for the best experience but the option would have been nice for those that prefer a keyboard and mouse. The game on a better screen suffers from it as much as it gains, as some cutscenes look absolutely horrible like the pre-fight cutscene with Charlie. However, the game on the PC is absolutely riddled with crashes, far more often and far more consistently than on the Wii or Switch ports, especially nearing the end of the game where a consistent crash stopped me dead in my tracks and killed a save file after the Captain Vladimir (rank 3) fight. The achievements in this port are also bugged and don't properly count some values or may not trigger properly. The bugged achievements I encountered that were solvable were: "Slay of the Dragon" for killing Ryuji, this achievement triggers at the very end of the cutscene so don't skip it. "A Brother's Nightmare" for killing Mimmy as Henry, this achievement also does not trigger until the end of the post-fight cutscene. "Spaced Out" for killing Captain Vladimir, as discussed above, the cutscene triggers for this fight may be bugged and kill a save file. Load up a backup slot before fighting Vladimir or you may have to restart the game entirely. "Desperate Massacre" for killing 510 regular enemies, this achievement's counter is bigged and resets upon starting a revenge mission (unlocked after beating secret boss Kimmy Howell). The way to fix this is to grind out kills before taking any revenge missions.  The bugged achievements I encountered that were NOT solvable were: "Minigame Masteroo" for playing all eight side jobs at least once, this achievement's counter is completely broken and does not count one of the jobs, I suspect it's the Scorpion one. "Maybe See a Doctor?" for using all 10 different toilets in the game, this counter is also broken and does not count one of the toilets, I suspect it's the one in the final level in Pizza Batt Tower. "It Was a Desperate Struggle" for getting every other achievement, this one is not unlockable for obvious reasons.       Overall, this port of the game isn't working properly and may be a coin toss in certain sections as to whether or not it crashes. The gameplay is fun and the story is great but the port isn't responsible for the good elements of the game. I reccomend this game if you're a diehard fan of the series like me and want to see how these ports work but for a newtimer picking up the series or someone coming back to the seires after a while. try to pick up the game on the Switch if you have one.

_childDocuments_.review: (First playthrough, no experience with playing the original on the Wii) NMH2 is an excellent sequel, improving in many ways. The most notable is the increase in graphics quality and more diverse characters. The combat has been reworked to feel smoother (and the special attacks have been significantly buffed). The paywall before fights has been removed, making it so you can go fight from fight quickly this time around. Money and upgrades can be collected by playing NES inspired minigames (grinding money takes a LOT of time however). Despite all that and the rare crashes (it's only crashed 3 times in total for my entire playthrough), this game is a definite must-buy for those who enjoyed the first and wanted more.

_childDocuments_.review: After reviewing the first game, I sorta felt a need to review this one as well.As a port, it's just as, if not more, bare-bones than NMH1. The options in the pre-launch config and in-game config menu reset after each launch, atleast the inverted Y-Axis that makes it not inverted to me. That said, I really don't fully understand a lot of the reviews about crashes as for me this game was significantly more stable than the first. I only suffered 2 crashes in 10.5 hrs. of play. As for the game, it cuts the annoying openworld and money making loop from the original, certainly for the better. While the "jobs" are still there, all but the scorpion job from the original have either been entirely replaced or remade into pixel-art mini-games that range from interesting to mind numbing. That said, unlike the first game they aren't actually required to progress the main story so exist more as extras if you want to grind for unnecessary sword upgrades or clothes. Additionally the scorpion mini-game has been overhauled, for the worst in my opinion, but that might not be the popular opinion. Either way its difficult to consider them a negative as they certainly only enhance the experience an feel of the game.Actual gameplay feels kinda dumbed down from NMH1, might be due to experience now, but I really didn't have trouble with any of the boss fights. Some were memorable for sure, including some returning characters, but there was a lot of chaff in there as well and the final boss was... uninteresting and certainly poorly designed. I can pretty clearly remember each boss in NMH1, in 2's case that would be a difficult challenge come one week from now. On positives new minor enemy varieties help the filler sections be actually engaging at time as well as the ability to swap beam-katana mid-combat allowing the player to change on the fly for specific situations. While you might think "I'll just always use my favorite" I found myself actually changing swords depending on the boss I encountered. The new beam-katana feel really good in general as well. The ecstacy system also gives the player far more control in how they rush to the actual boss. I will say I found the soundtrack far more compelling here with me about to search spotify immediately following this review. I sort of hesitate to review this game positively, but overall I did enjoy the experience. I just would say that I don't think this game is really worth your time unless you REALLY liked NMH1.

_childDocuments_.review: A note for ROTT veterans: if you're a fan of the original ROTT then you can skip this review. LE is easily the definitive way of replaying this game, hands down. That's all you need to know.Rise of the Triad is a semi-forgotten classic from 1995. Originally meant as a sequel to Wolfenstein 3D it turned into a crazy, quirky and clunky ball of madness that has managed to snag a number of fans over the years. As a member of the H.U.N.T. Team you assault a monastery full of insane Triad cultists to stop them from nuking L.A. You have an arsenal of weapons ranging from simple pistols and machineguns with infinite ammo all the way to Drunk Missiles, Firebombs and magical baseball bats. You'll explore labyrinthine Wolf3D-style levels full of traps, secrets and touchplates to obliterate enemies by shooting, blowing up and burning them to a crisp. On your way you can collect powerups (and powerdowns) as well as Life Items that provide points and extra lives.This is the remaster / re-release called Ludicrous Edition which is essentially a modern port for the original game. All I can say is that Nightdive and New Blood have knocked it out of the park. We can finally play ROTT on modern systems with all the quality of life features like widescreen, mouselook, uncapped framerate etc. Not to mention a brand new episode as well as restored cut content. Good stuff.Alright, let's not beat around the bush. This game is a trainwreck. It was very outdated even back when it originally came out - 2 years after DOOM and a year before Duke3D and Quake. Ouch! It has a truckload of problems, the gameplay can be really boring, the levels are mazes, all rooms have the same height and there are only 90 degree walls... But it is easily one of the most endearing trainwrecks ever made. Every criticism you may hear about this game is most likely true. But if you squint your eyes and manage to look past that, there's a lot to be liked.ROTT really oozes the fun that the team had while making it. It's obvious to me that its developers were well aware that their game couldn't really compete with the other contemporary titles. So instead they decided to just go all out and turn the crazy dial to eleven - to enjoy making it regardless of the outcome. And it shows.In this game you can turn into a God. And a dog that gibs people by barking. You can make your life miserable with powerdowns like Shrooms Mode and Elasto Mode. Sometimes when you use an elevator you'll literally hear elevator music. There are nonsensical bonuses and ridiculous cheat codes. There are flame traps, moving lava walls, fireball launchers in the walls, turrets, boulders, spinning blades coming out of the floor, gas traps, Gravitational Discs providing height variation in a Wolf3D engine, ridiculous secrets you'll never find on your own, 360 degree death cam when you die violently. Just to name a few.Not to mention that in many ways ROTT was ahead of its time. It had 5 different characters, jump pads (a standard in modern games), destructible and dynamic light sources, destructible windows (including being able to smash them by running into them!), enemies stealing your stuff, begging for mercy and trapping you in nets, first Capture the Flag mode, first vertical rocket jump, two routes through one of the episodes (in Extreme ROTT), heating up food so that it gives you more health, fog... I'm not even mentioning all sorts of easter eggs, jokes and other fun features. At some point you may start wondering if there's something this game doesn't have.If there's one thing that is by far the best aspect of ROTT it's the music. Lee Jackson has created some of the most memorable tunes ever for this game. Every track is amazing and that's not an opinion - it's an objective fact. The Ludicrous Edition also comes with an alternative version made by Andrew Hulshult for the 2013 ROTT reboot, which is a nice touch.So is it worth a recommendation? As always the binary rating system that Steam has doesn't work for a game like this. ROTT is awesome and terrible at the same time, fun but often really boring. If you're a casual retro shooter enjoyer simply looking for another great FPS to play then you'll probably be disappointed. Anything with Wolf3D-style engine is going to be a hard sell for most people. However if you're brave enough to tackle a game that's pre-DOOM in terms of technology then who knows?

_childDocuments_.review: Picture this: You're 7 years old. Your mom brings a bunch of CD's she bought at a dollar store from one town over. They're shareware discs that came out before you were even born. Most of them are games you've already played; Doom, Quake, Heretic, etc. There's one game you haven't seen before. It's got some lady holding a guy by the shirt and shooting somebody else on the CD. You put it in your old ass Windows 98 computer and what follows is the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane experience you've ever had. You're going 250 miles per hour while amazing synth music blasts your ears, some guy you think is dead gets back up and shoots you, you hit him with a bazooka and gore flies all over the place. Two days later the CD breaks. You can't remember what the game was called because you're 7 years old and you're stupid (like every other 7 year old). You forget about it. It becomes a dream, a vague memory of something your mind probably fabricated on one of the days you didn't take your Adderall. Years later you see some YouTuber who plays terrible first person shooter games named Civvie11 do a review of a game he actually likes called Rise of The Triad. That sounds kind of familia- ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. THAT'S THE GAME. IT'S RISE OF THE TRIAD, OH MY GOD.You see it's on sale on GOG for 75 cents and not only that but there's like ten times the amount of content there was in that shareware demo you played years earlier. You're in awe, you've been in an erect state for six hours straight, you have to go to the hospital for ischemic priapism. They drain blood from your massive throbbing ♥♥♥♥ with a needle. You're traumatized. Rise of The Triad nearly killed you because it made you so hard.Some years after that there's a remastered re-release of Rise of The Triad with even more bonus content and quality of life features added in. You're getting aroused again. It's raining and dark outside. You live on the edge of town, ten hours from the nearest hospital.

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, same universe! And don't get me started on the plot where Hitler's fall didn't stop the corporations that used him as a puppet to politely suggest a new kind of Armageddon. ROTT belongs in the DDD category, which stands for Demented, Deranged, Delirious. It's a Tom Hall project with Romero's influences, compared to it Doom is a completely conventional Satanic prance. For the sake of argument, of course. Originally made on a modified Wolfenstein 3D engine (presently it's on KEX), this game was conceived as Wolfenstein 2 by id. Tom Hall of Commander Keen fame left id and joined Apogee, led by another legend Scott Miller who had bought the licence and did... a thing with the property. More accurately, a bunch of deranged maniacs rolled out a freakish inside joke named Rise of the Triad. A game that barely fits into the confines of reality and, in its blatant abstraction, probably won't satisfy people looking for a sense of place in a shooter.I never looked for it, longing for something to push back on the impending walls of my shrinking world. Despite this predisposition, I averted my eyes from ROTT for a long time, its discomforting outsider art aura didn't seem compelling. Until one day I ran out of games, sat my ass down and tasted it. Sometimes appetite comes with eating. Until now, quite unlike other great shooters of the time, ROTT was a hard sell. Even I wasn't sure I still liked it. Thankfully, Nightdive pushed me to punish myself once more and I immediately saw the dusty artifact was handled with care. It pulled me into its gaping maw again. It looks more crispy than ever, the new lighting adds a cubic ton of volume to the world, improving the atmosphere. And it has all the necessary modern quality-of-life features like the FOV slider or UI options. Having numbers instead of vague icons is a game-changer. Also, several variants of OST on offer? I feel spoiled!I'm glad they got rid of that terrible near-death alarm and the monks' enormous health pools, which used to make later levels rather unpleasant. More unpleasant. These nuisances can still be turned on if you're a masochistic purist. Either way, no amount of fixes would make ROTT not an assh#le game. For one, enforcers are here to stay and those are just as bad. I recommend not going higher than Hard unless you think you could enjoy a combination of instakills and hitscan. The convoluted level design shall always be a major pain in the ass, too. You couldn't escape getting lost, you'll be cursing through your teeth. There's no solid foundation to point at, only an implausible geometrical torment. As if a fever dream dictated local designs, seemingly devised on the fly, born from a stream of inflamed consciousness. The fluid maze world is a bulletproof decoration, a surreal estimation that doesn't look like anything.You and the Nazis are in the same kind of hell made of glass and explosions. Oh yeah, transparent breakable glass! Woo-hoo! It blew my mind back in the day. Where did I see it next time? Duke or something? I know you aren't impressed, it’s hard to sweep anyone off their feet with the same technological advancement twice unless you run another techno-ponzi involving dehumidifiers. What's impressive is how ROTT's visual gimmicks become mechanics, then slide into your nightmares. The towering walls of stone and cast metal, bouncy pads, floating centipedes made of out-of-place round platforms. Repeated textures force the pattern to lodge into your brain. With your mind's eye, you'll be seeing these wood panels, strange stones with glyphs on them, and spinning blades swooping from the darkness long after finishing the game. It never washes away completely.God, ROTT sounds outright bad on paper! Let's make it sound even worse, shall we? Slippery platforming leads to finicky parkour, and there's plenty of that. Combat is collateral, you mostly solve levels. The less you try to guess the designer's intent, the less mad it will drive you. Savescum, you can't possibly survive all the fireball traps, blade traps, wall traps, lava walls, industrial presses, rolling boulders, trampolines, pits, lava pits, bottomless pits. The walls are shifting, a dozen warheads fly in your direction, you run away from one dumb way to die to turn around the corner and have an army of Daleks obliterate your face with exploding discs. Camera circles around your character, it's like they take a moment to realise they're dead before bursting into giblets, sending chunky blood splats and heaps of eyeballs in your face. But hey, at least those aren't always yours.Enemies are mostly developer-based humanoids in oversized uniforms. Soldiers of all ranks, monks, derelict robots, and such. Some men drop to their knees and beg for their lives or feign death... to get up and shoot you in the back. I find it curious, but foes aren't this game's strong suit. There's no wonder why ammo for pistols and even the MP-40 is infinite when you heat your meals with rocket launchers. ROTT is all about every way to shoot a rocket. You can only carry one rocket launcher at a time, yet it doesn't mean the game stifles you. Levels are ridden with different kinds of bazookas to use and discard, depending on your immediate needs. There's an Excalibat, a bat that sends a heap of exploding baseballs, then a FlameWall that shoots, you guessed it, a wall of flame which makes skeletons crumble with a cartoonish sound. Shoot crosses and lines of explosions, homing missiles, cluster bombs! Or maybe you'd rather turn into a dog? God? A pinball?Look, it's called LUDICROUS for a reason. Don't be offended by the cheekiness, this game is only childish. That's why it makes you feel like a panicked bug in the hands of a bored brat. When you get into the ROTT trance and synchronise with its flow, when you embrace being lost, you can start admiring its myriad of moving parts. Yes, the level design is delirious, I have no idea why it even works as it is. It's a bunch of constantly unwrapping nonsense on a grand scale! A balls-to-the-wall psychedelic stream of consciousness, it shifts and wobbles. It kills. The more I talk about it, the less sense it makes. You gotta give the game a whirl to get the feel for it. It’s unhealthy yet necessary to go tactile with ROTT. This edition is one of the biggest packages I've ever seen. 18 hours of gimmicky madness. Said madness isn't for everyone, but if you let it - it gets you good.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Rise of the Triad is weird. It doesn't do that much to engross the player with its visuals, it doesn't do anything terribly atmospheric, nor does it want tell a compelling story.What it DOES want to do is give you one of the most addictive classic FPS gameplay loops you'll ever encounter. It's simple; you have a number of infinite ammo but low damage weapons to depend on while you pick up limited use but high damage rocket launchers of various types. The key to success lies in striking a balance between their uses. It's simple to grasp, but insanely fun and addictive to employ.This game kicks immense amounts of ass and, once again, Nightdive proves itself the best at updating old games while New Blood and Apogee also prove themselves to be masters of their craft.

_childDocuments_.review: Rise of the Triad is an FPS created by 3D Realms in 1994. Tom Hall headed development shortly after being ousted at Id software during the development of Doom. It runs on a modified version of Wolfenstein 3D's engine and even began development as an official tie in to that game.RotT is a very confusing and bizarre game. It's the strangest of the 90s fps's in overall concept and is full of bizarre creative influences. The game's premise sets the player up as one of several special forces soldiers facing off against a criminal organization known as the "Triad". Much of the player's weapons vary in terms of time period, such as the player's pistol being a modern day beretta, wheras your smg is an MP40. Likewise enemies start off as Nazi like Axis soldiers but gradually get replaced with fantasy wizards. The game's environments are a mix of fantasy dungeons and sci-fi techbase stuff. The game also has a lot of things in it to intentionally break the fourth wall like "Dog mode" and the Excalibat. Much like Quake 1 two years later, no other game resembles Rise of the Triad aesthetically or in terms of tone.Where Rise of the Triad gets interesting is in terms of gameplay. Rise of the Triad's mechanics on paper feel like they shouldn't work. Most of the enemies in the game are tomato cans the player guns down by the hundreds. The player's pistols and SMGs act as workhorse weapons and have unlimited ammo. However the game as it goes on begins introducing new mechanics that throw some spice into the mix. Like ridiculously powerful enemies and environmental hazards that wipe out most your hp quickly alongside absurdly overpowered weapons that you stumble across behind push block walls. It creates this weirdly exciting rhythm to the game where you go from gunning down enemies by the dozens to finding a hard room and thinking of ways to even the odds with a powerful weapon hidden in a secret room around the corner. It's one of the more mechanically complex 90s fps's and it's very much hidden under the surface.This release of Rise of the Triad is really good. It contains almost everything that has already been released alongside getting multiplayer working and including a level editor. Plus Steam workshop. _childDocuments_.review: Rise of the Triad was a  game. They didn't have to go so hard, but they did. It goes the extra miles and has . 3 whole soundtracks, all the expansions, an extra modern episode made by New Blood and friends, the Return of the Triad gzdoom standalone game is also thrown it for reasons? _childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to blow smoke up your arse, Rise of the Triad is a bit of an acquired taste and I can fully acknowledge that. It's a product of it's time but it came out a full year after Doom and just didn't deliver something that was a comparable quality. You could say it already seemed antiquated despite how far it's engine had been pushed, a victim of circumstance considering how the genre and technology were rapidly evolving. There are aspects of this game that might drive you a little bonkers, the level design is just kind of a hodgepodge of stuff that might wear out it's welcome. It's very much closer to Wolfenstein 3D than Doom was when it comes to design, this makes sense since it was initially conceived as a sequel to Wolf and uses the same engine. It's your familiar structure of episodes each with a boss level at the end and full of key hunt mazes with push-wall secrets, item pickups such as weapons, "treasure" and health scattered throughout. The addition of jump pads, floating or moving platforms as well as environmental hazards or obstacles gives the game what it needs to not feel like it's just more of the same. The weapon roster starts with your basic pistol, you can pick up a second one to dual-wield and then there's the machine gun, all of these have unlimited ammo but your fourth slot is reserved for an explosive weapon or a magic one either of which you will end up having to swap as needed or after ammo is depleted. You also get a variety of interesting power-ups that last for 30 seconds like god mode, dog mode (yes dog, where you shrink down temporarily turning into a dog and your bark's got bite) and mercury mode which allows you to levitate. Watch out for the power-downs like shrooms and elasto mode, those are a bit of a nuisance lolWell then is it even fun to play at all? I personally think it is but it depends on what you like, I just hope I've explained with enough detail what you're going to be in for. Provided it's still available you can check out the demo if you're not sure but i think if you're a fan of retro FPS you'll know what to expect. I would say give ROTT a chance, this release is especially worth it! Part of what really makes me enjoy this game are the digitized actors and sprites as well as all sound effects and the music, it never gets old for me zooming around with god mode making those HUURRRRR noises. Blasting dudes into giblets also continues to be extremely satisfying. I must say this remaster is exceptional and I'm glad that it exists, Nightdive and New Blood have done a wonderful job here. The fact that i can play this with such ease on a modern day computer without any futzing around is very welcomed. Oh and the fact that this has The HUNT Begins (with Deluxe version levels) shareware release, Dark War full retail release and Extreme ROTT expansion all in one convenient place is so awesome, there's even an entire new 24 level campaign called The HUNT Continues as well as the inclusion of the GZDoom game Return of the Triad.EAT LEAD!!!

_childDocuments_.review: If Doom and Duke Nukem 3D are boomer shooters, then Rise of the Triad is a silent gen shooter. This game actually started life as a sequel to Wolfenstein 3D (and runs on a highly modified version of its engine), and the signs are all over the place - big, abstract, and labyrinthian levels that bear no resemblance to real-world locations, a low number of weapon slots (although the third slot has a variety of options available), pushwalls galore, and a selection of enemies that are supposed to be cultists but bear an uncanny resemblance to Nazis. Unfortunately for Apogee, id Software pulled the plug on the game before releasing Doom and taking the world by storm, requiring the team to completely retool the game as its own thing. By the time the game even released, Doom 2 was already out, leaving poor ROTT to be mostly ignored. However, this is a great game that has a lot to offer if you enjoyed Wolf 3D and want a way more advanced version of it. Instead of monotonous gray hallways, levels are alive with lots of moving tricks and traps, atmospheric skyboxes and lightning storms, and jump pads and moving walkways to add some vertical gameplay to the mix. There's even powerups like dog mode and god mode that are a lot of fun to play with. Although levels can be quite maze-like, the easily-accessible overhead map does a mostly good job of keeping you from getting lost. There's a TON of content here relative to other 90s shooters; 116 levels across the shareware episode, the original game (Dark War), the new episode for this release, and Extreme Rise of the Triad. That's not including the Doom mod bundled with this release called Return of the Triad, which features another 12 levels. I have not played EROTT or Return yet since the rest of the game took long enough to warrant a break, but rest assured you will get your money's worth here. Of course this all goes without saying that Nightdive did a fantastic job with this port. This is the definitive way to play the game and beats the hell out of launching DOSBox. There's tons of customization including which version of the fantastic OST you'd like and which HUD setting you prefer (which includes some all-new options that more closely resemble Doom). I highly recommend giving ROTT a try - just keep in mind the context of the game when it came out and what sort of experience you'll be getting, and you'll find an oddly addicting and satisfying game.

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest problem I have with Rise of the Triad is the levels you progress through. They have this weird sensibility to them. Like they were ripped from a Sega Genesis platformer. Just a mishmash of spring pads and moving platforms. I understand the appeal of verticality in a game engine that often didn’t allow for it, but the novelty is so overpowering here. There’s no theme either, so every level feels like every other level. So much so that it’s impossible to tell them apart -- or discern any sort of narrative going from one to the other. Enemies, weapons, and powers aren’t arranged in a way that gives the player a sense of progression. You’re not getting stronger. You’re not learning. You’re just stuck spinning your wheels in a series of endless drab labyrinths. It’s borderline adolescent in its design ethos -- confused and directionless. Just toys and ideas strewn about. Nazis. Cultists. Fire traps. God mode. Dog mode. Enemies are a joke, and so are the weapons. I remember playing this back in the day, wondering if I was playing some sort of cracked or modified second-hand copy. So little of it felt like a cohesive game.I love a good ol’ shooter, especially from this era. But I find very little to enjoy with Rise of the Triad. That saddens me a little, because I do have some fun memories of it. Guess the novelty wore off.Thumbs down.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start with this: Nightdive did a good job remastering this, with a whole new episode, a map editor, and more. Absolutely nothing negative to say on that front. They are an extremely talented team and deserve all the praise on this venture as possible. If you have played Rise of the Triad and liked it before playing this remaster, more power to you and this is easily the best way to play the game. , this review is coming from the perspective of somebody whose first time playing this game has been this remaster, Ludicrous Edition. So be warned.(Swear that I ain't fishing for clowns with this, hear me out lmao){Also ignore the 0.6 hours on record thing it hasn't logged half of my time)I waited to play the OG Rise of the Triad because of the numerous terrible community source ports that leave much to be desired, and I never wanted to bother trying it out in DOSbox, that ain't happening 💀. I was pretty hyped to play this because of how much I'd heard content creators like Civvie 11, among others, gas this game up like it's on par with Doom or something and, needless to say, I was disappointed once I actually got my hands on it. While on the surface, hearing of multiple playable characters with different stats, dog mode, and all this game's funky gimmicks sounded appealing, in function, I don't care for most of it, and the level design is extremely dated.The weapon balancing in this game is, frankly, some of the poorest I've seen from such a constantly talked about boomer shooter like this. You pick up some dual pistols at the start of the game? Look ma, RotT did dual-wielding the same day as Marathon!!! Yeah, too bad it's terrible. The pistols take forever to down the weakest enemies in the game and immediately become obsolete the second you pick up the MP40, which itself should be cool in theory. Infinite ammo automatic weapon, dope. Yes, dope indeed, but like said, only in theory. Besides the gun sounding weak, enemies take forever to go down with this weapon as well. Not AS long as the dual-wielded pistols, but combat with the proper guns in this FPS game is tedious. As monotonous as it comes.Ok, surely the rest of the weapons make up for this paltry showing? Nope, not even remotely in my opinion. The rest of the weapons besides the Excalibat (which is already pretty worthless in this game) are all some form or variation of explosive. They can all just fill in for each other really, I can't think of a single scenario where I thought "Man I could really use this other explosive weapon rn." They're all functionally pretty close and it doesn't make a difference which one you happen to have on you. They're all more or less effective against the damage-sponge enemies this game throws your way and are good for crowd control but that's the most I can give it. Can't say I really like this arsenal over anything any of its competitors were doing around the same time. Hell, even on the same day.It also has a weapon limit which is stinky, f*ck that amirite?This is where things really get bad. The weapon-balancing stuff I mentioned, I can take all that, but it's that in combination with the dated level design here that really gets to me and urges me to recommend against buying this game if you've never bothered with it before. Never since Hexen have I played a damn game so hellbent on getting me lost. Maps in Rise of the Triad are ginormous but also limited as it comes. Because this game uses an upgraded version of the Wolfenstein 3D engine, height variation in this game is more an illusion than it is a true property of the levels. GADs are strewn about the levels to create janky, unfun platforming challenges on occasions, and layouts are so labyrinthian that a minotaur would get PTSD and clinical depression trying to navigate most of RotT.It's not so bad in the expanded levels they added in the remaster because those are made by masters of this craft like DuskDev, who also come at it with something of a modern perspective, but the base game is still an absolute lost cause for me. Idk, levels here just feel too big for their own good and like how people that don't play boomer shooters stereotype boomer shooter levels to be designed like. Maze-like, hard to navigate because almost everything looks the same, likely completely unknown secrets because of how obscure they'd have to be in mazes as large as these, so on so forth.Maybe it's worth it for workshop/mod content, but with only good community maps cannot a good game make.Extreme RotT is terrible and about as fun as having your d*ck stapled to a freeway with a semi-truck running it over over and over again. Do not play it.Nightive did a great job remastering a very mediocre, dated FPS that contains odd balancing choices and unfun level design. If you already liked it, can't recommend RotT: Ludicrous Edition enough. If ya haven't played it before, stay away for your own sake and play something else instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I mean just watch the Civvie11 review video. This is pretty much the perfect version of this game. Which for me is the good old OPL music with the classic sound effects but you also have the option of using the ROTT 2013 soundtrack and renewed sound effects with louder explosions and more squishy gibs.And you can play it with a controller like a modern FPS game just like the Bethesda Doom remakes! What a joy. It works quite well, except when aiming up rockets will fire below where the cursor is. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not quite sure where to begin.  I still play the original Rise of the Triad on original hardware from time to time and still have enough hardware from that era in which I could run an 8 player COM-BATT game.  I will admit, it's been a long time since I played the original Dark War to completion.It should be noted that I still stick with version 1.2 of ROTT, however for Extreme ROTT I have a version 1.3 install just for that.  More about why later in the review.I do enjoy all the new changes that this remaster brings.  The new guards, new assets and enough to make the game feel like it got an actual 1.4 update.  I haven't quite explored all of it, but from what I've read there's plenty more than I've played.Plus, the default 90s controls were obviously lackluster back in the day.  The option to freelook is much appreciated.  Plus the original HUD did need a refresh.  I still use the old school one, but I do plan on changing things up eventually.The biggest issue, for me (and probably only me), is that when version 1.3 of the original ROTT was published the OPL/Adlib instruments (soundfonts, soundtrack?) were changed to that of Duke3D.  A preview build I saw of Duke3D uses "Goin' Down the Fast Way" was one of its tracks and it sounds exactly the same.I'm just not a fan of it and for some reason the original version of the music appears to be forgotten.  I've often played with the idea of using the Line In port and play the original music through that.Multiplayer I can't get to work?  Either no one plays or might be an issue on my end but whenever I check the online lobby I'm greeted with a blank slate.  No refresh buttons or any indication I'm connected apart from the signing in.I think it should be worth noting that I'm aware ROTT is id Tech 0 (or 0.5?) so as such the underlying engine would be based off of id Tech 1.  Some other games this sort of change would still be noticeable even if 100% of the original assets are present.  Here it's not an issue.While the single-player campaign, as far as I've played, has been rock solid.  There have been either bugs or oversights that weren't present in the original game.  Issues such as:Don't get me wrong, I enjoy ROTT and still listen to its soundtrack from time to time.  If there could be a patch or two that polishes this to be closer to the original I would be playing it a lot more often.  As it stands, I still would rather play the original game (and learn how to use an editor there, something I should have started nearly 30 years ago) if I had to make an absolute choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Admittedly I've never played Rise of the Triad before this. I tried many times using various source ports and they were all kinda crappy but at long last Nightdive has released a modern version so I can finally play this without any hiccups or hassle. Now I did play the 2013 remake a few years ago, but I didn't think much of it. It was janky but charming, clearly the devs behind it cared but didn't have the budget or expertise to make what they wanted.The original game doesn't have this problem at all though because this game is a blast. Is it weird? Sure. But I find a lot of its weirdness very entertaining. I mean, there's a literal dog power-up in this game where you run around biting people and doing bark attacks to explode enemies into gibs. I think the game's sense of humor is probably what sets it apart from any other shooter the most. It's quirky and strange but in a good way.Though that's not to say Rise of the Triad isn't unique in other ways, it definitely is. You'd expect the gameplay to be like Doom or Wolfenstein and while it sort of is, it has a few things that REALLY set it apart. For example you only have four weapon slots, the first 3 weapon slots have infinite ammo but are pretty dinky and not very good. The fourth slot though is for "special" weapons. Now there's tons of different special weapons you can find around that all have different gimmicks and quirks to them but are mostly exceptionally powerful. These have limited ammo though so you have to be careful when using them. You'll end up using the special weapons for beefy enemies and large groups of smaller ones, but if it's one or two regular enemies it might be best to use some of your crappy weapons to preserve special weapon ammo.The levels are also pretty wildly different from any other 90's shooter too. There's a lot of verticality complete with jump pads, floating platforms, bottomless pits and the like. Most of the levels revolve around the basic key hunting that makes up the vast majority of boomer shooters but there's also nearly invisible touchpads that activate parts of the level to progress. Thankfully they aren't too hard to find because they show on the automap.I figured I would enjoy Rise of the Triad and I'm glad I do. I'm also super glad that ports of these old FPS games are even a thing, I love retro shooters to death and a lot of them deserve good modernized versions for people like me to play who otherwise haven't been able to.

_childDocuments_.review: I need to preface this review by saying that this game certainly does not appeal to a lot of modern players. If you played wolfenstein 3d and didn't care for it you aren't going to get much more out of this game. The levels are maze like and the combat can certainly be repetitive at times. But if you liked wolf 3d, you'll most likely really enjoy this game. I have no nostalgia for this game and I still love it so far (having beaten the shareware episodes). _childDocuments_.review: This game really hasn't aged very well at all.I was excited when I saw all the rave reviews for this new updated version, especially since I recall playing this back on my Windows 98 literally decades ago.But this game really isn't very good.The simplistic level design isn't even the biggest issue. The gameplay itself is actually quite lackluster. You can only carry one primary weapon at a time (even Halo lets you have 2!) and there is no real strategy to the gunplay. It doesn't matter if you have a bazooka or heatseaker, drunk missiles, etc it makes no difference. The basic strategy of using the MP5 or pick off individual enemies while using the missile weapons for groups always remains the same. The difference is superficial.Enemy variety also sucks. All the enemies are just humans in different suits, and with certain exceptions like the monks it can be hard to tell the difference. I will grant that the game has personality, but it's not enough to make up for the above flaws.Interestingly, the game also comes bundled with a Doom 2 TC that's basically an unofficial expansion/sequel to ROTT, but ironically, the fact it runs on the Doom engine means it actually just exposes the original for its own shortcomings by being so much more technically superior in terms of the level design.In conclusion, it's cool they made this but it's not really worth playing. The levels are boring. The gameplay is boring. The enemies are boring. This game is boring. Only consider buying it if it's on sale.

However i'm sad to say it's a bit of a mixed bag.For a start Nightdive have done an absolutely perfect job with this remaster. They are so good at this they make it look easy.
