_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A bunch of cute girls + a bunch of pointless systemsGraphics: Average weeb game. The girls' models are good because it's Koei's game.Story: Not bad, there are some twists. Combat: I want to take it seriously but the game doesn't allow me to. It's turn-based + real time (the type I hate the most) like the developer's other games. Your camera will follow your character when they attack. It might feel cool, but It's very hard to see how much damage each skill does. There's a total damage on the right of the screen. But the number is cumulative. It shows how much total damage you did, not the individual skills which is not very helpful. Man, how do you take the combat seriously when you can't even have an clear idea on the effectiveness of your skills? And to be honest, the difficulty is low, you can beat the game whatever build you use. So, no, the combat looks beautiful, but it's actually shallow and unimpressive.Map: The maps are totally forgettable. There are a few elements that are being used over and over again: ruins + water + plain. Each dungeon looks familiar to the previous one. And most of the time you don't look at the actual world, instead, you look at the mini map. Because the mini map is all that matters. You go pick up those shining collectable items and you find your way to the next objective. There's nothing to discover. No hidden chest, no hidden path. If the mini map tells you there's no way ahead, then there's no way ahead. There are some interactive point on the maps such as walking across a narrow bridge or a roof. But you actually just press A and move forward. There's no fun in these interactions unless you really are obsessed with watching a girl T-posing. Tbh, even if you are, watching it 100 times still gets boring. Also, there's a small but annoying issue, after any dialog and map interaction, the camera's zoom level is rest. So, you have to constantly zoom out to better see the map.Stealth mode: Sound cool right? No, it's boring. Each enemy has a red cone of vision, you can see it by entering the stealth mode. They won't spot you if you don't enter their vision zone. You can literally stand 3 feet in front of an enemy's face without being spotted. Each enemy will patrol along a very short and programmed path.  So, there's no any actual variation in this so-called stealth system. You just wait there until the enemy turn around then you walk forward. Just like how you f wait for traffic lights every day. Oh yeah, there are some stealth mission. The developer wants you to have more time "enjoy" their beloved stealth play. I don't want to talk about this bs. In short, it feels like FFXIV Endwalker's stalking missions. If you know, you know. If you don't, congrats. you have not been tortured by this bs.Enemy: Surprise, surprise, there's no real enemy in this game. Unlike normal RPGs which all have some kind of "villain," this game doesn't have one. All it has are generic weird-looking monsters that try to slow down your story progress. The enemy in this game has 0 connection to the story. They don't talk, don't think, don't have any personality. They are just there because the game needs a combat system! The distribution of the monsters are also irrelevant. For example, in a normal RPG, you probably expect to see some wild animals or goblins when you enter a forest. Or some skeletons and ghosts when you enter an underground tomb. But in this game, the monsters have no connection to where they appear. The developer just designed some monsters with non-sense looking and randomly put them on each map. Additionally, each map has only 2-3 types of monsters. And the enemy compositions are exactly the same. So, your combat strategy is not gonna change throughout the whole map. You just use the exact same skills in the exact same order and repeat it for 40 times each map.Crafting System: Not much to say, it's tasteless. You won't actually need to craft any support items to beat the game. But you need it to develop the school to progress the story. You are gonna need a lot of f warm sand and cool sand. The developer intentionally made it this way so that they can sell you the $1 craft helping DLC.Dating System: A huge selling point of the game. You will date with each girl many many many times. It's fundamental because you need date them to level up their bonding (talent) levels in order to learn skills and progress the story. I don't particular hate this system since this is a weeb game after all. Who doesn't want to see cute girl interact with each other? However, as the story progresses, when new girls join the team especially toward the late game. In the early game, the pace is normal. You date with this girl one time this chapter, you date with another next chapter. But in late game, you will see situations like dating with the same girl 4-5 times in a row. Man, it's dumb. It's just rushing to make the girls that joins late catch up with other members. Developer, if you know this kind of situation would happen, just make some special adjustment to the characters that join late. For example, make them start at a higher talent level instead of level 1.Conclusion: If you have a burning desire to play cute anime girls, I get it. Every man has this kind of time. If you have to buy, you have to. However, if you can still control yourself and have any pursue to good gameplay and mechanisms, don't buy it, or wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Reflection: Second Light is a very enjoyable JRPG adventure. I first played this game on PS4. The overarching story is simple but you never feel bored because the strength of the game is its likeable and relatable cast of characters. You do not need to play the first game (Blue Reflection) or watch the anime (Blue Reflection Ray) to understand this game. The events of the first game are referenced but the whole theme of this game is focusing on the future and creating something new for the characters.The concept is very reminiscent of the Persona series - each chapter has both a dungeon exploring phase and a bonding phase for the main character to just hang out with friends. The bonding phase has tangible rewards for players as they can earn talent points after each social link event (called a date) and those points can be spent upgrading the characters' combat, support or crafting skills. During each date, players can choose their responses from the conversation options and different choices may lead to different rewards. There is no time management involved so players will not have to worry about the consequences of choosing one character over another to spend each day with. They can freely pick any party member and just focus on getting to know the girl. As the game is yuri-themed, the dates occasionally have conversation options that can allow the main character Ao to flirt with the character she is spending time with. This makes it even more fun to play the game because the different choices may lead to different reactions and scenes. Blue Reflection: Second Light is not a mere dungeon crawler; it heavily uses slice of life moments to drive character development. The dungeons are beautifully crafted environments that feel natural and none of them are too long. Even the reasons for going into the dungeons tie in with the game's focus on character growth. Players will get to know the characters better through both the dungeons and the social aspect of the game. The gameplay is quite varied for a game of this nature. Some chapters have a stealth mission where players have to sneak around enemies instead of fighting them. The stealth missions are not long and they encourage players to make use of the environment and their knowledge of the dungeon to reach the destination without being noticed. There are also some side quests that require the player to collect items from dungeons or craft things for party members. Blue Reflection: Second Light's turn-based combat is innovative and exciting. Unlike traditional JRPGs where the combat typically involves each character in the party taking a turn and choosing actions one by one, followed by each opponent taking a turn and doing the same, the turn-based combat in this game incorporates real-time elements. The turn order is represented by a timeline. The player's characters and the enemies all appear on one timeline. The player can delay a character's turn to get more ether for stronger attacks but that would result in the enemy coming closer on the timeline, and the enemy might even end up taking a turn first if the delay is too long. So the combat is more tactical and players can experiment with different strategies for each encounter. Each successful attack counts towards the player's combo and the more combos that player racks up, the stronger the attacks. The combo count may be threatened during boss fights, so the gameplay encourages the player to watch the timeline and not just spam attacks on enemies. Boss fights may also be won through one-on-one battles. These battles seem tough initially but after some practice, players will manage to get the timing of the counter attack right. On the overall, Blue Reflection: Second Light is a relaxing JRPG that does not require too much combat skill and also does not flood your quest log with excessive side quests. Recommended DLCs for the game: 1) BLUE REFLECTION: Second Light - Crafting Function - Ether Synthesis  (The Ether synthesis option makes crafting much easier so you won't have to keep returning to dungeons to find rare items. The price is also very reasonable). 2) BLUE REFLECTION: Second Light - School Development Facility - Summer Night Vacation (Who wouldn't want more dates? More dates = more talent points). The other DLCs such as the costumes and 2 additional dungeons are good but not as important. The season pass includes all the DLCs as a bundle. My only complaint is that the game does not seem very balanced. The normal mode is too easy, especially towards the end. The level cap should be raised and the enemy toughness should also scale as the player levels up and acquires facilities. Conversely, this also makes Blue Reflection: Second Light a great gateway game for players who are new to JRPGs. I would have also preferred the true ending to have a longer epilogue. Hopefully Koei Tecmo will make a Blue Reflection 3 sequel that continues the franchise, further explores the implications of the ending and shows us what happens to the rest of the characters. That said, Blue Reflection: Second Light is a massive improvement over the original game and is a major step in the right direction for the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to the first game, this was an enormously large improvement. Drastically revamped combat, more focused and engaging story, and skill progression tied to character development. The story especially stands out as they got rid of the useless NPC characters in favor of focusing on the main cast only so you can focus on the slice of life moments with them. In addition to this, Gust manages to borrow many of the quality of life features they started in Ryza 1 and 2 yet still make this game feel like a completely unique experience from the recent Atelier releases. There are still some issues with the game however: it's way too easy even on hard mode. You have to finish the game in order to unlock MUST DIE mode. The crafting items are very overpowered and monsters aren't tuned with items in mind. The Home Base customization feature doesn't allow you to place items where you want it which is understandable because there are stories tied with them, but still feels like a missed opportunity, especially since Photo mode is such a big thing in Gust's recent releases. Lastly, while the story has strong points and the characters are charming in slice-of-life moments, they can be really cheese during the more serious moments.

_childDocuments_.review: I find JRPGs to be the best at capturing the feeling of "young adult novels come to life." It would not surprise me if many teenagers who read young adult novels don't realize that they'd enjoy JRPGs. I'm a person who loved young adult novels, series such as Harry Potter, the stuff where a group of friends go on an adventure, and did not start playing JRPGs until after high school. Out of Gust's games I started with Nights of Azure 2 and Lydie and Suelle on the Switch, then Ryza 1 on PC. Ryza 2 was such a step up that I considered the Switch version to subjectively be an increase in quality over the PC version of Ryza 1. And Blue Reflection 2 is the highest quality Gust game I've played, and not just that, but one of the finest JRPGs that captures the spirit of young adult novels come to life.  It is a bona fide, high quality "mid tier" JRPG that is every bit as high quality as other mid-tier JRPG games from developers that may be more well known. True exploration where you can run with the left stick and spin the camera around with the right stick to admire the scenery rather than "fixed camera angles" like many mid-tier JRPGs used to have. A small group of friends that expands in size and gets to know each other. A comfy home base where the friends hang out, craft facilities and items for fun and to help in the exploration. Unique locations generated from the personalities and memories of the friends.  Going out to explore, then coming back to the comfy home. Some other games with the same feel and quality are "Rune Factory Frontier" for the Wii, and "Harvestella." Someone wrote here on Steam Blue Reflection Second Light feels like the "life changing summer camp experience" turned into a game.The cherry on top is that it is an all girl cast. I wish more games of this quality and uniqueness were made, and after also playing Ryza 3, I know that Gust undeniably now has the skill to create high quality, immersive mid-tier JRPGs that stand up with the other mid-tier JRPGs, they truly improved their craftmanship over the course of this generation. (And I did play BR1 afterwards, and BR2 feels like a generational leap in quality compared to BR1, in my opinion, Gust's games took the leap in quality starting with Ryza 2. In fact, if you are a person who feels like big budget JRPGs have been losing their way lately by trying to feel like HBO shows instead of Young Adult novels, put your money where your mouth is and consider Gust and Falcom games, and even some Square Enix mid-tier games too)

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I've finished the game proper, all of the stuff I said previously still holds up, but here are some extra thoughts on the whole thing:Music: the new tracks are still phenomenal, though I really REALLY miss the multi-phase music for bosses, as that mechanic is entirely absent in this game.Battles: They're like Ryza, but with it's own flair. It's very fun, as are the infight battles seeing as they're very active and snappy. The latter half of the game does get steamroll-y as your damage can scale up really fast once you start stacking fragments and school/item buffs. Bosses feel really weak compared to the original in almost every respect though, as they lack all the pomp and circumstance and get quickly recycled making them feel even less special.Story: I quite loved it, I thought I knew how the whole thing was going to pan out when reaching the back half but they did throw a few wrenches in there to shake it up. It's about as bittersweet as you'd expect.Characters: Each individual character story varied in depth, ranging from 'I've seen this a million times' to 'jesus, this is not daijobu' but each character does get mountains of additional fluff from the dates and chatter you see throughout the whole game to round them out. They really grow on you, and I got attached to every one of them, unlike the original game. I did often found myself just running around and cutting grass while thinking about what was going on in each of their heartscapes.Presentation: I absolutely loved the abstract designs for the heartscapes. Framing for the cutscenes, along with the music and overdone post processing (nuclear sun anyone?) gave it quite the unique look overall and suited the otherworldly vibe they were going for.As for some of the things that straight up sucked:- the stealth mission stuff just blows in every regard, thankfully there's only one or two instances where it's forced early on, with the rest of them being relegated to side missions you can take (or skip). Save scumming highly recommended if you do do those missions.- the back half of the game had some very obvious problems with proofreading, punctuation, and grammar compared to the relatively pristine first half.- the bosses paled in comparison to the og blue reflection, just full stop.Final thoughts: Second Light is a fantastic sequel, and anyone who likes slice of life style JRPG stories should absolutely give this a look (and the first one, also very very good).---Old Review---This is probably one of Koei's best PC ports to date. Looks great and runs great compared to the first game.As for the game, it's built off the original wonderfully along with adding a bunch of new systems that add a lot of flavor and character to the game. The soundtrack continues to be all 10/10 tracks, battling is a lot of fun, and the environments are very pretty and well detailed. The character design is also very nice, continuing the trend of cute girls doing cute things with each other. Honestly, it's met my expectations and more, can't complain at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This game brought me lots of nostalgic feelings and moments of a particular summer holiday, that time when I was hanging around with a few friends and an older cousin, was such an unforgettable experience. We all thought perhaps the world held only us then.The central theme of this game is Cute-Girls-Doing-Cute-Things in an enclosed place, and the usual magical girls slaying evil spirits. The plot is very straightforward even though it seemed convoluted at first glance, of course, there are a few twists to make the story engaging but still very predictable. However, the pacing execution is the key to make even a predictable feels enjoyable.Overall, the game has a clear goal set up since the beginning (one of foremost problems that its predecessor failed to establish)I don't really have anything to say about Graphics aspect. Art style embraced the first game's and improved even more, the result is a beautifully-crafted game. You can also tinker around the Photo Mode feature and publish pretty pictures.However, there are some small texture bugs with characters' hair.The Localization part is a massive step up from the first game, Gust and KT did a great job of getting a top quality localization team for this game.And about the Port, perhaps the best yet. This game came with a fully mapped KB&M buttons - which is a huge plus from me. The quality is very consistent, I have had not notice even the slightest drop in frames.I might be repeating myself countless times, but still, the gameplay is also a massive step up from its predecessor.They got rid of the old Speed Turn-based system in favor of an ATB-ish Turn-based, which offers more strategy approach and nullify cheesing to an extent. The Gear-escalating system blends very well into this aspect, although this can be repetitive for some people.And unlike the first game, your party won't fully healed after getting out of a fight and kept remain their HP through out expedition. Seems like a normalcy to JRPG games but it could threw some people (who came from the first game) off.Additionally, this game now has a Dating system. It isn't as well-crafted or impactful like Persona 5, but still a very nice cherry on top regardless. And through this, the chemistry of characters as well as some RPG elements is expanded upon so there is no harm in engaging with this aspect.Should you buy this game? Yes, you should experience this game for yourself, there are still stuffs that I haven't touched upon.You don't have to jump into its predecessor or watch Blue Reflection Ray anime (but should also consider them a try) to have a reason to play this game.Although, the game's quite expensive right now, maybe once it goes on sales you can consider getting this!Pros:+ Story, dialogues and pacing execution blended very well+ Engaging gameplay and strategically friendly+ Beautiful graphics, lighting and particles+ Localization and Port was handled carefullyCons:- There are some slight graphics bugs here and there- Gameplay can feel very repetitive and boring at times

_childDocuments_.review: If a third game is ever released, they will have my money the moment I can give it to them.I'm only recommending because the story, characters, music, and overall atmosphere of the levels were amazing. The actual game play was mind degrading-ly repetitive. Also, the true ending (or whatever it's called) is certainly  worth playing through the  game again.First off,  This game is obviously designed for controller first, keyboard/mouse never. You might get away with some strange keyboard layout, but you'll still have your fingers dancing all over it.This game basically has two core routines. The first is fighting demons and gathering random garbage. The second is use that garbage to build stuff and go on dates to raise character stats. That's all there is. The story is just there to give you a reason to go to this Heartscape to fight instead of that one. Even that gets undermined by the fact that sometimes the game just tells you to build more stuff before you can progress and leaves it up to you to waste the next few hours gathering materials from already cleared Heartscapes. Also, all the bosses felt the same, save for the one time you fight two at once and the final boss that has  phases, but even that just felt like  different battles with the same base boss type.I think my displeasure boils down to nothing felt like it mattered. You are given all these mechanics, abilities, and options, but "just YOLO it", is a perfectly valid strategy (becasue that's what I did on my second play through). The game turns from a JRPG into a "mash A to win" game. So much so that I bound A to a macro and used that more than the actual A button.Finally, why is there only one battle theme for 10 out of the 12 chapters of this game? The violin lead that opens whenever a battle starts got so annoying, so fast. I actually had to turn off the music or I was going to lose my mind. Don't get me wrong. The music is beautiful, but after hearing the same violin signaling a battle about twice a minute for the past few hours, it starts to get to you. On that note... how do you fail to implement proper volume sliders? The voice slider seems to do nothing. The story and characters were incredible. It was quite a roller coaster on my first play through and I really enjoyed it. I put 40 hours in over the course of a single week, because I was so hooked. All the characters had interesting personalities and memories that lead the imagination of the player really well. All the turning points didn't feel forced or out of place, while still being a bit surprising.The overall look and feel of the world was immersive. There were times that I actually just looked out over the endless ocean and wondered what I might find out there. The soundscape was done well and the music really helped set the tone of the locations.

_childDocuments_.review: There's not a lot of magical girl games out there in the marketplace, so despite my begrudging attitude towards turn-based combat, I decided to go all in and purchase both Blue Reflection games after seeing a bit of the story and gameplay.  Doing some research, I see that many mention Second Light as being a perfect entry point for the series, and would respectfully disagree.  Second Light is a very emotional game at its core, and I couldn't imagine going into it without having played the first game, as well as watching the anime, before hand.  While it's probably fine for many, the added emotional impact of seeing certain characters return, or seeing how some of them change based upon their experiences prior to this game, would have lessened the game's impact for myself.  What can be easily said is how Second LIght is a triumph and improvement of almost everything that the original Blue Reflection did.  It doesn't wildly change the formula, but enhances what already worked.  There's much less fan service to the characters, the different areas in the Heartscape feel more unique and BEAUTIFUL (parts of Uta's and Rena's are so pretty) compared to the pretty vanilla landscapes of the first game, and the way you can move around the school has been drastically improved.  In the first game, occasionally it was frustrating trying to seek out a particular character to speak with them, but now everyone is on the map and it's a quick fix and they are marked for you.  The "date" mechanic is also streamlined and feels more fleshed out, having 3 questions instead of one to respond to instead of one as well and ties into the school development and the actual plot of the game.  Second LIght makes you care about the characters, and the dates allow you to get to know them better, even if it occasionally borders on overkill with having to do like 10 in a row between story chapters.  It never felt like a burden due to the writing of the characters and genuinely wanting to know them better.  The battle system has been streamlined too, allowing you to have two characters on "autopilot" if you would like, as well as giving you the choice of who you want to use (as opposed to the 3 girls of BR).Admittedly, some things are different and not so great despite Second Light being an easily superior sequel.  The end of the game feels a bit grindy having to retrace your steps through EVERY Heartscape again before tackling the final area.  The music is again fantastic, but it does feel more 'chill' overall than some of the riveting moments of Blue Reflection - this one is different, but I would say it's still a very strong and attention grabbing soundtrack.  It also feels less RPGish at times, with the more generic leveling up system, that doesn't let you spend points like the first game did, instead that is relegated only to the points you get from dates.  The boss fights are less this time around, and don't have the same impact sans the final one, instead focusing more on smaller and more generic fights in each Heartscape.  The last nitpick is that of the story's conclusion.  I was FAR more invested in what Second Light offered in terms of the story and I absolutely loved it, but the ending was underwhelming when compared to the first game.  The final two chapters of Blue Reflection had me literally sobbing while playing through them, and while Second Light had plenty of poignant and touching scenes (many more along the way than BR had), the ending didn't leave me with that same sense of satisfaction.  It was a nice ending, but not at the level of the first game, leaving some loose ends in a sequel that may never come due to the anime tanking so bad.  All in all, Second Light and the Blue Reflection series quickly warmed its way into my top games of all time category despite some shortcomings.  Second Light has a great group of characters that I genuinely fell in love with while playing (Rena is simply the best), especially with the addition of returning characters to the franchise.  And for those looking for yuri content, you will find more than just bait, with a canon couple that really made this game stand out for me.  The way that they were portrayed was simply beautiful and I can't think of many video game couples that I felt so compelled to root for.  It probably didn't hurt that they were the two that I immediately attached to before knowing anything at the beginning, and as the story progressed and took its turns, it was so rewarding and satisfying to see their relationship blossom.  If you want a magical girl game, this is about as good as it gets!
_childDocuments_.name: BLUE REFLECTION: Second Light

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being a sequel to 2017's Blue Reflection, Second Light hardly feels like the same game - but not in a bad way.The short answer is “no, but it’s still recommended if you want the full experience”. Second Light features an entirely new main cast of characters and the story is mostly told without being too reliant on the first. I say mostly because the cast from the first do eventually make their way into this story, but it’s done in a manner that you would be able to understand even without being familiar with them.This extends to the anime adaptation as well: Blue Reflection Ray. I myself did not actually finish that anime yet I had no trouble getting to know the characters from it in the game – so again, you can just start from Second Light and be completely fine.Despite how simple the combat in the first game was, I kinda liked it. It was effective and perfectly matched the game’s laidback, slice of life feel. Second Light, on the other hand, completely throws that combat system out the window for an active-time battle system – similar to what we got in the recent Atelier Ryza games.Battles are far faster as a result and with the changes to the ether system, they only get faster the longer you’re in a battle. The MP system is removed entirely and now attacks, skills, and items all consume ether, which is regenerated at different rates per character depending on their stats. That said, I am a bit torn on this system. It is a completely different feel from the previous game and, while cool in theory, it does come with some problems.Mainly, it’s that it takes away a lot of the variety that the first game had with regards to its skills. Whereas in the first game, I was constantly scrolling through my different attacks and figuring out which best to use in a given fight – this game it is 95% of the time just going to be one of my basic attacks. I would enter a fight, spam A throughout the entire thing, and call it a day.Hard difficulty is not unlocked until you fully clear the game once, so you have to do your first playthrough on normal and I found it to be a bit too easy. Even after I intentionally kept myself underleveled by avoiding a lot of the enemies on the map, I still had no trouble clearing each and every encounter I ran into.Around halfway into the game, I stopped caring to even figure out the best party composition, which skills to unlock, and even what moves I was using – it hardly mattered with how easy it is and with how the ether mechanic is designed. Just keep spamming those basic attacks and you’ll build up your combo quickly, which in turn allows you to do more damage with your next basic attack and so on.Finishing up the game, I couldn’t escape this feeling that the battle system was just underutilized. It has all these cool mechanics, but the low difficulty and emphasis on building up combo quickly leave it feeling a bit repetitive.In the first game, the level design was some hot garbage – mostly small groups of pathways and platforms. In Second Light, they went all out. Now there are multiple areas per biome, movement options outside of just… walking, and some actual exploration elements, even if on the lighter side. The new areas are also far more dense, with more detail put into individual buildings and the overall geography being much more varied.Having to do fetch quest after fetch quest just to get to the next chapter in the first game was some incredibly boring stuff, so I was very happy to see that done away with entirely in Second Light. Now, side quests are just that – optional side quests. That said, they’re also more varied. Aside from the usual “craft this for me” or “kill this enemy for me”, a lot of them now have you build unique school development stuff – stuff that you actually can use outside of that individual side quest.There are even some side quests that straight up expand on individual characters by having you explore different areas with them to unlock their memories. You sometimes have to do some boring stealth missions, but it’s at least much better off than the filler that the first game had.It still has the same overall school-magical girl theme told across different character arcs, but there is FAR more focus placed on a larger, more connected story instead of just rushing things right at the end like the last game. Character arcs are almost immediately tied into this bigger story and the game does a great job balancing out character development with this larger mystery.The game as a whole takes a darker tone than the original and the pacing starts off slow, but ramps up around the halfway point once you start realizing the truth behind this world. It doesn’t go completely overboard either – in fact, it might actually be a bit too slow. Perhaps this is just because the game is longer (this one took me just over 30 hours whereas the first took just 20), but I felt like they could have shaved off a bit towards the end to make it flow better.Still an interesting story for sure (and definitely better than the first game), but not quite at the level that I would call it anything more than just “good”.I am a huge fan of the urban fantasy magical girl aesthetic and Second Light only expands on the first game in this regard with the improved world detail and upgraded visuals that bring it more in line with the recent Atelier games. It’s definitely not a shining example as far as actual graphical quality, but the setting, character designs, and overall theme are solid. The music on the other hand, while still good, I did not find to be quite as good as the first game.The first game somehow used 100% of my RTX 3080 Ti even with the fps capped to my monitor’s refresh rate, but this one ran just fine at 155 fps without turning my computer into a jet engine. There are far more graphical options to change this time too, so there is ample room to finetune settings if you need to.One recommendation I will make – do disable the game’s depth of field setting, it is WAY more aggressive than it needs to be. Otherwise, the only other problems I had were with the game always launching in windowed (which you can solve by hitting F9) and a game crash about two hours in. I didn’t lose much progress due to the new auto save feature, but any crash is worth mentioning.And surprisingly, the keyboard and mouse controls are actually NOT garbage this time around. There’s actual mouse support in the menus, on the field, and it doesn’t feel like it’s just emulating a controller. I still used a controller myself, but it’s one of the few Koei Tecmo PC ports where the keyboard and mouse controls would be a viable alternative – I had no problems with them during my testing and they are rebindable too.Blue Reflection: Second Light is an overall improvement over the first game in almost every regard. A more fleshed out story, a bunch of useful quality of life features, much better visuals, vastly improved level design, a decent PC port – it’s got a lot going for it. Unfortunately, the combat is a bit of a mess and the game is far too easy, making a lot of the new combat additions redundant. That, and while the story itself is interesting, it doesn’t come without its problems. Still, I had a good time with it in spite of these faults and would recommend it if you like Gust JRPGs.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: improving vastly on the first game, the music, atmosphere, beautiful environments and expansive characters all blend wonderfully to create another upbeat, mellow and ultimately memorable experience.the first zone in the game really expresses the undertones of the entire game well with the joys of exploration and adventure mixed with the fear and caution of mystery and the anxiety the unknown brings. it was also a ton of fun seeing familiar faces and noticing exactly how the stories connect and intertwine as well as hearing music from the previous game and instantly having an instinctual reaction when the battle theme played.the overall mechanics are an objective improvement and while at first i was skeptical about the new battle system, it proved to be a fun shake-up with interesting synergy nonetheless. a perfect sequel and what every sequel should strive to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Really great game. Takes every idea from the first that was kinda poorly executed and improves on it. It's one of those RPGs where the side content really does just slide right into the main game, and I love it for that. You still gain skill points by talking with the girls and completing fetch quests for them, but you gain actual xp from killing monsters now, so the leveling system is a lot better this time. Each girl has their own world, so there's lots of varied environments, although not a lot of monster variation. There is a crafting system now similar to the Atelier games, but not quite as deep. But lots of items to be used in combat. They have also added a facility building feature to the school that opens up new dialogue options with different girls and allows you to develop them further. The plot also is a little less straight forward this time. 20 hours in I kinda just now feel like I'm getting the gist of what's going on. Gust really nailed this one, I honestly might like it better than any of the Atelier games.

The story isn't great, but also not bad. It had its twists, but nothing to out of the ordinary. I was indeed a bit sad, that the game ended. (+1)+ Battle System is fun, if you don't have to fight too much. It is a turn-based / action-based hybrid system. Seems like it is geared to drag the battles a bit out. _childDocuments_.review: Against all expectations, Blue Reflection: Second Light has somehow turned out to be an absolutely incredible game. It's almost hard to believe that a game this good is at all related to the hot mess that was the original Blue Reflection.If, like me, you were drawn to the premise of the original game but ended up disappointed by it's poor writing, shallow characters and weak gameplay, then you will likely find Second Light to be everything you wished the first game had been and more.  As for newcomers to the series, while Second Light is a mostly self-contained story, I'd recommend watching the Blue Reflection Ray anime before playing it so you can get added context for the backstories of three of the game's characters. I wouldn't bother with the first game though, it's really not worth your time.In my opinion, Second Light is an absolute must-play for anyone who has ever considered themselves a fan of GUST's games, as well as fans of Yuri and the Magical Girl genre. It's easily one of the best games GUST has released in the last 10 years, and it has turned out to be my undisputed game of the year for 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: Gust has been creating fantastic combat system after fantastic combat system those past few years (Atelier Sophie 2 in particular might have my favourite RPG combat of all time), and Blue Reflection 2 is no exception - plus, this time, unlike in the first game, there's a challenging difficulty option in "Deathwish" that allows you to properly enjoy the great system.The game structure is more focused than the first one, and it drops the weird voyeur thing from it too that felt really out-of-place with the tone of the game. Though so far I'm not sure if I prefer the characters from this one or from the first, yet.I really enjoyed the first Blue Reflection, and the early impressions from Second Light is that it is an overall better game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have finished the game unlike most other reviews at this time. I assume you've seen the anime and/or at least know all the characters that appear in this game.TLDR: General improvement from first game but some subjective weak aspects.As a KT game with cosmetic DLC, I think even just the base game is very overpriced in my currency.I was apprehensive about having characters from the anime in the game, but they gave them enough development and backstory to justify it. That said, I don't feel that all the characters got fair development - stories and traumas from characters like Kokoro, Shiho and Kirara are absolutely forgettable, while other characters have very appealing and emotionally strong backstories, such as Rena and Yuki. I picked Uta for my ending cutscene but was unfortunately let down since her story felt kind of tacked on to the game and I was hoping to get some proper closure on her, which I unfortunately did not. It's a weak way of putting it but I'd say characters overall are 6/10s with some 8s.There are a handful of translation/spelling issues, and I was wondering whether different teams handled different aspects of the text since different things seemed to share separate consistency at times. Nothing worth complaining about overall though.Story was fine, it ties in a little with the first game but neither first game nor anime is entirely necessary to see. I think the premise was fine but the execution was kind of lacking, although I'd expect that from a game that's more focused on character building that story. Without going into spoiler territory, I'd just call it solid. The overall plot is often put to the side in lieu of the character stuff anyway.I thought I wouldn't like it based on the demo because the pause mechanics during battle are different (if you have it set to "manual", you can forget to tell your allies to make their moves). However as expected I got used to it very quickly and I think I prefer the faster pace. Knockdown has more impact here than in the first game, as does the fragment system and the talent system. Overall, battle system is a major improvement - it has been heavily streamlined and is more engaging, with a better Ether system. Even after finishing I'm still on the fence about the one-on-one system, it's nice but sometimes messed up my flow, especially since some enemies can trigger it on their own.Stealth was the main thing I disliked, there are some very annoying stealth missions (Uta, Yuzu/Lime) that I ended up save-scumming. Enemy detection is wonky (can sometimes see through objects or at strange angles) and their vision indicator is misleading (you can stand in the "weaker red" parts and not get seen). Was just frustrating at times being sent back to the start by what felt like unfair detection.I also don't particularly like the crafting/building loop, more than a few times I found myself going back to farm more "Warm Sand" to make and upgrade furnishings. There are 50 crafting teams by the end, which is too many, but I mostly ignored items throughout the game anyway. That said, I also feel that you can mostly ignore this stuff since you just need to do enough to trigger dates, no need to go for the extra bonuses from upgrades. The base difficulty (normal) doesn't warrant this, by about midgame you should be streamrolling all content until the end of the game without much investment into furniture.The final boss fight is very nice however I would still say that Daath is very slightly better overall. It was sort of introduced from nowhere and had little relation to the story other than being there because it needed to be (no explanation for it etc.) There are no game/save breaking bugs like the first game. Unfortunately there are also no real extras for finishing the game other than a quasi-NG+. The ending is purposefully ambiguous so again if you were hoping for particular character story tie-ups you won't get them.The music is very good, I'd say about on par with the first game for some tracks, while others were unremarkable. I couldn't pick between first or second for area themes, but boss themes from the first are probably slightly better (DNF FW15C III or Sayonara is still the best one imo). Generally good job by Hayato Asano once more.Standard Blue Reflection art, it's fine. If you liked it already it's pretty much the same. Personally felt that Uta/Mio/Hiori looked kind of strange in the proper artstyle but let's be honest the anime didn't do them justice either. _childDocuments_.review: *Exhausted yet satisfied stretch* So just beat it like 5 minutes ago, I like to review fresh while my feelings are running on the high of satisfaction, Blue reflection second light (which for all our sanity I will refer to as BR2) was a game I enjoyed a whole lot, did it have it's issues? sure and I'll get to them in the hopes if they ever do another game and see this that they fix those issues and for everyone who reads this benefit too of course but is it a funtastic game (yes that was intentional) despite that? you're gosh dang right it is so let's get to it dood!So to start the main thing about this game is although there's combat the main thing about this game as with  the last is relationships with the other girls is key, which means there's gonna be a looot of talking but it's not without it's perks, these net you upgrade points for both the protag and the other characters and to top it off I think the talking is nice, you get to know each girl, sometimes about their past, their problems and spoiler for the first game if ya haven't played it yet but our girls powers? run on emotions and bonds so it canonically makes sense, not everyone will like the text slog and honestly? to a degree you really don't need it either, I'll get to why eventually as it's actually one of the games problems but what's there is good and you should give it a chance, especially on whatever girl you like as a person dood.Let's see combat is next because I wouldn't want everyone who hates reading too much to be bored before I even start :p jk jk still the combat is done similar to an ATB ("Active time battle" I believe) in that you wait for your turn down the line but here's where it gets interesting, the gals are like well oiled race cars in that the longer they fight the more they shift to higher gears! a weird and yet apt description as the more you attack the more you change gears, 1 all the way to 5, what does this do? a few things, for starters it lets you use more types of attacks, as you reach gear 3 you also transform giving a rather cool visual change, to your attacks too at that, what's more the more you wait the more turns you can attack with, 5000 points, most attacks cost 1000 but go up to 3000 for a super attack dood.But wait there's more! as you attack you get a combo counter! as it rises you get a damage multiplier and after a certain hit count you can use the special I mentioned along with the 3000 points, you also have a support character who you can switch to, uses skills or even items so you can keep fighting with your gals, you have multiple attack types and weaknesses which pertain to both the player and the enemy and in fact will knock whoever is hit back on the timeline, if you hit enemies enough they will break allowing for free hits and on mid-bosses or higher will lead to another mechanic I'll talk about soon dood!Soon is here! so let's talk about 1 on 1 fights, if you break an opponent you can hit them enough to put them into 1 on 1 combat, the girl gets four moves, attack, dodge, counter and a unique to them skill which can heal or boost themselves, if you hit them enough times or kill them you will hit them with a powerful finisher move, this is fun but not without it's issues, it never happens often enough despite enemies being able to start a 1 on 1 fight themselves to get used to the style of combat, counters are pure guess based because of this, which isn't the worst, you don't need that but the real issue is I've never once hit them enough to activate that unique special attack, killed them for it yes but that kinda makes the attack pointless at that point dood.Okay that's combat done with, next is gathering and building! this is a main mechanic I wanted to talk about as it's quite important, you build facilities and they in turn give you permanent boosts as they are laid out around the main hub, this is a great fun idea as it looks visually fun, is great for building relationships with the other girls and benefits the player, possibly too much in fact as some boosts are really significant, which will lead me on to the bad aspects of the game which I'll talk about in a sec dood.So lets see here the bad of the game, honestly nothing much at all, in fact it's really my own fault so I'm not sure I can call it bad but upgrading facilities can make you too powerful, okay some peeps will love that but it kills all the challenge the game has to offer, to note the last boss couldn't even do 100 points of damage to be, my characters had 600+ and hard mode isn't available until after you beat the game, something the devs should really patch out and have unlocked from the start for this eventuality dood.Another bad aspect although not like you have to do it but most people will want to is that upgrading facilities requires gathering materials but a lot of those materials...come from enemies, early enemies, like things I could kill in one hit but the issue is it just requires soooo much, on top of that if you don't want to be doing that many fights then you better get used to crafting materials one at a time so they can take advantage of the 1-3+ bonus or free material uses or the like, otherwise you will create 21 planks rather than the possible 40+ you could have saving you time and a headache dood.That said these issues are more a problem for completionists, people who wanna max everything because it's in their blood but that said some people may want it because they think they will need it but suffice to say the issues is fine as long as you don't grind a lot and the final thing I will talk about is new game plus, it's not worth it, you keep half your TP and the only equipable items in the game which are frankly meh mostly and require more slots which you need TP for more slots, that's it, the things you crafted before gone (for story purposes though so fine to a degree) but what's worse? even if you craft them again they lose their upgrades, all that time gone but hey now you get to do it all over again for the "true end" at level 1 with none of the good stuff at all! of which to note that's just a single scene at the end, I hate to do this to BR2 but I'd suggest just watching it on youtube, it's a great scene but even I don't have the patience to do it all again dood.So all in all we have a stellar game, it's fun, I would suggest it to most people, it's active enough that it should fundamentally keep action game peeps entertained a little more than a basic turn based games, it's got a great story and fun characters, the visuals are great oh oh and there's a camera mode! the poses are limited due to censorship though <-> but otherwise it's one of my favourite parts of the game and I wish more games did it with such pretty and unique looking places in games, thanks for reading and hope you enjoy the game dood!

_childDocuments_.review: Before we begin, this is the sequel to the magical girl game of magical girl games, Hayato Asano is still best girl, and this game is simply really good.In short, this game is all about emotions, memories, and friendship. It also has the most "yuri" undertones I've seen in a game, but it's done pretty well. Every character is well-written and feel important to the plot, and the story may be a slow start (I was seriously doubting continuing at the beginning), but when it finally gets going (near the end of the first dungeon), it really picks up steam. Also, if you couldn't tell, I really enjoyed the music. Finally, there is some decent DLC packs to get- on sale, at least. A couple of extra dungeons, a near-essential crafting function (seriously, get the Ether Synthesis function for the extra couple bucks, it will save you SO MUCH pain in the late game), and a couple other goodies. Get this game on sale of course, I got it for 60 percent off, so about 32 dollars for everything including the four DLC packs, which, for 42 hours of fun gameplay, great story (after a slow start), and beautiful music- yeah, this one is great for people who enjoy magical girl media, or simply JRPGs in general. 9/10 game right here.

_childDocuments_.review: Major improvement from the first game, be it filler voice lines and more facial expressions to make the girls feel more alive, actual real time combat that still retains a ramp style combat, more QoL in making the game easy to pick up for newer and experienced players all make for a pleasant experience. Second Light also makes many references to the 1st game especially since Hinako (the protagonist of the 1st game) makes a returning appearance here too. The story is cohesive and detailed as a result which makes even remembering the tiny details enjoyable when relevant in a later scene. While there is a large cast of  over 10 characters, I find myself liking them all of them with each equally having their time in the spotlight. Seeing the school actually being 3D and explorable with the same layout as the 1st is a great step up.While the combat is definitely unique in that its real-time turn based in a sense, there are however questionable game design decisions that may irk the player. The hardest difficulty is not available until clearing the game (possibly designed with the New Game+ bonuses in mind), but even then you do not get rewarded more for playing harder difficulties such as higher XP gain or more loot. Achievement hunters will find that 30% of the achivements will require NG+ in order to get the rest and also discover that the exploration achivement can be missed if not careful. I had to do 3 gameplay's worth as a result to fully complete the game. QoL such as options already done being greyed out can make for a better NG experience. It is worth commending that Second Light went for a character focused gear system rather than skill focused for satisfactory and flexible gameplay.Blue Reflection still retains beautiful scenery of all sorts, from calming seaside railways to traditional Japanese shrines. The developers are so confident they even have an indepth camera mode so you can add any posable character and even enemies you wish in any ingame environment for photo shoots! As you explore the school, there appears to be animations of almost all actions as the girls do their daily routines. Examples include watering plants, finding a broom and cleaning with it, practicing festival games in a cheeky manner to even a full 2 minute stretch at the rooftop. GUST's attention to immersion is surely evident. It is worth noting that they toned down fanservice like wet shirts, changing scenes and more from the 1st game, which is up to preference. The biggest concern is that the game definitely prefers if you play with a controller, there is performance optimization issues with the PC version of the game without one. All in all excellent sequel where the aesthetics in story and characters are top tier with great gameplay, but potential performance issues and game design decisions warrant considering the game preferably on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty substantial upgrade from the first game in almost every way. It's not perfect, and admittedly, the last 10% of the game starts to fall apart through the narrative and its gameplay. In fact, this series could still use some improvements for future titles if they decide to make a third entry. But the fact of the matter is, they addressed a lot of my issues with the first game to make it an enjoyable experience. The characters are really fun, there's actually a proper level up system, and the school building/item crafting system is an absolute joy to tinker with. As someone who didn't like the first game all that much, I'm glad I gave the sequel a shot and wholeheartedly recommend it if you're still on fence.

_childDocuments_.review: Very boring experience to get through. I absolutely adored the first game, one of my favorite games on the Playstation 4. Therefore, I forced myself through this one, but the charm and soul of Blue Reflection just isn't there anymore. This game takes a turn for the worse making collecting and synthesizing a main component now. It wasn't nearly as important in the first game. Prepare to spend hours trying to find out which enemies collect what and backtracking so you can build your bases and continue the story.The first game had three main characters to focus on and a bunch of side characters that made school feel lively during your daily life cycle. This game has TWELVE main characters! Many appearing at a chapter by chapter basis. Every character has lost their memory and has a dungeon where you regain those memories. Within every memory, you experience their hardships in life. With so many characters, you never feel close to any one of them unless you choose to go on boring, non voice acted dates with them in an isolated school. You date them as the bland main protagonist, who has no interesting backstory and just likes to flirt with all the girls.The fantastical magical aspect of this game is put aside for farming and dating. In the first game, hell even the anime, transformation was a crucial moment with a big cutscene which allowed girls like Hinako with a damaged leg to explore and fight in the other world with their magical powers. Now in second light, all of a sudden, these girls can fight in their normal states and switch to magical girls after reaching third phase or "3rd gear" in combat. Which makes zero sense in the lore of blue reflection. The transformations in Second Light are incredibly underwhelming as well. It is a five second jump cut transformation that you can turn off in options after you get tired of seeing it in the middle of every battle. This is in contrary to the one time, beautiful, slow, gradual transformation from normal girl to magical girl that we experienced in the first game right before exploring the other worlds.This soundtrack was quite lackluster and doesn't come close to the incredible OST put together by composer Hayato Asano for the first game. I can't recall one outstanding song from this game, not even for the final boss.  It's all just mediocre really. At least compared to the first game.The dungeons in the first game were grand, spacious, with a certain color palette to them which represented the emotions the dungeon had evoked. The camera focused on the world, it's background and it's size, with the main character small in the center. Second Light has admittedly some beautiful locations however not a lot goes on in these worlds and they are so very small. The camera also focuses mostly on the main character and not the world.Last but not the least the combat. It's just a drag. Way too many enemies in this game and they can be fought the same exact way. It took me over half of the game to finally install somebody else's save that contained the locked, hard mode/must die mode. This made combat a little more fun since i could take advantage of the combo system that i never needed and use combo finishers against bosses. However the fights were still too many and never very interesting. The first game gave you a very chill, play at your own pace, turn based battle system that featured dynamic camera which showcased each individual girl pre & mid attack. It also focused and showcased enemies and their attacks when they retaliated. Battles were well paced, there were never too much battles, and bosses were a nice challenge without this new combo system from Second Light. SL gives you an always active battle system so you are always planning your actions quickly. The camera is fixated on the trio of magical girls, only swaying left and right, which is quite the downgrade in presentation in my opinion. So in conclusion, I very much disagree with the reviews that say this game is better than the first game. Maybe it took too much inspiration from the Atelier series. But I don't enjoy those games, and I did not enjoy my 50 plus hour journey with this game. It was honestly quite the chore and grind to finish. The story is NOT better. It had potential. The overarching story surrounding ash syndrome and what happened to the world was quite interesting. However the game almost never focused on that and instead focused on girl friendship drama for EVERY, SINGLE, CHAPTER.. It was unbearable by the end. Please do better Gust. Make Blue Reflection great again. And bring back Hayato Asano for the next game.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't quite know what to expect with going into a non-Atelier Gust game, but it's actually pretty interesting.  I can still see quite a bit of Atelier influence at times.  While the game is tagged "Sexual Content" and "Nudity", there is none of that.  There's no romance more than one canon couple, a few hugs, and handholding.  There is no nudity, the most fanservice you'll get without using DLC outfits are a few scenes with swimsuits.Visually it's pretty nice, there's a good bit of variety between environments since each exploration area is an idealized version of a specific character's memories or desires.  Character art is OK, it's a little odd seeing those who are supposedly late highschool or early college age in school uniforms.  A few characters (namely  have very similar looks and you have to really look carefully to know which one is which if you see the character anywhere except in a cutscene or close up.  Most of the others have enough visual distinction to know who they are.  One complaint is that it has the same distance/depth of field blur "feature" that Atelier Ryza 3 has, and it makes a few areas (such as the second and third heartscapes) very hard to see in.Music is a bit different from Atelier, but still pretty solid.  It is Gust after all.  Sound effects work, but some you can tell are obviously taken from previous Atelier games.Story starts interesting, and the discovery portion and restoring memories portions are quite good.  Unfortunately it starts to fall apart toward the end, and the ending itself is deeply unsatisfying.  Most of the character development is done via dates, which you need to do a number of with each girl to boost up their talent level and give you points that you will need to boost your party.  The other source of talent points are from requests, which are mostly fetch quests.  Talent levels unlock scenes, recipes, and new areas in the respective character's heartscape, so there is a value to raising them.  You'll need to do NG+ to max out all characters talent levels, as there aren't enough points to max out more than 1 or 2 character.It's not an Atelier game, so crafting isn't a big focus.  However, crafting is present and required to complete the game.  Acquiring new characters and their heartscape exploration zones requires that you build certain school expansions, which require crafted materials.  These school expansions also give you some sort of stat boost, an optional buff+detriment, or allow you to purchase consumables or get temporary buffs.  Consumable items are pretty useful early on, and on higher difficulties/underleveled play, but aren't really worth using late game when your character skills are so much stronger.Combat is an ATB based system, where you gradually gain Ether, which is used to activate skills.  Each character has a starting amount of Ether that is gained every second, a maximum value they can store up before it stops filling, and each skill costs a certain amount of Ether.  Most skills are 1000 ether to cast, with some costing 1500 or 2000.  Each skill will give you an increase (or decrease for some powerful skills) to the amount of ether gained each second (Ether Acceleration), and when you hit certain thresholds, you go up a "gear" which increases your cap.  Changing gears also changes what your skills do, some skills increase in power, others change their behavior (a very Ryza like thing), and some skills only show up at certain gears.  Some gears even remove access to certain skills, so if you need a certain buff make sure to hit it before you raise too high.  Hitting gear 3 will transform your character into their reflector form (essentially a magical girl transformation).  You want to raise ether acceleration and starting ether stats as much as possible!Other aspects of combat that are important to know is that there is a combo system, which tracks the number of attacks done before an enemy's super attack goes off and resets it.  Each 1 attack in a combo increases your damage by .25 times normal.  A 4-combo is double damage, and it goes up greatly!  One character you get reasonably early also buffs up your ability to build combo.  Attacking foes with their weakness will knock them back on the turn order, and hitting enough knockback will break them and stun them for a bit.  Bosses when stunned will put up a shield, that when broken will bring you into a 1-on-1 battle with the boss and the character who broke the shield.  This operates like a rhythm game, and are really frustrating to get used to.  If you can get used to them though, they're really powerful and let you pull off finishing moves.  The downside is that if you muss a counter or dodge and get hit, it resets your combo neutralizing your damage multiplier!  Finally there's a support character who will perform actions at certain "revolutions" around their support bar, such as performing a buff, switching places with an active party member, or using an item.  The buff actions can be random, giving you only a chance of using the buff, so it's not something you can depend on.  Item use is also done at certain times in the cycle, not instantly when done by the support character (active party is instant).  Overall support characters aren't a great mechanic.Combat is pretty tough at the beginning when you don't have great resources and only have access to gear 1-3, but late game the balance totally falls apart.  Shiho is, unless you specifically need help with knockback, a much better support character than Rena; plus she does higher damage in general.  Late game character Hiori has the ability to grant weakness to two elements, one of which is Shiho's element, and has the highest base attack and defense.  Both characters are also extremely fast to start with.  These two are the core of your team, with the third slot going to Hinako most of the time as her combo building and high speed is quite useful.  Kokoro can be brought in if you need her specific weakness.  Unfortunately Ao just isn't as useful.  Ao's main unique feature, protection from having your combo be broken, isn't useful later as Hiori also gets a combo break protector AND the three main powerhouses can just stunlock most bosses easily.Finally exploration, it's pretty Atelier in feel, discrete zones, with mini puzzles here and there, and monsters you either have to fight or can avoid.  Lots of crafting ingredients lying around, many of these will be needed for sidequests and required crafts.  There is a stealth element in regular exploration, if you attack an enemy that doesn't see you in stealth mode you'll get minor damage applied and make them easier to stun.  There are also stealth missions, one early one required, and several more as character requests.  These can be very frustrating and unfun, a couple late one are really terrible to do.  One of the big issues with stealth missions is that getting caught once will cause you to have to start over from the last checkpoint (some stealth missions contain no checkpoints), but the enemy movement cycles will NOT be reset properly, which can sometimes cause you to be unable to complete a particular segment without intentionally getting caught to try to get the foes on a better cycle.Overall, it's a decent RPG game.  The combat is fun, if a bit unbalanced late.  Exploration works, some parts are fun but others (opening doors in Kirara's heartscape and stealth missions) are terrible.  Character bonding events are nice, and there are a lot of them (well over 100).  The characters themselves are generally good too, I was especially fond of Kokoro, Shiho, Kirara, and the growth of late game character .  It's not an Atelier game, but definitely satisfied a similar itch.

_childDocuments_.review: Are you here for gameplay? Better look somewhere else. Otherwise, look closer. Provided you don't mind lesbians. I hope you don't.Blue Reflection 2 (or Second Light) can be played without playing the first game, or watching the (not very good) anime. There are recurring characters and themes from both, but I'd say in case of the anime it's probably better to not know it. Has a good enough chance to make you dislike the characters coming from it, because it's not well written. The first game I can't just recommend due to a lot of issues thanks to its non existing budget. If you liked this game, you could still check it out later.What about the DLC? Ignore. So far nothing worthwhile has been released. The DLC area has barely any story/cutscenes, and for that we are here.So, what's this about anyway? A bunch of girls, with more and more appearing, trying to survive in a strange little world they are imprisoned in. Outside of the protagonist, Ao, none seem to have any memories. You play through their so called heartscapes, to see their most precious memories and help them to restore their memories. These memories made out of fragments of a key event of their lives, usually involving hard times that made them able to become what they are today. They are generally kept believable and on the ground, so it's a refreshing and relatively calm experience. The music nicely underlines this with a lot of nice and calm music with some electronic aspects to otherwise often piano music. Pretty good music, mind you. You may also get a little teary eyed here and there, but it's never too heavy on its mood.Aside of that, you get to know the characters better. Everything really has story meaning in the game. Building facilities for your place or fulfilling quests character give you, don't just give you gameplay benefits, they also grant "date" events, giving you a closer look at the character(s) in question. Raise their ranks through both, and you get further events with them. There's not much romance, mind you, though one very explicit lesbian couple exists, but that doesn't concern Ao. She can play wingman though... and still hold hands with the involved girls. Okay, it's weird, but that's just Ao. You can make her flirt pretty hard with any girl, really. If you like that, great. If you don't, there's usually an option to not do so, but it may be hard. Ao is just that much of a huge flirt. You do these things usually at the beginning of a chapter and it can take 2 or 3 hours. During dates you can often also find optional events (marked on your map), which is a nice touch, aside of some obligatory choices slightly changing dialogue. Eventually you'll go into the next dungeon, and here we get to the less great part. The nice part of them is, that you can find the fragments and get enough little cutscenes to entertain. The not so nice part is, gameplay.Dungeons. Gameplay. Well, it's an Rpg, right? Right. First of all, if you aren't willing to use cheat engine to get the difficulty up to hard, or as of v1.01 deathwish, you can stop reading after this paragraph. It's so easy, you don't need to know if the mechanics are for you. It's gonna be boring, but you can dodge a lot of enemies in dungeons. There are also some stealth missions, where some later ones might frustrate. You can however save ANYWHERE in a dungeon, and pop right back to where you were, making it ultimately never more than a minor test of patience. Now then, you have cheat engine ready? Higher difficulties actually require that you really make sure to upgrade facilities and care about what skills you learn. (hint: Don't touch the flat stat ups, like attack + 3, and get the Yuki ether boost skills ASAP) That said, once you hit a certain point of the game, even deathwish becomes easy mode. In new game+ it should be easy mode from the get go. (the point you'd normally have it unlocked for) Because battle performance really matters little, I won't write much about the battle mechanics. Just one thing: Basically every fight is the same, which I consider a big minus. Some mechanics are also rather counter-intuitive (1vs1 is just a BAD mechanic, no matter how you look at it), and nothing is even remotely strong enough to live till you can use your "ultimates", especially given that enemies love to kill themselves due to triggering 1vs1. The endgame is also particularly stretchy, getting in the way of the story climax. Really, it's not great. Can be fun for a bit, but eventually you just cruise, as if it's normal mode.Still though, it's a good game, if you like cutscenes and getting to know a big cast that's well used and doesn't even really suffer from the "everyone has to say one line per cutscene" syndrome. Unfortunately there's also some bad news. The translation is a professional 4/10. While each line by itself is mostly correct, , in context there are way too many moments where the word choices do not make sense or downright clash with lines just seconds before. Being a liberal translation is fine and all, but then you need to pay a lot more attention to context, which they really didn't. The translation also likes way too much to write out what was originally only implied. If you played the first game, it's very similar to that. While it's a shame that the translation is so sub-par, there's still a lot you can enjoy. For a commercial product that relies heavily on its text, the translation may be disappointing. But there's way worse out there. This was simply a game that required more attention to detail, which it did unfortunately not get.

_childDocuments_.review: The second game is a much better…game. It's much more polished, with a better budget for everything: the script, the dates (so many dates!), the dungeons, the crafting system, etc.Now, the focus is still on dating the girls to get to know them better. Now you have exactly three options to select per date that would affect what fragment you'll get by the end, and as a bonus you get to see different reactions and sometimes cutscenes. By my count you can get as many as 141 dates per playthrough. That's not counting optional date events you can trigger while on the date, and group events.And, for what it's worth, there's some actual romance this time, and it's not just between the main heroine and other girls. Also, there's a handholding system implemented when you progress your bonding far enough!Item crafting is now required to progress some story events, and to unlock some optional areas in the dungeons. Plus, you get a separate school structure crafting to add to the school grounds (which work as additional dating spots).You also get more party members to build your team, plus an additional support slot for passive effects during battles.The combat system is also seriously expanded, with more skills, a gear system to unlock skill tiers, team combos, transformations, and additional one-on-one boss battle system.The music is mostly reused and slightly rearranged tracks from the first game (which is not a bad thing).One slight dig I have, is the outfit DLCs. There's not even one with casual wear this time around, which is a shame. All you can get is alternative colors for default outfits, and a bunch of fan service.The ending is also a bit disappointing, in that it's just a boss rush where you have to re-visit every dungeon and re-fight the dungeon boss. And then do it again in the end game dungeon. It feels like an unnecessary padding just to prolong the last chapter for a few hours.The ending is also kinda meh, and the NG+ changes for True End are so minor, it's not worth it to run again (but you probably will, if you care for 100% completion, because there's a bunch of bugged achievements, and you can only get half the fragments from dates in one playthrough).All in all, it's a very chill and enjoyable experience if you like the genre of cute girls doing cute things. And you absolutely do not need to play the first game, nor do you need to watch the anime before starting this game!
