_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Playtime: 4.9 hoursNot gonna lie, when I first heard about this game, I thought to myself, "Really? A card game?" I saw the trailer and I liked the art and the overall visual style of the game a lot but I wasn't sure how it would be. I then impulsively purchased it because it had a special discount, and boy, I am so glad that I did.This game takes everything which is so much fun of Solitaire and then enhances it 8 different suits with face cards which have different abilities. They can then be used strategically to clear a level of solitaire. The incredible music which gradually increases in intensity as you get closer to sorting all the card decks never gets old. It is VERY easy to just get lost in this game and singularly focus on it.I am not usually one for playing video games for hours on end, so I was shocked to learn that I had played this game for 3 hours in a row one night.The story told through the FMVs is fairly predictable, but it is fun regardless. Greg Miller gives a pretty fun performance and it was cool to see him in a different light than I usually do. Inel also makes an appearance as a suave agent and that is great too.A lot of people might get put off by the blocks of text which describe the "missions" you take on, but I enjoyed reading them. And soon enough, I started choosing missions which had good and noble goals, more than ones which gave me more XP. And this happened very organically. When I read that a mission led to protestors being able to express themselves on the streets, peacefully and safely... it genuinely made me feel good.This was my very first Mike Bithell game (only learned about him via the Play, Watch, Listen podcast) and I thoroughly enjoyed it. It definitely won't be my last.I am glad that I got and played this game, and put aside my initial biases because it helped me to find a game which I will return to a lot of times, whenever I am looking for a good game of cards.Now... time to collect the remaining three achievements!8/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Solitaire with a very slight hint of Alpha Protocol type story telling. As the title indicates the story telling has hints of an espionage thriller, however do not expect the great story telling. Plot twist(s) and the ending were obvious right from the beginning, however what is there is serviceable, The story does not outstay its welcome and it provides a bit of a break in between game levels.  The game uses  FMV cut scenes for story telling and surprisingly  acting  is  not cringe worthy,.Game interface very streamlined and different color themes can be applied to interface. They are unlocked as level completion rewards and can be changed in between levels. There interface is simple and there is some nice character designs that appear in the background while playing the game. The music that plays during the game play is has espionage film vibes, but overall it is kind of forgettable and and after playing for a while you kind of forget that is even there.  Overall you mileage may vary when it comes to game music and I would not be surprised if some players would just turn it off completely.  There are some attempts at introducing some new game mechanics to solitaire, but they can pretty much be ignored. First of all the game retains the basic mechanic of solitaire. Cards get shuffled randomly and then the player sorts them in order in four separate suites.  However instead of sorting four classic suites the game pretends your are sorting and coordinate various covert operatives. During the course of game play 8 operative groups get unlocked. Each one has a mechanic associated with them which primarily consists of shuffling mechanics such as reordering cards in the stack of bringing up a card that is buried deep in the stack on the top of the stack. It is also possible to make a wrong move and undo some of your previous moves, however on rare occasions that happened cards were not reshuffled drastically and it was very easy to redo moves . While there are attempts to introduce new mechanics the game does not do much with them and there is no onus on the player to use them. They seem like a wasted potential as they can be totally ignored while playing the game.  Overall it is just same old solitaire - I am not sure how much one can improve upon the basic concept.  Overall the game lasted fifteen levels or chapters which I completed in very leisurely  fashion in 5 hours. The goal of the game is to reach level 15 and for each level a player is presented with several different missions with each mission being worth a different amount of XP.  Depending on which missions a player chooses it might take longer or shorter. I ended up choosing missions with the highest XP.  The game story missions end after level 15. After level 15 the game unlocks random challenges, level replay etc.  Overall it is still solitaire, only wrapped up in slick presentation and some story telling elements. If you crave to play some solitaire in between "hardcore gaming" sessions or just want to take it easy for a few hours  then by all means give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Mouse controls are borked on an iMac 18,3 running OS 10.15.7. Double clicking turns out was apparently a normal control. So my first go with the game showed me it was broken: controls were unresponsive where I couldnt move cards and then all the cards would disappear from the game. I couldnt do anything. I've let some time pass, let some updates propagate and tried to play it again. The game no longer launches on my Mac. The icon appears in the dock but right clicking on the icon shows that its "Not Responding". Sophos Home Premium alerts me that is unresponsive too. I uninstalled and reinstalled to double check -and yep-  game no longer opens. App still appears in the dock but nothing related to the game shows on screen. Cannot recommend this game from my experience but screenshots and videos of the game look nice though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely the most impressive version of Solitaire I've ever played. The production value is excellent, and the music is sufficiently suspenseful such that I feel like playing a round is of higher stakes than it actually is, considering I can restart a round whenever I want. Gameplay and graphics are clean.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game if you have a few hours to kill and want to play a fun, easy card game. I love the care and polish that went into it, very easy to play, great soundtrack. Fun story and acting. There is a variety of powers (or teams) you get as you level up that keeps it interesting. That said, it misses on a few counts for me. Before each mission you get an intriguing description of the mission that is well written and draws you in, but the game does not incorporate the description into the game play in any way. Feels like a let down. The game also isn't hard enough. I never got stuck or had to redo a level. As a physical card player, that is a key part of games like solitaire, so I missed that challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: This has got to be one of the sleekest, most polished-looking & sounding solitaire games ever made, and I will die on that hill.Gameplay is what you'd expect, where the suit special abilities add that spice you're looking for. The extra mode Countdown is also a pretty refreshing take, where the energy of the soundtrack really comes into it's own world, keeping you on the edge of your seat trying to instead use the powers every chance you get.The story itself is a little meh? I feel like you should go into this game with a sense of imagination, where the card & mission descriptions conjure up the espionage the store page implies.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely well presented and interesting take on Solitaire. Who would have though upping the intensity of the music on Solitaire when you place that first Jack would feel so good.  It's nearly as a exciting as those "Cracking the Cryptic" videos on youtube.I tend to try and play the game by stacking face cards on their own stack and not using them for the developers intended purpose. But I'm sure there will be a vanilla mode added at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: There is something peculiarly satisfying about TSC - almost like the relief of untangling a bunch of interwoven yarn. Cleaning the board and arranging the crews can be challenging, confusing and stressful. But ultimately, there always seems to be a solution and it's usually a satisfying one.A specific shout out for the presentation. It is clean, smooth and extremely tactile. The colour schemes which unlock as you progress are also quite nice and keep the aesthetic feeling refreshed as time goes on.Is it "solitaire"? Probably not, but I think it plays on the game quite well and turns it into quite an interesting prospect with the various crews and underlying story. It fits.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: You could describe this as an interesting series light puzzles to solve, as you will win every hand of this game you play, it is just a question of how efficiently you do that rather than if you will succeed or not... at least initially.The more teams you unlock the more fun the puzzle becomes and previous teams that didn't make a great deal of sense start to become very handy tools to "pick the lock" of your current spread of cards.All and all, sweet, light, and beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Solitaire spiced up with some nice art, and some interesting "powers" to give you different tools for solving potentially unsolvable situations, then you'll probably enjoy this. You'll likely tear through the storyline pretty quickly, but it's an enjoyable way to spend a day or two. And at the fairly reasonable price point, this is a nice addition to your library.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: It's solitaire with some minor gameplay twists. What's not to like? If the answer is "solitaire", well, might be wise to look the other way. Otherwise, come right in.What The Solitaire Conspiracy absolutely nails is presentation. It's slick, it's stylish, there are customizable colour schemes, the character art is nothing short of gorgeous, and so on. The story and the setting were both gripping enough to make me beat the game in one go. I believe the overall experience would be considerably more satisfying if some agency was provided in the finale, but, well, I guess things are fine as they are.Overall, this was a pleasant way to top off my evening. Good stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: The FMV direction of this game is phenomenal - the downfall of most FMV games is the ability to blend the footage into the game well, and this game allowed for a perfect framework for that storytelling device. The performances were adequate - I felt as though a little more time could have been spent smoothing out some of the rough edges of both actors, especially in more heightened emotional scenes, however they were both still delivering great performances. (Greg Miller has a lot of potential to hold more star vehicle roles in the future, and this was also a wonderful showcase of Inel Tomlinson's work - always impeccable.) Music, phenomenal. Writing, impeccable. Art direction, gorgeous. The concept sounds like a stretch and yet, it's brilliant. Not perfect, but phenomenal. Buy! Now!
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: So, a friend of mine bought this on release and I watched him play it (including up to streamer spoiler town) and it made me want to play it. So I did. I beat it. I think it marries a very simple solitaire with a really fantastic premise and story. I think you guys did a great job, and I'll go back and play more in the other modes later.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Hats off the the dev team this is a very fun take on Solitaire! I play basic solitaire a lot when I am travelling, and I really hope that this comes to mobile or switch in the future. The acting is well done and the writing doesn't take its self too seriously while adding in some interesting mechanics to time tested game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a big fan of real-life card games, but virtual card games always catch my eye, and The Solitaire Conspiracy is one of the best. The campaign last a couple hours or so and gives you the basics for Countdown, which seems to be the aspect of the game that keeps on giving once you're finished with the core plot. A beautiful twist on classic solitaire that doesn't overstay its welcome, The Solitaire Conspiracy is a must-play.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: The Solitaire Conspiracy is another Mike Bithell classic! Simple enough to get into, and yet strategic in a way that is like solving a great puzzle, if that puzzle involved infiltration and spy networks. The main campaign does a great job of introducing the concepts and the gameplay adds enough measure of COOL into the familiar solitaire formula that it's like returning to a cozy bit of nostalgia with sunglasses on and bazooka in hand. It just makes solitaire slick and interesting in a way that I have never seen before. Great work from the whole team on creating a game that you can unwind with while still challenging your card-based problem solving skills.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: I don't play a lot of indie games but I have played my fair share of solitaire games in my day and I gotta say I love this new story layer as a backdrop to an otherwise ordinary and mundane card game. The crew powers help add a layer of complexity to the card strategy and the game's beautiful aesthetic makes it hard to put down. Also, the writing made me chuckle and it was funny to see Greg Miller in a game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the campaign today and have been dipping into the other modes. Such a good game, providing a really fresh take on a classic! The abilities of the picture cards make the gameplay really engaging, giving you multiple ways to complete a level. Having to avoid some of the cards adds a layer of complexity as well. Countdown mode is an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and anyone who has the achievement for getting to wave 15 is either a hacker or a literal wizard!Great music from Jon Everist adds a level of drama to solitaire that I'm sure every user of Windows 95 thought was lacking! On a related note the music is available on Apple Music (and I'm sure other streaming services) so go download it! Great performance from Greg Miller as Jim Ratio too! I listen to a lot of Kinda Funny content so was worried that might break the immersion a bit but it didn't. Really great job!An absolute steal for £7.99!
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: I mean, it's Solitaire, so if you're fundamentally not into moving cards around and figuring out how to get them into a neat order it probably won't work for you. But if that's even slightly intriguing, WHAT A VERSION. You've got an ultra-slick presentation, an interesting (if slightly cheesy, but hey it's spy stuff) story, and a really fun challenge in figuring out how and when to use the Jack/Queen/King of each suit's super powers to break the regular solitaire rules. Super fun, good price and fantastic art and music to round out the package. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: This game (as you may have guessed) is solitaire with a twist.Gone is your normal rule of red must go on black and vice versa, now cards are 'crew' based. The only rule is the cars must go on a higher card to stack. Should you 'secure' the Ace card, then the face cards of the respective crew activate and each crew carries a distinct mechanic to it (e.g. the first crew scatters the entire pile it is placed on across all the others). This actually forces you to pay attention to what you are doing, are you could place a king face card and end up having to fiddle it around as you having managed to bury a 2 underneath it.There are 3 game modes; Campaign, Skirmish and Countdown (the latter two available upon campaign completion).Campaign is the meat of the game (although if are good at logic puzzles it may only take you a couple of hours). Each 'level' is partitioned with an FMV sequence featuring Greg Miller and Inel Tomlinson to give the narrative, which is really well done and executed by the pair. To pass each level you play a game of Solitaire in order to fill up an XP bar, each "mission" providing various amounts of XP based on number of crews and the combination they are in. Prior to each mission there is also a little bit of flavour text for more narrative.Skirmish mode is free play where you can choose your own variation of cew decks (up to 4) and play a standard game. Countdown is a survival mode where you are playing against the clock, 'securing' cards will net you more time. I have managed about to wave 11 of this mode thus far but there are many people better and you will find yourself getting better with subsequent runs and your mind gets into gear.Graphics - really nice aesthetic. I would say its Casino Royale meets Cyberpunk, Each level pass also gives you a new colour option for the UI which is a nice touch.Soundtrack - Again really nice, but it is also my one gripe I would have liked maybe a few more different tracks for when I'm playing, or perhaps an option to change it (like a more relaxed song or two whilst in Skirmish mode for better repeat playability).Overall, solid game, easily worth the price of admission, and I think the card design could look great as a physical product (hint,hint).
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: - Quick to pick up, but the mechanics really make every game unique and engaging- Slick interface and solid artwork- I enjoyed that many of the card powers could be simultaneously beneficial and harmful. I thought this played well into the character descriptions, and gave the game more depth overall.This is a totally standalone game with no transactions, which I love. I'm looking forward to any future DLC, though, with more characters!
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this Solitaire game for the deep story and lore. Yes, you read that right.The Solitaire Conspiracy is a short, yet somewhat replayable, Cyberpunk solitaire game, the campaign actually has an intriguing story and throughout the missions you discover a rather deep and interesting world of espionage and subterfuge going on. And that is the most compelling part of this game, the world it opens us up to deserves to let us explore it more.The gameplay itself was fairly easy, though that may have been after playing through similar games, such as Shadowhand and Ancient Enemy. There's no time limit during campaign missions and at no point did I get stuck as I would in other Solitaire games, having all the cards face up and the numerous abilities certain cards give helped with that.It felt like the special abilities of some of the cards were rarely needed, it would have been nice to have a little more difficulty and situations which would have required more forethought and planning. I think a puzzle mode, where you have a specific set of cards and goal in mind could be very interesting. The gameplay is rather relaxing, unless you play Countdown, in which you gain time for placing cards in the centre and completing suits. This mode can be super stressful and will be where the replayability comes from, with both a friend and global leaderboards.The lore in the game is very in depth, each picture card represents a character and each character has a description that isn't really utilised elsewhere, I want to find out more about some of these characters and it's a shame there isn't more chance to introduce us to some of these people.Which leaves me wanting more. This game is a great, if short, solitaire game that is very relaxing and fun to play. It has a cool setting, characters, music, it's very stylised and the aesthetic suits the setting and theme of the game. Overall, it took me just over 3 hours to finish the campaign and earn the bonus achievements for the couple of additional modes, there is some replayability there, and I may go back and play some more, but I do feel as though I've beaten the game.If you have any interest in Solitaire games, I would recommend this one. It's only left me wanting more. I hope more games expand the universe and should the game be updated or a sequel released, I'll be here looking to play some more.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly what I want out of a £10 game. For the price of a cinema ticket, it has already given me ~twice the amount of entertainment I get from there (The main campaign took me about 3 hours). As an added bonus, there is a "competitive" mode where you can compete against the clock, and a skirmish mode for just messing about. I can definitely see myself putting in a lot more hours of just random games here and there.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been an absolute delight. The story mode was very fun (albeit a little cheesy) and I couldn't stop until I had finished it. Mechanically, the different crews available to you allow for some incredibly satisfying and smart moves. Highly recommended for any that are a fan of solitaire games, and even if you wouldn't consider yourself a fan, I'd still suggest picking this up.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: It's what you know, solitaire. But what you may not know is that you can exponentially raise the fun with game mechanics carefully designed. Every seed, many more than the usual 4, has a power, it comes with pros and cons and you can master it to do some genious moves.The game and its clean UI guide you in the first levels with a good tutorial that doesn't overstay its welcome and a curated spy-story. Once you beat the game you can freely play missions to find more about the details of the world.There are also two other game modes: Skirmish and Countdown. The first let the user play a game of solitaire with the seeds he likes, while the second is an appreciated marathon of solitaire with a score and a leaderboard at the end.Whatever you want to do, relax and pass time, or compete with a purpose, the game got you covered.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Production value: sky high. The art style, FMV, music, user experience is all phenomenal.Story: Fun and entertaining!Gameplay: If you don't care about solitaire, think of this as a puzzle game. If you care about solitaire, think of this as solitaire on steroids. It's familiar enough that it feels intuitive to pick up the difference in gameplay, but I'm genuinely impressed by the depth of emergent gameplay when the abilities of the various crews are combined.Replay value: Not sure I'd replay the campaign mode, but I already know I'm going to log hundreds of hours in the timed Countdown mode.I got this for free, but I was absolutely ready to pay full price for it, and will definitely do so if (when??) it comes out on mobile.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Gotta say, last time I played solitaire was on Windows XP. For some reason, The Solitaire Conspiracy had me curious. Diving in, I wasn't hooked initially. The FMV stuff is fun, as are the card abilities and worldbuilding elements. To me, this is all icing on the cake. The presentation is where the game shines brightest! Thanks to how smoothly everything melds together, flow-state inducer this game is!
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic, very stylish, slick and high quality and quickly addictive. I've not played Solitaire since my XP days (and not sure I even remembered how to play), but the tutorial does a great job of catching you up and getting familiar with the new mechanics with confidence. Already sunk a couple of hours into this and look forward to many more.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun take on the solitaire style of game with the Bithell and crew quality level.  I really enjoyed the mix of mechanics that made each match fresh, loved the art direction and specially the sound design. Whenever the sound would start to get intense because I was getting close to complete the table felt great. Short, sweet and polished. I will probably come back to complete all the achievements and check the other modes. For a world with more short well done games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short game! It does what it has really well, which is some cool takes on solitaire. You can keep playing past the campaign via a time-based mode and a standard one (so pretty much the replayability of normal solitaire). It's good! The modification it has to solitaire is pretttty cool.Now as for my own personal stuff: I'm slightly a solitaire addict (as of recent) so this was pretty perfectly timed, honestly. Also the atmosphere and world of the game is VERY cool to me, specific certain AI involved factions and certain TWA/Subsurface Circular references. I'm a sucker for robots and AIs and the like. Also I love a good asynchronous leaderboard sort of multiplayer, so naturally I had to strive for top 10 in the time-based mode! Basically this is pretty much as quality as ever and I'm glad to have got it :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: I am by no means at all a Solitaire expert, unless you class someone who spends times in lectures playing solitaire an expert, but this game is stupidly fun if you like Solitaire. Yeah it will have a fair few things that you are not used to compared to traditional solitaire but that's what makes it fun. It will take a while to get used to (I'm still not quite there yet) but it still doesn't detract from the fun. Having a story intertwined with a classic card game is something that I love. Greg Miller is fantastic in it and the UI/art style is beautiful.  Bithell Games has done an amazing job.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has no interest in solitaire I was sceptical going in... This game is amazing, the gameplay it's self is very compelling and the different special abilities of the spy squads adds a tactical layer beyond sorting cards. The art style and UI are outstanding and the level of detail it truly something to behold. The soundtrack is doing so much work while you play missions really giving the feeling of urgency and excitement.  The fmv cut scenes are a great bit of nostalgia for me bringing back memories of C&C games I played as a kid.This game delivered on its promise 110% and has made me a solitaire fan.  5* 10/10 game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: The combination of Mike Bithell, Greg Miller and Solitaire was too good of a prospect to pass up. I wasn't disappointed. Plays more like Freecell than standard Klondike solitaire; if this is an established version of Solitaire I've never played it before. And enjoyable experience and a well acted set of FMV cutscenes too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: The Solitaire Conspiracy is the new weird thing from Mike Bithell, which combines Solitaire with Team Abilities and an espionage Plot into a audio, visually and gameplaywise impressive whole.After a knock on your Head you find yourself in a Room, with only one Display in front of you. There you are greeted by Jim Ratio (Played by Greg Miller) who tells you that you were on a List of Candidates for the Spy Agency "Protego", which coincidentally needs your help. As they are currently locked out of their System after an attack on their System and only you have access to the C.A.R.D.S. System, which makes you the only one who can currently take it on with a Threat called Solitaire, who has a massive Network of Operations going. From that starting point on you climb your way through 15 XP-Levels until you gain full access to the System. On that way there are twists but not a WHOLE lot is happening within the 2.5 Hrs. long main story.Well, it's Solitaire. An all-time Classic. You have mixed stacks of Cards in front of you and have to sort them together into 4 Slots to win the game. But this is not Solitaire by the Classic Klondike Ruleset. You don't have to pay attention to colors or that the numbers chain together. You only have to make sure that the Number on your card is lower than where you want to put it. There are also Abilities to take into consideration. These 8 Crews come each with a Special Ability, ranging from "Sorting a Stack" to "Pulling the next required Card" to straight up "Blowing up a Stack and placing the cards around on the other stacks". All that combined makes this for a fairly easy Solitaire Experience, where one's Goal goes from "Just making it through." to "Doing it in the lowest possible amount of turns." If you wish to challenge yourself there is also the Unlockable Countdown Mode, a Survival Mode of sorts where you have to sort as quickly as possible before time runs out.For a game as simple as this, the Visuals are very much impressive enough. Both the Table and the Cards are visually pleasing, as are the Character-Arts for the different Teams. Along the Campaign you also unlock Visual Styles, all of which are pleasing in their own way so there should be one, which is right for you.The Soundtrack is good to keep you entertained as you plan your next move. None of the tracks were noticeable duds. A noticeable Element: The closer you get towards the goal of a Match, the more the music starts pounding and you start to notice that you are nodding to the beats or how you are really getting into it when the music turns up the tension.As this Bithell Short, the Solitaire Conspiracy is a good and fairly priced title to enjoy during an afternoon and beyond, if you wish to challenge yourself. It looks good, the soundtrack keeps you pumping and even with all the variations it's still Solitaire, a game you can always go back to. Very much recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Never ever ever ever have seen such production quality for a solitaire game. Usually within this genre, I would describe the design as a bit naive (nothing's wrong with that). That's basically is what made me to purchase this game. Within the game I was surprised to see that story is told through actual video footage, which again is rare for video game format. Another example how serious game developers have been about production value. Acting though a times gave opposite effect than intended. Criminal masterminds are not scary, because they put on their "angry voice" and "angry face". That behaviour is reserved for teens.Overall I recommend, but it took me only 2,5 hours to complete and get all achievements for this game, so maybe you want to wait for a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: Really makes you  like Greg Miller.Seriously, though, Microsoft, if you're reading this, get rid of your Solitaire and replace it with this.Playing this game feels like running around as an 8-year-old playing spies, where any random household object stands in for any tech or tool you might need. It's a popcorn spy story abstracted through C.A.R.D.S., where almost all the action happens in your head as you read the intro text and then imagine the scene through your own card play. (Except you don't have to imagine your own theme music, because the soundtrack is incredible.) I'm sure there's more surprises waiting for me but so far I love it. It's just fun, in every sense of the word.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: The Solitaire Conspiracy is so good, the visuals are so so slick, the soundtrack is fantastic and I'm going to download it on spotify immediately! the game play is simple enough that to pick up fast but there is definitely some depth to getting good. I've not had a lot of time to throw into it yet but I've loved every second and I can already tell I'm going to play this game casually forever!
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: First, I must say I'm not into card games. I usually find them boring. But in this case... add a beautiful futuristic UI, great music that builds up as you get closer to stack all cards, powers that shuffle cards in different ways and a spy story between missions... and I'm hooked.I just finished the story in almost four hours. Yup, it's short but entertaining, nice performances with Greg Miller and Inel Tomlinson, a couple of twists... and it helps you get the gist of the game and the different crews and their powers. And after that you can continue playing the campaign or try other game modes. I was interested just in the story, but as I said, I'm hooked and I will probably come back from time to time for a quick round.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a really fun solitaire game. The story is good, although you don't feel all too involved because of the discrepancy between the "action" and the card game you're actually playing. But the gameplay is smooth, the visuals are a joy to look at, and the music adds to a solid atmosphere. Finished the story mode in just under three hours, but will be returning to this as my solitaire game of choice.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review: We need your help, Spymaster. Join a world of near-future spies and take on a supervillain in this supercharged take on classic Solitaire. Precision engineered for replayable espionage action.
_childDocuments_.name: The Solitaire Conspiracy

_childDocuments_.review:
The Demon King has set his sights on Muscle Island, a hitherto heavenly and peaceful place where life was good. The dark figure has installed his army there and persecutes the population with the help of his generals.
Wasting their last coins in taverns, the mercenaries of the dreaded Golden Force take advantage of their last vacation moments when they receive a new contract: to defeat this evil new ruler and reclaim the mountain of gold in his possession.
When there is gold and the promise of a good fight, you can count on the Golden Force to save your loaves!

name: Botany Manor
detailed_description: Join Our Discord Botanical Friends About the Game Botany Manor is a first-person puzzle game set in a Victorian English manor. It's 1890, and you play as botanist Arabella Greene, who is working to finish her botanical research book 'Forgotten Flora'. Explore a complete historical English manor and its grounds, researching how to grow rare plant specimens from seed. There are many rooms and gardens to discover, all set inside a beautiful countryside surrounding. The manor is filled with mysterious clues for you to discover, including books, posters, letters and fascinating Victorian contraptions. The plants you grow are fantastical, but still inspired by real phenomena in nature, so some of them require you to think outside the box. Using what's available to you in the manor, you must create the ideal conditions for each plant. Room by room, you learn more about the life and career of Arabella, and the challenges she faced as a woman navigating her scientific career. Botany Manor offers a relaxing and peaceful environment, feel free to stop and smell the roses.

_childDocuments_.review: A rather short playthrough (I finished the game and all its achievements in less than 3 hours) but it's a rather nice afternoon of peaceful gaming time. Reminds me of Strange Horticulture, but with fewer plants and no horror elements at all.The puzzles are rather easy, made even simpler by the fact that there aren't any wrong clues or red herrings anywhere -- every clue is there for a reason, and you just have to figure out what plant it goes with. Each plant has quite a different story/theme about it, so it isn't all that hard to match them up. But I did enjoy the time I spent exploring the manor finding the clues, reading the letters, and putting everything together to collect some cool plants.If I had one wish, I'd want to be able to look at the clues I've collected from the UI without having to walk all the way back to where they were in the world to look at them again. The book had a record of what clues I'd collected, but this was purely the name of the clue and where I found it, without actually having any of the information. It would be nice to have a folder to pick up all the letters and snippets I find scattered around so I can look at them all again in one place.

_childDocuments_.review: Botany Manor is a lovely little game. But it really is little. It took me around 3 hours to 100% it minus a few achievements for solving puzzles wrong in humourous ways, and I was by no means rushing. For more context, the demo is 20% of the game. For the very short play time and little-to-no replay value, I do think the £22.50 standard price is a bit steep. Chants of Sennaar is £5 cheaper and gave me 3x as much play time, if we're looking at pure price-to-play-time metrics of course.With all that said, what little time I had with the world of Botany Manor was a truly wonderful experience. The game is one of those ones where its value doesn't come from any particular component, but instead how all those components come together. The graphics and art are simple, the story/world building is reasonably shallow, and the puzzles are well designed but unlikely to pose much of a challenge to anyone who's ever played a puzzle game before...But experiencing all those things *together* really makes Botany Manor greater than the sum of its parts. The graphics aren't breaking any boundaries, but the visuals along with the soundscape *do* excellently capture the mood of a quaint summer's afternoon at a grand countryside mansion. The occasional newspaper clippings and letters dotted about also help present information and context for the player character that the conclusion of the game has a nice emotional punch to it. And together those things gave me enough motivation to want to work out how grow my lovely puzzling plants beyond just solving puzzles for the sake of it.So I would really recommend this to a prospective buyer only if *the whole package* appeals to you. If you're here entirely for brainteasers and intend to plough through without any particular care for the environment the game is set in then this probably isn't for you.Personally, I loved it. Although I do think it should be cheaper or, preferably, longer.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me begin by saying thank you to the devs who kindly included a motion sickness toggle to their game. It was a relief after launching and seeing it was played entirely in first person to find this pleasant surprise as someone who has recently found themselves unable to play many games due to severe motion sickness.On the game itself, despite not being the most realistic graphics, I was thoroughly transported into the environment of the game. Its beauty and tranquillity was a welcome calm and even the most "stressful" of puzzles were eased with the sound of the calm music. Well executed environmental sounds including changes to sounds for footsteps on different surfaces added to the immersion.I enjoyed finding little pieces of lore and history, deciphering the story behind the protagonist, making the games ending all the more meaningful, knowing how much it meant, how much the protagonist had to go through to reach that point in her life.My only downside throughout the entire game was an issue with a puzzle not being solved despite doing the right things, just in the wrong order according to the games coding. But largely the puzzles are fairly simple, but not so simple as to feel unaccomplished when solving them and allocating clues to each flower in the book was a fun little mechanic I thoroughly enjoyed doing, ensuring to have every clue for every flower as a personal goal.This game was truly a gem to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of a neutral review since it has very good bones, but it definitely needed more. It really follows in the footsteps of games like "The Unfinished Swan" and "What Remains of Edith Finch" but it misses the mark when it comes to what made those games so satisfying to finish.I think the main issue is that it is basically a series of escape rooms. A lot of the "things" used to solve one puzzle would never be used again, which makes sense as it would mess up the hint system. But that hinders the number of possible puzzles this game could have. I imagine trying to keep each plant puzzle limited to specific areas was a lot of work for the designers as well as the art team. I don't have a huge problem with needing to constantly double back and re-read things. But there were definitely times where I walked through a room and was unable to interact with something because it wasn't intractable until the right puzzle started which meant that I didn't bother looking at it again. I don't think this was a good idea and I don't it's a problem to have too many proofs/evidence available in the book. It adds to the difficulty in a way that's not obtrusive. All that aside, I don't want the team to make a different game. I really did like this style of puzzle, but I think a game like this (where you can't reuse things from one puzzle to the next) would really benefit from repeatable side-games that don't require complex puzzle design and lean more into the "you're a botanist" angle of the game. Experiences where the outcomes would be unique to each player and an engaging/repeatable activity. For example: - designing and creating your own botanical garden and watching how plants react to different factors- a room dedicated to cross-breeding plants to get different visual varieties (perhaps even being able to even recreate the famous "too much purple" virus reaction)- creating tinctures or medicinal products from the various plantsThis would require creating a few new mechanics, but they would be ones that have a large replay value. Interspersed as a fun activity between the various escape room puzzles would give the player more time to just be inside the experience. Which I think is what most people here want and is a testament to the excellent design of the environment and audio/music by the team.Overall a great start for what I hope becomes a larger series by the team.

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolutely slept on game. This was such a nice and relaxing experience that only gets better the longer I think on it. For me, personally, it made me feel similarly to how Unpacking made me feel. In Botany Manor you're given a seed and some clues laying around and you must figure out how to make the seed grow and flower, all the while picking up clues about yourself and your life as well. A beautiful story that can completely pass you by if you choose not to engage with it. A game that simply asks you to pay attention. The visual style is to die for, the music is so beautiful, and the gameplay is engaging yet relaxing; what more could you ask for? I absolutely recommend this game, no matter the price tag. I personally think $25 is the perfect price for the game, especially after playing it.Small nitpicks (good and bad): Just some final notes I didn't want in the main review part.There was a single puzzle at the end with a  and I found that to be a randomly difficult puzzle. Idk maybe I just wasn't paying enough attention but there weren't any notes saying that the crank was missing or where it should go so I had to look that one up. Maybe if it's placement was added to a note that would help?Also the audio for the fireplaces is really jarring - if the radius for the sound FX was larger I think it would really help with immersion.ALSO OMG the track for running to the gate to check for the mail is so amazing and it always made me so excited to run all the way to the gate! And the slight change to it when you're going to  was absolutely gorgeous! I adored the ost so much! I can't wait for what y'all do next! c:

_childDocuments_.review: Botany Manor is a short, light experience.  It's colorful and possessing of a certain peaceful charm.  The puzzles are not challenging, and often basically amount to making sure you've clicked on the clues and then followed instructions.  Progression is highly linear (if somewhat contrived), and the puzzles are very self-contained.  There's a bit of story wafting along in the background as you progress through the pleasant environments.  It took me about 3 hours to play through, including a few minutes to go back and collect the last missing achievements.  While there may not be much "game" here, in terms of length or complexity, it's a pleasant place to be for a little while.

It's a lot lighter than Strange Horticulture's storyline full of demons and murder and cults, instead tackling a woman who is looking to break into the sciences in a British manor from several centuries ago before such a thing existed. _childDocuments_.review: Botany Manor is a charming yet short game about researching and growing plants, and each plant is grown by solving a series of puzzles based on information you learn about them.  This is a game that I love dearly and enjoyed playing a lot, but there were a few things that I think should be changed.  You play as a woman trying to publish her own botany book.  Botany Manor is where she researches all her plants, and every section is dedicated to a new series of plants for her to grow.  Along the way, you read small notes given to her from family and friends detailing about the life they've all lived, her achievements in her field of expertise, and about the hardships she has faced along the way.    With every new location you unlock more information both about the plants she has seen along the way and tidbits about her life, and the Herbarium you carry gets updated with every new bit of info you unlock.  It is a very linear storyline, so there is no way to get lost and unlocking new areas is the only way to move forwards.  There isn't anything hidden away, so don't feel like you have to look at every nook and cranny.Every plant that you research throughout the game is found and grown based on a series of notes and clues you gather through exploration, with each chapter giving you a set of plants.  Every plant has clues you have to put with it so you know the correct growing instructions, with some plants being harder to figure out than others.  This is part of where my trouble with this game lies.  As much as I loved the notes and being given clues about how to grow the plants, the Herbarium only updates with the location of the notes, not with the notes themselves.  This makes things incredibly difficult when trying to go back to locations to figure out exactly which notes you need, and which go to something else.  I can remember a fair amount of information, but sometimes the clues are given in a riddle, and with as many notes as we are given while we play, it is hard to keep track of what note is where.  While it's not a terrible nuisance to travel back to a location to read notes, there is only so much backtracking that can be done when going only one speed throughout the game.  Being able to pull up the notes through the book itself would be super helpful for those of us that lose track of where the notes are and to prevent some of the backtracking.  The game is founded on the ability to solve puzzles regarding the growth of each plant, which I found enjoyable.  The information required for each was readily available and easy to find, so solving most of the puzzles was decently easy to solve.  Others were not so easy and required a lot more preparation and research to solve.  However, I did not find the puzzles to be so difficult they couldn't be solved, which I appreciated.  It's just difficult enough to keep the game interesting, but not frustrating.  Those looking for a challenge unfortunately wouldn't find that in this game.The music for this game is something I found soothing with pauses occasionally interspersed into it to break up the monotony.  There are little noises that happen when you read an important note or look at something relevant to a puzzle, which made it so much easier to determine what was just lore or something that could help solve a puzzle.  The short little song that played whenever a flower bloomed was cute as well, and gave a sense of success by hearing it.  The achievements weren't hard to get and I appreciated the diversity in difficulty.  Of course, there were the achievements you got by following the story, but there were a few that you could gather by doing something incorrectly or just enjoying the scenery.  As an achievement hunter, this was perfect for me and I enjoyed finding the hidden achievements a lot.Overall, I would recommend playing this game.  There isn't a whole lot of replayability, but I did enjoy the designs of the flowers a lot and the layout of the manor.  This place would be a dream to actually have in real life.  The story was worth playing through, and brought up a lot of real-life scenarios plants could be found in and endangered in.  I do wish the game had the notes added in for easier gameplay, but I do think this game is very worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: It'd be unfair to compare my experience with this game with what I thought it would be, what I hoped it would be. Even more unfair would be to try to draw comparisons with recent titans like Outer Wilds or Return of the Obra Dinn. Admittedly though, with the mechanics and visual design and innovative rock-solid concept that Botany Manor initially presents, I find the unrealized  p o t e n t i a l  that this game has to be almost tragic. It's easy to see this game with the exact same mechanics and environmental interactions, taking a few cues from some other beloved titles, and positioning itself as a GOTY contender with staying power. Only worse than the potential this game has in my imagination are the frequent ways the game flirts and even demonstrates flashes of first-person puzzle brilliance, only to cut away in favor of a far more linear, miserly dispensed experience. First the good. Because there's lots of it here. I 'recommend' this because of its solid foundation, and I know there's a right audience for titles like this.  Like you might assume or glean from the trailer and/or already published reviews, you're needing to grow different species of flora, using the environment for clues as to how to meet each plants' particular needs to grow. Players will read clues from the items scattered around, all examined by player interaction, in order to determine where to plop down your seeded pot to successfully get it to bloom and tick it off your list. Each plant to grow can be thought of its own very (very) self-contained puzzle, with many (many) of the clues taking the form of written or drawn works - notes, letters, charts, advertisements etc that the player will pick up, need to remember the details of, and at times employ some genuine observational or lateral-thinking skills to put together to make progress. There are elements of great puzzle/problem design in no shortage here. If I were to try to explain to a brand newcomer why I love games like this as a genre, I'd probably suggest this game as one of the *very first* that they should check out.   I have to give a special shout to the vibrant and colorful environments and the subtle narrative pieces that the player is cleverly routed to through gameplay, giving what (I think) is a worthwhile story to tell. As for my critiques:I wouldn't want to play backseat dev or give too many spoilers in giving all my thoughts, but I can say that the experience is meticulously curated, though the manor is fully explorable, there is almost no 'openness' to the proceedings. What do I mean? As you progress, you open up new areas of the manor, but you are almost exclusively working within newly-accessed areas. Almost is there a reason to truly backtrack, not for clues, not for elements needed to grow your plants, not for anything. I remember two decent examples of a callback given via clue that sends a player back to where they were once to access a new area, but with both in isolation and with garishly obvious clues, you're funneled that way and denied your "aha" moment. For me the graver sin this game commits that I really didn't think it had to, was the way progress is compartmentalized - you never have more than 4 (3 real) plants to be hunting for clues how to grow at once. You have a book that is rigidly divided into chapters, each corresponding with new areas of the manor to access; you're literally just  arbitrarily mailed a literal key to new rooms after (almost) each completed mini to-plant list - which you have to leave the main manor and waddle all the way to the gatehouse to retrieve each time.  You aren't  even allowed to see the silhouettes of  plants in the pages of chapters ahead; they are literally blank while you're working on the current chapter. Not that it would matter if you were looking for an open experience because after the first few milestones, you know that all new plants with all their clues are going to be neatly contained within the boundaries of the newly-accessible areas. It's better to think of the game as 4 very, very miniature and pared-down open experiences, but what's worse is that even *within* new sections, plants and their clues are pretty tightly grouped locationally with a few very obviously intentional exceptions. When I talk about clever puzzle/problem design, I mean that almost none of it comes from locating clues or needing to know to which of your 3-4 open plants it refers, which is one of the many missed opportunities. The experience as a whole was still enjoyable, but dispensed in such small easy chunks that some of the interesting design is lost. I say this so that future players know what kind of experience they'd get. The only other fair critique I think there is to level is the baffling inclusion of a ROTOD-like (or Chants of Sennar) system where after you've seen a clue, you can assign it to the right plant out of your 3-4 open plants in your book. For example, if you see a taxonomy chart (not a spoiler because there is no such clue) that is a hint at one of the plants, you can indicate that 'taxonomy chart' is a clue to a specific plant where once you get them all for a plant, it locks in. This mechanic is completely pointless. 1. As I said before, it is so often so obvious which clue goes to which plant, that it's not like it's much a puzzle, with almost no way to mess it up or need to think or guess. 2. there is no way from the book interface to actually *view* the actual clue you're pinning to a plant, so it's not like it's useful for future reference/note-keeping. 3. For those aforementioned reasons this 'mechanic' unlikely to of any real help in deduction because you're unlikely to need it. 4. That I can tell, properly assigning clues is not a requirement as you can simply synthesize them in your mind and apply them to plant the plant and make progress. The benefit of this mechanic's inclusion completely escapes me. Finally, there are a few QOL things that the devs could have included - I already mentioned the addition of a player's ability to take notes or photos of clues, instead of needing to physically travel to them every time they need to refer to the contents. Another possible suggestion is an augment to the map system for such a labyrinthine environment. The one that's there now is only adequate because of how little backtracking is needed, but some easy inclusions would be an indicator of what room you're in something resembling a HUD. None of my other critiques here are fair or belong here as they're largely in the 'what could have been' or spoiler categories. Though, in short, I can say that the first tutorial plant, which I'd later find *is one of the only plants that* affects the environment in a substantial way, seemed to hint at the idea that you'd need to plant that plant again in order to make progress. This is also suggested by the different plant benches that each give you access to all of your previous seeds. Unless there's a major coup in the final half of the final chapter, I can say that you only ever need to plant each species once to tick the box, then you can forget about it forever. This was perhaps my biggest let-down of all. Finally, I do like the idea of readable objects that can be picked up by the player, but there is almost no observation of the environment necessary as all the information is contained neatly in the interactables. Another missed opportunity to cleverly use diagetic visual conveyances to inform the player. I know I gave a lot of critique here, but I am not ambivalent about recommending this game. It was an enjoyable experience, and I know that people who like solving mini-puzzles one or a few at a time would love this title, though people who like complex interconnected mind-vanias with backtracking and longitudinal and ongoing puzzle solving will be left potentially disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Botany Manor is a gorgeous little puzzle game about cultivating flowers that's perfect for getting lost in for an afternoon.Sound, general aesthetic, map, and puzzle design are all terrific.It's the sort of game that I wish I could recommend turning over to a kid for days of innocent flights of fantasy within imaginary gardens.I'm uncertain about making that recommendation though. For all its wonderful charm and delightful puzzles, Botany Manor showcases a darker theme in the background that makes direct commentary about women's rights and equality.These are important subjects that ought to and need to be articulated, but I'm uncomfortable about their injection into a game that is in every other way suitable for young children without reservation.This is a puzzle game where reading and comprehending most of, if not all of the interactable game objects(letters, journals, posters, etc..) is necessary to progress. The story of the main character Arabella Greene's mistreatment by male botany professionals is told through game objects in the same way as the clues needed to figure out how to progress the game. Arabella's story is explicitly about misogynistic professional cruelty against women and her specifically. The game introduces these story elements obliquely at first. As you progress more and more parts of the picture come together. Eventually the game leads the player along to the literal conclusion with its final letter, writing, "I look forward to visiting the school and meeting the talented students you have taken under your wing. Let's hope they carry on our fight."; a clear call to action not just for the fictional students, but for/to the player themselves to carry on this fight.There is nothing inherently wrong with that call to action, but it is a message of activism playing out in what is otherwise a game meant to engage flights of fantasy. I write this review only to prompt parents to consider the themes that the game will present before purchasing it for young children. To everyone else, this game is great, buy it, play it, lose yourself for an afternoon. Maybe do some introspection about historical inequality. Or don't. This game is worth playing either way.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is not particularly complicated or compelling. The puzzles aren't particularly hard. Even if you stop to smell the roses it's only about four hours long.Why then have I not stopped shaking my monitor asking for more? It's a little slice of tranquility and an oeuvre of beautiful art direction floating on a lily pad in the lazy afternoon sun. It's taking a sip of cold lemonade in the shade of a tree listening to the deafening hot summer silence.What's more, from the website I think that Balloon Studios is a one-woman show? A four hour game with a fresh concept that bites off exactly as much as it can chew and then swallows? And the mouthful is *this* big and *this* delicious? We are certainly spoiled for choice and I get that not everybody has the $25 in disposable income, but come on.I'd pay $60 if it signals the desire for Botany Manor 2. More plants, more gardens to explore, and more complicated puzzles but all with the same vibe? Easily. If you're on the fence and $25 is no object, open the front gate, ring the bell, and stay a while. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a beautiful game, the music and lighting are stunning. The mechanics are easy to follow. Unfortunately though it just doesn't have any further play-ability once finishing the game. On top of this as someone with a mental disability it was hard to follow clues as they were all over the place and not very linear. I found myself having to look up clues in order to figure out which clue was meant for what plant as sometimes you'd get multiple seeds and puzzles at once. If you're someone who enjoys a challenge and is able to read between the lines this game is definitely suited for you. For someone like me who thought I'd be having a fun little puzzle game that wasn't going to frustrate me to no end, I'd look else where. _childDocuments_.review: I remember back in the black and white days of the late 1800s, it was really difficult to become a botanist, but I'm so glad that the wonder devs at Balloon Studios, took on my great granny Arabella's struggle and triumph in the world of botany, and colourised her journey. BOOOO to roughmen that told her that she couldn't be a botanist because she didn't have a peepee. I think this was very rude of them, as she brute forced so many plants into blooming that those MEN couldn't even fathom. GGs Great Granny Ara Ara~! Art style and puzzles were very good and different for each plant, so there didn't feel like there was any sense of repetitiveness! My fave place was my little cave, because I could live my best Gollum life. Can't believe Eliza didn't tell us she was in the game, heart broken!
_childDocuments_.name: Botany Manor

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most beautiful puzzle games I've ever played! The graphics wow-ed me from start to finish and the lighting and sound design is phenomenal! _childDocuments_.review: The game is a little on the shorter side but in my mind the environmental storytelling and the simple enough to understand puzzles, along with the beautiful visuals made it well worthwhile. _childDocuments_.name: Botany Manor

_childDocuments_.review: Botany Manor is a beautiful and clever puzzle game about growing mysterious plants that require very special conditions to bloom. Puzzles are mostly medium-easy, but never boring; the hint-collecting system is also helpful in letting you know wether or not you have all the information you need to grow a specific plant, with the only downside being that the hint itself is not recorded, only its nature and location, so you may need to backtrack a bit from time to time. Luckily, the manor isn't THAT big, so that's a minor annoyance. Also, the game is divided into chapters through a simple but effective trick and you almost never have to go back to previous areas of the manor to solve newly found plants.The lore about the protagonist, gained through personal letters and other objects scattered through the manor, is also perfectly fitting (and a bit sad, from time to time).Absolutely recommended, if you're looking for a relaxing puzzle experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Botany Manor

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely, lovely game. It's so well thought out, everything makes sense and works so well together. The location is just perfect, I wish this was a real place and I could stay there with a few friends. So many cozy nooks, the house has so much character and the gardens are just lovely. The puzzles are very clever, I struggled a bit with the tutorial but once I got the hang of how it worked I never once felt like they were asking the impossible. And then there's the little side narrative through book titles, letters, cards and notes. How I love Arabelle Green, and how I feel for her and all women living in male-centric times like that. I haven't finished the game just yet, I 'solved' 10 out of 12 flowers, but I have a feeling our Arabelle will be fine in the end. I sure hope so, she's brilliant.If you're not sure yet, get the demo, it gives a very good idea of what you're in for. If you like cozy games without a hint of time constraint, that make you think and feel smart, this might be the one for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Botany Manor

_childDocuments_.review: Botany Manor is a well crafted thematic puzzle game. Set in a 1500's English Manor with an incredibly impressive garden estate surrounding, you'll make your way through the house and gardens as you discover and grow various garden plants in pursuit of publishing your very own Herbarium. The puzzles are well crafted, contained within chapters to prevent you from discovering any red herrings, and utilize every corner of the estate to solve. The art is vibrant and poppy, the music is soothing and never clashes with your thought process. The experience is short, but it never felt like it was over-staying its welcome. When I reached the end, I was wholeheartedly satisfied with the experience.There is a small sub-plot story behind the front and center puzzle mechanics if you care to pay attention to various letters and notes notes stashed around the map, and although you never meet any of the characters face to face you can definitely feel their presence through these devices.As a fairly seasoned puzzle gamer, I completed the full game in about 2 hours and spent an additional hour hunting down the 9 hidden achievements I had not gotten by the end of the game. I hope to see more from this developer!
_childDocuments_.name: Botany Manor

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game a lot. The puzzles were fun to solve, learning about the protagonist's life was quite interesting, and though it was a fairly short game it didn't feel unfinished or like it was missing anything. It also helped that I myself am interested in plants so I could really put myself into the protagonist's shoes. The graphics had their own unique, colorful style which was nice and honestly kind of refreshing. They added a bit of whimsy to the overall feel and I think that style really meshed well with the laid back, cozy vibe of the story. While I do wish there was a way to look at the clues I'd collected without having to track them down in the garden again if I needed to reread them (especially in the late portion of the game when you find quite a few clues for multiple plants at once), it wasn't overly bothersome to do so since the landscape was so nice to look at as I walked through it. I wouldn't mind playing more games from this developer if they're all this well-crafted.
_childDocuments_.name: Botany Manor

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of folks complaining about the price-to-gameplay duration ratio, which dissuaded me from purchasing for a while despite enjoying the demo very much. Honestly though, i'm so glad i just went for it. This is one of the coziest, most thoughtful logic/detective puzzlers i've played in a while. Super immersive environs, creative storytelling, and a poignant backstory without too much hand-holding throughout. Great job to the devs and thank you for sharing this delightful little charm of a creation with us. I didn't put a lot of hours into this but for the hours I did put in, I enjoyed the quality of the gameplay thoroughly. Very here for these types of clever journeys so clearly made with love. More please.
