_childDocuments_.review: Hands down, one of the best point&click adventure games I ever played. Maybe original STASIS is more gruesome and the atmosphere of hopelessness and horror, more chilling.. Still, Bone Totem excels in character development, world building and is far more streamlined, polished experience. Puzzles are logical, there’s no pixel hunting or any UI getting in your way. My only gripe - low budget jank is still here. I guess nothing especially annoying, it’s overall impressive work for such a small developer. Also, if that particularly annoys You, there’s A LOT of talking. Sometimes, a bit too much in my opinion… in the other hand, ALL characters are likeable so I can really forgive that small detail. If original STASIS is 8/10 for me… BONE TOTEM gets solid 9/10. You should play both, if you enjoy old-school point&click adventure games.

_childDocuments_.review: Point’n’click and sci-fi and body horror! Oh, my! Plunge into (literal) depth of darkness and gore with the next game in STASIS universe.Mac and Charlie (and their creepy robo-bear toy Moses) traverse the ocean surface making a buck picking up and disposing of salvage. While, arguably, all abandoned structures on the dark waters have a degree of ghoulishness to them, their latest discovery – a rusty oil rig – has it off the charts. Mac isn’t convinced, but Charlie is sure that they are in dire need of whatever money this could bring them, so Mac lets her persuade him to explore the rig. Little do they know it belongs to Cayne Corporation. Oh no! Well, if you played original STASIS (which you technically don’t have to, but it definitely helps) you know what happens when Cayne Corp. is involved. If you don’t know, let me throw some words at you – horrific monsters, gruesome deaths, even more gruesome not-quite-deaths, gigantic functioning body parts that can kill you, terrifying biogenetic experiments, something that’s called “human soup” and gore upon gore upon gore. There. I know I just sold you on this game.Another reason (besides tons of gore, let’s be honest) why you might be interested in Bone Totem is that the narration has surpassed even the brilliance of the first STASIS. As someone who is generally put off by purple prose, I’m astounded with this game’s ability to use three quarters worth of Thesaurus’ synonyms for anything horror-related and still not end up this showy example of writing, where your eyes glaze over by the middle of, stuffed with metaphors and allegories, sentences. How they managed to pull it off is beyond me, but they did and, just like the first game, Bone Totem turned out to be the one for the readers. Abundant (and superb!) descriptions of numerous details on every screen, wonderfully twisted plot and multidimensional characters are a testament to that. Sure, you can ignore all that entirely and be there purely for the visuals and gameplay, but you’ll be doing yourself a disservice. In the end, we all can use a reminder of cool, obscure SAT words, so we can show off in the next conversation and promptly forget them right after.Gameplay is point’n’click with a twist to the inventory system. All three characters (that will all have physically separate journeys) are sharing inventory space with each other, so swapping items between them is an easy breezy deal, and swap those you will, because Mac has an ability to break/bend/dismantle and Charlie – to combine and fix items. Both of those will be used frequently throughout the game to progress forward. Puzzle difficulty is nicely balanced to sit firmly in the middle, and it logically fits into the surrounding environment - an improvement over the first game which had a few extremely unintuitive puzzles that I still remember. Sure, it might be a bit “another locked door”-heavy as far as the tasks go, but not one door is being opened the same way, so it all works in an organic manner, just like the fungi on Deepsea 15.Graphic component is (surprised gasp!) magnificent. Deliciously morbid sci-fi horror worlds unfold in all their isometric glory. Some images that you get to see up close are so grotesque that it’s impossible not to stare at them with your mouth hanging open, not unlike the proverbial trainwreck – hard to look at but also hard not to. Same goes for FMVs that depict not just story-important cutscenes, but a myriad of ways you can kill off the characters (something you’d need to do if you’re interested in achievements) that all end in what I call “blood wall of STASIS” – expression that only makes sense if you allow words “awesome” and “gore” to be in the same sentence.  On occasion, I wished for the environment to be less dark (undoubtedly, a purposeful stylistic choice) just so I can gawk at all this insanity with ease, as edges of all screens and a good main portion of them are always enshrouded in darkness, but that only shows how much in awe I was from the world developers have created. By the way, the main menu screen with its first-person view of the rig made me almost crave for STASIS with a different POV. Hey there, The Brotherhood, I hope you are reading this.With the quality of the game so far, it will be a shock to no one that the soundscape is equally marvelous.  The tracks are very subtle and even subdued, barely there, on the very edge of your hearing and seemingly sample some of the famous works (I can attest to at least one). This is a perfect combo to have places like underwater stations or abandoned laboratories as close to silent as possible, while keeping the player audially engaged. What comes to the forefront here is sound effects, and, boy, do they come, bringing the atmosphere to the level supreme. If in the first STASIS effects were largely banking on growls, howls and screams to make it seem like something horrific was tearing through the hallways,  here, the emphasis is on sorrowful whistling, quiet (but no less disturbing) laughing, and a variety of dying gurgles and rasps that mingle with plethora of metallic, stone and water sound effects and occasional, almost out of place, guitar strums. This is masterful ambience. Voiceover is, of course, equally outstanding. Apart from, perhaps, too many “nnnghs…” and other “character in pain” sounds that, while justified, became overwhelming towards the end, this cast of voice actors did a phenomenal job hitting all the right tones, from robotic to fearful, disenchanted to worrying, creepy to hopeful. A+, developers.Captain Obvious here. With the report that I found STASIS Bone Totem an absolute gem. Fantastic writing with layers upon layers to story and characters, stunning visuals, balanced gameplay and splendid sound make it an all-around winner. As much as I’d like to recommend it to just about any adventure fan (and beyond), I’d have to make concession that this is hardcore sci-fi and body horror. The themes inside are disturbing and macabre, and the darkness of topics explored (narratively and visually) is up there, at the highest rung of the horror ladder. Everything is permeated with gore and is meant to provoke the most “interesting” reactions, so you must be sure you’re OK with that kind of thing before stepping into the game. If you are, however, OK with it, or maybe even a fan of the dark genres - this is something not to miss, for there are very few game experiences out there like The Brotherhood provides us with, and this one is, unsurprisingly, top notch.Now, did you know that human skin with tattoos can be used as paintings? No? Ok, well there you go – happy thoughts to ponder on when you look at someone with a full sleeve. Thank STASIS for that one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a fantastic journey start to end. Filled with an engaging and emotive cast, you find yourself invested quite fast. I really enjoyed the attention to all the detail in the world from lore to set pieces - what truly gorgeous and macabre backgrounds and art. Voice acting really sucks you in - Moses is best bear for sure.Further going back to a classic point and click adventure was the perfect bit of accessibility for me, as I'm currently one handed but I digress - this genre deserves attention and love.Thank you for a wonderful game.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable story, a less than enjoyable game. I think this would have been WAY more entertaining as a graphic novel or short story, the point-and-click elements add needless tedium to the plot beats and intrigue of the story itself. The puzzles are never puzzling but very often aggravating, requiring the player to look at *everything*, and in many cases, look at everything twice. Logic can be thrown out the window in terms of what might make the most sense, the only times I was held up while playing was when I made an incorrect assumption about what should or shouldn't be possible, where I could or couldn't go.The game appears to be riddled with AI art, in the computer image data, in many of the drawings and posters around many of the areas. I've heard that others who've noticed the same and made mention of this in steam discussions have had their threads locked or deleted. I find this really off-putting.These characters are so cliché it's almost hazardous to the mind, there is no real character development in Bone Totem, every person is, with the exception of your 'hacker', the same person at the end as when they started. The aforementioned hacker character does have some growth but is just so obnoxious and grating to listen to after a while that the expansion of their character is really overshadowed.By the end of the game I was sick of plot-via-PDA. It got so tiresome having to halt all momentum to spend 5 minutes reading through twenty entries in a new journal for every 15 minutes of gameplay. I ended up skipping the last several PDAs entirely, for the most part they only contain the threads connecting events together, the main beats are all happening in overworld dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: Stasis: Bone Totem is an ambitious and mostly successful sequel, though it does suffer from some unintuitive puzzles and lack of visual clarity. Like the original game, Bone Totem is a horror adventure game with an emphasis on body horror. The writing and voice acting are an improvement over the first game and there's a lot of interesting lore and character. It's not really scary because you're never in danger. Instead, it's more disturbing as you peel back more of the macabre backstory and discover the grim fate of everyone involved.In Bone Totem, you play as three characters simultaneously and you can freely swap items between them even when they're separated. In addition, two of the characters can either assemble or disassemble items to create new ones. This leads to some interesting puzzle design. However, it also leads to some ambiguity. Progression is often gated by one character obtaining items required for another character to solve a puzzle but this isn't always immediately obvious. Similarly, sometimes a character is gated by a scripted event that won't trigger until another character has reached a certain point. This all leads to unnecessary trial and error when it isn't clear that your character just can't progress.The visuals, while very detailed, are typically shrouded by darkness, This forces you to read descriptions of the environment, which quickly becomes a slog. You don't need to describe the environment to me when I can see it. Just remove the darkness and show me the things you're describing. The darkness doesn't increase the tension because you're never actually in danger (this is an adventure game, not survival horror) so it just becomes annoying. I was getting flashbacks to Doom 3 and Outlast 2.Even though most of this review is complaints, I did enjoy Bone Totem overall. The developers have crafted a twisted dystopian world that's basically cyberpunk horror. I'd love to see more of it and in this case, I mean that literally. There's no need to keep the environments shrouded in darkness 90% of the time. After Stasis, Cayne, Beautiful Desolation and Bone Totem, I think the devs need to step out of their comfort zone and take some more risks. Maybe add some survival horror mechanics like Frictional did with Amnesia: The Bunker. Bone Totem does add some new elements to the formula but not enough to make it stand out.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game and definitely wasn't disappointed - it's my favourite so far of The Brotherhood's work. I liked the new game mechanics a lot (e.g. switching between the three different characters, swapping items back and forth remotely) and the variety with the puzzles. It's always a plus when they aren't all just "pick this thing up and put it over here", which is the case with many point-and-click games. I will say that some of the puzzles are fairly difficult, but as always I would advise people to just be patient and use walkthroughs if you're getting really stuck instead of rage-quitting. The game has a really interesting story with plot twists and a lot of nicely executed horror (the body horror in this game is glorious by the way), so it's worth seeing through to the end. I also cried three times lol. I got way too attached to the characters in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend it to players who like to play adventure games. I wouldn't recommend this game to lovers of horror and stressful situations requiring frequent action. The whole game is based on the passage of 3 characters and their cooperation with each other. The atmosphere is excellent, the story is interesting although incomprehensible at times. The puzzles have 95% logic clues. In about 8 cases I watched the passage in youtube because I didn't understand the clue of the puzzle solution and the time of the hitting the spot exceeded a reasonable limit. The game is linear in terms of puzzle solving. On the other hand, you never know when a particular character has reached the maximum achievable pass within the available items and the solved pass of the other characters. I enjoyed that.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Why is no one talking about this game? How does this only have 500 reviews? 2023 continues to be the best year for horror in recent memory. This game instantly evokes Alien and Dead Space. Industrial Sci fi horror at its finest. With a phenomenal atmosphere, believable characters and fantastic writing. This is a must play for Sci Fi horror fans. I’ll update when I finish the game but I had to give this one a recommendation for the price as I was instantly enthralled.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for some puzzling, and an exploration of the soul and what the concepts of Hope and Belief can mean to people, look no further.Excellent characterisation that pays off in spades is paired with intriguing horror that hooks you very easily, before stepping on the gas pedal into the second half. Has a heartwarming message that I found easy to accept and didn't find particularly preachy.If you're debating the quality of the game, don't sweat it. Fans of Alien, Amnesia, SOMA, System Shock, and other fictional/fantastical horror-puzzle games will enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Not usually a point and click adventure enthusiast but the writing and voice work for Stasis Bone-totem are spellbinding. The rare treat of using visuals and story telling to convey intense horror without the need for jump scares or hiding in closets. One of the best dystopian sci-fi settings in games/books/movies. Definitely worth picking up and learning to be a strong and courageous bear.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Stasis: Bone Totem is the first game in the series I’ve played. The setting and characters pulled me in immediately. Great voice acting. Small cast. Plotwise the story is a well crafted journey. The gameplay feels like a return to old school adventure game this time without the headache.I also appreciated the ability to switch playable characters to solve puzzles in a way I’ve only seen before in Martian Gothic.-my only gripe is the use of what i assume is genAI photos for several art assets.(please don’t do this in the future The Brotherhood)Big recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid adventure game. Beautiful presentation, a unique story, and great voice acting. I also wouldn't consider myself a master of puzzle games, but I was able to complete this game without looking at a guide. The puzzles are logical and straightforward, but still require thought. This game is a sequel, but you do not need to play the previous games. The sci-fi universe presented here is bleak and unique. Humanity has evolved beyond finding the human body sacred, and this informs a lot of the weird technologies you will see in the game. The rich and dense writing in the game along with its excellent presentation really make the world come to life. I give this a very high recommendation to anyone who wants a good story.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good narrative based point and click type game. It's sci fi horror adjacent, and the lore is quite interesting, but the best part of it is definitely the characters, who are very well voice acted and developed. There are 2 other games in the universe released before this that I would definitely now like to check out now that I finished this one. If you are normally bad at puzzles, you don't need to worry with this game - the developer included a guide to the game in the install files and in the guides section in steam to help with all puzzles. I definitely used it when I got stuck however all the puzzles feel logical and the tangible way you interact with them in the world feels good in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. Loved the characters and the story. The fact Mac can tear objects apart and that Charlie can fix them was a nice touch. The puzzles often require you to search for information, but I never felt there were insufficient clues. You just have to find them.The first "Stasis" game left me with mixed feelings, but this was definitely a huge improvement in every way.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Another lovely point and click game by The Brotherhood.The atmosphere is superb. Great graphics, sounds, music and story. The voice-overs fits great.Had a great time with progressing through the story and there is a lot of things that one learns about the characters, events and such when reading the information you find.The puzzles were good.Truly enjoyed it from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: A point and click adventure where you control 3 party individually, each party have their own perk and later will be exploring their own unique area. The game unique mechanic is the QSD which let party swap item between them freely without restriction, allowing some unique puzzle solving situation. Furthermore the game has a ping to show all intractable so no pixel hunting in this game. However some of the puzzle solution is a bit out there and you may require some trial and error and just trying item on every character to see what works. You can't soft lock your game thankfully. If you take on a puzzle you get a question mark where the character will give a hint via dialogue. It won't give you the answer straight but will nudge you in the right direction.It takes place in a bio punk setting and as usual with the Stasis series it explores very uncomfortable and macabre theme. The game leans heavily into horror and your character needing to salvage parts from mutilated bodies are the norm.The game is very humanistic with its approach to the character, including the non-human bear toy, Moses. The writing and voice acting is top notch, I found myself caring deeply about the characters. It can be heavy handed with its symbolism, the child is named Hope after all.Despite the dystopian setting, the massacre and disaster that has happened the characters will try to push on with some hope, this is very much appreciated as the game isn't just doom and gloom. There is excellent character development as they try to grapple with their flaw and despair.Near the end the game has pulled the biggest heart pull I've ever felt when the character plays back a recording. I don't want to spoil the story, but the setup was masterful and made me cry.In summary.Excellent point and click adventure game with great visual, story and voice acting to sell it. Quite the macabre experience with its gore, bio punk aesthetic and death should you make the wrong choice. Puzzle can sometime be just trial and error, but the developer have provided a guide if you got too stump.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: A point-and-clicker. Graded on that curve, I think it's pretty good. But, I think it has also taught me that I just don't like this genre very much.The good stuff first: Bone Totem is well-acted, and the world is interesting. Dialogue and diegetic text are natural. The non-diegetic text is not—it’s absurdly overwritten, but in a kind of endearing way.  The plot writ large is good. I'd rate it a better-than-average abandoned environment sci-fi horror story. I probably won't remember it well a year from now, but as with a lot of good genre fiction, it's the small details that are most interesting.The Stasis universe seems, at first glance, to be a pretty typical near-future setting, but discarded logs and conversations gradually reveal it to be... pretty weird. Most advanced computing is done by organic superbrains grown in vats. Society is run by a single theocratic corporation, which itself relies on nine semi-self-aware AIs to execute its vision. Most people are horribly in debt, and are working it off through a lifetime of labor or by selling the rights to their organs to the rich. None of this is very significant to the plot, but these small dystopian flourishes do a lot for immersion.Man, though, that point-and-click adventure formula! Mechanically, you spend almost all of the game combing through environments for keys and locks, and then jamming differently shaped keys into differently shaped locks until something clicks. Thankfully, I felt that puzzle solutions did make sense 80% of the time. But the 20% of the time they didn't was still enough to feel really frustrating.By midgame, my inventory was overflowing with bric-à-brac without obvious use, and I would sigh heavily every time I entered a room with like four interactable dioramas. Just a bit too often I found myself sifting through my bags and applying objects to each other at random until something worked. Even larger setpiece puzzles rarely feel like they require much deduction; they merely function as tests to see if you've examined your environment closely enough, and were able to recognize clues as clues.So, yeah—I think Bone Totem offers up a cool (and icky! didn't even talk about that!) dark sci-fi environment to explore, but your enjoyment will depend a lot upon your patience for the point-and-click formula. I think I just prefer exploring environments like this in a more immersive, first-person mode, a la SOMA or Bioshock. Point-and-clickers definitely have their place. They're much easier to develop, for one, and they're more mechanically accessible to a wide variety of gamers. I am glad that games like this exist. I think it'll be a while, though, before I will want to spend another 15 hours stumbling around the ocean floor, trying to divine what combination of junk I need to jam together to fulfill the puzzle deity's obscure vision.

_childDocuments_.review: I will be completely honest I liked the story and the setting but besides that the gameplay is just clunky.I just couldn't get into the whole use this item with a different character thing. The game is just too short, too linear and particular for this sort of thing. I tried but I just couldn't get into it. Combining and breaking things sounds useful but it just ends up being annoying. Oh I played with Mac now I hit a wall, let's switch to a different character and play that until I hit a wall again, one last time for the third character. Let's see what we've gathered and what can I break or combine. Spoiler alert it's a mostly guessing game. Then there's the part where I have to wait through the whole dialogue playing before I can act with my selected character. You can skip it with T, sounds great until you realise that it doesn't skip the whole convo just this particular line. And there's a lot of Hmmmgh, Arrrgh or Uhhhh. So, you just sit there spamming T, waiting to play the game.Again, the first time around I had no issues, I read everything, I explored everything, I listened to everything and I somewhat enjoyed it but I wont be able to do it again. Some had some fun bits which helped explain the setting better but most were just uninteresting, waaay too long and felt like waste of my time.Another thing that I didn't like is that this game has these gorgeous and I do mean absolutely gorgeous backgrounds yet everything is so dark, you can barely see anything. _childDocuments_.review: Stasis: Bone Totem is an excellent adventure game with puzzle solutions that are logical rather than absurd, a horror plot that goes all over the place but never loses itself in its indulgences, and a damn good core voice cast. Interacting with puzzle sites or computers brings up a cool old school survival horror interface, giving you a closeup of whatever you're working with. Oftentimes the clues and ciphers for math/code puzzles are hidden in documents, so it really pays to let yourself be sucked in by the worldbuilding!Buy it, right now, if you're at all interested in anything you've seen or heard about this game. Every corner is dripping with love, care, and extraneous fluids.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent, horrific point and click adventure with a few flaws that make it just shy from perfect. This thing has some of the most ghastly, gory, visually disturbing imagery I've ever seen in a game, so if that's what floats your boat, you'd be a fool not to buy this thing. Relatively clever puzzles and an interesting premise backed up by a creepy soundtrack round it out. Buy it. Also, hail Moses. Praise be to Moses. Couple things I didn't like: 1) Character animations during cinematics. Instead of motion capture, it looks like it was all done manually, and not very well at that. For the next game, invest in a cheap mocap rig so your characters don't look drunk all the time. 2) Several times I was totally confused about what to do next. It seemed as if I'd reached the end of the available things that could be done, and even checking the hints didn't necessarily help. More often then not my progress was blocked because a specific character hadn't triggered a specific line of dialogue/conversation, and the interactive objects didn't become available until that audio played. I ended up having to check walkthroughs for the next step. Obviously this wasn't a problem for everyone.3) Unanswered questions. I feel like the story did a reasonably good job of tying up all the loose ends, but there were still a bunch of questions that were never addressed. C'est la vie.

_childDocuments_.review: Want to learn how to not end your adventure game? Then boy have I got the title for you :V -------------------------------------------------For the first few chapters Stasis: BT is a fun, cheesy little sci-fi horror title with that cute pre-rendered sheen all over it. Then in the last 2 chapters it falls off a cliff, literally and figuratively. Nonsensical plot points, new characters that exist purely for unneeded exposition, and everyone just starts repeating themselves endlessly. I didn't skip any of the dialogue up until this last section at which point I began to skip most of the dialogue entirely and didn't miss a single important plot point. It gets to the point of being stuck in exposition hallways that exist purely to listen to the characters talk. Except said hallways are too short so you walk to the end and then just stand around until everyone gets done repeating themselves or you skip the dialogue. This is made even worse by how simple the dwindling puzzles get. There are a few sections with singular puzzles you can easily solve as you only have a handful of "puzzle pieces" remaining. But they still felt the need to make you sit through the character expositting that, wow, it sure would be cool if the single door in this dead end room was open instead of closed. Oh shoot oh darn if only there was some way to SCRUB the RUST off this DOOR with some sort of RUSTED DOOR SCRUBBER.  -------------------------------------------------In conclusion I want to feed Moses into a woodchipper, feet first.7.8 out of 10, too much water.

_childDocuments_.review: STASIS: Bone Totem is a fantastic sequel to an already good game (the first STASIS). It's a point and click adventure game, quite puzzle-heavy. It's got a sort of isometric view, with beautiful backgrounds. The tone of it is sci-fi horror, the story a mix of stuff personal to the main characters, as well as revealing a grander mystery.GAMEPLAY:Classic point and click, quite puzzle-heavy overall. The puzzles themselves are mostly logical but there were a few times where I found it difficult to know exactly what I was meant to do. It's a game where having a pen and paper is handy, as puzzles are often reliant on clues you read about when exploring (often based on numbers). I'd classify the game as slightly harder than most contemporary point and clicks.You control three characters in the game, with a shared inventory, and you can switch between these characters at (almost) all times. One character can combine certain items to make a new, another character can break down certain items to make a new one. This all works pretty well.Interactive objects in the game are clearly marked. And the puzzles in the game are contained within separate UI screens. This does help alleviate the "click everything until something works" syndrome of some point and clicks.I enjoyed playing different characters and found that it worked well for the game. But there were some parts where I feel it slowed the game down a bit as you switch through them in search for something to progress the game. Most of the time the game does a good job with this though.VISUALSMostly great, and of extremely high quality. As with the devs previous games, stuff like cutscenes are simply jawdropping considering it's made by such a small team. Very reminiscant of Blizzard's cutscenes in their older games (such as Starcraft).Sometimes the otherwise very beautiful backgrounds lack definition. It can be hard to tell exactly where you character can actually walk. It's not a problem since it's not an action-game or whatever but it can be difficult to see sometimes. The game is very dark most of the time, which fits the horror-vibe and the setting obviously. But yeah, visual clarity could be better in some places.The game has a "highlight all interactibles" system which is nice, but it also leaves the game screen feeling quite cluttered when you use it.AUDIOMostly very good as well, featuring excellent music from Mark Morgan (and additional composers). There are some annoyances here for me though. The voiceacting overall is *fantastic* and, as with the graphics, a much higher quality than one would expect from a smaller indie game. Really good effort from the VAs.Some acting is rather "emotive" though, so you'll hear plenty of breathing for example. This works pretty well, but for the female character it became really obnoxious to me after a while. It's especially noticeable when you hear her through the radio filter, the constant breathyness becomes overbearing.There were also some repeating sound-effects, most noticeably a certain background-whistling, that annoyed me to the point where I had trouble focusing on reading the journal entries you find in the game.All in all, audio is very well done though except for these annoyances.STORYPretty fascinating. I will say that I found it to be a bit slow and uninteresting for the first parts of the game. It's a slow-burn at first, which I can certainly appreciate, but the "slow unfolding of horror" didn't quite hit the mark for me. However, once the story really does get going, I found it very hard to put the game down. Both the characters grew on me (especially Moses) and there were a few different layers to the situation which kept it all interesting and fresh.After finishing the game, I felt very satisfied with it. Both in terms of how it ended up and also in terms of game-length. It felt meaty, without overstaying its welcome.All in all, a really strong game and definitely my favorite from the Brothergood Games. A few annoyances here and there didn't stop my enjoyment, and it ended up being one of the strongest modern point and clicks that I've played. Very enjoyable, and highly recommended if you like the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Bone Totem is amazing!I really liked how well constructed "Stasis (2015)" was for a Point & Click game,and had high hopes for Bone Totem, after all the praise from MandaloreGaming's video.But this exceeded my expectations and I personally would call it the best game in the Point & Click genre!While I described the 1st game like the movie "PANDORUM (2009)", Bone Totem is like Pandorum had a baby with "The Descent (2005)".Bone Totem has beautifully crafted environment, claustrophobic atmosphere and superb voice acting.Direct upgrade to Stasis.The mystery is highly intriguing and playing 3 protagonists at the same time is just genius!When stuck on one, it is best to switch to the others and progress there,maybe even find an item that will help solve the puzzle that you were stuck on. Really refreshing!The reason why I call Bone Totem one of the very best in the genre, is because all puzzles and solutions are logical and are not plagued by the insane moon logic that has taken over the genre (to artificially prolong the game).Our time and intelligence is respected.The only negative I can think of are the missable collectibles. Especially when they clash with the one-save file achievement. What were they thinking?Great game!P.S. Moses is the absolutely bestest of bears !

_childDocuments_.review: Story/characters- Main characters are likable and go through compelling character arcs. Their performances are well done, and their dialogue feels very fitting of themselves and the world around them, and flows in a very naturalistic way. I quite liked all of the main cast.- Story is very compelling, starting with a simpler premise that gradually escalates with a grander scale and stakes. Pacing felt right as well, with no chapter feeling too long or short. The story was very personal to the main cast, while tying into the larger universe, which I also liked.- My primary story takeaway is that it's about . Overall I found that it was executed very well and strongly resonated with me.- World building is well done, with many details shown through dialogue, found diary entries, and environmental details. Key aspects of the game's universe were easily understood and felt organically taught to me, and helped deepen my understanding of the story and characters.World/environment- Good artstyle that's simple and mostly readable enough for gameplay, while having its own identity. The gritty, visceral, and industrial details of the very cyberpunk world are communicated wonderfully through the visuals.- Additional descriptions for world items supplement the art, being very well written. They communicated details that the art couldn't, and to my recollection, none of them felt repetitive, and were all interesting to read. Admittedly I only read half of them and skimmed over the other half.- Diary/PDA entries for a multitude of deceased can be found around the game, and they help to tell how routine life was like in this world, and how certain events transpired. They also help with the world building, and enhance or clarify certain aspects of the story. Piecing together the lives of the deceased and how they all interacted was also very enjoyable for me.Puzzles- Most puzzles are fun to solve and had solutions that were intuitive to me. There were a good mix of puzzles that could be solved relatively simply, versus others that required more progression and exploration to gather all the needed pieces/info.- The three playable characters have a unique skill that lets them interact with the items you pick up in unique ways. I think there is only a single and/or linear sequence of item interaction(s), so it doesn't allow for as much creativity as I initially expected, though it wasn't an issue once I adjusted my expectations.- Hints are done very organically, with each item having different descriptions depending on which character you are controlling. It hinted at different potential uses for items without being explicit, and also provided more insight into each character. Some puzzles have slightly more explicit hints where a character will say what they think they need to do, but keep it vague enough to not handhold you through the puzzle. These hints are also manually triggered so you can choose to not use them.Misc. stuff that I liked- No puzzles are timed, except for maybe one, and can be done at your own pace- No combat, stealth, or anything that'd require mechanical skill is present- Everything can be done with the mouse- Despite the grim world and serious subject matter, the game plays at a very relaxed paceMisc. complaints- Captain's globe and weight balancing (with the ) puzzle did not accept the correct solution the first time, and took several attempts for the game to register it as solved.- Some areas look inaccessible due to how the environment was drawn/lit, but ping will clarify this confusion. Conversely, some areas will have interactables that are not accessible in the currently loaded area. Either occurrence is minor and not a detriment to the overall experience.- Too many area transitions that incur a small fade to black, especially when some of the zones are very small with minimal interaction in them. There's probably a technical/gameplay reason for it, and the fade is very brief, so this is only a very very minor complaint, but it's something that's very prevalent nonetheless.In summation, I found Stasis Bone Totem to be a very good iso puzzle game, and it excelled at nearly every aspect, with only very minor complaints/bugs. I finished the game in just shy of 12 hours, and every hour was worthwhile. I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone that's interested in it.I am a very smart bear :)
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: The Brotherhood's Stasis: Bone Totem is a fantastic game and a great follow up to the previous games in the series. Technically speaking, it's no different from any point and click game. You go into an area and have to solve a series of puzzles to proceed to the next. The only big difference here is that you're controlling three characters. One being Moses, an AI controlled teddy bear. He's as equally adorable as he is terrifying. I personally preferred the structure of this game compared to Beautiful Desolation. That game was ambitious and came out very well. However, the more linear approach helped the pace, which the story went by quite quick. I loved the characters and their voice acting. Especially the previously mentioned character Moses. One of the best things about the game is the art direction and music which creates a fantastic sense of dread. The environment has so many wonderful gory details. A lot of which appears to be influenced by H.R. Giger. It looks impressive and I felt constantly distracted looking at all the small details. This obviously means that the game has a lot of atmosphere. Between the superb environments and the sound design, It's down right creepy for near enough the entire journey. I loved playing this in headphones. I did feel like a few of the puzzles fell into the non sensical department. This wouldn't have been bad if the hint system was more prominent. Not to tell you the answer, but just give enough of a hint towards the solution. There were times that it popped up when the solution was obvious and other moments where I wish it had. The best example for me is the bear trap on the door. I could have swore that I had already used it on the door a few times, as clicking on everything is the name of the game after all. _childDocuments_.review: Easily the best adventure game I've played in a long time. Possibly even the best adventure game I've ever played.There is so much to like here. The characters. The setting. The horror. The puzzles. The story. Everything is just so damn good. Well, maybe not everything, but I'll get to that later. For now, let me wax poetic about this wonderful game. I was a bit skeptical at first, when I was having some trouble with the beginning puzzles. The controls felt clunky. The characters were slow. Moving items around was a pain (It's not, but it felt like it at the start). I was getting bored fast. Finally, something just clicked. I think it came after I realized that you need to try every option available in order to figure out how to progress, even if that means back tracking a bit. For example, one of the characters Mac can break items apart to separate things and the other character Charlie can combine items. Sometimes you need to hand one of them all of your items and let them either try to break them apart or combine them to see what you can create. It gets tedious and some combinations make very little sense, but it's necessary more often than not when you're stuck. After the puzzles became easier I started to enjoy this game much more and I could finally take in the horror setting I was being treated too. I can't stress how good this game looks. The environment is the perfect combination of 2D and 3D models that many games these days either can't pull off or don't try to. It feels A LOT like Pillars of Eternity and certain elements like PDA's, terminals, and environmental interactions have a Fallout 2 feel as well. Looking at the developers Twitter account briefly, I noticed that Pillars of Eternity and Fallout 2 were listed under a Tweet that said "What are your favorite ISOMETRIC games?" so I think it's safe to say they had inspiration from them. In my opinion, this game is like if the developers took Pillars of Eternity, Fallout 2, I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream, SOMA, and Dead Space and put them in a blender. A near perfect combination. My only complaint in regards to the environment is I wish you could zoom in more on certain areas. The camera is player focused for the most part and you can only really zoom out, rather than zoom in. I want a better look at some of the crazy sh*t they put in this game.The story is very good as well. A down on their luck couple forced to take on a dangerous salvage job with their dead child's robot bear. An evil corporation/religion investigating an underwater cave system below the ocean. What could go wrong? Well, a lot, actually. I won't spoil anything here for you, as it's best you go in with no real knowledge of the story. I will say though, by the end you will feel many feelings about some of these characters. Especially the robot bear Moses. "I am a very smart bear now." Yes you are Moses.Overall, I think this is a fantastic game, but there are some glaring issues that could have been easily avoided by the devs. I am not sure if it was them cutting corners or they honestly thought it looked good, but using AI art was a terrible choice. It's obvious from the first PDA you find or terminal you use. The animated pictures used for the owners of PDA's you find are especially bad. Apparently everyone with a PDA on this deep sea expedition were 60+ years old with multiple face tattoos and a bad drug addiction. Some of the terminals you find with images are mostly AI art as well. At one point I came across AI art of the face huggers and alien from the movie Alien and then a Graboid from the movie Tremors. I am not sure if this inclusion was intentional as an Easter Egg or not, but when you're trying to figure out what happened in the story or solve one of the puzzles, things like that are just distracting or misleading. Mixing AI art and actual clues to solving puzzles into the terminals was a really bad design choice because you'll start dismissing most images you find in terminals as not necessary to the plot and one of those images might have been a clue. This happened multiple times to me and I wasn't very happy when I realized that a terminal 4 area transitions ago had a clue I needed and was mixed in with 3 AI images.Also, I can't help but feel that most of the PDA messages and letters you read were AI written as well. They just feel so inhuman and vague that I can't help but feel that a real person didn't write any of them. That's another thing that drove me nuts. The vagueness of EVERY single PDA entry. Nobody seems to be able to specifically say what is happening in any document you read. It's always alluding to something. I understand wanting things to be a mystery to the player, but after the tenth or so PDA alluding to the horrible things I am currently standing in front of, I'd like a little more clarity here. Even documents you find at the very end of the game contain this irritating vagueness.The dialogue of the characters can be a bit much at times. When characters talk to one another or themselves the game blocks you from interacting with the environment. You can't solve puzzles or move onto a new area when someone is talking. This is done for pacing reasons I am sure, but at many points in the story character dialogue isn't long enough or important enough to warrant blocking the player from starting a puzzle or transitioning to another area. Can't tell you how many times I had to sit there and either listen to Charlie say "Oh my God" or Mac say "Cayne's reign" for the billionth time before I could read a PDA. The last two hours of gameplay is also mostly listening to one of the characters moan over their comms every time you transition to a new area, so I don't blame anyone for using the Skip Dialogue button a lot here.The last knock I have against this game is the cinematics and oh boy they are bad. Very very bad. They look like those fan CGI videos that independent YouTube artists put out for games they like. Warhammer 40K has a lot of these. They clearly took a lot of work to do by someone by themselves, but they don't look good at all. The voice lines don't match up with the lips most of the time. The character movements are awkward and the camera is often at weird angles I think to hide some of this. There are also way too many of these cinematics. I think the devs should have scrapped 90% of the cinematics and just done the big scene transitions or events directly in the game engine instead. Being pulled from the game into a half baked cinematic and then back into the game again is pretty jarring. They could have saved their cinematic budget for the beginning and end of the game and gotten much better quality cinematic work done for them.Despite the issues listed above this is a fantastic game that I can't recommend enough. My complaints are minor in the grand scheme of things. $20 is a steal for this game and I got it on sale for $15. I think I owe the devs $5. I am looking forward to playing the predecessor to this game next.

_childDocuments_.review: In this current era of unfinished, procedurally generated AAA game releases which clearly lack passion or effort, every release from this developer has been an absolute breath of fresh air. With an astonishingly small budget, this game is an example of pure excellence in creativity, worldbuilding and storytelling. The environments are painstakingly crafted as showpieces to advance the story and immerse the player. The sound design and music fit the story and environments perfectly. The plot/setting is a very specific mix of science fiction dystopia and cosmic horror, taking some of the best elements from games like Dead Space and movies like Alien, The Thing or Event Horizon in order to tell an unnerving, mature story. This is a very specific genre of sci-fi horror which draws its power from the fear of some cosmic evil beyond human comprehension, and when executed correctly, it is (in my opinion) the most captivating and unique setting for a movie or game. The passion and dedication this team shows here to faithfully craft this exact setting and aesthetic so expertly is something that no amount of AAA budget can replicate.I've been playing games for 25+ years and this game ranks in the top 5 of all time for me. If you haven't tried the stasis series yet, I highly recommend it. In fact, not only do I recommend this game but I would argue that it's a solid 10/10 for what it tries to be and the small size/budget of the team who created it. I would be equally happy with this purchase at 2x the price point they are selling it for, and I eagerly await the next installment in this setting.

_childDocuments_.review: In a nutshell, Stasis: Bone Totem is an incredibly enjoyable point-and-click adventure game with a dark and eerie atmosphere that's perfect for horror fans. Despite its isometric perspective, it stays true to the classic adventure game formula, focusing on collecting items, deciphering clues, and solving puzzles.One unique aspect is that you control three different characters who share the same inventory, and each has special abilities to interact with items. This mechanic adds an interesting twist to the gameplay, as you'll need to collect items with one character to solve puzzles for another.The puzzles are mostly enjoyable and cleverly use the environment without becoming overly abstract. Some will deceive you with misleading information, while others will reward careful observation. Though a few may seem straightforward, they generally strike a good balance of challenge. Also be warned, if you are not a fan of reading, skip this, rather a lot of the clues to the puzzles are hidden on PDA's.The game's story is engaging, and the mysterious atmosphere keeps you motivated to explore deeper. The characters, while simple, have likeable personalities and contribute to the overall experience. The climax may not be mind-blowing, but it satisfactorily ties up loose ends and pays homage to classic horror movie influences.One minor gripe is that the game feels overwritten at times. Characters often pause gameplay to deliver redundant or overly dramatic dialogue, which can slow down the pace unnecessarily. Additionally, some text, including personnel logs and environmental descriptions, could benefit from trimming to improve the overall pacing.Nevertheless, Stasis: Bone Totem excels in its atmospheric presentation, reminiscent of eerie horror games from the '90s. The voice acting is top-notch, adding to the immersive experience. Despite its minor flaws, this game is a solid eight out of ten and a standout in the genre. If you enjoy narrative-driven point-and-click adventure games, this is a must-try.The developers deserve praise for their passion and dedication to crafting a unique and engaging sci-fi horror experience on a relatively small budget. The attention to detail in the environments, sound design, and music adds to the immersive storytelling.As an old-school gamer, I highly recommend Stasis: Bone Totem and consider it one of the top adventure games I've played in recent years. Its unsettling atmosphere, nostalgic visuals, and challenging puzzles make it a standout title. For those who enjoy narrative-driven adventures with a touch of horror, this game is a must-play. The developer's commitment to crafting an exceptional experience shines through, and I eagerly anticipate any future instalments in this setting.On a personal note, I am usually not one to pre-order or buy games upon release. However, my positive experiences with Metro Exodus and Stray led me to back Bone Totem, and I'm delighted with my decision. The game has provided over 10 hours of fun, and I'm still immersed in its world. If you enjoy modern point-and-click games or titles like Bioshock, Dead Space, and Alien Isolation, this game will undoubtedly captivate you.In conclusion, Stasis: Bone Totem is a fantastic indie game that exceeds expectations and delivers a polished, atmospheric adventure worth experiencing. For a reasonable price, you'll get an exceptional gaming experience that works smoothly from the very start.Don't miss out on this gem; give it a try and support these talented local developers!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is 3rd in the series: Stasis, Cayne and Stasis: Bone Totem - so I recommend you play the previous ones to get the gist of the universe and spot the references.In short, this is a great quality game! Play it if you like story-rich puzzle genre.The events take place in an anti-utopian setting, some time in the future (22 century, I believe).The corps took over lives of an average person, God is no more, instead there is Cayne.Cayne is the founder of Cayne corporation, which conducts all sorts of biotech and genetic experiments.You're going to play as a couple of scavengers who discover an abandoned Cayne sea rig.I don't want to reveal more of the story, so here is a cap on the quality/mechanics:* I did not encounter any bugs* my PC is potato, but the game didn't stutter at all, except for the cutscenes* the environment is quite detailed and nice to look through* no pixel hunting, since the game shows hot spots (on demand), also there are puzzle hints, if you need them* the writing is atmospheric, many objects have a description to them (but it may get tiresome to read it all)* voice acting is believable, sound is good, GREAT ambient sounds* it will take around 15 hours to complete the game (if you read all descriptions and PDAs)My only warning is gore. If you don't like reading/seeing gory stuff, then I think you better skip it.

_childDocuments_.review: Stasis: Bone Totem is a horror puzzle game based in a somewhat far future. The main characters, a couple, Mac and Charlie, come across an abandoned mining rig in the sea and decide to try and loot it. They soon discover there is much more to the mining rig than they originally thought. Pros: - Cool setting - Good environment artwork and short cut scene graphics- Some puzzles are pretty clever- Guide included for those who just want to play through the gameCons: - Didn't care about the characters much. Side characters were much more interesting than the main ones- A main mechanic of the game is that all characters can share items through some device (Quantum Sharing Device?) It feels very hand-wavy to me, but fine- What I really didn't like though were a few parts of the game where you literally just have to wait for time to pass. I'm glad they included a guide, because you could be going around trying to figure out what you're doing wrong for hours, just to realize "Oh enough time has passed that X has progressed." It's just a no-fun mechanic. They really should have included a "wait until X happens" button if they want to preserve the time aspect. But even so, there is one such part where it is established that time is of the essence, and then you have to wait a chunk of time for a key ingredient of solving that puzzle. While this isn't super common, it happens a couple times- Weird character reactions. It's like you just walked through four separate rooms with various gruesome horrors contained within, and you'll get to room 5 and the characters will still stop and talk on their radios like, "Oh my god! Is that a b-b-b-b-body!?" That all being said, I know puzzle games are not my genre at all, but I'll still give this a thumbs up because a good number of the puzzles were good and it has a cool setting

_childDocuments_.review: Spoilers ahead. When looking at an adventure game, I tend to focus on puzzles and their logic, the pleasant feeling of grasping a pattern, figuring out what a hint was for, what the designer intended but only obliquely pointed at. This feeling was, by and large, absent or irrelevant in this game. That is not to say that the puzzles were terrible - the logic underneath most actions was sound, hints were appropriately scattered (most of the time) and at no point does the game devolve into the 90s trope of needing a pigeon, rope, and a crystal skull to make a gun you can use as a key. But puzzles remained purely functional, often very clearly being set up just to ensure that each of the playable character progresses through the rooms and plot points in line with the others, and most of the times just requiring a certain object to be found by another character, or a clue that spells out the solution in the clearest way possible to pop up in a terminal somewhere else in the base. 9 times out of 10, if you are thinking about a puzzle, you are overthinking it.What makes this game special is also not the graphics. The design of areas, creatures and building is often very inspired and even breathtaking in its gruesomeness, but across a 15 hour or so game, there are only so many corpses and viscera you can see splattered across walls before it turns into just another interior design choice. The first ritualistically murdered man hits you like a truck - but by the end, you´ll just see the others as an item deposit box for Mac and team to use. It´s not the worldbuilding, either, which can and does appear confused at times - are we at the bottom of the ocean, under thousands of atmospheres of pressure? Then how are we walking around the air bubble with not even a jacket on?  Why does the hallucination of the Russian Orthodox character, depicting himself as Jesus, happen in a very clearly Roman Catholic inspired building? If CayneCorp arrived to the ruins following a signal, why did they never bother tracking it until they reached the submarine that sent it - and if they did, why did they just leave armed nukes hanging around? Why are some of the Soviet corpses, centuries old, effectively mummified, while some are skeletons and others in water barely look weeks old? Why did Cayne´s resurrection shake the world to such an extent that all modern religions died, when rogue anti-corporate groups can pull a virtually identical feat on random kids just to get leverage on a couple of scavengers? If Cayne wanted the MULE gone, why not send other teams to at least bomb the oil rig from a safe distance - and if they were planning on returning for the P139 and its promise of literal immortality, why not keep an eye on it with basic satellite surveillance at least? We do not know that our enemies have pre-colombian weaponry when we get on board, but Cayne does, and it does not seem like the group that would have moral qualms with going full conquistador beneath the waves. If being left with these sort of doubts on a game´s narrative and world leaves a bad taste in your mouth, there might be a lot here to dislike. Not a lot is cleared up, really, and nothing leaves you with the idea that a clear plot line exists in the background for you to reconstruct if you put your mind on it. You could let this game go.You would also be missing out on an excellent emotional arc for all characters. The selling point for this game is always going to be Mac, Charlie, Moses, Faran, Boynya and Calaban. The way they react to their past grief, their mistakes, their fears, their wants. The excellent voice acting does a lot, but there has also been an incredible improvement in the dialogue since Stasis 1, with the writers clearly finding the voices they wanted to channel all this time. Some lines will stay with you for a long time. "I am strong and brave." "My friend." "You just need to blink." "Here, strength does not matter. Only courage." "I am Numen." "In water, you are powerless." Suddenly, the world not making sense, the big players of Cayne, LEAF, the underwater tribe, the plant-turned-bacteria-turned-parasite, all cease to matter - their plans being surreal and senseless becomes a major way to understand the emotional turmoil of the characters, thrown in a world with no apparent meaning, where giants and gods can pluck your very soul and digitize it, enslave your family with a loan for medical expenses they made necessary, put your loved ones in a grave for a 0.1% profit margin, and bring them back as a power play in a conflict you are not privy to, and whose results don´t matter. The world never was meant to make sense. The people within it do.Is S:BT a game you should play? I am certain. 81% accuracy prediction.

_childDocuments_.review: No spoilers review:Great game, especially if you liked Stasis, or if you tried the demo and enjoyed it. You don't need to have any familiarity with Stasis to appreciate this, though -- they're entirely separate experiences, just set within the same loosely-connected universe.Also, works on Windows 7, for anyone else still running that! I completed it with zero technical issues.As for the actual gameplay, it's pretty simple: walk around, find items, change/combine some of them, put them where they go, move along. Almost like a walking sim, but with a little bit more going on -- but not much more. There's light puzzle elements mostly based on visual clues and occasionally on info found in PDAs scattered around, just like Stasis. You've gotta be in it mainly for the presentation and narrative, or else you're likely to find yourself bored. Also like Stasis, some of the puzzles are a bit obtuse to figure out if you're focusing on progressing the story and not taking time to think things through (which I'm often guilty of in these kinds of games), but for the most part, solving them is pretty easy.Some of the changes from the demo felt a bit off to me at first (all new VA, some writing changes), but then I gradually came to appreciate them, and before long was past where the demo left off anyway. I did enjoy the VA for Mac and Moses better in the demo, at least initially, but the new ones came into their own before long, and the VA for Charlie was consistently good -- much better than in the demo. And the new characters post-demo had *fantastic* acting.The story was good-to-excellent throughout, which is the main draw for this sort of game. And some moments were genuinely heartbreaking. The developments near the end are really, really well done, and the ending was satisfying. I've played a lot of games with dark settings, and mostly they don't affect me much, but this one really got to me emotionally in several different places, mainly due to the quality of the VA and writing. Not from the horror, but the tragedy. Really great stuff. That said, if you're looking to ♥♥♥♥ your pants in terror, this game probably won't make that happen unless you're newer the genre.Visually, of course, the game is incredible as well. Much like in Stasis, The Brotherhood really showed their skill in making impressive high-tech and bio-horror environments. Though if I had one complaint, it's that some areas are really dark and difficult to make out, partly due to the setting and partly due to this subtle fog-of-war-like effect where things further away from the cursor are a little bit shrouded. I don't think this shrouding added much to the game and I didn't find a way to disable it, but it was only a minor detractor and only in certain areas, so not a big deal.All in all, if you are up for a really good scifi horror story, this is definitely worth checking out. Try (or watch, since it doesn't look like it's still downloadable) the demo, and if you like what you see, you'll definitely enjoy the rest.

_childDocuments_.review: First two hours gameplay:  First of all have to say that I am pretty new to these type of games and specifically this franchise, so my review is from a very new player point of view.I honestly enjoyed this a lot, yes I had lots of struggles to find solutions to early puzzles (even had to look for guides once or twice) but I am catching up, understanding how the game is working and really having fun with it. By no means it's an easy puzzle game, you need to think, explore and pay attention to all the details in the game which makes it so interesting. The visuals and atmosphere is pretty cool and creepy, the story is very intriguing and I always want to know what is next and what is happening in this rig.The mechanics of switching characters is pretty new to me but very well done I think, yes it's little odd to transfer items between characters but overall I think it's working pretty well in game and make it more engaging. If you are looking for some engaging and tricky puzzles to solve while uncovering the sci-fi horror story of it, I think you'd like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Nowhere near as good as the original stasis. Puzzles are confusing and half of them make no sense unless you look up the solution on YouTube. Bouncing between 3 characters and being able to transfer inventory between the 3 makes no sense. If I can magically transfer inventory, just transfer the person itself. Listening to Moses tell me how smart of a bear he is every 6 seconds gets on my nerves. Macs heavy breathing on every statement that he makes and Charlie disobeying every command she's given. Got about halfway through and the story just became so nonsensical, that I just became so bored, that I quit playing. Not caring about the characters, the weird story-line, and having to figure out if I need to solve a puzzle by looking a picture from a PDA that I read a hour ago doesn't make for a fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really, really torn on this.STASIS: Bone Totem is a game with great writing and amazing characters. Moses is a triumph, and his relationship with Faran was incredible. There were numerous moments in this game which moved me close to tears. Vocal performances are up to the task and well, and you end up with a beautiful presentation. As a character story this game is a home run.Sadly, there's still some struggles with the puzzles. There's a hints system designed to help you along, but it's not great, and sometimes not even that accurate. One that stands out is a puzzle around sound where you relate the sounds of the puzzle wheel to the sounds of some pipes. The pipes are several screens away, so if you want to check the sound it's already a slog. If you get stuck the hint will tell you it's a sound puzzle, and then play the sounds back. Nice. Except, no, not nice, because it's not a sound puzzle, the first in the sequence relates to a drawing on a note, which breaks the sounds sequence for.... reasons? Not to mention there's two sets of every note on the wheel and no way to know which to use. This was my most frustrated moment, but the game has a number of them, especially later on.The game would also benefit from some UI quality of life improvements. Why is the inventory not simply shared at all times? Why can I note combined items by clicking them on one another instead of tediously transferring them into the special combine area? Why did they remove the really great UI feature from STASIS where items would show you whether they could be used with something without any clicking being necessary?The game is close, so close to being great, but the puzzles just frustrated me enough towards the end that I soured on the experience. Using environmental clues is fine, but they are too many screens away, sometimes buried in far too much noise to stand out, and sometimes just don't seem to make any sense even after you solve them.Despite all that, I'll probably get the next one, because you can see such a great arc of improvement since STASIS that I believe they will only improve on this.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I'm keeping this brief.The sound and music are amazing.The story just keeps pulling you in more and more, and the buildup is very well done.The graphics at first are odd but develop and create a really memorable world.Nice puzzles for the most part, there were maybe 5% where I kind of shrugged my shoulders and said "why".This is a very good game, I recommend it strongly.

_childDocuments_.review: While it's a very good video game, instead of getting to learn more about CAYNE, more about the future, it devolves into some gibberish about ancient civilisation and miraculous oxygen pockets under the sea.You cannot even google "CAYNE Numen AI", there is nothing out there, there is no lore available. There are these worshipped 9 Numen, so uber super amazing they are that there's not a single word about them. Final word of advice: do not wear headphones when starting this game, the intro video cannot be disabled and has such loud shrieking it can damage your hearing. Even after the patch that promises to fix this they failed to actually fix it.

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant point and click adventure horror game. Better than the first Stasis with a gripping sci-fi thriller story and engaging characters who you generally care about. The atmosphere and tension is expertly crafted, the setting takes clear inspiration from Alien with it's grim future aesthetics, and Event Horizon with it's visceral gothic horror. The gameplay is simple point and click adventure fare (pick up, combine/dissemble item, search everything) but the environmental puzzle solving is excellent with logical solutions for the patient, thorough players. There is a hint system if you get frustrated, but you can disable the hints in options.     The graphics are good with lots of really detailed, quality pre-rendered backgrounds, and nicely animated characters. The cutscenes are a bit janky looking through this is a small development team behind this Indie title. The voice actors put in great performances, elevating the drama and suspense, many AAA game characters pale in comparison. Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: This game has great voice acting, characters, graphics, story. Moses is an awesome character. However, the puzzles and reading material start overpowering everything once u get to chapter 2. IMO it drags the action to the pace of a snail. If you want to feel like a very elitist snail.....I give it 10/10 for effort and 7/10 overall.

_childDocuments_.review: Best part is when Cayne B. Totem kicks open the Soviet-era ritual doors and yells "It's Bonin' time!" and fires AI bears hugging Nuke warheads at everybody.The latest entry in the isometric point-n-click horror series, this one is pretty damn good.  Inventory sharing is excellent since you don't even have to switch to the person to take their ♥♥♥♥, so it makes mix n matching easy.  A few of the puzzles are kinda wonky/obscure, but overall they made sense and weren't annoying.  Probably the biggest negative is the game is so dark..as in difficult to see!  While the cursor is a light source(like in Dungeon Keeper), it should really be boosted to see all the background art properly.The best part for real is..(other than the gleefully sadistic deaths for everybody Brotherhood delights in) the fact that each inventory item has a different description depending on who is looking at it.  So a manly man description, sciency girl one, and bear child robot.(who is definitely the most entertaining)
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely another amazing game by the Brotherhood!  Very much felt like an improvement in every way from the first Stasis and Cayne. Bringing what they learned with Beautiful Desolation and more to the table. Very interesting story and atmosphere that really kept me wanting to play to the end.  No real jump scares or anything cheap. But in true Stasis fashion there is some quirky gruesome deaths that can occur. Ambiance and overall just foreboding feeling the whole time is great.  Really grew to enjoy all the characters and felt invested in them at the end.None of the puzzles were exceptionally hard, but I did have to look around a bit to make sure I found all the clues.  All the information is available to you to figure things out.  If you still need help there is even a in-game hint system to try.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent point and click with high production value. I thoroughly enjoy the swapping of the characters and the convenience of the transfer of the items. There is very little "abrasiveness" (think Resident Evil 0) in character swapping and item management.The theme is phenomenal and atmosphere is just-right. Tension is built and diffused in a worthy way throughout the story.An excellent successor to a great game. Looking forward to more installments in this series/universe!
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend STASIS: BONE TOTEM enough.  I played the first two STASIS games and enjoyed them, but BONE TOTEM blows them out of the water.  The story, graphics, voice acting, puzzles and overall atmosphere are insanely good, which is why this is now my favorite point and click adventure game of all time.  It's one of my favorite horror games now, too, and I enjoyed it more than SOMA since BONE TOTEM's narrative is on par with that great game AND it has better puzzles and characterization.  I know that not everyone is into this type of game, but this one may still appeal to you because it doesn't have the pixel hunting and moon logic puzzles that other adventure games often have. The ping system is really useful at helping you figure out where to go and it also partitions the game's descriptive narration so that you don't have to listen to a character go on for several minutes.  Indeed, BONE TOTEM's narrative felt much breezier than other adventure games I've played because of the way it's presented, so I never felt like any parts in it were a slog.  Having to manage three different characters is also easy.  Day of the Tentacle was the first adventure game I played that featured this, but you had to share items by going back to the time machine.  BONE TOTEM, however, uses a quantum storage device that allows you to transfer items immediately.  The story is definitely BONE TOTEM's best feature. While I was able to predict some events, others managed to surprise me and there were still twists and turns up until the very end.  While there is no reason to replay the game, I most likely will just to experience the story again.  I didn't think that modern day adventure games would ever match the classics from decades ago, but STASIS: BONE TOTEM has thankfully proven me wrong.  I'm greatly looking forward to playing BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION next.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Atmospheric and packed with detail and top notch voice acting.
