_childDocuments_.review: I've scrapped my old review as I feel it was rushed and don't feel I accurately got my love for this game across. Draft 2.I've played all 3 of the games in the stasis universe, the first being excellent, Cayne gets a bad rap (from a particular knight on youtube) but I don't know why, a free game that fleshes out the dark universe and despite what others say I kind of liked the voice actor for Hadley, her flippant attitude was more endearing to me than irritating. The third entry, Bone Totem, blows both of these out of the water.Graphically this is a huge step forwards, the scenery art, the character designs and animations are amazing and immerse you in the story. On the scenery front you'll be exploring a wide variety of environments that all blend together seamlessly. They're eerie and abandoned but still feel lived in, even with it being set in the future areas are familiar enough that you can picture how these places operated when fully staffed. I'm racking my brain to pick a favourite area but I can't, each has a unique feel...nope, I love them all and as you progress you'll constantly be wondering where you'll be taken next.I'll not go into the story too much, in fact, not at all, play the game. Needless to say I finished this in 2 sittings, it would have been 1 had I not fallen asleep at 4am during the first sitting. It hooks you early and the pacing makes it very hard to put down. As the game took me about 16 hours I'd recommend starting the game around 8am, then you'll be hooked and entertained for the day. Scifi Lovecraft gets me every time.The music and sound design is brilliant, background ambience will keep you on edge and the musical scores fit perfectly elevating the emotion of the story, or building tension as you progress. The highlight is the voice acting, I can't emphasise this enough. I've enjoyed the voice acting across the anthology, even the cheesy stuff, never took me out of the first and second game, but Bone Totem... it's something I'd expect from a triple A title (a good one). Without spoilers upon starting the game I was hesitant about the characters; Charlie, Mac and Moses. I made the mistake of judging a book by its cover, I rolled my eyes at the cliche tragic backstory and its impact on interactions between the 3 main characters, and when Moses was introduced I thought "here we go, the annoying side character". I have never 180'd so hard in my life. 15 minutes into the game and their backstory had weight, the character interactions were meaningful, and by the end I genuinely cared for and was fully invested in each (as well as characters you meet along the way). The writing is superb and the ability of the actors to convey emotion...chefs kiss. No cheese, not a slice of Camembert in sight. The conversations, even throw away dialogue, made the characters feel real. The way lines are delivered...I felt sad when they were sad, or scared or tense when they were, and this was all through the acting combined with such a well written script.I was going to give Moses his own little section here, a character who I initially disliked, but later found to be the most compelling character in the game. Alas, I shall not, play the game because my description will not do the character justice.Negatives? No, none. I did encounter one bug that....erm...happened right before the final cut scene and stopped me finishing the game. Why is this not a negative? Well I hopped on to steam discussions and made a post to see if anyone had a fix, ended up in the Brotherhood discord and my file was fixed within 15 minutes. Please note that I bought this game on the day of release so I'd very much doubt you'll encounter the bug. After finishing the game I was watching the credits and realised that the two gentlemen providing me with tech support were in fact the leads at Brotherhood and had made the 3 games I have completed multiple times and will do so again, which left me starstruck and I was immediately spamming my friends about it, which unfortunately fell on deaf ears as they all suffer from league of legends. Que sera, I was hyped about it though!The end. To summarise I hope the devs didn't see my first review - on a weekend in a hungover state I had thought to myself "oh I best pop a positive review on steam as a thank you for making such art and fixing my game" and proceeded to shart out 2 sentences that boiled down to "cool game lol". I hope my revised review better reflects my feelings about the game, and I shall sleep with a clear conscious. Bone Totem is my current gold standard for adventure games, and I eagerly await their next project so I can immediately wishlist it and buy it on day of release.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Infuriatingly hard without a step-by-step. I mean, rage-inducing. It doesn't go all out with stupidity like most 90s era adventure games, but I did find the logic of this puzzle or that puzzle still maddening.I am 100% positive nobody on Earth can beat this game without a walkthrough. OK, I am probably wrong, as I remember being able to defeat Myst back in the day sans walkthrough, but this game? AWG.I have to take it in small doses, with the walkthrough right by my side.However, despite this griping, the story is not to be missed. The story (so far) gives the difficulty a free pass.

Great atmosphere and story, and a great addition to the Cayne Universe. Cayne reign... Can't wait for the next game in this universe.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent horror adventure game narrative and a great sequel to the original all aspects have been improved from voice acting which between the characters carries the story amazingly to the models and backgrounds which are now 3D for the most part if you liked stasis or games about horror under the sea this is an absolute recommend
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: This game is perfect for people that like the Sci-fi horror type genre. The story is really interesting and had me reeled in from the beginning. You will need to read all the logs to fully understand what's going on because the dialogue alone is not enough. Graphics are excellent, a huge improvement compared to the first Stasis. The game is also very well optimized and all characters are very likable.My only issue with Bone Totem and all other Brotherhood games, are that certain puzzles and some parts of the game can be extremely ambiguous. Unfortunately, this causes me to get stuck quite often, which does interrupt the gameplay and immersion. It's also the only series of games that I need a walkthrough video queued up in the background so that I can figure out how to proceed. For the most part though, I'll get past that within a couple minutes and can continue on with the game for a while before having it happen again. Overall, I still really enjoyed the story so I think it's worth a playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I hate this game's puzzles so much. It all started with finding a code for the Chimera Storage Unit. I got frustrated, so I used the hint system and was given a hint to look through the documents. In other words: explore. After realizing that I must pay attention to the tiniest details, I continued playing, slowly solving more complex puzzles. But then I arrive to a part where I need to burn away bodies blocking my path. I had a lighter. But it would not do anything. I got stuck for ten minutes and finally used another hint. This was my hint: "I need to find a way to burn the bodies". This pissed me off, because I already knew that and tried desperately to get the lighter to work. I thought the game bugged out until I got bored and started combining random items. Turns out, you have to combine the lighter with a sampler of fluids, turning it into a flamethrower! Jeez, game, I wish that was more obvious! You couldn't've just told me that I needed to combine the lighter with something!But this was what made me quit and uninstall. There is a puzzle that requires you to use bio-engineering or something like that. Basically, we need to extract DNA from a creature and an egg to make it become male. I lost my mind over this puzzle. And the hint guide only kicked me in the balls when all it told me was: "You need to use the correct genes to make it male, dumbass. Look at the research notes." And the research notes don't offer any insight or clues on what genes you should be extracting. A bunch of genes are highlighted, and you're only genuine hint is "Start with A1". This puzzle is confusing, and if I have to look up a guide to solve puzzles, then-- I'm sorry-- but you made a bad game. Signalis had some tough puzzles, but there were enough clues in the environment and documents. I'd never looked up the answers to any puzzles in that game, and some of those puzzles took me a solid ten minutes to figure out; but I never got frustrated, because there was enough clues to help guide me to the right answer.There were other moments in the game that ticked me off, but these three I just explained really got to me.Besides the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzles, the game is great! But the fun and interest to keep going was sucked out of me from some of these annoying puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I got this off the recent Humble Bundle, and just going to say upfront that I hesitated buying this game due to hearing that it has AI Art. After learning they listened and switched them out, I was only happy to support such a great decision.I could probably talk about all the little things I loved about this game, but what I will say is that it is a major improvement over the first game in all areas, from puzzles, to voice acting, to story, to visuals. And despite a messy, but very enjoyable story, where I came to love the story most was in the characters and their dynamics, how they develop over the course of the game as they keep helping the other progress further on their paths. And the ping function is the best addition. I hope it's kept for future titles, as it made the bulk of my frustration with the first Stasis just disappear. This is a fantastic horror game that is worth playing. Not jump-scary at all, but something that will horrify you with its visuals. It took me a good 12 hours to beat it, and I don't regret any of them.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think this game did anything I didn't like. The atmosphere and artstyle are cohesive, immersive and incredibly well made. The characters are not only believable but also really captivating. The story goes through many plot twists and turns without ever getting boring and respects the player's intelligence. The puzzles and interactions for the most part make sense (I feel like there's still some slightly moon-logicky parts, but way less than I'm used to from the point-and-click genre).The sound design is spot on as well. I think if you don't mind body horror/gore you're doing yourself a disservice NOT playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is solid and doesn't fall into the adventure game trap of trying every item in your inventory on every object. A lot of care and thought has clearly gone into the world concept and it shows constantly in how characters interact with each other and the things they encounter. Handles its big reveals extremely well and paces its conclusion pretty much perfectly. Everything you could want in a horror/adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: There are traces of those 90's macabre Point & Click PC adventure games in Bone Totem.A great sf/horror story with no sugar coating, borrowing from Alien, Event Horizon, The Descent... with a technical lore that leans more on europeans biopunk comicbooks aesthetics than the blands and generics Hollywood SF universes we see in countless games nowadays.The puzzles are quite fair and, most of the time, logic-driven. It's not perfect, but the ambiance and story alone are what constitute a must play for fans of sf/horror and point & click puzzle games in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: An old-style point and click adventure with horror style "edgy" setting and "edgy" happenings. If that is what you are looking for, you will likely be very happy with it because it does deliver on those things very well. The atmosphere is done very well particularly in how the characters interact with it (or their outlandish lack of sane world reactions to the madness around them). The voice actors do a very good job of not making the rather delicate mix of feelings of the characters throw you off as ridiculous.Direction of tone and consistency are therefore the strong points of this game, as are the beautifully horrid environments you go through. The gameplay mostly consist of traditional puzzles, which appear to be on the more understandable side as far as point and click adventures go. The addition of multiple characters to explore with in-between, the gentle nudges via hints as well as the beautiful interfaces with the guarantee that you never use your items outside them keep the amount of bruteforcing low. Nevertheless, an impatient player will likely try to mash tomatoes in a severed cable to somehow fix them which does happen.The first weak point of the game - oddly enough considering the good direction of setting - appears to be the use of AI generated content that is prone to stand out. When you notice that something is AI generated your immersion suffers, and as some puzzles rely on you getting clues from artwork you may begin to feel cheated. What part of this is artificial horror pads made by a tin brain, and which part is carefully placed for me to find? Second is a plot that starts fantastically but ends in a rather predictable manner, if fitting for the setup. As previously mentioned the characters hint at a mature writer, but the overall direction of the story does not seem to follow. Nevertheless, the voice acting performance should be sufficient to make up for it and get many people a satisfaction in certain character developments throughout the game.All in all, this is a very good old style point and click horror game, it promises to be disgusting and bloody and it delivers solidly.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed just about everything about this game. I highly recommend using one of the Steam Guides to get through some of the puzzles if you get stuck like I tend to do. There is a hint system but there is an achievement to not use the hints. Took me about 8 hours or so to beat.I am a very smart bear.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun point-and-click adventure dripping in horrific atmosphere. Don't let the isometric perspective fool you - this is a classic adventure game through and through. Collecting items, studying clues, combining doodads, and solving puzzles is the focus of the gameplay. The unique gimmick is that you control three playable characters who all share the same inventory, with two of them having special abilities to interact with items. This means you'll often be collecting items with character A that character B can combine into a puzzle solution for character C. It's a fun wrinkle, but I'd say the main draw of Bone Totem is its relentlessly unsettling atmosphere and grotesque imagery. It crams a ton of horror influences into its playtime, touching on a bunch of different archetypes that're sure to tickle your fancy if you're a fan of the genre.The puzzles are for the most part very enjoyable and do a great job of utilising the environment in fun ways without getting too abstract. Some bamboozle you with information to trick you into overthinking them, others reward scraping through logs, a few require paying attention to visual clues, while a handful are fairly self-explanatory logic puzzles. None of them particularly blew my mind, and a couple disappointed me when I accidentally brute forced them before figuring out the internal logic, but none felt so obtuse or specific as to be unfair. The only point of genuine frustration I ran into (and the only time I ended up consulting a walkthrough) was ironically not because of a puzzle, but a UI interaction I had no idea existed because it was excluded from the tutorial. To spare yourself my pain: there is a point in the game where you'll have to use an item *on* one of your characters by dragging it over their portrait.The story is the other main component of the game, and it's also an overall positive, though slightly mixed bag. The atmosphere and the mystery are by far the most compelling aspects. Unearthing spooky revelations as you delve deeper into the depths is a strong motivator to keep pushing you forward. The playable cast have solid if slightly simple personalities and some basic character arcs to play out. Everything is very serviceable, and while the climax is nothing spectacular, it provides a decent conclusion to the story that echoes a lot of the classic horror movies it draws inspiration from.My only substantial criticism of the game would be that it's fairly overwritten. It's not too intrusive for the mid portion (which is by far the best), but characters have a habit of pausing gameplay to deliver dialogue that serves little purpose other than to repeat information the player already knows or drop exclamations like, "Oh God," "I can't believe this..." "What the hell is that?!" etc. At times it feels like every step of progress triggers a response like this. At least half of them could've been cut without losing anything of value and the pacing would've been much better for it. The personnel logs you read are incredibly verbose for what they contain, and many of them are exploding with an aggressive amount of authorial voice that feels like a writer trying to punch up a character's personality rather than a natural diary a real person would've written. The environmental descriptions also suffer from a lot of purple prose that reads like someone flipping through a dictionary to replace every word with an unconventional alternative. Fortunately the dialogue has firmer footing, and the voice cast do a great job of delivering their lines. Don't let this criticism turn you off too much - at its core there's an engrossing horror premise here and a lot of cool world building alongside some likeable characters and endearing performances. The execution is just a little ropey, like an explosion of creativity that needs a good pruning by an editor to tighten it up into something truly great.Overall, this is probably one of the best pure adventure games I've played in recent years. The atmosphere is stellar, the visuals evoke the unsettling, low-framerate horror games of the nineties, and it'll keep your brain tickled all the way through. A very solid eight out of ten, and definitely something I'd love to see more of.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I played the original stasis when it came out because it had clunky & obtuse gameplay that hampered its great atmosphere. I'm happy to say this one is a completely different beast, one of the best adventure games I have played and a truly unique game that everyone should try : - The art direction is stellar, with each screen bursting with macabre details & world building details- The plot and narration are very cleverly told, because the game trust its players to understand things by themselves while still giving satisfying conclusions to each of its mysteries. It's a frightening, sad and sometimes really beautiful story that really hits you hard- The puzzles are clear and logical, and the devs even had the kindness to write their own game guide for people who might get lost- Voice acting is really great especially for such a small size gameCan't praise this game enough, it's really a gem of craftmanship made by very talented & dedicated people, can't wait to see what they come up with next
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Stasis: Bone Totem is an excellent sequel to Stasis, improving on the previous game in basically every way. With an interesting plot that stays engaging throughout its roughly 10-12 hour runtime this is an incredibly dark journey with some surprisingly touching moments along the way.In a point-and-click adventure game the story needs to be strong to carry what can sometimes be somewhat simple gameplay. And the pitch black sci-fi horror of Bone Totem kept me working through every puzzle so that I could get further and see what fresh terrors were around the next corner. And being an isometric puzzle game Bone Totem doesn't rely on jumpscares and instead builds up a delightfully tense atmosphere through its excellent art direction and sound design.There are a few points where the game's limited budget shines through, but for the most part I found Bone Totem to be a smooth -if disturbing!- ride from beginning to end. And while some puzzles were quite tricky they never reached the moon logic of the genre's worst examples.All in all Stasis: Bone Totem is an easy recommend for fans of point-and-click adventure games and science fiction horror.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a big leap in the right direction from the previous two Stasis games. On the negative side, it gets a little talky at times, but if you're into that then good for you. However, the graphics are great, the story is immersive enougn, the difficulty was just right (no need to google stuff) and it was actually a lot longer than I thought it would be. Very recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: game great, buy buy buyThis game is wonderful.  It improves on so much from it's prequel, STASIS.  Sci-fi horror point and click adventure game.  Lasted over 10 hours. Click things, examine flavour text, interact with anything of interest, they may have something you need.  Solve puzzles either with items you collect or via clues scattered across the enviroment.   You play as 3 characters throughout the whole game, swapping between them to progress and make use of their specific tools via special means (one takes things apart, the other puts things together).  The puzzles were fine.  Some left me a little stumped but I got through the game without using a guide so I reckon that's the sign of well made puzzles.  (I am a smooth brain whose brain only gets smoother with each passing day, so I reckon most of you will likely have an easier time than I had)While I had a difficult time keeping up with certain aspects of the story, names and lore, (Need to start writing things down ovo'') it was great.  I got hooked in as soon the characters came across the first corpse.  The story is a lot more character driven this time round which I thoroughly enjoyed.  The supporting characters were also wonderful.Visually, it's gorgeous.  The environmental details paired with the fact that the characters torches can light up areas in a very convincingly real added so much to it's depth.  The character models look fantastic and fit in almost perfectly.  All the items you collect looked so good, all the wear-and-tear details etc.  The characters get their own personalised UI's too which was a splendid detail. Soundtrack was great.  Audio effects were great.  Vocal performances were great.  I especially appreciated how the music was tweaked depending on which character you were currently in control of. My only issue/gripe/dislike would have to be the characters animations in the CGI cutscenes.  They can look a bit off with some of their movements.  Facial expressions might not convey what they probably should, the lip sync was a bit off and looked pretty unnatural a-lot of the time.  It managed to take me out just a little which was unfortunate.  I totally get that it's a small team/limited budget etc.  It's a minor gripe.  Everything else about the game I loved.  I don't have any other problems with the game.I am aware of the AI imagery.  I have no clue if it was 100% replaced or if anything of the sort still lingers.  Other than the talking heads, i'm not 100% if they are still AI generated or not, I didn't notice anything.  I understand some of the boons to making use of AI generated content in games, but I feel it takes away far too much for it to be worth doing.  Just my opinion.Moses is best boy, very smart and extremely brave.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing point-and-clicks as far back as King's Quest I, and I have to say, this modern version of the genre with 3D cinematics; wonderfully developed, voice-acted characters; a long, gripping story; and lots of optional but very descriptive environmental elements really drew me in. I thoroughly enjoyed watching the story unfold, and enjoyed all the puzzles. My girlfriend accompanied me on this playthrough and she fell in love with the bear Moses. She also cried a few times throughout the story which made me appreciate how endearing the characters are. We read every log together and really enjoyed the atmosphere they created. Definitely looking forward to their next game!
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome. My best recommendation. Play Statis (first game) first, then Cayne, then this. Also, don't read about it too much. Immerse yourself and get lost in the story. This series is so good and to watch how the developers grow with each game is very cool. If you are mostly a FPS or ARPG player, this game may not be for you. But, story-based  and puzzle lovers, you will be pleased.

_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: The atmosphere, environments, narrative and (for the most part) puzzle solving are great and enjoyable. The sense of discovery as you read more and more about this place and what happened is amazing. My one gripe is that by the last quarter of the game, the puzzles either just feel like progression gates (where you need an item you haven't got yet from another character), or really obscure logic that doesn't feel rewarding when solved. Sometimes you just need to brute force your way through these things. Game builds amazingly, but in the end falters a little bit when it's trying to get you through all these locations and just gating progress.

_childDocuments_.review: Can not say this enough: if you have not played the game, PLAY IT.This game is a 10/10 from me. Even after a month since I first played it, I'm thinking about this game ALL THE TIME. The story is amazing and left me actually tearing up at bits. _childDocuments_.review: Presentation: 1/2Sound, music and voice are perfect and working together with the graphics department to convey a game overflowing with mistery and a creepy atmosphere. The only issue here is that it was very clear that a lot of AI generated artwork and facial animations on the PDA logbooks and I found those very distratcting and it took me out from the experience a lot of times.Length: 2/2Around 10 hours to finish. Lots of puzzles and awesome character moments sprinkled throughout. I felt the ending coming and it delivered on time. Gameplay: 1/2It's a modern take on old school point and click adventure games and I hope it comes from stay. Gone are the times where things are so cryptic that you'd need extra guides to figure out where to go next. The game is very straightforward in this aspect and it respects your time and intelligence. I however, had to check online a couple of times to figure out where to go or what to do BUT, upon seeing the answer, it was very clear that it was it was nothing but skill issue on my part. Failing is fun and the devs know this, as most of the achievements are dedicated for the multiple ways you can die during the game. If you die the game resumes immediately before the scene, so you barely lose a second or so. If only BG3 had a good autosave system and fast loading times...I'm deducting one point here due to critical, time sensitive moments that were hindered by a lot of expository / pointless dialogue. This happened very close to the end of the game, which was annoying as it broke a lot of my immersion.Story: 2/2♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Characters, worldbuilding, dialogue, twists. All top shelf, good stuff is here.Last Impression: 2/2I'll be thinking of Stasis bone totem for a long time. I'm considering playing the previous game in the series as well. I have started thinking of running a TTRPG campaign set in the bottom of the ocean. We'll see.Uniqueness: 1/21 point here because the story, characters and circumstances felt very fresh to me. I was invested in wanting to see where would the characters go to and it was very satisfying and surprising to see the story unfold. Truly a masterclass in storytelling here.Total Score: 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: This is a bummer, because I really enjoyed Stasis and Cayne. I simply cannot see this game sufficiently to play it. There are a thousand options to tweak in the menus, but bafflingly there isn't a simple brightness or gamma adjustment. So I'm staggering around in inky blackness, just dragging my character along all walls both in the hope of finding something interactive/collectible and simply to divine where the exits are to any room. Triple this confounding and unsatisfying feeling because it's guesswork as to which of the three (so far, maybe there are even more later) protagonists I should be playing as at any given time to stumble through the dark, and this game wore my patience away quickly. When I finally buckled after a half-hour of fruitlessly banging around in the dark, and I went to a walkthrough for a hint, it described a bunch of things I hadn't seen at all. Evidently I was supposed to have collected a depleted power cell? Great. Good to know. I'm not going to scrape along every edge of the environment trying to search for it any longer.

_childDocuments_.review: Now, to preface this review — something I rarely do — it must be said that this game is gross. Not just gross, but distressing, nauseating and genuinely hard to stomach at times. But unlike many other artistic takes on all things gross and slimy, solely to perturb and unsettle, like needlessly gory B-movies or over-the-top graphic novels (looking at you, Garth Ennis), Stasis: Bone Totem somehow makes it... well, tolerable would be a stretch, but it becomes somewhat understandable for this chosen medium and story. Filmmaker David Cronenberg's stuff (and his son's) always kind of pushed the limits of what is acceptable viewing, which many moviegoers might find fault in, and The Brotherhood (the developers of STASIS), I think, have done something very similar to this medium with this game.It's hard to settle on why the disgusting moments in this are easily hand-waved away (at least by me) as not simply shock-gore, but I believe it's because the Bischoff brothers established a world, even through their previous titles, where such terrible things happen infrequently enough not to be considered common, but not rarely enough for their veracity to be questioned. The world ushered in by Cayne's rebirth is cruel, fosters and engenders cruelty, and so cruelty is expected; the rules for this universe are established and followed, a facet of world-building on which many fail to follow through. I particularly like the avenue they took with establishing the umbrella corporation as a new, modern religion, one that promises a more tangible afterlife, despite its empty promises. There can be a lot of commentary between the lines, though never outright debated or spoken of in the game. Perhaps not subtle, but it's there.Depicted in this story are events and experiences frankly so inhuman and downright alien that it beggars belief, yet are presented to the player and characters as if, by some byzantine and backward logic, they make total sense. Given the facts and stories of those who suffer them, there are few leaps the player cannot make, both in the story and the mechanics. Sometimes, very rarely, the puzzles can be a little obtuse, requiring a bit of lateral thinking, but nothing like the extremes of this studio's earlier release, CAYNE.The characters — Charlie, Mac, Moses, and more — are believable, earnest when they need to be, taciturn when the scene demands, and it's all brought together by a great performance (in my opinion) by the voice actors. The audio mixing, though, got a little grating after a while, with almost every inhale and exhale peaking the in-game radio's mic during dialogue. Few scenes drag too long, which is a blessing in some audio performances. Flashbacks are a tired cliche at this point, but Stasis: Bone Totem handles them well by keeping them scarce, short, and mercifully bare enough not to belabour the point that, yes, these characters have a tragic backstory.The sound design and music are incredible, so thank you, Mark Morgan, for that. This is something the Brotherhood has always done well, I think, and that legacy carries over here. Each character has differing ambient sounds, most notably Moses, the AI toy bear, who has eerie lullaby music playing softly among the plaintive wails and screams of the damned. Creepy ♥♥♥♥.I'll also hold it here to mention that, in most video games, the added notes, PDAs, audio logs and various scribbles add very little to anything, a tasteless spice that just complicates a recipe. But in STASIS, there are almost no superfluous or extraneous accounts to be found. Each log and message speaks of some horrid aspect in this world, either by the direct influence of these things below the surface or the wandering left hand of the hegemonic employer. Some employees of this deep sea research station, so deeply in debt to the corporation, establish a gambling ring, betting on stolen sampling drones, leading to the ultimate failure of the self-destruct sequence. Or another worker, badly burned in their debt repayment, receives word that they are not sufficiently burned enough to warrant evacuation and treatment, so they abandon safety concerns until they are so disfigured they may leave. Or the maddening scrawls of survivors and what "sins they committed" to live so long. Hidden in most of these are the various hints and keys needed to solve most of the games puzzles. I read them all, or at least, all I could find. As gross as they can be, I loved them.The pacing of the story works well, blending seamlessly with the character-switching mechanic, so that each area and situation requires help from one another, even when separated. It never seems to drag, and each new area reveals darker truths about this place.The Brotherhood also expanded on the formula for CAYNE by including more rendered cinematics. They are shown very close to characters faces, which, I assume, was to impress a sense of claustrophobia or maybe hide animation issues. Unfortunately, this hindered some cutscenes, and it's hard to tell what happened visually. They are very short, so it's not hard to intuit, but still.Overall, this is what horror should strive to be. Maybe not all the time, but in projects like this, stories like this, it's not jump scares or chase scenes that instill terror; it's hoplessness, it's loss. It's being so far from home that you'd prefer the storm to what every port has to offer.If future releases by the Brotherhood continue to excel and improve at this rate, boy howdy, I don't think we're prepared for that.

_childDocuments_.review: The Bischoff brothers hold the highest quality mark, creating something that can already be called their corporate identity, while captivating with novelty and unexpected ideas. The guys make their games for a long time and painstakingly, but how much does the final result live up to expectations. And the definition of "handmade" fits their games perfectly. Bone Totem takes us back to the dark universe of their previous games, where body horror has sank its teeth into the sci-fi fiction of Peter Watts and Alastair Reynolds, while also crashing into the seething dark cult beliefs of a crazy future. I was again convinced that the authors know how to write science fiction, they know how to grope for the line beyond which body horror begins to be vulgar torture porn and stops working for the atmosphere. The game is 13-17 hours long and it's the purest hours of gameplay and storytelling. No tricks to tighten the timing, almost no backtracking, with excellent character development and deep-sea setting.The creators undertook a rather ambitious task, because we simultaneously play for three characters - experienced Mac and Charlie, and the creepy robo-bear Moses, whom you begin to love in just 5 minutes. And they coped with the task, taking into account the difficulties that you will face as much as possible a player who controls three different characters at once in three different locations. The maximum convenience for the player is provided - items can be transferred between characters very quickly, the special characteristics of the characters are clear and intuitively applied. And in general, the puzzles in the game are logical, in some places extremely difficult, requiring attention and study, the inventory is very rarely overloaded, all items will be used one way or another for passing. The character work is just brilliant. They are adults, they are wounded inside, but not broken, they are responsible for their actions, they do not hysteria for no reason, but they try to solve the situation in the ways that they have. There's more life in robo bear than some whole huge games, seriously. You empathize with such heroes, with them you want to go through even the most difficult path to the end. What I didn’t like was the search for collectibles. For 14 hours, I still didn’t understand how to look for them, either you step on them, or you have to physically take them, they don’t give anything particularly valuable (except for the achievement), so I pretty quickly abandoned it. Searching for journals and records is an almost identical activity, but how much more interesting and reveals the world of the game.I am impressed. This is a real gift for fans of dark science fiction, in which everything is worked out to the smallest detail. The guys have talent, any of their new project will immediately become one of the most anticipated games for me. Bravo!
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think there's anything I can say that can top MandaloreGaming's review of the game, but if you're somewhat hesitant about the issues raised in that review regarding AI, you can be rest assured that all AI art has now been scrubbed from the game. One thing I can say though is that when playing this, have a pen and paper ready, because you will certainly need it. I can also see why he thought the removal of AI art was a necessity for the preservation of the game's overall artistic fidelity, since a lot of art and lore found in the game clearly have a lot of thought put into it, and the addition of AI art for jibberish is just stuffing that's overall detrimental to the game's overall purpose.That said, I tend to not have the motivation to bother with leaving reviews (thanks, depression), but I highly recommend this game. I'm not a horror fan, I'm doubly horrified of sci-fi horror specifically (thank you, The Thing), yet despite that, this game's story just had a lot of heart that I couldn't really stop, another thing I didn't expect was for this game to actually get me to teary on a lot of moments, which is something you don't really expect from horror in general. One thing though that isn't mentioned in Mandy's review that I believe contributes to the game's strong narrative is the inclusion of Olga Moskvina in the writing team. For those unaware, she was also a writer for a similar game you might know called Disco Elysium.

The characters are great though, and when the ending hits it hits hard. There's so many different elements in the world created here and the mix of it all works fantastically well.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 10 hours into the game now and have utterly lost interest. Some of the puzzles it seems, cannot be worked out logically - I reached a brick wall with one of them and have had to look at a walkthrough for the answer. Looking at the answer, I feel I could have played for another 10 hours and not reasoned it through. The game seems to reward the player for just fiddling with things randomly until a solution is found; I've found several solutions this way even before I've worked out what the puzzle is. I started off initially enjoying the game before I realised it's limitations. The only desire I have to finish the game now is just for a completionist tick, but that's not enough and I'm going to happily walk away from this one.The gameplay and interface is clunky and revolves around walking from one interactive object to another and 'fiddling'. The character movements are painfully slow at times, especially underwater. The scenes look quite nice though almost all of it is non interactive and incidental.The plot and gamestyle is fairly cliche ridden and sits somewhere between H.P.Lovecraft, Alien and The Thing. The characters are standard fare - clever female scientist and idiotic annoying male.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting story with difficult puzzles, Lots of body horror, and gore, you need to be fine with quite a bit of reading. The cutscenes are probably the weakest bit but for a small team doing 3d animations. but the static art and environments are great. Lovecraft and Geiger were most likely influences
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely good adventure game made with beautiful chunky pre-rendered art. Puzzles offer a nice challenge, with every solution eliciting an exciting rush of endorphins. The items and gadgets are wonderfully creative. The three character system is a joy to use and cleverly evokes "Day of the Tentacle". STASIS is a hidden gem! And the best point and click adventure to come out since the genres former days of glory.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the previous statis games I was not disappointed by Bone Totem.It's simply a great sci-fi horror adventure, like reading a great book!I was afraid that the introduction of multiple characters would make it cumbersome but the system works really well and it's very nice to see how the characters experience the story with different perspectives.Wish there were more games like this!
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Slow and plodding and not always the easiest puzzles, but, in my book, those don't count as negatives! No, you get an interesting story and characters and plenty of enjoyment for your money, if you're into more classic, isometric puzzlers. Personally, I like the graphics as well: it all looks good and highly detailed, but without the typical modern trend of bombarding the players with non-stop, flashy effects.I'll have to check out the developers' other games, I think, and add them to my watch list.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful story in a bonkers, disgusting near future, and one hell of a ride.I think the game is a rough diamond that in many ways punches way above its weight class.It's not perfect, but the faults are by and large relatively superficial blemishes that are easy to forgive and look past, and more importantly the developers deserve all the support to reach even higher next time.I'm not even going to list said faults, because I don't think they hold the game back.Just try it for yourself and you'll probably agree!Instead I'll just quickly mention the highlights:- the story, screenplay/script and emotional core- fantastic voice performances- art direction and environments, lighting and integration- Moses, easily front-runner for best bear of the decade
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: This again proves that small passion projects manage to consistently deliver better games in terms of story, gameplay, and overall quality than today's AAA industry in many cases. It is kind of funny because this game would've completely gone unnoticed by me if not for GOG's newsletter, and I am really glad that I've stumbled upon this game.The game's atmosphere draws you in immediately upon arriving on DEEPSEA 15 as you discover what happened to this seemingly abandoned oil rig in the middle of the ocean. The story is intriguing and keeps you in suspense as you discover what really happened through reading PDAs left by the missing crew and character dialogues. The puzzles range from very easy ones to very complicated ones, divided between 3 playable characters that must help each other in order to proceed further into the story. Characters are well written, and their evolving dynamic throughout the story keeps you engaged and, quite frankly, makes you like them more and more. The art is fantastic and accompanies very well the atmosphere and setting of this game. At times, the CGI was a bit goofy, but it portrays well the situation that is happening on screen.During the whole playthrough, I only encountered one bug which was quickly resolved with the help of the developers on their discord who are, by the way, very friendly and passionate about this game.If you like games such as Pentiment or Disco Elysium with a SOMA/Alien twist mixed in there, I definitely recommend this game.Voice actors really nailed the characters of Moses and Faran.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with the game thoroughly. Some issues can be found like one grammar error, one puzzle is bugged and the timed sound effects don't always work correctly +   silly things that seem like mistakes to me.The story had some good moments and elements. Characters have enough meat around their bones for you to care at the end which is nice for a game I bought for Lovecraftian vibes.The puzzle minigames are pretty okay but relay on giving vague hints sometimes so you'll fiddle around longer. Once you know the rules it becomes a puzzle for a 5 year old. Other puzzles I found mostly satisfying but won't deny I started to throw my whole inventory at a problem or tried to smash the inventory or tried to mix the inventory up together. Sometimes the story would only continue by walking around which would trigger a cut scene, these parts waste your time because most likely you just think that you are missing something from a puzzle and keep throwing your inventory at random puzzles until you look up a guide and realize you had to walk 2 meters that way to trigger a scene.The art is great and the environments are grimy and moody. Most things here are off putting (in a good way) even our beloved bear. The environments also have text pieces attached to them describing different items and parts visually like in a book, I appreciate the time that was used writing these texts but honest to god there is too many of them and they more likely end up being distracting.I would say a must recommend for click and point enjoyers and for others I will mention the game but won't force it on them.And I must mention that this isn't a horror game, really. I'm a wuss but I didn't feel even an ounce of piss in my pants.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the first game for all it's faults and in many ways this is a massive improvement over the first in terms of graphics an puzzle design. Where it really falls off is the storyline and characters as well as general pacing. If I have to read one more PDA again, I'd peel the flesh off my own face too. The game seems determined to prevent you from simply enjoying the environments and atmosphere with endless dialogue from the characters and insanely front loaded exposition. Towards the end of the game you literally can't take two steps without several characters chiming in and dragging the pacing of the game to a total halt. It really feels like the writers had a hundred ideas they wanted to toy with and just decided to use them all, by the time I reached the end I just found the story exhausting.I wanted to like this game and I was enjoying it the first half, the writers just need to get out of their own way and let the horror speak for itself. Prediction Accuracy 100%.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very well made game. The world-building and the story was just as impressive. The plot is really thought provoking, as well as the ending. I would definitely recommend it. Another thing I would recommend is reading through the achievements if you're not a fan of replaying the game, but it's good for a replay once you know the story.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: STASIS: BONE TOTEM is an engaging, bone-chilling, and gruesome horror adventure. Departing from the original space setting from the first STASIS, we now follow Mac, his wife Charlie and the toy helper Moses on what appears to be a normal ocean scavenging expedition. However, as we progress, we encounter indescribable horrors within a seemingly abandoned oil rig, hidding a secret underwater base, which a dystopic mega corporation will do anything to keep its terrors hidden. Adding beautiful visuals, and an exceptional storytelling, STASIS: BONE TOTEM is one of the most underrated gems in recent horror adventures!
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Despite leaving a negative review for the first game, I will say that the devs have improved by leaps and bounds in nearly every way. The puzzles were fair and logical, and I came to really care about the characters, significantly more-so than with Stasis 1. While I finished the first game with a feeling of relief because it was finally over, I finished Bone Totem wishing the story could continue on. That's not to say the length of the game was too short. Quite the contrary, I found the length to be just right.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic point and click adventure game with a stellar narrative and art direction. The characters are brilliant, and Moses stands out to me as one of the most interesting lads I've seen in a while. The puzzles are actually quite intuitive for the most part, though I did need to use a guide occasionally. The only complaint I have is that during conversations, you mostly just have to sit and wait before being able to interact with objects. It would be nice to do so here and there, but it's a pretty minor issue. Buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: A very good and strong continuation of the Stasis series, but not without some minor problems, where the game sags near the end. If you had played previous installments and interested in the story - buy this game and don't waste your time reading. After finishing it, return here to discuss. If you had never played previous games - give Stasis (the original) a go first, then play Cayne, if you liked it.I will make this review almost spoiler-free for anyone unfamiliar (otherwise I will place the spoiler tag), but I will critique some things in vague terms so anyone familiar may relate or argue with me.I had played all of the games by THE BROTHERHOOD, haven't finished Beautiful Desolation for some reason or the other - I will most likely revisit it or just watch a good walkthrough (It's still very memorable, unique and worth the praise). For anyone new to this - Beautiful Desolation is not connected to the Stasis universe (AFAIK) as Stasis, Cayne and this game are, so it's kind of irrelevant, but in my eyes there's something that could be said about the design, themes and bit meh dramaturgy that started in that game and seeped here.There's a problem of escalation of horror, especially in Stasis universe. The first Stasis started kind of slow and the horror element rose throughout the whole game gradually. Things go from bad to worse with the little sliver of hope shimmering in the dark somewhere. There's a strong body-horror element with the dread of existential horror that makes it's crescendo near the end. Cayne just starts "In medias res" where you are kicked and bashed from the start not even understanding what the hell is this level of insanity around you with body horror given you in bulk non-stop making previous set-pieces seem like it's nothing. The Bone Totem presents it's first set-piece almost at the very start and it looks very gruesome, almost peaking on the horror chart and then there's little way to go. You can always add more of that kind of thing, but it doesn't have the same effect, it's just more. At some point you grow accustomed to it somewhat and when your character exclaims for the hundredth time seeing something gruesome, you kind of start to wonder if this character was present in the previous 99 situations or is this a hint of early onset Alzheimer's. Also it seems that this game is just longer and much meatier in terms of story and locations, so this problem is getting pronounced.I must say that I loved the development of the universe. The story doesn't spell some things out, but some comments in broad strokes give you the hint on what's happening with the world and Cayne. More of that! Also, maybe I'm just stupid, but I realized something about two previous games that was pretty much obvious, now that I think about it, but I just thought that some experimental work  in Stasis and something you see in Cayne was just another mad-scientist-extravaganza stuff, but those projects are sort of related and are key to the overall story. Somehow i bridged that gap playing The Bone Totem although there was nothing about it in here, just very vague comments about the universe developments.Voice-acting and direction is salvageable, but there's room to grow. Nothing tops Ryan Cooper as John Marachek in Stasis. He's selling every bit of the thing all the way and even enhances the horror of the story somehow. Same can be said about Sarah Anne Williams as Hadley - the star of Cayne. Sadly, I can't say that the characters in this game are as believable or selling it appropriately, except one. I don't thing that's there's a problem with a talent, but a direction and screenwriting. There's nothing to feel when the character just exclaims "oh my god" in every situation. There's no range of emotion or some special comment. Hadley reacted in various ways: shouting, commenting and even joking about some unspeakable horror set-piece, which made her character more elevated, the story, the everything! It just blossomed like there's no tomorrow. I get that we have stoic here, so minus one to emotions It's a shame really.There's a rule in dramaturgy - show, don't tell. I must say that there's a lot of jibber-jabber with heavy exposition dumps in a latter quarter of the game. Not good. Oh, I enjoy the story - make no mistake, but I think that there must be a better method of giving it to me in this case.Another rule is to suspend the emotions of the actor to give the onus of emoting on the audience. And it's hard to emote in a scenario where horror escalated pretty much from the start, the acting is bland and the chatter is constant. Give me some room and shut up about water being not the thing that you like for Cayne's sake! 100% prediction FFS.Funny thing is that the unspoken stuff is working like a charm - I already said about the universe, but there was some moments when you, the player know or sense that some action will mark a point of no return or will have a consequences that should be avoided, but the characters don't speak about it and just proceed, and then you see those consequences blossom and make situation worse story-wise. This is great! It makes me dread the whole thing and focus even harder on that tiny shining ray of hope at the end if there's any. What's not great is spoon-feeding me the whole thing in the end constantly, on repeat. Also there's this theme and study of a two and a half societies, basically. And one society kind of mirrors the other one - there's nothing spoken in the game about it, but that's a strong theme and an interesting thought. It's a shame that writers took another angle by giving us a cameo appearance of one famous superstar and ran with it. Don't really like that and I don't thing that it worked or was warranted. Also, the stuff with the prevention of some disaster doesn't really work - the world they are in are so utopian that there's no argument in my mind about the distinction on how exactly it will go to hell. And it can't, because in some sense it's already way worse.There's a two games worth of story here. The last two chapters is spreeeeeeeeead like one spoon of butter on a baguette. It's on-rails as it can be, the puzzles make less and less sense and it's basically a movie with some clicking in-between. I was interested in the story and that's what made me push through, but man could it be trimmed heavily. And it could be said about the whole game, I'm afraid - it would be much better with less dialogue, a bit less locations, less characters. The player will lose nothing and gain much more, being present in a more concentrated story, but that's a thought for another game (hopefully)You can still expect an absolutely stellar set-pieces and locations. The writing in journals is great. Although, given that there's so much of them, the authors may have to invest in a more advanced interface in the next titles - current interface doesn't show a headshot of a person (when you reading it after) and it's easier to remember someone by his or her face rather than by name. Also some links or text search would be welcome - I like to come back to these journals to match who texted who and what was where, but it's hard to track without such features. This stuff shines.Music by Mark Morgan, again. Enough said.Some puzzles are great. I thank the authors for the hints functionality - it's good and it's a very good design.Great story still and I regret nothing!

_childDocuments_.review: This game oozes with passion and creativity. With a dark, sci-fi horror atmosphere, set at the bottom of the ocean, I cannot overstate the must-play nature for horror fans. While the writing/dialogue can be a bit utilitarian, folks should remember this is a development team of only a couple people. And I am impressed by what they manage to achieve here - from the original Stasis, to Beautiful Desolation, to Cayne, there aren't many games in their style, and Stasis: Bone Totem is well worthy of a pick-up.In an era of broken releases and half-baked high-budget games, small developers like The Brotherhood should be praised for releasing a product they clearly show passion for.
_childDocuments_.name: STASIS: BONE TOTEM

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the best games that I have played for a long, long time, an extremely good example of very fine storytelling. _childDocuments_.review: Stasis: Bone Totem is, without a doubt, my favorite horror adventure game. It nearly perfectly lands all of the important bits -- narrative, character moments, environment, and gameplay.You play as Mac and Charlie, a husband and wife running a salvaging operation. They stumble upon a deep sea oil rig and decide to investigate, as it may give them a way out of their crippling debts. Of course, this is a sci-fi horror game, and everything on the rig is terrible, both man made and not. This set up quickly evolves into a very dense narrative with tons of well done twists and turns -- most of which are excellently foreshadowed through environmental story telling or logs that are optionally available to read. The character development and overall characterizations in Bone Totem are a huge leap forward from the original Stasis. It's hard to talk about with avoiding spoilers, but I was very pleasantly surprised by how much the game made me care about some rather non-traditional characters. Bone Totem also grappled with quite a bit more philosophy than the original Stasis, though it's not quite as in your face about it as some of my other favorites like Primordia and The Swapper.The environments you explore in Bone Totem are probably the best I've ever seen in an isometric game. There's excellent and disgusting detail throughout every screen of the game, with lighting  that adds a ton to the mood. The sound design and music are all excellent, with the main characters having slightly different variations on the same themes for each section of the game -- a very nice touch. The voice acting is also top notch, making the big moments of the story hit that much harder. I'm very impressed with the presentation for an indie game with a team of this size.It's tough to land the gameplay in adventure games, but Stasis: Bone Totem delivers here too. By and large, you have your expected set of environmental and item based puzzles, which, other than a small exception or two, are very well done and help you engage with the world. There are a couple of features that really push it to being at the top of the genre, though. First is the accessibility. You can always right click to 'ping' the surroundings, revealing all descriptions and interactable objects on the current screen -- no pixel hunting necessary, if you so choose. There are also optional hints available for the puzzles like many games. Each interactable object has a separate screen that pops up for the puzzle, and all items are used in these screens, which reduces the need to try each item on every object in the environment that happens in many adventure games. The second, and more important feature, is that you are playing as multiple main characters, with inventories that are connected via the 'quantum storage device'. This gives the game a very unique and fun flow, where, if you get stuck with one character, you can switch to another. Each character also has some unique way they can interact with objects or they environment -- breaking things down, combining items, or hacking. This is both nice for variety, and allowing you to have something else to do when you're getting annoyed with a particular puzzle.Anyway, that's enough gushing about the game. If the game appeals to you at all -- give it a try. You may also come away with a new favorite.
