_childDocuments_.review: I don't really post reviews. It's not my thing. That being said there's very few games that make me feel things. This game is easily on that shortlist.A group of dev's from Chile managed to create something beautiful that AAA developers couldn't even dream of producing. It's artstyle, while grotesque at first, powerfully asserts itself and endears itself upon the you, the winding and unforgiving lands, while harrowing at first, soon become your stomping grounds, and the cast of characters are all bizarre and unforgettable.It's really unfair that this game will be slept on, I just don't see it getting any attention, and that should be a crime, because it should be receiving the same love and attention that similarly thematic indie heartthrobs such as Outer Wilds and Undertale have had the privilege of enjoying. PROS:- One of the best original scores I've heard in video games soundtracks ever.- Level and world design that I haven't seen so tight and well thought out since maybe Dark Souls 1- Interesting Yakuza meets Souls RPG/martial arts combat that manages to remain simple and straight forward, but provides enough variety so as to not get stale during the average playtime of the game (I've found the combat here to be more entertaining than that of Yakuza's personally).- A wildly beautiful multi-media mashup artstyle utilizing cellshading, faux watercolors, and extremely unique color palettes.- You are rewarded WELL for exploring as much as you can.- Hidden Mechanics you'll be discovering all throughout your entire gameplay experience.- Simple challenge curve that you can grind levels to get yourself out of if you find areas too difficult, though doing SL1 style runs appear to be both viable and pleasantly challenging.- Despite being effectively Zeno Clash 3, you should have no trouble following the plot if you're unfamiliar with the series as I was.- It's only $30 bucks, and definitely worth it, even when not on sale.CONS:- The game's title isn't exactly the easiest thing to try to sell your friends on.- There are some bugs if you get unlucky. The two most prominent are AI glitches, and getting into animations that push you out of bounds or within barrier collisions. Though the devs seem intent on identifying and rectifying them when they can.- Many would probably not consider this to have a particularly high replayability. Though as previously stated, the player could easilly challenge themself with challenge runs such as Soul Level 1'ing the game. Additionally NG+ is rumored to be introduced shortly.- No Armor Transmog. There's so much cool armor in this game but you may find yourself moving away from Fashion Clashin' in favor of armor with higher stats that you may not be entirely in love with aesthetically. ACE Team, please consider a transmog system!!!Folks, it's $30 dollars. Please owe it to yourself to give this game a chance. I admit I slept on this game for months, I simply didn't want to play it when it was first presented to me. But from the moment I hit the intro zone, I knew I was playing something really special. ClashAOC has easily became my frontrunner for GOTY, early contender for GOTD, and cemented itself in my top 20 all time games list.Thank you ACE Team. There's no way you can do a sequel, but please don't abandon the world of Zenozoik.
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing surreal game overflowing with unique style. The distinct crosshatch shading combined with the strange environments and odd characters makes for a visual experience unlike any other. I have a great appreciation for ACE Team's commitment to creating characters that look weird and have unusual anatomy. I never knew I enjoyed punching strange bird men and giant three-legged elephants to save a cute little bird child with hands. What makes the world of Zenozoik unique is that it doesn't belittle its own weirdness or have self-referential jokes that poke fun at the wacky characters. Instead, it embraces these aspects, and has the player walk through the world to unironically explore and interact with its residents.The world is wonderfully complimented by Patricio Meneses score, which is used to great effect throughout the game. Often upon entering a new area you will be treated by a new track, and these always had me slowing down and listening as I walked into a strange new forest or mountain ruins. There are elements of sound taken from the Zeno Clash games which were a delight to hear, but there were also the new vocal performances. From the primal shouting and electric guitar in 'Pseudo's theme' that makes you feel like a badass, to the soft, but dramatic, female vocals in 'The boy calls'. I heard many instruments I didn't know, and many tracks feature a gentle piano that is used sparingly but was always a nice surprise. I've put in my vote for Clash: Artifacts of Chaos in this year's WSA Game Music Awards, and I hope to see more from Patricio Meneses in the future.The story of Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is a simple one and falls into the “Strong dude protects innocent companion” trope that has been quite prevalent in popular culture recently. That’s not to say there isn’t unique elements within the narrative, but the journey and growth the main characters go through is predictable. Without going into spoilers, I did enjoy the mysterious nature of some of the older characters, who drop hints about the world beyond Zenozoik. Fans of Zeno Clash will also recognise the themes of madness and insanity that are presented through the Corwids. You meet characters affected by the lifestyle of the Corwids and it is interesting to explore how these characters rationalize the bizarre behaviour of the forest dwellers. The Corwids are a living example of the chaos that Gemini hopes to eradicate with the One Law, and throughout the story, Pseudo’s adherence to the Ritual and participation in the power struggle of Zenozoik is questioned. These aspects of the story are intriguing, but few and far between, as most of the denizens and henchmen of the perilous land seek only to fight and thwart Pseudo on his journey.Like the story, the voice performances are competent and sufficient albeit simple. There are moments that let the main characters express stronger emotions, and at times Pseudo’s strong-willed defiance and concern are genuinely touching. The Boy’s innocence and sadness are well communicated through the acting; however, the voice can be a bit overbearing at times. I’m not sure if there were issues with the recording of Boy’s voice, but at times I heard mic-peaking and overall, the voice seemed too loud without realistic reverberation. Pseudo rough and serious tone is aptly juxtaposed with the Boy’s juvenile banter, reminding me of Kratos and Atreus from God of War (2018 Overall, the npc’s talk and behave in ways believable for the world they live in, and they service the story well enough. The casting and performances in Ace Team’s games get better with every iteration. The gameplay is fun and snappy, featuring many difference stances and customization for special attacks. While it falls into the ‘third person action’ game combat category, it oddly feels more like a fighting game. I’ve seen some reviewers approaching the game with a ‘souls-like’ approach, and express frustration with the game for being too ‘punishing’ and ‘clunky’. I too become slightly frustrated with some of the earlier encounters, as I felt like enemies stunned me too much and I didn’t know how to approach fights. It wasn’t until I started treating it like a 2d fighting game that I really understood how to make the most of my abilities. You fight in close-quarters, and you don’t have any dodge-roll I-frames to protect you, so you must rely on timing your attacks and dodges around enemy movement. I applaud Ace Team for the variety in special attacks which undoubtedly came with a lot of difficult animation work, which is all brought to life with the detailed character model of Pseudo made by Felipe Diaz. Depending on how you play, Pseudo can feel like a heavy-hitting brawler, or an elegant ninja. The boss fights were a highlight for me, Moon-Sun still haunts my dreams. I found they added extra challenge and spectacle to the combat, and I was always excited to encounter Gemini’s top henchmen. Pseudo will get clobbered, thrown, and smashed into the ground by these bosses, and it forces you to become more strategic with your approach. One mechanic I fell in love with was the enemy friendly fire. Enemies can hit each other in this game which adds a new layer to the group fights which always made me laugh. Are you fighting a massive guy with wide swings? Well just let him do the work for you by positioning yourself behind the other enemies! Sometimes creatures join the fray too, randomly or through an artifact, and this just added to the chaos. The Ritual system was a big draw for me when I saw the trailers, as it offered a randomized, chaotic aspect to fights that I haven’t seen in other third-person action games. For the first half of the game, I really enjoyed this mechanic. However, as I went further into the game, I used the ritual less and less. There are some fun effects like capturing an enemy to be used in a later fight, or restraining them with a rope, but in the second half of the game, I was so strong that the ritual become redundant. Not only was I becoming bored of the effects, but playing game would always take longer than the fights themselves. In my playthrough I did a lot of exploring, and was quite thorough, so the end game fights were not very challenging. I think there are too many boons to collect on your ritual belt, and that the Ritual mechanic in general should of either been streamlined or expanded. As it stands, it doesn’t ruin the game or anything, and you can even skip the Ritual in most fights, but I do wish It was more compelling.When you’re not fighting, you will be navigating a fairly linear semi-open world with light platforming and exploration. The night-time gameplay encourages the player to backtrack and seek out various body parts which act as armor. Like the Ritual, the night mechanic overstayed its welcome for me. I became burnt out of exploring the same area twice everywhere I went. But I must commend that most of this is optional, and the night-time environments are awesome to look at, with a mysterious and surreal ambience. Pseudo and his enemies are all re-created with strange, twisted bodies of wood and shadow, which combined with the eerie music creates a disturbingly beautiful world. The progression/collection system could have been streamlined, and some of the resources felt a bit tacked on or useless. I feel that there should have been fewer resources required to upgrade a given ability, that way the player has more incentive to try difference ones. As it stands though, you could still beat the entire game without upgrading your stats and abilities. The game rewards players for exploring the strange world of Zenozoik as you go from one camp to the next.Thank you, ACE Team, for creating this underrated gem and continuing to create the weirdest, most unique worlds to explore. (Full Review will be in the discussions tab, I couldn’t fit everything here)

_childDocuments_.review: This is absolutely 100% one of my favorite games of all time. I haven't felt this way playing a game for the first time since I ran into one of those 'special games' like UNDERTALE or Secret of Mana, one of those stories that stays with you forever.This game isn't groundbreaking and never-before-seen. In fact, its story is incredibly old, one of the oldest archetypes - Lone Wolf and Cub. But it does everything so well that it is a new and to-be beloved entry in the long history of story-telling.The gameplay is a fantastic evolution of the nu-brawler that they started in Zeno Clash; it was a smart idea to transfer to mostly Third-person and use First-person for special moves and abilities. It feels much less cramped and allows the enemies to be more aggressive and animated. You can see this in-game, when you use the special FPS mode, the enemies revert to a kind of Zeno Clash AI where they stand their ground more and move slower. It's to simulate Psuedo going super-speed but still, you can tell it's because the regular gameplay in first person would be overwhelming. Good game choice.I love the world and the art direction, it's the craziest it's ever been. Everything looks more polished; and while our resident Zenos are perhaps less disgusting than they are in Zeno Clash, they are by-far and above more strange and uniquely animated, including brand new Titan sized denizens and multi-limbed mutants of the Zenozoik lands. Things are a bit smaller than the sprawling cities of Zeno clash, it's meant to make everything feel more personal and more claustrophobic. A contrast between the more untamed wilds, which should offer greater freedom, and the crushing responsibility and burdens of our heroes.The gameplay is fun, everything is punchy and powerful. It feels good to beat the crap out of everything, which is what you'll be doing for hours as the game is quite a bit longer than you might expect. A lot of games like this, even the first Zeno Clash, are maybe 3-6 hours at most, with Zeno Clash 2 being 6-8. This game is about 12-20 hours minimum, unless you know exactly where to go and who is a mandatory fight. I recommend exploring the world, or you'll miss out. Seriously, take your time, please!The special moves are interesting, and there's only maybe two moves that aren't worth using with most builds if only because they're too slow. The  are so good though you have to force yourself not to use them. I also think it was a smart idea making your first move, Spin Kick, one of the most useful in the entire game. If you don't like a move but wish you did, be sure to upgrade it with figurines. Some moves change or gain a power spike with enough upgrades!The RPG mechanics are interesting but aren't as in depth as something like a Souls game or etc. I went for a perfectly balanced build and felt very powerful by the end-game of both my first playthrough and NG+. Both of them were fantastic times and I wish I could experience it all again. I rushed through the last 20% of the game my first playthrough because I REALLY REALLY wanted to see the ending and I just couldn't wait anymore, but I used NG+ to 100% the game, as you can see in my achievements. I regret nothing and it was a grand experience.The game's voice acting is top notch; all the characters sound as crazy and unique as you'd expect from a Zeno Clash title. The VAs aren't slacking at all, the emotional weight of the story is crushing if you let yourself get invested. The depth of Psuedo and the boy's voice acting cannot be understated. Psuedo perfectly encapsulates that one Uncle or Father you had that was hard to relate with and came off as rough and intimidating, but you know he loves you and would do anything for you. The Boy is a charming and lovable - and especially BELIEVABLE - child. Listening to  broke my heart to pieces and the ending speeches will stay with me forever.There's a charm to the enemies being the same cadre of mercenaries the entire game; it both shows in-universe the unbelievably stubborn nature and physical resilience of the Zenos. It doesn't really get old either because the game isn't hiding the fact that it's the same guys every time; they bring new tactics, wait in ambush, try to hide their numbers, etc. But you just keep rolling them over. While Psuedo isn't as powerful as other Zenos for one reason or another, he's certainly not weak. Most of the Aggressive Finishers outright kill the wildlife with his bare hands. Seeing the sentient goobers get beaten into the dirt and then come back for more later with bruises on their faces is both hysterical and intimidating. Nobody in this world knows when to quit, and that's admirable in some weird way. I do wish that  was more difficult, considering his importance and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' theme tune that plays during the fight. Some people might feel that the last boss gauntlet might be a little easy, especially if you explored everything at Night Time and got all that bonus XP. But NG+ really gives their AI and stats a needed boost and will provide even the biggest grinder a satisfying conclusion. Sorry, Elden Ringers, this game doesn't have %-based damage and health - you CAN outscale the content if you're determined enough.I saw some reviews complaining about the Dice Game you can play with your enemies. I understand if it's not your thing but some reviews complain about it being mandatory. That's not true at all; the game makes you play dice maybe 4 times the entire game and two of them don't even matter. All the other dice games are YOUR choice explicitly. The dice game is very fun and even though I played it as much as possible, I was drowning in Artifacts. Don't be afraid to use them; there's never a bad time to blind all your enemies with fog and watch them kill each other.However, speaking of music. It's ALL amazing and it's ALL on spotify and youtube and they deserve a listen. Especially since in game, if you're in the flow of combat, you'll kill the boss long before the songs are over. Psuedo's two themes especially convey such power and motivation that you can't help but feel bad for your opponent.It is  that all the Zeno Clash games - but especially this one - have had difficult sales. Maybe it's the marketing, maybe it's the audiences that aren't open-minded enough to play as funny worm-guy Bruce Lee but don't let yourself miss out. Do yourself a favor and play Clash: Artifacts of Chaos today because there IS NO other game like it right now. ACE TEAM try so hard with every title and they make beautiful rough gems that are underappreciated every time. I can't wait to see what they make next and it will be a complete tragedy for gaming as a whole if they ever stop.Play the game, it's worth the money even if it's not on sale. You'll get at least a dollar an hour, and that's better than any movie, that's for sure. Don't let this one slide by.

_childDocuments_.review: I heard about this game from Iron Pineapple's Souls-like game you've never heard about, and has kept this game on my radar since. I had my doubts as many reviewers had negative thoughts on the combat and how stilted it felt. But I pushed to pass this and had a pretty well gaming experience.There are a few things you need to know which the game explains once, and you're left with your own devices. Any attacks you land can be cancelled the moment it connects with the enemy, which opens up combo opportunity and makes even the Mammoth style (the slowest style in the game) lightning fast. Any attacks that land can be cancelled, ANY (From experience anyways, there might be some that could not be).Second, don't play this game like a dark souls game, as dodging here is not a perfect evasive tool, but rather use it to extend your combos by chasing the enemy, performing directional dodge attacks, or giving yourself space to breathe. What matters is landing your first hit on the enemy, and knowing when to back off during your combo string. Most enemies could be stunned and locked to death if they know what you are doing. Third, night mode. Pseudo could just take off his skin at the tent by waking up at night. That is important as night mode allows you to open up paths (pass thorn bushes and thorn guardians) for daytime Pseudo. There are also items only available in night mode, which a handy steam guide: , helped me a lot to 100% the game. Let me be honest, the story in this game is there just so to justify fighting people. It's not deep, and the epilogue is jarring and sudden with no build-up I felt that Pseudo and the boy should have had a heart-to-heart conversation after beating up the big bad. The characters, however, are interesting. Pseudo, the boy, Npcs, and the bosses felt like individual people. Nothing to complain about here.Autosaves, are good and also a bad implementation. It's good as it means I could reload my last save so I could experiment and try some risky ideas out before having to fully commit, or reset my progress when I found my performance undesirable so I can grind out perfection. It's bad because I was soft-locked in the town due to weird interactions with the pact artifact, and the Eo cutscene didn't trigger forcing me to start a new save. And also I couldn't have a save file before a boss I like to refight. Just nitpicks and glitches.But you play this game for the combat, and the combat feels just right. You could cancel your moves into another move, a variety of special attacks which spice up your combat, and the super meter when you want to kill something. The upgrade stat "Endurance" is... negligible, but that's probably because my play style is hyper-aggression so my guard meter is always low. There is also the issue of having to fight multiple enemies at once, but most enemies usually hang back while you focus on the big guy, or you can always attempt to blitz an enemy down with combos or your super. Some gank fights I did find annoying, but you have enough healing cylinders that you could survive it with no problem. Also, why do we fight the final 3 bosses multiple times before we fight them for real at the end? I get the secret shadow fights ("hard mode" of the bosses), but they just appear during day time as a roadblock with no explanation, and that kind of feels like the developers are just reusing bosses to pad out playtime. Why???  Then there is the ritual... the dice game before some fights... which you can just always skip. The debuff isn't worth it, the Corwids don't abide by that rule, and most of the time the enemy has better tools and dice than you. It's a cool idea, but not that strong.While I am rambling here, the map of Zenozoik is great. Shortcuts back to the previous area surprise me with how interconnected everything is, the uniquely beautiful environment design and enemy placement are not annoying and well thought out, exploration and secrets areas that reward you with upgrade materials or even a new special attack, map designed with the player's tool kit in mind: jumping and combat, and environment being around the height of Pseudo so you could peer over terrain to see where you are. It's a small map tightly packed with content.Music is... tribal? I guess that's the best way to describe it. It really suit this game's setting. "23. Pseudo returns" might be the best track as it gets you pumped up and the situation it plays during the game.I liked this game, enough to recommend it to other people. It's not that difficult, but you must master the combat to be able to dominate the game. A game will always have flaws, but a good game does so much good that you ignore the flaws. Clash: Artifacts of Chaos does that successfully. I rank this a Yakuza 5 out of a Dark Souls: Prepare to Die.

_childDocuments_.review: The story takes place on the mysterious and visually unique world of Zenozoik where you will encounter many interesting and special characters, but not always friendly. Like Gemini, others are also targeting Boy and it's your job to defend him and fight everyone until you finally defeat Gemini too.Watch a snippet of gameplay here: In this game you play as Pseudo, who is sent back to Zenozoik by his master,The law of the strongest has been in force here for years. Pseudo will have to take care of a little creature known as Boy, who you will get to know shortly after the start of the game.Boy is protected all the while by an old man whom he refers to as his grandfather. However, in Zenozoid, when challenged to a duel, you cannot refuse.You will then have to take care of Boy in a certain way.Pseudo has a dark past, the Kid is endowed with mysterious abilities, the creatures inhabiting Zenzoik live by decidedly incomprehensible rules.Imagine yourself as the hero of an old science fiction book, the author's fantasy, not yet distorted by modern artistic solutions, sometimes gives rather ridiculous and completely unbelievable versions of alien landscapes and the appearance of their inhabitants. Roughly the same impression leaves Clash Artifacts of Chaos.The game also has good support on the Steam Deck: Clash has a pretty good story and a pretty interesting universe that can be compared to the lore of the Zeno Clash games.

_childDocuments_.review: I can only describe this game's vibe as basically Jim Henson's Dark Souls. The Dark Souls 1 Influence is notable- a bonfire checkpoint system (literal campfires here), corpse runs, a estus-like health system, and shortcuts to previous areas you open up in its semi-open world, littered with chests and items, as well as a protagonist that has two forms analogous, a fleshy one and a "withered", reduced form.But it isn't a soulslike, not really. It has a ton of stuff to make it stand out. Notably is its wild aesthetic. The world is pretty alien feeling and most creatures look like muppets, but in a good way. You play as a do-gooder toughguy, trying to help out a weird bird-like little guy who's wanted by a local warlord. The combat is where it really separates itself from its Dark Souls influence. Because it ostensibly felt like a soulslike at first, I tried playing it like one, and was getting stomped by anything but the lowest level enemies. You have to be really, really aggressive in this game, more than any FromSoft title, even the super aggressive Bloodborne. You build attack power and fill a rage meter by basically getting into a flow state of attack-dodge-attack. Enemies that were flattening me if I approached them like this like a Soulslike were trivialized when I got into the combat flow. And when I say flow, I mean basically button mashing. In fact, the game became way less intimidating when I realized it wanted me to hammer on the attack and dodge buttons.All in all, a good game, really cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: The crown Jewel of ACE Team's game making experience so far. Game play is great, engaging exploration, a deep and satisfying combat system. Zeno Clash walked so this game could sprint.The Graphics are beautiful, in ACE Team fashion the art style is completely unique and really there is nothing else like it.Music wise the game strays away from the typical ambient fantasy tropes and pulls off a surprising amount of singing.Expanding on the World of Zenozoik (Players of ZenoClash will feel right at home) the writing stays excellent with lore, characters and a simple but well executed heartwarming story.The game runs GREAT, has an option to stream an open world with no loading zones or switch to zone loading for HDD. In my 15 hours of play I only encountered one minor bug. Even though there is a good amount of jumping around on platforms and from ledges plus enemies that throw you around the arena the game holds up and is not janky.ACE Team really delivered on this one, cannot wait for the next game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a master piece of gaming fun. The game starts off a bit confusing but if you bother to learn the finer points you will realize this is a great brawler adventure not really sure how to class this game out. But one thing is for sure combat is not slow. you need to figure out how to string together moves and play somewhat not button mashing. It is by no means Souls hard for anyone. The game music is the best gets you feeling like Earth Worm Conan Jim.Update: Now that i am 4 hours in 2 of which i restarted just to experience the first area a little better and find more upgrades. I am glad i did there were many secrets i missed because i didn't really learn the area.It actually gets easy to see the paths after you climb a location and scout a bit then try something if you can't reach. Try sleeping at the camp until night then you may find what you saw before you could reach it. Very nice.Update: After completing the game i need 4 achievements to finish. This is a game that is nothing short of an amazing tale. The game play and story are both enthralling and immersive. I completed it in roughly 17 hours. Again if you love exploration on a massive scale and figuring out the secrets of the universe your in I highly recommend this experience.Its more than a great contender for the game awards with its fresh take on what makes a compelling interesting ride, one in a sea of remakes (Which i am looking forward to) this is just fresh from the graphical style to having a engrossing experience. the presentation in this is top notch.

_childDocuments_.review: Although Clash: Artifacts of Chaos does drag its feet, the game still has enough positives to offer players. Best of all is the amazing visual appearance of Zenozoik and its many awesome inhabitants, combined with the great music, that make it worth playing for its presentation alone. Fans of the Zeno Clash games will get a kick out of the visual upgrade. As a third-person beat-em-up, the fisticuffs can be enjoyable despite there being too much of it and little else. The associated Ritual mini-game is fine but does not provide enough benefit or lasting value. While the many Dark Souls traits are obvious and make the game challenging, the levels are consistently annoying to navigate due to their indirect routes and confusing structure. Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is a good way to beat up strange critters in stunning environments, even if it doesn’t land all of its punches.

_childDocuments_.review: Zeno Clash was an awesome series that further enhanced the brawler type games. The first person view, the whacky world everything took place in, and the game mechanics were awesome. Add a few mini-games and there is a solid rounded game. Clash: Artefacts of Chaos is an off-shoot of Zeno (and have read somewhere that Zeno was meant to be more of this style). Clash: Artefacts of Chaos (CAC... heh) is a well rounded brawler game, but is meant for more hardcore gamers that want to explore without hand holding.CAC has solid . At first I found myself wanting the Zeno Clash style of battle. Soon after I understood the game mechanics a little better and understood how the game was meant to be played. It was certainly frustrating starting out in an open world and not having much idea of where or what to explore first. After a bit of frustration (and a lot of losses) the game started to make sense. There is a day/night mode where the player switches their character and allows them not only to battle slightly different characters, but also access places on the map that are not regularly accessible. This adds to the dynamic element of the game where it forces the player to seek out new options if a repetitive one doesn't seem to work. The  feel like an xbox 360 control scheme when the player is moving around, however the battle controls are actually quite smooth. I hated the fight scheme at first, but soon learned to use what the game tutorials taught me in order to properly take on multiple or difficult opponents. I can actually appreciate the difference between CAC and Zeno Clash. CAC is essentially an RPG brawler. The player's only access to location is through a map displayed on the loading screen. Beyond that, the player is on their own to figure out what to do, who to battle, and where to go. The player is able to pick up multiple items around the map that will help conjure potions, increase stats, or items for appearances. As the game progresses the player can find totems lying around the map in order to unlock new battle styles, and sometimes even new special moves. The player can choose to have two active styles and three special techniques. Additionally, the player can boost the stats of those styles and their own personal stats (such as strength and speed). This all comes together well when the player enters a battle. Before a battle does begin (and if a player has suitable items to battle with), there is a mini game that involves dice (or the One Rule of the land). The game has an impact to give the player or the computer an advantage given the outcome. This could include fog of war, poison, or other sorts of limiting factors. CAC's  are quite solid and follow a similar theme of the Zeno Clash series. I enjoyed the outlandish characters, style, design, and layout of the environment. Though the environment can feel a little clanky at times, overall it's visually appealing. The user interface is also laid out nicely and easy to use. The  were also well done. The music is subtle enough that it can relax the player, but also bounce to kick the player into ready mode. The dialogue, sounds, and effects are also well done. There is a satisfying effect when brawling and landing shots on enemies. Overall, I would recommend this game, but very carefully. Saves are sometimes far and in-between which could bother some players (especially having to pick up items that were previously picked up). I was resistant at first to like the game as I felt the fighting was a little too geared towards the AI having an upper hand, but as I got comfortable with the game (and became familiar with it) I really liked the brawl concept. This is one I would highly suggest doing your homework before a purchase. Surface level may look fun, but how the game was designed may bother casual gamers looking to button mash. Also feel like once you beat the game, this is one you're happy you've beaten and seldom come back to. Solid campaign if you're into that! Why a C+? Well, I'm an older gamer now and these hardcore games do need a good chunk of mastering to get through (and tries)!
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos tells a beautiful, yet heart-wrenching story of Pseudo - a stoic character with nothing to lose, or so he thought. The game is quite challenging, the combat is quite dynamic in the sense that you can choose your own style thanks to a wide variety of combat stances and special attacks. In addition to this, "The Ritual" mechanic is like none I have seen before and serves to either make an encounter with the enemy easier or much harder depending on the outcome. The soundtrack is amazing and perfectly fits the whole theme of the world. It is soothing, but also carries a tinge of sadness. If you have played any of the Clash games, you will understand exactly why this is the case.I absolutely recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is a lot of things, pretty much all of them good, and exceedingly so.  For fans of the Xenoclash games it is the return to Zenozoink that we've been dreaming of for nearly a decade, though it is also a departure from the unique first-person-brawler experience that was found pretty much nowhere else, as the 1st person view was relegated to finishing moves and finishing moves alone.  I wasn't thrilled about this, but I got over it pretty quickly because the new gameplay is just as stellar and feels substantially less janky moment-to-moment.  Gameplay wise I would call it a martial arts souls-like.  I know everyone calls everything 'souls-like' when a game has a map and is even moderately challenging, but it's actually accurate here.  You are usually fighting enemies that can out damage and out tank you head to head, so you need to play cautiously and play intelligently.  There's no penalty for losing though, besides just being kicked back to your last save, so feel free to experiment in each and every fight as much as you like.  As always the ACE Team delivers on another astonishing fantasy vision with some of the best character design I've seen in quite a while.  Everything and everyone is so incredibly bizarre and utterly alien, yet so human at the same time.  So much of the world feels like an alien world that doesn't feel like it follows the same rules of our own, but yet much of it feels so familiar at the same time.  It just feels good to play, and I won't spoil anything but having finished the story I can say it's nearly as interesting just to ponder it all.  This game reignited my own IRL sense of adventure.  I mean it.  Go play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Original review exceeded Steam's word limit, so here's a synthesized version.By far the most enjoyable ACE Team game, for me!I've replayed the first two Zeno Clash games in preparation for this, and the gameplay is vastly improved in every way. It's bolder and better.The combat is less unique, but more fun.The writing, disappointingly, doesn't really take the Zenozoik story in any new direction, but it is a much more eloquent treatment of the same themes, with tenuous connections to the other games. Certainly much better for new players, but I would have really liked to see more movement to the Zenozoik story - guess I'll have to wait for a sequel.Visually, too, it's far better, although I am not fully on board with the style - while I love the textural feel of it, it feels a bit *too* textural for a Zenozoik game, which relied more on quirky and identifiable models, if that makes sense.The music is very unique, and quite good, but once again feels a bit off for Zenozoik. The previous games used unique "ethnic" instruments to convey the culturally-alien (Xeno) nature of the games, which I really liked.This time around, voice and piano are very prominent - the voice is cool and unconventional, but the piano takes out some of the alien feeling, to me. Now, brief discussion around specific subjects:--- Souls-like & Exploration ---I feel like this is a misleading labelling. The game is neither difficult nor mechanically deep. What it does take from Souls, however, is the open level-design and the lack of a GPS system. I love this, and exploration was by far my favourite part of the game.The whole world is fully connected, and you need to rely on (and develop) your navigational skills alone, not following an icon on a map. Many paths are initially closed off, in each area, but you will open them up as you explore (in the riskier night form) as well as the connecting shortcuts across areas.The areas are very... maze-like, which is a positive and a negative. On the plus side, it's really cool to map out in your head and explore when you reach a new area, for sure. There is also a lot to collect in every nook and cranny (equipment, ingredients, stance and attacks, upgrades, etc.).On the minus side, it's a pain to backtrack through, and this really hurts the "end/post-game" if you're one to look for optional bosses and equipment. While in Dark Souls you're navigating very distinct areas, most of the time (ruins, buildings, etc.), here, being mostly "alien nature", it is difficult to remember where things were. Plus, when exploring the first time, it's easy to identify where you have been before (since everything is collected), but once you return, most things have already been picked up, so it can become more confusing.--- Skill points, Difficulty ---This is an interesting design problem that I did not expect to have.In Dark Souls, souls are the currency for everything, and they are risky to carry with you, since you lose them upon death. This makes levelling up very encouraged.In here, you level up through XP and keep your skill points for ever. This made me hold on to them. "Too good to use syndrome". By the end of the game, I had spent maybe 30 points, and had 90 points leftover, unspent.This brings me to discuss difficulty - the game is far too easy, after first few hours. It undervalues every other system in the game. Equipment will maybe give you 20-30 extra points, at most.Potion brewing, too, was too subtle and problematically opaque (next section) to be relevant.Weapons could be used, but their lack of integration into the combos made them awkward to use.And worst of all, this lack of difficulty applies also to the optional dark bosses. I also feel like optional content is a great opportunity to force players to delve deep into the game's system, to demand them to learn and use everything to their advantage in order to overcome the challenge. None of that here, a wasted opportunity.--- Crafting and Brewing ---This is a huge design problem.You get crafting materials from enemies and use them to purchase equipment and ritual upgrades. Enemies respawn "infinitely" so you never run out of materials; but shops' stocks are limited, they have a finite use.You get ingredients by gathering them in the world, but they do *not* respawn, so they have a finite supply. But, depending on how well you play, how much you explore, you may need to craft many potions. Beyond that, the brewing system is extremely opaque and unclear, making blind trial and error a necessity to learn it. You can imagine how blind experimentation and finite supply can go wrong.I don't know how this happened, but wires got crossed. Crafting supplies, having finite demand, could have had finite supply. Brewing ingredients, with infinite demand, should have had infinite supply.The low difficulty makes this largely irrelevant, but still.--- Ritual ---Neat idea in theory, not at all workable in practice.This is a mini-game you can play before some fights. It's a dice game, the winner gets to apply a penalty on the opponent.It has neat connections to the narrative (and is used with a great intent in one area of the game), so I would have loved for it to work.However - the benefits are rather subtle, it's not a very safe bet that you'll win the ritual, and it's very slow. Its most likely use would be in tough fights, but these are the ones whose opponents also have correspondingly better ritual "abilities", and the ones you may have to retry a few times. Replaying the ritual in such situations seems to waste more time than it aids you, not only may you end up with a penalty yourself, but it's a significant amount of extra time between retries.The result is that, from what I've read, most players (myself included), just decided not to use the Ritual at all, after the first couple of hours, once the novelty has worn off.So it is one more system that becomes irrelevant. Again, neat idea in theory, but didn't quite work.--- Writing and Story ---I'm a huge fan of Jonas Kyratzes (although I have not played the Talos Principle yet; my familiarity is mostly through his own indie games, and ACE Team collaborations).In a way, he didn't disappoint - the dialogue is far better, ideas are expressed beautifully, and often very funny.Unfortunately, the themes end up being largely similar to those of previous games. It's a full new game that doesn't really add much to the world of Zenozoik. It kind of moves in place. This sense was very disappointing.I must give credit to three little sections:- I loved the monologue of Word; not just how it related to the previous games and the role of his character, but also for the idea it made much clearer, to me, about the relation between anarchy, anarchism, and historical memory.- There was also a subtle line about the "mythology of when the stars changed"; this only makes sense for those who've played Zeno Clash 2, I think, but it plays brilliantly with the last point of historical memory.- The ending was great, especially in the role and kind of love between Pseudo and the Boy. I am one to care not at all for plots and resolutions, in most games (they are usually vehicles for themes and ideas and not as important in themselves, in my mind), but I must say that it was both unexpected and significant to the ideas of power, control, and, of course, love.--- Conclusion ---All in all, a huge improvement over the previous games, and a very enjoyable game.Design-wise, it is far from water-tight, but nothing that hurts it too much, at least for one playthrough.It adds little to the previous games in the series, in terms of story, but it does a much better job of addressing the same themes.I'd expect it to be a great entry for beginners to the series (a lot less janky), and I'm sure it will be enjoyable to veterans, even if it ends up disappointing the expectations set at the end of ZC2.

_childDocuments_.review: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is a great adventure fighting game, with more souls-like mechanics than you might initially think. Even though the visuals are striking and one of the biggest selling points of the game,  ACE Team managed have the gameplay feel complete as well, rather than just having the artstyle carry. The unsung hero of this game is the level design itself, featuring memorable enemy encounters and top-notch interconnectivity through shortcuts. The game is not without flaws though, as you will run into the occascional bug or polarizing design choice. However, none of them were of any real hinder to me. You can feel the love poured into this game and the sense of exploration never left me during its runtime which led to 100%'ing the game. Easy recommend.Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is an action RPG game that has you traversing a weird world while you punch the lights out of creatures with designs not even my nightmares could come up with. Despite of that, the game never feels out of place, as weird as the world itself or scary. You are a fighter, and you can use a mix of different fighting styles and special moves to give yourself the edge, as your final hit sends enemies ragdolling to the ground. Let's start with the most in-your-face aspect of the game: the artstyle. If you are like me and never played any of the Zeno Clash games (developed as well by ACE Team, set in the same world with the same artstyle, but not prequels), it feels like a lot to take in at first. The world is odd, enemies are grotesque and you look like someone had fun in a character creator and wanted to show their friends how unrealistic their character looks. Despite all of this, there is never any issue with "accepting" the art of this game. Everything I said still applies, but the game is not making a big deal out of it, so you probably aren't, either. You are a part of the world, and so are the enemies. They don't get any special introduction highlighting how many appendages, eyes or other features they have. You just encounter them and you fight them. It allows you to take what you see for granted, and there is nothing wrong with that.The visuals are good, and the gameplay is good as well. You have your standard action/adventure RPG loop of going from point A to B in a semi-open world. There are no quest markers or anything, but you will probably not get lost along the way. Most of the world is pretty linear, and very specific about where you can and cannot go. While you being stopped by an ankle-high wall or incline is frustrating, an alternative of putting high walls everywhere would take away from the experience even more. You're often climbing or descending through a level, and having the ability to look ahead or back is great.The level design is on par with the Dark Souls franchise. I do not know how they could improve on it. Every enemy you encounter, no matter how insignifant they are, is memorable. A plethora of shortcuts turn a 3-minute trek up into a 1-minute walk back. While not all of them are as relevant, they make traversing the world a lot of fun. I did grew kinda weary of literally every new door I encountered being unlocked from the other side, similar to your character making remarks about this whenever you try to open one of them.You will be doing most of your traveling during daytime, and pretty much the entire plot plays out during the day as well. However, you can also visit places you've already been to at night. This changes up which monsters you fight, and some areas are only accessible during this phase. Do not expect a level of "second world" like Lords of the Fallen or Enotria did, but there are some unique collectibles to get. If you die, you respawn at night and have to find your body. If you then die at night without succeeding, you lose all progress you made since the last time you saved. At times, it is mandatory as well to visit places at night to unlock areas for your daytime travels. All of this gives you more stuff to explore which is nice.Speaking of exploration, through the world you will find random plants and animals that you can put into your healing soup,  chests that you can open for goodies and upgrade items in the form of small wooden dolls. In a very odd design choice, these items are only highlighted when you are next to them with your camera aimed at them as well. There is no shiny from a distance. I understand if people dislike having to shove themselves into every wall and corner to see if there happens to be an item, but I liked it a lot. It gave the world a realistic feel, away from a video game. This was further compounded by savepoints being actual campfires that you need to light. You cannot get around the "Bonfire lit" memes, but you can see the smoke from the campfires from a distance. It feels rewarding to push through that one extra fight because you can already see that behind there, you can light a campfire for a savepoint. All praise for the visuals and world design aside, Clash Artifacts of Chaos is a game about fighting, and the combat is fine. There are plenty of different fighting styles to unlock, as well as special attacks you can do. However, you'll have to come to terms with it at the start, and it will always feel kinda clunky. You can get ganged up on in a corner or use some very cheesy cheese methods to stunlock enemies. It is not perfect, but the combat loop itself is still very fun. It did not get tiresome over the course of the game.The last gameplay mechanic that is worthy of note is "The Ritual". A game of dice where you and your opponent can use actions to modify the roll results. The winner gets to impose a disadvantage on the loser. It is a fun minigame that unfortunately has too little impact on the entire combat. It is fleshed out well, but I wish more was done with it.  The story itself is a positive. The voice acting is top tier and it has both its serious, cute and humorous moments. It is presented in a fine manner, both in quality and quantity. The main characters are great. There is nothing more I can add to it.In my 18 hours of playing this game and seeing all of its content, I have only experienced bugs or a frustrating gameplay element a few times. These include flying enemies standing still mid-air, me accidentally getting beneath very large enemies and them standing on top of me, and me walking off a ledge since some cutscenes still have you control your player character even if they are off-screen. Almost all of these gave me a laugh.The game is definitely not for everyone though. It is the type of game that I expect game journalists to give a 7/10, whereas it sits closer to a 9/10 for me. If you are a fan of souls-likes, you will enjoy the interconnected world, overall exploration for secrets, healing and the death mechanics. If you are a fan of fighting games, you will enjoy the combat and the many approaches you can have to it. If you are a fan of adventure games, the aforementioned exploration and story will be great. And if you like indies, this is one of the most unique artstyles out there, and that alone is also already worth it.If you got to the end of this wall of text, you are very likely interested enough to buy it. Give it a try, and try to stick with it through the first few hours. It is criminal that less than half of the people owning this game played it for longer than 3 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game that definitely went under radar. You can see by the screenshots how weird and surreal everything is. That atmosphere kept me surprised from the start to the very end. There was always something weird around the corner that kept my attention. Overall, I must have spent at least a couple of hours just looking at the environment, my character or other NPCs.The soundtrack is quite nice and they've added it in a way that accentuate the tone of the environment or of the situation. It's far from being some generic, low quality loop.The exploration and item finding has an old-school feeling about it and I think they've implemented it well.The voice acting is great. The first time I saw and heard my character talk was weird... but in good way.Combat does get a little repetitive. I ended up, most of time, using always the same combination of attacks. You do unlock quite a lot of different "stances" and special attacks along the way though. This might have just been me being used to my combat style and not wanting to change.The story is fine with some minor plot twists along the way.If you're just a tiny curious about this game, you should give it a try. You'll be surprised.

_childDocuments_.review: What a surprising little gem. The DNA of this game is a soulslike, complete with estus flask, bonfires, open interconnected world and deeply engaging combat. But it's set in this bizarre nightmare fuel dreamworld of peculiar locations and creatures. The creativity from the artists is phenomenal, a truly unique world and I'm unable to draw comparisons to anything. Underneath this peculiar setting there is a surprisingly strong narrative with wonderful characters, very well written with great voice acting. It's rare for any game to pull at my jaded heart strings, but I was fully invested in this tale of Pseudo and the boy.The game is very janky; the combat and hitboxes can feel awkward at times, some enemies glitch out, often the level geometry fights against you, and game performance isn't great. But after a while that just becomes part of the charm of the game. You can sense how ambitious this game is, how much thought and care they put into every detail, reaching way beyond what was feasible, so you find yourself accepting the frayed edges.By far the most impressive feature is the level design. I've not seen this level of craftsmanship since Dark Souls 1, and From Software should be taking notes. The game world is an ingenious web of connections, with each zone having a different atmosphere and landmarks. Buildings or features are shown in the distance, foreshadowing for when you explore them later on. Some areas are layered vertically and also loop back on themselves with handy boss shortcuts. It feels like the devs have refined the Xenoclash idea down to something wonderful. I'm hoping we get to see more from this series and these characters.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much in such a small package.Expect a 10-14 hour adventure per playthrough. With fantastic characters, out of this world whacky character designs and some brutal close quarter combat.Psuedo our protagonist is a hermit martial artist and mercenary, trained by his grandpa for since childhood. Preferring the life of solitude making small camp where fate takes him next. In comes a fateful event where at the end of it, he shoulders it to bring this small creature only known as Boy back somewhere safe.The combat is not deep but it can be as wide as you like. A generous parry system promotes practice, multiple stances that will change your generic attack patterns to be mixed with special moves (If you ever played Street Fight and done jab > jab > jab > shoryuken, you'll feel right at home.The game lets you know that Pseudo is not the strongest creature of this merciless land, dodging and positioning is as important as getting attacks in. These dodges whether backwards or to the side (which can be punished doing the wrong one against the wrong attack) they can be turned into a follow-up attack unique to each stance.Enemy attacks does something unique in this game and that is that they will hit each other. Positioning yourself to line up two enemies and bait the one in the back to wind-up an attack and smack the one in front  will net you some free damage.This becomes very valuable when you are facing off against multiple enemies. There is also a "night time" mode, where you can re-explore the areas you just traveled in Pseudo's golem/avatar form. It has its own equipment to collect (creatively put up in giant dreamcatchers). And its own enemies reflecting the ones from daytime. Night time adventures also grants the opportunity for some challenges optional encounters that will reward heaps of exp and/or unique gear and crafting items you can use for daytime adventures on Pseudo.Once you reach Act 2, the game becomes much more open of where to go next. Any place that isnt blocked by a turtle is free to approach and see what events plays out. The unlocking of shortcuts becomes valuable as you might want to backtrack later on. Seeing as there is no fast travel system you much dread such concept. But from the hub area to the edges of the world becomes a fast sprint once you pulled down bridges, unlocked doors and burned away brambles that once was in the way and I never was too bothered by the lack of fast travel thanks to this making all generic encounters avoidable (or just run past them).So yes, I highly recommend Clash: Artifacts of Chaos for being a game you can't quite find out there anymore. It feels like something that belonged in the experimental and whacky games of PS1 era (Spyro, Motor Toon Grandprix, Abe Odyssey etc) and I'm glad I got to experience the game.Becomes the world's mightiest thumb with the fighting style of choice and bring Boy to a safe place he enjoy as home.

_childDocuments_.review: Good stuff. But i am biased as i loved the in your face freakish violence of Zeno Clash games (And even more their lovely Abyss Odyssey) and therefore i am just primed to love the world of ZenozoikPro: + They actually managed to make the linear previous games now into a light exploration & parkour game. I avoid using here references like 'weird elden ring' or metroidvania as it is quite so light in those departments now that i have explored over half of the map. + The smack down never gets old. Beaten foes even come back again later asking for more. + Expanded moves and proper parry system with a generous parry window. XP point system and leveling. It is worth putting some effort into becoming a better fighter and learning new fight stances. + Get defeated by a boss/tough enemy? likely it was your own fault so re-think your strategy and try again. +- During nights you can explore the same area in a more limited fashion. You very quickly pump out all interesting stuff out from traders. - In the longer run exploration despite it looking so gorgeous in the beautiful world of Zenozoik is quite limited. _childDocuments_.review: Much like Pseudo's relationship with the Boy, the game's start is rough and rocky, but it blossoms wide open quickly enough to have the strong parts present themselves.The Zeno Clash series is consistently off-putting visually. It is a striking style that almost feels iconic at this point. It's not really a detriment, because it perfectly softens up the player to throw away many of their expectations. Expectations such as a parent figure being a father  mother, or violent conflicts beholding to no tradition before they start. It makes strange concepts easier to swallow, such an entire section of a land devoted entirely to those who think without reason or logical sense, or where animals are relentlessly violent with no regard to their own survival.Zenozoik makes little logical sense to us, but it functions perfectly as such within its own world, and the devs show little restraint in looking to dunk you in it. It's this effort that, consistently, lifts up the games from "Look how funny and silly these people are", to genuinely caring how the story ends. Fantasy doesn't make much sense either when you think about it, but we still care about the Mage, Rogue, Paladin, Cleric and Barbarian in our adventuring party.Mechanically, Clash is a new level, a massive cut above the first two Zeno Clash games. We've moved to third person, and we have a vast array of fighting styles and special attacks. And if the flying uppercut wasn't so exploitable, it probably would've been a rival to Sifu on how unforgiving the game will be if you don't interact with all of its mechanics during a fight. On one hand that's a shame, on the other hand I'm glad I didn't have to frustrate myself again just to finish a game. Sifu gets to hold that one over me, I don't need another one.If anything, that lead me to 100% this game in my very first run of it. Most of the chievo's happen naturally, with only three or four being left to do. Finding pieces of armor for my Night form was a bit of a collectible hunt, but it wasn't too annoying, really. Once you've opened up the map with all its shortcuts, traversing it to hunt the collectible pieces was hardly an effort.Speaking of shortcuts, it at first felt like the game took all the wrong lessons from Dark Souls 1 when it came to interconnected design. And that's largely because of the stoney mountain. Twice did I run into a "Doesn't open from this side" door, not realizing until much later that the way forward was actually right next to it, albeit a touch obscured. That's not great. The rest of the game doesn't really make that mistake, with its varying locales. If anything I felt that the interconnectivity was more akin to that of Hellpoint, though either way it can be traced back to DS1.The game really does not leave much to the imagination beyond what it shows on the tin, though. Varying fighting styles, and special attacks (read: Heavy attacks that are separated from fighting style), four stats that empower these in differing ways and strengths, as certain stats boost some styles/skills more than others, depending on their nature). Burn little straw dolls to empower these in a more linear way.It all feels a little Dark Souls-ey without really blatantly copying it, which is the part I appreciate the most. You sort of have estus, being limited to three(?) drinks that heal 25%, but this healing can be empowered along with buffs if you do a little cooking with up to four ingredients per drink. Death during the day has you scampering to your body in Night form as your last chance, interacting with it or first fighting off what killed you if necessary. Bosses and sentient enemies stay defeated (at least in the area you found them in...) while animal-ish monsters tend to respawn.Suffice to say, a lot of good lessons were taken from Dark Souls to create something different yet recognizable. It's the best way to do it, really.Night time on its own is also an excellent mechanic. Your Night form is wooden, so it can walk through brambles that your normal form cannot. Sometimes this leads to secrets, sometimes an actual requirement for progression, as dried out brambles tend to be connected to a guardian who'll despawn them when defeated. Conversely, Night form has a limited range, typically not allowing to venture much further than where you've explored in Day time. Some secrets and chests also only appear at Night. It makes the mechanic essential and different enough, while still feeling well connected to your normal form, as any fighting style and specials remain exactly the same during the Night.Nothing about this game comes across as hacked-together, cynical or cheaply thought up. For as off-putting as the world of Zenozoik is, it seems crafted with more love, inspiration and imagination with every iteration.I highly recommend people check out the two Zeno Clash games to see different perspectives on this strangely fascinating world, though they should know that the peak sits here, with excellence.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit biased, already being a fan of the first two games, but this was such a gorgeous spectacle, with a great soundtrack. ACE has really come a long way and this has easily become one of my favorite brawlers of all time. What little it borrows from Souls-likes is welcome and fits right in, but it doesn't slavishly follow the formula. Resources can feel very limited, but not unwelcomely so and there's also a new game plus with juiced up enemies. I loved that Pseudo isn't some typical polymath main character, he's a lonely hermit who's actually a bit slow to understand what's happening to him and his world, but when he cares he cares deeply and with passion.The gameplay definitely feels different from the two Zeno Clash games, with it being more 3rd person oriented and 1st person being a special move. The name says it: expect a spin-off not a sequel. It still feels very tight and satisfying, once you get the hang of it, and many familiar mechanics are still there though. You have a lot of options as far as builds go by the end of the game (just be careful spending those figurines). It was hard for me not to just jump into NG+ right after.There are some weird bugs sometimes, sometimes some deathplanes feel silly considering where you can and can't drop long distances as well as no good way to cancel a combo near a ledge, and sometimes it's a bit hard to navigate by landmark (not too bad, a lot was done with the limitations). I also felt maybe that the streaming transitions instead of loading zones option should have been made more clear, I didn't find out about it till near the end and it really feels good if your computer can handle it (check all the settings for this game thoroughly). I generally didn't have many other complaints though.I really dig everything it's going for overall as a spin-off to a series I love.

_childDocuments_.review: Here are the main problems with the game.1) The dice roll game is, go figure, very luck dependent. It can be skipped most of the time, but it still would be better if the RNG couldn't shaft you so hard.2) The game does that stupid thing where it forces you to walk sometimes for "cinematic" reasons.3) The combat is messy. It isn't like Dark Souls where you can identify patterns, sneak in a hit accordingly, and then get out of the way. It's more about knowing that you're going to get punched in the face after you try to throw a punch yourself, and just trying to minimize that damage. Not very elegant, and generally unsatisfying because of that. It also artificially restricts you to fight in certain perimeters which seems entirely pointless to me.4) A lot of the areas are samey and it's easy to get lost or go in circles.5) It has some cheese in it, e.g. enemies can swing their weapons through walls and stuff.Okay, aside from those downers, I liked it. It's an interesting world and exploring it is mostly satisfying, the characters are well written, and it's the perfect length.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best experiences I've had this year. I had trouble running it on PC (due to my graphics card drivers), and I just went ahead and bought a console version just to keep playing, that's how good this game is. It features one of the most creative, compelling and immersive worlds I've seen recently, presented with a unique, comic-book art style that is just gorgeous to look at. Part of what makes it so appealing are the character and creature designs, which approach the bizarre and surrealistic just enough to make them weird and exotic but believable and coherent with the world they are in.The narrative and writing in the game are just outstanding. Each character has such charisma and well-defined personality (which is enhanced by the amazing voice acting) that they're ALL memorable. From the main duo of Pseudo and the boy, whose story arc progresses just at the right pace, to each and every intelligent creature in this universe.The gameplay might be a bit divisive, but I really appreciated how it encourages exploration, from traversing the world, to collecting resources and figurines, and avoids holding your hand as much as possible (which unfortunately requires you to learn and practice some of the combat mechanics on your own). The combat system is as deep as you want it to be, meaning that if you stick with the same combat poses and special moves it will feel repetitive, but again, rewards experimentation, which is also why it features weapon durability just like Zelda BoTW did. Overall, fights felt really intense and satisfying, and you can feel the strength in every punch you throw (I really enjoyed the boxing combat pose)The music does so many things right. It takes the best of Elden Ring and NieR Automata and blends them together mixing powerful orchestrated pieces with Gregorian chant, memorable ballads and soft flute melodies which you'll find yourself singing, especially the main theme which is as beautiful as catchy.Finally, it's worth remembering that this is a game made by a relatively small team. It delivers AAA quality features to an indie / AA title and it shows to what an extent passion and good design choices can make a huge difference. I also want to mention how criminally underrated and ignored by the games media/press this game has been. If I hand't played any of the Zeno Clash titles before, I would've missed out on this game because I couldn't find no coverage or reviews of this game anywhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I have to say I really underestimated this game at a first look from gameplay videos and reviews.Just coming off my first session and I played 4h straight.So many great things about this game. Combat system is very well put together, not overcomplicated, but enough room for depth with chaining together different stances, different directional attacks and special moves with dodges and parries. Interesting fresh ideas, like the stamina deflecting 50% of damage with passive blocks.Hitsounds sounds straight out of Dragon Ball Z, that makes bashing alien creatures just feel right. If you are a fan of anime type over the top martial arts, this is definitely a game for you, the combat is very statisfying. Very nice level of difficulty, challenging, yet beatable if you use what options are given to you smart. I heard things like the game being frustratingly difficult, which I cannot agree to.The Ritual system is a very fun way to switch up fights, and can be skipped or tactically used, depending on what your opponents strenghts are. Also cool risk reward and completly believable to have such a ritual in a world centered around fighting and brute power.I was really suprised how much I liked the exploration aspect, there is meaningful loot, that actually let's you progress leveling your stances and moves, and crafting materials for things you wanna buy, or even complete armour sets. Also the Leveldesign actually caught me off guard. Pathways are very well connected, with lots of sidepaths, vertically overlapping lanes and plenty of shortcuts that make sense. Theres tons of hidden stuff to find, and in most places where you'd expect some hidden loot, you get rewarded for going there.Also great world building I get really strong Dragon ball/ Z vibes with the colourful pterodactyl creature. Sweet details, like the boy calling out creatures names when he sees it, so you get to know what they're called. despite, what a cute little sidecharachter! The Alien creatures and charachters in general just look so unique and fantastic. I guess the artistic style speaks for itself, it has this very surreal and unique look to it, I personally love it. Ontop of that you get a really great soundtrack.I read in so many reviews that it's confusing and you have no idea where to go etc. I can't confirm this. It sure is possible to get lost if you don't pay attention, no doubt. But there's plenty of Landmarks spread, so if you pay abit attention you can always orient yourself. The game basically teaches you this in the first sequence of exploration, where someone literally points you to a big bridge throning over a cliff. there's no minimap but honestly, the game feels like it doesn't really need it.The Day/Night Cycle switching up levels and enemies, and also adding new loot is really cool. When I saw gameplay footage of the thorn wall sequences, I tought it's just a simple way to switch up traversel, like in many other games. I didn't realize it actually limits you to only go trough in your night wood form and actually has a deeper mechanic gameplaywise.Honestly I was never so off with my first impression of a game. I really judged this the wrong way from gameplaymaterial and reviews. I was really doubting if I'd like it. And I totally love the game.And also a shame how this game gets 6s and 7s in many reviews. I think many reviewers are just too used to unchallenging and handholding type tripple A games nowadays. For me personally, this game even tough not perfect, does many things right. I'd rate it a strong 8, possibly a 9 from what I've expirienced so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Ten years after , Clash - Artifacts of Chaos welcomes us back into the thoroughly bizarre world of Zenozoik, this time with a . The resulting game may be more limited than its inspirations from the soulslike genre due to the lower budget, but it's an engaging experience from top to bottom, with some really well-implemented features and a world like you haven't seen before.: Pseudo, a grouchy hermit with a hidden past, and 'the Boy', whom Pseudo adopts at the start of the game. This setup was probably inspired by similar character dynamics we've seen in recent games like  and , but .This sidekick spends most of his time sitting on your shoulder (instead of turning the game into an extended escort mission), only dynamically flying off during cutscenes or when you start punching the crap out of Zenozoik's inhabitants. He even occasionally dive-bombs enemies during fights, and you can send him into certain context-sensitive holes to gather resources you wouldn't otherwise be able to reach. The idea of dressing the little guy in various clothes to protect him from certain environmental hazards feels a bit undercooked, but everything else about him works great. And .Gameplay-wise,  (if the dice favour you first). As someone who's always preferred the exploration and moment-to-moment fighting in soulslike games to the boss fights, I definitely approve. Much like in other souls games, the maps are very intricate and loop into each other, with unlockable shortcuts all over the place. For fights, you get to use strong weapons with a limited moveset as well as a variety of unarmed fighting styles and special attacks you can mix and match to complement your playstyle. All of these fighting styles have vastly different attack patterns, which rewards learning special moves and switching between different setups depending on the situation. Where Ghat’s moveset stayed mostly the same throughout  and , Clash - Artifacts of Chaos actually offers a lot more complexity and variety. .Much like in previous games, the art design is extremely varied and deliberately bizarre, though this time around, ACE Team have implemented a cross-hatching art style that I personally think fits the world of Zenozoik wonderfully. It gives the entire thing  (make sure to activate the 'animated lines' setting). ACE Team refers to this game as 'punk fantasy', and they've chosen the perfect art style to emphasize this concept during every single moment of the game.Clash - Artifacts of Chaos is a great experience if you're willing to give it a chance and don't mind the occasional rough edge. I've aluded to games like  in this review, but . For example, the little interactions between the main characters are often cutscenes with fade-outs and fade-ins, where a more big-budget game would probably have tried to add them directly into the gameplay or have cutscenes and gameplay flow seamlessly into each other. But as far as I'm concerned, , as well as a great achievement from a small studio with big ideas.
