_childDocuments_.review: Very nice game, sadly underrated. Recommended especially for fans of Oddworld. I write this review after doing everything in the game (except NG+).Things I liked:- Map design is absolutely exceptional. Very complicated with many shortcuts and interconnected side paths, ultimately cohesive and tight map. Feels like a proper adventure. Thanks to shortcuts you can cross in a couple minutes the map you explored in many hours. Best part of the game along with the god-like artstyle and positively bizarre designs.- Combat is nice, if a bit janky. It could definitely be harder. How fun it is depends on how you play, it can be very boring if you limit yourself to safe combos but entertaining if you start chaining moves and deflecting. It's ultimately not a very complex combat system but the game thankfully ends right as the gameplay starts feeling repetitive, which showcases the developers' wise mindset. The dice minigame you play before combat is cool and unique, and also doesn't overstay its welcome.- The bittersweet story is simple but catching. Pseudo is a relatable character and The Boy doesn't commit the usual sidekick's sin of being annoying, he's instead endearing and sweet. The dialogue, like Pseudo himself, is both bluntly serious and at times ironic, fitting for the setting, and it doesn't make the mistake of overusing puns and jokes (unlike many annoying games).Some things I didn't like, or would've preferred to be different:- Pick-up items (including upgrade materials) don't glow. Which means the game forces you to walk close to walls surfaces, looking at the ground for the "pick up item" pop up since the materials usually blend with the environment (especially the brown upgrade materials.......). This is *very atrocious* design and strong-arms you into looking away from the beautiful scenery. Having the items glow even slightly when you walked close to them would've fixed this without hurting exploration. - Like many games of the same genre, it is unnecessarily stingy with upgrade materials for your weapons (in this game's case, for your martial art movesets). The game is not complex or hard enough to warrant this, upgrading should've been limited to stats and maybe special attacks. All it does is limit the amount of fun you can have by experimenting with movesets, which is lame. - I think we should've been able to switch between all the movesets freely, without having to equip them. The game lets you equip only 2 movesets at the same time (and 3 special attacks), you can switch the 2 movesets between attacks and have cool results. If you could switch between all the 8 movesets freely during combat (using number keys), it would've been way more entertaining. Missed opportunity. Maybe, upgrade materials should've unlocked more stance slots instead of strengthening the stances themselves, as I said in the point above.- As far as I could tell, there's no way to attack using your standard fist combos if you have a weapon equipped. The game should've had separate keys for attacking with fists vs with weapons. Having a weapon on your back is visually cool but you're forced to use the repetitive weapon combos, which is why I would've liked separate keys.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic game!As someone who's getting somewhat tired of soulslikes that are just grim and dark, this game is a breath of fresh air. The world is vibrant, colorful, and very much alive. The art style is absolutely gorgeous, everything looks like it was hand drawn. The weird character design may take some getting used to, but it is an integral part of the world of Zenozoic, and after a while I wouldn't want it any other way.Every location has two versions, day and nighttime, with different mood, enemies, and sometimes loot. To progress, you mainly have to play at daytime, with occasional night missions. I really liked this change of pace, although it requires some backtracking that can get annoying. The main soulslike mechanic is that if you die during the day, you have one chance to recover your body during the night. Dying during the night means game over and you lose all progress since the last save. But save points are quite frequent, so it's not that punishing.The combat is a ton of fun, you have the usual light/heavy attacks, dodge and parry, as well as some unique mechanics. But don't expect it to work just like other souls games you've played before, I also have to admit I didn't figure out how to play properly until very late in the game, and I ended up cheesing a lot of fights before that. So if it doesn't click with you immediately, don't give up and maybe check out a guide. It honestly feels amazing to completely dominate a tough enemy dodging in and out and dancing around like a whirlwind. You can choose between several fighting styles that each feels different. Difficulty depends a lot on how comfortable you get with that system, if you manage to play as intended, it's not that hard.The writing comes from the hand of Jonas Kyratzes and after playing the Lands of Dream and Talos Principle games I'm convinced that anything this man touches turns to gold. This game is no different, although not quite as cerebral. The basic storyline could be compared to God of War, tough guy and boy bonding over the course of an adventure, but the whole thing is so much more than that and the themes and setting make it truly unique. The characters are all charming in their own way, and the finale moved me deeply. Also the music is great, it ranges from fun and whimsical to moody or mysterious and gives each area its distinctive feel. Only the combat sounds are a bit silly at times.I only have a few points of criticism. One is the map, which is very small and has few details. At least being able to zoom in would have helped, as the levels can get quite convoluted. The weapons break after a couple of hits, which means I never used any of them during my first playthrough. You can't even have more than one of any weapon type, if you pick up a weapon you already have, it just replaces the old item. Towards the latter half of the game, the majority of loot becomes useless, as each item can only be crafted once, and the resources have no other function. I've encountered a few bugs and the game crashed a couple of times, but nothing serious.All in all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes 3rd person action games with unique visuals and a lot of heart. It's become one of my personal favorites.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRPros:Interesting combatUnique and interesting worldPleasant storylineGreat musicCons:Parry system is nearly worthless. It's generally your worst defensive option. Multi-hit moves you use and enemies use invalidate any use of this incredibly weak mechanic.The map can be confusing keeping track of paths you've taken or when hunting for side content. It would be nice for there to be some direction, or maybe even a minimap to use. One of my favorite games of last year for sure. The game is visually weird but designed very well for an action-rpg beat em up.It is a pure upgrade over Zeno Clash 1 & 2. It takes all the elements from those games and expands on the fighting greatly by adding styles, a pre-fight mini game determining bonuses.Different fighting styles have strengths and weaknesses and you'll certainly find the type you like most playing with which is the most important.I think my two biggest cons for the game are the lack of a map/direction indicator and the parry system. The parrying is generally your worst option with many of the more dangerous enemies attacking with multi-hit moves that completely eliminate any advantage the parry could provide. You'll also notice multi-hit fighting styles you use invalidate the enemy parrying.While the design of the game is incredibly unique visually, it also makes it painful to traverse sometimes. Without any additional aids if you want to move through "side" content (mostly hidden or explorable things off the main path) you'll find yourself getting lost often.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid game that kept me interested with its combat, story, setting and art style. The combat felt stiff in the beginning, but as soon as I understood the pacing, it made sense. The combat is simple but interesting, there are no long combos or many special moves, but the whole system feels tight and deliberate. It was moderately challenging where I won most fights on the first or second try, but still difficult enough that the fights felt rewarding. It has souls-like elements but felt far from derivative mostly thanks to its new take on corpse runs.The setting is amazing and some of the best art direction I have seen in a while. The world is beautiful and grotesque at the same time, and the main character is so damn ugly but in such an interesting way. The world map is not that big, but it is interconnected in interesting ways. The story relied mostly on the characters and the quirks of the setting and it explored many interesting themes and open a lot up to interpretation in a good way. My only issue is that there are some pacing problem, there is a lot of walking back and forth and getting lost. The map is a bit complicated to navigate and it is hard to remember where you are going and how to get there. And about half-way through there is a fight that is WAY harder than anything else in the game. At first I thought it was an optional challenge, but it was not and it stop my progress for a while. Not even that final boss is nearly as difficult.Great and unique game, well worth it!
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: (Mild Mechanical Spoilers!!!)One of the best experiences I've ever had Ace team continues the excellence of the previous Zeno Clash games into a new design with fresh elements borrowed from multiple different genre's. It's blend of exotic locations and simple yet rewarding exploration made for a extraordinary game. This paired with a beautiful story about family and society makes for a heart wrenching narratives that rivals some of my favorite stories. It's combat Is rich with it's focus on customizing Pseudo's (the main character) move set so that you can create a character that is unique to your preferences. If you want Pseudo to be a burly brawler with slow windup attacks, or a nimble striker focusing on making quick hits to stagger the enemy. The ability to customize allows for player expression to be widely varying. The main feature of this game however is The Ritual a dice game that allows you to impose disadvantages on some of your Opponents but if you lose the can impose an effect on you as well. This adds a thrilling layer to each fight and further emphasizes you to explore your environment to find what new artifacts you can sick on your enemies. There are some flaws I think that the camera and lock on systems tend to be a bit squirrely. This is especially frustrating when you are about to land a hit but Pseudo zips past the character and swings wildly at the air. There's also has a corpse run mechanic where if you die you have a chance to recover your body and continue where you left off. The problem is when you fail a corpse run your sent back to your previous checkpoint which are disparate little camps strewn throughout Zenozoik. But when you respawn any of the previous consumables, upgrade materials and xp will be reset. This invariably forces you to scrounge across the map vacuuming up your lost progress and grumbling back to the fight that killed you. While this issue is frustrating by itself it isn't that hard to work around it certainly made me more cautious.  But this complaint is compounded by the lack of I-frames after being hit by an enemy. In a one on one fight this might cause a little extra damage to the player. But when put into an encounter with multiple enemies, suddenly the player is locked into an inescapable sting of attacks where a hit from each of the enemies takes away half your life bar. Enemies will also attack even when they are out of your periphery with no indication that they are making said attack. it makes some fights a struggle to work through. This all to say I strongly suggest you stick through to the end. I think the fact that I wanted to beat this and heck I might even complete it shows that despite it's flaws, Clash is something special and I think that Ace Team should be proud of what they have done. I can't wait to see what comes next from them and I love this game with my whole heart.

_childDocuments_.review: This installment of Clash changes from first person pugilism to third person. It is also now a soulsish mechanics and a father/son story. It keeps the fun world design ACE Team always brings.Let's just get to the combat, a little button mashy, but can have some depth to it. There is your basic 4 string combo, a hold heavy attack, a dodge, 3 distinct dodge+attacks (forward, left/right, backwards), and a jump forward attack. There are a bunch of different Fighting Stances that change your animations/damage scaling/properties of your attacks. All attacks are loosely the same thing, like the back dodge attack will always dodge back, then lunge forward to attack, but some are multihit or whatever. You have 2 slots to change between equipped stances, and 3 slots for special moves on the Y button. Stuff like Shoryuken or a teleport forward (if you get hit while doing this the game WILL stop recognizing movement inputs unless you die/reset). Once you get used to your stance you pick, it can feel really good just stringing combos together to knock around the ♥♥♥♥ outta enemies. Or even get long damage strings on bosses without getting it from including dodge attacks, it kind of rules.There is also a special meter that fills up and once you unleash it you will go into a first person mode. You have to do enough damage in a limited time and you will unleash a canned animation high damage super on the enemy you activated it on. I found this mode to be very annoying on boss enemies because you can get hit out of the super by a bunch of attacks and it is a waste of meter. Just made me mad everytime it happened.Before most fights against sentient enemies, you can invoke The One Rule. It is a game of Yahtzee where you roll dice onto a mat. Whoever hast he highest can innact the artifact they picked to the fight. Artifacts buff whoever won with numerous things like summoning an extra ally, causing enemy to cramp, a free hit, etc. After you roll, you can use Tchaks to affect yours or the enemies die. You can half them, subtract from the total, or other things in various shapes. The idea is kind of cool, and I like the strategy with the Tchaks, but it is also heavily rng dependent. You could just roll like ♥♥♥♥ and the enemy could roll great, or all you die could land close to eachother, or in a line, or in 1 quadrant for the enemy's Tchak to just obliterate you. You also don't really need to play the game by the halfway point I think cause you will be able to just beat them up without any help, and they can't have any buffs cause you didnt play it.The exploration is kind of cool, a little tedious cause there is a daytime/nightime versions of the map. In the night you play as a like a "dream" you and there are "dream" enemies. There are thorned bushes that only the dream form can go through and you need to go through them to open them up for the day mode. Along with Night Time variants of the bosses and armor you can only find at night, there is a lot of exploring the same areas twice over.There is also a bunch of pickupables everywhere, things like crafting materials. They don't have highlights so its a lot of spamming the pick up button while exploring, not very optimal I think. Some materials are used for trading merchants, no currency, just trade items for them to craft the stuff. The other stuff is used for mixing your estus's so their heals are actually good and maybe have a buff.The story is a classic father/son adventure thing. Pseudo meets a boy, everyone wants the boy for his powers, Pseudo decides to protect him. I like Pseudo's voice actor, just a good voice. There is some connection to the previous Zeno Clash games, but idk what they are cause I can't remember the first game besides 1 character that shows up; and I didnt play the 2nd game.Overall, I think it is kind of a messy game, but its definitely cool.

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down the most beautiful game I’ve ever played. The exploration can feel a little confusing and grindy but once you’re past those first few hours you  start to understand how the developers think, and moving quickly through the word is made all the more satisfying by it. Damn good story and decent voice acting (the game is fully voiced) although some of the mobs shout constantly annoying things and it gets old fast. But those few main characters are fantastic. The combat is fluid, creative and fun, and it runs about as well as I’ve seen an Unreal Engine game run on lower specs (I put medium graphics settings and high for textures and only had noticeable hitching during colossal boss fights and in one especially densely packed area specifically; I’m on Steam Deck) The environments are incredibly detailed and lush, the animations are smooth, and the weird character designs perfectly sell the absurdist world you’re traversing. It all contributes to making this by far the most stunning game I’ve ever had the pleasure of experiencing, and maybe even my personal game of the year (yeah I haven’t gotten around to playing BG3 yet but Zelda was pretty good). _childDocuments_.review: This game is really cool. Its a fascinating mash up of a bunch of genres into a combat system that is fun and flashy, if a bit simplistic and exploitable. Paired with the interesting and unique gameplay feel is a world that is truly odd. Fans of the dark souls school of storytelling where much is left unexplained and merely hinted at will feel right at home here. The difference is that while this style is often imitated, many devs forget that your world actually has to be interesting enough to motivate the player to puzzle out the meanings behind things. This game accomplishes that. The story isnt super complicated but the way some of the weirdest looking characters in any game I've played play the story completely straight and deliver lines as though nothing is amiss really helps engross you in the world. Overall, I'm very glad I gave this one a chance. There is decent build-craft opportunities with the different fighting stances and moves. Unfortunately I found the upgrade materials to be a bit too rare to encourage experimentation though so I kindof picked a setup I liked and stuck with it the majority of the game. Also similar to Dark Souls is their approach to level design. The entire world map is interconnected and this is both a positive and a potential negative depending on how willing you are to be lost and figure things out. I spent a good amount of time wandering before I knew where to go. Highly recommend you give this one a try!

_childDocuments_.review: The whole Zeno Clash series has to be one of the shiniest, most well-hidden hidden gem indie titles around. And though I also loved the first two games, this third instalment is probably my favourite.Clash: AoC does something with the series that I didn't think would be possible - it manages to preserve its utterly unique identity, while also polishing over some of the story and gameplay peculiarities that I thought were essential to this identity. What we end up with is a beautiful story set in a strange world, with greater emotional intensity, more compelling characterisation, and all-round better presentation, without sacrificing any of that crucial Zeno Clash weirdness. We also get more diverse and fluid gameplay, integrating a bit of a Souls-like formula that works very well.If I were to compare this game to others that I've played, I would say it is a cross between Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice and the Oddworld series. But really you will struggle to find another game quite like this one. I never really review games but this one deserves it. Give it a go!

_childDocuments_.review: The journey of The Boy and Pseudo is a beautiful blend of sweetness, melancholy, and blood pumping action. Clash's main loop consists of exploring a gorgeous and impressively intertwined world full of secrets and beating down the varied inhabitants within it. Exploration is split between two times of day, night time is used to unlock paths for day and has its own set of secrets to search out. Daytime exploration on the other hand has you searching for loot and challenging the many goofy inhabitants of Zenozoic through dice-based rituals & fisticuffs. Zenozoic in the day is a sprawling maze of biomes and dungeons, each looping back in itself in surprising and convenient ways. The sheer diversity of environments and the cleverness in how it all comes together is a pleasure to behold. Combat feels responsive and looks weighty, each hit pounds into the enemy with a thud and the visual variety in moves is spectacular. The main sense of depth in combat comes from stance swapping and building combo routes on the fly using dodge cancelling. Each combat style has a basic combo, 3 directional attacks, a heavy attack, a running attack, and a jump attack. On top of normal attacks the player gains access to 3 directional specials and a meter-based first person super mode that ends in a finisher if done successfully. There is also a parry system that slows down enemies and grants you a guard meter which reduces damage taken. This just feels great and calling out your enemy with the right move at the right time makes you feel like a lumpy orange butterfly. I really respect just how free-flowing combat feels and building custom combos that end in a meaty finisher is always awesome. The combat system could use a bit of touching up though, Despite there being encounters with multiple enemies frequently, the player is never given an area of effect attack or a way to control groups besides goading enemies into friendly fire. Stances also have differences in range, speed, damage, and stagger, but don't have any deeper intricacies that would make you change up your tactics or grant them a niche use. The Boy will also assist in combat at times and even receives a power, but I only saw him use it once in my whole play through, I appreciate that he has autonomy but adding a button for actions with the boy could have allowed for a stronger impact. Overall, combat has a great feel and good amount of depth but still is on the simple side and mostly relies on the  variety of enemies and the player mixing up their own tactics to keep things fresh. The Ritual is a cute minigame that you can opt into in most instances to add an extra effect to a fight with intelligent creatures. The ritual is played by throwing dice and using different tools to affect the dice is positive or negative ways. The ritual is a fun diversion and some of the artifacts you find can impact a fight in some really interesting ways, like summoning a fighter or tethering an opponent to the ground. I didn't use the ritual too often but I am so glad it is here, much of the story hinges around it being "The One Law" and it diversifies gameplay in a major way while providing tons of personality. The light RPG mechanics provide incentive for exploration and allow you to soften the difficulty with very slight incremental stat increases, as well as letting you dress up Pseudo (which was so much fun). The character stats for Pseudo is a neat idea, allowing the player to spec into glass cannon speedsters, Tanky sluggers, or meter-building meanies. I think that leveling the stances and skills themselves was confusing though, a lot of the fun in this game comes from throwing new builds together and seeing how it works, having some builds be worse because you didn't collect enough lil figurines means you have to handicap yourself when trying something new. Overall though, many of the RPG mechanics are superfluous and stat bonuses build slowly over the course of the game and don't weigh down your choice in playstyle that heavily. On top of character upgrades you have resources for buying weapons, armor, hats for Boy, and items for the ritual. I honestly found the resource system to be the most worthwhile part of the RPG systems. The ritual is heavily impacted by new dice, new tools, and new artifacts you find which does make it feel like the minigame evolves with the rest of the game. Armor also provides some choice in stats and often has big enough boosts that you can feel a difference and a set is even necessary to traverse a biome at one point. Resource collection also allows you to brew health potions with different buffs which can absolutely change the dynamic in a fight. Honestly, the RPG mechanics are quite bare and mostly serve to provide extra incentive for exploration. Lastly I'm gonna briefly touch on the narrative & music. It is simply wonderful, the game establishes its world instantly with stylish confidence. The characters all take the events seriously and the drama between them is well acted and compelling. The music does so much to further punctuate these moments and completely carry them in others. Each character seems to have their own style of music and vocals and it really helps to define them. Clash's soundtrack evokes familiar emotions while simultaneously feeling like its from another world. I highly recommend giving the whole OST a listen (shout out to "The Boy Calls" and "Pseudo Returns"). I could never get enough of the relationship between Pseudo and The Boy, they made me chuckle with their banter and cry multiple times with their heartfelt connection. Clash uses a well trodden dynamic but executes it so well, with such convincing animation and performance that it feels fresh. Nobody is seen as a joke and almost every character gets some moment to shine. I'll treasure this journey and these characters for a long, long time, hitting the credits felt like saying goodbye to dear friend. Thank you so much for another unique and unforgettable experience ACE Team, you all are wonderful and I hope you continue to create for as long as you have ideas in your beautiful and talented noggins.

_childDocuments_.review: I played and completed the original Zeno Clash back in 2009 on the Xbox 360, and have periodically revisited the franchise here and there for nostalgia. That being said, it never occurred to me how much I wanted a new entry in the series, nor how much I missed the surreal fever-dream world of Zenozoik until picking this bad boy up. If you're familiar with souls-like games, this one should come naturally for you. You primarily fight in hand-to-hand combat, making use of various combat stances that you learn through your travels, and melee weapons that do great damage but break pretty quick. Campfires take the place of bonfires, but act as more of a save rather than respawn enemies in your vicinity. Attacks are hard-hitting and immensely satisfying, and it does feel like a triumph when you beat larger, more formidable opponents. There is also a night mode, which you can access by sleeping or upon death during daytime with Pseudo, where you'll fight stylized tree-like night enemies, and travel through pathways that are inaccessible to Pseudo directly. It is also the game's most souls-like feature, allowing you to find your body and revive. However, upon death at night, you will game over and reset to a previous save. Zenozoik, while the setting of Zeno Clash 1 & 2, has never looked better than now, nor has it been as beautifully depicted. Seriously, the world in this game is GORGEOUS. Not quite open world, but open ended through wide regions connected by linear pathways. While many areas feel as linear as they are, some areas are very open and reward exploration. Find collectibles, new combat stances, alternate pathways, upgrade and crafting components, new and cool armor/weapons, ect. While I haven't completed the game just yet, the story has been surprisingly compelling up to this point. You play as Pseudo, a veteran martial artist who, while on his travels across Zenozoik, comes across a small owl-like creature mourning the death of his grandfather. After protecting him, he decides to take the critter, now known as the Boy, with him to try and get him back to where he belongs. On this journey you will encounter many more characters, some especially weird!Both Pseudo and the Boy are wonderfully acted characters and their banter is well executed; often light-hearted and exposition heavy, but sometimes genuinely deep and thought-provoking, which I would have never imagined coming from the original Zeno Clash duology. Clash: Artifacts of Chaos far exceeded my hopes and desires for a Zeno Clash 3, and despite some janky moments, it's gonna be a hard 10/10 from me. I sincerely hope the talented team behind ACE Team return to Zenozoik again soon, either in an expansion or a new installment.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this game with a major caveat about the gameplay. There is a lot of good, but I have some nitpicks too that I'll add as I cover each aspect of the game.-The level design. Each map area is unique and memorable, and paths twist and curve back around and open up in a way that is satisfyingly labyrinthine. Secrets are hidden in little nooks and crannies, but they also offer you new angles to discover the path forward or just appreciate the view. There are a few areas, however, particularly in the Corwid territory, where it is a bit unclear what it a path and what is a drop-off that will kill you.-The character design/ art style: Imagine if Alejandro Jodorowsky and Hieronymus Bosch had a bastard love child, and that child grew up watching too much Dragon Ball Z. These are the creatures that populate this world. If you are looking to beat up some freaks, you will not find a better game. The mobs are also more unique than your usual stock fantasy fare. Even the items are unique windows into a patchwork world (and the Mesoamerican flair is a cool touch). There was maybe one too many "big enemy" type guy for my taste, however, and I was disappointed to find bosses reused for the gates to Gemini's palace. I thought I was going to have to learn to fight new guys! Also, given how interesting the Corwids were in Zeno Clash, I hoped that there would be more of a variety of f'cked hobbies that they "just do". The guy who makes the birds blood was funny the first time, but overused.-The music is really unique and poignant. Lots of choir vocals, which I love, and strong notes of zeuhl in the battle music. It was a bit too loud, sometimes, so I just turned it down. Also some parts the music didn't quite match the action (or lack thereof), and it felt a bit like it was doing the heavy lifting.-Story: The worldbuilding is great, but story itself took a bit to grow on me. It's a pretty typical "reluctant guardian" affair, but that's not all a bad thing. Pseudo evolves from a cynical, begrudging hero into someone who protects and cares for those unable to protect themselves, and the Boy from being helpless and needy into a character with some genuinely thought-provoking questions and observations about the harsh world around him. Supporting characters were interesting, although I wish a couple were more fleshed out, . There were also a few character models in the town that I feel like were essentially set pieces that I wish had been given at least some blocking or a few grunts of voice acting.-The voice acting was great, by the way. Maybe a bit repetitive with some of the Boy's lines, though.-Gameplay: Unfortunately, this is where my biggest criticisms are. The actual fight fights start off challenging, with me only making it out by the skin of my teeth in a lot of cases. Some of them were punishing and even felt a little unfair at first, but once I understood how to pace myself and got a hold on the blocking system, fights quickly became quite satisfying. However, this only lasted for about the first 6 hours of the game, and then after beating the Director the game's difficulty level quickly dropped off and never recovered. A significant factor here is that, after leveling it up to the highest totem level possible (minus the special totem) I quickly discovered that I could cheese battles by spamming the long range attack and keeping a safe distance away from enemies. Worse yet, a lot of the mobs (including the candle enemy who clears the vines at night) could be attacked and killed from a distance without ever aggro'ing them. I know this is not how you're supposed to play a fighting game, but once I figure out it was possible it proved a considerably easier than learning to time my blocks more accurately. Really only enemies with long-ranged attacks and the Claw guy presented a challenge from this point forward, and in the first battle with Claw (I'm pretty sure that's his name) I got clipped out of bounds by one of his hits and couldn't get back in (so I ended up cheesing it again). By the final area pretty much all of my moves became overpowered, so that effort was taken out of combat and crafting armor/ weapons felt moot. I think if the issues with difficulty scaling-- particularly with the long-range move-- and enemies not getting aggro'd by attacks were fixed, this game could go from being a good game to an incredible game.A few other nitpicks, however. There could be, like... 33%-50% more mobs. A lot of areas felt empty, and at times I was doing more item collecting than I was fighting. The lack of mobs felt especially apparent right before the final boss, . The flying mobs, particularly the pterodactyl guys, were janky, and would scoot around in the are and not attack sometimes and their corpses freak the f'ck out when they die.And a few more not-really-nitpicks! The Ritual, Night Mode, and First Person Mode were all unique and fun ways to break up the gameplay, and I'd love to see those ideas fleshed out even more. I wish I had gotten to use the 'summon' totem more; as it stands, I bound Wrehg to it and when I finally used him on Gemini's ex-friend he got stuck in the floor :/ . Even with the difficulty of the game quickly dropping out, I still felt compelled to explore such a unique world and stick around with its weird denizens. I'm not usually into fighting games, but if you are or if you just like one-of-a-kind game worlds and you can get past some of the jank then this game is a recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: This game hits everything I want from a martial-arts action game. Stances, parry mechanics, special moves, combos, group combat and more. The Ritual minigame at the start of each fight was also really fun and had a good bit of depth to it, although I do wish the stakes were higher sometimes and unfortunately it becomes very easy if you get all of the upgrades related to it.It also delivers on an engaging storyline with a surprising amount of emotional depth and some simple character arcs that were really effective at being both believable and interesting. This is all supported by an interesting world with just enough lore drip fed throughout the game to draw you in to a living setting with depth to wonder about and so many questions that you want answered. On top of all this, the art style is impeccable, blending cel-shading, a great hatched shading style, almost watercolour textures and really interesting design of characters, levels, flora and fauna. The soundtrack is amazing as well blending vocals singing in an indecipherable language with interesting instrumentals that have a feel very distinct to the game. Obviously, nothing can be perfect and there were certain things I didn't love like the weapons system and the unpredictability of staggers. Additionally, I would've liked for there to have been things like challenges or short sidequests that yielded interesting boss fights or puzzles to add some variety but given I expected a sub 8 hour game and played 15 hours on my first playthrough I can't really complain.

The shift from first person to third seems like it might lose some of the identity of the Zeno Clash games, but the new perspective (lol) allows for excellent evolution of the beat 'em up gameplay into something slightly Souls inspired but delightfully distinct. The world, worldbuilding, and characters are all top shelf, just a delightful amount of visual and narrative creativity on display. Two notes: it starts out hard. Stick with it. _childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing as well as a bit relentless. It will from the get go let you know a very important lesson: Pseudo (the player character) is not as strong as the people inhabiting Zenozoik, the world of the game. Once you get the hang of it you will be able to dominate fights making you dance on the battlefield like a martial arts master and it will feel good, knowing that you are inherently "weaker". If you do not try to learn from your mistakes on the other hand , Pseudo will get stunlocked, reduced to mincemeat and you will be forced to redo a lot of fights.At the beginning of fights you can challenge intelligent beings into playing the ritual and like in the world of yugioh they cannot say no. Winning it can give you some helpful modifiers but if the enemy win they get to hinder YOU so be ready.The world is divided into day and night playing Pseudo in his normal and "imagined" form. The latter can get through thornbushes normal Pseudo cannot. However if normal Pseudo gets knocked out you respawn as "imagined" Pseudo giving you a second try if you can find your body and wake it up. But if "imagined" Pseudo dies its game over.The Story and its ending had me heavily emotionally invested in Pseudo and The Boy; The world is weird, fascinating and thoroughly enjoyable; the characters in it are strange and ugly and yet they fit in perfectly with the world that do not seem out of place.I love this game but it can sometimes frustrate you but unlike other games those moments are not to common and when they happen there are ways around it.Some tips to start you off with:Do not be afraid to backtrack to a campsite and rest as it will save your progress. They are plentiful but the path to the next might have a few tough fights between themDo not use all materials to make brews right away as SOME of them can be used to make other things you might be interested in. Keep at least a few in reserve until you know which ones are safe to use up. Don't worry the really important materials cannot be made into brews anyway.Play the game you will not regret it.Good Roads, Clear Skies.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m don’t know what it is about this game, but there is something about it that reminds me of games from when I was younger. It’s straightforward but incredibly enjoyable to spend my time with.+ The world is weird and vibrant with a unique art style.+ Character upgrades and skills are deep enough that your decisions matter but simple enough that you don’t need to do a bunch of outside research.+ Combat is straightforward but it works well with the array of gnarly enemies and their fighting styles.+ Navigating and exploring the world is fun (It feels a bit like solving a simple, but beautiful maze).+ Awesome cast of crazy characters.I’ve heard some people mention they had difficulty navigating around the world but I had no problem with this and thoroughly enjoyed the environmental mazes!In my opinion, this game is well worth the price. It was a nice reminder that a game doesn’t need a bunch of different bloated systems in it to be good. I never thought I’d enjoy this game to the degree I am when I picked it up. I’m sad at the thought of completing it and finishing up my time in this weird and wacky world.

_childDocuments_.review: So I get incredibly frustrated playing this game, but I'm still loving the experience.The art direction and visual style is fascinating - it's so distinct, with beautiful landscapes and remarkably ugly character designs.  To be clear though, the characters are designed to be ugly, not that the game itself is.  The enemies are super distinct in their weirdness and fighting styles.  I think the closest I can come to comparisons with these character designs would be the Oddworld series or the old Neverhood games, but that's selling both short - Clash is incredibly unique, and I would love to be able to just wander the world that this game presents.As far as audio goes, the soundtrack and voice acting are superb.  The main character, Pseudo, sounds like the uncle that will teach you how to defend yourself in school, and the Boy hits that kidlike quality without sounding obnoxious.  The other voice actors are also giving their all to having a varied and fun range of voices, accents, and random sayings.  The soundtrack doesn't overstay its welcome, and has some moments that are catchy, clever, and just as unique as the visuals.  It doesn't follow the trends of other video game soundtracks of the modern era, and largely goes its own way.Gameplay-wise is where I get the most frustrated.  Combat is MERCILESS, even moreso than games with a similar playstyle like Wolong Fallen Dynasty or Elden Ring.  Enemies hit hard, and you don't have i-frames when dodging or reacting to being hit - You can be flinching from a strike and then get hit by another followup attack.  Thankfully, you don't automatically get stunlocked like it sounds like you would.  The need for perfect timing with dodges and parries is incredibly necessary as a result of this.  However, there have been multiple times where it feels like my mouse clicks for attacks aren't registering.  This has led to many periods where I feel like I should have been able to hit an enemy, but instead find Pseudo just standing there letting himself be struck instead.  I've checked, and know that my mouse isn't broken or anything; my best guess is that the game has some kind of system in place to prevent what it might perceive as button-mashing.To add on to that, the death/revival system is a bit weird, and sometimes feels like more of a punishment than another death.  Let's say you die in a fight against multiple enemies, after taking several down.  You get revived, and get one more chance to defeat your targets to recover your body.  Your enemies in that fight all revive, as well.  You don't lose experience or items or anything, but you are on your last straw.  If you die a second time (in what the game calls "Pseudo's imaginary form"), it's game over and you have to start over from your last autosave.  Having certain segments where you are required to fight tough enemies while in this "one death and it's game over" phase adds to the frustration.(This part is also almost entirely a skill issue - I know I'm not the best at games like this anyways, but it's worth saying in the review)Even with that said, combat can be incredibly satisfying.  The different fighting styles and special moves that can be unlocked feel so distinct, and landing a perfectly timed hit that sends an enemy ragdolling is awesome.  It's really fun to set up attacks and land the perfect attack.  When it feels good, IT FEELS SO GOOD!All told, it's somewhat flawed, with a difficulty level that will feel incredibly intimidating to a majority of players, but it's absolutely worth facing down for the music, the visuals, and the unforgiving combat system.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm rewriting the review after 100% play-through because the first one doesn't do it justice. this game is THE GOATeverything about it is almost perfect, they don't make games like this anymore it gave me the same feeling when playing ps2 games when i was a kid (it doesn't mean it's bad).the art style is unique and i liked how i could control rendering style and make it more comicy and it's sure has it's own taste, the monsters and the characters are weirdly unique and they had good design and each one has it's own flavor in the world in the previous review i stated that combat was clunky, well it's not! i was just bad at it, after few hours i knew when to use aggression meter and dodge-attack the enemy to Ko! it was slow at first but very enjoyable at endgame! and there's a new game plus !The ritual or the ''one law'' is good and fun to use,it's luck and strategy based and it could change the tide of battle for both sides and i hope they add more artifacts so it will have more of an impact in the future the crafting system was okay it was nothing special it helps alot but i could survive without weapons and armor, the looting however was a nightmare. i had my camera glued to the ground and the corners of the map just because they're blended in and easy to miss it didn't let me enjoy the scenery i hope they do something about it, that's why items in darksouls glow! and at the end of the game i had so many small figurines! i thought i could convert them to higher versions but nope i'm stuck with 70 figurines in my pants the story was beautifully told, it has good writing and good voice acting and i was engaged with the journey because i wanted to know where does it end and i wasn't disappointed, the ending was emotional and beautiful! overall this game is a hidden gem and i hope it get more recognition

_childDocuments_.review: + Really unique graphical style that looks fantastic+ Inventive, weird fantasy world with a distinct identity and refreshing originality+ The ritual game you can play before fights is fun, easy to grasp, and has some skill involved+ Combat is fun and blows have a weighty impact+ Lots of fighting styles and special moves to mix up and find ones that work for you+ Character, creature and environment designs are awesome - really unique and stand out+ Interesting mix between day and night mechanics, and if you die in the day you get 1 attempt to try and recover your body in the night+ Simple but well-told story with some solid voice acting, good dialogue and themes+ The music is really nice and complements the world well- The very start of the game felt a little aimless as you have no real goal (but picked up quite quickly once it got going)- Traversing the environments sometimes became a slog due to how dense and convoluted they can be - it was quite easy to get lost and a bit frustrated and was made worse when backtracking and still not knowing your way around- Some QoL features missing such as being able to switch to melee weapons without going into the menu (which doesn’t pause the game) and the map being fairly unhelpfulI had a blast with this game - it tells a nice simple story in a not-so-simple land and has some solid martial arts gameplay beating up mutants. I’ve thought for a long time that a lot of fantasy settings play it too safe/samey (as soon as I see a new fantasy game featuring elves, dwarves, goblins and the rest of the usual suspects I start to get bored) when you can do whatever you want with it - it’s nice to see a setting that breaks the mould. The environments and creature designs were great, but the character designs were particularly fantastic and varied. Hoping there will be a sequel (featuring a Mutant Battle Royale mode where you can play as other mutants please!)

_childDocuments_.review: (New Review)I really didn't want to leave a negative review but this game is insanely buggy. If it were an Open Beta, this game would still be in an unacceptable state.Crashes on boss fights, winning fights only to end up stuck in the geometry and having to restart, beating giant enemies only for them to fall and their body blocks your way forward, killing enemies only for them to stand back up and now be unkillable while they keep attacking you, enemies spawning other enemies outside of your playable area making it impossible to fight them, these are just the MAJOR bugs that I have a problem with. I also somehow sequence broke the game and got all 4 Great Shield Artifacts to fight the final boss without ever unlocking the path to the Outsider/Coast area. The times my camera got stuck inside my body or went thru walls doesn't bother me at all, but losing all my progress over and over in a game with a terrible checkpoint system does.In this game, the checkpoints/respawns/bonfires will sometimes be separated by multiple areas and dozens of fights. Sometimes you will start at a campfire, go through 2 different Ritual NPC fights, 3 more Wild NPC fights, a new area, a cutscene, a boss fight, another cutscene and ANOTHER boss fight, and still not get a new checkpoint. Even sleeping at your tent isn't a checkpoint, even LEVELING UP isn't a checkpoint. As far as I can tell, the only reliable way to save your progress is to run all the way back to your camp and brew a potion.Also, the potion-brewing ingredients are limited. They're single instances across the map, you pick one carrot up and that carrot is gone forever, meaning EVERY single ingredient has a set quantity before you have no more. I can't fathom how this seemed like a good idea in a game where the only way to learn what each ingredient does is to brew them, drink the brew and then remember what they did.On the opposite end, there is an absolutely ridiculous overabundance of Materials for the shops. After the first armor set, I never once unlocked anything new in the shop that I didn't immediately have 3x the required materials to buy. They are EVERYWHERE in chests and bags and backpacks, and on top of that some materials drop from respawnable enemies making them infinite. And on top of THAT you can actually trade some of your Ingredients, which are FINITE, for more materials, for some reason.The first person fighting feels absolutely terrible. You always feel like you're punching them from way too far away, and sometimes even while holding forward and pressing against the enemy as close as the game will allow, your punches still won't reach. You also are still vulnerable to being hit and knocked out of first person mode so you have to dodge, except the dodging barely moves you and you can't see yourself anymore to try and get a good read on what's happening.I love the art style, story, themes and world of Zenozoik. The Corwids are one of the most interesting concepts I've ever seen in a video game, the fighting is incredibly fun when it works and you don't get all your work stripped away for no reason. But this game is just way too buggy with way too many glaring flaws for me to think anyone who isn't an insane person obsessed with the Zeno-verse like me would actually enjoy it.(Old Review)Very fun, the art style fits the world so perfectly and really makes you feel like this is an entirely alien civilization to our own.However it's pretty buggy and the nonsensical checkpoint system makes the bugs even worse. You would think that anytime you sleep at a campsite would be a check point, but it's not. So at some point I had a check point that was at a Totem 2 areas away from the fight I kept dying on, the only fight I could do to make progress. So I had to keep running through multiple loading zones for the same fight before I figured out that while sleeping isn't a check point, brewing potions for some reason is.The game is pretty hard and a lot of the sections can be a ton of fights in a row you have to overcome to make progress, I had multiple situations where I had to re-do entire areas because the game crashed or I won a fight, but ended up stuck on geometry and unable to escape.The brewing system is kinda interesting but the ingredients are normally too sparse to really want to experiment much, which you have to do since none of them tell you what they do. Even after you drink them, it's not written anywhere, you just have to remember the combos.1st Person fighting feels super weird and finicky, like you're striking for 3x farther than you should be at all times but cannot get closer because of the enemy's hitboxes.Also the parry seems to serve absolutely no purpose as it's 3x harder to do than a dodge, gives no movement unlike the dodge, and as far as I've seen you at best can get off one normal attack as reward and in some cases not even that, while you can literally attack WHILE dodging.This should honestly be a Negative Review but this game isn't very big and I want it to succeed so I'd rather lay out all the flaws without hurting their rating.

_childDocuments_.review: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is a game with a whole lot of soul and heart. The eternally creative ACE Team returns to the strange and wonderful world of Zenozoik, last seen in Zeno Clash 2*. While it's still a brawler, Clash: Artifacts of Chaos (mostly) moves to a more traditional third person view rather than the first person perspectives of its predecessors.There's clearly a lot of influence taken from the Souls franchise this time around with an estus equivalent, the ability to recover from death by finding your corpse in a strange nighttime reflection of the world, looping environments with many unlockable shortcuts, as well as light RPG elements in the form of equipment, minor crafting and stats and a greater emphasis on exploration and experimentation. I'd be hesitant to call it a Souls-like though, or even a Souls-lite, but the influence is certainly there. The combat is fun and you're given a lot more freedom than the prior Zeno Clash games. Your stances and special movesets are customizable with more being unlocked through exploration. You can have two active stances to swap between at any time and three special moves bound to the directions of your choice, which leads to a lot of potential mixing and matching. Moves feel like they've got some crunch to them, and the different stances and specials largely feel distinct from one another.Another part of the gameplay loop is 'The Ritual' which can be used to challenge most sentient opponents prior to fighting them. The Ritual is a simple game of dice, with each character rolling their bones and then using special items to either increase their own total or decrease their opponent's total. Whichever side wins gets to use their chosen artifact, which provide various beneficial effects to the victor such as allowing them the first strike with impunity or causing their opponent to be stung by hornets. It's a simple but pretty fun mechanic, but if ancillary dice games aren't your thing then The Ritual can be auto-played or even largely ignored entirely if you wish.Stylistically and graphically they've nailed it once again. With influence taken from both surrealist and classical art Zenozoik is one of the most unique fantasy settings around and perhaps my personal favourite. The music is also top-notch, featuring both remixes of classic Zeno Clash tracks as well as awesome brand new tracks. Pseudo's theme music rapidly became my favourite piece of music from the series.I'd also like to mention the voice acting - particularly that of Pseudo and The Boy. Zeno Clash's voice acting has never been a strong suite of the series, which is why the two main characters pleasantly surprised me with their performances. The Boy in particular (played by Anjali Kunapaneni) is very believable, and the back and forth dynamic where The Boy asks existential questions with a childish innocence and Pseudo trying to maintain a gruff demeanor when faced with questions that may not have a real answer is both endearing and also realistically played out. However I do have some relatively minor gripes with the game. The primary being that while the world map is large and there's a lot to explore, a majority of the areas you travel through are relatively cramped. Even out in the fields and plains you're railroaded through corridors with impassable rock formations and fallen trees. While I think Zeno Clash 2's world map was smaller overall, it had some pretty expansive locations in comparison. Another issue with exploration is that I found myself hugging every wall and trying to get my face in every nook and cranny looking for hidden items. Since there's no glowing aura or outline or anything around items (for better or worse), you can sometimes miss stuff surprisingly easy. - Update: A new game+ option has now been added! All in all though the positives far outweigh my few issues with the game. I think Clash is another great entry to the series and also a great place for people new to Zenozoik to begin. You can really tell ACE Team cares a lot about the world they've created, as well as their craft in general. They pour their creativity into every aspect of the game and the result is something... genuine. That's something to be treasured I think. *The Zeno Clash games are also worth playing. They're not required to play before Clash: Artifacts of Chaos however, as the stories are largely independent.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game with a very unique artstyle and overall very fun game play. Would recommend to the following people with a few caveats. There are a few nitpicks that I found very annoying to deal with throughout the game, which you can see towards the end but I would recommend this game If: First thing I found out was healing is very limited. You get 1, then up to 3, "flasks" that heal for a base of 25% HP but you need to craft them into stronger healing pots so you can get 50-100% heals. At the end I ran out of crafting materials to make them better so I had to scrounge around the world for stuff I missed so I would stuff for the final bosses. This was pretty annoying but when crafting you can make potions either give you more stamina regen or better damageThere is a very interesting "bloodstain" system in the game where you come back to life during the twilight hours and are now made of wood where you fight whatever killed you again in order to revive yourself. This is cool and also does not work very well as you are likely to have worse healing resources because you used one of the stronger ones during your alive fight and now cannot craft stronger ones. Also any enemy you defeated alive, are now back up at 50% hp. I think this could be a lot more fun if the healing wasn't limited. You can also wake up at night and roam around in a spooky/limited version of the world and do some extra stuff. I think this is a really cool mechanic and was a lot of fun to use and explore around in.You start with one of 3 different starting movesets and get 5-6 stances you get throughout the game. You also get 3 special move slots with about 10 special moves that allow you to do many different things. Overall very fun and varied with lots of interesting ways to do what you want to do.Dodging is more about moving out of the way of something rather than dodging through the attack. Dodging has very little, if any, i-frames and it was difficult getting used to that. You will fight the same 20-30 enemies throughout the game over and over and it gets tiring towards the end. Also fights tend to be 1v2-4 messes that results in you circling the group while they hit each other until there is 1 or 2 left. I ended up finding that you can spam 2 punches and then do a "special" to stun lock most enemies in the game and ended up using that for most of the final third of the game as trying to be fair was not working very well due to instant hit moves.Good for the most part except for when the story just kind jumps to the end. Because the game is open world, you can go in any one of 4 directions before being sent down the final path, but the final path is 4 bosses, 2 of which you've already fought before, and then it is supposed to be a super tear jerky moment but we didn't get enough build up for that and it feels off.Overall very good, I know a lot of this review was complaining and pointing out flaws but those, and some fps drops in some of the later sections of the game, were the only really massive issues I had with the game. It was a fun, unique world and the characters kept me interested in playing. A solid 7-8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Fun brawler set in an imaginative, alien world full of kooky weirdos to punch in the face. The game's basic plot is about Pseudo, a hermit who is pulled from his life of seclusion on a quest to protect a small feathered boy from seemingly every other person in the world, all of whom want to get their hands on him.Unlike the two earlier games in the series, Clash is primarily a third-person game where you combine light attacks, special moves and directional dodges to string together combos of attacks. Build up enough of your aggressiveness gauge and you can switch to a first-person minigame of sorts where you then have to rack up enough hits without taking a hit yourself to unleash a powerful finishing move. As you explore, you can unlock new stances and special moves which may or may not suit your preferred playstyle and build, with different moves and stances scaling differently with the different stats you can improve on. Overall I found the combat to be satisfying and not overly punishing. Worth mentioning is the lack of a difficulty setting, so some players might find it a bit too easy, especially in the second half of the game. To add an extra layer of depth to the exploration, Pseudo can also traverse the world at night in a sort of 'imaginary' form that conveniently lets him enter areas his daytime form cannot. Sometimes it did make the exploration feel a tad padded, in that you spend a lot of time exploring areas you've already explored, except for the small nighttime-only areas. There is some interaction between the two, where the nighttime exploration can allow you to access new areas in the daytime as well.Its most standout feature would probably be its art direction though, which combines the bizarre alien designs of the previous Zeno Clash games with a new stylized crosshatched look. The crosshatching can be toggled off, if you prefer the smoother rendering of the older games, which was a nice consideration by the developers. I enjoyed the design of the world itself as well, but in general the setting feels a bit more grounded than the earlier installments.Heavily recommended if you're looking for something a little out there or you just like punching things in the face.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is flawed, but oozes with passion and love that creates an unforgettable experience that is well worth the price tag.Now for my detailed review, which I will split into The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly.Also a forewarn, I have not played the Xeno Clash games before this. So if parts of my review sound pretty clueless, you know why.Self-explanatory. I certainly have a lot more good to say about the game than I do bad or ugly. To begin, the gameplay, visuals, and sound design.The gameplay feels really fun and it requires a degree of skill as you fight enemies with the incredibly useful parry mechanic. The combat isn't very deep, but ACE has still managed to make it feel satisfying to land parries and solid hits while punishing you for button mashing. On top of it, the multiple fighting styles can let you cater to your own style or just whatever feels good and the special moves can add a little extra spice to your moveset. I found the Corwid stance and the Spin Kick to be my go-to's for my playthrough. The visuals are really nice. The entire painted land of Zenozoik feels bright and colourful and the various areas in the game feel great to navigate, each with their unique appearance and iconic layout. I actually found myself seldom getting lost as I explored because the areas were either pretty straightforward or felt really well designed to the point where I knew exactly where I was in the area. The only exception was in the Zonectic Mountains because my blind ass couldn't see the damn climb spot and maybe the Amonkuali because I think that area was meant to be mildly confusing. As for the exploration itself, ACE did an excellent job making exploration, especially during the night, all that much more rewarding. I would often find a thorn wall and immediately look for the nearest camp to see if I could explore it at night just to see what's behind it. even during the day, there was a gigantic host of goodies to find across the world that gave you a nifty advantage just for advancing your moves or allow you to buy more things from the shops. There's also the diverse cast of enemies that might seem limiting to the game at first, but it kinda makes a lot of fights feel more personal. Even then, the enemies in the game are so numerous that you don't really feel any fatigue from fighting foes you have met before, and it's enough to keep you on your toes for a majority of the game. These enemies also feel really unique in terms of their designs and their varied personalities. They added a lot of character to the world of Zenozoik, populating it with all these weird characters that you can recognize instantly just from a single glance. A lot of heart definitely went into the way the game looked.The sound design was the icing on the cake and then some. The soundtrack was an absolute masterpiece to listen to with many of the tracks being iconic to the game itself, namely the fight themes you find throughout the game. Austral Music knew what they were doing and it made the game feel like so much more than just the fighting game where you play as a dude who looks like a shaved carrot. The music wasn't the only good thing, the sound effects are part of why the combat felt really satisfying. Every hit you landed felt like it had a lot of oomph behind it, even the stances where you slash or slap enemies felt satisfying to pull off all because the stances just  powerful, even when they weren't.I could talk about all the good in the game, but I still feel that it's important to address the flaws in the game because otherwise my praise would just fall flat on it's face with nothing to back it up with.My main gripe is the writing and the story. While I overall enjoyed the story in the game, there were moments in the game where it felt like there was a huge disconnect where not enough was explained. For example, the game felt a bit vague on what exactly the Boy's powers were early on, and it isn't until later on where you actually get a solid idea as to what it is, but it still feels like there is some inconsistency between what they said early in the game compared to later in the game. It almost felt like they were sitting on the script for a long time and didn't change it as new ideas were introduced. Another example was moments prior to my first example where the main character, Pseudo, is talking to the main antagonist, Gemini, and she somewhat explains her reasoning as to why she wants the Boy. She briefly mentions her illness, but never goes into it. The writing itself is not the problem. The moments between The Boy and Pseudo were pretty cute and interesting, albeit a little stilted for some lines. The issue arises when multiple story elements are introduced and are either never elaborated on or never brought up again, like the Amonkuali and how it's clearly ancient ruins but it's never fully explained or elaborated on. If this was a design choice by part of ACE team, then I can see why they wanted to do it, but it's an extremely delicate art of knowing when to withhold exposition and when to explain things that ACE team seemed to struggle with somewhat. There was only one point where there was a massive exposition dump, only for it to not really matter because it was only loosely connected to the story as a whole. It might have been a reference to Xeno Clash with how unfamiliar I was with the details, but it didn't really feel like it had a point other than to worldbuild. I think that was a long-winded way to say that the pacing in the game was mediocre. Here I'll put down some personal problems from the game that weren't necessarily bad but still bothered me regardless.One of the game's main mechanics is The Ritual, which is a neat thing that you can do while initiating a fight for an opportunity to give yourself the upper hand, or completely fail and leave yourself with a disadvantage. It's a game of chance and strategy that left me actually scratching my head on some rolls as I tried to figure out what my next move should be.  However, I felt that after a certain point, The Ritual just kinda became fluff and it was a better idea to not even chance the ritual and just fight. It was still fun, but I personally just avoided the Ritual late game in favor of just getting to the beatdown. And then there is the matter of the game being called a "soulslike" which I can definitely see why. Stamina management, parries, dodge button, lock-on, checkpoints, point-based level ups, and a death mechanic. Despite all these mechanics, the game never truly felt like a "soulslike" the way that something like Sekiro, Nioh, or even Elden Ring felt. I never really felt that the game was unfair in any way or was absurdly difficult. All the challenges in Clash: Artifacts of Chaos felt reasonable and achievable in one try with only some practice. While absurdly high challenge isn't always the hallmark of every Soulslike, Clash: Artifacts of Chaos just felt like it was using that tag as bait more than anything. I even recall in the demo that the game was meant to have a multiplayer mechanic where you could duel other players, which kinda ties into how some of the souls mechanics just felt like a relic of an earlier build, like the death mechanic where you get a second chance at a fight for an opportunity to get Pseudo to wake up. Fortunately, ACE team discarded any further relation to the souls games by scrapping the multiplayer mechanic, which was to the game's benefit imo. Thankfully, everything else worked out, so I don't know why I'm complaining.In conclusion, while the game suffers from some drawbacks, I still had a downright blast with the game that had an ending which left me in tears. I definitely recommend the game for a weird and kick-ass experience that i think is definitely worth the price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Another amazing game from ACE Team, full of charm and challenging combat.  I expected another Zenoclash, but was pleasantly surprised to find a very competant God of War-like that feels like a deconstruction of Sony's first party storytelling.  The relationship between our two main leads might not have the same depth as Ellie and Joel or Kratos and Atreus, but I still fell in love with them and wanted to see their journey through to the end.  I also loved the ending, for what its worth, and the combat is VERY fun.  There are a handful of encounters that are quite difficult, but generally there is a gimmick you need to exploit (like letting the big guy accidentally knock out all the little guys).  Also, you fight the same dudes throughout the game- bounty hunters.  I really liked this.  I felt like I got to know not only the characters from a narrative standpoint, but also mastering their combat styles and recognizing what to look for.All in all, great game, worth the money, support these devs!

_childDocuments_.review: I was interested in the game due to the freaks they showed and stayed for the super fun combat! Honestly the amount of effort and care they put into combat kept me in awe, there's 8 stances each with their own normal, charged and dodge attacks (Sides, forward, back) BUT on top of that each stance also has a sprint attack AND a jump attack unique to each stance! Then you have 7 special attacks of which you can equip 3, all of these you must find around the world but they're not too difficult to find and each is unique in it's fighting style! The world is at times confusing to explore but really beautiful and the story, while not too crazy still captivated me and caught me off guard in the end! All in all there's a ton of fun to be had and to explore!TLDR; Super fun gameplay and pretty captivating story! Had a blast pummeling my enemies and so will you!

_childDocuments_.review: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is a semi-open-world third-person-brawler about an ugly, belligerent mutant in a world full of ugly, belligerent mutants who reluctantly takes a boy under his wing, only to realise that makes him the target of some unsavoury, powerful enemies. It's a prequel to the Zeno Clash games, but you don't need to know anything about them to enjoy this title. It's a simple story (Lone Worm and birb?) beautifully told, with a ton of warmth and humour. The world it's set on and the characters that people it are wonderfully weird, with some outstanding visual design and a wonderful surrealistic streak. And everything is beautifully rendered in an illustrated style that mimics the more elaborate eurocomix artists, full of crosshatched shadows and scratchy line work. All of its surfaces are superb: the music is just as excellent as the visuals, with lots of very striking orchestral and vocal compositions. Gameplay consists of combat and exploration. Combat's slow and deliberate - it reminded me a lot of the lumbering combat in the first Dark Souls, except that here it emphasises locking on and cancelling out of attacks and dodges to manoeuvre around enemies. There's a lot of personalization as to the combat styles and special attacks you take with you, and an RPG-lite system of upgrades. I clicked with combat almost instantly, unlike with the Zeno Clash games, and the few times I had issues with some boss or another I just equipped a weapon... that made short work of them. The world of Zenozoik is split into large-ish discrete levels, with a few small open areas lot of interconnected pathways weaving in and out everywhere. There's Dark-Souls-style shortcuts, lots of hidden things to find (combat styles and the materials used to trade for armours and items) and a whole system where  you can explore the world at night with another form of your character, alternate enemies, and new hidden treasures. The game's unwillingness to hand out map markers or to signpost where you're meant to go might be the biggest point against it; I spent a lot of time trying to work out what I was meant to do at one point, but a new patch has come out since which should hopefully address that issue. I certainly had no major problems once I was done with the mountains. I'd be extremely surprised if this is not one of my favourites, or even my favourite game of the year. A great story set in a ridiculously imaginative world full of secrets to find and hilariously ugly faces to bash in? Oh hell yeah.(Note from the future: Yep, even with all the other great games released this year, this one is right up there.)

_childDocuments_.review: This game was weirdly engrossing. God of War / Dark Souls in a neolithic acid trip world full of deranged creatures (watch out for the lion with Nigel Thornberry's face). Combat is methodical but not slow. It can be challenging, especially starting out with a limited moveset, but I found it much more forgiving than a souls game. Whenever you fight a sentient opponent you have the option to invoke The Ritual, which is a little dice game where the winner gains the effect of whatever artifact they played (opponent gets stung by bees when standing still, winner gets a free first blow, etc). I mostly skipped these because the benefits don't outweigh the risks, except for the Pact/Summon artifact which lets you summon a previous opponent as an ally and is genuinely useful to take aggro in big fights.My biggest con with this game is the level design. Visually the zones are beautiful, and the flow of them is not bad per se (sometimes they're actually fun to traverse with DS style looping shortcuts) but the starting zone especially is plagued by a number of unclear invisible barriers and visual elements. I've heard complaints of people getting lost, and while I didn't have much of a problem with it I can see why. There's so many knee-high rocks, mushrooms, fences that look like you could easily jump but are supposed to be boundaries instead. It's not that you don't where to go, it's more so that you can't really tell where the game is going to allow you to go. That plus a number of awkwardly placed level transitions detract from the semi-open world feel this game is trying to go for. Overall though this was a really fun and charming game. The original Zeno Clash was one of the first ever non-Valve games I owned on Steam and ACE Team has been making interesting underrated games for a while now.
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: If you like action adventure games or beat em ups then this is a must play, the combat when you first start can feel clunky but once you learn to do directional dodge attacks and parries you can do a flurry of blows that kill your enemies quickly, it's very smooth. Stamina plays an important role as once you run out you take double damage and cannot parry properly so this forces you to pace yourself and not button mash your way through encounters.If you like freaky or otherworldly settings in your games then you'll love Zenozoik, mutants, chimeras, robots and flora, all twisted versions of things you may see here on earth. The cross hatch rendering style and colours make this game beautiful to look at and travel. The world is separated into different main areas, the town and areas to the north east south and west. Each of these areas has you collecting an important artifacts to defeat the main boss and their bodyguards. The level design of each of these areas has you going along a main path to progress the story and optional paths to collect items and unlock shortcuts.The story, although simple, is told great and you'll fall in love with the characters. The voice acting is great and it has some funny moments.This game also doesn't bloat itself with side content, there are optional nightmare bosses that give large amounts of xp, special armour and an extra health flask. There are also body parts to collect for your nightform scattered around Zenozoik.There are flaws however, certain attacks from enemy have telegraphs so short it's extremely difficult to parry or dodge them, however these quick attacks don't deal too much damage so it doesn't break the flow of combat. It can also be tedious to backtrack to your campsites to save but they are pretty common so it's never too long of a backtrack. The night time mode could also have been fleshed out more, at the moment it allows you to find your way back to your body and have another try at a fight before a game over and to also allow yourself into areas you cannot go during the day. These areas, once completed then allow you to travel there during the day. The devs have said this was original meant to feature a PvP mode during the night but needed to be cut.I got 100% of the achievements in this game and it was always a blast and took me about 15 hours.Over all I give it a 8.5/10, definitely worth your time. With how unique this setting is it is currently my GOTY. I'd love to see some story DLC and maybe an arena mode
