_childDocuments_.review: The Music and Story were superb, and I found the combat to be a lot more interesting and engaging than the previous Zeno Clash games. The multiple different stances and special moves you can mix n match, combo together, and the dodging moves that can be either used just to dodge or attack in different directions all feel great when you learn to use them together. The ritual system also was a fun and unique way to spice up combat and interactions with the enemies, and it's optional a majority of the time so you only play it when you want to.Ace team really knows how to make a wonderfully weird and beautiful alien world, and I cannot recommend this game enough, as well as the first two Zeno Clash games, and Eternal Cylinder.
_childDocuments_.name: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos

_childDocuments_.review: While I admit that the first couple of hours were clunky as I adjusted to the combat system, after adapting, I found it simple but satisfying; I enjoyed my time with the game overall. It had a simple yet touching story that, when mixed with the art style, had me wanting to learn more about the world of Zenozoik. I beat the game in a little over 14 hours, so compared to rising game prices, the $30 price tag is appropriate though I understand if you would want to wait for a discount. A few other reviews pointed out issues with player knowledge regarding mapping navigation and enemy strength. During my playthrough, an enemy strength indicator and an update to the game map were swiftly patched in. I found some combat encounters mildly annoying when you are put up against more than two or three enemies as I feel like the combat system works better for one-on-one duals. Recently I've begun to feel like games are trying to do too much when it comes to either game mechanics or story beats, which end up feeling like unnecessary filler or just a detriment to the game, so Clash felt like a breath of fresh air.Overall I rate Clash 8/10 and am eager for a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished and wow- absolutely phenomenal game. I brawled my way through as a Boxer/Corwid. For the Boy!Each stance was deep enough for varied combat, each special viable and unique, and paced throughout the world so as to not drown you in choice illusion. Combat never felt like a chore, or something you'd want to avoid. It's a testament to how important the core gameplay is in any game.The interconnected world design is something that -in my personal opinion- has out shined the standards set by FromSoftware's Souls games. They've managed to build these vertical, yet surmountable regions that connect sensibly. This creates a strong feeling of progression while you brawl your way through Zenozoik. I know this was game was independent of Zeno Clash 1 and 2, but it was nothing short of enjoyable seeing some old assets from those games be re-used. As a Zeno Clash fan, nothing scared me more than seeing "Corwid Territory" on the map as one of the regions. And I was right to be afraid, as the descent into madness via true freedom is still as maddening as ever.The cross-hatching art style, while some may be taken a-back, served the narrative and immersion well. It's not a downgrade by any means, if anything it's a piece of rendering technology that's used creatively AND effectively. You can turn it off if you desire, but I personally feel it would detract from what ACE Team were trying to convey with Clash.If I had any downsides, they'd probably be that I didn't use weapons that often, in comparison to Zeno Clash. It may have just been that the combat arts themselves were more than enough (and allowed more moves). Additionally, some minor bugs/stuck on level geometry that were quickly resolved by either waking up or reloading my checkpoint - nothing detrimental or progression-halting. I was part of both closed tests, and there were two cut features I'd have loved to seen (not sure if I can say what they were). But understandably, they were probably not fleshed out enough to warrant further delays, or fit within the gameplay.Thank you ACE Team for revisiting Zenozoik a decade later. I really love this universe, as do so many others. It has been my goal to get my friends invested into the games, and this entry might be the one that finally tef-ing gets them to jump right in.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I know this review may look a bit strange since its 33 minutes long. But in actuality, I've playing this game on Epic version until certain mission that I can't get passed due to very specific bug. Since Epic version still have that issue, I decide to f..k it and supporting the Dev for more by purchase on Steam (After all they'd confirm on discussion that the certain issue already resolved on this version). And I'm very please to see my save is properly transfer and my Achievement just popping up like a mushroom on raining season.Anyway, Let get to the reviewClash: Artifacts of Chaos is a spinoff on Zeno Clash. That wacky series you might have a chance to play since 2010s . The whole series is know for couple of thing, Which might not be all that positive. But if you are into something strange and very stylish. This is a game for you.In this game, You'll play as "thing" beating the living sh1t out of other "things". You see, in the land of Zenozoink. Everything are kinda "many things" putting together to the point you can't tell which is which. Luckily however, The "thing" we are in control here got a name, He's Pseudo.Pseudo is a hermit. He's living alone and might continued on that way until one day, He met with "The Boy" and got tangling into the plot that have a thing to do with very angry grumpy and power Siam twin and the rest of the inhabitant of Zenozoink out to get to the boy and that hefty sum of bounty. Pseudo then has to be a reluctant hero (at first) and see to the boy for his own best.Gameplay wise, Clash is like its previous predecessors (Zeno Clash). Its a full on brawling game with very satisfied Sound effect when you punching kicking beating the living crap out of your enemies. The game will be playing most of the time in 3rd person. The control is smooth and there are some life comfort like target lock, switch target and a command set move which is set up to be very easy to access.'- The combat feel a bit of Dark soul-ish. But to me personally, I think this game have similarity to Absolver than Darksoul.- Your basic attack will be determine by the style you've pick at the beginning or along the way of your adventure, Each style allow you to beat the enemies to your liking. (After all, The hitbox in this game is pretty much base on the whole area of the character, Meaning if your hit connect to the body part, Its a hit. And no other way around)- Your "Heavy" attack consisted of 3 button set up, One Button , Forward+One Button and Backward+One Button. I like this set up. Its allow for you to customzie the move you like and executed them in the most simplest manner without a need to remember to much combination.- When you hit the enemy to certain point. You'll accumulate the "Agressive" bar. This bar can be a life saver. When use, You are enter FPS mode just like in previous Zeno Clash. Then you beat the hell out of the enemy and finishing with very bad ass and powerful move.And then there are a ritual. Which consider as a mini game to determine buff/debuff before you start each brawl. After all, Even in a lawless barbaric land like Zenozoink. There are just ONE rule. And its the ritual. Which is still consisting of beating each other to pulp. But with a little more curtsy by playing a game before doing so first.- In Ritual You will start with choosing the artifact, The artifact will have its own properties which if you win the said ritual, The effect will be apply to the enemy and in vise versa if the enemy win the ritual- You'll have to play the dices. When the dies are cast you'll need to use the assign "Tak" or the effect which will be use on dies. The "Tak" can be apply depend on its properties. Some are area base, Some are one die only. There are variation of these "Tak" which you can trade and adjust to suit your need.- The rule on the ritual is simple. Whoever got the most point at the end, Win.So basically most of the time. You'll run around, exploring, collecting, trading and fighting, rinse and repeat. Which in coupling with a strange world and living things you have to beating them, I say its going to be very fun and unique experience and very fun too.Now for the not so good part:- Most of the time, You'll have to fight multiple enemies, And they are very very tough. It might be a bit tedious that you have to kite them around to get a shot at.- The ritual, Even with the RNG nature. Still feel like a fix match. If you really really want to win it, You might have to cheese and reloading alot just for that.But in overall, The game is great. If you are looking for a very wacky world where you get to beat the living sh1t out of the wacky things. This is your game.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid action adventure game, the narrative is great. I have no context on the previous games in this series so I viewed this game by itself and was super impressed by the world building. The laws of it's inhabitant is the most important part- There's a big theme about "being a slave to someone or some idea" and what it means to be free, and if it's even possible to be totally free. Honestly if I wanted to I'd write a whole analysis about the game's themes and writing, which I love.Art direction is super strange but beautiful in it's own way. The game feels like some mix of God of War and a Salvador Dali painting. All the people are these ugly chimera like creatures with unique designs.Gameplay has pros and cons. Early on it feels fairly challenging but then you start getting into the combat, figuring out how to combo and it becomes super satisfying when you start stun locking enemies from these combos + upgrading your character. One issue is that it gets pretty easy towards the end when you're overleveled. I even stopped having to craft healing potions cause I just wasn't losing any fights, even if I lost the artifact challenge. (Which also starts to become tedious towards the second half.) Overall I liked all the large group fights or boss fights.Biggest issue early on is that finding where you need to go can be a challenge. The devs have listened to this feedback though and added/are still adding improvements to make this aspect more reasonable. For me though, once you get your bearings with the map you start to navigate it easy towards the end of the game, which is the point. Another complaint is just the general janky-ness of it all. Constantly reusing the same enemies, scenes transitioning is a weirdly anticlimactic way, parts where you feel like it may have been rushed. If the game were longer these issues would dampen my experience more.Lastly- this is an OST of the year contender, I'm positive it will be atleast top 5. The soundtrack is perfect for the primal/tribal aesthetics of the world. Some tracks incorporating this opera singing or a foreign folk singer. Some tracks are just 10/10. Check out "Parting" or "the boy calls" for examples of such tracks. Personally it's on the level of Ori or Hollow Knight.Overall- Gameplay is fun but can get old/too easy towards the end. Artifact Ritual game gets tedious (Though the fact that the ritual game is kinda dumb is weaved into the narrative? Which is kinda sick and almost balances it out). Art is strange and weird. It's ugly in a beautiful way if that makes sense. World building makes me wanna read a graphic novel for this series if it existed. The story is well written with deep themes. Soundtrack is 10/10. It's not too long, though I kinda wish it was a bit shorter. You might get lost a lot. A fantastic, very low key indie game for 2023.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game with a really good yet not complicated combat system and decent story. Visuals are stylized amazingly well and I can see this game aging decades without issue. Only had a few minor bugs and 1 softlock that I intentionally went to find. Never had a death I felt was unfair, usually a result of multiple bad decisions on my part. If I had to say anything else it'd be two things : 1. I wish the game had a better map system, I never got lost but trying to figure out where I've been and where I haven't so I can explore new areas was a bit of an issue with how some of the level design wraps around on itself.2. Certain parts of the story, especially towards the end, feel cut up. Like there should've been an additional cutscene of dialogue in between the 2 relevant parts before they start. It never really hinders the story but it makes it feel like it's jumping a bit, like someone clicked to skip forward 5 seconds in a video or something.Overall solid 8.5-9/10. Very very good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool game with a fantastic and weird art style!In a way, it kinda reminds me of the old games from Shiny Entertainment, like Sacrifice and Earthworm Jim.You're basically a weird-looking warrior monk named Pseudo on a mission to protect a creature just named "boy". Since you're a warrior monk, you unlock and use all kinds of martial arts styles. You can switch between two of choice during combat, and upgrading them makes you stronger or more resilient, depending on what you upgrade. There's also a pretty big selection of weapons you can find or buy, but I've personally not used them much. The combat itself was much more fun without them in my opinion. The world itself is very unique and weird looking, but still has biomes you can recognize. During the day you do most of your exploration, but some areas can only be accessed during the night, by using Pseudo's night-time form. There are also never any waypoints or markers, so exploration is a must to progress. But since the world looks so good, it's a joy to explore every nook and cranny!There are some souls-like mechanics in the game. When you get killed, you switch to your night-time form, and you'll have to go back to your body to wake it up. Which means defeating those that killed you first, or else you can't wake up your body. You don't lose "souls" or anything if you actually die, and enemies don't respawn when you save at a camp but it can still be pretty difficult. I found the game pretty difficult in the beginning, but once I unlocked more combat styles it became much easier.All in all, I really recommend it! I think if you like martial arts combat games and old school games where they don't hold your hand and you have to explore, you'll like it as well!

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with this game. The world of Clash is just breath taking. And the music might be one of the best soundtracks I heard in a while. It's very fun and satisfying to fight and explore the world.There is a lot of interesting mechanics, like unlocking attacks You can equip in Your arsenal or fighting stances You can learn.Ritual is a very cool idea. Before fighting, You can start a short dice game. The winner can put some kind of impediment onto enemy. Like tying their leg to the ground so they can't move or having a free first punch.Overall Clash is a very fun, satisfying game with a fantastic world, incredible soundtrack and engaging story. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic extremely evocative dreamlike art combined with...a functional brawler that's... inspired by dark souls??? Sounds crazy on paper but it seems super confident at mixing these two genres. It has arcade-ness, energy, combos and crowd control attacks of a brawler and also need for careful positioning, dodging or parrying, flasks, leveling and resting mechanics of a souls game. It's does not seem to be as demanding as most games from either genre are so far. Hopefully the difficulty will escalate later on. Oh, and you can also challenge various enemies (not all) to a duel through performing a ritual that can modify the conditions of the battle... Said ritual is a mini game of dice with an extra turn based twist. After rolling dice, you and your enemy can plant flags on the dice tray that modify resulting values of the dice. For instance you can roll super high but all the dice are in close proximity to one another and your enemy could plant a flag lowering each dice result by 1 thus making you loose 3 points. The point of the ritual is that each side chooses debuffs and buffs that will activate during the actual combat depending on which side wins that ritual mini-game. There are a couple conditions/modifiers to choose from and they all influence the fight afterwards in a significant way. For instance, you or your opponent could spawn an additional npc after winning the pre-fight ritual. Or a visibility and z-targeting affecting fog could spawn it. Or a losing side gets a huge mobility debuff, etc. etc. NPCs banter thought the ritual mini game and the fight, it feels so organic it's crazy. ALSO YOU HAVE LINK TO THE PAST DARK WORLD TYPE/LEGACY OF KAIN SOUL REAVER ABILITY and you can shift into your dream-world wooden version that let's scout ahead in a limited radius from the camp you went to sleep. and that form can also pass through certain obstacles that your body form can't. ALSO YOU HAVE COMBO FINISHERS THAT ARE JUST ZENO CLASH 1 AND 2 FIRST PERSON BRAWLING... Crazy stuff...

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be summarised as Kung Fu Dark Souls, but with a very unique style and setting with a handful of neat mechanics that set it apart.Imagine if in Dark Souls before you started a boss battle, you could challenge the boss to a dice game where the winner could inflict any number of severe and interesting handicaps on the loser. That is one of the core mechanics in Clash and it really never gets old. As you progress in the game and the fights get more difficult and complex, so too does "The Ritual" (the name of the dice game you play) adding in more rounds, more dice, and more ways to affect the dice during play. I should add that taking part in the The Ritual is almost entirely optional, it's a tool in your arsenal to tackle tough fights or make them more interesting.The combat is very satisfying and strikes the perfect balance rewarding both slow and methodical  as well as fast and aggressive playstyles. There is a very large variety of both fighting styles and special attacks to find and choose from that can be mixed-and-matched to suit your preferred style of play.Clash also has some of the best hitbox-porn of any game I have played, if an attack looks like it shouldn't connect, it won't. This leads to some very cinematic and satisfying moments where you can come in under an enemy's strike and punish them before they can recover. I don't want to call Clash a Souls-like as it does so much to set it apart and make it stand on its own, but if you like Souls-Like games the combat and gameplay alone will make Clash: Artifacts of Chaos right up your alley.

_childDocuments_.review: A unique and colorful art style painted over a souls like designed world, where you have to navigate by memorizing landmarks. The writing and voice actors did a good enough job to get me engaged in the story, even though I feel like I had a prediction where it would go from the first hour.The music is great, it takes inspiration from Nier, and it pulls it off. The combat system seems to be a third souls like and two thirds its own thing. I am not an expert on judging combat. But I will just say that it felt new to me and was fun to learn. If you hate getting lost (like not knowing where to go) then this game may not be for you. I got lost at multiple points in the game, sometimes searching to up to 30 minutes to find where i needed to go. But even  if you don't know if your going the right way, you will be getting knowledge of the map, experience points, and materials. So it still feels like consistent progress is being made, Most of the time.If you love getting lost (immersion) then this game is absolutely for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Clash: Artifacts of Chaos is weird, but one of those kinds of weird where you can see the love poured into every part of it, the kind of weird where you know that this all made sense to someone... It is weird, but it is also wonderful.Now I will say that in recommending it you should know that you're walking into a game that is sometimes just a bit wilfully cryptic, the tutorials aren't great, the UI for inventories can be a bit bare-bones and if you don't like a game that is more than happy to let you be lost and confused sometimes, you will not like this. Clash's interconnected map means that learning to navigate it and figuring out where to go next can sometimes be confusing in a way that I can see turning off a lot of people, but yet it always feels less like an oversight and more just a part of the intentional weirdness of the whole thing. Especially the navigation part, I won't spoil it too much but this is a game that use the concept of actually telling you where to go as a powerful narrative device, it's the kind of moment that makes you realise that "oh....they really knew what they were doing here and were not afraid of losing some players in the process to do it right".The thing is it's now been a day since I beat Clash and....I can't stop thinking about it! The fighting was really fun, the style and presentation was exceptional for me, the music was filled with constant surprises and some really great moments... It all just sticks in the brain as something really memorable and cool and those moments of getting lost honestly felt like part of it by the end. Now I will say that this game's combat can be really punishing sometimes, and if you find it difficult I have nothing but sympathy because the game really doesn't hold back sometimes when it comes to difficulty, like it or not you're going to have to learn how to deal with group fights and block management, and when to get aggressive and all that stuff....but as you learn it, as you master it, you will find moments where the combat absolutely shines. Plus walking into a fight, challenging someone to a dice game, winning, and then making them have to deal with a random swarm of bees for it is never not funny.(Bonus thing that I wasn't sure where to write: when travelling across the world do remember to stop off at campfires whenever you can, they're your spawn points and forgetting to go to them and then dying can lead to moments where you have to run long distances again so just keep that in mind, when exploring don't forget to reset at a campfire when possible to keep checkpoints nice and local)I will say as well, personally, that I actually recommend keyboard and mouse for this game, it really doesn't feel as odd with it as I worried it would and locking on is very rarely a necessity, the controls for it feel honestly really good and responsive in a way that keyboard and mouse rarely does for this kind of game (although as of writing there are unfortunately a couple of keybinds such as c for your first person mode attacks and i for inventory that can't be rebound for some reason, it's not a deal breaker for me as I actually found the default bindings mostly fine but I know for some people that will 100% be an issue and it's perfectly understandable).And as for the story, it's neat, it takes a while to grow properly but it has a few moments of storytelling that stand out really well but beyond that it's just a cool excuse to return and explore the weirdness of Zenozoik once again. It has been forever since I last played the Zeno Clash games so my memory on them is fuzzy, I will say that the story is still perfectly standalone but I'm pretty sure there's a couple of moments that Zeno Clash fans will appreciate in terms of fleshing out this world a bit more as a prequel seemingly set a long time before the civilisations we see in the other ZC games. However it still stands on its own as was compelling enough to see me through to the end and I'm honestly glad I did as, while the story isn't groundbreaking or anything, I can't deny that by the end of the game I was genuinely attached to Pseudo and the Boy, and upon completing the game, I can't deny that I miss them a bit.So yes, I recommend it, it's not without flaws, occasional minor jank can occur with some ragdolls and at one point I punched a man so hard I accidentally phased through a door but honestly I don't want to give the impression that technical stuff is worse than it is, it ran smooth apart from minor stutters when going to a new area which never affected combat or anything, it never crashed on me, and glitches were few, far between, and very minor for the most part, it's a good, solid, and complete release :)The TLDR is just that I really liked it...I probably could've just written that xD....I really like it :)Also I can't stop listening to Pseudo's theme, it's an absolute jam so, regardless if if you get the game or not although I do personally think i's worth it, at least join me in enjoying a really good early-game song that I can;t stop listening to: Oh and final heads up, atm the soundtrack version is only in flac format so just know that if you do buy the soundtrack, anyway....Have a nice day everyone. Hope you're all doing well :)

_childDocuments_.review: Long-time fan of Zeno Clash, here - I’m only an hour in, and I can already tell that this is also for me. Mainly because there’s nothing else out there that I can think of, which comes even remotely close to fitting the very specific mold Ace have created and ran with.However - since the game definitely isn’t perfect, I’d like to address some seemingly-common complaints about it I’ve seen, and give my thoughts on them:And yeah, that’s really all the complaints I care to address - everything else really has been completely up my alley so far. To top that off - their support for the Deck is pretty solid, too! They earned that verified status!And with that, my review is pretty much done for now. I just wanna thank Ace Team for not giving up on their beautiful, funky lil “cave-punk” world, and let them know that I - and, hopefully, a large enough number of other weirdos - will always be there for them, every time they choose to revisit Zenozoik. One of my absolute favorite settings in gaming, and easily my pick for most underrated.

_childDocuments_.review: A good return to Zenozoik, no need to be a zeno clash vet to get in.  Gameplay differs from the Zeno Clash formula, 1st person fistfights are limited to a special combat mode you build up during fighting and the combat is more comparable to Zelda:BotW or the ever comparable Soulsborne type of games. You start relatively weak and need to gather EXP and special figurines to burn for skill points and to boost your fighting styles, fights are bit more strategic with the inclusion of the Artefact system where you and a sentient enemy play dice to see who gets spanked extra hard in the upcoming fight, it feels very fitting for the world of Zenozoik where people use savage beatings as currency and as friendly greetings.Quality VA work helps breathe life to Pseudo and the other characters making up the world of Zenozoik, plot feels like the Zenozoik version of Wolf and Cub, but that's just fine, people should copy that stuff more. A real find for a 30€ game in these times. Still waiting for Zeno Clash 3 though, because this game even for all of it's good points ain't Zeno Clash 3. It's just as good, but different.

_childDocuments_.review: *EDIT 3/13/23, after an original review that was very negative* Okay fine, you people were right and I was less right.  Granted, I still think it was a mistake to throw out the ZC 1 & 2 style of combat, but this game's combat is manageable with the right build (and thanks to the users on a certain anonymous basket weaving forum for recommending me one!).  I still vastly prefer the first-person brawling of ZC 1 & 2 over the third-person whatever-it-is of Artifacts, but the latter is growing on me now that I found a style that clicks.  I guess I recommend trying out all the different styles and seeing what clicks for you.  For anyone else struggling: I also take back what I said about the lore.  It actually does make sense and flow with the other games, but its still kind of a story that didn't need to be told.  From what I have been told and am gleefully anticipating,   Again, not really any details that people were dying to know.  But still neat.Characters are fantastic.  Pseudo is so charming, he's got that charisma stat filled out.  The boy is adorable and worth protecting.  Their bond is probably the one cute element that has ever popped up in any of the Zenozoik games; found family tropes like this are a dime a dozen, sure, but they handled it very well here.  Visual design of said characters is amazing as always, with all sorts of weirdos and wonders around every corner.    Map design can be confusing and easy to get lost in (although with how pretty the map is, this isn't necessarily a bad thing). but bravo to the devs for looking into ways to fix it (as of this new review)!  Music is absolutely perfect and really enhances the weirdness of everything.  It is a strange combination of janky soul and modernization which can very much be an acquired taste for some (I know I sure did have trouble acquiring it).  Campsite/save point placement, crafting and leveling are nowhere near as convoluted as they first seem and are actually very fair.  Its just a matter of learning how the game works, which can be very intimidating and difficult.I still prefer the first two ZCs over this one but you know what?  This is a solid GOTY candidate for 2023.  The game is hard to understand, yes.  It can be tough to adjust to the new combat if you prefer ZC over soulsbournes, yes.  But stick with it, and you'll find a gem of a game.(Usually I keep my old reviews when I completely change my mind on a game but honestly this time nothing I wrote applies to my new review (and its going to be so dang long if I do keep it, I'm tired of my reviews being as long as Anna Karenina).  I will tell you a summary of the old negative review: unhealthily obsessed with Zeno Clash, didn't like the changes in this game, struggled to understand the changes, got huffy, cried about trend-chasing, quit.  There, laugh at my ineptitude.  Now go play all three Zenozoik games.)

name: The Tartarus Key
detailed_description: The last thing Alex Young remembers is being at home alone in her apartment… so why has she suddenly woken up in this strange mansion? All the doors are locked by bizarre puzzles and traps, there are cameras following her every move, and she keeps thinking she sees… things… out of the corner of her eye. If she wants to escape alive, along with the other captives she discovers, she’ll need to use her wits in this adventure thriller. Inspired by the look and feel of classic horror games, The Tartarus Key serves up a mystery filled with twists and turns, and more than a few deadly surprises. Rely on brains over brawn to help Alex survive, but beware - not everyone might make it out alive. Features: Escape a deadly mansion filled with dangerous traps, and rescue Alex’s fellow captives… or fail, and leave them to a grisly fate Uncover three different endings, and dig to the heart of the mansion and the strange secrets it and your captors hold Solve puzzles and challenges reminiscent of escape-the-room games in a variety of unsettling and bizarre scenarios A tense, atmospheric adventure that relies on puzzles and plot instead of combat or chase sequences The Team: Leonor Parra: Founder of Vertical Reach and the artist making The Tartarus Key as atmospheric and unsettling as possible. Hates jump scares and vowed to make a game that's downright spooky without them! Kevin Colegate: The programmer in charge of making a game that plays as smoothly as you remember the classics being! A lover of retro games, he hopes The Tartarus Key surprises people with its blend of authentic vibes and puzzles. Josie Brechner: Josie Brechner (she/they) is a composer, sound designer, and musician from Brooklyn, NY. She's made emotionally-driven sound worlds for games like EXTREME MEATPUNKS FOREVER, Blossom Tales 1 & 2, Mixolumia, Best Friend Forever, Freshly Frosted, and now The Tartarus Key. She has toured the US and performed electronic music internationally under the name Visager. Music from Josie’s three open-source Songs from an Unmade World albums has been used in hundreds of projects around the world.

short_description: There’s no way out for Alex Young who wakes up to find herself locked in a strange mansion filled with puzzles, traps, and cameras following her every move. Whether she and her companions live or die, and find the truth behind their abduction, is up to you in this first-person mystery thriller.

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a campy horror story  that has free motion and relies on point and click for interaction and puzzles.  You awake as Alex - a young woman who finds herself in a strange environment with no idea how or why she is there. As you explore the house, you discover 5 other people who are also trapped. Your actions either save each or kill each, with achievements awarded for both outcomes. Puzzles open up additional areas of the house (which is quite large) and are used to extricate your companions from a variety of death traps. Most puzzles are fairly easy, with obvious clues. Some are mechanical, including a very creative slider puzzle. There were a few that I had to look up because I never found a clue or did not understand how the clue applied. Overall, the puzzles are fair and diverse. They flow naturally with the story and never felt 'added on.' The graphics are low resolution and there are no voice-overs (which I appreciated).  There is a LOT of dialog which can be read and clicked through. On occasion, the dialog has clues. However, much of it is chatter that (in my opinion) did not add to the game experience. Perhaps I am just impatient with those who talk constantly without saying much! The 'E' key is used to interact and advance dialog. During cut scenes, the 'E' prompt appears but does not seem to move anything along. Again, my impatience got the best of me as I punched the 'E' key until something else happened!The game auto-saves and has 3 explicit save slots. These are handy to use before starting a mechanical puzzle, in case you get things too mucked up and need to reset. They are also handy for storing progress at a couple of key points in the game to experience all 3 endings without playing the entire game through as many times.A map of the house is developed as you play which was quite helpful. There is also an achievement for visiting every location and completing the map.The plot has some twists and turns but is somewhat predictable with a satisfying set of endings. The developers did a nice job of closure by telling you about what happens to each character 'after the game.'Completionists should play through and rescue everyone, while taking notes on puzzle solutions. Then, a partial second time through, failing to save anyone, will not be much of a chore.I recommend this game to those who enjoy 'escape the room' mechanics and prefer a horror story without excessive gore or jump scares.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic, to put it mildly.The first thing to realize is that this is 100% a puzzle/escape room game. There's no combat, no jump scares. The only way to "lose" is (and this is a brilliant subversion) to fail some of the puzzles that the game presents you with. Characters can die, paths can get locked off, and the game allows you to move forward. That's rare and much appreciated.Now, puzzle games are hard to get right. There's a balance between making it hard enough to be a challenge but easy enough to be logical. A lot of games veer on the too-hard side of things, making puzzles that are incredibly convoluted or have solutions that only make sense when you already know the answer. I'm pleased to say that Tartarus Key strikes that balance beautifully. The puzzles take some time to think through, and are satisfying, without ever feeling like banging your head against the wall. Aside from that, every puzzle was genuinely fun to solve. I'll even say that the puzzles managed to fit into the scenes rather seamlessly. At no point did I feel like I was being interrupted by an unrelated toy the game wanted me to fiddle with. Additionally, and my god this is a great touch, your inventory stays limited to your current location, and the puzzles stay within the room. There is no running about trying to figure out if you forgot something six rooms ago that you need now. The game lays ALL of its pieces out for you so the only thing between you and the answer is your own cleverness.There is ONE exception to this.  But that's minor.The writing is good. It's not superlative, it's a perfectly functional story about a secret society putting people in the big mansion to watch them try to escape. The characters are a LOT of fun, with a good bit of dialogue feeling FAR more natural than most games of this type. There are multiple endings, and I will say the "true" ending feels somewhat rushed, introducing some elements and progressing through them rapidly, but that's an incredibly minor quibble. It's a puzzle game, the point is to sink into the atmosphere and get your brain going.The atmosphere is also great. I see some reviews disliked the music, but I found it fitting. It sets the tone for the scenes and helps it feel like a movie. The design of the main location is impressive as all hell and actually managed to feel like an actual facility that some crazy rich MFs would have built.My five hours were on a single playthrough, with only two times of "save scumming" to correctly solve a puzzle. The first was for the above spoiler, and the second was for a section where I kept thinking I got it wrong even though I hadn't somehow. Both were my own fault. Overall, this is one of the best short experiences I've had in years. Spooky, cerebral, full of personality. If you like a "horror game" that's more about a feeling of unease than outright terror and need a fix of quality puzzles, I recomment this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I was blown away by this game. What is essentially a puzzle solving / escape room game, it has the added elements of horror (without being scary) combined with a retro PS1 style of presentation. The scene is a creepy mansion whose layout gradually unfolds as you move from room to room, with many rooms having multiple puzzles to solve before you are granted access to the next. The complexity of the puzzles ranges from relatively simple (if you know how) to quite challenging – requiring repeated visits to get inside the puzzle setters mind. I found myself sometimes overthinking a solution and ending up frustrated, only to come back to it later only and spot a different approach. The variety of the puzzles and the impressive imagination of the developers make for a very engaging experience. The overall plot is also very imaginative and makes you wonder if someone has already snapped up the book or movie rights. Overall, a great way to exercise the brain and while away several hours.I was a little disappointed at the ending after my first play through, but came to realise that all the characters you encounter can be saved. By doing so, many extra areas within the game can be opened up, eventually leading to a much more satisfying ending. Therefore, ensure you save the game before attempting to rescue a character, so that if you get things wrong you can go back and try again. Several ending appear to exist, and I have even seen a YouTube ‘whole game play through' that misses a major chuck of gameplay at the end. This is truly a game with hidden depths!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I finished playing The Tartarus Key and really liked it.  It’s a horror-themed escape room game.  I say horror themed because while there are plenty of bloody scenes and chances of death, there are no monsters chasing you or jump scares.  No need to hide, run or fight.  Many escape room games can be somewhat formulaic.  Trapped in a house, puzzle, puzzle, puzzle.  Well, in this game, yes, you are trapped in a house, puzzle, puzzle, puzzle.  But in this game 5 other people are trapped in different rooms and it’s up to you to save them … or not.  So this is an escape room game with lots of dialogue and interactions.  I liked the character I played and thought she was funny and sarcastic despite the dire circumstances.  The developers also poked a bit of fun at the genre as you discover what’s really going on in this murder house.The puzzles were all completely doable if you pay attention to the clues.  That said, I did run into a few that were tricky for me and it gave the game a good and varying level of challenge.  There is one autosave and three manual save slots.  I had a lot of fun with the game and hope to see more games from this developer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game.  It's slim pickings to be a horror fan who also wants things to be *about something.*  In that regard above all others (but not to their exception), this one has been a rare treat.  Naturalistic dialogue, good puzzle balance, great central concept, solid-as-hell execution, and it took me 20 hours *with* some time afk--in other words, respects your time.  Also, I love a puzzle game that lets you *fail* the puzzles, get the others killed, and just sally forth like no business haha.  It does actually create some stakes in a game with no combat or HP or etc.So yeah, very solid project on all levels--and one that pleases me in particular when it says, among other things, "there is truth in all fiction."  If you like indies, horror, puzzles, heart, conspiracies and the occult, games that just feel good to play, any or all the above, this is a big recommend.(If I have a single gripe, there are options to turn the VFX off but I wish they'd go further, only the CRT filter makes a significant difference to me and it's not enough to keep it from being nauseating sometimes--I get migraines though so YMMV, most folks will probably be fine with it)

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a really effective demonstration of how a horror game can work with no enemies and no threat of player death or progress loss - it's lighter weight than some of its contemporaries but it keeps the tension high and has some fairly effective scares. Its puzzles are, for the most part, fun and interesting to solve (I like having to take notes and I was routinely pushed hard enough to have to) and though its narrative wasn't all that complex, I was curious and engaged enough by its mystery that I completed all endings.I do have one fairly significant complaint though, and it's that some of the puzzles are designed in a way that feels a bit cheap. At a number of points in the game you will be asked to solve a puzzle where your solution needs to be right, the first time, and if you test an incorrect solution, you will kill another character. It's these puzzles that often introduce an element that feels like some kind of 'gotcha', an EXTREMELY well hidden object without which the correct solution is impossible, or a hint of moon logic, as if the devs were afraid the 'death game' puzzles would be too easy if they were fair. I'm pretty good at this stuff and I managed to save only one of the four characters you encounter this way on the first playthrough - one was my fault for misinterpreting information I had, but two did leave me frustrated. Details behind the spoiler. That said the number of challenging, interesting, and satisfying puzzles in The Tartarus Key, coupled with its effective use of tone, tension, and atmosphere to create a horror experience without threat, are more than enough to recommend it. Check it out, just be prepared to do a second speedy run-through if one of the less-fair puzzles caught you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a pretty good game but it certainly has its problems. I really liked the art style and the general premise of the game. The PS style graphics and the horror theme is pulled off very well. They really nailed the way these old games used to convey emotions without facial features or complex movements.The puzzles started interesting but quickly soured for me with a lot of them boiling down to hiding the one hidden object in the room to get the "true" solution. There were some puzzles towards the end which were irritating too as they were not completely logical and you almost had to read the mind of the developer to understand what they want from the clue. Other puzzles I spent ages trying to combine cryptic clues to figure out a solution and after much frustration it turns out that it is actually super simple, no combining of clues you just had to somehow know there are multiple parts and the clues are used one at a time ().Another issue I have with the game I found most of the cast completely unmemorable. I found myself not caring whether some of them lived or died and had absolutely no reason to care about what they are doing if they do survive. Not a major issue but to elevate this game from good to great I would have liked to feel some connection with the characters.Despite these frustrations though I think the game is overall very good and enjoyable. I do think the full asking price is a bit steep but I do feel I got my moneys worth buying this on 30% off sale. I hope the developers continue to make games and improve on this excellent foundation.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, if you're looking for a good escape room puzzler, I can't recommend this game. While the aesthetics (visuals, music) are pretty cool, the game is bogged down with so-so "puzzles" and excessive, inane (imo) dialogue/interactables. A good puzzle requires some degree of reasoning, which ultimately leaves you feeling pretty clever. So far the majority of puzzles in this game just feel like manual labor. An early puzzle (SPOILER) requires you to read little excerpts about serial killers, which include dates in which they were active. Then you use that information on a display case of murder weapons, and you have to select them in chronological order. "Puzzle" solved.  The following puzzle is similar to that: "here's the data, now go input the data." In my playtime I don't think I ever felt clever finding a solution.The next hang up is that this game suffers from "writers like to write" syndrome. It's not that the writing is awful, per say, however it is in desperate need of an editor. I can't speak for their motivation, but the writers decided to try to add as many sassy and "witty" lines for Alex, the protagonist, as possible. There are SO many interactables in the game (ie. clicking on an object to get some sort of inner monologue observation from Alex) I was reminded of everyone's first RPG Maker game (at least in my household this is what we did as kids). Following the fall out of Whedonesque writing (Forspoken, anyone??) you'd think other designers would take note.Anyway, from a story perspective it's a little strange having Alex so quippy internally, when externally she seems to constantly convey she's on the verge of a nervous breakdown. The second, larger issue is that more needless dialogue isn't a feature, it's a burden. It blocks pertinent information. I'm less wanting to interact with your environment knowing that a majority of interactables will result in "witticisms" that serve no purpose to the story or gameplay. Is this object pertinent to the puzzle?... nope, it's just a rejected joke from Alex's failed stand up career. Even with the main story conversations I always felt like they needed to end much sooner than they did. A conversation going on too long because you wanted to get in another clever line is forgivable, but when it seems like every conversation is like that then the writers desperately need an editor. A specific example (SPOILERS AGAIN) I can give involved a blacklight in a closet that I needed to turn on to solve a "puzzle". It took me way too long on this because I could not even see the blacklight, which was positioned behind a shelf of cleaning products. Besides the fact that visually there wasn't enough to it to distinguish itself from the cleaning products, the cleaning products were yet another useless dialogue interactable and it was actively blocking my ability to interact with the blacklight. Think about it: they were prioritising useless chatter over a step to solve a puzzle. It's a very mind boggling design decision that wouldn't have been an issue if they exercised a smidgen of restraint.I picked up this game because I liked the look, I like escape rooms, and I saw the "Very Positive" designation on the store page. I wish I had read the reviews here a little closer, and even some top critics on OpenCritic (it sits at a 66, which is far more accurate, imo), because it *might* have clued me in that I wouldn't have enjoyed this game. However, I didn't see many reviews griping the way I just did, so I felt compelled to add my two cents. I can understand why other players enjoy it, of course, and had I bought this at a deep discount maybe I'd feel grumpy about the whole experience.TLDR: looks great but excessive, pointless writing hinder the experience, and puzzles are more manual labor than actual puzzles that require reasoning.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I'll go through my main criticisms first - the writing isn't stellar, which I see others have pointed out. Lots of "I literally can't even" kinda stuff. The puzzles are hit or miss, and fortunately it doesn't suffer from the obtuseness that plagues indie puzzlers and bad Escape Simulator maps. There are some problems with item finding - things that are only accessible from certain angles, that kind of thing. I'd say it's a step above its class, but still needs a lift to be great - it's good, not great.The visuals are fantastic. The environment models and the animations are the most "professional" part of the game. I kept the fake-PS1 filters off - this looks good as a low poly experience without the gimmicks.Finished with a bad ending, and unfortunately trying for a better ending means playing the entire thing over - no "chapter select" or such. There are multiple save files, fortunately, but if you don't go into your first playthrough planning ahead to get the best ending, you're in trouble.The horror elements are light, which was a nice break, actually - nothing popping up and screaming in your face. This game borrows a LOT from 999, and as another "diet Saw" experience, it has the same sort of light horror atmosphere.Overall, it was a nice time, but lukewarm - I'm googling the best endings, and I had a good time for its sale price. Would have hoped for more polish for twenty bucks, but a pretty good romp overall.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles are indeed the "find the data, then input it correctly" kind, but that seems the correct brand for Horror games, this isn't a pure puzzle game. It's a shame it doesn't follow Survival Horror rules of having the data or necessary object far away from the puzzle location. Here, . Very good atmosphere, I loved the soundtrack. There are no jumpscares or enemies, but it manages to be creepy enough to hold interest. , which I wasn't expecting. There's a lot of non-voiced dialogue, and a good portion of it you have to opt-in to trigger. I liked every line of it, every character, and every exchange, honestly. It can always improve for future titles, but what's here is well above average.
