_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a Psychological-Horror Puzzle game and it very quickly earned its place as one of my favourite games of all time. My partner and I played this game together, solving all of the puzzles, voicing all of the characters and constantly theorising on what the truth behind the mystery was. It was an absolute blast from beginning to end and overall it was a deeply memorable experience. The atmosphere’s on point and that is in no small part due to the game’s fantastic art direction, music and sound design as well as its writing. I was constantly on the edge of my seat waiting for the other shoe to drop and questioning what was going on. The focus of the gameplay is on the puzzles but despite knowing that there weren’t any chase sequences waiting for me, the tension was so high that I was still double checking every corner as I progressed further into the game. I loved the way the cutscenes were directed! The camera choices made it feel like a movie at times and the game’s PSX style really heightened the experience. The game makes you question reality as you progress through the story and begin to unravel its occult elements. Every new and unexplainable clue feels very much like a lure leading you down into the depths to the Angler Fish’s maw from which you can never return. But what is real and what is set dressing? How can you trust anything around you when the only other pair of eyes on the scene are watching through a voyeuristic camera following your every move? The game justifies all of its puzzles with its heightened Escape Room setting and I really enjoyed them. I can’t remember the last time I’ve needed to actually get out a notebook to solve something!You can fail certain puzzles throughout the game and it will continue on afterwards but you will be locked out of certain routes. You really have to pay attention to every piece of information the game gives you! Do not be overconfident like I was! I got everyone but William killed on my first try and then had to reload because my partner and I were too sad to go on without them. Be attentive! Read that extra note in your pocket! I have seen some other reviews mention that they didn’t get some of the puzzles but I had no trouble with the ones mentioned. I think difficulty can vary from person to person as there were some puzzles I have no idea if I could have figured out on my own (despite the clues being there) that my partner picked up on and vice versa. (I’m sure we would have gotten them individually with enough time though!)One really helpful detail is that your inventory stays limited to your current location! You’ll always have exactly the items you need on hand which helps keep everything on track. All in all, I think the puzzles are a perfect balance of challenging and logical and I never felt frustrated as I knew the answer was always in reach. I’d pay a lot of money to visit an escape room like this in real life. I loved the characters and genuinely cared about them all. The writing is really strong and the dialogue feels very natural. Alex, Torres & William were our combined favourites!I believe you can come across these characters in a variety of different orders as you play the game after you’ve met your main correspondent Detective Torres. (For example: On our first playthrough we met the characters in the order of C, W, K & R, but on my second I met them as W, C, R & K - which felt more like the natural order to meet them in). I wish we could have seen more character interactions between them all as they’re all wonderful and I have to wonder if there were more optional scenes that I might have missed out on as I know at least once when I went back to join the group I found Torres and William talking to each other. (Nothing prompted my return, I just got spooked by a tremor). I would have loved more opportunities to talk to the other characters with the walkie talkie throughout the game. It was a real comfort object knowing Torres was in my corner but it would have been nice to have the others call you or chip in on puzzles involving their respective talents. (Such as when  offers to at one point in the game.) I understand that would have taken a lot more work to incorporate as you can visit rooms in mostly any order you like, and while adding an extra section to the game that would have allowed the team to collaborate would be incredibly fun, I get that may stretch the world building a little bit given the reason the game gives for the puzzles existing as they do. The next section of this review will contain spoilers so beware! Overall I think this game is worth every penny. It’s one of the best puzzle games I’ve ever played and one that will stick with me for a long time. Every single time we put this game down I was looking forward to playing more of it, it has my full recommendation.  This game scratched an itch I didn’t know I had and now I have to go on living in a world with no more of it to play. My partner also drew some wicked cool fanart of Torres, so if my review didn’t cut it for you maybe some art of the coolest detective alive will!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: As a puzzle lover this has some great ones, and the atmosphere and presentation is really enjoyable, the characters are memorable and exploring the mansion is nice, My one gripe with the game is during sections where characters could potentially die they decide to give extremely vague clues and kinda trial and error "oops you should have known that" solutions that make these sections oftentimes exasperating.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: A well-put-together escape room game with some neat puzzles that doesn't waste your time, and really needs more eyes on it. The atmosphere is thick with sinister undertones, but it's not trying to jumpscare you.While the dialogue is well-written, it's almost too infrequent in the mid-section of the game. You don't really get the sense that the player character is building up a rapport with anyone other than Torres, and as a result the remaining characters don't feel fleshed out after your first encounter with them - with only a single bit of optional dialogue once they're in the dining room, and no radio communication.Otherwise, The Tartarus Key has a strong sense of mystery, and the route to the true ending is satisfying. Give it a try!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: As always, the astrology puzzle was the worst puzzle. Please make the text on that note more legible!This game is basically straight survival horror puzzle solving. Think 999 but with less route shenanigans. It's a good game, but 20 bucks for 3 hours is steep. You might have more difficulty with some rooms than I did, but I was blowing through 80% of the rooms in 2-3 minutes. The game has essentially no replay value as well, unless you want to get the other endings. I got it for 14, still on the high side for me but all 3 hours were pretty fun!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: By taking the vibes of a classic survival horror game but removing the combat and instead focusing purely on the puzzles, we're left with a series of escape rooms wrapped in the trappings of a creepy mansion. Most importantly, these puzzles are balanced perfectly, never too easy but also not so difficult that hints become a requirement. The Tartarus Key is a true hidden gem.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I bought it because of the Demo I played.It's fun and smooth.  After Demo time,it makes me sleepy.You are always in the way to the next room,solve the puzzle and open the door,it's tiring.Most time you are searching for things rather than solving the puzzle,and it's NOT THRILLING AT ALL.  Everyone you encountered cannot help you,  once their problems solved, they just stay there and watch you till the end.The dialogues and the whole plot are acceptable,but emmmm.....  The puzzles' are not quality-consistent,logic-consistent.80% of them are good, 20% could be annoying,there's a consideration there.You cannot expect a whole smooth feeling like other top-puzzle-games.   There're coding/program issues.You got stuck every time in-out a room,and sometimes camera reset to look-up-state.You got very stuck or even complete unresponsive during the stuck after some puzzles done, 1 time restart for me.      If the program issues solved,and a price discount,I would recommend you to have a try.Because the puzzle design idea is good,it's not brainless,task-like idea you would see in some 3A games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game. It's first and foremost a puzzle game. There are elements of horror, but there are no jumpscares, no being chased down by monsters, no combat, etc. The puzzles are mostly fair, however as they are so vague it is easy to confidently come to incorrect solutions.I have an issue with the graphics. I'm fine with low resolution textures, low triangle count models, etc, but this game takes it a bit too far with its shader effects. Affine texture mapping (undoing perspective-correct interpolation) and the low-resolution vertex origin ('vertex shake') in particular is not pretty. Thankfully you can turn these off, though there seems to be an inconvenient bug where the options are not remembered after reset. Some uncontrollable stuff is still a bit too far, like the dithering shader, cracks in geometry, and some lighting issues (some bits of geometry will seem highly reflective).The story isn't particularly interesting. The characters don't seem well fit into the story as I'd have liked to see, and they all seem pretty flat. I wish they chimed in more often, as they all seem to just stand around doing absolutely nothing as you run off to solve everything single-handedly. Even Torres who is around the entire story, and has a lot to say at the start, will also go radio silent. I feel like this would help a lot with some puzzles that are a bit too vague. This could also provide incentive to players to save everyone. There is something to be said, that of the characters that are ostracized or villianized (William, Charles to some extent) by others (Ruth, Torres), ironically, they all equally contribute nothing to their escape. Even Kai is absolutely pointless, both for the story (being 'selected' randomly out of desperation/convenience), & for the nearby characters.I'll leave spoilers here to unpack the story. Basically, the ending is rushed, butchers the characters even further into uselessness, and fails to explain the context and situation of Tartarus and the plot.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: a lot of fun, absolutely worth buying if you like to escape rooms.Long version: what you make of this game will depend partly on your expectations going in. If you're coming from the tradition of abstract puzzle-box room escapes like Crimson Room and, um, The Room, you'll almost certainly have a great time. If you're coming from the Japanese tradition of 'murder game' VNs - most obviously the Zero Time trilogy - you may not quite get what you wanted.The Tartarus Key is basically a series of completely separate escape rooms threaded together on a vestigial story. The atmosphere is A+ - pleasantly creepy without ever causing you to leap out of your chair and shriek - and the puzzles are varied and fun to solve. If anything they're a bit on the easy side: quite a few of them can be solved almost without breaking stride, while the hardest are on the level of 'a few minutes chewing your lip' rather than 'get a notebook and stare into space for an hour'. But that's actually not a bad thing, as it keeps the pace up and stops you ever getting bogged down for ages on a single vicious puzzle. If you like dials with symbols, cryptic notes, and opening a safe to find a key to a different safe, you should stop reading and just buy the game.What this really ISN'T is a narrative game. The story is just coherent enough not to bother you while playing, but falls apart as soon as you start thinking about it. The 'true ending' is cool but extremely rushed, with almost no time to develop itself. Alex, the protagonist, is fantastic - a genuinely believable and sympathetic human being of a type that most triple-A games usually can't manage - and her relationship with the first character she meets is well-drawn and charming, but the other side characters are very lightly sketched in. Which, again, isn't a problem as long as you don't expect them to be anything more. If you've played a puzzle-VN like 999, though, you may go in expecting the backstories and relationships of the cast to be a major element of the game, and be wrong-footed when that doesn't happen.(To be fair, I do worry I missed bits here. One other reviewer mentions going back randomly to the hub room and finding two characters talking to each other, and I was puzzled in-game when it sounded like one character was referring to a conversation I hadn't seen.  I never went back to the hub room except when the game nudged me to, because there was no indication that there'd be anything to see or do there, and I'll be a bit sad if I turn out to have lost out on a bunch of character stuff.)Overall, this is very much a thumbs-up from me - I had a great time and I'll be eagerly awaiting whatever the devs do next (especially as another member of the trembling 'love horror, hate jumpscares' fraternity). I just think it's worth being clear that what you're buying here isn't a character- or plot-driven mystery: it's an anthology of fun escape rooms, soaked in a lovely lo-fi occult-horror aesthetic.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: A sinister mansion full of mysteries, with very elaborate and macabre puzzles that remind us in part to the movie saga "Saw". But that's not all, "The Tartarous Key" also has a very varied and well-structured cast of characters with whom we will interact and make decisions that will completely change the fate of our protagonist.At the narrative level the game is based on secrecy so I will not go into details. I will only say that, as a good mystery game that is, it will immerse you fully in its history in an excellent way and all this with an ending that does not disappoint at all.A fantastic game to play with friends or alone and enjoy discovering all the secrets hidden in this mansion.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I very much appreciate what the devs are doing here and they have executed extremely well for a team of their size. The puzzles are pretty satisfying and for the most part are signposted pretty well. So much of how someone solves a puzzle is personal so I'm finding it hard to ask for more hints than already given on the ones I struggled with.I like the tension of knowing that my choices matter in certain situations in the game but at the same time I'm not one to save scum my way to perfection like others. I went in with this mentality of letting the dice fall as I messed up... but knowing what I know about the content that I'm not able to access unless I play again makes it feel a bit punishing. I'm wondering if there was a way to incorporate not cutting the player off from the content but just giving a less satisfying ending would have worked better. Bold gameplay choice that I commend either way though.The game is short so realistically I could play it through again to do this but I worry I'd lose the stellar mood and feel I have after enjoying my first trip through so much. Looking at the achievements, I'm in the minority of poeple who did a bad job helping people so seems to be a me problem. I kept telling my wife "welp, I let someone else die... my bad". LOLOverall, what a stellar effort from these developers. The commitment to no jump scares and other tricks and tropes used by horror games is commendable. A very memorable game that I will not soon forget.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a masterful little horror puzzle game. After downloading the demo I was hooked by the premise of the mystery as well as the enjoyable escape room puzzles it presented, and so bought the full game not long after. I'm incredibly glad I did, and immensely enjoyed the next five and half hours I spent with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished yet, but I'm absolutely loving this experience so far.  Clever puzzles and environments that have temporarily stumped me, but have never required me to seek answers outside of the game.  Alex (the main character) has some hilarious dialogue and commentary on her situation that keeps things fresh.  Atmosphere is deliberately retro and has RE-mansion-style flair, but still maintains some individuality.Strong recommend if you like puzzles, horror, or any mix of the two.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for an escape the room game, it is a really solid one. The puzzles overall are good and fair with only a small handful that felt a little unfair (and some of that is due to the PS1 aesthetic occasionally making some important hints hard to see). The visuals/PS1 vibe is absolutely nailed, though, the CRT filter, the texture warping shader, etc. Everything looks great.If you're looking for a scary horror game, this isn't that. It is only puzzles, and actually, I feel like maybe it could have used a few more overarching puzzles since everything is tied to individual rooms, or more periods of exploration rather than a non-stop gauntlet of puzzles. There are very occasional scares and the game 'messes' with you occasionally, like an endless hallway for example (which, btw dev, if you walk backwards through it you can see when it 'switches' back to normal which was a little not-smooth). There are multiple endings, but (unless I didn't actually get the best one?) the best ending is pretty straight-forward to get. By far and away my biggest complaint about the game is the dialogue. It feels like a Marvel movie or Forspoken or something--if the game had voice acting it would be insufferable. The blasé attitude that all the characters have as they let out little quips while their lives are in danger just makes the horror aspect of the game fall entirely flat. If the characters don't care about their lives, then how can you be immersed and invested? They're in a Zero Escape-type situation, but everytime someone's life is in danger they're making little bad jokes and zingers.There's also way too many characters. It is cool to see them hanging out in the common area but they literally all do actual nothing the entire game. There is a "radio" mechanic which seemed like it could have been a cool Metal Gear Solid type thing but it winds up just being kind of pointless. Maybe if Torres (the only relevant partner character) had been separated from you the whole game it would have been cool? Like that way in the back of your mind you're constantly wondering "who is this person actually?"One other little weird thing is the two times you have a partner character follow you they act like Watson in that old Sherlock Holmes game where they just teleport around which is kind of silly and I don't understand why they did it that way. There are animations for the characters in cutscenes, and the protagonist has an abomination model (and shadows of it), so it isn't like they didn't have the resources to make them able to have walking animations, but instead they make it so that the partner characters just kind of do that like Slender Man teleport thing when you look away. Not really a problem but just a weird choice.Anyway, this is mostly all nitpicks, the game was fun, the aesthetic was phenomenal, and the puzzles were overall good--so if you like solving escape room puzzles, it is a great choice!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I can't recommend this.The premise of the game is okay, but after less than 20 minutes, I got frustrated with the visuals.  There are options to disable them, but they don't actually seem to work.  Even with the "wobble" disabled, there are still objects in the environment that wobble and even with the texture warping disabled, there are still objects that have warping textures.  There's also an antialiasing options that would presumably disable the pixel filter, but it doesn't work either.I can't recommend a game where 3 of the 4 accessibility options are broken.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the most fantastic games I've experienced in years. I played this with a friend watching over discord stream, and we had an absolute blast with the story and excellent puzzles. The writing in this is so friggin good, filled with humor and charm and characters you cant hope but grow to love.This a is a tight, efficient experience that takes every part it had to work with and mixes together something truly special.Games like this are so important for this industry. Thank you to everyone involved in making this a reality. Absolutely recommend this for fans of puzzles, light spooks, nostalgic visuals and just excellent game design and writing
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Scratches the itch I've had for PS1 style horror puzzle games I've had ever since I played Echo Night. Great game, with clever puzzles for the most part. The only negative I could think of is run time, at  4.3 hours for my personal playthrough, it was a bit short. But I only feel this way the game was a great experience, and I wish there was more.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: A very engaging puzzle game. The ever present threat of something coming from the shadows adds a pressure of having to get the puzzles solved. The setting is fun to explore with plenty of small details that collectively make a very deep world. These flourishes that deepen the world however do not distract from the clues that you need to solve the mysteries. Each of puzzles feel like they are solved just in the right time of not taking too long to be frustrating but also just in time to have averted any mysterious threat. Really enjoying it and will be playing for a lot more. Can’t wait for the HD remake.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Really adored this game!I thought it walked a great line of the puzzles requiring thought, but not being so abstract that you're completely lost. On top of this, the writing and characters really entranced me in the mystery!For the price and length of the game (about 6 hours for one play through and another hour to wrap up achievements) I would say this in absolute gem of an indie title. If you're looking for a fantastic horror/puzzle game, you can't go wrong with this one
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: i've gotten two of the i suppose three available endings and oh my god, the tartarus key was SO good. the atmosphere and the inventive puzzles were perfect (except for THAT one, you know who you are). this, along scarlet horror, is one ideal game for horror fans not interested in games artificially extending their runtime by chasing you over and over again, nor the stress of being 100% unable to sit down and absorb the creeping terror.the color pallete, very autumn-y, offers a warm and arguably cozy feeling that clashes nicely with the suffering occurring before your eyes, and the many escape room like puzzles will tingle the back of your head just in the right place. the only real downside is that i wish there were more interactions with the npcs, only torres and william really stand out from the charming cast. the rest feel more like good ideas, but ideas nonetheless.the BEST game out there is you like horror and escape rooms.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Decent puzzle game. If you like escape rooms this is kind of like that. The story is nothing special. It's alright. The puzzles are challenging but fair. On occasion I felt like the solution was impossible only to realize I was either overthinking it or missing an item still left hidden in the room. This is definitely not a game you should try to complete in one sitting. Most of the game can be completed in 6-8 hours, but sometimes it benefits to take a step back, sleep on the puzzle, and try again the next day. The only issue I had with the puzzles are with the trap puzzles specifically. Sometimes you'll have to solve a puzzle in order to save a character. If you fail. The character dies. The problem is that if they die, you have to watch an unskippable cutscene, wait for the dialogue to end, and then reload your last save to attempt the puzzle again. Another option is to control, alt, delete. My only real issue with the game is one particular woke aspect. I normally gravitate towards indy games specifically to get away from the woke elements but surprisingly this has major cringe element. There is a character named Kai who refers to herself as they/them. There is actually a scene in the game where the main character apologizes to Kai for miss-gendering her. It also makes reading the dialogue weird when interacting with Kai because the dialogue is like this "They is feeling better now" instead of "She is feeling better now." Fortunately you can choose to just not save that character during one of the puzzle traps and I don't think it has much consequence on the story.It is just disturbing that insane left wing ideologies are slowly finding its way into everything. The character Kai also ruined some of the immersion in the game as I was now wondering what other agendas I would discover instead of focusing on the story and environments. The fact that William is a white dude who also happens to be a narcissist jerk didn't go unnoticed either. While the situation with Kai almost had me stop playing and uninstall the game, I'm glad I powered through. The puzzles and atmosphere were great. Wish the developers kept their ideologies at home.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Was enjoying the game until the planetarium, I know the answer, just don't have clue about figuring out cardinal directions on the dial at all, i'd have to input each answer until it worked, and I just rather not, hate any puzzles about cardinal directions and it's the second one.Won't give a negative review, it's a good game, I just personally found it impossible to figure out on my own thus i refuse to move on by looking up the answer to where the North is in the dial, Idk where north is in real life, don't make me try and figure that out in a game man.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: This game is OK. It does not deserve the current rating it has so I am doing my bit to correct that.The visuals of the game are good, if you like the style (I do), but this is about where the positives end.There are some good puzzles but often they are either way too simple, way too obtuse, or way too reliant on spotting something miniscule (especially given the low fidelity art style). For example there is no way of distinguishing which notes/books are actually relevant without combing each room with your mouse to figure out whether you can pick them up or not and the game is full of the same exact models throughout. More annoying is the ludicrous amounts of text and reading for what is some incredibly mediocre writing. The atmosphere set by the graphics are seriously undermined by the "ironic millennial" attitude of the player character and two-dimensional NPCs. The actual concept of the story I enjoyed but I think the over-reliance on dialogue (given it's quality) really let it down.This is exacerbated by the fact that there is no obvious way to skip sections of dialogue/cutscenes. The game half-expects you to do multiple runthroughs for different endings which results in attempting to skip large sections of dialogue and cutscenes that have already been seen, to little avail.There was also a technical issue where my save from the demo was transferred to the full game when I purchased it, but continuing that save kept sending me to the "buy the full game" screen, forcing me to start again.Overall I think the game lacks a holistic creative vision and this leaves it as an OK game rather than a good one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: SYNOPSIS: yes, all the "positive" reviews are wrong. Screenshots will be taken as proof in case developer decides to erase my review.Let's start with an anecdote: - once upon a time there was a strong wahmen in a mysterious mansion, who despises the "institution" of law enforcement, and engages in vigalantism out of a sense of "justice". - A black wahmen with three university degrees, who despises the evils of the health care system, and practices illegally, getting paid under the table without a license for the sake of saving those who can't afford treatment. - The protagonist is a homosexual, who, all by herself is able to solve the mysteries of the mansion. - A non-binary "person" with the pronoun "they", who, even according to the lore of the game, was shoved into the mansion at the last moment just to be there (this is word for word written in the notes). - The white guy who does nothing, and talks like a jerk - because hey, (((everybody))) hates white people right?! - acts like the biggest pain in the ass, while enjoying how he uses his influence to rise above the plebeians.So, the writing team got together and said: , : No? that's not funny? Seemed like that to me. There are excellent riddles that are a pleasure to solve. Well-written dialogue (not characters, the dialogue). And pleasant graphics, although this isn't for everyone.The characters and plot, as a whole, are obvious, but they develop in schizophrenic fits; they either start strong, or not at all, if that makes sense.The endings, of which there are three (either separately or together), don't give a complete picture of what is happening.The soundtrack is completely mediocre. I can't imagine why it was sold separately.And yes, this is not horror. More like a thriller. The game tries to scare you two or three times it seems, throughout the entire playthrough.At a discount for fans of the escape room type, it'll work. And only if you're a severely blue pilled, blue haired, multiple piercings, statue-destroying, ADL slave.P.S. yes, these ARE also my views, and i completely agree with them.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: What if a survival horror was all about the puzzles and none of the combat. I really enjoyed my time with it, the puzzles were well designed and avoided moon logic.On the downside, I found the PS1 style flicker filter a bit overwhelming when a lot of things were moving at once, and none of them flickering quite in sync. Luckily, that only came up a couple of times, in cutscenes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: A scare-less horror game. What if a survival horror was just puzzles. As someone who is can be a scared cat in horror games, I actually appreciate this version of a horror story, where it's more horror vibes and scenery, it's a nice alternative. The visuals were lovely for people who like PS1 style games. Of course, as a big fan of escape room puzzles, I enjoyed it quite a bit. I do feel though that at times the creepy atmosphere falters  in being sufficiently oppressive, and I wish there was more interactions with the characters, but outside of it was a pleasurable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: "The Tartarus Key" is a first-person horror puzzle game that draws inspiration from classic titles like "Resident Evil" and "Alone in the Dark." Players assume the role of Alex Young, who awakens in a mysterious mansion filled with intricate puzzles and hidden dangers.Pros:- Engaging Puzzle Design: The game offers a variety of challenging puzzles that require keen observation and critical thinking, providing a satisfying experience for puzzle enthusiasts. - Atmospheric Retro Aesthetics: Utilizing a low-poly, PS1-inspired art style, the game effectively creates a nostalgic and eerie atmosphere that enhances the horror elements. - Multiple Endings: The game features multiple endings based on player choices, encouraging replayability and exploration of different narrative paths. Cons:- Limited Scare Factor: While the game excels in creating a tense atmosphere, it relies more on psychological tension than on traditional horror scares, which may not satisfy all horror fans. - Occasional Obscure Solutions: Some puzzles have solutions that may be too obscure, potentially leading to player frustration. - Sparse Narrative Depth: The storyline, while intriguing, may lack depth and character development, leaving some players wanting more from the narrative. In conclusion, "The Tartarus Key" offers a compelling blend of challenging puzzles and atmospheric horror, making it a must-play for fans of the genre.Score: 95 out of 100 cryptic keys—Unlocks a masterful horror experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: On it’s surface, The Tartarus Key is a stylish adventure mystery whose interests lean occult-ey. The fuzzy dithering, wobbly vertices, and jaggy aliasing offer a visual flourish to augment the fantastic stylized model, texture, and animation work If that style is TTK’s surface, then its heart resembles an escape room. Starting small you slowly, room by room, explore a suspiciously spooky mansion. Each room can either push the story forward or present a puzzle of diabolical complexity. Well not quite. But i did find some pen and paper useful at one point or another. If you like puzzles, retro graphics, and a spooky story then don’t hesitate!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: This game completely replicates the feeling of completing several escape rooms in a row. This is a unique feeling that is different from a typical puzzle horror game. You also encounter several other characters that you may or may not be able to save which adds some stakes to several of the puzzles. The puzzles never felt too obtuse. There was one I had to look up and it was because I hadn't looked at something in the room or I needed to look at it after triggering something else.The story is pretty interesting and I liked the characters. After getting one ending, I loaded my last save to get another ending, and each ending told me something about what was going on that I wouldn't have learned from just getting one ending. There appears to be more endings available if you play the whole game again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Nifty puzzle/escape room style game with a PS1 aesthetic. Described as "Resident Evil 1 without the monsters" and that's not a bad way to think of the puzzles involved, although they aren't as elaborate as a Zero Escape-type game. A strong atmosphere definitely carries the game, and the graphics have a strong sense of style even if things can look swimming and strange close-up. Recommended for a short but enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is pretty good puzzle game.The story is that you woke up in strange mansion and you are trying to get out of there. The mansion has been set up with puzzles in each room and you progress the game by solving them.The puzzles aren't very hard and I was able to solve them without unnecessary frustration.Graphics are in retro PSX-like style and created pretty good atmosphere.I am not really fan of puzzles and I still liked the game so would like to recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: As with a lot of intriguing setups, the eventual resolution of the story isn't all that great and in this case, it's rather unoriginal. You'll guess very early what's going on and you'll be right about it, because it's the same story you've been told a dozen times before. The way to that ending is entertaining enough, though, and I appreciated that the game allows you to fail and not see the whole story. The characters are somewhat onedimensional, but there's probably not much you can do with them in such a short time anyways.Where the game shines is the presentation, because the graphics style reminiscent of early 3D games combined with satisfying colours and lighting just look stellar.Gameplay consists of exploring and a lot of puzzle solving and while they don't reinvent the wheel, they're done pretty well and at least the main puzzles require you to pay a lot of attention or you'll think you found the correct solution only to learn better when it's too late. I had a really good time playing this twice for the different endings, so I recommend it despite some narrative shortcomings.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Lets start with the good: The presentation and world look amazing, like something straight out of a PS1 but with deeply decorated rooms that don't feel empty. The engine runs and controls well. The puzzles are challenging enough that you can't just breeze through them, but in general they are a bit too easy.But the problem is that this game goes nuts on pointless dialogue. There's so many unnecessary chatting scenes that this game feels more like a novel than a game. That wouldn't be a bad thing if the writing actually added to the story, but 90% of the dialogue is just pointless unnecessary backstory and side conversations that don't advance the plot. All the characters have some pity-party story to tell that seemingly goes on forever, but so what? Who wants to sit there and read all that? I just want to solve puzzles and figure out what's going on with the mansion, not read through small talk and side conversations. The game starts out with a semblance of a mystery plot, like some maniacal mastermind has trapped you in a supernatural puzzle house, but without posting any spoilers it really doesn't go in a good direction after that. Even the true ending doesnt explain anything about what happened or why. This game is 90% story + mystery and goes all the way to jumping the shark by the end, but somehow doesn't manage to tie anything up. Its like the writers made a mystery so mysterious that even they couldn't answer it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I initially found out about the game because I saw an animated portrait of Torres and immediately fell in love with her design because its so difficult to find middle-aged, tough, scarred women in fictional media, especially one that's part of the main cast. Interest piqued, I found out more about the game, purchased it after much consideration and I ended up loving it so much more than I thought I would!Very brief review:- What I liked: > Fun puzzles, they're actually more straight forward than they seem but does require some brain juice. In that sense, the puzzles are pretty well designed because they're not overly complex or challenging but cryptic enough that you'd still spend some time writing notes to solve some of it.> Puzzles feel very escape room esque where anything you find in every room is specifically for the room they're found in, so it lessens the headache when you're trying to figure out if this flask has any use outside of the room you found it in.> Amazing and interesting array of characters of various backgrounds and expertise. (Im bias to older women characters) So, it was very refreshing to see Torres and Ruth! (I love Torres, thank you for designing her devs <3) > Story line was very intriguing and characters were written well so the dialogue flowed very well too which kept me excited to press on with the game despite how scary the atmosphere was (Horror eque stuff scare me cuz im a wuss tbh)> Atmosphere is amazing!- What I felt neutral-ish about:> The weeping angel movements of the NPCs, when Torres first started teleporting every time I turned around, I nearly ♥♥♥♥ myself (10/10 experience)> Duration of game was just nice but I felt it was too short!! I was so intrigued by the characters I wish we got to learn more r had more to explore about them!! (The Tartarus Key part 2? 👀)Overall feelings: Amazing game! Loved it hehehe, thank you for this wonderful game Devs (and for Torres muwah love her sm). If you're looking for a fairly brain-poking puzzle game with horror-ish vibes and PS1/PS2 pixel graphics with liminal spaces that isn't too long with great characters and fun dialogue, this game is worth the purchase!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The perfect game for those looking for that classic survival horror experience, just without the combat and item management. A short game with great puzzles, style, and atmosphere. Some may not like that there isn't any replay value outside of going for the various endings. For the money, there's little better.9/10 overall, my favourite game I've played this year.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun puzzle game and narrative. The puzzles make you think but don't break your brain. There is a lot of dialogue and the characters are good. The PS1 aesthetic is very charming and it is good to be in an age where what were once technical limitations are now appreciated as a graphical style with value in and of itself. Squeezing as much detail and charm out of such a limited style is an accomplishment and art-form in its own right.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key strikes a near perfect puzzle difficulty for me. I never immediately knew the solution. The puzzle would feel difficult at first. Then, after trying a few things, I would take a moment to think through all the clues in the room again and have my eureka moment where I solve it.The atmosphere is the real star for me with this one though. It was very reminiscent of Resident Evil 1, finding yourself in a mysterious, creepy mansion with something sinister pulling the strings. Not to mention all the flavor text for the creepy paintings and other grotesque subject matter you can click on that adds so much to the setting and adds to your understanding of the protag's feelings and motivation/thought process.My main disappointment was that the mansion was not as interconnected as I had hoped. When you enter a room, all you need for that room is in that room. So much so that you can't even access notes and items you gathered from rooms you are not currently in. I would have liked the mansion to feel more like one giant puzzle rather than a series of puzzles, personally.I wholeheartedly recommend this to fans of this aesthetic and/or genre. It's also at a great price! But I don't think this will wow anyone who isn't already a fan of this stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: It was good. Lots of clever puzzles, but a few tedious ones too. Interesting visual style. Cool, but very small, location to explore.Main drawbacks were that the story wasn't anything new, and while the quirky writing style was cute in the early moments, it being infused across the entire product made it very much not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game, although I HATE how you get a terrible ending if you lose ONE person in the playthrough. I lost the first guy, thought it wouldn't matter too much and saved every single other person in the game, but I still got a super bad ending. That means, to get the good ending, I need to replay the entire game. No thanks. Also, some of the puzzles had weird solutions, but I'm glad most of them were logical and good. The game has great atmosphere and the aesthetic is wonderful though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: This was a fantastic game that kept on giving.Striking retro PS1 inspired visuals, a very slick, focused game design, and puzzles that were challenging, but in almost all cases, completely fair.  These were the sorts of puzzles that left you really satisfied and fulfilled in solving, without being frustrating.The game seems like it's going to play like a first person adventure game, but I'd describe it more as a room by room escape room sort of feel.  But this adds to its focused design... you're not filling your inventory with items from one room to solve in another.  Each room is a distinct set of challenges, and you move on.The overarching story was mysterious, if flat in a few places, but the pacing was great.I really recommend this for people who like puzzles, games like the Witness, Golden Idol, Obra Dinn, etc, despite not being exactly those types of games.  It scratches a very similar itch.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Overall recommend. I definitely want to highlight the visual style - it is clear from the playing that a lot of thought went into it and it absolutely works. There are definitely some striking visuals dotted throughout, too, beyond the bits that 'just' look good.The story is fine - it would be nice to have a few more dialogue bits with the rescued characters, though I know where limitations do tend to come in (there's also one line of dialogue that doesn't quite make sense if you didn't botch saving a particular character though in a "huh, that's tonally weird" way rather than being outright ruinous). There is some 'workman-like'-ness to it, but story serving the game is a fine way of doing things.The puzzles tend to be on the easy side -I think I used a guide all of twice puzzle-wise, and in one case because I felt like there had to be some trick to a puzzle I was missing because the solution was too obvious (wait, three times, one of the store cupboard things stumped me). As much as the story serves the game, I think the difficulty level is kept low enough that there's still a degree of flow to the story. It keeps things moving.Not that it isn't also easy to make mistakes if you don't pay close attention - I got the 'bad' ending first playthrough (and double-checking that I hadn't missed something else for my second is the remaining guide usage)- and not that there aren't some clever puzzles. And some where you can get half-way and brute force it because you miss the very obvious hint (I think the nature of the puzzle meant that avoiding brute-forcing was impossible, and also not something the devs would have considered because the hint is quite obvious in hindsight).
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: If this game was released on PSone, it would probably now stands as a classic from this era.Really good puzzle game, graphics are amazing if you are notalgic from the PSone era, puzzles are well design and balance (at least for me who isn't a pro in riddle and puzzle game), and the story is... surprising. The soundtrack is also quite good.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I'd call this game creepy/spooky and gory, but not scary. There are no jump scares at all. I'm a chicken when it comes to scary games and did not have issues with this game.It has a good PS1 horror aesthetic with nice lighting. It has a strong cast of unique characters. The writing is a high point, with lots of flavor text, optional conversations, and overall a good, if not particularly unique, plot that kept me interested.The puzzles tend to be on the easy side, but I found some to be obtuse and require a bit of trial and error. But overall I enjoyed the puzzles. They fit in very well with the plot and setting.This is an easy game to recommend if you are a fan of escape style puzzlers. It runs great on Steam Deck.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a lot o fun. It's not especially challenging (though I forgot I had a flashlight for a couple of hours early on, which didn't help), but the puzzles are reasonably diverse and creative, and importantly they're always fair. This is a game that values your time in a way puzzle games rarely do - each puzzle is self-contained in one room, meaning vastly less aimless wondering back and forth, and the information and items you need might take a bit of searching-for, but not pixel hunting. I really appreciated that.I also appreciated that the game is spooky and atmospheric but doesn't employ jumpscares, time pressures or visual effects to create artificial 'horror', which I generally just find stressful and offputting. Though this game is only part of a wave of recent horror games making the stylistic choice of emulating PS1-era graphics, that choice is used to great effect, with the shimmering textures, z-fighting objects and short draw distance keeping me on my toes and not quite able to trust what I was looking at, tying in nicely with elements of the narrative.The story and setting have nods to a host of horror tropes and maybe some satire on game development itself, in ways I'd love to see expanded-upon further. The narrative hints at a greater intentionality behind the scenes of the game's events that we never quite get to see. Whether the studio's next game is a sequel to The Tartarus Key or something new, I'll be eager to play it,I'd have liked a slightly longer experience than the two leisurely-paced sessions the game took me, but that's a testament to its enjoyability and moreishness as much as it is a criticism.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a interesting mystery adventure with a strong focus on "Escape Room" style puzzles. The PS1 era visuals and the great soundtrack fit perfectly. Unfortunately the story was less interesting then expected and the constant chatter between Alex and Torres sometimes hurts the atmosphere. Most puzzles are straightforward and not very difficult, but often there are details that can be easily overlooked when you are not double-checking everything.Overall a good game I would recommend for people that like puzzle heavy mystery/horror adventures and Walking Simulators.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: This game chalked down to 3 things that either make a or break the game, depending on the player's preferences:1. The nostalgic graphics and dialog systems.2. The story being a very good story but not a great story.3. The puzzles in the game being difficult -> very difficult.Personally, I had to look up a couple of puzzles but very much enjoyed the game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good! I wish characters didn't become irrelevant after saving them, but only because I enjoyed them a lot. I get why it would need to be done this way from a scope perspective, but I would have loved more optional dialog (again, though, I know that's not for everyone, it's a tricky thing to balance)
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a first-person puzzle game where the player has been locked inside a giant mansion, and needs to solve "Escape Room"-style puzzles in order to make it out alive. If you're a fan of escape rooms, this might just hit the spot for you!The game is presented in a tremendously charming style. akin to horror titles of the early 00's. Despite this horror aesthetic, I would describe the game as more "spooky" than horror. You don't need to love horror games to appreciate this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: A very decent retro-styled, horror-themed escape room game. A sort of mash-up of Alone in the Dark, The Cabin in the Woods and any "death game" story you can think of.There's no jump scares but there are a number of 'creepy Watson' moments where turning around might reveal a surprise. Also the game is kind enough to give a lot of warning before allowing you to make any choice that will affect the game's ending.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic escape room game with an underlying mystery.Perfect length, takes around 5 hours or so to completeI'm a bit half\half on the "True ending", but that might just be personal preference.Reminds me a decent amount of "Song of Horror", another fantastic game. (But Tartarus Key has no jump scares or intense horror moments)
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: THIS GAME WAS INCREDIBLE!The story telling, the writing, the art style, the puzzles, the mind blowing moments and the revelations!It is going to aggravate some people, as the puzzles are very tough or you read too deep into itBut this story and the characters, you sink so deep into it that you just have to find out what happens9/10Make this a Movie or Mini Series Please!!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't quite bring the horror that you might be hoping for, but the horror theme makes for a nice backdrop to the escape room-like experience combined with the retro visuals. The puzzles are mostly enjoyable, and unlike Resident Evil or similar they're mostly confined to the room they're in - your inventory items can't even be accessed without being in the correct room which helps avoid the "try everything with everything" shuffle but also prevents things from feeling very interconnected. There is one major puzzle later in the game in particular that I felt was a bit poorly conveyed and resulted in me spending way too much time overthinking it, involving a certain  However, the game does give you a pretty good indication of when certain clues are relevant by bringing up the notes on screen while you're interacting with a puzzle, which also helps reduce the need for writing things down.There's not much sound in this game which is part of why it might have less horror than you may be hoping for, as even the ambient sound is lacking a bit for my taste. The visuals look good if you like the style, but you may need to use the zoom button from time to time to make some things legible.While the game doesn't have combat, it does have people you can succeed or fail in saving by solving puzzles. This does play a part in the ending(s), but honestly there's not much to not saving them and I might recommend simply reloading if you fail a puzzle unless you really want to move on.All told, fun game if you want to solve some puzzles - but make it spooky.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Challenging puzzles.Spooky atmosphere.Fun characters and story.I wish the ending had a bit more to it (I got the bad ending) and it just kinda... ended. Might have better results with the good ending.Totally worth a playthrough if you want a spooky game with no jump scares that challenges you more than most horror games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: It would be unfair to leave a negative review for this game since it does quite enough of things right, mainly hitting the almost perfect balance of having difficult riddles but not unsolvable without a guide. I solved everything by myself without having to brutefore any puzzle, and since it is an escape room game it's a major upside for me.The rest is kind of a letdown. I was really seduced by the demo, but I feel like the game doesn't deliver on its promise of an exploration game in a spooky mansion. The horror elements are always downplayed or subdued by the main protagonist, and are sparse enough to never really settle in. What disappointed me the most was the NPCs, because  Their backstory is paperthin, and since I was eager to scratch the Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors itch I really felt the lack of substance here.Finally, I basically solved all the riddles and finished the game in 6 hours, which makes the full price quite steep. I'd recommand waiting for a 10 or 20% discount before getting it, but if you go for it those 6 hours are quite pleasant.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Basically, this is your typical point-and-click game but in first person. The puzzles aren't too easy but aren't unfairly difficult either. Each puzzle is contained to a room which helps simplify things a bit. It's about a 7-hour playtime. I hope we get a sequel or similar games from the dev.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: **Updated, after completing the game**Don't let anyone tell you that chases, jump scares and combat are needed to make a "horror" game creepy and scary.  This game creeps me out so much without the usual tactics.  It does, however, have an underlying feeling around every dark corner that something BAD is just about to happen, shadows are sinister and your imagination is allowed to fill in the blanks. I LOVE that about it.  I'm old school, believing that movies like The Changeling (1980) are way more scary than the blood/gore movies of today, and this game delivers 100% of the same chills.The end of the game was not totally unexpected, but still an interesting way to finish the story.  If you pay attention to reading between the lines, there was a hint of something else going on in this mansion, so the "true" ending did explain that.  I still would have enjoyed to learn a little more about the group who pulled this all together, but the story was fantastic nonetheless.  Maybe I will go back and try for the good/bad ending, as I think there are three endings you can get.Ultimately, really great job, Devs, you have made a very cool game!!  I look forward to other games they create in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: We were expecting more from the ending(s), and would've preferred them leaning harder into the horror instead of the humor. We also had a few puzzles bug for us, like a color puzzle where one of the three "neutral" pieces were already colored in. But the mansion itself is a fantastic place to explore, and the cast is likable enough. This one is absolutely worth diving into: just be aware that the conclusion may disappoint you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Nice Escape Room-esque puzzle mansion game, with a well done graphical style. No sudden loud noises or jumpscares or anything, but more of a spooky vibe overall. Rooms are fairly linear so you for the most part find all clues and items you need within the room with the puzzle itself. Occasionally I would overlook a clue, but nothing too bad.I would recommend saving mid-game here and there (instead of only relying on autosave) especially before sections where characters need rescuing, since you can fail them.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: I really had a ton of fun with Tartarus Key. Vertical Reach nailed the atmospheric/psychological horror perfectly, the artstyle lends itself well to the presentation they were going for, and most of the puzzles were really satisfying and rewarding to complete (except the  one was kind of deflating).For sure looking forward to what Vertical Reach puts out next; hopefully it'll be another entry in this sub-genre!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: This game was an unexpected fantastic game!  Classic ps1 retro graphics, unique puzzles, amazing writing and character interactions, eerie feeling to the mansion, great lore and multiple endings; got some silent hill 3 vibes from some parts. I didn't mind replaying the game for all the endings and had a great time unravelling the story; truly a gem of a game, highly recommend to anyone!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: The Tartarus Key is a spooky puzzle game with zero chase scenes and few jump scares. Alex wakes up in a locked room in a strange mansion with someone's voice coming through a walkie talkie. As she explores the mansion and rescues the people inside, a greater story unravels that may give some hints as to how Alex ended up in the mansion to start with.I did really enjoy this game, it was an easy 100%; the characters are interesting, the dialogue is funny and the puzzles are logical and can be solved quite easily if you just think from a few different perspectives. I only really struggled with the stupid meat pushing puzzle and I mixed up two of the sigils in one of the puzzles, which resulted in death. The antidote puzzle was also kind of confusing for me, I really needed help with that one. I'm generally not a puzzle person, but the no-chase-scenes really drew me towards this game. The music is quite good, but there's no voice acting. There's no way to skip cutscenes except to quickly press E to go through dialogue quickly. The few dialogue options you have change nothing in information gathering or with the endings at all, I think they're just there to give you a feeling of having some interaction (outside of the puzzles). I found that the walkie talkie is really spammed A LOT in the first few rooms of the game, but there's not really much to keep the chatter going later on, plus Torres is the only character who really talks to Alex over it anyway.Once each character is rescued they have very little interaction in the game, just sit in one big collective room while you move onto next puzzles. It was a really short game, if I had idled less I may have 100% it in 6 or 7 hours. A really great game, overall, however, scratches an itch I never knew I had.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Really good puzzle/light horror game with no jumpscares , a great atmosphere and beautiful retro graphics. I really enjoyed how most puzzles had some challenging aspect to them but never required any insane leaps of logic to be solved. The quirky dialogue grew on me very fast, and I enjoyed all of the characters and their interactions with Alex. If you're looking for a puzzle game with a nice mystery/horror atmosphere and none of the usual jumpscaring/tension from most horror games, this is it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Cant't force myself to give this game negative review, but it felt like mixed bag honestly. In short:- Gameplay. Game is solid horror-ish escape room sequence, but difficulty is all over the place. Most puzzles are quite easy, to point some puzzles near the end were disappointingly simple. Few puzzles were designated by obscure goal, few others required seeking messages in weird places with zoom. Brightness setting is crucial, beware! Some non-linearity of gameplay is present, which was nice. Still, taking all possible outcomes into calculation clearly wasn't the goal of design.- Graphics. PSX-style models and textures with some trippy effect present. Debatable, personally I don't mind these. They work quite nice with horror genre and graphical design in this game is fond of details, compared to some other escape rooms.- Soundtrack. Music itself is fine, but it doesn't work with game for some reason. Also ambient/music felt too low in volume even with settings being pushed up by me. Sound design overall is average, I guess?- Story and characters. This is part which makes game to fall apart imho. Things logically kinda work out in the end - considering info we gather during walkthrough - but due to simple puzzles and somewhat weird writing endings and puzzles leading to them weren't climatic enough? Characters have different screen time and some feel much more important than others, while pair of them being clearly unimportant. They also don't really speak to each other, so my empathy to cast was controversial. I saw one optional scene of people discussing things in lobby, but I'm not sure how it was triggered, why it was triggered, and was it just one-time thing or game got some content you need to dig more to find. Feels like coming up with trivia dialogues and flashy cutscenes was taken with less priority than gameplay and final twist.All things considered, I don't feel like game was wasting my time, it was neat and somewhat rare experience of puzzle-only horror game. Still, for cost and longivity of development, I felt like game could have some additional polish and more characterization for it's actors. Buy if you are fan of narrative-driven puzzle games or horrors, but don't mind plot being somewhat cheesy. Otherwise you may be disappointed even more than myself.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review: Loved this game! The puzzles are diverse and engaging, I was amazed by the variety in which puzzles were presented. The story line is interesting, each character felt distinctive and unique, and I felt driven to help other survivors and get to the bottom of what's happening in this spooky mansion. Aesthetics were the icing on top as the blending of old CRT graphics and high quality icons made for delightful visuals. Would love to see more content or possibly a sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

_childDocuments_.review:
The last thing Alex Young remembers is being at home alone in her apartment... so why has she suddenly woken up in this strange mansion?

All the doors are locked by bizarre puzzles and traps, there are cameras following her every move, and she keeps thinking she sees... things... out of the corner of her eye. If she wants to escape alive, along with the other captives she discovers, she'll need to use her wits in this adventure thriller.

Inspired by the look and feel of classic horror games, The Tartarus Key serves up a mystery filled with twists and turns, and more than a few deadly surprises. Rely on brains over brawn to help Alex survive, but beware - not everyone might make it out alive.
_childDocuments_.name: The Tartarus Key

name: Nobody Saves the World
detailed_description: When the ancient Calamity re-awakens, who can save the world? Nobody! (That’s you, you’re Nobody.) Master the art of transformation to become a Slug, Ghost, Dragon, and more in this new take on Action RPGs from the creators of Guacamelee! Complete quests to discover and swap between 15+ varied and distinct Forms. Mix and match abilities in unexpected ways to unlock and complete even MORE challenging quests. Explore a vast overworld - on your own or with a friend online - while clearing shape-shifting dungeons in an effort to stop The Calamity and save the world! KEY FEATURES Transform into MANY FORMS: Unlock 15+ distinct Forms, from Rat to Rogue to Robot, each with its own unique gameplay mechanics. Mix & Match ABILITIES: Combine over 80 Form abilities to create powerful customized builds. Play as an Egg that can leave a trail of slime and shoot fireballs!!! We can't stop you! Unconventional QUESTS: Help the strange inhabitants of this world deal with their troubles. Each Form also has its own set of quests, which you can complete in creative ways. Evolving Dungeons: As you become stronger, procedurally generated dungeons increase in difficulty and complexity to keep you on your toes. Local & Online Co-op: Invite a friend to play through all, or part, of your adventure together! Endless Fun: Tackle an infinite, ever-changing endgame dungeon to unlock a new form, and build a glorious statue to celebrate your skills! New Game+: Put your Forms and abilities to the test against leveled-up enemies and dungeons with remixed difficulty modifiers. Awesome Soundtrack: New original music by acclaimed composer Jim Guthrie.

_childDocuments_.review: Humor didn't hit the mark for me, in-game advertising for paid DLC is pretty blatant. Combat feels very simple and as another reviewer put it, it's a "dopamine injector." Probably would enjoy it if you're a young or casual gamer - didn't have enough depth to feel rewarding to me. And the paid DLC ads are a huge turn-off. Get vampire survivors instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Nobody Saves the World

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fresh take on ARPG's with a little action adventure zelda-esc design.  If you've ever wanted to play an ARPG but are intimidated by all the item management, complexity, and the possibility of making a "bad" character then this is probably a game you'll love. If you approach this like most ARPG's, finding your favorite build and maxing that thing out you'll probably get bored. This isn't that kind of game. In Nobody Saves the World you're building a toy box. You can and should play with all of the toys and change their accessories around frequently.I've seen some other reviews saying this game gets a little repetitive and I can see that being an issue especially if you're expecting a more traditional ARPG.  Honestly, most ARPG's are a little repetitive. You start smacking baddies around and settle into a groove. Most ARPG's avoid this becoming dull with level ups, skill points, and item management to break that flow and have you making decisions about your build.  Nobody Saves the World leaves that power in the players hands by giving you the toys to play with, but it is up to you to go in and do so.I would recommend approaching this game with completion in mind because the game will reward your experimenting and teach you new synergies with its quest/experience system. Even forms I didn't like at first I found a niche use or a set-up that made them a lot of fun to run around with. I don't think that would have happened if I hadn't decided to do everything. Hint: buy the skill that sets your minimum speed higher and level it up, probably my favorite passive.If you are someone who likes to experiment and find synergies there are a lot in the game that are just sneaky enough to give that little "aha" moment, but aren't required as the game is pretty easy. If anything I've written down here caught our attention than give this one a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Nobody Saves the World

_childDocuments_.review: My gf and I are having blast at couch coop. She had never been so addicted to a game since Darksiders Genesis... It's almost scary! Anyway, an amazing game for couch co-op, 100% would recommend, with at least one experienced gamer - I wouldn't recommend for, say, two young kids ; the combat feels clunky when you start, and some mid to later dungeons need some solid understanding of the mechanics and general strategies. It's not an easy game ; it often requires patience, rethinking, and some light grinding. General gameplay and soundtrack are amazing : I'm often left whistling along the track, and it's a real joy to experiment with the (quite deep) class blending system. _childDocuments_.review: This stupendous adventure RPG boasts a large cast of goofy characters, over a dozen playable characters with unique skillsets, procedurally generated "dungeons" mixed together with a hand-crafted overworld, and an engaging progression system whereby the player advances by accomplishing challenges associated with each playable character. The player can switch between characters on-the-fly and can even mix and match their abilities to come up with player-crafted skillsets optimized for overcoming any immediate and dynamic obstacle/challenge that comes along. If you're familiar with Hades, I'd say it's similar to slowly building up a persistent roster of weapons/boons to which you can assign limited slots, but switch them out whenever you want, even mid-combat - and then being able to define around 8 of these "loadouts" at a time (i.e. each character) while *also* being able to freely switch between those characters any time. Dungeons will also have special environments that require you to think carefully about crafting a perfect solution. No single character combo is an all-in-one solution which is a great credit to the game's balanced skill/stat economy, huge variety in enemy design, and well-paced experience/growth system. With all that said, if you're someone who doesn't enjoy intense challenges, then there are some helper utilities: 1) you can do online co-op with a friend who's more skilled to help you out, and 2) you can gradually accrue money which can be spent to permanently increase specific stats.

_childDocuments_.review: hits just the right notes with a humorous RPG mixed with a cool combat system. Be warned though that this game is definitely better enjoyed with a controller over keyboard. The couch co-op introduced back in  is also here and is a blast with a buddy.DrinkBox is back with  (NStW), their take on a 2D zelda-esque RPG. The biggest selling point of the game is it's rather unique approach to combat. Players unlock different Forms throughout the game and with each Form comes new attacks and passives. Additionally, continuing to use those Forms will increase its mastery and grant even more attacks and passives. The spice that ties it all together is the ability to mix-and-match attacks from different Forms. If you enjoy min-maxing to try and find overpowered combos, this game is  for you.Addressing some of the negative comments about the game, I'd say that you should not let naysayers stop you from trying out this game. Is there a bit of grinding? Sure. But not more than any other RPG. In fact, there's a lot of nice features built-in to make the game less grindy and punishing. In regards to the combat, the player does need to complete challenges to level-up their Forms, but almost all of the challenges can be accomplished through regular playing. Since there's so much potential to min-max (and there are some hilariously broken strategies), the challenges force the player to break out of their mold and actually try different things or do a bit of lateral thinking. In fact, I'd go so far as to say that people who complain about the grind are simply  at the game.For everyone else, NStW is a medium-length RPG that plays just as well solo as it does co-op. The humor can be hit or miss, but even the jokes that don't land still give the NPCs lots of character. The only complaint I've seen that I wholeheartedly agree with is that this game  benefits from playing with a controller over a keyboard.: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Does have an extremely fun gameplay loop at its core, but I don't feel like the rest of the game supports that the best way it could.My number one issue is auto-generated dungeons. I don't want them in basically any game, when the first npc said "This dungeon keeps changin' when I leave!" i audibly sighed. By the third dungeon, you're seeing the same room configurations with a different skin, unsurprisingly. Given the 'grindy' nature of the gameplay, it gets repetitive quickly.My second issue is that, as the game ups its challenge, it seems to just be getting more annoying. At the halfway point it started feeling like I was spending as much time in menus rearranging abilities as I was actually fighting. Not to mention the screen can get really busy, and with issues like the Attack Up buff looking almost exactly like the Sharp ward at a glance, and some forms being very small, it's really easy to lose track of what's happening. A lot of deaths to accidentally switching to the wrong form, but not being able to see myself to know I did that.Less of an issue than the other two I mentioned previously, but I also feel that there could've been a few less forms, and unlocked them through quests instead of straight progression. There's still a hard wall at not unlocking Rogue and Monk until after the first three shards, so it isn't really 'open progression', and I feel like doing some sidequests for some monks to be able to unlock monk form may've helped me feel a stronger connection to it. I was really excited about pushing for the last couple forms, but felt really unsatisfied after unlocking them. Only maybe 3-5 forms have really unique-feeling abilities, the others are kinda different configurations of the same ideas.Overall, fun gameplay for about the first half, but really could've benefitted from a more of a traditional structure in the overall progression.

_childDocuments_.review: Mom always said I’d grow up to be a nobody… well it looks like Nobody will be saving the World mom! GET WRECKED!It’s like the perfect homage to the OG Legend of Zelda game with their own spin on combat and gameplay. It has the fun factor, combined with depth, and a constant sense of progression!Me and my wife’s boyfriend had such a blast with it. It was such a pleasant surprise, and surprisingly difficult in areas. It's easy enough for me to hang, but difficult enough to let my wife’s boyfriend flex his skills from time to time. It took us about 10 hours but I enjoyed the hell out of every minute. There’s no wasted time here. Just a fun game to play.It’s a dungeon crawler but you control a character (Nobody) who can transform into all sort of forms (rat, soldier, horse, etc.). Each one of them has its own abilities. To level up your class / character, you need get xp from quests which are plentyful in this game. Each transformation has 2-3 specific quests at the same time where you simply have to use your different abilities to finish it (for example kill 10 monsters with that ability). That’s the key to leveling up and unlocking new transformations / abilities. There’s just something so addictive about it. Even when I wasn’t playing, I was thinking about which class I would level up next time I would boot the game.I thought that there would be a lot of grinding but I’m surprised that there isn’t as much. I managed to complete it by unlocking all transformations available (except the DLC) and by that point, I had just enough stars to unlock the last dungeon. I did a lot of side quests and side dungeons too.It’s also harder than I thought. I died a lot but I liked the fact that there is no penalty for dying. You keep your quests progress which makes it easy to level up a specific class if you die and retry the same dungeon multiple times.It's exactly what I hoped Archvale was, but with that Guacamelee humor. It is a near-perfect game. It ticks all my boxes, the combat is extremely polished, class unlocking is fun and the class combination mechanic is extremely flexible, it is absolutely incredible. My biggest (and really only) complaint is the lack of coach co op. Like, it's perfectly designed for it, and the online co-op works great.If you have any interest in a fun game that doesn’t take itself seriously and has a lot of ways to change your build, go for it, or if you’ve been wanting to play something with an SNES Zelda vibe, this will be scratching that itch perfectly. I personally found it a great palate cleanser after finishing Sex with Hitler 3D. It is a great price for a great game from a great studio. 9/10
