Co-Op is perfectly forgiving, where you have to sort of "take turns" paying close attention, but 6 seconds later, your partner is back, and it's your turn to finally take a breath and throw the ball for the dog while your character dies (dog owners will understand what I mean).This was the perfect couch-coop game to play as a couple with "just the right amount" of difficulty for the majority of the game (thieves guild time-frame aside... maybe we're just bad, but those took way too many tries for us, to the point of us just wanting to 'get it over with' instead of 'enjoying the game').  The majority of the game though WAS just 'enjoying the game'.  We recieved "new characters" at a steady and healthy pace, even with two players, we always felt like we had something new to try or new characters to "work on" while we played.  We did all the side-content we could manage and outside of a few end-game trophies we can work towards, We really played the "full" game going in blind with no prior reviews, wiki-ing or anything like that.  It's just a great game that paces itself well enough to pick up and just be "played".I hope to see more updates, DLC's and continued growth on this game in the future, you've laid the groundwork for some healthy expandability from the players perspective by just throwing in more characters and elaborating on variations or alternate options to the endless dungeon for "endgame" to keep people coming back.The game just rocks - if you are on the fence but want a fun co-op couch game you can play with controllers, pause to deal with family-stuff (I.E. dogs), and play as underpowered or overpowered as your imagination and the abilities in front of you allow.  Know you can be:A super powered glowing horse that runs at light speed directly into enemies while electrifying them and knocking them into walls for extra damage (while on romantic horse adventures).A monk that has a legit naruto-style run and uses bunny magic to... summon a legion of bunnies (and sometimes tigers) that run at mach-ten and explode suicidal on the enemy while leaving health packs for you and your fam to pick up and do it all again.An egg.It's great!

_childDocuments_.review: The negative reviews on this game are absolutely insane. This is one of the best games I played in 2022 and one of the best I've played on Steam in the genre. This includes the DLC, which I walked into without realizing I had walked into it. Addressing some of the criticisms:Those are the three main complaints I saw. Please don't let them discourage you from playing this game. It was incredible. The dungeon crawling with the modifiers and different forms/abilities to surmount the modifiers made the gameplay so much fun. The randomization of the dungeons kept you from mapping it out if you had to start over. The soundtrack is honestly top 5 on Steam for me, maybe top 2 behind the theme song from Outer Wilds. Some of the challenges for the three guilds in the game and the DLC challenges were difficult at times, and really required quick thinking and a good understanding of all of the passive and active abilities in the game. The general world traversal wasn't ever too challenging, but exploring those facets of the game gave me the stress I was craving. You won't be disappointed.Ignore the popular negative reviews. If you like 2D ARPG's, play this. I would be genuinely surprised if you didn't feel the same way about it that I did.

_childDocuments_.review: You can tell this is by the Guacamelee team from the art style - and it has just as much character and attention to detail as those games. NSTW is an action RPG, but has a huge focus on unlocking abilities and characters throughout the game. You play as someone who finds a wand with the power to transform you into one of 17 different forms. Each form comes with a passive ability, and 2-3 unlockable active abilities that you can then use on ANY of the other forms. It allows you to create very diverse character builds. These forms level up by completing form-specific quests, which also teach you how to use the abilities well together and give you ideas.Aside from the form-shifting gameplay, it's basically a dungeon crawler with lots of quests and an overworld. The world is littered with dungeons that you need to beat to find stars to unlock the few Legendary dungeons, which lock progress in your form quests and make you assemble a build that works well. The world map is colourful and has several different biomes. Quests from the NPCs you meet are varied and interesting, and aren't simply just "go kill these". For example, one of them was a slug who's wife had died - and he'd heard of a slug necromancer who may be able to bring her back. Thanks to the form shifting abilities, you can combine the slug form with the necromancer's Summon Demon ability to bring her back to life.- The mechanics of the game feel unique - mixing different abilities from different characters to create unique builds- Some enemies gain 'wards' which is immunity to damage until they receive damage of a certain type. This forces you to change forms or use different abilities to break them- Dungeons have modifiers which make you think about how to build a character- Huge number of playable characters- Throughout the whole game you're constantly unlocking new toys to play with- Dungeons have fun modifiers- Incredibly polished, both in the UI, animations and gameplay- Huge number of abilities that you can mix and match across multiple characters- The game is a strange mix of too easy, and "keep bashing you head against the wall until it works". It's great that there's always something to work towards, but sometimes that means just getting killed over and over again until you level up a bit more- The music gets repetitive quickly. It feels like 10 seconds on a loop for the whole game- In between dungeons, it's pretty slow paced - it's mostly walking, or small easy groups of enemies- The dungeons aren't hand crafted; they're just procedurally generated rooms full of baddies to kill

_childDocuments_.review: DrinkBox Studios+ Steady-to-Fast paced gameplay+/- More action-oriented than RPG+/- Change forms to suit the game environment+ Quest-oriented tasks, more tasks completed, more XP- Some forms are more unwieldy and awkward to use than others.+ Casual game+ Upbeat village beats+ Spooky dungeons ambiance+ Appropriate background sounds (water lapping on the shore, crickets chirping, etc.)+ Has a "Don't Starve"-esque feel to the artwork+ artwork is simple but not boring to look at + Intriguing storyline- Fairly generic starting plot hook + Doesn't take itself too seriously+/- The game is made for controllers, but the keyboard works just fine+ Able to reassign buttons for the keyboard- Pricing is slightly steep ($24.99) for the amount of game you getThe game does a marvelous job drawing the player in with the introduction. It's a casual, action RPG with a unique twist of changing forms. Forms allow you to use different abilities to fight or accomplish tasks within the game. Nobody Saves the World has task-based quests that you complete to further level up various forms to gain new and improved abilities. With 15 different forms to choose from, you have a variety of choices to complete dungeons and slay monsters. Graphics reminded me of 'Don't Starve,' but the game's pacing is appropriate for an action-based game. The game is more action than RPG, but it leaves you wanting to continue improving your character. While Nobody Saves the World has some entertaining aspects, I didn't find myself drawn to replay the game. In addition, the price tag of $24.99 felt a little steep considering how much you get out of the game. Would recommend purchasing this game while it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't necessarily recommend *against* the game, but I can't recommend it either.First, it's a bit frustrating to control the character. It's a top-down 2D view, and you can only face in one of four directions — no diagonals. It's not a twin stick either — the direction you move is the direction you face. The game allows holding RT to stay locked in a preferred direction while shooting, but some attacks will lock in a direction anyway. There's also something to be said about the way characters layer on top of each other — there's some levels that really swarm the player, and it can be impossible to tell where you are or what you're hitting because things are in front of you and your form isn't one specific thing.Second, the game loop. The core mechanic is fairly interesting, and the quests aim for skill-based progression (which, in theory, I love). However, the way in which the player achieves these goals are an extreme grind. It's novel enough the first few times learning to hold a button to charge an attack. When it asks you to do it so that you hit 3 enemies at once 50 times for the third character in a row, it gets old. The game does, at a certain point, allow the player to mix and match skills to a certain degree. However, this isn't always rewarding — the skills require medals to level up, which are an additional grind to earn (a random drop, an end-of-dungeon reward for 3, or a hefty amount of money at a shop for 5; leveling one skill to the top requires ~15 or so.) The level of these skills matters more than the skills themselves in several cases, as there's multiple ways to overcome the various obstacles. To the game's credit, there's a lot of save points, and death is not much of a set-back in most cases.Third, the challenges. Throughout the game are several quests which are half skill based and half puzzle based. There is a certain amount of creativity in the quests themselves, and the ideas are great. The execution of several challenges is a bit overly specific. There's timed challenges with less than a second of room for error, a quest which as a reward reduces the players current amount of money (which is funny in context but also was obnoxious at the time), and several instances where quests require leveled skills to be reasonably attainable.Finally, the DLC — two branches of transformation are locked behind it. There's a few achievements which aren't attainable without it as a result. I don't currently have it, though I might grab it on sale in the future, so I can't say much else about it currently.In the end, I found the destination more fun than the journey — having all the abilities leveled up and being able to mix them is neat. However, getting there was an absolute chore. I spent more time while playing annoyed with the challenges than enjoying my accomplishments — the moment one was over, another more obnoxious one presented itself.I think that, for people who enjoy extreme challenges and a grind, this game is excellent. There's a lot to like here. However, for those who are not looking to grind long hours, or do not enjoy challenges which require an air-tight strategy, this game will probably not be one they choose to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't even want to play this game. It was not on my radar in the least. I'd seen it and dismissed it without thinking twice. Then I saw Skill Up's review on YouTube. Within the first half of the video alone he had changed my mind. This game caught me off guard with how charming, refreshing, and fun it was within the first two hours. I thought the gameplay would get stale at the game went on. Normally about 1/2-3/4 of the way through a game I'm starting to get bored and pushing through just to see the story. That can't be further from the truth in this one.This game felt like playing A Link to the Past(in terms of exploration and the map) with modern enhanced combat. Even the forms you aren't interested in at all when you see them will end up being something you love playing. "Horse"? Wow, that feels so out of place and boring, until it's not. Slamming enemies into other enemies with a kick to do bonus damage is so rewarding on many different levels. Positioning and planning are everything. Twenty minutes into playing horse, magician, zombie, ghost, whatever doesn't seem interesting to you; you will realize you're having just as much fun as the class you thought was your favorite. The further you go in the game the more you unlock. You can interchange abilities and passives between every class(aside from your Signature Passive which is locked on each class)and you're constantly rewarded for it by fun quests to complete and additional bonus experience for doing it.Want to be a ranged Robot that plays like an Archer, summons zombies, and bathes the entire screen in holy light? Yup, you can do that. Want to play an Archer that gallops around stunning enemies and doing bonus damage by slamming them into walls and other enemies while also poisoning them and then causing them to explode from that poison damage? Yup, you can do that. If you can imagine it you can play it, and you can beat the game with it.This was probably the most surprising game I'll play in 2022 and I can't recommend it enough. In my 33 hours I did almost everything in the base game - there is a New Game + after completing the game to provide additional challenge if you so wish. It won't take you a hundred hours, and you can probably finish it in as little as 10-12 if you so wish.

_childDocuments_.review: An ancient calamity has attacked the world and the one mighty wizard that everyone believes in has disappeared. Then there is you, an absolute nobody, someone who doesn’t have a single skill and to top it off doesn’t have any memory either. However, you will have to master the art of being a nobody and try to save this world, or at least attempt to find someone who can in Nobody Saves the World. One thing you can be assured of is that you’re going to be facing a mountain of quests. Some of them will come from the inhabitants of the world you’ll be traveling, but many of them will come from yourself.I have to say that I’ve played my fair share of games that love to grind, but this game takes it to a higher level. The thing, though, is that the grind isn’t just to waste time but to power yourself up and unlock additional skills and character classes. If you haven’t figured it out yet, perhaps you are more than meets the eye. You are still a nobody, but a nobody that can grow in power. Your main focus is going to be centered around class specific grind quests, something along the lines of “hit 25 enemies using your bite skill”. The more class quests completed the more powerful you can make that specific class version of yourself, and you can also unlock new classes once you have a high enough ranking in a previous class.There are a set number of dungeons that you’ll have to conquer, and some of the dungeons will be optional, but I will warn you that as you enter a dungeon, no matter if it’s a main or side dungeon, take note of the special effects. Some dungeons will have enemies that can only be harmed by a specific type of damage. Some dungeons will increase the damage of the enemies. There are many other varieties, so I repeat, check on what the dungeon will do before rushing in there. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve been burned by that little detail. Once you’ve completed a side dungeon you can always go back and take it on again. You will notice that the second time around they do scale to your level so don’t expect one hit kill when you take on a very early dungeon again.I really enjoyed this game. The characters you interact with are unique and humorous. The grind in the game actually makes sense. The types of classes that you can become was quite a surprise, and when you couple that with the unique abilities you can unlock and then mix and match with, you’re looking at a very unique experience. Sure, the start and the end to the game might be the same, but I would be very surprised if many gamers came close to playing the game the same way. There’s just that much variety stuffed into the game. So do yourself a favor and pick this game up, you can thank me later.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm both a roguelike fan and a metroidvania fan, and this definitely ticks some of those boxes.  In Nobody Saves the World you play as a Nobody, a blank shell being without a personality or memories.  You stumble across a magic wand that will let you switch between a large number of different forms, all of which have their own abilities.  After a few hours the game opens up and allows you to start combining anything but the primary attack from all of them.  All of these abilities cost mana and your primary attack builds mana.  Fairly straightforward so far.By the time that you can freely swap abilities from both your list of forms and a list of generic buffs the game truly comes alive.  Combat is driven by a mixture of elemental attacks and status effects.  For example: the rat has the ability to detonate every poisoned target on screen.  If you take the ghost and grant it the poison ability you then have a large aura effect of poison ticks that gets wider and wider the more things you hurt with it, and then you can take the detonate ability as a finisher.  But the aura is limited by a cooldown, so to get around that you take the rogue's ability to reduce cooldowns when picking up money and now you have a loop of damage and more damage that feeds into itself.  On top of this each of your forms will save your selected customizations and you can swap between them with a radial menu.  This keeps combat fresh for most of the game.  However when you start reaching the Necromancer, Robot and Monk you may not see much incentive to go back to older forms.The game is structured in a series of main quests that all require unlock keys.  These keys can be gained by going into procedurally generated dungeons that may or may not have rules.  These rules range from minor annoyances like mobs dealing extra damage to massive pains such as constant status damage or all attacks being responded to with rockets.  These dungeons also will have guarded enemies which are standard minions who cannot be hurt until they have taken some damage from a specific element first.  You'll always know what element is needed when you walk in and the mobs are clearly marked so the challenge is in putting something together that will fit the current difficulty.  Bosses range from wave type encounters to large bags of hit points and are generally not engaging.  The final boss is an exception to this for all the wrong reasons.  There are also some storyline dungeons that prevent you from changing your build or earning form xp.  These can only be completed once, which is unfortunate because they tend to be some of the best designed dungeons in the game.One major complaint is that you don't have a conventional leveling system.  Instead you have quests which are related to your forms and a few repeatable quests you can purchase.  These form quests grant you form experience, and when you level up a form your character level raises as well.  From there you can spend another currency found primarily in the dungeons on upgrades to your powers.  Many of these quests involve using the form's abilities: first as just repetition and then stacking them together or with another form's abilities.  Some of these will involve a lot of leveling before you can even attempt them, such as one for the Strongman who needs to level an ability up almost to the highest rank just to be able to afford to cast it enough times.  Others may seem difficult but can be completed in two or three full room clears.  These quests did force me to interact with the system and learn the abilities but unfortunately it feels like it added hours of filler on just so that I could see the last couple of forms.  There is no inventory management or equipment or potions: just the three currencies.  I really enjoyed about 20 hours of this game and finished it hoping to get back to that point.  The humor is hit or miss but the visual styles are wonderful.  But the real fun of the game is sitting down, finding the most broken combination you can imagine and wrecking dungeon after dungeon with it.  The forms are unique and well built to start, but the final few forms are so powerful it starts to make the game a dull slog.    Recommended, as long as the caveats wouldn't turn you away.

_childDocuments_.review: What a great game!- The game just feels great to play. Combat is fast and wild, and you are almost always brimming with a variety of abilities to spam. I can't count the number of times I emerged from chaotic melee with dozens of enemies that I evaporated with a potent combo. I literally cackled maniacally on several occasions.- The forms play and feel remarkably different. At least five times, I found a combination of abilities that I loved so much that I thought "Ok, this is the combo I'm going to exploit the rest of the game." Each time, it wasn't long before I found an even more satisfying combo, or more toys to play with.- Leveling up is fun and rewarding. Instead of grinding generic XP, each form has a list of quests which grant XP specific to the form. These quests repeatedly forced me to use abilities I'd been avoiding, and discover how powerful they were when used correctly. There's also a steady stream of upgrade tokens you can use to upgrade your favorite abilities.- Mixing and matching abilities rules. It's exactly as awesome and powerful as you think it will be, and there are endless combinations worth playing around with.- The art and world are fun and simple. There isn't much there plotwise, but the art is consistent and high quality.A few low-key pieces of criticism:- Many of the character advancement quests involve killing a bunch of monsters at once/in a short time, or with a particular combo. I often found it hard to find a large enough group of durable monsters to pull these off. There were a few times when I found a one-time encounter with a big mass of monsters, and I repeatedly let myself die right at the end so that I could keep re-running it with different forms.- It is easy to lose track of your character in big fights. This is especially true for a few fights where the camera is fixed, and you may be a tiny character on a screen with more than a hundred assets.- There appears to be no inherent benefit in getting the A rank in a form. A few forms require an A rank to unlock another form, but for most it has no mechanical effect whatsoever.

_childDocuments_.review: Very addicting, fun game in single player with lots of upgrades, options, synergies, and optimization for each form. This is a bit of a double edged sword though because those same qualities become annoyances in multiplayer, because every single time you want to upgrade a skill, equip a different skill, try a new form for the first time, complete a quest, check the map, or talk to a vendor, it brings the game to a screeching halt for all players as they are forced to stop whatever they are doing and watch one person navigate the menus which obviously can be incredibly irritating. Yes you can pick old forms out of a quick radial menu without interrupting gameplay, so why cant they do something similar for everything else? If you wanted to pick a different skill for example they could make it so you could hold down the A button or something plus the skill you wanted to change which would bring up a slider which you could choose a new skill from, I feel like that would be pretty simple. All things considered its still a pretty fun game, I just hope that theyll fix the glaring multiplayer issues. If they do then ill happily recommend it

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVED this game so much!! It's even worth playing ng+ for new (in a fun way) dungeon challenges. It's a nice stress-free game with a cute story to which I looked forward to playing it each evening for a couple of hours. It's also my first 100% achieve clear on Steam, if that says something!  Can't stress enough how awesome this game is for local co-op players, and undoubtedly online co-op, though we didn't play that way. My partner and I maxed out all characters to S-rank and it was really fun doing so. (HINT: You can find certain dungeons to get your objectives/quests done faster if you are smart about it). Absolutely recommended!)

_childDocuments_.review: This is just Cookie Clicker with extra steps.You're given something to do (kick 100 enemies, poison 50 enemies, bite 500 enemies, etc), you do it, you unlock a new thing to do, you do it... and... I can't think of anything else to say about this game. What happens if you die? Nothing, really. You keep all of the progress you've made. You're a wave crashing against rocks.There's nothing going on here. It's a list of brainless busywork. I guess some people are going to enjoy the dopamine hit of checking off box after box, but as soon as they accidentally think about what they're doing, they'll realize that they're not doing anything at all.Brainless gaming isn't always bad (hell, I play Truck Driver), but this game doesn't have the progress path or necessary vibe to carry that sort of experience; the developers didn't set out to make that type of game. Unfortunately, they did, and it doesn't work.

_childDocuments_.review: Its an excellent game and worth it.  Shouldn't be surprise from the Guacamelee devs. It has good humor, nice weird atmosphere, fun characters.  Gameplay starts slow but grows more and more complex and varied as you go.  Kinda like the final fantasy job system or Bravely Default, you can level up each form and take abilities from one form and place them on another.  Each form has its own stats and core abilities as well as unlockable abilities.You can really experiment and do some crazy things.  I have to say, they really knocked it out of the park with the options.  The dungeons themselves have varied obstacles, some random generation and modifiers that encourage different styles of play. The leveling is interesting and smartly implemented. _childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. This thing is chock full of original ideas well-executed that solve a lot of problems that most RPGs have. The innovative quest system basically eliminates grinding, and the shapeshifting mechanic is brilliantly executed, keeping the game fresh and challenging. The various monsters encourage players to play around with their build to get the best outcome, and it's all topped off with great art and music and fun, light-hearted dialogue and story. The only gripe I have is that I wish the quick-morph could be customized instead of having it automatically display your last eight forms. I didn't tend to use it in combat because the location of each form was ever-changing. If I could simply set my favorite eight forms, I would use the quick morph a lot more!

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad, but there was something that kept me from really getting into it.  It took me a while to figure out what that was...But first, the good stuff!- Game is quirky, art is vibrant, animations are fluid, combat is responsive.  Sometimes the humor is a little "meh" but it's overall lighthearted.Next, the annoying stuff!- Traveling around is a bit of a chore, even with fast travel points.  Nothing terrible, but I spent more time trying to figure out where to go and wandering around old areas than exploring new ones/doing quests/fighting, etc.- The ability to quick-change forms is nice, but depending on what you've changed into and when in the past, the locations of forms can change on the menu.  Since the game doesn't pause when you bring up the wheel, this can get frustrating.  Not sure if there's a way to select slots that stay until you change them on purpose.And now the thing that made me not want to keep playing!- The forms you can change into are just too random.  There's no connection to anything or anyone in the game and it takes me out of the experience.  At first you get an Archer and a Knight, which makes sense in a fantasy setting.  But there's   Bodybuilder?  Turtle?  I mean, there's fun to be had in those forms, but if I'm playing a Waffle one minute and the next form unlocked is a Toilet, what's the connection?  And I have to level up both forms in order to unlock the Tuba?  Ohhhkay, I guess?  And when there are no other waffles or toilets or tubas in the game, I wind up wondering "why?"I wanted to like this game more, and maybe it's less of an issue to others, but it made it hard for me to care where the story or character is going.

_childDocuments_.review: Kept me entertained until the end, the quests to advance the forms are varied and some require or greatly benefit from some cleverness. Good mood throughout. As you unlock more abilities through advancing the rank of your forms, you get more tools to have fun with, and there are some particularly interesting or entertaining combinations possible.I do have some issues with it. Many of the abilities just don't feel very valuable or good to use, and many of the passives are underwhelming. Every form is forced to use its base passive, making some forms strictly worse than others because of the dead passive slot depending on your playstyle preference. But that's just part of how the game works. That's not strictly a detriment, it's just something to keep in mind when constructing your loadout for each form.Haven't tried out NG+ yet. I don't know what appeal it might have, I don't have any interest in it.Worth the price for sure. They did a spectacular job of nailing the price point. Arguably better content than most AAA games that cost $60+.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw the announcement trailer for this game, and I knew it was something I had to play. And now that I'm not even halfway through the game, I can say that this is one of the best top-down RPGs I've ever played. With an art style that emulates the classical look of Don't Starve, mixed with the innovative mechanic of hot-swapping your characters for combos mid-fight, and a story progression game that make the player want to do more and explore the environment before them, every aspect of this game is beautiful and had a lot of care and attention put into it. I will say, it is a slow burn at times as you try to improve each individual character to progress, but I feel like it makes the mid- and late-game elements that much more satisfying. 10/10 game Drinkbox, can't wait to see where it goes.

_childDocuments_.review: A+This is an extremely fun game! You just need to give it 2-3 hrs to really kick in.You get the experience you want from a fast-paced ARPG, and like any good game, your desires are exceeded. The fun really kicks in after you've started unlocking forms from about the 3rd tier. Each form is genuinely distinct, they're not just faster/stronger remodels. And the mix & match skill system is awesome if you enjoy experimenting with strategies, this will so hit the spot. The world has a silly charm, with a gorgeous art style.Like most games of this style, gameplay footage makes it look like a mindless hack & slash, with no challenge. And unfortunately for the developers, this is the case for the first 2/3hrs. I expect there to be many returns and negative reviews from players who didn't get past this stage, and feel there was no depth or challenge in the combat. But, this is my experience with most RPGs, especially ARPGs. It's a tricky design challenge, you can't just throw all of the mechanics at the player from the start, because it's overwhelming. Or unlock everything too quickly and you get the same issue.Great job DrinkBox, 2 thumbs up!

_childDocuments_.review: So the game overall has been fun but from a controls perspective the game is made artificially difficult by the fact that all the movement is only done with the left stick on a controller. With the melee based characters this isn't too much of an issue but with ranged it adds in an artificial level of difficulty as you're constantly being forced to stop attacking and turn to make sure your character is facing the correct way. Other than that the game seems alright, I'd like to recommend this but I think the controls need to fixed first. Right trigger can hold your facing obviously but that doesn't do much to help a overall clunky control scheme. _childDocuments_.review: A friend gave me this gem of a game as a birthday gift, and it's been one hell of a present so far. If you want to look at it this way, it's a Ben 10 game on steroids. You have a wide cast of "transformations" to choose from and a wheel to select previous toons; each with its own abilities and passives (you cannot switch "signature" abilities and passives) and the game allows you to mix and mash them as you see fit (sorta like Diablo III) to fight, solve puzzles or quests (some quests have weird and specific wording until your brain makes the connection so you can arrange a certain character with a certain ability from another toon.)If you're expecting an endless rogue-lite, this ain't it, chief. Finished it with every single character maxed out (or "S-ranked") in less than 20 hours. A cheap, well-rounded, fun little game that anyone should play (with a controller.)New Game Plus looks like a fun time, too.

Very good designUPDATE after beating the game at approx. 20hr mark:I've never until now felt the urge or seen the point of a New Game +. Looking back at the course of beating this game first run through, I am flabbergasted at how well everything worked and how it wasn't frustrating at all despite being challenging. _childDocuments_.review: With "Nobody Saves the world", you get exactly what you expect of a game with this price tag. A game with a nice, well thought-out, core idea and then a little bit of story around that.While many games try to stretch the playtime, to a point where the core gameplay loop becomes boring, "Nobody saves the world" ends exactly at the point where you feel you are done: you can complete almost everything in less than 20 hours played, including side-quests and most of the collectibles and this is roughly at the point where you got to see all mechanics the game has to offer. you get to try out some final skill combinations in the final dungeon, and then the credit rolls and you can go home.There are a lot of good things to say about this game, but the most important is: don't skip this.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Saves the World is a simple, fun dungeon crawler with a few flaws that might be a dealbreaker.The premise is that you're a little guy who gets a magic wand that let's him shapeshift. Whenever you unlock a new form to shapeshift into, you also unlock unique active and passive abilities that can then be applied to any of the other forms. These forms span fantasy tropes like rogues and rangers to oddities like bodybuilders and killer bees. Onto the gameplay. It's an adventure game along the lines of a 2D Zelda game. You walk around, break stuff for money, talk to some people, do simple quests, hit levers to open up new areas, etc. I'm very bad at figuring out where to go in these sorts of games, but I had no issues with this game. So if you're into that sort of thing, it might be a little too easy for you. The combat and dungeon crawling is kind of like a bullet hell game but easier (...bullet heck?) Dungeons involve lots of enemies that walk at you, charge you, or shoot stuff at you. The gameplay isn't outstanding, but most of the fun is unlocking the forms, leveling them up, and making a unique build.Unfortunately, the forms and the dungeons are also two of my biggest issues with the game. Unlocking new forms is gated behind completing certain simple tasks (kill X number of enemies with Y ability) BUT ALSO story progress. Meaning that you cannot rush a form that you want to play as, and that character's passive and active abilities are gated until the latter part of the game. This doesn't make a whole lot of sense to me as a game about unlocking these characters to break down their parts and put back together as a unique new build. This is even worse with the DLC which is kind of impressive with how poorly implemented it is, but I'll get to that later.My second biggest issue is the dungeons, or more accurately, one specific gameplay mechanic: wards. Wards are shields that make an enemy invulnerable until you damage them with a specific type of damage (there are 4). I just do not find this mechanic very fun. I realize that it's meant to break you out of playing with one specific form/build, but I really wish they did it in a different way. It would even be fine if they took reduced damage. I just find the invulnerability to slow down the game by adding a rock-paper-scissors element that didn't need to be there.I think that these two issues wouldn't be an issue if the game was more along the lines of Diablo, with randomization and reasons to keep playing it over and over again, but it's not. It's a story game and it feels wrong to get a cool new ability when your time with the game is coming to an end. And it feels wrong to have dungeons pushing you to switch up your build when (I feel, at least) that the game is about finding the right mix of abilities that you like.The writing is not for me, but it might be for you. It's that sort of wacky, random, PG humor that a lot of indie games have. Sort of reminiscent of Ittle Dew but less charming in my opinion. It's not a dialogue heavy game, so it's easy to ignore.Onto the DLC, which is so poorly implemented that I'm not sure what they were thinking when they made it. If you want more of the same, it ain't it. It's a weird sort of puzzle gauntlet which involves you thinking up the best build for these little minigames. I don't like it at all, and the worst part is that it adds 2 new forms. Awesome, 2 new forms that I can unlock and incorporate into my builds, right? Wrong. First of all, if you already beat the game, then you won't even want the new forms because the game is over other than the DLC which you have to play halfway through to unlock them (and even then they won't be too helpful for finishing the rest of the DLC). So the longer you wait to play the DLC, the more of the main game that you're missing out on using these forms. So then just play the DLC first, right? Also wrong. To complete the puzzles, you have to already have unlocked many of the main game's forms and upgrade them. So the best way to play the DLC is to play the main game and periodically see which of the challenges that you can beat so that you can unlock the new characters as fast as possible so that you can actually play the game with them. It might be forgivable if the DLC was actually fun, but it isn't.At the end of the day, I like the game. It's sort-of a lot of things. Sort-of adventure, sort-of bullet hell, sort-of collectathon... And I sort-of like the game. It does everything perfectly competently, but no one thing outstandingly. It's a fun idea and I enjoyed my time.And hey, it's also a great game for Deck. Easy to pick up, make a little progress, and put down again.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello Friends,Today I will review the game NOBODY SAVES THE WORLD. This is about a amnesiac hero who must find out what happened to them. Their special ability is shapeshifting and using the powers of the forms they take. This can help with different situations, like puzzles, or passing by certain areas of the game. Using these forms correctly really helps the main character in certain situations in the game.The graphics are cartoony, and is made by the same people who made the Guacamelee game series. The game story is silly and funny at points, but the fighting is quite fun. The dungeons are similiar to mystery dungeons as their layouts change depending on different times the main character goes into them. There are also many forms to upgrade and umlock to fully enjoy the game. Some forms must be found to use, or do certain things to unlock them.PROS:- A cartoony adventure featuring a shapeshifting hero with many forms.- One you upgrade forms to a point, the player can make custom loadouts of which powers and passive abilities they can use.- Each form has quests to upgrade them, which may require specific conditions or killing so many monsters.- Unexpected suprises found on the world map.- Many side quests to complete and bonus dungeons.- New game Plus mode which carries over upgraded forums in the new game.- Co-op mode to play with friends to have fun.- Works on Windows 11 OS.- Controller works fine with the game. I used a ZEN switch controller.CONS:- The cartoony asthetics may put off some people for buying the game.- Some of the puzzles can be confusing to figure out.- The impossible dungeon can be well..impossible. It is very difficult compared to the rest of the game.- The music for the dungeons only have 3 tracks that keep playing over and over again. That is my only gripe about the music. At least you can get used to it after awhile.Do i recommend this game? YES. The game's silly story and goofy graphics may turn off people on buying the game, but the game is a decent mystery dungeon game with a main hero who can shapeshift to get out of certain problems. From the makers of Guacamelee series, which is also a great game with nice graphic style. I fully recommend you try both these games in that series too.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying I dislike leaving negative reviews, but sometimes, a game is just so awful, so deceptive, so utterly deceitful that I feel I must say something, to speak up for some of us who can’t spare the time, perhaps due to an unwillingness to give this trash fire of a game anymore of theirs, or just can’t spare the time due to life circumstances.I make this sacrifice for you my fellow gamers.Normally, I would say something nice about the game, to try to soften the upcoming blows, but there is precious little positive I can say about Nobody Saves the World.The one thing I can think of is that the game doesn’t do the typical lock you in each room / monster closet until you clear it, like Ziggurat, Enter the Gungeon, or Mortal Sin.In Nobody Saves the World, you can just wander the dungeon, though as I found out, there is not that much of interest to actually see!That itself is a damning statement towards the game, but it is an accurate one.Alright, here we go, my extensive list of suggestions / observations about Nobody Saves the World. May they be of use to you, and perhaps spare you the pain of actually playing this, as for me this one was downright PAINFUL!I’ll try and keep this organized.If anyone feels any of this is out of line or off base, let me know, I only made it about an hour in this one, so it is likely I missed a bit, but most of what I did see I did not like!Or in-game?On a PC game!?Terrible!This is never a good look.It’s like putting out a Playstation or Xbox game, and saying: “Plays best with mouse and keyboard” and not including basic support for the PCs most common controls.It reflects a total disrespect to both the platform, and the player base.It is something that should not be done.This happens if you make the apparent mistake of trying to play this with mouse and keyboard, discover that it is a PC game that totally lacks mouse support (GROSS!) and resign yourself to grabbing a gamepad and plugging it in.Just terrible!At least give players the options to turn the boring, mindless stuff off, if they’re the type who likes to figure things out themselves…I tried to skip it of course, first in the menu, (NOP!), then by just walking past the tacky wizard house, but NO! So Damned Linear!And of course, the Mandatory Tutorial is full of slow, super basic, demeaning crap that you can’t really speed up or skip, and that really seems to be nothing more than an attempt to run out the 2 hour Steam refund window; so transparently scummy….I’d refund if I could…Such a basic feature in most PC games, yet not present…Nop, it just kind of hangs out on the left hand side of the screen, just reminding me with that sad face how unexciting, linear and time wasting this trash game is. Don’t worry game: I won’t forget!If I had seen that prior to buying this, I would not have done so…It looks terrible: every time I look upon it I am reminded how terrible and poorly thought out this game is.You’re literally sealing the player into a room until they collect enough stars; at least in Mario 64, you have a CHOICE of rooms to go in!It seems even THAT is too much for Nobody Saves the World!You have to “Redeem” completed quests in the inventory, waiting for some slow, stamp /sticker thing to appear before the game will give me the damned star bs needed to exit the room! (it never actually gives you enough stars, but it still wastes your time!)What an unneeded, total waste of the players’ time!Yet more built in bullsh*t that seems downright designed to be nothing more than an attempt to run out the 2 hour Steam refund window; so transparently scummy….I begin to suspect the whole game, or at least that first vital 2 hour window, is full of that scummy crap… It’s to the immediate right the moment you get your first form, if you try to look right and see what else you can get.Just unbelievable…There is no collision on enemies here.Worse, there is ZERO speed reduction when literally running through enemies; am I a ghost? Perhaps to add a bit of weight to the combat and movement system, your speed could be reduced by 50% when you attempt to literally walk through enemies, perhaps representing your characters evading and dodging through their position?You can just play with your eyes closed, just hold down X and move left to right, zero skill or awareness required! Just terrible!It’s so mindless and boring!So, you get no exp from kills here, instead, you do tasks and get a “choice” of 1 upgrade for the current form; Then, why does the game say it does right on the steam page?It says “Shared/Split Screen Co-op”.I have seen zero options for that.I saw Online Co-op, but that is not split screen co-op, split screen co-op is local co-op.Again with the deception…You can just ignore enemies and run through the dungeon; as the combat is such boring, sleep inducing crap, that is precisely what I did!It was also slow and boring, with nothing interesting to see: no treasures to find, fun items, or good combat, just more mindless crap tasks and brain dead enemies to literally ghost through.So, I ran to the boss room, and it sealed up, and I closed my eyes and moved back and forth, mindlessly gnawing through the enemies; it was exactly as uninteresting and boring as it sounds.After that, there was another, bigger boss, but by then I had had enough of the mindless crap, and just exited the game; 1 hour of my life wasted.Ha, you failed to hook me for 2 hours game!Course, I’m still stuck with this trash, as it was over 2 weeks ago that I foolishly purchased it.

_childDocuments_.review: is a fun action RPG with satisfying core combat and amazing progression that is undermined somewhat by the most aggressive level scaling I have ever seen. The plot for this one is pretty simple and is basically just there as a pretext to move the action along. You play as the titular Nobody, a mute, bald, and naked man-baby-thing who awakens in a filthy shack with a bad case of amnesia. Following a sequence of mishaps and misunderstandings you end up in possession of a magic wand that allows you to change form, gaining the powers of numerous fantasy creatures and adventurer archetypes. Newly empowered, you’re soon roped into a fairly standard ‘collect magical McGuffins to save the world’ quest. While the overall outline is fairly thin, the plot is significantly elevated by a few memorable characters who have surprisingly satisfying arcs along the way. The game also maintains a brisk sense of humor throughout reminiscent of the Paper Mario series. I personally didn’t find any genuine belly laughs here, but the tone is so light and breezy it can’t help but be charming.  The primary draw here is going to be Drinkbox Studio’s signature art style, which is every bit as weird and wonderful as their previous work. When trying to describe it I can’t help but use oxymorons like ‘grotesquely appealing’ or ‘disgustingly cute’. Despite some similarities,  does manage to distinguish it’s visuals from the  games through the use of much bolder linework and an overall more cluttered aesthetic. On a purely technical level this is a fairly simple 2D action RPG without too many bells and whistles in the graphics department. There are a few subtle lighting and shading effects that are quite nice, but this engine’s primary flex is pushing a huge number of sprites on screen at the same time. Things are never quite as overwhelming as something like , but given the more detailed art style, I still found it impressive just how many enemies, familiars, and projectiles could fill the screen at times. All this chaos does come at a cost however, as I did encounter occasional slowdown even on an RTX 3090. Sound design and music are fine, but don’t really stand out as strong features of the overall package. The soundtrack is certainly appealing and generally does a good job of complementing the action, but I didn’t find anything memorable enough to catch myself humming along. Sound effects are just right, crunchy when smashing up the environment, squishy when pounding on enemies.The main appeal of  is its primary gameplay loop, which involves completing quests to build your character and earn currency that can be used to access the game’s main story dungeons. Unlike most action RPGs, simply defeating enemies does not net the player experience or levels. Instead, each form has a series of quests that need to be completed in order to advance it’s rank, with each improvement providing an overall buff to your character’s base stats and level. You start the game with only a single form, but through completing quests and ranking up you can unlock more advanced ones. Each form has its own unique abilities, which all have an elemental affinity that is necessary to damage certain enemies. Eventually, you unlock the ability to mix and match abilities between different forms, allowing you to compensate for weaknesses or find synergies that would otherwise be impossible. The quests do a great job of encouraging you to experiment with different builds, often revealing super effective combinations that might not have been obvious otherwise. Overall it’s a fairly unique spin on systems I’ve seen before in games like  or .As fun and satisfying as this form of progression is, it does come at the expense of disincentivizing exploration of the game’s modest open world. The game’s main objective is to complete a handful of story dungeons, which are unlocked with currency earned by ranking up your forms. Most of your character grinding is intended to take place in the many optional side dungeons scattered across the landscape. The problem is that due to level scaling, you can grind ranks literally anywhere, making it largely unnecessary to ever branch out from the first area. Many of the later game dungeons have painful ability restrictions and requirements, while providing largely the same rewards as the unrestricted early game ones. You do gain a modest amount of experience and currency for clearing an area for the first time, but I only ever really felt compelled to complete the late game dungeons for completionism’s sake. Level scaling also puts a damper on the satisfaction of character progression. I’m generally not a fan of this kind of system, and this must be the most aggressive implementation I have ever seen. No matter how much you grind your character, the majority of the game’s dungeons will always be scaled two levels higher than you. A few of the early areas peter off after a while, but even at endgame, with every non-repeatable quest complete, I still found myself below the recommended level for many dungeons. When the scaling is this overbearing, it really makes me question whether the developers actually wanted to make an RPG, or whether those elements were cynically included to heighten the Skinner box effect. Regardless of intent, it’s a bafflingly awful and unwelcome design decision that mars an otherwise excellent progression system.   Overall despite it’s flaws this game is well worth the asking price. It took me about twenty or so hours to complete the main quest and all side objectives, and there is a new game plus option available with retooled dungeons should you wish to extend the experience. The level scaling did hamper my enjoyment significantly, but depending on your preferences it might be tolerable. At the end of the day this is a recommend, and I’m confident anyone who enjoys action RPGs in general will have a good time with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough of this game and there's lots to love about this action RPG. It's my introduction game to DrinkBox Studios and I'm already looking forward to more. Gameplay is addictive, well paced and sometimes very chaotic. Dying is not very punishing, which I personally find fine (it only makes you start a challenge or dungeon again if you're in one). Difficulty can get up there in some very specific challenges where you have to use precision, fluidity changing forms and combos for different typing. I didn't find any over-levelling problems either and when you're too weak it's just simply impossible to go through some sections. Now as for levelling your forms, some were locked behind having to obtain movesets or passives from other forms (so if you don't enjoy a bit of grinding this isn't for you). There is also a shop where you can obtain passives and other progression items. The passives and abilities that you can equip to your forms are not limited to their typing, so there is a huge array of combinations and sets that you can make.Now for the art style, that's what really sold it for me. I don't really have many words to describe it other than fun and very easy on the eyes. My only problem is that when there are too many monsters, it's hard to distinguish which is which. Would have also loved for Laura to actually find a bestiary so that we could see the exact properties (attacks, description, etc.) of the monsters in this awesome world.Finishing off with sound and music. The latter is cartoonish and catchy, but after playing for an extended period I got a bit tired and had to switch it off. You did a great job though, Jim Guthrie. Voice acting would have been the cherry on top for me ;).Overall, it's a game worth trying. If the art and charisma of the characters and their puns doesn't get you, I'm certain the gameplay will. Now off I go to complete a NG+.PS: The map is bigger than you think, status moves are your frenemy and familiars are OP (go bunny!)

_childDocuments_.review: I realllllly want to recommend this game, but as it stands, I can't. Not because the story, the artwork, the progression, or gameplay is bad, but because the developers decided that there is ONLY one way to play this game. That is to say, its gamepad or bust. If you want to play this with keyboard and mouse, well, your ♥♥♥♥ out of luck as this game doesn't have ANY mouse functionality. The option to change the controls to fit your needs or wants is there for purely cosmetic reason. I understand developing a game to be best played with a controller (looking at you Dead Cells), but to not even INCLUDE mouse functionality in a PC game is absurd. Its not even like this was a console port, it was released on PC at the same time it was released on XBOX.Combine this with the fact that even with a controller, the game still plays somewhat wonky as your characters aim is tied to whatever direction your running towards. So if you want to backpedal while shooting at enemies, you first have to run towards them, hit the lock direction button, and then you can back pedal and shoot them. Though I will say this particular wonkiness doesn't ruin the gameplay, but is an annoyance that's easy to work with.So with all that said, if you have a controller, this game is really fun and I would totally recommend it. But with the developers purposeful decision to not even include one of the most basic and common input functions in a PC game, is so obnoxious and arrogant, that I cannot recommend this game. Or maybe I'm blowing this all out of proportion and the reason they left out mouse functionality is because they forgot to  the on button for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Saves the World is a game inspired by 2D Zelda games, but with some modern game design to keep it original. What sets the game apart is the class system. There are over 10 classes to unlock. Each class unlocks new active and passive abilities as you level up. Once you have unlocked a new ability, you can use that ability on a different class. The classes range from your typical fantasy RPG class to quite silly. Classes and abilities have what boils down to elemental types, which are required to break enemy wards. If an enemy is dark warded, you cannot damage them until you hit them with a dark attack. This is where the mixing of different class abilities comes into play.Like 2D Zelda games, NSTW is broken up into several zones that you gain access to via new class skills. Each zone is themed and has a dungeon to complete. Before you complete the dungeon, though, you have to do several mini dungeons. The mini dungeons have roguelite elements to them. Each time you enter a dungeon, the layout changes. Ultimately, this doesn't add much to the experience or provide any meaningful replayability to the dungeons, but it doesn't make them worse because of it.If you're familiar with Drinkbox's other games, you will find this game isn't short of their charm. The music, the art style, and the writing are in-line with what this studio has done in the past. If you liked it in the Tales From Space or Guacamelee games, you will like it here.My one complaint with the game would be the mini dungeons and, to a lesser degree, the main dungeons are kind of boring? I question it, because it's harsh to say, but I wish there was a bit more to them. The dungeons may have been better without the roguelite elements, but who knows what the decisions in development were at the time.If you like Drinkbox games, 2D Zelda games, action adventure games, and Saturday morning cartoons, you will have a good time with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Are you looking for a great game to play by yourself or with a buddy? Well look no further since "Nobody Saves the World" is here. A neat little package of shape shifting, stupid humor (the good kind), fun gameplay and great music.The gameplay consists of you taking on the forms of various classes, jobs and animals which come each with their own standard attack as well as 3 further skills and a passive. While the standard attack and stats itself are tied to those characters, you can use the other 3 skills and passives and mix them how you want on other forms.Want to play as a bee and use the fireball of the dragon, while constructing turrets from the mechanic and use the infected bite from a zombie to create more zombies? No problem!And the game wants you to combine those things. Because on one hand you get quests at the beginning to learn the skills of the form and later on you've to use other skills and passives to advance further and one the other hand the enemies might've shields against some damage types and having only one wouldn't help much. There is blunt, sharp, light and dark damage to mix.The designs of some characters and monsters are really awesome and the game is really cheap for around 20hr of fun. If you are interested in the dlc, which adds two additional forms and some cool puzzles, I recommend to get it with the base game. While you might not be able to beat the dlc completely at the start you should treat it as further side content while you progress through the story. If you do it after the main game you wouldn't have much use from the new forms while getting them slightly in the middle opens up more good combinations.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR I love NSFW, err, I mean NSFW! Err... NSTWWot I liked- Great artstyle, I really enjoyed NPC design (goofy & funny), pixies especially;- Very good writing. It does not have a lot of text, as an indie roguelite should have. The dialogues are short, witty and fun. Also you can get actual rewards (minor ones) for being an attentive reader;- A bunch of forms, a lot of them hilariously looking, each with its own abilities (4 active + 4 passive) You can mix and match 7 out of 8 abilities of ALL dozen forms;- This cutesie world: different guilds, exploration is just fun - there're areas you can get by flying / swimming with special forms;- Simple yet smart quests and combat puzzles, based on your classes' abilities;- Leveling up experience goes swimmingly as you progress from a tiny critter to a huge beast (going through a bunch of forms on your way up, and you do it all exploring the world;- Lots of dungeons, which are not only have randomised layouts but a ton of unique tiles;- Play as a transmuter!- Horse porn;- Animal racism.Wot I disliked- ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ keyboard controls - you have to hold a key to backpedal;- There's no way to tune you quick access panel or bind forms to shortcuts.To sum it all up, I just fell in love with NSTW. The originality of the idea mixed with standing out artstyle and a great sense of humour and some real solid writing. Even the awkward control scheme could not break its charm.

The quest system also feels like a huge chore, basically with the same missions to kill x number of enemies multiple times endlessly for each form that you are basically forced to do because it's the way to level up and make progress. There are also no quality of life options, especially when having to select other forms. So everything feels like a huge chore, repetitive and a waste of time.But I think this game is exactly about it. That quick dopamine dose and the feeling of instant satisfaction to just defeat a bunch of enemies and complete these little chores without a real storyline objective. Many people may like it to play casually.I was not having fun with it and ultimately decided to drop the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I pushed the 'add to cart' button as soon as I read "From the creators behind guaca...."  And honestly, based on screen shots and the description, this doesn't seem like a game I'd like. I didn't have fun with "Undertale" or anything that rides off on the back of charming characters, and not gameplay...and this game looks like the type of game that just charms you to death, and feels uninspired in the minute to minute gameplay.    I booted up the game, and I was thinking that this might be a return for the first half hour...However, I'm happy to say that this game is really friggin' good.  It's very "gamey", with all the charm and comedy of guacamelee as a bonus.   Switching through multiple characters to match the situation you're in is not a new idea, but this game does so beautifully.   This game is addictive.   It's a great mix of a hack and slash game with an adventure game, and looks far better than the screenshots appear.If you're on the fence about the gameplay, just give it a shot... It's nothing crazy complicated, but has plenty of nuance, and the game is constantly giving you ways to progress outside of the story.I'm having a great time so far, and I should have been in bed a hour ago.  Good job DrinkBox.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is genuinely phenomenal. The mechanics are fantastic- each form has it's own play style, easily customized as you play best. The quests to rank up are tough but manageable, and offer new styles of play for the form for players to try out. Moving and attacking in this game feel GOOD. Enemies and environmental objects feel like they have weight, and if you sink your little rat teeth into them, they crunch just right. The dungeon modifiers are clever and fun, the bosses are a great time, the world enemies are enjoyable, everything about this game honestly rules.Speaking of the little rat, the character design in this game is also fantastic. The world looks amazing in every stage of the game, with the corruption slowly building and manipulating the environment, but every environment looks different and engaging. I love the little background animals that exist in different zones. They're such good tiny pieces of worldbuilding. The forms each look incredible, and their movement and facial expressions are so so cute. I adore how the dragon floats, the rat's little chompers, the mermaid's happy face in the water, the little scuttling demons of the necromancer... the art in this game is absolutely incredible and this game would not be the same without it.I'm working on new game plus now and am extremely happy to continue sinking hours into this game. It's both a brain workout and a brain relaxer! It just feels good to play and fun to progress in. It may honestly be one of the few games I replay multiple times.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Saves The World by Drink box Studios (Guacamelee) was never something that was on my radar. It was one of those games that could've easily fallen into obscurity due to It's early year release date. So on a whim I took a shot in the dark buying it on Steam ($24.99). Full disclosure though, it's available on Game Pass if you've been taking advantage of that. Enough preamble, on to the game.Nobody Saves The World tries a lot of interesting things while still staying somewhat familiar. At a glance it's a top down, slap it up RPG. After spending about 10 minutes with it you begin to see what the appeal is. You play as...well...Nobody, an eyeless white humanoid blob? I think that's an accurate description. Not soon after meeting and taking control of Nobody you meet your inanimate cohort (as well as some colorful characters) in your adventure. A magic wand that allows you to shift your form. You start out simple, a rat. And soon you begin to unravel a tree of forms with varying signature moves and 3 other abilities. These abilities are activated the face buttons ala Diablo or Ultimate Alliance. At first your limited to your signature moves, the rat for example starts with a quick chomp that causes poison damage to enemies. This can be frustrating sometimes if your not feeling the signature attack, which i wasn't. The good news is each form has a level or letter grade and it doesn't take long to progress to your second ability. And without giving away too much, there’s a specific upgrade you get in the early hours that remedies that frustration even more.All this leads to another main concept of the game, quests. Quests come fast and loose, some are easier than others. There’s different type of quests whether it's related to you form (you must be in that form to see and complete them) or broad like kill 20 "baddies". Along with experience for your general overall level and your form level, they are separate, but you gain steady experience with both. You get wands which will allow you to open the various area dungeons that progress the story. In order to get and complete these massive area dungeons you'll have to complete quests and minor dungeons around the open world. Everything is labeled with a recommended level so plotting your course is somewhat simple. This also give you ample time to experiment with all the different forms. It does a good job of incentivizing using different forms, especially when they start to introduce "wards" more heavily. Wards are basically status effects that are attaches to all your abilities. Some enemies will start to pop up that need to be hit with light damage before they take any damage. Sometimes it's sharp, sometimes it's blunt, this makes for interesting (and at times frustrating) combat scenarios.That frustration never completely overtook the experience though due to excellent checkpointing and inconsequential death. I may have missed something, but when you die in the open world you respawn at one of the many scattered save points. Dungeons are a little more harsh, but there is a checkpoint right before the "boss room" so you won't have to re-run the whole dungeon if plans fall apart. Speaking of those boss rooms, every dudgeon has one. In order to clear a dungeon, you need to clear these final rooms. This was one of the disappointments I had because they're just rooms in which the normal enemies come out in different waves. The bigger story dungeons have a "boss" in this room, but it's just a giant version of a common enemy. My disappointment aside I was still enjoying them. It's not like they're the same room or there aren't some fun gimmicks thrown in every once and awhile. Off the top of my head there's about 25 or so truly unique enemies, more will crop up, but they usually fit into a type you've seen before. The general loop of quests and dungeons make you feel like there’s always something to do, at first it's a little overwhelming. Eventually when you clear more of the map and learn to navigate it using the fast travel portals it starts to become a more seamless experience. The gameplay of Nobody Saves The World can shift on a moments notice depending on the player and how they choose to unlock forms and abilities. Consistently engaging, and sometimes frustrated, but never bored.Another reason i didn't get bored was the idiosyncratic look it has to it. That individuality extends to dialog and story. The characters are face with a world ending threat yet it doesn’t take itself too seriously. Everything has a Nickelodeon esq vibe to it in the best way. Characters are constantly questioning what you are or why your wearing no pants. There are answers to all these questions and more throughout the story. The actual narratives not doing too much to blow you away, but it's a fun ride. I would be completely remise if i didn't bring up the soundtrack. Composer Jim Guthrie channels Supergiant composer Darren Korb (which I 100% mean as a compliment) with folk instrumentals mixed with synth and at time industrial. From the overworld theme to the dungeon boss theme, I was bobbing my head start to finish. By the end of my 27 hours I came away satisfied. The story wraps everything up in a nice and by the end I was so strong there wasn't much that posed a threat. It's a game that can be as hard as you want it to be, but still at times challenging. I can't say everyone will love it, but if you have game pass it's definitely worth checking out.5 Randy The Rads out of 7

_childDocuments_.review: The way the developer has integrated leveling with trying out new skills to create your own unique class and character is interesting and reminds me of older 'combo' games, but for the casual, dungeon crawling gamer. It can be frustrating, no doubt, to have to perform actions your character was not designed to do, to have to do them in order to advance and unlock other classes, etc., but it is always a doable challenge and that makes it fun for us.We play co-op 100% of the time and it has been largely great, with few connectivity errors on a 150d/20u connection and only a couple of crashes the developers were genuinely interested in reproducing. Otherwise, almost no 'bugs' in the game that a user wouldn't think was intentional. The challenges are still significant despite two-manning it, there are secrets you can find only with specific classes, and just about everything we've had to do has been interesting. A deeply feature-rich game.We do recommend using your controller, although we did find that with the newer xbox controllers, orientation is upside down if the user tries to use it with BT, so he had to plug in while playing. Mine is a decade older with the ifra dongle and works great. No issues. But it's going to be a lot easier to switch characters, which you will find yourself doing a LOT mid-combat, if you go with a controller.Only complaint is that when you switch characters, you lose less-used characters from the wheel (there are more classes than spots on the wheel) and have to manually fetch them again if you need them. I would prefer manual assignment because it's harder to switch to the right class in a pinch when it has moved positions. But it's such a minor QOL issue for us and might not be a complaint for other people.

_childDocuments_.review: I love shapeshifting in RPGs and this one really delivers on that front. I don't know why it's taken so long for someone to make an SNES style action rpg where you change shape at will. I enjoy the humor as well. It's like if you took "A Link to the Past" and added Earthbound's humor and the ability to turn into several different monsters. Each form has it's own advancement which is tied to various things (which makes it less grindy than if it was just XP based). An example is as the turtle you need to find a pond and swim in it for a bit to level up your turtle form. All in all one of my favorite recent games.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if this game is fun or not. And I'm being honest.I wanted to like the game, it's quite interesting. It opens up once you get to the customize-ability of classes.My biggest gripe with it I think is:The whole basis of the game is just a dopamine injector. How you progress theough the game is basically doing the daily quest for predatory free to play games that want you to log on to drive engagement. They do it because they know it works to make dopamine fire off. And in the same vein, you have to do something suboptimal to complete the quest by playing a class a certain way. This gets tiring with how many classes there are. And doing all of the "dailies" feels so empty. But also I feel like the game is fun but I'm pretty sure I'm just being manipulated. Secondary gripes:It depends on the audience for the game but I don't feel like I am part of the audience fir this game's combat system. I won't say there's no skill involved in the combat but it's far more focused on building something overpowered by gaining levels (by playing a suboptimal class in a suboptimal way for stretches at a time) and then shooting it off for a rest run. Seems more of a power fantasy than anything. I'm not the audience for that but you do you. The issues still exist regardless.The reason why I feel this way is the AWFUL visibility of your character and all of the enemies. It also doesn't help that the "quick swap" for swapping classes in this game is god awful. If you want to swap in the middle of a fight, it's best to pause the game completely and break the flow of combat. Why? Because the quick swap doesn't pause or slow the in-game speed down AND it takes your ability to keep moving. The developers recommend controller but are too stupid to map quick swap to RB + right analog stick (something that serves no purpose) but instead maps it to RB + left analog. That means if you want to quick swap optimally for combat, you should always pause. If you are quick swapping for traversal or not combat portions, you'll most likely be walking and it steals your ability to move. Absolute awful system.Just a nitpick but it drives into the first point of this just being a dopamine injector for dailies. There are repeatable quests just like free to play predatory dailies of "play x matches", "kill x enemies", etc. Which is fine for how they want their game to be but the quests are something you turn in the second you complete it because you won't get carry over progress. I kind of understand that it's weird if someone banks 25x repeatable quest but 1. who cares, 2. honestly not a huge deal. The trade off of doing it their way is that you have to pause the game and turn in the quest if you want to optimize progress. So "kill x enemies" while you're in a fight? Whoop. Better slam on the brakes right there pal. You better claim that quest in the middle of the fight so you can progress it while fighting still.

_childDocuments_.review: In this day and age, few are the games that truly try something perhaps not new but certainly different, and very few of those that do try manage to actually make it work. Nobody Saves The World is one such example, and its a damn good one.Zelda meets Diablo, but instead of gear and numbers you have forms (classes essentially) with unique abilities and passives that can be changed at anytime. That on its own wouldn't make this game stand out at all, however, the developer have introduced one deceptively simple mechanic: you can mix and match any ability or passive with any form/class in the game. This opens the door to a myriad of different playstyles and fantasies to play out.Want a Zombie monk that can call holy lightning while also lunching guided missiles? sure thingWhat about a fire breathing Slug that can pull an army of bunnies to fight for it and heal itself for its damage? why notThis is a clever and fun game, that offers complexity without ever being overwhelming nor an impossibly long grind to even began the "build crafting". At about 20 hours at its base game, Nobody Saves The World is worth every penny and gets my wholehearted recommendation to any that have even passing interest on it. Don't miss it!

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is simply loads of fun. I loved the fact that the game offers lots of "forms", which actually are classes that can be switched on the fly. Each class offers lots of build possibilities, which can also be changed on the fly.In fact, the game constantly floods the player with quests (which are more like achievements) for each form until said form is levelled up to the max. These quests entice the player to constantly experiment with the different forms and builds.As a result, the gameplay gets refreshed a lot and never gets boring.The game looks like a Sunday morning cartoon and reminded me of the Cartoon Network shows I watched as a kid. The soundtrack is fun and easily gets stuck in your head.The story in itself is pretty straightforward and nothing deep, but the humour is done very well. Which keeps it light-hearted and makes for fun situations and dialogues.Most of the characters are simply there to give out quests. There's a few which stand out and offer a little bit of story, but don't expect any character development or anything like that.The same goes for the world, the dungeons and the enemies, they're mostly the same throughout the whole game with different skins (often they're even the same asset in a different colour).All in all, an ARPG that focusses mostly on fun and not on complex systems.8/10
