_childDocuments_.review: A hollow shell of a human finds a wand of shapeshifting and begins a quest...It's hard to describe Nobody Saves the World without describing its components. The structure is a bit like your 2D overhead ARPGS and Zelda, but quite light on story. Explore the world, find dungeons, take on NPCs' requests, and collect parts of the great Macguffin. The hero can transform from his rather useless base form to animals, human warriors, and monsters. Combat is Gauntlet-style brawling. You have attacks, with each form getting a normal attack that generates MP and special attacks that consume it, as well as passive abilities. Some have cooldowns or cause an array of status effects, among other mechanics. Then there are the RPG bits. Nobody resembles some of the classic Final Fantasy Job systems in this regard. To power them up, you complete goals involving using certain attacks or combinations effectively against enemies. This unlocks more of their attacks as well as new forms via a skill tree. Those attacks and passives? You can combine them. Forms have a few set qualities, like standard attack, stats, and one passive ability that they always have equipped, but they can equip passives and attacks to their remaining slots however they want to create powerful combos or meet the demands of a particular situation. So those are the components. This game can be very hard to put down if it clicks for you. It's not all that long or difficult, though, so you may fly through it. There is a New Game Plus but despite throwing some interesting twists at the player, it probably won't take as long as the first run. I still recommend it to anyone who likes Drinkbox' other work, ARPG brawling or build customization.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a good game, and i find it difficult to put it down.  Its not over difficult, and its not super easy. You can die easily if you stand in one spot and spam attack, but its fair enough where enemies dont kill you if they sneeze on you. Multiple dungeons, huge map, awesome forms, all with different skills, that later can be shared between forms. Multiple damage types, used for enemy weakness, to break through elemental shields for certain enemies, and cool boss fights. Ive found a few towns, and some dungeons im not even close to level wise yet, which means ill have future things to do, even in low level areas. Dungeons have buffs, and debuffs for you and enemies, all different. Such as, all enemies plus 1.2 health, all healing heals even enemies, and tons more. Buy if you like fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I hope I remember to review after more play time. I played this on Xbox Gamepass and absolutely loved it so much I bought it here on Steam to make sure I had it. It is so goofy, and absolutely does not take itself seriously, which to me is all part of the charm. The characters are small and funny, and the gameplay is rewarding and challenging in its own way. What I mean by this is that you can absolutely hammer your way through with a couple of favorite transformations, but the fun is in developing each of them. Each of the 'Quests' for the transformations is clever and never feels like too much of a grind, and is rewarding when you achieve it. The game also actively encourages mixing things up to the point where the quests encourage you to try combinations you may not have thought of.
_childDocuments_.name: Nobody Saves the World

_childDocuments_.review: Game is very fun to play, It doesn't drag for too long and the system of quests, which had me concerned before the release, actaully turned out to be a decent instrument to engage player (assuming they are going to S rank every form which is the way to play if you ask me) not only to try every form but also check out interesting ability combinations. Rogue-like elements are barely noticeable (there are not that many dungeon to be honest), there are not many assets and some of them are recycled across demi-dungeons which isn't a big deal taking into the account their number. Dungeon modifiers are rather interesting and also try to engage player into exploring different abilities, I would say, try mostly successfully. Game is not challenging most of the times unless you are imposing challenge on yourself. My hardest time was when I was walking through the x9999 dungeon without dmg limiter passive which was actually an interesting experience. Main quest dungeons for some reason block form progressions which I find pointless as it only forces more grind throught regular dungeons and you don't really want to grind in this game due to little to none variety in terms of dungeon generation (if you ran it once, the only difference you will notice would be enemy arrangement and corridors' position). Also shopkeeper doesn't really sell anything interesting -- I suspect if one completely ignores the shop they wouldn't miss much, same goes for many ability upgrades as they are mostly manacost reduction or damage improvement -- both minor. However, what isn't boring is a gameplay core which is about utilizing different forms and abilities. It has enought variety to not grown old within game's length which is the biggest reason why I enjoyed my time with this game quite a lot. NG+ offered dungeons with more interesting modifier combinations (well, some of them were interesting) but at that point of the game it is facerolled with minions+fireball spam in 90% of the cases. In the remainder you have to use default attack of either dragon or robot to ignore everything thrown at you. However, this is something I would expect game to have at a normal game run (I mean, these modifier combinations). Also these modifiers have actually shown me how OP health pick up drops' are. I was getting through with my necro just fine without them, but when I entered a Dungeon where there were no healing reduction nor "no heal pick ups" I was basically immortal with zombie leech+use health istead of mana+fireball spam as long as there was something to hit. Finally I would like to say that this game could really use some "hard/very hard" difficulty setting which would cut player's health (I think you can safely half player's hp without any issue at all) add more deadly modifiers to every dungeon (like x9999 but with egg passive being banned or other modifiers forcing player to not be able to fit egg's passive; or wards regenerate+form locked with several ward types present). Skill ceiling here is definetely not as high as in smth like Doom Eternal, but at first glace there seems to be a big room for players and developers to push the game's challenge

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay. It's a relatively simple gameplay loop that gives the player enough breadcrumbs to carry through to the end. It feels a bit tedious and uninspired towards the end of the first playthrough. The writing is nonsensical random humor with a straight forward narrative towards the end. In short, it's an alright brain-off romp but ends up being pretty forgettable of an experience.This game starts off a bit slow and fails to take off. It feels like a bunch of check boxes from start to finish stretching a simple gameplay loop just a bit too far. There's fun there but it only applies to about 3-4 dungeons. I did not count the NG+ stuff because if it takes an entire playthrough before a game gets interesting, there's a problem.That said, it's not all bad. There's a lot of really good stuff like the overworld map design is filled with nooks and crannies, collectables which all go towards improving your character, and silly little side quests that have a lot of humor of the 'that was random' type. Depending on your funny bone, it can come across as charming or overplayed. The art style is great and fits the writing, world, and whimsical twisted nature of the game. It's the best part by far.The main carrot-and-stick of the game is hitting big 'story' dungeons, completing it with what you have, and unlocking more forms (classes) to add more possible tools to your belt for the next big story dungeon. The game does a great job of giving the player the freedom to be a minimalist and unlock just enough to beat the next story gate dungeon or grind for more tools up to a certain point. Form progression is locked behind those gates forcing the player to move on before more forms can be unlocked and more things can be grinded.This loop is split in two major parts where the later forms effectively gets ungated all at once along with a portion of the map. While this isn't necessarily a bad thing, the way to unlock these forms and their skills is very tedious and monotonous. It all boils down to:-'Use X skill Y number of times.'-'Trigger X status effect'-'Hit X number of enemies with Y skill'-'Use X status to break enemy shields'There's some slight remixes of the above like 'Use X skill to trigger Y status on enemies' or something to that effect. This is the same across all the forms and personally, I ended up just grinding it out in 2 dungeons in order to unlock the fun combinations.This is not a knock per se but to illustrate a point of design in this game. If the player min maxes or likes to be as strong as possible before moving on, it gets monotonous fast and it trivializes the dungeons. However, if the player goes through the game more organically and jump around different forms trying to complete the dungeons and objectives on after another, it's rather fun and the way I'd assume it was meant to be experienced. What's great about this design is it's up to the player how challenging things are. The flaw in the design is, for those who wish to complete as much as they can before moving onto the next story beat, they can easily trivialized the entire game and end up with a disappointing experience.The dungeon design starts off strong and ends up being rather samey. Modifiers like 'everything does 9999' or 'no mana regen on normal hits, status breaks grant X mana' mixes things up enough to custom tailor a build for. But those are few and far in between on the first playthrough. NG+ changes things up a bit with more modifiers but by then, I was already tired of the loop.The game manages to drip feed the fun parts of the game but not have enough substance to drip feed. So by the end, there's a feeling of emptiness. 'I really just went through all that and this is it?'At the end of the ramble, I managed to waste 30+ hrs doing silly tasks and unlocking/completing things. But at the end of it, the experience felt a bit hollow and as soon as I closed the game, memories of the game had already started leaking out of my coconut. It's sadly a bit of a forgettable romp of a game that never really manage to create a really memorable moment in the entire run. It's junk food for the gamer.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets a solid 4.5/5 and I'm confident in that having only spent 1.5 hours in-game. (the only negative thing I have to say about it is that the keyboard controls are a bit clunky and have a little bit of a learning curve.  I discovered this little gem after going on a action RPG, hack-n-slash tear with Grim Dawn and Diablo 2R.  (if you haven't played Grim Dawn, do yourself a favor and check it out.  Like this game, it's just so so good.)  This game takes a unique approach to the hack-n-slash genre by removing loot.  That's right, the floor isn't littered with items like usual, which was almost a deal breaker for me.  But once I started playing, I realized the class/ability tree made up for it. Instead of loot there are 10+ different classes, with all different abilities, that you can switch between.  Some classes give unique perks, e.g., the rat lets you fit through narrow passages. And you can level up each class, level up each ability, level up your main toon.  It's got a great skill tree/system that is just the right amount of complexAs for the graphics and sound, they are classic indie and well done.  The game has just the right amount of challenge.  I'm sure it's going to get more complex and difficult as I progress, but like most other ARPGs, the fun is in blowing up/smashing large groups of monsters, and there's plenty of that The only complaint I have is that the controls are a little clunky on a keyboard, which is probably why the game recommends a controller when you first load it.  I had to rebind W-A-S-D to move and up/down/left/right to use abilities as the default had them reversed.  Once running around, I got the hang of it in about 45 minutes.  Aside from that, this is cartooney hack-n-slash mayhem that was 100% worth the price of admission.  If you've gotten this far reading reviews, do yourself a favor and pull the trigger, you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Saves the World is an action RPG where you play "Nobody" who acquires the ability to change into different characters ("forms") at will. Nice cartoon-like graphics and a humorous story with good controls (I used an x-box controller). I still have a lot of game to go having unlocked less than half the characters, but the game play so far is great. There are dungeons/quests and map locations that seem impossible until you unlock a new form that gives you the ability you need. Part of the fun of the game for me is figuring out the the best form/loadout combo for a given fight or map location. Some battles require you to switch form mid-fight. NOTE: the tutorial trains you to hold LB and scroll through a wheel of forms which is super clunky and unnecessary. You can just pause the game with LT or the pause button to calmly switch your form and its load out before returning the battle. There is no button to quickly switch between two "favorite" forms, but I didn't need that once I understood that I could switch forms mid-battle by pausing.

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: A fun, charming, and addictive action RPG with unique mechanics.  Play as a form-changing nobody, complete, a lot of quests, and save the world.  Clever, colorful, and with a lot to do, it's a must-recommend for fans of "Smart" Action RPGS.Nobody Saves the world starts with you, awaking in a dank hut.  You have no memories, no pants, and no idea what to do.  When an accident grants you a magic wand that lets you shapeshift, you set out across the land to beat monsters, recover gems, and try to find out who you are.  The core of the game is your shapeshifting ability and leveling it up.  Your forms have different powers, and as you level up forms, new ones unlock.  These forms bring you quests to use your powers in various ways, unlocking new levels and of course, new forms.  Soon you can combine abilities - you can be a strongman that raises the dead, an arrow-shooting turtle, a knight that summons animals with a magic hat, and more - much, much more.You'll need these abilities as the wacky, colorful world is in danger.  You'll travel across a gigantic map, take quests, delve into dungeons, and try to figure out just what is going on with the mysterious Calamity.Combat is a major part of the game.  Initially simple, your different abilities and forms become necessary to deal with different monsters and environments.  Some monsters shield others, others have magical wards only broken by certain damage, dungeons have differene effects.  It takes awhile for these challenges to open up, but when they do you'll find yourself strategizing and thinking to complete your quests.Quest you will, as the reward loop is all about meeting challenges.  Complete regular and level up.  Get a new form or level one up and there are new challenges using the form's abilities OR combining them with others.  There's always something to do, something to discover, or a new way to use an ability.  This leads to a tight, compelling gameplay experience.You'll also get money and upgrade coins on your journey to purchase advances and upgrade abilities.  These give you new options and let you overcome challenges.However, the game has some "gateways" to the grind and some difficulties scale.  There's always going to be thought required.The game is not only fun, it's also gorgeous and funny.  Little humorous details about in the world.  Characters are weird and wacky.  Quests may not be what they seem.  Parody abounds.  Throw in the soundtrack and the game drips with atmosphere.Despite so many good things there are a few flaws:* The initial start is slow.  It takes a little time to get everything to open up.* Combat is a mix of frantic and thoughtful, and the at-times wonky aiming and frenetic mobs aren't always your friend.* The "quick shapeshift" control is near-useless as it's real time - but you can go to the menu and shapeshift just as easy without getting mobbed.Flaws aside?  The game is a blast and clearly made by people who get FUN.So who's it for?* If you want a colorful, smart action RPG - and love tight reward loops - you'll almost certainly like this game.  There's a lot to do, a lot of buttons to mash, and a lot of thought to put into it.  * It's a perfect gift for the same kind of person.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute must grab. I'm sure with other titans of the industry coming out later this year this game will inevitably be drifted under the carpets, but believe me when I say it is genuinely a contender for game of the year already. It's got a unique handcrafted world, hilarious dialogue, an in-depth skill tree, upgrades and levelling system all topped off with a ridiculously fast paced and engaging gameplay loop. I can think of one single thing wrong with this game, but even they don't subtract, they just don't let it achieve a full 10/10 mark. Firstly the voice acting, or lack there of. Now I don't mind no voices in games, but the amount of wacky "WAHs" or "Hmmphs!" is just too little as well. The only character (so far) that bleeds life to me is Randy, who's always making weird and interesting noises. I think a sardonic narrator for nobody or even just more stock standard grunting sounds could have livened up the dead noise whenever you talk to a character.All in all a solid 9/10. Truly a labour of long, with a long, fun gameplay loop that I'm sure will keep me enticed for 10's of hours more.

_childDocuments_.review: A hack-and-slash action RPG whose core gameplay loop is propped up by a unique transformation mechanic, yet at the same time bogged down by its implementation in some regards. The transformations themselves offer a wide diversity of playstyles and a ton of customization potential; but overall progression requires more grinding than some players might be comfortable with, and it's in serious need of some QoL improvements that have yet to be implemented despite over a year of fan outcry. Despite its flaws, the base game offered a fun enough singleplayer experience that I don't want to give it a thumbs down--but don't bother with the subpar co-op implementation, and maybe skip out on the DLC.  is an action RPG about a featureless being referred to as "Nobody", who suddenly wakes up without their memories in a world being overrun by the all-consuming Calamity. After stumbling upon a powerful magic wand that grants Nobody the ability to transform into different beings, they set out to stop the Calamity and uncover the truth of who they are and where they came from. Beyond the traditional adventure game exploration and hack-and-slash combat, the main gameplay gimmick that drives the whole experience comes in the form of...well, Forms. You have the ability to alter your physical appearance into that of another being--Rat, Ranger, Ghost, Magician, etc.--providing you with different stats, active abilities, and passive buffs to go along with it. Each one has their own quests that require you to use their abilities in various scenarios (e.g. hit 50 baddies with X attack), and completing enough of these will increase that Form's rank (from F up to S) and eventually provide access to more abilities and more Forms. Later on, you can mix-and-match active and passive abilities from other Forms, opening up a ton of new combinations to make yourself even stronger.This mechanic is the source of both the game's biggest strengths and weaknesses; and although I do like the overall idea, the execution is not without flaws.  even before you unlock the feature to mix-and-match abilities between them. Once you do unlock that, though, things get way more interesting: you'll find new active/passive synergies that can turn average Forms good and good Forms great; and if a Form has a major weakness somewhere (e.g. bad multi-target damage), chances are another Form's ability can help balance them out. It's at this point that , whether you're actively using them for their stats and signature moves or using their unlocked abilities to augment other Forms.Playing with new Forms and abilities is a lot of fun, but actually unlocking them is another story. , whether it's to increase Form ranks, increase character level (a separate XP bar that affects base stats across Forms), or collect Stars (a currency for opening story-required dungeons). Most grinding is for the sake of Form quests, which offers all three rewards; and these are often repetitive (e.g. hit baddies 200 times with X move) and can have requirements that are hard to come by naturally (e.g. hit 5+ baddies at once with X move). You have two options: spend your playthrough constantly overthinking about the Forms you use at every turn to ensure you're not squandering a chance to work on the more tedious quests, or spend what will amount to several hours of time monotonously farming a spot in the overworld so you can get those quests out of the way and play the actual game with one less worry. Many quests are also progression-gated so they don't appear until you've reached a specific point in the story, which is understandable from a design perspective, but can be annoying as some of these later quests ask you to do things you were already doing previously for no reward.While we're still on the subject of Forms, there's a particularly frustrating part to using them that, for some reason, has still gone unaddressed over a year after release: . Unlocking Forms will add them onto the wheel automatically until there are no slots left, and manually selecting one not on the wheel via the character menu will cause it to replace a random one currently on the wheel. Why you can't just customize this manually is beyond me, but it makes this very important feature a hassle to use since you can never memorize a menu that's frequently changing on you. This was a constant source of annoyance during my playthrough; and if there's a single thing I wish the game would get in the future, it would be the ability to let the player set the wheel themselves and lock it from automatic change.I also want to quickly mention a couple minor gripes I had that don't have much bearing on a singleplayer base game playthrough, but should be noted in case you're looking for more than that:; only electing to pass on the New Game Plus run that would've gotten me my last Steam achievement. I had enough fun with it that I don't feel comfortable giving it a thumbs down, but I really can't fault the other reviews that did, because the highs when playing don't always balance out the lows.

_childDocuments_.review: Really nice game. It is not that hard and it gives some ways to customize your player character using different forms. For example, you use slide skill to slow down enemies, throw poison lobs at them with a slime and you unlock beatiful mermaid who can travel through water and gives you new exploration abilities.Later some enemies have elemental shields that block all damage to them until you hit them with that element (just 4 elements) and you can quickly switch to another form and hit them to remove the shield or you can customize your form to have some abilities from another form (unlocked a little later in the story).Going through the form tree and unlocking all different forms and then trying to use them to complete the same dungeon is enjoyable.There is level scaling in the game which is there as usualy to keep all enemies and locations relevant. But there is also a shop that sells permanent stat boosts which are applied to all forms at once (but at different values) so you can overboost yourself over that scaling.Some (maybe most) dungeons are randomized but the global map is handcrafted. _childDocuments_.review: Loved this game, with some caveats.First, the good. The game knows what it wants to be: a grindy statsy zeldalike. Everything else is pushed to the back seat, which mostly works out for the better. The art direction (super meat boy meets zelda) is pitch perfect for the kind of story being told: funny, irreverent, doesn't take itself too seriously, but has the necessary amount of "feels" when it needs to.Now for the bad. My biggest complaint is that there is too little "friction". NStW has no inventory at all, which prevents it from having any kind of give/show mechanic. Instead of this, all quests are marked with an exclamation-point objective on the map. You're so handheld through fulfilling your quest objectives, you don't even need to pay attention to dialogue, characters, or landmarks. you simply go where the exclamation points are. This took me out of the world considerably. i think i would have been much more immersed in the game if i was forced to do a little more work. In other words, a little bit of friction can be a good thing, if it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Saves The World is instantly fun, but it doesn’t take long to get repetitive. It's a well polished, but shallow game. It feels like a step down for the studio that made Guacamelee!.The different areas of the map are weirdly random. There's a whale dungeon, an alien spacecraft, a nuclear power plant, a tree, and an odd blob monstrosity. The dungeon interiors are pretty samey, though, essentially reskins of the same basic components. For some reason they rearrange themselves like a rogue-like every time you enter. The randomization seems unnecessary, since you rarely visit a particular dungeon more than once. The dungeons get fairly tedious after a while, especially with enemy wards, and even moreso when they regenerate.Having different forms is a pretty cool idea, but there's no rhyme or reason to what forms you get. There’s no story reason for why you can turn into a magician or a zombie or a mermaid, you just unlock new forms as you level up the ones that came before. Because the game lets you mix and match abilities from different forms, each form ends up feeling pretty much the same by the end of the game. You will likely land on a handful of skills that you equip on every form.The level up mechanic is novel, and pretty fun at first, but like the other mechanics, it quickly gets tedious. Every couple of minutes you level up one of your quests and need to pause to accept it. This gets even more annoying late in the game when you're at the level cap and you don't get anything from accepting the fulfilled quest.There is a lot of originality here in the art, but not much cohesion. The character design is really fun and unique, but it's all undermined by the snarky dialog and rote humor.Finally, I kept running into this really annoying bug. I would occasionally start playing the game and find myself for some reason controlling two characters with one controller. I'd need to futz around with the controller setup and restart the game to get back to a single character.

_childDocuments_.review: The densest game I have ever played. Every singular component is simple enough, but so many things are interacting with each other against enemies that don't give you time to breath that it's exactly as complex as it has to be.I caught onto the bait and switch, but I can see others getting tripped by it. Have fun with the story.On the one hand, it's a perfected game. On the other hand, there's not much room to do more with it without completely starting over with the skills and passives system. On the other, OTHER hand, that's probably a good thing so that the game doesn't grow wildly out of scope like a malformed fungus, if you know what I mean.

There's only like 3 music tracks so music gets boring. The different forms aren't too crazy different from each other and there isn't much incentive to play as a different form unless you want to grind for new transformations. The story is as simple as it gets and most side quests are "go to this location" or "defeat enemies" with small tweaks or variations. The game honestly feels like a cookie-cutter top-down adventure game with leveling systems put in place just to keep you playing and is filled with unmemorable characters.Only recommend the game if it is on sale and you like to grind.

While trying to outsmart the game I decided to avoid one of the main story dungeons to complete some other side quests and mini dungeons to level up some more. When I returned back to that main story dungeon I realized the dungeon leveled along side me and I did nothing but make it harder for myself. I really don't understand the point of having levels if the thing I was trying to out level will always match or be slightly harder then the level I obtain. YMMV, so give it a shot, but be warned.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun top-down RPG which not only had a substantial amount of things to do and places to explore but also allowed for full player customizability of characters, allowing you to turn the slowest tanks into speed machines or magic boys into brawlers, but the levelling and balance was pretty fun across the game, this game made me want to explore and rewarded me for putting in the time to excel and rank up characters to make the best builds and have fun doing it.The game is lack lustre in some areas, grinding all characters to S is very tedious and many of the high end dungeons only allowed for full self healing builds, meaning I ran the same set up multiple times, even the specific damage wards weren't enough because I could easily equip all 4 damage types by the end. Some of the Final bosses were really easy and there isn't much end game stuff to do, mainly just NG+. This game deserves to get some add-ons later on, it is well made and has a lot to it, a few endgame or bonus areas could be added with some ultra difficulty conditions to really make you work, a bonus story such as the guilds could also be added, but a branching class tree I think is the most important, the mid game point I had unlocked or discovered all options, maybe alternate paths could be added to change the types of finishing classes you could have access to, i think 6 more classes would have rounded out the number more evenlyStill great game and I'm definitely gonna have some more fun with it

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the idea of this game. I saw it was kind of like an old school Zelda style game, there were multiple different characters you can switch to, the art style was nice, the music was fun, the humor was good, it all looks fun on paper. However, playing it is just OK at best. The visuals leave a lot to be desired in practice. Looking at screenshots and trailers, it looks very appealing. However, when playing, you realize some of the poor choices that get old fast. There's often so much going on screen that you can't even tell where your character is exactly. You don't know if you're getting hit or not because there's so many numbers and effects, enemies will stack on top of each other and obscure your player character. You can face one of four directions only and the direction you're facing is the one you're attacking in. If you move diagonally, it's pretty much a 50/50 in which direction you'll actually attack so you have to look at your character. However, with so much chaos on the screen, you can't even see which direction your character is facing, leading to attacks not going where you want them to go. You can hold RT to remain facing a direction but it honestly just feels so unnatural I found myself either forgetting to do it, or constantly letting go and pressing it again to try to change directions, that is, when I get the direction I want. Obviously going diagonally somewhere doesn't always turn me where I want to be looking.The game play loop is also such a grind. You unlock new forms by leveling up particular forms. As an example, the first form is a rat. You have to level up the rat to unlock a knight and a ranger. Then you have to level up the ranger to unlock a new form. You have to level up the knight to unlock a completely different form. The game is constantly forcing you to play new characters to progress and unlock other characters. The issue I have with this is that we all like to experiment in games like this. However, you'll end up finding characters you don't like but you'll feel forced to play them to progress to a new character. In other games, you find a character you don't like, just skip it and play something else. Not in this game though, deal with the chore of playing something you don't like just for the sake of progressing. Furthermore, the goals to level up characters later will change your play style and maybe you liked the original play style of that character and then you grow to hate it as you try to level up with a different play style that you don't enjoy. In theory, you could get a character you don't like that will change the play style to a style you enjoy as well but at that point, I just felt so jaded having to play a character I hate that it doesn't make it enjoyable.The idea to the game is really fun. I don't necessarily think this is a bad game but it's not a particularly good game either. I played it in co-op with a friend and after 3.5 hours we both had a "meh" feeling about it. If I played this solo, I'm honestly not sure if I would have gotten past an hour. Unfortunately, it's just not that fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I love the art style and the idea of switching characters is interesting, but the gameplay is just god awful.Controlling your character is bad - you can only move in the 8 cardinal + diagonal directions, even though the game insists that you play with a gamepad (which I did). No idea why they restrict movement this way, it's inexcusable, really.Because of the poor controls, combat is awkward and unnecessarily hard, so the game compensates by showering you in health. Fair enough. The problem is when you're presented with any kind of challenge, it becomes almost impossible to make progress and you're fighting the controls the whole time.Other examples. Navigation is already frustrating, but then again any small obstacle (or enemy) will stop you completely on your tracks. You have to pull back and go around, no sliding or avoiding possible. If you open the menu you can switch forms while the game is paused (after pressing like a million buttons) but when you use the quick access the game doesn't pause. Why? I've no idea, it makes no sense - why make the worst option the most effective?At one point the game leads you to a spot and there is this big challenge, all told within the story of the game. Then by the point you're about to start it, you're told "You have to pay the entry fee" and the game takes you to Steam to buy a DLC. I don't appreciate being misled like that.After like two hours of wandering around without knowing what to do, failing every single one of the challenges I encountered multiple times because of the obtuse controls and reading flat jokes I just gave up.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Saves the World is to SNES Zelda as Guacamelee is to SNES Metroid. This twist is that instead of swapping gear between arrows, bombs, etc, you swap entire characters, who can then be customized further to replace skills and add new passive bonuses. Gameplay balances between microquests for all of the various transformations that require customizing and combining abilities between them, and running dungeons with special properties and enemy bonuses which require certain skills to break wards, survive relentless damage, or avoid healing the baddies. Combat has a nice one-two punch rhythm, where you debuff the enemy or buff yourself, then go for the kill, and there's a lot of good variety in how that plays out.Some transformations are weak on their own but have great passives to give to others (bodybuilder), so you run their quests to level the passive, then put it on a hero who can put their unique skill to better use (zombie). Some transformations are great with nasty penalties (slow slug), so you get passives that fix their issues (speed boost). Juggling the needs of fulfiling the transformation quests, the enemies and special conditions of the current dungeon, and routinely swapping between transformations to get new quests that progress the overall character keep things varied.Credit to Skill Up for causing me to give this game another look.

_childDocuments_.review: The time wasting, jumping through hoops quest design that never ends really sucks the fun out of this game. You don't earn exp to level up your forms, like in a normal RPG, you have to do things with the class in specific ways, or combine the classes with abilities from other classes in specific ways, otherwise you're not actually earning EXP for the class and you're essentially wasting time instead of progressing. I don't know about other people but this really does nothing but active my Min/Max brain to the point where I just thought about doing the stupid combinations so I could level up more rather than actually combining the classes or playing the classes that I wanted, I was instead obsessed with just playing the game the way the game told me to because that's the only way the game rewards me for doing anything. These aren't like quick and easy challenges, they're very grindy and annoying like "kill 200 enemies while they have this status effect from another class, with this type of damage with this move." I could see if they were like quick little things that are more so about understanding your classes and figuring how how to effectively expand your arsenal, but they're not it's really about having the patience to; once you figure that out, play like that for hours even if you don't enjoy it or find it fun, or if it takes away from the way you want to play the class.

_childDocuments_.review: From the same studio that brought you Guacamelee! comes a bit of a unique one. It’s a top-down action RPG hack and slash adventure with a very cool form-swapping mechanic.So an immediate comparison I would make here is to that of Shantae. The core mechanic in Nobody Saves the World is that you’re able to freely swap between different “forms”. There are over 15 of these different forms and they each have a full slate of unique abilities to use in combat on top of their base traits like some being able to travel in water and some being able to go through tight spaces.It’s a very cool mechanic and is made only better by the sheer variety and detail behind it all. Some forms are faster, some forms are tankier, some are ranged, some are melee, some are a mix of both - there are plenty to choose from and they fit all sorts of play styles.That’s not all though, because shortly into the experience you’re granted the ability to customize each form further by equipping abilities from any of the other forms. You can get stuff like a horse with the poison traits of the rat or a ghost with the water spray ability of the turtle. Because each form levels up individually, you’re encouraged to hop around and not stick with just one form, but at the same time, this customization allows you to take some of your favorite abilities from one form and apply them to another - a very cool combo.The combat was already fun enough on its own with most of the base forms, but the addition of ability swapping really elevates it and especially so later on once you have most of the abilities unlocked and come up with some crazy synergies. And it’s not just the combat  - the quests and puzzles build off of this mechanic too. One quest, for example, has you destroy a bunch of targets using specific damage types in a limited amount of time and you’ll need to come up with some sort of form combo with just the right abilities to complete that task in time.The maps are a good mix of environments with cool designs, cool characters to meet, and fun quests to complete. Unlocking more forms gradually opens up more of the map, so exploration is encouraged too. And of course, the map greatly benefits from the game’s colorful art style. Great coloring, plenty of world detailing - it’s just an all-around good looking game and with some nice music to match too.My main complaints are mostly with the quality of life side of things. For example, the “quick select” wheel that allows you to change between forms is a bit finicky once you have enough forms to fill it up. In the event that you want to swap to a form that is not on the wheel, you have to pause the game, pull up the form menu, select that form, and hope that it does not replace another form that you also would like to swap to. I don’t know if my friend and I were missing something, but it seemed that the form would be put on the quick select wheel randomly, so it became a bit of a pain once we had to juggle all of these forms.I also wasn’t the biggest fan of how quests are tracked and submitted. To do so, you have to pull up a menu manually and submit them before progress can be made on the next part of that quest. This is a bit of an annoyance because sometimes you’ll complete one in the middle of combat and have to pause right then to submit it or waste the next several kills not getting tracked towards your next quest.I did run into a few issues with the multiplayer. Whether that be the occasional lag spike that lasts a while or the random disconnect forcing me back to the main menu - both were annoying. The latter could easily be solved by keeping at least one player in the game instead of booting both, but as it stands that is not the case.Otherwise, the game plays fine. I ran it at 1440p and 120 fps without any performance issues. The game lacks mouse controls but does have rebindable keyboard controls. They are a bit obtuse, but at least doable if you do not have a controller on hand.I went into Nobody Saves the World thinking - okay, basically top-down Shantae, but it’s a lot more than just that. Fun combat with plenty of depth, quests that actually do something unique and don’t just have you running to and from, solid music and colorful art with plenty of detail - it’s got a lot going for it in spite of some technical and design flaws. It’s fun enough as a singleplayer title, but an absolutely easy recommendation if you have a friend to do online co-op with.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Nice, simple, fun game. I wasn't as enthralled or sucked into the game's universe and story as I was the developer's previous game, Guacamelee. (Still haven't played the sequel to that either) BUT, I had a fun time with this game, anyway.It's fun unlocking different forms and trying them out. You can mix and match other forms' moves with your current form as well, allowing for a bit of strategy in an otherwise pretty mindless dungeon crawler. I say 'mindless' with respect in this regard, as dungeon crawlers, in my opinion, are at their best when you can zone out and basically autopilot through your strategies while cutting down hoards of enemies and collecting that sweet loot. That being said, this game doesn't have loot. Again, more mindless engagement. You spend no time picking up items and comparing them a la a traditional dungeon crawler, as it simply doesn't happen. No need to halt the action for a bit of item management. Monsters drop currency or health items, and sometimes drop upgrade tokens for you to upgrade your various forms' abilities. It has a top-down view/approach, and combined with that the gameplay is not unlike the original Legend of Zelda, wherein you can wander through the map, in and out of townships, and fight enemies along the way. Also, there are dungeons where you'll be doing most of your slaying in an attempt to collect stars, which are this game's story keys, essentially. Can't get to other parts of the story without these stars, you gotta go grind and get 'em.  There's nothing wrong with this feature or premise, it's just nothing new or unexpected. You can play co-op too with one other person, which is a feature I have not tried yet. I do not know how this performs, but it is an available option if you don't feel like crawling alone. The game recommends you play with a controller as well, and I agree with that. Playing on the keyboard felt a little odd, but it works perfectly fine. Just feels nicer to play a relaxed dungeon crawler like this with a controller on a TV or monitor. You don't need a keyboard or hotkeys, given how simple and straightforward this game's design is. I think that's where this game shines its brightest - in its simplicity. It's easy to pick up and play without much practice, and it's fun and ultimately challenging by the game's halfway point until its conclusion. Given its simplicity, though, it does leave room for some desires. Particularly strategy. You can beat enemies at higher levels than you, but a lot of it boils down to the tried-and-true method of dungeon crawling or looter shooters: THE GRIND. You gotta grind just a bit to get experience and keep leveling yourself up so you can advance. Sometimes the actual grind feels like its namesake - a grinding experience - but for the most part it isn't anywhere near as excruciating as other games (particularly MMORPGs or other online grinds, which this is not, of course). Plus, you have the option of playing with a friend to keep any "grindy" elements from feeling stale. I'd say, out of my 20+ spent in the game, maybe 1 of those hours felt grindy to me. Who knows. I could have just been in a sour mood at that time of gameplay, though, but I wanted to include the sentiment anyway in an attempt at transparency/honesty/whatever. As for strategy, I found myself wishing there was a little more, but that doesn't mean the game is COMPLETELY lacking. As I mentioned earlier, you can mix and match various abilities from the forms you unlock, which adds a necessary layer of strategy and variety in the gameplay.  Ugh, I'm getting tired of typing now, so I'll just summarize. Sat down to leave a 'like' and a short review, and this turned into a freaking essay. Guess I got carried away. TL;DR - Fun simple game that is worth your time; lacks some (but not all) of the "grindier" elements of dungeon crawlers in favor of simple jump-in-and-play mecahnics, which works in its favor most of the time. Although I wasn't entirely enthralled, I still enjoyed this game and recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A simplistic and cartoonish hack-n-slash, dungeon-crawler RPG with a heavy emphasis on character choice and build customization. Drinkbox Studios have created a mechanically rich game with just the right amount of simplicity and plenty of humor that kept my brain engaged the whole way through. Accompanied by a fitting fantasy-inspired soundtrack infused with some new-age synth groove.Nobody Saves the World is just a fun game; definitely not difficult, but not mindlessly easy either. It includes plenty of entertaining dialogue that is light-hearted but doesn't pander to children and a hand-drawn art style that keeps the tone cheery throughout.You start the game as Nobody, a literal blank slate of a human, waking to the apocalypse on your doorstep and an amnesiac mindset. After a brief intro, you are set loose to explore the world and find the one person capable of crushing this calamity: Nostramagus! You progress through the story by finding shards of a powerful gem. Which are located in various legendary dungeons around the map that are only unlocked using 'stars' acquired from finishing quests and demi-dungeons. Steadily gaining more forms and the power needed to help stop the destruction of your homeland.The biggest draw of this game is the large cast of unlockable characters you can switch between. There are eighteen in total, and all but two are a joy to play with; I was genuinely surprised by how engaging and fun each form was. You can play as a teeny rat with a poisonous bite, a quick bow-wielding ranger, a barbell-chucking bodybuilder, or even a familiar-spawning magician, to name a few. Each form has two signature abilities that bring something unique to the roster and three extra slots for both actives and passives, which you can fill with the abilities of any character you've unlocked. As you play with each form and finish their specific quests, you rank them up (from F to S), granting more skills to share amongst the cast and allowing you to upgrade their respective moves with orbs. So, you can end up with a zombie who releases a barrage of arrows, a turtle capable of stomping entire groups at once, or a horse who can pull rabbits out of its...mouth?!Mixed within these ridiculous combinations of abilities are four damage types and a handful of status afflictions to inflict on your foes. The latter includes things like, slow, stun, and fire; their uses are self-evident. While the sharp, blunt, dark, and light damage types are used to break the wards of enemies, which will negate all damage until destroyed. With all these choices, you (mostly) have the liberty to tackle challenges and your progression however you see fit.Unfortunately, there is one limiting factor: the form-specific quests are the most efficient way to gain stars to open the legendary dungeons. Consequently, most of your playthrough will likely be focused on playing inside these 'quest boundaries,' somewhat hampering the free-form progression the devs were going for. Form quests generally amount to killing things with X character using X move. They aren't all quite as bland as that though, and there is a lot to do, so you still have a good amount of freedom; moreover, they are all fairly easy to complete, and you can farm dungeons as much as you like to finish them quickly and get back to your favorite build.There are quite a few distractions that will beckon you off the beaten path as you journey to the center of the calamity: side quests, chests, silly dialogue snippets, and specially modified demi-dungeons. There is a good amount of extra stuff to do. Not to beat a dead horse here, but it's a relatively simple recipe with a tablespoon of humor and a dash of challenge thrown in for good measure. The quests range from escort missions to fighting around a single destructible item to translating the words of an expletive-spewing dolphin. Likewise, there is an abundance of dungeons to crawl, some of which have modifiers that will significantly alter your method of approach. These modifiers may seem daunting at first glance, but there is always a clear way to mitigate the extra adversity: you just gotta use your noggin a bit(or come back later) and remember that, unless stated otherwise, they affect both you and the enemies. Modifiers like increased melee/ranged damage, form lock, or regenerating wards are easy to deal with but must be taken into account to succeed. While, the more creative ones definitely made me think twice about my approach, things like: signature hits don't restore mana, no health pick-ups, rocket retaliation, and exploding corpses. I was happy to find that many quest and dungeon challenges could be overcome with keen use of your forms and abilities, encouraging creative build design.Nobody Saves the World took me twenty-five hours to complete, having scoured the map for collectibles and finished every side-quest and dungeon. But by the end, I had not completed the form progression for all my characters, and honestly, still wanted to play. So, I went straight into new game plus and had another ten hours of fun before the second rolling of the credits. The main change to this playthough is the story progression: you can now only gain stars by completing dungeons; thus, to open the legendary ones, you must complete every other dungeon on the map. And, every one now has multiple modifiers. I will say though, that I avoided doing anything except the dungeons; the rest of the game (story, side-quests, exploration) held no interest for me the second time around.Why do you play games? A question I often ponder. I don't feel right giving any kind of number rating or 'buy or don't buy' opinions. This is a game that is just fun. It isn't complicated and doesn't require much skill to finish; there is some funny dialogue and silly characters, and there is a great art style and soundtrack. If you've read the review and feel that you understand what the gameplay loop is like, then you should be able to form an opinion on your own, and hopefully, you'll know whether this game is for you. I will say though, that anyone looking for a game to play with a child, look no further. You've found an excellent all-ages adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine an RPG with 15 different characters (classes), each with a unique play style, attacks and perks. But instead of having to start a new run with each character, you unlock other characters by doing quests and leveling up. Once unlocked, you can switch to a certain character at any moment, depending on the situation and your favorite playstyle. When a certain character gets enough experience, you can assign it's attacks and perks to other characters, resulting in one of the most diverse game I've ever played!The game world is very well designed and filled with random generated (but unique) dungeons, challenges and plenty of different enemies and bosses. You'll also encounter a few neutral factions, which you can join for extra quests. It took me more than 30 hours to complete the game, but I enjoyed every minute of it. The game also looks great with it's sharp colorful graphics and the catchy soundtrack is excellent. I can't recommend this game enough!

When I started NG+, it was a requirement to 100% the content again for the NG+ run to count. I was hoping to avoid a lot of the fluff and just get to the main dungeons so I could wrap up the last achievement. But NG+ is intentionally set up to make for a more grooling experience. I recommend the game for the initial play through only.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever wanted to be a disgusting mermaid creature that turned people into zombies? Ever wanted to be a cute turtle that flexed so hard your enemies died? Let me tell you about NobodyNobody Saves The World is an RPG-lite dungeon crawling romp where you can turn off your brain, turn up the transformations, and fight waves of monstrous monsters while clearing dungeons and being a general badass. It honestly feels like you're playing a Saturday Morning Cartoon starring Nobody (that's you) and the many forms you shape shift into. That being said, the story of Nobody is full of tropes and cliches that you'd find in those shows. Typical  save the world (I'll see myself out) plot that we've all seen time and time again. That doesn't mean you wont enjoy Nobody, but just don't go expecting anything more from Nodody's story. The core loop of Nobody is pretty enjoyable! The more you play Nobody (and your various forms), the stronger your character gets. You unlock different forms by playing through the main story and you're rewarded for it. You beat enemies and you're rewarded for it. You clear dungeons and you're rewarded for it. . You can even mix and match abilities from other forms to cause absolute chaos! The scenarios I mentioned earlier? All that and more. Nobody knows how to keep the dopamine flowing.There are a few things to keep in mind when going through Nobody. I don't think the music is awe inspiring... It's just okay. The writing for the dialogue is really just gag humor so if that's not your thing you might find it irritating (there is horse romance and it's completely optional and hilarious). Local coop does not exist so if you want to play with others, you better hope your friends have the game. I had nobody to play with though.Do I recommend it?  Did I use this review to constantly repeat the word "nobody"? Do I regret it?

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome spin on Diablo formula, I did not expect such depth of building your character. The sheer amount of synergies and combinations is staggering. While Nobody Saves the World has no itemization, it uses multiple progression systems for your character and skills to give you that sweet sweet dopamine shot. Its difficult to explain what makes the core gameplay loop so great, there is nothing quite like it and developers did an amazing job designing various form your character can shapeshift into. At the same time your progression through the world is well paced and introduces something new whenever things start to get stale.Artstyle is just as unique as the gameplay and all characters, while not especially deep are quite memorable and have their own funny quirks. I mean just look at the screenshots, its all a mix of bat$hit crazy with cuteness. I love it!Music is very catchy and fits the tone perfectly. There is no voice acting, but it never bothered me. The sounds of various effects and interface are spot on, everything has these satisfying "clicks" and "pops", that hit just right and never get old.Story turned out to be pretty fun, nothing too deep of course, but it has its surprises and very lovable characters. Some quests were quite hilarious and creative. Its definitely worth it to explore every nook and cranny for upgrades and some out of the way quests. I have a fewminor nitpicks. Some quests are extremely challenging, like ranger shooting range, which requires absolute perfect shooting. I also felt that last three forms are unlocked way too late into the game. At that point there was not much left for me to do in this playthrough, so I had to grind some older dungeons to progress these forms, which was a bit tedious. Overall I highly recommend Nobody Saves the World to anyone who enjoys action-RPGs like Diablo and appreciates quirky artstyle and humour. Its progression is one of the best designed ones I experienced recently and it kept me glued to the screen for over 20 hours. There is also New Game Plus and infinite dungeons to clear, so your are getting a lot of game for a bargain. DrinkBox Studios just never misses and you should check out their older games as well, especially Guacamelee duology.
_childDocuments_.name: Nobody Saves the World

_childDocuments_.review: Because of how prominently this game is being featured on Steam right now, I've decided not to recommend this game because of a critical issue. But I will say that I do like the game.I like the open world and trying to find everything. The open world is really fun to traverse and scratches the itch Tunic last scratched. I like the music and some of the games charm (some jokes land, some don't). I like the level up system but sometimes the requirements for quests aren't clear so quest completion is bothersome at times. What I don't like about the game are the dungeons and the slow progression. You can't get the later forms until you get the higher ranks of previous forms, but the quests for those forms unlock after completing enough dungeons. The dungeons are bothersome, monster-filled mazes that cross the line of being too annoying to deal with. Some of them wall the player too much to the point where it's more fun to leave the dungeons alone and keep exploring the main map until you have to deal with the dungeons. I wouldn't complain as much if you could unlock the rest of the game without these dungeons and the greatest parts of this game. I've even come back to the dungeons being 4-5 levels over the requirement and still die in the first 2 minutes. My game actually crashed because of how many armoured enemies there were trying to kill my character after I decided to dodge through the mobs. This isn't fun. This is how you destroy a good game.Ultimately, Nobody Saves the World is a fun game with a critical flaw that makes the game annoying to play and I may not finish it because of this annoyance.

_childDocuments_.review: It's one of those games that's easy to learn and difficult to master. It looks simple, it's easy to get into, and the game loop is rewarding. I'm not a completionist but I got all the characters in this game to their maximum, that's how good the game is. It's not difficult if you don't want it to be, but if you're in for a challenge, you can definitely find it here.Have in mind that graphics are nothing revolutionary, but the gameplay is very satisfying. The story won't knock you out of your socks, but it's present. This game should be played for it's gameplay as it's its strongest value, and boy is it strong.Definitely worth the money even outside of sale.

name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales
detailed_description: Join our Discord About the Game Steal legendary artifacts to regain your freedom Etienne Quist, a once-acclaimed writer, loses his ability to write after he is found guilty of an unspeakable crime. In an attempt to reclaim his lost status, he is approached by a criminal boss with a cunning offer. All he needs to do is locate and steal a series of legendary items from books. Delve into remarkable book worlds, each with its unique rules and challenges. Should anyone stand between you and the artifacts, be prepared to persuade, deceive, or even engage them in combat. Explore different books and reshape their stories Each quest thrusts you into an entirely new world: medieval prison, snow-capped mountain, futuristic spaceship and more. Meet the inhabitants of each book and use them to achieve your goals — after all, they are not really alive... or are they? In your quest, you will not be alone, as your paths cross with a sentient caged page, whom you adopt as your partner-in-crime and trusted advisor. Solve unconventional puzzles across fiction and reality Test your ingenuity with unique puzzles that encourage thinking outside the box, as you freely travel between fiction and reality, gathering valuable items to overcome obstacles. Using the mystical power of ink, you can manipulate objects within the books, adding depth to your interactions and unlocking new paths to explore.

short_description: The Bookwalker is a narrative adventure in which you play as Etienne Quist, a writer-turned-thief with the ability to dive into books. Use your powers to journey between reality and book worlds, and steal legendary items like Thor's Hammer and Excalibur to restore your ability to write.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game, it's a combination of a puzzle and a story teller. You have to figure out how to progress through the story while getting what you need. Very unique concept.So the thing about this game so far is that it doesn't really make sense in its mechanics, and I'll explain. For example in every book you go in, you have the illusion of choice, and I say illusion because no matter what you pick eventually it will all bring you to the end of the book. Like there's no choice that you'll pick to where you'll die. That's the first major thing. The second major thing is that combat does absolutely nothing in this game. Like you fight things, and if you win, you get items that you then turn into ink, which doesn't do much, but if you lose, you just start over, so it's not a game over, its just a little bit more time. Which is pointless, because even if you win, the ink doesn't matter enough to do anything. Like you don't use it to upgrade anything, you just use it for an occasional quest and for those fights. And so I just feel like this game has a lot of great elements that are not being utilized correctly, so they feel very linear.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright. The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales is done and dusted. This was an interesting game with surprisingly good world building.In The Bookwalker, the known world is basically run by book publishers, and authors hold great power. However, those powers need to be watched, and so there are Book Police, who make sure authors aren’t breaking any laws, such as stealing objects from books and smuggling them into the real world, and likewise that they aren’t bringing characters into the real world.You play as Etienne, an author who was sentenced to thirty years of indentured servitude, wherein he must select a mega publisher to work for and that will serve as his probation officer. With good behavior and loyalty, he might be able to shave two years from his sentence.To enforce punishment to wayward authors, those sentenced are forced to wear special shackles which are supposed to hinder them enough to prevent them from using their author powers in addition to preventing them from authoring their own books. Which includes the ability to enter books (the walking part of the title) and affect the outcome of stories, if not outright change them. Or as mentioned, do things like smuggle objects out of said books for sale on the black market.Anyway, being as how Etienne is sentenced to thirty years of not being able to write for himself, he seeks a way to break his shackles and is offered an opportunity to have his shackles removed (illegally) if he’ll enter six different books with the goal of retrieving a specific item from each for his new benefactor. The items include the Sword Excalibur and Thor’s hamner Mjolnir.In his first mission, he encounters a character who has been trapped in an object and placed in a wholly different novel than the one he was written into. This character has amnesia, but is wise, kind, and becomes both Etienne’s companion and his voice if reason.Gameplay-wise, while in each novel, The Bookwalker is mostly a puzzle game with some simple turn based combat with a reasonable amount of exploration in point and click fashion. In the real world, you’re basically confined to your apartment building and will click on various items to add to the story. And, while in a book, you can leave the book anytime you want to come back to the real world in order to find objects that you can bring back into the book to help solve puzzles. There are seven books in total. Six with objects to retrieve and one more for good measure.The is no voice acting. Speech is handled in mumble fashion. The graphics are very nice with good variety and two distinctly different styles between the third person view in the real world and isometric view while in the books themselves. I honestly was so focused on the story and gameplay that I can’t really recall if there was music or not, lol. Safe to say that if there was, it wasn’t prominent.All in all, I quite enjoyed The Bookwalker, and the story resolution had a nice little surprise that was very satisfying. It took 6.1 hours to complete. You’ll probably need to play each chapter twice to get all the cheevos if that’s your thing.This game is fully Steam Deck compatible, and outside of one weird bug where the real world and book world smashed together, freezing the game, I encountered no technical issues. The autosave feature was generous, so zero progression was lost.I bought this on sale on Steam recently (recently as of the time of this writing), but cost vs value is there at full price IMO. It may not be everybody’s cup of tea, but I think it’s well worth experiencing and can definitely be considered an IndieGem.

_childDocuments_.review: The Bookwalker has a compelling concept, but unfortunately it's ruined through poor writing, pacing, and dialogue. On the surface level, it's pretty clear that English is not the developer's first language. The game's prose is quite basic and awkward in places - which is somewhat disappointing for a game about literature - but there are several far more fundamental problems that make me deeply dislike the narrative and the game as a whole.One of my biggest issues, and bear with me here, is that the game has some of the most bizarrely implemented moral choices I've ever seen. To give a concrete example, at the end of the first mission, you are offered the choice to either take a potion of immortality and leave, completing your task and satisfying your handler, or give half of it to a deranged, dying scientist for him to presumably pour on his long-dead lover's grave. This is about 40 minutes into the game. You have never spoken to the scientist up to this point, and you know he just shot several people and spent years committing reprehensible experiments on human subjects to make the potion. He's also a character in a book, while the player character is facing 30 years hard labour if he doesn't bring the potion back into the real world. If you choose to take the potion for yourself, you are chastised as cruel and immoral by your companion (who you had only met a few minutes prior), and then APOLOGISE to them and promise not to do anything like that again at the start of the next mission. You are not given the choice to stand by your decision, or defend your own interests as being more important than those of a fictional psychopath you never even really met. If you don't agree with the game's message that fictional characters are as deserving of mercy and compassion as real people, the game simply shakes its head in disapproval and makes it clear to you, through extended melodramatic exchanges between the main character and his companion, that you are simply a heartless sack of ♥♥♥♥.The game's message is so ridiculous that I'm not sure if I'm even interpreting it correctly. It's insane to suggest that authors have some sort of responsibility to provide their characters with safety and happiness, but that's really my read on the narrative, and it's reinforced by the melodramatic way in which you and your companion struggle with the moral implications of removing batteries from robots to progress through another book. It's a very difficult message to defend, and the game doesn't even come close to doing it justice! Each mission is so short that you have no chance to get invested in either the setting or its characters, and the only indication that there is any ethical dilemma here at all is that the player character and his companion angst and agonise every time they have to "harm" a character in any way! It's not thought provoking, it's just annoying and preachy.... All of that aside, the writing is generally quite uninspired. The player character and his companion have no chemistry, mostly trading tired quips and jokes from the instant they meet instead of establishing any sort of believable rapport. The writing is very spartan, giving very little lore or worldbuilding beyond what's necessary to further the plot of the mission, with the player character remarking on the clichéd or poor quality writing of the books he's in on multiple occasions. Does that mean that the developer made the books bad on purpose? Why? Why not have him be immersed in one deep and fleshed out literary world for the whole game, instead of hopping between shallow worlds populated by equally shallow and archetypal characters, with even the main character completely unengaged beyond the abstract dilemma of whether or not it's acceptable to mistreat fictional characters? This game leans heavily on its narrative and it just does not do it for me at all.It's a shame. The visuals are fantastic throughout, and it's clear a lot of passion has gone into the game. But it's a narrative-driven game with a poor narrative, and there's not much else of substance to save the experience. I haven't finished the game yet so maybe it pulls out some insane narrative twist later on that redeems everything, but I very much doubt it. The start of mission 3 certainly didn't inspire me with confidence.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great isometric RPG. Don't expect too much depth, as it's mostly linear with minor dialogue choices changing the plot of each book that you full dive into. The plot is what matters here, and the RPG battles are fun, having to manage ink, which is your mana, as well as health. Health items are limited and theres no healing abilities, only a shield ability starting chapter 2, so the battles are really strategic in making sure you aren't hit, or that you have the food to heal your wounds.The concept is great, reminds me of a book series I read called Libriomancer, but instead of simply taking items out of books, this character goes into books to try to retrieve an item out of the book. In his universe, this is a common ability, which gives books a whole new meaning.
