_childDocuments_.review: If you had your interest piqued by , chances are, it was because of its art style and certain UI elements heavily reminding you of .That could be one reason. The other, perhaps the very nature of these games—text-heavy and narrative-driven; and what better excuse is there to show off your writing chops and how big of an erudite you are than setting a game in not one, not two, but  (made up) books. These are the reasons why I decided to give the game a chance, and as such, I feel obligated to dispel some misconceptions you may also have, as this is where the similarities end., obviously, wasn’t the first game to concern itself with storytelling first while utilizing an isometric view, but that hazy, painterly colour scheme and those character portraits are quite reminiscent of it. , on the other hand, isn’t nearly as text-heavy, nor is it an RPG. Instead, it plays like a point & click adventure with turn-based combat and, to my greatest surprise, crafting. That might be enough to put some of you eager wishlisters off, but don’t worry— is still one well-realised idea. Let’s get some technical hiccups out of the way first: if you’re living in the future, where playing at only 60 frames per second is a frightening thought, then maybe hold off on the purchase for now. Something about  makes it hard to work with at high framerates, progressively making mouse movement choppier the higher they are. So, cap it with your preferred method before jumping in—though not even that will save you from some minor, annoying visual glitches during the game’s first-person sections.That’s right, that gif above isn’t just a fancy menu screen. Starting the game throws you into the shoes and puts you behind the eyes of Etienne Quist, a disgraced writer suffering from writer’s block. Times are tough—many of his personal belongings have been seized and there’s a big ol’ eviction notice plastered on the front door. To make matters worse, the writer’s block is quite literal in this case, I’m afraid. Etienne’s creative juices haven’t just dried up, but he’s been shackled with a special kind of armband, by none other than the Writer’s Police, for a crime he doesn't talk lightly about.Inside of  dystopian setting, it’s not a prison sentence that awaits Etienne but rather forced labour at a publishing house without much input on what goes into his writings. It is a grim fate that not many manage to pull through, and even those that do rarely ever go back to writing. And so, with a promise of his shackles being removed after six odd jobs, Etienne turns to bookwalking—an illegal practice of diving into books, stealing powerful artefacts from their plotlines, and selling them off to other, less imaginative writers who then use them in their own stories.It's such a simple, yet clever idea. It's not a wholly original concept (rarely anything is), but  manages to create a separation between the “mundane”—Etienne’s harsh reality presented through the first-person sequences— and the wondrous settings created for the novels he has to steal from.Each novel is as subversive as the very start of the game, the difference between the isometric plane of the books you visit and Etienne’s stuffy apartment. Creaky pipes jut out of the walls and all that can be observed through the windows is the brick façade of the factory next door. Take a couple of steps to the study and whoosh!—you find yourself inside a sci-fi rendition of an Arthurian legend or a retelling of Norse mythology with a corporate twist.  takes a sort of post-modernist approach to the classic framings it explores, but it’s more of a fun exploration rather than outright deconstruction. Thankfully, it never comes close to being cynical or irreverent in its observations. In fact, I’d say that the dispelment of irreverence is the crucial theme the game tries to land by the plot’s climax, but its aspirations fall a bit flat due to the underwritten character drama that carries it.The whole of  is, ironically, underwritten—the regime that keeps artists and their creations as another resource in check isn’t all that explored, the rules of bookwalking are a bit murky, and you shouldn’t be surprised if you don’t find yourself caring as much about its characters when the game so clearly expects you to. Praise multiple-choice dialogue, right? You’ll be able to paint Etienne’s sensibilities somewhat closer to your heart, even if most of the journey is rather linear. features a couple of additional mechanics to make the pointing & clicking a bit more engaging as you’re thieving around its tales. Unfortunately, it doesn’t take them far enough to fill up its narrative holes.The turn-based combat makes sense narratively, even if it’s a game of rock, paper, scissors that’s always in your favour. You’ll be able to see what action the enemies will take on their turn and are then supposed to pick one of your own that’ll do the best job of exploiting their choice. I didn’t get much out of it, but I can’t say it bogged the experience down. It was, at times, even a satisfying resolution to some of the problems Etienne faces. But, the crafting—and the puzzle-solving in general—might as well have had the game play out itself.Where one might expect to find puzzles, additional dialogue, alternate routes, or worldbuilding,  has crafting resources and junk. With crafting resources, you can make lockpicks and crowbars, which are used throughout the books to advance, usually by opening a crate or strongbox that contains the next plot-relevant item.Junk can be converted to ink, which lets Etienne rewrite something about the book you’re in through a special dialogue option. Ink also fuels all of your combat abilities, so an interesting choice could have presented itself were it not for the fact that you have the free ability to drain ink directly from enemies. The junk in each scenario is so abundant too, that you’ll always have enough for everything you need. I’ve never died in combat and I’ve never missed out on an ink-related dialogue option. It wouldn't have been a problem, were it not a replacement for puzzles and the sole reward for exploration.All of this, and I’d like to end on a positive note, would spell doom for the title were it not for its presentation and the idea that lies at its core. The whole bookwalking experience, at least on a conceptual level, is so well-realised that I still consider it a worthwhile one, shortcomings included. That visual of literally diving into the pages and the soundtrack bring it together for me, elevating the game when nothing else could.It’s these rich ambient tones—a serene song, yet with a strong dark undertone, treasuring the moment but also going back to that unfortunate chasm between escapist storytelling and the unromantic real world. The story will, sadly and eventually, end; and we’ll exit, or be tossed out, back into the difficult uphill battle that is the day-to-day struggle, perhaps richer for an experience.And that’s okay; ultimately what  is about, and the grounds I can recommend it on with no second thoughts.

_childDocuments_.review: Bookwalker is an amazing and beautiful game.From the indie creators of pixel-art game "The Final Station" which I enjoyed, they make such a fascinating and gorgeous game! I can't wait for their future projects !!The entire concept of traveling into books to talk to written characters and steal relics to sell them so they can be used in plagiarized works is novel.It's like the movie "Inception" but instead of diving into dreams, you dive into literature.Elementary ;)Bookwalker gives you 6 unique worlds to explore:1) The Alchemist's prison (tutorial world)2) Norse Mythology but modern and re-imagined by Simon Stalenhag.3) Harry Potter Hogwarts detective mystery.4) Legend of Excalibur but in space.5) Haunted Mansion.6) Sand world like DUNE but with SNOWPIERCER locomotive trains.Not only that, but when you "resurface" to the real world, game changes genre and now you play from a 3D first-person perspective.Such creative experimentation I only encountered in "Nier:Automata" and the new nun game "Indika".Bookwalker is a beautiful and creative project with amazing writing and sound.The game is polished, it has no apparent bugs or bad grammar. A clean and enjoyable experience.The combat is lackluster but remember this isn't a fighting game. The fights are only a small Optional part and served their intended purpose well enough.But the most important part is how the game asks moral questions and I was brainstorming for longer periods contemplating my choices.What's the difference between people and characters?Especially in a world where you can dive into the Matrix and written characters are indistinguishable from real people. The border between living and not, is blurred like it is in the typical Cyberpunk AI and synths discussions.I remember watching a Youtube video that discussed this topic and made up characters like Luke Skywalker have influenced and inspired us, unlike living people in our lives.Bookwalker was an amazing experience!

I'm not saying that it has to be Mass Effect levels of choice and consequence outcome. But if I make a life or death decision at the end of a chapter, you damn well better not pretend like what I chose didn't matter 2 lines of dialogue later.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I have not finished this game, so I cannot comment on the whole story, nor the endgame combat.Sadly, I cannot recommend this game. Don't misinterpret this as caustic criticism, however. This game is the only game I've played that's compelled me to go forward with writing a full-on Steam review.The Book Walker is a simple game, in its story and in its gameplay due to the nature of the premise and the game's limitations respectively. Story: Because the game goes out of the way to present the player with new and varying worlds every level, the writing runs right into the pitfall of re-exposition. The player is constantly being reintroduced to settings that, as far as I know, don't intersect or matter later on at all, which makes it hard to get invested in anything the story puts out to you when the levels, and thereby those settings, are gone in a flash. As for the player character, Etienne is written to be this relatable, MCU-level-quipping, bleeding heart longing for the good old days of "real" writers. Of course, the game up to the point I've played makes fun of this point of view, but it doesn't necessarily challenge it because of the story structure. The big theme of Book Walker is that fictional constructs are people too and we should want what's best for their well-being like any other person even if it means rewriting "fate". However, the game doesn't help drive home that the characters are real people when every dialogue option loops back to the same answer even when it clearly makes no sense or when the player interacts with an NPC and then they forget who you are in the next interaction. There are no heavy choices to be made in this game, just a linear path to follow, like a railroaded D&D game. As for the real world gimmick stuff, there's an impossible-to-ignore uncanniness to it all. Rather than have models that you can interact or talk to, a majority of the real-life portions consist of "talk to X door to get Y item/scripted-event to obtain Z item that lets you progress in the book." Your apartment is conveniently blocked off on all sides by giant walls so there's nothing to see out the windows. Characters are always conveniently hiding behind doors so you don't see the lack of models in the game. Both lend to an unintended eeriness. I feel like when I switch to the real-life segments, I've suddenly jumped from Monkey Island to PT. Overall, the inconsistent tone and preachiness of the writing rubbed me somewhat pretentious.Gameplay: The gameplay loop of Book Walker is disappointingly mundane. A majority of the game is point-n-click puzzle solving, but none of the puzzles are particularly inspired or thought-provoking, and are often more of a long, convoluted way of clicking "next line". Most puzzles will have you walking around the game's large maps for one specific item or interacting with X number of Y's until the game says "Congratulations! You've just unlocked the next line of dialogue!" When you're not doing fetch quests in disguise, you're scrounging around for crafting parts to make tools to open the various locked items in the game to obtain "loot". This loot, however, only exists to be used to craft more tools and, if not that, potions that refill this game's version of "mana". This segways into the tedious combat. Combat, like the puzzles, is just a convoluted way of getting to the next line of dialogue. It mainly consists of spamming the Stun attack so enemies can't act until you get them to 2-3 HP and you can finish them off with a basic attack. It's filler. It's a chore, both metaphorically and literally.There's SO MUCH HERE with the premise. I bought this game because there's so much potential behind delving into stories and breaking fate while also being this cool, confident thief. Unfortunately, like the protagonist Etienne himself, what I got was very disappointing. I hate to be so harsh, but The Book Walker: Thief of Tales is really not worth your time. Just play Disco Elysium instead.(I will be finishing this game and maybe coming back and editing this review if it, at all, does not reflect what I believe will be my final thoughts.)

_childDocuments_.review: There are meetings that should have been e-mails, and here we have a game that should have been a book. Another entry in the growing list of Disco Elysium inspired "narrative focused" RPGs, The Bookwalker suffers from the usual problem of the genre: lack of interesting mechanics. Mostly, you just walk around and click on active points, only rarely having to make a meaningful choice. To be fair, unlike most Discoids, this game does feature combats. They help relieve tedium a little, but the combat system is simple enough (compared to e.g. The Thaumaturge), and there is little penalty for losing.Another gimmick The Bookwalker adds is a transition between 3D and isometric modes. It fits the theme of game well: you walk around in 3D in "real world", and then dive into books, where everything is seen from 3rd person. Both 3D and 2D locations are beautifully done, but are very small.However, where this game fails for me is the crucial point for Discoids: the story. Earlier this year, I praised The Thaumaturge, because its real history-inspired storyline set in rarely visited region was enough to keep me going (along with a slightly more interesting combat system). Here, the story isn't BAD, but... As I said at the beginning, it would make a better book. Or maybe not, but at least in a book, the writer could EXPLAIN more. As it is, I have no idea about the world outside the protagonist's appartment building. Why you can't write a book without stealing an item from another one? Why is there writer police? Do items from books ACTUALLY work in real world, or not? Through the game, we get little news stories which make it seem that items we steal from books are used to write other books, and yet the ending kind of suggests a different use for them? Also, how in the world did the protagonist figure out identity of Roderick and the book to which he belongs? I surely didn't, and I don't think there were enough clues for the player to do that!I get that the game doesn't have time to explain everything. Nor does every book, although I'd be much, much happier reader if every writer was like Brandon Sanderson. But here I'm just left unsatisfied; hence, the thumb down.On the technical side of things, the game froze in a live lock for me half a doze times when loading a level, especially when I Alt-Tabbed during the loading, and I'm not impressed with the speed with which it loads its tiny one-room locations. Also, I feel like I spent more time waiting for one scene to fade out and another fade in than actually playing (well, this is an exaggeration, but really: these scenes are small and simple enough my PC probably could keep them all in memory and switch them much, much faster; this is especially annoying in book worlds where you have to backtrack more, the 5th being the worst offender).
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I would happily assign a maybe to this game because the concept of invading books to steal items from their plot is very interesting but the game itself is not, but we are stuck with "Yes" or "No" and I'm more inclined to "No".My main issue with this one is that is like a game from Telltale, you have a lot of interesting choices during gameplay that in the end amount to nothing, some different dialogue here and there or skipping a fight but the ending of every chapter has been predefined so nothing matters.You have 2 main sections on every chapter, your apartment that you will explore in first person view and the book that you'll explore in isometric view trying to emulate a point and click adventure with a bit of turn based combat.There is almost no challenge in this game and is more like you are driving the story forward with your presence while sometimes interrupted by the combat scenes that can be annoying and tiresome. The most difficult thing you will have to do is scour the screen to find a hotspot to keep moving the plot forward but most of the time is click and read through the dialogues.There is not much replayability except if you want to hear other dialogues also, the game can be finished in 6 hours more or less so I suggest to get it on a sale if you are really interested in the story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Bookwalker, an attempt to blend role-playing game (RPG) elements with a visual novel, had great potential yet failed to deliver on almost all fronts.Storyline:The game's storyline, which should have been its strongest point, is devastatingly disappointing. Out of 8 hours I spent on my first playthrough I got about 20 lines of dialogue actually explaining what happened to our protagonist and almost no worldbuilding at all. Gameplay:What about gameplay? Maybe puzzles and fights make up for the story shortcomings? Unfortunately, Bookwalker's gameplay suffers from the needless RPG elements and tedious puzzles. You need to progress to your objective? Oh no, something suddenly happened and now you need to backtrack 4 times. Don’t forget to fight uninspired enemies by clicking the same 2 buttons for all eternity. Such joy!Graphics and Sound:The game's graphics and atmosphere are its saving grace. The levels look fantastic, each of them distinctly different, detailed and provide a visually appealing experience. I loved how protagonists home changed between levels, it is a nice detail.There are no voiced lines but sounds are very serviceable. However, the music is forgettable and does little to enhance the game's atmosphere. Performance:There are no settings aside for resolution. I was able to play at decently stable 60 fps in 1200p on my Legion Go, with occasional dips to 40 fps in several areas.Conclusion:If you care about story at all, don’t buy this. Thinking back, I remember this style, the same developers made a game ‘The Final Station’ that suffered from the same weak, pathetic storytelling but great visual design. The gameplay was a bit better though. Now we can see that developers are unable to learn from their mistakes. Maybe it is just me, because both games have 80%+ ratings, I don’t know, but both of them made me angry enough to leave a negative review, which doesn’t happen often, make of that what you will.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, I really enjoyed this game, and I wanted to write a review, not just to recommend it but to congratulate the devs. I played the demo for this game a while ago and it stuck with me; moments from it kept coming back to my mind unbidden, which isn't something that happens to me often, and I really enjoyed the demo's story. I left a post in the forums complimenting the devs on their work back then, and now I've played the full game, and I want to say, I really enjoyed it!To set the tone: this is a shortish story-focused game, mostly puzzles and dialogue with some combat. It took me about six hours to beat it, it's likely it'll take you less. And... the game isn't perfect. My two biggest issues were the combat system, which was fairly easy (but I didn't mind much, because I was more focused on the story — and I'm also, um, kind of bad at videogames, so it was on my skill level lololol) and some inconsistencies with my choices; occasionally I'd make a choice in a chapter and my companion would act in the next one like I hadn't done that thing. (This was particularly bad in Chapter 2). However, these problems didn't take away from my enjoyment of the game.The story was where the real heart of the game truly lied, I think, and it was a real good story, well told (mostly, apart from that choices hiccup haha). I found the protagonist really interesting, his dynamic with his companion very sweet, the "real world"'s worldbuilding extremely intriguing yet never overwhelming, the stories they jumped into all incredibly fascinating (I'm so curious about what those books' "actual plots", so to speak, would've been), and I think the later reveals made a lot of sense (and some made me feel a lot of emotions, in a good way). The presentation of everything was great, too. Though to be fair, I'm also a huge book nerd, so maybe I'm biased (there's definitely plenty of books I'd like to jump into).I would recommend this game to any fellow bookworms, or anybody interested in having a nice afternoon with a one-off game about books. Great stuff!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: After playing games for the last 40 years, it really is difficult to find something unique. Developer Do My Best has succeeded in making something wholly original with this wonderfully executed isometric point-and-click adventure, "The Book Walker: Thief of Tales". The premise is interesting: you are a writer who has been sentenced for a variety of crimes that bar you from writing books for the next 30 years. Well, a shady offer comes along that promises to reduce your sentence, and thus begins your adventure. You get to jump in and out of different books, looking for items for a collector who promises to help your situation. Within these jobs, you have to explore, investigate, and sometimes battle your way to finding the required artifacts. The fights are turn based and relatively simple, even if you are defeated you get to basically pick up from where you left off, so the immersion isn't broken with the story. There is some light crafting involved, as you will need to make lockpicks, crowbars, and other assorted tools to help you get past locked doors, chests, and other barriers. The dialog is well written and perfectly placed. The game isn't overly verbose, which is quite refreshing as some adventure games have so much text that it's easy to lose interest.The graphics and locations are quite beautifully done and are accompanied by an atmospheric, at times ethereal soundtrack. A lot of thought seemed to be placed in every room, object, and encounter. There really isn't anything in the way of filler here. Everything has meaning and adds to the story. It's hard to think of any negatives to the game, aside from a minor graphical glitch while carrying a suitcase. I see another user has had this issue as well, so I know it's not related to my system. It did not take away from the experience from the game whatsoever. If you are a fan of adventure games, I fully recommend "The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales". It truly is one of the best modern adventure games, and hopefully we see more in this style from the developer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on the fence about whether to recommend this game or not. The premise is great, and I love the art style but the story is incredibly linear and the player is only given the illusion of choice where they're told to make a decision that could negatively impact the story and the characters left behind but that doesn't go anywhere. There is no alternative route and no real choices to be made. There is only one ending and the game railroads you towards it in under 6 hours. It's a neat game with a really cool concept, but the lack of actual impact on the story depending on your decisions leads to a lack of interest in multiple play throughs, at least for me.Also, combat felt like an afterthought, there's very little customisation for play style and if you don't like the combat then too bad because the dialogue options you think will help you avoid combat won't actually say what you intend because the 'choices' in dialogue all have the same answer and 9/10 times ends up with the MC being a complete nitwit and starting a fight anyways. So it's a decent game for a single playthrough but I don't find myself reaching for it again immediately because I know there isn't any other path to take, all 'roads' lead to the same destination.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't really know what to expect with this game but I was blown away. It is fantastic. The story is original and the characters are compelling and I really found myself rooting for them. I loved the mix of first person to point and click. It had challenging gameplay and the combat required strategy. My only con for this game is I wish it was longer. One of the best games I've played in a while it is absolutely a hidden gem and a must play. Please anyone reading please buy this game you wont regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully written game, and the puzzles with it. _childDocuments_.review: I was really unsure about this at first. The Steam reviews for quite some time were apprehensively positive and one or two of the negative ones made me think that I would not enjoy this game (based on what I usually enjoy). Then I got it on a sale, played for a couple of minutes and was still quite sure that it wouldn't be my cup of tea. The 21:9 resolution is vert-, so you should manually change it to 16:9 in the options. The characters voices being a muffled "Sim-lish" threw me off as I would have preferred no voices at all over this. And the first person sections at the beginning felt clunky and unnecessary. At the end of the tutorial you get a "choice" and I uncharacteristically (for me) chose the "evil outcome" (for lack of a better term) just because I was not invested in the characters (yet) to really care.But then I played the first chapter. Then the second. The third. And I noticed that whatever had painted my initial (mis)conception about the game evaporated. I was getting invested, heavily, in the story and the characters. The game on a purely progression level is a walking simulator with light puzzles and predetermined "combat" encounters (which are themselves more or less light puzzles than anything else, depending on how much stuff you have picked up and crafted beforehand) -- but the balance of the gameplay elements is so good that they enhance the story, or rather: the multiple stories (of the books and the overarching story of the main characters).Bookwalker overall has a really interesting premise in regards to the idea of what "book walkers" are, why they exist and what the consequences of their actions can be. Aside from that, most of the books had a really compelling internal story to tell and experience. Smarter people than me will probably find psychological worth in some of the metaphors, but for me it was enough that they were interesting and unpredictable. The best compliment I can give the game is that I was sad that it ended (after ~5-6 hours playtime), as I would have liked to experience more books of similar quality.Due to the linear nature I doubt that a second playthrough would have the same impact, so that is one thing to keep in mind when contemplating a potential purchase. That being said, my first (and only) playthrough was great enough that I wholeheartedly recommend the game to anyone who is more interested in stories than competition in games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolute gem. I loved every second of this game. It flirts between first person, point-and-click, and old-school turn-based combat. The premise feels wonderfully fresh and the retelling of classic narratives is excellently executed. You play as a writer that is forced to enter books in order to steal powerful items. It is a very cool idea that has been really well put together. I would highly recommend this to indie fans. I had a blast.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid single player game. Interesting worlds and the music reminds me of Disco Elysium but the game is nowhere near as text heavy as that. If you are just looking for a good narrative single player game with an interesting world and story then definitely give this a go. I finished it in 7 hours but I'll probably play it again a few times, definitely a game you'll remember and can talk about
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The  of the premise is good, going into story books and messing with the plot in order to steal stuff, but the details of the premise make two major mistakes:First: that the story books are made up, rather than being well-known public domain books, part of the plot is that these books are badly written by different authors, you don't get to deviously employ your prior knowledge of how the story is  to go to mess with things. What kind of person wants to immerse theirself into the worldbuilding of a cheap Harry Potter knockoff for forty minutes before leaving it and never thinking about it again? Because the books are written by different (imaginary) authors they can't really even be doing a "these worlds you're exploring are all different lenses into the same personality/philosophy" angle.Second: that diving into books and messing with them is apparently a normal mundane thing lots of people do. They make no effort to establish how that's supposed to make sense early on, and it takes the premise from "whoa cool magic power" to "did the game devs just hear about books second hand? You know they're supposed to be made of text that you read right"I guess the metaplot writing is going for a kind of "this guy is stuck with an unethical job and he doesn't like it" angle which is alright, but a story about being sad about a job works a lot better if the job feels plausible.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Do you wish to enter a vastly creative realm of books and inter dimensional authors?Do you wish to have a suspicious side kick dangling around your neck?Do you wish to be marvelled by the combination of different gameplay and design styles this series brings together seamlessly?Do you want to play a point and click choose your own adventure masterpiece?....Then LOOK NO FURTHER!I absolutely adored every moment of this game! The game play is so genuinely immersive and creative, and every chapter, environment, character and decision you make is engaging!On top of this! This game remedies every frustration I've ever had with point and click adventures!-no having to 'guess' what item combines with another-crafting that isn't tedious or confusing-clickable things are not infinite and when you do its actually useful or an interactive point-you can make different choices about how to pay different areas without worrying about being soft locked (completionists you definitely would want another play through tho haha)-decent walk cycle with VERY minimal backtracking-non repetitive chapters/environments-very difficult to 'accidentally' click something- i could ramble on about the ways in which other games could emulate this games brilliance!I only wish this game was longer!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Take a walk with this book!

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game with a great story. I enjoy the decision making involved and how it may affect the characters within the books and outside of the books. The ending was very nice :) Nice happy ending. 10/10 I definitely recommend this to anyone who is looking for a new game to play in the evenings with a cup of tea and some biscuits
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: This was an interesting play. I have some mixed feelings for this one.I really enjoyed this game as a narrative. It was an interesting read and plot. It definitely gave the player a chance to form attachments to the protagonists.I was heavily attracted to the transitions of POV to 3rd person view when in and outside a book. It kind of gave depth to the separation of realities (real world vs. book). Graphics were clean and the overall design was pretty good. Navigation was simple; Searching your surroundings and moving around by point and click. Crafting was a little unusual. Each book you enter you are forced to start over with crafting necessary items to obtain quest items, crafting materials, or scraps of food for health when engaging in combat. Combat was pretty mediocre. Turned based tactics was evident but I have to agree, was a little dull. Even if you made a wrong move and died, you get to start over at full health and ink and lose nothing really. But my understanding was that combat was not really supposed to be the meat of the game.Overall challenge of the game was pretty much too easy..which kind of takes away from the satisfaction of fulfillment.Honestly one burning question I had from the beginning of this play: Why tf did devs think it was ok to keep a fire extinguisher LOCKED in locker if it's purpose is supposed to be used in emergencies and readily available? Lmao guess I'm being too realistic.I still enjoyed this game regardless. I can't quite give this a thumbs down. Do I recommend this game? YesDo I recommend it at full price? Likely not 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game so bad because it has a lot of interesting concepts but they just...don't really follow through with them. The game play is fun but not exactly challenging, the book plots absolutely peaked my interest but the world itself is never really expanded on. It's disappointing, the ending was lackluster, and there were too many threads left hanging. As for buying it? Not at it's current price but if it's on sale and you're bored why not.

_childDocuments_.review: Great, unique and emotionally touching story with fantastic art and diverse settings. Character diversity is somewhat minimal in this game, as the main focus of this game is the exploration of MC's moral compass. Visuals and identities are unimportant by design in the game (to the point we don't know how MC looks until the epilogue). The diversity we do get is in the worlds we explore, the facets of humanity and the exploration of social responsibility of the individual.I'll go over TW & CN, Pros and Cons, Accessibility features, my general verdict and suggestions for improvements. Trigger warnings:Prison, corrupt justice system, experimentation, non-graphic death, ageism, bullying, unpaid servitude, dehumanisation.Content notes:Poverty, corruption, heartbreak, amnesia, empathy.Pros:+Fights are not too difficult but are unique enough to be interesting,+No perma-death,+No bad endings,+Achievements,+Beautiful and unique art style,Cons:-Some text is timed and moved too quickly for me to read-No accessibility settings-Autosaves (no save slot options)Accessibility: +Epilepsy safe: No flashing lights or flickering+No jump scares, loud sudden noises, etc+Good text/background contrast of conversation text -Poor text contrast and size for object descriptions (text hovers over areas of interest)-Lacks settings for text size, and speed of text disappearing from screen-No voice actingVerdict:The story-line was consistent despite the vastly changing settings and getting to know the characters was pleasant. The world-building is organic, never feeling like info-dumping and leaving enough to the imagination but showing you a great deal even through the canon 'real' and 'fictional' worlds.  This game takes us through 6 chapters (or book-worlds) with different settings, types of corruption and facets of human nature demonstrated within. It ultimately explores what it means to be human, and how to be empathetic to those around us through observing canon fictional characters. Although the main characters seem to present 2 sides of 'who counts as real people', I felt it was a bit simplistic at times because the playable character obviously didn't disagree. This made their debates seem confusing and as though the MC was inconsistent, or there was miscommunication for the sake of the theme. However, I guess it successfully explores that space between cognitively and empathetically viewing others as 'human' or 'real'. 'How do you treat people humanely? How indiscriminate should empathy be? How do we deal with negative associations without denying others or our own validity.' These are interesting questions and I think it explores and concludes this theme nicely.The ending was meaningful and ended without a cliffhanger or major unanswered plot-hole questions. There was a predictable reveal at the end, but as it wasn't a hammed up mystery it was a welcome conclusion.Suggestions:+Text size settings would be great, along with colour contrast or a soft contrasting background colour for text hovering over complex images to improve visibility. +Consider providing font options, particularly dyslexia friendly fonts.+It would be very useful to have Self-voicing (inbuilt screen reading) capacities built-in for these games. +Generally, having diverse disabled game testers would enable improved accessibility for future projects.As always, feel free to leave comments, particularly on accessibility features I  may have missed.

_childDocuments_.review: A short, straightforward point and click adventure with a good story and light turn-based combat. The setup and world of the game feel unique and worthwhile, and the characters you interact with are well-written. Graphics were quite nice although there were noticeable FPS dips during some scenes and no options to change anything significant apart from resolution. Overall the game pacing is a bit slow, and there's a lot of clicking-everything-to-progress (mainly to dig up enough materials to craft the items you need which basically act as keys to progress). In-built hint system is there to keep you on track, although no puzzles are difficult. Kept me engaged throughout its runtime, but I'd still say to get it when it's on sale. A nicely made and entertaining game and story overall though, kudos to the devs!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A nice game that took me by surprise. I am normally not into these kinds of games, but the story and exploration were interesting enough to keep me going. The combat is fairly easy and not to deep but serviceable enough. The story is where its at. With the different books you must steal from different stories. All brought together by the main characters own little drama. After the fourth book I thought, okay, now I know how it goes. That is when the game threw some new characters and storylines at me. I would recommend this game at full price if you are interested in the genre. However, if not, wait for a sale. It is short, sweet and I enjoyed every minute of it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A very weird an interesting game. Dive into books to steal famous treasures. Use objects from the real world to solve fictional problems as you try to earn your freedom as a writer again.Each level is it's own unique story that are often just as fascinating if not more so than the "actual" setting. Puzzles and combat are pretty straight forward, enough to keep it from being a walking simulator but it's hardly a puzzle or tactical battle game. For what is essentially a point & click there is a decent amount of non-linearirty to the way you progress and solve problems. It all leads to the end but the path you take can be pretty interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I was drawn in by the art style and the premise, but I had to say that I'm very disappointed by the game's actual execution of these interesting ideas. My biggest problem is with the writing: the protagonist is supposedly a writer (at least they used to be), but this fact is in no way reflected in the way they act or, more importantly, how they *speak*, and that just breaks the immersion for me completely. I finished the first story but couldn't push past it. If the lackluster writing in the beginning is put in there intentionally and somehow its quality will improve dramatically as the game proceeds, I might be willing to give this game another shot. Unfortunately, after reading other reviews of the game, it doesn't appear to be the case.As it is, I cannot recommend this game to anyone looking for a well-written and engaging narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A soft recommend, if the setting/concept of the game intrigues you then it might be your cup of tea. Like other reviewers have said its a cool idea but the experience is much less than it could have been. The game is a linear story with what seems like the illusion of choices, where you might have some different dialogue options come up but ultimately the overall outcomes probably don't change (though I can't say for certain).Not knocking what the devs have created, bravo the game ran flawlessly, it told a story and you transported me to some fantastical settings. Thank you. Perhaps it's just that just maybe my expectations were a little too high?!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I did not like "The Bookwalker". On one hand, it is missing most of the features of good old adventure games, as there are almost no puzzles apart from the trivial ones you solve on the go. On the other hand, there are too many artificial limitations and forced choices to consider it a non-linear role playing game. "Thief of Tales" is somewhere in-between two genres and does poorly at being both. The game is good looking, though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for fans of point and click adventures. It blends a variety of styles with some first person and some isometric exploration, casual puzzles and turn-based battles but it mostly works and keeps things interesting, especially as the adventures are contained within each 'book' so you get some new ideas each time. I would also recommend The Longest Journey / Dreamfall series, The Thaumaturge, and Gamedec.+Visuals, environments+Point/click elements+Real and book world duality+Exploration/adventure+Turn-based battles+Story-Barebones options-No key rebinding-No voice-Unclear direction at times-Hard to tell/see some interactables, no highlight-Some shoehorning/on rails-Autosave only-Backtracking-Few battle skills/options overall-Limited healing
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo for this a while back and really enjoyed the unique concept of diving into books and finding artifacts. It definitely intrigued me enough to pick it up the day it came out, and after some procrastinating, I finally finished it, and it was great!Now, granted, I had some problems. For one, the way exploration is rewarded can be very questionable at times. Occasionally, after you scavenged all of the crafting materials you could muster in order to make a crowbar or lockpick, all you would really find by using them would be trash items that convert into ink (a resource you will quickly have an abundance of by the halfway mark of each book). And yeah, the crafting system overall was a bit unnecessary as a whole, but it didn't take away from the game, so whatever.And probably my biggest gripe with the game is the combat, which can feel unsatisfying and bare bones at times. Mild planning may be required in the later fights, but strategy just gets thrown out the window when you get the healing shield upgrade (near the end), which not only shields you from a hit and heals you, but also has NO INK COST. Needless to say, I never died during my ~6 hours of playtime, and have no idea what the failure state is (if there even is one).Now, that sounds like a lot of negativity right out of the gate, but in all honestly, many of these gripes aren't omnipresent enough to noticeably harm the overall package. For instance, while the exploration may be flawed at times, it still feels satisfying to understand the pieces the game places in front of you and connect them together, revealing some great revelations and interesting ideas on the nature of writing. And while the combat seems shallow on the surface, there is depth to be explored, especially on some of the final encounters.Throughout the overarching story, you're an ex-writer with a weird name (Etienne) who's been tasked with working off his lengthy prison sentence by stealing artifacts from a variety of 6 books - some deriving their origins in myth, legend, space, trains, and other stuff. It takes a bunch of twists and turns with a gaggle of reoccurring characters, and is overall an enjoyable story to witness unfold.The art design in the 2D world is fantastic, and while some of the animations may be janky here and there, the models in the 3D world look great too. From the dazzling spiral book transition to the detailed and varied locals of each respective story, Bookwalker is definitely a treat for the eyes.Overall, a quaint little game that poses some great questions about the nature of creativity, all wrapped up in a fun, poignant, short package.7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I just completed The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales in one sitting, couldn't pull myself away from it. I bought it the moment it became available on the strength of the demo (which is the complete 1st section of the game). It's a surreal, hilarious, and very well-written adventure game. I'm having trouble thinking of things to write in this review because there's so little to complain about. So I'll write some disjointed positive thoughts instead: each of the worlds (books) present in the game are simultaneously recognizable as pieced-together while still being intriguing enough to warrant whole games of their own. The character dialog is charming and keeps you engaged in the tale of the unfortunate Etienne from beginning to end. The aesthetic (first-person adventure game into isometric CRPG-style) is darn tootin'. In a single sentence, The Bookwalker is as good as you *remember* old adventure games being. Easy 9/10; the only way I could think to improve this game would be to make another ten games just like it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales is a delightful adventure that will steal your heart! With its charming characters, captivating storyline, and clever puzzles, it offers a magical journey into the world of books. Very interesting idea, I especially liked books 4 and 6. Unfortunately, some books are frankly weak and not interesting. Still, the game deserves your attention.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a lovely premise that is ultimately hampered by excessive linearity and a subpar combat system. The game would be better served by having spent whatever time was spent on the combat into making more meaningful different choices (at least within 'books') and more engaging puzzles.Perhaps worth it on sale at around the $5 mark, but even the inexpensive intro offer of $13 feels like too much spent for too little meaningful product.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Playing it reminded me of older style games with narrative choices and puzzle elements. Although the game is fairly linear, and I would have wished having a bit more choices.The gameplay is in service of the story for better and worse, with an intriguing world building. Familiar with a touch of uniqueness.I could see it feeling like it drags out, but it is short enough to not have become an issue for me. It was a fine strange experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: After playing 2 of the 6(?) books, I lost interest to continue. It's clear that different dialogue hasn't been written to handle different choices you make; so the game feels flatter than the books you visit (perhaps there's a lazy twist that you are a book character?) Each world's background feels small and shallow - even if we view the visits as a short story précis of each ostensible novel.Combat serves no purpose, it's not engaging enough to be a game loop in addition to the main point-and-click dynamic. The art didn't do it for me either; too drab. Not sure what the point of the "crafting" action was - given how linear the game is, even when it didn't need to be. For instance, on the 2nd map, you have doors (power levers) requiring a set amount of tokens (batteries) to open - an incrementing amount tailored to govern which screens (and dialogue) you visit encounter first.Overall, the biggest problem with the game is that it needed about 5 times the budget to flesh out the premise adequately - every area of the game from dialogue to art to overall depth suffers from it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty good, shorter than I had hoped and a bit more rail-roady than what the demo made it seem to be, but I still enjoyed it quite a bit and I would recommend it, it's pretty fun and the story is pretty nice too. Though again I do wish it was a bit longer and more open with the choices you get to make (especially at the end of each book).
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: At its core it's a point and click adventure game. You are a write who has the ability to jump into books. You explore the book world, solve some mysteries, and even get into a little combat. There is also a meta world where you live outside the books, which has a very Dark City feel to it. You are being contracted by a mysterious collector to steal things from the books and bring them back into your world. But stealing things from the books has consequences for the characters within and you have to decide if this bothers you or not. The writing is excellent, as it should be for a game about books. Each book completes a nice chapter of the game where you can pause and come back later, though I played through them all. The meta world has a nice mystery to it that progress with each book and makes you want to keep going. I wish they had done a little more with the meta world story as there are lots of clues to tease you, but not much is explained in the end. I think the closest game this feels to me is the Time Stories board game, jumping between different worlds/times. Overall, definitely recommend if any of the above sounds intriguing to you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a very interesting premise where books can be experienced by diving into them and objects can be freely moved between planes but cannot persist for long. The protagonist is a criminal whose sentence is "writer's block", the inhibition of his creativity and prohibition from writing and publishing. In order to escape this punishment, the protagonist must perform a series of black-market jobs involving extracting key objects from stories, to fuel the works of lesser writers. While inside a given story, the gameplay is similar to Disco Elysium's, albeit heavily simplified in terms of exploration, conversation tree depth, skill checks, etc. However, while outside a story, the game places you into first person perspective and allows you to interact with your immediate environment. This degree of freedom is something I felt was sorely lacking in Citizen Sleeper for example, and is greatly appreciated. There are some moments where the game does not acknowledge your actions. For example, using a lock pick from a book to break a padlock in read life. Instead, this requires the progression of the main story line. On the other hand, small interactions within the apartment building you reside in (irl)  acknowledged. Such as residents posting up notes in response to you stealing food from the common kitchen area. While most missions are fun and entertaining, one in particular (book 4) does nothing to further develop the character. Meanwhile, the next mission represents a high point of the game, introducing a rudimentary but well put together time travelling mechanic. Quite a few minor complaints that can be easily addressed. For example, the dialogue choices can be selected via the number keys (as in Disco Elysium) but the games does not inform you of this. Can be addressed by simply numbering the choices. Another issue that I have is that the character can only run when the destination is far enough away from him. This does not make much sense and the game should allow you to run by double-clicking. Lastly, I would like to be able to see the conversation log in case I missed something while clicking through text.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: unique game in a sea of saturation. Takes elements from both turn based RPG and point and click games, layers it with heavy narrative. As soon as it started to feel repetitive, it slammed me with a bunch of story development. Really cool game, could have been heavier on the foreshadowing. One of my favorite things is that it heavily relies on text to convey what is happening in game. No bombastic animations or scenes. Great world building and writing. Recommend

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very straightforward and easy point and click game that I'd say feels more like a Telltale game in point and click form. However, I don't say that as a negative. While The Bookwalker isn't challenging, I'd call it a great palette cleanser game, where you get a cool experience that doesn't require a ton of effort to enjoy.The world of The Bookwalker reminds me a lot of the larger meta around the Myst universe, which you would have had to read the books to fully get the fiction of. Essentially, writers in this world don't just write books, but can actually enter and interact with them, as well as take things out and they appear to be treated as sacred works for that reason. This is very tightly regulated and controlled by the government as a result. You have run afoul of the law and don't know why at the beginning, but this becomes clear throughout the story as you enter different books with different missions.There are short first-person sequences in between books, but you spend very little time there. The majority of the levels take place in an isometric form, reminiscent of many point and click games. The puzzles are all very simple and there's no moon logic to be found here. The progression, discovery and conversations are what this game's really about. The art and especially the music are very well done and create a good sense of atmosphere, but also make things feel laid back and relaxing, despite the darker nature of the story. Each book is very different and you'll be in different environments, interacting with very different characters each time. There's definitely a critical path you'll be following, though there are extra objectives you can complete. Some of these are tied to achievements, but if they do impact the story at all, it's not clear how.A single run of the story takes about 7 or so hours and I think that's perfect because it means things don't overstay their welcome. Some people might find the relaxed and easy progression to be boring, but I really enjoyed this. I wouldn't want every game to play this way, but sometimes, it's nice to have something that's not high pressure and just gives you an enjoyable story and cool places to explore. If you're looking for that kind of experience, definitely give this a try.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Another hard one where I was kind of on the fence, but ultimately decided against a recommendation.The Bookwalker - Thief of Tales is a mixture between very few "Walking Simulator" Sections in 3D and mainly an isometric point and click adventure with very few tacked on turn based combat sections in it.The premise sounds intriguing but in the end the Game didn't do much with it.I think I'll just ramble a bit here.Technically it looks good (not great) but I had a few issues. In the First Person Sections - even though the Game is not really demanding - I had some stutters and also my PC got noticeably warm.Otherwise it ran fine.I really liked the Artstyle especially in the isometric sections and the story was really intriguing at first.But after a while the whole middle section felt kind of disconnected and pointless up until the end where it picks up again a little bit but also left me kind of disappointed when the credits rolled.The Story is just soso.There are not really puzzles to solve, you just click on stuff (which can be very relaxing) and read a bit of text. It is not overwhelming walls of texts that you read but just rather snippets and it just didn't feel coherent.As I said, Combat felt tacked on, I never died and it also felt kind of pointless to include combat at all. It was not meaningful and yeah, just couldn't wrap my head around why it's there in the first place.Apparently it is also a linear plot so your choices don't mean anything at all apart from maybe getting 1 or 2 different achievements and maybe 1 or 2 new lines of dialogue but the outcome - from what I read - seems to always be the same.After 9 hours of thoroughly exploring I also didn't feel the need for another playthrough.Verdict: Interesting premise, nice Artstyle but ultimately feels completely pointless. This is like a 5/10...
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Ironically, I would liken this game to a pretty darn good book.  It has some excellent story telling and very well written characters, and the world building is wonderful.  Honestly, I would've liked to have learned more about the world and the books within it, but the game only gives you enough to get a general picture rather than a detailed diagram.  The game was a bit short, which left me a bit wanting in the end, and although the big twist in the story was excellent, the ending was just a touch dissatisfying.  At the end of the day, I find myself wanting more, and I hope that this isn't the true end for this game.  True, adding more wouldn't really work for such a self contained story, the same could be said of several books I've read in the past, but that doesn't stop me from wanting more.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: This was truly a joy to play. I wanted a shorter experience without all the bloat of open worlds or overblown budgets, yet had an engaging story. This game was spot on for those things. And what a surprise ending as well! They managed to capture some of the worlds most iconic characters and include them in a delightful ending. Like a bow on top of an already wonderful present.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The Bookwalker is a game that at first is a little hard to pin down. But ultimately its gameplay boils down to that of a point-and-click adventure game with some occasional turn based combat.But to me the main selling point of The Bookwalker is its narrative and its worldbuilding. The writing is good, if occasionally a little clumsy (which I chalk up to translation issues), and explores some interesting ideas. The setting of the game is quite unique and presents what seems to be some kind of post-apocalyptic version of our world in which books are basically gateways to other worlds, and that writers are therefore very powerful.We take on the role of a man who has been magically hindered from writing due to the worst crime an author in this world can commit (although the discovery of what that crime was takes place deep into the story) and rather than work off his sentence legally he opts to become a Bookwalker. And that means that he steps into books and steals objects from them that he brings into the real world, but with the consequence that the plot of the book is forever changed.The game takes us through several books that explore different genres and themes and this gives the game a lot of welcome variety that keeps things fresh throughout the whole runtime.No single element of the game excels, but they're all tied together neatly by an engaging plot. As the credits rolled after a satisfying ending I felt pleased about my time spent with The Bookwalker.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. It's such a fun concept to go into the books. I also like how the art/perspective changes depending if you're in the real world or a book. The story was interesting; the game play was fun. The only small complaint I have applies to the steam deck, since I didn't play this on my PC. Sometimes the controls were off when maneuvering the MC around the rooms in the book in order to get the interaction prompts. Usually I just had to make a large circle and come back to the spot, so it wasn't a huge deal. Otherwise, it played flawlessly on steam deck.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: After doing 2 playthroughs of The BookWalker I can say that this game has an interesting concept of jumping into books, exploring those stories and stealing items from those worlds while interacting with the book's inhabitants. It is a narrative-driven point-and-click adventure with some puzzles that somewhat looks and feels like Disco Elysium but with a smidgen of turn-based combat. The isometric level design and overall art style I found to be incredibly charming to look at especially the protagonist's head being reminiscent of that of an open book with the pages serving as his hair. I found all 6 books to be pretty interesting such as Book 2 and 3 that I was left wanting to explore more about them as these books felt more complete, while others felt that they lacked detail or too short. Besides the main character and his companion which I enjoyed, I felt there wasn't enough depth and exploration to the characters you encounter and for the ones that showed felt a bit more fleshed out, we weren't given nearly enough time to appreciate them. The time spent in each book should have been much longer to give us more time to interact with the characters and explore more about the world they inhabit.Combat is very simple and doesn't serve much of a purpose besides a means to deal with enemies to progress the story. It's a very simple turn-based combat that gives you 4 abilities to choose from as well as a few upgrades to those abilities along the way. I think cutting out the combat would have been a better option and to have engagement with enemies be entirely text-based similar to Disco Elysium where you are given dialogue options on how to approach a situation. Another gripe I had with the game was the lack of choice in the narrative as you're playing through each book. In the game you are given a few different options in  situations, for example, choosing to help out a character or just ignoring them and walking away. My initial thought was that these choices would change the outcome but ultimately it has very little to no effect at all in each story and even more so by the end of the game.Overall I enjoyed my time with this game, despite seeming to be overly critical of the game-play and the story. It is a short but sweet game that will take 6-7 hours to do 1 play through, I think its worth giving a try for the price. I've read that the game pass version of the game has had some issues but haven't seen if they've been patched or not, but personally I didn't encounter any issues buying the game and playing it through Steam. The game has an incredibly interesting concept that I would love to see the developers continue exploring in a sequel or spin-off.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is absolutely worth playing. I want to get that out of the way right now. I have quibbles, and issues, but overall, definitely worth getting, even at full price.That being said, it does feel both short and rushed. The character development between chapters seems to be missing, with the main character switching his attitude towards characters on a dime. I'm not sure if this is because the writing for these missing character developing moments isn't there, or was cut, but the story as a metanarrative (like what the game is really trying to do) it's a little weak.The gameplay is pretty good if you like Planescape: Torment, or any other game that has taken inspiration from that. My only issue is that I wish there were more of it, more branching paths, more silly dialogue options, but I also understand how difficult it is to compound on systems like that, so that's fine.The deuteragonist was a nice touch, and I was a fan of the epilogue, but there was surprisingly little dialogue between the two characters after the first couple chapters.So, to wrap up, I would like this game a lot more if it were to expand on what's already there, but as is, it is absolutely worth your time and I really enjoyed myself.

_childDocuments_.review: as an aspiring writer, I recommend this game wholeheartedly to anyone who enjoys a unique twist on tropes in classical fiction.  [readers & writers will love this game]you play as an ex-writer, who embarks on an 'Inception'(film) like journey into 7 Folkloresque stories, each spanning 25-45mins.a casual semi-choice matters game with rpg elements that requires reading, and exploring.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I usually think that graphics come secondary to many other aspects of the game, but I'll make a notable exception this time. The small little details that are on every single map of the game are akin to a paining; the relatively slow movement speed of your character make it more poignant; it was a treat to wander through such a carefully detailed world, each one crafted to fit its environment so nicely, revealing little tidbits of world building that dialog doesn't touch upon, but sometimes insinuates.Graphics aside, the world is a very interesting one. One where writers have god-like powers within books, and where creativity is a commodity. I would gladly read a book or watch a show with that premise alone. I can't say the same about the characters. They're consistent and fairly deep, but their motivations don't quite convince me. That is to say, my actions within the game (being on the ruthless side) didn't reflect well with the dialog of the protagonist, who just seemed momentarily ashamed of the actions I was forcing upon him and then quickly forgot about them and reverted them.I understand the monumental task it would be make more diverging routes in a game like this, but I would preferred a bit of a nod toward playing a game more on the selfish side. The only other negative thing I can say is that it was a little too obvious who your partner was all along. I can't discuss more about that without spoiling it, and maybe other people haven't read the relevant books, so I'll leave it like that.That's not to say I'm displeased. I did not only like the art. Despite my criticism of very minor things about the characters, the development of the plot caught me about chapter 3. It was a bit of a slow burn, but I didn't mind. It was quite exciting to discover where all was going, although I will admit that the ending was a bit... odd? Boring. It was a little too boring. Either a tragic, a happier, or a more action-oriented ending would have fit much better. It feels like the protagonist just went on without doing nothing, having learned little, resolved no injustices, and wasted the vast majority of his life.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I've been really enjoying this game so far! The writing is sharp, with humor that lands well, and the atmosphere is perfectly set. The premise of infiltrating books to "steal" a unique item for a mysterious employer is engaging and adds a clever twist to the gameplay.Each session is about 1 to 2 hours [so far], focusing on one book at a time, which keeps things moving at a good pace without feeling overwhelming. With six books to explore the game delivers a solid experience in well-timed segments. The dystopian backdrop creates an atmospheric feel that pulls you into the game’s world without needing to spell everything out. I’d highly recommend it to anyone who loves well-crafted stories with a strong atmospheric feel!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: *Standing ovation, credits roll.*Fantastic work! Nice and easy puzzles that don't get frustrating, while giving you a few options to do things your way. There isn't a lot of combat, but where it does show up it's quite decent. But where this game shines is the story, presentation and atmosphere. This is a really well written plot, characters, and the execution is awesome. Makes me think of Disco Elysium or Planescape Torment, but lighter and more approachable without leveling and RPG mechanics getting in the way, while still executing a great experience.When I played the developer's previous game, The Final Station, I knew this team has potential. And I'm so glad they didn't disappoint.I wish them the best of luck in future projects. Just... um... let's hope there are no "Game Walkers" out there. Heh ^^
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: At first sight this game gives a feeling of Disco Elysium, with all that items/NPC to interact with, a narrator seems to know everything yet chooses to keep quiet and only give guidance in need. 10 mins later I figured out, no, this is just another linear game that asks players to be an errand boy running back and forth, finishing requests with little outlets. As a writer, player will have different identities and walk into each book, try to deal with the problem and bring back essential items to reality. Honestly, if developer focuses on put items between reality/fantasy into use this could be a fun game, however each book is as plain as an expanding of an article without an ending, rather than a standalone book with proper plot, characters has little/no personality, and no more info is given about the items you bought from/into the book.I have so many questions in each book. Like, identity and background of the scientist? Why is Thor's hammer in a factory? The function of wand, and a magic school needs an outsider handyman? With so many plot holes yet the game offers another new book for the player to enter, I couldn't bear anymore. Books written like this won't sell well, either.I stopped playing after book 4. Maybe eventually the game will explain from the first to the last game as a whole, maybe not, but based on what I'd experienced I don't expect an answer. No, I do not recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Super creative game with a unique concept and very diverse short stories in an isometric style. The real world is designed in a first-person perspective, and you can freely move around your house and switch between the book and the real world at any time. The stories themselves vary in length and offer an immersive gaming experience! I can only encourage everyone to try the game, even if you're initially unsure due to the style, as I was. On top of that, there's a great atmosphere! My only criticism is that unfortunately, your decisions only partially influence the story. It would be nice if decisions had a stronger impact on the course of the story. Nevertheless, an all-around awesome game! 👍👍👍
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: This game keeps you entertained giving you different worlds to exploreAs a person, who quite frequently abandons games I can say, that this one doesn't let you off it's hook until the end. It isn't a long game, but it doesn't need to be, if anything it's better this wayI was a bit frustrated cuz there are no save slots you can come back to(you can, however come back to chapters/books). Sure, the game is linear(choices affect the end of some chapters, but not the ending overall), but it would be nice to be able to check other dialoge options/complete achivements you missed without much extra time neededBut despite this con, this became one of my favorite games, I really recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the atmosphere of this game. Everything is so well put together, it felt pleasant from start to finish. I enjoyed each books and each of their universe settled in a detailed and very well articulated story. It's old concepts but each time revitalized by a great storyline and an unique gameplay.I also loved the connection between your exploration of the books and your interactions in the real world, with all the details hidden in between.Special mention also to the french translation being of high quality, you can clearly feel the interest for the game and story into it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The game does not feel finished, it's obvious combat system is way too easy to be what the devs intended it to be, some art is completely lacking (portraits of important NPCs while non-important ones get theirs, animations, modelisation of PC being in another state...) and the story is very linear (I don't think it's a problem but the game  has this vibe of making you think your actions have consequences: they don't). BUT, I recommend this game because I see the efforts the dev team made. I know budget and time are aweful and  they were probably cutting features and watching they ambition having to be cut down too. I liked the universe even though I would have loved more lore and more explanations for it to feel more cohesive. I loved the relationship between Etienne & Roderick, I saw some comments saying it was not good, I feel it was. Would have been better with voice-acting though, the trailer was kinda showing that there would be voice acting...I'm disappointed by marketing. Trailer from a year ago feels like a scam since lots of the content that is presented is not in the game. Trailer from a month ago must have cost a pretty penny and has nothing to do with the story, the content, the atmosphere, the personality of the protagonist. I guess if those trailer had been more truthful, I would have been more happy with the game. Please publishers, stop doing that, give more money for the production, do more gameplay trailers. I recommend playing if you want an adventure in a strange and compelling universe and you don't mind considering indie devs as people doing their best with big ideas and little money.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: In general, it's a good game to play. Great game play design, I really enjoy the exploring and turn based combat in the game. And the theme of game is very attractive to me. I was immersed in the  book walker's worldview in the game. As a heavy narrative game, you won't be lost in the game. Every purpose is clear. You'll be guided step by step in the game, which performed well in numerous heavy narrative game. But there are still some negative aspects in the game. The game laid a lot of groundwork but I didn't get enough game content at the end of game, which really disappoints me. It also makes me feel it's a demo. The words and stories in game is interesting but not deep and meaningful enough, which did not so well. In other words, you can finish the whole game even if you don't read the text at all. At last, I want to say it's a game with great potential. I'm looking forward to the sequel or DLC of the game very much. I'll give yes to this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales is a wonderful narrative game with an endlessly imaginative premise that hooked its fangs into me and held my attention throughout the entirety of the campaign. Each book you delve into is fundamentally different and provides a small slice of a universe that could very well be a separate title on its own, but – like a literary tourist of sorts – you hop in, do what you need to do, then leave, thus lending the game a satisfyingly episodic structure where nothing ever overstays its welcome. The writing is solid enough, and the light RPG elements and combat mechanics are simple but competently done, never really feeling out of place. Lastly, while the storyline and its themes – particularly Etienne’s past – could’ve used some more fleshing out, The Bookwalker still manages to stick the landing with an epilogue that puts the perfect period at the end of a genuinely entertaining journey. All in all, if the premise alone catches your attention, I’d very much recommend checking this one out.For more honest indie game reviews, check out our Curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, just a truly original and all around great point and click adventure game (without the actual pointing and clicking mind you). Really creative story that finds a unique way to genre hop between fantasy, sci-fi, horror, and more using literary narrative as a plot device. Every new chapter gives it new life and keeps it feeling fresh. As the game goes its fairly straightforward and almost holds your hand since the story is the main star. None of the puzzles sent me to the internet for clues and there's a reoccurring turn based battle system that felt engaging while remaining simple and easy enough I never had to worry about it holding me back. Again, great characters and solid story that felt immensely  satisfying when the credits rolled. Also just incredibly beautiful visually with such a unique style and vision all its own. Whatever these devs do next, I'm in. Great stuff here.
