_childDocuments_.review: Overall Bookwalker is well written and really fun to play. Even if he can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ sometimes the main character is very relatable, fostering empathy throughout the gameplay. The diverse and unique settings are presented in a very creative way which adds a lot of deapth to the experience making it a standout feature of the game. However the illusion of a butterfly effect mechanic and the inconsequential fights somewhat diminish the gameplay's impact, cause it fast becomes clear to the player that the decisions taken have limited to zero impact on the gampley and if you die or win the game just go on as always. So at the third fight you encouter you just find them a distraction to the narration itself. So in conclusion Bookwalker stands out as a very good storytelling that would be very enjoyble for players seeking pure narration game, nevertheless the unfulfilled primises of a dynamic decision system and lackluster combat mechanics make the game lose some good points. In the end I think those features could be competely removed and the game would have been still a very enjoyable game if not better.

_childDocuments_.review: a couple negatives:  - there's some sensitivity issues, in that the max sensitivity is much slower than desired; but it's only during unimportant phases of the game, so i can look past it. i am using arch linux as my OS in case it's different on windows or mac.  - without spoiling too much, the ending felt quite rushed in my opinion, maybe the devs were running low on funds and had to cut it short?  other than that, however, this game is really good. i recommend it, despite the listed flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The Bookwalker can often be fairly simple in its gameplay and the combat never gets complex enough that a clever player can't finagle their way into coming out of every fight untouched by the end, but there's something truly special about this experience, even beyond the incredible story. This is a game that you should sink your time into and explore, as it truly shines when you engage with the sidestories in each book. There's a lot of potential to be cruel and the game itself often forces the player into that territory as a matter of plot, but there is too a great breadth of possibilities for empathy and a fascinating exploration of the existences of fictional worlds and characters. I love this title and I want to return to it again and again.

_childDocuments_.review: It is rare when I leave a negative review. Even more so, when it is a small indie game, however I feel completely justified on this one. I was really happy to try out this game, as it was luring me with the promise of a good, fresh story, even despite negative comments about tech state of the game or clunky controls.The reviews mentioning gameplay issues were absolutely right, but I am more than willing to disregard those in favor of good story and narrative.This game have none.The premise is very creative, reminds me of the Inkheart movie, but seems to be a fresh take about the topic. Additionally it includes a hint of depressing dystopia world, that the hero is fighting against. Great ground for grand tale. Player have no real choice about protagonists view of the world and if we choose any choice that is against the vision of the creator of this game, we get a lecture why our choice is bad. _childDocuments_.review: "The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales" is an intriguing narrative-driven adventure that cleverly blends elements of fantasy, mystery, and a touch of literary magic. In this game, you step into the shoes of a "bookwalker" – someone with the unique ability to literally enter the pages of a book and interact with its world and characters.The game's visual style is a delightful fusion of the quaint charm of old books and the vibrant energy of the worlds within them. It’s like stepping into a series of paintings, each one telling a story that’s both familiar and fantastically new. The transition from the real world to the literary realms is seamless, capturing the essence of falling into a good book.Gameplay in "The Bookwalker" is a mix of exploration, puzzle-solving, and narrative choices. As you delve into various books, you encounter puzzles that require both wit and creativity to solve. It's like being a detective in a world where logic is intertwined with the fantastical elements of literature.The story is where "The Bookwalker" truly shines. As you journey through different stories, you're not just a passive observer; your actions and choices shape the narrative. This mechanic is a clever nod to the way readers interpret and internalize stories, making each player's experience unique.Character interactions are rich and thought-provoking, often challenging you to think deeply about the themes and morals of the stories you're exploring. Dialogues are well-written, offering a blend of humor, drama, and philosophical musings that keep conversations engaging.One of the most captivating aspects is the variety of literary worlds you explore. Each book is a different genre, offering a new set of challenges and characters. From the high seas of adventure novels to the intricate plots of mystery stories, the game keeps you on your toes with ever-changing settings and scenarios.However, "The Bookwalker" isn't without its challenges. Navigating the literary worlds can sometimes be as perplexing as understanding a classic novel’s symbolism on the first read. This complexity adds to the game's charm but might be daunting for those looking for a more straightforward experience."The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales" is a love letter to literature, offering a unique adventure that's as intellectually stimulating as it is entertaining. It’s an ideal game for those who love books, enjoy narrative-driven gameplay, and relish the idea of diving into the pages of a story to uncover its secrets.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly my only suggestion for the game developers is to charge more for this game!! Such a great gem of a game that is so rare these days. _childDocuments_.review: A pretty darned original adventure-game by the makers of The Last Station. In a fantasy world in which writers are legally regulated magicians who build stories by transporting themselves to another reality that they can mold and shape, a writer who broke the law is put on Writers Block by the authorities. He plans to get out of it by illegally diving into the world of other authors books to exact treasures and ideas from their fiction... to sell to other authors to put in THIER fictional universes. Plagiarism as a magical, reality hopping heist.  It's allegorical as hell, but pretty fun. Just be aware that it's a LINEAR adventure game, even if it tries not to feel like one by thrwoing choices and rpg mechanics. In this regard it is better than other modern Advernture games with a dash of rpg like Sunday Gold in that it never gets in the way. It's a narrative puzzle adventure game even if it might seem like more at times. Be aware that you dont really have much choice and you will have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Book Walker" is an excellent game with a weak final act, but its sense of immersion and storytelling skills more than make up for any issues. Rather than discussing the entire game, I'd like to highlight one of its most impressive elements: the hub apartment.Even though you don't explicitly learn where Etienne lives, the apartment provides key context. You may not know the specifics of his life, but the apartment reveals key details and settings that let you know about his situation. The grimy bathroom, the single cot bed, the kids playing in the distance. While you don't know much about the society he lives in, you understand it is bureaucratic through clues such as his imprisonment and his bathroom door being locked by the state due to unpaid bills. One striking detail is the dried herbs hanging in the hallway, along with the shared kitchen for the apartments. We import so much understanding of the culture just through that touch. Every book in the game is crafted with this level of detail and consideration. By the end, I was thoroughly engrossed and sad to leave the world of Etienne and Roderick.

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Beautiful isometric 3d graphics with a unique shader that makes them look like they're painted. There are lots of details on objects and places, nice color palette and atmospheric lighting conditions.- Amazingly designed surreal world. Each book that you visit is a whole new universe with its own style, design and places to explore. It's so imaginative and offers tensive, mysterious, dark atmosphere.- Great lore and clever main concept. You're a writer with the ability to travel inside books and fictional worlds. It takes inspiration from various well known tales and makes you be curious about what's coming next. The story feels a bit fragmented, but the storytelling and pacing are excellent and immersive.- Well written. Graphic novel style of narration and descriptions fit perfectly to the concept of traveling into books. Text helps you fully understand what's happening, the expressions and feelings of the characters. Dialogues are amazing with great sense of humor. You never get bored of reading.- Unique characters with vivid personalities. Some of them are really unforgettable. The protagonists are absolutely lovable and the relationship between them is fantastically crafted with a lot of high quality humor and memorable moments.- Gameplay has issues but also some interesting ideas. It combines nicely elements of point and click adventures, pen and paper games and RPGs with good balance. You use items to solve small puzzles, but also loot things form the world to craft useful tools. It's interesting that at some points you have to go back to reality in order to find things that can help you. - Nice, calm, dark music that fits great to every world and moment.- Although it doesn't get deep enough, it has its own unique way to open some philosophical, social and political discussions giving the player interesting food for thought.The bad- Turn based battles are simplistic and extremely easy. Enemies look generic, there are only a few mechanics or attacks so battles are getting boring after a while. They needed much more work and don't really offer much to the gameplay.- It has great lore, but the main story lacks coherence and feels a little bit fragmented. Side stories not always contribute to main plot. Also I found the first two books a little bit rushed with no major events.- Puzzles are fairly easy. They could have been more complex and challenging offering more creative ways of using items and tools. Most of them are just unlocking doors, crates and finding batteries. - Protagonist's slow walking can be annoying sometimes because there is a lot of exploration and backtracking.

_childDocuments_.review: What a cool game. There's just something about the idea and the world that really hit right and I played it straight through like a long movie.Bookwalker is a point and click adventure with a lot of window dressing. What I mean by that, is that at its heart it's about walking around, picking stuff up and talking to people to solve puzzles; and while you do that, you craft items, get into turn-based encounters and occasionally borrow items from neighbors. I won't say that any puzzle was particularly difficult, but moreso because there are very few if any fail states the choices and mistakes you make will influence the outcome of the area you're in. In that regard it feels more like a narrative adventure, which is not a knock against it because what I played was very enjoyable.The game pulls a neat trick by taking place both in first and third person. When you are in your apartment, you walk around in first person. When inside a book, you have your isometric third person view. This doesn't really change gameplay much, but it does break up sequences nicely and more importantly does a lot to really make the books you enter feel like a different world.Surprising no one, The Bookwalker is about a man who walks in books. Etienne, a writer who has been shackled by the writing police for writing crimes, is looking at being unable to write for 30 years. Unhappy with this, his friend suggests some...not quite legal activities to get the shackles taken off by some not so upstanding individuals. As a writer, Etienne is able to go into books and remove objects from them, objects that can change the story of any book they are taken from or inserted in. However, the shackles placed on him limit his writer powers so he often needs to move through the book's story and interact with its characters to acquire the item he needs.The premise is the shining light of this, and the world it takes place in is pretty fascinating. Don't ask too many questions though because while their is some really good fleshing out of how everything works, it's less concerned with explaining things and more focused on making the game interesting and fun. Nothing egregious to me stood out, just that sometimes you have to accept things at face value to let the story continue. The way writing works, how the writers of Etienne's time aren't the "original writers" and what the governing bodies that surround this world and publishing companies that scheme and control writer's works are all wonderful tidbits that are left mysteries. I wouldn't say no to a more expanded world in a sequel but as all you get for the game we have, it's more than enough to keep you intrigued without feeling like there are plot holes.The game is also visually wonderful, with a varied amount of set pieces considering you go into a number of drastically different books. I loved the look of them because it was always detailed and drawn so nicely. The only strike against it I had was that sometimes you would pixel hunt for interactable objects because there is no indicator of what you can or cannot click on without mousing over it. Luckily there's nothing so small as to be overlooked or hard to find.The Bookwalker is a tight 6 hours of story that I enjoyed following the whole way. It's not the hardest point and click game, nor the most in depth, but what is there is extremely fun and rewarding to see to its conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: The Bookwalker is a neat little point and click adventure game with cool ideas, and some experimental stuff going on.The gist of the plot is that the protagonist broke WRITERS LAW and is staring down the barrel of decades of HARD LABOR working for a PUBLISHER, unable to write anything himself or even able to associate with other writers. The only alternative available is risky, extremely illegal, morally dubious, and very cool: taking on jobs where you jump INTO a story, steal something valuable, and get out alive.The game is divided into specific chapters where you're assigned a book and an item to steal, and a big part of the draw for me was that there was a big shift in setting for each book. While you could argue that the tone of the game might not change that much throughout, you will be going to new and interesting places each chapter. Each chapter involves you exploring, making gear from stuff you find, and solving fairly simple puzzles. One of the things that makes The Bookwalker stand out from other point and click games is that there are turn based battles in them. Not particularly indepth or difficult but between skills that do different things costing ink to use and fighting multiple dudes at once you can't really sleepwalk through them either. There's other stuff that was actually a surprise for me so I'm not gonna get into it, but I really liked it.Speaking of difficulty I didn't find the game particularly hard, both in terms of what the game wanted from me, and also that I wasn't at the mercy of confusing moon logic at all times. You know what you need to do, its just about being able to do it and then doing it. You also have a partner of sorts who you can talk too whenever you want, both for plot stuff and a reminder of what you need to do, which can help you stay on track if you forget after leaving the game and coming back. The most frustrating apart actually was that there were things that I could interact with that I didn't notice right away. It doesn't reach pixel hunting levels of nonsense, but I do wish there was a button that highlighted things in the environment you can interact with.How the game is structured also lends itself to playing it in bite sized chunks, which isn't a big deal generally but just something that I always appreciate. Overall I think The Bookwalker is pretty good, not amazing, but a nice little game.

It takes a few to get used to, and it can be repetitious at times (having to craft the same items for all of the books rather than unique items for each story was a bit tiresome) but the STORY is what makes the adventure fun! I highly recommend this game for all fans of books!! it's a quick playthrough that will have you entertained for hours!!!

_childDocuments_.review: The Bookwalker was okay. The setting allows some people to jump in and out of books, and perhaps change them, or bring back things to the real world. Because of that, being a writer is a really heavily supervised position. Your main character was just disallowed from writing for 30 years for some unknown reason, but by doing illegal book heists where you go into books and grab valuable items, the black market is looking to get your shackles off you soon as long as you do what they say. Gameplay-wise, most the game is walking around doing puzzles so you can get to newer areas. They aren't very hard, and you have a little assistant to point you in the right direction anyways. It's more about enjoying short stories than actually trying at difficult puzzles. There's also a little bit of combat which is turn based, but again, not very serious. Also the upgraded shield is bugged. It says it persists between rounds but it doesn't. The main selling point of The Bookwalker is enjoying the worlds of several short novellas while also uncovering the greater overarching story of your character.

_childDocuments_.review: A point-and-click (light)/mystery game with a unique story and a lot of interesting ideas and concepts. I didn't think I'd like the characters as much as I ended up doing, and by the end, I was much more invested than I initially anticipated. It's a great game that, with a playtime of about 6 hours, might serve you as the fresh & excellent change of style and pace it was for me. Is it perfect? Not by a long shot. Parts of the game feel a bit tedious, and some mechanics are not really all that interesting. Importantly, most of the "puzzle" elements come from having to run between rooms multiple times. And I'm afraid I'm not as happy with the ending as I thought I'd be at around 60% of the game, when one of its biggest plot points is revealed. I'm afraid I thought I knew where they were going with the story at that point, and they didn't, and I still liked their conclusion, but not as much as I anticipated. The RPG elements in this are also fairly minimal, and a lot of dialogue choices are actually just dead ends that oftentimes force you to pick a different option after all.All of that being said, despite all its shortcomings, I loved this game and its story, and will definitely play it again. I really enjoyed the characters, the social critique and commentary on writing and publishing, and the clever plays on tropes, words and story beats. This is a smart game that knows what it wants to be and manages to create and maintain an exciting atmosphere all the way through.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a nice little game with an intriguing plot.The backstory is told in bits and pieces throughout the experience, but never bluntly, so as to keep the mystique until close to the end.The switch between first person and isometric view is a nice touch which ads separation between the "real" world and the other worlds. I only wish that the parts between the jumps were a bit more fleshed out as to allow us a closer look at our main characters world. It seems very interesting and it left me wanting to know more about the original writers and the world at large.I really hope that there will be a sequel as this is a really interesting concept that I have only experienced previously in Myst.

_childDocuments_.review: An engaging adventure game for the people who love books.  The first thing thats noticable is the dual nature of the game's graphics. The "real world" is rendered in the full 3D from 1st person perspective and it is a drab and depressive dystopian police state. The segments inside books are rendered as an isometric 3rd person, more similar to classical point and click adventures. These environments and characters stick to the theme of the book and look more colorful and stylized. The voice acting is extremely minimal, but the music sets the mood nicely.  For the most time, the game is basically a classical adventure, without outright puzzles, relying  more on exploration and interactions with objects and characters. There is a caveat though: the game is significantly non-linear and with autosaves only. Every decision sticks, so it really does not pay to select interactions without thought. Valuable tools can be destroyed if used incorrectly or fights may break out because of uncautios replies in dialogues and there is no going back. The fights are another break from the genre: they are turn based, often avoidable and neither particularly engaging nor bothersome.  The story follows a disgraced writer in a world where it is possible to infiltrate a story inside book and extract plot relevant items and even characters as a form of supernatural plagiarism (and vandalism, since the original book is altered in the process). The overworld has strong dystopian overtones and clearly takes inspiration from Eastern block police states. The books are more like archetypes of stories, making nods to several important genres and tropes of fiction. There are two main characters and I enjoyed their interaction and development and uncovering their backstory.

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely an old school point-and-click adventure that bets itself on the narrative.  And for the most part it bets well.  There's a cool mechanic where reality and fiction are separated by camera perspectives and really sells the idea that the books and the world of the bookwalker are two different places.  The 'books' you travel in are all very interesting.  In fact often I felt annoyed that I couldn't stay and play *those* games instead.  Not everything is great.  Re-used assets and intermittent blank character portraits give the sense that this game needed more time in the oven.  And I'm not sure how I keep getting knocked out in the last book when I've proven my combat prowess against the police.  Nonetheless Bookwalker is a complete package and worth the play.

_childDocuments_.review: Spoilers for chapter 1 follow.I love the distinctive aesthetic of The Bookwalker, and I'm enjoying learning about the characters and the setting. The premise reminds me of the Inkheart Trilogy of books, where certain characters have a hereditary talent to read books aloud and make their contents come to life, and later in the series they can enter books outright. In The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales, it seems that maybe all (or at least a significant number of) writers have this talent? And knowledge of these literary travelers' (or "walkers") exploits has resulted in widespread provisions in the publishing industry--such as requiring authors to spell pounds as "poudns" to prevent people from spontaneously generating money from literature. This is corroborated by the black market demand for walkers to steal legendary artifacts from books--though not for use in the real world, but for re-use in someone else's book? I'm not entirely sure I understand yet why this is necessary when one can presumably write a few lines to similar effect...? It seems like the devs are using this framework to create an extended metaphor for plagiarism, which I'm not opposed to. Here, the act of creative theft causes actual harm to the original source material (the MacGuffin item, once pilfered, vanishes from the text of the book it came from, though whether this persists through all print copies of the book remains to be seen).There are some distracting ludonarrative dissonance moments, like when the hint function advises you to interact with a cauldron you've yet to encounter, or a character's name is spoiled by the UI before he is properly introduced--and the scene where you learn his name is actually quite cute, so there is something lost there by revealing it before the intended moment, I think. Also, coming TOO close to interactable objects makes the prompt to interact with them vanish? I'm hopeful these issues will be resolved with future patches, but as they're minor enough and relatively typical to the medium, I'm learning to tolerate them for the time being.So far I've enjoyed most of the writing. The main framework and primary setting feels a little like Inkheart meets 1984, which I'm excited to engage with and continue learning about. Upon entering a book, it seems as if Etienne is subject to something like literary callbacks and the "rule of 3"s: at the very beginning of his first job, Etienne injures his knee, and further complications and misfortunes surrounding that injury befall him to humorous effect. Having given praise to the humor, I will say there are moments where I feel the sincerity of a scene is undercut by nonsensical humor--like the finale of chapter 1. Not only is an attempt at compassionate compromise marked with several bizarre and extraneous details, your companion, the person you're ostensibly compromising FOR, does not acknowledge the outcome of your choice in the second chapter(!!!) beyond begrudging you for putting your foot in your mouth when you argued it with him. Bro, I did this for you... I know you weren't watching but please acknowledge that I jeopardized my liberty and livelihood to make you happy. ):I restarted my game, also, because I broke my lockpicks in chapter 1 and missed an opportunity to open a locked chest as a consequence, and also I couldn't return my neighbor's sledgehammer and assumed I missed an opportunity to do so in chapter 1. But no, you are just doomed to inconvenience your neighbors and suffer the indignity of being the guy who never returns the tools he borrows. 😩EDIT: I wrote this between chapters 1 and 2 when prompted by Steam after 3 hours of play, and I'm happy to report that the writing amped up and rose to the occasion of all the story's theming and moral ambiguity in subsequent chapters. So while I was frustrated by some unusual choices and some jokes that fell flat in chapter 1, I'm really glad I stuck with it and played it all the way through the night, because I LOVE this game now, it rewired my brain, I'm obsessed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo only about a week before it came out and ended up loving the game. It was super fun and peaceful for me. Like other people have mentioned it has quite a bit of puzzles with a big storytelling element in and out of the book worlds. I've not played many games with turned-based fights, but I really liked it by the end of the game. I thoroughly enjoyed the friendship/banter between Etienne and Roderick, it made the whole game for me. The artwork and the constant switch between being in Etienne's apartment and the book worlds are amazing, I would definitely recommend you try it out. 10/10 Very entertaining game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Finished this just now and really enjoyed myself. If you're a fan of meta storytelling and anything that explores the horror of characters being stuck in a story someone is writing about them, you'll love this game. I liked some of the books the character visited more than others, but overall the writing was solid enough that I had a good time the whole way through. Also had absolutely zero issues playing this on the Steam Deck, worked perfectly out of the box with native controls!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing idea. The execution could have been a bit better, maybe with a bit more non linear way to approach things. Maybe closer to an immersive sim where, knowing that we are in a book, we can think about several approaches. But all in all it's an interesting little game that's well worth the small price tag !
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Good game with an interesting story, though a few shortcomings keep it from being great. It's beautifully realized, but a few aspects of the story don't seem well thought through or are too underdeveloped to convince. Puzzles are a bit too basic and the combat system is just ... there? A few narrative threads aren't followed after having been introduced, which adds to the impression this was somewhat rushed out the door. It's still engaging and makes you wonder what'll happen next, entertaining you until the very end.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've ever played. Gameplay, visuals, and story are admirable to say the least. But the direction the story goes and most importantly (to me) the writing for dialogue pushed this game above so many others. I felt a connection to the characters and their stories, as well as the NPCs' stories. The developers did a great job making our character's experiences in the books parallel with our experiences playing the game. Would highly recommend to anyone who appreciates more thoughtful, investigative, and exploratory games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful game. I think my only """""""""disappointment""""""" (*I'm not actually disappointed at all) is that there isn't more. Not like the game should be longer, I actually think it perfectly tells the story it was telling with brilliant pacing and amazing dialogue. The way that the world naturally explains itself through character dialogue is outstanding. But I just... wanna play more!! The idea, the game play loop, it's all EXTREMELY FUN. I hope there is DLC one day exploring another story in this universe, like Final Station had. That'd be perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely great game. Fairly short but at a price I think suits it. Visually great with a very interesting concept. Combat is by far the weakest point but its clear that it was in no way a focus of the game (think Disco Elysium with an incredibly simple turn based combat system). Everything else was really just amazing writing and storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Quite an intersting concept with the combination of point and click and first person view and engaging story. The level design for the point and click parts, which are the majority of the game, is absolutely beautiful. Great style and detail. Clear design, you don't search for an eternity with what parts of the room you can interact. The dialogue options can get a bit repetitive in a handful of situations where you return to a character several times, but it's not that big of a problem. There is no voice acting, which is not unexpected for a game with this kind of budget, but the writing gives a clear voice to the characters. I would have loved more interaction with the character's world to tie the story more together, but I really enjoyed the whole story. Haven't looked into how much the options influence the story, so I might do that in the future after I completed the story today. Very nice epilogue, really didn't expect that turn of events.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: What an excellent, evocative point-and-click adventure game! It lies at the intersection of Disco Elysium (dialogue, ambiance and music style) and Planescape Torment (graphics + Roderick reminds me of Morte). Its definitely a must-play for any fan of either of those two games. The idea of bookwalking serves as a great springboard for the developers to weave together different biomes (I think my favorite were books 3 and 6!).
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A very atmospheric and colourful experience. This game was shorter than I expected, but I had fun with what I got!Pros:-  Bookwalkers look insanely cool! Gold cosplay material right there. All the animations look smooth and polished, and the in-game art looks beautiful. Environments are unique and colourful. You'll enjoy how things keep switching up whenever you enter a new story.-  It's not overly complicated, but it is unique and intriguing. Especially Etienne's own personal journey. You will not be able to predict all the plot twists. However, whenever they  revealed, you won't be that surprised either. Short and sweet. I liked it!-  Roderick and Etienne are a dream team. I wish we got more time with them. Dialogue is good. Bad guys sound very evil, and our neighbour sounds very fed up with our shenanigans.-  The game runs smoothly; I didn't encounter any bugs or glitches. It was a joy running around just doing stuff. Puzzles are easy and obvious and don't take away from the narrative. There's zero chance you'll get stuck, but if you do - Roderick will help you out.Cons:-  Throughout the game, we get to experience multiple stories from which we try to extract unique and/or magical items. The idea is amazing and is executed fairly well. However, I wish we got more out of the 7 books we get to jump into. We always find ourselves on the outskirts of what's happening or right after the Big Event. This makes those individual stories feel a bit flat.-  I wish we had gotten more information on how the world of Etienne Quist functions. We get the general idea of who Bookwalkers are, some rules on how writing works in this universe, and what the big no-no's are. But it's not nearly enough to satisfy my curiosity. I want to know what happened to the Original Authors, how bookwalking came to be, how one  a Bookwalker. Lots of interesting questions and not nearly enough answers.Final score: 8.5/10. I had a great time, and I highly recommend you give this game a try!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique concept with subpar gameplay. The idea is genius and allows the devs to create pretty much anything they want. Gorgeous artstyle and all locations are well realized. The gameplay loop stays the same for the whole game. Get materials -> craft tools -> get quest items -> repeat, with some turn based fights in between. Wish gameplay changed between books, kind of like "The Hex" by Daniel Mullins. The combat is way too simplistic. You just spam your abilities with AOE that stun enemies and regen your mana. Puzzles are nice. Ending was kind of silly.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I am not the Point & Click fanatic. Not everybody on this planet is one. And not every game is capable of changing you into a P&C fanatic. But this game... Oh boy, it does at least kick you in the right direction. Despite the fact, that this game is pretty "young", I relly hope that the developers will create a sequel or at least a big DLC. I would be grateful. Whatever, buy this and play this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: It's own masterpieceThe idea and concept behind bookwalker is unique. I hope they come out with more content by continuing past the main story. I would love to keep playing levels inside these books. For example, a prequel about how Roderick ended up where he was. I love that I can also self-pace the game and play one chapter a day. The story's ending was also very good and it was compelling to not know what happens until the end. As I love books, this game was my most memorable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved The Final Station, you'll love this game. Interesting combination of puzzles and book stories. Mysterious plot will pull you (literally) into book stories, where you re-live the story and steal powerful artefacts to earn you writing freedom. Game has good 7 hours of gameplay to offer with 6 different books (stories). Achievements are fun to do and allows you to just have fun and not grind anything instanely (and at the same time they are not free to earn).If you just want to chill out, I can totally recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I was planning to first finish the game and then write a review but i'm in the third book and the verdict is already clear. This is a unique masterpiece. The stories are so different, interesting and beautiful... you'll have a great time. The graphics are super, the colour palette as well. The soundtrack is top level. The gameplay mechanics are very well designed, making your life easy, letting you enjoy the story. This is a 10/10. Do a favor to yourself and buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys short adventure games with well-done narratives and some puzzles to go along with. It took me about 7 hours to beat the game. It caught my eye during the Future Games Show stream and I played it on my Steamdeck shortly after release. The game runs perfectly fine on Steamdeck, by the way, so don't worry about the missing "verified" or "playable" status on the shop page as of now. To me, The Book Walker was one of the best games I played this year, so I'm looking forward to anything new coming from the developers in the years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following this project for a while since the demo, the world-building is amazing and the old feel of the real world is like an old library or bookstore. Without spoiling much you really come to understand Etienne's plight, and are with him every wacky, scary, and interesting step in his journey through worlds for his own personal freedom. One of the best indie experiences I have ever had and I hope to see more from this world!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about this game was, in my opinion, amazing. From the premise and characters, to the ideas brought to light in the game, to the literary references and pieces of inspiration found throughout the game. The only thing i did not like about this game was the ending but other than that i would say that this was one of the better indie games i have played.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: i really really enjoyed this game! its premise and how that ties into the gameplay felt new to me and kept me engaged pretty much throughout the entire 11-ish hours that it took me to finish it. however, the ending felt abrupt and some of the twists that led up to it didn't work as well as they could have.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful merging of both literature and video games, this is what the concept of storytelling is all about. The twists on real life novels, the emphasis on "show, don't tell", and the association of the first person perspective as "safe" then breaking the illusion... I can tell this was inspired by many, many forms of visual and literal arts. As a student of both literature and design this game satisfied my expectations in what I look for in a video game. I'm looking forward for more. Thank you <3
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Well, its not *bad*, graphics looks decent (at least in books, where you spend most of the game). Story is... alright? Quite short (4h), and different choices didn't look influential enough to warrant a replay. Funny thing, for a character/writer that is complaining about badly detailed characters in books, main hero is not that deep or well-written. Random tidbits he is giving about the world leave more questions than answers. Overall it's an alright game for a reasonable price. Check it out if you have some spare money.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking forward to this since playing the demo and it did not disappoint. It's chock full of mystery and has the coolest world behind it. The turn-based combat is super easy, so don't let that part turn you away. (I'm someone who normally hates turn-based combat and it was fine.) There are different options for how you handle things, but they do all kinda funnel you towards the same major plot points.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A very beautiful game with interesting characters, stories and world.It's pretty short but the price is well adjusted to this.It's very easy but it didn't really bother me that much.I feel there could be done more for some stories. For example the worldbuilding could be explained even more while you play (not just text dump of course). And the story about the downstairs neighbor could have been expanded a bit more.In general, after I finished the game, I still feel like there is some secret I haven't found or another ending I haven't unlocked. But based on the achievements I think that's it.I know I am saying mostly negative things but this is because I really enjoyed the game and I wished there was more of it. I will definitely check their other game as well.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Charming and fun! The world of writers that the game is set in is the highlight for me since it allows for infinite setting possibilities, and it doesn't try to explain the rules that make the outside world so interesting. I've only done one play through so far, but I plan on going back through it because I feel like there are things that I missed that I really want to find for myself!
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun story and setting, but the gameplay is lacking. The combat can be gamed very easily, especially with some of the later upgrades, and the puzzles, which is this game's main form of gameplay, aren't actually puzzles so much as they are walking from point A to point B. If you're coming into this game looking for a riveting turn-based tactics game or some challenging puzzles, turn back now. If you want to engage with a fun narrative and don't mind the writers not being perfect, then this is a good game to but.
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

_childDocuments_.review:
Etienne Quist, a once-acclaimed writer, loses his ability to write after he is found guilty of an unspeakable crime. In an attempt to reclaim his lost status, he is approached by a criminal boss with a cunning offer. All he needs to do is locate and steal a series of legendary items from books. 

Delve into remarkable book worlds, each with its unique rules and challenges. Should anyone stand between you and the artifacts, be prepared to persuade, deceive, or even engage them in combat.

Each quest thrusts you into an entirely new world: medieval prison, snow-capped mountain, futuristic spaceship and more. Meet the inhabitants of each book and use them to achieve your goals - after all, they are not really alive... or are they?
_childDocuments_.name: The Bookwalker: Thief of Tales

name: G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout
detailed_description: G.I. Joe and Cobra are back! G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout is a classic team-based third-person shooter where you play as your favorite characters from Team G.I. Joe and Team Cobra. Experience the action from both sides as you help G.I. Joe restore order and lead Cobra to world domination.  G.I. JOE VS COBRA - Play with 12 of your favorite characters from both sides including Snake Eyes, Duke, Roadblock, Storm Shadow, Cobra Commander, Destro and more in 4-player PvP and across 17 epic campaign story missions.  Includes voice acting for over 20 iconic characters in the G.I. Joe universe. COMBAT TOOLS - Fight for your side with 18 awesome weapons, 36 weapon skins, 12 alternate character skins and a series of uniquely devastating ultimate abilities. LEGENDARY FRANCHISE - Take control of the iconic G.I. Joe Persuader and Cobra H.I.S.S. tanks in your battle across classic locations like the USS Flagg and Cobra Headquarters. CO-OP & PVP MULTIPLAYER - Play the campaign with a friend in local co-op, or compete in 4-player PvP local matches in 4 Multiplayer Modes: Capture the Flag, Assault, King of The Hill, and Deathmatch Arena. *Local multiplayer requires the use of Steam compatible controllers connected to your PC.

_childDocuments_.review: This brings back so many memories - good memories. I used to watch a lot of G.I.Joe in my childhood, still collect the comics, and used to own a MASSIVE amount of the figurines before I gave them away (big sad).The game is a glimpse back at the good ole days of my youth, and a nice one at that.However, the game play is pretty basic. This would be my first hour of game play thoughts.To sum the game up:It is a basic third-person shooter with general running and gunning, and when you find the mini-bosses it is pretty intense. There is no real cover, other than couching behind small shields, but not like you would expect in a modern third-person shooter. Gears of War this is not.You get a computer AI partner in the game, and right now I feel they are worth nothing. Most of the times they are running around doing nothing. In fact I have noticed also that the Enemy AI appears to just focus on you (the player) and in most cases will just ignore your AI partner, since that AI partner is also doing nothing.As for multiplayer:unless you have local people to play with the game modes are no use to you because you can't play with other people other than split screen. To not have network play in this day and age just stuns me and makes me feel disappointed. I haven't tried the Remote Play Together feature yet, so I am hoping that this will work - however - I still feel it is split-screen and I don't think it would work all that great over long distances?? Verdict is out on that one - I will update if I can get chance to play with someone.As for the story and the characters: Well they are G.I.Joe characters. The voice acting is way over the top (I couldn't help but laugh the first time I heard Cobra Commanders voice - it was so iconic and really captured in this game). They have got most of the character voices very close to their Cartoon counter parts.The story is again over the top, which again is like the cartoons and comics. Without going into much, Cobra do something big, and the G.I.Joe team have to save the day. Cookie cutter type story from what I can see, but that is what you expect from G.I.Joe type stories :)So, as to my disappointments: Well the AI really is frustrating, and makes the game not as enjoyable as it should be. When you have a massive amount of Cobra running at you, guns blazing, it would be so much nice if my ally AI partner is doing more than looking pretty! Additionally the game play is so very basic, it is just running around and shooting. It reminds me very much of the old Doom/Duke Nukem games, where the game play was just about running and gunning and using your special when it charges up (okay I don't remember special charge up in Doom/Duke Nukem) Of course you don't play with the whole G.I.Joe line up (which is sad) and you are limited to just the main characters that I can see. The issue here is that if there are characters locked behind PvP, they can only be played when you have people with you in the same location, it reduces the game's value a lot.Additionally I am disappointed you can't just play your characters by themselves in a run and shoot type game. So I do feel this game is going to have a very limited amount of playability unless you can split-screen share with people. From what I have been told so far the campaign is only 3 hours long so it will not give much to people after that.So my final view of the game:If you are like me, the main reason to buy the game is this is probably the FIRST G.I.JOE game that has been around which is related to the comics/cartoon in a VERY VERY long time (if there are others please let me know). The last G.I.Joe game I liked was way back in the C64 era. I want to see more of this stuff, with better story length and with more multiplayer options. I hope that the Devs on this will add more to it, but since I believe it was a Playstation game released in October I doubt there will be anything extra added.As stated it would also be a lot more fun if you could play solo missions with your favourite characters.Overall I would give this a thumbs up - for those people who like "mindless action shooters" and like G.I,Joe. If you are not a G.I.Joe fan I would probably wait for a special since it really is your run-of-the-mill third person shooter game without basic things you expect now days (like cover, etc).However, because of the pretty bad ally AI in the game right now, I am *forced* to give this a thumbs down (I so wish there was a middle option!!) because it really does impact the enjoyment I had for the first hour. I mean, the AI is really bad, Roadblock would just stand there and stare at all the BATS coming at you, and do... nothing.
_childDocuments_.name: G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's kind of nice that a fairly recent game has been released from G.I. Joe, despite the well-known characters, typical action scenes and the entertaining animations, I didn't immediately get the nostalgic feeling I hoped to get from a game of this franchise, but the animations compensate the gameplay well in this area.Watch a snippet of gameplay here: Time to confess: most people who grew up between 1980 and 2000 look for ways to relive our youth as they age, like Saturday mornings watching cartoons in our pajamas.In the category 'crazy cartoons that almost made our eyes bleed on a Saturday morning', we loved the cartoon by G.I. JOE. which hereby makes a return in the form of Operation Blackout.In the campaign you go with two of your favorite G.I. JOE heroes or Cobra baddies at work.The game is made for co-op, but can also be played alone.G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout didn't elicit a wow reaction from me, but like most video games made from a franchise, you're faced with repetitive missions with endless use of the same attacks and combos, not ideal controls, but good graphics.
_childDocuments_.name: G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout

_childDocuments_.review: One word to describe this game: Meh.The voice acting is great and from what I've played so far the story is pretty good. I like the comic book style cutscenes. It really captures the feel of the cartoon. I kinda liked it at first.But the gameplay is just...boring. The gunplay is boring and samey. Run over here, shoot a bunch of dudes, interact with a thing, run over here, shoot a bunch of dudes but now you gotta wait for a timer to count down before the waves of dudes stop spawning. Do it some more. Rinse and repeat. Weapons feel weak and I don't feel like a badass. There's the occasional turret level with infinite ammo but it just isn't exciting. Bosses are huge sponges with no real patterns- they just walk one way then go the other way then back, all over the place. Achievements suck.Got it in a bundle for 3 bucks and you could do a lot worse. If you can put up with the blah gameplay there's a good story in there but for me it's not worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up watching GI Joe. I love the idea of a GI Joe video game that I have access to. I have access to this GI Joe game. I do not love the idea.This game is everything that you don't want it to be. It's got the names, but it doesn't have the personality. Simply put, it's just incredibly boring. Very disappointing. Avoid at all costs. Don't be like me and convince yourself that you're still going to like it despite all of the negative reviews. You won't.
_childDocuments_.name: G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout

_childDocuments_.review: The extra-wide dresser drawer packed full of my collection of G.I. Joe action figures is one of the most memorable parts of my childhood. If there was a Joe or Cobra out on the market, it’s likely that it was in there as I can only recall a small handful of them that hadn’t made it in. While my brother and I were at school, my dad would set up these massive battles that took up the entire room with bases, vehicles, supply stockpiles, and so on. We knew as soon as we walked in the door that it was time to go to war.So yes, I’d say that G.I. Joe carries quite a bit of nostalgia for me. I decided that G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout was going to be one of the next games that I’d review before I’d even really taken much of a look at the store page. It was the kind of spontaneous decision that could’ve ended in a disaster. Fortunately for me, the legendary heroes and villains came through for me once again and offered me an enjoyable experience, even if it was clear that there had been some changes over the years.There’s a lot that’s familiar here for those who know the G.I. Joe setting and it’s adapted quite well into an action-shooter format. Each character has one of six primary weapons, a secondary weapon, grenades, a melee attack, and an ultimate ability. A good amount of variety in weaponry makes each feel different than the next, with the classics like assault rifles, SMGs, and sniper rifles showing their faces, but also with electrical cannons and rocket launchers thrown into the mix. Grenades pack some AoE punch for when the enemy makes the mistake of huddling up and they come in a few different shades as well with some dealing immediate damage and others applying damage-over-time effects. Melee is either mediocre or absolutely exceptional depending on your character, it’s more of than not an emergency back-up, but you’d do well to not underestimate its use in the hands of those like Storm Shadow and Snake-Eyes. Finally, ultimates stand out from some of the others in the genre by both charging more quickly and being noticeably weaker than in something like Overwatch. They can certainly turn the tide of a close battle, but they won’t turn an utter rout into a victory either.The campaign itself is designed well and offers something that I would call a modernized old-school experience. It feels less like a modern shooter, with less bells and whistles, but more like those we used to play through an era or two back. Missions tend to mostly be clearing zones of enemies and completing simple objectives, though defending locations from enemies while a timer runs out isn’t rare either. Every once in awhile, you’ll even be able to pilot one of the vehicles and use their heavy firepower to your advantage as you race through a level, blowing up enemies and defenses that stand in your way. The on-foot shooter portion follows a straightforward path for you to complete it though there’s room to run around and explore to find collectibles, while the vehicle portions railroad you as there is only ever one way forward. That said, the simplicity here is a strength rather than a weakness, and I found it to be something of a walk down memory lane to something akin to the old Star Wars Battlefront games.Narratively speaking, missions bounce around between G. I. Joe and Cobra allowing you to choose between at least two of the roster to take into the fray. I always look forward to being able to play both sides of a conflict, particularly when it’s asymmetrical and I don’t have any complaints here. The story feels like classic G.I. Joe with Cobra finally pulling off a successful enough maneuver that they drag the world in a Wolfenstein-esque scenario where Cobra Commander has established his organization as the uncontested leaders. The Joes fight back and do what they can to restore peace and order to the world.The only real issue that I found with this title was that that the unnamed enemy fodder that you spend eliminating throughout most of the game is used for both sides. The justification that’s provided for this is that the Cobra B.A.T. technology was adapted by the Joes to field their own army of robot soldiers, although I would’ve liked to see unique-looking enemies even if each type still filled the same role. Instead, the relatively small variety of enemies that you face has little more than a palette swap when you change sides. The gameplay surrounding these encounters isn’t bad though, so it didn’t tarnish the experience too much, I just found that it would’ve helped add to the setting overall.It’s clear that G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout put heroes front-and-center and there are a handful of familiar faces here even if I would’ve liked to see more. Each side has six characters available, each of which mirrors the class of one on the other side. This means that both sides play relatively similar, though there are small differences between them that do manage to keep them feeling slightly different.Snake-Eyes and Storm Shadow represent the ninja class. They wield SMGs, move quickly, and have brutal melee attacks, though they’re fragile and drop quickly if they’re focused on by the enemy. Duke and Baroness are soldiers that carry rifles and have relatively balanced stats that let them perform admirably in any given situation, even if they may not excel; they’re the jack-of-all-trades sort. Lady Jaye and Cobra Commander are supports that bring solid firepower to a team but take longer to reload, making them ideal for backing up others but not for going one-on-one with a foe in a duel. Sci-Fi and Firefly are havocs, and as that name would suggest, they carry heavy explosive weapons that have a penchant for blowing things up with heavy damage and area of effect. Scarlett and Zartan are skirmishers, specializing in long-range attacks at pinpoint accuracy, though you want to keep them out of harm’s reach as they’re extra squishy. Finally, Roadblock and Destro roll up as your heavy strikers, locking down enemies with their close-range electrical cannons and excelling at eating damage that would murder the rest of their team. I enjoyed playing every class available and they felt balanced enough that I bounced around between them as I progressed through the missions. I would love to see the roster doubled, or even tripled though; even if the heroes’ characteristics are mostly decided by their class, it would be fun to see more of the legendary icons show up to fight.G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout is a surprisingly good third-person shooter that plays like a smoothly designed title of years past. I was willing to take the plunge and risk wasting some of my time on a G.I. Joe game to give it a chance, but I was surprised to find out how enjoyable it actually is. That goes doubly when you drag some friends along for the ride, either tearing through the campaign as a duo or duking it out with up to four. It doesn’t reinvent the genre or push it forward, but it’s an excellent experience to add to your digital shelf if you’re looking for some good old-fashioned run-and-gun in a good old-fashioned setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like every other game made on a licence of a famous cartoon, movie or comic book series, it's super mediocre. This is just a basic third person shooter with mild RPG features and some minor customization options. It reminds me of Agents of Mayhem gameplay wise, minus the open world, you play as different characters who each carry different weapons and have different skills(active skill and different kind of utility) with which you fight robots that either fall down in a pod or spawn in from a teleporter, just like in Agents of Mayhem. I have to note that this is one of the better budget movie/cartoon/comic series licensed games I've played recently(Jumanji and Zombieland were objectively worse and more of a cash grab) because this game has fan service and decent mechanics.With that aside, the game has a campaign, which is mixed between good guys and bad guys, their missions intertwine and you'll see every area twice with different objectives or sometimes from a different side. There are also a couple of driving missions but you don't drive, you just steer, it's pretty much on-rail shooter at that point. As you go through missions you'll be able to find weapon skins which will then unlock character skins once you have them all, they're super obviously placed if you've played games for a while you'll know exactly where to look. Just like cosmetics you'll also find comic book covers, which are super cool and finally, once you get all of the collectibles, you unlock some G.I. Joe cartoon educational clips, which are not that great(low resolution and super short) but they're still a fun addition.It features local COOP of the campaign as well as versus mode with no online option, besides remote play, which is a bummer. You might want to play with a friend because AI is braindead and will block your shots while doing absolutely nothing combat wise, enemies also ignore it to only shoot at you. Overall a fun little afternoon experience, grab only when discounted because there's not that much to do and unless you're a fan of G.I. Joe you'll not find that much value in it.

_childDocuments_.review: G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~G.I. Joe Operation Blackout, based on one of the most popular and commercially successful franchises of all time, features some of the most popular characters from the franchise in a fun, intensive arena shooter environment.As soon as I heard about this new G.I. Joe title, I was biting down on my hand to get a hold of it! Growing up in the early 2000s, TV series, Franchise and Toys such as G.I. Joe played a major role in my life. As soon as I started the game and hearing that classic ‘’ Yo Joe ‘’ from one of my favorite characters from the game, ‘’ Duke”, put me on a nostalgia overdrive. The first few minutes while playing is kinda blurry to me Not Gonna Lie; it kinda shocked me how many characteristics they managed to bring in from the actual characters. I won’t say they did a great job, but they did a great job! Plot: Seems to be another normal day at sea, onboard The Aircraft Carrier USS Flagg, when a sudden burst of radio chatter catches everyone’s attention. It’s another Cobra attack, but it’s not a single attack at a single outpost; no! It’s something big! Cobra and its forces have attacked all G.I. Joe assets at the same time on a simultaneous attack. While trying to get hold of his men, G.I. Joe commander Duke notices something odd in the sky; it’s a Cobra attack lead by Storm Shadow and Cobra Commander himself!They manage to take down all defenses and get a hold of Duke and other Joes from around the world. The Cobra unleashes a new form of weaponized device, called – The Blackout Sphere. At the push of a button, the world plunges into darkness; blackouts start occurring around the world. One by one, countries and governments fall into Cobra’s hands. With a handful of Joes still at large, they must regroup and fight back, finding and freeing their team in order to push back on Cobra’s plans. Only Joes now can stand up to the Cobra and his allies. Gameplay: G.I. Joe Operation Blackout features a fun, arena-shooter style gameplay, with solo and co-op game modes. In both cases, you will be allowed to choose between one of many characters from either G.I. Joes or from the Cobra. During each mission, you will be going for a specific target.  Each mission will be guided by multiple main objectives, as well as side objectives as an added bonus. You get to unlock and choose between 12 iconic characters from the franchise, 8 from each side of the fold.  You’ll have the opportunity to play as Duke, Roadblock, Shake Eyes, Lady Jaye, Sci-fi, and Scarlett from the G.I. Joe team, and from the Cobra side, such Iconic characters as Zartan, Baroness, Destro, Firefly, Storm Shadow, and The Cobra Commander himself. The gameplay is fun, simple and effective (apart from the run and jump machines), utilizing a great third-person perspective while implementing a simplified WASD movement: Space jump, shift run, and L-ctrl for crouch. Something that did catch my attention in a distracting manner was its run and jump machines. From the animations to implementing the movement speed of each character, it felt oddly unmatched with the gameplay and out of place. Although I faced no issues while running and jumping, the speed of each character and its one-size-fit-all jump animations kinda ruined my immersion. I was expecting something grander, at the very least from the two ninjas! I should have been allowed to be much much faster than the rest with these two ninjas, and with better jumping and vaulting animations! Each of these iconic characters has something unique about them in terms of their movement, how they act, their body language, etc which makes them special.  This was clearly missing, and I would have loved to see something like that being implemented. (Although there are these Taunts; okay, beggars can’t be choosers!) The game also features two iconic tanks from each side, which I am kinda upset about. The game features Persuader from the Joe side and H.I.S.S from the cobra side, both of which look nothing like the real thing! Having owned versions of both these iconic tanks, I was heartbroken to see these designs.Combat: The game features a simple yet effective gunplay system with its Left mouse to shoot and Right to aim. It’s a simple point and shoot that, added to its inaccurate fire, adds a fun element to the game.In addition to its fun gameplay with 18 unique weapons and 36 skins, each character gets their own unique Ultimate attack by hitting Q. Ultimate attack varies from character to character; some are effective in ranges, while some are only effective while an enemy is nearby. Same goes for tank combat; the difference is you will only be doing one thing, which is running . . . in similar settings. World design: Unique and stylish, in a toned-down manner from the intense G.I. Joe-type world design and scenarios. For the most part, the world looked and played out greatly.Being an arena shooter, you will be playing on a limited area in each stage of the mission, but having multiple stages gives an illusion of it being a larger world. Music and sound effects: Well-selected background music. It’s simple, it’s motivating and it’s catchy - I love it! Dialling it down a bit early on stopped it from getting repetitive. Absolutely enjoyed the sound effects, which were over the top and unique in a way; just how a G.I. Joe game should be. Dialogues: Cheesy and always over the top. Hey, the game did justice to the franchise; G.I. Joe dialogues are always like that and that’s the charm of it. Positives: + Decent plot+ Iconic 12 characters from my childhood+ Decent world design + Those Iconic cheesy dialogues + Great music selection + Appropriate sound effects for a G.I. Joe game+ Well designed characters+ Fun, simplified arena shooter combat Negatives: - Poor Run and jump animations - Poor weapon animations - Minor performance hiccups here and there- Not implementing the iconic tank designs- No trading cards yet Stand up and regroup, Joes; it’s time to take the fight to Cobra! 12 Iconic characters from the franchise will go head-to-head for either world domination or peace. ‘’ Yo Joe ‘’. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

Joe used to be called, which was a real AMERICAN hero. Like all good little terrorists, cobra hates the flag, america, everything, so they dispatched several good little cobra B.O.T.S.(the new cobra unit android unit that doesn't actually do anything cool like combat or anything but instead distills anti-american propaganda onto the internet all day to destabilize America.) to write a series of undeserved negi reviews.Now, let's get down to the nitty gritty, what is the actual game like? First of all, the pixel shaded graphics are fantastic, the characters look great, the controls feel great and the characters similarly felt great. The game allows you to pick between to fan favorite characters for either side of the Joe vs. Cobra operation. While the enemy A.I. Isn't great, the game eventually dispatches a boss of some kind to ruin your day. While the boss is no hardest boss in gaming, once during the first level on normal I got cocky trying to melee and was pwned. Challenge exists.As for the "dreaded A.I. Partner" I was told that the A.I. partner doesn't shoot, can't hit and has literally never killed an enemy character by these reviews. This is the impression I got. _childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game, albeit with some caveats.G.I. Joe: Operation Blackout is an old-fashioned third-person shooter with 17 missions, across which you get to play as twelve characters total (six each for the Joes and Cobra). The game is obviously a love letter to the original 80s cartoon, and given the comments the developers make in the art book, they worked with what they had and would've make a more robust game if given the choice. If you like G.I. Joe and don't boot up the game expecting a triple-A title, I think you'll have a good time.Pros:-Campaign spans both factions-Voice acting is fun and sometimes cheesy, but on purpose-Each character has 1-2 unlockable skins, which are callbacks to the comics, toy lines, and later television shows-Each character has 2-3 unlockable weapon skins-Unlockable comic covers and videos-2D comic-style voiceover cut scenes with voice acting are well-drawn-The AI is surprisingly good. Enemies know how to strafe and avoid shots, even on the lowest difficulty (four total)-Split-screen co-op campaign and PVP modes, if you're into that-Catchy soundtrack-Varied locations (Arctic, desert, G.I. Joe and Cobra bases, etc.)-Three vehicular missions, which spice up the gameplay-When replaying a level, you can choose from six characters instead of the two used in the first story playthrough (i.e. if Cobra Commander and Storm Shadow are Mission 1's playable characters, replaying the mission gives you the option of playing as the other four Cobra characters instead)Cons:-The game can be repetitive at times -- if I play it for more than hour in one sitting, I get bored of just running-and-gunning-There's seven total locations across which the levels take place. Six of them are returned to in subsequent missions but are reversed, meaning the starting point becomes the end point, and vice versa-Short campaign (8 hours for me, and I take my time)

_childDocuments_.review: this is what you would expect from a franchise game and that is to pump out mediocre games to milk a license. that said it's not a overly bad game it could be fun for a kid or to get your joe on. the game even lets you use modifiers to make the game easier or harder and this alone is a huge positive. devs tend to forget we are here to have fun not brute force some failed attempt at level design. giving the player option is a good thing and i wish more games did it. anyway outside that everything about this game is serviceable at best. the game is a bland 3rd person shooter where each character has a unique main gun and a off gun that you can switch with weapons you find around the level. they also have power moves, nads, some dashes, all basic fps stuff. your ai helper is useless and when you try to snipe long range targets once alerted they will dance when you put the cross hairs on them. the story is what you would see in any episode of the show (not great) and has you playing both sides throughout 18 levels. most missions only let you pick between 2 people since this has split screen co-op but each side has 6 characters you'll play, as the game goes on and 3 of them are vehicle missions. i do feel they should have split the campaign for the two sides though i have a feeling they didn't want to write 2 separate stories. it just does not feel right jumping sides and fighting the very characters you just played as in the previous mission.there's no upgrades, states or anything like that though there are some weapon and outfit unlocks as well as comic book covers you can find in levels.   finally i didn't run into any bugs but playing solo my ai buddy liked to run in front of me when i was shooting but maybe it's done to teach kids why it's bad? since knowing is half the battle of not getting caped by your friend(s). don't expect much as there isn't much here and i would skip the dlc. they only give cobra gold weapon skins, joes chrome weapon skins and 2 character skins (duke/cobra commander).p.s. this game was made for consoles so you'll have to mess with the setting to get rid of the playstation blur and make the screen wider.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly couldn't tell you why this game got so slammed at release. I picked it up in a Fanatical Platinum bundle and powered through the whole thing in one sitting - and it was worth every penny. Definitely a budget title, but between the self-aware humor, earnest appreciation for the IP, and damn fun action (even the vehicle sections!), Operation Blackout might actually be the first genuinely GOOD G.I. Joe game!? It basically is like if Volition's Agents of Mayhem was a linear action game rather than a sandbox grind, and it works so much better as a result!Bear in mind, the PvP and co-op are local only. This is like a lost PS2 game. Everything is unlocked through tracking down collectibles or playing through levels as particular characters. The only real downside is like many old PS2 action games, the final level has a rather BS difficulty spike. That said, overall, an absolutely great time if you can grab this game on sale. Didn't expect to say this going in, but yeah, "GO JOE!"Also, I don't understand why people are complaining about the controls? It works perfectly fine - hell the aiming even feels good on the Steam Controller and usually when playing TPSes that can be pretty wonky. It's not like there's any particularly unique layout, plus the game features full rebind support for controllers and keyboard/mouse if there's something truly troublesome to your input preferences. *shrugs*

Each character has their own weapons and abilities that they come with, but you can also change out weapons as you go through missions.  There are unlockables to find to keep things moving and once a level is beaten, you can apply mods to make it easier, harder or more fun in general.  I'm still working on completing the game, but I am enjoying myself so far and hope that others come to see what this game has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing G.I. JOE with low expectations. I'm not a G.I. JOE fan and I knew this wasn't a triple A game. I was hoping for at least a decent game. Let me tell you something, this game is way below average. This game sucks!Dear developers, don't make a co-op game if you can't program a partner AI. Your partner is completely useless and when I say useless I mean literally. He only shoots 2-3 times through levels and doesn't even kill anything. I thought Sheva's AI from Resident Evil 5 was bad. After seeing this atrocity, I can easily tell Sheva's AI is really good. Your AI partner is as dumb as a rock but enemies on the other hand are super smart. They can snipe you from across the map. As soon as you peak from cover, they start throwing everything they have at you. They don't miss, and they also completely ignore your AI partner. Because of this you can't use that dumb idiot as a meat shield. Your stupid AI partner is only good at one thing, getting in front of your line of fire. He always blocks your view and makes things harder for you.The soundtrack is generic as hell. Not a memorable song in it. Weapon sounds are awful too. Some laser weapon sounds are just sh*t.Levels are pretty bland and forgettable. Level design is utter garbage. Most of the levels include a boss fight. Boss just comes at you firing his gun at that's it. You throw a grenade, boss doesn't react. You empty a clip on his body, boss doesn't react to this either. It's a complete mess.Graphics is the only thing I like about this game. It has that distinct comic book feeling and I like it. Cutscenes are nice too. Other than that this game is a huge disappointment for me. If you are not a G.I. JOE fan, stay far way from this game.

This feels like it started as a mobile game and then the requirements to actually run the thing ballooned past what would work on a mobile device. _childDocuments_.review: Not recommended.It pains me to say stay away. It's not bad, but it is sub-par. I grew up with G.I. Joe and was hoping this game would be better. For what it's worth, the graphics are decent (reminds me of Borderlands) and I think the story has potential. However, everything feels low budget, from the controls, combat, character movement, static cut-scenes (was really hoping for it to look and feel like the old cartoons), terrible sound effects/audio quality and the lack of polish. For a deep discount, it might be good for die-hards, but my brother and I didn't want to keep going after the first co-op mission.

_childDocuments_.review: I just bought it for the Joe...The heart shows through here and there, but unsurprisingly, the game sucks.The sad thing is there were people who genuinely love the source material working on it. Where it really shines is in the background details, like spotting the Sear's exclusive Cobra recolored MOBAT, someone knew what was what with those little easter eggs.And honestly I wanted it to succeed so Hasbro would be compelled to make more (better) Joe games... but it came out as expected; low budget, rushed, extremely generic mechanics, (character choice is essentially a reskin with a primary weapon change, none of the weapons feel substantially different); short campaign that gets samey within moments...  I enjoyed the story and the comic panel cutscenes... but I still enjoy the original cartoon, so there's that.Skip the game, buy the Classified series figures these character designs are based on instead. (Got a whole collection myself).yoJoe
