_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: AS OF THIS REVIEW THERE IS A BUG IN WHICH HALF OF YOUR FLEET WILL RANDOMLY DISAPPEAR, ESSENTIALLY ENDING A RUNI'm inclined to give this game a negative review due to this, however there are several checkpoints throughout the run on a normal difficulty. Painful case being, twice this happened JUST before I reached the next checkpoint, meaning I'd have to replay the past similar few hours again. Does remain technically playable, but very much not enjoyable. In spite of this, the game is good. Do play and try it. Do bear in mind there is a prologue which plays a bit differently from the actual game, with the prologue being a bit offputting for me personally.The game does a poor job of explaining certain mechanics and features (often not explaining them at all), however I don't think that detracts from the game itself being good, especially once you understand how these things work. It certainly isn't for everyone, but if that were the case it'd likely be a bad game. Combat is beautifully done, with extra immersion in the case of glass getting bullet holes when you take hits, obscuring parts of the already poor vision.Story gets a bit repetitive with repeated runs, but it can be looked past. The world map is uniquely done, with interesting mechanics in the form of detaching units for sudden strikes, missiles and plane strikes coming and going between you and unseen enemies, and different levels of radar.The radio feature does get a bit annoying, especially when you lack a cipher key and the game keeps pausing for it, or a tarkhan that you already know the whereabouts of keeps letting you know he wishes to speak with you. TLDR: is unforgiving, has a few bugs currently (ships disappearing is extremely frustrating), does a questionable job of teaching certain parts, but is very unique, well made, and satisfying

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Highfleet is a delicate balance of careful planning, brazen raids, intelligence gathering and deeply fun and chaotic action. At its core, Highfleet has deep military inspired strategic gameplay coupled with physically simulated ships and visceral arcade combat. It features a fully functional ship builder where trade-offs actually shape your designs and costliness of your ships. Further, it has electronic warfare inspired mechanics (radar, cryptography, direction finding) to enable careful planning and manouerve of your fleet - either to intercept prize vessels, or to avoid your adversary.All this with a well crafted narrative, excellent lore and immersive visual and sound design. RPG elements also come into your playthrough in the decisions you make during random encounters and how they affect your relationship with your allies.  Highfleet scratches the itch that you discovered when you spent hours playing games like Sid Meier's Pirates, Space Rangers and Faster Than Light.I rate it 5 out of 5 Irradiated Bedouin Cities!
_childDocuments_.name: HighFleet

_childDocuments_.review: This game oozes atmosphere. It is one of the most immersive and fun games I've played in a long time.It's hard to describe to be honest, it IS a strategy game but there are so many layers and decisions to be made, along with a collection of very fun and engaging 'mini-games' that you can't just define it as being one genre.It's got everything; an awesome dieselpunk aesthetic, incredible sound design and music, fantastic combat that makes you pout your lips when you let off a salvo of heavy calibre rounds into an enemy broadside, and tactical decision making akin to that found in Silent Hunter 3.To top it all off, it has an FTL style campaign where you are both the hunted and the hunter. You try to evade enemy strike groups while hunting down strategic locations and important enemy transport vessels. Always on the search for fuel and ammo, your search carries you across a vast irradiated desert and through multiple locations.I absolutely love this game already, 9/10, I just wish there was a way to have Russian audio while retaining English text and menus!

_childDocuments_.review: Nice and original design, I had this game on the wishlist for a long time, and finally, it is here.I had to manually mod this game to make it playable for me:- disabled annoying sounds;- disabled annoying visuals (at least ones I was able to reach);- manually save game files whenever I want;I described these tweaks here: After mentioned tweaks and latest patches, the game still has terrible UX and needs further polishing and bug fixing, but it is playable, and it is great. There are many tactical possibilities, and with the ability to save-load-experiment it is challenging exactly like I want it to be.Older review from 2021-07-21:After 12 hours, I don't think I will play this game until a major update or something. The reasons are below:1. No saves.Every time just another roguelike game developer creates a game without saves/loads, it only means that he makes the player manually save the game data. The absent saves feature is only a missing feature, nothing more. I don't get how it is not clear for game designers after all these roguelikes we had. The only case when a modern game may have "permadeath" is the very short game sessions plus almost no punishment on the game over. Like we have, for example, in Hades. But in Hightfleet, you have a campaign that will take hours of hardcore and repetitive gameplay - without the normal ability to save and load.2. Repetitive and boring mechanics.The game has nice mechanics, e.g., working with radar reminds about all these submarine simulators. But after a few hours, you feel them repetitive and boring. Like "land on a platform, press buttons A, B, C, hear the same sounds"; repeat again and again.3. Insane difficulty without adequate compensation for your time and efforts.The game has "Dark Souls+" level of difficulty. You play on the enemy territory without your own economy, so every fight you win (I'm not even talking about losing a fight here) could be a game over because you will not have the resources to prepare for the next one. It is definitely inspired by FTL (Faster Than Light), but FTL gave you a hard but possible challenge you enjoy beating. This game is only making you give up trying.4. Ship fights will simply burn your eyes, kill your vision.The core mechanic of this game is ship fights. It looks nice on screenshots but not fun to play. Actually, the fight screen is an example of how to screw UX in every possible way: sensitive information on opposite sides of the screen; UI elements hiding your ship, making you avoid corresponding arena areas; you need to focus on 30x50 pixels areas to shoot; plus visual and sound noises all over. If you didn't kill your vision already, play this game to finish it off.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best game I've played since like, Star Wars: Rebellion, or Empire: Total War. Reminds me of old Microprose bigtime.. especially Starship Troopers: Terran Ascendancy (that was MP, right?). Finally someone is making modern games that have that old school feel with top notch aesthetics in all the right places. The depth of the "mini-games" or whatever you want to call them (radar intercept, character interaction, the story in general) is immense and is what keeps me interested secondarily.The combat is what keeps my autism locked in though. The shipbuilding, fleet logistics, salvage ops, and the vast array of different armaments and tactics they create are, without a doubt, the most unique and plain fun I have had in a game for years as previously noted; not to mention the physics and particle effects. This game will be one of the most popular games of all time if the multiplayer combat becomes a thing (I honestly haven't even looked to see if there is mp yet because I'm so into the campaign). This is also in large part due to the story being so engrossing. I'm a sucker for ancient megaliths, lost prophecies, and ancient nuclear warfare set in a time period I can't pin down, so to say its up my alley would be a bit of an understatement.In conclusion, it is a rare thing for a game to remove me from the world and plant me in its own and keep me there looking for more. I salute the makers of this game, it is excellent beyond what it is. It will create a whole new genre and I am loving it. Salve! Could we see a new 90s-esque resurgence of unique, affordable, and endlessly re-playable games that aren't trying to push a narrative? After playing this game; yes we will. Buy this gameBaaaam, Peanut Butter and jaaaaaaaaam(also, the art is just beautiful.. hope you all are doing great today everyone)

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this review, I have completed the prologue & am about to embark on my first campaign. I will update my review accordingly once I have had a chance to experience the game in more depth but I doubt my opinion about HighFleet will change much.---Kudos to the devs, this is a gem with very few rough edges!HighFleet just oozes atmosphere & immersion all round. You can almost smell the methane & feel the dry sandy wind flowing through your beard.The art style & direction is simply amazing, I can't get enough of that dither & the game just looks spectacular from the oppressive control/map screen to the battles & landing sequences with impressive smoke & dust effects, explosions & all kinds of over the top on-screen effects (which can be toned down if you find those too distracting, I personally love it). The audio is chunky, clunky & meaty & weapons feel like they pack the punch. The soundtrack fits with the theme and sets the mood perfectly.The interface is gorgeous, functional & easy to pick up all at the same time, if you've played Silent Hunter or Dangerous Waters you will feel right at home but even a novice should be able to pick up on it rather quickly as it isn't quite as complex as it seems on the surface (quite cleverly so). I initially thought the combat would be a simple arcade shooter mini-game but I couldn't be more wrong, the ships have a fair bit of inertia and landing shots does require more skill than can be thought at first due to the amount of action going on around your ship and having to avoid incoming projectiles and missiles whilst braving the weather.In my few hours of game time I have experienced a few minor issues such as a tutorial prompt getting stuck, and the Prologue ending with a Game Over upon completion but nothing that won't get picked up in the next few days/weeks.Overall, if you are after a rogue-like that feels & plays like a more mature & in-depth version of FTL, with a strong influence from older games, this is the title for you!

_childDocuments_.review: As difficult as it is enthralling, Highfleet  presents an engaging and visually rich experience that rewards the player that engages with the lore and is willing to do some work to understand and capitalise on the game's mechanics. Meaningful diplomacy and management, nailbiting tactical manouvre and frantic ship-to-ship combat in a rich fictional setting are the rewards for persisting with the sometimes obtuse interface.Variously drawing  inspiration from Harpoon, HBS' Battletech, Lunar Lander, Sands of Kharak, Dune and the Old Testament, the setting is fantastical in its concept, but has a coherent ruleset that gives the player an advantage if they pay attention. Factions and personalities the player meets can be swayed by persuasive speech that appeals to them based on their background in the game world. This information is not spoon-fed to the player and requires close attention to the choices presented and the responses to them. This favour can be used to reap tangible rewards in game in the form of intel, logistic support or rousing speeches to raise your fleet's morale.Combat is the other half of the game and presents first at the  operational-to-tactical level where the Action mirrors modern Naval combat where the constant struggle to see without being seen meets long range cruise missiles, ECM and carrier alpha strikes. Presented in a Situation map or overhead satellite view, this component rewards paying attention to enemy reactions to your actions along with forecasting how much fuel (and damage) you are going to burn prior to the next resupply. Once ships or fighters close to visual range, the fight becomes a rather unique side on 2D affair where ships swirl around each other with stunning tracer and missile trails going all over the place and thick black smoke marking impacts and failing systems (and eventually entire ships). Both these systems are underpinned by a reasonably in-depth ship customisation system ala Battletech where choices can be made in armour/weapons/fuel/sensors etc that affect all levels of combat and manouvre.Highfleet utilises a Diegetic UI (it looks like the physical control panels in the game's ships) which is very visually appealing but can get cluttered when there are multiple elements onscreen at once. In addition to this, some features are not clearly laid out via the prologue or other tutorials whilst others are. A good example is use of strike aircraft. When you buy an aircraft carrier, your deputy does not offer a tutorial as he does for other aspects of the game. The player is left wondering how to get the jets to do anything. In this particular situation the manual also fails to fully cover the subject, leaving the player to find out how to arm their jets by chance. This leads to parts of the game being needlessly unclear considering you are supposed to be a trained fleet officer. Discovering the inter-relationships between the Desert Factions should be a player responsibility.. Discovering that your Fleet's basic combat doctrine sees fighters only attacking with rockets and bombs (but not guns) should be something that you are expressly told. This being said, I strongly recommend consulting the manual if you are unclear on something.With luck, most of the niggling interface bugs and documentation ambiguities will be ironed out with some updates. I sincerely hope so, because Highfleet presents a multi-level game experience within a unique and compelling setting which demands your attention.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a first impression review after 17 hours, so, while this is more than most rants or early high praisers have played, do be aware.LOOKSLets get the obvious out of the way, the game looks and sounds gorgeous. The UI is very unique and like someone else said literally oozes atmosphere by itself. You feel like you ARE sitting in a dieselpunk cockpit and that feeling is fantastic. The sounds let you feel the massive weight and power behind your ship in strategic mode. In battle, you get very nice lighting effects and hits feel impactful. Debris sprays all over the place and damage is visible by missing ship parts. Weapons and impacts sound great as well. 2D BATTLESLet's get to gameplay and start with combat. There have been reviews portraying this as a cheap flash game and my review mainly wants to offer a counter-view. First of all, 2D shooters are what they are, 2D shooters. I don't know what you expect but if you don't want to play 2D shooters, don't play'em. Sure, the concept is simple. You steer your ship with WASD and you point and shoot. But there's way more to it than that.First of all, many outside factors play into this shooting part of the game. Mainly the characteristics of your ship and those of the others ships. You can design your own ships. Like completely. You have an editor where you can build ships to choose for the start of your campaign and while you have no opportunity for getting them mid campaign you can strip down existing ships you get down to the core and rebuild them.What this means is, how your ship plays and feels is very dependent on how it's built. A heavy cruiser steers slow and unresponsive and is usually not really made for battle, because even heavy armaments don't make up for the fact that you can't dodge ♥♥♥♥. At least that counts for vanilla heavy ships, I have seen player designs with armor literally the thickness of a football field and yes, you will probably kill all the influencers before they can chew through your armor.Then you have very light ships and everything in between, and there is a lot of minmaxing. More on that in the editor part of the review.Then there are lots of different weapons, you got very fast air saturation weapons great as point defense and against unarmored targets, you got nicely balanced ones which are fan favorites and you got the big guns with few shots that matter. So whatever style you prefer, you can play it. In battle you only control one ship at a time and you get to play the others ships participating in battle after your ship dies or retreats, in an order you choose beforehand. You also have special ammo which you have to choose beforehand as well but can be changed in battle between special ammo and standard.The AI controls 3 ships at a time against you. This might seem unfair but pretty soon you will see why that's balanced. Once you get the hang of shooting and either build better ships on your own or import superior community ships, you will make them cry.So after all the technical stuff, is battle fun? To me, yes, even though I am NOT a fan of 2D shooters or shooters in general. I played lots of them in my earlier days and barely play them anymore. But this is fun. Because looks and sounds are amazing, because you really FEEL what's happening and because skill and ship design plays such a role. You get little notifications how much damage you did (or took) and what subsystem was damaged. Fires can break out which can be quenched with fire control systems... which are limited to how many you put on the ship and if they have already gotten shot off or not. You also can install flares to confuse missiles and you can steer aircraft carriers and launch aircraft. All in all, definitely more than a flash shooter, whether you like it or not is of course up to you.OVERWORLD/STRATEGIC GAMEPLAYNext is strategic campaign play. I have limited insight here because I am not far into the campaign. This really is the other I would say 67% of the game. You have to get to a certain city on the other side of the map, while flying from town to town or in between towns, either evading enemy fleets or engaging them. You start with the ships you picked in a single fleet, but from there on out you can do whatever you want. You cant fly as a single fleet or you can split off groups, which is advisable. Because fuel.Fuel? Yes. Fuel. Fuel makes the world go round. Your fleet will need fuel to fly around, and any fleet will need a tanker, except if you decide do put giant fuel tanks on your fighters which is not advisable for size and weight reasons and because fuel tanks explodes quite nicely once hit. So you will have to scrap the remains of your killed influencers to buy fuel. Maybe ammo and ship parts and new ships too, but mostly fuel. Because fuel. Man, this is really stressful, I can only think about fuel. The campaign gameplay is very deep and complex and really overwhelming at the beginning which, paired with the fact that the 2D shooting part looks simple on first glance, is probably the reason for a lot of bad reviews. I'll say it right away, if you don't want to a) do an extensive research on your own beyond the game manual or b) don't want to learn on your own by doing a ♥♥♥♥ TON of mistakes and hopefully sometime learning from them, this is no game for you. It's basically a realistic strategic war sim focused on aerial combat in a dieselpunk dune-like setting. Just looking at information and intelligence is insane. You have a radar, infrared sensors, radio and ELINT and of course visual contact. That's just the number of possibilites for you to detect your enemies and for them to detect you. How and if you use those will decide your playstyle and if you will be successful or not. I'll not go into detail here because I have already extensively covered battles. But there is no handholding and little convenience. You will have to make notes based on your results from radar, sensors, intercepted radio messages etc on your map to get an idea where enemy fleets are or have been x hours earlier. This is extreme fun for me, I like doing my own calculations. Also there are missiles, different ones, also based on real missiles. You got missiles that need a ship with radar to paint the enemy. You got purely ballistic missiles and you got missiles that pop a vectored radar search on the point of the map you told them to and seek targets.SHIP EDITORThere's quite alot more to strategic gameplay but I'll leave that for you to find out. Lastly there's the ship editor. It comes with a testing mode which is really nice because you get to try out your own designs or designs of other players in combat and get to find out that your designs suck because people who are nerds in this game already know what to do. The editor is quite professional. It's got a few quirks but your options are expansive. You can build anything from peashooters to fortresses, from specialized ships like pure scouts or pure missile carriers to hybrids (usually not advisable though). There are limits though for the sake of realism. For example, if you put a thruster behind your hull, it will not work. If you cram your sensors between other parts, they will have limited range. This is displayed by areas that are either painted yellow or red, red if that area is blocked. You are also limited in how close you can cram components together. Also systems need crew. Crew needs crew quarters, compontents also may use power for which reason you will have to install generators. You have to worry about where you put what. If you put your fuel tank right behind your armor or even outside your hull, you get nice fireworks after the first enemy pops your cherry. So maybe hide it behind armor and less vital components, you get the idea. Would buy again.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game. It looks and sounds awesome, almost the entire UI being diegetic is incredibly cool and immersive, and I'm a huge sucker for any sort of airship battles. The campaign mechanics are complex but interesting enough that I was willing to learn. I didn't spend any time with the ship designer, but it's the sort of thing I would have loved to sink my teeth into once I got the basics down. Making you play the moonlander minigame every time you arrive at a town is a nuisance, but it's a small enough part of the game that I could tolerate it.Unfortunately, the real meat of the game is in the combat, which is not remotely enjoyable. First of all I thought this was going to be more of an RTS, controlling your entire fleet at once, giving orders to move and attack at the tactical level. Shame on me for not doing my homework I suppose. Instead you control one ship at a time in an arcadey, twin-stick style. When you decide the current ship has taken enough of a beating, you retreat to a randomly chosen place on the edge of the screen and the next one in your lineup will replace it. Shots move relatively slowly, inherit momentum from your own ship, and targets are constantly moving making aiming pretty difficult. To add insult to injury all you get for an indicator of where you're aiming is a tiny arrow right next to your own ship. The AI of course has no trouble leading its shots perfectly.The difficulty of aiming, combined with the fact that your ships trickle in one at a time against the entire enemy fleet, makes combat incredibly punishing even when you have the superior force. The one advantage you get is that you can restart the battle instantly, as many times as your ships' "morale" stat (10 by default). But this isn't a fun way to play a game, repeatedly taking a mulligan and hoping to land a few lucky shots before run out of chances. Being able to time-warp away my mistakes really breaks the immersion which has been so carefully crafted in every other aspect of the game. It doesn't match up with the narrative about a scrappy, outnumbered force trying to guard its limited supply of equipment and people. And it feels like a band-aid solution on a much deeper problem with the design. I don't mind a difficult game as long as it's an engaging challenge that's satisfying to overcome. But this game is just infuriating in a way that left me exhausted and salty whether I won or lost. I would have preferred if the battles were easier to beat on the first try, but with no restarts so the stakes for taking damage are much higher. Something as simple as a longer arrow and/or a visible mouse cursor to show me where my guns are pointed would go a long way toward feeling like I'm in control of the outcome, and less like throwing darts blindfolded from a spinning office chair.This was the first time I've ever tried to refund a game on Steam. They didn't give it to me because I'd played for 4 hours and the limit is 2. I'm not really annoyed about the money, but I've uninstalled it and don't see myself ever returning. In the end I spent almost as much time getting this game to run on Linux as I did playing it. For what it's worth, once I got it working (which required using ProtonTricks and the GloriousEggroll fork of Proton) the performance was flawless.

_childDocuments_.review: There is sooo much to love about this game (the art, the sound design, the gorgeous interface), but it ultimately kills itself on execution.  The problem is that there are lots of options... but they all suck.  This game is nothing more than a beautiful exercise in frustration.Want to try using airplanes?  Great!  You get no loot and will soon starve.Want to try using missiles? Great!  Same problem.Want to try using nukes? Great! FAFO.Want to use small, agile ships?  Great! They'll be blown out of the sky with one hit.Want to use big, tank ships? Great! Their fuel requirements will quickly bankrupt you.Want to use enemy intel to avoid fights?  Great! Except we just changed our codes again, so start at square one.But the cardinal sin is this:  Why would an overwhelmed insurgent force send their soldiers in one by one to be destroyed by the enemy like bad guy ninjas in a cheesy 1980s movie?  We have few precious resources against a foe with unlimited resources, and the game forces us to use them in the least effective manner possible.This is like if you took the X-COM games and modded them to only allow you to bring one soldier to each battle, with no other changes to features or game balance.Even on the "easy" mode, this game is punishingly difficult, and totally inaccessible to those without perfect senses and reflexes.It's such a disappointment, compared to what it could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: e: With update 1.1, the developer has addressed a lot of the issues people have. There are still options missing, but it is clear that effort is being put into making this game more accessible. Key rebinding is still missing, but the rest of the major grips were  - more or less - fixed.-----While I absolutely adore these types of games - and I adore this one as well - we live in the year 2021. This game has no keybind remapping, resolution options, widescreen support, or even borderless window mode. There are no graphical or accessibility options.Everything else in this game shines and is clearly crafted with love.  But as much as this game tries to invoke the feeling of games of ye olden times, it sadly also emulates their technical downfalls  and shortcomings.If you can live with this, buy it. It's great.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like Transarctica, Lander, Silent Service, and FTL, all rolled into one.The premise is that you are the heir to the Russian Empire in Planet Afghanistan, that a coup has taken place in your capital by rebel noblemen, and that you must scramble with your fleet and whatever allies you can muster to seize the rebels' nuclear power plant. The gameplay itself is a real time with pause game of cat and mouse in which you need to manage your budget and the time you spend in a single location, and lead your fleet (which you can split into strike groups), interspersed with real time battles with newtonian physics in which the ships in your group take turns fighting all of the enemy fleet at the same time.The graphics are both gorgeous and functional, with many retro (late 80s and early 90s) graphic effects enabled by default, although I find that dithering does not add to the game's looks and I disabled that one right off the bat (and indeed, the Steam store's screenshots were taken with that option disabled).

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome atmospheric game! Truly a work of art. The sound and visuals are incredibly well done and really pushes the tension. Rain, lightning, fire, smoke, clouds, night, day, fuel and scarcity of parts, limitations on powerful ammo, and lasting damage, all come together to create a tense harsh environment that must be tread carefully. Fights are fast, punishing, and has lasting consequences once they are done.  The choices you make seems to really affect the game and you frequently find yourself trying to get out of a bind. HighFleet plays like a mashup of Silent Hunter, Cortex Command, Hammerfight, Cryptark, and FTL, and does it fairly well. There are still some needed quality of life adjustments and features that are are an absolute must, but those should come. Microprose has done a good job with this one and I'm glad they're still around!

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic roguelite experience that reminds me somewhat of a submarine simulator (i.e. the overworld map where you'll spend a lot of time navigating between cities that offer various rewards such as new ships to purchase or cheaper fuel, tracking radio signals and avoiding patrols while managing your precious fuel and cash reserves) and an action game that heavily favours intelligent movement (e.g. putting an enemy between yourself and another enemy or their missiles, good use of afterburn and targeting weaker areas of ships) to match your itchy trigger finger.Featuring a very interesting setting and airships that truly control like the lumbering behemoths they are (I am reminded of the mechs and tanks of Ironcast or Valkyria Chronicles), this game also has some stellar sound and visual effects. Little details such as the screen blacking out as your ship pulls heavy Gs, the way your cannons boom and light up the clouds, and even the various beeps and warning sounds outside of combat when you're simply cruising around in your mothership—or the panicked footsteps of a crewmate warning you of a nearby threat—are all very satisfying.The music reminds me a bit of Black Sails at times (a compliment, if that isn't clear), and even landing your ships is a joy in this game, particularly when you're only left with one landing leg and have to try to "prop up" the other side using a wall or you've blown several engines and you have to prevent your ship from spinning during your descent. And yes, it is even quite amusing when your landing fails and pieces of your ship start to explode and don't worry, the game allows you to retry many things including combat and hard landings without penalty, as far as I can tell (unless of course your mothership explodes or the bridge gets destroyed as that is where your character is). When your campaign is over, you are given a rating and your best rating will give you additional funds to buy ships/hoard for fuel or special ammo at the start of your next run.Rest easy that the game does tell you all you need to know in time while also giving you the leeway to experiment and discover things on your own too. I am still enjoying figuring things out for myself after 13 hours and seeing what works and what does not, and I find myself devising different strategies to try on my next run.As with any great roguelite, I am enjoying my miserable failures as much as my hard fought victories; highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: I suck so bad at this game. In my roughly 34 hours I have managed to:- slam irreplaceable ships of all sizes firmly into the ground- hit my own strike fleets with cruise missles- drive a Lightning directly into the open maw of an enemy strike group- leave countless men stranded in the desert with no fuel- go bankrupt at least a dozen times while strike groups close in, arming their (what feels like) hundreds of cruise missilesAnd yet this game has stolen my heart in a way few games have. The immersion, the interwoven strategic systems, the combat, the graphics, the audio design, it's all great. The feeling I get from this game is a lot like the old Silent Hunter games. You are severely outgunned in a hostile environment with limited intel, and every move you make feels weighted. The slightest misstep and you will lose hours of progress. Very rarely did I have a set back that was not caused by my own oversight or incompetence. This game keeps you on your toes and rewards you for good strategic thinking and punishes you severely for being (like me) a dumbass. I didn't even mention the story, which for any Dune fans out there is a wonderful rip off. I found myself really losing myself in my role as a Duke's son leading a fleet of loyal tarkhans into the jaws of death on a likely futile campaign of resistance and revenge. Oh yeah and there's nukes.Buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent enough game initially, but has only gotten worse. No updates with any content. Developer is focused on "balancing" combat (at glacial pace) by crippling fun play-styles rather than reinforcing others. Don't get me wrong, it is fun and feasible to play through the game with plodding bad ships (Sevastopol) and fast ships with few guns, using the exact same designs as your enemies use. But this is not interesting for long; ship design is essential to really varying a playthrough.Schizphrenic part nerfs, the crippling of multi-gun functionality and homogenizing structure statistics have all contributed to reducing both creative fun and gameplay variety. I don't see a point in ship design anymore. You might as well get used to the vanilla ships. At least you can pick up more of those during a playthrough.Many hours spent in this game designing new, fun ships, and having novel playthroughs due to different fleet compositions. And that fun is something I can't have anymore with a legal copy. Overall, what a shame. Pray for mod tools or something, then maybe someone will add CONTENT.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello,I can't really recommend this game for anyone right now. The game looks really cool, the physics seems cool and the effects are nice, but the tutorial gives off a completely different vibe than the rest of the game, and after some hours, I realized I was just doing the same thing over and over again.First off, the tutorial.What do I mean that it gives off a different vibe? Well the game starts with a lot of dialogue, and you can choose how to reply kinda like Mass Effect or Dragon Age, and it gives you positive and negative relations with people depending on what you say, this makes the first impression feel like you might be able to make alliances, allies and enemies based on how you behave in a more social manner. That isn't the case, those kinda conversations almost never appear after the tutorial whatsoever except for some pre-defined events.Now the repetitive gameplay.At first it seemed really cool and fun, but after 6 hours I realized I was just doing the same thing again and again.You start a new save, your goal is to attack a specific city. What do you do? You drive to 1 town, then send your quick units in first to take them off guard, then after the attack you land and refuel, then you go to another town, send in your quick units to take them off guard, then after the attack and you refuel. Then you go to another...... Yeah you get my point here. You do this all the time until you beat the main town and your done. There are pre-defined events that occur, where after 18 battles or so it will be permanent/semi permanent night time and so on. But it doesn't really matter the same strategy goes anyway. There are ship building, you can build/customize ships and buy new ones... But you are still just doing the same strategy over and over. So after 6-8 hours I just don't really boot up the game anymore EVEN THOUGH I WANT TO because I know I'm just doing the same thing over and over. I like the game, it's just... Not that in depth as far as I've noticed. And is only fun for the first few hours. Hopefully the game gets patches and improves in the future but as of right now, I can't recommend the 20$ price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh yes. I've been anticipating this for quite some time, and it didn't disappoint.Currently, there's a bit of jank and some bugs. It needs a few more QoL passes to really iron them out, but once it gets those (dev is actively working on it), it's going to be absolutely legendary.All that said, I absolutely love it. However, this game is  for everyone. It is  dense, complex, and punishing. There's a lot to learn, even for experienced strategy players.  But if you're willing to put in the effort to learn the game systems and mechanics, it's a hell of a reward.The aesthetics are incredible, as you can see in the screenshots and videos. Sound design in particular is PHENOMENAL. Hammering the ♥♥♥♥ out of enemy ships with heavy artillery cannons is viscerally satisfying in a way few games of this kind have been able to pull off.The landing sequence is one of my favorite parts of the game, which is funny since it involves no combat, just positioning and orienting your ship onto a landing pad. But you get repair speed bonuses (very important) if you land in the tighter spots, so there's a real incentive to pick the challenging ones. And it only gets more tense if you're landing a ship with some engines missing. The visuals and sound make the whole thing feel incredibly immersive.I feel like I've only scratched the surface of the gameplay, having lost my first campaign attempt within a few hours. But each time you do lose, your next campaign starts with extra cash, which is really nice. And on top of that, there's a Hard mode, which I'm nowhere near ready to try.Further, the Shipworks editor lets you build custom ships which can be purchased right at the start of a new campaign, so you can have an entirely custom fleet right out the gate and go nuts with it if you prefer your designs to the stock ships. However, if you make an ultra dreadnaught ship, you probably won't be able to afford it, so build wisely! Extraordinary meme potential in the editor, too.Overall, if you're on the fence, give it a few more months for patches. If you think you'll like the gameplay based on what you've seen, and you're not deterred by intense, complicated gameplay, I'd say check it out.[Edit] After about 63 hours, I finally made it to the endgame. Jesus . This game is incredible, and I'm genuinely scared of what comes next. Best horror game of the decade.

_childDocuments_.review: As the others say, there's some rough edges to this game. _childDocuments_.review: A perfect game, absolutely inspired. A great work of art born in a beautiful mind.This is not a product constructed to fill a specific niche. This is a personal project, brought to the world by a person convinced of his vision. The unprecedented attention given to tiny things in this game, things that only a handful of people will probably ever notice continue to astound me.The fidelity of the systems, layered gameplay, the extensive meta and freedom that this game grants you to exploit it's systems, to construct your own custom made strategy to achieve victory deserves to be held up as current benchmark for the industry.The game is both operational and tactical. Some decisions you make will not affect you untill many many hours of gameplay later, while some are split second, one-keystroke-away-from-annihilation affairs that will leave you white knuckled and swearing. A well placed shot that causes a magazine explosion will turn the tie of battle and open window of opportunity for you to exploit to push for victory; or (if you find yourself on the wrong side of the gun barrel) will leave your entire campaign in shambles.Observe the cold moment of realization that things you previously didn't think of as important, reveal themselves to be the chain of terrible mistakes with which you unknowingly backed yourself into a corner.If naval/aerospace combat is something that interests you. If your favourite day to unwind after a long day is to watch Operations Room/Montemayor on YT. If you enjoy putting yourself in the shoes of the generals and admirals of the days of yore and reliving the forgotten campaigns from centuries ago. This is a love letter to war in all its terrifying awe and beauty

_childDocuments_.review: HighFleet is a fantastic little game, if you can get past a couple of quirks. The developer has a very strong, specific vision of what this game is and seemingly made no compromises on that vision. The downside is that includes things like any sort of modern options menu. Speaking personally I would love to be able to switch the audio language to Russian while keeping the Text in English, but you can only toggle it all the way one way or the other. The upside is that the vision for the game is *very good*. It's all based around a tight flying combat game that feels super satisfying. The campaign map is challenging but rewarding. The immersion factor is off the charts. Definitely give it a try if you're on the fence.

_childDocuments_.review: The all-time best ever flying submarines in the sky game ever made. Although I have spent most of my time obsessing over ship design, "submarine airship game" is the best description for this FTL-like rogue-like UNFORGIVINGLY Difficult game I can come up with; in campaign, you spend a lot of your time trying to manage 15 different simple things (signals analysis, threat tracking, resources and fleet management, navigation, combat, landing, and then the global story/factions/political overlay of story driven decisions). The ship editor will drive you on the express train to crazytown; every. single. decision. carries huge implications for your campaigns when you start running custom ships, and this gets into the infinitely complex fleet design (what roles do you want your ships to play is critical, and the game lets you figure out your own ways to fail). This is one of my favorite games of 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: This was and is my first dip into what some would describe as sim games. I have NOT been disappointed with my purchase, nor have I been disappointed with my time spent in the game thus far. I could describe many things that I enjoy, but I believe the quickest way for me to summarize is this:I received Battlestar Galactica, Homeworld (Deserts of), and Star Sector "vibes" from the game - perhaps it was the music and desert for Homeworld, and Battlestar Galactica and Homeworld for the premise of the style of campaign I was running - quite literally, sometimes, running for my life while making quick stops to repair key components while strike group(s) bore down on my position. Star Sector definitely hit me with this game, especially in the combat - the combat is on a 2D field, but it's visceral, unforgiving, and very engaging.At some points, if you're new to sims, or not... I believe there will be frustration in learning the tactical screen / map's controls and all of the many subtle nuances to the game. For each that I learned, I was able to immediately devise several ways to make use of it - I had epiphanies for each, which in some way felt like a mind bloom. The game can cause you to grit your teeth AND then feel so ridiculously rewarded when your strategy / plays become fruitful.I hope, to some measure, something that I wrote has you interested enough to give the game at least a two-hour try. This game deserves at least that. Immediately, it has rocketed to my favorite game this year so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game. 70 hours of solid gameplay.This is the hardest game I've ever played.Story reminded me of Dune movie. You are Mark Sayadi, either the saviour of Gerat, or the destroyer.Strategical aspect of the game happens on a radar screen. You have tools, such as circle drawer, eraser, pencil, and ruler, to mark your map and gauge distance. It matters. If you know a certain ship that holds valuables is at a certain point going 90km/h at a certain direction, you will know where it will be 10 hours later as long as it doesn't reach its destination. Your fast ships can get him pretty easily. Other times, you know the group you have to avoid are going certain way. This way you can avoid their potential destination.The HUD may seem tedious at first, but everything is useful. Missile launch order at the top right, aircraft slots at the bottom right, you will use them at some point.Tactical part of the job is when you're engaging enemy ships in close combat. There are two types of ships, fast and fragile, and slow but tanky. However, if you know how to build ships, you can design your own to be the best of both worlds: fast and tanky. And with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ of firepower.During combat, there are two pieces of HUD, one at bottom left, and the other at bottom right. If you're new to the game, you might think they are useless and just obstruct your view, however, they are some of the most useful things you can look at. The bottom left shows the condition of your ship, the bottom right shows the targeted enemy's. If you see a hole, abuse it, you'll take the ship down way more quickly than just hitting where you get to hit. Armor is shown as bright white.It took me 65 hours to finish the game. It took me a bunch of game-overs, losing hope, and deciding to end the run, only to successfully come out of one of the toughest battles of all time. That boosted my confidence, and I eventually carried that run to the finish line. The finish line is where you have to use everything you've learned on the field. If you didn't learn much, you'll lose over and over and over again.How I found this game? Someone recommended that I listen to Tanc a Lelek. I wrote some of the YT comments, and I got the game after a PC upgrade. Oh, and you will need DX11 to run this game. My i3 Laptop couldn't run the game.Fly safe.Post edit: for an unforgettable experience, turn the lights of your room off, put something anti glare on your eyes, and then light up the sky. Each Sarmat shot will light your whole room.

_childDocuments_.review: My friend, do you like Diesel punk? What about 2d, action packed, tense, ship to ship combat? Does the idea of using an array of sensors and intel to seek out (or avoid) incoming missiles, aircraft, or strike groups composed of multiple ships the size of your flagship interest you? Do you wish to inflict an ABSURD AMOUNT of warcrimes via NUCLEAR BOMBARDMENT from a strike group burning enough LIQUID METHANE to effectively counteract the cooling effect of a nuclear winter on a global scale? Then my friend, this game is for you.I paid full price for this game and I regret nothing. The first couple of playthroughs were kinda rocky, me largely ignoring recruiting other tarkhans to join my cause, and not having the damnest clue about how sensors work, as well as the importance of using Aircraft Carriers and Missile Carriers to my advantage. (For the love of god keep that active radar off and only send out individual pings if you need too) However once I got the basics of combat and sensors down the game got a lot easier, and much more fun. This game can be very unforgiving, but at the same time rewarding. Especially as more events unfold later into the story, where you as the Tarkhan of the fleet have to make decisions for the betterment of your fleet. These decisions can also affect how the people of Gerat (the country you're attempting to liberate) see you. Whether you take on the image of a prophet from god sent to punish the rebels for heresy, or the image of a hero just trying to unite Gerat to end the war once and for all is up to you. The setting and immersion in this game are another feature I quite like. First the setting, the setting is in an alternate timeline where several large kingdoms rule the world and conduct warfare largely through the use of massive airships powered by burning liquid methane. The game kinda gives off a diesel punk Dune vibe and for some reason I just absolutely love it. The immersion is great too, something about looking at the map on the bridge and trying to plot your next course of action, all while listening to the hum of the engines as you fly between cities is amazing. Not to mention the tension and panic you feel as one of the crew runs down the hallway to yell "Thermal signature detected" or hearing "radar emission detected". All in all, its just an amazing mixture of sound design, setting, and game mechanics that put this game above many others I have played. Bottom line: Its unique, its fun, and it offers a nice challenge while offering some control of the challenge with three difficulty modes. While it lacks in the tutorial department for things like using long range missiles, aircraft, and advanced sensor tactics, its still an amazing game. I rate it a 9.5/10, only docking it for the lack of tutorials. Would recommend to anyone who thinks this game looks remotely interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird game, some parts of it are great, other parts defy belief on how terrible they are.So in this game you travel along a map with your fleet of flying russian ships, trying to reach your end goal to have a big battle. Not that different from FTL. You can't beat all your enemies because they outnumber and outgun you, so you need to be sneaky about it. Travelling off the more used routs, using radar to avoid the tougher enemies, hit cities with surprise attacks with your smaller ships then raiding it for supplies. Intercept enemy messages on the radio.The game even have a ship editor that allows you to create your very own ships and put it in the campaign to play around with it.All great stuff, but then it comes combat...Now, combat isn't bad on itself, but it takes all the complexity of the strategic map and completely ignores it. You fly on a 2d plane, with a single ship no matter how many ships you have in your fleet, and attacks the enemy that is always outnumbering you 3 to 1. Really brain dead stuff, WASD for movement, mouse for aim and shooting and that's it. With the worst part being that combat is half the game and you can't make anything to make it more tactical, it plays like an old flash game.It feels like one team did the strategic map, while another did the combat, without ever communication to each other what type of game they were making.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with an incredible design that is about right. Yet it is, stifled by a lack of settings options to add flexibility for graphical options, accessibility settings, and keybindings. Additionally the existing settings menu suffers some UI problems that should be revisited (Settings saying one thing when they actually mean another). Personally, I think it should be redone and line up with the design of the strategic layer UI.That said, the actual game is fantastic. The game is split between its strategic and tactical layer, with the strategic layer possibly needing getting used to as you avoid (or seek) enemy squadrons, track signals, and engage your enemies with strategic munitions. The tactical layer give additional depth and is incredible both visually and mechanically as you clash with opposing ships, firing your cannons, defend against missiles, and evading enemy fire. 8/10. -2 for the settings lacking flexible options and UI.

_childDocuments_.review: Huge learning curve. Your enemy has free access to all of the infrastructure (Repairs, rearm, refuel) you would otherwise have to fight to use for a relatively small amount of time before the locals report you to the patrols of heavy ships, aircraft carriers, and rocket carriers searching for you. Play through the prologue, otherwise you'll be clueless when bombarded with the radio, knobs, switches, buttons, dials, navigational tools, and alerts. All of which are essential for going undetected and calculating not only enemy movements but your own. The current top review doesn't account for the fact that you're heavily outnumbered, a single fleet among hundreds hunting for you. If your entire fleet of precious ships all of which are expensive and vital were controlled by AI, you would have a bad time paying for repairs as the games AI cannot dodge enemy fire as well as the player can. Every time you meet an endgame, your highest score is accumulated with start points on that save file as extra points for you to purchase more ships to be able to have a better chance of survival. Progressively through a series of failures you'll learn how to properly use the mechanics of the game to your advantage, and which ships make the perfect fleet for you to survive and complete your mission. Even late game on easier difficulties, you will still be outnumbered, so practice aiming and dodging, don't sell or use your nukes, and never turn on your radar. Only the experienced survive war in Gerat.P.S - I suggest if you want to create your own ships that you play the game a little to get a feel for what necessities you need for your ships based on their role. The Flagship for the most part should be left alone. The shipbuilding community in this game is pretty immense, you can find all sorts of ship designs and downloads as well as guides online.

_childDocuments_.review: *slaps roof*Yeah I recommend it, even at full price!You know when you've been playing badly done, unfinished, unpolished games for so long you forget how gaming experiences should be... And then... then...And then Microprose comes around, unzips their collective rusky pants and slap Highfleet onto the table...Yeah the quality of this game is WAY HIGHER than 99% of the crap that's being sold in steam today. TOP NOTCH 2D AERIAL COMBAT. They made other developers look like amateurs and beggars. Not a SINGLE crash or bug WHATSOEVER on my 80+ hours so far. That's actually legendary impressive for 2021. You just feel the guys that made this game really know what they're doing.Don't expect too much of it though for its high quality it balances out with the fact that it's not very deep at all. And in this case it is good for the experience, because I swear it's so well done that replay value is through the roof. I'm on my 3rd campaign right now, and even though I know what will or may happen, combat, careful navigation, radar avoidance, ELINT and all that stuff you need to survive the mission makes it so it never gets dull. Even if you get tired of the campaign there is always shipworks, a creative mode that allows you to build whatever ship your heart desires and then test it against any specific challenge the campaign may throw at you. And you say this is a good ship, I want this ship in campaign. Guess what... You give it a name, save it and it might show up as a hireable merc in the campaign. And it's all very carefully balanced because you actually have to pay a lot for your OP ships.It's a difficult game, but not frustratingly so there is no free retrial so you must plan very carefully; you either succeed at the first try or you fail and take serious penalties for trying again. This makes the choices you make have real tangible immediate impact on the course of your mission.Oh and it's got a lot of sweet details meant to enrich and immerse you in the experience, such as every single graphical element is functional and has a purpose, or for example if you ram an enemy ship in combat you take a serious morale penalty.This takes me to what everybody else is currently doing: Many current games lack the adequate challenges to actually be difficult and not just frustrating. This game is not frustrating at all, it's just hard BUT you can master it and enjoy it a lot. For example destroying a cruiser with a corvette or some similar hard to accomplish feat shouldn't be doable at first, but after learning the aiming principles and how to properly manouver to avoid ordnance and volleys you WILL eventually kill that cruiser with even the puniest of ships.I usually loathe 2D games but this one deserves the spot as my favorite modern, most enjoyable 2D game. Money well spent! I really recommend you to buy it, the gaming community needs more of this kind of quality product and one way to get more like this is to vote with your wallet.Thank you Microprose!

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying: I have played rogue-like games before. This one is just punishing. The art and lore really made me want to push through, but the actual gameplay is just a non-stop barrage of uppercuts to your junk. I get that you're supposed to be hunted, and that you're supposed to out-gunned and desperate. Believe it or not, though, there are ways to make that fun. The way you break codes and intercept signals is pretty cool, and there's a lot of innovative things that they did. However, this game just throws you into the mix with probably one of the worst explanations I've seen. They just expect you to get your ass kicked to learn how to play. After I played about half-way through on Normal, I switched to easy. Even if you do everything right, sometimes you'll just get bullied by these entities called strike groups. You'll play it safe, but get stuck fueling while they move in and beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of you. In a stand-up fight, you can take them with a bloody nose and some damage. However, every strike group has infinite ammo and they just SPAM you with cruise missiles. There's no reward for killing this foe. Nothing to make it worth your while. You just take damage and get ♥♥♥♥ loot. Sure there's depth, but this level of punish-the-player is lame. It's not fun-- the entire reason I play games. I don't want to have to take a slide rule and a pencil to plot points on a map like a naval navigator. I'm not here for this sweatlord ♥♥♥♥.  I played a good amount, so I'm not going to ask for a refund, but I don't think I'll buy a title from these guys again. I need some time to decompress before I decide to rally and try again.

_childDocuments_.review: Highfleet is like having 7 different flavours of ice cream in a single bowl and 2 of them are sorbet. It's a dangerous proposition, but it might just be crazy enough to work. I love the big swings being made by this developer to make something really unique, so if you're on the fence, please do give it a go.The strategic layer is a submarine sim style cat and mouse game. Your capital ship is big and slow and you need to stay off the beaten path with it, while sending squadrons ahead to clear out towns or pick off supply convoys to keep your fleet going. The running costs of a gas guzzling flying fortress are no joke.  It requires patience and planning and the constant stream of intercepted communications can feel overwhelming when you're just trying to refuel and repair between outings. The combat is much more action oriented. The game switches gear and you're darting around in a corvette, perhaps one of your own designs, punching holes in enemy ships, evading fire and missiles and causing the enemy to blow one of their own up. Then there's a diplomacy card game, a salvage system, a cipher/decoding minigame, a reputation system, a lunar lander style minigame for getting damaged ships into town. If you don't like one or two of these, they might result in a little frustration or boredom here and there. You can avoid some of them or adapt your strategy to compensate for not being great at some aspects of the game, but I do get the sense that having the particular set of skills to enjoy and to master every aspect of Highfleet could be rare. Don't let that deter you from trying your hand at this one though.

_childDocuments_.review: Weird, difficult and brilliant.Strategic portion reminiscent of Silent Hunter, but with giant rocket-engine-powered airships.Tactical part that is a beautiful and chaotic bullet hell, using ships that you can freely customize.All in a unique world, culturally inspired by Central Asia and cold-war Russia.I love this game. I've been following the development for at least 5 years and I'm incredibly happy with the finished product. It's difficult (downright roguelike, with Ironman being the only mode), but also incredibly rewarding once you figure it out - which doesn't mean it gets easy.You're a captain of a strike fleet tasked with defeating rebels - who are no pushovers. Quite the oposite actually - they are looking for you and will hunt you down given the chance, so stealth is quite important. You manage your fleet composition (down to being able to modify every single part of your ships), fuel reserves, morale and plan your next moves - which include direct, tactical, bullet hell combat.While it features a ton of various minigames - manual ship-landing, radio signal interception, code cracking, card-game-like social interaction, and more - those are neither too easy, nor get too tedious and repetitive.One of the best parts is the fact that it leaves a lot to the player - for example, you technically need 4 numbers to crack the enemy encoded messages. That doesn't mean you actually can't crack the code earlier! Let's say you have a single number - that means we're left with a lot of combinations, so we could spend the whole day turning those knobs - but wait a minute! Thanks to you capturing a radio station earlier, you know there's a strike force "IGOR" around, and the number you put in shows an "I" at the start of the message! Now you know the first 4 letters of the message, and you start turning the knobs to match that knowledge. A minute or 2 later and you've cracked the code! And there's so much more stuff like that - analyzing those radio messages to learn not only the recipient location, but also additional info not written out for you. Fuel transport? Maybe it's heading to refuel a strike force that you had no clue about? A new codename? Could it be just another transport, or an armed force?My only, rather minor complaints are that the tutorial could be expanded a bit, especially when it comes to RADAR and some tooltips could provide more info (eg. cruise missile speed, gun accuracy, etc.) - but other than that - I highly recommend this niche, unique, and - most importantly - fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: How to even classify this game? There is a strategic layer, with processing SIGINT (radar, emission detection, IR, decoding intercepted radiograms), planning of routes and intercept courses, managing logistics of the fleet and ordering strikes by means of tactical misiles (multiple types), drones (multiple types, multiple payloads) or airships (multiple types, multiple ammo types). Then there is the combat itself, with physics based movement affected by the ship's mass, its thrusters and their placement (or destruction), firing angles and countermeasures. Then there is a ship-builder, where you can build, edit and test these ships. And there is a light RPG system that affects recruiting allies and some story events.  The game is strictly 2D, but very well made. The whole dieselpunk and oriental stylization is very atmospheric and strongly reminiscent of Dune. The grimy atmosphere is reinforced by various effects like smoke, fires and rain during combat, or glitches when ships take off or take damage. The interface in the strategic game is represented by actual knobs, levers and gauges, that must be manipulated. The sounds support the immersion even further, with blearing alarms and reports from the crew. And then there is an excellent music,  which shows up mostly during important fights.  The game's campaign has rogue-like elements: after a failure, you get awarded more resources for the start of the new campaign and on Normal and higher difficulties, saving is severely limited. There are many and complex mechanisms in the game. Reading the manual is a must, I strongly recommend watching some tutorial videos as well. Full disclosure: I have played on Easy difficulty, with free saving into limited slots and enhanced survivability in combat. The game was still challenging, but I managed to finish the campaign on the first try. I only needed to load back a few times.  It was an intense and a very atmospheric experience. Maybe its ending could use some expanding.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of my friends have been confused by this games thinking of it as an FTL rogue like, or even a side scrolling shooter. So with that in mind I am going to make it clear what this game actually is so you know whether you want to play it or not. First of all this game is a mix of three primary genres that make up the core game play loop; strategy, management, and bullet-hell.The strategy and management aspect come into play on the campaign map where you lead your fleet of diesel punk flying warships across the dessert of Gerat as you repair, arm, and fuel your fleet as you try to retake the capital city. Off the back it sounds a lot like FTL but the difference is how you go about it; unlike rogue-likes you are not limited to a certain number of paths and combat is not always certain. The map allows full range of movement and the game puts the decision on you to locate enemies and whether of not to engage enemy forces and how you go about doing so. When combat is engaged you take control of an individual ship in a 2D bullet hell mini-game, this same mini-game occurs when defending against cruise missiles and fighters from aircraft carriers. The thing is you only engage with one ship at a time against 4 of theirs. This may seem unfair but in actuality its far more balanced then it appears. You have the choice of the order your ships are deployed and you can build your own ships prior to the start of a campaign. The one thing I recommend when getting into this game is be ready for a learning curve and to read the manual, the game has no keybindings in the options and many of the capabilities of your fleet are listed in the manual. Understanding how your radar, EWR, IR, and jamming systems work is the key to victory and will allow you to make it to the capital safely. Understanding the difference between the types of missiles your firing and those coming at you and how to deploy your carriers fighters will soften up the toughest of battlegroups and keep your ships alive. If you do get the game and the gameplay is giving you a hard time check out Caracel's youtube channel has some excellent guides that really help clear up the tools you have at your disposal.  And with that good luck and clear skies!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun and there's clearly a lot of effort put into it, but the player's experience isn't really something the developers seemed to consider. Such as today's update which seems to have removed the main menu button which I used when my estimation for how many ships I should send went wrong, or if I randomly happened across a somewhat beefy aircraft carrier.The tutorial is lacklustre and doesn't explain everything in-depth, there's not even a tutorial for the ship building so I've got no idea how to make certain looks like how Sevastapol's warheads are hidden behind tubes that're actually just hull blocks, what's needed, what's a explosive hazard/danger, etc.I'm sure once the game's been polished and the developers implement more requested changes and start being more open about updates, I'll enjoy the process a lot more. _childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for FTL with a hell of a lot more depth, this is for you! In depth story, in depth game-mechanics, in depth strategy, in depth visuals. On the map there is a vast array of mechanics that you need to consider, such as radar, coms interception, jamming, plus so much more. Once you deploy your air craft units into combat, its almost like a twin stick shooter as you float around trying to blast down other enemy ships.If you are looking for an engrossing fleet management game that has a different story, it's worth the price (especially if you're looking to sink a large amount of time into something). But if it's only sparking your interest, do give it a crack on sale, you won't find much like it.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess the developer and reviewers consider this to be 'dieselpunk' when, really, it is 'dunepunk.' Is that a thing? If not, I just made it a thing. Anyhoot, I will give this game a strong recommendation with a strong caveat. It's fun. It's immersive. It's got style for days. The controls and mechanics are not actually hard to learn, but really hard to master. There are a lot of different things you have to do, repetitively, and, unless future updates include some quality-of-life fixes, you need to be prepared to play these quasi-minigames A LOT. Ship landing. Aerial combat. Find the hidden frequency to decode enemy communications to either avoid or setup an ambush. Those kinds of things. There is a pretty fun dialogue game, where you choose cards that act as conversational actions. That's been pretty fun. Let me be clear, the whole game has been fun. I really, really enjoy the world created, the mechanics are good, if a little repetitive, and there is a lot of challenge. You jut need to be aware going in that you can't auto-resolve anything. YOU are in command and have to control every single action. If you're into that kind of thing, then go for it, I don't think you'll be disappointed. If repetition wears on you, then maybe give this some time to see if those quality-of-life changes are made. I cannot stress how deeply awesome the style and wordbuilding are. The developer really went above and beyond, and, compared to some of the big AAA games - Cyberpunk I'm looking at you - knocked it out of the park. This is a lived-in world, even if you see most of it via the 10,000 foot view from your mega-ship. Again, I give this a strong recommend, with the caveats for certain player personalities. Now, go forth and lead the empire!

_childDocuments_.review: Highfleet caught me off guard as something that has it all; visually stunning, mechanically challenging, and has an amazingly immersive story and world. If you liked FTL then I thoroughly recommend you try this one. Oh yeah and the soundtrack is amazing too. They really did an amazing job at making a polished game in every possible aspect. Even the tutorial is good!The game comprises of a bunch of different minigames within that all require their own thought and planning, and I never felt like things got repetitive throughout my playthroughs. The progression was well paced and got more and more challenging towards the final stretch in a good way, and rewards you for planning ahead. Saying that though, it's also extremely satisfying being able to react to the curve balls the game throws at you.From a world building perspective, the game is extremely immersive, and I cannot express how much I loved the Russo-Roman-Ottoman mix that the game worked around. The way the story progressed kept me invested in my companions and the actions I made along the way. Huge props on making such a distinct scenario.The visuals in the game also absolutely blew me away. I'm in awe at how the team were able to perfect every minor detail of every corner of the screen.It absolutely baffles me how such a small studio was able to make such a completely polished game. I have nothing but deep respect for the devs for managing to come up with such an enjoyable set of game loops that all fit together in a neat package. My GOTY for 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: (Review updated August 10th to be more positive after two updates have fixed many issues)This game rules! The launch was in a really bad state, but the underlying game was so good that crashes to desktop and other bugs didn't stop me from completing the campaign. And now all those bugs are almost entirely fixed!I can't really think of a game that allows the use of tactics, strategy, signals intelligence and logistics to fight a war like this game does. I've done little but play this game since it was released on Tuesday (now it's Friday). I absolutely love all the moving parts the game gives you - fuel, ship design, different weapons and ammo, long range missiles in several types (active radar guided, radar emissions seeking, also conventional, tactical nuke and strategic nukes!), carriers, fighters and bombers... the list goes on. You'll even have to engage in diplomacy. These are all wildly qualitatively different tools and it's up to you, the player how you deal with enemy weapons while also using your own. I would say if you're interested in this game you should just grab it, but do be warned - it had some serious bugs on launch, and still has a few issues. Series issues such as crashes to desktop and really bad performance problems from savegame bloat have been  fixed to the point where there are 99% odds that you'll be able to complete a game without having your save rendered unplayable by repeat CtDs or other bugs. (Removed old problems that have been addressed by the first two updates)I hope it gets a ton of sales, I'm also totally onboard for the next chapter of of the story teased by the ending to this game, whatever form that may take.

_childDocuments_.review: Build and buy dieselpunk airships, then navigate your growing fleet across the campaign to find allies, screw up speech mini-games, discover hidden cities, and engage in tactical nuclear warfare with cruise missiles before closing to pilot your ships in close combat. Gameplay can be punishing to learn, especially because the game's great atmospherics do not help you make sense of intense fights. Monitors glitch out, epileptic folks get seizures from the flashing lights, and if it's not storming or cloudy, there's a haboob (Does not involve boobs, too much manly diesel machinery) , but what else would you expect from an gritty post-apocalyptic airship world? If you want clean, go to the drawing board, which you will probably visit many times as you attempt to create decent ships. That's not too tough, just remember to hold shift when placing identical parts. I got away with a flying armored brick that had 12 guns and did 90% of my fighting. Aesthetics are optional. Fortunately, you can test these ships before embarking on the resource dog of a campaign where you really cannot afford to waste stuff, including time. People liken the experience to FTL, but if you're good enough you can turn around and shatter the rebel fleet if you want to. Hide the rest of the time. Send carrier strikes, go radar dark, decode enemy transmissions to plan a step or two ahead, or just bull right through with iron guts and luck, it's up to you. Just be warned that if you draw too much attention, you're going to get hit with like fifty cruise missiles, so don't skimp on flak. To reward you for all your hard work, the game has some cool incentive systems. Obviously, you get stuff for exploring thoroughly and fighting, like tasty salvage or derelicts. You can land your ships manually for better repair efficiency in the towns, encounter semi-random story events that affect your relationships, and your allies will help a brother out if you need it, contributing various strategic goodies. If you save their favors, though....nice surprise. Still no boobs.  There's even a bonus if you die repeatedly in the form of additional starting credits when you begin again, erasable for hardcore. Every ship you kill and good action you make will contribute to that bonus, so it's worth trying, though I killed myself a few times when things were too slow or hopeless just to go back with better stuff, and hopefully better luck as the map is semi-random too. All in all, I strongly recommend this game to anyone who loves airships, dieselpunk, and/or fun games that are challenging but not impossible. If you're still having too difficult a time with it, there is mod support and you can edit files with no penalty, so there's that. But don't do that at first. Get into the engine grease and dive right in to High Fleet if you think you can rise above.

_childDocuments_.review: Realistic Theme: ✓Game feels gritty and often you will be thrown into hopeless situations if you previously planned poorly.Replayability: ✓Each time you start the campaign a new world map is auto-generated.Different random events happen in different cities which can have a positive or negative impact on your fleet.Karma System: ✓Determines who will assist you as you traverse the world map.Visual Novel: ✓There are different scripted events that randomly occur while you play and there is a morality system.Depending on your previous actions it influences your odds in certain scripted events.Unit Customization: ✓You are able to customize your own starting ships, so players have a wide variety of unit customization.Tactical World Map: ✓You are free to traverse the world map as you see fit.Depending on your play style the game plays like a Multi-directional shooter, RTS, or Missile Command.Certain game mechanics are left vague and it is up to the player to learn them on their own.Be warned a big portion of the game is managing limited resource: Time, Fuel, equipment, moneyGame becomes significantly easier if you are able to build an optimized ship outside the campaign.ExampleFirst play through made it halfway, but did not manage my fuel well enough.Got surrounded by multiple large fleets.One enemy fleet destroyed using jets and 250 kg bombs.Another destroyed using convention combat.Third fleet approaching, my fleet is highly damaged and Jets are being serviced.Could not win conventionally so used two tactical nukes.Game went from a multi-directional shooter and tactical real time RTS to Missile command real quick.Nukes solved the immediate crisis of the 3rd large fleet, but the enemy fired 7 nukes at me. 3/7 were intercepted by my interceptor jets once they were serviced.Another 3/7 were shot down in real time.1 made it through and wiped out my main flagship and it was game over.10/10 Would start a nuclear holocaust again.

_childDocuments_.review: I love everything about this game. The combat is weighty and physics based. The music is thematic and sells the dire situation. I love the art and graphics, there are some really top of their class effects for clouds and smoke in her, almost looks like a realtime fluid sim.The game combines a lot of gameplay elements into something so incredibly cohesive that nothing feels very abstracted(despite very much being so.)The tactical gameplay on the overworld is also pretty unique in modern games. You really do feel like your controlling these fleets, and making consequential decisions about radar use, splitting ships, resources etc. I guess theyre so consequential because if you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ rains down hard.Also worth noting this game reminds me heavily of the devs previous game(hammerfight.) From the world of tribal technology, the style of action gameplay mixed with text-based story and finessing loadouts, to the combat itself with physics based massive flying machines smashing into eachother.
