_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this game to drop for almost a year. Its a great game that is so frustrating you'll want to tear your hair out.One word sums this game up perfectly: Annoyance.The graphics 'glitches' ARE ANNOYING AF. You can choose a LOT of glitches, or LIGHT glitches, but you can't F-ing TURN THEM OFF. I get its supposed to add charm and atmosphere, but there is usually so much going on screen it just adds a visual burden to process it, and for me, takes away from the game experience. Sometimes weather effects are thrown in that are so over-the-top it feels like your on acid. Maybe its a Russian military thing, here in the West our sh*t just works - we don't deal with crap displays, and therefore don't feel the need to model them in a video game about the future.The game literally feels like your playing a Commodore 64 title on an emulator. Also, apparently Microprose and the Russian Dev don't realize that in 2021 most people have ultra-wide 2K/4K displays. The UI is just ginormous. I want to see my current position/RADAR (aka the CENTER OF THE SCREEN) but there is so much CRAP surrounding it. Again, its supposed to be part of the atmosphere/aesthetic but it just annoying.It took me almost an hour just to figure out how and where to land my ships safely without wadding them into broken metal hulks. This is the first time in-game a player actually gets to control one of their own ships. The game tells you just use W, S, A, D! No tips, no practice, no guidance on where or how to land. Yes, you can re-try without penalty again, and again, and again...Scrolling is a joke. Newsflash: people use the SCROLL WHEEL on their mouse to scroll. Not physically moving the mouse to the top or bottom of a screen WITHOUT a mouse cursor for any kind of reference I might add. I had to watch a YouTube video just to figure out I could scroll to the side on some screens!This game is incredibly hard. I love hard games IF they give you a chance to figure them out - but the documentation sucks with a tons of things not mentioned, or very complex subjects just glossed over. There is NO difficulty slider/option.You can build and modify ships, but there is NO WHERE in the game where things are explained. Ships appear to be random collections of junk that you can click on, remove, upgrade or replace. There is no rhyme or reason why you'd want to remove or add anything, nor of how or why you'd want to in the first place. You're presented with a metric F-ton of options with no clue about how a individual item is better or worse than anything else. You don't know how or where to place them, what prerequisites there might be, ammo used or needed, etc.The save system sucks. It was (supposedly) implemented to combat save-scumming, but in a game as convoluted as this, coupled with the laughable documentation - its needed just for sanity's sake. To bad. Suffer.Again, a great game that needs a TON of polish. It will reward you after you smash your head against a wall a few times.The last time I had this much trouble trying to figure out a game was when I played EVE Online for the first time in 2007.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite not being first person, it is an incredibly immersive game with me often feeling like I was truly in the captain's chair staring at the monitor (ngl kinda accurate irl). Even the main menu has a reflection.It's story is pretty engaging, sometimes affecting your journey to Khiva, and is of an all out war between the Romani empire and a faction referred to as the Gathering, of which is a group of many great houses, set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland that is the barren desert of Great Gerat. Your goal is to reach Khiva, a city that has a massive generator that you want to use as a bargaining tool.The combat is quite unique with many mechanics and playstyles limited only by cost, parts and your ideas. Want massive battleships? You got them, want a carrier fleet to strike from afar? You got it, want fast corvettes to dodge enemy fire? You got it, and so on!This is not a game for those impatient or with gaming journalist level skills, it will test your abilities, in combat as you fight a guerrilla war on tactical and strategic levels, diplomatically to see your memory skills and knowledge of the game world, and economically with near constant low amounts of money to purchase fuel, parts and ammunition. Fortunately there are several difficulty levels if you were worried, Easy, Normal and Hard.By far one of the best parts of the game is simply in the sound design, I don't think I can name a game that's been able to surpass the quality of sound this game has. Everything is perfect or near perfect and even sometimes gives audio cues that can aid you. It is truly capable of capturing the deafening roar of enormous salvos. The sound design adds a ton to the immersive feeling of the game along with many banger tracks in the OST.The art design is also incredibly well done, most specifically lighting. Don't let the monitor view style dissuade you, search up a video on youtube (specifically a night battle) and just watch the stunning visuals.Unfortunately if you were wanting to play this game, perhaps with a friend, you cannot. This game is single-player only as the single developer would have to make a new engine and it is not in the game's vision.10/10 game, would panic when ELINT goes off and Pyotr stares into my soul

_childDocuments_.review: Steep learning curve, incomplete tutorials, incomplete manual. You will be watching lots of youtube videos which try to explain the more arcane aspects of the game, most of which end up saying something along the lines of "I'm not totally sure if this is how it's supposed to work".Super cool ideas but there are some serious gameplay issues that have to be addressed. I dig the dieselpunk vibe, but for the love of everything diesely and punky, why does every single interface have border on illegible? the Radar screens do not need to be 80% snow in order to achieve ambiance. the flight HUD does not need to wave and flicker every 1.3 seconds to get the cool old timey vibe. Oh lord, the fights in the rain with explosions, yeah okay I get it, make visibility harder in bad weather, but please, is it not within the realm of imagination that windshield wipers could be invented in this universe? Perhaps the biggest issue is unintentional retreating from fights. Nothing is worse than being 20 minutes into a scrappy dogfight, clawing your way past superior odds, piloting your last ship, about to deliver the deathblow volley..... only to accidently fly too close to the retreat arrow forfeiting the battle. The arrow you didn't see because of all the rain, explosions, blackouts, smoke, and camera shake. This game is in an odd state right now. Super fun and one I'd like to get in to, but so frustratingly unusable at points that it makes you quit and play something like FTL for a while.Can I recommend it to most people? No. Is it bizarrely compelling? Yes.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is self indulgent contest of masculinity with fantastic levels of overcompensation. It furfilled my lifelong dream to have a 40 cm beard and a 180 mm barrel, thanks Highfleet!Youtube is filled with videos of different death-bricks (that's how average endgame cruiser looks like) that barely move, slow enough for the enemy to write a will. And then they open fire and everyone wishes they didn't. Because it sounds exactly the way it looks - absolutely terrifying. Sound design and design in general in this game are fantastic! The game is very strategic. You are required to have a fleet of different ships designed for different purposes. You can configure them in the editor, but that process is clunky.If you are tired of obscuring the sky with gunfire, you can also put aircraft on your airship. So you can bomb some locals while bombing them. Or you can nuke them with some ballistic missiles killing as much as 50000 civilians per nuke. Being war criminal is fun!Or you can deliberately skip the fun by refusing to boil people alive, nuke them or engage in slave trade. But the outcome is the same. Your ideology does not affect the ending (at least in version 1.16), which, frankly, is unfinished. However, some RPG elements, such as the reputation/alignment bar, are present in the game. Yes, you have to negotiate and give speeches. Your customized death-brick can kill every enemy fleet, but you can't win against all their fleets at once. Thus, you must use stealth and scouting to prevent them from ganging up on you. Use aircraft to spot enemy fleets or destroy their strategic missiles. Use your own missiles to weaken them before engagement and so on.The game is difficult. It requires you to master and utilize many things at once and doesn't explain the mechanics well. This is one of those games (like Academagia or Warframe) that demand you to discover and understand the meta, read guides, watch videos etc...Useful spoiler below:

_childDocuments_.review: Sound and graphics are top shelf for a game like this.Tons of interconnected systems that make sense as a whole.Managing it all is really immersive, never a dull moment.Tough and unforgiving - your mistakes will be punished severely.But.. every time you lose you get more money to start with next time, based on how far you got.I've lost 5 or 6 long campaigns already, but each time it was clear why it was my own fault. _childDocuments_.review: Amazing atmosphere, art and sound effects.  I both love and hate the combat.  There are a few things that really bring the game down for me.-The battles forcing you to fight one on three.  The AI really should have to follow the same rules and send only one ship at a time.-The insanely accurate AI while I feel like I land hardly any shots.  I've seen people say to just got to go fast and dodge, but what if you are in a cruiser?  It just feels terrible piloting big ships.-The damage effects.  Holy cow are these annoying.  You take one little shot and your screen fills up with these giant bullet holes.  I kind of like the glitching screen, but hate when the action gets covered up.I'm really on the fence with this one. _childDocuments_.review: An RTS Rouge-like with heavy thematic immersion, RPG elements, and interesting strategic options on a VERY large map with a complex information warfare system but... the battles are a weird lunar lander bullet hell with a sharp difficulty curve.  Cruise missiles and planes are expensive and have limited effectiveness and I'd prefer not to be trapped in an irritatingly small box while outnumbered even if I bring more ships to the fight.  I've honestly tried to make it work, I've built custom ships with guides and trial and error to try and make the messy brawl that is the main fights less painful but they're still mind numbingly similar even if you make something that can win them reliably.  Using cruise missiles tends to be far too expensive and hard to restock for the amount of damage they do.  Planes are slightly more cost effective but tend to be too flimsy if the enemy knows you're coming and also expensive to replace.  The game just seems to want you to play a certain way that feels annoyingly ham fisted despite how amazingly detailed the information warfare and strategic gameplay is.If the combat arena was bigger and had more ships at once, it could have some strategy to it and I wouldn't feel like I'm circle shooting every battle until I hit something important enough times and then move to the next.  If the game had map based artillery volleys or better strategic weapons, I could just avoid the part I don't like and play it like a strategy game.  If I could autobattle, I at least would have an interesting fight scene to watch as the visuals are pretty good and then I can take a coffee break or do something else for a moment instead of being forced to play the same annoying minigame over and over until I either run into something stupidly hard to kill or spend the next few hours slowly plotting out plane and missile ambushes until I get unlucky too many times and lose too many resources to continue.The game isn't hard if you play it "right", just horribly tedious since trying to use strategic weapons means you run out of resources because you can't salvage most the loot from your kills unless you're right on top of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute masterpiece of a game that is that is immersive. Whats supposed to be a strategic air combat sim slowly dwelves into a survival horror as all the ELINT sensors scream at you and you contemplate whether to turn on your radar for that little moment only to realise a strikegroup is trailing on you fast. My only issue is with the ending however, all the effort and immersion boils down to an abrupt ending where the story is seemingly cut. Don't know if the developers plan to produce more content for the end game but its set certainly set up for more content. Eitherway, 10/10 would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely effen LOVE HighFleet! I can tell you that HighFleet has thoroughly impressed me with its combination of intense combat, strategic resource management, always running on fumes to the next town , and a unique and beautiful dieselpunk world. The battles are overwhelmingly challenging and overpowering with visuals and sound, leaving me with hardcore PTSD, but what left me with even more PTSD was hearing “Heat signature detected” and already panicking. I cannot recommend this game enough to those who crave a deep and thrilling gaming experience. I have lost countless hours to HighFleet, and I will keep coming back for more.And then when you are done suffering, turn up the difficulty to hard and truly enjoy an anxiety wreck fest.11/10 would launch Nukes again.

_childDocuments_.review: It is still cool game for a first couple of runs, there are cool sounds, music, visuals, few gameplay mechanics to master and some creativity. And yeah, I guess optimization is underwhelming for low-end. But this game could be easily a lot more exciting and with ton more of variety. Yet it is very original and quite good on its own, so I probably can recommend, however...For 1.5 years all what was changing is balance, vague mechanics and some building aspects. Now ships designs from game's point of view are more reasonable (armor makes sense, large weapons, etc), yet  new was added, as if this game is already perfect from content side. Everything already works well, but there is not a lot of everything, despite the fact that in game files and even in development builds we have seen many intriguing things which were already implemented. Even if they work not perfectly or disbalanced it still will be enjoyable, it is a singleplayer game (forget about multiplayer) after all.Variety is the weakest spot of this game.In some degree this is roguelite, and this game really need campaign setting and preferences. Because now the only replay value is progression in learning curve. Every run is completely the same... even second battle is completely the same. In shipworks mode settings for the fight are lame, you can not truly generate interesting battle cases.I do not even know what to say about this , just how you managed to make so original game and do not know what to do with it after release when you have so many feedback and insane popularity boost thanks to Sseth... ~feeling discouragement I am~

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not played in a straightforward way, you do not simply move on the map toward the enemy and fight. You are a small, outnumbered and outgunned force. You need to hide out in the desert and split your fleet by sending attack squad toward cities that you already weakened with missile and aircraft strike. But don't hide too long in the same spot or you'll get ganked. Watch your radar and send scout ahead, only send fuel convoy to city because moving your bigger ships only to refuel would mean losing money. Its a really rewarding game and the mechanics comes naturally when you get that you need to play in a different way. But don't hide too long in the same spot or you'll get yanked. Watch your radar and send radar scouts ahead, only send fuel convoy to city because moving your bigger ships only to refuel would mean losing money. It's a really rewarding game and the mechanics comes naturally when you get that you need to play in a different way.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the groundwork for a phenomenal game, just needs a few patches ironing out some of the annoying parts like micro-managing your detachments (its a bit fiddly), or coordinating air strikes with the arrival of a sudden strike detachment. Bombing runs being automated has the unfortunate side effect of the AI focusing one enemy ship and dropping nearly every bomb on only that one.As it stands, its already a hell of a lot of fun, the combat feels great and is quite challenging, although the visual glitch effects in both combat and the campaign map are quite agressive and can get annoying and a little strenuous.The World seems quite interesting, the story kept me interested so far, although story progression seems to be dependent on your vertical position on the campaign map (the game also seems to rate you on a "% of the way to your target"), as well as how many places you visit on the way. This led to me kind of stumbing over a story trigger that suggests to have started a failstate timer?The Campaign management is quite interesting and requires you to keep track of things like rough enemy positions, enemy callsigns and ciphers (being able to manually set cipher presets in the game would be rad, as of right now you gotta write em down yourself and manually punch em in to read old notes), the map tools are a nice touch and pretty fun to use.At time of writing I am 10 hours in, currently ~3 settlements away from Khiva. There were a few smaller and a bigger story twist so far, so I can confirm it doesnt just fizzle out.tl;dr: It's a lot of fun already, although a little rough around the edges. If the aesthetic of the game appeals to you and you dont mind keeping track of some things yourself, this game might be worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: The year is unknown and the surviving population of the old Earth are engulfed in civil war—the type of civil war that enables game developers to keep the ideologies vague and the names sinister-sounding. You play a Tarkhan captain tasked with capturing a key rebellion city in hopes of bringing the rebels to the negotiating table. But it’s not going to be easy as generations of mistrust and bloodshed hinder any potential progress. There is a bad feeling all around.Arriving at the mission objective, the young captain finds survivors, hears their stories and then is led into a virtual reality version of a close encounter of the third kind. Through narration, he is told about the history of the war and the secret of life on what used to be Earth and continues his journey in the most unexpected way.I watched the cutscenes with pleasure that was frequently interrupted by frustration. The three key game mechanics (arcade shooting, strategy, and an RPG lite component) are very well done. But why does the game amble so casually between these high points? Why must I constantly worry about fuel or have to navigate levers and button pushes to simply get from one point to another?And why, oh why, in a game where stories of past galactic battles, are we given just one ship to control against an armada of enemy ships? While I enjoyed HighFleet, I can’t imagine why I had to go through so much to accomplish what I felt like was so little.The game misses too many of its marks, especially early on. But I kept going because it had so many extraordinary things in it. It’s as if the developer, Konstantine Koshutin, rises to the occasion with its slick graphics and presentations but falls slightly when trying to execute them. An old friend of mine verbalized his simple definition of a good game: “If the game is missioned based, make sure there are more good missions than bad ones” Thankfully Highfleet does more good than bad.Despite some of these annoyances, the game does breathe new life into the traditional blast ’em up tropes. Highfleet takes a little extra time to show off its laser beams, steering wheels, and hydraulic joints on its spaceships to make piloting one seem unique. And the feeling conveyed when landing a spacecraft goes the extra mile to show the player the emotional stress and natural obstacles that one must overcome while solving physics-based dilemmas. The game may not be the next Homeworld, but on its own, it is pretty darn good.It’s interesting to consider how HighFleet would have fared a decade or two ago when hybrid games like Battlezone and Uprising ruled the roost. I’m sure it would have had limited visibility due to it not being from a big named developer but would have most likely achieved a cult following simply by word of mouth alone.Of course, access to good games—and this is a good game—is what matters, especially during a pandemic that is forcing many to stay at home, but I wonder if it will get the same traction as it’s buried in an overcrowded Steam service. I certainly hope not.Overall, I absolutely enjoyed Highfleet. The storytelling is rich with a fantastic legacy featuring deep themes and an admirable structure that, at times, immerses the player in a real cosmic struggle. It’s a game that is not only fun to play, but demands to be replayed for many of its features will be overlooked the first time around. It’s a special game from start to finish and one of the best of 2021 so far.

_childDocuments_.review: For full review go here: Game's strong points are in its unique conversation/worldview system and ship builder. It has an interesting landing mini game which can get tiresome to some and a nice ship vs ship combat if you do not mind always fighting 1 vs 3 despite how many ships you have ready to go.This game is notoriously difficult to learn. One person told me that he had spent 20 hours just learning. Underlying mechanics under the HUD are simple, but you will have to learn it in the worse way possible.In any game will be made a lot better where you can actually design your own units. Highfleet is not an exception to that. Though, I do have a nagging suspicion that developer's favourite food is spaghetti as you could judge from his code in this mode. Engine is bugged, often not creating right elevations for your guns. Other times it fails to connect wiring to your parts. Doing the exact same thing somehow manages to fix all the issues.This game has an outstanding visual representation which punches way above its weight. Amorphism of various HUD elements into its real life analogues adds to an atmosphere. Weather effects, landing under difficult conditions, high caliber impacts. These things are amazingly presented in this game. Game has a lot to offer to a dedicated gamer as it has a lot of depth in its mechanical gameplay. It will take many hours just to learn how to play just by following tutorials online. Then you have dozen hours long campaign and shipworks adds a lot of replayability to the main game mode. To select few, it will be a matter on making the best ship designs online.To everyone else, I can't recommend this game. I did not had fun in this game. Game does a very poor job introducing player in its own gameplay. Vanilla ships often are extremely bad. Sevastapool (Your vanilla flagship) is actually so bad that many consider it to be a main factor why campaign is so difficult in a first place. If you are someone who wants to just have fun with its game, this is not it. You are looking at, at least 20 hours learning curve. Afterwards in-game mechanics become just tiresome.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a brilliant Rogue-like that is well worth the asking price!A fantastic world deep with lore for those wishing to find it. Great physics, brilliant combat, punchy weapons and effects. It's quite clear this game is a labour of love, and it shows!It's hard as nails, but incredibly enjoyable. The manual and tutorials are on point, easy to follow and the game can be understood if you pay attention. The UI also might seem overwhelming, but you will be guided on its finer points as you progress. Make no mistake, this is a game that requires time, patience, and skill. If you have these and are willing to invest in multiple play-throughs (as is the core of all RL's) you will be rewarded. However, if you suffer from epilepsy though, best stay away. Flashes, intentional screen glitching and tearing all add to the aesthetic of this game, especially in combat. But it will have sufferers fitting on the floor at the main menu. Whilst others have expressed this as a complaint to not recommend the game, I personally see the opposite. Without this, the game would be visually dull in combat. I would advise watching the game on YouTube first to see if it an issue.Nevertheless, I will be playing much, much more of this game. Rogue-likes typically don't hold my attention beyond the first few hours. It takes something exceptional to do so. HighFleet is one of those games, and I'm determined to beat it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is almost hard to recommend due to the learning curve and obtuseness of some mechanics, but the experience once you start putting things together is excellent. Managing your strike groups, working with the sensors and intel you have, every flight and fight means something. There's nothing quite like figuring your way out of a terrible situation on the strategic layer, weakening an enemy strike group with a well-placed airstrike or cruise missile, and then finishing them off in combat. A must-have for naval warfare nerds and anyone else who likes military strategy games.

_childDocuments_.review: Great strategic game with ship to ship combat similar to star control.The campaign itself feels a bit similar to FTL but with far more story and atmosphere.You control a fleet or fleets on a strategic map, you can detect enemy radar, fire missiles, launch aircrafts, decode messages. Stealth is important factor in this game (launching strikes with fast aircrafts before enemy transmits your positions, keeping radar off etc).When you get into ship to ship combat it's a simple 2D fight where skill plays very important role. Because you see indications of enemy fire, with good pilot a small ship with great acceleration can defeat much bigger enemies.What's great: * atmosphere with stylized visuals, ambient sounds, interesting story characters and dialogues * skill based ship to ship combat * strategic map combat and planning  * fun plot twists * it's hard, expect to need more than one start. On the plus side you get bonus funds.Less great: * campaign up to Khiva can feel a bit repetetive  * sometimes it's hard to predict response of some NPC and you are left guessing what response to pick * ship designer is there, but apart from ships you take in the start of campaign you won't see much custom designs. You cannot customize flagship.  * important weapon and ship part stats are concealed and you are left guessing or you need to check GUI elsewhere to infer it * story ending (we need follow up)

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a damn good soft-sim that melts your eyes and drowns your senses out in the heat of combat. It makes me think of the MechWarrior franchise & Airships: Conquer the Skies with the building and customizing ships. The combat itself is something else. You constantly fight outnumbered and in enemy lines with no reinforcements except the airships you send in. It requires planning and tactics during combat and outside of it.You can win combat encounters through a variety of tactics:1. shear firepower. 2. Take your time and fire at the weakpoints of the enemy. (Careful though, you're on limited fuel and you better make those shots count.) 3. Hit and Run. (Airplanes and Interceptors.)4. Use special ammo which costs money that is limited and wreck havoc on the enemy.5. Retreat after you've put your own ship through the ringer and bring in the next to begin the next bit of carnage.6. Bomb the enemy before take off.7. Use the enemy's missiles to your advantage and cause them to Friendly Fire.I will gladly start a nuclear holocaust and be the one to finish it. DEUS IN NOBIS

_childDocuments_.review: The meme about single devs and their passion projects seems to be holding true. Quite a solid little strategy game that has a very gritty and definitive feel to it. 72 hours in and on my 4th campaign...Pros :  - Difficulty. It's nice to have a challenging / punishing game that doesn't hold your hand nowadays - Great artistic style, and I really do like the way the UI was done.  - Good transition between the tactical and real-time combat aspect - Enough depth to keep things interesting, definitely good for a few playthroughs at least - Ship builder is fun and lets you explore various strategic options as far as your fleet comp goesCons :  - Limited music. Coulda used more tracks. Music that's there is "ok", but low on the production quality.  - Choices in-game end up getting rather predictable, and feel like their impact is relatively minor to the over-all story. Maybe on hard-mode they carry more weight to the gameplay, but in normal, I felt like I could just pick whatever answer and that it wouldn't matter all that much. *** Balance ***. I think the current balance diminishes many aspects of what the strategic game-play *could* be, and many strategic features seem to be either cost-ineffective, or downright worthless once you wrap your head around the game mechanics. To pick one example...I cannot see a reason to ever send even the A-100 cruise missiles at a strike group...as they're just too good at shooting them down. (1 in 4 typically makes it in). At the same time...why would I ever send a cruise missile at a tactical group or garrison, when 1 single strike ship can do the job? Simply not satisfying or cost effective any way you slice it.  - All hail, the mighty CWIS.

_childDocuments_.review: Really unique game. You are a fleet of airships flying over an endless desert (think Dune). You have a mothership, which is nice and tough, and also a horrible fuel guzzler, slow, takes ages to repair and update and is home. The tactical map of the game plays like a ship/submarine simulator. The combat is not turn-based, you get to fly the ships real time. Combat is not 3D, but don't let that deter you. It's nice.The coolest part is that you have a ship designer. You can design a ship, then have it built or convert an existing ship to your design. This takes time and resources, but you get to experience the design choices you made in combat first hand. You built small and fast interceptor craft? Do they have enough range (fuel tanks) to raid that convoy passing 90 km away? Oh you can send a custom-design tanker craft along with your interceptors. You want a nice long range AWACs type craft in front of your fleet? You can build and fly it.You can even strip down your mothership and make it into a small corvette. But then your fuel capacity will suck and your range will be abysmal.Oh and the clack-clack-clack sound of the autocannons loading... That stays with you long after you finish the game. I can still hear it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to say recommend because I like this game and its concept so much but like many others which have posted reviews here reported it is broken and crashes alot.The good:- Once you understand what your doing this becomes a very good strategic game about waying up the pros and cons of your actions:  Do you strike with effective yet expensive to run and maintain aircraft carriers?  Do you use your slow heavy battleships which will gaurantee a win but will allow time for the enemy to order  a strike group/missiles/carrier strike groups to your location to destroy you? Do you send your fast strike group ahead to stop the enemy getting a transmission off and hope they can  win with limited firepower and without taking too greater damage?  Do you hit with cruise missiles and accept the extra repair time its going to take to re-load your missile  ships along with the fact that the enemy will report they have been hit by missiles? Do you use nuclear missiles and start a nuclear war, forcing you to dread having the enemy ever reporting  your position for fear of retaliation.In my experience using fast strike groups most of the time and saving the battleships for strike group confrontations is the way to go but you may find a different way.- The first time you play through its kind of fun not knowing what to expect.The interesting:- There seems to be a ship building mechanic to build custom ships which looks interesting but is poorly explained and complicated looking, I'm sure I'd enjoy it if I was into that kind of thing but I dislike assembling IKEA furniture with relatively easy to follow instructions.- Rescue/salvage operations after defeating an enemy fleet, good risk reward system with limited time and many objectives which cannot be all fulfilled however its frustrating that you cannot enter cities while rescue operations are underway and you will come under attack from missiles and aircraft often during a rescue operation. Also prepare for your kindness stat to go through the floor when you prioritise stopping the ammo or fuel from exploding and possibly killing the survivors over rescuing the survivors. Or alternatively priortise getting safety equipment on your crew to prevent them potentially dieing in greater numbers than the number survivors you could rescue in a harzardous situation.- The combat, on one hand I enjoy the asteriods style combat on the other it seems unfair my ships can only attack one at a time while they can field three ships against you. If you fight three heavy cruisers using nothing but proximity fuse ammo prepare for a very long time to repair your ships that will get torn to shreds no matter how well you play.- The stylish overlay and graphics on one hand makes it hard to see whats going on but on another adds to the challenge.The Bad:- Crashes, the end game crashes all the time, pretty sure I could have defeated this game if it would stop crashing when certain battles occur.- While you are on the subject of the end game ****Spoiler warning***** - Tarkhan negotiations to gain allies are frustrating and most of the time the game does not give you the verbal options which would obviously appease them based on their appearance/demeaner. This can be circumnavigated with gifts if you have collected enough from rescue operations

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely incredible.A mixture of so many other games that I have loved, and some I've only dreamed of, over the years.But it is also infuriating.- No manual saves. Why?- An ingenius, beautiful, but ultimately impenatrable UI- No Auto-landing (I know it's risk reward for a repair bonus, but christ-alive it's exhausting & janky)- Gorgeous, visceral combat; but you face a fleet within only one vessel at a time.Wait for a a few months of polish on this diamond caked in gore and diesel.EDIT:Persevering with the game because there is so much good there, but it's still so frustrating to play; even if you go full hardcore-gamer- Not being able to save when you want/need means you cannot play it casually. You can't pick it up and put it down at need. This is 2021, life happens. You can't ask someone to lose progress because they can't save their game at a particular point and have to eat/sleep/leave the house, etc.- 16 hours into a campaign, and now facing *huge* optimisation issues. Whenever a map loads, or I select my flagship, or there is a screen load, it can take over a minute per load. A full minute! Sadly now nearly unplayable - as approaching a town, winning the combat, landing a ship or two, repairing at the Shipbuilders, purchasing fuel, and then taking off again can take 30 mins - most of it waiting! _childDocuments_.review: Originally refunded it and left a negative review. Realized I was going at it with the wrong mindset, came back, and learned to appreciate it more. Here are some things I should've known before going in, and some things potential buyers should keep in mind.PLAY IT LIKE A ROGUELIKE. Not recommended if you're basing your expectations on Carrier Command 2 or a naval strategy sim. Treat it more like FTL, where your early campaigns are expendable. You will inevitably lose everything to a simple miscalculation or just bad luck. You are constantly at a disadvantage, so think of it more like you're commanding a submarine than a fleet of rocket-propelled gun-bricks.COMBAT IS AN ARCADE GAME. If you want a game where fleet composition and mutually-supporting assets are vital, and where circumstances allow a clever commander to dictate the terms of an engagement, you will be disappointed. You go into a small arena with one of your ships at a time and engage in high-octane lander swashbuckling. All the methodical strategy in the overworld suddenly disintegrates as soon as you enter battle.GIVE THE SHIPWORKS A CHANCE. Do NOT ignore the ship-building element. While the dichotomy between the strategy and action is jarring, the action is still a lot of fun, and tinkering with different designs and fighting without putting a campaign at risk can help draw one in.

Looks like a 2D shooter and you'll be doing some 2D-shooting, but everyone who blamed this game for beeing nothing more than the sum of a bunch of minigames; including 2D-shooting is horrribly wrong.There is so much strategy involved on the strategic map, like radar range and radar detection range, IR spotting, preemptive strikes, negotiation for hearts and minds..Had to rewrite this review after couple hours and the more I delve into I begin to realize how well everything works together. _childDocuments_.review: This game is what happens when you take an awesome idea and do not follow through on the implementation. Its overextended - there are so many things going on that it seems “really deep”, but they missed the “fun”. To be clear - this is not a fun time – you have no indication of what to do until you fail multiple times to learn “the right way”. Its either frustratingly hard or boringly easy. You die for some unknown reason, then you win with an easy button.I’ll start with the good:Great concept and excellent immersion – graphics and style are top notch.The pacing rides the line so you’re always frantic but not quite overwhelmed.The size of the world means your eyes are useless – it’s like being in a submarine – all intelligence is indirect (radar, triangulation, communications interceptions, math). They nailed the strategic touches – being in the air increases your radar signature, disabling your radar prevents detection, attacking at night improves your stealth, etc.The combat mechanics are captivating. You’re jousting with other massive hunks of metal while aiming your guns and trying to hit soft points. Its intense and nailing your target is an accomplishment.Unfortunately, the game becomes frustratingly difficult because the mechanics are not thought though.Spoilers:Every battle is 1 v 3+. Its called highfleet but your fleet can’t join. The enemy fleet gets 3+ at a time. You end up playing a weird meta where your light ships unload as much damage as possible before you run out of fuel forcing a retreat, so your next slow and powerful ship mops up the mess. This is comical at the “final” battle where the enemy capital ship spawns with 2 support ships against your … newb ship. I ducked and dived around the capital fire to kill the other ships just to retreat so the rest of the fleet could take pot shots at the enemy (each retreating) until I won. Cruise missiles and fighters are completely out of place. Given how captivating the player-controlled combat is – it’s a joke that a few cruise missiles or some bombers can destroy capital ships in a few seconds. You make a powerful fleet and run the enemy just to be ripped apart by a cruise missile or a suicide bomber. It goes both ways - once you learn this trick you can obliterate the enemy. I’ve been extremely outnumbered just to spam cruise missiles at short range. For some reason they stop defending themselves after 2 missiles…. OK easy button. On the flip side, having to “defend” against 6 cruise missiles in a row is awful. The unit you control to defend can’t be chosen, and your allies shoots down your own AA missiles. It’s just random. If you get hit you ALT-F4 and if not you continue.The “big bad enemy” called “strike groups” are a paper tiger due to the broken cruise missile mechanics. It broke down to finding enough cruise missiles so you could lure them to their doom. I killed all the SGs using cruise missile mechanics. The end game is awful – you make it to the “end” at the capital city of wherever the hell we are. The capital has no gear to repair your ships, despite being the pinnacle of post apocalyptic technology. If you knew this you would bring all the crap you sold previously and easy button the end. Otherwise you’re screwed since they spawn magical 10x nuke carriers to bombard you – see the cruise missile discussion above. An added FU was spawning an extra strike group because i killed them all. Now that I'm in the know - 1) bring plenty of nukes to the end to destroy the magic carriers, 2) leave one strike group alive wondering the wastes, 3) capture cities around the capital so you can plant radar units to find the nuke carriers. I guess I could play it again to min/max the end game but… F that.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun and surprisingly deep rogue-lite game about leading your fleet of smoke belching 10000-ton sky battleships through hostile territory to strike at the enemy capital. The main campaign is a lot of fun, and it takes some thought to get through, both in regard to the composition of your fleet, and the game plan for dealing with enemy fleets. The story is there, but not really the highlight of the game. It takes the form of occasional text boxes and artwork, as well as meetings with other fleet captains. What is very nice, however, is the presentation. The artwork looks cool, and the sound effects as well as visual clutter like smoke, fire, raindrops on the screen etc really amplify the cool-factor and immersion of commanding and fighting in dieselpunk skyships. The ships at your disposal are fully customizable during a run, and entirely new ships can be constructed between runs, and included in your starting fleet when you begin your next one. Combat between ships takes place in a real time 2d battlefield, while management and the movments of your fleet(s) is handled on a separate strategy layer. After some playtime, and a few failed runs, the ship designer adds a lot of additional depth to tailor the game to your chosen strategy. Overall the main game drew me in, but the ship designer made me keep playing long after i had finished the campaign. I found a lot of enjoyment in designing the perfect ships for my starter fleet, fitting my chosen playstyle. Scout ships for detecting and avoiding enemy fleets, tankers to keep the fleet self-sufficient for long periods, light raider craft to capture settlements and conduct piracy, heavy cruisers to brawl with enemy fleets, aircraft/missile carriers and much more. Conclusion: Sky battleships cool, good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Highfleet is a game much like its predecessor, Hammerfight. A set of gameplay and style elements put together in a way no-one has ever really thought of putting them together, flying in the face of years of genre conventions. Except it's nothing like Hammerfight.The first thing that strikes anyone looking at this game is the visual aspect. Highfleet is one of those games that slips into its setting like a comfortable suit and wears it with confidence. The graphical art is an intrinsic part of the experience, whether that's the amazing character art, the purposefully clunky, fiddly UI, or the gorgeous smoke and dust effects. It's all there to inundate you into an alien world that nevertheless echoes our own. This inimical visual style is accompanied by appropriate, mostly understated music and good sound effects. These giant ships look like they should make a lot of noise, and they do. Roaring engines, blaring alarms, and the constant whine of giant engine gimbals during combat. You are not a nameless character attacking a nameless world to establish a highscore. You are Duke Sayadi, heir to the Romani dynasty. You are on a mission to end a way that is poised to swallow the world, and the deserts of Elaat you are trekking your way through. These might be the end times, and you might be a prophet. Success relies not only on the careful managing of your resources, and your skill as a warrior, but on understanding this land, and yourself.Underlying the soulful, artsy side of the game is a simple gameplay principle: Doing stuff costs stuff. At its heart the overworld aspect of the game is about resource management. Moving costs fuel, damage costs repairs, and engaging in combat costs morale. All of them cost time. You must move towards your objective, but you must also ensure you can take the objective when you get there. You must gather allies, and you must ensure that you have money in pocket so your expedition does not become stranded. Highfleet is one of those games where there are enough systems at work, and they are divergent enough, that it takes on a feeling of satisfying realism. Resource management, in other words, is not a simply paper, rock, scissors endeavour. It's a soft skill that requires taking into account a bunch of maybe's, leveraging risks towards potential reward. A hidden city, for instance, might be a good place to recuperate and hide from roaming Strike Groups. But it has to be found. If you are lucky, you will have intel. If not, you will have to comb the desert with ground radar, investigate likely sigantures, and be mindful of your fuel and plan B should you not find any city. Or say you have defeated a Strike Group and want to loot its juicy, expensive weapons, but there might be a carrier or missile group close. Sitting on the ground will make you very vulnerable to air or missile strike, but the window of opportunity to loot the battlefield will be lost if you take off. Ah, but you can launch your own fighters to fly cover, but will have to pay for that in turn-around time when they return. These decisions are the constant in Highfleet, and while a certain amount of brute-forcing may be possible for good combat pilots and designers (I feel like I've been particularly successful in designing a heavy interceptor that makes part of the game much easier than they would have been), it's paramount that you pay attention to how and where you deploy your forces. And yes, you can design your own giant skyships. This is another core gameplay element that the game flat-out expects you to at least dabble in. Some of the core designs are good, some of them are terrible, and a wise Tarkhan will pay attention to this.Even after putting a fair deal of time into it Highfleet remains a hard game to describe. It's kind of a roguelike, but not really, because save points are one of the resources you need to pay attention to. It's a light strategy sim, but you play a character in a story and talk to people. Hardly anyone ever mentions the talking to people, but you do. One of the resources are the Tarkhans, influential commanders who come with their own ship and assistance, who you will have to convince to join your cause. This is where Highfleet silently and humbly takes a leap that AAA games have been snoring on. The Tarkhans have personalities made up of how much they like certain concepts, and the things you say to them will convince them or anger them based on that. But that's not all. You and your crew also have opinions on these, which saying and doing things will have an impact on. And having high scores in these will be important for story events. In other words, playing an opportunist who just tells people what they want to hear has consequences, essentially giving you weak stats. Sticking to your guns and telling a Tarkhan something they wouldn't want to hear will make you stronger. This also extends to the random events you encounter, of which there are many, and several of the larger ones have randomized outcomes. All of this is underpinned by an intriguing setting and story, on which the presence of the Tarkhans you recruit and the decisions you make have an impact. Plainly put, there's a lot to see here, and the way the story and characters are set up is as involving as the resource management aspect of the game, in part thanks to a clever mechanic that I've frankly been waiting for in games. Namely, the things you say and do build your character.Highfleet is a unique game in the true sense of the word. Nothing quite like it exists. It's a serious game that demands to be taken seriously, which scares off some of the people who have tried it. Any other game with subject matter as ridiculous as giant, methane-burning airships engaging in aerial combat over science fiction pseudo-Afghanistan might have felt it necessary to soften the blow with humor. Highfleet does no such thing. There are still some minor kinks to be worked out, and some of the design choices might not be optimal. And admittedly, there's a feeling that there should have been more. But having already put in excess of 100 hours into it (which certainly didn't feel like 100 hours), I'm not sure that feeling is justified by it being true, or by me just wanting there to be more. because I know that when I've wrung the game dry of new experiences there won't be another game to give me more of the same.So yes, I recommend it. And yes, this is a fair price. Because this is the sort of game that just isn't safe to make. It definitely scares some people off, it's not super-easy to pick up, and its soulful setting might not resonate with everyone. The deserts of Elaat are not for the faint of heart. But to those adapted to such climes, they shine with a beauty not found anywhere else.

There's no indication.Can you buy any of them? No, you need specific missiles, but you're not told that.After you click on a missile type there's a subtle indicator showing which ship it's valid for. So click through 10 types to find which missiles fit which ship.Going into combat:You're shown a roster of 4, of your, ships.You drop into combat and see 4 ships on the screen. They must all be yours. So where is the enemy?3 of the 4 ships are now firing at you - because you only drop into combat with 1 of your ships, and the enemy can spawn next to you.Retreating:There's an on-screen indicator telling you how / where to retreat to swap ships.You're meant to battle with 1, while the enemy battles with multiples, which is dumb.If you reach the "Retreat" indicator, it often moves elsewhere and it's unclear how to retreat initially.Refitting your ship:You're not told how, and there are tons of parts immediately available.Okay, you click something, it removes a part, so you drag it back on - but you're charged a maintenance fee to do so.So you're being punished for not knowing how the game works at the most basic of levels, and it's not explained.---"It's not explained" seems to be the design philosophy of the whole game.And "it's not explained, but you have to do it well, or else" happens again, and again, and again, and it very quickly gets tiring.The presentation is fantastic, the game is dripping with atmosphere, and the concept is uniquely cool. But it's far more hassle than fun. One of my most immediate thoughts was "I can't wait for some other developer to rebuild this idea into something sensible."

_childDocuments_.review: Immersive and frustrating are the two best words to describe HighFleet. It's a game that pretends to be an arcade-y shooter but in reality it's a very advanced naval warfare simulator, the only thing I can compare it to is Pacific Threatre of World War 2 and the huge game of cat and mouse between American and Japanese carrier groups. At first you will have no idea what's happening, you'll get slapped by cruise missiles, pinched from two or three sides by enemy strike groups and missile-carriers. But progressively you'll start to use more tools to your advantage, you'll start noticing details that you paid no mind earlier. Just today I was able to destroy whole enemy strike group without my main carrier force being even spotted, using only two fast-moving radar and ELINT-capable ships and twelve light fighters with 250kg bombs. All of that, thanks to simple tool of compass. If you've ever wanted to employ actual Art of War in a game, this is it. From what I've gathered AI legitimately does not know where you are and has to look for you just like you look for them, with their radars, ELINT and calculating your movement with the data received from garrisons radio-ing in for help. The world is beautiful, the immersion is off the charts, the frustration spurring you on to get better is there. If you like Rogue-likes, Sekiro or Dark Souls you'll love this game. If you just want to shoot at dumb AI with cool ships, you should probably look elsewhere.

People who enjoy ship building and engineering in games will love the customization systems here. People who want an RTS that has a level of espionage and mystery to will love the on map planning and experience. People who love making the most out of few given resources will love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be the first time I've ever written a review for a game that I've asked to be refunded. I just want to warn people who might have the same misunderstanding about what this game is that I did.I bought Highfleet expecting it to be a strategic simulation game about fleets of giant, lumbering diesel-punk airships blasting away at each other with enormous cannons. It definitely has that aesthetic. Unfortunately for me, the "simulation" part of the "strategic simulation" that I was hoping for never manifests. Combat, the main crux of the game, is essentially a twin-stick shooter that uses your "fleet" as a series of extra lives.It feels pretty pointless to assemble a grand fleet when that fleet never functions as a unit. Instead you control an individual ship, all alone, against the enemy fleet. You can tag-out by flying to an indicated spot on the map to switch to the next ship in your fleet, but you will only ever have a single ship actively fighting at once. For me, this destroyed any sense of immersion that the game could have hoped for. I did not like twin-stick shooter combat. The twin-stick shooter combat seems to be about 80% of the game.I don't usually write reviews for games that I wouldn't recommend, and I'm sure there are some people who would truly like Highfleet. I was not one of them and I don't think that anyone who buys the game with the expectations that I had going in would enjoy it either.

_childDocuments_.review: So I've been playing it a while.The game isn't bad, and once you understand what is going on through sheer force of will and endlessly getting your ass handed back to you on a silver platter, it all makes a little more sense.Every negative point I had regarding the game can be boiled down to a complete lack of any sort of tutorial beyond Pyotr giving you a few pointers.  After that, you're dropped into the world and you think you have it handled, but with each consecutive game, you find out you've bare scratched the surface.The game needs a better tutorial and to display all information relevant to you, it's already an information heavy game, I think I can handle knowing the health and speed of a KH-15 cruise missile.Anyways, 10/10 would develop stockholm syndrome for this game again.ORIGINAL REVIEW: What a god awful combat system.The game starts off pleasant and tactical, and quickly devolves into bullet hell and save scumming because you're only one ship fighting off 4-5 ships.  This wouldn't be a problem if the ships were quick and nimble, but they're not.  Even the smallest ones handle like fat whales in molasses, so what should be a slow ballad of dodging fire and shooting down missiles, quickly turns into a god forsaken cluster♥♥♥♥ that's about as close to trying to get a cow to square-dance as I imagine I'll ever get.Also, I love the art style and atmosphere.  IF ONLY I COULD ENJOY IT instead of staring into a landscape and trying to make out which blob is my ship and which direction my guns are pointed to I can shoot at the other blob.  Why would you purposely not let me zoom in so I can more effectively knife fight the other ship WITH THE SHIP MEANT TO BE KNIFE FIGHTING?!This game is trying to be too many things at once.  Be hammerfight, be bulle thell, be something, just not everything at the same time.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this game is a very rough gem. It nails the aesthetic and theme of everything, from the artwork, ui, immersive mechanic, and stunningly beautiful graphic. It has also a very tight and hardcore dogfight where it would punish you for your mistakes and rewards you for utilizing everything you've got at the right time. However, the campaign map (one you see from your radar ui) and what micro you do there is as important as the dog fight it self and you won't enjoy the game if you only like one of them.In the campaign map, you'll need to manage a lot of things starting from resupplying your fleet with enough supplies for the next destination, managing strike groups to intercept or silence the enemy before they can alert reinforcement, and plan out your route wisely to avoid or engage the enemy by intercepting encrypted enemy messages. Mind you, just as how hardcore the dogfight could be, same also apply for the campaign map. You alerted the enemy because you keep your radar on near the enemy? good luck dealing with the 7 long range missiles heading your way, accompanied by multiple enemy fighters. oh and enemy Strike Groups are DEFINITELY going to your location now.Now for the bad part, while the game has a beautifully aesthetic ui, it doesn't function as good as it looks. everything just sort of blend together and there's a lot of visual noise that it would take you a while to know what button does what (or if something even is interactable). Some of the ui also feel slugish at times and it lacks some QoL improvement (especially in the ship building section). And on top of that, there's a constant effect of explosions and stuff that sometimes it's very hard to tell what the hell are you looking at during a dogfight. And as it stand now, it still lack ultra wide support which would in turn make everything stretched out.Definitely not for everyone, however it is easily a 9/10 if you into this sort of strategy and 2d side-scroller dogfight and also able to look pass the jank-ness.

_childDocuments_.review: game is an absolute gem, tons of heart and depthedit: came back to add commentary (at ~129 hrs).  Highfleet is a game with both beauty and brains.  The core of the game is navigating your fleet of ships across ~19,250 km to the enemy's capital, no wait the core of the game is the air ship combat where you fly thousand ton ships at 500 km per hr across the sky blasting down your enemies with various fused munitions dodging smoke, flame, and the now ruined burning hulls of your enemiesno wait the core of the game is the ship designer where you can lose countless hours tweaking ship designs and creating your own: fuel consumption, firepower, sensor suite, engine thrust, ammo storage, crew quarters, fire suppresion systems, on-board fuel storage, overall fiscal costno wait the core of the game is tweaking your campaign fleet's overall composition: fighting out a campaign, thinking of how you could change a ship here, design a new one there, and then restarting the campaign to bring along your new custom designs from the start.  High fleet is a game that's really the above mentioned series of smaller games (the campaign's fleet map, the tactical sky battles, the ship designer, the fleet composition) and each of these has such stellar design: easy to get into, lots of depth to explore.  High fleet can feel difficult to grasp at first, as if it's putting itself in front of you without actually divulging any of its secrets.  The overall game loop though makes the journey well worth the effort, as mastery over one section of game (eg fleet movement in the campaign) compels mastery over another section (eg tactical air combat) which inspires improvements elsewhere (ship design) which you can then realize at the start of the loop again (taking custom ships back into the campaign)

_childDocuments_.review: If anyone should come across this review please note I have now re-installed the game four times and played 300 hours of this masterpiece.The complexity of the gameplay is very confronting and confusing at first, but once that settles you learn every single element of the game has its own place and all of your decisions and actions matter as you move through the main story.I must have died 50 times trying to beat the game on normal, running out of money, completely running out of ships and relying on my capital ship that gets blasted to bits, or dying at the very end of the game when victory is so close.I don't know exactly what it is about the game that is such a big draw for me exactly. I like the rain and calm of the towns, I like organising a strategy and seeing it pay off like leaving a Mockingbird at a far corner of the map to draw a strike group so I can sneak past, I like how the game slowly switches from scarcity at the start to complete abundance at the end.If this isn't a game to be cherished, which one is?

_childDocuments_.review: i think highfleet is probably my favorite game ever at this point. i'm still young by the standards of a lot of the ppl i know who are into stuff like this (am 19 at time of writing) so maybe i lack the proper frame of reference for what this medium of art and entertainment SHOULD be.but i can't help thinking that highfleet at least comes extremely close. the artwork, presentation, and setting are magnificent (i made up my mind to get this game after a few screenshots i saw on twitter) and tactile. to give one example, big explosions are used judiciously in a way that's rarely true of other games. the result is that, when you hit something actually explosive (ammo or external bombs) it's exorbitantly satisfying.even with seemingly a fair bit of content cut from the release (k.k. et al, PLEASE. I WILL DO ANYTHING TO GET MORE) the amount of creativity possible in ship design, combat, and overall decision making is fantastic. if you want evidence of this, join the highfleet fan discord to see ppl debate which gun is truly the best (they virtually all have supporters) or building cracked-out custom fleets to cross gerat at supersonic speeds. there's even a small but very talented modding scene.highfleet has a difficult learning curve, admittedly, which would be my main source of hesitation for recommending this to a wide audience. the flip side is that you're forced to teach yourself in trial by fire to find your own rhythm and footing. for me that's probably one of the most compelling reasons to play a game, especially when it's structured to encourage that (see my backlog of space engineers stuff for a better perspective of how this happens in an admittedly much worse game, lol). if you have streaks of creativity and perhaps masochism, or maybe are just enamored by potential answers to the question "what if the soviet invasion of afghanistan was led by house leto from dune and carried out by massive flying gun bricks?"...you have unequivocally come to the right place ; )

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. I give it a recommendation, because it's a unique work by an obviously eccentric one-man developer. We need more unique and strange games!How to describe this game? Comparison to FTL is somewhat warranted, but only to a certain extent. This is strategy game, but that label doesn't really encapsulate it either. You manage a fleet of ships (of your choosing at the campaign start) as you traverse a desert planet that's sort of blend of Arrakis and Kharak from Homeworld. The ship management, repair and armament is the simplest part. You also have to manage radio, radar and infrared signals intelligence, which are mostly baffling due to the way they are (or aren't) explained in tutorial. Maybe others will take to them more quickly. I feel dumb complaining about it! Some aspects of your controls just are not adequately explained at all. Particularly how to use aircraft - and I question how useful these actually are. There is a diplomacy element that happens sparingly enough that it feels like a totally different game when it does. These are rather difficult because you need to pick your speech options based on what will play best to your counterpart's personality and worldview, but you don't know anything about these until you suss it out by trial and error, by which point it's likely too late. A big deal of luck is involved.There is a lot to like in this game. However my biggest impression from it is that I just did not enjoy the combat at all. For how complex the rest of the game is, the combat is too simple, but also seems like it's not giving you enough information. Damage is modeled on a part-by-part basis for each ship; there is no clear indicator of your ship's overall health or of the consequences of damage (or of your enemy's health) - I've been on fire and finished a combat without losing anyone, for example. You see a schematic of your ship and your target ship to see a bit of this modular damage, but it's not like you can target the bridge, for example, specifically. In combat you and your opponents are just flying 2D circles around each other and you shoot what you have at them. And the combat is so zoomed out that the bridge is maybe 4 pixels large, so you really can't aim at desired weak points. So the combat hints at having this strategic layer will a lot going on underneath, but all you can actually do is Asteroids-level gameplay.

For example, in explaining the Infrared Scanner, the manual reads as follows:  "Detail Screen - IR sources will be shown in greater detail in this screen."  No ♥♥♥♥.  Tell me what the heck it does in practical terms.  This game and manual are FULL of instances like this; wtf moments left fully unexplained. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a real masterclass. The game mechanics is a perfect balance in terms of complexity and engagement. It's simple conceptually but depth comes as you put theory into practice. The constant scarcity and looming danger throughout the game will have you thinking about logistics, taking notes to decrypt messages, triangulating potential dangers and weighing your options. The artwork, atmosphere, story and UI is very immersive. Don't let the graphics fool you into thinking it's an arcadey game. It's more military wargaming but simplified. Though I have to say, the dialogues with tarkhans do feel a bit unpredictable and constrained but I feel it makes it more "human" and adds to the atmosphere of the game.One slight I would give this game is it needs a bit more work in the quality of life department. It is a little tedious to move entire sections of the ship around if you change your mind on a design. A "blueprint" mode especially in campaign is sorely needed since you have no way of changing/managing different variants of a ship in your fleet.Highly recommend this game even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the ship builder and the customizing that you can do while playing the game at the ship works.  The game play is pretty immersive as others have said.  If a light blinks or a knob turns, they both have a purpose in the game and mean something.  The various mini-games from combat, radio messages to landing are all pretty slick ideas in the game.This game is clearly very good, and very popular.  But a few things just cause me to say "I'm not having as much fun as I think I should be having right now."1.  Missles.  The ones fired from far away toward you.  Very, very difficult to deal with and has catastrophic effects on your ships when you can't intercept them.  Not 1 in a while.    3+ back to back.  AA and guns from 2 ships hit the missles 2+ times but nah, you're still getting rocked.  Cool mechanic?  Yes, kinda.  I could just suck at this part of the game and even so, it's a deal breaker for me.2.  Radio messages almost non-stop.  After a while I just quit trying to tune in and just click the auto button.  It's not like the messages ever come in clear.  The same vital data missing from every message when you don't get it 100% correct.  And even when you do get a message, big deal, it's out of reach for you to deal with or the message is incomplete enough to mean nothing to me.3.  Intel.  Telling me about ships 10 cities away is great.  But just seems like a tease for what you can't be worried about immediately.  4.  With you RADAR off you can't see the targets anyhow, and if you bump into a Strike Group or Convoy it's dumb luck (good or bad). The game isn't a bad game...  It's just a few issues that are significant enough for me to shelf this game and uninstall.  There aren't 1000's of people who say it's the most amazing thing  in forever..Just not to me.  I did get my money's worth out of it though.

_childDocuments_.review: Oof.  What can be said about this game?  I've played Souls games so I'm not afraid of hard.  I've beaten Battletech so I'm no dummy when it comes to strategy.  But Highfleet is hands down the most unrelentingly meanspirited game I've ever played.  I gave it the old college try as well.  More than 20 hours and dozens of "die retry die retry die retry" as well as slowly figuring out each little doohickey and ship the game does very little to explain.  And look.  I get it.  You're fighting a guerilla war.  But my experience has mostly been "Go here.  The enemy found you.  Go there.  The enemy found you."  Even if a fleet isn't a strike group, this game's version of a boss fight, it'll be something that'll tattle on you to bring the closest strike group to you, which is often not that far away.  There are nuggets of brilliance here, but it's buried under layers of unintuitive mechanics.  Finding transport ships, the only decent way to earn money, has mostly been down to stumbling into them, even with the radio intercept and decryption tools the game gives you, and even then it's often barely enough to offset the cost of fuel and funding your war machine.  And that's not even mentioning other odd design choices like why you have to amass a fleet, but you still fight the enemies one ship at a time, yet your foes have no such restrictions, or why picking a difficulty isn't a handy options menu selection but is instead a little dial tucked away in the corner that defaults to normal every single time, or why meta progression is tied to how far north you made it the last run, which for me was barely more than a few cities in, or why the ship classes make no damn sense in the universe, especially when your own ships seem flimsier than its classification would suggest while the enemies' strike group ships seem many times stronger than their classification would suggest.  I also found myself becoming more and more unable to overlook the game's various bugs, like disappearing images or npc ships landing upside down.I gave this more than 20 hours of gameplay and have decided that other games are more demanding of my attention.  I won't delete it from my library.  It'll just sit uninstalled for now.

Half Dune half Lawrence of Arabia and then an extra half Soviet-Afghan invasion make for a fascinating setting and art style.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically the people giving this game a negative are just bad or want it to be something it isn't. Here's the QRD.What this game is:A Stealth Bullet Hell with RTS elements. It's also very hard and intentionally unfair (life isn't fair, cry about it. lol)What this game isn't: A typical command and conquer style RTS, though that'd be really cool with some tweaking. I recommend Airships: Conquer The Skies who want a game with more classical RTS elements and is similar to this. What I like: The mixture of stealth, bullet hell, and RTS is completely unique. There's nothing like having your favorite ship that you have been decimating everyone with and ranked up being blown up by some random missile 1250km out. There's also nothing like getting better at the game after watching so many prized ships die in a fiery glory, and learning how the scout and counterstrike or destroy them before they even get the chance. The end game is to become a demigod with a nuclear arsenal to rival the nation that destroyed yours. What I dislike: Ship builder that promotes homogenization, and lack of aesthetic custom options (though to be fair the game is beautiful). No multiplayer (the only way allied ships would work in it's current state imo but apparently there's a dlc in the works?). Tutorial system that doesn't quite get into enough nuance. Here's the expanded QRD.-This is a stealth game. You're engaging in guerilla warfare against a nation that has destroyed your own with no other goal than retribution through MAD. You are outnumbered and outgunned, and always will be. This game makes you feel like a cornered dog. It isn't like Total War or Civ Or AOE or w/e. Taking and holding vast swaths of land is not the objective. Neither are large scale engagements (hence all the people complaining about 3v1). As much as I would like this game to be that, it just isn't. Here's to hoping for a sequel that incorporates those elements. -This is not an RTS in the traditional sense. The RTS elements come from understanding the tools in your HUD, the roles of your ships, and logistic management. The HUD includes three different radar systems and a built in pencil and beam compass to plan intercept trajectories and strike ranges. Your ship role is also extremely important as using a ship for the wrong thing can ruin your playthrough entirely. Resources are scarce so you have to make everything count. This means leapfrogging from fuel point to fuel point with your big ships and causing chaos and diverting attention using your own strike groups made of smaller ships. You are a commander in charge of basically every aspect of your unit, from communication (hud interaction), the logistics (scouting and evading enemy strike groups, resource management), but will you will not be doing is commanding grand armies. The battles are still epic anyway, and people whining about difficulty just need to get good or choose a different game.

detailed_description: Join Gail, a simple villager, who must heed the call for adventure when a great star ship appears in the night sky and abducts all the adults. As the new oldest member of her fragmented community, she must set out to solve this great mystery. Little does she know of the grand adventure before her, the evil lurking in the shadows, and the role she will play in the fight for Earth’s very existence! Features: - A narrative-driven single-player adventure filled with charming characters, vibrant towns, and dangerous dungeons. - Over 10 different weapons & tools with which to combat enemies and solve puzzles. Fly with rocket boots! Blast with bombs! Play the flute! - Fight against over 50 different enemy types and 12 boss encounters. - A world brimming with secrets! Find 33 Energy Gems, 55 Heart Pieces and 111 Moonstones. - An achievement system, with 33 badges to earn, for players seeking extra challenge and replayability. - Over 60 original songs ranging from mellow piano and orchestra to raging synth/metal rockers and bagpipes! - A main campaign length estimated at 30 hours of playtime. 50 hours for completionists. Solve the great mystery of the Phoenix!

_childDocuments_.review: From the dev blog:"SO what is next?What isn’t next… is Phoenotopia 2. As you may have heard down the grapevine, the game couldn’t be what you call successful. No one’s earned even minimum wage on it.Maybe there’s hope in the game’s long tail. A year or two down the line… maybe. I won’t hold my breath though. At some point in the past few months, I finished processing (or grieving) and it’s time to move on.The game has at least earned enough for us to continue our modest operations. As long as we don’t expand the team, and we don’t take another monster six-year dev cycle like what Phoenotopia took, we can continue. We’ll have to be smarter and faster. Perhaps the most valuable thing we gained from all this is experience.".This game is soooo underrated, Devs deserve much more.

_childDocuments_.review: Every few years, there comes a game that reminds me why I play video games. A game that reminds me what they're capable of, the unique emotions and experiences they are capable of providing. Phoenotopia: Awakening is one of those games.This game was an absolute joy to play from start to finish. From hour 1 to hour 100 of my first, 100% playthrough and beyond that. Phoenotopia: Awakening is so packed full of fun things to do, cool stuff to discover, secrets to find that I'm still eager for more after over 130 hours of playtime.Every single aspect of this game is bursting with charm and passion and I would give almost anything to be able to play it blind again. It's that special kind of game that will stick with you for the rest of your life.It's quite possibly my favourite game of all time. It's not for everyone, but it's more than worth a try. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia Awakening is a really good Metroidvania that I played and put a couple hundred hours in when it first came out on the switch. World has a lot of secrets and is really pretty and fun to explore. The music is beautiful, the characters and dialogue are cute and the story is pretty good. The only major gripe that I have is the difficulty and it is recommended to use the accessibility options in the settings to make the game more bearable if it’s your first playthrough. The game doesn’t hand hold you and expects that you explore and speak to everyone(which you should since NPCs are pretty funny a lot of the time). $20 is pretty cheap for what this game had to offer so anytime it goes on sale there’s no reason to not buy this beautiful game.
