_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore Phoenotopia Awakening. I bought this game purely off of seeing it in my discovery queue and thinking the artstyle was really good and that it looked fun and I think buying it was one of the best decisions I have made in my entire history of gaming. Giving this a proper review is going to take a while so strap in, this is gonna be long.The first thing to go over with this game is the story, and without giving you any spoilers, I think the story is really good. The initial driving force to set you out on your adventure of all of the adults in your hometown being abducted after having such an idyllic beginning really sets the tone well and motivates you on your quest. The story elevates and progresses really well over the adventure as you learn more about the world and the history behind it, with some new information as you progress being potentially shocking or awe inspiring compared to how the game's insanely cute art style sets your expectations.The gameplay I think is overall very good with a strong inspiration from games like Zelda 2 with how the world is structured into a top down overworld with side scrolling areas. The combat is definitely much better than that in Zelda 2, but definitely could be seen as mildly clunky with the delay on some attacks. I don't mind the slight delay at all, and combined with the stamina bar, it kind of reminds me of Dark Souls combat, as it shares these aspects. Puzzles are scattered everywhere throughout the world and there are some really clever ones that made me admire how cleverly they were put together, with maybe only one puzzle in the entire game I thought was too cryptic, and it was for optional stuff. Overall the gameplay is quite solid and I enjoyed myself throughout, but that's not the biggest selling point of this game.Edit: I have read some other negative reviews of the game to see what people had problems with in this game to maybe give some extended information here, as most were linked to the  sprinting mechanics. The game does have a bit of a pressy feel with its sprint mechanics as landing from a sprint jump will cancel your previous sprint, and you need to hit the button again to keep running after landing. Some criticized this as being annoying, and the tutorial for this being a little too tight. I can agree with the second complaint, the room that taught this should have had a bit more room for error, but I didn't have an issue with the sprinting working like this. I got used to it pretty quickly and you don't get tested too harshly on it in required areas past the tutorial, which is admittedly strange. I'd recommend trying out the demo before diving straight into the game for this reason if this sounds like an issue.Edit 2: I figured I should also comment about the game length as that can be an important detail for some people. Phoenotopia Awakening is a fairly long game with a lot of content, with my 100% playthrough clocking in at about 50 hours. I personally am fine with the length as I enjoyed basically my entire time with the game, but I know some may consider that too much of a time investment, and others may think it's good value for dollar to playtime ratio, I'll let you draw your own conclusions if you like as this is entirely subjective.This is the biggest thing that has gotten me to hold this up as probably my new favourite game of all time. The presentation, being music and visuals, is absolutely phenomenal and had me loving exploring and finding new locations all the more than I already would have.The pixel art in this game I think is probably my favourite I have ever seen with how well everything is stylized and how cute everything is made as a result. It took me about 5 minutes into playing the game before I was already gushing to friends about how the game looks, which is saying a lot considering I don't often get that way over graphics. From the bustling town of Daea to the incredibly relaxing Moonlight Ravine, this game gets atmosphere down so well that it joined the ranks of Okami and the Ori games to get me to genuinely tear up purely off of the atmosphere that the graphics and music provided.Speaking of the music, this is one of the best soundtracks of all time to me. SillyTheWilly did a phenomenal job here and has made something I don't think I'll ever grow tired of. The boss theme is one of the best normal boss themes I've ever heard with me cranking the volume up super high whenever it started playing. Basically every area has a song that matches the location perfectly, with some as previously mentioned getting me to tear up. I've played many of the area themes as bgm for DND sessions as well and I've had some comments on how good the music was there too. Just overall a phenomenal soundtrack that deserves all the praise it gets and more.Phoenotopia Awakening is a true masterpiece in my opinion, and one of the most underrated games I've ever played by a massive margin. The fact that at the time of writing this there are under 1000 reviews is criminal as this deserves so much more recognition. Even before finishing the game with 100% completion today, I was already recommending many friends to check the game out, as well as gifting it to one of them, as I want as many people to experience this magical game as possible. I will absolutely replay this game in the future to likely get all of the achievements simply because of how much I appreciate it. I'm looking forward to any future endeavours of yours Cape Cosmic, you have a loyal fan right here.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that seems destined to be on one of my overlooked games of the year list. It's not flashy when it comes to the trailer, it's art style is good but not eye appealing, and its first impression of gameplay doesn't seem to pop compared to other games. But I'm here to say that would be a mistake. Phenotopia Awakening is a game that understands how to assemble a series of mechanics together to make an alternative yet fantastic experience that will reward players who adapt to the game's mechanics. The dash having a real momentum really ups the challenge of both platforming and combat, and sub-weapons actually have strengths/weaknesses to make them actually sub-weapons (and not abusable). Combat can be tricky if you try to fight recklessly, and the game rewards you using your mind rather then your reflexes in many cases, which is really nice to see. Combine that with a great variety of different puzzles and combat scenarios, and you have a game that you can bite into.The story does well in highlighting the world and not making it all about the protagonist, but actually feeling like she's a part of a huge adventure that happens in conjuction with other's stories. Granted, you may get bogged down in some of the text (there's a lot of talking here), and if you're someone who needs action every couple of minutes to feed your adrenaline addiction, this is not the game for you. It's a game where you will have to explore, find a side story, maybe do some grinding to get some money and food, and then figure out exactly where to go next. When the world opens up, man does it open up, to the point where it can really feel a little bit overpowering. With that said, it's a game that you can easily get lost in, wondering where the time went.Give it a try, and you'll find a game that you'll want to see where it ends up taking you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the Zeldallvania we didn’t know we needed.And just like in Zelda 2 you fight with something akin to a butter knife at the start.The game despite it’s flaws is fantastically fun. Unless your lacking a bit in the head then maybe this game will be a little too frustrating for you. It looks like the cutest casual game ever but it’s surprisingly hardcore. This is absolutely a "puzzle game", tons of well hidden secrets, punishing platforming, stamina/resource management and bosses who ragdoll you around the stage.The game will charm your pants off and make you love the world. The secrets are well hidden and the game strongly encourages you to research old areas after you've gotten a new ability.It really bugs me this game isn’t as talked about as it should be. Incredible puzzles, unbelievable charm and five-star soundtrack.It's deeply cozy for real. I love how much work went into making the cities actually feel bustling and populous, while still clearly having their own identity!I often look up guides when gaming despite not wanting to spoil the experience, but something about phoenotopia made me more patient, more willing to keep trying. It might be because of that fun, quaint atmosphere that I wanted to keep exploring, keep experiencing without ever slowing down. And the moment when you first enter the big city (forgot its name) is probably one of my favorite gaming moments. It’s the most fun level to explore in the whole game, at least. I 100% the game and  honestly have no regrets.Truth is game lays near and dear to my wife’s-and my heart. I remember playing the flash game for hours with her, trying to get further into the game, and seeing her fight the bosses was truly amazing. I couldn’t wait to relive those same memories with her again on this game. Of course, unfortunately she now mostly plays with her boyfriend, but it was still a great nostalgia trip.And I find the harder difficulty of the game as a huge plus. Nothing I dislike more than am otherwise great game that is just a cakewalk. The challenge is what makes a game addicting, and I’m so glad the devs gave us that challenge. It's a beautiful game, and the early patches resolved the combat balance issues that put off some. Give it a try if you are at all interested in 2d action rpgs with pixel art. Best game I've played in a few years and I still don't understand why it's had less attention.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is really hard to communicate; it would be so much easier if you could read my heart. _childDocuments_.review: This game is polarizing.On the one hand, 'Phoenotopia: Awakening' has a lot of character. On your journey you will travel through a wide selection of incredibly vibrant and unique locations and areas, filled with lovable, funny and sometimes touching characters. The type of story it tells isn't anything new, but the execution makes it feel fresh. Writing, art, tech and music are all amazing at best and still good at worst, so there's a lot on offer here.However...This game is fundamentally flawed in terms of game design. Almost every element of the game's core design is busted in a way that makes the exploration/combat sections feel like a frustrating slog to get through. The only reason I (and many others) stuck with this game was because all the exceptional elements I mentioned before kept me pushing forward.Combat is likely the worst offender. I'm completely baffled by the design decisions behind the combat system, which is completely directionless. Your character's attacks have little reach and you can quickly activate a run to speed up your movement. These mechanics are perfectly suited to a game with 'rush-down' combat, until you factor in other mechanics. You can't attack out of a sprint, instead you do a little roll (which doesn't give you invincibility). You can do a jump attack while running, but the jump attack has a ton of build-up (unlike the regular attack). Everything costs stamina, which recovers very slowly. At the start of the game this can be a major frustration as even the weakest enemy has to be approached with extreme caution to prevent you from running out of stamina and getting hit. And ooh boy, you're gonna get hit. lotsa enemies use charge attacks where they run straight at you at high speed (sometimes while off-screen). If you're charging a heavy attack or using any type of attack that has a build-up, your window to dodge is gonna be impossibly small. A lot of times getting hit feels really cheap, because you had so little time to respond. This is only worsened by the fact even the tiniest amount of damage will launch you backwards, often into another attack. You do seem to get some invincibility after getting hit, but not immediately, making it really easy to lose large amounts of health due to a single mistake. This is fine in a game like Spelunky, where its almost always completely your own fault you got hit, but here it feels mean. All this combines into an identity crisis personified as a combat system. Is it a high-action rush-down fighter? Is it a slow and methodical souls-like? Is it a wacky physics-based game? The answer is all the worst parts of the above.I touched briefly on enemy design and this is a large part of the issue too. These enemies feel like they were designed for a different game and in general just serve as an annoyance rather than a challenge. Enemies don't have patterns to learn, each of them only has two attacks at most (save for the bosses). These attacks include the aforementioned off-screen hyperspeed charge attack, acid attacks that are fired in wide patterns and leave behind damaging pools that will prevent you from getting close to the enemy, enemies that explode when you hit them, enemies that explode when they hit you, enemies that pop out of the ground when you walk over it without any hint suggesting they're there and then explode, enemies that stun you for way longer than necessary leaving you open to even more attacks, enemies that actively move out of the way of the direction you're aiming and moving while shooting at you, enemies that will fire volleys of projectiles that can take out half your healthbar in one attack (thanks knockback!) and more! They can also knock you out of the room you're currently in, resetting your progress for that room. THIS ALSO APPLIES FOR AN OPTIONAL BOSS. If all that wasn't bad enough, these enemies are often packed close together or combined with platforming. Its not fun to have to tediously jump up a vertical shaft bit by bit only to get your progress reset when a single enemy projectile hits you.Speaking of platforming vertical shafts, lets touch on level design. While the various towns you visit are full of character, the same can't be said for the dungeons/levels. Navigating these spaces can be difficult due to the lack of markers placed around the levels. I do my research so I know the dev mentioned he should've just put in a map and I have to disagree. The dungeons are largely a linear critical path with a couple of side branches for key items or collectibles. The lay-out isn't complex enough to warrant a map, it just needs clear pathing/player guidance. The issues with the combat and enemies are partially caused by the level design, too. For a game with such a restrictive stamina system you'd think there'd be a little more space between enemies so you have room to maneuver. This game doesn't agree with you, and insists that enemies be either closely packed together, be close to hazards so they can knock you into it, or be actively trying to stop you from completing what was already not a very fun platforming section. Platforming is generally okay as long as it doesn't involve climbing up vertical walls with a certain item (usually while getting shot at) or if its a timed affair like the parkour challenges. The same can't be said for the puzzles. I don't mind taking out a notepad and doing a Sudoku, quite enjoyed it in fact. But more often puzzles are either complete time-wasters where you have to slowly push several blocks into the correct position, or require perfect execution of several actions on a time limit (which is made very tedious due the movement systems).You know what the worst part of all this is? Its so close to greatness, but these fundamental flaws tear what could have been a 9/10 game down to an incredibly frustrating 6/10. I think Quell (the game's creator) did a fantastic job in so many areas, but design is just not his strong suit. My love for the good parts lead me to investigate what went wrong and after reading his devblog I think I have a decent grasp on what went wrong;Quell has a hard time looking at the game from an outside perspective. He's played the game so much that he isn't able to objectively look at its features anymore. To his credit he admits to this himself in his devlog. However, being able to do this is an incredibly important trait for a game designer. This wouldn't be as bad if he had a decent QA system but this was also one of his main problems (though I'm not entirely convinced he completely grasped the issue). He mentions the game receiving negative reviews because of its 'high difficulty', which was caused by him only letting a handful of speedrunners test the game. This could be interpreted as him being a little condescending, as the game isn't as much difficult as it is unfair. Lets not pretend people didn't like the game because they refused to gitgud, this isn't exactly Dark Souls. Things like the lack of player guidance, unfocused combat/movement systems and the reverse bell-curve difficulty (or unfairness) lead me to believe Quell lacks an understanding for the fundamentals of game design.That's not to say I think he's a bad guy, or even untalented. In fact, I'm eager to see what he'll create next. I just really hope that he either reads up on game design theory or finds a competent game designer to help him out.In the end, this is very negative review was not written out of hatred, but love. This game came so close to greatness only to have the experience be soured by such basic mistakes. I really hope Quell reads this and is able to learn from these mistakes  instead of feeling attacked, because that wasn't my intention. If he does, please get a designer to help you update this game. Don't leave it in this state, it doesn't deserve to be left like this.PS. I know you're probably attached to the name but I think it might be holding your sales back.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended only if you've got all of the patience and spare time in the world, even if it's on a deep discount. I'm a generally patient person who doesn't easily get frustrated by video games. The moment I realized that the consequence for failure in this game was going to be the old school "increasing amounts of either standing around waiting and/or grinding for healing items", I couldn't enjoy the game anymore.Pros:-Game is huge-Lots of interesting and varied puzzles to solve-Lots of nooks and crannies with goodies to find-There's a flute you can play whenever you want-Movement seems rough at first but you get (somewhat) used to it over time-Unlockable items genuinely open up the world in brand new ways each time you find one-Fishing mini game +++++-Most bosses are enjoyable and/or cheesable if you're getting frustatedCons:The penalty for failure in this game is taking little bits of your time over and over and over again-Ragdoll after hit is gratuitously long and you bounce multiple times unless you dodge-cancel the first bounce-Tons of areas and minigames where mistiming a jump/getting hit requires you to wait/run 15-30 seconds before retrying-Lots of later enemies cannot be staggered but can chain-stun you to death-button-mashing QTEs when restrained will never get you free fast enough to matter-all healing is done with food and/or a song that can heal you 99 damage (not a full heal later in the game when your health is higher) that you can't play again for *fifteen minutes*-food has to be bought or farmed from enemies, then cooked-average cooked food items can offset one, maybe two hits. many enemies can hit you multiple times in a row even with increased superarmor turned on in accessibility options-limited inventory slots means you'll want to focus on upgrading your inventory ASAP or make multiple trips back to town at every opportunity to get more healing items-besides the teleporters that get you from main region to main region, there is no fast travel (really thought all those angel statues were gonna pay off eventually)This would've been worth a couple weekend rentals as a kid, I work full-time now and found myself getting more frustrated by this game than enjoying the time playing it. There was a time when I'd probably have put another 50 hours into this game looking for every little hidden detail/mastering the wonky physics used for movement, but at this point I'd just rather play a good game that I enjoy instead of an alright game that revels in wasting my time

_childDocuments_.review: I first discovered this game through the Flash version, and lurked Quell's Dev Blog ever since I heard Phoenotopia was being made into a full-fledged game.Even after I 100%-ed both versions, I still think about them from time to time.(For those who want to compare versions, the 4* difficulty in Awakening is the closest to the Flash game imo).Although not as spectacular as some well-known indie-game titans, it is nonetheless a quality work made with both patience and love.Good worldbuilding, great music and varied gameplay mechanics all contribute to what could have been an altogether successful game. A shame it released with a bad timing and got overshadowed by "Skul" at the time.TL;DR : Great game, 10/10, would recommend, cooked Mystery Meat again ;)

_childDocuments_.review: I have spent well over  on this game since its initial launch, would be lying if I say I don't like the game. .From world-building with the gorgeous pixel arts, soundtracks and clever NPC dialogues, to the exploration-focused gameplay that involves constantly finding well-hidden collectibles and solving unique puzzles,  gives me the adventure I have always wanted from video games. It is definitely my personal favourite of all time.Pros:+ 30+ hours of enjoyment, 50+ for full completion+ Distinct- and beautiful-looking areas/+ Hundreds of Zelda-fashion collectibles (equipment, techniques, heart pieces, chests, etc.)+ Nimble main character and tight controls+ Variety of combat options+ Cleverly written dialogues (from comedic to deep and emotional, good stuff)+ Great attention to details in world-buildingCons:- Not enough maze-like areas/dungeons- Game can get too easy if you are an avid explorer- You can only hug Lisa once- You cannot throw more money at QuellsThis final section is where I elaborate on the [Pros and Cons] listed above. I also talked about  on reddit, so give it a read if you're interested!(I will simply refer  as PHOA from this point forth)An average game of this genre can usually keep you entertained for 10 hours, and 15 ~ 20 if you are a completionist. The original  (a free Web Browser game) is already this long, and PHOA is at least twice as substantial. I am pretty confident that PHOA is unrivalled in terms of quantity alone, but what about its quality?The sheer variety is the strength of PHOA, and it is the main reason why exploration feels much rewarding here. In terms of aesthetics for example, all the areas have their color themes picked from all across the color wheel (see for yourself in the 2017 ). It's hard to imagine how many colors they managed to fit in one game. Coupled that with the many fittingly amazing soundtracks? Having a big emphasis on exploration, PHOA has hundreds of collectibles scattered around the world as well. This game reminds me a lot of ALBW where I can find treasure chests and Heart Piece power-ups around every nook and cranny, and here you even have 100+ Moonstones to trade for tool upgrades, just like the Maiamai! Despite their differences in terms of genre, I am definitely getting a similar sense of wonder from both adventures!Besides the unlockable  and , most of the time you will be traveling on foot, and I really like the movement system in this game. This may sound childish, but it feels surprisingly fun and free to run around towns and areas, to the point where we even have mini-games dedicated to that (called "Free Running Challenges"). It gets even more satisfying when you discover the few hidden movement tricks that let you almost run indefinitely, making normal running like its own obstacle course!The game has its challenging moments, but you'll probably have no trouble if you are patient enough. The essence of combat boils down to "how you approach the enemies", which is quite different to the reflex-tests that most other side-scrolling platformers offer. For example, if you are surrounded by a group of wild boars, you probably want to lure and focus on eliminating them one by one, as opposed to rushing in with your baseball bat.It's also worth noting that enemies have no active hitbox unless they are attacking. So if you don't like close combat or throwing projectiles, you can literally run past pretty much all foes. Anyway, the game rarely forces you to use any specific weapon, and each weapon choice is good for certain situations (excluding the  ultimate weapon of course).Reading in this game is some of the most fun I've had. From the tutorial NPC that yeets you onto a bench to "teach" a technique, to the lore NPC that tells you about how the restaurant had to change its name after man-bear-wrestling became illegal for safety reasons, the writing in this game is simply full of life. Sure, some people may get overwhelmed, but it's not like you  to read most of them to progress or anything, so I'll take this gladly!Oh, and there are of course many Side Quests here. When it comes to quest rewards, you don't just get shiny new items, but also some of the best dialogues in the game too. While the bandit quest line might be fan-favourite to many, mine is the backstory of a nameless sentient robot (it kinda resonates with my mild depression, don't tell anyone). Needlessly to say, the game has a  diverse cast of characters.In addition to the assets and the writing, the designs are also pretty well thought-out. Treasures are in the form of antiques because you are exploring a ruin,  keys are one-time-use because it's a gemstone to be inserted, Prickle Fruit takes longer to cook because it's hairy and can be burnt easily like IRL, et cetera. All these small details may go unnoticed by many, but I argue that they do add up to help immensely in keeping this an immersive experience.This game is  with puzzles and riddles, and most of them are standalone with clues either next to them or right outside the room. There are many  clever ones that I like, don't get me wrong, but I wouldn't mind seeing a few complicated Divine-Beast-like dungeons too.This is another part that "bad reviews" confuse me - The game is not really hard or unfair. Obviously, the more you explore, the more collectibles you find. Some come in forms of money (used for buying certain tools and inventory expansion), some come in forms of Heart Rubies/Energy Gems that raise your HP/stamina cap. If anything, you are near unstoppable when you can . The reward for exploration  have empowered players too much near end-game.The animation when Gail hugs Lisa is so cute, and you only get to see it once per playthrough? Also, trust me when I say the most frequently asked questions from Discord are "Is any DLC planned?" and "When is the sequel coming out?". Guess it's safe to say that most of us are excited to see what's coming next from the team!^ This ^So please consider buying it to support the dev!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this game, but WRITE STUFF DOWN. There's a ton of stuff to backtrack and explore/get later... cracked walls, song stones, upgrades out-of-reach, just a LOT of that kind of stuff. If you don't write down everything you discover, you're going to spend a LOT of time backtracking and trying to find it all. There's no map, no task or points-of-interest logs, so it's up to YOU to keep track of it all. Otherwise, a cute and clever game with some design challenges (so far as I can tell, your melee range never increases, for example... it's just better bats.... and the damage reduction from better armors tends to be tiny). I'm still enjoying it... but wow, I wish I'd written everything down.

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a fantastic little game, I'm actually really impressed that it's only $20! There's a ton of stuff in this game for such a small amount of money, and unlike the vapid, shallow padding you find in most AAA titles, this game's content is so lovingly crafted. Collectibles are cleverly hidden, and I found myself going to the fortune teller to find out more heart gems and moonstones are in that dungeon I was certain I scoured from top to bottom. The puzzles are great (though I found one or two of them were a bit TOO hard), and I found myself writing down notes and diagrams to try to figure some of them out.And that's without even touching the story and the world-building, which is top notch in my opinion. It's involved enough to be interesting, but not so dense that it bogs itself down, it really hits that sweet spot that a lot of other titles miss. The mood is often lighthearted and wholesome, but it has a bit of a dark side too, especially when you start learning about what happened in the past. The characters and dialog are charming and delightful, I found myself falling in love with so many of them. It got to the point where, when I was told that two of the characters had been sent off to be killed, I immediately went around talking to everyone nearby to see if there was a way to save them. My only real gripes are with some of the controls, and maybe the symbols used for the songs. You have to use the quick select menu by moving the right stick over the item you want to equip and then clicking the right stick down to select it. It's not terrible, but it's easy to mess up when you're in a tense fight. The symbols used for playing songs aren't really intuitive, you just kind of have to memorize which symbol corresponds to which direction, which is fine once you've got it down, but even near the end of the game I was still struggling with it just a bit.Also the sprint is a bit weird, because it's not like a Mario style game where you hold down the sprint button and you'll always be sprinting, you have to be touching the ground and if your feet leave the ground for any reason, even if you're dropping down a very small ledge, you stop sprinting and have to manually press the sprint button down again. It's not the worst ever, I was definitely able to complete all the free running challenges, and even got the Lunar Key (even if I had to watch a video of someone doing it first). In fact, I nearly got all the items in the game, save for one energy gem. I just couldn't beat the last shooting gallery challenge. Also I didn't fight the optional boss, since I figured the game is going to require me to get 100% items.In conclusion, if you love side scrolling action/metroidvania-likes, gorgeous pixel art, and a heartwarming story and characters, this is probably your jam.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I only played this game for just under two hours and I want to persevere and love it but the controls are infuriating. The character's sprint jump is a commitment, and with all the tiny platforms I overshoot constantly. All I want to do is jump from a couple tree branches to a ledge in one of the first screens of the game and I'm messing it up way more often than I should. After the jump the sprint has to be reset for no discernible reason, and the tutorial for this is incredibly tight; you have to master this immediately, there is no difficulty curve. The roll after a sprint being triggered by the attack button instead of just hitting sprint again has gotten me hit countless times during the first boss fight. If you try to jump and turn to do an aerial attack the character will face the initial (wrong) direction. Since there is a slight animation lag in turning on the ground you may also attack in the wrong direction after pressing the right direction if you're too quick. The aerial attack also has a lag to it and doesn't protect the character's head, which wouldn't be so bad if not for the previously stated issue and the (starting) weapon's very short range.Combining healing items and alternative tools/weapons within the same system caused me to repeatedly start a heal instead of aiming a slingshot, which wasn't horrible until the first boss fight. In a Zelda game a boss would usually only require one additional gimmick along with the main weapon, so having to work the right stick (therefore momentarily abandoning the jump and sprint buttons) in order to swap to a potato, find an opening to survive the eating animation, then swap back to a slingshot is a lot to process while trying to keep an eye on boss and boss add animations.Instead of grab grabbing it instead prepares a grab... you need to press another button to actually grab. I understand that this is because there is a push/pull function, but you could simply hold the button to push/pull and press the button to grab.A very minor and personal complaint is Up can't be Confirm/Talk, as it will cause a conflict in the control check after controls are fiddled with. I admit this is only due to way too many hours in Hollow Knight, but since the doors are Up I don't know why Talk isn't also Up.There's also a stamina system, which you can turn off for normal attacks. I beat the first boss once with it on and once with it off. The difficulty changed very little but having stamina off for normal attacks was much less frustrating. It seems like an unnecessary system in a flood of other systems to keep track of during an active battle. Sprinting through town also takes stamina, and frankly I don't understand this design decision in any video game. No player is having fun when they have to take several breaks to let a bar fill up while simply traversing the world.Cooking raw meat is fine but I need flint for a fire that will always be within the same area anyway, which is busy work for the sake of a minor heal, at which point I rather just run with raw berries and herbs only so my tiny inventory isn't full of raw materials being hoarded for a fire.Oh, I also had a bat fly through me and hit me three or four times. I think one of the difficulty options minimizes this, but I don't know why this aspect would be optional. Being juggled always sucks.Everything else is incredibly pleasant as heck.Art is great.Animation is great.Music is great.Sound effects are great.Story I can't say, as I only beat the first dungeon, but the conversations up to that point are clever and often cute.I want this game to do very well but personally I can't play it further as-is or wholeheartedly recommend it to others as it's too frustrating to traverse the beautiful world. Regardless of my complaints, I appreciate the experimentation and am very much looking forward to future releases from this developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: A criminally under-rated indie darling on the same level of CrossCode. There's a lot of history relating to this game originally being a flash based game and getting a new coat of paint and lots of love for over a decade, but I only wanted to quickly touch on that. At it's core, Phoenotopia Awakening is quite the game for those of us seeking a classic experience in a new way. Not quite exactly like CrossCode, Phoenotopia feels familiar yet just different enough to intrigue those chasing nostalgia. The art design in this game is a pure joy with unbelievable amounts of details in small things that you could easily miss. The story & characters are extremely fleshed out and I've been enjoying seeing people from earlier segments in the game in different areas. Exploration in this is remarkable with it's world design.  Any time you see something out of place, make a mental note if you are unable to reach it. You'll be back, I promise. This is a solid puzzle game as well, I've had to write down a few things to solve puzzles which is extremely rare these days. Do not google/use a guide until you've completely hit a wall you just cant get over and have come back to a few times to try and solve. The overall game design is extremely well done though the combat is a little janky until you adjust. Some may not like the amount of back tracking in this game, and that's fair. Phoenotopia Awakening is extremely hands off in assisting you, it will give you clues but you will need to remember them and do them at your own pace. Steam Deck Owners FYI: The game runs extremely well on deck, not sure why it says outright unsupported for it. There is no Sync & Achievements do not work, but the game plays great on it. You will need to adjust resolution up to fit screen but really needs to be set to yellow instead of gray for support on Steam Deck. TL;DR If you crave that indie feel in the same vein of CrossCode, don't sleep on this. The names hard to remember and doesn't stand out, but the game itself is certainly overlooked and well worth your time. Would recommend writing down anytime you see blue text & puzzle notes.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but the controls feel like they're designed for a completely different game than what you're actually playing.. Your movement when sprinting is unresponsive and your movement when not sprinting is slow, but the enemies all move and attack fast or have multiple projectiles (some of which detonate into further projectiles). You have a stamina bar that's spent on every action you perform other than walking, but you have no dodge or block and a very limited parry that only works on specific projectiles with no telegraph. Getting hit by almost any attack locks out your controls for at least half a second and can send you flying if the attack is arbitrarily forceful (as opposed to damaging) enough, but the conditions for triggering mercy invincibility are so asinine that it may as well not exist and the only way to recover from the flying animation is to have previous experience with either speedrunning or playing 2d fighting games competitively. You're expected to hit midair opponents in combat, but your ranged options glue you in place while aiming and the first of your ranged weapons uses a timing-based aiming system like it thought this was supposed to be a Paper Mario clone. You're expected to aim incredibly precisely out of combat, but the targeting reticule is glued to the end of an invisible selfie stick.Special mention to the spear, which you can't even aim but are still expected to hit precisely with it during combat to have platforms to stand on, when it has a delay before you throw it. And if you're within what feels like the entire top third of your jump height it'll be too high for you to stand on it, and you're only allowed two spears at a time and can't just undo the new one without breaking both. Which is especially awful if you're in the middle of a long climb.Then there are the straight up mean game design choices. Birds in the desert stealing your money in increments of 10 when there are multiple required purchases of over 100 currency; many NPCs with extremely specific multi-stage fetch quests, but no map or quest log; jumps across tiny platforms while being shot at, when any damage at all knocks you down and makes you start over; throwing 4 enemies with different attack patterns at you in a confined space so any attempt to avoid one attack sends you into 2 more, which stun you long enough to get hit by a follow-up from the one whose attack you dodged in the first place; an NPC in the third town who all the nearby NPCs  imply is a scam artist, but actually sells possibly the single highest-impact upgrade in the game... You get the idea.And if you're going to design a boss for an action game that has thus far been punishing enough to make the player want to bring as many healing items to boss fights as they can carry, what you should  do is let the boss cancel attacks into a dash that, if it hits, locks out the player's controls for almost  while he steals one of the player's healing items and uses it on himself while taunting nonstop.The accessibility options barely help - you can skip the cast time on healing items and mitigate stamina management issues, but the available healing remains bound to your inventory size and you don't get any new means of avoiding or mitigating incoming damage.I did mean it earlier when I said I want to like this game. The characters are charming, the art is gorgeous, the music is stellar, the writing is generally entertaining. But whenever you have to use both precision and speed at once, like during a fight or certain puzzles, all the fun gets sucked out of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: While the overall game is ok there are some really GLARING design mistakes. Basically everything relating to the economy of the game is broken. The inventory is limited to 8 different items at a time unless you spend a lot of gold to upgrade that (300 gold nets you + 5 slots ooooh!). Which I did the first chance I had... but then I was out of money and realized that I needed to buy a couple of key items to progress but was out of money. There are constant random encounters spawning on the map but fighting them gives no benefits. It just hurts your hp and wastes healing items. They rarely drop money or items. A complete waste of time and makes one wonder why they exist in the first place since you can easily avoid them. Also there are lunar relics that you need to bring to a special collector but that person is in a late game section of the map so for most of the early game you have to run around with them taking up space in your inventory. Forums suggest just throwing them away because they respawn back at the dungeons... because yes that's what I want to do in a metroidvania: reexplore the dungeons I already found all items in because the inventory is artifically limited. And ofc there is not a single chest you could store items for later or anything. A lot of people praise the game for being very long but that is more due to it being drawn out and grind rather than it having a lot of content. You have to invest a lot of time upfront to get anywhere.Edit: also late game the combat becomes obnoxious as your ranged attack options are really bad to control. You have to stand still to shoot your crossbow and it does very little damage compared to the spear but its the only thing that can attack flying enemies; and take a guess what is the primary enemy type at the end of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: You can get hours and hours from this game because there's so many areas to explore and so many secrets to find, and so many sidequests to do, some of which have their own little stories to them. And just when you think you've seen everything, you find out you haven't. The story is also good, I like the part about midway through where you have to find your way into the dungeons and eventually reach the top of the towers, and the scene that happens when you go back home after that is really good and has some great artwork.My main complaint about the game is that the accessibility options aren't that good for people like me who REALLY suck at games since I still died to the first boss a few times, and the second area has a sudden increase in difficulty with money being hard to come by without loads of grinding, not helped by the birds that can steal it from you, and places where you have to spend it to progress. I also couldn't do any of the timed puzzles, or the trials in the second area, I have really bad timing and coordination skills, and there's no accessibility options to help with that. Thankfully, there is a mod available which makes things much easier so I could enjoy the story and the music and exploration without getting frustrated, it disables Steam Achievements but since I wasn't going to get all of them anyway I decided it was a good trade off.So I would recommend this game if you like difficult games, and if you don't, I would recommend it if you like exploration and sidequests and the story, but also advise you to use the cheat mod if you're getting too frustrated and don't want to watch a Let's Play (I have yet to find one without commentary since I prefer ones that don't have it).
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: A true gem. Games like these remind me why I love video games. This game has all of its mechanics nailed down tight. Wonderful aesthetic, with charming visuals and music that will take you in. A lovable cast of characters that are just fun to be around. It has been a LONG time since I have played a game where I actively want to talk to every NPC I see, but this game has that. The story and world it is building are top notch.The exploration is also phenomenal. The platforming and puzzle challenges are some of the most interesting I've seen in a long time, and every time I solve one I feel my brain bulging and get the loveliest satisfied high. They really encourage you to look for everything you have to hand, and push yourself. I will say that some challenges are "gated" behind certain upgrades and so forth, but these are usually obvious when you see them. If the solution isn't coming to you and you have other paths open, exploring more might yield the piece you need.The area I see getting the most flak is the combat, which I can somewhat understand, but don't agree with the dislike. I think the combat is doing its own thing, not really emulating the style of other games that closely, and thus takes some getting used to. But once you get into the groove, it can be quite fun. It's a mixture of stamina management, positioning, and looking for the right windows of opportunity to attack. Some encounters can be quite challenge - the bosses are a stand out! Surprisingly difficult, but in a good way! - but as with the puzzles, once you figure out how to beat them, the feeling is incredibly satisfying.TL;DR - This one is the real deal. Fun exploration and combat in a rich and charming world. Big recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia: Awakening is a very underrated metroidvania with huge amount of content, which sadly doesn't get the attention it deserves. It may start slow, and the combat system may need some time to get used to it, but as soon as I finished the first dungeon, the game got me completely hooked with its very clever puzzle design, charming cast of characters, rich world, and a absolute banger of a soundtrack.I absolute love the puzzle design, and how it offers a fixed solution, and a unorthodox solution, if the player is creative enough to explore the tools at their disposal. And what impresses me more is the huge variety of puzzles, which even if a section makes use of the same tool as solution, you don't see any kind of repetition elsewhere, which makes the exploration very fresh and fun. I explored every corner of the game, and even after 45 hours of gameplay, I didn't feel annoyed or tired because of a puzzle of platforming section.The level design is great too. Everything is so well hidden, in a pretty clever way, that makes the exploration and backtracking extremely fun and rewarding.I saw a review complaining about the lack of a antagonist, but I have to disagree. The story present itself in such a manner that a central antagonist is not needed. Without entering into spoiler territory, as soon as you finish the first dungeon, the game tells you what you need to know, and then everything else develops itself around it, and it works greatly because it has a pretty great cast of characters that carry the story without having a central antagonist interrupting your journey every time. Every city or specific location has its own kind of problems, but everything wrap itself naturally without dragging the story around.  In short, Phoenotopia: Awakening is the most fun I had with a metroidvania since Hollow Knight. It has content for any kind of players, and even optional content for those who loves to collect anything (including a awesomely designed super boss for those who collected every life and stamina upgrades). Cape Cosmic should be praised for all the love and effort that they poured into the game, and I truly hope that we see a continuation of the story in the future. It has a huge potential, and the ending sequence really screams for a follow-up game.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia feels like an amazing classic SNES zelda/metroid/jrpg fusion with tons of content (30-40 hours or 50+ for completionists). There is a lot of combat, puzzles, exploration and plenty of backtracking to do when you obtain items or powerups that open up previous places that were once unreachable. I downloaded it because I had a craving to play another pixel rpg and I'm glad I decided on this one.Story- AlrightJust like any other zelda-type game, the story isn't too deep. It's simple and it works, not much else to say about it. Conflict happens and your character's goal is to fix said conflict. It would be better to make more of the areas and bosses more involved with the main storyline though.World Building&Characters- Top TierThe world is fantastic, there's a ton of different areas that all have their unique theme as well as type of creatures and people who inhabit it. As for the characters, I usually can't be bothered to read filter text, but Phoenotopia had me reading BOTH lines of dialogue NPC tend to say, and not only because it was sometimes required for some secrets/quests. The writers went above and beyond in this game, and the humor hits where it is attempted. You wont be getting super close with side characters but you'll love them for the lines that they do have.Combat- Decent with flawsCombat is for the most part alright, but it also has most of the games actual flaws. It's typical 2d platformer combat, but where its different is usually for the worse. For starters, stamina is ridiculously bad in the beginning, and I advise anyone who is playing to absolutely go to difficulty settings and enable "stamina regens more quickly", and at least for the early bits also enable "normal attacks dont use stamina". No idea why some RPGs have you start out as someone weaker than the average human being, but until you get some energy powerups you're exhausted in less than 3 seconds and finding yourself able to do nothing but stare (or walking away). Secondly the knockback in this game is atrocious. There should be attacks that really make you fly back like getting hit by a boar charge, or an orc swinging a club, but you're playing as a human pinball and nearly every attack sends you flying. Thank the lord that they decided to make contact damage not a thing in this game, as it easily could have made all of this 100 times worse and maybe even irredeemable. Ranged attack weapons also really suck till upgraded, but I'm more of a fan of the bat so its not that bad to me.Puzzles- GreatThe puzzles in this game are what I wish more mainstream games could also learn from, but they're not mainstream because they require braincells so that wont really happen. Phoenotopia has you actually thinking in order to solve the puzzles blocking extra treasure, and even sometimes for the progression of the story. The main tool for this is usually the flute that is used sort of like the windwaker in LoZ:windwaker, except its not only for songs but also for inputting the codes that solving said puzzles give you in order to open pathways and loot.Music- IBoughtTheSoundtrack/10Music is a hard hit, and absolutely fitting to the area it plays for. Even areas I didn't like being in had some nice music to ease that pain. It has a whole lot of different ranges, going from classic 8 bit, to mellow piano, and even synth metal themes. I have some of them saved to my phone.Controls- You might have to rebindI started playing it with default keyboard controls. Don't do that. I later changed to custom keyboard+mouse, and then just used default controller. Aiming is really terrible with keyboard, great with the mouse, and pretty decent with an analog stick. One weird part of movement you'll have to get used to is that running has actual inertia. You will have to slow down before coming to a halt, skid if attempting to 180, and if you run jump, you're committed till you land, which is kind of odd because you have free movement in the air when normal jumping. There's also a lack of coyote jumping (being able to jump for a few frames after walking off a platform) so you're conditioned to jump a bit earlier till it isnt much of an issue anymore, but imo all platformers should have coyote jumping. The air attack has a long delay compared to the frame 1 bat swing on the ground, and outside being funny when Gail is stunned and rubbing her head after a headbutt, that attack is absolutely worthless and not worth picking up (you probably wont find it without a guide anyway). Lastly theres different jump heights you can attain from how long you hold down the jump button, but the smaller jumps are pretty strict on frames. Not SSBM short-hopping strict, but you'll get the wrong height jump quite often.CommentsOne of the biggest flaws to me and my 50 hour playthrough was that there is no option to respawn at the beginning of the room/boss room like other games have. Hell if there's a cutscene at the boss, you have to go through the respawning loadscreen, wake up from the bed at the save area, run to the boss, and then go through the dialogue again before your next try even starts. The biggest QoL would be to respawn at the boss room and have the dialogue skippable 2nd attempt and beyond, and I have no Idea how this didn't make it in to their accessibility patches. It would really get rid of a lot of the unnecessary frustration. Altogether the game is a gem, and I was really looking forward to the sequel, and was sad to see that it may be extremely delayed or even canceled due to lack of funding. This game deserves a lot more attention, and although it may have big flaws, it also has big strengths. 8.5/10, I hope to play Phoenotopia 2 one day.

_childDocuments_.review: To put it bluntly, I'm not the type of gamer who has much affinity for releases that make frustration a calling card; with a backlog like mine spending considerable time bashing my head against a digital wall just doesn't hold much appeal. So here I am, writing about a game that made me curse at my screen more than any other I can immediately recall...which, not only did I finish, but logged 70-plus hours on the game's clock and racked up a 97 percent completion rate to boot. Moreover, afterwards I immediately searched out and played through the original Flash-based Phoenotopia, just to get a better sense of where Awakening came from...oh, and also double-dipped when a DRM-free version came out.So yeah, whatever misgivings I might have about Phoenotopia Awakening there's something truly special happening here, and I'll do my best, hopefully without spoiling too much, to explain what it is.You take on the role of a young woman who's spent her entire life in a small town, but abruptly finds herself obliged to set off into the wider world and piece together its mysteries; let me tell you, this game makes darn sure that the player feels just as overwhelmed as she does. Outside of the general direction you need to take to progress the story you are granted precious little guidance, not only in terms of where stuff is but how any of it works; there's plenty of space to cover and lots of things to mess with, but you can forget any sort of map, quest log or other such reference to help you keep track of it all, unless you doodle it up on an IRL piece of paper yourself. To figure out which way is up you're expected to constantly and consistently explore, experiment and extract every bit of incidental information you encounter as you wander, and this takes a LOT of time and effort.This sense of slow, gradual struggle extends - and how - to the game's combat; while moving about and attacking generally feel solid enough, an ever-looming stamina meter limits how much time you can spend on the offensive, and your range and speed seem almost constantly outclassed by your adversaries, who will ruthlessly ambush you, snipe you, gang up on you and chase you down from the word "go". If that wasn't enough, you'll frequently find yourself not only knocked back upon taking a hit but careening helplessly between nearby hazards, damage piling up all the while, before a bit of mercy invincibility finally kicks in to give you a fleeting moment to regain your footing...or, just as likely, mess up your counter-attack timing, eat another haymaker and start the dreadful sequence all over again.In so many words, there are times where this game will make you want to yank your hair out; I couldn't begin to list the times other titles got me half as hot under the collar as this one did and wound up swiftly ejected from the disc tray, never to enter it again. But this time around, surprising even myself, I didn't quit and move on to something else; I kept going. Kept dying, and retrying, until I could finally progress. Why?Because I don't think I've ever played a game where being able to keep going was just so Simply put, if you're the sort of gamer whose favorite part of a given playthrough is the "I'll ignore the storyline and just meander around for a while" part, you're in for a rare treat; as much of a struggle as it can be to make your way in Phoenotopia's world, every last tidbit you do manage to get your mitts on is uncannily satisfying to obtain and renders you even more curious to dig further, no matter what. This extends not only to the platforming and puzzles, but even the often-brutal battles: as elusive as such mastery is, few pleasures can compare to FINALLY learning to spot a once-inscrutable enemy hiding in wait for you, charging up a full-power attack as you approach and sending the cheeky bugger flying across the screen with a perfectly-timed, wonderfully visceral .While this manner of experience is admittedly subjective in nature, looking back on it now I still can't help but marvel at how natural, how giddily organic it felt to open the world up, bit by bit; nearly every time I'd pass through a previous area I'd find myself, at least once, suddenly thinking  and it's rather amazing to recall how frequently and endearingly my curiosity and persistence was rewarded. Moreover, despite its considerable length the game very seldom feels like it's padding things out; every new place you travel to has fresh sights, sounds, threats and treasures to experience, and the thrill of discovery never truly fades. To wit, even during my very last play session with the game, before I headed to the final boss I took an "eh, why not" detour to a particular puzzle that had stumped me for several dozen hours prior; sure enough, I noticed something I'd missed before, gave it another shot and at long last managed to check it off the list.Out on the periphery the grueling portions of the journey are further softened by Phoenotopia's uniquely inviting vibe; while many games of this ilk tend to revel in their cruelty, constructing worlds full to bursting with oppressive and foreboding atmosphere, the developer here chose to buck the trend and keep the overall mood light, humorous and cartoonishly charming. Darker undertones certainly do exist, especially if you peer into enough distant corners, but you're far more likely to remember, and be urged onward by, the game's incorrigibly quirky bit players, from important secondary cast members to the countless nameless townies you'll chat up, and the array of silly antics they present for your amusement.Said characters, and the world they inhabit, are for their part rendered in a somewhat "blobby" pixel art style, which limits the amount of inherent detail present in any particular sprite or setting (and can occasionally make background and foreground elements difficult to parse), but also lends the visuals a strikingly "gentle" air, never failing to look anything less than pleasant, and frequently quite pretty. The accompanying soundtrack reflects the game's eclectic roster of influences (note that the game is not a "pure" Metroidvania, though I'll leave it to you to experience just how), featuring everything from peppy chiptunes to somber piano melodies to minimalistic ambience to a boss theme that wouldn't be terribly out of place in a Ys title.As grand of a time as I had with this game, I must acknowledge in the end that my memory of it is a bit tarnished by my judgment that it does cross the line one too many times from "sticking to its vision" into "refusing to get out of its own way". If you prefer games that "get to the point" this one is obviously not what you're looking for; Phoenotopia Awakening is best experienced by going in as blind as possible, prepared to very slowly immerse yourself in everything it has to offer and re-approach things from several different angles when you find yourself either stumped or unceremoniously smacked to the Game Over screen. If this setup sounds even somewhat appealing to you, do not hesitate: Cape Cosmic has ABSOLUTELY earned Phoenotopia Awakening's full asking price.In a nutshell:

_childDocuments_.review: Without a doubt, this game easily takes my favorite indie game of the year.It's an amazing gem of a game similar with similar gameplay mechanics like Hollow Knight, with cute pixel graphics, a very expansive world, and tons of exploration to be had, along with many many difficult challenges. One thing I really love about the game is just how much love and life is poured into the world and the characters. Every town and area are filled with NPCs and characters that really paint the picture and give it personality. The story in this game starts simple, but there's so much that gets built upon it. In a lot of games, I'm the kind of person to skip a lot of NPC dialogue.. but I ended up reading and talking to every NPC in this game. None of the dialogue is boring. Every line of text I've read in this game has personality. There's just so much life poured into the game and I love it so much.The music is fantastic too. The game is loaded with amazing songs left and right. The music gives ambience to each area. I could listen to the OST all day and not get tired of it.The boss fights are very fun and pretty difficult. The battle system is simple, but has tons of room for mastery. There's so many ways you can approach the fights in this game and boss theme is a massive banger too. Each boss has their own flavor, mechanic, and environment. Every boss I fought was such a blast and I wish I could fight them again from the beginning. The puzzles really make you think too. There's so much to do in this game, and tons of puzzles. The game really makes you investigate or get creative with the puzzle solutions. Sometimes it does get frustrating when trying to figure out the complicated ones, but all of the puzzles in the game are very fair- and it feels really good when you figure out it out and this game does a very very good job at making you feel that satisfaction.And then you have the world and exploration. There's a lot of backtracking you can do as you progress and obtain more tools, and it's not just a simple backtrack and obtain-an-item kind of thing either. Backtracking reveals so many new areas that were hidden even in the very first dungeon in the game. It's as if there's a dungeon within a dungeon, and it's very easy to get absorbed in the exploration. It's one of those games where if there isn't a wall, there's always a new path.Honestly, this is legitimately my favorite game this year. It's such an hidden gem of a game. I've sunk a ton of hours and even though I've beaten the main story line, I continue to play the game because there's always something more to do. If you've gotten this far in my review, I will say that this game is worth every single penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: The first 90% of this game is absolutely stellar, one of my favourite gaming experiences in the last decade. However, I would be remiss to mention that this game absolutely does not stick the landing, and fails to deliver a satisfying and rewarding conclusion on a narrative or ludonarrative level. If you feel you can stomach that, I would highly recommend you buy this game on sale. If not, you should consider carefully whether you should buy this game at all.

_childDocuments_.review: The first time I played Phoenotopia (the flash version) was six years ago. Then in the last year, I happened to find out Phoenotopia Awakening (the extended version) was coming soon which made me so excited and got it as soon as it's released. I knew I was going to love it and it even exceeds my expectations and makes me so happy. _childDocuments_.review: This game is truly a underrated classic. This game feels like a fantastic blend of Metroidvania and Zelda 2. Movement is a bit clunky, not in the sense of unresponsiveness but momentum is continuous; you cant make a 180 midair for example. This game is a fantastic gem and is endearing in all the right ways.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, the game is not a metroidvania. This isn't actually a statement of judgement or quality, just a mislabeling of the tag system. It is more similar to Zelda 2 than anything else. With that out of the way, this game is just a huge bummer. It's got an amazing look, a fun story, and interesting exploration but none of that can make up for the combat being absolutely terrible. The sluggish movement and extremely short melee range makes engaging with enemies extremely challenging but not in a good way, in a way that makes it feel unfair and unpleasant to deal with. Later on ranged options become available but they aren't much better, with aiming at any distance being hard to judge and also planting the character in place unable to move while doing so, making the always very fast enemies even more likely to hit her and sending her ping-ponging across the ground into multiple unavoidable followup hits.There are accessibility options available but none of them actually do anything to address the key problems with the game. Yes it will make it easier if food can be eaten while in the menu, if multiple attacks in a row don't decrease in damage, if normal attacks don't consume stamina. But they won't slow the enemies down, they won't make the character actions more responsive, they won't decrease the amount of damage the player takes, it won't stop the player from getting trapped into animations, or make them able to turn in midair. Not that turning in midair would help, since the current air melee attack is shorter range and slower to trigger than the ground one.Even playing with all of the options on the combat was an unenjoyable slog, and while most enemies can be walked past or avoided there are still mandatory boss encounters that will require the player to engage with it. Combat is a huge part of this game and the way it has been implemented ruins the entire experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: the exploration/dungeons in this game are fun, and the art is beautiful, but the combat and especially the boss fights are just so bad, in a way that feels really weirdly mean-spirited. its not that theyre too hard exactly; hard games can be really fun, but when the combat controls are this clunky, difficulty becomes tedious, and the accessibility options dont fix it

_childDocuments_.review: I'm legitimately impressed as to how thoroughly this game has left an impression on me in terms of how vividly I remember exploring each and every one of the unique locales. I never even finished this game yet because I stopped playing halfway through for various reasons, and that was like a whole year ago, and I *still* have all the different areas fresh in my memory even though I only have like 20 hours playtime. It's special.
