_childDocuments_.review: Today I am going to tell you about Phoenotopia Awakening. I've beaten it twice, both times with 100% items, and one of them doing a 0% sub-4 hour speedrun before getting 100%. This is a game that is extremely good and not everyone is going to like.It's a metroidvania. Any comparisons to Zelda 2 end at the overworld and random encounter design. The majority of the game is comprised of small areas (and large ones) that are broken up by the large map you move around in. From the very beginning, you are able to run around anywhere you can see and explore it. The sense of exploration in this game is pretty unparalleled. If you can think to go somewhere or try to reach a spot, even unconventionally, there's a high chance you can do it. The only guidance you are given is a general idea of where to go, and you need to talk to NPCs to learn more about each area. There's always someone to talk to who will tell you something to try. You just go do things, and there are a ton of things to do. Related to this: there is no map. This is something that may put people off, but the game is designed tightly. Each area you go to has clearly distinct rooms and doesn't suffer from the lack of map in any noticeable way. If you know where you want to be, you can get there. At most, you may want to note down places of interest to return to later. You explore in the overworld, find small areas to explore in 2D, and that's the formula.The gameplay itself is solid. You can run, jump, crawl, roll, and hit things. Combat involves beating things up by spamming hits or playing it cool and going for aerial/charge attacks, which are more effective. People who run in and spam only light attacks are going to have a bad time. You can also prepare for exploration by cooking food (dropped by enemies or the environment) and buying better gear. Money is well-balanced; if you explore, you get enough money to afford things you want without much issue. If you don't, you're not going to have any. The exploration itself is usually finding a new place and doing puzzles in it, with combat generally scarce outside of overworld encounters. Most of your time is going to be spent looking for things and solving environmental puzzles that are almost all well-designed. Some answers are hidden in the background, some are logic puzzles, but there's always something to see. The pacing of major usable item upgrades is also done really well. You'll be getting a new tool to use in a pretty steady stream.The music is extremely good. I don't know why the game has the right to have such good music, but it does. Some of it is stuff I don't care for, but even the tracks I don't like fit very well, with only one or two exceptions. And there's a lot of music. Tracks are generally not repeated and are unique to their area. I bought the soundtrack and kept about a fourth of the music in the game. This is unusual for me, and I almost never keep more than a few tracks out of an OST. The amount of variety in tracks is really bizarre in that I have no idea how the composer was good at creating such a wide spread of music.For the graphics, they're pretty nice. Character sprites are more basic than they maybe need to be, but they're perfectly readable and well-animated. The environments all look good, as you should be able to see in the screenshots on the store page. This was originally a Flash game, which I did not play, but all of the graphics are retooled and clean. Visual information is clearly communicated to the player any time it needs to be. I don't have a lot to say about graphics—they're not that important. You can see them for yourself.The story and writing itself: every NPC has something to say, and usually it's a joke that ranges from "okay" to "kind of funny", and that's totally fine. Some of them exist only to be jokes, and some will give you useful information while also being jokes. The presentation of dialogue is good, and there's none of that really obnoxious feeling you get from amateur writing. You know the type, where everything is trying super hard to be trendy and wacky. That doesn't happen here. The humor is enjoyable throughout. The plot beats themselves are actually good. Everything follows a natural progression, beginning with your entire village being abducted and going logically from there as you look for solutions. The scale of the story is a gradual build that's done very well, and while the actual events themselves are nothing incredibly special, it's nice to just have a game that's honest about what it wants to be and do. Phoenotopia doesn't try to be more than it is, and it drops many hints as to where it's going the entire time. It's the kind of narrative that begins small and grows bigger and bigger until it's encompassing some very large territory, but it plays it close to the chest the entire time without completely tripping over its own feet. It's something I wish more stories were capable of.I can't really overstate how good this game is at letting the player do what they want. You want to go explore something? You can probably do that. You want to ignore the main story for a long time and sequence break to a new area you shouldn't be, detouring for 5-10 hours? You can do that. You want to just go fish for a while? You can do that. There are constant rewards for exploring. There are legitimately only two complaints I can leverage at this game, which are that some enemies can remove your hair dye for absolutely no reason other than causing annoyance (since you can reload the loss away anyway), and the speed of stamina regeneration would probably have been better served as a percentage than a flat value, as lategame stamina regen can take 10 seconds. There are ways around this, of course, but it's still a little excessive. That's it. Everything else I just really like a lot. I've played loads of metroidvanias, and this is up there with the best of them on the merit of its exploration prowess alone. There aren't many games that give you this kind of feeling.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: When looking into Phoenotopia: Awakening (PA), I saw that it was a remake of a free Flash game, one which I hadn't played before. That was launched mid-2014, and with Flash fading away, that may have inspired the developer to recreate PA for Steam. Looking at the trailers and reviews, it looked like a charming Metroidvania, and with a few years of experience to work off of, I hoped for an experience that would have buffed out any rough spots. Unfortunately, my mood soured with PA pretty quickly, in spite of the interesting premise.There appears to be some discrepancy on how people would describe PA, whether it is or isn't a Metroidvania, or if it's more of a Zelda II kind of game. Personally, I see it as a platformer that emphasizes exploration and dungeon-crawling, which is what I expect out of most indie adventure titles. Regardless of the best genre to call it, I find that although it hits some good points, it doesn't deliver well in those areas. For instance, I've grown accustomed to chatting with every NPC I can, but that isn't enough to advance the game in PA. The sequences of events, of which person you speak to when, is so linear and specific, you could miss out on being able to progress because of not doubling-back to someone you already spoke to numerous times. What I disliked most with PA was the game's combat system, which is a common complaint amongst the negative reviews. If you play PA with all combat modifiers turned off, which is how I think it was intended to be played, swinging the bat drains stamina, even when only breaking boxes. Worse than that though, almost every action you'd take is based on this stamina bar: dodge-rolling, sprinting, throwing bombs, etc. Your options in combat are limited, as all of them revolve around the same resource, stamina. You don't have an inventory of arrows and bombs that can be used as you see fit. Using one draws from the same pool as the close-range melee attack. The only actions that don't rely on stamina are basic movement, jumping, and eating. The controls get complicated in PA, and serves as another problem I have with the title, because I don't think it was designed very ergonomically. An example of this is the sprint mechanic. When you hit the button, Gail sprints a certain distance, but this isn't something you can hold down in order to run faster. Instead, its primary use is for making longer jumps, or dodge rolling. In order to do that, you trigger the sprint first, and hit another button afterwards. This technically works, but I'd rather just be able to run normally, and trigger a dodge roll as needed. This is overly complicated.As the game begins, Gail rounds up the children of the village, and dives into a nearby temple, to check out a meteorite that fell nearby. On the way back home, an alien saucer swoops in and kidnaps all of the adults, leaving behind only the children. Admittedly, this is a good hook to establish the plot of PA, as there's important, personal stakes on the line. Players know enough about what's going on to care, as Gail heads out to follow the few leads available, so she can rescue the kidnapped villagers. I'm curious how it all pans out, yet am also unwilling to beat the game in order to see the story unfold. Personally, I think this is an indie game that has great visuals, as I find the pixel graphics vibrant and detailed. It's easy to determine what items are in environments, settings don't look tired and repetitive, as the backgrounds have enough variance to look organic. Additionally, the layered environments give areas a sense of depth. One area that falls flat for me is the character models, as I find them easy to mix up. Were it not for such flashy hair colors, I think they'd blend together.When listening to PA's soundtrack, I'd say it's well composed. It covers a broad range of tones and tempos, which helps build different feelings about the environments Gail travels to. I'm a fan of instrumental music, so I can easily slip into it and enjoy myself. A simple downside is that many of them aren't very long, so they loop upon themselves fairly quickly. 🌟 There are gameplay options that can be turned on and off to adjust the difficulty, to some extent. You won't be able to increase your HP, or weaken enemies though.🌟 I found the visuals and story went well together, which both drew my interest in the first place, and held my attention as I played.🌟 Based on the progression stats from the loading menu, there's quite a few secrets to hunt down.❌ Another problem in combat stems from how getting hit by an attack momentarily stuns the PC, and can lead into being juggled for multiple hits, with no ability to dodge or respond. You'll only get invincibility frames after getting hit three times in a row! With a starting HP of 30, you can take a large chunk of damage because you got hit once. Oftentimes, the number of enemies is more of an issue than their damage output.❌ It's not uncommon to find an item that seems pointless and will waste a valuable inventory slot, until you're able to do something with it much later. Also, with how many items there are to buy, some of which are required for progression, PA is rather tight-fisted when it comes to loot.❌ Not only is there no auto-save feature, you can only save at predetermined save points. This makes it easy to lose progress.🔍 Don't hesitate to drop weak healing items if your inventory fills up, as a cooked item like fish is much more useful than raw berries. Also, when you get to Aria, buy at least four inventory slots.🔍 Since PA won't track information for you, it'd be worthwhile to either jot down notes or follow a guide to know where you'll want to backtrack and when.🔍 You can walk through bosses if they're not in an attack phase. This will be necessary in order to deal with their patterns and counter attack.Even though this is an indie game, I still have certain expectations when it comes to modern-day releases. Considering how it's a remade Flash title, I'd expect them to have ironed out the flaws. Despite this, there's no map system, no quest markers or objectives list, optional treasure items occupy precious inventory slots, you have to speak to specific NPCs at certain times to progress, etc. Overall, I find that PA hasn't been designed around its own mechanics very well. Making the simple change of whether or not your basic attacks use stamina unbalances the game completely. It's either much more difficult or easy depending on which choice you go for. Although it has charming visuals and some interesting ideas, it lacks a level of polish I'd require to stick it out, and isn't a game I'd recommend playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia Awakening is basically a modern-day Zelda 2 if it were an actual Zelda game, filled to the brim with inventive puzzles, fun combat, and a metric ton of hidden things to find. I played it to completion when it released on Switch last year and it ended up being my game of the year. It's hard to get across just how much content there is to find in this game, and almost all of it is unique and fun to solve. The combat system starts out fairly basic with only a short melee attack, but your options expand as you find more weapons throughout the game. That main content of the game is the puzzles, and there's a ton of variety there. Every area manages to have new unique gimmicks; I found myself still being surprised with new puzzles even at the end of the game. For presentation, I really enjoyed the art style and the soundtrack is fantastic. All in all, this is one of the best indie action platformers I've played, and I've played a lot of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Spectacular game!Well made, well designed, well polished, with good gameplay, story, characters, music, puzzles, combat, graphics (if you like pixel art, which I do) - the works.Lots of hidden content to find and off-the-main-path areas to explore, something I personally love doing. Usually when I had an idea that I thought might lead to some hidden content, it turned out to be correct, and that's really neat.Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Clunky at it's best, Asinine at it's worst.I ploughed through best I could with the game's sheer ambition impressing me all the way through.You've got this Zelda 2 base game with lots of ideas, dungeons and cooking, sidequests, villages and cities with loads of NPCs and some big story you following all the way through. I let it all impress me, I was never really sold fully but i hoped that eventually I'd start finding it fun like all the reviews were telling me.But eventually I snapped, there is a clunkiness that seeps through the whole game. COMBAT. Jesus Christ it's these tedious spammy affair that's been strapped on with a stamina system like it's pretending to be Souls-like, but all the enemy's are dead stupid 1 attack drones that will toss you around like a ragdoll, I quit when all the enemy's became acid spewing robots, tnt on wheels and giant targeting turrets. No game, carrying a key through an acid lake teeming with these enemy's does not sound like fun.And the more I look back the I see this clunkiness is everywhere. From the weirdly stiff character movement to puzzle design that's either basic switch pushing lark or just asking you to solve a sudoku puzzle, I don't remember the part in Zelda where I had to solve a crossword. You've clearly got a character artist who did the promotional art and occasional cutscene, but then all the story is told through these emotionless square eyed blobs that constitutes all the characters in pixel art.What worked in a 2 hours flash game becomes asinine in a 30+ hour epic adventure. The fact that the playtime was sizeable for an indie game was what caught my attention but with gameplay like this I'm going to have to cut my journey short.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I really really really wish I could love this game, the story is charming, the setting interesting and the art is pretty and has tons of detail, but wow is the combat tedious and the bossfight that steals your food items with lightning fast attacks just sealed the deal for a negative review (who thought ransacking the players items randomly was a good idea?)There is even some real innovation in this game like one of the best equipment wheels I've seen in any game, but it's overshadowed by some absolutely bungled equipment and what can only be described as malicious design decisions, all while being patronizing at the same timeBring the patience of a saint or give it a pass
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game took a while to really grow on me. There's a lot of strange design choices and the combat doesn't always feel great, especially at first. But I gave it a chance, and before I knew it 30 hours had gone by and I was completely immersed in this world. It is beautiful, and contains one of my favourite maps of any game, littered with secrets and puzzles in every corner. My time with this game is not done, and I am eager to jump back in and explore the areas I missed considering I only finished it with 57% completion (and I thought I was being pretty thorough...). If you just want to go on a classic pixel adventure, exploring ancient dungeons while solving their many mysteries, you need to give Phoenotopia a shot. It is a criminally overlooked gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I remember really digging the flash version of phoenotopia. And while this game is very interesting and all with wonderful artwork, storyline, music and whatnot, the combat ruins it all for me. I guess it is a subjective matter and depending on the gamer they might find the battles to be amusing. The problem is that the devs somehow managed to make every single fight with enemies a grueling mini-boss fight which demands the utmost attention and energy from the gamers. And this game is not short of its enemies. It could be because I am not really a good gamer but for someone who has blasted through the original flash version several times, and all difficulties and achievements for rainworld, if I am two seconds away from dying of anger whilst playing at the lowest difficulty, I would say there is a problem with this game too not just the gamer.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game is criminally underrated... every aspect of it is truly spectacular. You are ALWAYS rewarded for going out of you way and trying things out, the game almost never tells you any strategies or gives you any hints as to how you beat bosses or tactics you can use unless you find them yourself... and the game rewards you for trying out clever strategies to beat its bossesThere are multiple difficulty settings to fine tune how hard the combat will beThe spritework and characters are immaculate... the music is phenomenal and the puzzles are legitimately difficult... but they feel rewarding when you figure them out yourself instead of just looking up the answers... some of them can be a bit rough... but thats only like... 2 of them out of 20 ive done so farThe game plays like a sidescrolling Legend of Zelda game, but still manages to maintain its own identityIts just good... if you've read this far... just buy it already!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This is a 90% fantastic game, but the other 10% suffers from egregious design and implementation flaws that are so un-fun they mitigate the fun of the rest of the game.The worst offender is a variety of enemies and dungeons which are designed around concise timing and dexterity (common for the genre), but are hindered by clunky controls that work against the player and inhibit the actions necessary.  Several "accessibility" options exist to scale the game's difficulty, but they all address parts of the game which can be adapted to with skill and none address the parts of the game that cannot be overcome as a result of the game's mechanics.For example: you can turn on i-frames between hits to avoid being juggled by enemies, however the knockback many hits generate results in an input loss of roughly the same duration the i-frames are effective for, rendering them relatively pointless more than half the time.Bottom line: fantastic game which works against itself in several infuriating ways to undermine itself.  I would not recommend the game based on this.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: 1-hour Gameplay First Impressions:We are all here to determine if this particular product will be a gem worthy of your time, or another forgettable affair like many before it, right? So, what's your poison of choice:- Music?This game will have you lost in a pure symphonic euphoria the moment the main menu lands. After playing, I happened across the fact that the OST will go on sale eventually. In my heart, I've pre-ordered the soundtrack, and when it goes on sale, I'll own it for real. It's good.- Combat?After speaking to literally everyone in town, I went outside. Enemies appear on the over-world and roam about; some will even chase you across the map, so be careful out there! I spent about 5 or so minutes whapping boars with a bat while dodging their attempts to steamroll me or Goomba stomp me. I died in spectacular fashion.I had this experience so you wouldn't have to. You're welcome.Keep in mind, I'm playing on the highest difficulty, so your experiences may vary. During the course of that trying battle, I learned alot about how combat will work. First off, you have stamina. Your stamina drains when sprinting and attacking (extra stamina is consumed if you jump after sprinting); each successive attack after the first deals decreasing damage until, ultimately, you can't attack at all. You can also charge your attack to deal massive damage; it's pretty quick but will necessitate well-timed use because getting hit interrupts it. Also, ♥♥♥ bees.- Exploration?Dunno, man. I only got an hour in. However, the over-world map already has several visible locations and my wanderlust was kicking in pretty fiercely. Oh, how I long to end up in-over-my-head in a place I don't belong...- Art design?Oh, come on. The trailer showcases everything you need to know on that end.- Not in Early Access?Oh, baby. This is, most assuredly, the full package.All in all, (for me, at least) this one's a keeper. If what you've read here didn't help you make up your mind, consider this:
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I just realized that I didn't review this game yet and it's a cardinal sin for how good it is.First, the game is gargantuan, it is not only vast but also tightly packed with collectibles and things to do everywhere, puzzles, people to meet, stories to discover... As such, you can really immerse deeply in its rich world. And what a world ! The pixel art and the color palettes used are a feast for the eyes ! There were frankly a few times where I just gazed to these beautiful environments.I have one warning about the difficulty though, while I personally found combat to be fair and fun, there where a few times where I felt the difficulty spiked pretty hard. That said, there are a few accessibility features available, things like energy bar recharging faster, more i-frames when hit... Nice things to have but not the gamebreaking type so feel free to use them, you can also switch them on or off anytime. I played the game without using them but I can imagine they can smooth your experience if you're stuck on a hard part.I loved every second I spent on Phoenotopia and I really think it's a shame it's not more well known (pretty sure the game didn't sell well sadly), so yeah, huge recommendation here.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia: Awakening is a wonderful game with some polarising design choices. Personally, I absolutely loved this game, but I think the mixed reviews are completely understandable.Pros:Cons:All in all, I think my complaints about the game stem from design choices that lead to a lot of time wasting. I understand some people's frustrations about the combat, but I personally didn't have issues with it.Despite my complaints, I loved the game enough to get all the achievements and leave a review (which I normally don't do). I hope we get a sequel someday.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has been following this game's development for over 3 years as a fan, its hard to say I'm not excited and a little biased when I give this game a positive review. However, after giving it some legitimate playtime, I can concretely say this is one of the best Indie Adventure games out there, with strong game mechanics and beautiful pixel art that embraces simplicity.Some things that could need reworking are the controls, as sometimes it can be awkward on keyboard/mouse to grab, throw and use directional input at the same time.The minigames are really well done, with certain timed sections as well as Fishing and Cooking minigames that are reminiscent of Stardew Valley's minigame aesthetic. The story is JAM PACKED with amazing fantasy plotlines and cute moments between characters. This game is absolutely fitting for it's Indie Game 20$ pricetag, and you get a LOT of content. As my hours AFTER review will surely show, theres alot more yet to come.Try it out! Support Indie Developers! Play the game!!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the best games I've had the pleasure to play. It's worth every single cent and minute invested on it.The game has a constant sense of wonder and exploration, as you discover new places. There is a world map where you will find bustling cities, mysterious ruins, beautiful fields, forests, deserts and many hidden locations. There are tons of secrets and missions everywhere to keep you busy for at least 50 hours.All is packaged with an amazing pixel art, wonderful music, lots of creativity and perfect game balance. With this title I rediscovered why I play games. 100% recommended, it's the quintessence of a hidden gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game does have flaws - like combat is unforgiving, early exploration is rewarded by inventory clutter, and the last act includes an endless slog - but they're outweighed by its everpresent undeniable heart.  The massive world is excellent, its complex and cohesive areas don't at all suffer from the game having an overworld.  Characters are great, upgrades are great, art and music are great.  The many puzzles are creative and there's surprisingly strong humor.  This game is joyous.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. music, combat, world, story, puzzles. All fantastically done. As someone who really only stays glued to competitive fps games. (with the exception of souls games) this was definitely out of my comfort zone but either way i still enjoyed it. HIGHLY RECOMMEND. Its sad that most games nowadays try to milk you for every penny you have. Only to then feed you the same garbage recycled game play year in and year out. The future of gaming looks grim sometimes, but this game gave me hope again. And more importantly its the first game to expand my taste beyond just mainstream triple A. <3

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've played in a long time. Absolutely a joy to look at. Tons of fun to explore, with some fun characters. & even some accessibility options that allow you to play the game your way. Combats' pretty challenging but very rewarding. But easily THE best aspect are the puzzles! Just challenging enough to get you using your noggin, but not enough to leave you banging you head against the wall. Overall, 12/10 would absolutely recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: /!\ /!\ /!\ SPOILERS /!\ /!\ /!\This game is a masterpiece, clearly a hidden gem considering how little spotlight it had and how poorly it sold. Really a shame!Phoenotopia looks amazing, I couldn't help myself but take dozens of screenshots while I was playing. Last time I did that was when I played Gris.The gameplay is simply fantastic, there are tons of smart interactions in the game design, the puzzles really test your spatial perception: whether it's activating a switch by angling your slingshot the right way, using projectiles to knock moonstones off their platform, piling up boxes and bombs to gain barely enough height to reach a platform, or completing parkour sections full of arrow traps with well synchronized jumps.The puzzles where you need to play the correct song with your flute gave me Zelda Ocarina of Time vibes. I liked how musical notes were often hidden in the background, and I had to spot them to know what I would need to play with the bandit's flute.The GEO dungeons especially had really different kinds of puzzles. One time you'll have to solve a jigsaw puzzle, the next time it'll be a sliding picture puzzle, then it will involve switching lights in the correct order. There's even a puzzle similar to sudoku.The game always managed to hold my attention with all its brainteasers.Cooking mechanic is based on reaction time, it's simple and engaging. I noticed there was a frying pan on display in the Antique Shop near Daea city, but I never managed to obtain it during my playthrough. I suppose it would have modified the cooking minigame in a certain way?Btw, I like how we immediatly drop cooked meat when we kill a mob/animal with an explosion (bomb or spear). Pretty cool that they thought about that!The Gear Ring allows you to quickly switch up between 8 different items, it's always a good thing to have a weapon wheel in any game I play. It's very ergonomic and it saved me a lot of time from navigating through the menus.And I'm thankful that we can use all our weapons as much as we want, without having to worry about ammo.It's very satisfying when you struggle while exploring an area for the 1st time, having to use your gear in a clever way, dealing with all the enemies and barely surviving. And then when you revisit the same area later in the game with a new ability, you can make it through in a much simpler way. The abilities that you get for traversal exploration are really game-changing. I was so excited to backtrack everytime I got a new one.Phoenotopia Awakening is very charming, and has a lot of light-hearted moments. I never got tired of listening to "Merry Fellowship" everytime Gail came back to her hometown after a mission, checking in with her brothers & sisters to see if they're okay. The game even manages to be funny sometimes. For example, when Gail and Fran use the teleporter for the 1st time, and Gail thinks Fran died during the teleportation as she watches the pile of dust on the ground, before Fran immediatly appears out of nowhere with a big smile on her face.The game also managed to do the exact opposite on several occasions. I was very anxious during that moment in EDEN's Lab, when you're quietly exploring the rooms and reading notes about those harpys in their stasis chamber. As you progress, you suddently hear glass breaking, and when you turn around, you notice all the harpys broke out.Those moments, whether tense or joyful, are always accompanied by excellent music. My personal favorites are "Merry/Mellow Fellowship", "Boss battle", "The White Towers", "Katash's theme", "Wheat Road" and "Caves of Mul".You can't put markers on a map to remember points of interest. So I had to write down informations on a notepad regularly to not get lost and not forget things like treasure chests, entrances to dungeons, or song stones. There are tons of stuff to do and optional content, so having a quest log and a map available at all times would have been useful, but it was definitely manageable without it.I loved the last part of the game that consists of 3 Boss fights back-to-back. The first one against Mother Computer was the most challenging fight in the entire game. Then you have this amazing showdown with your own shadows, and finally the duel vs Katash.I have to say this last battle felt a bit anticlimactic. I had encountered Adam earlier in the lab, and I thought I would have to fight this monstrosity, but instead it was a second duel with Katash.I'm pretty sure (and I hope) that I will have to fight Adam when I'll come back to this game to get the true ending, and I can't wait for it.I unlocked the first ending after 60 hours with a completion of 62%. I played enough and I don't want to push myself, so I won't go for 100%. However, I will surely come back to this game in a few months to do some more things. Notably exploring Aurantia, beating Katash' 2nd encounter, and accessing the locked room at the top of Pristine City to fight Phalanx.I don't know how they did it, but the game was never boring, never frustrating, never too hard, never too easy, never repetitive, never bad. There was the right amount of everything: fights, exploration, puzzles and platforming.Really, as I said earlier, the only thing that people could have a problem with is that it can be difficult to keep track of everything. But it's really not that big of a deal if you pay attention, and of course if you write things down on a notepad or a piece of paper.This is why I give this game a perfect score. This is one of the best games I've played this year! I'm still a bit salty that this game is so unknown...10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game really surprised me. I've had my eye on it for some time but finally decided to take the plunge and pick it up. What I got was a strangely addictive platformer with a cute and charming style all it's own. Combat is a bit weird but the game makes it work. I liken it to each major encounter having a "rhythm" that you need to tap into and once you find that rhythm you can get past it's many sticking points. Where the game really shines is in it's puzzles and overall world design. I really enjoyed going off the beaten path and finding items and other pick ups. And while I mostly enjoyed the puzzles I felt a couple of them were a bit TOO involved with finding a solution. But that's just me. Overall I feel like there's so much potential here for "more" and it makes me kinda sad that the game ended where it did.And all these years later there's no sign of a sequel which is really too bad. Give the dev some love I really feel like this project deserves it.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe I'm biased, but this truly feels like a worthy remake of the original flash game.It's beautiful, the soundtrack is "out of this world", and this is a bit of an unpopular opinion (I'm really putting it all on the line here, if I don't come back I want 'I only had to look up three things to 100% my inventory' on my gravestone), but I really do LOVE the (current patch's) combat system and most of the boss fights with accessibility options turned off.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has played the original Flash game back in high school, I was incredibly excited going into this remake. And all I can say is that this remake surpassed many of my expectations and subverted others when I played it.Pros:-The combat is pretty solid all around, especially late game when you start unlocking more stuff.-The art style is very charming and the 8-bit characters and environments are very distinct.-The music is REALLY good and memorable.-The enemy variety is huge and the constant shifts in enemies as you go on is pretty nice.-The amount of areas you can explore is really great.-The puzzles are pretty challenging without being obscenely difficult.-The progression was fair and balanced for the most part.-The dungeon design is overall really great, even if they aren't the biggest dungeons ever.-The story is MUCH better than the original.Cons:-Some parts of the combat needed work, especially with the base attacks and some of the bat abilities.-Some puzzles were unnecessarily difficult, and if you know, you know.-Some enemy attacks needed to be toned down due to how much high damage or stun locks there could be.But overall it's a really fun experience that brought me back and really makes me hope that there IS a second game, ever. It's the most fun I've had in a while, so much that I sometimes even forget the concept of time to where HOURS pass without me knowing.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful Zelda/Metroid adventure! In general, the game's got it all: an interesting mixed-technology world like something outta Star Ocean with an intriguing plot, charming characters with amusing dialogue that never felt cringe, refreshingly actual challenging combat and puzzles, a huge world to explore with tons of sidequests and places that give great rewards to keep track of and come back to, an addictive sense of progression with new gadgets and abilities, and so on! Like I said, it's the total package and anyone looking for a great Zelda-esque adventure should highly consider picking this up.Some points to consider:1) Combat works, and does have a lot of nice things to it like no old-school contact damage (enemies can only hit you with clearly telegraphed attack animations), but it can be a bit frustrating due to 1) stamina constantly running out and taking so long to regenerate 2) your melee attack being very short and stubby which forces you to get right in enemies faces to not whiff 3) no iframes, even for the dodge roll manuever, which makes defense feel very awkward 4) enemy attacks feeling overwhelming as they can send you ragdolling around and can wombo-combo you due to no post-hit invincibility. As said, it's balanced for this, there are a lot of great fights, and there are accessibility options, but even when I accepted it for what it was, it still felt so annoying at times.2) The game doesn't have any sort of marking system or a quest log to keep track of all the stuff you're doing, so if you play this, I highly recommend you have a notepad handy like I did. I enjoyed this prospect, but it can be difficult to keep track of everything if you leave the game.3) The cooking system seemed nice at first, but I was sick of it by the end. Cooking food is practically always a net positive compared to raw food, and there's no sense of expression through recipes or customization or whatever, so it just becomes tedium you always have to go through the motions to do, killing the pace. It's kinda like how, unlike most survival games which have cooking be a challenge at the start but eventually automate it to let you focus on greater goals, in this you always need to make time for cooking and fishing and are never free from it (some people may like this though, I suppose!)4) The moonstone currency system can be a bit frustrating in that I thought it was only used for unlocking fast travel, but suddenly the game pulled a fast one mid-way and offers upgraded gear which costs moonstones as well, meaning I felt cheated as now I had to decide between convenience and fun in a battle where both choices felt bad until I eventually get enough stones for everything I wanted.5) I enjoyed the journey and everything so it didn't sour me too much, but the ending did fall a bit flat to me as many things were handwaved offscreen or left unresolved.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on the fence on this one. I guess I would recommend it to fans of the genre, and it is a good game, but it does have issues which make it notably less enjoyable.The biggest pain point for me is the sheer amount of time-wasting. Travel is cumbersome, puzzles and bosses reset, there's no fast travel or mini map within dungeons you've already completed... at every turn it seems like there's a design decision which was made to make the game longer rather than better.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly underrated game, it kills me that it took me so long to finally pick it up and play. The music and pixel art are gorgeous, some people in the reviews seem to have problems with the gameplay but I never had any problems or annoyances with it throughout 100% completion (including beating the game without any upgrades on hardest difficulty). If you do have any though, the game has plenty of ways to alleviate them with it's customizable difficulty selection and accessibility features.Easily one of those games I wish I could play for the first time again, sucks the devs didn't make enough money from it in order to warrant making a sequel like they wanted. They deserve success.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I'll admit there were a lot of things that bothered me with this game, but there is a lot to love here. My expectations were on a roller-coaster of being blown away and then disappointed/frustrated and then blown away again on repeat. The size of this game genuinely impresses me and what's good is really good here. This is a grand journey, oozing with personality and charm.

_childDocuments_.review: While the art and music are very good the controls are terrible.  There are puzzles that require very precise jumps and dashes, but the controls don't work like most other platformers. At first I thought I was lagging but eventually found a post stating it was intentional."As for the sprint jump, it's intentionally non-controllable. It presents a tradeoff vs the regular jump - it gets more distance, but gives no control. As for how the sprinting works, that's another intentional design choice. I had in mind Mario Kart's "boosting" mechanic - in that game, you have to press "jump" at the apex of a hill, and doing so would result in a speed burst - it's not possible to simply hold "jump" and auto-get all the speed boosts in mario kart. I've, similarly, designed Phoenotopia to be very "pressy". So to maintain a high speed, you have to disengage and re-engage in the sprint button constantly, knowing when to let go and when to press. It's too late to change the mechanic now, but I've taken notes that a good chunk of people aren't fans of the system and will take that into consideration for the next game (if there is one)."Because of this exploring feels like work.  It becomes hard to tell if I can't access a certain area yet or if I'm just messing up the jump.Same thing with combat.  It feels like there is a half second lag between me pressing attack and actually swinging.  I really wish the controls were better.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia is a good game in my eyes. The dialogue is funny, the story is fresh and fun, and the gameplay is a challenging but rewarding experience. I played the original flash version of the game and I must say, pretty much everything about the new version is better. Phoenotopia: Awakening is a much more polished game than the original flash version. The graphics, dialogue, and game mechanics have been seriously touched up. New areas and items have been added, as well more secrets and collectibles. Phoenotopia has a difficulty most people may not be prepared for. There are sections that feel distinctly bullet hell like, but most of the game doesn't hold that level of difficulty. In order to properly enjoy the game at a reasonable difficulty, exploration is necessary to find health and stamina items. The highest difficulty may not be for everyone either, despite how it's the way the game was originally supposed to be played. Despite this, I enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: A very ambitious game that pretty much hits it out of the park with everything it tries to do.At its core it's Metroidvania gameplay but with the structure of a more traditional RPG, and does both parts of that formula well. The combat is fun and feels pretty well balanced. The puzzles are good and quite varied. The exploration feels rewarding, with lots of fun things to find and varied level types. Bosses feel well designed, and generally avoid the trope of "wait around for the boss to do the attack that lets you hit them".On the highest difficulty the fights that are intended to be hard generally demand one or two retries but never pose a brick wall (at least for me, though I consider myself a good player). The only exception was one boss who took me around ten tries. But if you are having trouble, there's a variety of options you can toggle to make the combat easier; the difficulty selection at the beginning just picks from a few default configurations (with the "max difficulty" just turning them all off). Some of the optional side content is much harder though.There's a variety of side content and minigames, of varying scope. Pretty much all of them are fun, well designed, have appropriate length and reinforce the tone and style that the game was going for. The same can be said for the levels.The story is fun and endearing, albeit not award-worthy. Visuals, music, and dialog are all pretty great. Expect a childish tone of adventure despite the high stakes (except in a few specific areas where they intentionally invoke a much darker atmosphere).In terms of length, it took me ~35 hour to beat on my first playthrough with 50% item completion. There's two full hidden levels which add a few more hours onto that, and a huge number of smaller side areas/puzzles/quests/secrets which will extend it much further if you're a completionist (even a few optional bosses). Fortunately if you are hunting for 100% there's an NPC who gives hints to stuff you haven't found yet. Also there's 2 challenge achievements which require a full second/third playthrough.Overall, this is a title that shouldn't be missed by Metroidvania lovers.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: The game has some charm and is overall quite well presented, but in it's current state I really cannot recommend it. Problems with the game range from bugs, a lack of polish, and some questionable design decisions.Text boxes will often draw off screen. Solutions to puzzles sometimes don't feel like the correct solution and feel like you've cheated it somehow. Scaling issues with the pixel-perfect camera cause random columns of pixels will occupy more screen space than other columns of pixels. The way in which you run in the game is extremely weird, it's hard to explain but feels clunky and your character is overall pretty strange to control. "jump" and "talk" share the same button, so you cannot jump if an NPC is standing close to you.I think the game has some potential, but should have probably spent another month or two being polished. I cannot recommend this game in it's current state or at it's current price point, I suggest either waiting for a sale or for some of the games problems to be solved before purchasing.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend it because of really just one major reason: Grind. This game is grindy. Grindy in an absolutely not fun way.If you don't mind beating up enemies for hours to gamble for drops to sell, so you can buy the dang key item to progress, the game is fine, if quite clunky on the controls. Looks are very charming, it offers some freedom and exploration (although the clunky controls will make you dislike combat and precise platforming) and is overall decent. The grind however is, as far as I'm concerned, ruining a lot. Everything costs way too much money and this isn't helped by your inventory being super small. You can increase the size, but that costs, you might've guessed it, tons of money.I have to think if I really want to continue this game. _childDocuments_.review: Not so much a metroidvania, even though some elements are there, as a wonderful oldschool adventure game with modern ideas and innovations added. This on top of being game full of soul, imagination and brimming with character, And one that needs to be explored and investigated to really see half of what's there?Despite looking very all-ages, and for the most of the time acting like it, it can be quite tough and difficult in places though; those optional areas and challenges in particular. _childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: A sidescrolling science fantasy epic of immense scope, heart, and quality,  is the greatest  spiritual successor available.  It has fast, strategic gameplay and a story that manages to be lighthearted and genuinely engaging in the same moment.  Every surface gleams with polish; every facet oozes pure love.  The only question that remains is this:  do you have room in your life to control a superhuman, pink-haired (non-SJW) chibi-woman for upwards of 40 hours?  Probably more if you leave it on hard, the game's original mode?     (I love how playing Gail feels like controlling a ground squirrel -- little, dense, and fast -- and also how she pings off surfaces like a rubber ball when she takes a hard knock.  It adds to the whole anime feel of the thing.)
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Ok this game has a huge identity crisis. It's tagged as a metroidvania, but even if Phoenotopia was influenced by that genre, it's blatantly not true. The overworld, towns, NPC hints, linearity of dungeons, and scattering of optional areas to stumble upon in the map resemble Zelda 2. But more importantly is that at no point over my 6 hours played have I felt like my character has progressed in any meaningful way. There's a general sluggishness and clunkiness imparted into every aspect of the gameplay that comes from several weak designs colliding at once - the lethargic stamina bar is an obvious flaw, but that didn't stop people from loving Secret of Mana. Instead, every interaction of movement, platforming, resource management, and combat are at constant clash with each other. You move slow, but your enemies are fast and small; your attack has minuscule reach, deals even less damage, and is barely improved by the extremely sparse weapon upgrades; platforming and box-pushing are everywhere, but you never get a ledge grab, or double jump, or wall jump, or anything that would make navigating previous environments easier or more satisfying. You have no block, no dodge, no i-frames, and get thrown around by a number of enemy attacks, despite the abundance of combat. You don't get Link's directional aerial attacks (or variety of spells) from Zelda 2, nor the usefulness those abilities entail - instead your aerial attack and ranged items have uncomfortably delayed responses that share no rhyme or reason. Bosses present bizarre difficulty spikes where they spam arena-covering attacks, simultaneously encouraging heal-item spamming while punishing the default setting of having to eat mid-combat as if it's monster hunter.Look I could keep going here, but I'll settle for saying that the "game" part just isn't fun. It's slow, tedious, limp, and stays that way - it's the first 30 minutes of every mediocre metroidvania when you have 0% percent of your arsenal, except that it never gets any better over the course of 6 hours. Maybe if the story was more engaging I'd be able to push myself further, but it's given me such a breezy and gossamer adventure so far that there just isn't enough in the plot or the characters to latch on to.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the exploration in this game.I enjoy solving the puzzles in this game.I have a good time going into towns and speaking with the townsfolk.I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate the combat in this game so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ much. It's almost mesmerizing in how frustrating is. You have to be pitch-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ perfect in some of the fights in this game. Sometimes you have to fight waves of enemies and you can get stun-locked into oblivion. I'm talking going from full health to near dead in a span of five seconds.Yes, I am aware there are difficulty settings you can change. But those do nothing when your equipment is woefully inefficient against bosses who are among the biggest sponges I've played in a game. Unreal how one awful aspect can sour an otherwise good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Easy = Still way too difficult. Everything requires WAAY too much money to purchase and the effects of those items are practically useless as they do not provide any real defense or attack benefit. _childDocuments_.review: I really loved everything about this game other than... yes, the combat.Seriously. The art, story, characters, ambiance, music... phenomenal. But the combat? _childDocuments_.review: Ive been craving a new metroidvania lately and while I didnt buy this game expecting it to be one, it certainly scratched that itch. Its technically not a metroidvania, more of a sidescrolling rpg, but it has weapons and items to find and unlock, rewards for going off the beaten path, revisiting old areas later, all of the staples of a good metroidvania are here.Also the music is amazing and the areas to explore are gorgeous!The game says its not steam deck supported but it works perfectly fine. just adjust the resolution and turn on smooth follow in the settings.

_childDocuments_.review: Contrary to what some say here, this is a very well balanced masterpiece.It's very simple in the matter of movement and combat mechanics at first, but it isn't necessarily easy to master, and those elements become a lot more fun as you progress.If you miss a game that respects you and your ability to play it like the old days, this one is for you. It brings a lot of that joy from the olden times, but with a lot of modern quality of life and game design improvements.IF YOU ARE NO LONGER IN YOUR PRIME OR NO LONGER HAVE THE PATIENCE FOR GETTING GOOD AT GAMES it's fine. It has difficulty options that can make the game gradually easier, all the way to a walk in the park, and that is completely fine.I'm still playing through it slowly, and enjoying every second of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant adventure game, the exploration aspect is the strongest point of this game, it rewards players being curious and attentive to the world around. The visuals are also one of the best, with gorgeous pixel art all around and animations. The combat gameplay is simple but effective, if somewhat limited in options in the early game. The Dungeons are extremely good, with the main drawback for most being the bosses, mainly due to some of them cranking the difficulty to an overkill level compared to the rest of the dungeon. The game does feature numerous difficulty options to help but the experiences for most bosses still leaves to be desired.Finally, the writing is excellent, the sidequests are all quite clever and lots of attention was put in all the extra information laying around in the world. The main story is well made, if a bit unclear at the early game and faltering at the end.Still overall it's a highly recommended game for anyone looking for a brilliant 2D adventure game and looking for a good challenge with puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game and seeing its lack of attention, I feel compelled to leave my thoughts. I thoroughly enjoyed this game from start to 100% completion and I'd definitely recommend it if catches your interest. Its story was interesting and the world is packed with enjoyable locations, writing, and secrets. This is one of those games where you can really see the love put into it through all its details (e.g. Gail's animations are downright adorable). Also, the soundtrack is one the best out of any game I've played, period. I've never experienced a soundtrack so consistently great.The only real downside I'd consider is the admittedly fiddly controls at times and that the combat is quite simple. I still had a lot of fun with it, but anyone expecting a super in-depth combat system may be disappointed. Regardless, Phoenotopia Awakening is definitely an underrated adventure game packed full of charm.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun game, except for the combat. Devs have added some accessibility options to help reduce the difficulty, but it's still gruelling. If you're not good with combat games then get ready to load up on food supplies to just tank boss battles (and some of the more annoying non-boss battles). And if you love difficult combat games, this game is definitely for you!Otherwise, the graphics are beautiful, the plot is good, the background music is pleasant, the puzzles range in difficulty from easy to normal to hard (you don't have to do them all and any required for progression shouldn't be too hard), the exploration is fun, and there are tons of side quests (get ready for back tracking galore). The fishing mini-quest isn't bad (easy concept, doesn't take too long, meaningful rewards), as fishing mini-games are normally a real turn-off in other games.I've finished it once, despite some very frustrating parts, and I will go back and play it again after letting it "cool off" for a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated! Phoenotopia:Awakening is a fun, immensely charming, challenging experience full of adventure, puzzles, and good times. The flow of the game is deeply immersive with charming characters everywhere you look, fun jokes, good wit, a staggering level of internal consistency, and a story that's always going in interesting directions. The world is large and chocked full of things to explore, puzzles to solve and secrets to find. Combat is challenging but masterable. If you're having a hard time with one of the game's optional challenges, come back later and you might have some tools to aid you! There's so much to do, so much to see, so much to HEAR, and it's all wonderful. A game that's not afraid to put huge chunks in optional areas. There are moments of genuine joy in this game, and I'm confident it will leave an impression on you.10/10 My personal game of the year for 2020. Cannot recommend enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic. This is what I hoped indie games would be when I first played Cave Story about twelve years ago.Lots of exploration with cool little secrets and puzzles sprinkled all over, charming visuals, dialogue, and sound, and the movement has a few little intricacies that you can master to get the most out of your character.There are a lot of reviews complaining about the combat, but I haven't run into any problems beyond having to switch from d-pad to control stick for crossbow aiming. _childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia: Awakening is a Zelda-like with engaging puzzles, interesting secrets, great music, and compelling atmosphere. While cartoonish and exaggerated in nature, the plot and characters are fun and charming.The main focus of the game is exploration. The world is overflowing with a variety of secrets to find and puzzles to solve, with rewards ranging from money and common collectibles, to powerful unique items and interesting side quests. The most difficult puzzles (all optional) even required I use a pencil and paper to draw and write on. There is no quest log or waypoints, so figuring out side quests often is quite intrinsically rewarding, as you've got to figure it all out yourself. The main complaints I've heard about this game are:1) The controls are janky/unintuitive because you can't turn in mid-air, sprint-jumps have a pre-determined arc, and you need to press the sprint button again after landing from a jump to continue a sprint.2) Over-reliance on stamina; sprinting, rolling, nearly all of the key items, and all melee attacks use stamina. This, combined with (1), makes platforming and combat overly difficult.3) There is no map screen while in dungeons, making them arduous and confusing.Combat in Phoenotopia: Awakening is relatively slow compared to other contemporary 2D action platformers. Most enemy attacks are either slow moving, or come with both audio and visual tells well before the attack happens. This means that the impact that (1) and (2) have on combat is less than it may appear. You are "meant" to take to combat with caution and an analytical eye, making sure you make the correct movements at the right times. Of course, good reaction time is important, it is just not the end-all-be-all. As for the whole "being unable to turn in mid air" thing, the aerial melee attack is more of a high-risk, high-reward thing (it does relatively high damage). It is safer to stay on the ground and use ranged weapons to attack things in the air.Even if you consider the combat overly difficult due to the controls, the game still can be accessible to you. Specifically, as I've already discussed, the main focus of the gameplay is on exploration. Similar to Super Metroid, (another came criticized for its janky controls), as long as you are regularly seeking upgrades, tanking your way through combat encounters is fairly viable. This becomes especially true if you stay prepared with healing food. While food takes time to eat, different foods take different amounts of time. Specifically, taking a dozen of food bits that heal only a little but are quick to eat can be quite easily used to heal in the middle of some of the hardest fights. The game also does not have much precision platforming, so the pre-determined arc of the sprint jump is not really that big of a deal. If you want more control, a regular jump will give you that.As for (3), most dungeons in the game have quite simple layouts, with many unique-looking rooms. I can see why the lack of a map could be problematic for some, but I personally didn't have any issues with it. I actually found it kind of fun; the absence of a map screen means that the level design has to do all of the heavy lifting to be interesting, memorable, and navigable.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game for lovers of exploration. Just a rock solid and varied adventure that rarely gets boring over its 60+ hr 100% runtime. Great level design, music, visuals, and more deliberate combat/mechanics that layer well together to make some interesting puzzles and exploration. The story at the forefront isn't the strongest but the minute to minute dialogue is fun and is just another way the game keeps you hooked. Again if you love exploration and secrets pick this up. The amount of secrets, bosses, and large areas that are completely optional is impressive and goes well beyond what you would expect for the price tag. Definitely a labor of love.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best Metroidvania in 2021. Just finished it after 50+ hours and I have literally no idea on how could a gem like this fly under my radar for so long.Think "Cave Story" with better story, better NPCs, more environmental variety, and Zelda-like items and puzzles. Positives:-Great worldbuilding and lore.I personally liked how it is exposed to the player: By exploring areas and interacting with NPCs outside the main story path. Collecting tidbits of info from conversations, journals and simple environment observation.-Great sci-fi main story. Though it starts deceptibly cliched and simple. The town of the protagonist, a young girl named Gail, is attacked. And everyone in it is kidnapped. Only Gail and the kids of the local orphanage are left, since they were playing in a nearby forest when the deed happened. So she grabs her baseball bat and slingshot, and hurries to seek help at the nearest town. From that point things escalate, and in her search for the missing adults he starts to discover hidden and dark secrets about her civilization.-Quirky, cartoony, and yet very well written NPCs.-Rewarding exploration and sidequests.-Very clever spatial reasoning puzzles.-Awesome '16 bit' era music.-Great stamina based combat system. Though it requires a bit of practice and is kinda hard to get initially.Using the melee attack or any other combat equipment drains the stamina meter, which recovers over time. Initially only the short range melee attack is available, though the game introduces better and ranged combat items later on.Enemies don't deal contact damage, so the short range is not really an issue. Also, jumping or moving has no stamina cost at all, the trick is knowing the attack patterns of each enemy, approach them with the best positioning and weapon, flail at them until the stamina runs out and 'dodge' their attacks by merely jumping or moving out of their attack hitboxes. You can also heal during combat by eating food, though it leaves Gail open to attacks for an instant, or a long while depending on the food.- Minigames: There are several minigames and activities, such as fishing or cooking to prepare different healing and boosting consumables. The fishing minigame is specially fun and clever.Negatives:-Pixel art design is kinda hit and miss. Some enemies and environments are awesome, but for some reason the main character has an extremely simple design.-No maps at all. Areas are easy enough to remember and navigate, but it still would have been a good feature to have.-No journal to keep track of sidequests, good ol' paper and pencil are required. Not that bad, since they also help with the most complex puzzles.Fair warning: The game is old school HARD. Though it has a great panel of accesibility options to enable/disable, so you can customize the experience to your liking. Eg: Greater stamina regen, no stamina cost for the regular attacks, auto-save, etc...Seriously, if you enjoy story-oriented metroidvanias like Cave Story or Iconoclasts, then give this one a chance, it deserves way more recognition.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games like Zelda, the length you get from this is definitely worth the price tag. My first playthrough finished at 31.5 hours, and 55% completion.My recommendation is play without guides or spoilers, don't worry about getting everything on the first go, and prepare to take notes or screenshots if you think you can't remember something that looks important. There's a LOT of very easy to accidentally pass side content and secrets, and no journal menu or markers to keep track of objectives in-game. However I don't think anything of consequence is actually permanently missable. If you are a completionist you can leave looking up secrets with help to post-game. There is also an in-game hint system that gives riddles towards side quest and loot locations, that you gain access to near the end, if you don't wish to resort to straight up guides.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Truly the best game for me. Reminding me of Zelda games with solid game play, lore and music, the combat is always challlenging, not because the boss and enemies are unfair, but each and every one of them are designed with unique ways to dealt with them, so you a never feel over power and boring, every encounter seems fair. That is rare for RPG action game.  There are a lot of puzzles. I truly mean A LOT, almost 200 puzzles and each one of them is uniquely designed and tested. And there is no bug, not a single one. This shows how much the developer actually put care and love to this game.There is only one minor downside, at first 2hrs of the game, the combat is hard due to you not used to the combat and there is no upgrade, untill the first major village. Then you have to grind for an hour to get enough gem for weapon upgrade. Most negative comment because of this.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following this game since it was just a flash game and I have never stopped loving it. Phoenotopia is a metroidvania style game that is EXTREMELY challenging, even more so than compared to when it was just a flash game. You can reduce the difficulty by toggling on or off various options if you are feeling overwhelmed but don't go into this game expecting the difficulty of an average action platformer. The game expects you to use every tool you have in combat. This (in my opinion) makes progress in this game feel extremely rewarding as you won based on your skills. This game is also blessed with an amazing soundtrack and beautiful pixel art that accompany you every step of the story. If you are looking for a unique and challenging action platformer with terrific music and charming art then I would ask you to give this game a try, it might be just what your looking for!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game is criminally underrated, and it truly deserves more exposure than it has gotten. Many others have commented on the game mechanics and basic story premise better than I could, so I won't comment on those other than the fact that combat is not meant to be easy.Phoenotopia is a work of art. There's such an intense depth of heart and soul poured into it, and it clearly shows. The visuals are gorgeous, the lore is deep and fascinating, and the soundtrack is a work of art unto itself. It's rare for music alone to consistently bring me to the brink of tears, but this game manages it.I've fallen in love with the world. There's always something fascinating, beautiful, or just valuable around every corner, and there are SO MANY CORNERS. Never has a game so richly rewarded exploration for me, and even 100 hours in you might still find something new or figure out a puzzle you couldn't quite crack before.I could honestly gush on for a long time. Every part of the game has had immense care put into it, and I only wish more people could experience it. If it looks even a little interesting to you, PLEASE try it. It's a beautiful experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Top 10 Best Games I've Ever Played In My 31 years of Life. (Sooo surprised at the polish of this game)Pros:-Story: Amazing-Side Quests: Amazing-Music: Amazing-Combat: PERFECT (Saw a lot of comments saying the combat was too hard?? What?? I played on hardest stars difficulty, 100% hearts, 100% energy, 75% moonstones, beat extra secret boss at the end of game with all no problems...Honestly the combat feels really balanced and smooth for a skilled gamer which is very rare to find in games today)-Timing: Amazing. took me 63 hours to full clear this game. It's funny because I went in not wanting to play for more than 20-30 hours and the game is just that good that I ended up doing all the side quests and collectibles without ever once getting bored or tired, I'm still shocked I enjoyed this game that much.Cons:-None........Well, the secret extra unlockable Boss-Fight for getting 100% hearts and 100% energy at the end of the game doesn't give you anything for beating it, so it was a little bit of a let down... theres a room before the last boss fight of the game that gives you infinite free food and in my opinion this free food vendor should of been behind the secret extra unlockable Boss-Fight room, but hey you can't win them all. I would like to add however the extra boss fight is the best fight in the game and is incredibly rewarding in itself to complete it, Good Luck!!!***This game is more for the completionist skilled gamer even though it still can be thoroughly enjoyed regularly. The reason its more for the completionist skilled gamer is because by taking a little time to farm and do side quests throughout the game you increase health, energy, and can purchase the much needed upgrades so you can continue the game smoothly.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe this game isn't more well known. Amazing story with lots of twists. The gameplay is a wonderful mixture of platforming, combat, and puzzle solving. I actually have pages of notes because some of the puzzles require that to solve them.A few of the fights and platforming sections had me ready to ragequit, but you can always come back later when you are more prepared instead of beating your head against the wall like I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I already played this game back when it was still a flash entry in Newgrounds, and cleared then and found it amazing.I was looking forwards to the sequel for a looong time, checking on the author's blog every once in a while and, even though I was a little bit disheartened that he opted for a remake instead of a sequel, it makes sense. Not everyone plays flash games, even more so now that the app itself was terminated. I knew the rough history line and was not disappointed, much to the contrary, was extremely pleased even though I sort of knew what was coming.There are significant changes, much more things to do, items to hunt and quests to pursue so even for "old timers" I really recommend it, not only as a support for the dev but for a great experience overall.Now, if you want to know about the game, think of it as an old 2D scroller, plataforming zelda-esque RPG. You have items to collect and increase your health and energy bar, you will have tons of different weapons to use in specific situations or against specific enemies and can adapt different ways of gameplay accordingly.Very interesting overall, even though the characters do not interact that much or that heavily, I would say it is a game more focused on combat and puzzles / platforming rather than on its lore which is not super complex nor super time consuming to clear the game.I like it, maybe I would like to see some small alternative endings showing the progress of the quests (if that is not much to ask, which is probably is, even if it is just a small extra on the final credits scenes).
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia Awakening is a truly amazing game. I genuinely don't think I can think of a single issue with the game. The story is quite good, and the gameplay is thoroughly fun, especially the movement. I played the original Flash game Phoenotopia, which I also loved, and would still recommend it if I didn't feel that Awakening was such an improvement. And if Flash was still supported.In short, this game could've been $60 or even $80 and I still would've recommended it, as I feel like it's an all-around better game than most recent AAA titles.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: For me this is an instant favorite.The pixel art is fantastic, kinda minimalistic, but detailed at the same time, just the right sweet spot. The sound design fits the different environments perfectly. The world is huge and full of secrets right from the beginning, e.g. the first dungeon has a second boss to come back for. The  game is quite open and doesn't hold your hand where to go next.Still the game is not without flaws, but nothing game-breaking or that cannot be configured. And the developer listens and improves the game constantly.

_childDocuments_.review: the art style is amazing and gameplay is pretty good for the most part. but, for me at least, the combat system can be a bit infuriating at times and the ending is also a bit mediocre. i also don't like how the stamina system works. you start with a small amount of stamina and through collectibles you find out in the world you get an increase for your stamina to have way more in order to sprint, use gadgets, or attack. but your stamina bar recharges at the same exact rate it does from the beginning of the game throughout the entire game. so it turns into a waiting game for your stamina bar to refill later on in the game. i also don't mind things like new moves/attacks you can use being barred by puzzles or bosses but the health and stamina upgrades are a bit much considering they're not really optional if you want to have a fun time in the game and not get one or two shot later on. you can also really easily get stun-locked later on in the game and there's not much you can do when there's multiple enemies attacking you and you have barely any i frames. i'd give it a 6.8/10. get it if it looks interesting to you but the combat drags the game down a bit
