_childDocuments_.review: A truly endearing, indie gem that evokes the same wide-eyed wonder I felt when playing Super Treasure World/Adventure years ago. A Zelda II inspired metroidvania, Phoenotopia Awakening feels like nothing else I've played in a long time. The level of depth in the world, characters, and story ultimately make up for some half-baked combat in the latter half of the adventure. I would love to see a sequel to this someday but the quality of Phoenotopia alone means I'll be playing the next Cape Cosmic game, whatever it may be.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Summary, would I recommend the gameYes! But, it only feels so complete unfortunately. The story is somewhat compelling, the game contains some snappy events that made me chuckled, but nothing outright blew my mind or made me feel like I was playing something revolutionary. That's a high bar to set, but after seeing so many good indie games, it does feel pretty average. If anything,  I would say this game does well at re-visiting the olden days. It feels more like a GBA game moreso, with all of the rose tinted glasses busted out. Some of its frustrating aspect did not make the game too enjoyable at certain points.What's the good?The story, while containing fairly average writing, does have a good concept! Without spoiling direct story, something clearly unnatural is happening on this world. The game made it obvious what sci-fi themes are present early on, but did decently pace other elements over time. I will say, however, the story does not end too well. Upon further reading, it appears the devs do want to continue an overarching story in another game that will likely be in development for a while... It doesn't fall absolutely flat; however, the ending left me with more questions than answers. If that was a mystery met by a dlc and had a story as trippy as Katana Z, maybe I'd understand it. But this doesn't feel like that type of story. It lands average, with more told through dialogue and some early story exploration intriguing you, but it didn't go far enough.Gameplay:Both ok and occasionally bad (more of the annoying rather than difficult variant). The bat? The melee attack mimicking most modern close combat oriented metroidvanias? Is a toothpick. By the end of the game it is probably the last weapon you should be using to even have a leg up. The game revolving every item around a single stamina bar was not a good idea, especially how any action that depletes it resets the timer to recovering any.This part isn't hard to explain. You Metroidvania. It's as simple as that. It works until it doesn't, as while fighting one enemy is farily good, fighting large enemies or multiple enemies gets bad really quickly. The bosses in this game needed way longer in the oven considering they seemed designed to work against a much faster character type. Getting a no-hit run would feel like luck, if I could put it bluntly... The other stuff:The game does ok on theme. The pixel art does alright, but it's not mind boggling.The music is fairly ok, but some of the mid-game themes you'll probably want to get out of your head after a while. The main theme is a good 5 stars.Dev interaction: I have no rating here. I didn't hear if there's enough story surrounding the game's creation. All I know is that this is technically a remake of an original game that drops its subtitle. It was much more inconclusive. But by the word of how long I heard it would take to make, it seems pretty unfortunate. But they don't sound like a focused dev group. Some of that's just life. I hope they're able to put their best foot forward at it!Conclusion:It's alright.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: What a unique, charming, but difficult little game. With secrets and puzzles galore, it's such a pleasure to find and conquer them. Getting a new skill/item and remembering an area where they might be applicable was always worthwhile. While I initially thought of it as another 2D Zelda clone, I found myself caring for Gail and the supporting cast much more than I ever have with the LoZ. My biggest gripe with it is with the difficulty, and it's a shame because I can't recommend EVERYONE try it unless they're ready to dedicate a significant amount of time to mastering the game mechanics.Not very hopeful that we'll see a sequel, but I do hope we get to see Gail again one day~

_childDocuments_.review: a flawed gem but it's a gem.  one of those games that has a way of really sucking you into exploring its world. _childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia: Awakening is a demanding game. It demands that you fight smart. It demands that you pay attention. And it demands that you pursue optional content, if you want to keep up with its power curve. But if those demands don't turn you away, then you should absolutely play it - it really is something special.Phoenotopia's most-criticized element, by far, is its combat. It's definitely unforgiving, and it punishes reckless aggression with brutal knockback chains. However, it also gives you some interesting tools: light/heavy/aerial melee attacks, a number of ranged weapons for different situations, and some incredibly useful consumables (STAMINA REGEN). The end result is surprisingly strategic - figuring out  to attack is often more important than skillful execution. One last thing to note: completing side content (collecting life gems, finding Ouroboros Scrolls, etc.) will make you much stronger, and thus, make the difficulty more manageable. So do that!Outside of combat, Phoenotopia has a lot to offer. Exploration, light platforming, item-hunting, puzzle solving...and the puzzles, in particular, are great. They're demanding, like everything else - you have to write stuff down, figure out patterns, pay attention to background details. But they're incredibly satisfying to figure out, and I didn't find any of them to be frustrating or overly cryptic.On the one hand, the game's central plot is a little messy. It awkwardly shifts focus at its midpoint, leaves some serious loose ends on the table, and ends kind of abruptly. But Phoenotopia isn't really  that central plot. It's more about exploring the smaller stories of each area (which are consistently great); about interacting with fun, well-written characters; and about discovering more of the world's secrets. The payoff on those fronts is much better - so ultimately, I walked away satisfied.Also, despite the weaknesses of the central narrative, the game has very solid pacing, with some moments of great tension and some long, well-earned breathers. If this element was weaker, the game's back-and-forth transitions between cheerful fantasy and ominous sci-fi would feel abrupt. But instead, they work very well, and the game never exhausts you with too much of the latter.The sprite art is great, especially in motion, and the backgrounds are gorgeous. The music is also lovely: it nails the adventurous mood of a desert town, the serene beauty of a far-flung beach, and the looming danger of an ancient lab. Combined, the effect is enchanting, bringing out the same sense of wonder that the best Zelda games do. I have just one small criticism of the game's art direction: sometimes, I can't tell what's part of the background and what's not. Luckily, this problem is mostly confined to non-combat areas, so it's not a huge deal.Did you know this is actually a remake of a 2014 Flash game? I played that game back in the day, and I thought it was a flawed gem. But Phoenotopia: Awakening fixes every problem I had with the original, while expanding on everything that made it good. It's everything a remake should be, and it's well-deserving of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the bastard child of Salt & Sanctuary + Stardew Valley that I never knew I wanted (yes, the original Phoenotopia came first, but I haven't tried it.)  Phoenotopia: Awakening is a sprawling, imaginative, platformer that strained my combat ability and frequently surprised me with its creativity.  Though it wasn't perfect, it was a good use of $20.- Pretty sizable map that takes a while to explore.- A lot of detail and content in a world that feels very lived in, with extensive side quests.  It's also pretty for pixel art.- The universe merges scifi, post-apocalyptic, and medieval fantasy genres fairly well without taking itself particularly seriously most of the time.- NPC dialogue is solid across the board and warrants a chuckle at times.- There's fishing, and it's optional!  There's cooking, and it's... less optional!- Even basic attacks will throw you across half the screen.  Groups of enemies/bosses will often be able to chain hits or yeet you into hazards with little difficulty, which can get frustrating.- Even though there's a ton of content left after credits, the actual postgame is poorly implemented.  Basically you get sent back to the room before the final boss and the world you walk around isn't any better than when you last left it.    There is apparently a sequel coming out, so this may be alleviated.- No minimap, which makes thorough exploration a little more tedious when you inevitably run around in circles.- Combat is punishing.  Poor timing or putting yourself in a bad situation will get you killed outright.  Bosses are hard.  Most healing can't be done on a whim (unless you choose to enable it in the menu.)- There's a lot of backtracking as you unlock new abilities, pretty par for the course in this kind of game.- Plenty of puzzles, ranging from "move the boxes around" to "find the right way to travel through this entire massive area with minimal use of the keys hidden throughout and one map hidden in the background."- If you want tough platforming, you can find it.  For the most part it's not mandatory.- Money feels precious; the game isn't too generous with it and you'll want to buy food, weapons, even inventory space.If you're looking for a game to be in your top 5 ever list, I don't know this is it.  If you've finished Hollow Knight or Ori and want something else to scratch that explore/save the world/die frequently itch, this will do a good job satisfying that.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: All I can say is that I've been waiting for this game to come to steam for so many years. And it's finally here. Personally, the flash version of this game got me thru some rough times during high school years so it holds a special place in my heart. I don't know what about a pixelated, zelda-inspired 2d platformer, and sometimes rage inducing game that I love so much about, but I do know that it impressed me so much when I first played through it. It was one of the first games where I thought we didn't deserve it for free because it was that good. I'll be honest, when I bought the switch version the difficulty on there was way too much for me. And even Quells himself admitted the beta testers he hired were mostly highly skilled platforming masters so the standard was set a bit too high for comfort for average players like me.I still love the game nevertheless. And I'm happy I can finally give it the monetary support that it deserves and is worth. I guess the only thing that's frustrating about this game is the save points. It doesn't have the feature anymore where you can pay in order to restart from the most current save unlike the flash version so dying is kind of a pain especially when you have some progress in your pockets up until that point. But other than that I love everything that's been enhanced, added, and polished from it's flash powered predecessor. I've been following the dev's blogs for years and I'm glad they timed the release close before the death of flash( rest in peace December of 2020, always remember). I've been recommending this game to anyone whenever the topic came up ever since so long ago, and I'll happily continue to do so.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the original on notdoppler, and with flash games having more or less died off with fragments surviving, it's nice to see games taking it a step further and becoming even more than what people thought they could be. Phoenotopia Awakening takes nostalgia and doses it up with refinement that brings even more life to an older game. Various changes, new mechanics, revised music, and plenty more content all work hand in hand to make this game stand out. There have been a few minor issues with using a controller to aim as opposed to a mouse, but they tend to not really take anything away from gameplay. Been waiting for the game to come out for a long time, and having a blast so far as I see how much more there is to offer now.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I love the premise, I love the genre, it sounds great and it looks pretty. I was so disappointed on so many levels though that I just can't bring myself to keep playing it. No other game I've played tries this hard to waste the player's time. It's all just so tedious.Everything takes forever. Want to sell some items? Go to the menu, equip the item, stand under the machine and use it, wait for an animation, then run and pick up the coins it threw everywhere. You have to do this for every item you want to sell. Almost every system in the game is like this, and it makes everything feel like a chore.The stamina system is so poorly balanced. I spent so much time literally just standing in place waiting for my stamina to slowly regenerate. You start with a pitifully small stamina pool, and when you get more your regen speed stays fixed, so you still end up sitting around waiting just as much. Some of the later tools cost tons of stamina to use, too. Trying to climb a tower with the spear is just tediously slow.The level design further reinforces this trend of making things as slow as possible. The levels in this game don't really wrap back in on themselves. There are a few shortcuts here and there, but by and large you go through the area to the end, then it warps you back to town. That's great, but it's not there when you backtrack for items, so you end up just walking back and forth through the entire area.This is holds true even when it doesn't make logical sense, like at the top of the windmill towers. Despite it regularly allowing you to fall from one screen to another, if you try to jump off the top it just gives you a bit of damage and puts you back up there. You have to enter the tower and walk all the way down. The enemies don't even respawn, so you just trudge back down through the empty tower. Why?Finally there's the controls. I don't understand why interact and accept are the same key bind. If I want to bind it to A on the xbox gamepad, since A is accept in like every game ever, and have jump on A, again like every platformer ever, then I'm constantly talking to people when I'm trying to jump around town. I either have to move jump or accept to something else. Both go against decades of precedent and just feel super awkward.Aside from that, movement feels stiff and clunky. When you dash jump you're on a fixed trajectory, so it's easy to misjudge your distance and have to repeat jumps or entire sections if you fall. When you move in air it doesn't change the direction you face, so it's easy to end up facing the wrong way and miss an attack opening or miss a switch or something. All of this means that I ended up fighting the controls more than the enemies, and you guessed it, that makes everything feel slow.There's a core of a good game here, but some questionable design decisions and some very rough edges just keep it from realizing that potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of a neutral leaning towards negative review. A fun, good-looking, challenging puzzle game brought down by one glaring flaw that you have to deal with throughout the game - the combat. I love challenging combat platformers (and challenging combat games in general - see Sifu, Sekiro, Dead Cells), but the combat in Phoenotopia is incredibly unintuitive and frustrating to the point I have no desire to finish the game even after reaching what I think is the halfway point. The combat feels heavy, there are no iframes, no parrying or blocking, and there are a bunch of odd pauses after completing an action like a jump. Sure you can learn the sequences of bosses and beat them easily enough, but it's just not the same type of challenge. I can see why people like this but I personally find the combat to be a massive turnoff. I even tried pressing through because I really enjoyed the rest of the game, but given combat is a large portion of the game I just couldn't do it anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: good game, but the game itself is annoying in the absolute worst kind of ways, pointless delays for everythingsleeping might be fine but loading a game? dying? get over your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ selfcooking takes forever, controls are janky at points, getting any significant amount of money seems impossible, to the extent that newbie guides recommend not upgrading your stuff. wow. just make a method that can make a decent amount of cash that requires decent effort fishing for 7 gold is super stupid, and crossing the bridge to collect berries is even worse. some enemies not only can attack you through i frames, but stunlock you because of it, fun.a whole hell of a lotta janky ♥♥♥♥.EDIT: the random encounters are so pointless - all you have to do to fix the economy and random encounters is spawn a chest with 10-100 gold located somewhere in the random encounter. that would improve the game by LEAGUES!EDIT 2: Just beat the game, this is a good game worth your time, 100%. The mechanics, story, gameplay - everything is well refined and well thought through. there is a lot of environmental storytelling which i love. The game does have a lot of jank, almost too much to ignore.... almost. it is 100% playable through the jank but there are very distinct times where i don't feel like "I won" moreso that "Jank didn't happen so the game LET me win".I know this isn't the place to do so but i would like to make suggestions to remove some of the jank...Spoilers possible pass this point, beware1. Make random encounters worth something, whether you get a reward for clearing the entire encounter map, or hide a treasure chest with an appropriate amount of rin somewhere.... this would solve the economy and random encounters. Random encounters are useless and i never felt like i had an abundance of money regardless of saving, regardless of money hunting, I did every single optional thing i could, every side quest i found, every temple i went into is 100% complete to my knowledge. I beat the game with 478 rin and i still feel poor. I hunted fish for a couple of hours, I hunted gold dragon scales for about an hour and a half, still couldn't buy everything.2. The recycler seems like the answer to the money problem but it isn't, you would have to sell your food to get money, which in the mind of the player is pointless. sell food to get money to eventually buy food. there are "treasure items" but they are SOOOOO worthless, amberite ore is worth 5 and golem cores are too. neither can be obtained in mass amounts and both take up space. A possible solution could be making any treasure items stack to a high amount, like 99 or something, so picking them up isn't a choice between life and death.3. remove the "waking up" animation from death, it is absolutely infuriating to lose to a boss then have to wait a single second on gail acting like she is above you. might be petty, but i hate this.4. if you are just under the water's surface, up against a vertical wall, and try to jump out towards the wall you get stuck in this stupid cycle of wasting all your energy and doing nothing. I wish there was a slight coyote time after leaving a platform in order to jump right after leaving a platform. this leads to a more strict game which you miss jumps that you feel like you should have made (regardless if you actually should have)7. the sonic spear allows you to create a platform to stand on when it is in a wall, you can have 2 of these spear platforms out. Two. it is possible to throw a spear at the peak of your jump and not be able to get to it. the next spear thrown will remove the one you are currently standing on. forcing you to restart a tower climb, immensely annoying and this is simply solved by allowing 3 spears out at one time. whether it being an upgrade or the default amount, this was one of the most annoying things in the game.8. The crossbow and slingshot are hard to aim consistently during battle, i do not know a solution for this, but i wish they were easier to aim. Any suggestion i could make would have negative aspects to it. Like my initial reaction would be a slight autoaim helper, but that has heavy downsides, i do not know how to fix this problem.9. a minor annoyance i had when fishing for moonstone fish i would often be at the edge of the water, the moonstone would then sink to the bottom of the body of water, unreachable. every other item you get from fish floats, and i understand that moonstones have physics attached to them for some of the physic based moonstone puzzles so of course they sink, but you could have them just automatically collect when obtained from fishing. it's a minor annoyance but could be fixed easily.10. you can grab bombable blocks and try to push, pull, or lift them to no success. at the beginning i thought i might get a strength upgrade but it never happened, why can i grab them? what is the point?11. Cooking kinda sucks, near the end i kinda just forgone cooking because of how long it takes, this has a few mediocre solutions but no perfect solution. I got the frying pan which makes cooking easier but doesnt help the amount of time it takes. Maybe, an answer could be that after cooking the same "recipe" several times it permanently removes an input needed until eventually, if you cooked fish 100 times you can cook it with a single button press. _childDocuments_.review: As a whole, I really enjoyed my time playing this game and it definitely deserves more attention. I'd say the best part of the experience is the atmosphere. The combination of the gorgeous pixel art with the developments in the story and best of all, the soundtrack.I think the combat does get really difficult towards the end teetering between challenging and unfairly difficult, but overall it's still a memorable experience. Story is fairly interesting, though the highlights I would say are the exploration and the soundtrack ngl. In someone else's words, "it fills me with childlike wonder," and that makes it worth it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game with a %44 completion and I hate to say it but I have no desire to ever play this game again. It is so close to being an instant classic for me but it falls flat in so many areas that I don't think I could ever recommend this to any of my friends.-The combat is weak and the worst part. _childDocuments_.review: This is not a metroidvania. It's more of a platform action/adventure with a lot in common with Zelda II, and general 2D games which traverse between action platform/puzzle segments and overworld exploration.And it's a really, really neat game with lots of charm and competence. Some people are complaining about the combat. Meh, it's good for what it wants to do. If you want floaty hack and slash go play Bloodstained. There's upgrades, puzzles, quests, backtracking with powers previously unheld, secrets. This is the kind of game I want from Indies. You don't see many of this ilk with actual content beyond 10+ hours. I'm 20 hours in and don't think I'm near finishing

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give Phoenotopia a negative review based on a purely subjective experience. Objectively, this is a decent game, clearly with a lot of effort, skill, and love put in. The graphics are beautiful, the story is rich, the music is good, some mechanics are interesting (e.g. encounter transition mechanics). There are lots of interesting puzzles, good humor, and charm. And there are dozens upon dozens of hours of content (based on research I've done). Unfortunately, this research is second-hand, since personally I've abandoned this game after 6 hours. Why did I do so? The little things. There are just too many quality-of-life problems that might be endearing to the old school players of 90s RPGs, but are neither common nor really acceptable for a 2021 game. Such as: no in-game map (very unusual for a metroidvania, where backtracking is very common), no quest markers, and no diary or quest journal system. Unless you want to refer to guides/walkthroughts, you need to play this game with a pen and paper, and pay a lot of attention to the text, to remember where to go and what to do. Some puzzles also semi-softlock and require a full game restart to reset the environment, rather than just revisiting the area.The other big issue is the movement and combat mechanics. It's just too slow and clunky. Fighting and dodging is hard (not because of challenging enemies, but because of crude and sluggish controls), the weapons are difficult to use, and the overall pace (both combat and progression-wise) seems just too slow/repetitive. Despite being a beautiful, well-crafted world, it just wasn't fun for me to stay in. Despite getting a lot of the "big picture" things right, the game just has too many small flaws and pain points for my taste. By all means, if you're the patient gamer willing to do whatever it takes to find a solution and overcome obstacles, pick up this game and don't let this review deter you, as you'll get many good hours out of it. For the less determined gamer, or someone more used to modern video game conveniences, you might find this game just too demanding.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: My first impression of this game was very strong.  For the first 10-15 hours, it's a very charming and enjoyable Zelda 2-style metroidvania with nice pixel art, great tunes, and a surprisingly interesting story for the genre.  But as the game stretches on its weaknesses become overwhelming:- The gameplay is just OK.  The controls aren't that tight and there are some odd design choices, like the need to release and then press the sprint button again when landing from a jump.  There's also a Souls-style stamina bar which seems misjudged in a game of this type.  It mostly serves to cause a lot of frustrating waiting around as it refills rather slowly and will even drain when using items for puzzle-solving purposes.  Combat in particular is not a lot of fun.  Gail's weapon has a comically tiny range, she bounces around like a ping-pong ball when hit and can be juggled in extremely annoying fashion.- Save points are haphazardly placed.  Sometimes you will encounter them frequently, sometimes there will be 20 minutes of difficult gameplay challenges between them.  This leads to a lot of annoying repetition, and makes it feel like the game has little respect for the player's time.  Other features add to that feeling, like the bosses that have long dialogues that need to be repeated every time you fight them.- To an even greater extent than I implied above, the game is unbelievably bloated.  It took me 30 hours to see the credits roll and I only achieved 49% completion.  The gameplay is not good enough to sustain this amount of content.  There are so many items and upgrades to collect and they all feel insignificant.  For example, there are 55 health upgrades to find and they each increase your health bar by a tiny amount, no more than the damage done by a single hit from a low level enemy.  There are dozens and dozens of moonstones and other trinkets to find, and which require hours spent traipsing all over the map to find the people who will take them off your hands.  I finished the game with at least half a dozen unique items I simply had no idea what to do with and it didn't seem to matter.  All of this bloat ruins the pacing of the game as well.  Sometimes so long would go between plot developments I would lose track of what was going on.I genuinely think there is the seed of a great game here, but more polish was needed and a huge amount of fat needed to be trimmed.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most charming game I've seen in years. The townsperson dialogue made me laugh out loud. The music is delightful. The art makes me happy. The combat almost feels like a Souls game. Even the world map blew my mind. This game captures a special spirit that I haven't felt since the SNES-PS1 era.Update: It's STILL awesome. The quality of the towns and NPCs and combat and puzzles and balancing has maintained if not improved even into the third area/town. Get this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: The best Metroidvania since Hollow Knight.Great visuals, great music, great puzzles, great overall level design, and quite a lot of inspiration from the best Zelda games. I was absolutely hooked from beginning to end. The biggest surprise for me was the length; this game took me almost as long to complete as La-Mulana 2 at about 56 hours.The combat can be a bit difficult, but if it's too much for you, the developer has added in a difficulty/accessibility option when you start a new game which can also be changed at any time.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like Zelda 2 done right. The adventure is very well paced with tons of secrets and puzzles to discover. The story and characters ooze charm and personality as well. If you're looking for an adventure game, it would be hard to go wrong with this one.The only major problem I encountered while playing was the game's combat mechanics. Combat is very sluggish and unfun. Fortunately, if you take the time to explore the world, there are plenty of hidden weapons, accessories, and combat techniques that trivialize every required fight.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: A metroidvania with some nice puzzles but also some very frustrating mechanics, like having to carry quest items in your very limited invertory for a long time, having to choose between spending collectables on upgrades or fast travel and a boss that steals your healing items and heals himself instead...
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Best game I've played in a long time but the combat with all modifiers on is seriously awful and unfun, with the biggest problem initially being your tiny range combined with hitboxes that are very unforgiving.  Realizing that you can walk through enemies without taking damage definitely helps, but everything needing stamina just isn't good IMO, especially when getting hit just once is so unforgiving due to how you get bounced around. I turned all of that stuff off and the game became much much more enjoyable.  If you don't like the combat initially, just go into the accessibility options in the game menu and turn it all off, there's nothing shameful about doing it and the game definitely doesn't become too easy by doing that, in fact I think it's just about right considering the fact that you can easily spend 40-50+ hours on this and not 100% it.  Is it a Metroidvania?  I guess.  Who cares, the label isn't important, It's just really good.  I play Metroidvanias almost exclusively these days and I loved it.  I've seen complaints suggesting that areas need maps, but I don't really think they do.  There's only one area (with the bugs) that I could have used a map, but even then the individual areas just aren't large or complicated enough for you to need a map to get around.  The puzzles are very good too IMO.  40 hours in and I'm not even done, and I haven't even tried to get "everything", just most things.  Still missing a ton of stuff that I may or may not even get.  I bought this on a whim and don't regret it, best purchase in awhile actually.Updating my review with 55 hours total played:  Love the game even more.  There was a lot more content to get through at the time I wrote this review, which surprised me.  There are a few huge optional areas that were fun and interesting.  The optional boss was also very good, as was the last boss, and the ending was satisfying.  I still only managed to get about 80% of the Moonstones, so there were still more items to collect.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I actually have no problem with the combat, which is what most of the negative reviews are calling out, and checkpoints only healing half your health. So why am I leaving a negative review anyway?-Items don't work how they sensibly should. The slingshot's aim is dependent on your timing and not on aiming the control stick, and the flute's note symbols have no logical connection to the directions you have to press.-Aerial enemies are incredibly hard to hit, because of the aforementioned problem with the slingshot, and dodge even by the standards of aerial enemies in games in general.-Buying everything requires absurd amounts of money farming.-The inventory space is far too small even maxed out.-And the biggie: the cooking minigame (and bear with me here). It's bad enough that you have to reignite campfires every time you restart the game, but for the hardest levels of the minigame you can't miss at all. That was unacceptable even back in 1979 and certainly is now.

The lack of a mini map and questbook just makes it more tedious and less fun.  I've written less stuff down for a JRPG on PS1.  As a completionist who always gets 100 percent, I didn't feel bad putting an end to my journey.  Get it on sale if you really want to.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic game.Took me about 50 hours to 100% it, so much content, and I never felt bored once.The fact that they're only charging 17,99€ for it is in my opinion almost criminal.One of the best metroidvanias I've ever played, definitely on the same level as Hollow Knight and other well-known indie metroidvanias (in my opinion).9/10, would absolutely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: A real hidden gem metroidvania on Steam. I think the worst thing going for it is the title since I still cant spell Phoenotopia without googling it first. I heard it didn't sell too well at launch which is a shame as the developer deserves some success. I figure one more positive review couldn't hurt. _childDocuments_.review: Had played original Phoenotopia on NG years ago, it'd became one of my favorite games, so I was thrilled to know there's gonna be a remake and bought it as soon as it released. Some might criticize about the controlling, yeah, imaging how I felt beating original Phoenotopia with keyboard only, every time fighting bosses made me wanna kill myself. Now we got controller, thou some bad keys binding at first, fortunately dev has fixed it in the new update.Exploration is the best part why I love this game, every time re-visiting a place I might find something haven't found before, so I won't say it's grinding, but quite enjoyable. ( and re-visiting is time-consuming, yes.) Most puzzles aren't too hard, therefore not very challenging, but hey, we already waste  a lot of time running around, moderate puzzles are good enough. Combat is as horrible as original Phoenotopia, even with controller, but since my love is about exploring and puzzles, I can live with that.Overall I like this game, brings back good memory and fun to play. Surely needs some more tweaking, like maps or easier way to cook or combat system, etc. Could be better, but metroidvania or not, if you love the good old exploring little flash games, you will love it, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I love metroidvanias, based on the original Metroid and Castlevania series.  This game exemplifies the characteristics of the genre and creates an aesthetically pleasing and enjoyable gaming experience.  The quality of visuals and audio is outstanding and adds an extra level of depth to the game.  The level of secrets and optional side quests is tremendous, I'm about 17.5 hours in so far and I have about 35% of the total game completed.  It is by no means an easy game to play, when you begin the game, combat can be tricky due to your lack of health, stamina, and good equipment, which can make it slightly frustrating, but as you progress it gets much more fun.  If you love the genre, and even more so if you want an amazing game to play, this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing gem of a game that has a lot of relatable gameplay elements to Cave Story and Hollow Knight notably. -Immersive world with a large and bright cast of different characters and backgrounds that you can get invested in. The dialogue for even pointless NPCs is often witty and full of life-A storyline that by itself isn't super innovative or original but definitely kept me invested and wanting to know more -Well-balanced combat system where your character has visible flaws that you need to work around and find your own solutions for. It's not as enjoyable/flows as well as Hollow Knight combat but the balance between your melee and ranged options and their strengths and weaknesses helps make the combat refreshing and relatively unique to the game-Massive amounts of sidequest content from exploring. Easily 3/4 of the game is optional but worth doing to help your character strength through the main story quest. Almost any venture I did trying to explore hidden nooks and crannies or unique NPC interactions rewarded me for it in some way. -Relatively intuitive puzzles that were just the right level of challenging but hardly ever unfair and are everywhere-Gorgeous soundtrack with a good, small focused mix of notably piano, flute, and digital sounds where they were appropriate. The sound design too in terms of sound effects were generally immersive for the feeling of the game and hardly intrusive.-The pixel-graphic aesthetic with vivid colors looks great and is animated in a very pleasing way
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: !!If you struggle with the combat, change the Accessibility Options. In particular, turn on 'regular attacks don't drain energy' and 'energy starts recharging faster after use'. This will make the combat more like other games. I've played almost every major metroidvania. This game just blows everything out of the water. The environments have a ton of detail and personality and interesting things happening. The NPCs have stuff goin on and they're fun to talk to. It's all well paced, looks amazing, and it's very charming and funny. The only metroidvanias on the same level are Environmental Station Alpha and Hollow Knight. In my opinion, of course. The combat is excellent, but it's different and really hard. It gets easier when you realize that enemies don't hurt you just by touching you. Don't be scared to drop the difficulty. It's fun to play on the easiest level and just enjoy the story. It reminds me of Spiritfarer. It's got some vibes from Stardew Valley and Earthbound too. But the biggest influence is Zelda. Just great vibes all around. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: More than worth your time and money if you like exploration-heavy action platformers. You could call it a metroidvania as it has progression based on items/abilities that give you access to new places, but that would be somewhat misleading because it doesn't have a map. Rather it has numerous smaller areas of all sizes connected by an overworld. In this way it's directly inspired by Zelda 2: Adventure of Link. The inclusion of a flute you use to play songs for various purposes is another obvious Zelda influence, and should be appealing to fans of those games. Some of the dungeons are conventionally designed, requiring navigation like the dungeons in Zelda 2 or normal metroidvania maps, while others work a little differently. There's a great variety in the environments and puzzles. And if you like collectibles, there's a ridiculous amount of items of varying degrees of secrecy. At the time of posting this review, I'm fairly close to the end of the game and have found a little over 2/3 of the health/stamina upgrades and the moonstones used for other types of upgrades. I've backtracked quite a lot, talked to every NPC, and found all kinds of stuff, but there are still a handful of important sidequests that are leaving me absolutely stumped. Maybe this is a good thing to you, maybe not, but it will scratch that itch for finding secrets on top of having an above average amount of content.The setting and story is very interesting, and relatively rare in gaming. If you think it looks generic, or childish, don't be fooled. It gets crazier the further you go. It has to be said that the music is outstanding.However, if there's one thing that truly sets this game apart it's the tremendous amount of heart and soul in the world and the characters in it. NPCs interactions are funny, charming, and relatable. Apparently it has a ~100,000 word script. Evidently it was made with a lot of love and depth of humanity.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia Awakening ultimately is a charming game that suffers from some very serious problems relating to the combat and antagonist. Its worth your time, but it isn't for everyone.The world and characters for this game are just charming. There isn't much more to say, I enjoyed the one-off villains, the Supporting characters are likable, and the questlines are interesting and unique. Atmosphere is certainly down with the towns and Dungeons. However, there are a lot of filler characters. I honestly could not tell you the names of most of the Bandit leaders, other than the one you go to in order to get some upgrades, despite them all having distinct personalities and appearances.  The best parts of the game is definitely exploring new areas, Gaining access to more and more of the area as you solve puzzles and talk to characters. Its just a treat to put the pieces together, and while it is annoying on a second playthrough to have to retrace your steps exactly, the first playthrough is wonderful. It also ties into the worldbuilding, as the two go hand in hand. The combat is less than desirable. Its not bad, but its not good. By the end of the game you can demolish any enemy with the right upgrades, so combat isn't necessarily difficult if you know where to look for upgrades (With the exception of the Secret boss, which you need all health and stamina upgrades to fight, and is great). The problem is just that the Stamina mechanic is poorly implemented. Alternate weapons (Which are your main damage dealers against endgame bosses) devour stamina like there is no tomorrow, and it takes an eternity to come back, and using anything during the recharge causes it to stop, and since there is a delay between using a weapon and stamina coming back. Stamina recharges at the exact same rate at the end of the game, as it does at the beginning. This leads to a lot of waiting, unless you constantly stock up on an item that drastically speeds up stamina regeneration for 2 minutes. Its not hard, its just annoying As I've said earlier, the game isn't very hard towards the end, when you have all the games collectables at your disposal. The hardest bosses (Excluding the Endgame Superboss which is intentional) for me weren't the last ones, but instead the 3rd (Great Sand drake) and 5th (Katash). Because these were both punishing bosses situated a long way from towns, meaning that upgrades weren't readily available, so I just had to ram my head against them until I got good enough to beat them at my current power level. I played the entire game without any of the Combat modifiers that are supposed to make the game easier, and the difficulty felt spikey. The 1st, 2nd, 4th, and everything past the 6th just felt easy (Once again excluding the endgame superboss). My only real complaint with the main story is its lack of a substantial main antagonist. The closest thing the game has is Katash, the leader of the Alien forces searching for the same weapon that the player. And he shows up twice (3 times if you count a brief appearance of his shadow through a window), one for each of his boss fights. And even he is subservient to an Unseen "Master" who is hinted through statues and lore text to be the main villain, but is never seen. So the Villains fall into the category of "Vaguely threatening presence that vaguely does bad things"TL;DR: Good story, but lacks a strong antagonist. Combat has a poorly implemented stamina mechanic and difficulty is spikey. Overall, Make sure to search the overworld and towns for upgrades before you go to any dungeon, and don't be afraid to use the accessibility options. Don't play it for the combat, play it for the exploration and characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game with nothing but improvements compared to the flash version that came out years ago. Those who criticize the game by saying how the range and choice of weapons are limited, how it doesn't have a list of objectives or a map or how the game is unfair or punishing in general aren't taking into consideration how these are all deliberate design choices made for a certain playstyle and atmosphere. Maybe it's because you're too used to being handheld and coddled by modern popular games and the only reason you play them is for gratification. This game is an instant classic and the devs deserve every support they get. Buy this game and recommend it to everyone you can.

_childDocuments_.review: Methinks this game is underplayed!  I was checking up on possible upcoming game updates and I read Phoenotopia's developer blog.  It seems that there won't likely be any further major developments or sequels, primarily because there haven't been enough sales to do much beyond keep the lights on over there.  Well, this is a travesty...I say TRAVESTY, sir/ma'am/mx!  So here I am, come to extol the virtues of this game and hopefully help to better reward its creators for their endeavor!!WARNING!  Very minor spoilers...teeny tiny, really...hardly worth mentioning.VISUALS: Charming, gorgeous art style.  Its quite colorful, so if you demand moody, limited color palettes and pixel art that is super abstract or realistic, this might not be for you.  This is pretty cartoon/anime, but I think it's well done, especially considering how far it's come from its earlier iteration.  And yeah, it's super cute.  Get over it.  Don't be that machismo that don't do 'cute'.  Make room for a wee bit of cute in your digital diet.MUSIC:  Solid, catchy, front-and-center, energetic melodies.  I mean, part of the game's mechanics kind of rely on memorable melodies, so you will likely be occasionally humming these as you go about your day after a play session.  There are also a few pieces that go a long way to provide great ambiance as well.  I really appreciated the mysterious and somber, even lamentable tones lent to the early game temple, especially once I leaned a little bit about its former occupants.  It really is rare when a piece of music makes you stop moving and ponder the fate of a people.  My only gripe is I that I found myself yearning for a bit more subtle and subdued ambient stuff to counterbalance the bright and bouncy stuff.COMBAT:  Controversial, considering some other folks' appraisal of the system, but I like it and I have it on hard mode.  Mind you, you have to practice (God forbid) to get super accurate and efficient with combat and not get your apples handed to you, but I enjoyed the challenge of this particular blend of combat mechanics.  I also liked that so many weapons have a useful utilitarian purpose essential to the game's platforming element (more on that later).  Combat progression is simple and coincides well with story progression.  You can put a little extra time and effort gearing up to get ahead of the curve if you like, or you can often wade in with sub-optimal gear and still survive if you are patient and skillful enough.  The movement mechanics feel good and the things like dash, roll and special attacks flesh things out.  Energy management is critical, which may annoy some, but to me it just serves as an incentive to explore and grab energy upgrades.STORY:  I have yet to finish the game completely, but I am nearing the end and I've liked it so far.  One thing I am a sucker for is a world littered with remnants of fallen civilizations.  If you like that sort of thing, this game should scratch that itch.  I usually dislike the cool-trumps-logic medieval fantasy/sci-fi tech mashups (looking at you, Final Sci-Fantasy), but in my opinion, Phoenotopia makes it quite palatable and gives you a decent logical reason for the coexistence of the two elements. I also think the game strikes a good balance between making the protagonist important, but also sharing the spotlight with other key players and even the people she knows and cares about that can't come on the adventure with her.  I find myself caring about the concerns and fates of various NPC's.  As for the dialogue, it definitely slants toward lighthearted humor, but it does a fine job of it.   Almost everyone has some witty or silly thing to say as a reward for talking to them and those beady eyes everyone has just make it all the more humorous to me.  Plenty of folks drop snippets of history and lore or helpful hints to mill over.  If you are a "repeatedly check in on npc's and past locations so I don't miss anything" kind of player, like me, I pity you for you have a lot of people to talk to and a lot of dialogue to go over.  But you know, that's how it goes.  Its one of those things some of us both love and hate about RPGs; It can be genuinely rewarding to be thorough and check back with folks every now and again, but half of those NPCs gots nothin' new to say.PLATFORMER ELEMENTS:  This game will have you running and jumping every which way, using your dexterity, brains and items to solve puzzles or traverse through the game world in general.  The puzzles certainly aren't the hardest brain-melting, callus-bursting mind teasers I've ever encountered, but some of them can be quite tricky and clever.  Still, nothing unfair.  If you wan't your character fully tricked-out by end game, you're going to have to deal with the cleverest and trickiest of them. PROGRESSION:  This game is built around progression gates.  You find an item, solve a puzzle or do someone a solid and your world opens up a bit.  You can go more places, do more things, survive new challenges and occasionally return to old haunts.  Tis a pretty common mechanic (if you say 'Metroidvania' out loud while you read this I will slap you through your screen).  What I personally love about this game is you can fudge things a little.  There are more than 1 or even 2 ways to solve some puzzles.  There are unusual (and probably unintended) ways you can use items and push/float/throw/stack things around to get the results you want.  There are a few progression steps I have been able to skip because I was a clever boy and figured out how to get to where I wasn't s'posed to get.  Luckily this didn't result in any game-breaking (a testament to good programming, I'll venture), but I did encounter one odd inventory/menu bug because of it.  Still, the gameplay rewards and sense of accomplishment far outweighed one little bug and a crap-ton of patience.  Speaking of patience...EXPLORATION AND SECRETS:  I love a game that rewards you for poking around, keeping a sharp eye out and checking back every once in a while.  There are LOADS of secrets to discover and many totally optional areas you can only enter by returning to places you've been before.  This adds depth to gameplay and, sometimes, to lore as well.INTERFACE:  The HUD looks good is pretty simple to understand, but the menus could stand a bit of polish, especially with respect to navigation.  Something to help keep track of quests might be nice too, but given the fairly linear style of the game, it isn't strictly necessary unless you demand to have your hand held.  Just pay attention to what people have to say and keep a notepad handy for when someone mentions something intriguing or important and you'll be fine.ALL IN ALL:  What I really appreciate with Phoenotopia is its distinctive blend of flavors.  None of its components are new or done in an earth-shatteringly brilliant way, but it is a solid blend.  I get the feel that this is a passion project that has been in development for a long time,  done by folks who are paying homage to some great games by blending their key elements into a coherent, competent and FUN game.PRICE:  As the cinemas in your area open back up, buy a movie ticket and grab a soda and a popcorn while you're at it.  You will hopefully be entertained for 1.5-4 hours, depending on the movie.  You will likely have spent more money on that than you will on this game.  If Phoenotopia Awakening seems, by this review, akin to your tastes, you will likely be entertained by this game for much longer.  I cannot yet vouch for the game's conclusion and haven't read any spoiler reviews, so I am in no position yet to promise a rewarding conclusion, but $20 buckos ain't much to ask by my measure.  And if it goes on sale?....pshhhhhh!  Give it a whirl.  Hell, throw that fliff around and grab a copy for a like-minded friend you can flex on for being an inferior energy gem hunter!    Arbitrary numerative assessment score: 7.5/10...I guess.  Just buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good! It really hits the nostalgia feels. If you like metroidvania type games I definitely recommend it! It's a shame this game isn't reaching to more people that would enjoy it. Retro yet beautiful, and the soundtrack is phenomenal. It's a little bit of 8 bit, but also mixes in modern sounds, some tracks are very beautiful, such as Ava's Lullaby and Wheat Road. If you like Hollow Knight and Celeste, why not give it a try? The devs put their heart and soul into making this game so it's hard to see such effort and talent go unnoticed.However, it is inspired by retro games, so therefore it does try to bring back the difficulty of them. It is a very challenging game at times. And I consider myself a pretty casual gamer, considering I don't like to get into the competitive scene or 100% everything but for some reason this game kept pulling back in even when it frustrated me. I think while the devs do intend for a challenging experience, I think they should add more difficulty options to appeal to more players. We do have a fair bit of accessibility options but some still might find it too difficult. Maybe even add checkpoints. While I understand it's trying to emulate that feeling you get when one mistake could cost you all that progress like Castlevania and Metroid did, we are not in that era anymore... newer players don't keep at it if they lose their progress. Back then, there weren't many games, we didn't have a choice but to keep playing since there wasn't much else to do. Now with so many other games, if a player gets frustrated, they might move on. I think adding checkpoints and lowering enemy damage for the easiest game mode could really help this game succeed in sales. I want this game to succeed. It might not be how you intended for the game to be enjoyed, but getting more players interested never hurts!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: You get punished for getting punished. This is a more bitter negative review since I like the game and can recognize the love and effort to put into it. I particularly appreciate the life put into the characters and the time it takes to read their dialogue and learn about the life of each region. However the amount of time you spend enjoying the story you spend twice or three times as much time getting tossed around like a ping pong ball. Basically if you get hit, you get sent flying/ bounce off walls/ bounce off the floors which will inevitably result you getting hit again. Of course if you get hit again you get launched again and the story continues. Getting hit also doesn't have invincibility frames so any multi-hits will all land and nuke your health. Basically this game is brutal and unforgiving when it comes to making mistakes. Can I live with that? Sure, but it's definitely frustrating. What I can't live with is the fact that there are multiple rooms set up to take advantage of this. While trying not to reveal too much, I'll just say there are a bunch of puzzle rooms designed with this ping pong mechanic in mind; meaning that if you get hit once you have to start over from the beginning while also taking a bunch of hits by getting tossed around. In terms of the other aspects, combat felt a little clunky or lacking and some boss fights didn't feel that engaging. I honestly do love the story and the character this game has. Lots of cute moments, interesting character interactions, some comedy mixed in. The artwork is nice and the environments are diverse and well made. Just taking time to enjoy the characters sometimes makes me forget the atrocious battle mechanics. But I will always be reminded when I move onto the next section. TLDR: Game is a lot more brutal and punishing than I expected. I would be fine with that if it wasn't abused the same way so often instead of making a new design or mechanic. Frustration with this just barely exceeds my appreciation for the artwork and story writing.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I just closed the game because I lost 50 min of progress because there are almost no save points in the castle. Don't mind me, I can recover my progress later. I lost 50 minutes of playtime, I can use a bit more of my time to give some feedback. Hope the developer reads this and get a better understanding of why the combat mechanics made people (me included) so upset.It is a nice game storywise, has a lot of mechanics for crafting/cooking which normally aren't explored by most platformers. There is no map for tracking your current position in an area, but it doesn't affect gameplay that much. Puzzle solving is a plus. No option for petting sheeps and chickens.The main problem of the game is the combat mechanic (there are also fewer save points than necessary in the castle, but lets talk about what bothered me the most - I think that for the advancing of this story, combat shouldn't even exist). You can check on most negative reviews that the game is kind of unforgiving. Well, I play tons of metroidvania games, and what bothered me the most on this game is how different (in a bad way) the character respond from a tipical metroidvania character. There is no problem in utilizing the mechanics that are nicely done on other games, right? No reason to reinvent the wheel, and to fail in the process.You have either a short range melee attack or a ranged attack that requires precisely timed shots (which can be deflected by enemy fire). That includes the following projectiles: stones, javelins or bombs. Short range for melee attack is lame when you have no dodge mechanic, and not all enemies get stunned when attacked.When you get hit, you have no invulnerability frames. That means you can be hit multiple times until you react the ground for Ukemi. I am ok with being knocked back (hello curse of the moon), but being on a receiving end of a combo is not ok. 2D platformers REQUIRE invulnerability frames after being hit. Even Cuphead (which is known for being unforgiving) has it.Maybe I didn't pay enough attention to tutorial and stuff, but the command normal down+L2 was never presented to me, and it helped quite a lot to dodge (USE RIGHT AT THE LAST MOMENT POSSIBLE TO PREVENT ENEMY AUTOCORRECT). It could be binded on R2 instead of a command normal though, I am currently using R2 only for teabagging.Once midair, you can't change the direction the character is facing. Therefore, if you need to intercept any projectile or hit an enemy, you have to wait until you reach the ground.Enemies have auto correction on their attacks. If they are charging an attack and you go to their back, they follow you instantly (why is it charged if the enemy can change its direction midway?). Projectiles throw by enemies also ignore platforms (but not boxes).The basic air melee attack has longer starter time that the ground melee attack (which most metroidvania games doesn't have - this is the reason why jumping and attack midair feels much more confortable than ground ones on games like Momodora, Hollow Knight or Bloodstained). There are some bosses that require the player to hit an basic air melee attack, and the feeling of having a higher startup on the air is awful. The air attack is just too slow to work.It also seems that grinding is required if you want to get better armour and weapon. The gold you earn following the main quest isn't near enough to get your upgrades.I am still playing the game, this list might increase.I have no hope the developers will ever fix these issues, but if they do, I will be more than obliged to recommend this game.Edit: I've completed the game after 28h for 32% game completion. Most of the money I got in the game was spent on food in order to survive the bosses, since in some cases it is better to just facetank everything to rush the boss ASAP. No reason for learning the boss mechanics, because there is none.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start with the pros. In my 3 hours with this game, I thought the art and music were absolutely phenomenal. I particularly loved the boss theme that played at the end of the first dungeon. I felt the first dungeon was decently paced, and the end boss wasn't too difficult or too easy.After this point, I started to see more of the game's shortcomings. The segment that takes place immediately after the first dungeon, without spoiling too much for any that are undeterred, requires you to travel to the next town and do, frankly, far too much busy work. It felt like the pacing of the plot fell to a crawl at this point, and I started to lose interest. My progression was gated behind a series of fetch quests and other busy work before I could move on. Every time I thought I was making progress, the game would find another reason to halt my progress.After an hour or so of fairly boring busy work, I finally had the maguffin that I needed to be able to progress, so onward I went. On my way, I got caught by a random encounter with some brand new enemies I've never seen before which killed me in seconds before I could figure out how to combat them. Frustrating, but alright.Respawn back in town and turns out I hadn't saved in a while and got set back by about 30 minutes. 30 minutes of boring busy work that I have to do again.Should I have been saving more often? Yeah, probably. Arguably its my fault. But it just made me so frustrated that I quietly closed the game. I have no desire to repeat everything I just went through.Am I salty? Maybe. But nice pixel art and great music alone do not a good game make. In 3 hours I was unable to get invested enough to be willing to repeat some tedious tasks I had already completed. I can see that a lot of love and polish was put into the game, and maybe some day I'll give it another shot.In summary, Pros:-Great art style-Phenomenal soundtrack-Decent puzzlesCons:-Pacing is all over the place-Combat can be a bit frustrating because of how touchy it is-Story progression gated behind money. If you don't have money for some mandatory story items, you are forced to grind-Random encounters are frustrating and tedious to deal with for little reward-Movement is okay, but sprinting doesn't feel great with the stamina meter, especially in town. Sprint-leap forces you to jump a set distance, can't adjust trajectory5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Summery: This game excels in,Metroidvania explorationPuzzlesWorld buildingDialogueArt and animationFull Review:A truly great metroidvania style game that excels in so many aspects. The mix of 2D side-scrolling maps that are connected by larger overhead maps gives a lot of freedom of exploration. The level design for each area is very well done both mechanically and thematically. There is an abundance of things to find as well as secret areas sometimes even within other secret areas. And like a true metroidvania, your first time in an area likely won't be your last as you find more ways to explore and platform.As you gain more key items that let you explore, the more puzzles will open up to you to solve. You'll encounter many within dungeons and required areas but those are only a fraction of that amount of puzzles that game offers. Some come in the form of environmental puzzles, some are platforming, others are simple minigames.But the world itself is actually one of the strongest points the game has. It is, again, exploration but instead of power-up and items, you're learning more and more of the lore. I would say you're heavily missing out if you're not talking to each NPC and seeing everything they have to say as the dialogue is extremely strong in this game (some of the strongest I've seen in any games recently). It's witty, charming, funny, and even thought provoking at times.And as you can already see from the preview images, the game has a very pleasant pixel art style. While, art styles are subjective, I personally really like how the games looks and even has a surprising amount of frames in the animation for a pixel graphics game making everything look very smooth.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a metroidvania labor of love that provides such a unique and full experience that I don't think you'll be able to find anywhere else. The worldbuilding and aesthetics of the game are charming and memorable, the gameplay combines platforming and exploration with puzzles and secrets beautifully, and the combat system takes some getting used to but it has an incredible amount of creative expression and depth later on. The challenge only adds to the experience, making you really feel as though you are putting forth effort to succeed, which pairs incredibly well with the sort of post-apocalyptic setting.Every nook and cranny of this game has something interesting and potentially significant to see. I remember from the very moment that I stepped out from the first area, I was enamored by the scope of it and intrigued by the possible areas you could go to. There are secrets to find immediately when you start it up, and every one of them is rewarding once you uncover it. All the secrets barred by puzzles are creative and do a great job of teasing your brain, and the melodic aspect of it was something I felt was unique and satisfying (even when compared to the melodic puzzles from games like Ocarina of Time).If you can get past the initial shock of the way movement and combat feels, and really get to know how Gail moves, what you have here is a lengthy and truly fulfilling experience. It nails the core pieces of a great game while giving each part a unique spin (story, gameplay, aesthetics, content), and every single hour you put into the game feels just as fresh as the first. This game is absolutely worth your time yet is remarkably obscure, so if you read this review all the way to this point, you should get it! Overall 9/10, fantastic diamond in the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals are charming and the soundtrack is very nice. Puzzles were fun, although some were... challenging.But at the end of the day this is a video game, a platformer with combat and RPG elements, and to me it fails to mesh everything together in a pleasant way.Take the dash/run mechanic for example. In most other platformers you have a "hold button to run" a la SMBros, or "tap button to dash" a la MMX. This game combines both: you hit a button to dash, but then you have to hold it to continue running. This doesn't sound so bad until you find yourself in the heat of battle and suddenly your character dashes headfirst *into* the enemy instead of away from them. This was much less of a problem in MMX because in those games you could animation cancel your dash by letting go of the button and just hit the opposite direction on the d-pad. You can't do that here, as there is very little in the way of animation cancelling. Shot your crossbow? Wait until animation completes before you can jump or run, lol. There's also the very laggy aerial melee attack animation (as in, the time between you pressing the button to attack and the character actually swinging their weapon), the need to re-press the dash/run button after every jump, and the fact that they actually mapped the "aim crossbow" button to the dash button (at least on KB, which I am using because I have no good controller). Also, the melee attack range in this game is a joke; apparently you get a decent melee weapon later, but I didn't even get to that point before getting fed up with the awful controls. The end result is a platformer with unresponsive controls, and it really takes away from my enjoyment of the game when half the time I'm fighting the controls on top of trying to fight enemies.And before I forget: it's 2021, I thought we were all past the water = death trope platformers used to have. I mean, I'm a *bad* swimmer, but even I wouldn't flail around like a moron every time I get into water higher than my waist.TLDR: Great visuals and soundtrack, fun puzzles, but unresponsive controls and questionable design choices sucked a lot of the fun out of the game for me. In the end I uninstalled the game without getting past the second world area (desert), that's how much I was put off by the stupid controls. Very disappointed in this purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/5. A masterwork RPG. Worth full price.Phoenotopia is big on exploration, lore, characters, puzzles and secrets, with simple yet engaging combat system. The world and its puzzles & secrets are laid out expertly. Its lore and visuals are consistent. The music is great. Everything is just perfect.There is no quest menu. You must engage with the world and remember people, names, places and events to progress in the main story, and even more so for secret unlocks. As a vague example, you'd have to talk to a lot of people around town, who will give you nuggets of information that give you the general state of things. Guided by your own curiosity, you will use this information to find secrets and solve puzzles as you inch toward your goal, which often conveniently ties into the main story.Combat is simple, but has depth due to the way you interact with enemies. Projectiles can be destroyed by hitting them. Enemies are not immune to environmental hazards. Enemies will perform certain actions, not at random, but depending on how healthy it is, what you are currently dong or where you currently are. Enemies aren't just damage soaks. They flinch and have knockback. Your attacks have weight. The gameplay begs you to outsmart the opponent. Enemies don't just touch you to damage you, they all have attacks that you can see and dodge. It just works.The economy in this game is expertly crafted as well. They have a food and cooking system, that is actually VITAL. Inventory space is short, so you have to decide what you hold, use and discard. Eating is nuanced in an interesting way. Heavier foods heal for a lot, but take literal mid-combat seconds to consume, leaving you open while you try to heal. However, liquid foods, which are rarer to come by or harder to craft, can be consumed quickly, so they are better for combat, for example. Money is similar: it is scarce, making spending money a decision to weigh carefully. Do you want extra inventory slots or do you want that new weapon? Do I really want to spend money on this shady NPC who 'claims' to have useful information? You have to actually think about these situations! In most games, the economy is so bloated that you can throw money where-ever and it wouldn't even matter.This game challenging and makes you think.All that being said, difficulty may be a concern. If you're not one to pay attention or maybe you just forgot some key information, the lack of a quest menu may become a nuisance. Without the right leads in mind, you can easily get stuck, not knowing what to do, where to go, or how to progress, if you don't pay attention. Also, some combat scenarios can be very challenging. Keep in mind that there are a variety of perks you can enable to make the gameplay more accessible at any time. Settings, such as getting invicibility frames and having more stamina (you need stamina to attack or use abilities). ---Overall, I love this game. Definitely my favorite RPG to date. I've been a fan of the game since it was a Flash game on Armor Games. Since Flash died, this remaster is such a welcomed release. If you've played that version, note that this game is that, but with more features and new or reworked content, on top of the graphics update.Also, its not a "metroidvania". Maybe in a very loose term... but do note It takes way more from Zelda than it does from Metroid or Castlevania. Phoenotopia is an open world, 2D action RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: I first found Phoenotopia on the Newgrounds page and fell in love with it years ago. It was a game that I kept coming back to and even made a Newgrounds account for so I could get all the achievements. When it was announced that there would be a sequel to it, I knew I would happily pay full price when it was released. It was so good that I wanted to support the creator.Phoenotopia Awakening expands on its predecessor and offers a lot more gameplay and story. Even having played the first game multiple times, I never got bored playing this one.The game itself reminds me a lot of Legend of Zelda. It's fun and suits a casual player like me. I still haven't finished the game as life got busy, but I will absolutely go back to 100% it later.The art is so cute. The soundtrack is darling. The story and world aren't super original, yet it feels fresh and incorporates twists and new content to a story we've seen before. It's similar to the different games in the Legend of Zelda series that build on the same basic plot points. The controls take a little getting used to. I'll admit that I recall the original Phoenotopia's controls were more more manageable because they were simpler, but I think the new controls aren't terribly taxing; they just need some getting used to. It evolved along with the game and its platforms. I imagine it's easier if you have a controller, but I did not.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, but it is NOT a metroidvania. It's more of a Zelda-like platformer, insofar as you frequently come across areas you can't access yet, and you need to remember to come back once you've gotten some new item or another. But it's quite linear, at least in the first 6 hours of the game.The game is really pretty, the dialogue and story are fun, the music is great, and once you get used to the movement and combat (it felt extremely awkward at first but after a few hours I can dig it) you'll be good to go.That being said, a dungeon minimap would be hugely appreciated, and maybe a little less grinding for cash to be able to get weapon and armor upgrades. I'd much rather have been able to find them in the main dungeons or by doing side quests rather than just having them all available for purchase, if I ran around farming enough.Edit: So yeah this game should have the Metroidvania tag removed and the Puzzle tag added in. So many puzzles. Are they good puzzles? Yeah. But... I'm not the world's biggest puzzle fan. If you aren't either, maybe avoid this to be honest. If you are, you might well like that aspect of the game! I'm gonna soldier through since this game has a lot of good stuff going for it but I honestly don't think I'd have bought it knowing then what I know now.
