_childDocuments_.review: This game is good not great.Game looks good and has a good soundtrack. You can tell that a lot of care was put into the world. I really enjoy the platforming and puzzle aspect to this game. A lot of the puzzles are really clever and fun to try and decipher. The biggest issue for me is the combat (I played on 4 stars until after the castle). There just isn't enough precision to do a lot of things the game is asking from you on the higher combat difficulties. Turning the character around is such a battle and sprinting is such a huge commitment. When there are 1-2 mobs on the screen it generally works fine, but as soon as more enemies come it turns into a huge cluster. Moves have too much self stun to really avoid a lot of attacks coming from different directions. Damage repeatedly comes in chunks equaling 30% of your health pool due to lack of i-frames and enormous recoil. Game was much more enjoyable when I just turned all the combat perks on.A few minor annoyances are the controls and the rarity of money. I get confused trying to remember what buttons to press to do certain actions. Money seems to be extremely hard to come by and a lot of the side quests require large amounts of it (plus buying gear upgrades).Overall, solid game. Definitely recommend checking it out if you like side scrollers.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fantastic. Its a  bit like Zelda 2 in its style but also its got some really good flare of its owntheres a lot of enphasis on puzzle solving and exploration and by that i mean theres lots of stuff to explore thats very fun to explore. The first dungeon is a good example you go in the first time, you beat  the boss, get the thing and notice that theres more beyond the boss arena like more stuff to get afterweards. All throughout the dungeon there are things that you cant get past at that point in the game and you arent required to come back to the dungeon later at all but if you do youll find some more treasure, harder varitions of the types of puzzles you solved your first time around and at the end youll find another boss and some... interesting loot. The loot is actually worth a lot more lore wise than as a "tangible rewards" (though you do get a good reward later by giving it to someone).Also, that last boss fight at the very very end of the first dungeon? Entirely skippable if you have the right tool by that point.This brings me into the other thing i loved about this game. the progression in terms of its exploration is actually not that strictly to what you have on you. Theres lots you "cant get to" that you actually can if you use your tools in a tricky (and a bit convoluted) way which the game never tells you and that I just figured it out on my own and that felt really great!It goes both ways too. you can get to certain places earlier both by getting enough of a certain collectible early enough in the game or by exploting your tools in clever ways and actually if you have other certain tools by the time you tackle some exploration segments you can use those to both skip puzzles and or solve them differently (more than once i actually just used the tools in a way to solve the puzzle in an entirely different and easier way that just felt right for me).Its somewhat like metroid where you can do a similar thing at some points but it felt distinct and memorable enough in this game since what you were bypassing or "outsmarting" were often times actually puzzles and not just traversal/platforming challenges.The world and lore as well as some characters are very very enjoyable as well! The art  is charming, the soundtrack very memorable and the combat...Well thats one of few things i have issues with. It has a stamina bar that gets used by pretty much evertyhing except jumping (unless its out of the water) and if its empty you cant do anything until it refills past a certain point. this does get annoying in combat and specially in puzzles where your tools and attacks are used for sovling stuff but you gotta sometimes wait 2-3 seconds till it recharges which is a bummer Also the game could definetly use some form of quest log or something. I sometimes lost track of certain quests I started and some quests I kinda knew were avaible but I didnt start them since it required to like talk to the same character 3 times to start it. Kind of a bummer but the wiki kinda saved me through all that so meh, its fine.All in all this is an amazing game thats extremely easy to recommend and very enjoyable! Not perfect, there are a few issues but none that soured the experienced for me at all. Any fan of games like Zelda 2 should definetly check this game out.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is nothing short of magical in my opinion, and it's a crying shame that it's flown so far under the radar.Before I get into anything else, let me just say that I've completed this game 100% on multiple different platforms now, and I can say without hesitation that it's in my top 3 favorite games of all time. Here's my TL;DR- This is a Pseudo metroidvania, exploration, and puzzle game with unmatched atmosphere, solid gameplay, and solid combat. While the story is linear and it's not "technically" a metroidvania game, every ability you get unlocks a massive amount of new exploration, puzzles, and upgrades to find.Atmosphere: Simply unmatched. The artwork is unique, vibrant, and super charming with each and every area being unique & distinct, accompanied by music that is downright mouthwatering, some of the best I've ever heard in a game. The world is huge, dense, and incredibly alive- there are hundreds of NPC's that populate the gorgeous locations and every single one of them has a minimum of two lines of dialogue that directly contribute to the world in some capacity, no throw away lines.Story: Fantastic, but a little distracted. I love the concept and every aspect of it, but the main story (your entire village getting abducted by space pirates) is more-or-less ignored and instead you work to save the world from a separate force of hostile aliens. I think it works well, but it's a shame that this game wasn't popular and probably wont get a sequel following up on that Combat: Subjective. I loved it, but it does earn some criticism from most people and it's not undeserved. Unlike most 2d games, your character has momentum. You can't turn in the air, and once you've started moving in a direction it takes time to slow down and change directions. It lends meaning and weight to the movement system which I enjoy a lot, but others hate. What I do agree is kind of bad is that when you get hit there are no i-frames, and you REALLY bounce halfway across the room. Its very punishing for getting hit, although  the difficulty settings do let you adjust this combat quite a bit to make it much easier (which I recommend most people do). Overall, I think the combat is solid and people who nit-pick it are trying to work against is and play as though it's the same as other games when its not. You need to learn it and work with it before you see how well it actually works.Exploration: Phenomenal. There are upgrades to be found in every single nook and cranny, and every single movement ability you get will unlock dozens upon dozens of new items to find. Some of these are VERY difficult to find, but if you like exploring I think it's more than worth your time.Final verdict: One of the best games I've ever played. The amount of love the developers poured into this game is clear in every single scene and the experience absolutely reflects that. For me, this is a classic that I'll never forget.

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia: Awakening is a solid 9.9/10 for me.There's a lot I enjoyed in this game. The story is engaging. The world is huge and packed full of interesting characters and rich lore. There are a ton of puzzles, minigames and side quests outside the main story. The constant sense of wonder and exploration is probably the strongest aspect of this game. Even though the rewards for exploring are usually just one of three types of collectibles, it's more about the journey than the destination. The feeling of accomplishment when you finally crack a puzzle or uncover a hidden secret is great and present throughout the entire game.In terms of presentation, the art and animations are incredibly cute, both for the pixelated sprites and the backgrounds. Great use of color, too. The dialogue is charming and full of little jokes sprinkled in. Some NPC dialogues change after certain events, which is something that most players won't even notice, but it's a nice touch. The soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal. I love how some tracks have "calm" and "busy" arrangements that transition smoothly into each other as you enter or leave a fight. I also love how the in-world flute songs are tied to the soundtrack (e.g. the GEO song and the Royal Hymn) and how themes are revisited in different tracks (e.g. Moonlight Ravine, Boss Battle and Mother Computer all quote the main menu melody). None of this is groundbreaking or anything, it's just done really nicely. (As an aside, I love that the composer went with relative minor instead of parallel minor for the "sad" Panselo theme. OK I'll stop nerding out about the music now.) In terms of gameplay, I found it to be mostly smooth and satisfying. That said, I can see why most of the negative reviews focus on the controls. The sprint-jumping takes some time to get used to, and the tutorial for this mechanic is way too hard. The awkwardness of the controls becomes even more obvious during boss fights and the target shooting minigames. I played on PC and I found that aiming with the crossbow was nearly impossible without the mouse, which was weird and clunky for a game where I didn't need the mouse for the remaining 99% of the time. Then there was the "accidentally detonating a bomb I meant to throw" problem and the "accidentally throwing a box I meant to put down" problem. Maybe it's different on a controller, though. I know the game was originally designed for the Switch so maybe there is some unavoidable awkwardness when using a keyboard.Despite all of that, the controls didn't really hurt my enjoyment of the game. If I had to point out a problem with this game, it would be those stupid sliding picture puzzles, and the one with the screens you have to turn on. I have no idea how you're supposed to arrive at the solution other than guessing correctly. Most of the puzzles in this game are really clever and involve solving a riddle or using your tools to overcome an environmental challenge, and then there's like two or three which are "hit the correct switches the correct amount of times". Thankfully, these are optional puzzles.My other major complaint is that there REALLY needed to be savepoints in the middle of the  and after the  fight. The first isn't too bad because you can backtrack to the previous savepoint, even though that's still annoying to have to do. The second is atrocious design. If you want to  and you die, you have to repeat that entire segment! That's three boss fights in a row! At least reopen the doors or something.

_childDocuments_.review: If there's one gripe I had about this game, it's that the combat can get extremely annoying. The MC's attack has a range of slightly longer than an ant, you practically have to hug the enemy to do any damage. You can also get bounced mercilessly by certain attacks, which adds salt to injury.ANYWAY. That said, I enjoyed this game immensely. It's easy to pick up, the storyline isn't too confusing, great art, wonderful music. Many sidequests, which is always a plus. but nothing too much that they deter the main story. Also, I LOVE the puzzles. Some of them can get frustrating, but for like 95% of them, they're enjoyable.The game mechanics are okay. The Gear Ring is super helpful, and I love the tools that you get. Not really a fan of the energy system, but eh, you get used to it. I guess one other thing that struck out a bit odd for me was how for the fishing rod and crossbow, using a mouse is extremely helpful, but otherwise you never use the mouse at all, only keyboard. Could get jarring how you need to switch between the two, but again, you kinda get used to it.Also, screw the Ancient Vault. Nothing else in this game has made me so angry.One last thing. Why is perro a chicken?? Why is it not a dog??

_childDocuments_.review: It just isn't fun. I like difficult platformers. I like everything about this game on paper. I was enjoying it, despite it being frustrating at times. Until I got to one particular platforming section beneath a well. The timing of arrow jumps has to be pixel perfect. When you die, you have an annoying walk through town, and you have to reopen a door with a combo of button presses each time. To get back to the challenge takes about as long as your next attempt will take before you die, and takes you out of any rythm you might have had. For a reaction-time grind like this, you will need to try over and over. In my opinion this is either bad game design, or just malicious. Either way it sucks. The game doesn't respect you or your time. I uninstalled it after about 30 attempts at that section.

I love learning more about this world and seeing more sights!The boss fights are really exhilarating, but were frustrating and felt really unfair until I managed to survive about 3/4 into the fight. _childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia is a stunningly beautiful and immersive game. There's a ridiculous amount of dialogue for a metroidvania style of game, and the backgrounds and environments are surprisingly detailed. All paired with a fantastic sound track.That being said I don't think this game is for everyone. The game seems to take heavy inspiration from legend of zelda 2 for the nes. The quests instructions in the game are pretty minimalist, leaving the player to figure a lot out on their own. And on top of that the combat and platforming can be pretty challenging even when just traveling from point A to point B. There will absolutely be points where you die and lose a significant progress and it feels like an old school through and through.The game has a wonderful sense of exploration. The puzzles are challenging, and there are secrets littered everywhere. Getting a new item is exciting and you are constantly rewarded for trying strange things and going off the beaten path.Overall I absolutely love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is a rare gem. Great visuals, combat, sound, and story. There lots of little thoughtful touches that make a big difference, too.I played on challenging difficulty and enjoyed it as a veteran of platformers and metroidvanias. Phoenotopia Awakening punished me with hilarious ragdoll knockback, no invincibility frames, and limited energy to perform actions. Git gud, collect powerups, and learn new tactics from NPCs. By the time I beat the main questline I felt powerful, satisfied knowing half of that strength was my own reflexes.There's a ton of stuff to find: powerups, secret weapons, optional dungeons, even optional bosses.There are a lot of well-done puzzles. Not all puzzles are for everyone. Personally, I loved the logic puzzles, but not the not the more sleuthy puzzles. There's tons of info in the wiki and elsewhere to help you enjoy what you love and bypass some of the rest.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cute game with a cute style and animations, and it's one of the games that I really try to enjoy, but it doesn't hit me on the right spot.Some of my thoughts I had while playing through the first 2 areas:- The game feels very generic and lengthy, or at least has a very slow start, There wasn't much going on and you stay with the same equipment for a long while. Several gameplay elements introduced in the first area seem to stay the same over the rest of the game, and in some cases also start to feel redundant. Grinding enemies for money also becomes stale with the same basic equipment over 8 hours.- There's only 1 item slot, which you use for all your secundaire items and healing items. The circle helps a little to quick swap them, but that swapping has to be done continiously. I think the game would play much smoother if you had one or two more active item slots.- Combat itself also has it's issues, mostly the energy requirement for a basic attack, the main attack been a very short-ranged bat against rather mobile enemies. and the rather beefy enemies that drains through your stamina quick.The Story introduction and the music is nice, as well as the aforementioned artstyle and animations, but the rest...idk, they don't appeal to me as much as I had expected from the trailer.

_childDocuments_.review: honestly, this game is a masterwork. deservedly one of my favourite games i've ever played, highly recommend. the story is pretty good, the sidequests are fun and enjoyable, the music is , and every character you interact with is great, all the way from the early game to the final bosses. it's not afraid to get dark at times, and it's certainly got quite some depth, more than you would expect from such an on-the-surface charming pixelart game. the lore intrigues me, and it all integrates into the world amazingly. many questions are left answered to a sufficient degree, and quite a few more remain for future entries (which i do  hope are made) to answer. there's a few things that seemed to come out of nowhere for me, but they're astoundingly few in number.overall, seriously, get this game. if it's on sale, great, if it's not, better start saving. if you're a fan of metroidvanias, that's just more incentive. if you're not... well, i can't force you. but know that i am staring at you across the expanse of the earth and desperately urging you personally to reevaluate. 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Adventure, exploration, side-quests upon side-quests, upgradable tools and weapons, flute-playing, platforming, collectibles, hair-dying, puzzle-solving, fishing, upgradable songs (not joking), bat-swinging, boss fights, countless varieties of food, cooking, teleporting, attack-charging, dashing, leaping, swimming (eventually), and so  much more wrapped up in absolutely gorgeous pixel art both background and foreground and music that can haunt, relax, tense up, and enlighten the mood whenever required. Imagine Samus Aran, Simon Belmont and Link decide to have a three-way marriage and the result of their care and rearing is this beautiful, empathetic, full of energy person whom all the villagers trust and hope can lead them to prosperity forever more. Once again, I am not joking: if you like any of the respective classic games those three protagonists are known for, you will have  to like about Phoenotopia Awakening.Note: i actually have 24+ hours on this already (and still not finished at time of writing!), I simply forgot to connect Steam online when playing. If you want proof, check the screenshot in my profile.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a delight from beginning to end. _childDocuments_.review: Charming and ambitious Zeldroidvania with a fun (if incomplete) story, cute animations and lots of clever, tricky puzzles.I recommend setting all the difficulty options to Easy, since combat isn't the game's forte and the extra difficulty only really adds clunkiness to an already kind of clunky combat system.The main appeal of Phoenotopia is the exploration and puzzle solving, and both of those elements are great, full of clever, varied solutions and clever brain-twisters. Most collectables are actually accessible as soon as you see them, so there's not actually that much back-tracking.The game also gives you more than your money's worth. It took me around 40 hours to achieve 75% completion.Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is good, but not great. It's held back by a number of small issues that minorly inconvenience the player. Accessibility options can help with some of them, but not all (as someone who played without them, I suggest using them unless you're achievement hunting or always play on hard mode). I think the most annoying issue is the fast travel system, which is much slower than it needs to be and is locked behind optional collectibles that are also used for item upgrades. Another issue is there is no quick way to retry many challenges immediately; you have to see their dialogue from the beginning. These are different ways that the game makes it longer to traverse and backtrack with no extra challenge, and quite frankly it took me a while for the game to click for me. But once it did, I stopped caring about these issues, and just started enjoying myself.The presentation is gorgeous. There are some legitimately amazing areas that I had to take in once I saw them, and I'm not the person to do that in games basically ever. The soundtrack compliments the graphics wonderfully. The load times are very fast, as one would expect from a pixel graphics title, but it's very welcome here. Dialogue from all of the NPCs is charming, and the world felt like a standout character. They really made me adore some of the sidequests in this game. There are some fun (mostly minor) sequence breaks that I was able to do, which makes me think this is probably a good speed game for anybody into that. There are goodies all over the place, so you'll find a bunch without having to go out of your way, but there are even more off the beaten path (sometimes even in places I thought the devs would have ignored!). The equipment you get is pretty cool; my favorites were the Bombs, Spear, and then the more late/endgame stuff. There are some really fantastic screens to complete, and there are some really awful ones (mostly optional at least). I loved it, and I hated it. But really, I liked it.Story spoilers and thoughts on the ending that I'm still keeping really vague:
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a while since a game really allowed myself to hunker down and enjoy it. Between the aesthetically beautiful world 'Phoenotopia: Awakening' brings with it's myriad of melodic scores of tunes & music that will likely continue on with me the same way Link's ocarina has with others. The developers for this title managed to turn what seems to be simple gameplay mechanics into a web of intricate puzzle designs keeping it fun throughout my entire adventure, while managing to keep it coherent in escalating levels of difficulty, having felt both extreme levels of frustrations & accomplishment after the fact.  The eccentric characters you meet along the way as well as well as those you've yet to encounter, I'm hopeful I'll be able to see a sequel to the title in this lifetime. I'd be curious to know what happened to Nana from the orphanage ;(I found myself both fulfilled and left with a gaping void once the journey came to an end.  Hopefully once I muster up the courage like the boy wanting to seek sunken treasures in the Moonlight Ravine, I'll be back to try the Zero Trial achievement!Thank you team at Cape Cosmic as well as Flyhigh Works for publishing, a time well spent and a metroidvania to be remembered for the ages.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a fan of the original flash game, so getting this game was a no brainer.In terms of artstyle, atmosphere, immersion, and of course music the game knocks it out of the park!It pretty much blows the original out of the water (aside from a few music tracks that didn't make it into this game that I miss).The characters feel more "alive" here than in most other games with their varying and well-written dialogue, and the music really sets the mood of each area you visit. Plus they sound great even outside of the game. A real sense of.... how do I say this? It's sort of like a nostalgic feeling for a time gone by.The gameplay for the most part is good (aside from a certain jumping section in a secret area) and is certainly better than the original flash version. The only thing I have a gripe with is the controls. I am aware that they were made with a certain feature in mind (which I barely used at all) but in the longterm of the game it had a bit of a detrimental effect for some items. Specifically the Crossbow item.It would have been much more intuitive to use the mouse for aiming rather than the arrow keys. I didn't have a problem with this in the original version because there was basically no item that needed mouse aiming in that version (though the slingshot would have been easier to use if it had it). Here it's tied to what is going to be your primary ranged weapon once you get it.Now for most of the game you don't need precise aiming in a speedy manner, but when you do the control scheme isn't going to make it easy.Other than that the game is pretty much my game of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: The post-apocalyptic medieval world feels enormous and lively, and actually is enormous. There must be hundreds and hundreds of NPCs across all the different towns and locales, each with their own story to listen to and often quests and tasks to help with. Although the game is focused on one "nation", you get the feel for a much larger world outside. Within the nation you explore so many diverse sub cultures and social groups that it's hard not to love everything about the world of Phoenotopia. The more "serious" questions about the past and the war that reset history are also slowly explored if you put in the effort to seek them out. The tone of the world is a bit lighthearted, and sometimes this is sharply at odds with some of the darker and more serious subject matter, but this isn't a catastrophic flaw.The plot doesn't quite live up to the worldbuilding. When you look back at it from the end, the plot development is very simple and not particularly engaging. In particular, near the start of the game, you are given a task of "find what happened to your village", which isn't even addressed or developed until you beat a large 10 hour segment. After that point the pacing picks up, which is great, but there aren't really any narrative twists to add spice.The real-time platformer-style combat consists of selecting the appropriate weapon, dodging attacks and projectiles using jumps and rolls, and returning fire, all the while managing your stamina bar. Even more advanced techniques are unlocked later that provide a nice variety and power at the cost of difficulty. My only issue with the combat is the emphasis on knockback attacks. Many enemies can knock you a screen or two away, often into other enemies who do the same, putting you in a kind of stun lock. There is a technique you learn for avoiding these "tumbles" but it's really quite tricky to perform. In addition, being knocked so much  results in you being knocked off-screen, which resets all the enemies' health and might as well be an instant death. If only there were a system to stop this.There are truly hundreds and hundreds of useful collectables in this game, ranging from stat powerups, to moonstones, to stashes of gold. The moonstones in particular have very intriguing and fun uses, and unlock items that really impact gameplay. Later in the game you unlock a hint system for finding collectables, which is really invaluable for completionists. I only wish the hint system included some extra collectables not in the "main three" such as .Consistently amazing. In addition to the catchy themes you might expect, Phoenotopia has some creative ambient tracks that really innovate on what you expect say "beach music" and "farm music" to sound like. Even the music in the final area, which in this genre is traditionally dark, aggressive music is really fun .Phoenotopia has a fully-fledged enonomy, with buying and selling of items, money from quest rewards and chests, and a  of things to spend money on. I enjoy the "simplified" economy in this game where weapon and armour upgrades are all strict improvements on the previous level, so it's just a question of  you unlock them, you don't need to optimize your build for different enemies. The same applies for the selling system - you always get the same amount for the same item, regardless of where you sell it (with a few minor exceptions), which helps to keep this simple and fun. Cutesy pixel art. There are some phenomenal landscapes in the game: the Moonlight Ravine, and two certain underground lakes spring to mind. The cityscapes too are very detailed and engaging. But the characters themselves aren't particularly inspired. Even Gail, the protagonist, doesn't really have any iconic features.There are some really diverse and mindbending puzzles in this game. Given basic building blocks of "block pushing", "switch toggling", "music playing" etc emerge some really creative ideas. The sheer amount of puzzles in the game is unbelievable, including the main storyline and countless side quests. Even more impressive is that none of them seem repetitive, and every new area has a new type of puzzle for you to try. Phoenotopia uses the rule of 3 quite a lot, whereby it introduces a puzzle mechanic with one trivial puzzle, and then tests your understanding with two harder puzzles, and this consistently works well, allowing you to pace yourself. Particular note goes to the "GEO" puzzles, all of which pull this off perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I've played flash Phoenotopia and followed the game development for years so I might be a little bit biased/nostalgic. If you've ever played flashtopia before, get this asap, it's 10 times as polished while keeping roughly the same story.Highly recommend for anyone interested a cute, relaxing metroidvania styled game. Lots of exploring pretty locations, lots of fighting and especially collecting items. The story is rather generic, you are a smalltown girl and have to save the world from unknown danger but it's delivered very well through the course of the game, constantly adding in new faces and background lore about the world as you progress. Ending could have had more work though.The artstyle is stunning and one of the best I've seen in indie pixel games, Some areas really make your forget about the objective and just make you want to admire the view. The soundtrack just adds to this and comes with quite a number of tracks. I don't think I disliked a single track.One thing I especially like is how many side areas and hidden places there are to explore. Entirely optional of course but usually they contain a hefty sum of cash or a boost to your stats and sometimes even interesting lore about the world. I also liked how your power level grows quite significally in some parts of the story, unlocking new and quicker ways to deal with enemies or to find hidden areas.Some people say the movement and jumping is clunky but I didn't notice that at all in my playthrough, you get used to the controls pretty quickly. Some minor negatives I would say are some equipment items are pretty unnecessary and cycling through them can be a chore sometimes. Some boss fights are pretty tough and some puzzles could take some time to crack through (if you're really not interested in puzzles there's a community member who has made extensive guides about every puzzle and then some). There is also no map of any sort. Your memory will be your biggest friend here as there is a lot of backtracking. I actually kind of liked this, as I won't be constantly bringing up a map and can instead focus on memorizing this beautiful world.None of these things affected me in a big way though so I wouldn't worry about those.Now some things that might actually affect you: Farming money can be quite boring but it won't be needed if you explore for money and don't buy random junk. Some areas can be particularly annoying to traverse through *cough* Mul Caves *cough* White Towers *cough*, especially if you want to 100% them, but collecting enough stat-boosting items and food will mitigate annoyance levels to a degree.Overall, Phoenotopia: Awakening definitely deserves more attention, a real indie gem to take your mind off the real world. Reason it hasn't been heard of that much is because of it's bad sponsorship/advertisement.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia: Awakening is one of the best "Metroidvania?" I have played. (Not entirely sure if it's categorized as a Metroidvania, it's kinda like a side-scrolling Zelda with Metroidvania style mechanics) The game is one I also feel is hard to master with the combat. Some enemies in the game gave me ton's of trouble, partially due to my poor aim and timing of certain mechanics I believe. The game also has an insane amount of content for an indie game. I realize that this is a remake or remaster of its original game, but I still find the amount of content impressive with the variety of enemies, weapons, items and things to find throughout the game. Also, I found the music in the game to actually be quite nice! Overall, I believe this game has a lot of charm to it, it gave me some major nostalgia remembering some of the older Nintendo games I used to play like Zelda, and a variety of SNES and Gameboy Advance games. Even though I struggled with the game (I guess that's what I get for disabling all of the options that make combat easier, but hey, it makes the game more fun), I thoroughly enjoyed playing through it.

_childDocuments_.review: Charming game with interesting puzzles and challenges. It definitely has a Zelda-like vibe even though the gameplay is more metroidvania. The difficulty is affected by enabling or modifying certain control mechanics like stamina usage and I-frame duration. It's best played with a controller, and it does take a bit to be able to get used to combat let alone master a balance between fighting and dodging. Still, the controls aren't too tricky, and it's fairly doable to finish the game even with some difficulty rules added.Getting through the middle part of the game can be rough, since you have to deal with having food on you to restore health, and with a small inventory space unless you grind for money. At some point near the late game you'll find a way to restore hp passively without having to eat or rest somewhere.The story is surprisingly deep and interesting, featuring a unique theme of a post-post-apocalypse where civilization resets(middle age-ish with science) but remnants of the old world still remain(modern/futuristic technology). A bit unfortunate that a continuation to the story is unlikely in the near future, so try not to get hooked too much to the story.Overall it's a really fun game to play, and even the soundtrack is really nice to listen to. Good to get on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The Cave Story inspiration is very clear, and I loved me some Cave Story, but there are a considerable amount of mechanics and plot events in this game that are massive time wasters. Every new town starts you off with a mini quest that seems to more or less force you to get familiar with the town by making you find people scattered all over it. Would much prefer to just continue the story and explore on my own.The combat energy/stamina mechanic implemented in this game also doesn't really feel like it does anything except make you waste time. I can see how they may have been trying to go with a "Get your attacks in, and then recharge your stamina as you avoid attacks" kind of a situation, but it often becomes just an awkward stare down as the enemy doesn't attack and you wait for your stamina to come back...With that said, however..... this is a very very very enjoyable experience. There's just so much to explore, so many secrets, great enemy and weapon variety, great boss fights, great puzzles, a nice variety of characters, dialogue, and personalities, some absolutely fantastic music and pixel art, and a method of back-tracking I haven't really seen done in other games where new movement abilities are provided as you progress, but I really liked a lot.You will spend a considerable amount of time that will feel like overkill in towns on your first run, as well as cooking food, managing your inventory, and just waiting for your energy to come back, but if you like games that offer lots of exploration that feels rewarding to do so, this nails it.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy. This is one of those games where everything, EVERYTHING, is fantastic, except for one single element which is absolutely terrible and makes the game a real struggle to get through or even recommend.The obvious: God this game looks beautiful. Lineless pixels, colorful and varied aesthetics, smooth animations, it's a delight to look at and that alone makes exploring its many, many areas a delight. The sound design and soundtrack are great too, tons of memorable tunes and a huge variety of styles - maybe not an all-time great, but it was enjoyable start to finish. The game even does a solid job lore-wise; I admit I'd struggle to call the story itself great, especially with its bittersweet and inconclusive ending even in the best case, but the lore of the world and Gail herself does feel worth digging up, especially with how tucked away some of it feels, like you're uncovering secrets best kept buried.And on that note, the gameplay. I'm going to avoid... The Topic™ for now but what this game excels at, it really excels at, and that is: EXPLORATION. This is -not- really a metroidvania in a typical sense - while it's a 2D sidescroller with combat, there are only a small handful of movement upgrades or tools that aid in exploration - most other things are more geared towards combat. But this game has so many diverse areas and so many secrets tucked away in its map, the vast majority of which feel perfectly fair and can be a DELIGHT to work out. Imagine it's late game, you're following a hint that the game's in-game hint system gives you pointing towards one of the last few collectibles you're scrapping out, and that hint leads to discovering an entire hidden area containing some of the hardest puzzles, platforming, and combat in the entire game, rewarding you with a huge lore dump -and- two upgrade items in one. I didn't even -like- that area but it's so cool that it's there! And there's just all sorts of things like that - environmental music puzzles, secrets hidden based on the sound of your footsteps, a map-spanning trading quest that leads to one of the best items in the game, and FISHING PUZZLES. The mad lad put FISHING PUZZLES in the game. On top of that there are so many optional challenges - races, box breaking minigames, target minigames, mazes, puzzle mazes, riddles, combat rooms, platforming gauntlets, often hidden in clever ways and often in completely optional but delightful to explore areas.And every location has its own atmosphere - highly populated cities teeming with life, often containing a dozen or more internal quests, isolated but homely locations, secret dungeons, gloomy sewers, all in what ultimate is a fairly compact overworld that's so nicely connected via fast travel that it really only takes minutes to get anywhere, and despite lacking a map it's rare to get lost. And, again, in-game hint system that has such a miniscule fee it's basically free by the game's standards. In terms of sheer scope and density I could barely name a game that does both this well - Environmental Station Alpha is my measuring stick for density, and Hollow Knight for scope, and while this doesn't quite beat either in their own metrics, Genuinely the only games I can think of that outdo this game's sheer amount of content are the La-Mulana games, and I don't think -any- game could even attempt to best those. We're never getting another game like that again and that's fine. it does both so well the overall result is just as if not moreso impressive. it's a damn shame that the game plays like crap, then. Like, okay. The platforming is mooostly fine. You move at a decent speed and you have a run option, alongside some more platforming tools you acquire at around the halfway and three-quarters points of the game that fill out your repetoire and make Gail pretty athletic all things considered. But there's so many... nuances to the platforming that feel like they were put in place simply to make the game more demanding, not to make it play better. When you jump while running, you're committed to the arc - okay, I've seen that before in the aforementioned La-Mulana - but when you land, you have to re-press run? And if you land after a longer fall, you have to time a roll or get stuck in place for a second? Oh and you have to re-press run at the end of a roll or you get stuck in place for a second there instead? And a second time immediately after because you're stuck at normal walk speed? So let me get this straight, if I've performed a running jump and land from a high distance, I need to 1. time a roll, 2. time a roll cancel, 3. quickly tap run AGAIN, and if I fail any of these steps it breaks the flow of movement?  Again, it feels like intentionally overcomplicating something that could easily be accomplished in a more simple matter - if it ended at step 1 I'd really have no problem - after the roll, I'm running again, a reward for timing that one button press correctly. The weirdest part is none of this is ever necessary? Every platforming challenge in the game can be accomplished without worrying about this. The hardest room I can think of, the Lunar Key room, is still lenient enough that you can take that moment of time loss every so often and still be fine - the real issue is that any mistake punishes you with like 50 points of damage for no real reason, but, whatever, there's a save spot literally one screen away, not a huge deal.But then there's the combat, which has its own annoying nuances, and is THE part of the game that I hated interacting with almost every time I was forced to in any significant way. Gail is just not a good fighter. Her melee weapon is tiny, her ranged options are all very unwieldly - 360 degree aiming with a very short-range reticule never ever felt natural - and the air attack is the most pathetically slow move I've ever seen, you practically have to attack the moment your feet leave the ground to have a chance at landing a hit. So you've got a character who's already kinda sluggish unless you've mastered every aspect of the platforming engine, with slow, imprecise attacks. And damn near every boss requires such fast reactions and near perfect movement to dodge around, while often also being way more mobile than you could dream of being. And there's so, SO many enemies Gail is just not physically up to par with, either. I eventually just stopped using the bat outright and mostly fought with the crossbow and spear because, well, at least I can hit things without taking five billion damage in return that way, even if it's painfully slow and costs stamina.And the unnecessary nuances come into play here, too - you get juggled like a ragdoll from basically any hit unless you can perfectly time a button press the second you land on the ground - and good luck reacting fast enough to taking that hit, because you fly fast! Oh by the way only one NPC in the entire game tells you this, in a weird spot, where you have to pay money to learn this technique. So it's just. Not tutorialized properly. So yeah, expect to get juggled, a lot.  The game tries to have a three-hit limit after which you stop taking damage, but it doesn't always kick into effect, and just makes Gail feel even worse of a fighter than the already low standards she sets the rest of the time. I basically ended up face-tanking my way  with food items through what I'm sure are very well designed bosses for a game where your main character is more mobile of a fighter than Gail - one boss I literally just stood in front of and wailed away at with my bat until I won and it was easier than trying to fight it seriously. Only the one superboss you need near 100% completion to even challenge is relatively immune from this and even then I'd bet you could facetank it with enough top-tier items too.<continued in comments>

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia is a bit of a mess, clearly not the work of developers experienced in making action platformers. The controls are a bit clunky, menus aren't super intuitive or convenient, aiming ranged weapons is a pain, the melee weapon is short, and the stamina system isn't integrated well enough into the game to really add much, though at least it doesn't get so much in the way that it drags everything down.But, Phoenotopia is something I haven't seen in quite a while; the last two games I remember like it are CrossCode and Treasure Adventure Island. It's a game in which the developers' passion and vision drip off every screen of the game. The world feels alive with possibility, there's something for you to do or see around every corner, every NPC has something to say that someone enjoyed writing, every dungeon has little quirks and mysteries that make it feel rounded out and like more than just a series of tasks to perform. Bosses have gimmicks that make you use your head, and despite playing on the hardest difficulty I've only died once to each of them - once you understand the idea behind the boss the fight just kind of comes together as long as you execute correctly, and the game is fairly forgiving as long as you're going in the right direction.The music is phenomenally good, perhaps not as ear-wormy as a Shovel Knight but a beautiful blend of ambiance and melody that reminds me of Valdis Story. The graphics are lovingly polished low-res pixel art in a style that's both cute and easy to read. The main character is animated with plenty of personality. Every part of the game feels like it had not just time and attention but real affection put into it, and it carries through to the experience. I'm not as far in the game as my hours (37 at time of review) indicate thanks to leaving it on while I sleep or go out to do things, but the time I've spent playing it has felt engaging in a way that only the best games from my youth did - not a time-devouring, hyperfocused way like a cyclical roguelike or a nail-biting way like a Yoko Taro game, but comfortable, happy, fun, like coming back to an old friend and just enjoying time together.If you like pixel games, platformers with RPG and puzzle elements, Zelda games, or anything in that general style, give this game a try. It really wants you to enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: A flawed gem if you like metroidvanias that focus on exploration.The visuals and audio are fantastic, and it's fun to seek out secrets just to see what new areas they'll lead you to.The story is ok but still compelling thanks to worldbuilding with a few fun twists, and there's a ton of NPCs with lore or amusing dialogue - your mileage may vary, though. Most NPCs are good-natured idiots and I found their banter entertaining, but it might be a lot of boring text for some folks (there's *a lot* of optional dialogue in this game). It's all very cheerful even when it's trying to be serious, which is kind of nice in the dark timeline we live in.There's a ton of secrets and collectibles to find, and most of the puzzles hit that sweet spot where they're just difficult enough to leave you feeling like a doggone genius when you do solve them. I completed most of them without the wiki and I'm very not smrt (I especially liked the many song puzzles that require you to figure out a specific melody).The game doesn't have a map which makes remembering some of the secret locations tricky, but there's a fair amount of side quests that'll have you traipsing all over and make you stumble back into whatever you forgot (and late game there's an NPC that can give you hints on whatever you missed). The world is also a lot bigger than I thought and unless you're dashing through everything, a first run will take a decent chunk of time (while I've been hunting for secrets somewhat thoroughly, getting to the end took about 25-30 hours).Unfortunately the game has a major flaw and that's the combat.It's not too bad for most of the game, but there are a few combat-heavy areas that are just frustrating to go through due to odd design decisions and controls that are nowhere as precise as the game expects them to be. The boss fights as well range from average to Frustrating® - as long as you're stocked up on items none of them are particularly hard, you just take damage in ways that often feel cheap.There's many little quirks of control that add up to some frustrating fights. For example, you cannot turn your character in midair; you still have air control, but your character will only strike in the direction when you initiated the jump, which is frustrating when dealing with some of the fiddlier flying enemies.Attack animations have a few frames of delay between the button press and the action, as well as some frames after, making quick reactions feel clunky and often resulting in taking hits.Most enemy attacks (especially later in the game) will send your character flying, and while there is a 'recovery' move, the timing is finicky and you'll often end up bouncing around taking more damage before you even get to use it. You basically get a lot of stunlock damage chains like in Spelunky (less lethal here, but irritating).This is all made worse by the Stamina bar, which takes forever to even begin refilling (2 whole seconds, which feels a lot longer than it sounds) and the recharge rate is so slow that you'll spend a not insignificant amount of time just pootling until it's recharged. The game has consumables to help with this, but it feels like a bandaid over a glaring design issue, especially since the stamina items are not that common and you have to go out of your way to get them.So basically, if you're looking for tight combat, this is probably not the game for you.It's not catastrophically bad and you get used to its quirks, but even then it never feels particularly good (it's a shame because you can see what they're aiming for but it's just not there).I highly recommend enabling the 'difficulty' modifiers in the pause menu - I played most of the game without them, and rather than making the game easier, they resolve basic QoL issues. I really wish I'd played the game with them from the start - one of them speeds up the stamina recovery delay, which vastly improves the flow of the gameplay (especially since there is no ingame upgrade to this). The only one I'd leave off is  "allow instant eating of food" which kind of breaks what little combat balance there is (healing items are rated by how long they take to activate - like variable speed Estus Flasks).And yet despite all that I still thoroughly enjoyed it and by the end I just wanted more to explore. I'll probably end up trying to 100% because the exploration and puzzles are so entertaining, and it's just got such a wonderful atmosphere to bask in.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't quite bad, I just don't think I'll ever bother to finish it. The art direction is fantastic, but it can't really cover for how iffy the game feels to play:* The sprinting is just weird. It resets when you land (even if you're still holding down the sprint button). And pressing the sprint button causes you to start sprinting in whatever direction you're facing (even if you're not currently inputting any movement). In theory this could be useful, but in practice it just make the running feel really finicky. Sometimes you hit the sprint key too early and start sprinting in the wrong direction. Sometimes you're trying to run and jump between platforms, and you mistime repressing the sprint key so instead you do a non-running jump and fall short. I can't think of a single other platformer that does this, so I'm not really sure why they went with this weird sprinting mechanic.* This game has Metroidvania-like backtracking but no dungeon map. So you'd better have a really good memory to keep track of all the places you can go back to!* The range on "sword" attacks feels a little too short. This makes it hard to maintain any sort of "safe distance" when fighting. This isn't bad on its own, but the (early) game also seems to focus on mechanics that slow your movement while fighting. For instance charging an attack cuts down your movement speed significantly, all-but guaranteeing you'll get hit if the enemy is moving even a tiny bit. Another example: one of the standard attacks has a huge amount of input delay (leaving you vulnerable that whole time) so if you don't time it just right you're almost certainly going to be hit.* The first projectile weapon in the game has "bullets" that are so slow it's legitimately hard to aim. Luckily it's not needed for anything fast-paced (as far as I know), but it's still just feels unnecessarily difficult to use.The above aren't really killer in any way. I'm sure it's possible to train up on all of it and eventually have a good experience. But I'd struggle to justify doing so. There are so many other beautiful platformers that don't make these mistakes (Ori and the Blind Forest, Hollow Knight, Rain World, Dead Cells, Gato Roboto, etc) that I'd really rather just find something else instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Zelda and the Metroidvania genre had a child, and then that child learned how to fight from Dark Souls. This is unironically one of the greatest games I have played in the last few years rivaling Hollow Knight.The abilities are fun and at times caught me off guard as I would expect to get one thing only to be sideswept with another. The games story is intriguing, fun, and beyond fascinating. I love the setting of this world torn between technology and the middle ages, I love the characters that I ran into and more than anything I love this game's sense of humor. I literally fell out of my chair on more than one occasion laughing at some of the jokes that got thrown my way. Most of all though is the sense of scope and exploration. For anyone that loves the feeling of trying something clever and getting rewarded for it, then this is the game for you. Secrets and mysteries hidden around every corner and most all of them are challenging but doable without a guide. There is the one or two odd ball ones that could be overlooked at times (Like musical sudoku) but even those can be figured out with ease once you have get a small clue.Lastly the games combat is just superb. The stamina mechanic is extremely well balanced, and I love the need to use time to eat food making boss fights frantic and chaotic. Nothing ever feels impossible but it also far from easy. For me the challenge was just at the right level and had me dying for more. But I think what I appreciated the most was the games approach to accessibility and difficulty. Rather than artificially inflating enemy HP or Damage, instead they allow the player to manually tweak the games mechanics in their favor, like removing stamina consumption from normal attacks or allowing healing immediately from the menu. It allows the game to maintain its own vision and difficulty while allowing anyone to freely customize their experience. As someone that overly studies and analyzes game design I could not be more in love with this system.All in all 15/10 game, I loved it from beginning to end and by god do I plan to 100% this monster of a title. I will be following these devs very closely for their next title for sure, I will spread the word of this amazing game, and I will hope that one day a sequel may come to exist.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely worth a play.It's a fun, cute fusion of Metroidvania and RPG. Beautiful art and music. Excellent world building. Surprisingly, it's a post-apocalyptic setting, so there's tons of environmental storytelling. The plot is a genuinely amusing adventure with pretty challenging platforming combat (difficulty is variable). The story and the music have an unspoken, very deeply melancholic undertone where it regards the bones of the old world. But the experience of the game is just delightful.Protip though--the cooking and fishing minigames were clearly meant to be part of the difficulty curve. If you don't embrace them, you're going to find yourself out of money, out of healing, and probably frustrated at the pointless grinding you have to do for coins. Also, search everything, and make sure you know the full move set going in.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorites, but not without its faults. It's charmingly cute, a big plus for me, and is a cool world that's fun to explore, another big plus. I can definitely see myself doing it again.I played it on "maximum combat difficulty" and the only qualm I have with that is the stamina system being too restrictive. Attacking uses a lot of stamina and means you spend a lot of fights dodging waiting for the bar to fill back up.The item system was kind of annoying, both the actual inventory and usable items. The inventory is very VERY small and there are a lot of item types early that fill it up quickly. Otherwise, only having one item equipped at a time is unfortunate, especially after one item  proves to be so often relied upon as its both better for a lot of late-game combat and leaned on a little too hard in level-design for its ability to create platforms.The story's pretty great but I'm not a huge fan of the ending. I was kind of surprised that the game ended when it did, I was legitimately expecting at least one more area after what turned out to be the final boss. I felt kind of let down and that the story didn't get resolved.Even with those qualms, I very much want to see the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I played and loved the original flash game years ago and have been awaiting the reboot(?) since I found out there would be more. I do have a few minor nitpicks like I think a basic map of the cities would be helpful just like on a billboard or smth, and if you have dynamic lighting off then the . _childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I first played the flash version of phoenotopia on newgrounds years and years ago. It was challenging, had an engaging story, and a well built world that called for exploration. It was one of my favorite online games and it's fully fleshed successor has kept its promise. It's a cute game but you can't sleep through it, you have to play it and paying attention to not only the gameplay but also the story definitely pays off. You can complete the storyline in under ten hours pretty easily, but 100% will take much longer and is actually quite rewarding. There are some teething issues but Quells has worked hard on those and I haven't had any hiccups since the initial visual hitches were fixed. Play the demo to see if it's for you, but I bet it will be

_childDocuments_.review: Its a much harder game than its cute art style would lead you to believe, but it's worth it to get good at it because theres a lot to see and do. It features a large zelda 2-esque open world map to explore, combat thats a stiff challenge, and puzzles that are just hard enough the give you that "aha!" moment when you solve them without being frustratingly complex. _childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Colorful, immersive, emotional. Challenging but somehow I managed to collect all the items and solve all the puzzles (only with minimum help a few times).The best time I had in a while. _childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: I was so overwhelmed when I saw Phoenotopia Awakening was released. I immediately bought it and its the best decision I've ever made. I've always been a big fan of Phoenotopia, I remember playing it countless times to see the secret ending over and over again. It's always been my all time favourite game, no game gave me that much joy, interest and fun. The story is more than a girl with adventures. It has a great story line, thrilling secret places, lots of emotion, good pixel visuals, great music and game play. No game will ever give me that much satisfaction. Then this game happened. I was always waiting for part 2, I was so excited and curious about it. Now I almost finished the game, and I can say they outdid themselves. The game is even better this time, with heavier storyline, fuller visuals, more tools and weapons, harder boss fights and many many puzzles. I absolutely loved it. I dont even wanna finish the final boss and end the game. All I can do is to give all my money for the amazing game and thank anyone who had a job in it. Thank you. I would gladly pay for part 2 if there is a chance. Also, (spoiler!) the ending is very, veery satisfactory this time. The betrayal in the first game was really saddening and unexpected, now in this game it is totally fulfilled in the way I wanted and it was also unexpected again.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game with a ton of love and details poured into it.Though it may not be for everyone since the game need some heavy polish on the quality of life department. Healing and preparing for battles are a chore since you have to actively hunt/grind for heals, and the stamina system (which can be partially turned off) is unnecessary for such a fast paced game which makes combat becomes a chore of dodging until you have enough stamina to attack and even normal enemies at the same level as you require at least 2 to 3 stamina bars with the best upgrades (weapons, tools and stamina) you can get when you face them to take down, so be sure to turn off the stamina system before you start or you will start hating the game very fast. And there are many more quality of life improvements need to be made that I will not mention since it has spoilers.A hidden gem is what I would use to classify this game. It may feel like the game hates you at first but give it some time and you will love it like how one would come to love Darksouls. TLDR: "Welcome fellow masochist and appreciators detailed arts. You will feel right at home."
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: + amazing story + challenging gameplay + nice variety of calm exploring and action-packed combatThis game is a gem you should not miss. It is outright amazing. If you're looking for downsides, many people seem to find combat too difficult, which I simply cannot understand:Every enemy in the game has a very limited number of simple attack moves, which they just use one after another. When you meet a new enemy, just take a few seconds to observe what he is doing. You should be able anticipate his next move(s) and kill him without even getting hit once.If that is too much for you and you just want to bash your way through mindlessly (which the game wasn't designed for), you can still do that by simply picking minimum difficulty! It is a real mistery to me why combat is criticised so often...Anyway, with the only "downside" of the game being one that probably arises from ignorance and hastiness, there is really nothing that should keep you from buying and enjoying this jewel! _childDocuments_.review: Great game. Actually managed to recapture a bit of that feeling of playing Ocarina of Time for the first time on N64. Combat leans towards the more difficult side of things, but it almost never felt truly unfair. Exploration was good too -- often, I felt clever and rewarded for paying close attention to my surroundings and experimenting with the environment (even if I was occasionally disappointed by the actual rewards themselves, relative to the effort put in to acquire them). I was most impressed by the puzzles in the game -- not only did they usually strike the perfect balance of being neither too easy nor too difficult, but they were also presented in such a variety of ways that the process of solving them never became stale. In fact, it was the first time in a very long while that I actually felt motivated to bust out pencil and paper to figure out solutions. Overall, I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a true masterpiece. I'm not sure that I've ever enjoyed a game start-to-finish as much as Phoenotopia. The play style resembles a mix of Zelda and Metroid, with a story that is part Final Fantasy and Earthbound, all with a delicately balanced utopian/dystopian flavor... the result is something totally unique.Every aspect of this game was done with excellence and care- the script was engaging and humorous (it was actually worthwhile to talk to every NPC, even as each typically had at least 2 layers of dialogue), the music was spot-on for each terrain, and the graphics were incredibly intricate in the pixel style. The physics are perfect- character movement is free and agile, and the ability to smack enemies across the stage with a hard strike never got old. The wide range of weapons, tools, and abilities lent itself toward an even wider array of tactics, and the primary healing mechanism (collection of various foods, which could be cooked to improve properties) was fun and engaging.Perhaps most impressive is how enjoyable every minute of play truly was- it took about 48 hours over the course of a month or so for me to casually work through to the end without attempting to grind for every achievement (90% completion on the casual run, then another 4 hours to go back and get 100%). With every added ability/tool that allowed access to different areas within old regions, it did not feel like a grind to return; I enjoyed the opportunity to re-explore the past areas knowing there was some reward to attain (even if small). Part of the intrigue is the many layers of rewards possible- in addition to the standard units that increase maximum health/energy that are found in many games, there were a large number of additional abilities, tools, weapons, and side storyline tidbits that made each exploration interesting and worthwhile.Well done, developers- I'll eagerly await the sequel, and hope you'll have the support needed to continue the story!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenotopia: Awakening

_childDocuments_.review: After finally finishing the game I can I say this is the best game of its kind I've played in about 15 years. This game leans heavily into exploration and gameplay and is fairly lite on progression (there's enough). The way this game captures the feeling of exploration is unmatched. My last session was 17 hours long, and all of that time was pure exploration. If I had to guess 3 most important things, I'd say: big world, rewards for side tracking, no hand-holding (i.e. quest markers, maps, navigation). That culminates into you running around blindly, finding areas, solving puzzles and ALWAYS being rewarded. Most similar games screw up in 1 of those aspects.I mentioned the game is "big", but it's done through world density rather than size (although size is respectable). Every area, house, NPC and object feels like it is worth interacting with and so far over half of all areas I visited featured at least one platforming section, hidden area or a puzzle of some sort."Big deal, lots of games do it" I hear you say. Well, that they do, Billy, but Phoenotopia has few key game design choices that make it feel more rewarding than competitorsA common complaint is unfair combat, which I can definitely see at higher difficulties. Your basic attacks include short reach melee and various ranged weapons, which all leaves somewhat defenseless for some time. There's no damage on-contact, so you can safely walk all over then as long as enemy attack doesn't connect with you.. Main difficulty in fights stems from positioning yourself well enough to attack after enemy attack animation ends (which often leaves them too far to reach in time before next attack) and not get hit when next one starts. So far there was one exception: are just as easy to read as normal enemies, but safely positioning yourself for an attack is significantly harder.To evaluate combat I first need to address the difficulty, which can range from casual game to unfair souls-like, due to the way difficulty scaling is setup. Honestly, I think these developers deserve an award just for taking the time to design difficulty settings, which are not just stupid enemy HP/damage multiplier.There are 5 levels and I've tried 2 of them. This 1 enemy type cancerous. You wouldn't call it hard, it just slows you down... a lot. Luckily it's mostly localized in 1 area.Few areas in game are annoying for combat reasons. In all cases enemies are still easy to read, but I faced a few situations where they felt impossible to avoid due to numbers.This is subjective, but I figured I'd include it, because I loved it. The game features adult humor (contextual humor, no NSFW stuff), which ranges from comical life situations to subtle jabs at similar stories. For example: you find this band of musicians that pass a remark along the lines of "We found (girl's name) in a forest suffering from amnesia. Can you believe that?". This cracked me up, because that's exactly how a good portion of games start.Other stuff that might interest youFew minor negativesIn case my opinion about the game was not clear to this point. I think it's a masterpiece. I'll probably buy a random friend a copy, just to support these developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Great world design, charming art, fantastic music, and tight gameplay. It's a really well designed game, with stunningly good puzzle design (and I am not a huge fan of puzzle), engaging exploration, and well designed, difficult boss fights. All of the game mechanics are well-thought-out, and contribute well to the gameplay. I particularly appreciate the innovative mid-fight healing system.As a bonus, the game has remarkably good accessibility options included, if it's a little too challenging for your tastes. I found it just as difficult as I wanted it to be, but it's nice to have the option open for others.It's definitely not a metroidvania though! It's a linear game with lots of optional exploration and secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure what to expect with this game, but it's been an amazing journey so far. It's not really a metroidvania, because the world is broken up into smaller segments connected by an explorable world map. There are also towns and houses other places to find in addition not dungeons.The game is chock full of side quests, puzzles, minigames, and secrets to find. Think a side scrolling Zelda, all the upgrades and tools are found, bought, traded for, or won from a game. There are also some Immersive Sim moments, some things can be accomplished in multiple ways, i.e. bribing a guard or finding a secret to gain entrance.The graphics and music are very lovely. The little animations of Gail waking up or bouncing off sheep amuse me every time. This is such a massive game with so much heart poured into it, if you are even slightly interested, please give it a try. Yes, it can be difficult, but the accessibility options make things more manageable. Be warned that the game doesn't hold your hand and there are no maps or quest journey(though I feel both would be welcome additions.)This has been a game for that captures that sense of wonder that I found so prevalent as a child, and I can't wait to see what else there is to discover!Indie Curator Page

_childDocuments_.review: You will find yourself recognising many adventure tropes. A young hero set out into the open world, on a journey that has consequences on worldly events. It all started when a starship came and rudely abducted all the adults, and so recruiting the help of others, you plan to get them back. The stakes are still relatively small for me, but I am sure to learn the “fate of the world” stakes any moment now... If only I took a break from exploring and collecting moonstones. Unfortunately, I get distracted way too easy by new landscapes and recurring characters like The Travelling Melodies.It is a vast world with lots to explore, in true Metroidvania fashion. Any that adore the genre will find a happy home here. Even within the first hour, I spotted cracked rocks and corridors hidden in darkness. I smirked, “Yes, I will be returning to learn your secrets”.  When you’re not exploring for secrets and lore, you will be fighting for your life in the challenging but rewarding combat. Button mashing the attack button will get you nowhere, you will need to study your enemies patterns and fight smart. Yet another excellent reason to love this game.  There are; underground bandits who live with armadillo-like sand monsters, huge towns filled with beautiful windmills, hi-tech laboratories with robots and secret underground ruins of a lost city reminiscent of our modern day. With so much to discover and humorous dialogue with characters you meet, you won't get bored. Each new location looked different from the last, with great effort in adding narrative details to show off different cultures and lands. The music assisted in the atmosphere at every opportunity, boasting an album of 60 gorgeous tracks.

_childDocuments_.review: Full review: Metroidvania fans will feel right at home with Phoenotopia: Awakening, a modern answer to the 2D action-adventure born from the passion provided by the genre. Some may seem surprised at the volume of content available in a seemingly simple indie game. Yet passionate indie developers around the world have shown that with enough work, anything is possible, even triumphantly fun games such as this one. It's all that an adventure should be: you look back at all that you've done after so long and realize that none of it was wasted.+ Fantastic detail for visual storytelling+ Combat is generally fluid and fun+ Item collecting and exploration never grow old+ Whether main or side content, there are tons of things to do- Controls aren't always the most precise- Characters are pretty weak overall

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia follows in a similar vein to Hollow Knight, Rabi-Ribi, Sundered: Eldritch Edition, and, strangely enough, the Legend of Zelda 2. It beautifully (and I do mean that quite literally) ties together classic platformer mechanics with a tight control scheme, and many, many well thought out puzzles that are just the right level of difficulty, and keep you thinking throughout the whole game. Something rare in most any game these days.I've seen some other reviews complain about how big hits send you flying, but that's actually a part of player skill, and it is explained multiple times by NPCs that you can negate this by hitting the dash button just as you are landing, and though the timing for this does need to fairly precise, the game does explain how to safely practice this skill until you've mastered it.Did I mention the controls are tight? I'll be honest, slight gripe, everything is a little too tight. I don't really mean the controls, but the battles. Aside from most of the Legend of Zelda 2 style overworld battles, They're built like puzzles, which is great, I love the approach from a design standpoint, but once you figure out the puzzle, it's nice to have a little wiggle room for user error, which there is not much of for many of it's fights and challenges, especially along the main story line. They're tough, and while it's possible to beat all of them without taking any damage, some of them feel like a small Touhou fight. Even early on, the game doesn't hold your hand. That said, the puzzle mechanics to the fights don't get Rabi-Ribi levels of complex, and even when you do get hit, the fights are still rather doable, so long as you've figured out the patterns for the fight, and haven't completely refused to explore a little.The game plays a lot like an RPG, and I was actually a bit surprised, given the overall style, to find that there is no leveling system, and you don't really need the Rin (this game's currency) you're awarded for fighting all that much either, so aside from the occasional need for item drops, the game actually encourages you to avoid fighting when possible, and it's here that this little gem shines. I thought I was being clever avoiding fights here and there, but it quickly became apparent that the levels are carefully designed and very well tested, actively rewarding you for what would have in any other game been seen as clever, out of the box thinking, both with the more obvious faster or better way around an obstacle or group of enemies, and collectibles often directly used for character upgrades. It's no ordinary metroidvania, and I love that it actively rewards you for gaming it.Despite knowing that the difficulty the challenges in this game presents may seem daunting to some players, this is easily one of the best releases since Hollow Knight. Well done.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the best games I've played in a long time, and I outright disagree with the negative reviews criticising the combat, movement or puzzles in this game.Both the combat and movement have depth and a learning curve. Mastering both the combat and movement gives you a huge boost in performance when tackling bosses and parkour. As for the puzzles, when strictly following the main path they are simple yet rewarding. The difficulty ramps up when doing optional content, as it can get much more complicated and they don't hold your hand. Some of the puzzles even have multiple ways of solving them which further pushes the immense amount of freedom in the way you play. I'm not saying that the combat, movement and puzzles are for everyone and i'm not saying if you dislike these aspects you should change your mind or your wrong. I just felt compelled to write this review, after seeing people criticise aspects of Phoenotopia that I truly enjoyed and wouldn't want changed.Thanks for reading

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenotopia: Awakening is the closest thing to a 2D Zelda game that I have played. That being said, it is also a distinct game. - In traditional Zelda games, to progress through the game, the player MUST have the proper dungeon item. They may also get optional pieces of heart to increase their life. - In Breath of the Wild, all weapons are optional. However, finding good ones doesn’t require the player to go out of their way. There are both heart pieces and stamina gems, but the way to obtain all of them is clearly from beating a shrine.- In Phoenotopia, there are 3 types of "heart pieces", (one for energy, one for life, and one for optional weapon upgrades)  and most pieces of equipment  aren't required. There are also optional songs and optional battle techniques to improve combat prowess even more Because of this, the main focus of the game is on exploration.  Looking around for collectibles and solving puzzles is almost required to move on past the increasingly difficult combat challenges. Thankfully, it doesn't feel like a chore. Every treasure chest is cleverly placed, and each upgrade makes you feel increasingly powerful. The amount of content in this game is INSANE for a $20 game, and I have spent over 80 hours on the Switch version.Furthermore, the graphics are good with smooth animations, it has a very good soundtrack, interesting story and worldbuilding, etc. If you enjoy the Legend of Zelda or exploration, this game is well worth the price.
