_childDocuments_.review: The Epic Store exclusivity deal was a slap in the face. Don't do that again, Ska Studios.With that out of the way, the game is good. Great, even. More than a worthy sequel to Salt & Sanctuary.There's your metroidvania-style exploration, tool acquisition opening up more exploration, non-linear progression with some backtracking and such. A lot of platforming. Done well, some good challenges and overall interestingly designed areas to traverse, but with that said: Prepare for bullcrap. Some of it optional, much of it not. You will, in all likelihood, be knocked off of high places more than once, which often kills you outright and can potentially cost you a lot of salt (experience) and silver (semi-useless currency), though if it should happen, in fairness, you can always get more of both later if you need it. Salt can be recovered from where you died, unless you die again; silver, you lose half of what you were carrying... so spend it ASAP, after you unlock some merchants, and don't worry about it until then.There's also your 2D-ified soulsy combat, with blocking, timely block-parries, parry counter-crits (underwhelming in this game, to be honest, and they don't work at all on a lot of enemies) and a lot of rolling away from devastating blows, blasts and traps. Also you can hit things with your own weapon now and then, if you time it right. You die, learn, die, get better, and eventually you die less. Your character gets very incrementally stronger but the slope is as long as it is slow; along your journey, you can grow more than strong enough to beat down whatever you like.Into this ties the gathering, crafting and upgrading. There are materials used for healing potion charges and ranged weapon ammunition replenishment, kind of monster hunter vibes there. Also you track down bizarre, towering mages, fight them and absorb their essence, while also collecting some crafting and upgrade materials. Loads of different mages, which you chase down, fighting their minions as you go, until they make their final stand. There are non-mage boss battles, but most bosses in the game are mages; there's great variety among them, though, and each brings its own attack patterns and minion types. From mage and minion materials, you craft weapons, armor, accessories... all kinds of neat things that grant a variety of protection types, attribute boosts, special and active abilities. Example: A fiery Highblade (katana) can, with the appropriate character ability learned, ignite its blade in order to apply burning damage over time as it strikes. Combine that with a ring of fast stamina recovery and an amulet of fast climbing, and you begin to see the possibilities.All in all, the game is a rich and rewarding experience - if you're prepared to go in with the necessary zen mentality of accepting death as part of the cycle of learning and all that.Highly recommended for fans of the original, or anyone wanting to try a fun, oddball mix of Dark Souls, Monster Hunter and Castlevania spanning several vast, darkly beautiful realms.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of people compare this to Sanctuary, and I don't think that's helpful. This game isn't really a SEQUEL, except for sharing many systems and names with the first. Instead, this game merges the souls-like combat and RPG levelling from the first, with monster chasing and farming systems from Monster Hunter-type games.There are still traditional bosses who gate the metroidvania-esque upgrades which allow your player to access new areas and treasures, but they are much fewer in comparison to the mages (the monster hunter monsters), and honestly the bosses that I've fought so far are fairly plain in attack design. This leads to people who come expecting this to be primarily a souls-like to be disappointed.On the other hand, the mages are actually quite varied, each with their own "element", summon monsters, and attacks. They DO teleport around a small area while you chase them and get a couple attacks in. I personally don't mind that, as it gives the player some time to heal, buff, and deal with summoned monsters. They also usually just teleport slightly off screen, so you're not out of the fight long. One system I personally don't like as much as in Monster Hunter is the grinding. In which I mean that so far, there is virtually none. After killing a mage for the first time, their drops, combined with quest rewards, are usually enough materials to make the 1 or 2 items from their "tree" you want. And if you don't have enough resources, I've found that killing them one more time - which is usually quicker than the first time - will get you enough. I know a lot of people don't like the grindey nature of MH games, but I wish there were slightly rarer drops that give you a reason to fight each mage a few more times.Overall, I think this game is a better MonsterHunter-like than it is a souls-like. I like this game as a MH-like as much as I liked Sanctuary as a souls-like. And that's saying something, since I don't think there are any good MH-likes available.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of Salt & Sanctuary (played multiple runs all in co-op with my partner), I was initially a bit worried hearing that Salt & Sacrifice was apparently a bit different. Other reviews made me think it would be a massive departure from the first, and it is different, but there's less different than I was expecting. Overall, progression isn't tightly tied to Mage Hunts anyway, so there's no mandated grind.If you liked the first, I think you'll have a lot of fun with this one! Keep in mind though, I'm playing with online co-op (which has been flawless), and that has added a lot of fun as we discuss builds and where to explore next. Some bosses might be less enjoyable solo, but going hunting Mages together & exploring has been really great!Wishing all the best to the developers, thank you for a great game :)

_childDocuments_.review: I previously played this game on the EGS, so while my playtime seems low, this review comes from the perspective of someone who has beaten Salt and Sacrifice. If you want me to say whether I like this game or not, well, yes, I do, and I hope you do too. But my review comes with a caveat.If you are looking for a proper followup to Salt and Sanctuary that expands on what that game did right while alleviating or abandoning what it did wrong, you will not like Salt and Sacrifice.Sanctuary was a metroidvania with soulslike mechanics, while Sacrifice is more of a Monster Hunter-like with soulslike mechanics. Instead of one big interconnected world, you are sent into smaller, still interconnected worlds that, while still well designed, fun to navigate and containing some really fun boss fights, aren't connected to each other, making this less of a metroidvania and more of a Demon's-Souls-but-2D kinda deal. Additionally, instead of making the big-ticket Mages isolated story bosses you need to destroy, they're structured like a Monster Hunter hunt. Beat on them, they run away, you chase them and beat on them more, they run away, rinse and repeat until they finally stand their ground in an isolated boss arena.You are very much meant to kill the same type of mage over and over to grind out materials to make and upgrade elemental weapons. Which is a system I enjoy wholeheartedly, don't get me wrong, I'm a total sl*t for grindy games. But probably the most frustrating aspect of the mages is that they will spawn enemies exclusive to them during the chases that makes that chase so, so unpleasant sometimes. As much as I enjoy the hunts, it gets annoying really fast. This game definitely reeks of being a game that more heavily rewards multiplayer than single player.That being said, there are still aspects of Sanctuary at play here. The leveling system is the same, there's some new weapon types and a whole new set of throwing weapons, you still get abilities that expand how much of a given area you can explore, the combo system is still present(albeit a bit watered down seemingly), the gameplay is still as weighty as ever, and there are still unique bosses that are one and done affairs that are pretty darn cool. And there's some neat lore reveals for fans of the first game.Ultimately, Salt and Sacrifice is a followup that fails to be a proper successor to its predecessor. It's more of a sidegrade to the original game, doing some things better, some things worse, and doing some new stuff that won't always land. But on its own terms, I like it a lot. I just hope the next Salt game is a proper followup to Sanctuary.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played prior versions, but the game presently post patches is plenty of fun. It's not Salt and Sanctuary 2, but Salt and Sacrifice, so I expected as much; something familiar but not a sequel. So I treated it as such, and really enjoyed my time with it.Honestly I was very surprised, I went in with an open mind and thought it was more familiar than not - there's plenty of exploration, backtracking with new mobility options - the usual fare. I played three characters somewhat simultaneously, all different builds but keeping their progression generally the same so I could see the differences between builds. They all have their ups and downs, but I felt that stronger two-handed weapons are unmatched in damage output. Heavy armor and poise are also pretty fun to use together in both tanking and attacking through enemy hits.Mage hunts are fun, and an interesting addition to the formula. Because the enemies they (infinitely, until killed) spawn alongside them also drop crafting materials, I never had to really "farm" a mage to make whatever gear I was looking for. This meant they didn't overstay their welcome / get boring. Personally it was interesting for me to see what designs were coming next.There were a couple minor frustrations, but definitely nothing enough to soil the whole experience. Most issues I had just came from seemingly-odd late-game difficulty scalings. Lookout for the , that's quite a rude fight because of how small the arena ends up being, coupled with the enemy's tendency to create a lot of area denial and very high damage output. It's an optional boss, so it gets some leeway with me but was far and away the most frustrating encounter.Loved the music, I was surprised to hear that Mr. Silva didn't score it; Maclaine Diemer did a pretty good job of doing his own thing but keeping enough of that Ska Studios sound in there that I wasn't sure at first. I can't speak much for the multiplayer components sadly, but only because I like single-player games and didn't engage with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Not as good as Salt and Sanctuary and very different in a lot of ways, but still a great game, specially after the new update added fast travel to several checkpoints.Combat is fun, and I much prefer the timed block mechanic of this game compared to actively having to parry in the first one. _childDocuments_.review: After 100% completion, I can honestly say that this game is excellent. Is it perfect? No. Are there valid criticisms? Of course. But the game is not nearly as bad as many reviews on Steam make it out to be. Apparently, many are still salty (yes, pun absolutely intended) that the developers did not make the same game twice. I like Salt and Sanctuary, but I am equally glad that Salt and Sacrifice is its own game. What to expect from this game:(1) A plethora of different gear and weapons with a multitude of damage types (physical, fire, cold, poison, light, dark). You need to hunt mages and their minions for materials; the materials allow you to craft both armour and weapons. Some items can be found in chests, some can be bought with in-game silver from merchants. In some cases, you can unlock merchant items by killing non-mage bosses. There are named mage hunts, unnamed versions of the same hunts (tougher than the named versions), and fated hunts (which require tomes to unlock for each main area and reset every 24 hours).(2) Quite a lot of platforming. As you progress through the game, you receive more tools to explore the maps.(3) Soulslike combat in a 2D environment. Weapons have different attack combinations that cost stamina. You can attack, block, perfect block (parry), dodge, and jump. As you kill enemies, you receive salt (currency for levelling your character); if you die, you drop your salt in the place of your death and have a chance to retrieve it. If you die again before collecting it, it will be lost for good.Criticisms:(1) Poise has been useless so far, but the developers are currently working on making it more useful than it has been. In simple terms, even with high poise, you get ragdolled around like a toy pretty easily and stagger as much as in Dark Souls 3.(2) In some locations requiring a lot of perfect platforming, ranged enemies and mages can stunlock you to death as you have no iframes during such actions as ladder climbing and jumping from platform to platform. You can get knocked off platforms and literally fly across half of the map. (This is not an exaggeration.)(3) If you get knocked off a platform and die due to gravity, your salt will be where you died, that is to say, where you landed instead of where you were knocked off, which can be rather far away from where you were and need to go. In some cases, it is not worth trying to recollect the salt.I am going to update this review in case my criticisms get addressed with further patches. In the meantime, I still highly recommend this game if you like soulslike combat and 2D platforming.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for quite a few hours looking for an excuse to write a positive review. Sadly, Salt and Sacrifice is not a good game. If I wanted to compare it to Salt and Sanctuary, its predecessor, they wouldn’t even be in the same league. So I’m going to try to explain why this game is mediocre at best. It’s a metroidvania trying to be Monster Hunter, but it falls short. Boss fights are nothing more than a sad exercise in button mashing without much strategy, and almost all fights feel the same with little variation. The maps have a lot of verticality, which would make it interesting that you have to chase bosses to hunt them down, if it weren’t for the fact that absolutely any enemy (boss or mob) can send you flying with a simple attack and send you back in a rather frustrating way, if the fall doesn’t kill you. That is, if you haven’t found a trap in the middle of the map, which is there only to troll the player. One of the common mistakes that these types of games have is that they boast of having great difficulty when the reality is that their difficulty does not lie in their mechanics, but in the statistics of the enemies, which is quite frustrating. When I finished the game, I thought that a new run in NG+ mode would give me a new perspective, since the first run was too easy for me. However, I found that the enemies scale in power much more than my character can. This makes boss fights impossible in some cases where two or more bosses are in one part of the map and, in addition to the enemies that each one summons, there are also enemies from the map itself. If I can’t even see what’s happening on my screen, it’s not difficult, it’s unfair.Salt and Sacrifice tries to be something new, but falls short and fails to shine in any of its aspects. The combat is decent, but there is nothing better than in Salt and Sanctuary. The lore, as always in these games, is cryptic enough that I didn’t even understand the story well, and it invites little exploration. The level design is decent. Overall, it’s a game that scores 5-6 out of 10. And if compared to Salt and Sanctuary, it’s a “don’t waste your money” out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking to get this game because you liked Salt and Sanctuary, STOP AND READ first!  This game is not like its predecessor.  I'm currently 34 hours in and will only complete this game because I spent money on it.  I don't find it fun or entertaining, just frustrating.  So lets get into it.Compared to Salt and Sanctuary:It does not contain in interconnected world where you can move from on zone to another.  It seems as though the developer abandoned their original ideas to follow those that are proven or expected to enhance game play.  The sanctuary         system is not in this game, preferring to use a dark souls 3 hub.  It is the only place you can level, craft, enhance equipment, and move from one zone to another.  There are NPC here, but outside of purchasing a few items they are almost entirely PVP based.  Unlike the previous game NPC do not enhance, upgrade, or transmute gear.  They literally included these NPC to talk to, dialog that is exhausted almost immediately.  There are almost no eldritch horrors bosses to fight.  The main point is to hunt down mages, that once defeated appear through out the zones mostly getting in your way.  Which wouldn't be too bad if the only real way to gain experience wasn't gotten from them and them alone, mobs drop almost no EXP!  Lastly, when compared, the interesting movement and and abilities from the previous game have been dropped in favor of those from other successful titles.  Floating up wind currents, used in Ori, fail as they are never low enough and don't actually send you up is you have any horizontal momentum.  Grappling hook, used in Halo, are basically uncontrollable and often send you flying where you are not trying to go.  The grapple points are also often place horrifically.  Magic is almost gone, this game uses weapon arts, like in Elden Ring.As a stand alone game:I think this game is just abysmal even when you don't compare it too Salt and Sanctuary.  I would say that it can be described as either unrefined or rushed.  Bosses are not really that unique, they all seem to fit in the exact same hit box with very generic differences, they all summon minions and their move sets are fairly easy to see.  I think they were included in the world, outside boss arena, to solely pad out the game time.  34 hours is very long for a 2d game, especially when not fun, and I still haven't beat it.  Control and movement wise, I use the same controller I use for every other game and this game just seems to have issues.  It's not the very common occurrence of the game putting attacks exactly where you are dodging to, like input reading. Its not the dodge being too far to the point where it regularly puts you out of range to attack, especially when this game seem to seek to only ever give you enough time to strike once before you need to dodge again.  The real issue is that it seems to loose button inputs.  Need to grapple to avoid falling to you death, failed to accept button input.  Trying to use a ranged weapon art requiring you to hold block then press Y, get interrupted and get locked into a stream of melee attacks that drain you stamina.  Honestly, the thing that makes this game so frustrating to me is the damage sponge enemies, the utterly excessive traps with no visible triggers, and over reliance on enemies that that hid and pin you down to stab you to death.The developers had such a good jump off point with Salt and Sanctuary, but for whatever reason abandoned it and ended with a game that was enticing but ultimately enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great game, finished two playthroughs. On the first I took my time, did everything and ended up with a high level character. It got a bit easy near the end, but it was still a bunch of fun exploring, customising, and being strong enough to take down multiple mages at at time. Then on my second character I did more a rush to the end boss and was happily surprised to see the difficulty get nice and challenging, especially in the 'regular' level bosses, where playing more of a glass cannon build can be rewarded with more of a quick boss rush style ending. The game is fun. It looks and plays a lot like the first game, Sanctuary, I'm a little taken aback by how many reviews claim it's "not anything like Salt and Sanctuary, etc.." By my impression they are very similar games. Where Sacrifice adds handful of new game features, which all seemed pretty decent to me. I think more or less during the majority of the game you are running around doing the same things you did in Sanctuary. I love it! It has the same addictive nature. The environments are large, gorgeous, and full of details. The monsters are very diverse and challenging. There is a larger selection of items. The combat and build accessibility is refined. In my opinion Sacrifice feels like a very well made game that the developers put a lot of time and love into making.

_childDocuments_.review: I took the other reviews with a grain of salt (no pun intended) and thought maybe it's a matter of taste. Well, if it is, my taste is I absolutely hate this. In the first area I mostly had fun - a bit like Monster Hunter, good pacing.The second area was a bit iffy. Often frustrating, many unfair situations. If the signature of Soulslike games is "tough, but fair" or "if you die, it's your own fault", then this is not a Soulslike, and it begins to become evident here. Fighting multiple mages at once is fun at first but rapidly becomes a chore or a war of attrition. You attack them, maybe you die or retreat to get supplies, but it doesn't matter since most of the fights are persistent. Even so, most gear is crafted from mage parts, so you're going to be grinding. On top of this sometimes a mage may become completely entrenched on a platform with no way to climb up without being knocked back down.By the third and fourth areas the problem was very evident: Running through the entire hub every time just to go to a different area. Too many traps that are too hard to see and too hard to dodge. Most of the traps just send you flying off a ledge, but tend to juggle you. There's also terrible platform layouts combined with frustrating controls - dodge and grapple are the same button, for example., or how grappling itself doesn't work straight up and has no direction control, or how inconsistent air attacks can be done.I paid $10 for this but I still don't think it was worth the money. I hate to say it but my life would have been better if I didn't play this game. There's some good ideas in here for sure, but the execution is just not fun - this game is more like a job.

_childDocuments_.review: the bones of this game are decent since the last game was good but the rest just feels like one really bad design choice after anothermenus feel almost intentionally poorly laid outyour fire link shrine area is absurdly large for no reason. last game all your vendor"s used to fit on one screen essentially a few steps away from where you warp in where here you have to run up several cliffs to get to the only place in the game you can level up at.speaking of vendor"s the only thing you can spend money on is buying experience consumables or armor worse than what you start with.this game suffers pretty bad from the (what the heck did i just pick up syndrome) every time you kill a boss since almost all your equipment is craftedwhich brings me to bosses, which is pretty much all you do in the game. you fight (mages). every main quest you have, every side quest and every hidden quest is go kill a mage.  You have to chase them as they jump all over the map after a few hits 5 or 6 times before finally turning into a health bar boss fight. _childDocuments_.review: Can start this review off with the fact that, this game has a pettable cat. - 10/10.Anyone to compare Salt & Sacrifice and its sequel, Salt & Sanctuary would tell you the same thing - You must be crazy to leave a negative review of this game by comparing it to Salt & Sanctuary. They are both incredibly different games. That yet still both work cohesively well together, and yet with very different gameplay & focuses. However, and still further yet, both remain incredibly fun and cohesive, immersive, fun games with interesting worlds & story-building.This is my second purchase of Salt & Sacrifice after it's post-Steam release off of its Epic-exclusive purchases. Everything from its unique, beautiful & atmospheric art style to the design for the enemies, bosses & items the Inquisitor will be using to slaughter their way forward to devour wretched hearts, to mini-bosses and small details go a long way. The bosses are quite fun, and there's quite a lot. Story-telling is everywhere, the world presents itself really well, and there are NPCs who will tell you all about the world, old gods, and inquisitors path to ruin. The progression is almost Monster-Hunter esque with the mage hunting and craftable mage rewards, unique to each one in design and function. Weapons also have runic abilities, and are quite well done in both visuals and function. Build theorizing lacks a little bit in variety, and there aren't a whole lot of weapons for each weapon type - But this is is game that is constantly expanding and improving, and has more than enough to make up for it as is - Co-op is incredibly fun, the game runs well and has AMAZING sound design and music at times where it is present - The UI is incredibly simple to move through, and works really well to compliment the rest of the visuals. - Game difficulty is well-centered, a good mix between too hard, well mixed, or easy. It sets the player up well for success, typically giving you the effective weapon type to hunt your next mage before you have to, and the difficulty is extremely well-paced for newcomers, with learning curves that are pretty feasible - Rolling is generous, and they even go a step further to let you grapple onto Mage faces and destroy them up close for even more openings, a feature I did not expect them to utilise so incredibly well with player utility items used in and around for map exploration.Salt & Sacrifice offers immersive level design with more emphasis on exploration & metroidvania elements, there's wall jumping, grappling hooks, a glider to soar through wind currents, and even a 'luminstone' to reveal hidden platforms to traverse. There are tons of unlockable alternative routes to go through, and it makes the maps just so much more cohesive. There is convenient fast travel after non-mage bosses, and the new update 'Traitor's Tomb' expands both the story and content much further, there is much more polish. For a team & studio as small as Ska Studios, of which people fail to realise is not a Triple AAA company or large team, are crazy to think that this game isn't big for how much work goes into it. It nails replayability, difficulty, and diversity. Each update heavily improves its functionality, flow & fluidity, and polish.I do not have anything more than lots of praise to Ska Studios, another Ska Studios project that goes above and beyond my expectations and beliefs of what they are capable of, constantly improving both their own work and their games. With lots of community feedback that they feel they are very tied to, and how active they are in listening, responding to, and working on improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Soulslike, but in 2DWot I liked- Same cute art style;- Real deal DS-style online feature. You can help others, invade, protect or be invaded;- Various enemy types;- There are like 4 big maps to "explore";- Some bosses actually have many cool moves;- Fighting mage minibosses is quite fun. And there are many mage minibosses;- You see most equipped gear;- Monsters fight each other;- Cool gestures. Unique 2 player emotes.Wot I disliked- Weapons have few moves and veer towards spamming;- Combat feels unresponsive: your basic dodge seems to be designed for dodging huge monsters, so it's pretty useless in fighting normal-sized enemies, and huge enemies quite often are too big to be dodged, so dodge is pretty useless against them either;- For some reason the skill tree occupies only 40% of the screen and on top of that it is zoomed in and cannot be zoomed out. Very unfriendly;- The skill tree looks impressive when you see it for the first time, but you soon understand that it contains 2 things: stats and weapon/armour proficiency - nothing more;- "Exploration" in this game deserve quotes - it's bare bones: open a door to hunt for a mage, hunt a mage to open a new door, repeat;- You cannot track the mages you meet in the world which makes running after them confusing;- Inventory management is a step back from your regular cumbersome unfriendly soulslike game;- The game provides you almost no respec option - that's too cocky for an indie game;- Game's too long. You have to hunt for the mages too much and the fights are not that different;- Enemies can gank you at respawn;- They make you watch through the end credits;- Bugs, glitches;- Coop might be broken: you are invaded or sent to people who sometimes are way out of your league.To sum it all up, the biggest problem of this game that even though it looks nice on the surface… the surface is all that is there. All the mechanics are 1-inch deep, all you see in first 10 minutes of the game is basically all there's there.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This is Salt and Sacrifice's combat mechanics with a new gameplay loop and a greater emphasis on crafting to find your optimal weapons and armor. Solid 7.5/10 for me.Salt and Sacrifice is the successor to Salt and Sanctuary, but it is not a direct sequel either in terms of the story or in terms of the gameplay mechanics. People going into this thinking this is just going to be a direct sequel that builds on the lore or continues the story or even in terms of the world will be disappointed. People have likened the gameplay loop of Sal&Sac to Monster Hunter. I don't have any experience with MH, so I can't really say whether this is true or not. I'll just do my best to explain the experience:You play as a criminal who had the choice to either accept execution for some crime or become an undying Mage Hunter. Choosing the latter, your curse is to go about hunting these powerful magic users and to stop whatever force is behind the creation of Mages in the first place. Rather than having one huge world map like Sal&Sanc, there are multiple smaller areas to explore. And I do mean "slightly". Each of the maps that you can explore are pretty sprawling in their own right, and all of them have areas that can only be accessed by finding the right tools and upgrades in later areas. In most instances, these areas lead to optional bosses or treasures, making it rewarding for remembering that your new tool had a purpose from several worlds ago.As you go from world to world, you find the mark of the Mages' influence, giving you the ability to track them down on the map. Rather than tracking them directly to a boss arena, you fight them all across the map, chasing them back to their arena where you then have the final showdown. Destroying the Mages and their minions will award you crafting materials, each mage having an armor set, several weapons, and several amulets and rings that boost various aspects of your character. Given that there are over a dozen weapon types, it becomes a bit of an interesting surprise as to when you're going to find the next best weapon or armor you are after. With the right stat investment, however, most weapons within a class are pretty balanced to one another, such that the fun of finding a new weapon may be that it more closely matches the stat investment you were after or its damage types give you more versatility against different kinds of enemies. It is here that I will address the complaint of "grinding". I personally did not find the game very grindy at all. You can re-fight mages using a variety of methods the game provides, and I think overall I spent maybe 2 of the 42 hours in my initial playthrough grinding mages for one specific top-tier weapon. I'd consider that a reasonable percentage of game time, overall.With the bevy of weapons and armors in each class, the game felt like it gave me a lot of room to experiment and tweak my build for what I liked. No matter what way you are building there is going to be at least 2 main-hand and 2 off-hand weapon types that complement your build in some way. Then it's just a matter of gittin gud and putting the mages to rest.There's also a healthy amount of bosses and side-quests that are completely optional and entirely missable. In my case, I missed 10 achievements on my first playthrough, 3 of which involved NPC side quests, and 4 of which involved bosses I just completely missed. As if the allure of trying out a new build with new weapons wasn't enough of a reason, this gives the game plenty of replayability and shows how much the game rewards exploration.Finally, the story. I would say that the story here is even more bleak than its predecessor. The devs did a good job of spreading the lore into multiple aspects of the game, from optional dialog to the enemy design to the weapon descriptions; heck, for the true lore-gluttons, every node on the skill tree offers a blurb of text. And when you get to the end of the game, if you've taken your time and spoken to the people along the way, you'll be sufficiently moved by the endings and their implications.In the end, this was a fun game, and in my mind, a worthy successor to Sal&Sac. I liked this enough that I will absolutely be doing at least one more playthrough to get all the achievements I missed and try out some weapon types I didn't get to try yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, doesn't deserve the hate it's getting. It's not Salt & Sanctuary 2, so don't go in expecting it to be. Still mainly a Souls-like with the combat and build making systems being pretty much the same as in Sanctuary, but with a few Hunter-like elements thrown in. Sanctuary might be 2D Dark Souls, but this one isn't 2D Monster Hunter, not at all, so don't go in expecting that either. It's its own thing, a bit experimental I'd say, but it turned out well.A lot of the issues other people complain about have been fixed with the latest update. Or maybe never existed in the first place? Idk, I only started playing recently. Bosses juggling you around isn't really something that happens. There are a few combo attacks, but they usually deal around the same damage in total as a single normal attack.  With some of these reviews I wonder if people even know that you have iframes on rolls, because honestly, they're making it out to be a way bigger deal than it is. The biggest danger is getting stunlocked because multiple enemies attack you at the same time or getting punched off a cliff (although the fall damage is extremely forgiving, you gotta be in free fall for a couple of seconds for it to be lethal). And while multiple enemies can swarm you, they will also fight each other, so just use that to your advantage. 75% of the time enemies will be pre-occupied when you arrive and you can just attack from behind.As for the gameplay, basically there are 5 different locations, each being a big and open map with various sub-areas that are interconnected like in Sanctuary. But the main locations are disconnected and accessed via a hub, like in Demon's Souls. The exploration is very similar to Sanctuary, with some backtracking to access pathways that require specific tools. There are regular bosses spread throughout each map, but the main combat loop comes from Mage hunts.The hunts can be divided into 2 parts. First you accept a mission to hunt a specific Mage (there are a total of 21 different types) and proceed to chase it around the map. During this stage the Mage will rarely actively attack you and instead mainly spawn minions. Regular enemies, other Mages and their minions as well as hazeburned enemies (which only spawn while a hunt is active) will all be on the map alongside you and the Mage you're hunting. It's basically a free for all brawl. Once the Mage receives enough damage it will flee to another nearby spot on the map (always an open spot, they never spawn in tight hallways or something, the game has lots of big rooms) and if you repeat this enough times, you'll enter stage 2. The chase phase really isn't too troublesome, there is no time limit and you can even rest at a "bonfire" and restock your "Estus" in the middle of it without losing your progress. In the second stage you'll enter a proper boss fight with the Mage. Once you get close enough to it a health bar will pop up and walls will be erected around the area, so you can't run away or get punched off a platform. This is where the Mage will actively attack you with its full moveset and no longer spawn minions, although if minions or other enemies were present at the beginning of the fight they will stay there (and possibly fight the Mage alongside you). Mages as well as their minions drop materials specific to that kind of Mage, which you use to craft gear, same as in Monster Hunter.The new DLC adds a 6th area to the game, but outside of a boss rush-style arena (which is an awesome addition) there are no Mages here, it's purely Souls-like in this case. You unlock it pretty early on, but it's kinda divided into 3 sub-areas with big difficulty differences, so I think you're meant to leave it after killing a sub-area boss and returning later once you're stronger. It's not a small DLC either, it has various hidden paths and a total of 4 bosses (one being a secret boss). The setting is probably my favourite in the entire game and it adds to the already very interesting lore. Honestly, the only complaint I have about the game is the balancing in terms of raw numbers. At some point, roughly halfway through the game, everything seems to be turning into a glass cannon, both the player and the enemies. You start 1-3 hitting all the mobs and a lot of boss/Mage fights are over within less than a minute, whether you win or lose. Which is a shame, because some of them have cool movesets that would be rewarding to learn and master. But in practise you mostly end up killing them before they get use to all of it, or they kill you ofc. If everything did like half damage, the game would be more fun imo. Hopefully a future balancing patch will change this. Other than that, it's a nice game, with unique gameplay and a banger OST (the Mage theme goes hard). I have done 2 complete playthroughs so far and unlocked every achievement, all of which was a fun time. I definitely plan on making more characters in the future for various different builds as well.I do still prefer Sanctuary and I do still hope that Ska's next game will be more like that again, but I don't think Sacrifice was a waste of a game. I would also like to see it getting a sequel at some point, ideally with better damage balancing and a bigger grind. Perhaps even higher difficulties/ranks, like in Monster Hunter, instead of NG+, since I found a bunch of fights, particularly the Mages, were too easy (but part of that was the damage you deal ofc).

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying the game, but I'm very much doing so in spite of its design, not because of it.This is a metroidvania without a map. Intentionally so. And it doesn't do anything with that intention. You don't find a deeper appreciation for the game's mechanics because it's missing a map, and you don't engage with the game's world in an interesting way because it's missing a map. It's just missing a map, which sucks.Worse, this is a metroidvania about backtracking. Hundreds of times, with default enemies that give basically zero exp, trying to remember which of the dozen identical doors just unlocked because you cleared a miniboss or which of the dozen identical heaps of rubbish still has ghost juice on it that you need to rub to fight the next miniboss.70% of the game is tedious memorization and backtracking without a map. I'd love to know what the design rational was for this so I know what types of thinking to avoid.So then, is combat better?No.It's weird to think about the Dishwasher games, because they had fluid, fun movement tech and were genuinely enjoyable to control. Then the developers made Charlie Murder and the controls were less fluid and more janky. Then Salt And Sacrifice, where the controls are janked to straight to hell. You do fortunately have some hyper armor when you've been knocked flying sometimes, which is good because even with an aggressive poise build most normal attacks from anything will send you flying. Enemy attack hitboxes are also the size of the moon and not clearly communicated by animations and *can* juggle you if they find their way past the hyper armor, which they do often. Your attacks, on the other hand, have hurtboxes smaller than their animations. No, I don't know why. Everything is scuffed, everything sucks, but combat does get a little more enjoyable when you play cheap.Salt And Sacrifice is a game about using your tools to overcome crappy situations. The controls are a crappy situation, enemy hitboxes are a crappy situation, so you cheese ranged weapons and consumeables to supplement your melee attacks.And there's even a difficulty curve to this. The better you get at cheesing the game, the better the game gets at making its hitboxes awful and limiting the fun you can have playing it.For example, ranged attacks use consumable resources which you have to farm. Why? You already have a limited capacity you can carry without going through a lengthy crafting animation. You've already limited how much a player can spam them in combat. If they're meant to be powerful but scarce, why do you get one or two arrow crafting mats from every generic mob you fight?The controls for firing ranged weapons also feel *awful*. I can't stress that enough. Hold LB + aim with right stick + fire with X. TF am I supposed to be pressing X with? My tongue? So you end up doing a *lot* more jumping neutral shots than aimed ones because even though gravity is cranked up 1000% on your projectiles and they immediately drop like a brick once they're out of your bow, you can kind of time them into an enemy that's walking towards you.Despite, y'know, *all* of this, Salt And Sacrifice does have some cool elements too. I genuinely like the aesthetic and the setting, and the Monster Hunter style minibosses are a cool mechanical element. The skill tree is *alright* (though highly committal for reasons I don't understand,) and the parts of exploration where you're not tediously backtracking feel engaging. With some aggressive patching, this could be a game I'd recommend to any soulsvania fan.As is, you need a pretty moderate tolerance for jank. If you have that, you'll have fun. If not, and if it hasn't been patched by whenever you're reading this (11.29.23 posting time), you're going to bounce off hard.Edit: One last thing, which I'm including in case it helps someone out. The running kick is a better opener than any light attack. Also, light attacks are for stunlocking enemies that can be stunlocked. If you want quick, reliable combos with decent damage that you can tech roll out of in a pinch, you want the heavy attacks, which don't stun. No I have no idea why Salt And Sacrifice is like this.2nd Edit: Rolled credits. The game was noticeably easier after discovering that your heavy attacks are for fast, non-stunning hits, and that your running attack should always, *always* be your opener for melee. That said, grab hitboxes are massively scuffed, hitboxes in general are scuffed, the game is just scuffed. And it looks nice enough that the stiff controls and weird hitboxes feel extra bad---everything that isn't the gameplay is pretty polished. My review is still a thumbs up, but barely. There's better janky soulsvanias. Probably get this one on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been getting a bit of flak and while some of it is deserved a lot of it is not, so I will go into the good, the bad and the ugly.The Platforming is a direct upgrade to Salt1, while sometimes challenging and sometimes frustrating, but ultimately fair in the end. The walljumps and inquisitor tools you pick up over time not only allow the game to more effectively build in verticality, it also rewards players for returning to older maps and explore them for additional goodies and loot. In the end a friend and I went through a trial area that tested your ability with the games platforming.The Cooperative play in the game is absolutely seamless, Attacks that enemies do as well as everything else that you can hit are all performed clientside, allowing you to play without issues with friends in cooperative play. I've played with a friend on another continent without any observable lag on my end.The fact that a modern game has the capabilities to be played with the minimum requirements being essentially  without issues is honestly great. A friend of mine from brazil plays with the computer equivalent of a rusty toaster that dies when having discord and chrome open at the same time, and his computer ran the game without issue. The fact that it runes on hardware that's practically 20 years old is impressive to say the least.The combat is done well, it is reactive and it neither feels too strong nor too weak. Poise works for smaller enemies and allows you to tank a hit or two, but heavier opponents require either dodging, blocking or perfect blocking (the game's equivalent of a parry). I have to deduct some points for how some of the boss attacks seem a bit spammy and they ALL have the ability to ragdoll you, and it can get a bit jarring sometimes (looking at you  ). Though ultimately the game has been extremely enjoyable for me.The map design is honestly as always excellent. The hand-drawn art really brings forth the place you're in and it is clear when you know you can get to a place or not. The Doors that open up after certain bosses are clear in when they are accessible. But it is also confusing and often by the time new passages open up you will forget where they are. This leads to a lot of backtracking and getting lost, but I feel this was intended with how many secrets are strewn about.Note: With this I do not mean coop. I mean multiplayer through the used of multiplayer items in-game.The multiplayer while not dead is somewhat slow, sadly. It can take a while before you are being summoned for cooperative boss hunting, or invading someone. However I believe they do a decent job at multiplayer balance. Seeing as you can be summoned at any range of multiplayer, but get scaled down to the level of the player.Armor feels like it is improperly balanced, namely heavy armor. It feels like the defenses do not give you enough to make up for the loss of evasiveness that light dodges give you. With some of the bosses light armor with light rolls makes it much easier to defeat them than medium or slow rolls do. I've finished the game with heavy armor and a medium roll, and especially in the DLC for some of the bosses light armor was a necessity.Note: With this I do not mean the final bossDuring the final boss after defeating him, you have no choice but to go into NG+, losing all key items. While this was likely predictable, it was still in a bit of a sour taste, as I wanted to do a few more . This means that by defeating the final boss, I was locked out of some end-game content, which was a tad jarring for me. All in all, I believe this to be a good game. While not as good as Salt & Sanctuary in terms of boss fights and lore, it is still a greatly enjoyable experience. I will give the game a solid 8/10 up until the end after the final boss.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fairly different from the first one. Story is nothing to write home about and aside from the repetetive grind for ressources propably the worst part. Addition of Multiplayer (many other reviews say it has problems) and amazing boss-design is the best part.+ As mentioned leveldesign is good, areas connect to and fro via shortcuts or metroidvania items. The game also is not one interconnected world like the first game and instead lets you use a portal to reach different areas via a runesystem. Those areas are fairly big thou and are made up of quite diverse areas in and of themselves.+++ Enemies look amazing and the higher their tier is the more attackpatterns they have (trashmobs > ranged > challenging variants > minibosses > proper bosses / mages), there is monster infighting which I like a lot. Had 4 mages duke it out and I was the victor at the end, really nice.You guys should cut down on the hazecursed enemies those are spawning endlessly all around you during magehunts and will attack you and the mage. Or make them NOT spawn near ledges it makes some jumping puzzles impossible as they will attack you as you are approaching and will just knock you to your death over and over.+ The mages are quite divers and are mostly fun to fight, but...- The magefights... oh boy. The bad part is that someone had the foolish idea that there should be bosses that run away from you like in monsterhunter, but it doesnt work in this game. Monsterhunter has amazingly choreographed combat and interactible traps and the like, this game has nothing like that.I had it happen that mages ran away into areas I had not yet unlocked which is dumb, there literally was a boss and a whole section between me and the mage. One way to go around this problem by the player is to explore first and clear as much as you can before farming, but a patch would still be nice.- To top it off you have to redo magefights, with them fleeing and all that, over and over for crafting and upgrade material. You will get a pointer to the mage and a heartbeat as a signal but this doesnt work in freeroam straight away. No problem during a quest to hunt one, need an item to unlock those for a map thou > generates new quest every day. But have fun getting one that has the tier of items you need...My character has reached level 100 and I got enough upgrades so that I can do the fights really fast most of the time, but mindless grinding shouldnt be needed to enjoy yourself (I upgraded and tried lots of weapons and this also artificially raises your playtime a lot.If you look up the weapons then the whole magic of finding out what you can get from defeating the mages is gone... Come on, make us hunt them once and give a simple way to fight them again after or something else to get materials.- The mages can summon creatures at any time during the fights and those guys can be as dangerous as a miniboss. This can be very frustrating because there is NO cooldown or limit, they just spam those guys out and some even buff the mage... Had a Mage  summon a floaty boy which gave him invincibility (remember those eyballs from the first game, those) and he summoned a second one while he was running away, the first caught up and made it very hard to keep figthing the actual target.The mages also have  of attacks that are AoE and will hit the whole arena and they are also able to spam these , get hit by the first shot of a machinegunbarrage and you might eat the whole thing depending on poise. Fix this via cooldowns and add more melee > which would let the player actually parry them (you cant ). CORRECTION, you can parry, but it will not happen much. Most mages dont attack melee enough to break their stamina! Bad design.- Juggling of your character is real and it ruins the experience when it happens, same with being flung off into all kinds of direction, especially off of things... Having a fight against a windmage on small platforms combined with incredible "throwing" ability of windmagic is no fun and the summons can do it as well. Making the damage lower each time you get juggled is ok as a fix, but the spam needs to stop as well. At least blocking works but the are NO shields in the game and only vanguard weaponclass gets the privilege of blocking 100%, hope you have high stamina for that thou.+/- The devs have been really sadistic with some of the placements of traps, ranged enemies and destructable groundsurfaces. Very hard to see activators. Be aware!By the way parrying works differently than the first game, you perfect block now. Need to do it multiple times in a short timeframe for the break of the enemy-stance to happen!+ The whole armorsystem and damagetypes have been changed. This is a weird one, they removed slash, piercing and blunt damage (its all physical now) but added a lot of other damagetypes instead that are mixed. This adds the need to have some alternate damagetypes at hand for some fights. The mix of damagetypes is also amazing! I like the possibilties!Did some testing some bows say poison but dont poison and one has a spore status effect which works. Is this a bug? The frostbow works well for applying statusdamage? I can be poisoned with multiple types at the same time thou, even stacking poison??I did some testing and only runearts can poison on a weapon that has poison as damagetype, weird and confusing for the players.+ I have a bow that deals light+fire damage for example, this is really cool but I feel like there are physical variants missing that are viable for use, even higher tiers are lower damage (need to check after update, scaling changed). There are concoctions which can be used to add elementaldamage to your weapon and it seems to work with any mundane weapon.+/- Something about regular weapons is that compared to the mageweapons, which you craft, have a weaponart while regular weapons cant. I have not seen one that has an ability. Missed chance, add the ability to find arts and perhaps even change scaling through them! Yes that would be like Elden Ring but that system is amazing and could be build upon! Please consider, also add more of those weapons. + Heavy weapons interrupt properly now in the latest patch! Thanks devs.+ Armor, poise does work how you expect it after patch, but there is a weird thing about light armor there is only some that have poise, is this intended?Heavy armor has really good poise but is  heavy... have fun spending points on encumbrance, you will likely mix and match or level your stats/use item effects.- Before I forget, character creation... You cant see the stats of the classes and cant tell what your starting gift is... perfect design choice . Fix that asap. You can guess from the name what you will likely get but that is bad design. Make it clear!Long story short, the devs have been on holiday while the game was out on Epic, well I guess as there are no means over there to report bugs (funfact there is in game) to them or tell them grievances (no forum on Epic) that is how it had to go.I am teasing, the whole situation feels like a joke. You had a year to tweak the game to make it fully enjoyable and messed it up. This game can be fixed with little effort (first Patch was ok so far, but still ways to go)> Add cooldowns to things, make the materials (higherlevel magefights) easier to access and fix what seem to be bugs. Think about adding some more fun gamemechanics like interactibles on the map! I like the game. It has so much cool stuff, but the issues are just frustrating! Careful thumbs up for now!

_childDocuments_.review: Gotta say....with the latest patch the developer has really addressed a ton of the complaints I've had with my experience playing. The game still has some fundamental design issues that would make me hesitate to recommend this game to someone who usually doesn't go out for this genre. But if you're reading reviews for this game, you obviously know what you're getting into, and I can safely say that you'll get your money's worth.ORIGINAL REVIEWSuper disappointing. Everyone said this is NOT Salt and Sanctuary II. Sadly, they were right. Game feels like it predates Salt and Sanctuary. Such a huge step backwards in so many areas. I really want to love this game. I loved Salt and Sanctuary. I want to love this developer. I want the developer to make more games in this genre. The developer clearly has a talent for 2d souls like games. But there are just so many confounding choices that were made in the development of Sacrifice. I want to chalk up the game's faults to a compressed development time and rush to release to meet Epic Game Store requirements. But the game has been post release for 1.5 years and it's just now hitting Steam in a state that feels shockingly identical to it's original release on EGS. Which is to say, this game has really lost the thread of what made it's predecessor so well loved.Let me start with some things I like about this game. Love the look. Game looks great. Animations are on point, weapons look great, bosses look awesome, and the levels look good as well. Skill tree and character development are straightforward and easy for any new comer to get a handle on. The crafting system feels like a real hit. I think the dev really nailed the crafting system and I'd say it's absolutely an improvement over Sanctuary. Being able to craft multiple pieces from each boss by downing them more than once feels great. No more waiting till your new game plus to try a different weapon crafted from the same boss. Early game play feels great. There were a number of hours early on where I was like...I dunno what people are talking about, this feels like Sanctuary 2. Seems great. I definitely had a lot of fun starting out with this game.Now to the problems....The scaling in this game is just so far off the mark. There is a point in time before new game plus, where even basic enemies are deleting the player in a single short string of 2-3 hits. And I'm not talking light armor, 25% roll here...I'm talking full on upgraded heavy armor in every slot, soft capped 40 END and capped at either 50% or 75% roll. And it's not simply that Vitality is nearly worthless (despite running close to the soft cap). And it's not simply that even basic enemies do too much damage in a single basic quick strike (which they absolutely do). It's the fact that you combine this with the reality that even wimpy basic enemies have more poise to withstand interruption than a player in full heavy armor using a greathammer/greatsword/twohander. I cannot count the number of times, my 'quick' attack animation which started before the enemy's attack gets completely derailed and interrupted by their basic quick attack. Additionally more than half the time you actually do land damage first, they still manage to get their attack damage out, when conversely you do not in the same situation reversed. Fighting regular enemies in the game becomes a massive chore after the first 3 areas. It becomes so annoyingly time consuming and frustrating that there is simply ZERO reason to give a f*ck about actually playing the game, other than doing the bosses. Ok fine, so we'll just skip all the regular enemies because they're time consuming, frustrating to deal with, and worth virtually no salt to kill anyway. Oh wait....here we are, running through the rest of the game just trying to skip straight to the next boss. So if you like speed running, this game probably still has some value. But basically once you're halfway through the 4th area, everything just becomes a chore. The fun has all evaporated away. The bosses fights themselves feel like sh#%. The bosses in Sanctuary felt difficult but fair. And honestly I spent a lot more time wiping on them than I have in Sacrifice. But a number of the bosses in Sacrifice have just been a complete luck fest. It's simply a matter of attempts before the luck of the their attacks and placement allows you to get in the necessary number of hits. There are just too many bosses that create unavoidable damage situations for melee. It's like the dev just didn't want you to play melee. It's crazy. This game just BEGS to be cheesed. I've taken my heavy armor STR twohander/greatsword/greathammer build and had WAY better results just hitting bosses with throwing axes form distance. I wish it was a git gud situation. I really do. I know I could certainly improve. We all can. But even though I'm not spending as much time wiping to bosses in Sacrifice as I did in Sanctuary, they feel so much less satisfying to defeat. It's just a matter of so much luck involved in the difference between defeating a boss w/o getting hit once and getting put in a situation where this is no way to avoid taking a hit to get subsequently 100-0 w/o the capacity to recover. There are so many design decisions that really sap the fun out of the game and I think a lot of other reviews have really highlighted these issues. I don't want to belabor the negatives endlessly despite my desire to rant about all the frustratingly baffling choices that brought this game in it's current state to my desktopI really wanted to make my first run though the game as melee which the general consensus was that it was significantly more challenging. Sadly it does not feel commensurately more satisfying to play. Conversely playing a ranged build allows you to avoid dealing with a lot of the design issues since cheesing mobs/bosses form distance makes them ridiculously easy.The idea of Mage hunts was a really great idea. But wandering mages resetting on death just leads to massive frustration when so many of them can take you from 100-0 in a single attack or chain. It really is baffling. There is essentially one way to play this game. Skip regular mobs, go straight from one named mage hunt to the next named mage hunt. Skip everything else. Skip unnamed mage hunts, Skip wandering mages. Skip fated mage hunt. None of the activities in this game reward you for your time. Which would be find if the moment to moment game play were satisfying. So if you find it satisfying rolling past every normal mob, and shooting bosses form the other side of the map, boy is this game for you.But if you want to play a melee build. And you want to fight your way through the game. And especially if you're deluded into thinking you'll have fun with 2handers....better check back later to see if the dev has come through with some changes. Or just wait for Salt and Sanity. I know this dev can put out a great game. Sanctuary was not a fluke. I'm going to choose to believe that getting into bed with EGS tied the devs hands somewhat and that next time around the dev will have the time and freedom to give us a game from the heart. Am I deluding myself in believing this? maybe. But despite my heavy disappointment in Sacrifice, I still hope this developer will continue making games in this genre. And I will hold out hope that Salt and Sacrilege will be even better than Salt and Sanctuary.

_childDocuments_.review: Its like if you slammed salt and sanctuary and the worst aspects of monster hunter together. It's level based salt and sanctuary, but most equipment is locked behind "Mage" drops, which you get from hunting mages. These mage hunts are awful. Repeat numerous times, before they decide to stop and just fight you with only a couple attacks they have that they just spam over and over. In monster hunter, you can learn the monsters attacks and learn to avoid them. In Salt and Sacrifice, you can't. They come out with next to no warning. This applies to monsters too. The mage will spawn some monster that instantly grab attacks you, and by the time you kill it, the mage has run away, or spawned another monster to grab you again. It's the monster hunter equivalent of having a monster spawn a jaggi every time you hit it, and it constantly runs away, until it eventually stops and just spams a handful of moves it has, that come out with no warning.The game has an idea, but the idea just doesn't work. Salt and sanctuary and monster hunter just do not mix. I'll be refunding, and reinstalling salt and sanctuary instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game on Epic because I liked it. Bought it again here so I can enjoy it on the go with the Steam Deck (and I just simply prefer Steam)It is not like Salt&Sanctuary, which seems the point most people complain about. It has a monster hunter style "mage hunt" system, which can get tedious/boring if you play it for too long, in my opinion. For me it is a game I play for maybe one or two hours at a time, then take a break. The graphics are a clear upgrade to Salt&Sanctuary, the animations are good, you can pet the animals in camp. It looks lovely. The latest big patch changed a few things, how you lose salt/silver when dying and how you can get juggled by the enemies, it was overall a very good patch and addressed quite a lot issues. Overall I do recommend this game, but don't compare it to Salt & Sanctuary, because it feels nothing alike aside from the devloper and the art style.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty much crap. That comes from someone who liked the first game in the series "salt & sanctuary". While the first game had it's fair share of problems, it always came around with something that's actually good, be it charm or some nice exploration or fun weapon/rings combinations.Salt and Sacrifice feels like a quarter of a game. Like they really had an idea for the first map of the game and started designing it, then after a while the ideas or the money ran out, and they put together some uninspired stuff, mixed up with whatever, wrapped it up with poorly thought mechanics and game design and shipped it. The combat ranges from passable to frustrating, be it because you can't block most stuff without taking damage or depleting all your stamina, be it because your dodge puts you in a different postal code than the enemy attacking or because everything dishes out a ton of damage. The game devolves rapidly into identifying the enemies you can stun lock and kill with light attack spam or the enemies you must dodge farther away than the hit (so you end up somewhere even close to hit the enemy back) and hitting 2 light attacks, never more. Almost every boss, elite, whatever can be beaten by this pattern... dodge in a further distance, hit 2 light attacks, repeat. And it's not that it's a cheap tactic that you use to win, it's literally the only thing that works. Dodge is wonky, you can't combo, blocking is too much risk for little to no reward.In conclusion, this is what happens when you have some good ideas, but lack focus and polish to turn those ideas into something fun to play. They took the roots from the first game and ruined it trying to go for some Monster Hunter shenanigans that's not polished or developed either. The exploration is boring, the combat is bad and the unique mechanics detracts from the game instead of complementing it.Very disappointing. Oh, also the art is kinda bad. The first one was ugly as sin... this one is a little better, but still very ugly...

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give a cautious recommendation. Firstly I enjoyed It enough to platinum it both on PS4 and PC that said its not without its issues. The Onlines pretty dead but the covenants are cool if you get lucky enough to encounter people their is also no lvl cap to assist or invade I've been invaded and assisted by lvl 999 players at lvl 31 and vice versa. The Game itself has a nice soundtrack, atmosphere and combat, Also unfortunately a lot of cheap gotcha moments with both traps and enemies. Getting Chain grabbed to death in Altarstone by the British there was not fun. The player model is way too easily ragdolled by a bunch of things despite poise/heavy armor which can be frustrating and the stamina and endurance systems aren't doing enough always felt like I'd run out of stamina even at 20+ will and equip load is honestly kinda ♥♥♥♥ lvl 40+ endurance will get you a midroll though if your not going super heavy with armor which is too much stat investment imo. The Mage fights are fun and can get outright chaotic and evil and They do fight eachother and also have unique minion designs for each mage though obviously some model and move reuse it does get tedious constantly chasing them though. Finally perfect block (you should still block occasionally) instead of parry just feels kinda awful give me back my salt and sanctuary shield system. The skilltree is large the weapons are fun the glyph (magic) system is you'll either love or hate it but I enjoyed playing more with them unlocked rather then not.

_childDocuments_.review: Salt and Sacrifice is an amazing game. Ignore the negative reviews complaining that it’s not Salt and Sanctuary 2. It's a different game.My wife and I were a little disappointed on our first playthrough on the PS4 because it was so different than Salt and Sanctuary, but it grows on you and we both now appreciate and love Salt and Sacrifice for what it is. After playing through both games as much as we have, we’re actually glad SKA Studios mixed up the formula a bit for this one.Chasing Mages around the map may feel annoying at first, but once you start to know the maps and the Mages, know where they will go next, and what to expect when you fight them, it becomes a lot of fun. The level designs are a fun mix of platforming and enemy encounters just like Sanctuary. Because they were purposely built for chasing Mages around, navigating through them has a good flow to it and feels natural. I also really like that nearly every weapon has magic abilities. It makes each weapon feel unique and opens different strategies for combat. One issue we have with the game is how unbalanced the player builds are. DEX builds are terrible and make the game significantly more difficult and frustrating. My wife always plays a Mage in both Salt games because she likes to stand back and toss magic while I melee the bosses. I like to try different builds with every playthrough.After completing the game with several different builds, we found mixing a strength and endurance build with a strength and magic build to be the best co-op combo for taking down Mages.If you were a fan of Salt and Sanctuary, Salt and Sacrifice is more than worth its asking price. The combat feels more refined and the change in gameplay and systems gives it its own personality. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!
_childDocuments_.name: Salt and Sacrifice

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRThe game's good.But takes some getting used to.I'll get this out of the way first, this isn't a Sanctuary 2 like I know a lot of us where hoping it'd be. And if you go into this game right after Sanctuary, you'll get hit with a learning curve. It's not steep, but it is noticeable. And I'll just say, gone are they days of face-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the big monster bosses to death before the second phase starts.I'll get the meanest issue I had out of they way first.Mage-Fights.Most of what you'll be fighting boss-wise are the mages, and you'll be fighting A LOT of them of all shapes and sizes.Unfortunately, while they all look different, they each follow the same pattern of spawning a few minions for you to kill, before running away a couple times before the real boss-fight starts, which's where the monster-hunter aspect you may've heard about comes into play. And the most thinking you'll do in in these "chase phases" of each fight, is leading other monsters/mages in to pull aggro from the main mage you're hunting. But that's about it.Unlike most of their scripted, non-mage counterparts there isn't much strategy to fighting the mages themselves. Other than keep dodging or blocking attacks until there's a gap in their spell-spam. And if possible exploit their elemental weakness.Killing the mages and their minions gets you your materials for elemental themed weapons and gear. And one of the few aspects I actually like from fighting the mages. You'll get a bit of dialogue from each one before they truely die. Ranging form angry last words, to crumbs of the overall story.The other thing that really grated on my nerve was the platforming. It all works 99% of the time, but ever now and then you won't grab a ledge, the grappling hook won't grapple, or that stupid sail-cloth won't work and you'll plummet to your death... This was an issue in Sanctuary too. Fall damage in 2D games is always annoying, andIt's upsetting this wasn't addressed in some way. (At least the wall-jump is built in from the start this time)Especially when your platforming around those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ green knights, that can jump almost anywhere and EVERY hit from their glaives send you flying! >:(♥♥♥♥ the Mireguard, I'm glad their stupid swamp was destroyed!Also there's still no dedicated map mechanic, and more that once I've had to google one to remember a quicker route somewhere.With the negative stuff out of the way, I'll move on to what I actually like in the gameExploring each area from top to bottom is just as, if not more so rewarding than before. Knowing the terrain you'll be fighting on when hunting mages can at times give you an advantage over them. And there's enough landmark-like locations so you're less likely to get lost. That said, a map will defiantly help with subsequent playthroughs in getting to latter stages faster.Combat's just as enjoyable as before, and the dedicated ranged weapons are a nice change. No longer will you have to lug around a bow in your second weapons slot just to pull enemies out one at a time.Early game magic isn't limited to just fire and lightning spells. And if you see a mage use a spell, chances are YOU'LL be able to use that same spell with one of the weapons you craft from the materials they drop.So all and all, the weapons are way more diverse, and fun to play around with.Wish I could say the same for armor...The old system is still here, and heavy armor is almost always more of a hinderance than it's light counterpart. Not taking hit-stun with poise is cool and all, but avoiding damage altogether is just always going to feel better. And this next point is a nit-pick, but design wise I don't care for most of the new armors. Fashion-Souls this is not.I suspect this's due to the new PvP aspects of the game, and being able to know exactly what your up against when you get invated/hop into the arena. But I can't say that for sure.This one is small, but the inclusion of more NPC's dotted around the explorable zones in a nice touch. Even if most of them are PvP faction people. Really makes the world you're in feel alive. And a place you're actively fighting to save. Even if in typical souls-like fashion, all seems lost.Story-wise it runs the same vein as Sanctuary. Bits of lore scattered though item/enemy descriptions, and short story segments in the skill tree. There's a few things hinted at  in the Traitor's Tomb "DLC" area that came out recently that may or may not elude to your created-character not just being some random criminal off the street. But it's nothing concrete, and you're meant to draw your own conclusions about it.Overall, if you liked Sanctuary you'll probably like Sacrifice. But be warned, it's not a direct sequel,  there's less Dark-Souls in the formula this time around, and the grind for certain weapons/skills/equipment is real.Also don't ask my about the PvP/Online stuff. I haven't bothered with it, and don't plan to.That ♥♥♥♥'s for try-hards.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this for a while now, and while yes, it's not really a Salt and Sanctuary 2, it still is fun in its own right.So hear me out for a bit.Salt and Sanctuary is among my top 5 favourite games, Sacrifice? not quite, but it is a game that I enjoy and would see myself playing with other equipment sets, as I did with Sanctuary.So yeah, I'd agree that this didn't need to be directly linked to Sanctuary, as it probably made people think that it would be the same gameplay wise, which it isn't. At it's core it is a Soulslike yeah, but the inventory and Monter Hunter elements are what make it different, instead of a single fully connected world that you explore, you have a hub area, from which you can go to 5 (At least as far as I've seen, haven't beaten the game yet, but I'm close) Areas, which I'd say are love or hate, I'm fond of them.So here I'll list things that were in Sanctuary but won't be here- Sanctuaries as a whole, NPCs are found in areas and only then do they come to the main hub- Since there are no Sanctuaries, there are no Creeds or Religions.- AIR DASH (smh on this one)- Salt Charged enemies after you die to them- Weapon Transmutation- Standard Parry ( Changed for a "block just as you're being hit" way less op imo)- And other stuff I can't recall atmNow, stuff that Sacrifice introduces (That you might consider good)- Actual Online (Co-op, Invasions, Temporal Help, PVP stuff, lots of ways to go about it)- Greater inventory slots, and 2 new equipment slots for a necklace and knife- Better (in my opinion) Ranged Weapon System ( Ranged weapons use their own slots, and are not shot until you press the attack button, also more variety on the kinds of weapons)- Major Focus on Elemental Damages- Running (If you run outside of combat it doesn't consume stamina, this small detail is so delightful, because I've never seen it before)- Option of setting a checkpoint without resetting the enemies- Storage for itemsIn conclusion, is Sacrifice a bad game? No, I don't think so.Does it pale in comparison to Sanctuary? Yes, the tones feel completely different, and Sanctuary made more of an impact.But as stated before, the gameplay differs quite a bit from Sanctuary, so within its own right, it is a fun a cool game.All things said though, I do want a Sanctuary 2, hope the folks at Ska Studios don't forget about the old ways, if they want to make another one of these, that's fine by me, but just, also keep the Dishwasher/Sanctuary like Games please.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't typically play hyper difficult games; I've never played other Souls-like games;- I enjoyed this game.  It being a 2D game made it more approachable for me — not that I have difficulties in playing 3D/FPS games.  The speed at which you can get back up to confront the same boss and navigate the Metroidvania-like landscape is quite enjoyable.- The ability to play cooperatively (and without strangers) cross-platform is a big plus for me!- The "on-boarding"— in-game explanation of what-is-what, think tutorial — is lacking, the game assumes you're already familiar with other Souls-like mechanics;  i.e. "What does  do and why is it the other attribute with an icon next to it?!";  And most wikis on this game continue in the same vein, every-gamer has obviously played every other game; Why can I refund some skills but not others?!?- For a brutal game — blink at the wrong time and you're dead — I was surprised the game displays decorative doodads in the foreground which may hidden or otherwise hinder your vision (and I'm not talking about indoor/outdoor transitions);  But it's not  prevalent to render the game unplayable;  Still…

The level of difficulty right off the bat does not allow for gradual progression to build up your character, you practically have to grind for hours against low level enemies just to prepare yourself for a boss fight.
