_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I never review games, but I had the urge to make an exception here.I want to start by saying Salt and Sanctuary is one of my favorite games of all time. I loved that game from the word go, and beat if numerous times in various ways. Even for the shortcomings that game had, there was still so much heart there and nothing that outright killed the experience or my adoration for the game itself.This is not that game, nor is it a sequel. It's a hollow shell, the empty flesh suit of the game I love, draped over some grotesque bubbling mass trying to imitate the motions of a Monster Hunter game.While a 2D monster hunter clone sounds good on paper, this game really did not execute on that vision at all.Many other people have articulated better a lot of the grievances I have here, so it seems a waste to just repeat the same points you'll see on any other negative review here. I'll just say I agree with more or less all of them.I just felt the need to say that this game didn't just disappoint me, It legitimately broke my heart.
_childDocuments_.name: Salt and Sacrifice

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could just leave a review without a score because it's so hard to do with this game.The recommendation comes with GIANT asterisk, because while I personally had fun I don't think that many people will and games is such a disappointment compared to Salt & Sanctuary.The heavy oppressive atmosphere from first game is gone, the cool unique bosses are replaced by just a handful of notable examples and everything else just being Elemental-Force-Of-The-Month mages that feel very same-y, and whats worse, starts showing up during normal level exploration immediately.Fun crafting system from first game where you transmutate your basic weapon to eldritch artifact is replaced by generic monster hunter mechanic of grabbing tons of same weapons but doing different elemental damage so you can dispatch mages weak to that element faster.This game just feels at times like your generic AAA slop that was manufactured to meet as many current popular trends as possible without really wondering if it's gonna work.Monster Hunter is popular? Let's add hunting Mages over and over again for materials.Dark Souls is popular? Let's add souls invasion and co-op systems - because yes that is here too, and I don't know why.Due to that, metroidvania aspects are now left lacking as game is now hub-based so the feeling of finding new areas and finding connections between them is very diminished considering you just teleport between them using your hub teleport and they are not connected otherwise.At the end this game feels like it's lost it's unique identity and that's really sad considering S&S1 was phenomenal.I still had fun which is why I'm recommending BUT I only had fun because I like -vania games, Souls games, and Monster Hunter clones. If I disliked any of those genres I'd probably dislike this game too, so if you are not like me you'd best avoid this, especially if you liked S&S1 as you'll only find disappointment here.
_childDocuments_.name: Salt and Sacrifice

_childDocuments_.review: Better character progression and upgrade system compared to Sanctuary. Upgrades are more accessible and you don't have to squander upgrade materials generally speaking. "Magic" is much more accessible than in Sanctuary due to it being attached to weapons. The story is not AS good but it's not bad either, it's quite sufficient. The levels are dope as hell and the bosses are great. Honestly love that you get to fight the bosses as much as you want instead of 1-offs. In my estimation, the main reason people seem to not like this is just because it's not Salt and Sanctuary, which is pretty unfair. It's not trying to be Salt and Sanctuary and that's why it's not named Salt and Sanctuary 2. I love Sanctuary and I love this too. My largest complaint is the game is well-designed for PVP but it's not precisely, as one would say, alive.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I have mixed feeling about this game. I change my review from thumb up to thumb down for 2 times.EDIT: It is not as good as Salt and Sanctuary, especially the game sometimes force you to do mage hunting missions. Hunting mission feels tedious at first, but after you build up you character, it feels a little better. But I would say the pacing has some issues regarding mage hunting missions and difficulty curve.Base gameplay is fun for first 3 hours. It seems the cancerous in-air combos coming from enemies are removed. For the time being, I have not seen a more than 2-hit combo coming from enemies. So combat is still like the first game. The exploration, I would say it is worse than the Salt and Sanctuary. I skip encountered Mage Hunt opportunities for most of time, in favor of opening shortcut and finding items. So it is not super troubling for me, as I could decide when to start mage hunt at my own pace.However, after 3 hours you beat the initial 3 mages, the mage starts randomly showing up and enhanced version of some of these mages are very tough and probably unfair (Water mage is spamming bubbles all over in your tiny screen and and hit boxes are crazy). I would say as the mage encounters are not very fun and sometimes frustrated to see so many enemies in screens (which you have to carefully push through). It feels really bad to see so many annoying distractions. What makes it worse is that progression of the game sometimes tied to hunted mage count, it is kindly ruins the fun of any Soul / Metroidvania game. Imagine in Souls' games, you had to collect a fixed number of things to progress!However, after a few hours more it is more comfortable to mage hunting and it feels easier.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: buy it on sale, it's a fun game but short.Just beat the game at ~24 hours.  I will recommend the game and don't agree with all of the bad reviews/feedback on the game.  It's more like Salt and Sanctuary than other reviews would have you believe.  However, there are some gameplay additions that make it feel different:1) Hook mechanic like Sekiro.2) A bunch of bounty type side quests for specific mobs to get items for gear like Monster Hunter.3) A HP bar penalty if you die like Dark Souls 2.4) A reduction of useable potions if you die to the same boss too many times in a row.5) There are 1 shot mechanics, which is stupid af.  You will get juggled by mobs and it's obnoxious.I don't like 3/4 but the 1/2 additions are okay.  However, the world is much more about exploration and upgrades vs a new ability automatically opening up a new area.  The new weapon types and variations allow for a few various play styles (including a caster type).  It's a rather short game.  I have 46/56 achievements with my completion at 24 hours and could probably 100% the game in another 10 hours max.Having said that, it's a welcome addition to the Salt series and I appreciate the devs taking some risks with new game play options.  I hope they work on a 3rd and learn from some of the challenges/issues with Salt and Sacrifice.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm guessing all the negative reviews are because folks wanted a replica of Salt and Sanctuary - this one, while similar, borrows a lot from Monster Hunter. _childDocuments_.review: Alright, I don't do these normally, only other review was more of a joke one, but I'm going to try and write one of these, as I have a very good grasp of how this game works at this, played it when it released over a year ago, played it again at the end of last year, doing ng+ and then ng++ getting the platinum, and I finally got to experience the co-op and pvp invasion system with the steam release.As it is, I would describe this game as a cross between demon souls and monster hunter. Not dark souls. Demon souls.This itself is for a variety of reasons, the "Worlds" being smaller and disconnected from each other but more focused and tailor-made for the vibe each goes for, with plenty of really cool sites and vibes, the multiple stones you need for different upgrade paths, each tending to connect with a another depending on the kind of weapon/clothing, the focus on actually visiting later worlds before actually wrapping up earlier ones, having gained not only new mobility related tools, but also new and improved gear, (one could say that that one is more metroidvania-esque, but with the focus on different elemental damages and resistances, it reminds me more of world hopping in demon souls to get a proper damage type to trivialize another world, or when you have to kill and archdemon in order to get past the tower knight arena.). I could probably articulate it even more, but honestly, just the general vibe of both this game and salt and sanctuary make me think along the line of "flash demon souls". and of course, this game and it's predecessor have the customary, somewhat annoying, somewhat charming, jank to go with that sort of vibe, although I have never been one to be actually dissuaded by it.But enough of that, let's actually get into the meat and bones of the game. there are more "classic" bosses, and then there are the mages themselves. the normal bosses are simply the, go to the arena and fight them, type of deal, not much to say on the front, a lot of them are pretty cool, and invite a bit of curiosity into the story of the different areas, like the hag boss with the puppets stuffed with the souls of children ( no, you get no context.), or the two that remained. The mages, on the other hand, are really where the monster hunter inspiration bleeds in. generally, you either find a area of distortions and corpse's left by a mage, and you start a quest to hunt them, or you find them milling about in the worlds as your exploring them. either way, you fight them, they summon some minions, you either kill them and deal damage to the mage, and they teleport to a new area, or you focus on the mage themselves and deal enough damage that they teleport away anyways and your left with minions in the aftermath. Or, you know, there's the third scenario where either the worlds inhabitants are disgruntled with the mage appearing and start wailing on them, or they get disgruntled with you instead and they wail on you. or a mix of both, because their caught in the crossfire of the mage and you. After the mage is finally cornered and properly dies of a forcefully induced heart attack. you get to loot the remains of the dispersed magic, and make gear from it. rinse, repeat. it's a simple loop on paper, but anyone who has played monster hunter know it's much more chaotic and fun in practice.Now, there one thing that I would critique about this, and it is that this sort of gameplay loop does not lend itself well to 2d, especially with the customary vertical and platforming of 2d games. However, it is handled fairly well, and anyone who likes monster hunter or loves to see a boss get shredded because they decided teleport to the two heavily armored guardians in the blasphemers vault, and then found out that, it was in fact, not a good idea, all while you stand in the distance, will have a lot of fun with the actual gameplay, especially once they've found their forever weapon and armor (my favorite mages and their gear are the electromancer, and the dracomancer!).Now, the game play loop aside, there is co-op and Invasions and pvp, and OH MY GOD, somehow, by some Vor-Yuile begotten, profane miracle, they have managed to finally do what no one else seems to have truly accomplished. They actually made really good, non-jank online seamless invasions and co-op, and the factions are actually really fun too! Now, before I hype anyone who understands what in any gods name this means TOO much, keep in mind that the net code and servers are dodgy at times (I swear it's curse, and you just can't convince me otherwise at this point), so your fun may be cut short. That, and some of the factions take longer to join on a session do to the requirement of an invader in the first place (fortunately, these ones get equipment that lets them get summoned whenever, where-ever while they wear it, so their not just waiting around). You have blueheart runner's, who aren't there to kill the host and and co-op buddies, but are encouraged to be hunted down by them because the bluehearts spawn various dangerous entities while fulfilling their task, which are annoying at the best of times, and really nasty at the worst. you have the sheriff's, who hunt the blue heart runners themselves, as a bit of push-back, because the the blue heart runners can just run instead engaging with the host forever. there are the shroud alliance and the chaos hunger, which are normal invaders and abnormal invaders respectively. shroud is just out to kill the host and the chaos hunger is out to kill or help anyone kill anyone else, as long as there is killing that can be done. there are the oathbound, who are there to help stop the shroud alliance from murdering the host, and there are the dawnlight guard, who are your co-op faction. all around, really fun, and it has been a blast doing invasions and co-op. There is also an area that let's up to six inquisitors fight each other in a free for all, or in a duel (I have not been doing this one yet, the invasions have been too fun so far to stop.).honestly, I hold the game in equal regards with demon souls and salt and sanctuary, and other games I tend to hold close to my heart and come back to every now and then. without the co-op and pvp, it's as good as salt and sanctuary, worth playing through every now and then. with the co-op and pvp, its much better, and I would be willing to play this for months on and off for the sheer chaos and fun of it all, especially because (last little bit about the co-op here) you can password in a friend for co-op, and the two of you can share your progress completely and seamlessly until your done co-oping, AND you can still get a random co-op friend and start getting invaded while doing that, if you so choose.Honestly, after having said all this, I can't recommend this game enough, even though there are in fact flaws, like the before said monster hunter chaos not doing so well in 2d, or some of the random haze-burnt spawns on hunts making traversal to mages way more annoying than they need to be, or you know, some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane final mage battle placements in the later areas (trust, no one saying this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ actually know what their talking about half the time, because I can attest my self, you haven't seen ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game design in this game until you've fought the nameless diablomancer, or god forbid you fight a fated biblomancer in the temple of embers. THAT, is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and everything else is rather fine, whether in comparison or talking about "Muh character gets juggled to death" or not.). But flaws aside, it's just a really great game, with really great online features, and with a really great story. I would probably talk about the story and lore a lot more, but I have enough respect and faith in other people to not spoil them in favor of them just wanting to find out the story on their own, or with another friend.Alright, see ya, I've made enough of a wall of text, already had to trim this alot, lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Salt and Sacrifice is great. Just like Salt and Sanctuary and the other games Ska Studios makes, the game is very much so worth your money. While I can understand being mad over it having been Epic Exclusive starting out, something that is a terrible decision in my opinion in nearly every situation, but the game is great.I've heard people upset that mages flee. This game takes a monster hunter inspiration with its mage bosses, them being like the monsters that spawn in the field and the minions they summon being used to further defend them from your onslaught, as the mages and their minions are friends to nobody. Not even other mages. Can it be annoying? Yes. But is this a problem? No. Not at all.As for those who like salt and sanctuary more, I suppose I can agree. I went into this game looking for a good ol' Ska Studios game, and this game manages to hit a nice blend between Salt and Sanctuary and The Dishwasher with its gameplay, at least for me. Granted I forced Salt and Sanctuary to have a Dishwasher feel by speccing into light armor and multiple weapon types for good movement and speed fighting.Also you can pet a cat deer and a deer...deer. Is nice.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I want to love this game, and in a lotta ways I do, it really really really does not want me to enjoy playing it. I am a huge Salt and Sanctuary fan, and hope any comparisons I make below ideally are made between genuinely comparable portions of each game. I have not beaten the game, and will still try to, but I have developed feelings strong enough to feel like I needed to leave a review.Pros:-The levels, while not a fully open world like sanctuary, are still massive and sprawling and I found quite fun to explore. There's lots of platforming that visually spices up the exploration, as well as some really stunning areas I've seen (Dreadstone peak and altarstone in particular look great).-Enemy placement, while just boneheadedly cheap in some spots, is generally fair enough only get you once with the surprise and keep you on your toes without feeling like you're dying  and are also visually quite pleasing, fitting each level's design in a way that is reminiscent of sanctuary, but in a less desolate kinda way.  -Combat is quite changed, but not in a way I find disinteresting. It keeps the souls style stamina bar and rolls, but weapon classes almost feel more like monster hunter weapons in how niche they are (like staves having specific spells tied to each on and still functioning mostly as a melee armament). Each class I've tried out has a fair few combos that I get use out of regularly in different situations, and I find myself properly wanting to and actually using the different weapons and gear I make/find-The art is more or less a straight upgrade from sanctuary, as far as I'm concerned. It's the same style but detailed in the right places and with a helluva a lot more polish. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ love it.The ConsOk it's not actually a list of cons it's just a big con with a lot of moving parts. The main gimmick of the game, hunting mages? Completely unfair and incredibly frustrating. Brings the game to a screeching halt and is genuinely so bad that I find it hard to keep playing a lot of the time despite absolutely loving the rest of the experience. It's specifically that the mages are bosses on their own and are dangerous on their own, but now they also teleport all over the level (with all the regular mobs that are also there) while  spawning their own mobs and actually fighting themselves. This is just frankly too much ♥♥♥♥ going on, and it's so incredibly easy to get blendered in the blink of an eye. This is exacerbated by the fact that you get thrown by so many attacks, and any long distance you fall after being thrown you take full fall damage for, and the whole duration of the animation you're being thrown you are completely vulnerable to any enemy attack as long as it is not from the original enemy that threw you. And if you might remember, there's like trillions of enemies ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everywhere if you're fighting a mage (which is required for both progression as well as getting access to a lot of the sick weapons in the game that I've found so far). It's so ball-bustingly miserable that I find myself rage-quitting quite literally every time I have to deal with a mage after and hour, and it takes multiple sessions to get through any hunt. Nothing is quite as ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful as fighting your way past the same set of enemies (because you cannot ignore them, it will ♥♥♥♥ you) 15+ times only to make one mistake and ToD'd within a minute and have to do it all over again. I have no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clue what they were thinking when they were balancing the mages but they throw such a massive wrench into an otherwise fantastic game that I cannot in good conscience say I recommend this game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Salt and sanctuary was a game that I personally wasn't that big of a fan, clunky platforming, lack of map, questionable design choices hindered my enjoyment of the game, however despite these shortcomings i still really liked the art style, atmosphere and the bosses. I was kinda excited for salt and sacrifice since it had a lot of potential, but that was not the case. This game does so many things wrong and it's baffling how some of these mechanics made it into the final product. I played this game last year when it first came out and the experience was not pleasant. I had some hopes that some of the problems would at least get fixed with the steam release, seems like it was foolish of me to think that. My main gripe with the game is its idea of difficulty. The game thinks it's a good idea to have enemies who can bounce you around like a rag doll while you can't do anything about it. The game thinks it's a good idea that every enemy should two shot you, it thinks that it's a good idea to have 5 enemies in one spot who you can't just ran past them. It was bad on the release and it's still bad even though they had over a year to at least balance these problems. Mage hunts are still as tedious as ever, they never feel fun to do, and the game forces you to do them to progress the game. Some of these mages are horrendous, especially in the last two zones. Regular bosses are unmemorable and are easier than regular enemies in the zones that you are fighting them. I would only recommend this game if you have a friend who can play with you, it makes the experience slightly less frustrating. In conclusion i do not recommend this game, what a shame

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first game and so far, I love this one. Feels similar enough while offering a new experience.I think a lot of people are expecting a Salt and Sanctuary 2 and this is not what this game is even if they have a lot of similarities. The combat feels very much like Sanctuary but you run around a lot more, hunting mages and to me, it was a lot of fun.The learning curve can be steep and unforgiving. Sometimes, the RNG will get you and that can be annoying and frustrating but it is to be expected from this kind of game.As a reference, I'm really not a fan of Soul games and I played Sanctuary a lot (New game +2) and so far, I am enjoying my time playing Sacrifice. It is its own game, not a sequel to Sanctuary so if you have played it, please, give Sacrifice a chance by not comparing the two. They have similarities but they are also very different. Just appreciate the chaos of the hunts!//--- The game loopYou start in town, which is its own instanced level. There is a bit of exploration to do but it is mainly to interact with the npcs there (you unlock more as you discover them).Then, you use a portal to travel across different maps, where you will hunt mages. Hunting mages involves a lot of tracking and moving around the maps to find them and eventually, eliminate them.If you are curious while doing so, you can encounter npcs, new gear, ingredients for crafting and new "abilities" that will allow you to access previously inaccessible locations, allowing you to go back to previous maps to unlock whole new parts to explore.Eventually you can invade other players and you can also offer aid in pve. (You can get nice rewards doing that.)--//When I got higher level (30+), that's where the chaos and the fun got even higher for me. When you encounter packs of monsters fighting 2-3 mages that spawned at the same location, each with their own summons fighting each others... Pure chaos and fun.I mostly played coop cross-play (me on Steam and my friend on Epic) and we didn't have any issues, desync, lag or any problem joining each other.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Salt & Sanctuary, one of my all-time favorite games, and therefore bought this game in the hope of finding a game with improvements over the previous chapter. Instead, Salt & Sacrifice keeps pretty much the same gameplay, worsening almost all other aspects. First, it is NOT an open-world; you have to use a teleport to access macro areas (these macro areas contain interconnected micro-areas, but the feeling is much worse than in S&Sanc).In addition, the last areas have UNFAIR bosses (based on the pseudo-random pattern of the moveset, some attacks cannot be dodged at all). Another thing that bothered me a lot is the random spawn mechanism of common enemies during a boss "hunting" phase: it will happen sometimes that the enemy will spawn in front of your face, or during the boss fight, thus ruining your run (attempt) at random. It is a real shame, because Salt & Sanctuary was a diamond in the rough that simply needed polishing... The only thing it has improved in is playing with other players, nothing to say about that.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who never played the previous game and was looking for a coop game, this one isn't a recommend. Mostly because the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemy random enemy placement that chases you till the end of the world, while also juggling you off the cliff with the occasional boss fight (that later turned into regular mobs) are just frustrating. The coop works fine, almost like Nioh and some part are even kinder, which is better than Dark Soul coop. It's just that most bosses do the same attacks (there are around 5 areas with each having 6 bosses, 5 of those are not unique and are just different elements), the armor that you get only have number difference instead of unique skill, and the enemies will juggle you a lot.Bosses also have attacks that are too fast with spammable AoE, making heavy weapon almost useless due to its slow attack speed. I was able to play one because my other friend plays a light armor, so that if a boss attacks too fast they would be the one who carried the boss. Even with the balance update (that made the game from frustrating to tolerable, it's just not that good).My suggestion for the dev, stop any development on here or finish up quickly and just focus on the next sequel (or game). Also, don't copy other games without thinking "oh, what does this do to our player". Dark souls game is a very flawed games that have been reviewed by many people from a rose tinted glass. We have been getting so many souls like these past few years that another indie soulslike/metroidvania would not be a great choice for your next game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, but it could've been better. I recommend it if you want new experience. otherwise, get it on discount.I waited for a time for its arrival on Steam purely because Epic Games is...Epic Games. Much of my excitement was...slowly diminished and by the time I hit the last area, I can wholeheartedly say that there are much potential that got buried under a few problems. Allow me to list some.Exhibit 1: The Mages.They are painted as dangerous beings that I found quite...cowardice. You hit them twice and they summon their minions, then fly away after attack once or twice. This repeats too much time for my liking before the actual boss fight start. Then you face with more often then not, two results: you kill them very fast, or they kill you very fast. The different here is that unlike you, they use cheap, petty moves that once hit, just combo into another attack. Most of the time, I don't feel rewarded for killing a Mage, it comes more as a "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's done". And then you look at the list and now you realize you have a lot of the same thing to do. Some of the Mage is quite good and fun to fight. Most of them is middling. All of them is a chore to pursue.Exhibit 2: Blocking enemy.You can guardbreak enemy though you most often won't. Barring the basic goblin with the sword and shield, the moment an enemy guard, you may as well walk away. Wailing an entire stamina bar at them won't budge at all, and you more often than not, may get punished for that. The problem exacerbates when most of the summoned minions from the mage also have the same blocking problem. And being punished for playing the aggressor only to be heavily punished by a blocking small fry feels like ♥♥♥♥.Exhibit 3: The world itselfIt maybe due to the fact that Mages can roam around, but the world is much, much more empty then I expect. Now putting enemy literally everywhere isn't a good idea, but some of the area gives the feeling that "something should be here". That "something" can be some mage. But you, more often then not, won't see one there. Oh, and the trap. Traps are put in place they should be put. That's good. You won't see them though. They are so well-hidden that you won't notice them until you are already hit by it. And even after that, you still won't notice, because they blend too well with the environment.These are some of issues I have with the game. There are more problems with the game, but I think these are the core problem that should be fixed. I like this game, so I would like it to be more than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a good game? Yes, for the most part. It has issues, like enemies (and especially bosses) being too spammy, enemies being able to attack while spawning in, some enemy attacks having active hit frames before an animation even starts, having to chase down mages as they jump between rooms constantly, enemy attacks being able to just juggle/combo you to death sometimes, there's a bunch of flaws in the game that seem baked in or deliberately kept, a lot of which I would argue are pretty bad, and shouldn't be there. And yet I find myself unable to put it down because it has the sort of things you'd want from this game. Getting stronger, and beating stuff, as well as defeating certain things more easily than you did in the past, is pretty satisfying, if you like seeing a build slowly come to bear fruit, this game is pretty good at that. The co-op is actually pretty good, and it has a lot of quality of life things that bigger games be they bigger scale like Fromsoft or other indie games, lack.Is it a good sequel to Salt and Sanctuary? No. In fact, I would argue it isn't actually a sequel at all. Instead of a souls-like metroidvania, this is more... Metroidvania Monster Hunter with souls-like mechanics. As a sequel to that game, it's actually quite frankly worse in a lot of places. Gear is so limited in so many ways compared to the first, and even build and playstyle variety is cramped down in comparison, you can't mix and match weapons with shields anymore, nor can you 1hand or 2hand weapons anymore. Factions feel more like game modes rather than a character roleplay aspect that actually affected some important things like in the first game. The metroidvania style unlocks are more utilised as area gates and shortcuts, and not things that can also help you out in a fight or make movement more fast and fun from what I've seen thus far. Even the character creation felt like it either didn't add more from what it was in the first game, or had less to it (If you liked the creepy smiling face, I'm sorry, it's not here.) than the first game, you don't even get an in-menu explanation for what your starting item is from your crime choice.  I'm not really a fan of the timed blocking having replaced parrying either, the timing doesn't always feel quite right, and enemies are so spammy that I've found it considerably more rewarding, easier to do, and viable to just stagger bosses and enemies than get good with timed blocks. I think longevity wise, I'd play this more just because the co-op is significantly better in Sacrifice, especially now that you don't have to use remote play or parsec as proxies through local co-op like in Sanctuary.My feelings for this game are mixed. As its own game, I would say it's solid but has many flaws, as a sequel to Sanctuary it's taken too many steps back compared to forward, and some of those steps are in such different directions from the first that despite feeling like you're playing a Salt and Sanctuary in some ways, it's strange that it's even labelled as a 'successor' to it. I do appreciate that it's not called Salt and Sanctuary 2, but I still understand the feelings of disappointment that people have with this game that it's not really holding up to the first, because in a lot of ways it really does not. In some alternate universe where this was called something else, or Salt and Sanctuary didn't exist, I think people would've liked this a lot more.That all being said, I do recommend the game, but if you're expecting Salt and Sanctuary 2, either go in without thinking that, or skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the first game; this just isn't it.I have currently defeated two bosses, both forgettable and easy. I have found no secrets despite hitting every wall. The dodge rolls further past the enemy than my attacks reach, and there’s usually not enough time to catch back up to them before they start swinging again. The parry is gone, and now you just have a timed block that acts as a stagger, rather than the original system of block + attack, which just feels awful paired with the dodge roll. None of this was an issue in the first game. As well as this, the hub is super confusing to traverse, and is way too big. You have to go back to the hub to level up as well as do various other things, splitting the original camp in the first game into multiple areas. To travel back to the camp you have to teleport back, and upon reaching it, travel up to level up, then travel down through caves towards the portal, which you then have to put 5 specific runes in each time to unlock the ability to teleport back to your original location. This issue gets worse when you realize that there are two functionally different save points, one that you can travel to, and one you can travel from, meaning if you haven’t unlocked the former you have to carry on until you do, or lose progress in the map. This is functionally similar to Dark Souls 2/3, but made even more tedious, while the first game was functionally similar to Dark Souls 1. This whole system is just made unnecessarily inconvenient, and adds nothing to the experience. While I haven’t got much hours, I do not want to go over 2 hours and lose my refund period, and I don’t see myself enjoying this game after reading the other reviews describing more flaws than I’ve experienced so far. If I had to compliment this game, I do enjoy the grappling hook + wall jump. If I had to nit pick, I prefer the jump + dodge = fling yourself far bug in the first game, even though it wasn’t intended, making for some fun/fast movement. I just don’t see the appeal of this game. The combat isn’t anything special either compared to other games like Blasphemous 2/Hollow Knight. While Salt and Sanctuary was my first 2D souls-like game, and holds a special place in my heart, it’s been long enough that the standards for games like these have raised so much that this just feels out of place.

_childDocuments_.review: Salt & Sacrifice is a fun experience, whether solo or with the built-in multiplayer capabilities. The crafting mechanics for creating your own gear place the players' success firmly in their own hands, and the platforming of each stage adds a twist of risk to every area you play in. The addition of elemental strengths and weaknesses is a strategy bonus to any playthrough.I didn't play the predecessor, Salt & Sanctuary, and it's my opinion that the number of negative reviews for this game based on it being a sequel are similar to the reviews given to Dark Souls 2, which is saddening. A game shouldn't be getting mixed reviews because it isn't identical to previous games in the series, and taken by itself, Salt & Sacrifice is my favorite game of its kind.7 out of 10, but only because I'm not finished discovering all it has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my review of Salt and SACRIFICEI'm not really sure why people are giving this game a negative review based on the fact that it's not "Salt and Sanctuary"... You wouldn't yell at a chef for serving beef stew after he originally served potato stew. They both have their own merits and downfalls. You certainly can't fully discredit either for being unlike the other. That's just asinine. TL;DR: This is more of a 2D Monster Hunter set in the S+S world, and it's definitely worth playing through, especially if you have a few friends to play with or find some along the way.~STORY~Salt and Sacrifice is a overarching story about Sacrifice. A world plagued by mages, and the more of them you kill the more seem to keep coming up. It all ties together by the end, if you pay attention. It's a decent story considering I still can't tell you what most of Souls-likes are about.My main troubles with the story points are my main troubles with any souls-likes with stories. I can't seem to find when or where the characters will show up in the world. That part requires a guide for me, as it has in all the Souls games as well as Elden Ring.~GAMEPLAY~The actual gameplay isn't what most souls-likes are. It's more of a 2D Monster Hunter game. You hunt monsters with friends, you collect materials, you craft weapons with said materials.The gameplay is smooth as butter. You choose an initial "class" which basically just starts you off in different places on the skill tree. You have many different weapon types to choose from, a lot more than the previous entry, and it's a lot more robust in terms of skills, magic, abilities, etc.The other awesome fact are the different "tools" you find that helps you unlock different areas. It's a great system.My gripe with this system is that armor still has 2 types. Light and Heavy. You have to unlock them in the skill tree. But bosses can only give you 1 set. So you'll end up not able to get an armor because you wear Light Armor and not Heavy and vise versa. It doesn't makes sense in this kind of game. Armor shouldn't have been split into 2 sets like this, or behind a skill tree unlock. The game is hard enough having to upgrade all the armor it doesn't need all this extra to weigh it down.I do love the weapon system here, even with the unlocks in the skill tree, it's a lot of fun to get new stuff and try out what their skills are.The downside to that(or upside depending on how you look at it) is that boss skills are bound to weapons, and you don't inherently get them or anything. The upside to that is that you swap weapons and you have new stuff to use without having to bind the skills individually. The downside is that your weapon type might not come with good skills. The real tragic downside though is if you don't have the skill tree unlocked for using focus skills, then they're just dumb weapons that don't have any skills. That doesn't seem right, but it's the way it is.The game is too damn difficult for a monster hunter game though. Like in MHW, you kill these huge monsters and they are all initially hard, but then you get better gear and they feel like "Oh yeah, I could totally trash this mob in my sleep", I found a lot of mages aren't that. Especially because they are  leveled depending on the zone. So a sanguimancer will always 2-3 shot you. Despite farming him and being decked up in fully upgraded pieces of HIS armor, he'd still mop the floor with me if I wasn't immaculate in my timing. There's something so sour about that. The monsters mages spawn also go up and become really tough towards end game, despite your cool flame resistant gear or whatever, those little dragons the Dracomancer spawns can still two shot you somehow....The skill tree: Why? I have yet to really notice if dexterity or strength do much of ANYTHING in relation to actual attack numbers. Can anyone confirm? Do they? I felt this way in the earlier entry too. I upgrade gear and that makes a difference, but it seems the game doesn't actually care or the difference is so minute it might as well not care. So as it stands it's just a way for character customization and devoting yourself to one skilltree, instead of multiple.~ATMOSPHERE~I'm gunna lump music, ambiance, sound, and general vibes up here.It's a 2D platformer, so there's only so much the dev could have done to really spice things up. Random mobs don't really make a lot of noises other than their attacks. Mages are silent also. Would have loved to hear more roaring and hollering. But I guess that's because it's a multiplayer game? I dunno. With that having been said, there's nothing quite as satisfying as seeing the screen shake, the heavy guitar and drums swell as you rip the heart out of a mage and crush or devour it. That's VERY satisfying, even after the 40th mage.All in all my play of Salt and Sacrifice was very rewarding. Having beat it I will go back to play NG+. I somehow missed two types of enemies, and that's maddening, lol. I also didn't complete any of the NPC quests. It was definitely worth it for the reduced price from having owned S+Sanctuary. Having played it doesn't make me appreciate the former any more, like some may claim. It's its own game, and deserves the respect it was built with.P.S. Two dudes basically made this whole game... I don't see why there's all this hate for the fact it's not what they were expecting. That's sooo rude. They worked night and day on this for probably a few years, only to have a thousand die hard Sanctuary fans give it a heck tone of flack because it wasn't what they wanted.Well, message received, if the dev bothers to make another game(or can afford to) then I'm sure S+Sanctuary 2 will come out. It's basically a different genre of game anyways :P

_childDocuments_.review: This game is dreadfully mediocre because it takes a few different influences and meshes them together poorly. I'm not going to elaborate on everything here, but here is my basic gist of the game.The Good: Cooperative gameplay, weapons, items, world-building, characters.The Mediocre: Wandering mage hunts, enemy placement, platforming.The Bad: Single Player, PVP, character building, enemy design, perfect guards, stamina system, equipment loadsWhile it has been stated that the game takes influence from Monster Hunter, it's pretty much just in the way you gather items and make your weapons; otherwise it's a souls-like through and through. Most of the bad is the enemy design crapping on everything else. Most regular enemies have 1-3 attacks while mages have somewhere around 3-6. Most enemies constantly attack, and attack quickly, not leaving much room for anything really. Mages will chain attack after attack until you are dead, sometimes releasing multiple delayed ones at once (screw the sanguimancer and electromancer especially). This makes for boring, frustrating single-player gameplay, and just okay gameplay cooperatively, because playing with other people is fun.Here are the other main gameplay problems: Stamina is way too easy to deplete for how quickly enemies attack. With the speed of enemies in this game, it probably would have been better to just eliminate it all together, because you will all too often find yourself out of it, while the mage releases their never ending onslaught. You also lose so much stamina failing a perfect guard, that you basically need to be perfect at it to get anywhere. There's also the fun of having a slower reaction time to doing something else on a regular guard as opposed to a perfect. Stamina punishes the player, especially when alone while enemies are free-ranged spam lords of the worst caliber. The other problem is how long it takes to break enemy guards. Even with some pretty heavy weapons, tons of enemies will guard several strikes and then send you flying with a speedy strike.The roll is too long for how much platforming there is, and too slow if you want to wear any sort of armor without equipment load gouging. You'll fall off of many platforms rolling because it covers a ridiculous distance for the type of game this is. If you have a moderate or heavy equip load, most mages will catch you with another attack right after dodged the first one because they are too slow. Heavy characters really only work well in groups for a good chunk of the game.Single player just seems tacked on with how the enemies are balanced. They are made to smack around groups of people, and nothing changes when you play single player. It can all be accomplished alone, sure, but it's not fun, just annoying. PVP is much the same, there are a few factions, and it's just, who can spam quicker, or who's got that poise.Good souls-likes usually have a few flaws in some areas, but shine throughout. Salt and Sacrifice is full of irritating flaws, with the saving grace that playing with other people is enjoyable. It's the only reason I keep playing the game, other than my enjoyment of building characters. There's definitely a good game in there, but it really should have been baked and tweaked because the character speeds and enemy speeds are at war with each other. Really this game acts like it wants to be a hack and slash, but is bogged down by its souls-like and Monster Hunter influence. If they really just slowed down the enemies a bit, it would be much better. It's obviously balanced for multiplayer, but I'd prefer an overly easy multiplayer experience and a relatively tough single-player over what it is: A pretty easy multiplayer, with a hot garbage annoying single-player experience.This game only gets a recommendation because I'm still playing it for jolly cooperation.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. Is it Sanctuary good? No. But it's good. most of my problems lay with the fact that a lot of combats feel similar. While I didn't get a lot into the Runic Arts part of combat, the movesets of the weapons were somehow both too fast and too slow with little variation between moves. I also feel like this game isn't Salt and Sanctuary 2, but rather a totally different game that drew some inspiration from the original. When I bought this game, I expected something that expanded on the concepts of the first game, but got something totally separate. The familiar weighty combat has been traded for flashy movesets, and the beautifully crafted world disappeared in place of a level-based game, more like Demon's Souls than anything. The enemies are numerous and hit hard, and a lot of the bosses have frustrating, screen-filling attacks that shred your health.While you may think that this all amounts to a negative experience, I found the thing that fixes it all: Multiplayer. Having another Inquisitor joining you on your journey turns this frustrating game into a wonderful time with a friend, and allows you to revel in the flashiness and charm. Not only this, but it allows you to split a boss's attention, effectively negating the aggressiveness of enemies. A Souls-Like experience is traded for a Monster Hunter-esque bananza, and anyone who is a fan of local or online multiplayer needs to try this game out. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Not been playing too long but I was a big fan of the first game. Although this game is indeed quite a bit different from the first game I still find it really enjoyable. The fun combat and Metroidvania style platforming are back and the animations look and feel much improved upon from the first game. The game is similar to the first game in many ways but also much different. Its still a souls like but now there are boss enemies that you have to chase around the map while they spawn enemies around them until you reach a certain point and they stand their ground and fight you and you kill them. I may be in the minority but I honestly have really been enjoying this. Its put a really interesting twist on the side scrolling souls like formula that they really nailed in Sanctuary. Personally been having a ton of fun and I recommend it if you like the idea of chasing the boss around and collecting materials from their minions they spawn to make gear and weapons.  I found it really awesome. Been playing some on Co op too and the Co op is really great. Got it 35% off during the sale and don't regret it at all. I understand why the reviews are more mixed considering how different the game is from the first one, but at least for me, all the important bits were still there (i.e. gaining souls to level, fun builds and weapons/spells etc..) plus a new twist with the Monster Hunter style boss fights with the mages. TL:DR: In my opinion, been a really great game so far. Different then the first for sure but still similar on a fundamental level with some Monster Hunter boss chase elements thrown in. Would definitely recommend though. Especially on sale. Had I bought it at full price it would have still been totally worth it. Thanks Ska Studios for another really fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: Salt and Sacrifice is parts of Salt and Sanctuary, and Monster Hunter sandwiched together. With some interesting results.+Art is unique and nice to look at. +Wide variety of bosses, both "Salt" bosses and "Mage" Bosses +Soundtrack is okay, minimalist if anything. Creature and sound effects are good.+Hate it or love it. Salt has a way of ping ponging and throwing you off a cliff or send you flying 50 feet across the screen. Just laugh it off.+Variety of craftable armour  sets and weapons which are looted from the different mages across the game. Each with their own weights, stats, and art. Scythes, Daggers, Wands, Rods, Swords, Hammers +Hub world (I.E Dark Souls 3) , Shortcuts unlocked+Quite a number of varied classes and an expansive talent tree.Now for the negatives-So, mage hunts are a mixed bag. When you start a mage hunt you follow a trail and start attacking the mage, he retreats and you follow along. Eventually you will box it in an arena and have to fight it. The game is usually generous with save points, with a small run back. Hate it or love it i guess is your call.-Now even while you are on the hunt for a mage, there are other mages that can spawn on the map. This can be both frustrating and chaotic as you can either get dunked or the mages and their minions will attack each other.-Biggest gripe I have with this system is, when you down a mage he kneels and you get a prompt to hit a button to "assassinate" it. Only issue is if there is an additional interactive element nearby you usually get drawn to that instead of killing the mage. This is a very case select scenario though. Just a small grievance I have.Overall a different game than Salt and Sanctuary. Much less Dark Souls and Metroidvania, more Monster Hunter and semi linear gameplay route. Still has it's many moments of fun and two endings and new game +

_childDocuments_.review: Think this is one of those "It's a good game, but not a good *series title* game."After a bit of play, I can see why Sanctuary fans are disappointed. I think if they just titled this game something else it would have saved them a lot of heartache and allowed more expansion/exploration of mechanics, because a lot of choices do feel anchored down to the idea of being a "Salt" game.While Sanctuary is more of a Soulslike, Sacrifice is closer to a Metroidvania where you spend more time expanding secrets and traversal options than you do exploring a vast-feeling interconnected world. With that said there is a bit of an identity crisis because you can feel they weren't entirely willing to commit to being a Metroidvaina so it sits awkwardly in the middle of the two. This wouldn't be as big of an issue if it weren't that the game is still advertised as being the former. If you're on the fence, give it a shot but go in with the expectation that this is NOT a real sequel to Salt and Sanctuary.

_childDocuments_.review: Salt and Sacrifice is an ambitious expansion on the style and gameplay of Salt and Sanctuary, and the developers handled it well! The formula feels new and innovative without losing the core gameplay that I loved so much in the first game, and with the recent balance update, the difficulty feels fair. The boss fights are hectic, with a real sense of spectacle, and their craftable weapons feel powerful. The level design is a little too sprawling for my tastes, with the main “worlds” not connected, but it doesn’t detract from the overall experience. Fun game! I would recommend playing it on couch co-op for maximum chaos.UPDATE: I finished the game. Twice. And I LOVED IT. Everything feels really good, from the combat to the exploration (I think there are still some secrets in the DLC I haven't found yet) to the progression, and I actually enjoy the PvP. In a soulslike game! The chaotic 6-player multiplayer is one of the reasons I'm still playing this game, even after finishing it and trying a lot of the weapons and builds. Bang-up job with the game, Ska, and you have my utmost respect for sticking with it and fixing all the fixable mechanical problems people were complaining about. I look forward to whatever you decide to make next!

_childDocuments_.review: Following the previous beloved tale of "Sodium Deficient Dude Kills God"...We join yet another severely sodium deprived dude who has gotten so desperate to get their fix, they decide to commit a random crime, and because they are sodium deprived, they screw it up and get caught. The penalty is one of two options: enlist in special forces, or die. Quite the difficult choice, there...Our protagonist chooses the former, and their mission is then given to them: There's a bunch of mages screwing up the ecosystem! They are screwing it up so bad the game has become less of a soulslike and more of a Monster Hunter World-like! So it is our protagonist's job to.....KILL EVERYTHING THAT MOVES!As our hero/heroine dwindles the numbers of mages, the gods that are in charge of developing this world suddenly realize they were supposed to make a soulslike, and crank the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ meter to 11 as you approach endgame! We're talking juggling, one hit kills, quick moving bosses demanding precision reactions, and more move spamming than a Down-B Kirby in Smash Bros.And then you kill Gwyn and either link the flame and make the gods feel special or kill it and piss them off something fierce. GG.I don't think it's horrible, but I also came in knowing it was not going to be very faithful to the original. (Thanks previous steam reviewers!) If you want my honest opinion, it's an acquired taste, but it at least warrants one playthrough. Just to, at least somewhat, scratch that itch that Salt and Sanctuary left us with.Rating: Dark Souls II/10

_childDocuments_.review: The first time I played this game I absolutely hated it. Like a lot of people, I really really wanted and expected a similar experience to "Salt and Sanctuary". So going into this at first a lot of things were different/new/confusing and I ultimately didn't play it much after the release.But after a few months I decided to play the game with fresh eyes & not compare it to their previous game- and so far I've already sunk over 10 hours simply because I love Jolly-CoOperarion. :praisesun:Salt and Sacrifice seems to want to focus on an Dark Souls feel and overall Jolly Co-Operation and Invasion aspects of the game. If you've played anything made by FromSoftware you'd recognize a lot of things inspired from their games in S&S.A main hub or "Firelink Shrine", a literal sunlight Covenant ("Affirm the Dawn" is such a cute reference to "Praise the Sun" 🥺), BOSS WEAPONS 🐦‍⬛📣, Solid Invasions only when you choose to summon friendly Phantoms- not to mention the naked red phantoms that can one-shot you.I always get a chuckle out of the naked f*cks with a stick kicking my *ss, just like in the actual Dark Souls games. :praisesun:I also always get a smile when myself and 2 others spam the block or jump button anytime we gank & kill an overpowered red.A CAT YOU CAN PETIt's the little things in life lads.I also really like that Salt & Sacrifice has Cross Play & an Password system so you can connect to friends easily. There's also a covenant item that makes area monsters attack red phantoms!Overall I'm very happy with Salt & Sacrifice & I would happily recommend it to anyone who loves Souls-Like games.BUT- If you have played Salt & Sanctuary before PLEASE don't expect Salt & Sacrifice to be similar to it. It's a completely different experience altogether but it's a happily welcomed one & I'm so happy that I gave it a second chance. 🖤

_childDocuments_.review: A warning if you're going in thinking this'll be Saltier And Sanctuary or something, this is more akin to a 2D monster hunter than to a dark souls.  Salt and Sacrifice keeps the same aesthetic and combat style from its predecessor but reimagines it into a whole new setting with newer mechanics.  The biggest thing is mages.  You hunt mages.  You track mages.  You corner mages.  You kill mages.  You craft weapons out of mages.  It's mages all the way down and is the crux of combat and the purpose behind exploration.  The game is definitely enjoyable if you don't go in expecting another soulslike, but it does have its sore spots that might turn you off.  It almost certainly did for me. For one, knockback is everywhere.  Almost every enemy has at least one attack that'll send you flying and literally bounce you like a basketball off the ground, leaving you in a prone stat that, while keeps you invincible while you're on the ground, makes retaliating tough because most likely enemies will just knock you around again.  You see this as early as the second region with the aeromancer- the wind mage.  You fight him in a tree canopy high above solid ground and while his wind blasts don't hurt they'll toss you out of the area and kill you with fall damage.  It can be infuriating and by far the worst aspect of the game since you knocking enemies back doesn't have as much impact other than satisfaction you spiked them like a volleyball.  Even if you aren't immediately killed from fall damage, enemies tossing you off castle towers or floating platforms or from giant trees or into hazards is all over the game from moment one.  It could just be the downside of a 2D game but it's certainly tuned up from it was in Sanctuary.  That said, as I write this there is a balance update that should hopefully alleviate these issues if you're in heavy armor and wielding one of the heavier weapons.Speaking of which, another issue to consider, albeit much less infuriating as the one above, is weapon variety.  In Monster Hunter, from what I've been told as I haven't played it myself, all monsters' materials can make all weapon types.  So if you wanted a flame greatsword or an ice greatsword you're set.  This isn't the case for mages.  Some mages lack the katana options, or dual dagger options, or great weapons, their armor sets are either heavy or light armor but never both, their ranged weapon is only one type so if you're trained in, say, a bow but all they have is throwing knives you either have to respect or you're SoL.  It makes weapon options more limited because if you wanted ice daggers or a wind greathammer you'll be disappointed.  Personally it isn't a dealbreaker for me since even early-game weapons can be upgraded to  be feasible end game.Now, despite this I give it a thumbs up because while the knockback is annoying as all hell (I remember a recent incident of fighting a large knight on a tower when all his attacks have knockback hard enough to launch me like Jigglypuff at 300% despite wearing heavy armor so it took me 10 minutes to beat him because of the constant climbing back up to get another shot at him) and the limited weapon variety is disappointing, they don't strike me as dealbreakers.  Just something to get used to.  The core gameplay of hunting down roaming mages as they rampage through the maps while exploring massive areas that only grow larger the more travel options you obtain doesn't seem to get old.  There's no minimap but damage a mage hard enough before it escapes and it leaves a bloodtrail of sorts you can follow to the next location, and enemies normally found on the map by default aggro towards mages, who in turn aggro other mages in the area, creating a moshpit of chaos as 4+ mages in one section all summon minions and beat the crap out of one another.  There was at least one instance when fighting the venomancer- poison mage- where a nearby knight enemy that was fighting it for a bit literally leaped into the arena with me mid-battle and started slicing the venomancer up when I was nearly dead.  Not only did he get me the win but the poison from the venomancer killed him afterwards so I didn't even need to worry about him aggroing me now.I'm rambling, bottomline is if you want a 2D monster hunter with more than a few sprinkles of dark souls for good measure, give this game a shot.  Just watch out for knockback....

_childDocuments_.review: I'm kind of torn here, its a great game with some gigantic issues. I'll first say that the first one is better and if you haven't played it then don't play this one first. Full disclosure I'm not finished with the game and don't really know if I will finish it, I enjoy the exploration and love how bosses now drop materials so you can craft their weapons and armor. That being said, the bosses aren't great. I don't mind the mage hunts but they do get tedious, maybe the devs should tune down the sheer amount of them that you have to do. Plus, for goodness sake, stop spawning nameless mages during mage hunts! At times I've been fighting 4 different bosses at the same time. A lot of the non-mage bosses are complete BS, I'm talking about dragons who can cover the entire arena in a fire attack that you cannot dodge. Oh and that attack insta-kills you even with the best fire defense armor available at the time. This is only one example, there are lots of bosses that have attacks like this and fighting them pretty much comes down to hoping that they don't use that one attack that ends the fight. That all being said, some of the bosses are great and fun to fight and the worlds are great to explore. You can find NPCs hidden in the world and get them to come back to your "not firelink shrine" and become merchants or quest NPCs. All that being said, I enjoyed my time with the game and don't regret playing it for as long as I have, but I don't really have any desire to beat it. TL;DR Pretty good game if you liked the first one but be ready for some extremely unbalanced and unfun bosses.

_childDocuments_.review: Salt and Sacrifice is the follow-up to Souls-like dark fantasy RPG, Salt and Sanctuary. In a land plagued by powerful and twisted Mages, the condemned Marked Inquisitors take up the hunt. A once-peaceful kingdom is plunged into chaos by encroaching tides of Mages: merciless embodiments of elemental chaos. The Marked Inquisitors, a doomed force of the condemned, once again mobilizes to stand against the existential threat of Magic. A buried secret threatens to bring an ancient empire to utter ruin. As a Marked Inquisitor, you’ll journey through the western frontier: pursuing, hunting, and obliterating the Mages that roam the realm. You may be bound to the Inquisition, but your choices are yours.

detailed_description: Steam Deck About the Game Saviorless presents a captivating 2D platformer set in a stylish dark fantasy world. The game features exquisite hand-drawn artwork and animations that enhance the visual experience. Players take on the role of Antar, a determined child aspiring to become a Savior. Embark on a journey through the treacherous path to the forbidden land, the Smiling Islands, overcoming a multitude of obstacles along the way. A strange world to explore Dive into a captivating narrative-driven platformer featuring distinctive scenarios, enemy designs, and a variety of characters, all crafted in a complete hand-drawn animation style. Experience an atmospheric and mesmerizing soundtrack, enhancing your journey through enigmatic and visually breathtaking landscapes. Three playable protagonist Engage in dynamic gameplay that seamlessly transitions between diverse characters, each possessing distinctive abilities and facing specific challenges. Antar Embark on a journey as a recklessly curious child, determined to unveil the secrets of the islands through exploration and puzzle-solving. Explore ancient ruins, all while evading the lurking dangers that threaten your path. Savior Embody Antar's fierce masked avatar and face hordes of bizarre enemies and formidable bosses that haunt the realm of the Saviors. Brace yourself for high-speed, unforgiving battles against all obstacles standing between you and your destiny. Nento A merciless hunter obsessed with control, who will do whatever it takes to become the unexpected protagonist of this story, even if this means annihilating everything that stands before him, even his followers. Game Features Unravel a mystery : Can you unearth the secret behind the Smiling Islands? Fight nightmarish monsters : Kill the aberrations that try to stop you from becoming a Savior. Collect the pages : Your story won't be completed if you leave some mementos behind. Explore the islands : Feel the melancholy irradiated by the glooming landscapes and crumbling ruins scattered around the Smiling Islands. A broken narrative : Unravel what keeps Antar from reaching the Smiling Islands and face an unexpected twist of events.

short_description: Embark on a journey to The Smiling Islands, the realm of the Saviors, where an enigmatic guide beckons. The seasoned narrator has shared this story countless times, yet none have graced the miraculous land. Can you seize your narrative and ascend as a Savior?

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, but hand-drawn graphics, a dark fantasy world and challenging combat and jumping passages promise interesting gameplay. It is the brainchild of Josuhe H. Pagliery, who got the project off the ground in Cuba despite adverse circumstances (no state support, no reliable internet, no other developer studios in the country) and has invested seven years of his life in the development of his dream project.The story is set on the Smiling Islands, a menacing world full of monsters and deadly dangers. The name "Smiling Islands" is highly inappropriate for this cursed region. Over the course of the game, you take control of three different characters - firstly the long-haired young lad Antar, who would rather avoid enemies than fight them. He is determined to become a Savior. When we play his avatar as a Savior, we control an agile fighter with a mask. Finally, there is the hunter Nento, who prefers to eliminate opponents in close combat. Each of the three has special abilities and plays very differently, with the battles requiring quick button presses rather than any particular strategy. They are certainly not the highlight of the game. The highlight are the puzzles and the platforming.In the first sections, we jump and climb with Antar as we make our way to the Smiling Islands. Antar can duck and pick up an item to use in marked locations. The enemies are relatively stupid and can often be lured into various deadly traps. In the first small boss fight, we briefly play the hunter Nento, who has to defeat a monster that rolls up into a ball, and then continue playing with Antar. Such changes occur more often in the story. When we die, we restart shortly before we die. The number of lives is not limited, there is no penalty for dying. This means that the overall level of difficulty is not extremely high - at least if you are patient and keep trying. The levels becoming more and more challenging as the game progresses. The level design is quite varied and always brings new ideas, and the somewhat strange but fascinating and well-presented story motivates you to keep playing. What's really going on with the Smiling Islands and the disgusting giant worm infestation? Overall, the gameplay reminded me a little of the old classic Another World, but the playability is much better in a sense that you do not die as fast. At least at the beginning, dying is not so easy.A clear recommendation for fans of classic puzzle platform games. It is not a Metroidvania, you won't find backtracking, complex maps, collecting resources, an inventory, a skill tree, reviving enemies as soon as you leave a room. What you do get, however, is a well-made indie game that offers a unique graphical style as well as an exciting story, some puzzles and, above all, challenging platforming as well as hack 'n' slash gameplay in linear levels.

_childDocuments_.review: This was surprising. I had played the demo years back and almost wrote it off, as there are many cinematic platformers that leave a way stronger first impression. Still, the cool character/enemy designs and animation made it worth staying on my radar. After finishing the full game, I'm glad I never forgot about it. The developers perfectly understand what constitutes a good puzzle-platformer. Level design doesn't run out of ideas, keeping you on your toes, and there's an intriguing, well-presented story to propel you further. Better yet, I've seen gimmicks here that I don't recall from others in the genre. Most of the environmental art is too clean for my liking with its geometric design, but I found myself immersed despite that, thanks to solid atmosphere by dynamic music and animated elements in the background. Combat is button-mashy; fortunately, encounters don't tend to drag so it's not a big problem. My only real complaint would be that checkpoints could've been tweaked slightly to prevent seconds wasted after death.Until I read other reviews, I wasn't aware that this is Cuba's first indie game. I'd have praised it regardless of its origin, though the devs should absolutely be proud.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravo Cuba! Saviorless is short, but sweet. It feels like a cinematic platformer with more arcadey platforming controls. There's a clear focus on narrative and trial-and-error sections like Another World or Inside. Also like those games, there's a lot of blood and gore. The death scenes are brutal. It's a dark setting with an ominous tone. The obvious highlight is the presentation. This is one of the most beautiful games I've played this year. The art direction is inspired. The backgrounds are crammed with meticulous details. The animation for every sprite is so smooth like an animated film. It feels like a fairy tale you'd see in a picture book with an extremely dark tone beneath the surface. It becomes increasingly more disturbing as you progress and learn the secrets of the setting. Nonetheless, "dark" does not describe the visuals. It's very colorful with nice shading. The sprites are very uniquely designed and menacing. It's a solid puzzle platformer with some welcomed combat sections that were fun. There are multiple endings depending on the collectibles you get throughout each level. The soundtrack is just as amazing and I'd love to buy it if or when it becomes available. It's atmospheric with some lovely melodies. I will say I had some difficulty following the cryptic narrative. One of the most glaring aspects is the translation. I can see some awkwardly written lines of dialogue that feel like they were ran through a translator. I still enjoyed my time with it though. For $13, this is absolutely worth getting. I got about 4-5 hours in my playthrough. (7/10)

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good platformer overall, with some downsides.- Nice art with smooth animations, and the imagery has a great level of creepiness/weirdness to it. I especially like the radiant heron and the aquatic monsters in the wasteland.- Not too wordy, leaving room for lots of environmental storytelling.- Interesting locations with solid level design and varied mechanics.- Short and not too tough overall, but has a good difficulty curve as it goes on.- Some of the previous issues have been fixed with the newest update, including a level select and better checkpoints.- The biggest downside I have is that the story doesn't really deliver on its interesting premise, and both the endings are very anticlimactic and unsatisfying. The short length and slow player movement will also be a turnoff for some people.

_childDocuments_.review: Saviorless ReviewBy Thom Stone on  HIGH Clever challenges and the animation is pure eye candy.LOW Few autosaves, unwieldy controls and an opaque story.WTF I can’t spoil the ending — I have no idea what happened.While I was deciding on what I wanted to review, I spent an afternoon watching promo clips for new and upcoming games, and my first reaction to Saviorless was sheer awe at the hand-drawn art and animation.Certain frames looked as if they could be illustrations in a children’s book or a graphic novel, and the overall atmosphere reminded me of a Guillermo del Toro film featuring beautiful settings and grotesque creatures in equal measure.When I actually got to play Saviorless, I was struck by the clever, puzzle-like level design as I hopped, glided and climbed to find levers, keys, NPCs and collectible pages.One NPC known as the Chronicler condescendingly tells the player that they can start over if they don’t get all of the pages in an area and alludes to the convoluted metanarrative aspect of the experience — an omniscient narrator permits two fledgling narrators to control different characters who have the potential to alter the story and (if I understood it correctly) players can take over the narrative and unlock different endings by collecting all the pages.Other reviewers have compared Saviorless to metroidvanias like Hollow Knight or Blasphemous, but unlike those titles, players don’t gain any new powers or abilities that they can use at will. Rather, the player spends most of their time controlling a powerless young boy named Antar as he pursues his quest to reach the Smiling Islands and become a “Savior.”There is a certain appeal to simply platforming, tactfully avoiding enemies or using the environment to one’s advantage, but thankfully, the developers mix things up about a quarter of the way through by having the player take control of the main villain, named Nento.It was a relief to finally be able to attack after only being able to evade for so long, and the epic accompanying music, appropriately called “Nento’s Rage,” made it all the more satisfying. That said, it was only a taste, as players don’t get to experience everything Saviorless has to offer in the way of combat until about halfway through when they reach the Smiling Islands at last.Another way the developers mix up the gameplay is by having players defeat one of the first bosses, a fuzzy blue rhinoceros-like creature, and then having them control it and use its ability to roll and crash through walls.There are also many creepy sub-areas, like one section infested with giant worms that track the players’ movements as they pop out of the ground or the ceiling –they made me jump more than a few times. There was also an underground lab where creatures were being dissected and I learned the sad truth about how Nento’s madness had spread to his fellow hunters from scattered notes.I particularly enjoyed one part where players navigate a series of trees and treehouses, but one of the most frustrating parts of Saviorless was being chased up the inside of a tree by an ax-wielding hunter. After at least a dozen tries, I barely reached the next save point, which brings me to one of the main problems I had with the experience — poorly placed autosaves.The vast distances between save points during the campaign could be ridiculous. I would often get close to what I could tell was the end of an area, only to go all the way back to the beginning because I failed to stick the landing on a crucial jump. Speaking of which, another issue I had was with the controls.The slow, unwieldy movement in Saviorless didn’t bother me much at first, but as play became increasingly difficult and response time became more and more important, I grew furious with certain animations like coming up off of a ladder, or recovering from a fall since speed made all the difference between progressing and starting over. I would also run into problems with making Antar crouch instead of stand (or vice versa) which got me killed quite a few times.By the end of the game, I had figured out how to navigate the slightly awkward controls and I especially enjoyed the final area where I was able to float my way around flying monstrosities and face off with Nento, now represented as a dynamic boss fight with an inventive mix of fighting and platforming.When I finally beat him, I found myself in a new environment fighting as something or someone who wasn’t Antar or anything else I had seen before, and then… it was over. I got the sense that it was supposed to be unsatisfying — perhaps because I didn’t collect enough pages? — but I personally don’t find it motivating when a game punishes me for not doing more.I can appreciate the philosophy that Clever Head seems to share with From Software in the way they reward curious players with fragments of lore to piece together and form a better understanding of the world, but after only five and a half hours I felt a bit shorted and deeply confused by what had just transpired. However, the fact that I was left wanting more spoke to how engaging Saviorless is overall, and how much potential it has for a sequel — or DLC, at the very least.Saviorless isn’t perfect, but this beautifully animated, enigmatic world offers an incredibly artful and engaging experience that I would ultimately recommend.Rating: 8 out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a sucker for hand drawn animations and something about the game was intriguing so I gave it a chance and I must say I’m not disappointed. It has this weird bad dream vibe. On one hand you know it’s not real but on the other it’s a little bit disturbing. I would say this is the best part of the experience is the atmosphere and visual design.Gameplay is OK. In a way it feels “oldschool simple”. There are no skill trees nor unlockable upgrades but it was nice to just focus on playing rather than figuring out what you want to unlock. First half may feels a little bit too simple but closer to the end it shows its teeth. Also variety is there. It’s not just jumping and climbing ladders so don’t worry and even those parts become a bit more challenging and interesting with time.Story is weird and I would say it’s a little bit too vague. There are some cool ideas and it fits the overall vibe of the game but the whole concept could be explained a bit better.To sum it up, it's a macabre version of Gris. Simple yet enjoyable gameplay is driven by striking visuals and unique atmosphere.Things good to know:- It took me 4h to finish it and I would say it’s a perfect length for such an experience.- No issues on Steam Deck (once it didn’t want to launch but resetting SD solved the problem).- You can replay chapters if you miss some collectibles.
