_childDocuments_.review: There are games you continue playing into the wee hours of the morning because of the story.Others, you lose yourself in them because they are just so absorbing.And there are some that have you playing them so late (or early) simply because they bring out that stubborn part of you and have you growling and saying "Oh, no, THIS is getting FINISHED!!".Now, I'm not complaining or disrespecting the game. Far from it. To me, the fact it made me stubbornly and doggedly play it until the end in one sitting is a great compliment.The gameplay, the art, the music, the unique... "narrative", all fit together like a work of art. Difficulty is just right. And that is good. This game is the kind of game I'll be replaying again and again when I need something different and refreshing.So my congratulations to the devs, this is clearly one hell of a passion project, and one that I'll continue to enjoy long after I've platinum the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The word that assotiates with this game is "UNEARNED". This team has spent 8 years, but in the end every part of the game is severely undercooked, but behaves like it is finished and top-notch. The best part of the game: fresh style and nice atmosphere. At least, in some places. Promo materials could convince you that you'll get loads of cool surreal art, but in reality there are mostly endless repetitive platforms and patterns. And really only four types of monsters (with different sizes and colors): running ones with lots of hands,  flying or crawling triangle ones, crawling or jumping worms (with optional tentacles) and different "ugly ghouls" in robes. And only five levels, sharing a lot of graphics, but colored differently. Understand me correctly, I love surreal art, but all of it in this game could be printed on a couple of A4 pages. This kind of story could be called "fake it until you make it", except it is only "fake it". Somebody really tried to make believe they have a complex story with meta-narrative and twists, really really tried... but did not make a story in the end. There is some island... with herons... and saviors... but they kill everything... and there is a villain... he is even worse... or no... and there are narrators... Because if we literally show narrators it will make our story deep and multilayered, right? Story does not make sense and no character is likable/unlikable or interesting. Looks a lot like a typical "story" devised by an artist, who "feels" colors, shapes or whatever, but doesn't have a slightest idea what a cohesive story is. There are loads of short-form festival animation that is of the same kind: very "artisty", but nonsensical and really hard to watch.   Maybe done by the same artists as a story was. At least, in the same manner: they took some good puzzle and platforming ideas from another games, but could not construct a cohesive gamedesign. Slow and almost stealthy platforming can suddenly switch to fierce "boss battle" using completely another character, no preparation, no previous playing as this character. Character dies from any tiny spike, like in Limbo, but checkpoints are so infrequent you will replay the same levels again and again. With frequent checkpoints or save function (or very skilled player) this game could be completed in 30 mins. Also, with every repetition you will go through the same dialogs and slow cutscenes, sometimes dozens of times. Again, all of this is completely unearned, because neither the story, nor characters are developed enough to push you through such hurdles. There is no sense in n-th repetition of boring sequences or grindy fights because there is nothing to gain after that. No skills, no items, no interesting achievements, no comprehensive story bits. First, we meet this boss who is apparently the game's antagonist Nento, but he looks different, has different size and his donkey head is not recognisable until the final animation. Also according to the achievement he is "awakened", but he was not asleep before. So, it all starts with confusion. Then starts the Chase. Three phases of precision platforming (deadly "moving wall"-type) with all sorts of deadly obstacles. Precision sometimes is pixel-thin (especially in the vertical phase), one millisecond of stutter and you are dead. And no checkpoints except for between the phases. Depending on your skill, you can spent hours on this part.Ooff, maybe now we can get some satisfaction and finally destroy this annoying Nento? Well... sort of. Your "savior" character for the final fight is weak and has no extra abilities. Nento has again three stages and all sorts of attacks, including rising knives from all the floor surface and dashing left and right at the same time. Most of the fight he is invulnerable. Oh yes, and you can die immediately after the battle because there is no checkpoint for another couple of minutes. You think you'll get a beautifull long cutscene or new gameplay element or something? Nope. 2 second animation of Nento exploding and you off to the ending. Ehm, but maybe now we'll get a satisfactory ending for the story? There were so many mysteries and subplots thrown in during the game... And again, not at all. There are three endings, bad, good or best but : you just become a saviour of... a guardian of... or a narrator of... of what was it again?, it very much feels like a game made in one year by one good coder and one slightly-better-than-mediocre artist, who for some reason thinks that (s)he is a great writer and gamedesigner. Bizarre situation, underwhelming result, maybe you had fun for eight years, good for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent little story-driven platformer that's drenched in atmosphere.   You take control of a young, powerless boy who sets off on a quest to ascend and become a "savior".  However, not everything is as it seems.  For most of the game you're weaponless and powerless.  It plays a lot like Limbo and Inside, where you need to rely on light puzzle solving and fast reflexes to help move ou forward.  As you come closer to finishing your quest though, the game introduces some light combat.Pros:+ Beautiful, haunting graphics+Intriguing, cryptic story+Several unique, visually stunning bosses that are fun to confront+Forgiving checkpoint system (based on some reviews I've read, this could be due to a patch)+Two distinct endings with a very generous "chapter replay" feature that will help you unlock both of them quicklyCons:-Very short-Relatively simplistic gameplay (not really a con for me, but I can see others being a bit bored)-The endings may be a bit too cryptic for some to enjoyThe Pros easily outweigh the Cons.  If you're intrigued by this games visuals and premise, I encourage you to give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was AMAZING! Saviorless had such creative graphics, story concepts, and gameplay elements.           The hand-drawn graphics are one of the largest appeals to this game, and they help to enthrall the player in the world that Saviorless presents them with. There's just something so inspiring about the grand landscapes and bizarre character designs.          The story was also very unique. It had a very From Software-like feel to it, being grim yet hopeful in the bleak reality it sets. The story can be somewhat ambiguous at times, but it definitely adds to the mystery and intrigue of the game. One issue I did have with the story was that it felt like it could have been longer for sure, but that's not to a fault. This is an indie game after all, and every detail takes a tremendous amount of work (but I wouldn't mind seeing a sequel of any sort that could continue the story woven in such a fantastical world!).          Lastly, I also want to talk about the gameplay elements. Most of the game is a basic 2D platform/puzzle solver. The puzzles are environmentally based, so they're not difficult by any means. However, they do offer a good challenge and make you stop to think for a second. But what I really want to talk about is whenever the game rewards you with gameplay that makes you feel like you are PART OF A FANTASY SETTING. They're small segments that require just a slight deviation from the platformer aspect of the game, and some are almost purely an experience of the world you are in. Riding fantastical creatures through the ruins of a mechanical paradise, controlling ancient machinery as you descend deeper into sacred abysses below, flying past spiked traps in a tram as abhorrent creatures attempt to claw their way in: several great moments that in this game that will make a player take a mental step back from the small areas they traversed by foot and realize the true scale of a world that their actions affect.          The one and only complaint I have of this game is really more of an observation. There are only a few areas where the difficulty seems a little too hard, and I hate the idea of someone putting down this wonder of a game for good from a small, inconvenient section. They're nothing too bad, it just seems like a few things require a small amount of tweaking to make the game feel a little bit more accessible.Wow, what an awesome game! This is definitely one of my favorite indie games, and I am so proud that Cuba can call Saviorless its first. This is an amazing precedent for future Cuban indie games and studios, and I hope to see nothing but success for Empty Head Games and the indie dev teams that follow in their footsteps! Thank you for such an amazing experience!

_childDocuments_.review: What starts off as a simple puzzle platformer gradually ramps up the macabre into incredibly dark and violent territories. This game shines visually (thanks to imaginative hand-drawn style) and creatively (world and creature design). There are quirky narrative devices that make it stand out, too, even if the story itself is not very original. When it comes to difficulty it gets harder and harder in the most natural way. There are boss fights aplenty, but in most cases they are all about avoiding the bosses as your moves are limited to jumping, crouching and occasionally dashing and one type of attack. _childDocuments_.review: Saviorless is a mostly great puzzle platformer game with an intruiging narrative and nice visuals that is hampered with frustrating combat sections. Most of the game is very enjoyable, especially when you have to platform or solve puzzles but when combat becomes a bigger focus later on it loses some of its appeal. Not that the combat is clunky or anything, but the mechanics are quite punishing due to imposed time limits and swarms of enemies. Still though the game is worth experiencing for the story and the atmosphere, in no small part due to the artistry on display. The enviroments are gorgeous and varied and the soundtrack was immersive, sucking you into the world. I hope they sell said OST later down the line as it was personally my favorite part about the whole experience. _childDocuments_.review: A short game full of beautiful art, an intriguing story and simple but very effective and sometimes addictive mechanics. This is a surprising first game from the studio and you guys should definitely play it. At first, it's a slow burn (still fun and engaging though), but once you obtain the savior form, all hell breaks loose. That mechanic is really great, it incentivizes to take on full attack, almost like that health mechanic in bloodborne. I think it could have been introduced earlier, but the last part of the game really shows how well it can combine the human and savior form, using all we have leaned up until that moment. The animation is really fluid and dinamic, and the art is amazing, from bloody and haunting to calm and beautiful. The combat is surprisingly fun, even if it is extremely simple, and it can be a little tricky in some encounters (in the good way). The puzzles are really simple and the story is not as complex as it wants to appear, but it is still a very unique tale. You can tell the passion, the heart in every animation frame and astonishing background. I can only hope these guys keep on creating, because if this is their first try, just imagine what they could come up with in the next ones.

_childDocuments_.review: Rather than adding another short opinion to the list of reviews, I have attempted to document the things that might sway your purchase (for better or worse). Although this game was crowdfunded, I was not an early backer; I'm just a fan of the genre and the R-Type series.Moreover, please forgive the "1.5 hrs at review time" indication above. I began this review with basic, core information as early as I could to help answer a few major questions I felt some excited, potential buyers might have moments after the game launched. But I have since been continuously updating this review as I've progressed further.    • What separates the R-Type series most from other side-scrolling shmups is the inclusion of a "Force" -- the large orb you see hovering in front of your ship. All ships have such a Force that the player can leave attached, launch forward, leave out in space, and recall back to them at will. During the Force's return, the player can also fly ahead of the Force and back into it, effectively attaching it to your ship's rear instead. In all cases, the Force will emit its own (friendly) projectiles, invincibly block/destroy most all incoming (enemy) projectiles, and usually serve at least one other utilitarian purpose unique to your chosen ship's loadout (e.g., working as an independently flying companion when not attached to you, or projecting an even larger shield to deflect more bullets with, etc). On paper, this feature might seem novel at best, but in practice, it defines a major portion of R-Type's unique gameplay, strategies, and customization. Watching any duration of any gameplay videos of either R-Type Final or R-Type Final 2 should suffice for learning the significance and value of a ship's Force (and the player's ability to manipulate it).    • Kazuma Kujo (the game designer and producer for several R-Type releases, including R-Type Final) nailed the audio and visual presentation of R-Type Final 2, making the nostalgic portion of the experience all the more rewarding for former R-Type players. Moreover, the diversity in ship weapons (be it melee attacks, bouncing lasers, droppable bombs, sidekick projectile emitters, heat-seeking missiles, auto-aiming turrets, and everything in between) remains true to what I expected from a modern R-Type title.    • The 16:9 aspect ratio "upgrade" (from its predecessor's 4:3 aspect) measurably improves gameplay by allowing you to see upcoming enemies and obstacles in greater detail from further away, etc.    • Beyond your basic 8-directional shmup controls, the in-game ship mappings include a rapid-fire button which, as expected, fires your basic weapon at the maximum rate your weapon allows (negating any need/advantage of rapid button-mashing). You are also given dedicated buttons for slowing down and speeding up your ship's agility (that is, how fast your ship can navigate the screen-space and avoid incoming projectiles/obstacles, not how fast you progress horizontally through the level) for quick escapes or precise dodging on the fly.    • You pick from 5 difficulty settings at the beginning of each run (Practice, Kids, Normal, Bydo, and R-Typer). These seem to simply adjust the number of enemies/projectiles on-screen at any given time (and perhaps their health).    • There are options to play at up to 360 FPS at 4K resolution.    • You can change the controller icons used to Keyboard, Xbox, PlayStation, and Switch styles.    • You are offered fully remappable controls for both keyboard and gamepads.    • While there are no colorblind-related accessibility settings, I have not had any situations arise where obscure color-coding played an important role.    • The interface seems to indicate room for 99 flyable ships in total, however, it is my understanding that not all 99 are currently present and unlockable. (The developers are quick to advertise their intention to add new content to the game post-launch, so take that as you will.) Regardless, each ship has its own projectiles, uniquely meaningful upgrades, powerful charge shots, interesting Force mechanics, and so on. And it is this diversity in customizable ships (and the gradual unlocking of them) that drives a big part of the game's "fun factor" and replayability.    • The "R Museum" (a giant warehouse showcasing your entire ship collection) from R-Type Final is fully-realized in 3D, complete with a ground-level first-person mode for exploring and viewing your collection, and a focused view to see all your individual ships from all angles while you read immersion-friendly descriptions of their loadouts, etc.    • You start the game with 3 ships unlocked, and all ships appear to be customizable. The customization interface offers 8 body colors, full RGB canopy selection (~16 million colors), 61 *extremely generic* decals that can be rotated and positioned anywhere on your ship's body as you see fit (with more optionally unlocked later), 12 missile options (with only 2 unlocked initially), and 12 companion "bits" (smaller projectile emitters that closely follow your ship, of which only 1 or 2 are unlocked initially), all provided and saved on a per-ship basis.    • Beyond the initial 3 ships unlocked from the start, new ships and modifications are unlocked through either crafting materials gathered in-game or bought via currency earned in-game (sans a few exceptions locked behind game progression accordingly).    • 4 ships are locked behind (all lowercase) passwords entered in the R Museum:     • The length of the game is decent for an arcade-style shmup at the intended (or harder) difficulty, as countless lives will be lost as you learn the ins and outs of each stage. (The struggle of progression is similar to challenging "Mario Maker" levels, if that means anything to you.) But I suspect fans of the easier modes will find its 7 current levels unexpectedly short and unrewarding.    • As can be gleaned from the promotional videos and screenshots provided in Steam, the background during gameplay is bright, detailed, and interesting *almost* to a fault. While I do not believe it has measurably affected my performance in a level yet, I wouldn't be surprised to learn a portion of the playerbase was struggling to distinguish the foreground threats from the background art at the reflexive speed the game requires at harder (and thus "busier") difficulties. An easy fix would be the introduction of an option that allowed players to either dim the background significantly or toggle it off altogether.    • The game requires text-typing in a few select areas (naming your "pilot", inputting backer codes if you have any, etc), and attempts to leverage an in-game keyboard to accomplish this. Unfortunately, this was clearly a rushed "feature", as its implementation is beyond clunky and mandates you to use your mouse every time it comes up (even just to close it, which confusingly is done by clicking the "Enter" button on the virtual keyboard, regardless if you're trying to back out of it, return to the previous menu, or submit the text you've entered). Until this is fixed, using your mouse to click the "Enter" button is a simple workaround for this one-time issue.    • It's perhaps an insignificant shortcoming, but the initial 61 decals available to customize your ship with have an unreasonably copy-pasted clipart-esque aesthetic. It genuinely feels like a barebones pack of public domain emoji (which is *certainly* not the work of any of R-Type Final 2's artists). Fortunately, you can unlock more pertinent decals with in-game currency as you progress.

_childDocuments_.review: This review will be updated in time as the game is updated. I want to recommend this game, as I have been a fan of R-Type since the first few games over 30 years ago now. But right now the game has issues, issues that can hopefully be fixed! Right now the game is buggy, has lag issues during key moments of fights, and has menu glitches that make it impossible to interact with the game if you alt tab out and tab back in. Currently, I have not gotten to any of the final paths of the game (It has branching paths beginning with level 6 depending on a choice you make at the end of level 5, similar to the first Final). However, the reason for this has not been because the game is too hard or I'm bad at it or any complaints with the levels themselves. When I reached level 5 the first time, I died to the final boss on it, alt-tabbed out to check a discord message, and when I came back the game wouldn't do anything. I could not hit continue, I could not select a fighter, nothing. Controller and keyboard become completely unresponsive, no matter what button I pushed I just got nothing or an error sound from the game. So I quit it, and retried. Same thing happened when I alt-tabbed again. The menus are also buggy when looking through the bydo labs and the other gallery sections, not properly responding to directional inputs, leaving your input in a spot it wasn't upon exiting out of a menu, etc. Just now I played again, got through stage 6.2, and the game crashed for the third time today trying to load stage 7.2. tl;dr Game is good, but currently I cannot recommend it due to constant bugs and crashes  hampering the experience, among other minor nuisances that add up to tedium across the experience. Even barring all that, as much as I love R-Type, this has less content than R-Type Final on the PS2 and costs $40 plus a $20 season pass for more levels, all while having far less ships than its predecessor. The graphics are phenomenal, but the content is a bit lacking right now, I hope to see more in the future that will change this to a recommended, because more content is still being added, both paid and free. Biggest things that need to be fixed are menu errors, input issues, and the crashes. tl;dr, again:If you love R-Type, get itIf you just like schmups, wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: R-Type fan since Delta and Irem Software Inc enthusiast:This, is a crowdfunded 900k game on Kickstarter, that looks like about 50k was completely invested on itLet's get some things clear first: The game plays much like R-Type Final 1, minus the dead time. If you remember playing it, you remember sections of the game that were like 40 second transitions with nothing to shoot. This doesnt happen in this game, it's faster paced, i'd say the gameplay feels better in Final 2 than Final 1, but at the end of the day there's really not enough enemies to shoot, This is the most "puzzle-like" R-type on the series,  it's all about ship positioning and memorization, slow transitions, and shooting 2 or 3 enemies if you're lucky. On that note: the stages are like 50% shorter, and the bosses.... well, look it up on youtube, it's really low-efffort.... like really REALLY low effort. Bosses are a definetely 1/10 without exaggeration, maybe 2/10 because at least they tried something differentThe graphics are all over the place, first things first: This game runs on Unreal Engine 4, so expect the ships, lighting and shadows on this game look supreme, it really looks great. Unfortunately, that's about the only thing that looks good about this game. 3D models, assets, enemies, background objects, surfaces, basically everything about the stages after the first stage looks.... god-awful. It's insane to me that R-type 1 which is a game made in 2004 looks better than this. Usually i would't mind graphics if the gameplay suffices, but it detaches soooo much from the experience that there's no way in a million years this game could look like this in 2021. Irem would've never approve this game's pressentation on it's current state.On regards to this game as-is and not having R-type final 1 as a refference (or any other shmup for that matter):I don't know if this a game worth your while, it's very short and relies on repetetive gameplay, enemies will come from the foreground, from below, from the ceiling way too fast (memorization is imperative), and some cannon/turrets fire instant-death lasers without a a sound cue or beam charging. All of this is expected of shoot em up games in general, but this game takes it too far. The best way to put it, is that it was developed in a way that you just KNOW something's off, the difficulty curve is all over the place, enemies sometimes have more health than they should really have, sometimes less, sometimes their patterns are either overly-artificial, or straight up brain dead. You probably have read this a million times but YOU CAN'T SEE THE ENEMIES BULLETS well enough.This is a good effort by Granzella... if you think that 25% percent of effort is enough to make a somewhat decent game, which this game is not.Stick to Final 1 and Delta

_childDocuments_.review: I was so damn excited to hear the news, a new R-type game in coming and not just that its coming to Steam. So being a life long PC gamer (and PC Gamer only since early 2000s) I couldn't contain myself and counted the days till the release of the game. Unfortunately all my expectations have been crushed. While this is in no way a bad game. Its not a great game either. And if I could speak freely (yes everyone is welcome to their own opinions) this is not even a R-Type game. Let me explain.For me R-type is two things. Grim oppressive atmosphere. Huge towering enemies and mechs and space ships that always keep you in awe. Take R-Type Delta for example or R-Type II, each and every level is an assault on the senses. Really high stakes imagery and total apocalyptic world vibe that  is somehow gorgeous to look at. This R-Type has some kind of plant enemies theme and it doesn't work for me.  Remember that opening level of R-Type 1 on PS2. How the camera placement was inverted, glass shattering and huge mechs and spiders enemies crawling into sight while you had to survive all of it. That was a challenge. The real deal!  This game's first level is so damn easy slow paced and uninspired. The later levels have no soul to them.  The music is fine and rather enjoyable. The actual visuals are sometimes jaw dropping good but not in the level design department. The levels are mostly the antithesis of what R-Type is all about. THE HORROR ..... IS MISSING!!!!!!!!!  THE HUGE MECHS ARE ABSENT MOSTLY!!But I understand it might be so that the phallic imagery and horror of the previous games was not what the devs of Final 2 were going for. Perhaps they wanted to do something entirely different while keeping the R-type characters and weapons intact. I don't know. But to me its missing that unmistakable R-Type appeal of most previous titles. Anyways you can disregard my opinions if you are so inclined to. And I don't mind. Neither do I hope that this title should fail commercially. On the contrary I hope the best for the devs and game. This one is just not for me. And lastly I really hope the devs decide to port the classic R-Type Delta and Final 1 to PC soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty much just an uninspired re-skin of the original R-Type Final, with even more boring levels you mostly just hold down the autofire button in while getting "gotcha'd" every couple of minutes just because you're so out of it you stopped paying attention. When series producer Kazuma Kujo said he wanted to do something new with the widescreen format of modern screens I can't imagine how all that potential got squandered when Darius has been doing better with even wider screens for years. I think it's telling when most bosses have a safe spot and a timer where all you lose out on is score if you let them unalive themselves. The game just seems like it doesn't want you to play it, which is pretty insulting (and also embarrassing for myself due to how many hours I've sunk into it).The satisfaction of unlocking new ships wears off pretty quick, since it's now a system based on very few "resources" that are awarded when completing levels, even on the harder difficulties. I'm just glad they haven't made the materials and currency purchasable with real money, but I fear that if I speak too loudly they'll decide to implement that in one of the next big updates, like when it will DEFINITELY, REALLY (trust me, guys), become the epic successor, R-Type Final 3 (which I feel is just an in-joke at Granzella at this point).The DLC is also way overpriced for the number of levels and their respective qualities, often ruining what made the original levels so fun with more downtime to sit in one spot and hold the fire button and completely botched, uninspired remixes to back the "action." The only thing I can slightly praise is the graphics, but they still pale in comparison to other 3D shmups and come down to just being generic (like, Delta's PS1 graphics by comparison have aged like a fine). The engine is not well optimized either, usually making you put up with an entire level of stuttering just so it can get all of its textures loaded or something. Maybe its just my PC, but why is this the only game that does that for me?Some of the lore implications are cool (like the final levels), but there is little of a useful glossary/etc. in game that gives a complete timeline like R-Types on the PS1, or clarifies the existence of characters that are mentioned throughout the series (beyond a little nudge nudge at the beginning of the game by name-dropping Jade Ross). I doubt that the R-Type series is going to live for much longer past this entry outside of rereleases of the first and second game every decade to please the '80s babies, so it would be nice if they just made this "Final" entry one that fans could use as an easy reference to other titles in the series. Final 1 made some attempts at that, but mostly everything outside of the 100+ ships from that game are nowhere to be seen in this sequel.Despite all this complaining, I can't say I HATE this game, but I certainly don't like it. If you're a die-hard R-Type fan, you already own this and either hate me or begrudgingly agree with some of my points. If you're a die-hard shmup player or just nostalgic, don't waste your money. Maybe if the price ever drops below $10 (or your equivalent currency).

_childDocuments_.review: (Background: I was introduced to the series with Super way back when, loved it, and played and loved Delta and Final 1; I played all 3 of those  the day before Final 2's release to give myself a solid reminder of how things evolved and what Final 2 was about to be tacked onto the end of.)For those who have forgotten, R-Type Final 1 came out for the PS2 in 2003.  Yes, 18 years ago.  However, I believe very firmly that Final 2 is a beautiful ode to that which Irem had established R-Type, in general, had evolved into by the time Final 1 had come out, in a much sleeker and more pleasing aesthetic than Final 1 offered (my God I hated Final 1's menu aesthetic and sounds, and Final 2's are great).  In essence, I'd argue Granzella did  drop the ball on how it  to play an R-Type game - I think they got the overall feel correct.As  feel, not only should I mention that the ships seem to control fine, but difficulty is part of feel as well, and yeah, R-Type has historically been on the hard side; Final 2 is merely no different in that regard and thus also hits  nail on the head - "R-Type" and "particularly easy" just  traditionally go in the same sentence together, so you simply  go into Final 2 expecting the game to just keel over for you.  Effort is required to beat this game.  For what it's worth, I felt that Practice difficulty here feels to me about as hard overall as Baby (the equivalent difficulty) did on Final 1.The stage design also seems pretty spot-on for general obstacle placement and difficulty of navigation; it is good modernization of the notions of what Irem themselves previously put us through in Delta and Final 1.  I will also give HUGE praise to stage 6 of Final 2 for the wheel cycles being  and giving you extra opportunities for entrance/exit that you might not have thought you'd have: some previous games - R-Type III being the worst offender by far - had situations where Irem was  unfair with cycles, automatic doors, walls, or other hair-pulling stage design elements; Final 2 never throws any wholly unfair stage design stuff at you, and I see that as fantastic.I think the main takeaways here should be:* We should count ourselves  lucky that after  we even  a new mainline R-Type game , regardless of who made it.* We should be happy that Granzella has managed to get it as right as they  - I agree with their cheesy tagline that Final 2 is "the best R-Type we can make now."* I recommend that any fan of R-Type in general play Final 2; I feel that any actually-reasonable human being familiar with the series won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is coming from someone who grew up playing old school style sh'mups and very much enjoys them but who is, frankly, not very good at them. So with that said, I definitely recommend this game.At its core, this is a horizontally scrolling shoot 'em up with an emphasis on upgrades, strategic use of your pod upgrade, one hit kills and checkpoints. It isn't a "bullet hell" type shooter but rather there is more emphasis on enemy patterns and learning routes and approaches through levels rather than dodging huge swarms of shots.Pros: I think what I most appreciate about the game is that there are a lot of difficulty levels so those who are more casual fans of the genre can still enjoy it and those who are more into these things can crank up the difficulty. I am also really enjoying the 99 unlockable ship aspect of the game and I really am enjoying trying a lot of different ship types all with unique in-game upgrade paths and abilities. For me, the game was definitely challenging at first even on the easier difficulties but once you start unlocking ships and "turn the corner" on getting some unique and more powerful upgrades you can really start digging into the game, and start gradually ratcheting up the difficulty. I don't imagine I'll ever finish it on the "real" harder difficulties but I'm still enjoying the sense of accomplishment from getting better at the game, finishing it on an easy difficulty and then start working through a harder difficulty.Cons: some aspects of the game are a little opaque like what "dose" is exactly and how one gets "dose" and also how the game calculates the resources you are awarded at the end of the level. My biggest "con" is that the base game is a little on the short side (though the length is pretty in line with past series entries) and there are a couple of levels that honestly look and feel unfinished (I'm looking at you level 3). Finally, you might curse a lot...On the whole though, I think this game succeeds at being what it is supposed to be and was very enjoyable to someone who is a fan of the genre but also not an expert. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Gen X gamers, prepare to be struck right in the feels. Jokes aside, Granzella did quite a good job here. Using a modern graphics engine, R-Type Final 2's graphics are impressively shining. Alongside, the gameplay really stands out, as it keeps the R-Type spirit intact. No quirks or flaws whatsoever. Furthermore, some improvements are also introduced: there are no more speed-up power ups (kind of personal opinion, but hey, remember avoiding them in older R-Type games?), instead you can select your craft's speed on the fly, depending on the situation. Also, there are plenty of difficulty settings to choose from. The game can be a bit hard and unfair on higher ones, but that's always been the case with R-Type. As with its predecessor, the game features many unlockables, not only ships to try out, but also cosmetic items and on top of that, a ship customization feature, to make it look more to your liking.  To sum up, R-Type Final 2 is a must have, for the series enthusiast, but also an excellent memory based hori shmup, for those who want to try their luck on one. Recommended! (9/10)

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly a masterpiece of horizontal shooters (in the making?)... but if R-Type, to you, is huge bio-mechanical bosses and H R Giger style imagery in the first few levels, you might be best sticking to earlier releases. I think the strength here is gameplay, with a focus on mastery of control, learning enemy behaviour and quick decisions about the bit's position or function.I enjoy the patterns and the need to alter your speed in places for finer control. It's very satisfying identifying enemy weaknesses or finding a spot on screen where you are less likely to die. The graphics are lovely, but having got to level 3, it feels the design crew gave up a little (but I have only seen a small amount of this level - I love R-Type, but suck at anything past R-Type Final 1, unless I ashamedly choose 'baby' difficulty). My son loves the music and it is a very fresh sounding, enthusiastic soundtrack. Not as dark sounding as as Final 1, but a competent piece of work, with engaging arrangement and a positive and modern vibe. The sound effects are great with nice, fizzy crispy explosions and boost / laser sounds.The bosses have great attack patterns, but visually, look a little boring (at least on level 1 and 2) compared to earlier incarnations of R-Type. For example, level 1 - the Bydo boss  you see on the very first R-Type, but part frozen, slumps to the right of the screen, covered in ice. The much smaller stomach parasite is the only noticeable feature. The level 2 boss is a couple of rectangles floating around another rectangle. Great fun learning to beat that boss, but the design doesn't inspire me.Final small gripe - the 3d camera panning effects can seem a bit robotic and not very smooth or organic (i.e level 1 approaching the structure, the ship turns into the entrace and the scenery rotates around the ship as it approaches - and then abruptly stops. I would have liked to see a less abrupt, smooth, gliding transition.)Over all, it's my favourite R-Type. I feel it would knock Gradius V off the my top list for awesome side scrollers if the above bits are addressed, in time. It's very fun to play, and I would think the younger generation of players will be taken by Yuki Iwai's positive and solid music score, the ability to customise your fighter, learning enemy patterns and behaviour and the fun of learning how and when to use your boosts, dose, speed changes and bit. My son is a big fan of Final 2 already, although is very new to the genre.It is a tad expensive to buy (I got it in a Steam sale) but I find that there is a lot to like about this game.
_childDocuments_.name: R-Type Final 2

_childDocuments_.review: I believe this game had a pretty troubled development (including three separate crowdfunding campaigns), but I'm glad we got it in the end. R-Type Final 1 is one of my favorite shoot-em-ups so I'm glad to see just another R-Type in general.All the ships are lovingly rendered, though the stages come off as a bit samey and simplistic (only played up to stage 4 as of this review). There's a lot of nice little touches. The bosses are pretty creative, and riff on other bosses in the series which is nice.Final 2 has... differences I'm not sure about. I like that the stages are shorter and you get a ton of credits by only playing a couple hours, and I LOVE that you don't need to play ships for a certain amount of time, you just grind the three currencies to buy them. Which... is its own thing, but at least I get to choose what ship I want while I grind.On the other hand, I feel like the game is a lot stingier when it comes to checkpoints; not in the amount, but that you'll restart and have to navigate the stage without a Force for a while. At least it means I have to get good.I don't think it's a perfect game, but I wasn't expecting it to be. I wanted another R-Type, and another Final at that, and I think this is a great fulfillment of that vision. I can't wait to see the stage variants and all the little secrets Granzella's put in.
_childDocuments_.name: R-Type Final 2

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game for a while, I can say without issue that it's a solid shoot'em up and a good R-Type title.Its original levels follow a more simplistic design compared to R-Type Delta and Final, and are overall more linear and, "videogame-y" rather than having the feel of a 3D adventure like the previous games, but they're an overall fun experience, with bosses that are in my opinion very creative and very, very fun to fight, the highlight of most levels.The difficulty of the game varies a lot between the five settings, allowing for a more relaxing and easy experience for less-skilled player (such as myself), to incredibly challenging at the higher difficulties, providing an experience suitable to all players.The weakest part of the game is without a doubt the graphics - although the game can be truly gorgeous to look at in certain moments (especially in regards to the ship and the effects of their weapons), many stages present occasional low quality textures if not models, with stage 3.0 being the most egregious example. It can (and 3.0 straight up will) look jarring, but at least for me it doesn't take away from the overall experience of the game.I haven't played long enough to explore the depth of the ship variety, but for what I've seen they did a stellar job in that regard. The various vehicles maintain the same feel as their R-Type Final counterparts, their models and particle effects are beautiful and the customization, while not flawless, allows for some very fun tinkering with the look of your vehicles.Unlocking the ships is way different than in Final, where you were required X minutes of playtime with another specific vehicle for most of them; here, you have to buy them with currency obtained by beating levels, which means you are no longer forced to fly ships you may not like for long periods of time, but you're also not rewarded for failure anymore - whereas in Final you could die over and over and over in one section while still making progress towards the unlocks, here you'll need to reach and defeat the boss to earn the currency... But on the plus side, you can progress even just by playing your favorite ship this time around.Overall for what I've played, this game is a solid 7.5/10 - despite its flaws it's a very pleasant and fun experience, and I plan to keep going to see all this game has to offer. And while more content will indeed be welcome (not that this game is lacking in that department, quite the opposite), I'd love to see some graphical tweaks in the future to make the overall aesthetic of the game become truly beautiful to look at.

_childDocuments_.review: In the sense that people wanted another R-Type Final, you're pretty much getting that; 2 plays much like the previous, with all its ups and downs.The slightly touched-up functions of the old Wave Cannons you know and love are positive for the most part; Andromalius gets a particularly welcome upgrade from this, as the shockwave continues to inflict damage for a split-second to catch another minor Bydo or two as they advance. Barrier Wave goes faster and further than before, although it's still around as bad as it's always been offensively so don't lose that Balmung.Dose builds up a bit faster - a lot faster in certain specific areas (the bio-goop walls you have to destroy in some regions counts each individual little block as a 'hit'). There's a little something in Stage 1 regarding how early you can build it.Speed is reset to 2 when you die which is slightly annoying but minor.The ship models are beautifully detailed, a real joy to look at. The weapons have this odd style to their coloration (the original Photon-Belts in particular) but it doesn't look bad, kinda grows on you after a while.The sound... sounds about right? It sounds like R-Type Final for the most part. Not gonna win any awards there but it's the same old atmospheric elevator death muzak you remember. The effects don't seem out of place, though at the same time *because* of it we're reminded of the series' age.Two minor points against though:- Couple of the stages feel particularly short, 4 in particular (boss was fun though).    [Edit: Stage 7.1 makes up for this: very long, and damn-near breathtaking]- The stages are also prone to very similar-feeling tunnel sections, so I'm hoping the resurrected previous-game stages will help there as Delta and Leo in particular were usually great in that respect. We'll see if Fire Cask Factory retains its infamy.(Edit: OKAY YEAH IT DID THAT WAS BRILLIANT)Game's not fully optimized for all systems(hopefully that's a 'yet'); I get no problems other than the system running a little hotter than the requirements would suggest, but some folks on the forums speak of slight stutter at the start of a stage (nothing compared to what the console players are apparently experiencing though).Not really surprising for... almost any game launch nowadays though when we think about it, but "everybody does it" does not make anybody doing it better.If you didn't like the original, you're never going to like this. If you loved the original, absolutely give this one a shot.Just remember, it's been over fifteen years for most people; we're the ones who've changed.

_childDocuments_.review: While not my personal favorite in the series, it's still an excellent game, and certainly wins out over previous titles in terms of replayability. While the main campaign is pretty small (11 stages, with only 6 or 7 being played at a time depending on your route), the DLC (which thankfully is fairly cheap) offers tons of new stages, several of which are remixed versions of stages seen in previous games. Plus, there's a ton of new ships to unlock, all of which have unique movesets to fit any possible playstyle. I do have a few critiques. For one, while most of the game looks beautiful, especially the DLC levels, there are some stages and bosses that aren't exactly a treat to the eye. Stage 2's boss looks like you're fighting angry legos, Stage 4's boss is just a wrecking ball (which can be bullied really easily) and the entirety of Stages 3 and 6.1 look weirdly glossy and unfinished. Second, the credit system is outdated and redundant. Due to their arcade roots, shmups have always had this issue where they can never seem to grow out of having limited continues, despite it very clearly being an outdated practice who's only purpose is to add artificial difficulty to an already difficult game. What baffles me is that console ports of R-Type I and II, along with the two SNES games, all had unlimited continues, and then the 3-D games decided to retroactively shoehorn them in for no reason. In Final 2 they're especially useless, because once you complete the main campaign, you get unlimited credits anyway. So why not just not have a credit system to begin with and just let me have fun playing the game without an arbitrary "♥♥♥♥ you go back to the beginning" if I die too many times. I paid for the game, I'm not feeding quarters into an arcade cabinet, so let me enjoy the game in full. Thankfully, the credit system can be rendered moot fairly easily, but it's just an annoying hoop to jump through and it shouldn't exist at all. TL/DR: R-Type Final 2 is a fantastic entry in the series, and while it does make a few archaic design choices, it is a very enjoyable experience, and I'm glad that the series is still alive.

_childDocuments_.review: Seen a lot of reviews blasting the game for the difficulty. This is a thinking shooter where memorization and planning are just as important as a quick trigger finger (or a slow one if your charging a 3-loop Wave Cannon) similar to how Dark Souls rewards observation, experimentation and action with success. RTF2 does the same. Bearing in mind that with 99 ships to unlock not all ships are created equal and some are awesome to play, while another shoots (good for clearing out enemies btw) fireworks or a giant honking cannonball. You got plenty to experiment with not to mention fine tuning your R-series craft for looks with a decently robust ship editor. Music is techno-y with a few tracks that are really nice. Graphics are what I expect and do the job. Though as noted in other reviews I'm thinking stage 3 was half baked or the fact that it is an AI lab the bydo are constructing said warships and it isn't done yet (shrug) Either way most bland out of the stages I've seen. The ship graveyard is an eye opener. Controller support works well. Any mistakes I made was my own blasted fault and you get punished if you screw up and die. As it should be. Overall. It's a buy for me. If your a completionist (basically this game boils down into Poke-Type gotta collect 'em all.) and want to unlock all 99 ships it's gonna take you some time. At least 40 hours of gameplay which would pretty much be an entertainment value of $1 USD per hour which is acceptable to me. This is for: Fans of shmups, Folks who like difficult games, Gluttons for punishment, and Completionist. This Isn't for: People who get pissed easily, People who hate shmups, People who hate punishing difficulty curves, and People who don't find enjoyment out of Dark Souls or other self-rewarding difficult games.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very glad that this game even exists. Granzella (which, as far as I can tell, is made up of many of the same devs that made the original R-Type games) brought back this dead series in a Kickstarter, and has been very good at delivering what they promised. They released the original R-Type Final 2 campaign, and has been very good about supporting it with DLC and content updates. While the vanilla game was pretty serviceable, it was clearly made on a budget, and some levels look pretty barebones. They clearly focused on gameplay, which plays just as well a typical R-Type level.But what makes this game really shine is its post-release content. The vanilla game launched with a handful of ships, but the devs have continued to release more and more ships for free (except for a few backer-only ships) on a continuous schedule, so now you have a huge variety of ships to play with. I think it currently has just as many ships as R-Type Final 1, if not more so. The DLC level packs contain remakes of previous levels in the series, and they tend to look far more detailed than the levels of the original game. You can clearly see the devs finding their footing with this new engine and doing more and more with it as they go.R-Type Final 2 is mechanically very solid. It's true to other games in the series in that while it's generally less visually flashy than many other shooters, there is more of a tactical/puzzle element to it in that knowing where to put your ship and where to place your ship's force (the orange glowy orb thing attached to your ship) is extremely important to surviving certain sections. Keep in mind that this does mean that memorization plays a somewhat larger role in this game than in other shooters.R-Type is not like bullet hell shooters in that it doesn't give you a tiny hitbox. Your hitbox is slightly smaller than your actual ship, but it's still huge if you're used to bullet hells. So while the game doesn't shoot that many bullets at you, it's harder than it looks because you will take hits very easily. Your force helps offset this because it's able to destroy weaker enemies on touch and can also block most bullets (again, playing into the tactical/memorization component of the game).Speaking of difficulty, this game can get extremely hard, especially in its DLC stages, even on Normal difficulty. The game gives you infinite continues (I think it's an early unlock?), and expects you to use them. It's not uncommon to get stuck in an area and wind up dying repeatedly while you try to figure out how to recover from the checkpoint. This is an YMMV sort of thing - you might want this level of difficulty, or you might find it frustrating.The large variety of ships is really nice, and a soft way to adjust the difficulty of the game. Some ships are clearly way more powerful than others, so your ship choice can make the difference between breezing through a level and struggling through it. The game lets you set a roster of about a dozen ships when starting a campaign, and you get the option to swap ships between levels. Some ships play very differently from each other, so you can pick ships that complement the way you like to play. Some ships have an extremely powerful wave cannon (your charged shot), and you wind up relying mostly on that instead of shooting normally. Some have great normal shots but weak wave cannons. Some ships have really good forces that can carry you through some areas all by themselves, while you just try to stay out of trouble. And the most powerful ships (which you can get after unlocking all other ships) let you customize all of those things into a single ship.Ship unlocks run on a currency/resource system. You get resources from clearing levels, and you spend those resources on unlocking ships. This is a much better system than Final 1, which forced you to clear stuff with  specific ships to unlock specific other ships. Having said that, the game does expect you to play through it multiple times and/or grind the most "lucrative" levels to get enough currency to unlock everything. Other thoughts:- For the most part, the game looks very pretty. Your ship's wave cannon charge creates a glow that shines on the level around you that's pretty satisfying. Some of the DLC stages look really good, especially when you recognize their original SNES or PS1 incarnations. It's nice to play an old school side scrolling plane shooter that's in full 3d/60 fps.- Having said that, most of the explosions are kind of underwhelming for some reason. Boss explosions are particularly bland. - Speaking of bosses, I found most of the bosses not particularly fun to fight. A lot of them are designed around just surviving long enough while the boss is invulnerable and waiting to reach a point where the boss shows a vulnerability for you to shoot, and personally I didn't find it that interesting. Some are downright tedious.- Stage 3 in the vanilla game looks like crap for some reason - so much so that it's almost a meme among the community. Maybe it was rushed.- The music is serviceable but mostly unremarkable.- The way the DLC levels pull from all over the series can make level progress in DLC campaigns feel disjointed. While in a standard shooter campaign you get the feeling you're flying deeper into enemy territory with each level, some of the DLC campaigns have you playing stage 3 from one game, then stage 6 from another game, then stage 1 from another, and so on. It can feel like you're going all over the place, because you are.- Some of the level recreations also recreate the drawbacks of those levels as well. For example, R-Type Final 1 has a problem with long periods of downtime between waves in levels, and that happens in the remade levels here as well.- On the other hand, some level recreations were improved. The stupid vent section the recreated level of R-Type 3 now has tells before they fire, which was sorely needed because there used to be a lot of straight memorization deaths in that section.- The graphics can get a little too visually busy at times. Sometimes it's hard to tell what parts of a stage are part of the background and what's something you can actually interact with.- The game runs fine on steam deck. It stays at 60 fps for the most part, though it does lose frames at times.I wouldn't say this is for everybody because it's a very specific style of side scrolling shooter, and its level/enemy design does lean towards a slower and more planned out approach than some people might like. But if that *is* what you like, then this game has it.

_childDocuments_.review: R-TYPE Final 2 is an absolute gem of a game that brings back the nostalgia of classic shooters while introducing exciting new features and visuals. As a long-time fan of the R-TYPE series, I couldn't wait to get my hands on the Steam version of R-TYPE Final 2, and it did not disappoint.First and foremost, the gameplay is incredibly satisfying. The controls are responsive and intuitive, allowing for precise movements and quick reflexes, which is crucial in a game like this. The challenging levels keep you on your toes, testing your skills and strategic thinking. The familiar enemy patterns, coupled with new and unique foes, provide a perfect blend of nostalgia and fresh experiences.Visually, R-TYPE Final 2 is a feast for the eyes. The graphics are stunning, with detailed environments and beautifully designed enemy ships. The attention to detail is remarkable, and the explosions and special effects are a visual treat. The game runs smoothly on my system, and the art direction perfectly captures the essence of the series.One aspect that impressed me greatly is the amount of customization available. R-TYPE Final 2 offers a vast array of ships, each with its own unique abilities and playstyle. The upgrade system allows you to fine-tune your ship to suit your preferences, providing a sense of personalization and replay value. Experimenting with different combinations and finding the perfect setup is incredibly rewarding.The soundtrack deserves special mention as well. The music perfectly complements the action on screen, pumping up the adrenaline and immersing you further into the intense battles. The sound effects are crisp and impactful, enhancing the overall experience.The developers have also shown great dedication to the game's post-launch support. Regular updates and patches have addressed any issues and introduced additional content, ensuring that R-TYPE Final 2 remains a polished and enjoyable experience.Overall, R-TYPE Final 2 on Steam is a must-play for both fans of the original series and newcomers to the genre. It successfully captures the essence of the classic shooter while incorporating modern elements that enhance the gameplay. With its stunning visuals, tight controls, customization options, and a fantastic soundtrack, this game is an absolute blast to play. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an exciting, challenging, and visually captivating shooter experience.

_childDocuments_.review: F*Ck Level 4.1. It was damn near impossible on Normal. And it is just damn impossible on R-type Difficulty.So here goes my review of this game. You have to keep in mind that Final 2 is a record of battles. Now the reason why it is a record of battles is b/c no one could come up with a good story to tell. Final 2 is one of the most, if not the the most, difficulty disjointed shooters. Level 1 is a joke it is so easy. Level 2's boss... I mean what the heck is that? a couple boxes doing circles. Level 3's Battleship stage is low poly for whatever reason, and the boss is a red nub. Then you hit these branching levels, and may the Shmup Gods of Old & New help you if you stumble into 4.1. I spent 2hrs getting thru in on normal without upgrades b/c my ship went Kaput due to the number of enemies, bullets, and random spirits whizzing by. Hardest level by far.Anyways, so here I am 20-30hrs later. I've done a crap load of stuff on this game. Many challenges for achievements. And I got all these ships, and I'm thinking. I'm gonna go show lvl 4.1 who the mothertrucking boss is. But my f'in geebus. I get to phase 2 of the fish boss, hit it with a Dose, aka, bomb that took 1hr to charge...no joke. And this fish looks fried, but the damn thing doesn't die. And so we do this pink cloud explosion dance again, and go into a 3rd phase, and damnit he hits me with a blue circle laser b/c I'm positioned for his puff ball shots that he did in phase 1 & 2, but he doesn't do it. And being one d-pad click too far over kills a brother. And my gawd. If that isn't r-type for you. It's just survive a bit, die, memorize. Survive a bit longer, memorize, repeat, repeat, repeat.So anyways, the hardest level is smack dab in the middle of the main story. Therefore, keep in mind that these are "records" b/c level difficulty is a roller coaster. No progression. Heck, all half the Level 7 bosses are a joke b/c they are just sitting there letting you blow them up. I blew up my first final boss (7X or 7Y) in about 10 seconds, and I said, WTF????. If the base game missions are too easy and fun... oh boy, pick up the DLCs b/c difficulty jumps in parallel with level design. The DLCs are on average more detailed and prettier than your 2nd cousin. Several stages also have stronger R-type vibes... granted, they are homage stages so that makes sense.Okay, so bosses in this game kind suck. Most can actually be beaten too easy using a ship with a rodless force (basically a sidekick that runs around shooting whatever it sees). So you can use this one particular force on Normal ...maybe even Bydo difficulty, and your sidekick will attach itself to the boss and blow it up fairly quickly. This strategy does fall apart, and you will need to adjust to more powerful ships and in-game store "cheat" tickets to fire quicker charge shots or keep power-ups if you die.  I really think the game could have used a few more old school bosses that are static on the right side of the screen and do different bullet patterns/attacks. There are just a lot of bosses that attack from behind, and on higher difficulties (and me not watching youtube strategies) I've just had to resort to timing out the bosses on R-type 1-3 difficulty which are the harder difficulty levels.Achievements. Are you a perfectionists nerd? Well, you need to buy DLC 1-9 to get all the achievements. On top of that, some achievements are beyond ridiculous. Beat 300 levels w/o dying on R-type difficulty. Beat 1000 levels for another achievement. Idk if you've counted the number of stages yet, but with all the DLCs it's like 30 something stages I believe. So you can do the math on that one. Another achievement is make it thru 7 stages without taking a hit. Over on the TrueAchievements site, several individuals hit 160hrs+ to hit Perfect Game.  No thanks.Okay, now I've listed many negatives. And that's b/c I want you to know what you are getting into. It's r-type hard that is slopped together, rather than, a difficulty progression.Do I like this game. Yeah. I do. I even bought the stage passes on sale. I don't normally buy DLCs. And originally, I was appalled by the 9 DLCs, but I was like well, it is like 30 something levels total, so I dropped bout fifty dollars on this game which is the only game I've spent more than $20 on since Half-Life: ALyx and Zacarria Pinball Plat Edition.So yeah, good game, but it could have been a great game had the company put out a more polished and coherent base game.

_childDocuments_.review: y can't r-type turn aroundR-Type fans are going to want to play this regardless of what I have to say. Just go in knowing that the quality of the stages (I haven't touched the DLC stages) is roughly on par with the PS2's R-Type Final 1. That is to say, not nearly as good as the classic R-Types (we don't talk about Super R-Type in this house) but still Very Good for a horizontal shmup. I find the stages slightly less interesting than Final 1's, but there's also less slowdown and empty space in Final 2 compared to Final 1.Those on the fence--let's say you're interested in shmups but aren't sure if this is for you--I would ask, do you like Collect-a-thon style games? Because the gameplay-reward loop is heavily favored towards replaying the game, getting good at it, and using the acquired resources to unlock new ships, which change how the game is played and thus require you to re-adapt to the stages you previously thought mastered. For new players, I heavily recommend getting the free (as of this moment) DLC "April Fool's Prototype" because the early ships the game gives you are bottom of the barrel, and the Fool is no fool. The game should be beatable by a patient newcomer with that ship. The paid DLC "Mariko" is another good early game ship that plays differently from the April Fool's Prototype you might also be interested in. Either allow you to beat stages, which allow you to earn resources, which allow you to unlock the other ships that make the game easier (and thus allow quicker access to more resources).If you have no patience at all and just want something you can play through without thinking about or spend a bit of an afternoon on, I'd give this a Hard Pass. If you're committed to learning a single shmup and investing the time required to unlock the 100+ ships in the game, this is the shmup for you.

_childDocuments_.review: "R-Type has returned!" says the store page, and that's about all there is to this game. Final 2 is so oddly named because it's a direct sequel to one of the very best PS2 games, R-Type Final, and most of its ideas come straight from that source, for better or worse. Expect a difficult struggle as you fly through stages old and new, advancing through a tech tree of spaceships.R-Type goes back to 1987, a time of many spaceship shoot-em-ups (or shmups). In it, the screen scrolls to the right, and you wobble around a side view of the action and shoot down the enemy ships. Two primary features made R-Type notable: a charge shot known as the "Wave Cannon", and the powerup system tied intrinsically to the "Force". Like many shmups, there are powerups corresponding to different weapons, but here, they're not for . Instead, they summon and upgrade a ball of energy called a "Force", and the Force opens up a lot of interesting strategies. First, it deals contact damage and absorbs enemy bullets, which is handy in a game where you die in one hit. Second, it can attach to either the front or rear of your ship, and fire lasers corresponding to the color of the weapon powerup you've got (yellow lasers shoot vertically, blue diagonally, and red horizontally). When the Force is attached to the left, its weapons fire to the left. Third, it can be tossed off the ship at the press of a button, left to float around the screen and fire sort of independently of your actions.These elements add forethought and strategy to a twitchy genre. Do you keep the Force close and use it as a shield, or fling it away to attack from new angles? Do you rapid-fire, or charge up your Wave Cannon for huge burst damage? R-Type is a slow-paced shmup, but that slow pace is there to give you time to plan. By the time of R-Type Final, those core gameplay elements have been refined. Where you once only had one ship to choose from, now there are over 100, bringing new Wave Cannons and Forces with them. For example, the "Cerberus" introduced in R-Type Delta boasts a Lightning Wave Cannon that homes in on enemies and arcs through multiple targets, and an Anchor Force made to be thrown and stuck to large enemies. The Cerberus is here too! It's a lot of fun to iterate through the R Museum, to unlock new ships and try them out, to notice parts of stages where a certain Force or Wave Cannon makes it much easier (or harder...) to get through. You get old faces like the Cerberus, cameo appearances from other Irem games like Mr. Heli, and some buckwild ideas like the Platonic Love. At the very end, you gain fully customizable ships that can use any Force and Wave Cannon you want. This encourages wide knowledge of the game and rewards that with the ability to cook up some busted combos. As nicely as R-Type Final 2 scratches that itch for a less twitchy and more tactical shmup, it doesn't do much that Final 1 didn't. There are a few new ships, but most of the 100-plus craft are direct holdovers from the previous game. Whereas Final 1 mostly gave you new ships after certain amounts of play time (in general or with specific ships), Final 2 has a crafting system, where beating stages rewards you with four different currencies, three of which are spent to unlock new ships...but it still comes down to playing the same game over and over. Branching paths offer different configurations of the back half of the game, and lead to one of three endings. Many of the new stages of Final 2 follow similar progressions and themes to Final 1's, and all the DLC stages are actually throwbacks to past Irem games--including Final 1. Longtime R-Typers won't see very many new things here, but new players can see a wide swath of R-Type history represented in one easily accessible place.Well, I say "accessible", but this game can be harsh. R-Type games have sometimes been called "memory shmups" because it's less about reacting and more about knowing what comes next. The past stages in the DLC are the biggest offenders--sometimes they even appear to offer a branching path between high and low, but taking the high path just gets you crushed against a wall every time. Enemies can appear onscreen from any angle without warning, so sometimes moving near an edge of the screen gets you into a sudden crash. The new stages of R-Type Final 2's main game rely less on these cheap shots and checkmates, but they're still there. You die in one hit, and are sent back to a checkpoint with all your powerups gone (which sometimes sets you up very poorly for the next attempt), so these traps are very punishing. Worse, some special effects can make it difficult to even see incoming enemy attacks. Destroyed enemy ships and some of your ships' weapons have the same color scheme as the enemy bullets, while spherical blasts like Balmung missiles and the Shock Wave Cannon can entirely occlude the action. Between tricky spots you have to memorize, and the possibility that you literally won't see them coming, it's easy to feel like you're being punished for a mistake that you had no way of knowing you were making.I didn't mention the tickets in my first iteration of this review, but I've realized, these things matter a lot. When choosing your difficulty, you can open a submenu for additional options. Four special options correspond to the tickets you can buy with real or in-game money, and the only one I use regularly is Arms Warranty. With it, you  lose your powerups on death. It feels like Final 2 was balanced around using that one. Each ticket only lasts for one run, but higher difficulties give so much currency, one ticket pays for itself. With Arms Warranty, the game is still hard, but no longer punishing--especially once you unlock infinite continues. Beating a stage unlocks it in Score Attack, so you can play just that one or add it to an "original course" of seven stages in the order of your choice. And you can use Arms Warranty there too! This all combines to turn the grueling vibes on their head.Speaking of vibes, one thing R-Type Final 2 is missing is atmosphere. Over time, the R-Types have leaned more into horror, incorporated themes like "man is the real monster". Delta has a sort of Pyrrhic victory vibe all the way through (especially for the Cerberus), and Final starts every stage with a little blurb from the pilot as they gradually lose their mind in the face of a war with an unbeatable enemy. Notes in the R Museum (almost all copy-pasted from Final 1) go into detail about how the Force attached to your ship is actually a Bydo alien embryo trapped in a torture device, and some of the ships are torture devices for the pilots. Stages went from abstract space stations and tropey hives to facilities and even cityscapes that underscore that this is, in fact, war. I'm making it sound more heavy-handed than it actually is, but I think it's neat that the series evolved its excuse plot into such melancholy. Final 2 feels very gamey; it doesn't interact with the series lore, and when it does, it's not doing anything Final 1 didn't already do (better, imo). Even the visuals are...the lighting engine and overall style can make everything look like toys. Maybe this isn't a huge deal for you, and you're just here for the gameplay, and that's fine, the gameplay is tight. But if you're a series vet looking for more of the lore or the horror of R-Type, this ain't it.R-Type Final 2 is simply more R-Type, as its name and its store description imply. Granzella hasn't iterated the R-Type formula in any meaningful way, but this is very much a case of "if it ain't broke, don't fix it". The core gameplay loop is incredibly good, challenging reflexes and tactics in equal measure, and offering lots of different playstyles in the form of new ships. If you're interested in R-Type as a series...I would still recommend Delta or Final 1 first, if you can acquire them somehow. But if you just want a shmup on Steam, this is one of the best.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to start this off by listing all of the bad:-Alt+Tabbing is a gamble. It will sometimes leave the game in an uncontrollable state.-There are some performance issues that will arise from time to time. Usually this is in the form of frametime issues.-There is an issue with textures on assets. -The menu system can be buggy on some occasions. -The PC Version is still stuck on version 1.0.1-Stage 3 seems weirdly out of place. It uses a minimalist art direction and clashes with the rest of the game.-Price point for this package should have started around $25-$30.-Graphical Settings are non-existent.-Projectiles can get very hard to see when the screen gets busy.-Some bosses feel like afterthoughts.-There is one laser in the game that just... disappears when you disengage it. It is very contrasting compared to how amazing the animations are for other weapons in the game. -The currency system for ship acquisition is kind of busted since Etherium is so hard to come by. It makes the other currencies pointless.Even with these issues I did enjoy the game. GAMEPLAYI enjoyed the mechanics and varying styles of play offered by different ships and their Force. Some of  them drastically change the way you approach stages/enemies. Some specializations include: area of effect, long distance, close combat, utility, etc. They really did a decent job in making different classes of ships feel unique. They also put in a type of risk/reward factor into how scoring is handled through the use of Force and Dose. The stages included in the base game and the first DLC are enjoyable and look great (aside from the aforementioned stage 3). The difficulty for this game is handled beautifully in my opinion. Not only do enemies become more aggressive, but their numbers/patterns increase as well along with some other surprises. PRESENTATIONAside from some aspects of the UI being glitchy, the design looks great. The museum is a tad clunky in my opinion, but overall it is handled competently. It does take a few button presses to get into the game, but it's that bad. During gameplay, indicators are clear and stats are Sound design and music sounds good. Some tracks are better than others, but it fits the overall atmosphere of each stage. PERFORMANCEWhile the game does tend to have some stuttering issues for me, it runs smoothly for the most part (Usually my stuttering occurs after alt+Tabbing and/or Alt+Entering a few times). This is one of the rare shmups that allow you to play at above 60FPS and I love it. I lock everything to 120FPS and the response time and smoothness of animations does wonders of the gameplay and aesthetics. While the game doesn't allow you to control graphical settings it does allow you to ramp the game up to 4K. If you have a decent rig, you should be able to handle 4K 120FPS without issue. It's an amazing way to play the game. GRAPHICS (Outside of Stage 3)Lighting and particle effects look amazing in this game. Stage assets look amazing. Enemy and Ship models are detailed. It feels good to see a modern Japanese shmup with some production value. The only issue is that there is some minor texture pop in. The game also doesn't seem to be using the highest available textures on the player ship, but it's not very noticeable until end stage close ups.  Overall I enjoy R-Type Final 2. It is missing ALOT of content that was promised, but hopefully that gets rectified soon. This is a great base to build from and I feel like they can really propel this game into a modern shmup classic with a little bit more work. From the screenshot I've seen of a future DLC stage, I'm hopeful for the future of this game.PS: Please fix Stage 3. It is almost a meme.
_childDocuments_.name: R-Type Final 2

_childDocuments_.review: 30 credits later, finished the main stages - Excellent game, exactly what I've come to expect from R-Type, I would go on to say that this is so much better than its predecessor, R-Type Final.There are some things that could have been improved, some textures are a bit poor and stage three looks rather... bland, I wish the capital ship you fight had more detail to it.The pacing of the game is great, unlike it's predecessor, has very few empty sections, performance is great and I'm overall pleased with this, I will undoubtedly continue to play this for many years to come.Review update:- I'm sorry to say but I can no longer recommend  this game, initially it felt great but now the more I play, the more I see what's wrong with the game, the balancing is just... lacking, not for the sake of difficulty but rather inconsistencies with prior games and how the respective ships handle. There are bugs - Lighting wave cannon is bugged dealing lower amounts of damage the higher the framerate is (meaning at high framerates, the damage is very very very weak).Let's also talk about bits - in a whole playthrough, there are only 3 bit pickups, Stage 1, Stage 4 and Stage 7 - This means you can only have a fully powered up ship by Stage 4, in Prior games you would get one bit pickup in every level or every other level. Furthermore, they don't retain their movement characteritics of previous games and in particular from Final where shadowbits can be used to "whip" around the figher when using exaggerated movements.Next we also have hitbox issues - you're going to get pissed off with this one, the hitboxes are a large blob that do not match ship models.Now I'd like to talk about DLC 2, in particularly the "Crazy Machine" stage from R-Type Delta. There are just so many things wrong, from powerups, terrain, audio and overall balance not matching the original, here are some examples:-Powerup pickup order from the original were:-Red, Blue, Missile, Blue, Yellow, bit and RedNow:-Red, Yellow, Missile, Blue, Yellow, Blue (this should be the bit), Red and Red (new boss phase) - so we've lost a bit and the early pickup increases the difficulty of the section played through.Other differences include the following:-Gains doesn't get interrupted when you damage/fire the force at him, the turrets fire shots that ignore the force now, terrain (bridges in the opening segment) can kill the ship now (In Delta you could ram them and the cars on the road) and finally the music, it's not the complete song and it's been remixed with what just doesn't feel right.I hope these criticisms and issues will be addressed in later patches but I fear that these  will fall on deaf ears, not to mention the poor/slow support the PC platform is currently receiving (such as lack of transparency with store content and delayed patches).
