_childDocuments_.review: ntroduction:You Will Die Here Tonight is a survival horror game that plunges players into a tense and claustrophobic atmosphere, reminiscent of the genre's golden era in the 90s. Combining puzzle-solving, resource management, and heart-pounding encounters, this game seeks to resurrect the classic survival horror experience. Pros:- Atmosphere and Tension: The game excels at capturing that 90s horror game vibe so well- Challenging Puzzles: You Will Die Here Tonight features a variety of challenging puzzles that are both creative and rewarding to solve. - Playing smarter not harder: The game has a good way of encouraging you to make smart decisions to get ahead.Cons:- Forced Death: The game requires death, which is fine but is some places it takes away the feeling of risk.- Confusing Map Layout: The map is neat but also a little bit off putting- Sparse Storytelling: The story is great but sometimes it gets a little dry and you feel a serious lack of story progressionConclusion:You Will Die Here Tonight is a commendable nod to classic survival horror, capturing the essence of what made the genre so captivating. It’s not just a game where you might die tonight—it’s where you’ll live the horror of yesteryears, earning a solid 9 out of 10 S.T.A.R.S. in the survival horror genre.

_childDocuments_.review: You Will Die Here Tonight is an indie, Resident Evil-like horror game, played from a top-down perspective. You play as 6 members of a special forces team called ARIES, obviously inspired by RE's STARS. And like their first game, your mission is to investigate a mysterious mansion filled with traps, zombies, and oversized spiders. Gameplay is similar, you will have to explore the mansion to find items needed to progress, and can only save at a lamp. But the story is more than it seems.What makes this game unique, is firstly the combat. Unlike RE's automatic aim and shoot, entering combat will bring your character to a first-person view (but you cannot move) and fight the enemies from that perspective. Secondly, it's a roguelike game, where if you die, you'll have to continue as any of the remaining characters. Key items stay, but you can loot your teammates' corpses for ammo and healing items. And each character has a different ability, like how Ashley can make medkits, Eric can upgrade weapons, and how the bulkier characters can deal and take more damage but move slower.To properly finish the game, you'll have to play it more than once, and you'll get a new objective clue for subsequent runs from the KRKN computer. But it's not a big deal, since the game itself is short, and you actually keep your equipment, which makes later runs easier, faster, and more fun. It's also not too difficult, and you can actually revive your whole team if you have found K Coins. If you're into Resident Evil games, especially the early ones, you should definitely try this title.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

Check it out, it ain't bad.

_childDocuments_.review: First off let me begin by saying this game is too short.  I wish the main story could be extended by a few hours at least and that it was more tangible.  The gameplay in my opinion is quite fun.  I enjoy the pov mechanic in battles reminiscent of a light gun shooter (makes me think of time crisis 4's mechanic of holding off enemies coming from all directions).  I like the gun play and puzzles.I just wish there was a lot more to explore in the game in addition to more in depth looks at each character's motivations.  I get that the starting Doctor is supposed to be special but I felt no real interest in playing as her during the entirety of the game.  I ended up mostly playing as the weapons expert and the medic, finding their reactions to the events of the game to be a lot more entertaining.  For the price this game is really good especially if you want to scratch the resident evil itch.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game concept that mixes top down exploration with stationary first person combat that feels similar to playing a light gun with a controller all within a theme that's clearly inspired by Resident Evil. Unlike RE, this game has auto-save on death and you will frequently straight up  if you stumble your way into a puzzle's fail-state instead of having opportunities to fix the situation and live. The game is 100% designed with this abrasiveness in mind though and won't make you restart the entire game with a new save file or anything like that so just remember to take a deep breath and resist the urge to throw your controller through your screen.As for gripes, some boss fights fell particularly flat, combat on really weak enemies feels throwaway, and the comedy just did not do anything for me. I also am a weird freak that kinda likes the flawed as hell, awkward, red-headed PS2 step child of the RE franchise, Dead Aim. Because of that, I just couldn't get that fantasy out of my head of how cool it would be to play through this game with my Sinden lightgun. That said, I still had a good time playing through this with a controller and would recommend giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a really good surprised, I had hoped it would be a nice trowback to Resident Evil, and not only did I get that, I got so much more.The story had a very interesting twistIt's a really good looking game for those who like retroThe atmosphere was sooo good, there was several moments that got me on edge and a few moments that I actually jumped!And the gameplay mechanics, from the combat to the part of the game that... lives up to it's name, I enjoyed it all very much.This is a gem and the true horror is the fact that this game hasn't gotten the attention it truly deservesI 100% recomend

_childDocuments_.review: The most refreshing and fun survival horror experience I have had in awhile, plus it has plenty of laughs!!Honestly I see no "Flop" points about this game, I think it is extremely well done, the action flows good, and the combat is pretty damn good and entertaining as well. _childDocuments_.review: It’s an interesting twist on the classic survival horror genre and wears it’s inspiration on it’s sleeve.The good- The puzzles were fun and creative without overstaying their welcome.-The characters were all interesting and I was invested in trying to keep them alive. Seeing the reactions that each character had to various situations made replaying through the game a delight.-The aesthetics. The game is gorgeous and gory making lovely use of retro-esque visuals while not compromising on the quality of assets.-the arsenal of weapons are fun if limited. The feel good to use and sound nice enough. The one exception is the shield which I'm fairly certain is a joke item and is intended to get you killed.The bad- It’s a rather short game, I was able to beat it get the majority of achievements and the true ending in about 8 hours. This means a couple things one the excellent characters don’t have much of a chance to interact and the enemy variety is rather small. This wouldn’t be so bad if there were more reasons to replay the game. As is the only reason to play the game again after seeing both endings is to see the character reactions. And while those are enjoyable they can’t carry a replay of the game by themselves.-Communication is the most glaring issue I have with ‘You will die here tonight’, In my opinion the games does a terrible job of communicating with the player. This is consistent throughout various aspects of the gameplay, boss fights, puzzles, and certain items.	During certain boss fights I was absolutely certain I was missing some key aspect of the fight as I was just sending character after character to their deaths hoping that I could do enough damage so that the next character would be able to finish it off. I’m referring to the giant spider boss here. Or a boss would do something and I’d have no idea why it happened. I’m thinking specifically of the 3 knights fight , the first character I used was slaughtered but with my second and third I noticed the boss would occasionally freeze even after beating them I have no idea why.	I praised the puzzles before but these is a small exception the moth and the butterfly puzzles. My main complaint about these and how they differ from other puzzles is that there is no way to tell that you’ve completed the puzzle successfully. I’m fine with the puzzle killing the player if they fail to complete it properly but confirmation of completion would be nice. As is I ended up accidentally resetting one puzzle after putting in the correct combination.	I mentioned the shield before. I think it’s suppose to reduce damage but if it does I certainly wasn’t able to tell. A visual indicator or a clanging sound when the shield is being hit would have been an excellent fix.	Finally K-coins having no explanation for what they do I ended up hording all of mine and only finding out after I had completed the game what they actually did. It’s understandable why they don’t include anything on the actual item description but it would be nice if there was something more descriptive on the game over screen explaining what they do.While I have been more negative in this review I overall really enjoyed the game and I’m looking forward to what this team does next. If you enjoy the classic resident evil games you’re likely to enjoy this. That said if you’re on the fence and this game is on sale I’d highly recommend getting it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has absolutely no business being as fun as it is. It's perhaps a little short and lacks the depth of content you might expect for the price tag, but what you get is a game that looks and sounds fantastic, tells an interesting story and layers on some really thoughtful puzzles. The way the game transitions from top down to first person is essentially seamless, and the combat itself is a really interesting and initially quite engaging change of pace. Unfortunately it did get to the point where the lack of resources and ability to dodge/effectively block hits made it feel a bit one dimensional - if and when you miss you are basically just waiting for the enemy to hit you, and since you can't actively dodge you're basically forced to start your heal/reload knowing full well you're going to take damage or die. That said, it took me until quite close to the end of the game for this to matter at all because the novelty of the combat lasted a long time. Visually the first person view is stellar, the zombies have this mixture of slight pixelation and colourful detail, their animations are fluid and realistic and the 360 degree encounters are able to make you feel a sense of urgency without also feeling cheap. The top down view is a bit more basic, it by no means looks bad but it's comparatively sparse and the animations for the player characters are a little awkward. I also felt at time that the game could have used a line-of-sight system to draw you in a little more - the house sounds threatening, but you'll quite quickly realise that for the most part you can see enemies before they become an issue, even around corners, I'd really have loved, especially in the back half of the game, to not be able to see enemies coming if they are around a corner. The ambient sound in the house is compelling enough to warrant a bigger spot on the stage.While there is a meta-progression system it's limited by the games length - I only upgraded I think 2 guns and that was because the second run through I basically knew exactly what to do and where to go, so I never had the right person in the right spot to upgrade anything else. I'd really have loved for the house to be a longer experience, the enemies to be more varied and perhaps for there to be a certain amount of forced deaths to justify the idea of starting over and upgrading things further. It's hard to feel like you need to upgrade gear when you kill 90% of the enemies in one to two shots.The story is pretty decent, there are a few twists and turns but I will say it felt like it fell victim to the general lack of content in the game. To bring the story to a close they had to get through quite a large story development, have the player deal with it and bring it to a grand conclusion within the space of about 10 minutes of game time - if this had a bit more runway it would maybe have felt like a more natural end, but because I could clear the rest of the game without needing to restart it felt like it just went 0-60 basically from nowhere. It also felt like the story of the house itself was only partly told - I'd have loved a bit more visual stuff, maybe some narration of the notes you find or some more background on the antagonist and why we're there. There are good reasons for a general lack of background on the house in the story, but whether the narrative justifies the lack of content or the lack of content informs the narrative is not especially clear. Ultimately though I hope you can tell that I'm nitpicking hard here - what you have is a genuinely fun and unique experience that takes the bones of Resident Evil (when it was actually good) but layers on an engaging combat mechanic plus an interesting exploration loop and I genuinely enjoyed every minute of it. If you're even remotely interested in this genre I'd really urge you to buy and play it, if only to support a developer that is trying to do something interesting. If AAA can extract £100 from you for formulaic, uninspired reruns of the same game every year you can spare £17 for this. Definitely recommended and I hope the devs make more.

_childDocuments_.review: It's alright.Decent(if a bit weird) story, mostly decent characters and the gameplay has an interesting twist with the combat, even tho it does kinda get a bit stale towards the end (way too many single enemy fights in a system that shines when fighting multiple enemies at once).The puzzles were alright, and as the title of the game implies, quite a few of them will try to kill you if you fail. But also, in spite of the title, I somehow managed to avoid dying to any of the puzzles, or any of the regular enemies.But I did die quite a bit when fighting bosses. Boss fights were a bit frustrating at first, but then I just embraced the fact that You Will Die Here Tonight and it got a bit less frustrating.I don't think this game is particularly replayable, but it's fun and interesting enough for a single playthrough.I will leave two pro-tips:1) Don't worry about dying. You likely will die here tonight, but it's alright, just roll with it.2) All you need to do to use the  is press space(or whatever button pulls out the melee weapon on gamepad), you don't need to time an attack or anything, just have it out and aim at the attacking enemy. _childDocuments_.review: Boy, did I enjoy "You Will Die Here Tonight"! In a year stacked with great horror games, this unassuming 2D indie title is among my favorite. Well, that's actually not saying much, after all years pass by and games-of-the-year lists get forgotten... but I really think "You Will Die Here Tonight" will be one of my go-to horror games in the future, and I'll be returning to it every once in a while. I like it because, for one, it's a neat gameplay idea to have a group of playable characters who can die and be removed from the plot permanently. I've seen it attempted in "Until Dawn" (kinda worked), "Song of Horror" (barely worked), and "Obscure" (didn't work at all), but "You Will Die Here Tonight" is the first time when I actually felt the tension without a single note of frustration. Each death felt like it was my fault: I could have been more careful, I could have prepared better, I could have given more attention to subtle environmental cues. Yes, there are some instant death traps, but they are foreshadowed quite well. The game is a lot easier than it seems initially, but it withheld key information from me long enough to make me sigh with relief when I realized I'm about to make it to the end. The story is a bit hard to follow, but I was intrigued by it; when I replay the game, I'll make sure to pay more attention. The exploration is pretty great and fairly non-linear, though I think puzzle solutions are always the same. "You Will Die Here Tonight" could have squeezed more time out of its gameplay loop if it had more RNG, but to be honest, I've had so much fun throughout its 4 hour runtime that I don't really feel like complaining.

_childDocuments_.review: Resident Evil Gaiden was always one of my favorite entries in the series, and to see a modern love letter to that game finally release was the shock of a lifetime. The varied and interesting traps and death scenes were also fun to discover (and necessary for achievements and to a degree story progression).  Some might find it a little short, but I felt like it was perfectly paced and didn't wear out it's welcome at all.  Highly recommend grabbing this, be it on sale or at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: A really really good game.Not exactly survival horror, as it showers you in resources. Instead, 'You Will Die Here Tonight' is really good at playing with your expectations if you've played the original resident evil.The good:-The first person 'on rails shooter' combat is really fun and really suspenseful, I would love to play more of it.-The game feels great to control over all. Thank you for refraining from using tank controls.-All but a couple of the puzzles are actually really fun to figure out. I never really had to resort to moon logic for anything. Great job on the puzzles!-Having to move on to a next character after dying rather than re-loading is REALLY effective at making things tense. The way the into mission was handled really helps build that tension as well.-Each character having somewhat different strengths and weaknesses, as well as their own flavor text for some descriptions, is just great. It really makes them dying more impactful.The bad:-The shotgun puzzle is rather unclear, and could use a light rework.-The spider boss is weirdly overpowered. It is MUCH harder than anything else the game throws at you by a huge margin. Even the final boss is a chump compared to it.-I wish the game were longer. I've hit 100% achievements in about five and a half hours.-Tension can be somewhat undermined by just how much ammo you get. There's very little reason to avoid fights once you get decent with the pistol. In contrast, it's usually best to clear enemies constantly so you only have to deal with one enemy at a time.-The character writing leans a bit too comedic for my tastes. I found myself wishing the characters were written from a more genuine angle more often than not.

_childDocuments_.review: An homage to early Resident Evil and it brings arguably one of the most overlooked mechanics from it back from the dead. It brings back the combat system of Resident Evil Gaiden where you move along a 3D plain but when you target an enemy it brings you into a combat arena that you will then shoot enemies in, almost like a mobile House of the Dead combat system. It's freaking amazing and I wish I saw it more. The other neat mechanic is that you play as a team. When one of you dies you will switch to any of the other team members you want, and each of them has a specialty as well as a neat personality attached to them. It will probably take you roughly 2-4 hours for a play through as well as a bit more for cleanup/endings. Because of how much I adore these kinds of games and for it bringing back a long lost mechanic I like the $20 amount but for what's here for those not nostalgic $10 is a great buy for a day off play through.

_childDocuments_.review: A cool and very intriguing mashup between resident evil one, but also the arcade light gun game House of the Dead. Basically, you explore an area in top down, but you engage in combat like a light gun shooter. It also distinguishes itself by effectively giving you 6 characters which act as your lives. Instead of having a game over when you die, you just wake up and resume the progress made by another survivor in the mansion.So enemies that a previous survivor killed won’t respawn, but also the ammo you used to kill them doesn’t regenerate.All your survivors die, well… it’s game over and you start the game again, only this time better prepared for all the cheap deaths out there. The game has some problems but otherwise is a solid short experience. Its combat is clunky and the game is very short for its $25 price tag.  They also made some choices with regard to difficulty that made the experience a bit too easy? Like infinitely respawning ammo at the home base. They also have a cool system of finding the corpse or infected survivor, but you rarely have to interact with it. On the flip side, taking down a boss feels like it’s supposed to kill at least one person to make enough progress to actually beat it. The difficulty alternates between cheap death and hand holding, and never quite hit that survival horror sweet spot. When you add in a specific non-renewable resource, the magic is gone.Regardless, it’s a fun and unique experience that could have been improved if they just stuck to their guns and changed some aspects of the difficulty. Definitely pick up if it’s on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly good survival horror game that continued to surprise me from start to finish. I hadn't been this frustrated and attached to keeping a character alive throughout an entire campaign just to see what their reaction would be to everything, especially with Mike and Erik. The mechanic of losing characters can be subverted with K-coins throughout the mansion. These can allow you to switch characters to see alternative outcomes or to use a character's strengths and abilities to tackle a challenge, but the attachment is still there. Dev team is small and like the original Resident Evil, they had to cut out a lot of alternative scenarios and story elements, so I expect them to come out with a Director's Cut or a similar release at some point in the future. A lot of folks seem to compare this to RE Gaiden and HOTD, which is apt and I can see why. There are a lot of competitors within indie survival horror and this game stands out, even with its shortcomings. There is so much potential here and a lot can be added in the future, so I definitely recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: It always pains me to see games like You Will Die Here Tonight. Games that aim to do true classic survival horror with some new ideas but fail miserably. Though, at least in the case of You Will Die Here Tonight the end result is still quite serviceable and with some updates and fixes might become slightly better. Though it won’t fix any of the issues that are making this project deeply flawed on a fundamental level. And my experience with the game went from mild curiosity to genuine, though sometimes annoyed, engagement. Only to plummet into frustration as I stopped playing it right during the final sequence of the game and refuse to attempt it again, because it’s horrendously designed.So what is You Will Die Here Tonight? It’s a quite well designed classic survival horror game with an isometric perspective that in many ways reminds of Resident Evil Gaiden. Sadly, that includes some of the bad things about RE Gaiden, but for the most part the title figures out how to take that extremely flawed and often frustrating game and its ideas and turn it into something that is actually working. Due to the isometric perspective, as you might expect, no combat is happening in that main view of the game. So when you get attacked or aim a weapon in the direction of an enemy (with a clear line of sight), the game switches to a first person view. In it, you’re locked into place in a jRPG-like battle arena space as the enemies are approaching you while you shoot them. The amount of enemies in that battle space corresponds to the amount of enemies that were aggroed and in the vicinity and the distance and their state of aggression in the isometric view is estimated in this battle view. Oh and, the battle view covers the full 360 degrees of rotation and enemies can attack you from all sides.When you’re not fighting enemies, you’re exploring the very Resident Evil 1 inspired mansion, find weapons, upgrades, ammo, healing items and solve puzzles to get equipment and key items. Most of which is done really well and exploring the locations is genuinely fun. Except for one big thing that in a typical survival horror game would be pure bad design – the game is exceptionally rude with its enemies, bosses and traps. In many spots you’re not given any second chances or ways to undo whatever you did when clicking the interactable spot, so if the game asks you if you wish to do something, you say “yes” and it trap hasn’t been disarmed yet – even if there’s a delay for the trap, you cannot undo your action.So how is the game excusing this behavior? It’s also a time loop rogue-lite-ish game. In a concept that is introduced right from the beginning, you have a team of 6 people and as soon as one of them dies, you just switch to another. All of them have some unique perks, one of them has a unique quest and two can give you permanent upgrades. All of your key items and equipment within one loop is preserved between characters and between whole loops all of the equipment is always kept, but the events and key items are reset. Which… I guess it could be cool? Maybe? I’m not much of a fan of rogue-like/lite games or permadeath, so I’m not one to say if this idea can work in theory or not. But what I can say is that it doesn’t really work for this game.The big problem the game has is that, apart from some especially rude and unforgiving moments, it plays like a proper classic survival horror game. To the point, where it seems far more natural to ease the moments and build in a normal save/load system than find more ways to excuse it’s main gimmick. On my very first attempt I’ve finished about 85% of the whole time loop events, including all secrets, with just one character without dying only to die to an especially obnoxiously long boss. Partially because I couldn’t upgrade any of my equipment as you can only switch characters when they die. So as soon as that character died, I switched to another to finally do all of the upgrades and then went so easily to the end of the game that I decided to die intentionally by the end just so I can switch to the other upgrade-necessary characters and do the other upgrades. And an even more frustrating thing is – despite having this team of 6 characters, most of them don’t even have anything interesting or special about them.Apart from the story, I suppose, which serves as the main excuse to have this gimmick and… Wow is it terrible. I mean, the characters are horribly written, which seems to have been done intentionally – to create a gallery of tropes. But it’s not charming or funny, it’s just dumb. And then you have several layers of stories, none of which have any proper resolution or even proper progression, apart from the big twist for the true ending path, which explains the whole time loop thing and… again, it’s so stupid and poorly done I don’t understand why the developers got hung up on it so much. And yeah, since I did drop the final path almost near the end I had to watch the rest in a video just to see if I’m missing anything that makes things better. I wasn’t and I wasn’t about to waste more of my time doing laser dodging in an isometric game with invisible collisions and no way to judge distance.It’s a shame that the developers decided to sabotage their own genuinely solid, if a bit too reliant on classic survival horror tropes, game for the sake of a story twist and a mechanic that aren’t any good. Because for the most part the game was really well put together. Yes, they’d need to make enemies less plentiful and less aggressive, make some boss battles a bit less long and slightly rebalance a few traps. But if they’d do that, we’d have a simple but extremely well made, very stylishly looking isometric survival horror title that proves that Resident Evil Gaiden could’ve worked with few tweaks. I especially want to praise the people who did the pre-render cutscene visuals to look like a perfect recreation of the PS1 CGI feel, but with modern resolutions. And the normal game had me thinking that Parasite Eve or Blood Omen could still work even in modern very high resolution games if approached smartly.Nonetheless, I would still recommend not ignoring You Will Die Here Tonight. Some of it’s more minor annoyances might get improved with updates and the main chunk of the game is really good, especially if you’re a sucker for classic survival horror. Sadly, I don’t see a way to remove the core issues of the game as removing the main gimmick would require rethinking the whole story structure, while moving harder into the gimmick would probably make the core survival horror gameplay more frustrating. Still, a very good attempt and I’m highly interested in what the developers can create next.

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels like a RE-flavored rogue lite, in that the level design/atmosphere/sound design/art direction/puzzles/cheesy dialogue all feel very classic survival horror, but there's no inventory management whatsoever. You're never actually in any danger of running out of resources because you can just run back to the item box at any time to fill up for free and handgun ammo is infinite when you can't. Dying doesn't actually set back progress at all and even if every character dies they all reset for free as well. All in all, still a super fun, well-polished little game that's absolutely worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare that a game actually makes me want to give the devs MORE money for their game, but You Will Die Here Tonight managed to accomplish that. With innovative gameplay, nostalgic graphics, and amazing sound design, the game pulled me in from start to finish. The writing was also well done, and kept me intrigued throughout. Overall, it's a unique experience that is satisfying from beginning to end.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: Resident Evil 1 loveletter game, where exploration is in an isometric perspective, and combat is in rooted first person. You have multiple characters to play as if one dies, and you continue to progress where they failed, though they might not be dead anymore. Do not expect to beat the game with your first character, and you should not you aim for it. It does horror well, and the switch from isometric to first person stayed unnerving throughout the entirety of the game. The story is decent and serves its purpose, but the real beef of the game is the exploration, puzzles and combat. There is a true ending if you do a specific series of events. There is no randomiser or ng+ modes, but those would just be cherries on the cake.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent isometric tribute to the original Resident Evil, with a really neat spin on first person combat. The combat is fun and challenging, and the characters have personality and charm. I recommend this if you're a fan of the genre even at full price. Game would be better when achievements and maybe NG+ or unlocks are added in later. I'll have to check out the other additional endings too.

Don't miss out on this and show the devs some love.

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect game.. Amazing game design combining all the great stuff we love from RE except none of the annoying elements that used to come with them, such as:1. oldie exploration without objectives being too difficult to remember,2. super exciting arcade shooting without the horrible sense of direction during down time,3. fighting with limited resources without locking you out for using up ammo by mistake,4. lets you upgrade/ choose your loadout to an extent without a forceful trade-off in item management,5. death traps and puzzles but has mechanism to completely having you re-run everything.6. has sort of a meta-gameImpeccable.Make moreeee please!PS love the several small elements that alluded to RE1

_childDocuments_.review: YWDHT captures the feeling of a classic Resident Evil (not remakes) of the mansions, puzzles and the traps that are littered throughout the environment. If you are successful at reaching certain points with particular characters, those upgrades will carry across the loops.Only thing that was strange was the ESL-like dialog along with the random generated names though I'm not sure if that's just a homage to the translation choice that happened way back when too. (Miserable pile of secrets, anyone?)

_childDocuments_.review: You Will Die Here Tonight is a really interesting idea with some very uneven execution. Essentially Resident Evil meets House of the Dead meets Cabin in the Woods, this pretty much plays like fixed camera Resident Evil with (very entertaining) first person combat. The biggest change to the Resident Evil formula is permadeath and an almost roguelike looping system. You start with six characters, and once one of them bites it, that’s it – no loading a save, do not pass go, do not collect 200 machine gun bullets. You start again with one of the other characters with your guns and items intact – though you will have to scavenge your ammo from the corpse of your teammate. If all six characters die, then you start on a new loop – you keep your guns and upgrades, but all key items and progress is lost.Each character has their own strengths and weaknesses, as well as their own missions – some of which are necessary to see the true end. While it is possible to complete the game with the true ending on a single loop, it is unlikely unless you are using a guide as the game is extremely lethal. Even outside of dying to the  fast enemies that can kill you in 2-3 hits, every trap will one shot you, and while it is often obvious that there’s likely to be a trap the inability to experiment at all can make it unclear exactly what is required to not die. There is a particular (thankfully non-lethal) puzzle where even after looking up the solution the language used was so unclear that I felt none the wiser. It's in these roguelike elements I think that the game does end up fighting itself a bit. On a new loop, going through the exact same puzzles, the exact same corridors and fighting the exact same enemies just isn’t interesting even if you will be able to do it much more quickly the second time round. Permadeath just doesn’t gel that well with hand crafted puzzles and encounters.I do think that there’s a lot to like here though, and I don’t want to sound too down on the game as I did enjoy my 5-6 hours with it. The first person combat is much more interesting than the point and delete combat of early survival horror games, there’s some great atmosphere and the deliberately lo-fi visuals are very charming. The story, while not exactly original is an interesting twist on the haunted mansion formula. Tentatively recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: Perfection. Beautiful love letter to Resident Evil.I only wish it were longer. Right when it starts to build steam and REALLY get you hooked, well, that's the end. Short and very sweet. This gameplay format was genuinely so fun and if this developer repurposed it for a longer survival horror story, I'd throw money at them.

_childDocuments_.review: A very cool top-down survival horror with a RE Gaiden style combat system and really clever progress and character permadeath system. Looks delightful, spooky atmosphere, satisfying exploration and puzzles, multiple endings. An absolute treat for classic survival horror fans, and a cool twist in the story too.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: You Will Die Here Tonight ReviewYou Will Die Here Tonight is a love letter to older survival horror titles like Resident Evil. When you are playing the game, it has an isometric third-person view. When you initiate combat, it goes into a first-person mode. The game's graphics look like a game made at the tail end of the original PlayStation's life cycle, which is a compliment because it looks great. It invokes all those nostalgic feelings.You go to a mansion to track down a killer. Upon entering the mansion first thing you find after waking is a note saying, "You will die her tonight. Anything you find might help the other escape. On the back is a photo of your team saying, "Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it." You will soon find out that is true. When a character dies, another can gather their inventory and add it to their own. Once the second character goes down. You realize there might be a time loop involved. Your character says their line again and thinks about how they have said it before. This whole set up is enough to pull you in and have you interested. That is all I will say to keep it spoiler free. The story is interesting and will keep you wanting to find out what comes next. The story should be experienced, not read about. Once all characters have died, you restart with everyone alive and progress carries over. You will have all your weapons and items from the previous run. This roguelike element allows you to experiment if you are having a hard time with a puzzle and it kills you. It can also help if you stumble into a boss fight you aren't ready for. While the game is difficult, the roguelike element helps keep the difficulty manageable.You Will Dies Here Tonight is a throwback to 90's survival horror, and you can see that in the puzzles. The puzzles will remind you of Resident Evil quite a bit. Most puzzles are not that difficult, but sometimes you come across puzzles that will make you frustrated. I ran into a puzzle with statues that you have to move according to a poem. The poem doesn't help much in understanding the orientation of the statues. I struggled to make sense of it but ended up moving them around until I got it right.When you initiate combat you go into a first person mode. You can aim like a traditional shooter, but you cannot move. There is a button to escape if that is possible with the encounter. When you switch to combat woth a group of enemies they won't always be directly in front of you. You can spin 360 degrees in combat mode, which makes encounters much more intense. You start off with a Handgun and Tactical Knife. You can find other weapons in the mansion. With the first three hours I had found a magnum, shotgun, and grenade launcher. You find ammo through traditional means such as, breaking boxes, breaking vases, and just picking up boxes of ammo. The one frustrating thing to happen in combat is getting infected. You have six doses to cure the infection, but it felt like every other encounter I was gettimg infected. I feel the amount of infectious bites should be lowered to raise the enjoyment for the player. The game is difficult enough that lessening the chances of zombie virus infections wouldn't ruin anything. There is no voice acting for the characters. You get your dialogue through text boxes, but it isn't overwhelming. The sound design really makes the atmosphere creepy. You can hear enemies shambling around and their monstrous voices. Sometimes you hear creepy music playing in the area that starts skipping, adding to that uneasy feeling in the pit of your stomach. The weapons also sound great while firing.The switch from third person to first person is such a unique mechanic. If you packaged this as an original PlayStation game and had me play it, you might trick me into believing I'm playing one of the most innovative PS1 games ever made. If nostalgia is always pulling at you and you find yourself playing older titles, wishing they still made games this way, look no further. They do make games like back in the day. The game isn't perfect, but I feel every survival horror should pick this title up. This isn't just a hidden gem. This is a diamond in the rough.The game does so many things right, that when it does a little bit wrong, you are able to ignore it. Not only will it fill your nostalgia cup fully, but it will also scare the pants off you. The story reminds me of a good book. The more you play, the more you can't wait to turn that page and see what happens next. The combat is intense, but a lot of fun. If you love Resident Evil and the old Alone in the Dark titles, this game will make you feel right at home. Spiral Bound Interactive has delivered a solid survival horror game at a great price point of $19.99.Edit: $15.99 until November 7th.This review is expanded on

_childDocuments_.review: People say Resident Evil 1 but this actually feels more like a modern twist on Resident Evil Gaiden on the GBA. You run around in the overworld exploring and solving puzzles while combat resolves in a separate first person shooter instance ala House of the Dead. The game itself is actually quite good. Atmospheric and tense. It's unique feature is its lives system where each character functions as a life to progressively finish the game similar to old Survival Horrors like Sweet Home or Nightmare on Elm Street.Only downside is really janky kb&m controls that take a bit to get used to.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: Game is pretty brutal until you figure everything out. Has hints of Resident Evil DS in it's combat with an overhead view like Resident Evil Gaiden. Every fight is an event. Enemies can spawn all around the character forcing you to have a strategy in mind when going up against multiple combatants. Characters have their own unique personalities and traits ranging from a Fast running medic to a slow and bulky weapons specialist.Each character also possesses a unique ability such as stocking a med cabinet or modding weapons. i was able to full complete in about 6 hours. I do feel that at some point i was pulled out of the core experience, and i'm sure those who have completed the game know what i mean. Overall, it's fun, and has a lot of character outside of the materials it takes inspiration from (and in some circumstances, directly pulls from)
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed it. Briefest rundown I can provide:Isometric Exploration and PuzzlesFirst Person Arcade style shooter combatAlthough it may appear to be just some kind of Classic Resident Evil at first, it's got a unique story. I feel like the game play is an interesting enough mashup to help it stand out from other games.Doesn't appear to be any unlockables for completing it at this time - but I still had a lot of fun with the journey.  One of the Developers has stated that it's roughly 6-8 hours of game play for the average player,and I'm inclined to agree as my experience was roughly 8 hours at a dawdling pace.The only negative things I have to say is that I ran into a few bugs that ranged from irritating to having to reset the game.  The lock ups only occurred maybe 3 times in my 8 hours of play.  I saved often, and the issue was always resolved upon booting the game back up.The 'Irritating' bug was getting ammo upgrades before getting the weapon seemed to render them useless.  I was not Soft Locked by this, but it was irritating to see the upgrades sitting in my inventory, yet having no impact.I got it on sale at a steal, but I wouldn't shy away from full price if I hadn't. Worth the price IMO - especially later on when they've had a chance to iron some bugs out.
_childDocuments_.name: You Will Die Here Tonight

_childDocuments_.review: I loved it.However, I must warn anyone who plans on buying based on the demos that pretty much all the demo content is absent from the final game.What you're actually going to get is a kind of roguelite Resident Evil 1 homage.Just when I thought I knew what I was getting, well, let's just say there's a rather dramatic twist.

Has a great PS1 era vibe, combining the likes of Resident Evil and House of the Dead.It isn't anything like I was expecting it to be, and the twists I've already had are what make this game so good. Definitely recommend giving this game a try

name: BRAVELY DEFAULT II
detailed_description: 『BRAVELY DEFAULT II』+『VARIOUS DAYLIFE』Bundle BRAVELY DEFAULT II and VARIOUS DAYLIFE: two great games from Square Enix's Team Asano in one bundle! Bundle Contents BRAVELY DEFAULT II (main game) VARIOUS DAYLIFE (main game) About the Game Fire, Water, Wind, Earth, nature's masters, The Crystals' power exceeds the hand of man, And if unleashed, would bring down death, disaster, Calamity and blight upon the land. ―― Ancient quatrain of Kingdom Musa Guided by fate, it’s up to you to stop the forces that threaten these heroes and all of Excillant. A new entry in the “Bravely” series A new world, a new story, and all-new Heroes of Light 'Four new Heroes of Light emerge' Seth A young sailor who drifts to the continent of Excillant and is the main character of this story. Meet Gloria, an exiled princess whose kingdom was robbed of its Crystals, and set out on a journey to recover them with her. Gloria The princess of Musa, a kingdom that once watched over the harmony of the world - but the loss of the kingdom's Crystals led Musa to destruction. Having fallen into despair and gone into hiding, she decides to embark on a journey to retrieve the Crystals. Adelle A mercenary for hire. She travels with Elvis as his bodyguard in his search for an asterisk. Elvis A scholar who travels the world. Embark on a journey in search of a particular asterisk needed to unravel the last spellbook left by his master. In addition to a traditional, turn-based battle system that combines jobs and abilities, you can enjoy innovative and strategic battles unique to the Bravely series by taking control of your turns via the Brave and Default system. Brave and Default Brave Points (BP) dictate how many actions a character can use in a single turn. Players can have characters 'Default' to stock up to three additional BP to use in a turn, or characters can 'Brave', to use more than one BP to perform multiple actions. Balancing stockpiling and using BP is a key component in battle strategy. Jobs and Abilities Each character can exhibit both a primary and secondary job class, with each job specializing in different abilities. Combining jobs allow you to handle two abilities simultaneously. You can create an all-rounder balanced in offense and defense, or perhaps a character that specializes in magic. Your tactics and how you develop each character are up to you. Acquire New Jobs “Asterisk bearers” will often block your path forward. By defeating them, you will obtain an Asterisk that enables you to change jobs.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a high quality game but with a very niche appeal, being a more modern take on the classic  job formula. If you loved games like  and , this is more of the same, just with better visuals, smoother combat and various quality-of-life improvements. Don't be spooked by the II in the title, the game's story and setting have no relation whatsoever to  and , which are still 3DS exclusives and .And while there's a decent amount of story, it's not the focus. This is a gameplay heavy JRPG for people who love job systems and experimentation. There's no "story mode" either, the only difference between casual/normal/hard difficulties is enemy speed, i.e. how often the enemy gets turns, you still have to exploit weaknesses and the damage taken/dealt will always be 100%. So if you're unwilling to engage with the job mechanics, you will not be able to progress, as bosses can wipe you in just a couple turns if you don't know what you're doing. It's largely impossible to overpower bosses by grinding levels, you need to build a sensible party, e.g. the classic tank/healer/physical attacker/magical attacker.If you've never played a Bravely game before, the main gimmick of the series is the brave/default system. Brave lets you borrow up to 3 turns, while default banks the current turn and puts the character in the guard stance. So e.g. you can default for 3 turns, then brave 3x to execute 4 actions at once. This lets you deal a lot of damage while still guarding most of the time. And you can also choose to be brave even without any extra turns banked, which will simply make your character skip the next turns (but without guarding), this is a gamble that can pay off if you know those extra turns will net you a victory.The game offers 24 jobs to choose from, each with a unique outfit for every party member. Of course, given this many options, the balance can be shaky. Some jobs are must haves, some are great for their active abilities, while others are only worth it for 1-2 passives. Your main job will decide your stat scaling, weapon proficiency, active abilities as well as give you up to 2 specialties (unique perks, e.g. white mages can AoE revive and remove status). You can also choose a sub-job but it will only be used for its active abilities (barring some late game exceptions). And you can also equip up to 5 passive abilities from any jobs you have learned. Compared to previous games, buffs have been nerfed making bards quite weak, and turn order is now individual instead of global, meaning characters with high speed and low equipment weight get more turns.Some players complain about puzzle bosses, but I didn't find this to be true, outside of some late game exceptions. The vast majority of bosses are beatable with any party combination, provided it's within reason. You never need to switch to a specific job to beat a boss. However, it's worth noting that the game relies a lot on counters, but at the same time you get a passive pretty early on that makes you immune to physical counters, and magical counters are pretty rare.The game offers mostly excellent quality-of-life with 4 combat speed options (adjustable on the fly) plus a button that lets you repeat your last turn's actions which is useful when fighting trash mobs. However, there are also some notable UX issues, such as dungeons having no maps and the battle info screen only listing weaknesses but not immunities and resistances (although, those can be looked up in the lore menu). Also, the quest log only keeps track of active quests, you can't see what quests you have completed.Audio and visuals wise, I thought the game was excellent. The characters look very cute and diverse, the models are high poly with very detailed textures despite the semi-chibi art style. The towns are 2.5D and look like oil paintings, while everything else is fully 3D. The soundtrack in particular is really good, it was composed by Revo, the same musician that worked on the previous Bravely games, and it's full of bangers. Just listen to  or . The localization is very high quality and done in the same style as , featuring a plethora of British accents and regional slang, which is very fitting for this kind of game.Side content wise, the game has 100 side quests, which can range from basic fetch quests to high effort ones with fully voiced cutscenes and exclusive dungeons and bosses. The post-game is sadly lacking but there's a New Game Plus mode that allows for some interesting challenges such as a level 1 run.Overall, Bravely Default II is an easy recommendation provided you're into classic JRPGs and value complex turn-based combat over story and characters.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, the port of this game is really good. Everything works and looks great, even better than the Switch version, which is a welcome surprise. But is this game for you? If you ever played really old-school jRPGs with job systems, and turn based combat, like Final Fantasy III or V, or Octopath Traveler and you really enjoyed them, then most definitely yes. Bravely Default as a series is basically a huge love letter to this style of games, and if you are veteran FF player, that can't stand new entries in the franchise, then this one is definitely for you. If you don't even know what I'm talking about, I will try to list everything you should know about the game below:- You control party of 4; - During the story you learn new "jobs" which are basically classes like warrior, mage, archer etc.; - Any party member can get any job, and change it on the fly so there is a lot of customization and experimentation;- The fun actually comes from finding the most optimal party setup and synergies between jobs;- The game is about 60 hours long, if you only want to get to the ending, but it will take about 100 hours for 100% completion;- The world is set in a typical jRPG High Fantasy setting with Goblins, Orcs, Dragons, Mages, Knights etc. Think Dragon Quest or Early Final Fantasy games;- The story actually covers themes like Warriors of Light (basically chosen ones) and Elemental Crystals, so really archaic stuff, but it has got some spins to it, that I won't spoil;- Battle System is turn-based but with a titular Brave/Default System;- Brave/Default works like that: Every action you perform costs 1 turn. "Default" command is basically a "guard" from other jRPGs but additionaly you save an action up to +2 actions. With "Brave" command you can perform multiple (max 4) actions in single turn, but if you abuse it too much, you will have to wait additional turns, while being a free target for your enemies;- Balancing this system is essential to the battles and it gives them even more depth, making player take more "high-risk, high-reward" approach;- Side Quests are really basic, they are all basically fetch quests like "kill x enemies" or "find y Item";- The game requires you to grind, it could happen even on the easiest difficulty;- Really, don't let the cute chibi graphics fool you - this game could be actually really hard, if you have no idea what you're doing.So would I recommend it if you are new to the genre? You really need to decide for yourself, if you are ok with the things I mentioned above. Some people might get the wrong impression that this is another casual Switch game, and if you want to just force your way through the story by just smacking enemies to death with basic attacks, then I would advise not to buy it. There are some much easier games that work much better as an entry point to the genre (Most notably Dragon Quest XI), but if you are up to the challenge, then I would highly recommend it.In conclusion, I believe Bravely Default is one the best Square Enix franchises (I actually played all three games and loved every second of them) and nothing even comes close, if you want to go back in time and enjoy jRPGs in their old-school glory.

_childDocuments_.review: Here I stand, atop a summit of countless bodies before and ahead of me, a master of warfare through five different methods of extreme cheese.Like so many final fantasy games, part of the fun here is not in playing the game normally, but in breaking it like the shell of a crab. I'm not here to tell you how to do it any more than I'm here to tell you the plot.Bravely Default 2 is what happens when someone decides Final Fantasy should come back but their bosses say they can't call it Final Fantasy because the only people allowed to make Final Fantasy are the hack director/writer or the guy who clawed his way up by taking the dumpster fire of FFXIV 1.0 and turned it into the most successful MMO in the world.I am convinced that's the only reason this series is called Bravely Default. That and the difference in mechanics, I suppose, but it's not as if the mainline FF series doesn't have radically different mechanics between many of the games.The music is what you wanted. The art style is great. This is what happens when someone wants the energy of the old, expressive SNES sprites with a modern 3D model style because their boss won't let them bring in the sprite artists who got thrown into the gatcha mines to make phone gambling content for all eternity.I hate so much about many of the directions modern square enix goes in. I love Bravely Default 2. This game is everything I wanted it to be and more. Look nothing up. Know nothing going in. You can't permanently miss anything, so you can just go back for stuff later if it really bothers you. The feeling of satisfaction and surprise in getting new jobs and finding out all about them and what kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥-up broken nonsense you can make out of them is half the thrill. The other half is a competent and serviceable classic final fantasy storyline told by people who love the old games but don't want to just copy/paste them.This is the ♥♥♥♥ a lot of other series' should/should have done. Update what you're making with new, fresh ideas that significantly change what's going on without losing the core and heart of the series. The literal only reasons you can tell this isn't a Final Fantasy game are the name on the title screen and the lack of moogles, chocobos and characters named Cid, Biggs or Wedge.If you like Final Fantasy games, get this game. _childDocuments_.review: is a well-made JRPG that feels like it was plucked straight from an alternate timeline where Square only kept releasing refinements to the Final Fantasy 3 and 5 formula. It may not be for everyone, but those who love retro turn-based 'classic' JRPGs will feel right at home.But the game is far more than  another JRPG cashing in on nostalgia. BD2 improves a lot upon the classic turn-based battles seen in older final fantasies and introduces some welcome modern twists and quality-of-life changes. The core of the gameplay is the job system: as you gather jobs you learn more and more abilities that you can use to augment many, many aspects of the gameplay. Eventually you can mix and match the best aspects of each job to create some utterly ridiculous builds which is part of the fun in this game. To match that there are some truly challenging boss fights, especially the optional ones, that require you to know the ins and outs of this system. Alongside all that, there's a nice little collectible card game here which is surprisingly very fun. The minigame reminded me a bit of Triple Triad from Final Fantasy 8, but it's different enough to be its own thing.The game also looks quite nice: towns are beautiful prerendered diorama like structures you explore, enemies all have a distinct visual style and the multiple costumes you unlock for each job are fun to collect and discover. Musically it's pretty standard fare except the various battle themes which sound really, really good.I quite enjoyed the story here. It seems rather simplistic at first but it goes in some darker directions and has a bit of a meta-commentary thing going on too, which was nice. Plus the vast majority of side quests fleshed out the world and characters much more than I expected.The PC port is fine enough. It runs at high refresh rates and supports high resolutions properly. It runs without any stuttering or loading hitches. One of my original issues with the game was the initial lack of cloud save support but that seems to have been fixed now, which is great!A very fun game that toys with retrospective ideas while being modern enough, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to JRPG fans.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default 2 is by no means a perfect game, but it's certainly worth taking a look at if you love JRPG's.Bravely Default 2, despite its name, feels less like a sequel and more like a spiritual successor to its predecessors. Bravely Default II takes a step away from Bravely Default and Bravely Second and feels much more like a standalone title - which is good. The story feels a bit generic. The gameplay is similar to the other titles, but has enough to where you can keep things interesting through experimentation. If this is your first game in the Bravely series, you'll have no trouble jumping straight into it as you don't need pretext of any kind whatsoever. Is it a good port? Yes. Is it worth playing? Yes. Is it worth $60? Debatable because you can find the Switch version for cheaper. If I don't have a Switch but really want to play it should I buy it at $60? Yes. Should I wait for a sale? If you can manage waiting it out, absolutely.The story follows a similar path to the other two installments in the series: four Heroes of Light in a quest to save the crystals to restore peace to the land. In that sense, it has a very classic JPRG-esque feel to it. That being said, some story beats feel a bit contrived and there isn't as much, for lack of a better term, "magical allure" when compared to its predecessors. Bravely Default II's story plays out much more like a generic fairy tale and feels like much of its overall atmosphere is fairly grounded in reality. In comparison with, say, Bravely Second which features things like otherwordly presences, it certainly feels more grounded in reality. It's campy, lighthearted, but is able to add gravity to the mix when the story really calls for it. My main gripe with its story is that it felt like some story beats were constantly hammered throughout the story - some a bit too much. Spoiler regarding that exact thing: Aside from that, the direction of the story is fairly linear, and like I said earlier in this review, it plays out like a fairy tale, which is nice in its own way.The gameplay will be, of course, familiar to those who have played the previous two installments. Bravely Default II features the classic turn-based formula that is nearly synonymous with classic JRPG's. However, there's enough variety with the Brave and Default system that you can do all sorts of interesting and fun combinations with the variety of jobs you get. For those unfamiliar, you can "default" which in this game equates to guarding, which allows you to store a turn in the form of "BP." You can then expend this "BP" by using the "brave" command to take multiple turns at a time. It's an interesting formula and it keeps general combat pretty fresh as you figure out ways to best effectively utilize the Brave and Default system. As with most JRPG's, you might need to grind a fair bit not only to gain EXP to increase your level, but to gain JP to increase your Job's level. Grinding can be fairly repetitive and is honestly one of my least favorite things about this game in particular due to the fact that at some points, especially when you get to the harder fights, it's pretty much required. There are certainly things that do make it easier, but still, be prepared to grind a fair bit.The art style is reminiscent of the first two games but feels like it got a breath of fresh air due to the massive graphical leap from 3DS to Switch and now PC. There's a very "homely" and "warm" feel to the overall art style of the Bravely series. The port is excellent! I've played through it on Switch, and there are a lot of improvements. Frame rate feels much smoother on PC. Loading times, especially for the menu and map transitions, are just so so so much better. Overall 10/10 port, they nailed it on this one, at least for me - I haven't run into any issues whatsoever.Overall Bravely Default II takes a bit of a step away from its predecessors in both story and gameplay. It really does feel like its own separate entry in the series, and if you told me that it was just a spiritual successor I'd believe you. That being said, is it worth the buy? Honestly at $60, I'm not too sure. And I only say that because at the moment you can find the Switch versions of the game for cheaper. If you're eager to check out what the game has in store - absolutely go for it. If you can wait for a sale, then definitely wait.

_childDocuments_.review: The two most important questions are:1) Is this a good game? -- Yes2) Is this a good port? -- Yes1) Metcritic has it sitting at 76. If you're new to the series you need to know that it's a (largely) traditional JRPG with an hybrid active time battle + brave/default (turn-borrowing) battle system. You control a part of characters, you unlock jobs as the story progresses and you can freely switch jobs for each character at will to face the many challenges along your journey. Bravely Default games are know for both subscribing to many JRPG tropes as well as finding fun and clever ways to subvert those tropes and serve you something you haven't seen before. Bravely Default II is no exception to that heritage.2) This port is exactly what I was looking for. They removed the 30 fps cap, allow for 4K resolution, and since it's PC the load times are way better. Full button remapping is really the only option worth mentioning. Graphics settings are locked (for now--I'm sure someone will mod it) with the exception of resolution.tl;dr -- Solid port of an already great game. If you love JRPGs pick this up. If you're not sure if you like JRPGs it's a fine introduction to the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has played both prior entries in the series, I can give a glowing recommendation for this game to both new and returning players.For New Players;- Fantastic JRPG teeming with possibilities and combinations through the Job system- Pleasant Visuals and Great Voice Acting- Beautiful Soundtrack- Multiple Difficulty options- Action Time based combat, rather than Strictly Turn based (Your party members and enemies will receive their OWN turn based on their agility stat, rather than all commands being placed at once)-Party Members can 'Default' or Defend to save their turn, and 'Brave' to use multiple turns at once-Intriguing Story with some Standout MomentsFor Returning Players, an Un-Objective Blob of my OpinionsPersonal Ranking for the Series (Which I'm in the minority for btw)Second > Default > Default II (All of which are 9/10s MINIMUM to me)Default II has an excellent story, but myself and many others agree this game's story peaks during Chapter 3. I think the stories of this game's two predecessors is superior. The characters I personally believe are generally equivalent, as I like all the casts thus far. Important to note that the cheesyness of Second's characters has been drastically toned down, which I very much appreciated. Seth is mostly a blank slate unfortunately, but he does have some spices of personality here and there as a sailor, but not much compared to Tiz. Every other party member in this game feels like a person who has existed prior to the game starting. Ringabell and Yew both had a lot of their backstory fleshed out and experienced by the player, however Agnes and Edea, for example, more or less boil down to 'I was with the Orthodoxy' or 'I was at the Duchy' for 16ish years respectively. Not a slight to Default, but my point being that every party member in this game has the same treatment as Yew and Ringabell did (minus Seth). The story and characters more than supplemented the gameplay, but I felt the ultimate antagonist was somewhat meh.In terms of gameplay compared to the predecessors, I find myself very happy overall. Mostly positives with like one gripe and some bickers. The switch from pure turn based to action timers a la FF4 was implemented superbly. Agility was far from useless in the prior entries, but now it is further accented. Sneaky Thieves and Cunning Ninjas (Phantoms) now accumulate more actions than other party members and enemies as a battle progresses much like that in Mist Walker Studio's Blue Dragon (please port it to PC it was so good). Having a slow healer was actually not a bad idea in the past two games, as your healer could heal damage the enemies did that very turn. Now it is imperative that your supports have at least acceptable speed in order to keep up. On that notion the difficulty of this game. The difficulty of this game is nigh perfect, but it is NOT perfect. Breaking the game with Salve Maker or Beast Master is pitifully easy and on the other end of the spectrum end game bosses generate way too much BP for free. Prior to the endgame however, the difficulty was almost perfect. Bosses were interesting and challenged me to strategize, while at the same time not forcing me to use a certain team comp.Alright now that gripe. So as someone who really dives deep into this class system I noticed something. Job's stats in this game SUCK. Default and Second usually had stat modifiers for Jobs to range from -40% to +40% with some outliers. With most jobs, the average stat total would generally be positive. Freelancers are +0% across the board for a +0% average, which is the same in all entries. However take Black Mage as an example. Black Mages get a whole +15% intelligence (actually refereed to as Magical Attack in Default II, but I use the terms interchangeably) in Default II compared to their staggering +40% in Default I. If you add up the averages of their added and subtracted stats in Default I, you would be pretty close to -10% to +0% overall. Not the case in Default II. Black Mages have TWO positive stats in Default II, MP at +25% and Int at +15%, all at the cost of a bevy of negative modifiers for the other stats. Overall I would say the Jobs don't receive good stats until Chapter 3 and even then some classes idunno about. Red Mage is designed for utility, and in Default I and Second, they had a bevy of small increases to their stats to reflect that. Good Int, but not as good as a Black Mage's. Good Mnd, but not as good as a White Mage's. So since the Black Mage in Default II gets a measly +15% modifier to their Int now, Red Mage gets a -10%. Like what? Dude. Their healing is +0%, but Red Magic does static healing anyways. Like the issue here is that a Freelancer, the first job in the game, is a better statistical Red Mage than a Red Mage. And no don't bring up MP as a stat because Red Mages have a crisp -20% to that too. As per their title, JOBS should have an innate proficiency to their skill list. I could go on and on about these classes' innate stats but I won't. The game IS designed around this new philosophy so it isn't an issue gameplay wise, which is why I call it a gripe. But seriously guys why did we give MONK -20% Speed??? IT'S A MARTIAL CLASS THAT USES THEIR FISTS AND LEGSAlright the bickers. Job selection is smaller than Second and I think that's perfectly fine. The weapon selection, however, I do find somewhat lacking. Bravely Second honestly had too many weapon types and I found myself defaulting to Katanas for my physical attackers too often. Rifles and Bows constantly conflicted with one another, not to mention GreatSwords were just Axes for wussies. Default II in my opinion cut back a little too much. Katanas, Swords, and GreatSwords are all now just Swords which I'm not too miffed about, but still Katanas were cool man. Knuckles? Just use your fists dweeb. And only your fists, because Knuckles as a weapon type no longer exist. No Rifles I was alright with tbh. Staves and Rods being combined is where we start pushing it. Rods were defined for magically offensive roles, and Staves for magically supportive (and occasionally martial) roles. It somewhat promotes a One-Size-Fits-All mindset for my magical characters which is somewhat lame. The rest of the weapon types stayed which is nice, but I often found myself defaulting to Swords in Default II, as Spear, Axe, or Bow proficiency is somewhat hard to come by. Daggers still suck lmao.Small Note; Giving White Mage a B-Rank in Spears was awesome and it should always stay that way. My early game White Mage was putting up some meaty DPS while looking stylish AF.Last bicker for those that didn't tldr this. The job outfits in this game are very hit or miss.Speaking of, TLDR;Game Good. Plenty of content for the price, but if you are apprehensive about it, but it on sale. Like most JRPGs, the gameplay takes a while to get going, I.E past the 2-hour return window.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default 2 is the sort of the game which takes every trope and cliché known in the JRPG series and cranks it up to 11. Despite the somewhat predictable story, it somehow manages to be a compelling and deep RPG. The asterisk job system does a fantastic job in making you want to grind away and level up every class to experiment with builds. Towards the end of the game, the possibilities really open up, and provide multiple ways for you to tackle the fair amount of challenge and optional content in the late game. The game is very self-aware of its clichés and builds upon them well. Despite the bog-standard story, it has its moments of brilliance, comedy and genuine tragedy. BDII doesn’t try to reinvent the wheel, but instead makes the best wheel there is. The predictable story and gameplay elements are a familiar comfort, as the nostalgia factor really kicks in and makes you realise how much you have wanted to play a classic JRPG in the modern era.  What the game is good at, it does extremely well. Grinding is made painless thanks to its enemy lure items and battle speed mechanics, and repeatable battle commands. The engaging card game and plethora of side quests also provide a welcome distraction when things become too repetitive.I would have liked to see a more mature story, a greater variety in side activities, and a more expansive soundtrack. Still, the overall presentation of the game is cohesive, and does not try too hard to be more than it can be. Overall, I felt it was an absolute joy to play through, and a must-play for anyone who likes traditional JRPGs.
