_childDocuments_.review: When I wrote my initial review, I played ~6 hours and was skeptical of the game. My opinion has changed for the better in the intervening ~82 hours and I... kinda recommend this game, but not as part of the series it stems from:It is an alright game, but not a great Bravely game. I played Bravely Default and Bravely Second years ago on the 3DS and they were the reason I bought this one. This is heavily influencing my view of the game, especially my list of negative points.- It has good performance overall, though one optional vulcano-themed dungeon was kinda laggy for me. The game lost the high detail background textures of towns one time at around 36h playtime and had one blackscreen at 70 hours (both fixed with a restart).- The story is sufficient for me, though this is a matter of personal taste. I like the usual theme of "There is no black/white morality". Side missions giving more insight into main story characters, sadly many are easily missable because they are somewhat hidden between fetch quests.- No microtransactions, unlike the previous parts.- Two accessory slots instead of one, I like customisation and this, together with the Bravely series combination of classes and passive abilities, provides it.- Each character and enemy has their own turn in battle. The higher their speed attribute, the faster their turn comes around again, with some element of randomness involved. This makes it basically impossible to plan out complete turns for the whole team.- Special moves cannot be customised and have unskippable animations. They cannot be used together with Brave actions (= extra actions) during the turn they are used. They provide a stat boost that lasts as long as the special music plays, with further special moves by other characters adding further boosts and extending the duration. Sadly, the "each character and enemy has their own turn" mechanic makes this unpredictable. I have almost never used them.- Less information about mechanics. Many skills are described as “weak”, “fast”, “powerful” or “very powerful”, which does not help me in making decisions on using them.- Spells are now part of the Job (= class) progression instead of being purchaseable in shops. While this is justified by the lore of the game, BD2 is missing many of the classes and abilities of the previous games, which I think is a lost opportunity.- No further information about Status effects in battle. There is a menu that displays information about friend and foe, but it has only ~six lines for buffs and status effects. It’s easy to surpass that number due to equipped items plus battle buffs plus enemy debuffs, which causes the menu to loop through multiple pages of effects, without any possibility to stop this or get a description on what a status effect actually does.- No information about enemy immunities, resistances or counters in battle. Weaknesses are recorded after triggering them for the first time or scanning an opponent, why not the rest?- The Brave action queue UI covers the name of support-abilities and immunities etc of some enemies- While the game stores the last actions taken by a character in a fight, there is no programable moveset and no "autobattle" functionality like in the previous games- While the Job costumes can be deactivated, this is an all or nothing setting, there are no custom outfits for each character like in the previous games- Buns (items which permanently boost a single attribute by 1-3 points) are easier to farm than in the previous titles, where they were rare drops from bosses. In BD2, they can be farmed very efficiently from common encounters, up to 4 of a single type of bun per enemy per fight. In a vacuum, this isn't a particularly bad thing, in my opinion, as similiarly to power leveling each player can deceide for themselves whether or not they want to go through that grind. But I believe this design decision is strongly connected to the cap of attributes in the game: Each character can have a maximum of 9999 HP and 999 in every other stat. This is the ceiling unlimited bun farming hits eventually. Higher stats are still stored by the game because the 'pure' stats of a character seem to be separate from the attribute modifiers a job provides, but in battle, 999 is the limit. Sadly, this also includes temporary stats provided by buffs, which can make buffing pointless in postgame fights.- Similar to BS, BD2 has a (Spoiler about postgame content!)  can have. In BS, this was accomplished by  In BD2, there is a point in the story after which  From what I've read however, starting a NewGame+ will reset this mechanic again. Why? The point of NG+ (for me at least) is to experiment with all the cool stuff I've collected previously. Why gets the (debatably) coolest stuff taken away from me? I already know the story, I already know the challenges, let me experiment ffs.- Less difficulty customisation. The regular difficulty of normal/hard can be set, yes, but not the frequency of monster spawns. Exp/jp/money gain can only be disabled by finding and equipping specific accessory items, which is a waste of equipment slots when the previous games had this setting as an game option.- "Seth", the protagonist character, is a blank slate. I write his name in quotation marks because he can be named by the player at the start of the game. He gets stranded at the beginning of the story and aids Princess Gloria, the rest is history or rather, the plot of the game. He cares for the other characters and has some cute moments with Gloria, but suffers from the "bland protagonist every player can imagine themselves as" syndrome. His origins get barely expored, he follows the story while never attempting to find his way back home,  and his name cannot be called by the other characters.- No log of completed side missions. At one point I thought a particular  quest was only available in an earlier chapter and that I missed it, turns out I just had to complete another quest first and the third party questlist I used had no information about this dependency.- The camera PoV on the worldmap can be turned to look at spots the default camera angle does not reach. This is oftentimes done to discover treasure chests and I assume works pretty well on the Switch. It’s less comfortable on PC, as the usual controls are on and around WASD, but the camera is controlled by the arrow keys. This would be less of an issue if leaving a dungeon or city wouldn’t re-angle the camera on that exit, which forces one to readjust unless one wants to run blind, wheter by a backwards PoV or by the map covering up to a third of the screen.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review as someone who's played both Bravely Default and Bravely Second.The combat is better. Real time turns allow for fluid decision making and allows for comebacks mid fight without having to resort to raw leveling.The story is good. It initially felt more lackluster compared to the first 2 games, but that is because we are walking into BD2 with expectations and preconceptions. For first time players of the series, it will be just like our introduction to the first game.The cast of characters also felt lackluster, but that is also due to spending 2 games with the same characters for BD1 and BS. I realized I was attached to the characters when I tried to switch to japanese voices and found it too weird and not like Seth, Gloria, Adelle, Elvis at all.The big bad feels less big and bad than the final boss in BD1. As this is a new world, it feels like they tried to make the scope of this game more grounded than the first 2 BD titles. I also feel like the initial Bravely Default games were darker and grimier. Our very first introduction to those games was a whole village getting destroyed, and betrayal. The introduction to this one is tamer in comparison and it doesn't immediately thrust you into the intense dark mood of the first 2 games.Overall still a 8.5/10. The strength of the Bravely Default series is the gameplay and this is no exception. It is a more than solid, and very enjoyable addition to the series.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up on sale, and its one of the best JRPG's I've played for a while. Instead of writing chunks of text, I'll just summarize what I liked and suggestions for improvements with no spoilers.Likes:1) Your jobs/classes are contained in an 'artifact', and the way you unlock new ones are always very fun in Bravely games.2) The voice acting is really good, and I love the variety of British accents from the different nations.3) Once I collected a few good cards and made a deck, the in-game card game was decent.4) Very well thought out multiple endings. They are all valid, and connect very cleverly.5) The post-game was perfectly done, because side-quests can be done whenever. No items/story are missable.6) The worldbosses were challenging, but not challenging enough to need to grind for hours.Suggestions for improvements:1) Please add a side-quest log for the ones you've completed, this is a VERY big oversight.2) When entering an area, it would be useful to know the name of the dungeon when you walk in the door. This way players can walk in, and walk straight back out if its not correct dungeon. There are no quest markers when looking for items or lore, so we currently need to Google the names of the previous dungeons to know which is which.3) Minimap position needs moving to the top when enlarged. It's very easy to run into monsters you can't see because it covers the literal area in-front of you where you're walking.4) If you've viewed the 'new' shop items from vendors, if possible, globally mark these as 'read' in all the towns (not just the one you're in). If you go into a previous/new town, you're constantly being told there are new items until you've marked them as read 'individually' in 'each' town.5) If you're in the overworld, it would be useful to somehow know your ship has maxed its voyage (via notification).6) More of a nitpick, but showing locations of 'opened' treasure chests on the minimap is just generally useful.I don't usually take the time to give feedback on a game, but because I enjoyed it so much I hope these suggestions make it better for everyone else. This game is definately worth buying.

_childDocuments_.review: edit: It has come to my attention that this game was not made by the same studio that did Bravely, Second, and Octopath, but by a studio that made a mobile game. No wonder it's so different.finished the game in Hard mode and quite a bit of grinding, trying to get all the cards of NPCs i find and do all the trials, etc., and am writing this right after beating the gameNote that I played Bravely Default 1 and Bravely Second: End Layer.----Reasons I find the game meh:1. The lighting is really weird. When I first booted the game I thought it looked terrible. Combined with the upped graphics, it just looked like odd clay dolls in an animation Youtube channel. Took me a while to get used to, but if you're used to how much more blended the first two games were, this will be a bit jarring2. I don't mind grinding, it's part of Bravely, and it's fun. What I DON'T LIKE is taking off the ability to save Party Sets into Favourites. WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ MAN? IT'S LITERALLY IN THE FIRST TWO GAMES, WHY REMOVE IT? Grinding in Bravely is actually kinda fun, but switching sets manually every time you want to go from a Grinding Mode to a Story Progression mode is NOT fun.3. Not much challenge once you're in late game. There are these things called trials which you can optionally do in the late game, and they are brutally difficult at first. But once you start grinding some job levels, you end up gaining actual EXP as well, causing you to be overleveled fast, and nothing in the late game scales to that. WHY NOT THIS ONE???? Yes I hate the fact they're now items you gain in later chapters.5. The main character's name is Seth. It ruins immersion when the game itself won't speak our character's name. Should've made it like BD1 and BSecond's Tiz and Yew.6. There is literally no connection to the other two Bravely games. I expected some sort of thread tying the world back to Luxendarc, but no. This game can be called literally anything else and I wouldn't bat an eye. I know Square Enix likes to do this kind of ♥♥♥♥ where it's all different worlds, but I thought Bravely would be an exception. Oh well.++++Reasons to play the game:1. Bravely Default had great music imo, but Bravely Second's was... okay. In particular, BSecond's character Ultimate theme songs were absolute horse radish, and none of them were memorable. I liked the story====While my negatives are blown out of proportion, it doesn't stop the fact that the game's still pretty fun and I enjoyed it, go play it! but you'll be a bit disappointed if you liked the previous two Bravely games.

_childDocuments_.review: Without considering the previous games in the series, this game is a functional and satisfying JRPG. I found it easy to spend hours playing through the story and grinding for the best end game gear, If you are looking for some classic JRPG comfort food, this can be for you. However, when you consider it alongside the other games in the series I feel more lukewarm towards this installment. I didn't find myself quite as invested in the characters or story this time around. I partially attribute this to the lack of additional garnishes such as rebuilding Norende, the optional high level bosses, and the scope of D's journal. Overall, I enjoyed my time with Bravely Default 2, and am content with the product I received for my purchase. However, as time goes by I think I will be returning to the original Bravely Default should I ever have a hankering to return to the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game for the classic turn-based combat and the job system. They're both there and exactly what I was looking for. If that's all you care about you can buy this game and be happy. And honestly, I'm so desperate for those features in a game I'll keep playing. However, the writing for this game deserves special mention in that it jumps off the screen as absolutely the laziest, most generic work for a production this size that I've ever seen. It would be more forgivable if they had tried and failed to write a better story, better characters, better dialogue, even better character names.... they did not. It feels like they used a boilerplate to generate the plot and never changed a word. They did not try and fail; they never tried at all.

_childDocuments_.review: BD2 stands out as one of the rare, nearly flawless games I've encountered in recent memory.While it isn't entirely free of imperfections, any flaws it possesses are minor and primarily subjective IMO. The combat system, for instance, has sparked debate since BD1, but many players enjoy it and find it unique (rather than detracting from the experience).Personally, I feel the main storyline presented a simple but engaging narrative from beginning to end, avoiding both excessive complexity and unsubstantiated fluff. Bonus points for making side quests and side characters very charming too.I also enjoyed the variety of options that the job/asterisk system offers (both mechanically and visually). On the topic of game systems, discovering hidden elements throughout the game was not only fun but fundamental to the game experience.One aspect I particularly appreciated was the unconventional difficulty curve. Unlike most RPGs, BD2 throws you right into the action with a higher than average initial challenge, which gradually lessens as you level up, refine your builds, and progress through the story. This translated the fantasy of gaining strength into a tangible gameplay experience, while avoiding handholding or making power levels trivialize content later in the game .Lastly, the multi-ending structure and end-game content, without being particularly challenging or conceptually flamboyant, are some of the best I've seen in the genre. Can’t go into specifics without entering spoiler territory, so I'll leave it at that.Without hesitation, I recommend BD2 not only to JRPG enthusiasts but also to any gamer who's dipped their toes into the genre before.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has serious chill-out-ittude. The music is relaxing, the visuals are great, there's party chat, heck I've spent about an hour just cutting grass. The battle system has a great risk/reward element that makes even basic encounters a little bit spicy. To just say it: the game has the cozy feel of and old-school Final Fantasy game, and one that comes close to a Dragon Quest game. If you're a fan of the older FF games or DQ, don't hesitate to pick this up. The port is actually, well, good! There's no arbitrary frame locking and it runs buttery smooth with almost instant load times on a NVME SSD. I hesitated picking this up on Switch because of the frame rate and load times, but I'm really glad I picked it up on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default 2 feels like a soft reboot of Bravely Default but with different issues to it's predessesor. Overall my opinion was that I only had the drive to make it through this game BECAUSE I had played the original. When I imagine this game as a standalone without being in the BD franchise, I likely wouldn't have finished the game. Bravely Default had twisted the tale of four crystals into something unique. Bravely Default 2 takes the same tale and plays it straight... like a Final Fantasy game of old. In short, BD2 abandons the previous BD games and sets forth on a new weaker journey as a sequel.Soft-Reboot:The original cast (Tiz, Agnes, Ringabel, and Edea) are replaced with near-clones (Seth, Gloria, Elvis, and Adelle) and take a very VERY similar tale if you've played the original game- where you keep thinking 'Hey I've seen that before'. However BD2 is a far weaker experience than the narrative in BD1. Without going into too many specifics, in BD2 Seth and Gloria are still complete strangers and Seth has no real cause to come to her aid (in fact only hearing about her situation by chance). This is drastically different from the relationship between Agnes and Tiz, where Tiz protects Agnes from a clear threat in the immediate moment despite him being a simple villager. There's just tons of better writing decisions that were made with BD1 that it's frustrating to experience weaker versions of similar events in BD2. At the end of the game I was laughing... LAUGHING at the dialogue from the characters. And not in a good way, like the Gloria info dump outta nowhere. Also the entire game takes place in a single continent. Gone is the world from BD1 where you had a sprawling world with multiple continents. Now you just have one super continent that has every biome in the world... welcome to Pangaea home of the Five Kingdoms and lack of imagination.Quests:For some insane reasoning the Devs decided to NOT add indicators to show that Quests are available in each city (on quicktravel menu). So not only do you have to revisit each city, Quests ALSO follow the day/night cycle. For reference there is absolutely NO way to quickly pass time to night but you can sleep in the Inn to have it become day instantly. I've played RPG Maker games that have this exact option, this is just horribly sad that you can't go rest at the Inn to skip to night- BUT MORE-SO: WHY THE ♥♥♥♥ IS THERE A DAY/NIGHT CYCLE THAT AFFECTS QUESTS AT ALL. Who asked for this. The quests don't matter that they're done at night it's just so infuriating to even differentiate the two. Furthermore there are also quests in extra side areas that are a chore to travel to. Such as the Gambler Den, the Prison (Halcyon + Savalon), the orphanage, the science institution (separated into two parts, one requires you to go in and out of a dungeon), the Serpent Grotto (also at the end of a dungeon with half a shortcut), and even the outside world. And as if just trying to find the quests wasn't bad enough, the quests are also more similar to MMO styled questing than an RPG. AKA the quests are literal fetch quests, talk to xyz, kill x amount of y, kill x boss, etc etc with very minimal rewards. The comparative to the original is just completely heartbreaking. The original BD had ZERO quests of this nature and every single sub scenario was a boss fight that rewarded the player with an asterisk. So in many ways the original game had no 'side' quests since the player was going to want all the asterisks regardless. Here the side quests are entirely skippable outside of two which gives asterisks: 2 out of 100 quests.Dungeons, and Side 'Bosses':Dungeon Quests don't unlock appropriately and you'll leave an area without going to any of the side dungeons. I'd go through a Dungeon to collect all the chests and unlock the shortcut before leaving. At this point the enemies within the dungeon are still queued up to be hostile and are considered strong to my player level. It's not until AFTER I complete the entire next area at some point the dungeon quest becomes available... and all the monsters are frightened of me for being too high level. Personally I wish the Dungeons had been completely optional explorations with a boss at the end. Instead there are side bosses which are scattered throughout the over-world, pretty comically at that. I'd bet the first optional boss 99% of players bump into is the Axolotl on the beach, which is a ~lvl 20 boss in the starting area. Each area has about 2 optional bosses that would've been better off shoved into dungeons instead of me having to memorize where they are on the world map.Mini-Game:The card game (B&D) is a ridiculous grind-fest (it's optional but still). The game rates the rules, points, and ranks of the match which gives you points to spend at the end of the game to take cards from your opponent. Once you get all of your opponents cards you can set whichever rules you want and play to grind out more points to more easily get cards from other Players. This game gets unlocked in Chapter 2 but for some reason you can't hit max rank until Chapter 5 and you can't get all of the cards until the final chapter. At this point the game will reward you with an item... that might have been useful long ago. In some ways the game could be fun, but because you need to grind so many points it turns it into a frustrating experience instead of simply winning the opponents card and moving on.TL;DRIf you played the original you won't be impressed. If you've never played Bravely Default give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default II is a turn-based RPG that refines the formula established by early Final Fantasy games. I find it most similar to Final Fantasy III:For context, I haven't played much of the first Bravely Default, so I won't be talking about that game in this review. You don't need to have played the previous games to enjoy BD2, as they are completely separate. Let's get started.If you enjoy oldschool RPGs, this game was made for you. It's a game where you control a party of four characters on a journey, and you're free to change the Job of each character as you unlock new ones. The roleplaying element given to the player there cannot be understated. You are naturally given a lot of choice in how you want to tackle combat and how you want each character to look. How long will you stick to the Freelancer job? Will you switch jobs based on the location you're in? Or perhaps based on the personality and backstory of each character? Maybe the Berserker outfit seems fitting in the snowy region. You ask yourself these questions as you play, because the game lets you make these decisions for yourself.An important addition to the formula is the equipment weight limit per character. You can freely choose to roleplay a character not wearing any hat or helmet and not feel like you're handicapping yourself, as you can use the weight freed up from that decision to give them a stronger weapon, for example. You can also hold on to early equipment for a long time, as there's always a use for it. Early armor is more lightweight and offers a lower "Chance to be Targeted" to the user, so you may want to keep those for your less resistant characters.It should be said that I wouldn't recommend playing on Hard if you wish to fully engage in the immersive roleplaying aspects mentioned above. That option is there for those who prefer figuring out what the optimal strategy is against every boss; not for those who wish to stick to their choices and merely adapt a bit. You can change the difficulty at any time, so if the game seems too hard at any point, don't be afraid to lower it. It affects how often the enemy gets a turn, making more strategies viable.There are many important quality of life additions, such as the ability to fast-forward animations in combat (4 speeds to choose from) and to skip the intro cutscene when entering combat, making repeated combat encounters not feel slow. You never feel like you have to wait for the game to let you control it. It is a video game after all, and you always feel in control of it. There are also no random encounters, which makes exploration more interesting because you can run from fights physically instead of being forced into a fight every few steps. That is a huge change in philosophy that modernizes the formula without getting rid of its essentials, and it is very appreciated. This lack of random encounters means that you can explore some dangerous areas for sweet loot found in chests without grinding first. Beware of nasty surprises, though.Note that this game is not going for the same level of freedom as Octopath Traveler, as you cannot remove a character from the party, and you cannot explore the whole world from the start. Seth, Gloria, Elvis and Adelle are always present, always participate in the story, and have conversations with each other much more often. You certainly don't have to imagine that part. I don't think the game is better or worse for it, it's just a different approach to RPG storytelling.Speaking of, the characters are very charming in this game. The story feels humble and mostly traditional, but where it shines is in character and voices. If you play in English, each character has a different accent or tone. Gloria's tone is more formal, for example. I love Adelle's voice and personality the most, but even the main character, which is typically mute in this style of RPG (Dragon Quest's protagonists are mute to this day), is his own character here. He's a sailor, so in battle he lets out "yarrs" like a pirate, because why not. It's fun.The music by Revo is, for the most part, amazing. The battle music is phenomenal, especially when you catch the parts that are inspired by classic FF battle music. It is given its own exciting touch. The overworld music is incredibly catchy, and I adore all of the dungeon and forest music, which ranges from funky to mystical and beautiful. Each track was clearly crafted with a lot of care as it fits perfectly with the region it's used in. Unfortunately, it does stumble around the Wiswald region due to one particular instrument that is annoying to listen to. Only two songs are affected by this instrument, but you do hear them for a while.The BP debt mechanic is very interesting and adds intensity to battles, as you need to be careful not to go all out at the wrong times or you'll be left helpless for multiple turns, yet sometimes it is best to do so. Along with the quality of life additions I mentioned earlier, it actually makes grinding quite fun, as you can go all out in regular battles and end battles in one turn. Of course, regular battles would grow stale if grinding was that easy, so they added a JP multiplier as an incentive to engage in consecutive battles. It makes sense that you'd get more Job experience by exercising restraint and executing things smartly in a challenging situation. Similarly, there's also an underdog EXP bonus if you go against tougher enemies, encouraging you not to pick on weak monsters and making tougher fights more rewarding. Excellent stuff.Back when BD2 was first announced, I thought it looked a bit bad, at least on Switch. However, playing this game in HD changes everything. The enemy designs are incredibly cool, the animations at 60+ FPS (and without motion blur) have a lot of flair, the town backgrounds looking like paintings are wonderful, and the overall "clay-like" art style is very pleasant to look at, as it doesn't overwhelm your eyes with too many details. It also stands out from the overused anime art style, making the game feel very unique in 2021.Whether you've never experienced an oldschool RPG before and would like to enjoy what it felt like to go on an adventure back in the early days of the genre, or you're smitten by this style already, I highly recommend giving this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who is really picky about JRPG's, I wanted to leave my own review. To get it out of the way, I highly recommend this game for people who love old school JRPG style games. This will give you a modern FF5 feel for sure. The job system is a blast, and really intricate and fun to try different combinations (and also challenging at times).First thing i would recommend is to play on HARD. This will make the game a challenge and much more strategic than simply spam strong attack, heal, win. This will force you to understand the class strengths, the active and passive abilities of each class, and how to optimize. Be warned though, this game is not "easy" if you choose the hard difficulty. Yes, the story is generic(ish) but I love that they have some darker themes of death and chaos. it certainly is not just "evil empire do bad things and we do good things so we must stop them from bad things". It shows some pretty disturbing scenes from the villains that makes it feel more violent, scary, and impactful to stopping them. Great quality of life additions, like 4x battle speed, fast travel by carriage from each town, auto heal in menu, and very clear  icons on where to head for side quest. Also, the OST is fantastic. Get this game.

_childDocuments_.review: For context I loved the original Bravely Default and Bravely Second.Bravely Default 2 is mind boggling. Going for a full ATB system where every battle has 6 enemies in it is jarring. Every single encounter takes ages to get through and they’re technically unavoidable. In dungeons the pathing is so small even if you run away you’re nearly forced to run into them.The boss battles are always a huge spike in difficulty even if you grinded all the way through.The ATB system mixed with the above is extra frustrating. You have to spend so much time focusing on equipment and what makes you slower, constantly malign trade offs but it’s so boring. Additionally you have to add in time for grinding JP so you can get additional skills like countering counters. It’s flabbergasting how much padding is in this game.Why is everything in this game such a slog? It really makes it a miserable experience.In a world where there are a million RPGS including the original I can’t say I’d recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I feel an immense lack of polish in this game in a lot of aspects (except the soundtrack, which is stellar like always). If you haven't played the previous games, I suggest playing them for a better experience.* The UI transition from dual screens to one didn't work very well. The UI, especially in battle, feels displaced and amateurly made.* Some character models, sadly, are... ugly, it's hard to get used to them. We don't need beautiful graphics, but they needed to avoid uncanny character models.* They added dozens of forgettable fetch-quests, instead of keeping like the previous games, which only had meaningful sidequests with relevant rewards.* They changed the battle system to lean more toward improvisation than a planned strategy: while this is neither bad or good, I personally prefer the old style (on Bravely Second, you had a lot of customizations for automatic, repeatable commands, now only a "repeat last command" option exists - which was a good QoL for grind-based games like these).* A lot of Job abilities/skills were nerfed or simply removed in this game, limiting strategy. Magic is now learned through Job Levels and they fill the spots of many removed abilities from the previous games. Some remaining skills like Protect were nerfed to increase 15% DEF for 3 turns instead of 25% DEF for 5 turns, making them feel useless. It feels like they had trouble balancing the game, and ended up just cutting a lot of things as a means of solving the problem.* The English dub was impeccable on the first two games: on this one, I'm not so sure...* And the story - as I didn't finish the game, but watched a good part of it - isn't out-of-this world enough to compensate for the other downgrades.As someone who loved the first Bravely Default, unfortunately this wasn't the sequel I was expecting. I hope others can enjoy the game more than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like the design team listened way too much to the critics of the original game, that it was too easy, and decided to crank up the difficulty here- and they did that through some very controversial ways.The first is that bosses are damage sponges. They take forever to kill and, essentially, require a team specifically made to take them out. What this means is that in the early chapters you'll be grinding out jobs to specifically counteract whatever gimmick/weakness the boss has, which winds up overleveling your characters to the point that overworld monsters aren't even worth your time.The second is that job abilities are basically worthless early on. For example, the White Mage job learns a passive ability called "Drain Attack" that will heal your character for a portion of the damage they do with a regular attack. Sadly, the amount seems to be percent based, so in the early game you're basically healing for nothing meaning you're still going to require a dedicated healer to maintain your team.Third is that damage seems to be paltry.  Either the equipment stats were tuned improperly or stats don't seem to matter as much, the damage you do feels terribly weak. Combine this with these passive abilities that don't really come online until late in the game as well as the damage sponges called bosses, makes a game that feels  grindy and tiresome for little benefit.Overall the game feels "difficult" in the sense that it was made to take longer- more grinding, longer boss fights, and more trial/error. To me, that doesn't make a well designed game nor a game that is difficult- it just makes the game exhausting to play.I'm personally reminded of the game that Bravely Default takes its inspiration of- Final Fantasy V. FFV is a great game and allows you the freedom to do, basically, whatever you want with your team and make it work. The game can be difficult, but leveling up your characters, getting new passive abilities/spells actually feels worthwhile. For example, the Monk from FFV gains the ability to "Kick" doing damage to all enemies on screen- the Monk from Bravely Default 2 gains... The ability to sacrifice 1/5 of their health to do a slightly more damaging attack to one enemy.Bravely Default 2 doesn't balance risk with reward well, and nor is it designed in a way that, I feel, actually rewards players for their time spent. I don't recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: is everything I could have ever wanted in a SS/SE JRPG that represents the "old world" in both art direction and mechanics. It is one of the best titles to carry the torch forward in place of the classic turn-based JRPGs I grew up to love. Simply put, it's a more modern take on something like FF3-3D but overall a much more pleasant experience.To start off, the combat in this game can be tough, but fair. Hard mode presents an actual challenge and that sense of difficulty can last all the way until the final credits roll. With that said, this game still manages to feel rewarding even if you choose the JRPG-staple route of grinding. It's a game that lets you grind without feeling the burnout associated with it. BD2 achieves this by providing consistent releases of dopamine in the form of measurable progress in the game's 20++ interchangeable jobs that you can mix and match to great effect. One of the other hallmarks of good JRPGs is allowing players to achieve a snowball effect under the right conditions as a reward for deeply exploring game mechanics. This comes in the form of taking advantage of the game's fleshed-out job system that lets you utilize moves from primary and sub-jobs, enabling passives from multiple jobs, among many other features. There is a balance that the game expertly maintains between that snowball potential and the base difficulty of hard mode—both spectrums of course remain optional so you can set the tone of your own experiences.One of my favorite things about this game is the vibrant implementation of picturesque explorable cities and towns. The closest thing I can draw on from my limited gaming experience is the beautiful cityscapes of FF9. The beautiful backdrops in this game can be fully appreciated with the built-in panoramic view that I often used just to take in the sights. My favorite location in the game is the small yet homely town of Enderno.The 70+ hours it took to complete this game was pleasant all the way. The game ran great and though the graphic customization options were limited, it was just enough to highlight its beauty to the fullest while maintaining a stable 60fps on my RTX 2080.I recommend this game to those who love turn-based JRPGs and the art style of the earlier PC ports from SE (FF3 3DR). Fingers crossed they release the rest of the games on Steam!

_childDocuments_.review: This is an awesome RPG that reminds me of old school games like Final Fantasy III! The story isn't ground breaking, but it does what it sets out to do well enough. I've gotten a little tired of new turn based RPGs, and this is coming from someone who's been playing them for 25 years (Super Mario RPG was my first). It feels like they are only turn based to try and fire that nostalgia response. A lot of RPGs were turn based back then because of technological limits, not because of an artistic choice; if you're going to have a turn based RPG today, then it needs to feel like it was purposefully designed to be turn based and feel like it innovates somehow. The Bravely Default Series does just this; the risk/reward system from deciding whether to brave or not/how much to brave adds a significant layer of gameplay on top of the well done turn based combat. If you're looking for a game that feels both nostalgic and fresh, with a decent enough story on top of it, then this is it.One warning though: like the old school RPGs it's based on, this game does demand a certain amount of grinding. If you are tight on time, then maybe you should play on easy. If you are really tight on time, then maybe it's not a game for you. While I absolutely love this game, I could see it taking months to beat if you only have 2-3 hours a week to play, even on easy.

_childDocuments_.review: Years ago, the Kingdom of Musa that once watched over the world, lost its four crystals, this lead to it's destruction, it fell apart and into despair. Now Princess Gloria along with Seth (your character name here), Adelle and Elvis you set off to find the four missing crystals in the hope of returning the Kingdom of Musa back to its former glory. The game starts with a small intro underwater, “I am that which whispers... Which carries... Which connects... This thread of life... Adrift... Untethered... It must be woven back into the fabric of the world... Remember... Remember who you are... (choose your game difficulty here). Now go... Return to the land... To your destiny... Cry out your name...” (name your character here).  There are three game difficulties to choose from, Casual, recommended for those players who wish to enjoy the story with easier battles. Normal, is for everyone wanting a standard game and finally there’s Hard, which is recommended for everyone who wants a game where the battles and enemy turns come around much quicker than the other game difficulties. You are able to change the games difficulty at any time should you be struggling or want tougher battles. After you’ve chosen your name and difficulty the game will start. You find yourself washed up on a beach with the waves lapping again you as the sun beats down. As you come to you notice two figures looking at you, an old grey-haired man and a younger woman. They are speaking about some crystal and a light which lead them to you. The old man is Sir Sloan and the young lady is Gloria, Princess of Musa. They take you to Halcyonia, where you awake in an Inn and after talking with Gloria and Sir Sloan your adventure begins. Making your way around Halcyonia or any other town you’ll find shops, other places of interest and folks standing around doing whatever they’re doing. You can get a better look at your current location by zooming out. This will show you where places such as shops, Inns and folks which may a job for you to complete. People with a quest for you will have a blue speech bubble instead of a normal white one. Talking to them will allow you to accept or refuse the quest they offer you. Indicated by a yellow and black diamond shaped icon is a key location which you are required to visit as it’s part of the story. Other quests are indicated by the same icon although it will have a different colour in the bottom corner of the icon to indicate a different quest. Leaving a town or city will take you out into the open world, out here you’ll find creatures roaming the land and if you get close enough, they will attack you for the most part. Upon encountering an enemy you’ll be taken to the battle screen, here you will combat the enemy you have just encountered. There will be multiple enemies to fight and there may be other creatures other than the one which you initiated combat with. So, you’ll have to beware of who you fight with as there’s no way of knowing who’s going to be in your next encounter. These creatures won’t always attack you, instead they will run away from you. This happens when you are too high a level and too strong for those enemies, you can still initiate a fight if you run into them. Combat consists of choosing from various options when it's your characters turn which is decided the Turn Gauges which are displayed under your characters Health and Magic points as a bar which fills yellow. Once filled it will then be the turn of that character. The character you start with will have the options, Attack, Miscellany (this will depend on the characters Job), Brave, Default and Items; other options will come available as you take on new Jobs.  Choosing Attack will allow you to perform a physical attack using the weapon which you’ve assigned to a character. There are several types of weapons which you can choose for your characters, Daggers, Swords, Axes, Spears, Staffs, Bows and Shields. The characters can hold a weapon in both hands, so you could have a sword and shield or a spear and dagger, it’s up to you how you equip your characters. Selecting Default will allow your character to go on the defense for their current turn but it will also give your character a Built- Up Power point. You can use these Built-Up Power points by selecting Brave, this will allow you to use up to three points at any time allowing you to perform multiple actions. You are also able to select Brave up to four times and then perform multiple actions without first selecting Default. However, when you do this, it will skip your next turns depending on the number of times you selected Brave, this can come in handy if you find yourself in a pinch mid-battle. Miscellany is the abilities of the Job type Freelancer, which is the main Job of your main character to begin with. With the Miscellany you will be able to use abilities such as Examine which will allow you to reveal an enemy’s Weakness and their Health. Examine is the first of the Miscellany abilities, you will unlock new ones as you win battles and earn Job Points. Once you have levelled up enough then your character will become a Master in that Job. You can also have a part from your main job a Sub Job, this is a secondary job which you can use in combat and will provide other abilities. However, your sub job will not level up like your main job does so you will only have the basic abilities of the sub job. You can swap main and sub jobs around so that if you have a mastered job, you will still be able to take advantage of its abilities even if it is set as a sub job. There are several different types of jobs in which you can assign to your characters, Freelancer, Black mage, White Mage, Vanguard and others.  To unlock new jobs, you will have to find Asterisks which can be found after defeating some shady characters. There are also Passive abilities which you can also unlock and select and fill up to five slots for abilities which take one slot out of the five you have available. As your character jobs increase in level, you’ll earn new passive abilities, some of these abilities will have different values and will require more than one slot. There will come a time when you will have multiple enemies move on to you to initiate combat, when this happens it will trigger Consecutive Battles. This is a normal battle however upon completion of the first battle another one will commence straight away. You can have multiple consecutive battles and in doing so you will gain better rewards and experience points multiplied by a factor depending on the number of battles you competed against. There are Monster Treats which you can use to bring in more creatures so that you can create more consecutive battles. Positives  + Very nice graphics + Decent story + Multiple character jobs options + Has achievements + Has cards + Full controller support Negatives  - Camera angles a little awkward Help Princess Gloria, Seth, Adelle and Elvis, the new Heroes of Light to recover the missing crystals stolen from the Kingdom of Musa and return the Kingdom back to its former glory. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default II is a solidly built, visually appealing JRPG that is carried by its fantastic job system. I enjoyed my playthrough, but it's story and characters are notably weaker than its predecessor (Bravely Default on the 3DS). There are also some changes to core systems from the original games that I can understand would push players away who are looking for the traditional experience. I still recommend this game (at discounted price) for its overall quality, and also because it's the only Bravely Default experience you can find, unless you are able to play the originals: Bravely Default & Bravely Second (pls remaster pls).----- Thoughts on System Changes -----The game is now ATB with individual character speed stats. Previously, you would plan out the moves of all 4 characters before playing them out. I didn't find too much of a problem here as it allows the developers to design different boss mechanics (ie. counters), but understandably it is different. Monsters now appear on the overworld requiring you to hit them first or suffer a combat penalty . The 'first strike' mechanic is simply lazy in my opinion, it punishes the player more than it benefits and serves to lengthen the game. There is now also a weight system to your equipment, which I personally enjoyed, as it forces me to make some choices and not just use the most expensive equipment. Again, some find this tedious.There are some objectively good changes however. They added a whole new card game, which is much appreciated even though I did not consistently partake in it. The job system allows 5 passive abilities to be added to your character from any job as long as you have the ability unlocked. This is arguably the most fun part of the game as you can customise and plan out your character with combinations that work. To help this out, low level jobs also get an exp boost, making the grind much quicker. ----- Story & Character Thoughts -----The story is too safe and formulaic, especially when combined with the generic, template characters. Gloria is your angelic, altruistic princess. Seth is kind of a blank slate representing the player character. The two side characters, Adelle and Elvis,  just happen to have personal interests aligned, so they accompany you on the journey. I appreciate that they at least kept the dark themes, which was prevalent in the first games.-- A note on voice acting: Part of what makes this game high quality is the generous amount of voice acting. I played the game through with Japanese VA, because the mix of accents in the English I found to be too jarring. I think Elvis has a heavy australian accent and Adelle was like Irish or something? -- A note on UIOther than the minimap being terrible, I think it's overall pretty good, especially coming from some other jrpg's that have terrible menu/ui designs.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some old school designs implemented which can be kind of frustrating as they equate to cheap tactics. One hit kills, enemies that drain MP and the need to time your sword strike against a charging enemy can be kind of frustrating. The brave system can be a mixed bag as a result also since some enemies will unleash a bunch of attacks at once leaving your party badly battered or even half dead.  There are some other odd game choices like the ability/item to scan an opponent. It tells you details like HP and weaknesses, but not what they are resistant or immune to. Also, the side quests each have a number, but it only flashes that number up just as the quest begins. There is no log showing all the quests you have completed so you can't easily see if you missed a quest or not. Still, the story is fairly entertaining and the characters are interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a fair few turn based JPRGs in my time, and I can honestly say this is right up there in terms of how much I enjoyed it. Played it pretty much the whole Christmas.Graphics:The background environments along with the cute character models really work well, along with the effects in battle and other little bit, they fit well togetherGameplay:Honestly the best part of the game in my view, the fact you can level up each job, your character level, collect all the BnD card game, complete the monster lore book there is so much for you to doStory:Nothing too special here if you ever played any final fantasy game before, You get introduced to crystals early on and you can pretty much imagine how its going to go. I did however enjoy a few little things near the end of the game where things are a little different (dont want to spoil anything)Sound:The thing which music and sound is that if its done badly you will notice it, if its done good or at a standard most of us are used to then you wont even notice it. This game for me didnt really stand out for its music, but did enjoy the little tunes when you go into each town and area.Cons:I would say the games too easy, but I did have problems facing some bosses but only because I wanted to level up each class. There are also some classes and abilities that can pretty much kill any boss but again finding how they work is half the fun, you can change the difficulty throughout your gameplay if you want.The only MAJOR thing I didnt like about the game was scrolling through the menu, and sometimes it flipping to other menus if I used the joystick....that was it....so nothing major, just something that slightly annoyed me.When to buy:Do you want to buy this game at full price? In my persona opinion I would say no, as good as it is its not worth £49.99 (not many games are) however it is worth £34.99 or lower.

_childDocuments_.review: Sigh.I'll start off with the basics... If you didn't like or had a problem with Bravely Default 1 you won't enjoy this one either.Every problem the first game had is still present.The good:*The characters are honestly better than the first game's in my opinion. None of them immediately had me assigning the "totally annoying party member" title to them (thus far anyway)*The battles look cool and the characters actually match sizes (no more 11ft tall foes that are supposedly regular people)*The job system has some new jobs to play around with (which is nice)The bad:*The Brave/Default System: So I have a serious problem with the fact that most bosses in this game counter the very system the GAME IS NAMED AFTER! MANY of the bosses tamper with or hard counter actually using the brave/default system in some way, this becomes most immediately apparent in the chapter 2 boss fights. The bard frequently counters attempts to attack him by putting you to sleep, if he does this in the middle of a brave combo you not only get your combo cancelled you also lose all the brave points you put into it. This is repeated by the beastmaster except she uses silence rather than sleep. However the most annoying boss for this HAS to be the thief, he literally counters usage of the Default command by STEALING YOUR BRAVE POINT. This means the ONLY way to use a brave combo on him is to go negative and skip future turns... Fun.*G-R-I-N-D-I-N-G: This is not an RPG you can simply play, battle your way through the dungeon and fight the boss (even on the easiest difficulties) You're expected to take the time to fully master every new job as soon as you get it as most of the boss fights expect you to use the new job's strongest abilities to beat themThis becomes most apparent in chapter 2 where you fight a boss gain the thief job, and then immediately have another boss fight as your next story point with no handy dungeon between... go straight there and you will get absolutely destroyed (even if you mopped the floor with the previous boss).*The "equipment weight" system: In most similar RPGs you CAN still go to areas above your current strength, you can offset your level difference by simply buying new strong equipment in the later towns provided you can survive to reach them... The equipment weight system doesn't allow this, essentially it's a level requirement system which FORCES you to grind extra levels so you can actually wear that new armor.*Money!: Normally I wouldn't be complaining about too much money in a video game but... there's almost nothing to actually buy! Simply passing through a dungeon and fighting anything that you run into will (usually) leave you with plentiful cash, and you can always take the Zelda approach and simply cut grass instead... The first game's Merchant job being so early in the game forced you to have some care with your finances if you wanted to actually use it but this game? Nope! Consumables aren't all that wonderful either as you can buy Star Pendants which raise your characters' HP by 500 but the same town only sells Potions which heal only 250... not exactly ideal.*Dungeon Treasure Chests: Hoo boy, this is a personal pet peeve of mine in MANY recent RPGs... Most dungeon treasure chests in this game contain... The same crap I could buy in the previous shop?!?!? Why? As my previous point stated I already had a full set of that (admittedly mediocre) equipment due to the infinite money, why on earth am I being given more of it? This leads to little to no incentive to explore the dungeons fully to get the treasures which leads to less encounters which leads to less EXP which leads to... more grinding. Yay.In short, this game has been compared to FF5 so many times, but it's not even in the same department in my book.Sure it has a job system, but unlike FF5 it's a soul-crushing experience where you can't have fun with experimenting with the various jobs and build a party using your favorites. Instead you need to spend an excessive amount of time mastering everything in order to min/max and make progress.And yes I have 8 hours on record with this game at the time of this review, of those I would say half of them were strictly grinding.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the game having some clear flaws littered throughout, BD2 still manages to be a great entry into the series.The gameplay strikes a balance between BD1 and Second with the jobs largely being re-imagined versions of ones from BD1. Many of them aim to retain some of the simplicity from BD1, but with a bit of new flair along with some influence from Second's outlandish variations appearing here and there. This ends in every job, barring one arguably, having some sort of use or setup that lets them shine if the player is willing to experiment. It also results in the game feeling noticeably more balanced compared to past entries whereas in BD1 most jobs tend to be a mixed bag between extremely niche and absurdly good, and in Second you can find strategies to decimate the game fairly quickly. Despite this, for classic players coming back you still get some of the game breaking strategies you're used to but for early~mid game you have to actually go out of your way to do so. While I still personally prefer Second's combat for the amount of creativity and wild strategies they allow the player to get from early on, BD2 still offers a lot to the player to keep them satisfied until late game where they let you go wild. One problem the game has is though its that many of the side quests feel bare bones. For each area there's usually a few that let you see your party interact, or fight some special enemy but the vast majority are just standard fetch and kill quests. It made me miss the more straightforward and less game-bloating asterisk gathering side quests of the older games that are honestly quite rare in this entry. The game also has a card game style minigame that, while not horrible, is nothing to really write home about. Although it does have a pretty great track playing throughout.The soundtrack, which has REVO returning as the composer, competes with BD1 for the best the series has to offer, which is a huge compliment not to be understated. The game has an astounding 62 tracks in comparison to the 46 from BD1, and I can't say there's even one that I found to not be at least good and most ranging from great to surpassing some of my series favorites. Tracks like the asterisk boss themes, overworld theme variations, and the ones that litter cutscenes consistent standouts almost every time. To add onto this, the soundtrack manages to make interesting callbacks to motifs from BD1 while still feeling like it has its own identity throughout.While the models along with certain textures certainly let you know that this game came from the Switch without shame, the game's costume design with its Jobs, along with its actually pretty solid 3d environmental design in some places, and of course wonderful 2d art spread in towns helps distract you from it.Finally, there's the story. Unfortunately this is the part that certainly seemed to get shafted by what I assume was COVID dev time problems the most. At a certain point, the story starts feeling extremely rushed with some important plot points either being forgotten, feeling unexplained, or just becoming narratively irrelevant by the end. Luckily, the phenomenal main cast really carries the weaker parts of the story, especially with some select side quests that let these characters have moments to shine outside of the main plot. The only exception to this is, unfortunately, the main character. By the end I felt like I knew less about Seth than I did about some NPC who told me to kill random snakes for a fetch quest. However, characters like Adelle and Elvis both shine as arguably the best ones to come from the whole series. Gloria is also fantastic, although it feels like to get some of her best moments you have to be willing to go do some of her sidequests.Overall, despite its flaws, I would say that BD2 might just be my new favorite entry in the series for all the things that it does relatively well and gives me confidence in how the series will proceed from here.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default 2 was a really great game to me honestly. I enjoyed the jobs, the story, the characters and pretty much everything else you'll see while playing. I will say some side quests, namely the fetch quests, were awful in how much back and forth they wanted you to do, though the side quests for main characters did have funny/sweet moments that gave me a chuckle and smile. The only reason I'd say wait and see is if the price ($60 USD - got mine on sale for $53.99) is too steep for you as most people don't like to pay THAT much money for a video game. I get that. I'm glad I still did it though because this is the first JRPG I could stomach in a really long time considering most of them are fan service for straight men or generally have characters that make me want to stop playing. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A very fun game with its own shortcomings. However, if you look past those, you can definitely have a good time! 7.5/10 overall.I've had so much fun with this game, and I've put in so many hours!However, I would be lying if I said this game didn't have shortcomings. For one, the story and characters are not for everyone. They're incredibly generic, and a lot of the story and characters lack depth of any kind with little to no development since the story begins and ends with them being practically the same peoples. With that in mind, I actually didn't mind that since I don't play too many JRPGs, but I do understand that this would bother some players. There are also a couple of "quality of play" things that I would like to mention. The "Lore" book option doesn't actually allow you to see the location of where certain boss monsters are in case you watch to have a re-match. I found this challenging since I had to search from their locations online, even when I had faced them before. Second, there is no way to actually flag a certain point on a map. The only flags they give you are ones that they already set for you. You can turn them on and off, but that's about it.During the prologue, after three hours of grinding so I could get used to the game, my game glitched and sent me to an area that you can only access in the second half of the game with no way of returning to the main city. This was a major problem, and I had to restart from the beginning after about an hour of trying to figure out how to make my way back (when there was no way).Lastly, this may have been based on the system which I was playing on (which is really slow), but there were a lot of lag moments and times where my computer was heating up and not responding to the point where I had to restart or force end the game. This slow processing also made the art look worse, and I was already hesitant on the art style. The bobble head characters were inexpressive or corny and at times laughable (even during death scenes). Also, once you've cleared one area of the game, congrats, you've seen all the base designs for every single monster you'll see for the rest of the game. They just slap a new coat of paint and call it a new enemy.For the positives, I have many! I, for one (and maybe the only one), enjoyed the story and characters. The story and characters were so mind-numbingly simple, and what was not broken they certainly did not fix (although some broken things they also didn't fix). While I do enjoy a complex story with compelling characters, I can also enjoy the simplicity of these stories and characters. And after playing Octopath (which felt more like a random bunch of people happening to be in the same place at the same time), seeing these characters interacting and not switching out really added to the cohesive feeling the cast had. Even though there was little development, you do actually get to know some of these characters more (even if it's a very cliche background). And since I don't game or indulge in these types of stories often, there were about two plot twists that surprised me.Gameplay was really fun. I like the system they built, but like Octopath, a lot of it depends on the items and jobs you have equipped (which isn't bad at all since that's one of the main points of the game). Unlike Octopath, this game allows for absolute flexibility between main and sub jobs which I found really cool. I feel like there should've been a bit more balancing between jobs though to keep it a bit more fair. Besides that, I'm pretty sure any partaker in a JRPG would know exactly what's up with the rest. Since new jobs are introduced as the story goes along, it felt a lot less repetitive than Octopath (although Octopath also has a lot of strengths over Bravely Default II). The music was alright. While it was great at times, I felt like the whole open-world made it so that there was a lot less variation than what I felt would've been necessary for a game like this. Especially since nothing really changes (same old grinding with the same old enemy models and the same old characters), it would've been nice to have more variations in music.The voice acting was hit and miss for me. I played in English for the entire game, and I will say that it wasn't bad all of the time, but there were a few pivotal scenes that really missed the mark and stuck out like sore thumbs while others were just bland. I can't exactly blame the direction of the voice acting given the bobble head models and the lack of expression on their faces in the first place, so that may have been the reason that the voice acting didn't really work for me. I enjoyed the variation of accents though. The extra flair of colloquial and regional dialects helped enrich the somewhat bland models and made the story and characters more enjoyable in a funny way. It adds more quirks and nuance to the lines they say, so while it's not the best voice acting I've heard from an acting standpoint, it's still worth putting the game on English for one playthrough just for the sheer laughter I had because the voice acting was ridiculous at times. If you want a serious playthrough though, I'd recommend the Japanese voice actors for that since they honestly feel like they put a lot more effort to make the characters sound more emotional in a few scenes.Story and characters: 6.5/10Art: 5/10Gameplay: 8/10Music: 7/10Enjoyment: 9/10Overall: 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: A really solid port from SE.  A good throw back of sorts JRPG, it really feels nostalgic.  BDII features standard RPG combat with a twist, which is in it's name, called Brave/Default.  When you Default, you defend and accumulate Brave points, which can be used consecutively, up to 4 times (and you can choose whatever action for each.  However, unlike Octopath Traveller, in which you build action points no matter if you perform a regular attack or defend, you only build brave points by defending.  Using Brave borrows from future turns, so keep in mind you can exhaust yourself, so balancing is key.  Otherwise, BDII features some of your old standard SE JRPG tropes.  Red mage, BM, WM, and a wide assortment of other jobs.The good:Great musicGood VAWide cast of charactersVisuals look good at high res, especially considering that this IS a port (it may look and feel better on the Steam Deck)Game plays smoothlyUltra fast loadingYou can fully rotate the map and tiltThe bad:No true 32:9 ultrawide support - as with all switch ports (so, I'm forced to play at 1080p)Combat system can be divisive - being forced to defend to build your attack counter - though this is part of the games hook/strategy (for better or worse)Party does not recover HP or MP after waking? up in the inns after cutscenesCan't say I'd recommend this at $60, but It really is an excellent product.  I'd definitely highly recommend this when it is on sale.  Especially 33-50%, which I'm sure it'll hit at some point during the fall or winter sales.

_childDocuments_.review: Hope you are ready for a list. So i picked up this game on steam because at the time i didnt have a switch. All in all i have VERY mixed feelings of the game.  Ill start with the bad first and then move on to the good. So first bad thing i have issue with is that this game wasnt... really ported that well... I got the game and immediately was saddened to see that when i booted it up all the beautiful backgrounds i saw in trailers and such were blocks. I couldnt see any of the backgrounds or much of the environments at all. The characters were fine and the spells looked ok but it broke my heart to not be able to see the landscapes and such that i saw when looking in to the game.Second reason i had issue with the game has to do with the Boat System. Now dont get me wrong. I love the idea of it and use it every time. HOWEVER unlike the switch version which allows you to use it for 16 hours at a time the port for steam only allows you three hours and on top of that there is no way to actually make your game "Sleep" without leaving the game running and your computer. Atleast there is no way that im aware of. And now moving on to the positives. I love the characters and the world they explore. The main characters always have good banter and the npcs actually are important. Most of the npcs you come across in the game are ones you will end up talking to later on in  the game. They arent just locked to that portion of the story. Everyone is important.Next part is the game does not hold your hand in the least in terms of its story. It gets HEAVY and very dark at times. I will say if you are sensitive about certian topics then you might wanna be careful about this game. It goes places you wouldnt expect for a game that looks so unassuming. I love being able to mix and match your jobs and abilities. Taking abilities from this class and using it to make this one stronger while also on top of that giving you a sub class where you can have all the spells from one of the other jobs. I love games that include this kind of feature and wish there were more. More or less that concludes what i can think of off the top of my head about the game. If im being honest you should try and get the switch version if you can. However if you cant then you should try and pick up the game. Even if its on steam. Maybe you wont have the same issue i do with the blocky looking environment. And even if you do this game is still worth playing. For the story and game play.

_childDocuments_.review: Follows similar design principles as octopath traveler (since this game is developed by the same developer). _childDocuments_.review: Absolutly one of the best classic like turn based jrpg's to come out this year. It's basically what if final fantasy 5 was made for this generation. The job system once you unlock a few classes is fun to mix and match and see what works and what doesn't ( pro tip mastering the bestmaster class and the beserker class for everyone as soon as you get them and capturing a bunch of monsters right away will help a lot with late game stuff and tank your way through the start as well ) I've hold off on playing tales of arise for this game and im pretty glad i did i would have played this eventually regardless. The sound track of the game is also one of my favorites. Game play is your basic turn based rpg with a small twist you can build up brave points which will allow you to attack 4 times in one turn. _childDocuments_.review: What happened to this series? Bravely Default is one of my favorite games--the gameplay is so tight and fun, and the art is super stylized and cohesive. I know I'm someone who cares a lot more about how a game looks than the average person, but I absolutely cannot stand how this game looks. Some of the stylization is there--especially in the town design--but the shaders are godawful and the characters look plastic. Without the saving grace of the extra sylized chibi designs from the original game, they look SO weird, especially with some characters having fully modeled features and some being flat and doll-like. The cutscenes are too ambitious for the amount of animation they were actually able to do and end up feeling stupid. The voice acting makes it all even worse. It feels like a middling indie game in terms of art and voice quality, honestly. The gameplay is good, nothing different from the first game but feels clunkier and slower.If you played Bravely Default or Bravely Second and loved it, I honestly cannot recommend this. If you just want a decent turn-based RPG and don't care about how it looks, maybe you'll enjoy it. But coming to this after Bravely Default, and seeing how lovely games like Octopath can look in the same genre, I'm super disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adored the original Bravely Default, and was fairly mixed on Bravely Second. When I first played this on Switch (early tester and retail) I was pretty mixed on it. Now that I've finished the game a second time, I'm much more positive about it. I would recommend it if you're looking for a long, classic JRPG adventure.It's great to see the game in 4K on Steam with its wonderful watercolor background and art style, it really is a highlight of these games.My main critiques are that it suffers from the issue the original games did, which is a lot of grinding is required and at times there's very clearly a part in the game direction script that says 'and then we pad the game here, here, and here'. Though it should be said it's nothing like the original Bravely Default in that regard. Additionally, whilst I like the character designs, and think that they're an interesting modern interpretation, because they're so doll like you rarely get impactful facial expressions during cutscenes. This can make the game feel a bit soulless at times, in spite of the voice cast (both EN and JP) doing really good jobs (mostly).In terms of performance, with an RTX3080 and i7700K in ran smoothly, but it caused both to throw out a ton of heat. By which I mean, it was comparable to Cyberpunk 2077. I'm happy for the port, but I wish a bit more was done on the optimization front.

_childDocuments_.review: As a lover of traditional JRPGs with no prior experience with the series, definitely worth purchasing. If you have to choose between the steam and switch version, buy on steam for the better FPS. Unless you really want to play it mobile for some reason.I have seen people complain about the game having a full $60 price tag, but for me I enjoyed my triple A gaming experience. I also bought it when it was a 10% off launch sale, so maybe wait for a discount if the price is a barrier.Now for the game: I do not traditionally care about graphics, but I have to say, the environments and dungeons are gorgeous. 10/10. If I had to sum up the battle mechanics, it would be a mix between Golden Sun and what Xenosaga 2 should have been, but nonetheless they are pretty fun. The game play and class building allows for a lot of different builds and strategies. Hard mode is actually hard, in the early game. After you get the beast master class though, the game becomes less about strategy and more about brute force. It literally breaks the game, so avoid that if you want to be "fair". Mid to late game I had to actually relearn mechanics to defeat some of the bosses, because it was such an auto win class to use. However, in a way the broken class feels justified because the dungeons became a pain over time, slogging through the monster battles. Besides the cool looking graphics, the dungeons/random encounters lack depth and are very same-ish. Got pretty boring I have to say.Story is an 8/10. Nothing stood out but it was not particularly bad. There are some moments where it seems super random or dark, which I was not expecting. Some of the characters you want to learn more about get no further spotlight which was a huge letdown. Lots of open ended circumstances concerning the plot. Music is a 10/10.So overall if I had to give Bravely Default II a rating considering everything, it is a 9/10 for me. Super happy I gave it a shot, and hopefully you do too.
