_childDocuments_.review: Verdict: If this is your very first JRPG because you're 12 years old but you love anime, this is a good game to get you familiar with the extremely quaint retro tropes and history of the genre. If you play RPGs because you like rich stories and fascinating settings and the personal drama of character development, this is not that. There is none of that here. If you like tactical complexity and mechanical depth to reward your mastery of the game's systems, there isn't enough here for that either. It might be worth 20 bucks if you can get it on a very good sale for a weekend of brainless fun, but it's absolutely not worth more than that.It's a beautiful game. I mean, Squeenix has the cash to just throw a thousand artists at a project. Effects are snappy and glittery, animations and facial expressions are quite legible and smooth. Textures are gorgeous and go well with the "miniatures in a panorama" camera / environment style. The hyper-cutesy chibi character designs are reminiscent of Golden Sun. And Bravely Default 2 is still a childrens' game, but they probably wanted it to be targeting young teenagers instead. The dialogue is ... basic. There's a lot of it, but nothing particularly interesting or dramatic is ever said, which makes it boring to trudge through unless the audience is working on their reading skills (and there's mediocre voice acting for those that need help with sounding out the words). Characters have no personality beyond trivial babble about inanities like oh how delicious is the food in this town, M'Lady this and thank you for doing nothing whatsoever that. It's worse if this isn't your first RPG because the Mary Sue complex absolutely ruins most of the player characters. The last remaining has no other personality beyond being an obsessive alcoholic buffoon with a (very) fake Scottish accent. The best I can say about the plot is that at least there isn't any painful, misogynistic lecherous gooning - which was a refreshing surprise, given that this is an anime title.The balance is all over the place. Because of the terrible action economy design, bosses are forced to employ anti-fun mechanics that completely nullify and bypass any of your own available abilities or action economy. For example, Bernard who is infamous for not even needing to do anything because his reactions one-shot any of your own characters who perform any actions while he just defends with default to stock up for a triple-kill / theft rampage. While one-shotting your MP so you can't do anything that wouldn't provoke his reaction. And while he's fast enough to take two actions for every one of yours. So the only possible strategy available is to farm minotaurs for thirty hours with beastmasters to one-shot him in the first round of the fight by burning yourself into -3 BP with all four characters to blast him with 16 summons. Although it's technically possible to do that, it isn't balanced, clever or fun gameplay. It's just an automatic win for doing the hard-requirement grind to progress the plot past him. It's just cheese and borderline exploitation. It also clashes with the aesthetic of the entire game which is otherwise juvenile and casual in the extreme. Children might not mind working ten hours to see a cutscene, but adults probably should be getting paid for working a full shift of tedious drudgery.The combat is basic barebones primitive 1990s Final Fantasy / JRPG fare. The only attempt at evolution is the slightly flexible action economy allowing you to stock up actions or go into debt to manipulate and time your bursts. Which is fair because enemies can do it, too. But bosses have mechanics to bypass this framework entirely which renders all your stats and tactics meaningless except for the one gimmick "solution" you are required to use. Overall, the game requires absolutely intolerable amounts of just mindless grinding. It wouldn't be so bad to grind if the process weren't so mindless, but here we are. In the 2020s still just setting heavy objects on our controllers to hold a button down to auto-grind overnight on nameless random encounter trash. Which is a much more damning critique of Square Enix than the design team realizes, obviously. It's just tragic to see the studio famous for doing nothing but JRPGs so completely fail to produce anything new or interesting for more than three decades in that space (active time battle action economy came with Final Fantasy 4 back in 1991). The details of inter-class balance in the game are hidden at first but become fairly apparent as you begin unlocking classes. Not only are the classes boring (none of them except beastmaster have anything more complicated than "push button do 10% more damage than your autoattack", and the beastmaster itself is a half-assed Pokemon trainer except without anything that made Pokemon fun), but their costumes are uninspired as well as sharply clashing against the aesthetic of the rest of the game. Trenchcoats with newsboy flopcaps and fedoras (yes... actual fedoras...) may have been the height of fashion in the 1920s but are painfully out of place in sword-and-sorcery fantasy.With a competent gameplay design team, the juvenile dialogue could have been forgiven (much of it is thankfully skippable) and the painfully cliche plot () could have just quietly receded into the background. But while we're here, can we take a minute for uncomfortable disgust at the fact that Squeenix literally just copy-pasted the plot of 1987's Final Fantasy 1...?

_childDocuments_.review: I SO BADLY wanted to ignore the critics with this one. I LOVE Bravely Default and Bravely Second. Second especially added so much to the series gameplay wise and QoL wise. Bravely Default II feels like a punch to my gut.The Art Direction feels like an attempt to maintain the same style as the first 2, but the 3D elements feel so cheap and off-putting. They are chibi styled, but everything is shiny and weirdly high def. It doesn't sit right with me. 2D elements are great, but that's not what I'm looking at 70% of the time.The game moves SO FAST. In the first 30 minutes you have met and gathers all your party members, gotten 2 jobs to mess around with, and have been overwhelmed with tutorial windows. Nothing is eased in, nothing is introduced in easy to understand chunks. HERES BRAVE, HERES DEFAULT, HERES WEIGHT, HERES ATB, HERES JOBS. Just hold on a damn minute! Let me take this in at my own pace! Which reminds me...I have always hated ATB. Having a "waiting" meter sucks, and turns the game into a hectic mess. It's either too fast, too much, or it's slow as piss and doesn't make a real difference in JRPGs. Some people like it, I do not. Adding ATB to the Brave/Default system feels AWFUL. Braving or Defaulting feels like a punishment. On top of all of that, they added a WEIGHT system like this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dark Souls. Which also affects the speed of the ATB meter. So heavy characters take LONGER to get their turns back and just stand there and get hit more often than they would in the old system used in BD/BS. I hate it, I hate it so much! Now gearing characters is a frustrating experience! How did you make setting gear frustrating!?The plot feels like an afterthought. It specifically feels like an intentionally bad retread of the original game. It's like no one cares about what they are doing! Your plot hook is literally "gather important crystals and asterisks". I don't even know WHY I need to do it. Just that I have to. Also all the elements added in Bravely Second that made that game an amazing sequel, The game feels like a grind, an intentionally unfun "♥♥♥♥ you" kind of grind. And they give you an overpowered NPC in the first 2 hours to do all the work and basically be the reason you beat the first asterisk fight at all. I was taking my time and trying to be smart, but the boss healed too much, and did so much damage that had I not had the overpowered NPC to do 1000 damage when I was barely hitting 100, and raise/heal my team instantly, I would of game overed 12 times over. The worst part about this game is that this MIGHT be the death knell of the franchise. There might never be another Bravely game ever after this, and that is upsetting as hell. I don't even know why they took this route with the series. It was never about being a difficult RPG with no plot. It was a goofy Final Fantasy with charming music, characters, everything! I get that the plot is basically over for Tiz and the gang, we don't need to go back to Luxendarc for a third time, but at this point I doubt we'll be going back to the Bravely series at all.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Bravely Default and who somewhat enjoyed Bravely Second, I can say that this is a significant downgrade to the previous games in the series. The story is generic, the character relationships are paper thin with the only development within side quests, the music is not nearly as good as previous installations, and the gameplay is somehow worse then the previous games due to being unable to turn off encounters and bosses being able to counter everything your character can do. It's no fun when this game relies heavily on HP for skills and the boss can attack in response to you using those skills, and also no in-game way to figure out what that boss counters.Overall, it fails in nearly everything a game of this genre should do.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default II is an excellent addition to the series and I am overjoyed to see it arrive on steam. For those who have played this on the switch, there are some other great reviews which go over the quality of the port. For those who have played other games in the series but not this one, can rest assured knowing that this is a solid entry in the series and worth the time to pick up. However, with this being the first entry of the series to be released on steam, I want to focus on how this game is from the perspective of someone who has not played any of the previous titles.The bravely default very much likes to carry itself as a classic JRPG game, and a huge part of that is in how it presents its story. This entry in the series starts with a completely fresh set of characters and world, so there is no story lost from getting in to series from this game. The story itself is a slightly fun twist on the classical "4 magical crystal mcguffins". Throughout the story bravely default wears this classic influence on its sleeve, resulting in some "true to form" cheesy dialogue and character motivations. But the game is fairly self aware of this and will poke fun at itself at the right moments. That's not to say there aren't some more interesting story threads to tug on (especially in the process of the true ending) but it doesn't feel like the game is presenting a story more complex then it has the structure to support.This game continues the "bravely default" combat system, which is turn based combat in which characters can bank and borrow turn actions. How this works is each turn a character  is given one action, they can "default" and bank that action for a future turn while reducing damage taken on your current term or they can "brave" and use up a store of points for additional actions that turn. To me the most interesting part of this systems is that the game allows you to "borrow" points by braving in to a negative count of points, being inactive for future turns as your points restore back to zero. This is a godsend for doing a bit of grinding as you can easily brave in to negative numbers to quickly wipe out encounters, and makes boss battles a bit more strategic as you balance both the bosses points along with your own. Each character can have one main job and one sub job, these jobs are unlocked through beating bosses that hold this job throughout the story. Jobs have a unique list of abilities, the difference between a sub job and main job is that a characters stats (hp, attack, speed) are based on their main job, with the sub job only giving access to abilities. Along with this each character gets "5 passive ability slots" that can be filled with various passives gained through leveling the jobs. What results from this is a really interesting way to combine jobs both within a specific character along with the rest of your team. This to me is where a lot of the fun is, in theorycrafting a perfect team to take down some specific boss.The game continues the generally great art direction of the previous game. If I had any complaint about the game it would be in the individual character models, this kind of "chibi" style worked amazing on the low resolution 3ds screen but look a bit bad at times on a nice large screen. However the generally beautiful environment more then make up for this, and I found myself quite impressed with the graphical fidelity in my first couple hours playing. In terms of difficulty, I did not find any specific challenge to be overly brutal(even on the hardest difficulty). With that said I felt like there was a considerable difficulty spike at the start of chapter one(after the prologue), which did result in some frustration but this was quickly remedied after gathering the jobs for the chapter and having more flexibility with how you design the team. On the topic of grinding, I did not feel like it was overly required. If you properly explore the dungeons of the game and fight enemies as you explore that usually is enough "grinding" to beat the boss, as it gives you both experience and some much needed stats boosts through discovering new items.  If you do find yourself at a wall, it's easy to take a step back get some monster bait and hammer out an hour or so of grinding which is more then enough to get you over the next challenge. For some perspective in my 80 hour playthrough, I only found perhaps 3 times in which I needed to dedicate time to grinding.If any of this sounds interesting I would highly encourage you to give it a shot, the price point is well justified as a single playthough could easily hit close to hundred hours almost all of which being actual story/side quests/world events.

_childDocuments_.review: So let me be clear: This game has a very specific itch it is trying to scratch, and niche it is trying to fill. It is extremely good at scratching that itch, I would say equally or better than any of the previous games this team has made (The Original Bravely Default, its direct sequel Bravely Second, and Octopath Traveler are all by this same team, and if you've played any of them, you can tell, they all play very close to exactly the same, and I mean that as an endorsement).This is a JRPG about puzzle boss fights: You have other fights, and they do not matter. The other fights are actually the most engaging they've ever been here from any of the games I've listed above, thanks to some good experimentation in getting you to do something other than just spam all your actions at once to win the encounter in a huge burst, but they're still very much secondary to digging into the juicy turn-based boss fights. You are supposed to probably loose your first attempt, but in doing so, to figure out the boss's mechanics, so you can rapidly and easily re-build your classes and equipment from top to bottom to tailor-make your party to beat each boss. It is genuinely a ton of fun, and I have been absolutely enjoying my time with this entry.It is also , by the way. The almost 60 hours in, while inefficient and involving me leaving the game on while I did other things occasionally, looks like it's gotten me maybe halfway into the game? And considering how much extra length the first Bravely Default pulled out of its ass by surprise, it might be significantly less than that, we'll see.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of only a handful of JRPGs I've played, and I loved (almost) every second of it. I can't say how it compares to the previous Bravely games, but I can say it is a lot of fun if you're new to the series like I was.First off, the music is stellar, better than the first two games I would say. Revo continues to outdo himself yet again with songs like the Rimedhal and Holograd town themes, The Wicked Ones, Shadows Cast by the Mighty ~ Swift Judgement, and my personal favourite, Eyes that Gaze into the Nexus ~ The Ones who Gather Stars in the Night. The game is almost worth it for the music alone!The battle system is also excellent. I've heard from veterans of the series that the battle system is a bit different from previous entries but for a new player like me, I thought it was great. The only thing I could nitpick is if there were a better way to tell when the enemy is about to act, although that might make battles a bit too easy.The story is just good. It's not particularly mind-blowing (aside from a couple moments near the end), but there also isn't anything outright wrong with it. If you want a deep story this might not be the game for you but overall I found it enjoyable.From what I've seen of the previous games I think this game might have the best voice acting in the series. There was only perhaps a couple characters that I thought sounded a bit off occasionally but that aside it was very good (shoutouts to my scottish boy Elvis).The only issue I could have with this game is the lack of much postgame content. There are a couple challenge battles with extra-powerful weapons as rewards but that aside there isn't much to make you want to keep playing. However the challenge battles are hard enough that they might take you a while.Overall this is an easy recommendation for me to anyone looking for a JRPG, if you don't know what to try next PLEASE give this game a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: Square did a great job with this port! The graphics look much nicer and the game runs really smooth (supports uncapped framerates)! There's also a lot of different jobs to choose from and the characters are all fun and interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default 2 was not the game I expected. I didn't expect to enjoy a rich pleasant story about four heroes bringing hope and salvation to the world. I didn't expect the side stories enjoyable to play through. I didn't expect to put in more then 100 hours into the game. I didn't expect any of this, and I was pleasantly surprised by all of it.The story is fantastic. The narrative is saturated with beautiful music, and great voice performance: It makes for a story thatcan carry you through it's high and low points: I admire the kindness shown by Gloria when she cares for the people around her. I'm with Elvis when he becomes enraged when he learns of how his village has been used for a child's painting obsession. The whole story is filled with great story moments, funny character interactions, and it does it at a pace that never felt like it dragged on.What surprised me the most is the job system. In Bravely Default 2, you stay with the same four characters,which each have access to 20+ jobs. As you play through the game, you unlock a new job to play with, and each adding a different approach in strategy. If you want a job that has a variety of spells and ways to bypass enemies immunity to spells, the Black Mage 3 elemental versatility works well with it's second speciality to bypass immunities. If you want more damage, then the red mage second speciality to double cast any spells was a surprise for me. What you have is a system that allows for diverse strategies that the player can use and never have to be stuck in one part of the game. Any challenge can be overcome, and every enemy will fall to you.I bought this game twice at full price on two different systems, and I recommend it to people who do like playing rpg's.

On PC, it's such a massive upgrade compared to it's original release. While not as deep story wise as  the previous games, this is still a very solid entry  into the BD franchise, and the job system in this entry is fantastic - there so much customization and depth with it's options - the subjob addition reminds me a lot of how it worked in Final Fantasy Tactics. Totally worth playing through again, especially this time on Steam Deck, which, has perfect native support!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of JRPGs, and Bravely Default II is certainly one I can recommend.The Bravely series has a very unique charming style, which I understand can initially put off people new to the franchise, but has definitely grown on me as I played through the original Where The Fairy Flies. The music is absolutely sublime, Revo is an absolute godsend and I'm so happy he returned to compose for this game. The Brave and Default-based combat is still fantastic many years later as it makes for more 'playing it safe' and 'going all in' scenarios, and the job system allows for a variety of different playstyles by mixing and matching different skillsets together. The story takes a while to get interesting but it's got a lot of quirky, goofy characters that make it a fun ride all throughout.There is a lot to do in this game in terms of achievements, truly for the completionist at heart, so be prepared to put several hours into mastering a trading card game. Yep, we've got that too.Very happy to have gotten this on Steam. Now port the original WTFF and End Layer, you cowards.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a good game, but stay with me if you want to know why I can’t recommend it.Short story – too many minor, but nevertheless flaws for a such expensive game. It sometimes fails at the simplest things and I wonder if it’s because of budget, Switch limitations or laziness, or maybe each of above.The idea as I presume was to give spiritual successor to Final Fantasy V, which was based on the job system. It’s here, there is classic elemental crystals story, which old FFs fans already know, but by all means it’s not bad. Thing is I play games for gameplay, not for the story. If you can’t deliver engaging plot don’t flood player with cut scenes. Exposing average story with so much unnecessary talking is irritating. Bravely Default II is infected with modern games disease – stretched storytelling and side quests. This game has probably the worst side quests I have ever seen: Going back and forth few times between two npcs, just to listen short ridiculous excuse, often with lot of walking or even teleporting to different cities.There are lot of small things, which could have been fixed with little effort, yet there are not here. Starting with basics – you can’t chose language before starting a new game. Just why? Why do you have to get through intro and then suddenly have it in-game option menu  instead of the starting screen? Speaking of which for some reason default key-bindings are for WSAD on the main screen instead of arrows. Keyboard layout is definitely not convenient. There are too many unnecessary inputs. It takes time to customize it for a comfortable experience, but fortunately there’s no limitation for customizing it (unlike some games which give you only a pool of inputs you can set). Lazy port one might say, but also lazy design. The boss battles in this game are challenging and satisfying, but again - small thing – every boss battle has the same background area. It doesn’t matter if you fight boss in sewers, desert or some warehouse, every time it’s the same uninspiring background. Another little feature I have trouble with – screen tutorials. They are everywhere and they state obvious things, while missing deeper explanation of game mechanics. I miss level up stat increase summary screen as well. You don’t know what has changed after leveling up. Yet another basic feature this game doesn’t provide, which older jrpgs classics had. I also can’t comprehend why Bravely Default 2 starts with such huge digits. Everything is inflated at start. Few hours in game and you already have over 1000 hp, while in classic jrpgs you usually started with small numbers, above or around 100. It would give chance to feel progression, because inflated numbers are just numbers. Whether weapon gives 10 or 12 damage can be huge, but with hundreds and thousands it feels flat. Last, but not least, I was baffled by a short day-night cycle, which lasts like few seconds here, believe it or not.Are above flaws game-breaking? Absolutely not, but for a such high price I expected polished product, which won’t be inferior in any way to its predecessors. I would change few other things here and there, but anyway... it's time for good things. Combat is great, there are lot of jobs, some like white mage or black mage are definitely must-have, while others are lack-luster, like the beastmaster, who uses captured monsters as consumables, meaning you can’t just capture monster once and use them later any number of times you want), Brave/Default system and combat speed shorts grind, each monster has different weakness not only to elements, but also weapons, graphic of monsters is beautiful and exploring world map is satisfying, because of grass cut mechanic, which sometimes can give you really great rewards. Also equipment system is more complex than other jrpgs, which adds another layer of depth to already complex system.Presentation is matter of taste – you can like or hate characters design, but blurry borders is something I must mention as Switch version has option to turn them off, while PC is missing it. Music is, I would say: averagely good. Nothing you would listen to outside of the game, but still okay. Original voice acting on the other hand is very good for a such budget game.Overall score: 7/10 (7.5 if you’re from Carrington family and don’t care about the price tag)Younger brother of FFV, who feels smarter and for most probably more handsome, yet somehow you feel that he doesn’t have this special something older one was giving you. Just the little things here and there, irritating you on each occasion (like lack of preset settings for equpied jobs, abilities and gear).Bonus: Mini game here, similar to FF8 and FF9 is another example how minor things can spoil all the fun. Computer "thinks" too long, so duels drag out (you can't change combat speed like in regular fights), there's lack of animation where exactly opponent makes move, so it can be chaotic. _childDocuments_.review: Wish there was a Neutral rating...Wanted to like this game so much as I'm a huge JRPG fan and enjoyed Octopath Traveler a lot. Pros are the class system which are great, but the "Brave and Default" system I found to be... boring. You're meant to save up your points (Defaulting) and then spending them all to act multiple times in a row (Braving) - and you can go into Brave debt (skip turns). Sounds cool in theory. But in practice it just turns into random battle: Brave and go into debt to kill everything in 1 turn! If there's any survivors.... you may die as they get abuot 4 turns" --- Big battles? "Guard for 3. Big attack! Guard for 3. Big Attack x2! Sit around for 3..... Guard for 3.." you get the point. Overall, I think it'd be great if they accumulated passively - but I found the act of being forced to Defend (more than I'm attacking) to be more annoying than innovative. Now the class system, abilities, and the full shabang are solid. And the battle system is definitely praised by some. But for me: I found the innovation to be boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game last week Thursday and left on a trip the next day. I had 86 minutes played at the time, and was unsure if I wanted to keep the game. Had I known I still wouldn't like it after all this time, I would have grabbed a refund while I had the chance.Story:The story is very generic and cliche. Maybe JRPGs just aren't for me anymore, but you see every twist, turn, and death coming a mile away. Don't even get me started on the dialogue, which is very boring and occasionally cringey. At times, I found myself asking, "why would you say that". The first instance that stuck with me (not the first I saw), was in the cabin with Sir Sloan. He shouts Princess Gloria's name and says the signal phrase, throwing what amounts to a flashbang to blind the enemy. I expected him to naturally slide the signal into the conversation with the enemy, but he shouts Gloria's name then the signal, which would have immediately put a normal person on their guard. About an hour in I began to feel the urge to just skip the dialogue, which I sometimes did. Characters:Every villain feels like an edgelord or mustache twirler. The main characters are rather bland and generic, Gloria and Seth worst of all. They're your typical, "hero that wants to help everyone he can" and, "princess that's too pure for this world" archetypes. Gloria lost her kingdom, but she hardly seems to care most of the time. Seth was a sailor...that's it. Elvis is a little better, but he seems rather one dimensional. He's suppose to be a scholar, but we never see that shine through. He just loves food and drink, and there was mention of him being highborn (another trait they do nothing with). Adele likes food and drink too, with the difference being she's the mercenary. Maybe there's more to them, but I doubt it. As it stands, I couldn't care less if any of these characters die (one of the side characters dies early on, but I'll let you guess who).Gameplay:The gameplay isn't bad, though I'm unsure about the Bravery and Default system. It feels like you're basically just playing around with the turn order. Why would I default, then get two actions next turn when I can just use an action now and an action later? I could understand it's use if the enemy telegraphed some of their more powerful moves (Defaulting now so you won't take a massive hit, then dishing it out next turn), or if using Bravery increased the damage you took instead of taking a turn away, contrasting Default. Maybe I'm not using it correctly.The game is grindy. I expected a bit of grind from a JRPG, but they really went in on the grind here. There's a reason everyone tells you to max out Freelancer first. The enemies barely tickle your exp and jp bars unless you continuously battle them. Even then, you need to get 4 or more battles for it to be "worth" it. Although, to be fair, continuous battling isn't difficult as long as you have bait (when I stopped playing they weren't purchasable from the store). I will say, however, that I like the main and sub job system. It allows you to mix and match job skills which can be rather fun and useful, though some pair better than others (a main Black Mage with a sub Freelancer deals more magic damage than a main Freelancer with a sub Black Mage). Honestly though, this is basically a Final Fantasy game, so you expect the jobs to be interesting if you've played anything in the series. However, I've heard the jobs in the previous Bravely Default games were more interesting, and I would have to agree. I wonder what the Merchant would have played like...World:I don't really have much to say on this one. The world is okay. There are chests throughout each area, and a Freelancer skill that tracks how many are left in your current area. You can cut the grass, though I personally never felt like it was worth the effort . There are even side quest, and I also never felt like they were worth the effort. The rewards were usually items I had in abundance, and you don't get exp or jp from them.There are dungeons on each map, one of which you usually have to go through for the story. My main problem with them is the lack of a minimap. Some people had a problem with the narrow paths forcing you to battle some of the monsters in the dungeons, but I became overleveled grinding that optional fairy boss, so the enemies usually ran away. Speaking of bosses...Bosses:A lot of bosses seem to rely on counter attacks, which I've heard makes them difficult (in a frustrating way). Again, I was overleveled, so I can't say for sure if the counters are a problem. Although, I was rather disappointed after unlocking the monk only to find out I wasn't gonna get all those fancy counter attacks. As far as I can tell, the story bosses all unlock a new class (a fitting reward), but the optional bosses don't give anything but exp and jp. It's like they were made just to grind, and they aren't even good for that. Sure they give more exp than the average monster, but the battle usually takes so long that I'm fairly certain you're better off doing continuous battles (hopefully with a Wiki-Wiki). I don't even remember at least getting an achievement for them, though it may have happened and I just forgot.Conclusion:Honestly, this game isn't horrible. I didn't even mention the messed up faces, but that may just be something on my end. I think there are some things that people can find enjoyable, and maybe the game just isn't for me. However, I wold argue it's not worth $60. I wouldn't even advise you to purchase it on sale (which I did), just because of how generic and boring and safe it is. There are far more ambitious games out there worth your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: hands down one of the best rpgs ever releasedyes, it's a jrpg, but definitly playable by people that tend to focus on crpgsthe combat system is classical (FD) turnbased, with a kinda active time battle par, which determines when which char gets his turn (determined by the speed attribute). but the system comes with a twist: the default and brave system. default serves as for one as a defensive commande, but it also gives an additional action for your turn (you can stack up to 3, vanilla); the brave command on the otherhand spends these extra turns (which can lead to 3 additional actions for each turn, vanilla), you can also debit these brave-actions, which in turn will lead to your character beeing passive and skipping his turns until the "debt" is void (-1, means basicaly you skip a turn).this sounds more complicated than it actualy is. it's very fast to execute, and since enemies can use the same mechanics leads to vastly improved take on the classical turn-based jrpg combat. bottom line: combat is brilliant, far beyond the jrpg-genrethen comes complexety: similiar to FF Tactics and co. there's a fully realised Job-system here. mix and match, level individual jobs, comibine the active commands of 2 (one main, one sub), pick from a gigantic list of passive perks (each job also comes with it's own unique job-passive, which later on you can combine 2 of). it's one of the best rpg-character-systems, very polished, very motivating. then there's the art and grafical quality: screenshots and videos don't to the game justice. it simply looks incredible. each individual area is designed like a panaroma-window, full of detail, day/night-lighting, even the overworld-map looks alsmost handpainted. the character models are incredible clean, polished and full of detail, which also goes for your enemies. it's hard to describe, but this might be one of the most artistic games out there. the soundtrack blows most other classical orchester ost away, it's a genial mix between tunes ala Secret of Mana, classical fantasy (flute and co.) and Square-typical orchestral highs, mixed with guitarr-riffs for the more "action"-moments.the story is nothing to write home about, but the writing great. all important dialogue is fully voiced, even in combat. the writing and voice-actors did a perfect job (kinda reminds me of the "newer" Dragon Quests). each character feels unique, interesting and alive thanks to the amazing voice-lines. while creenshots might suggest that conversations only take place in a sude 2D plane, in reality there are fully directed 3D cutscenes, battles, plot-scenarios, it's all animated, voiced and looks just great.an absolute must have for every rpg-fan

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent job-system based JRPG. Each job has its own artwork and is used in cutscenes, so you can try to undercut the seriousness of the plot with silly costumes.I'm surprised by how good the voice acting is. I don't hate it which is very unusual for me, usually I find just the text boxes to be a superior experience.Basically the job system means that you can change anyone's class very easily and you can combine pieces of classes to make hybrid characters. Do you want to make a mage that hits hard with their fists? Main job a black mage and secondary job a monk. Or maybe a tank archetype that knows a bit of healing magic? There's probably something a bit broken if you explore enough.There's XP for each character (as normal for an RPG) but also there's JP for each job. As each job levels up it gets more possible actions and more passive abilities. You can use any learned actions from any 2 jobs, but only the main job gets JP. You can equip any 5 passive abilities from any jobs that the character has leveled up enough.

_childDocuments_.review: TlDr; Bravely Default II is the worst Bravely so far. Play Octopath instead.This game changed the battle system in a way that made it waaay less fun to play, and in my opinion defeats the purpose of the defaulting system. Instead of your planning your teams attacks and them occurring one by one in a constant order there is now a speed system. And now because now that speed is a factor, one character might get 2 or 3 turns before your slowest, which completely screwed up my combat sense. Also now there is equipment weight. Introducing equipment weight to a game that didnt have it before is insane to me.There are also now counter moves! Meaning that for any action you preform on a random enemy or boss, you have the chance to get counter hit for a ton of damage out of nowhere. And there is no warning at all, and for bosses the counter often occurs when hitting their weakness, DEFEATING THE POINT OF THEM BEING VULNERABLE! The game on normal is harder than the previous games and grinding is more tedious. If the game wasn't a complete slog to get through I'd have kept going just to get all the jobs/costumes but it wasn't worth it.Im not the biggest fan of the art direction in this game but its not awful. It's a minor gripe. The job system is the same which was the biggest draw for me to BD is the same at least.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Go play bravely default or bravely second on the 3ds, a second hand 3ds with a copy of both or either games will give you a much better experience than playing bravely default 2(The only good from the game)So far I've enjoyed the graphical overhaul compared to the previous two games and some of what I enjoyed in the previous two games has returned in bravely default 2. However the gameplay has suffered immensely compared to the first two games, which has left me not wanting to finish this game.(The biggest problem with the game)One of the main features of bravely default was always the "brave" and "default" mechanic, i.e. defaulting/guarding to accumulate points then braving to consume the points to take extra actions within a single turn. It *was* great back in the first two games of the series since it added an extra layer to strategy without being completely overwhelming to learn. However bravely default 2 completely ruins this mechanic with another mechanic they added into this game, counter attacks. And oh boy you will definitely run into this a lot.Some enemies will counter attack when hit with certain attacks, or if you use certain moves regardless if it was targeted at them. Not a completely bad idea in and of itself, however when you consider that counters interrupt your turn and can trigger multiple times when you are braving it discourages the use of the brave mechanic. If you choose to brave multiple times and trigger a counter, which will happen a lot during certain bosses, they can just counter attack you to death easily. (Bruh)This just discourages you from using the brave mechanic completely during certain fights, reverting the game back into a rather generic fantasy inspired turn based RPG, something that is a dime a dozen these days. The only time it "feels" safe to use the brave mechanic is during random mobs, which I expect to rapidly change in the coming chapters.(Seriously)*NEVER add a mechanic into a game if it removes more from a game than it adds back. How many times must this be said to game devs out there?*(Counters in older games)Whilst there were counter attacks in the 2 3ds games, it was never as over bearing as it is in BD2, where every boss has some kind of counter, and at endgame they still haven't done anything particularly interesting with the counter mechanic. At the halls of tribulations pretty much everything has "counter any ability" granting an extra brave point to them for doing pretty much anything. Not really anything interesting, just leads to enemies sweeping you.(So much grinding)You could change your characters job and grind that out, if job grinding wasn't so tedious. Admittedly this was a problem in the previous two games, however the choice was on you as the player to explore the job options out there. Here it feels downright mandatory for progression since some bosses/enemies will completely invalidate certain jobs, leaving you with essentially 3/4 party members who actually contribute, or worse if you run multiple characters with the same problematic job. So back to more and more grinding, just so you can actually fend for yourself.(Difficulty spikes hard)The early part of the game when you're learning everything isn't easy on "normal" difficulty, but it isn't too punishing either. This will *very* quickly change as soon as you get to the 2nd chapter where bosses hit hard, and abuse the hell out of status aliments, constantly keeping you reviving, healing, removing status aliments. Only for the cycle to repeat once again, assuming you didn't get party wiped. (Conclusion)In the end you're left with a generic RPG, with horrific amounts of grinding that's mandatory and a game that expects you to know how to tackle a boss before you've even fought it. Expect the unexpectable seems to be the moto of the game, and it's left a poor taste in my mouth.The money you would spend on this game, would be better spent playing the 3ds duology, forget this game sequel exists.

_childDocuments_.review: It's just boring. The combat system letting you store up actions or use up to four at once works really well for boss fights, because you have to think about the consequences of going into an action deficit, so you need to really think about each move. But when fighting random mobs, which outside of towns is what you're going to be doing the most, the system emphasizes the worst of turn-based combat. There's almost never a reason not to go all out, because you'll almost never fight a random mob that you can't defeat by having all of your characters take four actions on their first turn. Furthermore, once you've been in an area for a little bit, there's generally not a lot of reason not to have all four of those actions just be Attack. So think about a game with turn based combat where most every mob is defeated by just doing a regular attack. It's slow and boring. Now multiply that by 4 and you have Bravely Default II.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally, I had this game on the Switch, until my copy stopped working because of...reasons, and so here we are now.  This game, in my opinion, is one of those "it's pretty meh but gets better plotwise in the second half" kind of RPGs.  The first few chapters honestly don't feel very interesting and I didn't get too invested until the sequence at the end of Chapter 3.  I'll be honest, I wasn't too big on the characters in this game and still heavily prefer the Bravely Default 1 cast, and in some cases, the Bravely Second cast, but maybe that's because Tiz and Edea are returning characters.The main antagonist (before the real one we get no real info on until over halfway through the game), honestly was really weak.  He clearly went to the Walhart School of "solve conflict with even more conflict" and failed his class.  Backstory on this guy was hidden behind a sidequest and told to us by another character instead of getting the information organically.  I feel like Gloria specifically suffers the same fate, having most of her main development locked behind sidequests.  Speaking of sidequests, why was there no quest log in this game?  On top of that, you can only set markers for 3 sidequests at a time?  Why?  These were honestly some pretty dumb design choices.This game having zero relation to the past two games I think hurts it a bit.  Making the Asterisks more important to the overall story instead of just being an excuse for the job system was nice, but what baffles me is why only two are optional when almost all the others are given via the story.  The story was passable.  None of that "fight 4 bosses 4 additional times for the true ending" nonsense from Default or "press Start in the first fight unprompted" from Second, but it's way of guiding you to the true ending was a step in a better direction, even if I was a bit iffy about it.But one of the main draws of games like this and Final Fantasy V or X-2 is the job system.  Part of the fun is finding ways to shatter the kneecaps of your various foes by abusing the system to your advantage, and in a way, this game does allow that sort of freedom.  Some of the earlygame classes have things in them that can help smash the difficulty, like Thief's Godspeed Strike or Beastmaster's second specialty, which can lead to insane stat boosting if you're proactive on capturing monsters.  I feel like White Mage did get a bit of a nerf, especially with the massive nerfing Spiritmaster got compared to Default where it served to amplify White Mage's abilities.  Black Mage is still bleh and there's no Spell Fencer equivalent this time to use.  I also wasn't too big on how certain useful passives, like Pierce Default or Angelic Ward are locked to being specialties instead of just being passives you can equip like in the old games.That brings me to the one thing that grinded my gears the most about this game, and that's counters.  This system is objectively the single worst part of the game.  First, only enemies can do it.  Second, you won't know what they counter until it's too late and you're already getting smacked for performing certain actions, or the enemy gets free BP to set up their moves.  Worse, every Asterisk holder starting from the second boss on and regular enemies included, have counters.  Don't equip Counter-Savvy and waste one of your precious passive slots?  Too bad, time to taste constant pain.  The final boss was a major offender of "counter borderline any action" and it was awful.  Rematches with the Asterisk holders literally allowed them to get free BP as a counter to ANY action sometimes, which could lead to a certain Arcanist blowing your party to hell with high powered magic that not even two heavily boosted Beastmasters could endure.Now, I don't want to say this is a bad game.  It's...alright, but earlygame can be pretty grindy if you want those JP Up passives to make life easier in the future, and there's the matter of raising up jobs.  I would honestly say play it if you really, really like games with a job system or are a fan of Default and Second.

_childDocuments_.review: A classic style JRPG in the vein of Final Fantasy. It's got everything that the old FF games do, like jobs (though here you unlock them by beating bosses like Megaman), cheeky party members (Elvis the drunken mage is a hoot!), and FIRAGA! It's just a bit more modern looking while still retaining the classic gameplay and storytelling. Of which there is a lot, and most of it's voice acted! There are a handful of piddly bugs like equipment stat changes not displaying correctly in certain places, but nothing major, and there is grinding required to progress, but it's not insane if you tailor your party's jobs to the enemies you're facing. Now I swear I heard some music from Megaman in the boss battle theme, and from Metroid in the underground waterway...

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting game. When you're greeted by two goofy characters named Adelle and Elvis, you can't help but wonder... It has a Final Fantasy reminiscent style job/sub job system. You can choose which passive abilities you want from other levelled jobs, which is very cool. The possibilities are endless, and you can play on your own terms.Once you get past the goofiness of the beginning of the story, it gets a lot deeper, so don't worry... just keep at it and you will soon find yourself immersed in an amazing story with tons of sidequests and grinding. For those of you without much time to play, you will have an option to help you level up, and it's introduced very early in the game so just play for a couple of hours and you will see what I mean. Remember, this game does let you play on your own terms though, so just play it the way you want to.I definitely recommend this game because of its stellar turn based combat system and polished gameplay. Just think Final Fantasy, except a little goofier.Oh, and mow as much grass as possible. You will thank me later.

_childDocuments_.review: BD2 is an incredibly bland JRPG with no obvious audience. It's too hard for genre beginners, too badly designed for veterans, and too boring for pretty much anybody. The story is the same generic crap we've seen in a thousand other games going back to the very first Final Fantasy. The dialog is mind numbingly boring and the side quests and dungeons seem to be designed to waste as much of your time as possible. BD2 is not fun to play. Bizarrely, it very often hides critical information from you. You can see what weapon/element monsters are weak to, but not what they're strong against, what they will counter, or even what level they are. There's a card game, but you can't even change your card deck outside of the duel menu. You can only see some stats of items in some menus, and the "weight" system is one of the dumbest JRPG mechanics I've ever seen.The game also expects you to run back and forth constantly, mostly for very underwhelming rewards. There are many times where you'll find yourself running down a long dead-end path for a single chest which contains a consumable you could have purchased in the very first town. Side quests will most often give you rewards from several towns ago. This is absolutely lazy game design that was done better even 30 years ago.But most puzzling is the fundamental brokenness of the game. It's as if the developers didn't play test it at all. For example, one of the earliest classes you unlock has a special trait to gain stat bonuses based on the (uncapped) number of monsters you capture. If you do this AT ALL, this class will immediately overpower every other class in the game multiple times over and turn the rest of the game into a trivial mess.I bought this game and I wanted to see it through, but boy, was it a chore. The single best thing about BD2 is that you can skip 99% of the cutscenes and party dialogs (of which there are MANY.) Which is strange given that there is no remarkable content of any kind. Don't buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this make me wish I thought less.Deciding whether or not a JRPG is right for you within the first few hours is typically difficult, and I rarely find myself being turned off so fast and hard by a game's opening attempts at establishing its characters. The first game also had some trouble in its opening for me, but it's gone from weird and awkward to just kind of effortless - In the bad way.Main the Character is washed ashore presumably after a shipwreck (a la Adol the Red in Ys) and so the potential for literally any possible character dynamic is presented: They're new to this place, they are seemingly without any prior connection to it, they could bump into anything. So, what do we get?After a brief opening, you go back to the shore and instinctively save a passerby from some random low level enemies (like a true hero) and get noticed by a pair of adventurers who seem to dislike each other - Not enough to brew any clear enmity between them, nor at a state of ribbing levity between friends, just this awkward state of having no chemistry with one another yet both being lumped together because of reasons. They immediately team up with the protagonistThis isn't to mention the hilarious contrivance of being found on the shore initially by the Princess' most trusted knight and thus getting embroiled in her story in the process. I suppose I should thank the game for its brevity, but if the story is to have any weight or impact to it, it feels like it should take a few moments in between to breathe, or just forego the preamble entirely and start in medias res with the hero already in a party.How you are swept up into the story is rushed, the character's relationships to each other feels rushed, and then you rush right ahead into an (at least in the game's point of view) unwinnable fight, only for the spooky wind crystal of fate to show up to tell you it's time to be a real G and survive this no matter what. This, to me, completely erases any stakes the game might of had by showing that I could be saved by Crystal Ex Machina at any point in the story. As far as writing goes, that is where I mentally departed from the journey, no longer able to take it seriously, since it wasn't going to spend time developing its ideas at the start of the game (the most important part of the game to reel in a new player) and thus was unlikely to bother doing it later either.I can't help but compare it to DQ11 from the previous year, which also has many interjections from fate and weird little contrivances to bring its characters together, but since so much time is devoted to making you care about the characters as they are introduced (and before such contrivances are even made known) it's much easier to get invested in their story. I could go further back into games like FFX where the protagonist is given literal hours of game time to be presented as a fish-out-of-water (apt too, really) before finally being adopted by a pre-established party mostly due to foolish reasons, reasons that the characters themselves even take time to debate with differing levels of scrutiny.These examples aren't the absolute best that the genre has to offer, but for BD2's attempts to be so lacklustre in comparison shows that though the plot might be important to the game's direction, the writing that takes us along the plot was not. This can, of course, be totally valid if the gameplay picks up the slack.It does not.I had some fun in the boss fights, but the regular overworld encounters seem like they're impossible to balance by design. The game's main Brave/Default system mechanic means that all of the player characters are capable of doing around 5 times their usual damage output at the start of a fight, so either the enemies need to have massive health bloat to combat this (which would be boring and awful) or they all become inconsequential mashes of the attack command.Senselessly beating on random encounters is a JRPG staple, but I'm not sure I'm happy with it being made even more redundant, when little indie games out there like Crystal Project are finding ways of making every battle between you and the next checkpoint feel like engaging ordeals, without slowing the game's pace at all.The music's pretty good, but that's to be expected, and good soundtracks are more important when attached to a memorable experience that they can evoke, which this game doesn't appear to have.If you're here for emotional storytelling, a plot to sink your teeth into, and lovable characters to get mildly obsessed with for the next few months, this ain't the one. (Try DQ11)If you're here for interesting gameplay systems that aren't just standard PS1 era JRPG fare with one entire extra thing slapped in that harms the general experience more than helps it, this isn't for you either. (Try Crystal Project)If your standards of enjoyment are lower, then maybe you'll like it, lots of other people seem to.I can say that it is at least functional, and feels pretty alright to play - You aren't going to get a deeply inferior experience or anything, it's not exploding with bugs and broken features, though I wouldn't recommend getting it at full price.Aside from that, my best recommendation for everyone, regardless of who they are, is to just google "Classic JRPG" and then play whichever ones you haven't yet, you're likely to find more gold in those results than anywhere in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming hot off the heels of my first ever Final Fantasy VI playthrough, I was excited to move on down my list of FF games, next of which would have been Final Fantasy IX (Skipping 7 and 8 as they seemed predominantly Sci-Fi themed). I instead decided to make a pitstop in a more modern take of the Older FF formula in Bravely Default II to see what these types of games are upto in the current day. And I unfortunately do not like this game and was unable to bring myself to finish it although I gave it a VERY long time before coming to that conclusion.The Brave and default system is different, but it takes way too long for you to get classes that actually do interesting things with it, and the only other advantage I can see from a system like this versus the ATB system or just straight up turn based is that you can blast enemies that you are way stronger than by taking the max turns right away. The job system seems interesting at first, because you have a main job, which is the one that gets all the XP and uses it's specializations, and a secondary job, which gives you access to all previously unlocked abilities in that job but again, it takes way too long for you to get jobs that feel like they synchronize well together. The fact that passives can carry over between any class is cool, but made me grind sometimes just to get a job's passive for a character that sometime's didn't end up being worth it.I also found gear to be quite boring up until the later half of the game as most of it were just stat increases and for the most part didn't feel like it affected your characters too much. I was really missing the gear from FFVI that's for sure. The accessories were alright though, and those for sure had a bigger impact on your characters a lot sooner than gear did. I also never really enjoyed that your damage from the "Attack" action was quite low unless you were one of just a handful of jobs that had better damage off standard hits, but only one I ever used had damage comparable to abilities. This is less of a criticism really and more just that I miss big damage from attacks from FFVI.The story is just sorta "eh", not awful, but also terribly uninteresting. The one time I felt the story became interesting was during the Snow city where  but absolutely hated how they handled the subject matter. I could not believed what a dropped ball that entire saga was. Practically the entire city was complicit in those crimes and once it was over the authorities basically don't get blamed at all, the citizens pretend they didn't play a part in it and just all blamed the one named character involved, but since they had a family the main characters were forced to forgive them and in fact actively worked to make their legacy look good. The whole thing just felt gross. The Characters themselves are also quite boring and don't have much input beyond the classic "This is wrong!" "Yeah we have to stop this!"I was also slightly disappointed by the aesthetic as Bravely Default I & II have incredible art. There is something that's just a little lifeless about all characters and I can't tell if it's the animation, models or the textures, but after dozens of hours it I knew it wasn't merely "Oh I'll get used to it". I just don't like how the game looks. Monster designs too.Now the main thing that just irritates me in this game is the Boss fights. They were fine at the start but once I hit Bernard I stopped enjoying them. For the most part it seems like these Boss fights are all just damage checks as there were no clever ways to defeat them like in FFVI and you are just meant to overpower them. For a few, I found I NEEDED certain jobs to be in the party and that meant leaving the boss room and grinding the jobs i needed so they were at the level of the boss. I found plenty of success with class combinations that were fun between these fights so it felt awful to be forced into these required combinations that were often less fun and just involved weakness spam like this was pokemon or something. After all this I just realised I wasn't having as much fun with this as I was with Final Fantasy IV where I would look forward to coming home and booting it up and playing until the very final minute I could milk out of the day before going to bed. I was sick off work for a week with COVID and struggled with the thought of starting this game and playing for most of the day towards the end. I decided to pop into Final Fantasy IX real quick to see if I was crazy, if maybe this genre wasn't for me after all. Lo and behold FFIX charmed my pants off in the first few minutes and was a wonderful breath of fresh air.I do not recommend Bravely Default II and Final Fantasy VI is still the GOAT

_childDocuments_.review: Do you love classic JRPGs?  Do you long for the golden era when men were men and women had at most a bikini and a cape?  Do you want to experience a rich, emotional story with deep battle systems loaded with tons of options and endless replayability?Well too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bad, because this game has none of that.  This is a game for sweaty minmaxers who like to think that just because they looked up the one broken class combo on line that trivializes the game that they're actually smart and their lives have value.  They're not smart, their lives don't have value, and no, daddy is never coming home from the supermarket and it's all their fault.Everything about this game is awful.  Starting with the battle system.  Bravely Default 2 has a pretty rich job system, but unfortunately it's tuned for the one or two broken combinations in the game.  You have so many choices, but they boil down to: build the party you want to play and get curb stomped, or play 4 beastmasters and trivialize the game.  It's even worse by the absolute joy destroying counter system.  No matter what you do, bosses in the back half of the game will counter with stuns, silence, death beams, etc.  There are skills that mitigate this, but it just further railroads you into the ONE TRUE BUILD (beastmaster + anything).  It's not just attacks.  Debuff the enemy?  COUNTER!  Buff the party?  COUNTER!  Heal?  Screw you, COUNTER!  Guard?  THAT GETS COUNTERED TOO BABY!That's ok, you might say.  These games are about the story!  It's got a deep, rich story, right?   RIGHT!?WRONG!Bravely Default II has one of the shallowest stories ever to grace video games.  Note that I said video games, not rpgs.  The story is basic and shallow and it's filled with one dimensional characters who barely put in the effort to meet the low standards of generic rpg tropes.  Motivation?  HAH!  I'm evil, that's motivation enough.  Nuance and emotional depth are for suckers.  In this game it's clear from the color of the clothing you wear if you're good or bad.The overall story arc is lame as well.  It's basically the tried and true "go to city A, solve problem, then go to city B, solve problem, etc".  Nothing is surprising or interesting.Of course no rpg is complete without dungeons, and boy howdy does Bravely Default II have dungeons.  Do they make any logical sense?  Of course not.  Are they fun?  Only if you like mazes and think minimaps are for wimps.  The dungeon aesthetics are boring and samey as well, and the only dungeons that are mildly interesting are optional.  The rest of the game's aesthetics are meh as well.  The character models are super deformed cutesy, which some people like I guess.  The monsters are boring.  The music is generic fantasy.  The only good thing in the entire game are the city maps, which are absolutely stunning watercolor works of art.So in summary, this is a terrible game.  I finished it out of pure stubbornness and I hated every second of it past the second hour.  Do yourself a favor and give it a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first read up on the game the common theme was that the game itself is difficult, but worth it if you're able to overcome these challenges. At first I was put-off by these remarks, I figured I have enough games to play and the last thing I need to be doing is spending money on a game I might not even enjoy. With 84 hours into this game I can say that I was honestly happy they were wrong.. for the most part. At first, yes, this game is hard. When you don't have any of the good classes, you're low level, no real abilities other than the basic melee/caster abilities it is a bumpy ride. I'd say the game starts getting progressively easier roughly around the middle point of chapter 2. I'm willing to wager that a majority of the reviewers that claimed this game was hard didn't bother grinding all that much, as with me I spent probably a good four to five hours per chapter grinding my levels/job levels. It also helps if you do the boat mini-game thingy as it nets you a lot of nifty rewards that can help along the way such as Experience/Job Point orbs, money, booster items etc.Now to touch the bases of a review:Graphics: Simple character textures whimsical in a way but nothing that pops out. The backdrops are well drawn, but with the way the camera is placed some areas can get confusing. This game really shines on it's environmental textures though, really clean, and colorful and with all the little added effects makes it look simply a joy to look at. Sound: Sound effects were pretty spot on footstep sounds changing on the fly depending on what kind of surface you're walking on whether in a town with a static back drop or in a dungeon. The music was calming, in a way the music style brought me back to the old 16-bit days of RPG's with their magical bits, which I appreciate as a lot of RPG's it seems tend to go for a more robust orchestrated soundtrack or one with heavy guitars which, to me don't really suit the mood of the game itself. I will say though the battle sound effects weren't all that great. While most of the weapons made the sound effect you would expect a weapon like that to make it just felt hollow, a lot of it is drowned out by the characters talking so it wasn't a huge deal but there were time where I'd want a sword hitting a piece of metal to sound like it was hitting metal not just some generic slashing sound. So in a nutshell the sound is pretty damn good outside of the battles themselves.Story line: Standard JRPG fare with a few twists and turns but the character development and acting in the game, IMO, is top notch. I always got a kick out of the accents used with the main characters along with the in-game facial expressions. Game play: The game is hard at first as you're relatively under leveled and unable to do some of the better higher damage dealing abilities which in turn requires some level of critical thinking early on. There are a ton of side-quests, mostly just fluff but some of the rewards from these quests are actually useful. As of this review I have 84 hours into the game, but I'd say a good 3-4 hours was spent AFK on the title screen so at the time of completion I had 37 achievements and all characters at level 99 with >50% of the classes on each character maxed out, I played a lot of the in-game card game and got about 75% of the cards in the game, and to add I did numerous sweeps of each town and areas looking for any missable quests/chests and I will say a vast majority of the play-time was enjoyable. A lot of games go this length  yet offer maybe half of that in actual fun game play, with this game I'd say a good 65'ish hours of my playtime was pure enjoyment. As for replayability I doubt I'll be returning to this game soon as I have five games that I'm actively playing and trying to complete so I want to focus on that but for those that love to net each and every achievement unless you're an absolute pro/masochist you'll need to do at least two playthroughs to net all achievements. If I had to put a score on it I would give it roughly a 9.5/10 while it's not perfect (battle sound effects, issues with the camera panning up and down in the field, and difficulty spikes early on) It's definitely worth the asking price and definitely worth checking out if you have even the slightest interest in JRPG's.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start this by saying that I love Octopath, Bravely Default 1 and Bravely Second, and Bravely Default 2 manage to completely baffle me on how... bad it is. I have not play the Switch version so this PC port is the first time I ever play this game from start to finish.Story first since what is a JRPG without a good story? I'd tell you what, its became Bravely Default 2. I cant go into too much details since I will spoil the entire story if I want to talk about how bad it is. But my 2 key complains is that the story is really generic and making alot of nonsense plothole all around as well as the lack of interaction between the characters that make them feel very distance from each other. In Octopath we have this system where once something in the story happen there will be a prompts asking you to press a button and it will begin a cut scene of the characters in your party talk to each other about what just happen. It make sense in that game since the game dont know which characters you have at which point of the story, but bringing that same system here in BD2 make no sense as you have all your 4 party members very early on and having those very skippable dialogues (even if you do read through all of them they are all of very little consequences) as the main interactions between the characters do not sell them as friends, it put them very squarely in the "acquaintances" zone. This make the relationship they have or atleast what Square Enix expected us to believe that they have become very unbelievable. Gameplay wise... the job system was cool... for 5 minutes, until you realized that there are very little viable jobs as level them up is a giant grind (you can only lvl up main job, not sub job), attack magic fall hard in usefulness as the game goes on and even among physical damage dealer job only a few are actually viable. You might think that the weakness of the enemies would promote the use of the correct weapon or magic type, but nope, even with correct weakness and the enemy have halves damage for the physical wpn, physical often still out damage magic anyway for little to no cost of MP. But the worst thing that they do about the battle system is that there's no real benefit whatsoever for the weakness of the mobs to be exploit, since all the harder boss in the later part of the game specifically have counter against whatever weakness that they have, so its often much better to just ignore their weakness and go for the strongest physical attack you can perform. Equipment is also such a chore since the wpn sold in shop is often the best you can get at that point in the game, so it became a very simple process of just grinding money and buy all the newest stuff and put them on. Weight system is just plain annoying since over weight decrease your stat, but it became less relevant as you grind up your level.Music wise... BD2 continue to disappoint as its OST is 1 of the least memorable I have heard from Square ever. I couldnt really put my hand on why I dont seem to recall any OST in the game as soon as I close it until I reach 1 of the final dungeon in the game where it have areas that represent each country, and I realized when walking through each of those area the OST of each of those place played, and they are all the same OST with just slightly different tone. Very generic fantasy OST with no stand out track as far as I can recall, such a shame since Neo TWEWY released recently have such a banger OST, similar for Octopath and previous BD game.Graphic wise... I dont think the chibi 3D style they are going for match the world? unlike Octopath where it have a consistent art style, BD2 feel very disjointed in how it present the city, the world map and the player characters. Overall, all I can say about BD2 is that its very... generic. It do the bare minimum a JRPG do with a very generic art style, music, battle system as well as the story, which I would honestly would even put under the bad side instead of average due to so many problems I have with the scripts. If I have to give it a score out of 10... I'd say I would give it a 3/10. I would not recommend it. I'd much rather just go back to Octopath on my Switch or BD1 and Bravely Second on my 3DS instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Hoho boy, that one is such a failure!The goddess has created 4 elemental crystals, which control powerful forces of nature, and bestowed upon rulers of Musa kingdom to safeguard them. However, with Musa being destroyed, those 4 crystals are lost of stolen, the world is in peril. It falls upon an exiled princess Gloria, a sailor Seth, who has lost his memory, and two stray adventurers Adel and Elvis, to restore stability to the realm, saving nations and continents affected by rampant elements.Bravely Default is your typical JRPG, with most of combat system borrowing from generic Final Fantasy origins (think Cure - Cura - Curaga progression). The combat is ATB as well, but here is where the trademark feature of the franchise comes in: the brave/default system, which allows you to store or borrow turns, making your character to perform several actions in a row.You can change character class any time outside of the battle, and character may use actions of their primary class and their subclass as well, allowing you for greater flexibility, combining related classes, for example, a black and white mage. Leveling up classes also unlock character-wise passive abilities which may greatly improve their life.The party progresses through the world, avoiding (or heading heads-on) random encounters, exploring labyrinths, and fighting bosses, thus unfolding the truth about crystals.At first, this does not sound bad, at least, that sounds pretty much your average JRPG stuff, shouldn't be much worse than your average JRPG, right? Well, at some points things go south. Monsters feel too boring, and there are too many of them. Does not add it that, since authors need to balance player's ability to do 4 turns in a row at the start of the battle, monsters  has a lot of HP, and a lot of damage, too. At some point,  monster on the map had instant death ability. Random encounters in dungeon respawns almost immediately, just after the spawn point gets off your screen.All this makes progressing through dungeons a tedious and boring grind. This is reminiscent to Wizardry 8, yes, indeed, but even W8 was not  grindy, and death cloud could have been countered much easily.Items, and by extension, thief profession, are almost irrelevant - they will (and should) be replaced with spells, and there is no crafting in the game, save for one available to one class, from resources procured by this very class. May be, there were plans which were scrapped for budget reason?The story is rather generic, and, while I usually do not have reservations against standard plots, it's simply not captivating enough. Yeah, right, lost memory, wandering princess with a sence of duty, couple which does not realize their feeling to each other; great, but this could have been done much better, it simply does not click where it should.The visual, though, is adorable. The style of model somewhat reminiscent of chibi characters, awesome cities, nice visual effects. And the grass, indeed - you have it all. It could have so much potential...Music is okayish, it is almost not too repetitive, and even with me being very picky, I didn't really turn the music off.However, playing Bravely Default is just not fun. You need to brave for a lot of grind, and even then, the game is pretty default to begin with. May be, you should look somewhere else.

_childDocuments_.review: Man I loved the first two games... unfortunately this isn't it.They basically redid all the same stuff, pretty understandable it being a bravely default. Problem is they decided to add a twist with things like counters being a theme on basically all bosses. And guess what happens when you add a mechanic to a well balanced game that was never designed to work with it, and then you double down on it to oblivion? Does it really make sense that several bosses counter every default action you do with +1bp?This is the perfect example of a game ruined by adding things without thinking on how they affect the whole.Edit after around 20 extra hours: I went back to the game and enjoyed it for a couple extra hours. "Enjoy" here is a misnomer. I really wanted to give it a second chance and see the error of my ways, but there's just no way. On top of all the previously mentioned issues, which are definitely there and way worse, you end up grinding a lot to get jobs up to par for bosses that you don't have the right ones for, which isn't really as fun as in the previous games. Not to mention the jobs themselves feel a lot more lackluster, and the same goes for the game in general.Think that's not enough? Well, here's the worst part: most bosses you will NEVER defeat on the first go. This is fine and maybe shuoldn't be expected, but the real problem is that all bosses apply status effect and have game-breaking counters that you NEED to play around, but in most cases you can't do that until you lose, change gear for better immunities, change jobs for the right strategy and go back in. That's not even to mention that most bosses you'll end up googling cus it's not super clear a lot of the more complex mechanics or things they'll counter. It's not a rare thing to go into a bossfight, fight for about 10-20 turns, realize it was never possible to win with your setup, reload, spend 15 minutes changing things around,, go back in, realize that the boss either didn't actually work the way you thought or has a different, worse counter for whatever your new strategy is, rinse and repeat till you end up googling it, grinding the jobs up, and doing 2 or 3 tries the way god intended.All in all, no matter how many times you've played the previous games, just going back to those for the upteenth time is way better than spending any amount of time on this insult of a sequel.
