_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this one, the combat was fun and interesting with all the various jobs the game provides.I really appreciated the fact the game makes you choose how to develop your characters in a sense in terms of the jobs you give to them. Like I made the hero the tank, shielding my allies and absorbing all the damage. Gloria my healer that was crucial, if she went out of the fight I was practically doomed, Elvis and Adelle were my damage dealers.The story of the game is not bad either, there were a few moments where I was genuinely impressed and wasn't it expecting it at all.Then there is the OST, that one is just a masterpiece, there is not a single track in there that I disliked. There are 5-6 boss tracks I believe for just the first part. Then when you get to all the other endings I believe there are like 3-4 more and the final boss track is just sublime how it all ends.I also got some complaints about the game, the fact there is no side quest tracker is just annoying. You can see which ones are active but as soon as you done them you got no way to know you done a side quest or not unless you always go around every town and their interiors. Like they went their way to number these side quests and everything else has a logbook available (like monsters, items, etc) so this feels like a massive oversight. The same goes for the music player, there simply is none in the game and since this OST is so fantastic it's a darn shame.
_childDocuments_.name: BRAVELY DEFAULT II

_childDocuments_.review: Heavily enjoyed my time.As another installment in the bravely default series if you have played one of the prior then you can for the most part expect how the story will go, sadly they all follow a very similar formula but at the same time that is by design as the entire series is supposed to be a call back to the older final fantasy games.The game has a lot of issues for sure, but thats mostly due to it being 1, a switch game, and 2, the studio isnt really that rich so you can tell they lacked budget.This mostly shows in a lack of music tracks (although they never got old and the few they had are great)Lack of monster variety, it never really bothered me but i think there is maybe like what 20 unique monster types? and then the higher level areas just have them re skinned or with new particle effects.The few cutscene animations arent the greatest in their of quality, mostly due to again a lack of budget and it being a switch game.I think the biggest problem overall is the lack of balancing for all the various jobs, they have a lot of fun jobs but theres like a few outstanding ones that are just so absurdly powerfull using anything else is literally just handicapping yourself, its a bit of a shame.The story is good, i enjoyed even tho it was mostly predictable. There were a few twists and turns that made it a lot more fun, also the devs like to mess with the players ill leave it at that...Graphically i personally enjoy how it looks, the dungeons were for the most part fun to explore as well aside from a select 1 or 2, There are a bunch of "rare monsters" you can find around the world map to challenge yourself with, depending on how early you tackle them however the drops you get might make you a bit too overpowered for the next few bosses so be vary of that, eventually you will get side quests to kill them so you can save them until then if you wish.The jobs although the balancing was bad like i said they were still fun to look at and use, i enjoyed mix and matching some abilities seeing how things work together.The grinding if you do wish to go for it, there is a certain rare monster that you can eventually grind really fast in the mid game which basically lets you max out a job in 6 minutes or so, meaning there really isnt much of a grind if you wish to go for that. If you dont grind at all as far as a i know the game is reasonably challenging unless you choose some of the weaker jobs, then you might struggle heavily, i do wish they balanced it better.But overall i had a very very fun time with this game, i ruined my sleep schedule over it completely.If you enjoyed the previous bravely default games like i did then you should really enjoy this one and i would heavily recommend it.It took me 60 hours to beat it all, including all side quests, and all the side bosses.However this is due to me being massively overpowered for the entirety of the game, you can add on extra 10-15 hours to that if you actually have to do the boss fights, which from what ive seen of others playing it are fun to do the normal way.I might personally start a new game plus and force myself to not overlevel in order to enjoy the game that way.Tl;dr: If you liked the previous games or like jrpgs with the style of the old final fantasy games then you will enjoy this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Technical:  The port seems pretty minimal in terms of settings, but solid overall.  I have a decent rig, so I'm not sure how it scales, but it should be able to run well on lesser hardware.  Gameplay:  This is a throwback style game.  It takes a lot of inspiration from the early Final Fantasy titles (mostly 1, 3, and 5 I think) including 4 elemental crystals that maintain balance in the world and a job system.  Much of the gameplay boils down to light exploration and battles, there are some vanilla side quests and a card mini game, but if you don't like the combat in the game I'd say skip it.  Generally speaking most encounters are not horribly difficult, but the bosses are where you have to pay more attention and plan appropriately (I'm playing on normal difficulty).  There are 20+ jobs in the game, and you earn levels in jobs separately from your character, and you can also mix and match elements from jobs to customize your party.  To me this is where a lot of the fun lays, in concocting mixes of jobs that break the game in entertaining ways.Art/Story/Music: Music seems fine, but nothing super memorable so far.  Art is decent for a lower budget switch title.  The characters are throw backs to the NES/SNES chibi style, but they are the monsters have some pretty good textures.  Backgrounds of the towns in particular have a very quaint story book feel.The story is pretty much in that early FF style, 4 crystals and so forth, but the writing is pretty good and the voice acting is nice.  There are options for Japanese or English voice over, but the English is actually pretty good.  A lot of characters have British, Scottish, or Australian accents and deliver their lines well.All in all I'm not sure it'd be worth 60 bucks to everyone (I'm really enjoying it personally though), especially since some big RPG's are coming out within a week of it's release.  But this is a comfy blanket of a title and would recommend those who have even a casual JRPG interest to give it a shot on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravely Default 2 Review One might assume from playing any rpg that Bravely Default 2, is just another game; same old, same old. This is however far from the truth as db2 has some fairly unique takes on old rpg mechanics. Some people who not being knowledgeable with the 3DS versions of the game might assume the story is childish compared to a Final Fantasy or Tales of Zestiria, however for many of the series fans that simplicity is part of what sets it apart from the pack, yet when combined with the fore mentioned mechanics and art design is what makes it special. The Art Design  The bone of contention eh, the old games were to be brutally honest hand drawn and are still to this day ageless, this new game does seem dated from the get-go with the hand drawn backgrounds replaced by computer designed assets. It still looks okay and I have always stressed games don’t have to look superb to be wonderful timeless games. Some exception might include Parasite Eve, which though great looks awful and is unplayable by my person in this current day, much like the original Devil may Cry but that is due to very bad tank controls, which they could have fixed in the remaster but did not. Core Systems I have mentioned a few pros and cons at this point and this handily led to the core systems or experience of the game, the job system and team strategy of previous entries is all here, battles still take consideration and thinking ahead, some basic spawn battles can wipe you out if you won’t know the weakness or are woefully under leveled. That said as a complete package for a fan of the series and being 5.3 hours in this time is well worth £45. Other Value considerations  I can see why others consider this to be overpriced, I am not one to buy day one releases except on rare occasions, my history with the series however gives me an extra push despite having a massive games backlog. However, for a mass audience of the downgrade in presentation and high price point is not particularly attractive.   Db Fans : 8/10 buy Rpg fan: 6/10, wait for a 40% off sale

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Bravely default on the 3DS, I enjoyed Bravely Second on the 3DS, and this is just more of the Bravely franchise. At first I thought I was going to dislike the change going from being able to enable/disable earning JP/XP/PG(gold) and ability to turn random encounters anywhere from entirely off to 200% more likely that the first game had allowing you to grind when you wanted to but be able to focus on the main story when you wanted to. I worried that this change to having enemies on the map and without those toggles might make if so you end up way over leveled if you want to max your jobs without maxing your XP, but no with how you can chain battles together in this one (chaining was a thing in the other ones bur was done differently) and how chaining only multiplies the JP earned it actually makes maxing out your jobs without over leveling really easy, right in the very first map there is a spot where you can easily gather up 8 low level enemies to chain in about 1-2 minutes, and doing so if you have the JP UP skills equipped you can go from 0xp level 1 of a job to level 6,8,10,11,12 in 5 fights, meaning between set up and execution you can go from new job to level 12 in under 15 minutes earning very little XP...yes level 15 ends up being the max job level later but for most the game it is 12, it is stupidly easy to max your jobs out without over leveling.Fantastic addition to the Bravely franchise, if you liked the first two games you will like this, if you didn't play the first two games you can still enjoy this game, there is no need to play the first two first, the story is totally stand alone, though you should play the first one because it is a great game, but it is not required to enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't think of a recent Square Enix port to PC lately better than this...  From the smooth gameplay and great graphics on a pc with all the classic RPG elements of chrono trigger, final fantasy, breath of fire, secrets of mana, some octopath, this is a must play RPG on the pc if u like classic RPG games.  Many will say the bosses are hard, but I think it's just right and those who say they are hard have not played older generation rpgs where u just die over and over and need to grind.... It's the challenge and journey of grinding, leveling up and finding loot to get stronger in fights that gives these type of rpgs charm.  Add what I just said to modern graphics, great soundtrack, story, and you have an excellent RPG that's memorable and fun!

name: MONSTER HUNTER RISE
detailed_description: Featured DLC About the Game Rise to the challenge and join the hunt! In Monster Hunter Rise, the latest installment in the award-winning and top-selling Monster Hunter series, you’ll become a hunter, explore brand new maps and use a variety of weapons to take down fearsome monsters as part of an all-new storyline. The PC release also comes packed with a number of additional visual and performance enhancing optimizations. Ferocious monsters with unique ecologies Hunt down a plethora of monsters with distinct behaviors and deadly ferocity. From classic returning monsters to all-new creatures inspired by Japanese folklore, including the flagship wyvern Magnamalo, you’ll need to think on your feet and master their unique tendencies if you hope to reap any of the rewards! Choose your weapon and show your skills Wield 14 different weapon types that offer unique gameplay styles, both up-close and from long range. Charge up and hit hard with the devastating Great Sword; dispatch monsters in style using the elegant Long Sword; become a deadly maelstrom of blades with the speedy Dual Blades; charge forth with the punishing Lance; or take aim from a distance with the Bow and Bowguns. These are just a few of the weapon types available in the game, meaning you’re sure to find the play style that suits you best. Hunt, gather and craft your way to the top of the food chain Each monster you hunt will provide materials that allow you to craft new weapons and armor and upgrade your existing gear. Go back out on the field and hunt even fiercer monsters and earn even better rewards! You can change your weapon at any of the Equipment Boxes any time, so the possibilities are limitless! Hunt solo or team up to take monsters down The Hunter Hub offers multiplayer quests where up to four players can team up to take on targets together. Difficulty scaling ensures that whether you go solo or hit the hunt as a full four-person squad, it’s always a fair fight. Stunning visuals, unlocked framerate and other PC optimizations Enjoy beautiful graphics at up 4K resolution, HDR with support for features including ultrawide monitors and an unlocked frame rate make to make this a truly immersive monster-hunting experience. Hunters will also get immediate access to a number of free title updates that include new monsters, quests, gear and more. Enjoy an exciting new storyline set in Kamura Village This serene locale is inhabited by a colorful cast of villagers who have long lived in fear of the Rampage - a catastrophic event where countless monsters attack the village all at once. 50 years after the last Rampage, you must work together with the villagers to face this trial. Experience new hunting actions with the Wirebug Wirebugs are an integral part of your hunter’s toolkit. The special silk they shoot out can be used to zip up walls and across maps, and can even be used to pull off special attacks unique to each of the 14 weapon types in the game. Buddies are here to help The Palico Felyne friends you already know and love from previous Monster Hunter adventures are joined by the brand new Palamute Canyne companions! Wreak havoc by controlling monsters Control raging monsters using Wyvern Riding and dish out massive damage to your targets! Fend off hordes of monsters in The Rampage Protect Kamura Village from hordes of monsters in an all-new quest type! Prepare for monster hunting on a scale like never before!

_childDocuments_.review: If you have been a monster hunter fan then the game will speak for itself. Playing with a controller is a must although this game is on PC. Compared to MHW, they have each others pros and cons. Pros being that MHR has more fun mechanics with the wirebugs and new moves that really freshen up the combat from MHW although the combat is still fun in worlds. The new features give the game more life and lore to the game when you usually turn off your brain and just hit big lizard most of the time. Cons are that MHW is still visually superior to MHR. But the graphics are okay but nothing too crazy and can seem like a downer since MHW is very beautiful to look at. The music is still top selling point but the extra effects of slashes can really be blinding. With four hunters doing a quest and all of them hacking and slashing can cause a lot of visual clutter where it is super bright and can even cover up the whole monster. So if you are photo sensitive please be careful. But my true rating would be 8.5 out of 10 due to minor gripes.

_childDocuments_.review: MHR's graphic may not superior as MHW, but the gameplay mechanics are better. As someone who started playing MH series from World, I suggested anyone who want to participate in Rise to wait for sale or until Sunbreak released in summer. However, if you're really into Japanese culture and some melodiously OST, just join now!!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Hate to give a negative review on a Monster Hunter game but I have one solid reason to do so. I have played every Monster Hunter game released in the US and this one has a ton of improvements to the basic mechanics of the game. Wirebug is great, new monsters are cool, stances are awesome, and a lot of things are going in the right directions. HOWEVER the endgame is absolute trash.Bruh before the monsters would get steadily harder and get different mechanics, or they would just add more monsters. Its why I have almost 300 hours in every monster hunter. This one I dont due to Anomolies. What they are is the exact same monsters at high level, with like 4 times the health, and red spots on them you have to target so they dont explode and one shot you. Sure you do more damage while hitting the red spots but check it, some weapons just suck at hitting them. With duals you can hit all the legs and chest spots, but some monsters you cant hit the head or tail easily. Greatsword some monsters you cant hit the spots since you have to big of a hitbox and cant be precise enough. There is no good answer for this problem and you have to be able to destroy them all or the monster explodes and kills you. Even setting aside the how annoying it is to hit a red marker on a monster with certain weapons, trying to kill monsters that are essentially super health sponges that explode is just not fun to me. Wirebugs they can keep, i even like the turret/tower defense. It gets bananas in the event quests. _childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Rise is a solid addition to the series - and one of the more friendly games if you're new to the series or the genre. I loved it on the switch enough to buy it again to play with my PC friends. If you like this genre, and want a game that doesn't take itself too seriously, you'll like this game. They took most of the control-improvements from MH:W and spiced things up with new silk-bind moves to add variety and mobility to most of the weapons, although the theme and style definitely lean more toward the older games, which I personally prefer.Three important notes if you're worried about certain negative reviews on steam thus far.1. If you're experiencing crashes, failure to launch, or inexplicable frame-stuttering - UPDATE YOUR GRAPHICS DRIVERS. This resolved some D3D device crash(when launching) for me, and made a massive fps improvement for one of my friends.2. The DLC is entirely optional cosmetics. You can enjoy the game fully without purchasing anything beyond the game itself, and there are plenty of cosmetic options and gestures even without the DLC (although some of the DLC is pretty cool, if a little overpriced).3. The failure to save issue is being actively worked on by the devs. If you're worried, come back in a week or two and I bet they'll have it fixed. For what it's worth of the 6 people I know who got this game, none experienced the issue, so it seems to be at least sort of rare.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Rise gives me mixed feelings. What’s great about MHR is the combat. Having the choice to switch a move set is a perfect way to change the weapon playstyle. The wire bug is another feature that I like too, you can use it to dodge, swing around in the air, use it in a combo, and etc. The wyvern riding is ok. I was never good at mounting or wall bang the monster back in World, so it's a feature that I don't utilize too often. However, I think most people will enjoy this new feature. I also like how weapons and armor look in this game. The colors on them are a lot brighter and look more appealing to the eyes. I think rampage quests are ok, if you can find a full squad. It was confusing at first until I played with a group, observed what they did, and understanding what they were doing, rampage became more manageable. The palamute is a pretty good addition. Having them help you traverse across the map makes gathering and chasing the monster a lot more convenient. However, they are not my favorite when it comes to fighting monsters. I'd stick with my palico!Now onto the things I dislike about Rise. One major thing that MHR lacked is good updates. Back in MHW, small event quests would be released from time to time with decent rewards, but then MHW would release huge event quests with amazing rewards like kulve taroth siege, the witcher collab, arch tempered monsters and the infamous behemoth/extremoth. All of those event quests made MHW way more exciting and gave me more hope for future updates. So far, Rise does not have any good updates that are comparable. There are so many downgrades in Rise, such as the lack of an interactive world, some of the areas are shallow/bland, the soundtrack is weak, the limited players in lobbies, no upgraded houses, can’t catch endemic life, some layered armor are sold and not earned. Most people already know this and it’s been discussed thoroughly, but I will bring it up once again. The endgame is not great and since this game was released in march 2021. I’m surprised they did nothing to improve this, with the time they have until the pc release.In conclusion, should you buy Monster Hunter Rise? Yes, only if you can find it for a cheap price. Since this game is originally from a portable console it feels like the developers did not put enough effort into this game, compared to the last game. Sunbreak is coming out soon, but I am not too optimistic about this dlc. It feels like it’s going to have the same issues as Rise: future updates and longevity. But only time will tell.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing MH since the 3rd gen games. I enjoy this game more than I enjoyed MHW Iceborne. For those new to the series, this is a terrific jumping-on point that has streamlined much of the quirks of MH into a more arcade-y package. Tracking monsters, managing your farm, the annoying fly mechanics form MHW, and gathering are either a one-button deal or removed entirely so that you can focus on the stuff that matters. Many complain that the game is too easy, but most MH games are pretty easy until the G rank (or master rank) expansion so we'll have to wait until Sunbreak releases to really assess this. Regardless, this game is fun. The wirebugs, unlike the clutch claw, actually make the combat more exciting rather than butchering the pace and forcing you to play a certain way. The environments are not as gorgeous or detailed as in MHW, but they are much more spacious which allows more room to fight and accommodates larger monsters like the leviathans which is a huge plus. Overall, this is my favorite version of MH purely due to it being a fun game. It may lack the massive endgame of Iceborne, but its already fun and will only get better with the new content in the summer.I have played this game for about 100 hours on the Switch prior to this review and completed all of the content released before 3.0, which includes things like the rocket dragon. The PC port is incredibly good, just as good as one expects from Capcom at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: so i started with MH world, and then went back to GU and 4U so take this review with a grain of salt but they COMPLETELY BUTCHERED everything i loved about the weapons in this game.i have always used the same 5 weapons throughout the franchise: Charge Blade, Greatsword, Hunting Horn, Insect Glaive, and Gunlance. Almost every single one of these has had the fun sucked out of them.I'll start with CB. first off, compared to world and GU the turning during an AED now is ridiculously sensitive. you can accidentally turn 45 degrees and THEN do the attack. on top of that if you want to do decent DPS with a UED build you just have to spam counter peak performance, because why wouldn't you? its a long guard point that fills your phials that cancels into UED! and if you want to use something else, your only other option is the new bootleg savage axe mode compared to what we had in world. It goes away when you sheathe, and you can refill your phials by attacking because why not. guard pointing normally has no purpose now with the 3 silkbind counters this weapon has, and instead of feeling like a dance this weapon now feels clunkier than greatsword.Speaking of which, the reason for this one isnt as factual as the others. The main problem is this weapon lost its feeling of OOMPH, feeling like you just ABSOLUTELY CAVED THE SKULL IN of some unsuspecting monster on the receiving end of a True Charge Slash. The hitlag is gone, the screen effects have been replaced with lamer ones, and the monsters just dont flinch as much as they used to. Now there is a new benefit for rise GS, that being the new immovable behemoth playstyle with Adamant charged slash and Rage Slash. I would be all over this if it weren't for two things: you can now get stunned when armoring through a move, and 2: rage slash has the same problem as UED on charge blade where the turning sucks.And now hunting horn.My boy...Look how they massacred my boy...This weapon has literally been neutered compared to its 4U and world counterparts. Before it played as a weapon that applied a wide variety of buffs, varying from each individual craftable weapon that applied 3 in a row in one long animation that could be used to do damage. But now? This weapon became so easy there isn't even any risk vs reward anymore. the encore animation is now so short and applies the buffs instantly so EVEN IF you get hit after doing it you still got your buffs off. And it gets worse! one of the switch skills makes it so you dont even need to do the performance to apply buffs, they all just get applied the moment the correct notes are played. the moveset is alright i guess but now the best in slot damage move is a slow hit that does damage. No option for more support, no option for something like the echo attack in world that allowed for new melodies for more buffs, just a straight up attack or a useless cocoon.Insect glaive is simple. It now has no niche. The draw before was incredible mobility allowing you to bob and weave around the monster while still doing damage, on top of the customization of the kinsect. Now every weapon can fly around, and has about the same level of customization.And then there's gunlance. Rise gave the lances the short end of the stick in every way, from DPS to shielding to switch skills. Gunlance is a bit better than lance but it's not by much. The reason why there are problems now is because of 2 main things: shielding now does an UNGODLY amount of chip damage, on top of guard being a level 2 decoration now, and secondly gunlance just got a flat damage nerf that can only be restored with a silkbind move, ground splitter. This attack disguised as a 'buff' just restores the shelling damage back to world level. This lasts for 30 seconds and goes away when you sheathe.So that's really it. The monster roster is really good at least, with sunbreak we're getting astalos, seregios, gore and shagaru magala, all that. The fights themselves are centered around having full spiribird buffs which takes a good 5 minutes before the hunt to get and around using wirebugs, so a lot of pins and stuff. This might be just me but a lot of attacks in this game that are unblockable don't look unblockable at all. In world for example you had unblockable attacks be pins, or huge laser beams, or supernovas. Now some random moves are for no reason. Skills also got a nerf in general, with level 1 decoration slots being next to useless with critical eye, attack boost, guard, etc all becoming level 2, along with some skills such as guard up, critical element, resuscitate, etc all becoming level 3, making it even harder to fit them into a build.There are some things done right however, with being able to join a hunt without the host having to watch the cutscene before you join, and decorations becoming craftable (talismans are RNG now instead) TL;DR: If you want a good time playing Monster Hunter go play world or GU, you will simply be playing a better game.Edit 1 in response to comment: Yes. 4U charge blade was stupidly OP. Yes, it was nerfed in GU and then restored in world. I am aware. This has nothing to do with how unfun and clunky it is in rise. Insect glaive CAN fly more than any other weapon, which is nice but it really has diminishing returns. World insect glaive for example could move around very easily mid fight, but not to the level of rise Insect glaive. However there is a point where being able to fly around BETTER isn't very useful, and rise insect glaive has hit that point. Yes, being forced to choose your decorations for level 2 decoration slots is a good thing, but not at the expense of level 1 decorations being near useless.I want to specifically address something said about hunting horn. "Hunting Horn was crap to play till rise... they simplified the weapon and made it more attractive so I can't seem to understand where is the wrong about that..."Taking away a weapon's depth is only a good thing if it is unnecessarily complicated. Hunting horn in previous games, especially world, very much incentivized careful positioning and learning the timing for your performance during the fight. Rise just completely got rid of it. The weapon, as i said, is now much worse for support due to losing so many of its melodies, meanwhile all it gained in exchange is less complicated gameplay. It's a net loss, in my opinion. Which is what the comment said as well. I personally love the doot stick, which is why seeing it treated the way it was made me leave this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Monster Hunter since Freedom Unite, that's 14 years of Monster Hunter, and I can say this game is definitively the best MH game in my opinion.Monster Hunter World had some serious problems that made me still feel that MH4U was still better, however Rise has RISEn to the occasion, implemented huge QoL changes, brought back the return of older and cooler armor sets, has a huge list of monsters, added a riding companion, removed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ investigations to find your monster, removed the nightmare RNG of decorations in MH World and simply allows you to create them, added new cool abilities for every weapon, simplified the story, and made cutscenes skippable.However, it's still a little lacking in the armor models department. They nerfed lance (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ WHY? Lance was never all that good in the first place, it finally stopped being trash tier and became decent in World. Now it's back to trash tier), and while I personally think this game looks way better than MH World, with it's washed out colors and eye-abusive overuse of bloom, a few people have complained about the low resolution textures. I'd also like to see armor sets be a little bit more complex in how they're built for skills. Rampage is a great concept for a game type, but was executed so sloppily it's only sometimes fun.Overall, none of the negatives prevent this from being the best MH game so far, and a fantastic entry game for anyone interested in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: As a MH player who was introduced to World, and played through Iceborne and picked up Rise. I would most definitely recommend this game to new hunters of the series and still past hunters but I think they won't like it as much as old games if you loved those ones. Don't get me wrong when it came out on PC it felt very different to World and so some adapting was in order. I quickly grew to really liking it getting over 100 hours, but fell off when I got to just before of the base endgame content. So here's my pros and cons of base rise. Pro's: - New uniquely styled monsters- New Wirebug and Switch Skills Mechanics- Very stylistic approach to (BANGER) OST and cutscenes which was very nice to see- Lush map environments- Quest management, I love the ticks especially for event quests the amount of times in world I couldn't remember if I had done something omg- Likeable characters and a good MH story of protecting your village as the best hunter aroundCon's:- Lengthy tutorial mostly text based, which led to confusion of certain mechanics and what you're actually capable of depending how much attention you pay (I sped through it on stream and it still took me 2 hours until I finished my first actual large monster hunt, as someone who plays a decent amount of games I can't imagine how long it takes for casuals, definitely a single player experience at first)- Confusion between Village and Hub quests (could've been from lacking attention in a tutorial XD)- Confusion about intricacies for Rampage quests and how they tie into the games content overall (I never figured out how apex's even worked or why to hunt them outside of event quests)- Secret or intricate mechanics I would never have known about without a guide- The need for guides to best optimise yourself from spiribird collection to talismans etc.I think I didn't reach HR100 or maybe even 50 because I wasn't anywhere near as motivated to play the game as I am now with Sunbreak and SB is the main reason my play time is what it is now. I still really enjoyed the game but there was so many elements to it I just got lost in it all I think but that was over a year ago so it's hard to remember. So time for the Pro's and Con's for that.Pro's:- Amazing additions to Switch Skill mechanics including the Swap Scroll mechanic- Cool Dango skill levelling (Hopping Skewers) and usual orders now being more prevalent and specialise with different loadouts- Fantastic additions to the monster roster- Great new vibrant maps- Centralised top tier Hub with banger music- Of course another BANGER OST- FREE TITLE UPDATES GO HARD, I mean who doesn't want new monsters/content, etc.- Semi-simple endgame farming just need to learn how to best optimise yourself- The grind never stops (I love it at times and other times I get exhausted)- Way more motivating to play the game and help HR players, never have I been so social in a game community and found a community/place to I treasure in the gameCon's:- The grind never stops (like I mentioned even once your done with endgame like augmenting or reaching max AR there's still so much you can do from learning weapons, to fashion, to building new or unique sets or meta ones so this point will vary from player to player I mostly few it as a pro just at times I do get exhausted from it all having 100% the game and on my way to reaching MR999)- Speaking of grind reaching max AR took a decent amount of time for me even once getting really good investigations I'd recommend finding people of higher AR willing to help you out and give you investigations at the highest level you can accept (AR186 can do AR190)- Past con's such as spiribirds don't affect me so much anymore as Spiribird Call makes up for it- Now the main issue I see besides grinding with the playerbase is the complaint of the power creep and that's purely because of the type of game Sunbreak is, it's taking Rise and building on it for the target audience of past but mainly present day hunters either coming from World or being introduced to Rise. But the scaling of monsters like anomalies and the recent risen elder dragons dealing one shots to counteract why we're so powerful leaves a sour taste in many hunters mouths but personally, I don't find it an issue this is just a "con" I would like to address from my perspective. From my perspective it takes skill, game knowledge, and mental/ in game capacity to be able to fit so many skills on a build. you can search up a guide anyways if this isn't your forte. That's only half the battle for myself as I know it takes my skill as a hunter to then hunt those monsters without getting destroyed, there's only 2 or so moves I've not been able to survive in a game where you can fully upgrade defence, add on defence skills or eat for dango defender, stockpile buffs easily and keep those buffs up throughout the duration of a hunt, have followers alongside you giving buffs and healing, and having a weapon with a counter or ability to i-frame, dodge or block an attack it purely comes down to learning the fight and so I don't have an issue with it because if they didn't give us stronger abilities and harder challenges it wouldn't feel like we're making much progress or that we're not getting stronger alongside the new challenges presented to us.Long rant over, thank you for reading if you get this far, if you're thinking of buying the game I'd recommend getting SB once you play through the game and think you're going to invest more time into it past the story, as its a huge amount content added on and QOL improvements as well. Happy hunting!! <3

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I finished what I believe is the meat of the game (unlocked HR rank, for those curious), it's a good time to write some thoughts.Monster Hunter: Rise is a port of a Switch game, and unfortunately it shows. Graphics are a step down from World, gameplay is faster, the maps are smaller and the monsters are easier. The wirebug, while admittedly fun, breaks the balance of the game to a tremendous degree, and I wish it wasn't introduced. I miss actually tracking monsters (they now show up instantly on the map, no investigation required). The level of content is sorely lacking compared to base MH:W (right before Iceborne release, at least; I don't know how barren MH:W was on launch).With that out of the way, MH:R is still quite a fun game, definitely worth trying for MH fans and is perhaps a better intro to the series than MH:W for newbies to the franchise. Co-op is a lot more approachable too than MH:W's convoluted multiplayer system, and I loved most of the new monsters. It's also more mobile than ever, if that's your thing (not mine exactly, but I imagine for a lot of you that's a plus).While I don't think I'll get nearly as into Rise as I did World, I'll enjoy it while it's here. I absolutely don't regret buying it, and I'll get the expansion when it comes out later this year. I just hope the next game follows World more closely in scope and challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: 9/10 a great update to the franchise, with some frustrating class nerfs and porting issues.So, I played MHW and frankly, I hated it. Most of that was my choice of weapon (insect glaive), but a lot of it was also that it was my first MH game and I kept getting really frustrated with aspects of the game-on the gameplay side, the size of the map and the monster's habit of constantly roaring and running made hunting feel like being trolled. On the story side, it was extremely frustrating how utterly inept at storybuilding they seemed to be. It was like they pretended to have a story, to have a reason to give a ♥♥♥♥, but in reality? Nope.MHR has fixed a lot of those issues for me. I went with HBG this time, and found it much more to my liking, so yay. The maps are smaller, but still large enough you can get some fun out of exploring them. They've added some collectables to the maps, and the addition of endemic life is a real boost. The big thing is the Palamute. It's awesome. You can get to monsters faster (you also don't have to freaking track them anymore, so thank hell for that), and when they run you can chase them down much easier. The addition of Wyvern Riding and silkbind attacks are fun as hell. On the story side, there is less story, but it's actually competently done, which really reduces my irritation. It's very bare bones, but at least now when they have a "oh dear, character x is in trouble!" moment, that character 1. HAS A NAME, and 2. is someone i've had at least some interaction with and therefore give some small ♥♥♥♥ about. If you're not that into your MH games having story, don't worry- I've just hit high rank, and outside of the little "Monster Introduction" cutscenes (which have some TRULY terrible poetry voiceovers), there's been a grand total of maybe 4 or 5 cutscenes, none of them longer then 3 minutes. You're here to kill monsters, not watch a movie.Now, that being said they have made quite a few changes to the classes. If you're a lance main, they done did you guys dirty. Quite a few of the monsters have slightly different movesets and behaviors as well, so if you're a long-time fan of the series don't necessarily walk into fights thinking you know everything, which for some of you might be a real positive. If I had to gripe, I'd say that this game was very clearly NOT designed for PC. I use an MMO mouse, and rebinding MB4 and MB5 took a bit, but more importantly this game has problems with lag spikes (not super often), and some dropped inputs even on high framerates. Also, I would have liked the maps to be a bit bigger- I know they were working with Switch limitations, but it doesn't take very long to have unlocked and fully explored all the maps. There might be additional maps unlocked the further you go into HR, but so far no sign of anything. Personally, I really like what they've done with this game, and hope that they keep a lot of these QoL changes going forward!

_childDocuments_.review: I will assume that if you are looking at Rise that your introduction to MH was MHW, and your are now formally addicted to MH and wanted to check out this MH Rise game to try and fill your fix, but if you are looking at this game as your introduction MH that is also good. Now for my actual review of the game. MH Rise and very fun and addicting game, and has some of the fastest game play in MH (Not THE fastest, just one of the fastest), and is really challenging to a degree and can really give you a rush. Rise itself is essential MH but boss rush addition as there is not much else to do in this game besides grind to get better gear, and try to get better at fighting the monsters, which is my biggest flaw with this game, but despite this I still love MH Rise for what it is. Now to link back to my initial weird start to this review, if you are retiring player from World or MH in general, be warned this game does not provide much beyond the fights ( which some in the community would like to argue that MH has always been a boss rush series, I do not see it this way, if you want to play it for the fights then fine, but I do not think that is all MH has to be or should be.) so if you are in MH for the challenge and the fight, boss, etc then play MH Rise, if not still give a try as it is a really fun game, but if still no go try playing some of the older games. Now if you are completely new to MH as series a lot of the for mentioned stuff does still apply in some capacity, if you have already bought game have fun and go at your own pace (this goes for anyone with this game and just life in general.), but do not think that all MH is boss rushes, unless that all you want it to be. After to finish Rise or get through to a point where you are happy go play MHW which in my opinion is better than Rise in certain aspects, and such, environment building, ecology, monster iteration, and go play older MH games too they are really cool, but if you are new and have not bought Rise yet, I think you should think about getting World first as I feel it a better introduction to new plays of Mh an then go play Rise or the older games. If not and you really want to play Rise first go ahead it is still an amazing game and it really beginner friendly just like World, so don't worry to much but still and play World and other MH game when you get a chance. I hope clunky weird review helped and some have the day, and life that you deserve.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Rise is the most current Monster Hunter game released to date.  The combat is fluid and faster paced than older editions of the long running franchise. _childDocuments_.review: Hello. I dont have many hours in the game yet, I havent reached Sunbreak yet. I have 600ish hours in World though. I havent played any of the MH games before World. All i can say is, its a good game, i would recomend it but it just falls short. World is so much better, if world is 10/10 this is a 7.5/10.. im kinda disapointed. I mean its a good game but, I did expect more for some reason. I dont even care for the DLC drama and stuff, who cares about layered ♥♥♥♥ when the weapon designs are good already? The armor aswell. I like the monster designs too... Especially the bubble doggo so far, love it.But i have a few things i have to rage on not gonna lie. I play LS mostly and I see people saying "rise is so much more tight on controls"... like, are we playing the same game? Just an example, LS iai sheathe or whatever its called, is so slow compared to World... not the sheathe itself but the way it flows... after you full spirit combo in World and u put in the command to sheathe, it does it INSTANTLY.... in Rise, after the spirit combo, you like need to wait for half a sec before you input the command for sheate otherwise it just ignores you... I dont know man, doesnt feel very good to me. Very weird/bad flow comparably. I also see people saying "hitboxes are fixed" like really? Hitboxes in Rise are jank AF. They are all over the place... sometimes something connects when it shouldnt, sometimes the other way arround. World seemed so much better on that. Also capcom FK u for ruining SnS where you cant adjust directions after each attack, you ruined it for me.In World, when you helm splitter and ARE IN THE AIR, if the boss is doing something on the GROUND like swiping or spinning horizontally, IT DOESNT HIT YOU. In Rise for some retarded reason, when you helm splitter and ARE IN THE AIR if the boss ON THE GROUND farts, you get hit and interrupted, which is the most stupid thing they could come up with because it doesnt make any sense... Also it feels like dodge iframes are weird or non existant. Like regular dodge, not superman dive/foresight slash. And yes i know that you cant iframe thru some attacks, but just the breaths and swipes, which in world seemed so seamless and sensible to dodge, in Rise seems way off on timing and hitboxes. And yes, i know evade window exists, but im talking about just the base dodge. And yes, i know the evade frames and stuff are basically the same as in World, but that just proves my point in the worse character controlls. If i can dodge something consistently in World RN with no problems, i cant dodge it in Rise, its not a skill issue, but im sure someone would have something to say on my non empirical evidence xD. It just feels so much more different and well, worse.And i see alot of people saying "you get used to it" or, "youll get better after getting used to it" which is stupid. Why did capcom change so much stuff from world, when it worked just fine? And im not talking about wirebugs (which i like) or monster vareity or movesets or UI or DLC moneygrab or whatever. Im talking about the way your character controls, moves, default keybind setup, the unnecesary 2 ♥♥♥♥ scrollable quick inventories, that coulve just been 1... Why reinvent the wheel when a round one works ya know? Im no game dev, or marketing guy or whatever. Just a sweatlord living in my moms basement, but im confident that if they would take what World was, toned down the graphics to better fit Switch, added wirebugs, doggos and more monsters, they woulve had a better game, with less complaints. All that said, i like the game and would recommend it to everyone, especially if you didnt play World, but if you are picking between Rise/Sunbreak or World/Iceborne, i would go with the latter. Peace.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the overall experience, however if you want to max out your health/get bonus armor/attack/stamina during hunt, you need to collect the spiribirds. Also in base Rise there are Rampages, which appear a few times in the story. Think of it like Monster Hunter Tower Defense. However it would be much easier if I had anyone to play with, instead I soloed whole base game and Sunbreak story. After 200+ hours, I have only one useful talisman with slots. In the Sunbreak expansion I got maybe a few iffy talisamans, rest was basically useless.I played mostly with long sword, great sword, and sometimes with other weapons. Basically every weapon type plays differently, has unique attacks and switch skills. If you are bored looking at the same armor all the time, there is a layered armor system, so you can wear one set or armor, and see another. Wirebugs are a nice addition to the game, as well as some palico variety and addition of palamutes. In Sunbreak palamutes got some nice bonuses, like few extra item slots, and sniff'em which allows to easily mark different spots on the map. Also for palicoes, there are unlockable options for swapping support skills and skills like status up, element up, given you have at least one buddy with the skill unlocked. Monsters have many different attacks, some of them can catch you offguard. They get new attacks after unlocking High rank and Master rank versions.Have a nice day.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long standing fan of the Monster Hunter series so obviously, I may not be the best to tell you about the cons of the general concept.This specific addition to the franchise pros and cons according to me are as follow:Cons:- Graphics quality is lower than in  MH: World. To be considered is that this iteration originated from the Switch platform, which offers limited performances in that regards.- While some menus and interfaces have been streamlined/simplified, it does mean that you have less agency in how you, the player, can customize your experience (again mostly when compared to MH: World's interface) Ex: how one can move around items in the item bar and save presets of their fully customized item layouts.- The music is very good, but a lack of diversity without paying for extra downloadable content means the available tracks get repetitive rather quickly.Pros:- This game feels like a piece of art, the artistic work put into this game is just phenomenal.- You will run into monsters that you may be familliar with from other Monster hunter games and their adaptation is rather faithful (albeit, as an experience hunter you'll maybe find Low-rank to be rather... easy when compared to what you remember from other games.)- The newest monsters, in most regards, offer a genuine new experience based on this game's specific gimmick (wirebugs).- This iteration offers a freedom of movements never experience in a M.H, game before and it will most likely grow on you as it was well implemented imho. Overall, it feels much more fluid than what we've seen in MH MH: world.- This game feels like a proper continuation of most successful mechanics and QoL improvements we've seen in MH: World and it adds some of its own, meaning this game feels far less "niche" or "tedious" than some older iterations.- This game is definitely a good entry point for any new comers to the franchise, it is arguably one of the most forgiving entry in lower-rank, such as MH: world was, except this game has far less annoying NPCs and tutorials (still many pop-us sent your way however, be advised of the reading you may have to do)

_childDocuments_.review: It's funny seeing people complain about difficulty in objectively the easiest Monster Hunter game in the series. I'm sitting around HR 65 at the time of writing this and haven't fainted a single time. In fact, my problem with this game is that it's way too easy and that's mostly due to the utility of the wirebugs. Monsters simply haven't been given enough counters or damage to deal with the new wirefall mechanic. Instead of being properly punished for making a mistake, I can immediately propel myself out of range and heal; or right into the monster to take advantage of the opening that should have only been there if I dodged the attack. Sure, the new skills are fun and movement has never been so fast and fluid. But I'm not satisfied when there's so little to overcome. The only wall I came across was at HR 50 because the Allmother gets a bit ridiculous towards the end of the battle, that's it. Additionally, instead of giving us an endgame gimmick like randomized quests and tempered monsters, there is practically nothing to do. I believe the intent here was to make sure you buy the expansion, this game cannot stand on its own like World, Generations, and 4 could. And don't get me started on rampages, they are impossible to fail, repetitive, and boring. The hub was butchered again too, there is no incentive for camaraderie, just respond to an SOS or go solo.

_childDocuments_.review: Reverting my review to a positive review now that the Steam Deck launch issues have been cleared up.Rise is a great game, a faster paced and more arcade-like alternative to Monster Hunter World. Where World's approach is that of a methodical hunter, stalking the monster, learning it's habits and weaknesses before ultimately mastering it, Rise skips a lot of that, and focuses on the fights themselves.The addition of the wirebugs makes for hectic combat, with monster speeds amped up to match the hunter's newfound agility.My only complaint would be the spiritbirds - meant to simulate the "prep" phase of a hunt without requiring much in the way of thought, they eventually turn into a bit of a slog, a mandatory 2 minute phase of every hunt that's always the same.Otherwise, a very strong entry in the series, and a great complimentary game to it's sibling of the fifth generation.

_childDocuments_.review: Starting off: this is a good game. I've played every Monster Hunter game I have a console for, so some could say I'm a veteran, and I still enjoy this game. There are, however, some things to note. First off, (and yes, I know this is controversial, but hear me out) this game is quite a bit easier than every other monster hunter game I've played (MHWorld, MHG, MH4U, MH3U, MHS, MHS2). The main reason for this, I think, is the wirebug mechanic, which I personally am not a huge fan of. One of the things I've always loved about Monster Hunter is that no matter what you're fighting, from a blue velociraptor to a T-rex with a flaming sword tale, or from a fire spitting chicken to a dragon prophesied to destroy the world, you were just a person. There weren't many things you could do that could be seen as "superhuman". It was just you, your own skill, some items, and your weapons and armor forged from past victories. In MHRise, however, you're basically dragon-slaying spider-man. I think that is what makes this game so much easier than the rest, and, honestly, it takes away from the game big-time. If this is your first monster hunter game, great. Monster hunter has every bit of potential to be just as, if not sometimes harder than, Dark Souls (even in this game, near the end), so this is a good beginner level MH game. All things considered, the game is good. It's simply not the monster hunter many have grown to love. My rating: 7.5/10Monster Hunter Rise: Sunbreak review:Ok, now that Sunbreak has come out, some things have changed. Starting off; this game just got a whole lot harder, as I kinda figured it would. Before I get to that, though, lets talk content. MHRise: Sunbreak has added a pretty good amount of content, as it should for a 40$ expansion. However, I just reached Mr4 and have only seen around 5 new monsters, and I think only one of them wasn't leaked beforehand. Therefore, it seems that most of the new content is in the gameplay itself. There is a new kind of quest, called follower quests, where you can bring certain characters with you on hunts, such as Hinoa and Minoto. There have also been a lot of additions to, well, just about everything. There is even a new option when picking pre-hunt dango that levels up (or down) the food skills according to a certain system. All in all, there is a load of cool new content to explore, but unless it picks up a lot near the end, there isn't much in the way of new fights to use it in. Now, back to the difficulty. In MH:World, the monsters did change a bit from Hr to Mr (High rank to Master rank), but not so much that the fight is all but completely different. In Sunbreak, however, that isn't the case. Many of the monsters got several new, and arguably crazy, moves and behavioral patterns. Now, while this is great, Capcom did go overboard on some things, as they usually do. Certain things, such as some of the new moves simply being to strong, are just over-the-top. The thing I noticed the most, however, were the shady things the monsters are able to do. Now, these things have been in every monster hunter game I've played, but I don't think I've ever seen it ramped up this much before. Most of these things are in the AI, while some are in the monster itself. Some of the more notable ones are: 1) the monster knows when you're vulnerable (sharpening, healing, stunned, etc.), and almost always starts targeting you, 2) the monster knows exactly where you'll be and exactly when you'll be there and fires projectiles right there. this happens when sprinting straight or if you dodge before the projectile is actually moving through the air. And 3) The monster can sometimes (I haven't quite decided how frequent it is) start or stop certain animations to surprise you or deny you an opportunity to heal or attack. This happens in ways like the monster hitting you away or running to use a tired animation, keeping you from capitalizing on it, or the wind-ups and and ends of attack animations just being cut off. Again, this stuff always happened, but it's become much worse in Mr. All of this comes together to make the game a lot harder, but in several cases, not a good way. Personally, I hate cheating AI, and that's being polite. I would, however prefer it was to hard than to easy, 'cause then what's the point? The real problem, I think, is that Capcom just can't stop themselves, realize when they're starting to go to far, and reign themselves in. The perfect example of this is Alatreon in MHWorld: Iceborne. This fight would have been amazing if they had realized that a move that not only wipes your entire team, but is also incredibly difficult to stop, is in fact a bad idea. They just do what they want, call it good, and sell it. And often times they don't listen to their community, either. The defender armor/weapons, for example. These are meant to help new players start the game (which ultimately just takes away from the game, really), but in doing so, these new players are completely unprepared for the 0 to 1000 difficulty spike when the defender gear becomes obsolete. They made this mistake in MHWorld: Iceborne, everyone hated it, and now they've done it again.Ok, sorry about that, I kinda went on a rant there. Now, I know I made some strong arguments there, but don't let that scare you away just yet. Ultimately, Sunbreak is really good, and I am enjoying it, personally. Sunbreak is a good expansion with  a lot of cool bells and whistles, just not much to use them on in the first few portions of the game, at least. This would normally be fine, but with a price tag of 2/3 the price of the main game, it is a little disappointing. The price of 40 USD added to the main games price of 60 USD brings the total to 100 USD, which is not a small sum for most people. I have yet to reach the end-game, so the monster-content problems may very well change, but you can't be certain. There will, however, be new content added in future updates, so that's something. I think the primary issues are 1) the lack of new monsters (again, I have to stress that I could be wrong as I haven't reached the end yet), and 2) the aimbot-level AI. All things considered, Sunbreak is good, but i would wait for a sale. Some of the extra monsters might have been added by then (if no already, if you're reading this in the future), and you'll save yourself from what some may call overpricing. My rating for Monster Hunter Rise: Sunbreak: 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the worst, absolute worst, monster hunter games I've ever played.Worse than Freedom Unite, worse than Portable 3rd.This is also coming from someone who has been playing Monster Hunter games since 2013.If you're coming into this game expecting it to be as fluid as the controls for World? You're sorely mistaken.If you're coming into this game expecting it to have the keyboard and mouse settings to be easy and without breaking your wrist? You're sorely mistaken.KEYBINDS. Can't change them. You're stuck with what the developers have as presets and lets be honest--Capcom doesn't know damn about what keyboard/mouse users want for their control schemes. Buttons everywhere. Secondary mouse buttons that require you to be using a "Pro Gamer" Mouse with so many extra buttons just to be able to do all of the extra crap they require you to do.In World, you could pull open the aim option for the Clutch Claw with the V or CTRL buttons, and then launch your clutch claw almost immediately afterwards by clicking the left mouse button.In Rise you have to use the tiny buttons on the side of your mouse, and even then, its finicky and doesn't like to work. If you're using a melee weapon? Its fine. V and then mouse click. If you're using a ranged weapon? HAHA good luck trying to find out which stupid button does that.In summary: They designed this game to be played on nothing besides a controller. Not using a controller? Good friggin' luck playing this game properly.Next, the combos: The combos in World were fluid, easy to use, easy to remember, and weren't complicated. In this game its like you have to do pre-combos to get to the combos you want, and you can't skip the pre-combos like you can in World. A good example being the sword and shield: In World, you can hit both left and right mouse buttons twice to get the launching combo. In Rise, you can't just do that--there's additional steps to build up to that combo. Which makes it more difficult to pull off.The artificial difficulty in using your combos makes me think the developers were trying to turn this into a fighting game rather than a monster hunting game--just... why? World's controls were fine. Why did you have to try and change them?Next is the 'deluxe' armors/weapons you get to help you along on your journey. Summarized? They're trash. Sure they're stronger than what you can naturally get in-game but the damage they deal is so pitiful that its a far cry from the ones you get in World. I can use both weapons from both World and Rise; and hunts end 3x faster in World than Rise.And now here we go with monsters--monsters in this game have had their defenses and health upped up from previous games. And monsters were 'changed' as well. Normally, you'd consider Arzuros a beginner-tier monster with easy-to-identify patterns and slow movements. Not in this game, he's a 2-Star Quest monster in the Village, and he can easily kick your butt if you aren't paying attention. Even -with- the upped up gear from the deluxe edition.The Wire Bug mechanic. Just bad. Plain bad. Imagine Monster Hunter with Switch Skills that are horrible to aim with, as you can't see where you're going since I can't find the button to aim with, and you usually miss with them even so, and even when you land with a 'Switch' skill it deals such pitiful damage that its only really useful for making monsters 'wyvern ridable' which is not mounting. You just jump on the monster, ride them around, smash them into other monsters or walls, 'dodge' back onto them, and repeat.Boring, dull, this isn't mounting, this is pseudo-riding them as a controllable mount. Its cool in practice, but just sheer trash in execution for me.In summary, they tried too many new things with Rise and Sunbreak and honestly? I consider this game a write-off. Not worth the price for either games, even during a sale. The games could be on sale for 90% off and I'd still pass on it.I couldn't even get through Rise to get TO Sunbreak because of how jank it is and how often it just ticked me the hell off with its horrid controls.EDIT: I forgot to add a few things.The food. The food in this game is disgusting to look at and not at all appetizing. All you get is forms of Dango, which is some kind of weird pasty ball thing covered in melted glazes of some variety that are colored differently. It looks awful. I'm not sure if this is some kind of cultural amazement over in Japan, but I always remembered looking at the food in Monster Hunter games and going "That food looks soooo good" and it'd make me hungry looking at it. Dango just makes me feel reviled at the sight of it so I skip every cutscene involved with it. Sorry if the developers spent ages on them, but they're just god-awful to me.The Story and NPCs.The NPCs are bland. Nothing about any of them stands out to me--they follow a lot of cliche anime tropes with characters just yelling at a wall because they're too 'weak' and then have that inner spark suddenly that makes them go 'I can do this because I have family and friends at my side!' and its so cringe-worthy to watch.The story itself was not interesting at all to me. I won't go into detail to avoid spoilers, but the end-game bosses for Rise were just... unimpressive. And confusing.The "Apex" monsters. These aren't Apex Monsters. The only monsters worthy of being called Apexes should be the ones from MH4U, these are basically just Tempered/Arch-Tempered monsters because they act fundamentally the same with near-one shot abilities if you get hit at all.Rampages!What's a Rampage? Tower Defense. That's it. All it is. You fight a bunch of monsters with greatly decreased damage and health that come at you in massive waves, using defenses and side paths through your base and you gotta beat them before they shatter down your defenses and auto-fail the mission for you even if you have faints left.They break up the gameplay of this game, and I'm glad they're not required beyond a few single-player story missions. Its an extremely boring mode for the game and one of the absolute -worst- ideas Capcom ever conceived for this game. Its so bad I'd say that I'd rather fight a Rajang than deal with a Rampage, and I hate Rajang.Bad in concept. Bad in execution. Just bad overall. They'd do better with coming up with a new system and just removing Rampages from the game entirely.

_childDocuments_.review: With the release of Sunbreak I have decided to revisit my review of Monster Hunter RISE. I still consider the game to be one of my favorite games overall. I was formally introduced to the Monsterhunter series throughout Monster Hunter World, although I had before this seen some videos of earlier games. I was introduced to the game with the same friend group I played this game with. The game offers exciting monsters to fight, acting as a boss battle simulator of sorts. The combat is where the game shines, offering a very satisfying experience and allowing you to feel like you're fighting an epic monster. There are a multitude of weapon types to choose from, offering a wide variety of play styles. RISE introduces Silkbind Attacks, acting as a sort of super moves for each weapon. In addition RISE has added the Switch Skills that allows additional customisation of one's playstyle.RISE has for better or worse simplified the downtime between the action. In Monster Hunter World you had to track down the monster through following tracks. While this could be seen as a bit tedious to have to first find the target, removing it also somewhat reduces the fantasy of an expert hunter tracking their prey. A staple of the Monster Hunter franchise is gathering resources during hunts such as herbs for crafting potions and ores for crafting weapons of armor. This process has been simplified, however this change can only be seen as a positive. One of the best changes in RISE has to be the Wirebugs. These insects are what allows for the use of the Silkbind Attacks, but also a form of grappling hook that can pull you up in the air. Chaining these together allows for impressive airtime and fast traversal from location to location. You can also use these to pull yourself away when you get knocked into the air by a monster, however you must be aware that this loses you invincibility frames you get from being knocked down, so you must make sure not to pull yourself back into an attack by the monster as this may result in your death. The wirebugs act on a cooldown and should be treated as a resource that can be spended on the valuable wirebugskills or use them to break your fall. You have a set number of bugs (that can only temporarily be increased) making maging your bugs important, since certain attacks have a followup if you don't wirebug.Monster Hunter RISE is definitely one of my favorite games, however I am still on the fence if I like it more than Monster Hunter WORLD (the best reference point I have for a Monster Hunter Game). While the combat is enhanced by the Switch Skills and Wirebugs the fights feel… short. The game is clearly easier than WORLD. The game may be more beginner friendly, but no monster has really served as a roadblock to get stuck on. Most quests have only taken one to two attempts. It's not that I like to fail, however a monster that kicks your ass feels more intimidating and feels much more satisfying to beat. Another problem the base game has is that some content is locked behind hunter rank. Your hunter rank is increased by hunting monsters. My friends and I played the game tired long before we had all the monsters unlocked, however this led me to try out Join Request. It is actually really fun to play with randoms. I had dabbled a little in SOS hunting in WORLD but not to the extent I did in RISE. This ended up being the way I completed all quests in the game. But this brings us to the problem at hand. To complete all quests and side quests available still didn't bring me to the required hunter rank to unlock the last missions. I had to replay way too many quests to unlock all the quests. It was fine but this can definitely lead to burnout, especially for players who have not already set their mind to complete every optional quests.Now for the DLC. SUNBREAK in addition to the new story introduces a new level of difficulty. All monsters in this difficulty have some new moves and some old moves have been altered. Most monsters are much more satisfying to fight. In addition there are a couple of new monsters, some of which may be my new favorite fights in the game. However the progression is a bit weird, because in the beginning there are barely any new monsters. But unlocking new missions takes only a few hunts to progress anyway. It's only later in the DLC that the new fights occur. I get that this is because most new monsters are relatively strong, however this makes the beginning of the DLC not feel as exciting as it basically becomes a repeat of the base game. _childDocuments_.review: Undoubtedly one of the worst installments in the franchise to date. There are some mechanics in here from the outside looking in that seems fun and interesting like the verticality of maps being added with the wall running and wire bugs, or perhaps the silkbind moves that add additional strategy and gameplay elements to each weapon archetype. HOWEVER, almost ALL of these ideas are HORRIBLY implemented and hinder the gameplay rather than build onto it. The verticality is the biggest unnecessary addition to this franchise I've seen in a long time alongside when swimming was implemented in Tri (which I didn't mind personally, but I totally understand the hate for it). You will accidentally run up walls mid combat with wire bugs, you will try to implement a wire bug attack from mid air into the mix of a combo, and you will miss 70% of the time because the monster are not adapted with the wire bug mechanic in mind. I feel as though none of the monsters outside of the new additional monsters were reworked to allow wirebug implementation. It is slow. It is clunky. Monsters from previous iterations will destroy you if you rely on the wirebug, which is sad because it is the staple mechanic in this game. Nargacuga, Rathalos, and Barioth are prime examples for monsters that were not adapted to wirebug gameplay. Monster Hunter hitboxes are notorious throughout the series for being janky and unforgiving. This game absolutely takes this to the next level. You'd honestly have to experience it yourself if you have a chance to play the game. Explaining this does no good to try and convey how big of a fault this game has with hitboxes. The locales are very vast and large which isn't a bad thing, but with the added vertical element to every map as well as the incredibly convoluted map itself, there is too much of an opportunity to get lost on all the maps. It will be frustrating until you unlock the fast travel camps, and ever then this problem may still persist. There are plus sides to this game. The new monsters are very exciting and all have interesting and unique designs and move sets. I'm a fan of the Magnamalo and Rakna-Kadaki. The locales look great and all have a unique feel. The addition of the Palamute is a welcome change as well. I want this game to do well and I want to enjoy it as much as previous games, but Rise just doesn't do it for me and I cannot recommend it.Play World if you haven't and are new to this franchise. It is superior in every sense.

_childDocuments_.review: To preface this review, I've been playing Monster Hunter since 3U, so I'm a bit of a veteran that played the older style. That said, here's what I got:Pros:+MHW style of weapons with a few positive changes to a few of the weapons+MHW style of item usage - i.e. glug potions and eat meat while jogging, etc+New mechanic of Wirebugs is great for both movement and weapon skills+Wirebug skills for weapons bring back some of the fantastic Hunter Arts that MHGen had+Weapons also have "Switch Skills", which lets you replace a certain attack a weapon has with an alternative. This gives you tons of ways just to play a single weapon. The switch skills can range from changing the wirebug skills to just any of the regular attacks. Each weapon has 3 set switch skills in total.+Nice variety of monsters that doesn't make you feel like you're fighting 100 clones of the same monster with a different skin plastered on+Interesting new areas with a couple massively remade old areas that would give MHTri veterans a nice nostalgia trip+A huge variety of endemic life called "hunting helpers" that you can collect in a mission to assist with a hunt+Can now inflict elemental blights on monsters (-but not with elemental weapons), giving new status effects you can take advantage of+Companions: 1)Can recruit many cats of different types with random skills to try to get a cat with the perfect build, and 2) DOGS: They assist with attacking, using equipable tools to deal damage or support you, and YOU CAN RIDE THEM FOR FASTER MOVEMENT.+Unlike World, you can do multiplayer quests without having to wait for someone to see all the cutscenes, easy to just jump right in with the squad+Interesting story, but not as cutscene heavy as WorldCons:-Single player campaign is a separate mode from the multiplayer, but it only covers low rank and the story from it LEADS into the high rank multiplayer content. -Multiplayer content does not scale depending on the number of hunters, so if you try to solo it, the monsters are HP sponges-No sliding attacks or much useful terrain.-Can't choose an option to sell all money items for SOME reason, even though that mechanic was in World!-No option to just upgrade currently equipped armor, which is WEIRD, since that was ALSO in World!-Still no return of prowler :(Neutrals:>Tower-defense-like missions called Rampages. They are necessary and feel VERY different from the usual game, but they don't take up much of the game.>Endemic Life called Spiribirds are scattered around each map to give a buff for the mission to HP, Stamina, Attack, and Defense. While nice, the content seems to be built with them in mind and, unless you're really good, skipping them may cause you to faint pretty easily (as I've seen with the many randoms that neglected them)>Hunter connect is a nice way to easily join up with a usual group, but you have to uncheck "automatically send invitations" when you create it because you can't change it after it's created, and this makes you get TONS of hunter connect invitations from people who neglect to do this.>No mantles, which many of them are replaced with various hunting helpers and wirebug uses, but not all of them.Overall, I've enjoyed the game. It's best if you can have at least 1 friend to play with regularly if you're both decent at the game. Even better if you have 2-3 others to make a more complete squad.

_childDocuments_.review: I played rise for about 106 hours on pc, and probably about 40 hours on Nintendo Switch.I played the expansion (Sunbreak) for about half of those 106.Rise is a pretty good MH game.  It has taken criticism and maybe it's all true, but it's still really fun anyway.  If you already like MH or want to get into MH for the first time, it's good.Rise has flat simple maps compared to the layered maps of world.  Having played at least 100 hours of both, I like flat because, after 100 hours of chutes and ladders, the layers just become a nuicense.Rise has less "hunting" and more "fighting".  You always know where the monster is.  Maybe this is good, and maybe this is bad, or maybe it's a bit of both.  I feel like it's sort of both, because hunting was pretty unique when you had to find the monster, but it was often frustrating and time consuming, and rather shallow compared to the fighting.Rise is very easy until Sunbreak.  This might be good or bad, but overall I think it was a bit too easy for my taste, but I still had fun seeing everything.Rise has less grinding than previous entries.  For instance you might need to beat a monster 4 times to make his armor in Rise, vs in older titles, you might need to grind the monster 20 times.  It's basically just different and depends what you want.   I like a little less of doing the same thing again and again, so 4 times seems fine to me.Note:  I played the entire thing single-player.

Weapon variety is also insane this time around with a bunch of possible playstyles for most weapons now due to switch skills.  Rise is no doubt more "arcadey" than World but it's not a bad thing, and it works very well for what they were trying to accomplish. When in doubt, just play both games, as one does not take away from the other like many want you to believe. That along with the plethora of new monsters and two new maps supplies you with a bunch of content. There's a lot of monsters to carve, and there's a lot of fun to be had doing it.
