_childDocuments_.review: I've only been a fan of the MH series since Tri. That said, I feel that I have enough experience with the games that I can give an honest review.This, even though it is a port, is extremely disappointing for an MH game after its predecessor, World.The controls are jank as hell; this is to be expected from a port, but it's still extremely annoying and quite a turn off from exploring around. The Wirebug system, while pretty neat, is also janky. Starting out with it can be difficult, especially if you are trying to get to higher places.Speaking of which, since the map design is following that of World, it can be difficult to navigate. MH games in the past, besides World, used instances as the map rather than one giant instance as they are now. This change is viewed both negatively and positively by different members of the community, but for the most part, the giant instance is refreshing and makes it much more immersive. However, it can be difficult to navigate the map when it is very unclear where your objectives are in terms of an XYZ grid. There seems to be nothing that tells you how high something is above you or how low.All in all, it's okay. But honestly, I would recommend World over this, at least for PC and until this gets some proper fixes and updates. World, coupled with mods, is a much better version of the MH series to get into.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: I've played an extra 20 hours! As more context for the below, I've already played through MHW twice across two systems. If you're making a buying decision, go to Monster Hunter World.Upfront, I enjoy this game and will continue playing it - BUT I can't really recommend it.In essence, I think the constraints of the Switch and a few of the base design choices limit Rise being as awesome as it could be. Here's a couple of things:Mounting monsters: is cool but puts a massive amount of control in the flow of a hunt in the players hands, in Monster Hunter World the Turf Wars could bring a sigh of relief or significant anxiety depending on what you're doing. Monsters running into each other in Rise is always good for the player. I like player options but it makes many hunts feel the same.Aesthetics: I might get grilled for this but Monster Hunter World is so incredibly detailed and outright gorgeous at times, MH Rise feels like a step back (I know this is due to Switch vs Console horsepower but when playing on PC I don't care where a port came from).Matchmaking: Public matchmaking in MH Rise absolutely sucks, since they were still in development and have had a year in release all post Monster Hunter World being able to show a list of active hunts a player can pick from I can only assume they didn't think it was important.As I said up the top, I'll still keep playing. I had MH World on console and played it to death, if you really like Monster Hunter then this is probably going to scratch most of the itch - but don't be surprised if you find something that irks you a bit. _childDocuments_.review: Having played through this game with a friend earlier this year, we never quite actually finished it; we beat the base game after Sunbreak came out, and then we ended up getting distracted with other things during Sunbreak.That being said, we definitely had a fun time with it, but at the same time, while it was a step forward in a number of ways, it felt like a step back relative to Monster Hunter World in others. Gone was the whole "hunting" aspect; you pretty much just rush down the monster, with little feeling for being a hunter. And the maps were quite mediocre compared to the ones in World; not terrible, but just kind of lackluster feeling.And of course, the plot was garbage - shockingly, somehow even worse than Monster Hunter World's plot, with the NPCs not leaving any impact at all on us as players.The thing is, though, actually killing the monsters was a lot of fun - the monsters were interesting to fight, the new monsters had neat designs, and the additions to the weapon mechanics made them fun to use and play with. The wirebug mechanic was an interesting take on being able to zip around the battlefield, and changed the gameplay from the "latch on and grab" that MHW ended up having a lot of.This is the core of the game, and it does work well - and it is fun to fight them with other players. You get to bring a cat and a dog with you if you are alone, or you can bring one or the other as a sidekick if you play with other people, which adds an additional layer of strategy to your loadout.But we did get tired of it by the end, as the game felt like it outlasted its welcome and required a bit too much grinding to get all the gear we wanted.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS FEELS LIKE MORE OF AN EXPANSION THAN A FULL FLEDGED GAME. I don't really do reviews too much (except for games I tend to play a lot), but coming off of MHW into this I have to speak on a few things:GRAPHICS=Took a downgrade from MHW. It seems more like a mobile phone game and less like a PC game, if that makes sense. MHW was and STILL IS a beautiful game. The rocks and game edges look jagged EVERYWHERE and PS2-like, and I've noticed some screen tearing in the village, which is odd since it doesn't occur out in the field, no matter how powerful my GPU is or how much I adjust the in-game graphic settings. Thank God for the modders who have already released enhancement packs since Capcom's too busy counting zenny to notice. CONTENT=There's a crap-ton of things to do, and the people in the village always need something, as they lazy as hell and always ask you to do it (since they never step their sorry asses outside the gates). There's a ton of monsters to beat on vs MHW, and they have some unique abilities (looking at you, Bishaten). I love the addition of Palamutes and they are now my favorite aspect of the game. The map design makes more sense in this game (although somewhat smaller and confusing at times than MHW's maps) and everything is a lot easier to understand, thanks to the 500 tutorials the game throws at you as you play. Gathering has a more simplistic approach (which I welcome), and I love that riding your mount allows you to continue doing stuff without a break in the action. The wirebug is kinda stupid to me (but makes sense) and I miss the Clutch Claw from Iceborne already, and I hate SPIRIBIRDS WITH A PASSION.I hate they kinda took the mystery out of looking for monsters, you basically see their icons on the map at all times, so nothing is hard to find and you can speed run through the quest fairly quick. The map sometimes feels big but it's also empty as hell so I feel like it's a waste. Compared to MHW it feels rushed. I miss the old way of monster mounting, but the Rampage mode is a welcome addition.CONTROLS=The controls are solid, but this interface is TOO cumbersome at times. I hate the way they swapped the quick items list and it forces you to use the radial menu more, which I barely used. If you prefer long range weapons from the go you will hate it at first because of the adjustment. I won't tell you how many times I got smacked by a monster because I was drinking potions/sharpening in error when I really was trying to swap ammo/drop a trap. Coming off MHW, it's a pain, and you can only adjust the settings so far to mirror the previous game (if you swap between the two frequently like I do). The Sunbreak expansion adds a bunch of useless switch skills and to be honest during the major fights you don't have the time or delay to pull off all the moves in sequence they added.Overall it's a good game, just not $50 worth (I'd say $40-35 at the most). It has some nice additions, but they lost a few good things along the way. If you're new to the series, play this one first then play MHW (w/Iceborne) and you'll think the latter is the upgrade.

_childDocuments_.review: Comparing Sunbreak to the base game is easy. It's an improvement across the board. If you're hoping for a comparison to Iceborne though, that's a bit harder. Sunbreak has better build diversity, greater viable weapon variety and the combat is amazing with a few exceptions. Unfortunately, the RNG systems in place are pretty horrific for anyone obsessed with optimisation. Additionally, Capcom is slacking on meaningful event quests and rewards and the quest design in general is pretty dull.One major change between the games is the focus on world building and atmosphere (or lack thereof)... Where Iceborne's environment was packed with life and minute detail, Sunbreak's is sparse and uninspiring. Despite the efforts clearly made, Sunbreak falls short on many of the secondary aspects of MH and certainly lacks the special sauce that Iceborne had in regards to immersion.Despite its numerous shortcomings, Sunbreak delivers an amazing experience in regards to the core of MH, COMBAT and SET BUILDING... The wirebug system isn't perfect but it does allow for a faster tempo in each fight and raises the skill ceiling of each weapon considerably. Set building is a dream too. If you ignore "Qurious Crafting" it's still the most diverse endgame when it comes to usable sets and weapons (excluding poor G.Lance mains). Add the qurious system and you get an even deeper pool of viable gear that will have you farming essence like it's 2019 crypto. Unfortunately, you'll be stuck with sub perfect augments but they're useful nonetheless. Also, Malzeno is one of the best boss fights in any game ever.I rate Sunbreak 9/10 where it truly matters and 7/10 over all.

_childDocuments_.review: Can say a  about this title into the series, but I think the primary way to gauge how good a Monster Hunter game is is how much you will miss this title when the new one inevitably releases; and if there's one thing to say about Rise, it's that I am  for them to keep a lot of the mechanics they introduced when the next title is released. WIre Bugs, Switch Skills, Palamutes all gave Rise an extremely unique feel that no other title has given me. Rise feels a lot faster, both in and out of combat, to the point where it's extremely difficult for me to actually get back into World, even with the graphical upgrade that the older game has.Rise isn't as pretty as World, and that's fine, because what how makes up for it is just hours upon hours for pure fun, no matter which weapon you use. I can only hope that the next game manages to achieve the same level of enjoyment and addiction that Rise gave me.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate, 4 Ultimate, Generations, World and Rise. It's by far my most played series ever and all them are great to some degree. Each one has something interesting it brings to the table and each one has something that doesn't quite work out. I'm not sure which I would say is my favourite, but I do know that Rise (and Sunbreak, which is part of this review) is a very strong contender for that title. It avoids having any feature I dislike as much as, for example, underwater combat or the clutch claw that plagued some of the previous games in the series. It, at least with Sunbreak, has the best endgame the series has ever had along with some of the most fun and fluid combat.Initially made for the Nintendo Switch, Rise lacks much of the environmental detail that the previous entry in the series had. Environments are less dense and less immersive. Other sacrifices have been made too. In World, you could follow many of the monsters around the map to see what they got up to. In Rise, monsters are more hostile. While these may seem like negatives, I'm not so sure they are. Yes, the detail in the Ancient Forest, the first map you see in World, is great. But after going there so many times, navigating it to just get to the monster can start to become frustrating. Checking out a monster's behaviour is intriguing at first, but when I'm hunting my thirtieth one, I have long since stopped caring. I don't play Monster Hunter for immersion or exploration. With the amount of time I spend playing these games, everything that isn't the core gameplay just fades into the background for me at some point. Through the technical limitations imposed by its initial hardware, Rise mostly streamlines the experience, leaving a focus on its excellent gameplay.I played through the base game using a lot of the Switch Axe, a weapon I last used in Generations. It's a brilliant version of the weapon. The new Rapid Morph skill is fun and it means you're frequently switching between the two modes, something the developers haven't always got right with this weapon. I switched over to the Sword & Shield for Sunbreak and that was an even better experience. I was let down by the weapon in Iceborne, it being overly reliant on spamming one move that was not in line with the style of play I usually expect from the weapon (fast hits with little animation commitment). Rise returns to how I best like to play the Sword & Shield, complete with a satisfying counter and good gap-closing move.The monster roster is impressive, featuring the classics, some of the best third and fourth generation monsters and some welcome new favourites like Garangolm, Lunagaron, Malzeno, Rakna-Kadaki and Magnamalo. Some of them have undergone agreeable reworks, like Kushala Daora who is significantly less annoying than it was in World. There are some disappointing omissions, such as Brachydios, Odogaron and Gammoth. But that's not enough to mar what is a very strong collection of monsters.Perhaps the most disappointing feature of the base game was its endgame. There wasn't a great deal to do and the Rampage mode was a failure, trying to cross Monster Hunter with tower defense and not doing a good job at it. It was tedious and almost impossible to fail. Thankfully, the developers apparently agreed as the mode was ditched for Sunbreak. In its place is a phenomenal endgame, largely based around anomaly monsters. These are challenging without getting out of control with HP bloat. They have a DPS check that punishes you with an explosion that stuns you, but doing enough damage to avoid that feels achievable enough. The best thing about Sunbreak's endgame is easily the variety of it. Each anomaly part is dropped from several different monsters, letting you choose which of them you want to get the part from. No other Monster Hunter endgame has you fighting as many different monsters as this.  Augmenting armor is RNG heavy, but not so much that you feel like you can never get what you want. Any time I wanted a particular roll, I was almost always able to get it. I played though this as each update was released, so I never felt like the grind was too much. I do acknowledge that if you were getting into it now, the grind may seem intimidating.It's not a huge issue, but one area Rise falters is Spiribirds. These are little birds scattered around the map that can give you boosts to stamina, attack, defense and health. That last one is the most important because you can no longer max out your HP bar by eating or using a Max Potion. This didn't bother me in the base game but some of the endgame Sunbreak content hits hard enough that it's advisable to run around the map collecting these. In a game that otherwise removes this kind of distraction, it's a chore that feels out of place. Still, this is not as big of a flaw as the failings of other games in the series, like the aforementioned underwater combat and clutch claw.The next Monster Hunter game will no doubt take some of Rise's advancements and leave some others behind, as Monster Hunter always does. I hope the flow and fluidity of the combat, especially with the Sword & Shield remains, even if the switch skill system will probably be dropped. I hope the relative lack of hardware limitations from the newer consoles doesn't lead to additions that distract from the core experience. Regardless, I'll be there on day one. No other series nails third person action game combat quite like Monster Hunter does.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have never played Monster Hunter and like Dark Souls, you need to play Monster Hunter. The same tight combat (albeit different controls that take some time to get used to, but they're WORTH IT. The controls are laid out this way on purpose, your APM is much higher in MH than DS and the layout helps that), with even more dense RPG mechanics, insane levels of customization, weapons that are sooooooo fun and diverse with intricate, yet subtle combos that will keep you coming back. I have played with the Long Sword for 300 or so hours, and I am STILL learning things, lest we forget about the 13 other weapons that are all just as intricate. The expansion just improves on the game, it feels like MHR1.5 in the best way, it is an almost entirely separate game from the base game with sooooo many more mechanics, and even better Monster fights. This is THE BEST Monster Hunter game, and an incredible starting point to the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Rise is an excellent game that I've spent over 100 hours playing, all alongside my girlfriend. The gameplay is engaging, with a variety of monsters to fight, weapons to master, and teamwork that makes it incredibly rewarding.However, the DLC introduces a significant difficulty spike that dampened the experience for us. The sudden jump in challenge can be frustrating, especially if you're used to the more balanced difficulty curve of the base game. While we enjoyed our time with it overall, the DLC’s difficulty bump was definitely an enjoyment killer.

_childDocuments_.review: At the end of the day, it's still Monster Hunter so it's hard for me to dislike it, but God was it a step back from World. The textures on the monsters themselves are great, the weapon and armor designs are a serious improvement from the ones in World, and it brings back many fan favorite monsters that were missing in World, but it's ultimately a mess. Starting with my issues for gameplay, Palamutes. The Palamutes created a problem and sold themselves as the solution, the maps are absurdly large, but there's absolutely nothing interesting to see or do in them aside from go to the monster you're there to fight, and for some that's enough, but after getting to exist in a living, breathing world in MHW, it just feels bland, palamutes also allow you to sharpen while moving in combat, effectively negating having to try and manage your sharpness. Why care when you can just ride around in a circle when you get kinda low and be untouchable? Next is wirebugs, don't get me wrong, I love the switch skills and being able to have different moves swapped into your base moveset, but the ability to just fling yourself out of any and all danger with them kills some of the strategy in favor of flashiness. Why lay on the ground to keep my Iframes when I can just launch myself out of the way of whatever is coming at me next? With wirebugs came wyvernriding, wyvernriding is straight up garbage. It replaced the great mechanic of mounting that has been around since 4 and 4U with something that is A. harder to pull off and B. ultimately accomplishes less for you, the inflated damage numbers in this game means that that 500ish damage you got from wallbanging a monster 3 times is way less than if you had spent that time just hitting it with your weapon, and sure theres the knockdown, but the original mounting caused the same thing AND dealt more damage with the mount attack, even mounted punishers do less damage than just hitting the monster. Now moving away from gameplay, theres the jank. I fought 5 HR monsters today with MR gear, in those 2 quests I was teleported into magnamolos mouth 5 times while standing behind him while he was attempting to grab someone else, had Rathalos shoot 10+ fireballs through his own body to shoot out of his ass to hit me while I was behind him, and had some serious deja vu to dark souls with my camera when fighting bazel. I also fought a rajang and believe it or not, he was the least janky of them all, he honestly felt better than he does in World, so good on him. I touched on hurtboxes from monster attacks with magnamolos grab, and that is the biggest offender for sure, but all of the monsters save for like, great izuchi, have some of the worst hurt/hitboxes i've seen in ANY game EVER. There is so much that hits you that looks like it shouldn't while in World, Gen U, and 4U the hitboxes on most monsters are unbelievably tight. The only monster I can think of with bad hitboxes at the moment is fatalis, and he's been like that since Monster Hunter, so I'd say thats more of a fatalis problem than anything else.TLDRBuy MHW:I if you're looking for a monster hunter game to play, it's more well polished and more enjoyable to actually exist in as a world. Or emulate Gen U, or 4U, or any of the other games. Really I just recommend all of the monster hunter franchise except for this one, it has too many problems.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're on the fence because "this isn't Monster Hunter World 2", I invite you to try it anyway. _childDocuments_.review: I've played Monster Hunter since MH3U on 3DS, and this is my favorite yet. The developers have refined the series to the point that I was able to get my most reticent friends into the series. + Great quality of life improvements - less gathering, fewer small monster hunts, less co-op tripping, better multiplayer lobbies, swapping out your gear mid-hunt, refilling your inventory mid-fight, fast travel points, and a bunch of other things that alleviate the slow pace of play that made the previous games difficult to get into.+ Lots of fun monsters, be they old from the series' roster, some with new movesets, and new monsters are interesting and engaging+ Switch Skills add a ton of variety to old, beloved weapons+ Movement has been improved upon beyond Worlds' changes, and it feels pretty good to move around the map (not Warframe/Prototype/Saints Row 4 levels of fluidity and fun, but fun nonetheless)+ No sieges, no randomized weapons+ Maps are dense, with lots of little nooks and crannies to discover and interesting gameplay elements+ I've somehow put 200+ hours into this- Rampages, a tower defense mode, are an odd choice that aren't to my taste, though some folks enjoy it.- It's still Monster Hunter, so while the learning curve is eased once again, it's still steep- There are still very rare drops that are necessary for some buildsIf you've wanted to try Monster Hunter, or have bounced off it before, it's never been more accessible and fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Tbh I can't really make up my mind whether or not I'd recommend this game, I think it depends on the audience.Sometimes I like Rise sometimes I don't, I feel left and right about a lot of the changes made that seem to be aimed mostly towards a younger audience.I like Rise but not so much that I think it's worth 90CAD + the expansion coming out in Summer.If I could go back 30 hours I might of rathered skipped this entry and just waited for a more griddy and bigger Monster Hunter however, it's also nice to play this in the mean time before the next big Monster Hunter.If your really on the fence about Rise and can't decide I would recommend trying it for 2 hours and see how you feel afterwards, otherwise if your coming from World and that's the kind of Monster Hunter your attracted to then I say just skip this one unless you have the cash to spend comfortably and you really need to get your Monster Hunter fix.(For reference my specs are: Asus 1060 6gb gpu, I7, 16GB DDR4 Ram and I get 120-144 fps on a 144hz monitor max settings.)

_childDocuments_.review: Coming back to this game to be that one guy that uses the insect glaive from MW:W to mount the monster?Well, let me tell you, that was completely nerfed. Now, instead of being that guy, you now have to either get your target to win a battle against another monster to be able to beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of the monster you're targeting, lose the battle to be able to ram that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ into the wall multiple times, or use an ungodly amount of wirestring moves to be able to mount the ♥♥♥♥♥♥. On the bright side, you can now actually control the monster when it happens (And it's sweet bliss every time you do so) but now unless you get lucky enough you'll only get a mount or two before the monster's weak enough to capture or you outright kill it. No, it's not removed, but it's pretty darn close to. I've been using wirestring moves the entire time and the only time the monster actually gets mountable is with a monster battle 95% of the time. And that further gets ruined when you get cucked out of the mount hitting f repeatedly and someone else gets it to ram the monster into the wall one time and falling off.That being said, I love this game. Capcam did another hell of a solid in the Monster Hunter franchise. It might have been limited by the hardware of Switch, I get it. It might even be easier than world because of the gameplay on Nintendo Switch. This series has never failed to innovate, and this game is just continued innovation in the Monster Hunter series. I remember when I played Monster Hunter Freedom unite back in like 2012, to Monster Hunter 3 Tri, and I have seen it come a long way. The graphics is amazing. The music is astounding. I've made a pact with myself to listen to the Bunny Dango song every time because it's just that great. It's just a weeb's dream of a game, and you'll be sad if you buy battlefield 2042 instead of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game brings new elements to the genre while keeping the core gameplay intact.While I do miss the inclusion of tools like a pickaxe, fishing rod, and bug net, the combat system more than makes up for it with its smooth and satisfying mechanics. The attacks and movements feel great, and the loading times are impressively fast.Although the world itself may not be overly exciting, the weapons and monsters are interesting and offer a lot of variety. The hub-world is also an improvement over the previous game.It's an enjoyable and exciting experience overall.
_childDocuments_.name: MONSTER HUNTER RISE

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing wrong with the game as is, but for me this misses the mark when compared to my favourite entries in the series (monster hunter freedom 2, portable 3rd). As someone else has said, it's a good game, just not a good monster hunter game.Egg on my face for not playing the demo first, and wasting too much time in the character editor and settings menu before getting to any real game-play.TLDR: far to easy to be engaging, too visually busy, missing a lot of elements that made monster hunter special for me.The game has issues with readability: The UI is cluttered, objects, creatures and characters get obscured. The over use of glowing indicators for interactive elements actually makes things harder to see for me as I have issues with my eyes, which is specific to me but there's no option to turn it off. A lot of this means I actually can't comfortably play this game, despite that it's really easy, so I can only imagine how easy it is if you can actually see.There's not a lot to the moment to moment gameplay:There's a little *too* many quality of life tweaks that essentially mean everything is a little too convenient so you end up blazing through everything without ever really paying attention to anything, everything is scale-able, you can zip zap zoop everywhere, you don't need tools for the most part to harvest fish, or mine. You essentially have ESP by default, locations of anything relevant are marked on the map so you don't really have to *hunt* anything.This is subjective and a personal opinion, but I don't want to explore in rise, the maps, to me, feel sort of slapped together, not a world I want to explore. The maps are just areas to get stuff to make bars go up, monster hunter was always a grind but rise feels like busy work.To top it off it's too easy:Yes, I have played a lot of the older titles and that will have some impact on difficulty for me. However I can kill enemies in rise by standing still and hitting them a couple times. Damage dealt by small monsters is completely negligible and they die so quickly you don't really get a feel for what they're like to fight. Compared to older titles small monsters must have about 25-50% the hp.I have played a small bit of monster hunter world, and that seems to be a lot better for me, even though I have some similar issues, The monsters in world don't go down as fast, the map is pretty and interesting to explore and the game moves at a slower pace. So for modern Monster Hunter I will likely stick with that game.In the end, Monster Hunter is different now, and that's great! We still have the old games to go back to, and more people than ever are playing the new titles. But it's just not for me,

_childDocuments_.review: I am a Fifth Fleeter (In MH terms, I started with Generation V which is World/Iceborne, which from henceforth will be shortened to Worldborne), so consider this review to be something of a newcomer's perspective of sortsNow with that out of the way, Monster Hunter is not necessarily for everyone. It never did try to be that. It is a series that prides on methodical deliberate moves with high emphasis on planning for the situation at hand instead of reacting to whats ahead of you. But Rise/Sunbreak takes that and turns it on its head somewhat. The game is designed to be the best entry for someone trying to get into MH and it shows. From the movement to the combat to world design. Also, this game was originally made for Switch. That factors in on the design aspect of this game as well. Its faster paced than other MH games. Its unique mechanic, the wirebugs, are implemented pretty well for the most part. They serve multiple purposes, are rechargeable but different moves add modifiers to the recharge. That adds a lot to how the game flows. The narrative was never a strong point about the MH games and it might as well not even be here for all there is. It is a very run of the mill "save the village in peril, hero" story. But something new to any MH game is the introduction of actual named characters with their own personalities, motivations etc. The main draw for the game however, is the same as every other MH game, which is, the monsters. The game has returning iconic monsters from previous entries, along with some additions from World sprinkled in. The ecological focus that Worldborne had has been completely dropped to the point where you no longer even need to track monsters. They show up in the map the moment you spawn in. This is a mixed bag of sorts as any veteran can tell you, tracking monsters and preparing for a fight was half the game in any MH title prior to this. But, you cannot disregard the time saved for you to get stuck into the main draw of the game, its gameplay.  As mentioned above, the combat in this game flows a lot faster. Your attacks are swift, precise and stylish. There are 14 weapons to choose from and they have extensive upgrade trees each. All of them are unique and play differently. The wirebug also has different moves depending on the weapon being used. The beauty of this, is that all weapons are designed to be viable from the start to the end. The amount of info a player has about mechanics in the game has also significantly increased. You can, at any time, go to your Journal and check all the necessary info, from where to hit for maximum effectiveness to elemental matchups to status matchups to what kind of loot you can expect depending on which part of said monster was focused on. Gathering is also faster all items are gathered in 1 gathering loop. Almost all surfaces in the game are runnable on and you also have replenishing wirebugs that allow you to swing off literal air. You also get a choice to take 2 pets into a solo hunt with you, one of which, can be a rideable dog called palamute, which can drift around corners at high speed. In MP, you will have to choose either the utility focused Palico or the fast and nimble Palamute. This is iterated further on, in Sunbreak. The one controversial addition to this game are the Spiritbirds. In earlier entries, increasing your Health and Stamina meant having to slot in certain skills or wear certain armor. In Rise/Sunborne however, you run around, collecting Spiritbirds that increase your max Health, stamina, Attack and Defense for the duration of the hunt. While this mechanic incentivizes exploration, collecting spiritbirds before any hunt can get tedious. Speaking of Sunbreak, it is designed as the Hard mode+ of Rise. In MH terms, its the G/U expansion. The ceilings are raised in terms of difficulty. It has separate Master Rankings apart from the main game's Hunter Rankings. If the content in base Rise was a bit touch and go in terms of how engaging it was, Sunbreak filled in the gaps. More Skills, more armor designs, more everything. I would go so far as to say that If you are getting Rise, get it WITH Sunbreak for the complete experience. Other DLC that the game has to offer is mostly cosmetics. The items that do make a difference in terms of gameplay are character and pet customisation tokens. You do not need those in any way shape or form to complete, compete or excel in the game. Mod support is definitely is there but the recent  activation of post launch DRM rendered a lot of mods outdated. But, we have seen a lot of them return since. As this is PC and you are on Steam, there definitely are some nice QOL mods out there. The community is friendly for the most part but can get elitist from time to time. You will definitely be judged based on your choice of weapon and your efficiency in a hunt in certain circles. But thankfully, they are the minority. Overall, should you get this game? YES. In an age filled with subpar releases, disappointments and straight up lies, MH stands one of the few series that did not get afflicted by the generational rot that a lot of other AAA series have fallen prey to. At best, this is a good MH game. At worst, this is still a good game. If this is your first MH game, welcome, Hunter. If this isn't your first MH game, welcome back, Hunter.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Another solid entry in the Monster Hunter franchise. A lot of folks cut their teeth on World, which was a very ambitious release meant to bridge the gap between Monster Hunter Veterans and newbies to the series, so if that was your first foray, expect things to be a bit different. At its core, the gameplay loop is the same: Hunt monster with weapon, use monster part to make better weapon, hunt better monster. If you're there for the story you'll enjoy it, but as is usually the case, it's not incredibly deep or amazing. Still a very fun narrative and the english voices are very entertaining to say the least (But we all know Monhun language is best).If you like RPGs and games that reward you for reading, practicing and grinding, this game will be your bag. You can play it solo or you can hop into the Hub (Or the Outpost in the newly released Sunbreak DLC after you progress far enough in the Gathering Hub) with your friends and have a good time. The Village Quests you do are designed to teach you the basics of the game and get you used to hunting the monsters, as are the tutorials given. Lots of fun armor and weapon combinations to try, a training yard, and dual companions make the solo hunts very fun and some of them are quite a challenge. Grab some Dango, sharpen those weapons and get out there, Hunter.Also, Fiorayne is best girl.

_childDocuments_.review: 8.4/10Well, I actually played RISE and SUNBREAK for over 800 hours on my NS, and recently purchased the PC version since it was on sale.I've been playing Monster Hunter since the PSP days, and after almost 20 years now, I haven't missed a single game in the series. Simply put, RISE is made by a different team than WORLD, so if you're new to Monster Hunter (and the first game you played was WORLD), then you'll find that RISE and WORLD are so very different.RISE's style is more traditional Monster Hunter fare, which will be relatable to many veteran players, and while the combat is much more exhilarating, it comes at the cost of being too fast and spartan, and abandoning the excellent map design and ecosystem design found in WORLD.Also, the base game has very little content, and although the DLC (SUNBREAK) saves the day, it still can't hide the fact that the game is empty and has very little content.However, RISE still has a lot to offer if you judge it only by action game standards.As a final note, . However, I don't really care about the quality of the graphics, but rather the substance of the game, so as a port, the PC version is still good enough for me.However, if you use the keyboard and mouse to operate, there may be a lot of uncomfortable and uncomfortable, it is recommended to use the gamepad to operate, the experience will be much better.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Rise is one of the more divisive games in the franchise. A lot of players who play the Switch version of the game have been complaining about the amount of content, and I can see that happening in the near future on PC as well. This is simply due to the lack of any randomized quest feature. Which I can agree, I do think that a randomized quest feature should be in the game. But I think people are forgetting the amount of content that the base version of MHW had.I was told to avoid MHW for a plethora of reasons when the game first launched. Tedious cutscene management between individuals players just to do one hunt with friends, an "extreme" lack of content, among other things. Sure MHW had investigations, but it had less monsters than MHR has, and very little reason to do investigations. The only reason you would do investigations is to grind for decorations, but decorations in the early game of a "live service" Monster Hunter, become obsolete not long after the games launch. Investigations were your option for after you completed everything there is to do. Which is something I can respect, but it is worth noting that the feature of "putting a target on a random monsters head for you to go hunt" is not currently present in MHR, and that seems to be a turn off for a specific group of people who are looking to grind the game nonstop. Especially the PC crowd. The very same "not a lot of content" critique is repeating itself with MHR currently.Personally I believe that this is a solid entry in the franchise, and shouldn't be overlooked just due to no randomized quest feature. It's a good 200-300 hour Monster Hunter experience. With cleverly hidden secrets to find in gorgeous maps (some of which are reused from the first MH I ever played, MH3/MH3U, and they have been reworked to fit the new gameplay engine extremely well), great combat, and the same Monster Hunter charm that is loved by fans of the franchise. The only critiques I can really agree with when it comes to the game are the following:-Rampages aren't very fun. I can honestly enjoy "siege" quests (Lao Shan Lung, Dah'Ren Mohran, etc.) but rampages aren't the most enjoyable type of siege quest. It goes for a more "tower defense" style of approach. Technically you were defending structures in other siege hunts, but it's often more exciting to take down one giant monster that is a threat to a structure that it interacts with, rather than a bunch of normal monsters you have already fought charging towards a gate.-The game is "too easy" for veterans of the franchise. I can honestly agree with this statement, because the new mobility and wirebug attacks that have been added to the game, make even the most difficult hunts trivial for people who have been playing MH for many years. The ability to wirefall, and be insanely mobile, has removed a lot of the danger from some hunts. I personally feel that both wirefall, and wirebug attacks, should have much longer cooldowns across the board. They are both too spammable. In speedruns, you will often see players ONLY using wirebug attacks on certain weapons.-The story isn't very memorable, but what MH game had a memorable story besides 4U (Based)-Monsters invading your hunt is only a positive now, as it allows you to mount a monster and then use it to take down the monster you are currently hunting. Being invaded by monsters such as Deviljho and Rajang made for some of the most memorable moments in the entire franchise, as their presence was often much more threatening than the monster you were currently hunting. The danger is now completely gone, leading to monsters showing up during your hunt feeling too forced/scripted.Don't allow people to tell you that this game doesn't have much content, because it still has several hundreds hours worth of quests and side quests to do, with more to come. Its still extremely charming, fun, and engaging. It still feels like the Monster Hunter you know and love. Just don't go into the game expecting a several thousand hour grind, because that isn't what this game is.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from MH3/4 Ultimate and finding all following MH games boring, tiresome and a waste of money this Monster Hunter RIse is very fresh for meSome of the positives are : Mounts which can be mounted during combat aswell, you can gather and carve whilst riding and it's speed is really nice when you sprint you can almost outrun large monsters relocating to a different zoneNo annoying handler or an ennoying "new frontier" where you get all these tedious exploration quests , you operate from a village that's been settled for at least 50-70 years Everything in Rise can be fast paced, loading into a mission takes literally 3 seconds or less and so do all other load screens (on a nvidia 1070) which makes it feel instantaneousThe graphics are very nice too , I don't even have HDR but i feel like i get sucked into combat which enhances gameplay alotI don't know if this is new to rise : Custom spirit skills are added to every existing weapon type. One example is a quickstep dodge for Bow users which you can use whilst ADS'ing. It's insanely nice to just flow with the combat without any downtime and keep constant pressure on large monsters with a Bow thanks to thisI'd say this is a nice buy even for Dark Souls fans, the gameplay can be as fast (finally) as you want or as slow which gives me freedom to play as i wantthe HUD or overlay whatever it's called (the healthbars and other item info on your screen during combat) is also not distracting and sloppy like it was with World.World was innovative on some fronts but Rise just perfects it all. Even the background music in all village areas is customizable.Emphasis on the fast paced load times ; this game just does everything instantly, opening your stash , loading into zones or accepting quests, it's all super fast and saves you alot of time. You can literally be ready for the next mission and inside the next mission 30 seconds after you came back to town and that's including restocking , eating and accepting the new quest and subquests5/5 stars and worth the 60 eurosBuild variety allows for at least 1000 of exciting gameplay for sure.

That is great and i love it. Also you can now ride your dog and it makes traversal so much better. As for story it is kinda just their to get you to the next monster to hunt. Second, the game play loop is one that will start to get pretty stale unless you change weapons a couple of times in the middle of play due to you not really gaining anything but a stat buff in the way of combat. give me more cool moves and maybe an ultimate i can pop at later levels to make me feel like i am getting stronger instead of just giving me different looking armor so i can take slightly less long to kill the next boss with the same stuff over and over.Other than that, its alright, solid 7.5/10

Capcom also already addressed the bugs, which they're working on. Expect a patch coming in the next hours, maybe days.Update: Yep. Still great.Another Update: All these people claiming Enigma ruined the game are following in the footsteps of fearmongering 'influencers' trying desperately to cling to views and relevancy by spouting ridiculous lies and unproven facts. The sole reason Capcom updated the game to run Enigma DRM was because the Denuvo license ran out and Enigma costs a fraction of the price yet does the same job. They didn't 'add' DRM, they simply switched to a different one.Mods broke? No ♥♥♥♥, they do every update. Took them less than 3 hours and REFramework was up and running again. Steam Deck and Linux support was fixed within 12 hours. No performance issues or stutters whatsoever. _childDocuments_.review: Rise is not the worst mainline Monster Hunter game to date, but it still can't compete with the glory days of the oldschool games. This is a direct evolution of World and it sort of tries to meld World and old games together, to mixed results. Now, Rise still is a great game, because the core gameplay loop is still really fun and satisfying. I'm just gonna list a few things I like and dislike, from the perspective of someone who plays Monster Hunter for over a decade now.Good:- The story takes a back seat in Rise again. It's there, it has some cutscenes, but it isn't World-levels of storytelling. Some people won't like that, but I feel like that's how Monster Hunter should be.- I don't know how to really describe it, but it "feels" a bit more like a Monster Hunter again. Maybe because it doesn't have that realistic approach.- The new monsters are fantastic, be it for the mechanics, the fight itself or simply the design. There isn't a - single one I actively dislike. - Same for the maps. The new ones and the revamped old ones from Tri are great. They removed all the clutter that plagued World and thanks to the added mobility they're really fun to explore.- They also brought back actual weapon designs, too bad the monster from World are stuck with their tacked-on weapons.- Village and Hub quest got seperated again. Again, many people won't like that, but I think it's giving both areas a reason to be there. I personally were never in the Gathering Hub in Astera, because why should I?This also means you can now play with your friends without seeing every monster cutscene beforehand, since the game thinks you've seen it all in the Village or you don't care and just want to bonk stuff- The Wirebug is a fantastic new addition and makes traversing the maps so much fun.Okay:- The Wirebug may be great for movement, but for combat it is overkill for me. Silkbind attacks are pretty much Hunter Arts but without any real cooldown and the Wiredash prevents being pinned down or ever getting in a combo from a monster. The game is overall even more streamlined and casualized than World, which isn't inherentely bad, but rather than being a hunter in an Action-RPG it feels more and more like being a superhuman in a Action game. The new icon that pops up the instant a monster is ready for capture or how you have some sort of spider-sense and instantly see where what monster is on the map, and, for slaying or gathering quests, see the exact point where the small monsters or the materials you have to gather are. That last one really bugs me.- The palamute is a cool new addition, but I wish it was a bit more helpful. It can bring you really fast from A to B and being able to use potions, whetstones, etc. while riding it is pretty neat, but in the actual fight you're still better off with two palicos. Hopefully they expand on the doggo.- Same as in World, we've gotten a ton of cosmetic DLC, which is never great, but as long as it's cosmetic it's like fine whatever- Searching for tracks and leveling up your research level is completely removed. I'd rather have it be added again, but as a sort of side thing to level up and make things easier, but before they put it in as neccesary main mission it's better to remove it entirely- The endemic life also got kind of a cut. There aren't that many anymore, so the world feels kinda "barren" again. but every endemic life can help in different ways with your hunt. Luring monsters, making a healing cloud, inflicting the monster with blights, etc.No:- Farming is more or less not really requiered anymore. You can get full armor sets with two to three hunts if you don't need a rare drop and it takes a lot of out of the timesink Monster Hunter is. Many people will love that change, saying it's "not as tedious" and not a "grindfest" anymore, but that's what Monster Hunter is; a big 'ol grind session.- I don't like the Spiribirds. They were a cool little gimmick at first, but it's charm fell off quickly and now I'm annoyed that I have to walk like five minutes through the area collecting birds before even going to the monster. Some people say use it as a difficulty slider, but I rather have the old system with the canteen and using max/ancient potions when carting back- Rise added a new mode, called the Rampages. They're tower defense-like quests you have to do a certain points in the story, and they are absolute garbage. They are long, boring and also kind of a cluster♥♥♥♥ in the end. And Capcom must've seen it too because every monster exclusive to Rampages has gotten a normal quest by now- Wyvern Riding is just a worse version of mounting. At first it is kinda cool, but after a relatively short time it just gets infruriating. It's just long and convoluted, the old mounting mechanic from 4U-GenU or even World were a lot better- The weapons are kinda hit or miss, depending on what you usually use. The Gunlance feels better than ever and the Longsword got it's usual buff, but the Hunting Horn is completely massacered and doesn't even resemble the old one, and I've heard weapons like Greatsword or Charge Blade are also worse than before.Overall Rise is a fantastic game. Like World, it does some thing better than the old games are some things many times worse. But I guess I will never get games as great as pre-World again. If you like Monster Hunter, you'll like this game. If you started with World, try the demo first; I've seen many people who absolutely loved World and absolutely hated Rise. If you want to get into the franchise, I would still recommend World. Even though Rise is more fun gameplay wise, I feel like World eases you into the basics and the gameplay loop a lot better, even if it's a slog in the beginning.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge Monster Hunter: World (MHW) fan, I wasn't particularly excited or interested in Monster Hunter Rise when it was first announced. The graphics seemed like a significant downgrade, the gameplay didn't look quite right, and it just didn't have the charm that MHW gave off. After investing nearly 1,000 hours into MHW and completing everything, I decided to give Rise a chance. Although it started a bit slowly, I quickly began to appreciate the game.Rise is definitely not of the same caliber as MHW. It's much less immersive, the hunts are fast and furious, and the gameplay heavily relies on wirebugs and movement tech. Despite these differences, it is still a good game, and I enjoyed my time playing it. It remains a Monster Hunter game, so the core gameplay loop is unchanged. I did enjoy some of the new additions, such as the extra movesets for each weapon, the expanded monster catalog, and the variety of new builds and customization options. Although I have some grievances with the game's design choices, I do recommend playing Rise if you are a Monster Hunter fan. For new players to the series, I believe MHW is a better entry point.Before I finish this review, there is one glaring issue with the game that I can't forgive CAPCOM for – you absolutely need to get the Sunbreak DLC to fully enjoy the game. The base game is, frankly, a very shallow experience, and it is clear how rushed and unfinished it is compared to the DLC. I only recommend picking up this game if you can get both the base game and the Sunbreak DLC together.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: Most of my review will be heavily centered around my playthrough of the game on the Nintendo Switch, but I will take into account the differences I have experienced on my current playtime with the PC release. Monster Hunter Rise is a new mainline Monster Hunter game that I think offers veteran players plenty of new content to chew on, as well as providing the best entry point for newcomers to the series. Typical to the Monster Hunter formula, you start off in a new land as a newbie hunter, where you slowly rise in the ranks as a Monster slaying machine. It's a tried and true formula which has enticed me ever since my first Monster Hunter game, and I have been returning to each new release as they come out, each better than the last. If you are wondering if this game is for you, I’ll say that I think Monster Hunter Rise is the best entry point into the series, and you should absolutely pick it up on PC. The controls are tight, and there are plenty of weapon options to give you lots of variety. Many of them are easy to learn, but hard to master, you will be improving your skills with each weapon after many hours of gameplay, feeling more and more awesome as you continue to improve.Monster Hunter Rise differs from previous series, as it has incorporated much of the quality of life improvements from previous games like Monster Hunter World, and streamlines even further, allowing hunters to spend less time on tedious tasks and more time enjoying the point of the game- fighting bigger and badder monsters. The "hub world" is smaller and easier to navigate than Monster Hunter World's map, making getting around fast and fluid. New players will be less confused as to where to go, which is helping many of my friends who are new to the series, focus on learning how to fight rather than learning where everything is on the map. Multiplayer with friends much better VS Monster Hunter World, since it often would prevent players from playing together until after cutscenes, certain quests were progressed through, etc... It was cumbersome for no reason. Rise goes back to the original formula, where they split up the single player and multi player components into two quest givers, allowing players to jump straight into multiplayer within minutes of starting the game. No fuss- just playing with your buds right away. This is fantastic, as the frustrations around World's multiplayer prevented new MH players from enjoying the game.For the PC release specifically, I noticed that Capcom gives you a generous amount of gifts early game, likely to celebrate the games release, or to help boost new players. They give you a very generous early-game armor set, and plenty of golden eggs to sell for money, making early game a breeze. Don't let this experience represent the entirety of the game however, as the game does get increasingly more difficult as you progress through to harder and harder monsters. Eventually, you will outgrow the starting equipment and will need to farm monsters to get new armor and weapons. As a veteran player, I appreciate the gear as it can get me to the "meat" of the game faster- the harder, more challenging monsters! But for a new player, it may take away some of that early-game challenge. Some will appreciate the help, while others may feel the game is too easy and be turned off. I won't say it's a negative, but it is something to note. You could always choose not to use it.Monster Hunter Rise as a game is fantastic, and the PC release is nearly everything I had hoped for. The game runs far better than Monster Hunter World, allowing me to play at 4k 120hz consistently. Monster Hunter World was far heavier on a PC. Compared to the Nintendo Switch release, which was locked at 30fps, It's insane how nice it feels to play at a higher framerate again. Even just 60fps feels like a world of difference. I do notice that some cutscenes will be locked to 30 fps, like the title screen or eating food at the hub world, but it's not a big deal. I also don't recommend players turn on Depth of Field in advanced graphics settings, as it seems broken at the moment and doesn't focus where it should. White the game doesn’t offer the same high graphical fidelity that MH World has, the game doesn’t look bad graphically, and offers excellent art direction and design. The weapons are much MUCH improved over the template designs that MH world offered, each giving you a unique design. While World certainly looked better, the gameplay improvements made over World are a tradeoff I’m willing to make. I will say that I can tell that some small enemies (at a distance) run at a reduced framerate, like Monster Hunter World did. Not an issue, but I wish the PC release allowed us to disable this, since Rise runs so well.   MH Rise multiplayer has been very solid for my friend group, and hasn’t dropped or crashed on us once. The same can’t be said for Monster Hunter World, which had frequent multiplayer related issues that took many patches to iron out, and never became fully “solid”. Rise in comparison, feels much improved. I will say that sometimes you will see fast moving players “jerk” around as the game updates player positions, but the game never outright disconnected anyone, and during actual monster fights, they feel solid.   To summarize, MH Rise offers plenty of content for both new and old players. While some players may be disappointed that the graphics don’t exceed that of MH World, the art design and gameplay will not disappoint. The multiplayer is excellent, and the game feels as solid as ever. Monster Hunter games have always had a thriving online community of dedicated players, so the game will stay active until the next big MH release. While many new players will be slightly overwhelmed in the beginning, Rise is likely the best entry point for those new to the franchise. I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: At least it has no handler in it. This review will have me comparing this game with Monster Hunter World to point out the two approaches these 2 games have and not meant to say this or that game is better than the other one. This game gives me GU and 4U vibes with more arcadey style gameplay.Overall, I like World more for the experience, immersiveness, and also the side things you could do besides hunting. And I prefer World's combat pacing that's hanging in between Gen 4 and Rise. Not too fast and not too slow either. However Rise is amazing too. I love the returning maps from Gen 2 and 3. And i think they did a great job remaking the maps into the current gen. The combat is more fast paced, and some weapon got some great improvements and QoL, although there are also weapons that got too streamlined which makes the weapon felt more shallow like the hunting horn. The new things like wirebug and switch skills fits nicely with how open the maps are and they look pretty flashy and cool. Although a little overpowered and makes air attacks too easy to do. The combat feels less grounded overall with less interaction with the environment itself compared to World and almost no environmental traps/hazards that the hunter can use/exploit against the monsters. Environmental slopes and ledges are now useless with the addition of wirebugs. Although hazards from endemic life is still there like paratoads, flash flies, and etc. The addition of palamutes is a pretty nice change and I consider better and faster than raider ride in World. And I love the combat support the palamutes offer. Being able to take 2 companions with you is a nice return so for those who want to have 2 palicoes with separate gadgets again, you can. Or you can also take 1 palico and 1 palamutes if you want both. The progression system for the companions is also returning to the old system from Gen 4 with different abilities you can train and unlock based on what role they are like Trapper, Gatherer, Healer, etc. Which is a nice improvement from World's palico system. The visuals looked really great and almost World levels of graphics especially knowing that it's a port from a Switch. When it comes to colors, they are more saturated and arguably better compared to World. There are some visuals that felt like a downgrade like the hit visuals with swords and impact weapons looked a little less chunky. As for audio, the music is really amazing. With more cultural styled tracks especially the Desert theme being my favorite. Some audios for certain weapons like longsword slashes felt like a downgrade overall, with less crunchy and meat like sound present like in World. Although audio for impact sounds for hammer and hunting horn is definitely an improvement from World with the Bonk sound being the focus and the crunch sound slightly toned down. So, hitting the monster's head with impact weapons is very satisfying and rewarding. As with any monster hunter game, the story itself is nothing to write home about, however it gets the job done. Not as interesting as World's story. A little too short but not too bad. The monster rosters this time has more monsters than World when it's on early release. And definitely has more monster variety overall over World. The returning monsters like Basarios, and Khezu is also a welcome addition and a nice nostalgia hit. Overall, if you're focused on jumping on the gameplay immediately and looking for adrenaline rush fast paced combat, this game is for you and I highly recommend it. Rise allows you to skip cutscenes while World have unskippable cutscenes whether you have seen it before or not. So World have a slower start and progression. So if you don't care about the story, Rise lets you just skip through all the cutscenes even if you haven't seen them before. However, as first impression, if you're looking for a more grounded experience, slightly slower methodical combat, and want to immerse yourself as a real hunter in a living breathing ecosystem, World is nice game to start at! Also apologies for the messy writing of this review. Hope it helps you decide which games to pick first.

_childDocuments_.review: Nominated this game for best soundtrack and I still think that while I've had a lot of fun with this game multi, the music is probably its strongest aspect.I've been a MH fan for a good while now and while I wouldn't consider myself a hardcore fan by any stretch, I've played several entries and this one has me...kinda confused? Or it did until I played World, anyway. That game is quite the experience if you've played any of the prior MH games. It definitely feels very "get this game into Western eyes and Western hands", which isn't necessarily a bad thing but I'll tell ya, the fact that mounts were introduced in *this* game rather than that one is a real shame because even with teleports, navigating those maps is a nightmare. It's very interesting, though.But this is about Rise and while I don't want to go too into depth I will say that it was a lot more Monster Hunter than I was expecting compared to World which simultaneously felt like a huge departure and very at home. This is also probably the easiest game in the series, even if it's hecka fun while being that. The mobility in particular feels fantastic and this is a strength that the game displays loudly and proudly. Wirebugs are just fun and I'll be sad to see them go even if I wouldn't mind them being replaced with something similar later, albeit with less potential for fall recovery.So idk it's a fun action RPG with a lot of hours packed in and a ton of QoL from the previous games, possibly my favorite MH possibly but the reason I even made this is because I wanted to talk about the soundtrack. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LOVE the soundtrack to this game, so many tracks that I just jammed to so often and that doesn't really happen for me with this series. Like, I think certain themes are memorable, like the main theme of the series, Proof of a Hero, and hunt themes that you hear a lot (lots of fond memories of the Tri themes, specifically).But this game really had me from jumpstreet. Opening the game and just hearing this soft earworm and then getting into the game and going into the hub and vibing to the dango banger and then going to the hunts to hear any number of good songs. The one that stuck with me most ironically was the  which is the first one you here and is just so up my alley, especially as the song reaches its climax (that part just sat in my head rent free for weeks). I think the song that really pushed this game in particular up there for me is a fight towards the ends of the game that ends up being the fusion of two other pivotal fight themes. It's melancholic, really well orchestrated, and especially in the chaos of the battle just feels fantastically fitting. Easily my favorite song in the game.Anyway yeah, this OST's a keeper. _childDocuments_.review: I'm a player who who started playing in Monster Hunter Tri, and has played some of MH3U, MH4U, and MHW. I find this game extremely fun. While it has dropped some features in favor of quality of life, and it does feel slightly easier than past games. It still brings the same enjoyable formula to the table that has the same, enjoyable gameplay loop as previous titles. The monster design is still impeccable to me, Some monsters have been given new attacks, which have refreshed some fights for me. The addition of wirebugs has made combat different in a way I find really enjoyable. Zipping around with unique moves was not something I'd expect to do in a Monster Hunter game, but boy is it extremely fun. And as someone who has mained Switch Axe as soon as I unlocked it in Tri, the quality of life and fun it breathes into my favorite weapon has made me love my weapon even more.And then with the addition of Sunbreak and the most recent Title Update, we've gotten harder content that brings back some of the difficulty I remembered from my previous experiences in the series. After farming HR for long enough, the monsters in Master Rank bring back the fear I was lacking in fights too. I feel rewarded when I fight the monsters I thought I had mastered previously now that they can once again punish me for my mistakes. And the upcoming Title Updates seem genuinely promising for more hard content.And to top it all of, the final big elder dragon fights at the end of Low Rank, High Rank, and Master Rank that are the tradition of the games are an amazing experience. I won't go into detail to avoid spoiling what there can be to spoil about them. But all 3 of them made me squeal with excitement as I went through them. My only prior experience of these kinds of fights was just with Ceadeus- which was exciting but tedious and slow fight for me. So these new, mmo raid-like fights were a breath of fresh air. They quickly became some of my most favorite fights to do in all of the series for how different, fun, and intense they all felt for me.I really reccommend giving this game a try. I think it genuinely stands as a great title in Monster Hunter's series of games.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get this straight, this is a Monster Hunter game, so there is a lot of grinding (but less than World, as I have experienced so far). The monsters are all unique in their own way, which is expected. Some have similarities to others, whether that be in move-set or design, however they will still be a unique experience. WITHOUT Sunbreak, the game alone is really addicting and enjoyable, but could be lackluster if you only know what World is like, but for people who have played the other games, this game is still full of content to enjoy. Keep in mind that this game is not friendly to new players for the reason that everything can be easily learned (okay most things, some weapons are a bit confusing), it is also very much not friendly to new players because this is not a game for everyone; you need to get into the habit of specific things, and need to be able to get over the grinding aspect, and also need to learn a lot of new topics that are likely going to be confusing to you, but that's fine, we have all started at some similar point. In comparison to World, this game is both better and worse. For the aspects that are better, I would say game-play (both in general and the loop), farming, enjoy-ability, and the community. Starting with game-play, RISE seems to have addressed some of the issues a lot of players had with World, including the Clutch Claw (CC); players had an issue with this because of how much it slowed down the combat in World, so seeing it gone and replaced with the Silkbind mechanic is a very, very good improvement on both movement and combat ability (there have been other issues that were changes, but I don't want to make this too long, so I'll give one for each subject). Next is farming, which in comparison to World, items seem to be acquired slightly faster or have better rates, which in turn makes you get your targeted items much faster. Third is enjoy-ability, to which I personally find in the uniqueness of each hunt; each monster spawns in a random spot of their locale, and it feels they can also be more aggressive, which forces players to adapt and find new ways around each monster individually, which is an amazing feeling. Finally, the community, which is so much better and nicer than the World community; not to mention, they are (in my experience) more willing to learn new things and are better overall. Great people, and I love hunting with each and every person I've met so far (except for the toxic few that I've met).Now for the downsides. So far, personally, I only have two issues. One issue is being solved in the DLC, so I wont even get into that, but the second has definitely got to be the graphics; it is a direct downgrade from World (albeit VERY beautiful) however this doesn't actually bother me much because this IS originally a Switch game, so don't get upset if the graphics are not beyond World(ly).Overall, in my experience, this game is a must-buy if you enjoyed any of the Monster Hunter games. If you're a veteran of the series, then there's no reason you shouldn't buy it. If you're new, make sure you have an experienced player help you out (or go in alone and learn, if that's what you would prefer), but don't expect everything to be catered to you, because this game is very harsh, and you can make it as easy or hard as you want by choosing your own gear and play-style. I give this game a 9.5/10, but being unbiased to the series, I would then give it a 7.5/10 since it takes time to get into.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDRAmazing game. If you are interested in Monster Hunter game, this is a good entry point. ReviewA lot of OG monster hunter fans have several issues with Monster Hunter Rise, and some of them are quite valid points. However, even if this may not meet the standard of the previous MH titles, this is still a great game, and I recommend it strongly. The main cons I agree with the OG fans are - Lack of contents : Don't misunderstand. There are still ton of contents. I already played 120 hours, and I still have a lot to do. The main issues were the absence of DLC monsters and APEX gears. And I can't quite pinpoint it, but this game feels unfinished compares to World without Iceborne. However, this is something I'm certain that Sunbreak will fix completely.  - Difficulty : Wirebug made the game a bit too easy, and CAPCOM nerfed the monsters a bit too much. Of course, Sunbreak will fix this.  - Overpowered player : This was my main problem with MH Rise. In the past MH titles, monsters were fearsome being because how limited our capabilities were. And that made the hunt more satisfying. However, with addition of Wirebug, the monster now feel more like stronger trash mobs in standard RPG game. This is not just talking about the difficulty. It's the overall atmosphere and the progression. The game is still fun, but they weren't as satisfying as they were in MH World. I'm afraid this isn't something Sunbreak will be able to fix. I hope it will though. Anyway, those three are minor cons compare to the greatness that this game offers. MH Rise might not satisfy the hardcore and extremely skilled fans, but I think MH Rise could serve as a solid bridge that brings in newcomers and more casual players. I strongly recommend MH Rise. Oh and my 6 year old Laptop with GTX960m is running this game at medium setting with 90 FPS smoothly.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - A great game, but it has both good and bad decisions. Solid 7.5 - 8 / 10. Feels like an Arcade version of Monster Hunter.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------This is the MOST grindy Monster Hunter game I have played, only bested by the JP only MMO Monster Hunter Frontier.However, there's a lot of cool ideas and there is still a lot of fun to be had. Such as the vertical movement, special attacks and if you get the Sunbreak Expansion, new basic combos for each weapon to change up your normal gameplay.The mobility is awesome with both player movement and the new dog companion being a mount. The weapons feel slick and fast. Monsters are much more active and can be incredibly aggressive now.Combat feels awesome, especially when fighting regular monsters. Hits have good weight, each weapon has many options and it's a ton of fun to land some counterattack, or a big move and have the monster stumble and fall to your mighty blow. Or maybe you tapped it with your hand and it collapsed, either way the gameplay is still as solid as ever in any Monster Hunter Title.On one hand, they're now more engaging, but on the other hand a lot of the monsters individual personalities feel lost. If you're not a completionist, the game should give you about 60-100 hours with friends easily. If you're alone, your gameplay time may vary.The endgame in Rise is mostly just fighting the same monsters you've already been fighting, but they have a titanic health pool instead of a normal one, and they hit REALLY hard. You're grinding for a specific material that only drops off this special version, but only about 2 or 3 each hunt. Then, once you grind that same monster enough, it gets stronger and now drops that same item, but STRONGER, and you have to grind that item too. It gets insanely repetitive and boring.After 100%-ing the game with my wife, I uh...I have a final statement.I have finally earned my freedom.

_childDocuments_.review: IS MONSTA HUNTA BAYBEEEDespite having only played Generations and World a little bit, I'm really having a lot of fun with RiseIt runs well on my PC, it's stylized beautifully, there's an immense level of charm and attention to detail in every aspect of the game, and I'm finally getting much more accustomed to the mechanics and gameplay loop. I didn't get super invested in World, but I'm enjoying Rise a lot more...A lot of that enjoyment probably has to do with the aesthetics(all VFXs and artstyles are pleasing), as well as the weapon choice. I enjoy myself some Hammer gameplay, and Charge Axe is cool, but Longsword is the type of gameplay I like.To this point, being able to pick your weapon(which vastly changes the gameplay mechanics) to suit your preferred playstyle(and aesthetic), as well as switch skills(moveset), feels very satisfying. The amount of customization(and fashion, after hitting lategame), get a +1 from me.The combat is reminiscent of the Souls games for me(though slower), where due to heavy animation lockout, picking your timings and good positioning becomes essential in maximizing damage uptime(getting hit = not hitting) and preserving resources(heals/buffs are semi-limited). Learning a hunt well becomes a very rewarding experience once you've got the patterns down pat. Your mileage doesn't really vary on the last point, despite all of the different weapon types, since every type has a way to create an opening, dump damage during said opening, and smaller moves to poke at the monster.Side note, using tools to incapacitate monsters is a core mechanic of hunting. Learning which monsters are vulnerable to which tools is invaluable(some monster notes do point out specific weaknesses, but said monster must be hunted first). Although I only have played a scarce amount of multiplayer, the dynamics of combining classes immediately becomes evident and satisfying. Different weapon types prefer staying at certain enemy positions. This means that either a) you have a spread of weapon types, meaning all positions are spread and each player can maximize their gameplan, or b) you have similar weapon types, meaning that the focused body part stagger is high, allowing for more damage openings. Basically, you can play around your teammates regardless of party composition.The high variety in weapon elements and armor effects creates a very deep system that requires good planning. Playing around your specific gear's strengths feels very satisfying; the only caveat being that, specifically for mid-late to lategame, grinding for gear is somewhat(or very, your  mileage may vary) necessary in order to complete armor pieces and weapons that you want for upgrades.Overall, the thematics are a 10/10(attention to detail and charm are at max), gameplay loop is satisfying and fun(but not for everyone imo), and variations in content keep the game fresh. Like Elden Ring, the game is fantastic solo, and immensely better multiplayer. I just got to the DLC 60 hours in, and I don't plan on stopping anytime soon.9/10, you get a palamute AND a palico. Only downside is that every inhabitant in Rise eats nothing but dangos. GIVE ME REAL FOOD PLEASE
