_childDocuments_.review: I had mixed feeling about the first game, which made me hold up getting this one. While playing Nirvana Initiative I quickly noticed I liked this entry much more, and it kept me entertained until the very end. It didn't reach the Zero Escape levels for me, but was very good nonetheless.This game is designed to be standalone. Even if you decide at the beginning you want to see the spoilers for the first game there are very few connections to it anyway. There's one scene in particular later on, that I think is a spoiler, and you will see it regardless of your choice at the beginning. Despite that, and despite the fact I wasn't that big fan of the first game I think it's better to play the games in order.This game is much more linear than any of the Zero Escape Team games to date. There are flowchart splits, but you're forced to choose certain path when you first do them. Only after doing the first route you're allowed to continue into the other one. This is done by giving you text-entry prompts, where you won't know the answer without certain passwords found in the story. This fixed the biggest issues with previous game, where both main routes had to repeat a lot of scenes and dialogues. And by choosing the wrong order you might have gotten into more boring route. Here the pacing is much better, and the game is allowed to explain everything only once, and grasp your attention quickly.The game has exactly the same loop as the first one. You will go to multiple locations and exhaust all the dialogue options. They will give you nearly no information on your investigation. Then you'll grab a person and enter their dreams to get actual information and move the plot forward. There is a bit of data, and a lot of character stories during those investigations, but they can still be very tiresome. The issue is you have so many rooms to go trough each time you are allowed to free roam, and it stops the story. I guess that's the vibe they wanted for this series, but I would like to see a bit more excitement in those sequences. There is some though, you don't know when characters will randomly start dancing.Similarly to the first game the main gameplay sequences are kept in Somnium, the dream worlds. I really disliked the Somnium gameplay in the first game, so I went with Story difficulty. That meant I could try stuff around in the dream world and figure out how things work. I didn't like the time mechanics, coupled with quite random and often illogical nature of Somniums. The game will give you "keys" to the somnium as you do wrong actions inside. They explain the rules of the Somnium slowly, which helps you make the right decisions. But it's all still just a guesswork, and I'm still not a big fan of the regular dream worlds.Fortunately later on the game introduces new elements into the gameplay. Again, thanks to more linear story, they can introduce those elements as the story progresses. Later on you'll be able to gather items and use them, or have to solve escape-room like puzzles. Unfortunately this is all tacked on a bit, so there are issues with the UI. In Zero Escape games when you collected certain items you could review them anytime, to solve puzzles. In Nirvana you have no way to access those items while in text input screens. So if you go to the password menu and see it has 8 characters, and notice you haven't figured it out yet the only way to get out of it is to cancel. But then the characters will discuss the password and spoil the solution for you. That made me just screenshot all the hints, and then view them trough steam screenshots... I wanted to solve the puzzles on my own.There is also a new additional game mode - VR investigation. In those sections you'll control one of the protagonists - Mizuki or Ryuki, and you'll be able to use thermo vision and x-ray vision to uncover secrets on the crime scenes. Then once you gather enough knowledge you'll be asked to retrace the steps of the criminal, and answer some crime-related questions. I found those to be fun and engaging, but again, you couldn't access the hints trough the UI. So you'll see a full-screen pop-up showing you a hint you've collected, but then you have no way to review them. One of the hidden room puzzles is really hard to solve without ability to check the items...This game re-uses a lot of characters and locations from the first game. Many of them are completely unchanged from the original, which makes the sequel feel a bit cheap. I felt like maybe 30% of the scenes you could go to were new places. Even some Somniums are based on locations from the first game. For example one Somnium uses So residence reskin. Even though the game happens in 6 years timespan the places don't change. You'll visit the same restaurant, and it will have exactly the same menu, exactly the same posters, and exactly the same looking character, with no changes in their looks. There are only handful of NPCs that show any signs of aging. It all gives the feeling of a pretty low budget. Or they used it all for the dance sequence.As usual for the writer Kotaro Uchikoshi later on there are big twists and turns. Without spoiling anything, this wasn't my favourite twist. It matches the game themes, and makes some sense, and even explains some creative decisions, but still it felt a bit cheap. I liked the revelations from Virtue's Last Reward and Zero Time Dilemma much better.The game looks really good. The load times are instant. The backgrounds are on a simple side, but they are packed to the brim with objects. The character models are very well made, although they are animated in a bit of a stiff style. I also really dig the music.The game, as usual for Zero Escape Team, concerns itself with some sci-fi and supernatural elements. You get discussions of the world possibly being a simulation, and many scientific and para-scientific factoids are referred trough the game. I really liked the ideas explored in this game, although I with there was more focus on it. There are also some things that happen that require huge suspension of disbelief. Some of the characters from the first game take a backseat this time, but others appear fairy often. You'll be able to meet most of the old gang, and if you haven't played the first game you might get a little lost. Now as for spoilers. Notice that those are TOTAL SPOILERS, that will discuss ALL THE SECRETS. Do not read unless you completed the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I personally feel this is an improvement on the original in several ways. Firstly, it answers a lot of unanswered questions from the first game. Secondly, it's designed to avoid the issue in the first game where you constantly hit on dead ends until you stumbled into the one route you're supposed to do first to unlock another route, which would unlock another route, etc. This game requires you to discover things that unlock new routes at certain points in the game so you never end up trying to keep track of multiple route events at once.The characters are a mix of old and new, and I find it hard to find any real fault in them.The Somnia are a bit weaker than last game, being generally easier and with fewer excess options. This makes them easier and a bit less entertaining.Story-wise, I think this one is marginally more interesting than the first game. I liked both a lot, but this one is a bit easier to follow once you understand the twists, whilst keeping them unexpected.

_childDocuments_.review: A disappointing follow up to what I had considered a really good game. Characters were bland and returning cast had been reduced to caricatures. The twist lacked any gravitas, with the developers seeming to say "gotcha" rather than deliver anything satisfying. Action scenes were excessive, boring and many were unnecessary except to show off Mizuki's only character trait. Many of the assets from the first game were reused for this game and the new locations they added had the same magic of a default Unity map. Wasted my money, should have left it at the first game. I am not interested in a third game if they continue to deliver this kind of lackluster writing and story.

_childDocuments_.review: Nirvana Initiative is another great visual novel game by Kotaro Uchikoshi. The soundtrack is just as good as the first AI Somnium Files game, if not a bit better. The voice acting is top-notch, just like in the previous game. The animations were improved upon from the first game, which is nice. The graphics are good enough for a visual novel game. Granted, I don't personally care too much about graphics in the first place. I found the somniums to be more interesting than the previous game, but I also found them to be a bit too easy when it came down to ending with more than a second remaining. I basically never even worried about running out of time, unless I was screwing around just to see what would happen.  The humor in this game is on the level as the previous game, which is, in my opinion, some top-tier witty writing.Ryuki and Mizuki are great main characters; although I personally prefer Date. I like that the sequel decided to have different characters get the limelight, though.I opine that the story is more interesting than the previous game, but I think a very particular twist in the game could've been handled a lot better than it was. Without spoiling anything, this particular twist didn't seem to have any hints towards it at all, unlike in the previous game, where all twists were hinted at. This big "twist" came off as more confusing than a mind ♥♥♥♥. The only other "twist" I found an issue with was one regarding a specific character, which I don't think holds up particularly well against a magnifying glass. These somewhat lackluster twists are done more poorly than in the first game, at least in my opinion.I found the branching paths to be inferior when compared to the first game too. The branching paths from the first game had more diverse endings that always left you with questions that could only be answered by continuing to play through the game. The branching paths in this game are all entirely just character driven. By character driven, I mean the branching paths just focus on a very specific supporting character or two and almost always give them a happy ending, but they don't actually do anything in service to the overall plot of the game, unlike in the previous title. It's nice to see a supporting character get more screen time and development, but if it doesn't do ♥♥♥♥ for the plot, then it's kind of just irrelevant. The first game's branching paths built upon the story, left you with questions, and also developed the supporting character, or characters, in question.My final criticism is with the ending battle scene, which was filled with a bit too much fanservice and plot armor. Without getting into spoilers, all I'm saying, is that everyone except for Ryuki, Mizuki, Masked Woman, and Date didn't need to be there. You could've had the same conclusion without the other people.Anyway, Nirvana Initiative is a genuinely great visual novel game. I just think it falls a bit short narratively when compared to its predecessor, but that all comes down to personal opinion. I consider the first AI: The Somnium Files game to be a 10/10. I give this one an 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to the first game, the story is bigger in scope, but not as well told. Without spoiling - I'm not sure what to think about the "twist" in this one. Is it stupid, or brilliant? Or brilliantly stupid? I dunno.There's still anime tropes gallore - maybe even too much at times (looking at you, Date). And the gameplay, while better in some aspects, has some really unnecessary additions - who really wanted a tamagochi-style mini-game that's only used for farming in-game currency to unlock in-game costumes and two achievements?And why can't I HOLD DOWN the skip button like in the first game to click through already read/picked choices without stopping? Now the skip button stops working after a dialogue box sequence ends, so you have to awkwardly re-hold the skip button down every time you click on a new thing or a character, just to skip already read dialogue! It's annoying!Overall, a low 7/10, or a high 6/10. Even with all of it's annoyances, I still really like this game. Not as much as the first one, though.

_childDocuments_.review: I love team Zero Escape's work, I like investigating and the branching stories and everything. But I gotta say I am creeped out by the societal implications of the fundamental feature of this game. Syncing. In this game, you're a cop. You can "wink sync" someone to read their thoughts. And you routinely arrest people of interest --not even suspects-- for hours at a time, take them back to your lab attach them to a machine that forces them to go to sleep, where you can connect and go into their dreams. I have played about 7 hours and I am conflicted. I find it quite troubling the lack of concern for the consent and rights of these people to have the cops plug into their minds. Like it's fantastic, love it, very fun, but damn guys. Like, yikes.

_childDocuments_.review: Kotaru Uchikoshi at his best. Building on top of the world he introduced in the original Somnium Files, he delivers a compelling mixture of mystery and well-grounded scifi which culminates around 90% into the storyline with an absolutely astonishing, carefully crafted and surgically executed PLOT TWIST that is impossible to arrange in any other media.Now, mind you. I played lots of mystery VNs. I eat 4th-wall-breaking stories for breakfast every day. I'm even familiar with most other Kotaru's works. But the defining point of this story left me completely astonished for HOURS.Sure, it's a very controversial plot twist, and while I loved how unique was the way it interacted with my expectations, you will see in other reviews that some players even found its mechanics insulting. But like it or not, you have to appreciate the storywriting effort required to pull that off. I say this game is worth playing through just to admire how every seemingly unimportant part of the story was designed to match precisely, like a piece of a puzzle, into the larger narrative. Every detail has its purpose, to come crushing down on you when you finally uncover the real mystery.Unfortunately, these surprises constrained the story heavily in some areas. In particular, character development suffers a lot. You will spend lots of time with familiar friends from the original game, but don't expect them to grow too much.Those two most perverted characters from Somnium Files return, but are given much less screen time, so there are significantly less sex jokes - which is a major improvement of this sequel. I'd say there is much less anime cringe overall too, but you're still required to watch an absolutely mega cringe song not three, not four, but five separate times!English VAs are amazing. Sadly, Date's back to (minor AI:TSA spoiler) , but we get much more of Mizuki, whose VA steals the show again - but Aiba and Boss are back too, and I was also impressed by the voice work for Tama and Ryuki, the two new characters.The Somnias are significantly simpler and less challenging than in the first game of the series, but this game doesn't pretend it offers difficult puzzles, so that's fair.The game makes it look like it's possible to play it without knowing the story of the original, and I suppose it's kinda true, but don't do that. Being familiar with characters and the fictional world is absolutely necessary to enjoy the story. The sequel skims through all the concepts introduced in the first game, and therefore it gets confusing and hard-to-follow unless you already understand how AI-balls, Psync Syncs, Revolvers, ABISS etc. work.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy where do I even begin. The NirvanA Initiative is... a mess. A total, completely bonkers dessert after AI1's main course. An Uchikoshi-salad, if you will.And this time around, just not as good. I have to be honest here, I was torn up to the very last second if I should give it a positive or negative review, but I feel like I need to make a statement. I've been one of Mr Uchikoshi's fans for years and I diligently support every product he puts out (you know, beside ZTD, which I still regret giving a positive review in retrospect) and as a loyal fan I feel like its important to be vocal when it actually matters.To start off, it's important to note that this game isnt directed by Uchikoshi himself, as opposed to the original AI1. He was only responsible for the scenario, just like in Ever17. And the difference is night and day.I entered this adventure well aware of this fact. When you dont see Uchikoshi quoted as "Director" things get a little weird.Indeed, this is the case here. The NirvanA Initiative has his name written all over it, but its being handled by someone with dissimilar priorities. In other words, the execution.In my old review of AI1 I framed it as being "okay". With that, I meant no disrespect to Uchikoshi's vision: when he's got the wheel, he can steer the ship whenever he wants and the magic just happens. He has a very peculiar way of writing those 2 characters he's actually comfortable with, and the chemistry, multi-layered facets of their personality and playful banter is always on point. Whether its Sigma and Phi, Junpei and Akane or Date and Aiba, he's got it. You want to see and hear their interactions, solve mysteries and puzzles together, get to know them and see for yourself what kind of whacky story he'll pull out of his rear this time.In Nirvana Initiative however... you cannot do that. Because the magic isnt there. What Uchikoshi does best, beside writing about escape rooms and their freaky puzzles, is building up personal stories, smaller in scale but then explosive at the end, with big reveals and twists. Nirvana Initiative has none of that, despite the stakes being increasingly higher till the final climax.But lets start with some positives, because there are quite a few.First, there's more to do in the Somnium. There are new collectibles which unlock specific outfits and a minigame.The Somnium themselves have seen a major upgrade. No longer will the player randomly click on everything hoping for the best, in a world where there's literally no logic to it. You can clearly tell where to go and what to do, even when in doubt you have ample margin to try again and get hints at every corner. Somniums themselves are way shorter and smaller in size which could be argued is not strictly a positive, but I found it refreshing. It is much easier to tolerate them and even enjoy exploring.The VN sections have seen a good deal of adjustments as well. They are all shorter and intuitive, you'll just have to exhaust every option available in a dialogue and move on to the next area. Whenever a major twist happens, there will be intermissions addressing the player character with a large recap of events and double summary checks to ensure beyond a shadow of a doubt that they've got it right. Moreover, the hints to the big reveals are far easier to spot and truly scattered everywhere in Nirvana Initiative compared to the first game. This may be another point of contention, as not all will find it a good thing. But I for once welcomed it. None of the major twists felt like a total asspull... for a while.The visual aspect of the game has also seen a major upgrade. Scenarios look much better, the lighting has seen a large overhaul, as well as texturing and  choreography of the action scenes. The team finally got it, if they dont have the budget to show something too elaborate, DONT show it. Combat sections are still really silly, but at least it feels less amateurish.And now, for the negatives, which to me outweigh the positive by a large margin.As I've mentioned before, Uchikoshi's writing is at its best when the focus is on character interactions and personal stories. He just nails that childish playful banter between a strong male and female protagonists, he builds up tension, expectation, love-hate relationships, he gets their thoughts across well, and can give them crazy traits while still maintaining their personalities grounded in reality just enough to make them believable. When the time comes to be serious, they cooperate as a team and do their job. In other words, really good chemistry. Nirvana Initiative has none of that. The new characters Ryuki and Tama have too little time to develop any meaningful relationship, bits and pieces of Ryuki's past seemingly give no background whatsoever beside some silly one liners on the side, and he's overall unidimensional, submissive and boring. Tama is just barely above that.Granted she has more screentime than him which is ridiculous, but that's just part of the problem. They are not written to be the protagonists in their own game. Moreover, the "real" protagonists of the adventure - Mizuki and Aiba - are not written to work with one another. They are two strangers interacting with each other for a brief period of time and it feels like they never truly connect as partners nor as people. Aiba is the foil to Date's perverted self, but Mizuki cant be like that. Likewise, Mizuki cant be a foil for anything Aiba related as her story arc is already complete.Whenever the characters have nothing interesting to say or do, the game throws at the player one of two things: a 2 minutes long song that features cute girls dancing, or a combat scene with obnoxious QTEs. ...and given how little the characters actually have to say to one another, you can expect both occurrences quite a few times, also cranked up to 11, much to the player's annoyance.The results are predictable: adding to the already boring interactions and nonexistent banter between Aiba and Mizuki, or the very mild relationship between Ryuki and Tama, the Somniums and investigations being shorter and A LOT more linear than the previous game become a problem. Suddenly we have a super linear, less interactive, on-rails approach to the usual Uchikoshi formula which this time around doesnt even require actual thought on the player's part, as almost everything is spelled out for them if not outright solved by the characters themselves.Regarding the structure of the story: we are looking at  all over again. No  thi time around, beside a very mild mention which is never addressed again. As for the flowchart, it has been created to accomodate the game's mechanics. The story itself is being altered to fit the gameplay, while in the prequel the situation was reversed. Now the locks are incredibly easy to reach and open via a single thread.The director tries to toy with the idea that multiple timelines akin to the Nonary games can be superimposed to 's own plot devices, but that is not as effective here. On the contrary, if the player has finished the previous game, the concept of timeline alteration which should be very familiar suddenly has a completely different meaning.The only "new" element is that Blick Winkel is back at it once more. It's like taking a dusty old hat out of the closet from 20 years prior and putting it back on without so much of a sweep to get rid of the most obvioust dust marks.That is not to say I didnt like it, but it's existence came kinda out of nowhere and at present has no explanation.All in all, a pity indeed. Regardless, I'm looking forward to the next game which will conveniently exclude the plot points of this one beside the last 30 minutes. Hopefully that one will be directed by Uchikoshi himself and some more lessons will be learned. For now, two steps forward, one jump back.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really liked the first game. That one had a very meticulously written story, where as you uncovered more clues it would put everything else you'd seen so far into a different perspective. Almost every little detail mattered, if only to contextualize some of the characters' actions.nirvanA Initiative is, unfortunately, the complete opposite of that. 75 % of what's happening on screen is entirely irrelevant to the central story of the game. And it's immediately obvious as well, not just after the fact.The Somnium parts in particular are incredibly disappointing. They were THE central plot element in the first game in order to uncover the truth and push the story forward, while still keeping you guessing more than halfway through. In this game, however, they are basicly just gameplay parts for the sake of having gameplay. You spend half an hour listening to a random one-dimensional character's inner feelings which has no bearing on anything. And then, if you're lucky, you get one little sentence or detail at the very end or even after the Somnium that contains relevant information for the murder cases. Except, more often than not, it's something you already knew or figured out from contextual clues. Because the game is all but subtle and likes to pretend it didn't literally just tell you that exact thing several hours ago.Learning about the new characters and their motivations is nice and all, but how much can you really care about characters that have just about 0 plot relevance up until the game finds an extremely contrived way to shoehorn them into the story. Seriously, there is a moment where one character steals a dead body they find. Who in their right mind finds the victim of a murder case and goes like "Hm, I should take this with me and try to blackmail the killer", while having absolutely no idea who the culprit even is!?It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like that that surrounds every one of the new characters to give a false sense of plot complexity.AI: The Somnium File - nirvanA Initiative is, by all means, an extremely simple one or two hour story at its core, stretched to 30+ hours of gameplay and cutscenes. Worst of all, there is essentially no mystery. There is nothing to figure out, nothing to unravel, no foreshadowing, no clever twist. Everything that happens is either entirely obvious or completely redundant. As I said, 75% is meaningless filler. Another 20% are additions that solely exist to fool the player and for absolutely no other reasons. Like, the big twist literally only affects the player. It's the Uchikoshi thing again, where the plot has to bend over backwards to try and find the most contrived reasons to have ever been imagined to hide the utterly pointless twist from the player. For almost the entire game it keeps you wondering why there are so many ginormous and obvious plot holes that just keep piling up. To the point where you just can't give a ♥♥♥♥ about anything anymore and just want it to end.And then the big reveal is dropped ...... and it doesn't change anything. It just explains why the story telling is so unbelievably ♥♥♥♥ in many instances, while simultaneously leaving even bigger plot holes unexplained. It doesn't change the player's perspective in any substantial way. Watching or playing through key parts of the story again with knowledge of the twist just makes it even worse, while adding a "well, they sure got me there, hu" moment every now and then. I can't stress this enough. The characters have to try so hard to hide information from the player. None of which they have any reason whatsoever to do. Not that it's acknowledged at any point. They just do what they do and say what they say. It's the same thing that bugs me about the Zero Escape series. It's like Uchikoshi is fully aware of the rules of mystery story telling and then goes out of his way to break every single one of them. And it makes it look like the story was written by a 6 year old.There is a scene in the game where the detective knows that one person saw the culprit's face. Like, they know for sure. The first time this person is interrogated is 6 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ years later! Nothing in the game can explain the level of incompetence here.There is another moment where the culprit is literally surrounded and incapacitated and their face is revealed to the good guys. Then the scene just ends abruptly with no conclusion. The next time the culprit is mentioned is when they already got away and the good guys are looking for them again. ??????????It's amateurish, is all I can say about this.Honestly, if you liked the first game, don't buy this one until it's AT LEAST 50% off. I can't really recommend it.

Honestly it hurts to say it because the amount of work and dedication that was poured to make it work must be enormous, but it just didn't feel as interesting, and at some point the yarn ball falls apart as you unravel it.The characters had some great highlights and some less interesting ones, with a pretty disappointing It also suffered from a case of mcguffin eggs, where you'd have motivations and events happen to justify what justifies those to begin with, not really having a reason beyond "because it's needed to explain this".On a more meta side, I wished we'd see the After weighing it all, the quality of the somnia and some highlight characters make me lean in favor that it's worth it despite the flaws. _childDocuments_.review: My game of the year. It trumps the first game in almost every aspect except comedy. While the first game is funnier, this game still has funny moments and it's a step up in both (new) characters and story telling, which is more important to me. This game has two downsides, the biggest downside to the game is that they wanted to make this game accessible to people who haven't played the first, which was not the right call in my opinion, it leads to questions you may have where you think "whatever happened to this thing, or that character?" This happened multiple times throughout the game, and I didn't get my first question answered until 4 hours into the game.The other downside is that the character dynamic between Mizuki and Aiba is not nearly as strong as Date's and Aiba's from the first game. You will likely enjoy playing as Ryuki and Tama far more, as their character dynamic is on par with (if not greater than) Date and Aiba from the previous game.Despite the downsides, it's (new) characters and story are extremely memorable for me, much more than the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel nobody asked for to a visual novel that already worked really well as a self contained story (though you don't *really* need to play the original game since the game even asks you if you want to turn off spoilers from the 1st one).Is it better or worse? Honestly I'd say it's 1 step forward and 2 steps back. The story pretty much changed from a murder mystery to a sci-fi police thriller if that makes any sense. The twist while foreshadowed felt like it came out of left field because of the amount of contrived coincidences and the like for it to work, though on the plus side it made me want to read it again to catch the details so good work on that I guess? On the other hand the pacing began to feel repetitive around the halfway point and the fact that you're pretty much locked to a specific order of endings due to having "information gates" in every single branching path makes it feel way too restrictive.In terms of the quality of the story besides what I've already said, its...alright? Sans 1 or 2 things that happened nothing really left me with a sense of "THAT'S SO STUPID WHY WOULD YOU THINK THAT WAS A GOOD IDEA?" The old characters were still good to interact with but some of the new ones are pretty hit or miss. At the same time the plot feels way less personal than in the original one (sans for 1 or 2 characters) since it sorta kinda happens to them if it makes any sense, so a lot of the scenes didn't have much emotional impact.In terms of gameplay the Somnias do feel better this time around due to having a better hint system and the answers actually following a better logical sense so you'll end up banging you head against the wall way less than in some of the original Somnias. However the amount of QTEs with the same music repeated did become obnoxious after some time. Also some parts really fall down into the pixel hunt annoyance from adventure games (which I'm pretty sure it was also in the original but it felt way worse this time around).Though at the end of the day despite all the shortcomings I still enjoyed my time with the game, though I really don't want to replay it anytime soon, if ever.TL;DR. Worse than the original but still enjoyable (at least to a point). Still WAAAAAAAAAAY better than Zero Time Dilemma.Rating so far from this and Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward > 999 = Somnium Files > Nirvana Initiative >>>>>>>>> Zero Time Dilemma

_childDocuments_.review: I really hate to say this since I love Uchikoshi and his games. The first AI game is one of my favorite video games of all time. But this game does not compare in the slightest to the first game. Ryuki's side was pretty good, but Mizuki's side was pure garbage, and that's a shame since the game wants us to put more thought/effort into Mizuki. This game was honestly just disappointing. _childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed the first game, was looking forward to this one but can't wholly recommend it. The largest positive in the sequel is the production value which has gone up tremendously, especially in character animations and overall visual quality. The crux of this game, and the series, is wholly dependent on whether or not you find the characters, and more importantly, the plot engaging. At the end of the day, I believe I liked both more in the first game than the second, even though a lot the characters from the first title reoccur. From the first sequence I was a bit put off by the killer in this sequel. While the first game featured the Cyclops Serial Killings, an antagonist who would remove the right eyes of their victim, this title features a killer that vertically cuts one half of their victims' bodies, down to the molecular level. While this might seem like a gruesome feat, it comes off as more bugs bunny comedy than silence of the lambs. The pacing of the story is pretty bad. A slow-burn detective story where clues come in drips, works for a 2 hour movie, or even a season-long narrative such as true detective, feels like a frustrating chore in this narrative. You will go into preset stages to speak with npcs, but one out of every 4 dialogue choices has the possibility of getting anything that will move the story along. It wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't for the fact that in a lot of scenes, you have to exhaust all possible dialogue choices including exposition narratives about a character you may not care about before the game allows you to exit out of the scene to choose another place in the map to repeat the cycle. At some point your superior tells you "don't worry, if you can find this person you will crack the case!" only to have 15 separate locations pop up on your map, forcing you to visit each one and speak to everyone in the scene before continuing. At some point in the game you will narrow down a lead, inexplicably getting them into a machine that allows you to access their memories through a convoluted process. Often times there's no segway conversation between sets, nothing that shows the person agreed to this enhanced interrogation - it's literally "hi, I want to talk to you... you're comatose? no problem!" then a cut-scene to you and the witness sitting in a chair in a lab. While on the surface you feel like the 30 minutes spent solving completely obscure puzzles will get you closer to an answer, the reality is that many times you're unable to confront the person with the knowledge you gain from these sequences, as they will be unresponsive, or vague, even in the face of direct questioning. After 5, 10 hours, the process is just frustrating as your boss threatens to demote you for not cracking this complex case in 24 hours, your witnesses are on the verge of cracking before some outside force conveniently halts their testimony leaving you with a modicum of information, or your mentor pops in every once in a while to literally say "I know who's behind all of this but I got better things to do I'll tell you later". At times it makes you feel like you're the only person in the city that cares about the case at all. In the first 2/3rd of the game you'll spend your time with Tama, your AI companion. Her personality is great, and she brings some well-deserved chemistry with Ryuki as they try to uncover this mystery. Unfortunately, unlike Aiba, the protagonists AI in the first game, Tama is inexplicably outfitted with DD breasts and a police officer cosplay outfit as if she was attracting customers in a red-light district. After 5 hours of unnecessary up-skirt shots while rotating the camera in an attempt to search for clues that were hidden behind Tama's comically large breasts, I desperately fumbled through the menu using my eyeball currency to buy every costume imaginable to cover the girl up. Thankfully, one out of the eight or so costumes that were unlocked had a sweater and a pair of pants, but the only time it was applicable was in the Somnium sequences.If you've read this far and it hasn't turned you off of the game, buy it. It's your title. For me, I feel like the story, characters, and pacing of the first game were superior to this one, and can't fully recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been anticipating this sequel for a while since I'm a big fan of the original game and thus wanted to get my hands on this gem as soon as I could. Fortunately, in my opinion, the hype wasn't for nothing and I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing this game. Nevertheless, I do have my qualms about some parts of the game and will briefly gloss over them in this spoiler-free review, while also mentioning what I think makes this game so great.The bad:- First things first, you shouldn't play this game if you're looking for the most graphically pleasing interactive experience. Don't get me wrong, the environments are pretty nice and the looks are far, far, FAR better than those of a crappy roblox game, but to be fair, the expressions of the characters aren't very well-made. They look pretty weird sometimes when idle and do even more weird stuff when the character speaks. The lip-syncing also seems like it has a delay which doesn't make face movements any better. Moreover the braids of Mizuki tend to glitch sometimes, leaving a weird strand of blue through the portrait. Though saying all this, I gotta admit it really didn't bother me a lot during the game and it's not like you look at the character's face that much while they're speaking since you'll mostly be reading the text.- Fighting sequences and QTE events don't feel right. It's hard to describe, but you'll definitely know when you see it for yourself. They look pretty awkward and have weird pauses that don't feel logical at all. Also the buttons used for the QTE events are so random you basically have to look at your keyboard every time they pop up.- In a certain somnium at a certain time, the game tries to go with something resembling stealth. I'm not gonna say much more since I don't wanna spoil anything, but you'll know when you get there. This section absolutely ground my gears and despite liking the game a lot, I almost quit then and there. The only thing keeping me going was the music at that point. I don't consider myself to be an irritable person, but this section drove me nuts. But don't worry about it too much, this was the only tiny part of the game that was really annoying to me.The in-between:- The game features a kind of weird sense of humour, just like the first game. Personally, I liked it, but I've heard some people are put off by the timing and context of the weird jokes. If you liked the humour in the first game, then you don't have to worry about a thing. Keep in mind though that if you notice you don't like the humour of the game the first few times, it won't get any better.- There are certain segments in which people will dance and sing. It doesn't happen a lot, but  enough for you to say "Again?". Gotta say, it's not my jam, but to each their own.Side Note: For those who particularly hate them; they're skippable.The good:- The attention to detail the devs implemented here is insane. I already had high standards because of the first game, but I'm still blown away every time. I'm not giving any examples because that would lead to spoiler territory real quick, but you'll definitely see for yourself.- The writing is impeccable. No words to describe it. Just give Uchikoshi his two horses already.- They improved some of the somnium mechanics of the first game while keeping the same atmosphere.- Contrary to the facial expressions I mentioned earlier, the voice-acting is great.- The music is also incredible. They recycled some of the better tracks of the first game and used them in the current one (an example being the music at the kumakura office, nothing too major like reusing entire themes) but added a lot of new tracks too which slap just as hard as the first game. Beware that if you consider buying the soundtrack of this game that the tracks used in the previous game but were reused in this one aren't included in the OST DLC for this game! (at least as far as I know, if this is wrong please correct me)- You can ask Kaniza's name even more than ever before.All in all I'm really glad I bought the game even though it's priced this high, since it was absolutely worth it to me. I hope this game suits your tastes and that you will have a great time playing it if you considered to buy it after all.I wish you the most wonderful of times playing this game and solving its bizarre mystery!

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like the relationship this game has to its predecessor is very similar to that between VLR and 999:From a technical standpoint, it improves in a lot of ways - Somnia, which I thought were generally pretty tedious in the last game, are now much more playable, with their underlying themes and logic being simultaneously more straightforward and more interesting (if maybe a bit overcorrected to linearity). Both in and out of Somnia, the player is tasked with a lot more direct deductions, which feel quite satisfying to nail (although if you can't get one your progress grinds to a halt because the hints are never helpful).Narratively, the story is much bigger, which is a curse as much as it is a blessing. The central twist is much bigger, and must have required a genius-level amount of engineering to write around even if it hangs off of some obvious contrivances, but it feels like a lot was sacrificed in setting it up. There's a bit in the first game where (AITSF spoilers)  AITSF could never be accused of taking itself too seriously, but it knew how to suspend your disbelief enough to actually care about what was going on, and managed to deliver some actual emotional beats despite its absurdity. When this one tried to do the same thing, it elicited either a groan or a fit of laughter every time.I think this boils down to characterization, mostly. Every character in AI had their own thing going on, which caused them to affect the plot in different ways. I think the new cast in Nirvana Initiative is still quite likable on the micro level, but their arcs basically all boil down to "how could I  be loved when I have [NEGATIVE TRAIT]???" which gets repetitive fast and only has a satisfying resolution once. This isn't helped by the returning cast, who (aside from Mizuki and Aiba) don't have anything to do except take up screen time rehashing their inside jokes from the prior game (which, to be fair, I still laughed at most of the time). The game tries to make it very clear that you don't need to have played AITSF first to jump in, but I'd still recommend doing so, if only so you don't spend this game wondering why half the cast seems completely superfluous.Do I recommend it, in the end? Yes, but I think it really depends on not just  you liked AISTF, but . It's sort of like DRV3 in that respect - if you embrace the anime nonsense for what it is, you'll probably love it, but if you're actually invested in the existing world and story you might come away more frustrated than entertained.

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to dictate my thoughts from speech to text so forgive me if this is illegible. I would say I had a good time with this game. I think that I love what this game is trying to achieve more-so than what it delivers. For example, we have these action scenes that take place which are glorified quick time action events. Now sometimes these can be fun because it breaks up the monotony of what we're reading and adds action to certain scenes and engagement for the player. However, I didn't find that with these ones and if anything found myself just wanting them to be over with. I think there are two reasons for this. The first is that they failed to go for the spectacle in these fight scenes and a lot of them felt very repetitive due to the “Action, get surrounded, another character has your back, action resumes” dirge these scenes became. The second is that I felt they undermined what the story was trying to achieve. For example, Ace Attorney is a fantastic visual novel game that is able to keep you engrossed with the level of storytelling available in the courtroom drama. It doesn't need to cut away to some jammed in action because we haven't had a fight scene in a while. I think the sooner Spike Chunsoft learn this lesson with this medium the better these games will be. (Which I find crazy to say because some of their earlier works don't ham-fist action scenes in because it's unnecessary and would ruin the tension of the story and yet with this game they kind of do it which doesn't really make a lot of sense.)All of that being said, I think this games overall story is better and arguably has a better twist than the first. I didn't see it coming and was ecstatic to be taken by surprise. There are a myriad of twists and turns which are all fantastic. My main critique would be its use of troops and the fact that it undermines some of its master level storytelling with cringey applications of cliches. Think of the classic “these characters are perverts” which dominates some Japanese narratives. To an eastern audience this may be funny, but I think undermines the credibility of the story they're trying to tell which as I have said multiple times before, I think is a stroke of genius. If a story like this was told without those cliches I think it would receive a lot more praise and would be something I would wholeheartedly creatively cheer for. I'd also like to quickly mention that the humour in this game is plentiful with multiple jokes getting a verbal and physical reaction from me balanced by pop culture references which I can’t really hold against the game. I think this message has gone on long enough and I could probably sit here and say even more yet I think anymore and I would become a cliche in which my own critique would be valid to levy against me.I leave with this, both of these games are worth playing. Neither of them are worth taking seriously. I love them equally as much as I love High School Musical too. And for the record, High School Musical 2 sucks and I love that film. How’s that for taste?

_childDocuments_.review: As a standalone game I might have been able to accept nirvanA Initiative, but as a sequel this really does not work for me.It's hard to get into a lot of the complaints I have without giving spoilers, but the story keeps you in a state of confusion for the majority of your time with it. You push forward hoping for the big revelation or twist that makes up for it. And as expected, there are a couple of major ones, but instead of an a-ha! Moment if feels like you’ve been trolled. It’s one thing if a character in the story is unreliable but here, the game design itself actively misleads the player about several key elements of the plot and so much of the story was written around this gimmick that it doesn't feel coherent by the end, at which point I had mostly checked out.Sure it's fine to look back later and figure things out, maybe even a little satisfying but I feel like you’d almost have to play the whole thing again when it’s still fresh in your mind to get the full experience and that’s a lot to ask of a player. The original game was enjoyable at any given time just from the investigation and character interactions- it didn’t feel like you were always waiting for some massive revelation to keep the player motivated. Even more problematic for me are the way the characters from the original game are used in the sequel. Some are there for flavor and don’t get to do enough. Others act really out of character from what we saw from the first game’s ending. There are some major things we learn in AI2 which we are expected to believe those characters in AI1 already knew during the first game, which just doesn’t add up. I would go as far as to say that it tarnishes that experience if you let it, so I’m doing my best to consider this a separate entity or alternate canon. On the plus side, they did a better job with the gameplay elements this time around. There are more somniums, they are more varied in terms of gameplay and puzzle solving, there’s a lot less random trial and error, and they feel more like dreams these characters might be having.I may have to revisit the game eventually for further analysis but right now I’m having trouble seeing past my disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Play the first game  instead, as it's a pretty fun Uchikoshi adventure VN with light gameplay sections, a tight cast and a decent multiple route murder mystery to keep you entertained, that with few exceptions stays mostly down the earth without venturing too far into the loony zone. It also works completely standalone and didn't particularly leave anything hanging for a sequel. If you instead hate yourself, play .Nirvana Initiative's plot manages to be less intense in terms of drama compared to the first AI Somnium Files, while simultaneously amping up the number of extremely arbitrary plot contrivances to move things along, suspension of disbelief and tone breaking moments (especially during the infamous QTE action scenes), and several very convoluted major twists that appear to exist solely for the sake of having twists. Would-be plotholes concerning central mysteries on the other hand get quickly handwaved away with a handful of sentences. This game's story feels like the writer was grasping at straws to forcefully come up with another variation of one of his famous  twists, except this time it's given next to no actual in-universe plot justification to be included, nor does it affect any of the actual characters and major parts of the main story. It's random crap stitched together with a glue.The new characters aren't particularly likable enough to carry the story, while old ones don't get developed in an interesting way either that factors in their experiences from the first game, as the game (by the intro's own explicit admission) exists in this weird limbo where the devs wanted to satisfy both the old fans and rope in a new audience: thus the events of the previous game are given only lip service. However, I'd wager the stuff that is featured here (such as reappearing suspects) is enough to spoil several parts of the previous game for newcomers, without giving enough screen time and context for said characters and their relations to make their appearance in this game integral to the main plot, or to make them appeal to new people. Same is true for some of the first game's major plot mechanics and locations. Both old fans and newcomers lose. The devs should've either turned this game into a proper sequel that requires playing the first AI Somnium Files, or a completely different story with a new cast taking place in the same setting, with maybe a reference or two to the previous game.Actual gameplay sections were probably the worst part of the first game, and Nirvana Initiative hasn't really developed them that much further to make them enjoyable. Time limits and puzzles still do not go particularly well together, especially since the devs' apparent solution to combining the two was to make the latter very easy and potentially brute-forceable, only tempered by some amount of dream moon logic and potentially wasted time in between. Route structure is also less interesting than the first game due to increased linearity, and many of this game's short non-canon routes feel like increased padding for the sake of various twist deliveries that could have been easily put into the main storyline, rather than being proper alternative endings in themselves.If you want actual brain teasers (and a better plot), play the writer's 999 series instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Where Nirvana falters in comparison to Somnium is in its character building and overall pacing; however, these are facets that were toned to near perfection beforehand, and are only 'pretty good' now. Where Nirvana flies way over Somnium, and most other games I've played, is in the deliberate and meticulous structure of its narrative, paving the way for twists that eclipse any and all expectations I held going in.I absolutely hated Nirvana when I began; I disliked the way it handled many of Somnium's cast, and I really bristled against the new player character. However, by the time the (real) credits rolled, I was applauding these same components, and now speak just as reverently of Nirvana as I do the original game, maybe even more so. Saying I can't wait for a third game is a severe, borderline offensive, understatement. Absolute masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Mori's 3-Part Review:1. Bare minimum information and recommendations to improve your playthrough2. Background information on me and my playthrough3. More extensive non-spoiler reactions Part 1: Recommendations for YouIf you're like me and you try to get all the extra scene dialogue, then please, if you take nothing else from this, give yourself time to play this game yourself. There is actually so much content here, I really want you all to take your time to experience it as you go. The game is just too long to binge in a reasonably short amount of time, and if you do binge, you're going to lose a lot. My recommendations:1. Give yourself time to play the game. Let it sink in, and take notes- it'll be rewarded. The game is literally too dense and too long to binge reasonably if you like 100%ing. 2. Get invested in the characters and pay attention to them, not just the (admittedly stellar) mysteries. 3. Explore the game, its mechanics, and its dialogue yourself. Don't be afraid to restart a Somnium several times; the more options you pick, the more meaningful information you get. 4. If you're a puzzle lover then try to solve the game yourself. You're going to have a blast if you manage it, and the game has tons of built-in hint systems to make it even easier, fairer, and more fun. 5. Try to go in knowing at little as you can. The marketing has already done a great job. Focus on finishing the game and bringing it all together. 6. On PC, force anti-aliasing on using your graphics card to make the game prettier. Game ran and controlled smoothly with few bugs. 7. You don't need AI1 to play AI2, but I think AI2 does spoil AI1, though you could still enjoy them in reverse order. 7. If you're sensitive to horny then just read less background dialogue in Ryuki side. Gore is pretty toned down, and there isn't any single huge CW. You can stop reading now if you don't want your playthrough tainted by my reactions/expectations effected. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Part 2: Who am I, and how do I play?I'm an Uchikoshi fanatic. I've played all his English-translated games, and visual novels are my favorite genre of game. I've played a lot of visuals novels, but Uchizawa's are my favorites. I usually try to 100% complete all the scenes and see all the bonus dialogue. I've also played a lot of other genres of game, and I do like fun gameplay, but the most important things to me tend to be: A. An interesting story is absolutely what gets me investedB. Bunches of novel ideas like unique plot points I haven't seen before, philosophical ideas, or puzzlesC. Characters that I at least don't actively hate; I can like a game for the above two, but characters still matterD. Deep personal connection, usually formed by connections to real people or how a game shaped my life Those are the ways I rate my top games. For the last 8 years, my top 2 favorite games have been the same: My top favorite game of all time is Remember11. I love the plot, the ideas, the twists, the characters, and it's what got me truly invested in Uchikoshi. It's very much a mystery game first with an unravelling mystery and themes I love to explore. My second favorite game is Virtue's Last Reward. I love the interactive moral dilemmas. VLR's use of the Prisoner's Dilemma jumpstarted my interested in Philosophy which led me to major in Philosophy. I don't like the characters as much save for a few, but it's still very important to me. Now, let me tell you how I've played AINI: I've basically been playing non-stop since June 13th. Take this with a grain of salt because I've been documenting as I play (the average main story playtime seems to be 20-35 hours, with 100% likely taking 50+), but right now, I have 97 hours of playtime. I have not gotten all the dialogue, achievements, or fully explored the abundance of extra mechanics. Instead, I have a 616-page reaction document full of constant laughs, cries, screams, passing out, and most of all love. Part 3: My ReviewThe R11 #1 and VLR #2 holy duology held true for 8 years. Also, AI1 isn't one of my favorite standalone games; it has huge personal connection for me because of the community and the AI1 ARG, but it wasn't my favorite as a game. I gave all that background because I want you to take me seriously when I say this:AI2 is my new favorite game. The #1 spot has been Easily dethroned. The themes, twists, characters, ideas, gameplay, visuals, voice acting, fair mystery, presentation, mechanics, and comedy all of it resonates together perfectly. I don't even tend to value gameplay or visuals, but at many times, this game is fun to play while looking genuinely beautiful and cinematic. The story reads like a proper Uchikoshi + Nakazawa return to form. The mystery is fair, interesting, meaningful, and complex told satisfyingly. There are many deep ideas, concepts, and themes utilized in thought-provoking ways. Gameplay-wise, there are tons of mechanics that are utilized to make each Somnium unique; they all feel designed by love, fair, and reflective of the character through gorgeous symbolism. They blow the first game completely out of the water. Each one is its own experience to explore and a visual delight. There are also tons of mechanics for you to discover that make AI2 a fun game to play. The animations, voices, and directing are cinematic; this game is actually breathtaking a lot of the time. It's backed up by great and charming character writing- despite the fact Mizuki is my favorite AI1 character with 0 contest, I grew to like much of the AI2 cast the same amount. AI2 is a story about halves and splitting, but also love and coming together- please, see it through until it's whole. I hope and believe you will all fall in love with AI2 like me; AI2 is all I've ever wanted. AI2 is my dream game come true; it's a gorgeous love letter to all Uchikoshi fans who love Zero Escape's puzzles, Infinity's mysteries, and AI's characters and humor.

While it's not strictly necessary to know about the ARG I will still recommend you watch  If this is your first AI game I would first recommend to play the first game as this is technically a sequel. If you do not want to play the first AI game, know that the game will cleverly remove any spoilers of the first game if you did not play it yet, so while it is recommended to play the first game first, you won't be spoiled on it either by playing this game first.I really enjoyed the jokes in the flavour text in this game, even if they are pretty stupid most of the time :).  The somnia are much better in this game because the internal logic is made more clearer and each somnium is different from each other.Some characters didn't really need to be in this game, but were only there for fans of the first game though.Hoping there will be more games in this series in the future.

(So you can also listen).The story is SO GOOD, and you're rewarded by paying attention to every tiny detail.SERIOUSLY, you're don't even understand to what degree. Nothing is redundant. Some themes return fro mthe previous game, but for the most part, it fits the themes and the atmosphere.Some of it was kinda reptitive, and I sort of cringe at one particular song, which is why I gave it an 8, But other than that, Nothing to complain, perfectly fine.Play it. _childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by emphasizing just how much I've struggled to figure out my feelings for this game. I have.... some complex thoughts about nirvanA Initiative (which I'll shorthand to AINI for simplicity). This game is one of those rare cases where Steam's "thumbs up/thumbs down review system" can't begin to even so much as generalize my thoughts... This runs deep, REALLY deep.I don't think AINI is necessarily a bad game - you can tell so much passion was put into this title (as with all of Kotaro Uchikoshi's works), there's still plenty of things here to appreciate & truly value; But saying I "love" this game is a hard stretch. It reminds me a lot of my feelings on Psychonauts 2 (which is ironically also a sequel to a beloved original title where you explore people's minds) - Both are games which have a lot of respect for its source material; I can't hate these sequels, yet when I get to thinking about them, I also can't help but be reminded by how much more in love I was with the original.I guess I'll start off with the easy-to-explain positives, since I already stated earlier that there's plenty to like:[1] Mizuki & Aiba have a seriously stellar dynamic, it even tops that of Date & Aiba's dynamic from the 1st game's (of which I will shorthand to AITSF) for me. It made playing through the Mizuki Route an absolute joy.[2] The new characters are all great; while they might not seem like much early on, I was surprised at much I came around to liking them by the end (ESPECIALLY THE MASKED WOMAN DUDE, LIKE WOW, she is just an incredible character IMO).[3] There is a special reward to those who beat the game, & it is hands down one of, if not, the greatest completion reward I've seen in a videogame ever (longtime Uchikoshi fans will appreciate this ;) ).[4] The OST is GREAT - while some tracks return from the 1st game, most of them are for the themes for returning locales; the rest are new songs made for new locales/characters/Somniums.The Somniums are mostly 1-up'd as well. Returning players will feel right at home here, with their role serving the same purpose as before. However, the gameplay of Somniums has been completely overhauled & revitalized from the 1st game - AINI's Somniums exchanges the abstract surrealism of AITSF's Somniums in favor of more directly telling you what the person's mind literally feels & thinks.This change allowed the writers to come up with more creative scenarios that have a much more lasting/fun/immediately more impressionable characterization of the person's metaphorical reality (Komeji's & Kizuna's especially stood out to me in this regard. Their Somniums echo'd a lot of my own personal experiences... even just writing it here is giving me chills).On top of these Somniums being more interactive, there's now a total of 5 Eyeballs you can earn in each Somnium, not just 1. Plus, once you unlock all the routes of a Somnium, you can go back & do an Unlimited Psync, where you can replay the dream without the stress of a timer (a much welcomed feature that allows you to find the funny gags of some interactions).The reason I say the Somniums are only "mostly" just upgraded is hard to explain; I sometimes feel certain scenarios can get a little too over-the-top for something that's supposed to be taking place over the course of only 6 minutes; A part of me liked how much more abstract the Somniums were in the 1st game; The change to make the information in Somniums in AINI more literal means the whole "dreams are just a distortion of reality, don't take it too literally" thing has less meaning in this game, so they're more used as hard evidence in this game, which.... I dunno, I guess I just liked that the information was more treated in the 1st game with a grain of salt.I can see why the writers wanted to make this change. After all, there is a lot of plot to this game. Like, A LOTTT of plot. Like, "I think they bit off more than they can chew" a lot... which I think is the root of where a lot of my problems with AINI come from.This is due to a few reasons (of which I will keep vague enough to avoid spoilers).[1] The biggest one for me is making Ryuki a playable protagonist, & having his story cover the first 1/3rd of the game. A lot of Ryuki & Tama's dynamics feel like a watered-down version of Aiba & Date's, with Ryuki serving as the straightman to Tama's perverted antics... Only, it lacks the same soul that the former 2 had. It's that soul that saved me from fully cringing at Date's unnecessary weirdness, as Date & Aiba would often spin the punchline away from the perverted comment, & into a metatextual commentary about their relationship with each other. It's that soul that managed to make me laugh when Aiba would lie about there being a porno mag at Date's feet, all so she could enhance his reaction speed tenfold.Ryuki & Tama lack this soul. If their dynamic was more unique & didn't mirror Date & Aiba's dynamic so much, I guarantee you I would've loved these 2 a lot more (& I say this confidently, as there are times when we see these 2 be their own pairing with each other. Those rare scenarios stood out to me & are my favorite moments from them). [2] The reason for Ryuki & Tama having their own side is so they can explain the events of the story 6 years ago in the past, back when the Half-Body Serial Killings first started. Meanwhile, the Mizuki Side follows Mizuki with Aiba, exploring the case as it gets reopened years after it had first started. The reason the game is formatted like this is to set up a spoiler that, while incredible on paper & in theory, doesn't really add anything noteworthy to the core of the story, alongside having some noticeable plot holes... Yet despite this fact, this is something only Uchikoshi would be able to make work as well as he did. I've no doubt the man seriously racked his brain trying to figure out how to make all the pieces fall into place, & his efforts should be recognized for how far he got.(Though I'd be lying if I said it didn't give me similar vibes to DRV3, in that it makes me want to replay the whole story just so I can catch all of the countless details that elude to this spoiler & were hidden from me in plain sight.)[3] As much as I hate to say it.... this leads me to AINI's story. A story I want to love. A story that does a lot of great things. A story that does have elements worthy enough to warrant a sequel to AITSF.But it's a story that I feel is confused on itself. It's a story that doesn't know what it's trying to say. It's a story that proves what I had only kinda felt about AITSF's ending, that being "As much as I loved this journey, I don't think I need more - I think nothing more needs to be said".There are 2 separate things AINI is trying to say by the time the game ends; Yet with how everything plays out, it can't officially comment on 1 without undermining the value of the other. & both are subjects so keenly intertwined with the game that it ends up just coming across as confused.This is on top of the aforementioned plot holes (which spread a little bit further than what I had previously eluded to), the humor sometimes relying on the 1st game's jokes as a crutch, the excessive & off-putting gaming pop culture references, the sometimes slow/weird pacing, especially with the QTE's, things like fortune-telling that feel out of place in this sci-fi setting (all of which are honestly nitpicks in the grand scheme of things compared to the paragraphs I had written prior).Despite everything I have said thus far here... I still am not sure how I truly feel about AINI, & whether this is a game I could recommend to fans of AITSF. Even as I write the conclusion to this review that I have now spent over 2 hours writing, I still am not sure whether to give it the thumbs up or thumbs down on Steam... I think the only thing I can say confidently here is that I am going to be thinking about & processing AINI as a whole for a long time to come.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. There are some problems, though, mainly that the puzzle part of the game is somewhat flawed. The in-game characters you control solve some puzzles that are actually interesting, but you usually don't. There is so much hand-holding that sometimes they solve the puzzle automatically, without even asking for your input.With that out of the way, if you focus on the storytelling, then you'll see how amazing it really is. I think it's better played when you have some time to spare, with patience, reading everything, and trying to make sense of each piece of information you get, as you go. You'll certainly be awe-struck after a specific revelation close to the end of the game.The game deals with murders, torture, and some heavy themes, but it does not take itself very seriously. Basically, every interaction in the game has some jokes mixed in, and some are actually hilarious. There are also some very absurd scenarios inside the somnium sequences, like a Pokemon-like mini-game and a cooking show, that are somewhat funny.But again, the main thing here is the narrative. The way the nonlinear narrative is presented here can truly amaze you, and I think it's especially incredible that it can have this effect even if you played the first AI: The Somnium Files game and the Zero Escape series, because it has its own thing that is not present in any of these games (or in anything I've ever seen, really).

_childDocuments_.review: Uchikoshi's at it again. With these games I feel it's usually best to go in as blind as possible, so here's a short, sweet recommendation to start: If you loved the first AI: The Somnium Files, you'll like this one. If you haven't played that game yet, I suggest you check it out first. While this game is set up so you don't have to play that game before this one, I think it's better if you do. If you're not sure whether you want to try THAT one, I recommend checking out the Zero Escape series. Fans of the director will feel right at home with his newest title.At the risk of slightly spoiling potential players by giving them a sense of what to expect, I'll say more: for someone who's played other Uchikoshi titles (namely the Zero Escape series and the previous AI installment), this game will feel familiar. These games are known for including some mind-melting twists, but if you've played some of them already it probably won't be quite as shocking this time around. There are twists here, and they're cool and interesting, but instead of thinking "Holy s***, I've never seen a game do something like that before," you'll think, "Huh, that does feel like something these games would do." This may also be part of a trend with games in general pushing the boundaries of how they tell stories. The more games there are that take bold approaches to storytelling, the less impressive each successive game feels that takes similar approaches.Not to say that the story here is lacking--there's a lot to love, especially for fans of the first game. For my part, once I started I didn't want to stop playing until I was finished. The game kept me engaged the whole way through. I never felt bored with it. Some of the conversations were a bit underwhelming, and some of the characters got on my nerves at first, but with this game as with the last one, I think you're likely to warm up to them as it goes on. That goes for the game's weirdness, too. Like the first game, there are some extraordinary things that happen with deep story justification, and there are other absurdities that just seem to come from nowhere and go nowhere. The game is more enjoyable if you can just say, "okay, sure, this is happening," and take the latter in stride (and try not to think too hard about fight choreography).I did at a couple points feel frustrated, but it wasn't too bad. I feel that if you get stuck on a certain question or prompt in this game that you absolutely have to clear to go any further, there's no shame in looking up help for it online. Just try to find the answer on you own first, and be careful not to sequence break on accident (though of course, feel free to do it on purpose).The game's central characters, the protagonists Ryuki and Mizuki along with their AI-Ball companions, are all fun to follow. Between them, I think the game does a somewhat better job with presenting Mizuki's side of the story. Not to say that Ryuki's personal story is bad, but I feel like Mizuki's gets wrapped up in a more satisfying way, while Ryuki's was less so. There are reasons for that, and if I had to pick one or the other, I'm glad Mizuki was the one who got the most focus, but I feel like it would have been possible to give Ryuki's side some more closure and resolution without detracting from Mizuki. Again, though, both are suitable main characters and each carries their part of the story well.This isn't my favorite Uchikoshi game (I think Zero Escape: 999 still holds that title), but it's still a good one, and I enjoyed my time with it. If you want an(other) anime murder mystery with plenty of over-the-top humor, a cast full of weirdos and some quiet, thought-provoking moments sprinkled in, here you go. It's not groundbreaking, but it's good enough for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first AI game on Xbox Game Pass and was instantly hooked. It was an incredibly fascinating example of a non-linear narrative in a video game and I had to try the sequel out.After playing through Nirvana Initiative I can say that I found the experience overall to be just as good as the first game, but there are some flaws you should be made aware of.The narrative in this game is a little more linear than the first one, with only two main routes. There are still splits here and there for different endings, but there are less of them and the extra endings resolve much more quickly than in the first game. However, the plot is very "twisty" just like the first game, and if you enjoy that feeling, you'll still get it here. There is a point near the end of the game where suddenly, "it all makes sense" and that moment is something that few games have ever gotten right.The Somnium levels are much better than the first game, following a greater sense of logic and with a stronger narrative focus. Even better is the addition of an unlimited time mode after clearing a Somnium for the first time, the "funny" interactions between Date and Aiba were some of the best parts of the first game and now you have a chance to experience all of them without worrying about the time limit.The characters featured in this game are very well fleshed-out, even beyond the main characters (Ryuki, Mizuki, Tama, and Aiba). I especially found Ryuki and Tama's relationship to be very satisfying from a character development perspective. While most of the characters from the first game get sidelined to tertiary status, the new supporting characters are great. There are even some tertiary characters from the first game that become main characters in this game, which is pretty cool.The visual presentation is a little better overall here too. The art style is the same, but the GUI and HUD have been tightened up and they look great.Now, flaws. The biggest of these for me was that, like the first game (but worse), there are certain points where the plot just goes completely off the rails into absurdity. I was generally on board right up until probably the last 40 minutes or so before the final credits roll. I basically put my controller down and sighed. It wasn't bad, but just completely absurd and unbelievable. Very "anime".In keeping with that, other things I didn't like were the generous repeats of the same dance number which you could fast forward but not skip. I also very much missed the "clue collecting and presenting" of the first game, which made it feel like a little less of a visual novel. It's still present here but it's really only used well once. The "virtual reality" sections fill that void a bit, but you aren't challenged as much here.Generally though, it's more AI. And that's already a good thing.
