_childDocuments_.review: Another great game from Uchikoshi. While not completely on the same level as the first game, it's still very interesting and enjoyable in its own right. Comparing it to the 999 series, it's probably below VLR but still much better than ZTD (Which I honestly still found plenty of fun to play though). It even has a spoiler toggle if you haven't played the first game, so that's nice.Minor spoilers continue below...The story is relatively linear this time compared to most of Uchi's other games, with only a couple of branching paths. This probably makes it more enjoyable for the average person unfamiliar with these types of games, but I found it just a bit too standardized compared to other games from this dev. There's definitely still twists and unusual reveals, but ones that you'll have to think over to get the full effect, as its pretty sudden with little buildup besides your own observations. Some are done better than others, which may put some people off, especially after the first game.Due to the above, most dream sequences are fairly linear. They do seem to be easier than the first game in general in terms of time management, but each one is more unique, with its own gimmicks, and the key system helps confused players understand how each one works (though I must admit, I almost never used them myself besides for additional lore). One might be more investigative, with clues to pick up and store, and others might be a quiz or monster battler. There's difficulty settings available too if you still feel pressured, but the ability to replay them with no time limit is nice for finding collectables.There's a few other differences and additions compared to the first game as well. The first is the 'VR' investigation mode (VR not actually required), where you recreate a crime scene to see what a criminal did there. If you've ever played the Investigations spinoff games of Ace Attorney, think of it like Kay's 'Little Thief' sections. A fun addition, which seems to mostly replace the 'interrogation' sections from the first game. Another addition is the ability to solve puzzles outside of somniums. Unfortunately, there's little QoL here to review clues, unless they're present in the log, and you might find yourself being asked a question suddenly. Highly recommend having a notepad nearby to solve these. There's also small additions like a tamagotchi minigame, which is alright.Overall still a very enjoyable game, but not quite at the level of the first one. I would still recommend getting this whether you're a new player or old, and if you ARE new and liked this, definitely try the first game! Looking forward to potentially a third game in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: From a technical aspect this game is very good - I didn't have any crashes or bugs that were an issue.Ultimately though the story was just not nearly as good or clever as the first game and once you start getting to the end you quickly realize it's not going to suddenly get any better.There is one big twist as in all the Uchi games, but it pretty much flops in this one and doesn't have any real profound impact on how the story goes - it's basically just a bait and switch on how info was presented to the player and doesn't recontextualize anything for the characters or the story overall.All in all, it's probably worth playing through but you'd be better off waiting for a sale - I'd feel like I did well if I picked it up at around $30 or so.  It took around 23 hours to finish the entire story and I don't think I'll ever need to reinstall it again.BTW they do shoehorn in a couple lefty political messages so if you're trying to avoid supporting that kind of thing there's your heads up.

_childDocuments_.review: I still enjoyed this game and don't regret playing it.  If you're just looking for the journey and are happy to go along for the ride, it's still worth it.  That said...[Note: this review is plot spoiler free, but presumes an understanding of the way Zero Escape games are made which might be their own sort of spoilers]This is Kotaro Uchikoshi's weakest game plot wise.  It breaks several of his "rules" for mystery writing he's adhered to in the past and it feels measurably worse off for it.  Too many things are explained in a way that feels "unfair" per his conventional rules.  In the past, Uchikoshi's games managed to avoid feeling contrived in spite of their countless plot devices by ensuring everything had a clear purpose and the red herrings had an in-universe justification.  This time, it felt like the narrative took a more liberal attitude of "Yes, we know, but we need this for that other thing so just be cool and go with it".The Psyncs are actually a lot more interesting in this one, and credit where credit is due: they are moving in the right direction there.  The wide variety of changes and different flavours felt interesting and they all felt like they were reasonably constructed for the right amount of challenge/tension.  Notably less moon logic as well.Again, it was still a fun ride overall and the dialogue / characters / scenario is exactly what I knew I was signing up for... but the sloppy approach to constructing the mystery undercut the rest of the elements in a manner that feels unpleasant.  I would still recommend the game to the type of people who would play it just because of the dev team and are willing to be forgiving (which is where I fall), but I wouldn't recommend it to other people.If this interests you, play literally any of the other Uchikoshi games (which you absolutely should if you're considering it) and then decide if you are so eager for more that you're willing to overlook some things just to get it.---I also feel compelled to note that a central aspect of the game is a mysterious video which allegedly has a hidden message.  The game explains this message, but it never explains HOW the message was hidden or how someone was expected to decipher it, just what the answer is.  This is the first time in any of Uchikoshi's games that a mystery was never given a real solution.  Even if there's no imperative or reason for the player to personally solve a mystery, an in-universe explanation should still be given for how the characters who did would hypothetically have done it.  If only so the player can go "OOOH, dang, I see how that would have worked... That's neat!"

_childDocuments_.review: edit: I have cleared the main story of the game. The game would take around 40 hours to complete if you click on most dialogue options and do a bit of side stuff like I did (I clocked at 50-ish hours because I leave the game on at times while I do other stuff). Everything I said below still holds. I also would like to add the following comments/complaints (3., 4., 5.and 6. contain heavy spoilers about the endings):1. Most things were explained but the logic felt strung together and almost implausible even considering the game's setting2. The ending was quite underwhelming and predictable in my opinion 3. 4. 5. 6. All in all, I would probably give this game a 7/10. But considering it's a sequel of a game that is executed relatively well, I will give this a 6/10. ---I am somewhere around the 80% mark and can safely say that I am quite disappointed in this game (which is a shame because I was so excited when I heard about this sequel), the reasons being:Cast- Despite this being a longer game, there is not much development with the characters introduced in this game- Tama makes me cringe every time Plot- The main story is great but it is not as interwoven with the characters as the first one (although I think this is bound to happen to a sequel so I don't mind this as much)- The psyncs are very linear and didn't really evoke any emotions in me (with the exception of a particular psync). Also, a lot of the psyncs aren't necessarily related to the main plot- The story branches off at points that didn't really affect the narratives that significantly. I personally feel that the branching narratives in this game only serve to let you collect certain clues to open up other routes, whereas in the first one, I feel like they are indeed different timelines- Interactions with things in the environment in the first half of the first half (if that makes sense) are close to none. Almost every dialogue is generic- Also in the first half of the first half, there are multiple spelling and grammatical mistakes in the dialogueGameplay- As mentioned above, psyncs are very linear so they are not very challenging. I didn't like certain psyncs in the first game being too much of a trial-and-error thing but I feel like the devs toned it down too much this time round- With a certain psync, the choices in almost half of the psync don't even matter. - Aiba's/Tama's room doesn't really do anything. The convos are repetitive and are not that interesting- So many bugs! Several examples are:1. The camera keeps panning to the right even after I have stopped moving my left stick (XBOX controller)2. Every time the first key info pops up in a bubble in a psync in the second half, there is no response after I press the A button. I have to unplug the controller and use the keyboard to tap space to get rid of it3. After taking a steam screenshot using F12, the game does not register when I press the X or Y buttons. I can't really recommend this game because having played the first one, this feels half-baked and does not have much character. _childDocuments_.review: Nirvana Initiative is definitely a much less cohesive experience than the first game, but it does so many crazy things that I simply can't bring myself to hate it. It took a lot a huge bets, some of them paid off, some of them didn't, and the end result is quite fascinating.Without going too much into the spoiler territory, what I liked:- The Twist™ was pretty good, although somewhat heavy-handed.- The investigation sections were a nice addition.- Some of the puzzles were quite clever and reminded me a lot of Zero Escape.- Tama 10/10, best dommy mommy. The two things that irritated me the most were:- Even though there's a spoiler mode for people who played the first game, it still treats the returning characters like they didn't get any development, sometimes to a hilarious degree. I would much prefer if spoilers were hidden from promotional materials for obvious reasons, but the game itself was treated as a proper continuation for those who are already familiar with the backstory.- There's way too much filler here. It took me about 50 hours to get all achievements compared to 36 in the first game, and half of those additional hours could have been easily cut without any damage to the experience. The narrative slows to a crawl every time the game asks you to visit a bunch of the same places (some of which are recycled from the first game) and ask a bunch of the same people questions to get the same "I don't know" again and again, and it just gets a little exhausting after a while.Overall though I've certainly enjoyed my time with Nirvana Initiative, and I'm looking forward to another sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: while i was able to enjoy the game, if you haven't played the first somnium files game i actually would NOT recommend you play this game. i'll be getting into the "why" shortly, but if that's all you needed to hear, you can stop reading now!despite there being a "spoiler free" mode, the game still fails to serve as a narrative completely without reference to the first one even though it claims to be. there are also characters, plot elements, background information, and overall depth and complexity that the first game brings about that would make the second game a much more enjoyable experience overall.what's that? you've already played the first game and are wondering if the second game is worth giving a shot? that's where things get a little tricky for me. were there parts, plot lines, and characters that i DID really enjoy in nirvana initiative? yes. would i recommend the game to people who enjoyed the first game? yes. did i enjoy nirvana initiative as much as i enjoyed the original somnium files OVERALL? no. without going into specifics, one thing that i really enjoyed about nirvana initiative is the depth that they gave pre-existing characters from the original game and the way that they expanded on some of their narratives, as well as the general narrative and direction that the plot took. due to nirvana initiative focusing more on two primary routes as opposed to very many fleshed out shorter routes, i personally found it difficult to get through the game sometimes. if you're expecting the structure to be similar to the original somnium files game, ultimately, it was the investment in the protagonists that kept me playing further.i found myself compelled by both protagonists stories (as well as pre-existing characters that were brought into nirvana initiative), but i can't say the same for a lot of the newly added side characters. even the character(s) i disliked in the original somnium files game i found i enjoyed miles more than the ones i disliked in nirvana initiative. even characters that i was more fond of seemed to lack the depth that the side characters had in the original somnium files, causing this overall hollow feeling to a lot of the cast.i also found myself continuously annoyed by the number of convenient occurences / plot devices that were used. in the original somnium files, the game did an excellent job of tying together seemingly unrelated narratives and offhanded comments into a fully fleshed out an cohesive narrative. from what comes to mind, in the original somnium files there WERE no coincidences; almost everything felt intentional when the big twist at the end had been revealed. in nirvana initiative, there are multiple things that i can think of off the top of my head that felt like they existed SOLELY to move the plot in a specific direction while serving no other purpose, but to prevent from giving too much away or spoiling aspects of the plot i'll leave it at that. at the end of the day despite my grievances with the game, i don't regret the time i spent playing nirvana initiative. i do, however, wish that certain aspects of it were better executed than they were.i personally feel like if more time was spent working on the game and the dev team didn't try to make nirvana initiative work as something that could be played completely separately from the first somnium files game, the main issues i have with it might not have persisted.

_childDocuments_.review: The Nirvana Initiative improves on its predecessor in every way, bringing in twice as many interesting, layered characters that all get their time in the sun, crazy mysteries with twists i never saw coming, intelligent writing, vastly improved puzzles, impeccable voice acting and the best soundtrack of the year. I am shocked to say this, but I think the package as a whole outdoes Spike Chunsoft’s previous works. Whatever Uchikoshi’s next project is, whether it’s AI 3 or something else, we all need to be there day one. No one else is making games like him, and, frankly, I'm not sure anybody could if they tried. I recommend this game to everyone, even those who are normally averse to visual novels, though I wholly encourage you to play the first game before sinking your teeth into the Nirvana initiative.

_childDocuments_.review: A very slight recomendation, only for people who enjoyed the first game.If I had to describe Nirvana Initiative using one word I would use the word "cheap".The reused assets? Locations, music, character models? Cheap as hell.The story contrivances, plot holes, retcons, dumb twists added for "gotcha" moments? Cheap.Using the same jokes, characters, plot beats as before? Kinda cheap.Why would I recommend the game then? Mostly because it's still fun, in a way the first game was. It's a very dumb, yet entertaining ride that has a few cool, shining moments. But again, don't expect anything terribly clever, well-thought out or anything of this sort. The writing is stupid as ♥♥♥♥.While playing the game you can't escape the feeling that the writers first put together the scenarios the wanted to show and then, secondly were thinking of the ways to somehow jumble them together so they kinda fit. The amount of times you are shown something completly stupid or unprobable and are immedietly interrupted by a "in-universe explanation" is staggering. "See? We thought of everything!" say the writers, while telling you something dumb as ♥♥♥♥. Do not try to use your brain here. It's all contrivances.And the last sequence of the game? I literally had to fast-forward throught it to bare it, it was so dumb.Of course, the broken clock is right twice a day. There are some intriguing and cool things here and there. The ARG videos are well made and set a certain kind of mood. Some somniums are great and overall their quality increased compared to the first game, the structure of the game makes you feel like you're being actively gas-lighted and certain plot points really set your brain spinning, trying to unravel it all. Unfortunatelly, pretty much all of them are red herrings and instead of them you get a terribly non-interesting story filled with an enormous amount of plot twists (the kind that is there just to make the writing seem clever, while adding nothing to the story). There was an abundance of potential here but the writers chose an easy way out.Overall, if you thought you'd like to play some more of the the first game, then you're in luck, because this one is literally just that. More of the same. It's nothing more and nothing less. It's probably just a little bit dumber than the first one, and that's saying something.

_childDocuments_.review: I am left... conflicted. Not about the game's quality, but about its resolution.nirvanA Initiative is better in pretty much every way (or almost every way) to the original.Somnium segments are now all truly unique and different.There is now a new gameplay type segment similar to somnium - VR investigations, in which we gotta collect clues and recreate what happened at the crime scene.The puzzles in general are much better and less reliant on pure dream logic.The detective aspect of the story is much more intriguing and headblasting than TSF's.Hell, even the new main karaoke song is arguably better than Invincible Rainbow Arrow was.The only aspects i could say are debatable...The game is much more streamlined than the original, which on the one hand provides us an even better and bigger concentrated detective story AND it allowed somnium segments to get truly unique... And on the other hand, there is barely any branching in the story now, for the sake of the story that is presented and the way it is presented to us.As for the conclusion of the game... AS i said, coflicted. Because there is more than one conclusion, and i'm not talking about diverging endings. All i can say is... after the conclusion we ultimately get, it's doubtful that we will ever get another AI game, as it just can not continue on from something like that.And the whole revelation is just... I just don't know what to think.All i know is that i do not want to delete this game. I can not delete it. I shall not. And i shall go back.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed it more than the first game and I'm looking forward to more if there ever will be. Even if it can be some casual side-stories of random case solving I'd be down. As expected, all of the new characters are just as lovable and I really enjoyed Ryuki as much as I had enjoyed Mizuki from the first game, if not a bit more (which means I still love them both a lot; Date's pretty funny too XD). In the first half I nearly laughed 3/5 times I pressed the A button, especially at the beginning. 2 hours in and you're already back to being fully immersed into the silly and crazy world that is AI: The Somnium Files.As for the content, many of the characters held beliefs that were very realistic by understanding them in laymen terms. Talks about synchronicity (which is more than just thinking about a person and suddenly running into them. I've had some wild experiences that I cannot refute), simulation theory, and all this nice juicy stuff in general. The most verbal comprehensive understanding of Carl Jung's work in the game was when Date was talking about his porno mag powers XD with the libido theory of Eros, the serpent, and the death instinct from Freud. Anyone who uses the term psyche instead of mind or cognition has my instant attention and esteem (most people refute the idea of a psyche).Many of the dreams reflected much of what you can read about in Jungian psychology which kind of failed in the first game but in this one, it was more amazingly well-crafted. Kizzy's was the most perfect example with fantasy thinking from volume 5 of Jung's collective works involving fairy tales. In fact, many of the ideas that the simulation theory proposes as evidence can also be explained as psychic phenomenon as well, including the multiverse theory which, in my opinion, is related to synchronicity and ESP. Carl Jung had also written about how the psyche is responsible for people's sightings/panic of UFOs and general occult stuff. So I most certainly had fun with the story :DThis game has my most favorite set of characters from any game! If you ever need any help with the case, just remember Mama's pair of white milky balls :)

_childDocuments_.review: When I was playing this game, I had mixed feelings about it. Some aspects of it were really good, while some of the worst aspects of the first AI also makes a return. Pros: +This game had one of the best starts out of any uchikoshi game period. It hits you super hard and fast and it doesn't take like hours for anything to start happening like the previous games.+The mystery in this game is as good as ever because Uchikoshi has always been and still is a master of misdirection and bullshitting you to your face without you realizing it. When you reach the end everything just works. It just works. Everything snaps into place very cleanly and satisfyingly. +Voice acting and sound design are really good. They really sell the mystery and atmosphere of the game. +The Somniums are a more creative and well-designed this time around. However, this is a double edged sword, and we'll get to that later.  +Answers some dangling questions from the first game and expands on the cast. Wanna know why Mizuki is a 12 year old gorilla? Play this game. Cons:-Uchikoshi's worst habits from the first AI comes back in full force with even more ridiculous fight sequences and even more somniums. -The ridiculous fight sequences are back and they are as terrible as ever. Nothing takes me out of the story faster than these things. I cannot describe how much I hate them. Uchikoshi never did this with his previous games, so why is he so hellbent on writing them so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ often now? This is not an action movie; it's a mystery visual novel. Pick one or the other. You can't keep destroying suspension of disbelief with these things and expect me to still take the story seriously. -Holy ♥♥♥♥ are there a lot of somniums in this game. Grandma forgot whether she took her thyroid medication this morning? Strap her to the chair immediately and psync with her to find out. Then, when you're inside her brain, you gotta learn all about how she met grandpa and how much sex they had in the 80s, then how grandpa passed away from lung cancer in the 2010s, then how she cremated grandpa and scattered his ashes to the wind, then how she watched her daughter give birth to you, then how she cried when she watched you graduate from college 20 years later, then finally at the very end of the somnium you find out that yes, she did take her thyroid medication this morning. - A lot of the ""plot twists"" feel as if Uchikoshi just pulled them out of his ass. A lot of solutions to dangling plot threads also felt very contrived. While this is not too bad of thing because as I've said earlier, everything snaps into place very cleanly, it still really pushes suspension of disbelief. I feel like Uchikoshi's philosophy for writing mysteries nowadays is that as long as the solution cleanly answers every single question posed in the mystery, then it doesn't matter if the solution pushes suspension of disbelief just a little. I was fine with that in this game but Uchikoshi is walking a really fine line between writing an actually good mystery and parodying himself. In fact, maybe the entire AI duology are already Uchikoshi parodying himself. I don't know.  Overall rating: I'd give it a 7/10, just like the first game. The mystery is arguably a lot better than the first game but the pacing is even worse thanks to the fight sequences and how many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ somniums you have to sit through. Some of the answers to the mystery are also questionable, but the core of the experience is still solid, as this is an Uchikoshi game after all.

The script writing gave me whiplash as sometimes it was great and other scenes I didn't even know what the writers were thinkingQuick run down of my thoughts here;: The puzzles/soniums are great here. Felt nonsensical but was still grounded to logic somewhat. Made me solving the puzzles actually deliberate compared to the first game lol: Great: For a 3D VN there is no competition: There is a LOT of filler content in Ai Somnium that has little to know relation to the main plot outside of giving specific characters a shine. While I think this is fine I just thought they were poorly written or just boring really. At least the first game had considerably moving side characters. The main story picks up a bit at the end though even with all these interruptions via lots of plot twists and mysteries. If the full game was like this it would be a 10/10 but there is a lot of mid in itWhat I do love about it though is that its a mystery VN that respects your ability to solve and interpret stuff without feeding you an explanation immediately after. Any mystery story that lets you deduct things hours ahead of the reveal is respectable and way more fun imo. I know this might sound like a negative review (which it kinda is) but I did enjoy it a lot. Anyone who played the first game should definitely play this but those that didn't I am not sure.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember how difficult I found it to describe the genre of  when I played it about two years ago. In the end, I thought calling it a “goofy sci-fi thriller” was the most appropriate, as it was a unique mixture of a futuristic murder mystery, downright silly slapstick comedy and puns.Well, this sequel is just like its predecessor: we still have the terrible and dirty jokes, the musical numbers (even more than last time), a group of nonsensical characters who should all go and see a therapist… and, on the other hand, an extremely complex, engaging and often really, really dark story. This is exactly what I was hoping for, so I wasn’t disappointed at all, and I hope we’ll get more episodes for this franchise (but next time maaaaybe they could tone down on the musical parts a bit…).The graphics and gameplay are OK, they haven’t changed much to be honest (I still found the visuals a bit lacking in a few locations), but in a game like this the plot is what matters the most, anyway, and yeah, as I already mentioned, it’s great with twists that will leave you speechless, and searching the discussion boards and wikis for answers. Be prepared for a wild ride that messes with you in ways you can’t even imagine!With all that said, if you didn’t like the first entry, you’ll probably not like this one, either. And if you haven’t played either of them yet, but you’re curious, I strongly recommend playing the previous game first (even though you don’t strictly need to know its story for this one).

_childDocuments_.review: AI: THE SOMNIUM FILES - nirvanA Initiative had a rough time trying to succeed in the shoes of its predecessor which was already peak in many ways. And I'm here to say that I think it very much succeeded in doing so, creating a new narrative that is completely stand-alone for people who haven't played the original, yet very endearing to people who have, which is in my mind a difficult sweet spot to hit.Mizuki was an extremely under-explored character in the first game, so to see her be the protagonist of this game is a perfect way to alleviate that. We also unlike the first game actually deal with two protagonists here, which plays a key role in the way information is presented to the player and lends for an interesting narrative.The sequel suffers from a lot of the over-the-top anime fight scenes, and if you can suspend your disbelief and kind of just ignore any and all action sequences that happen in the game, I'm of the opinion you'll enjoy the actual story being told a lot more.I genuinely didn't expect a sequel to the game, since the first game wrapped up nicely, but was very happy it did get one, and specifically, one that mimics so well the parts that made the first game great. If you enjoy Japanese comedy, thrillers, and don't mind a few janky mechanics, you'll enjoy this game a lot.Though uh. Maybe grab it on a sale. That price point really is rough to justify.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as there is good with this game, there is so, so much bad with it.First and foremost, game looks good and plays well.Characters are fun and bounce off each other.That's where the good stops, unfortunately.The plot is the main selling point of the game, and I was heavily engaged with it throughout the first few hours of playtime. Unfortunately, that all stopped when we start getting into plot twists. ***SPOILERS AHEAD***Alright soYou know how the main gimmick of the game is that you have to figure out how the bodies "travel through time"?Turns out none of them did, so all of the hype was for nothing. It was all a matter of perspective. A trick of the light, if you will. All of them were discovered within hours of each other, not years. The biggest reveal of the entire game is that the mystery didn't exist.And we're not done yet. Remember how in the first game Date grew as a character and had stuff going on? Well congratulations, the mans got amnesia. AGAIN. Hoo ray. So he's absent for most of the game and doesn't have a dynamic with Mizuki. Oh boy.Okay so why is the killer doing this? What is their motive? Well turns out its so you the player can type a specific code at a specific time so that way a character can break the fourth wall. Thats it. I'm not joking, I'm not making things up. That's the entire reason. Just so she can do a hand wavey "I PLANNED EVERYTHING" and then immediately leave.Honestly all this game really made me feel was dissapointment with Uchikoshi. Zero Escape was a really engaging and fun experience that made me turn my brain on during gameplay. Now it feels like if i think about things for more than 5 minutes, everything breaks apart. _childDocuments_.review: is a sequel to the much acclaimed  and improves upon its gameplay in pretty much every way. You need not to have played the original to dive into this one which is great for accessibility but devastating in other ways which I'll talk about later. If you haven't experienced Uchikoshi's work before, be prepared for a joy ride of unexpected twists, lewd humor, philosophical discussions, and memorable characters with subverted characteristics. This is a visual novel with exploration and puzzle elements. The meat of the game is in its cutscenes and dialog, with the player being able to choose different options when interacting with characters and objects and hopefully gleaning useful information about the ongoing "Half-Body Murders" investigation while doing so. All dialog is fully voiced and audio is available in both Japanese and English. You play as two different characters, Ryuki and Mizuki, with Ryuki's story occurring 6 years in the past while Mizuki's story lies within the present. Both characters have an AI that lives in their eye socket, an "AI-Ball" that serves as their partner, navigator, driver, file storage, and smartphone all in one. The interactions between Tama and Ryuki as well as Aiba and Mizuki are genuinely funny and enjoyable, especially within Somniums. Speaking of Somniums, this is were the puzzles and exploration elements are located. Somniums are a dream world that contain hidden information within an individual's mind. The premise is that you dive into someone's mind using a "Psync Machine" and once inside, you play as your AI partner as they explore the Somnium, interact with different items, and unlock "Mental Locks" that slowly reveal more information about the person. There is a time limit of 6 minutes however and each choice you make shaves off precious time so you have to think carefully. Thankfully, there are "positive timies" that you can earn and utilize to shave off the time cost of your subsequent choices and hints that are provided as you explore the Somnium and experiment with different choices. While the solutions within Somnium aren't always "realistic" or "logical" they make a lot more sense than the ones in the original game and are satisfying to complete rather than frustrating. Another improvement over the original is "Unlimited Psync" mode, which unlocks after you successfully complete a Somnium once and gives you unlimited time to explore, which helps a lot with finding hidden eyeballs and messing around at your leisure.Other gameplay additions include VR Mode, Wink Psync, and Eyeballies. VR Mode is a simulated recreation of previously seen crime scenes that you can explore to help further your investigation. You interact with objects to find new information about key pieces of evidence and there are various viewing modes such as X-Ray and Thermal to find new clues. After finding everything, you compile your findings all together in a humorous "reenactment video" that your AI films for you. Wink Psync is a shorter version of psynching that you can use during the story sections. It provides a short 6 second look into a character's thoughts. You can only perform it once per scene however as it is power intensive on your partner. As for Eyeballies, there is a minigame within the pause menu that is reminiscent of the old Tamagotchi pets where you can "raise" your Eyeballie into different "adults" based on your answers to various questions.The game took around 32 hours for me to 100% it, which includes earning all achievements and collectibles. There are multiple endings and some require you to go back and make different decisions to progress. Luckily, this is easily done with an intuitive flowchart which allows you to jump to any event or Somnium you've done previously. As for collectibles, you can unlock various outfits for Tama and Aiba by earning and spending eyeballs from completing Somniums and raising Eyeballies. Unlocking more achievements within the game unlocks more outfits to purchase as well. By finding hidden eyeballs (there are 5 in each Somnium), you can unlock concept art of characters and objects within the "Dream Album". There are also other secret goodies to unlock for long time Uchikoshi fans but I won't spoil them here!This is my 6th Uchikoshi game and the story feels a little less tight on this one. Without going too much into spoiler territory, a lot of the characters from the original are retconned and their relationships are downplayed in order to preserve the twist of this game. At the very beginning of the game, there is a spoiler toggler that asks questions about the first game so veteran players can receive new tidbits of information and inside jokes that reference the past without ruining it for new players. While this is a good idea in theory, it wasn't executed too well. I felt that this game sacrificed too much in an attempt to draw in new players rather than expanding upon the original like a true sequel would. The mere presence of old faces doesn't make this a sequel, preserving their growth and relationships from the original does. A minor concern is the unnecessary addition of jokes during serious and tense moments, which ruins the immersion sometimes. Most of the humor is well-placed and cracked me up so I'll give them a pass on this one. Another annoyance was the overuse of QTEs during fight scenes. While they are relatively forgiving, they don't really add much to the scene and can be removed entirely with no effect on the overall game. Finally, not all of the Somniums were enjoyable. Some of them forced you through a slog of puzzles only for them to produce information of very little importance which is frustrating when you are actively invested in the game's mystery. Overall, it was a pleasure playing through yet another Uchikoshi mystery! As always, I was mind-blown by the twist and actively went back through the game to try to find moments of foreshadowing. The cast is generally enjoyable, although the original characters did take a back seat to the new ones which is understandable yet mildly irritating at times. I had many moments of laughter and learned quite a bit of new philosophical topics (especially from Tokiko). 8/10, definitely worth the purchase if you're on the fence about it :)

_childDocuments_.review: Short recommendation: buy when discounted for more than 60%As a fan of 999, VLR and Somnium files, I was eagerly expecting this game, but... Let me list the good parts first:- Curious plot twist (it doesn't make sense, but it does surprise)- Enjoyable characters and fun interactions (at least the ones from first game)- Interesting mystery (again, not to say that the solution felt satisfying but it was interesting)The first few hours of the game were quite enjoyable, but the more it went on the more flaws became pronounced and the game felt pretentious:- Somniums feel like slog and rather than enjoy the bizarre dreamworlds while trying to discover the true nature of the case, we now just follow some bizarre hallucinations (plus somniums with enemies or time moving at realtime speed just doesn't work when it goes against core concept of "time moving when you do", especially when controls are questionable at best). Worst part is that new characters don't have ambiguity or anything interesting about them to discover in somniums.- QTEs... They were bad in the first game and now there is more of them (especially frustrating when playing on pc). Feels like they just wanted to have more action scenes in mystery game (WHY!? the first game had a few action scenes and they were fun but now there are just too many and they are more of a slog than a fun distraction like it was before).- The core mystery has a rather unsatisfying answer as plot focused so much on meta elements that the actual core of the case did not feel meaningful or exciting (when it became clear who was the culprit, I felt nothing but disappointment)- The main plot twist does seem interesting at first but after thinking about it for a bit you realize that there was absolutely NO REASON for the twist to be in the game other than to have a plot twist. It's there to misdirect player into thinking there is some grander mystery, while in truth the case is just a simple murder, which is mysterious not because the murder is elabourately executed, but because we aren't told crucial points of information that characters (which we play as) actually know. This kind of plot twist is simply pretentious and bad writing.Overall it just feels that they took some random things that were done in moderation in the first part and went overboard with them (dances, QTEs, action scenes, surreality). Overall the game feels like a serious stepdown in quality of the story from the first game and while it is interesting to experience the story, I definitely don't think it is worth the full pricetag of a AAA game. If it cost like visual novel or indie game of around 10-20 euros/$, then it would have been good, but as it stands, it's overpriced.

_childDocuments_.review: *spoiler free*While I do recommend playing this game if you played the first, I have to say.... I'm disappointed. The good: the Somniums actually make sense as opposed to the first game and feel like 50% proper escape room 50% creative dream logic, which is ideal for the conceit of the game. The themes and solutions are so much more consistent with character motivation this time around. The characters are solid, and the animations and music were quite great for a visual novel. Voice acting is superb. The bad: The game is incredibly linear. Not only that, but the story just... is not great. The actions of characters don't really 100% follow their motivations, and what characters should know relative to their timeline does not always show up in dialogue. Characters seem to do things just because the game devs needed to achieve a certain situation vs characters acting in-character. I loved the Zero Escape trilogy, so I have no problem with unexplained plot elements, but the difference with this game is I have zero desire to understand the remaining mysteries after the true ending and epilogue. The difference is that I don't believe in the narrative cohesion of the AI: TSF universe whereas I did for Zero Escape.  Overall: Get this game if you are a fan of the first one. Do not let this negative review dissuade you, you may like it and I want to support the devs. However, if you want a tight story (Apollo Justice, Life is Strange, 999) rather than a loose one (Danganronpa series, Kingdom Hearts series, Higurashi), then uh, yeah, may not be your cup of tea. Random complaint: The quick time events are abundant, last forever, and, on mouse and keyboard, have some frustrating logistics (like doing arrow keys, then mouse, then wasd, so you have to move between regions on a keyboard in a way that is much more challenging than using a gamepad).

_childDocuments_.review: Christ, where to even begin? The amount of meandering this story does with no meaningful progression makes Virtue's Last Reward look like a riveting thriller. You're kept completely in the dark about the plot for the vast majority of the game after the second Psync or so, and you spend that entire time interacting with some very boring, very predictable characters. All of them are more shallow than Ota in their personality and motivations, and even spending 30 hours with them, I never felt anything for them. This includes Ryuki as well, who's supposed to be a deuteragonist. Kizuna: She's a stuck up rich girl with no personality other than having exceedingly high standards in men. She likes to dance. That's it. Lien: He likes Kizuna. That's literally his entire personality. He used to be a thief so he knows how to pick locks. This means any time you see anything locked, you're about to get a 20 minute conversation about how much he loooooves "Kizzy." Ryuki: Mentally ill detective who likes Date. He loses association with reality constantly, and does a ton of stuff that would get most police officers taken off the force permanently. We never really learn anything about him other than the fact that he wants to solve the case, and that he doesn't solve it (yes, the prologue shows you that he fails, then you're tasked with doing his ENTIRE arc, knowing full well he won't succeed).Gen: He likes Amame and cooking. Noticing a theme here? Almost all of the new characters don't have anything to them other than "cares about this other character, and maybe one activity."Shoma: Dislikes his dad and himself. Likes robots. Komeji: Probably the most developed of all the characters, but ultimately has even less going on than someone like Hitomi from the first game, who was very much a side character. Chikara: Transparently evil mad scientistTokiko: Transparently crazy crazy ladyNobody changes much throughout the story, and nobody ever tells you anything about the case, either. In AI 1, if you got certain characters in the right situations, they'd talk your ear off about heavy details of the case. In this game, you get some suspicions about a character being involved in something shady (by MIND READING them, because they don't tell you anything, ever) and then ask them about it. They deny it, always. You then Psync with them, and the Somnium is just whatever location they spent the most time in with a few extra props or some ooze on the wall. Every single Somnium is some sappy "unlock their feelings and heal their heart" nonsense that often has NOTHING to do with the case at all. If you're lucky, at the end of the therapy session, you'll get one sentence or note they happened to see. And the plot twist of this game... my god, it's the dumbest thing. One of the biggest mysteries of the game is how one half of a body was turning up six years after the other half while having different times of death. The answer?  But it wasn't the *flowchart* that made it confusing. It was the characters themselves literally wondering "how could these bodies appear so far apart but have different times of death?!" So the twist only works if everyone's an amnesiac or something? I have no clue how they wouldn't be aware of That encapsulates this game in general. It's 90% slice of life, meaningless bullsh*t with characters that are unlikeable. Then you finally get some plot progression after 20 hours, and it's something that has no real bearing on anything. Like  Sure, it's weird and "shocking" but how the hell is it even relevant to the plot? It's literally not. All it does is illustrate that  which is something you learn in the second Somnium in the entire game. Overall, this game was simply an exhausting mess that wasted my time. The first game was so good, it's honestly insulting to call this by the same name. Even after beating the game, I have no clue what the purpose of the overall plot even was. What's the message here? That  How does the bisecting even fit into the overall themes, if there even are any? The characters themselves ponder this at the end, and nobody can come up with an answer.The meme ending where you  was by far the most enjoyable part of the whole story, despite being a self-defeating sci-fi cliche, and basically just a reference to Zero Time Dilemma, a far superior game.

_childDocuments_.review: So I read some of the reviews here and I agree with basically everything from people pointing out the wrongs of the Nirvana Initiative compared and not compared to the first game. None of this is true for Nirvana Initiative. I couldn't get into the plot in the first part and in the second I was only getting more confused the deeper I dug into the game. The thing I like the most in Uchikoshi's games - the flowchart and multiple story paths - don't exist here so I couldn't even enjoy this. There are only two branches on the whole flowchart and they are very short and don't provide much unique story.I surely didn't expect to dislike this game when I was turning it on for the first time, but here we are. _childDocuments_.review: Another great mystery experience from Uchikoshi.The half-body mystery is quite long and there are less routes this time which may be a turn off to more choice-focused players but you NEED to stay for the twist of this game, it is so insane that I can't even conceptualize how this story was written. Let alone how he figured out to present the game in such a unique way. Be PERCEPTIVE, this game benefits the most when you're catching what it's trying to sneak past you.Think about the presentation of scenes and when they happen, and the specific way characters interact with each other and even how they describe things they look at.The characters are a bit more stubborn and less fleshed out this time, leading to a lot of forced somniums because they won't just tell you something that would help you solve the case because they need to be aggravating. I also feel they don't hit the emotional highs that the first game did, which may be because the story is less focused on emotion this time around but it was worth noting that they just weren't as endearing to me as the first games cast. They're still a good cast at the end of the day, though.Theres a lot of unearned and just poorly shot action scenes but I guess they're better than A1's as you can actually follow the action. It's still shlocky and kinda cringey to experience especially with more forced dance numbers but if you can look around that part of the game, this is an insane story to follow, especially with a friend experiencing it with you. The QoL changes and presentation in this game is insane, it refines a lot of things from AI1 and overall makes the game more convenient to play with new unlimited somniums so you can actually see all the choices in full without worrying about a time limit. I feel like they were kinda lazy with the models in this game but there is an actual reason for them reusing how characters look so do keep an eye on that. It's not solely because of laziness. Overall, just a solid fun and engaging experience that had me on the edge of my seat until the end.

_childDocuments_.review: I would definitely recommend this game so long as you know what you're getting into. The writing is great - it's the most compelling thing about the game - but it's also extremely *anime,* which will either make or break it for some people. Lots of deus ex machinae and serious suspension of disbelief, but the great characters shine through and the mystery at the heart of it is very intriguing - there was a major in-menu plot reveal towards the end which dropped my jaw to the floor, and it's rare you get that sort of thing these days. Technically speaking, a lot has been improved from the first game; the Somnia, the game's dreamy escape rooms, are much more interesting overall, sometimes interesting new gameplay features that are unique to particular ones. The game also runs fantastically compared to its predecessor. If you're at all familiar with Kotaro Uchikoshi, I would definitely say to give this a go, though, if you've never heard of Spike Chunsoft or Zero Escape, there's a very good chance it just won't click.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw "Missed Potential" mentioned somewhere and that pretty much sums up the game, I'd say. I'm going to start with some more objective changes to the game, and talk about the story (or, specifically, the mystery) later. I will not be spoiling anything specific, but I WILL be spoiling some things I wish I knew going in. In general, I think the first game was far better, but I'd probably buy a 3rd game if it came out.-The Somniums are better. I don't have strong feelings about this one, since I didn't mind them in the first game - I treated them more as a psychological showcase than actual puzzle rooms. Here they manage to also be more logical and mystery based, but I still had to reset about as much as before.-The QTE's, and action scenes in general, are more about action than humour or fighting smart. I can see how some people like the first change, but the second one makes the simple animation and choreography more glaring.-The story is far more linear. In the first game you had 4 endings to go for (on of them cut short, but far enough that I was fine with it) in any order, and the game turns linear in the last 20% of the game or so. Here, it's mostly linear, with a few hours in the early and late middle where you go do side endings. Again, I preferred the first, but I can see how this story might've needed this change.So, now onto the spoiler stuff. Personally, I wish I went back in time to tell myself this, but, you can ignore it if you want to go in blind.1.  2.  In the first game, I the plot twist felt like something natural to the world, and something you can start suspecting early on. It may not even have been part of the initial idea for the game.In nirvanA Initiative, it unfortunately feels like the writer had this "really cool idea" for a twist, and made a story about it, but then had to use a lot of duct tape to have it make sense. An impressive amount of duct tape, applied with plenty of thought, that I would gladly examine years later on a replay, but duct tape that makes it look forced and kind of ugly regardless. More importantly, it's yet another case of a mystery solving game taking out the solving part, by making it a real pain to figure out (and it seems it's not just me who thinks that). The moment-to-moment mysteries of "how did X do Y?" are fine, but when it comes to the grand *TWIST*, I'd say you only get substantial hints in the last 30% of the game. Compare this to the first game, where basically every ending you get early on, provides a good tip for the mystery that can make you go "I knew it!","Oh, that explains it!", or "What does this mean?", or all at once. Combine this with the fact that, even besides the plot twist there's tons of info dumping and red herrings (again, compared to the simpler story of the first game), and you get kind of a hot mess.Honestly, even if there'd still be duct tape, I'd accept a bonkers story and twist if it worked as a good mystery, but, this just didn't do it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll continue buying Spike Chunsoft games and continue enjoying their stories.  Most stories have great "mind-game" feels that make you think, they're creative and often times have great humour.This Somnium Files... I'm glad I played it, but it had nothing on the first game.  I won't spoil anything but this story, although had the bare minimum of "make you think," it was a total cop-out.  So many convenient things occurring to "make it work," it was a total let down.  There's a certain amount of convenience I'll let slide, especially if it's funny/goofy and just there .  These conveniences were totally necessary to make the story work, and it was just... a slap to the face.  It made the story seem really weak overall, and not what I'm used to from Spike Chunsoft.However, it was a great story overall, if you subtract the conveniences and just "pretend" some other factor was at play.  It did make you think, but not as hard as the first Somnium Files.Another gripe with this Somnium Files is that the Somniums were very, very linear.  There was little-to-no deviation necessary in each Somnium.  The camera intentionally focused on what you needed to interact with next, and (with limited exception) the only things you could interact with usually were the next item towards an unlock.  There were only two Somnium's that really "stood out" and that was Iris's Pocket Monster themed one (because you kind of had different options.  Kind of) and Chikara's Labratory (because you had to solve some puzzles with body halves).  Otherwise, most other Somnium's were linear with little deviation or distraction and could be solved on the first try (The "Mysterious Girl's" Somnium was a total bore, because you would auto-fail if you made the wrong decisions or failed timers.  It was an interesting theme but ultimately punishing, which is contrary to Somniums).Overall, I do look forward to more Somnium File's titles, but I do hope they put a bit more effort into their story.  Make me think, please, but don't throw a curveball or climax at the player/reader that's just plain moronic (For example: In Somnium Files 3, limit the number of characters having amnesia to zero).

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't really a game too worth reviewing, largely because it's a sequel well-targeted towards fans of the first game, which really should only be played after playing the first game. Thus:1) Have you played through AI: The Somnium Files?If no, consider that first.2) Did you enjoy AI: The Somnium Files?If so, you'll probably enjoy this.If not, look elsewhere.This is largely an incremental step up in the complexity and depth of the mechanics and overall mystery from the first game. As such, it works fairly well as a sequel; fans of the first one can enjoy a few good steps up. There's still a good amount of weirdness (albeit with less of Date perving), and a few touching moments scattered about.Since I've been comparing it to the first game so far, let's move on to what the first game does better. This game is significantly less focused than the first game. Part of this is a pretty broad active cast, part of it is due to the nature of the overarching mystery, and part of it is due to the multiple protagonists. It's a bigger game, and it's hard to point out any one thing that should have been cut, but it does still suffer from the downsides of a larger scope.Other negatives of this game are largely negatives of the first game, and I recommend going to that one first anyway, so I'm not going to go into much detail here. It's a visual novel, and not one with too much in the way of agency; be ready to read a lot of text or listen to a lot of (fairly well-voiced) dialogue.

The first game had like 10 interactables a level and half of them had something funny or dumb to say, this game suffers because it doesn't really have as much, there are levels, non-serious levels, where there will literally be no dialogue for the environment (this was mainly the case in the new locations, making me think that the devs just really had no ideas how to make the new locations as interesting as the first game's)- The lack of player freedom. I thought the first AI Somnium Files had a story that no one could predict who the murderer was, but most things in this game are plausible at least to figure out who did what if you pay attention closely. The twist is unique and brilliant. I like the new cast of characters while still showing the old characters. Uchikoshi likes throwing in random philosophical and scientific ideas in his games, but it gets more focused now on simulation theory.A negative I will say about the game is that it starts off slow. Sometimes it makes you go to all these locations when you know there is no point in visiting them. I guess that's how you build relationships with these characters. It is one of those games where it takes until the end/epilogue to make you love it.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about this game? It sometimes gave me a pretty hard time rating it, as during my playthrough it went from a 6 to an 8 and back... but also to an 8 again where it also finally finished. To go into some more detail and get some questions out of the way: The first game (Ai: The somnium files) does come out on top when compared, so if you haven't played the first game yet, you should start with that. Now one thing I have to say is, that they, in my opinion, really seemed to have put more thought in the gameplay part of the game. The puzzles are mostly fun and there's a great variety within them. Still, if you're looking for some real groundbreaking gameplay, that's obviously not the game for you. The game is also very out there when it comes to graphics or more fitting "design choices". It doesn't always take it self to seriously to the point where it can get a little annoying or weird. Still, it does a good job at creating tense and chilling sceneries, but you gotta be open for some... let's say "japanese" design choices. Another driving and important aspect of this game are it's characters and this is also it's biggest drawback sometimes. While the first game did a really good job at creating a complex construct of relations and chemistry between those characters, this game fails at this from time to time and to an extend that almost made me stop playing, tho there ARE also very well build moments, which, in my opinion, made up for the slip ups.The next very important point is the story... it's... crazy. very. crazy. and you gotta be in for that, otherwise you'll have a hard time having fun with it. If you've played the first game, then you probably already have certain expectations, but it's way more crazy than that. At this point I can very much understand, that it'S almost impossible, to make it absolutely theory- and doubtproof and I was fine with that. In excahnge you get a thrilling and really exciting story. It sure has it lengths here and there, but if you want an unresponsible amount of twists and something to satisfy your lust for something mad, it's perfect for you! Tl:Dr Now, let's sum this up:-First game>this game-VERY crazy story (positive) with cool premise-good gameplay to stimulate your neurons-some childish and "japanese" designs which make it less credible and serious-somewhat cheesy-LOTS of reading but everything is voice-acted-annoying characters from time to time, the chemistry isn't always fitting, to much emphasis on staying in a clichee (it's rare tho)I personally enjoyed it most of the time! I hope you do too.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot of things to criticise, but man, this game is fun.Upon your first few moments in the game, it's clear that it was developed with passion and love. The 3D models look gorgeous, the UI is great, there are all sorts of cool features from trivia entries to a tamagochi minigame. The game obviously doesn't take itself seriously most of time (which you can tell since it gives you a random dance scene 5 minutes into the game!), which paired with the hilarious jokes and non-sensical humor, makes for a fun experience. Even when it switches to a more somber mood, it knows when to go back to be light-hearted; it never feels too heavy to play. Usually, anyway- the game can really pull on your heartstrings at times, thanks to the stellar way they handle character building.Although the writer, Uchikoshi, is known for his ‘twists’, there’s definitely an argument that he’s an amazing character writer- after all, why would you care about the ‘twist’ and the story if you didn’t care about the characters? Not only are all the characters beautifully designed and unique in their own ways, but there’s also hours of fully voiced banter and quips you can get by clicking on random objects in the game world. As a result, characters in Nirvana Initiative feel more ‘alive’, like they fulfill a role other than advancing the plot- honestly, something a lot of games nowadays fail to do.Instead of controlling one pair of characters like in the previous game, in this game you control two teams: Ryuki with Tama, and Mizuki with Aiba. Although I had some doubts, the two newcomers, Ryuki and Tama, are amazing- it's just a fun time when you're playing along with these two. For Mizuki and Aiba, all I need to say is that she hasn’t lost any of her trademark snarky-ness that made her the fan-favourite character from the original. The voice acting, in both Japanese and English is phenomenal.You're locked out of doing Mizuki's route until you finish Ryuki's, which makes for quite a linear story compared to the first game- in total there's only about 4 branches. In a way, it makes for a more consistent experience, but it does feel like a bit of a downgrade. However, considering there was even a ‘recommended’ fan route for doing the original, perhaps it’s understandable they did this.Nirvana Initiative adds investigation sections, which are amazing- letting you freely use x-ray and thermo vision to figure out the mystery in 'the real world', unlike the previous, where most deductions happened in the dream world, somniums, which typically don’t hold to real-life logic and physics. And speaking of somniums, the new puzzle sections are now designed in a much more intuitive way, more fleshed out and memorable.Now for the bad parts: Uchikoshi’s love of the ‘twist’. Uchikoshi is infamous for what he calls a 'regressive' writing style, where he comes up with one of his trademark twists, and works backwards to create the whole story. While that may have worked in simpler games in the past where the propelling force in the story was finding out ‘why’, it's a little bit detrimental to both Somnium Files games. As I mentioned earlier, Uchikoshi (and Okada) have made a compelling cast of characters here, which sometimes get cast aside for Uchikoshi to chase the ‘twist’. It doesn’t help that we have about double the cast of characters, which dilutes the time we get with each one, and less story branches, which in the previous game was a great way to quickly delve into and develop a character.Then, the quick time events; why do these even exist!? Some of them are fine as they’re part of an interactive mini-game, but there’s more than a couple of fighting cutscenes where Mizuki beats up a bunch of faceless grunts, and they don’t really have any purpose. They're just really cheesy, and not in a good way.Regardless of all this, I can guarantee that you’ll have a great time, as long as you like the humor and you’re willing to suspend your disbelief a bit. Even if you don’t match my glowing opinion of the game by the end - and admittedly, I am a bit biased as an Uchikoshi fan - I’m sure you’ll have a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: A deep dive into a new fresh set of characters, and yet still have those lovable past characters I enjoyed from the previous game. Now while people may think, 'this is extremely confusing, why is this man powered up just from a porno mag' or 'this little girl can fight like a pro', there are reasons for any. . ./most/ things that happen in the game.This time we branch into two POV's. Mizuki and Ryuki. Both ABIS agents, both clearly great at what they do. Some people wonder why Ryuki was even added on, but to me I thought it was good of him to be added. A man who has mental issues struggles to keep sane while he tries to solve this case, and we watch as he slowly dwindles into madness. He's trying his hardest. : ( What I love most about AI is that I'm left with more questions than answers after I get to a certain ending. It makes me want to dive into it more and try to figure out why this happened. You HAVE to pay attention to as much as you can from the story to help you out in the puzzles, so play close attention to the story! ( I like writing out little notes when the MC pauses or the scene is emphasized in some way ).Uh, also? The HUGE amount of references in this game??? From Jojo to Pokemon, it would tickle me fancy when I would see something familiar and get a good smile out of me. This game is silly for a murder mystery, but that's good for me honestly, since I was never good with all the dark stuff in crime investigations. ( I still cover my eyes on some creepy bits though haha. ) I'm a huge fan of the soundtrack, love the personalities of the characters, and makes me see just how it shows that everyone has something to hide, and whether you can trust them or not. . .For a sequel to Files, I think they did a pretty good job so far. Of course not every game comes without some issues, but I enjoy playing it overall. With Mizuki being the new ABIS agent, we get to also know more about her and the people she's made connections with along the way. Give it a chance. While it may not be everyone's cup of tea, I really do enjoy the story. And remember, the flowchart is your best friend!!!

_childDocuments_.review: (full version with screenshots can be found here:  )nirvanA Initiative is the sequel to 2019's AI: The Somnium Files. That was a very good detective game that was nonetheless slightly disappointing because, with Uchikoshi and team having previously made three of my six favorite games ever in the Zero Escape series, the bar for his work had been drawn a lot higher than "very good." AI had largely solid characters and some standout comedic moments, but the mystery at the core of it all wasn't nearly as deep as even 999's. It was also held back by a grating protagonist and dream sequences that, while cool, were sometimes so illogical that they defied description as puzzles. AI2 has, thankfully, taken all those criticisms to heart. Start with the protagonist. While our old friend Date is still in the game, his role is far smaller and his personality has been dialed back to something more reasonable. Instead, we get a protagonist for each half of the game. New character Ryuki takes over for the first part and strikes does a good job of getting players introduced to the new characters, changes to old ones, and the foundation of the game's mystery. Then we swap to playing Mizuki, probably the first game's most popular character, and everything is unsurprisingly much better for her increased screen time. Aside from the other members of ABIS and AI-assistant Aiba, nearly every other character with significant screen time is brand new and nails their role. No one feels like a hanger-on or as if they exist for one part of the plot, and everyone is likable by the end. The dream sequences have been similarly improved. Most no longer branch the plot, which sounds like a negative but actually allows them to be more narratively cohesive and for more to be in the game without exponentially growing the number of endings required. More importantly, dreams are now far more clearly tied to the character in question and often have their own unique (but logical) gameplay to progress the scene. You're still choosing actions and trying to reach the end in under six minutes, but those actions now usually have predictable consequences and are more interesting. Silly stuff is present, but it's almost always obvious. Instead of just being visually interesting spaces for trial and error, dreams are now home to some of the best story beats, humor, and even gameplay and haven't even had to sacrifice any of the visuals. It's one of the biggest improvements in a gameplay mechanism I've seen between a game and its sequel. That just leaves the mystery itself, which is the core of the game. I'll say right away that it's still a long way from being as captivating as Virtue's Last Reward, but this time I don't mind. No, I wasn't constantly thinking about whodunnit even when I wasn't playing and yes, I'd figured out all but one or two of the major plot beats before they were revealed, but AI2 isn't really trying to be the next VLR. This is a story that's far more about the characters and themes than the mystery. It's fun trying to figure out who the big bad is, of course, but it was the interactions and relationships of the cast that kept be going. There were a lot of laugh-out-loud moments and even though AI's credits sequence set a high bar, AI2 does not disappoint. I also love how many ways the theme of halves is used in the story and even the structure of the game, but that's impossible to discuss without spoilers. The last thing of note is that even though the game encourages players who haven't played AI, I personally would not recommend jumping right to this one. The story is mostly unrelated beyond the presence of some identical characters, but you'd still be losing a lot about their personalities and would miss out on quite a few easter eggs and jokes. Besides, for as much as this may have sounded like I dislike the first game, it's very much worth playing for its own sake.

_childDocuments_.review: As a writer, Uchikoshi does something that maybe for some is a big ask. There comes a point where he essentially puts his hand on your shoulder and says "Hey, I'm going to cut you a deal. I'm going to give you an amazing twist that will make you reconsider how you feel narratives work, that could possibly change how you think about stories in general. All I'm asking in return is you accept a few things I tell you for granted." And the things he will ask you to accept will be absurd, but if you do, if you can choose to engage with the fiction in its own internal logic, you will have an unforgettable experience.Is it perfect? No, I do find some of the humor cringey and I wish some characters got more time to interact with each other. But is it worth playing? Yes, absolutely. If you are into games for their stories or are interested in non-conventional storytelling structures this is a great game for you to play

_childDocuments_.review: This gets a thumbs up based purely on the enjoyment of the story and nothing else, because the story is great.  Characters are great.  Voice acting is great.The problem is the everything else.  This game, made by the Zero Escape devs, is purportedly a mix of visual novel and puzzle game, but just like the previous Somnium Files game, the visual novel is overemphasized, and the puzzle aspect is greatly diminished, to the extreme detriment of the game.  I used to love getting to tackle a new puzzle room in previous games just as much as getting to the next story section as a reward for clearing them, but now you just dread any gameplay section.  They come in one of two flavors:- The psync sessions where you race against a clock to unlock mental locks in order to discover the secrets inside someone's mind- Press X to Not Die quick time events in cutscenesThe latter is just awful.  It's not gameplay.  It's just annoying.  Get it out of the game.  The former is weak and flawed fundamentally.  Puzzle rooms should not be timed.  You should be able to explore the entire puzzle, understand its mechanics, and then use the tools to produce solutions.  There's very little of that here.  Instead you just go to the next object highlighted by the camera and select typically the option that takes the most time which will be the correct one.  Almost every psync session follows this pattern, and it's just not engaging.  The puzzles have gotten even easier than the previous Somnium game too.  It's clear the devs need to seriously work on this aspect of their games.  Bring back legitimate puzzles that are interesting to solve, please.This game also lies in the beginning suggesting you don't need to have played the previous Somnium Files game because the events here have nothing to do with the ones that happened there.  This is just wrong.  This game is as direct a sequel as you can get.  The characters almost all transfer over, and they reference stuff from the previous game constantly, in direct or indirect ways.  You need to play that game first.  There's also a huge amount of asset reuse, especially the environments.  It just feels...cheap.It's not worth paying full price for this game.  It's a sale target for sure.
