_childDocuments_.review: Some sequels fall flat. Some sequels hold their own. And a handful of sequels end up being gems that impress the fudge outta me. Oh boy, did Nirvana Initiative fall into that third category! I have no regrets for spending nearly afternoons playing this amazing successor to AI. From the wonderful cast of old and new characters, to the new features, to the incredibly creative Somnia and finally to some of the most INSANELY baffling twists, this was SUCH a treat to play. Now, as I review this, I’m not one to toot my own horn… but I think I did a fairly bang-up job of talking about gameplay stuff in my Somnium Files review. So, I’m going to speak about this game in comparison to the things I noted about the first game.Some initial pointers: First off, the game asks you when you start playing if you’ve completed the original AI game, with the intent to reveal spoilers from the first game if you have, or not show any spoilers from the first game if you haven’t. I thought this was a neat feature and I’ve never seen it implemented elsewhere – though, I will say that playing the original AI enhances the experience, and I can’t recommend playing this one without playing the first. Also – this game has some new bonus features! One is the Eyeballie feature, which is basically a Tamagotchi that you grow by answering questions every 20 minutes. Another is Aiba’s/Tama’s room, where Aiba or Tama (depending on the protagonist you’re playing as) acts as… kind of a therapist, I guess? They ask you if you have any worries about things like relationships, work, school, money, etc., and offer advice to the player. And you can dress them up. It’s golden. It’s what every Aiba simp wants. If only it could be 100x more interactive T_T But alas, maybe in the next installment it’ll become a reality... I’m not lonely, I promise…Synopsis! Nirvana Initiative takes place in two time periods: one almost directly following the Cyclops Killings, and one six years after. ABIS agents Mizuki Date and Kuruto Ryuki are tasked with investigating a new series of killings, known as the Half Body (HB) Killings, perpetrated by the self-proclaimed “Tearer”, whose victims are left at their crime scenes, bisected cleanly in half. Much of the investigation methodology follows the original game, where both agents interview key personnel and psync with individuals to get insight from the unconscious. That’s all your getting from me in this paragraph. You should otherwise go into this game blind. Matter fact… why are you reading my review when you could be playing this work of art?!Characters! There are few things more trepidatious than playing a sequel to a game and wondering if the new cast of characters is gonna try in vain to outshine the original cast. But fear not – that is not the case here! I found the new cast to be a very delightful addition. I found Ryuki to be a great MC – determined, but not aggressive; sensible, but still quirky; and leagues less perverted than his predecessor. Although, Tama definitely picks up the slack in the dirty joke department. I consider Tama to be like a horny Esdeath who loves comedians like Aiba loves bugs. She’s oddly aggressive towards Ryuki at times, but overall clearly cares a lot about him. And my god – the Tama laugh is a pure treasure. The rest of the new cast is great – I didn’t find anyone to be super annoying, and those I found initially annoying grew on me. I won’t say much about my thoughts on each one but my favorite is totally  As for the old, you fortunately get to see most of the returning cast, as both their original characters and their 6-year-aged models. Mizuki, as a protagonist, gets more fleshed out, and I actually quite liked her this round (she was on the lower end of my favorites list in the first game). Everyone else is as lovable as ever. Aiba especially. She went to my #2 favorite with this playthrough. I absolutely love that the running jokes continue at full throttle in Nirvana Initiative: the Kumakura lanterns, Mama’s TV, forgetting that one inspector’s name, the sofa, etc. Jokes I thought were corny from the first game became ever-so-charming in the second. As far as cons about the characters… hmm, the only two gripes I have are 1.) not nearly enough Hitomi T_T, and 2.) Ota get a f&#%ing haircut!Gameplay! Overall, I thought most things related to gameplay were either the same or better in Nirvana Initiative. The normal investigation sequences play out pretty much the same. There’s the addition of the “wink psync”, which allows you to look into someone’s recent thoughts for six in-game seconds (which sometimes amount to a whole two minutes of monologue). Sometimes the wink psyncs progress storyline; other times, they're more so comic relief bonus content (e.g. wink psyncing with Kagami and vicariously experiencing his dating app woes). Outside of investigations, they did make a few other gameplay changes, some which are quite significant. Interrogations were taken out completely – which I was indifferent about. What Nirvana Initiative DID add was a VR simulation segment, which is basically an AI recreation of the crime scene that you investigate in third-person. The point of these VR sequences is to find clues (using regular vision, x-ray & thermo) and then determine how everything played out, in a similar slightly reminiscent of the “Closing Argument” from the Danganronpa games. Though I had nothing against the interrogation sequences from the first game, the VR stuff was a dope inclusion. It’s also very low-stress and easy to get a hang of. Lastly (before I talk about the Somnium segments), the QTEs were also noticeably better. I felt they were more fast-paced and required more inputs from the user. I actually felt excited doing the QTEs! They’re still not the greatest when compared to other games that are QTE-heavy, but I have to applaud Spike for the improvement.So yeah, the Somnia! Ah, I’m pleased to say that this also felt like an improvement. While there were still some frustrating moments , the Somnia of Nirvana Initiative were much more fun than not. Where Somnium Files had a pretty consistent “guess the right action to unravel the story” style, Nirvana Initiative made some VERY clever use of the gameplay mechanics. Some examples (I won’t mention who the Somnia belong to):  This was probably the one thing that impressed me the most – actually, no, the second-most – about this game. Overall, the Somnia were much more palatable in this game.Visuals & sound! I can’t really speak much more about this from what I shared in my review on the OG, except that everything in this department is pretty much consistent. The sprites are probably a tad cleaned up and the movements are a little less stiff (maybe? Or placebo effect?), but overall nothing changed with visuals. The music is also still rad – some returning tracks, some new ones. Some of the Somnia have some REALLY good tracks, and I’m personally in love with the eerie Naix theme – SO GOOD.I ASTRONOMICALLY recommend Nirvana Initiative if you loved the first game. There are enough changes to make the new storyline and gameplay fresh, but enough retained from the old to still feel at home in the world of AI. As usual, my words don’t do it justice… playing the game yourself is the only true way to behold its glory. I’m also trying to hold back on some of the spoilers that made this game astounding… so please, play it before I can’t resist and involuntarily divulge them!

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing ride from beginning to end and a very excellent sequel to the first game. Tons of quality of life and presentation improvements over the first game and while the plot is written carefully to not intersect too much with the first game (so that new players can get on board here if they want to), I feel it does a great job of developing the shared characters and world from the original in interesting ways.  I also think the new story and the new characters on the whole stand out excellently on their own and justify this as its own game without needing the first to prop it up.I have a hard time deciding if I like this more than the first game or vice versa, but at minimum I can say if you liked the original at all or have enjoyed team Zero Escape's other works you'll probably love this.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game. I do think the predecessor's story was a bit more tight and cohesive, but this game's plot juggles a lot more and finds its mark for 99% of it. That aside, characters here are so strong in both with characterization and voice acting that I'd recommend picking the game up just for that. Most characters are over the top in their own unique ways, but they're generally grounded in the world as they find it. Usually at any given time, especially given each protagonist has a partner they can talk to with their thoughts alone, someone is reacting and recognizing what someone said or how the situations they find themselves are, offering both narration and personalized insight. Between that nuance in writing and the full voice acting, everyone feels alive and like a real character and it just makes all of the story more fun. I know VNs are known for having strong writing and characterization, but I want to emphasize I think it's been executed extremely well here. I would also describe the puzzles and somniums as generally more pleasant and challenging, and the graphics and animations as improved over the original. This game is markedly more trippy in the new somniums, which I enjoyed. Overall its better, and ultimately the original having what I think is the tighter story just means I'll recommend you play both.

_childDocuments_.review: ------Intro------I have been privileged enough to receive a review code from Spike Chunsoft for AI: THE SOMNIUM FILES — Nirvana Initiative, who graciously agreed to give me a review code to prevent spoilers on the AITSF subreddit. I wanted to give you a review of the things that other reviews probably won't mention. Technical details, presentation specifics, etc. This review doesn't actually go over any of the plot events whatsoever, so it is 100% free from spoilers and is able to be read for a completely blind playthrough.I am obsessed with this game series, and as such, my review will be written from the perspective of a fan of the first AI: THE SOMNIUM FILES.------Presentation------Character portraits and models look cleaner than ever before, and individual elements of hair, earrings, etc. are all rigged to jiggle when they nod their head in a portrait or in-game, look down, and whatnot. It is very dynamic and looks great. Additionally, Boss, Ritsuko The Receptionist, and Tama all have breast physics, in case you were wondering. I suppose this proves that Boss does not canonically wear a bra at work. H̸̰̋e̷̯̓r̶͔̃ ̶̣͋p̶̰͝o̷̩̐ö̵́ͅr̶̠͐ back...The new animations look phenomenal. The characters all have a gorgeous fluidity about them, and all cutscene animations and most S̵̗̪͑ő̷͓m̶̜̌̔͘n̶̝̹̓̔̎i̵̛̩͙̥u̷͍͍̪̾m̶̻͕̂́ ̸̡̊̇̽ animations are motion-captured, making them look excellent. Combined with the stellar voice acting and snappy dialogue and localization work, it really did make me feel like I was watching a well-choreographed movie at times, not playing a VISUAL NOVEL, of all things!------Technical Details------I played the Steam PC version. It ran perfectly well on my RTX 3060 TI ć̸̩a̵̢͑r̴̼̆d̶̠̈́ with 32 GB RAM and AMD Ryzen 9 5900x... but most people will not have a setup like that. It seems to be about as performance-intense as the first game, but with better lighting and animations.One odd quirk is that the game launcher does not allow for anti-aliasing, which had to actually be forced in the NVIDIA Control Panel for me, and I'm sure the Intel and AMD Control Panels work the same. (Set anti-aliasing to  override to fix this. I have reported this issue to Spike Chunsoft.)AI Sight has been significantly improved. In the previous game, when a flashback to a character speaking occurred, the game would load the scene that character resided in. This resulted in 5, 10, or 15 second long flashbacks when a character would speak about a p̶͇͐ą̸̋s̷͎̔t̵͕̏ ̸̼̋ event. Some events were prerendered, but most were rendered in real-time, resulting in long load times for Date to recall a single line.Meanwhile in Nirvana Initiative, flashbacks work by a character portrait and model appearing in an AI Sight black void. You'd think this would be jarring, but this method of flashbacks get the message across the same way as prior and has the added benefit of instantly loading, not stalling the dialogue.One nitpick, though, is that the few prerendered cutscenes in the game have a jarring amount of visible compression artifacts. I assume the bitrate on the videos is low, but these artifacts are VERY distracting, even on my cheaper, 60HZ 1080p PC monitor, and I hope that the developers address this in a future update.------Writing------As expected, the localization and voice acting are phenomenal, with actors, voice director, and localizers doing a bang-up job. This was a passion project, and I could feel that in the cast's performances, as well as the localization work. Every character felt like a person with thoughts, feelings, etc.Nirvana Initiative is hilarious. I could not stop giggling throughout the game... Arguably, AITSF:NI is funnier than the first game. The jokes are generally less dirty and far more clever, which, in my opinion, makes the dirty jokes that are there much funnier.Characters rarely swear, and when they do, it is used for emotional impact or humor. It's a metaphorical spicy condiment, and they only apply it to dialogue is supposed to be spicy, so when a swear word is in a line, it feels much  more î̴̘͍̯̰͔m̴̲̰̓̀͝p̸̻̘̘͈͇̔͌̅̃ͅȃ̴͓̯̘͇̪̱͙̑̄̓͝c̵̛̜̞̻̥͊̈̉̐̏͝t̷̨̜͈̱͆͑͗͗͆f̵̨̲̮̥̠̦͝͝ú̶͈͖̙͖̓̅̕͝l̸̖̦̙̐́.------Overall Story Reactions, No Spoilers------I was enjoying the game itself. I loved the characters, and thought the twists were pretty great.Then, it happened : the Uchikoshi Moment. The moment where all of my perceived notions of the game's narrative broke, and my jaw hit the floor, leaving me genuinely gasping and giggling like a schoolgirl at the events unfolding on my screen.The game is good. The game is really, REALLY good. You will love this game if you enjoyed the first game.------Misc. Fan Concerns, Addressed------- There is a minor, touching tribute to Brad Venable, voice actor of Kagami in the first AI: THE SOMNIUM FILES, as Kagami has been re-cast. I will not spoil it, but it did make me tear up a bit when I noticed it.- Tama is interesting, and not just a horndog. _childDocuments_.review: A good game, worth its playtime. However, I do feel its inferior to the first game. _childDocuments_.review: Any fan of mystery, detective stuff, or oddball humour has to try this.It's weird with a slightly off the wall and dark sense of humour. _childDocuments_.review: A lot of things were fixed from the previous entry and some stayed the same. Let me start with the good: this game's mystery is on a 'different' level. The past entry was a cute whodunit that revealed information on different timelines. This time the game is a lot more linear, or so it seems, there are several big twist that you can *definitely* see coming if you pay a lot of attention to the way characters talk. I didn't get all of them, but I enjoyed the game a lot regardless. This game explains everything about the previous one that seemed 'off', it creates a solid 'reality' for all the characters to live in, and then it breaks it. Amazing stuff.This sequel feels longer, some Somniums are OK while others are not, the controls are still very janky, but at least every stage seems a lot more balanced, you can skip entire parts of a stage by writing down some notes. If you're a fan of having a piece of paper while playing a game, you will enjoy the puzzles in this one. A lot of stages require you to figure out codes, which might be good or not for you, some I enjoyed, some others I did not, specifically the ones that you have to solve while something is chasing you. The UI is still sometimes confusing, make your choices slowly if you don't want to get mad.I enjoyed a lot of the endgame. I could have kept playing this game for a lot more. I loved the messages and themes. I'll buy the next one for sure. If you're a fan of the scenario writer, there are a lot of references to past games, which I'm now inclined to check out. Thank you for this Uchikoshi.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you played the first game? , then go play that instead; while this game generally doesn't spoil the first one (unless you let it), the original does a better job at establishing the world and I think it's better overall. , I'd say this game does not hold up to the first one, although it does do certain things better. In general: the investigation/somnium gameplay has some improvements, but the story has pacing issues, there's a big twist which comes out of nowhere (and is recycled on top of that), some characters serve no real purpose and the ending is... well. I didn't like it. I'll explain myself a bit more if you'd like.I mean, that's what we wanted, right? More of what made Date's adventure so great. Diving into dreams, strange, gruesome murders, clever culprits, insane twists, dirty jokes, dancing...? And of course the colourful cast of characters, connected to each other in unexpected ways. And this game does deliver - on all mentioned points.Although the ratio is off. The game's main dance number makes an appearance FIVE times. You can't skip it, unless you turned on "skip first time scenes" in the settings. It's cute, but it was far too much. As for dirty humour - Mr. Porno Mag does some Porno Mag stuff, but since he's not the main character anymore, you don't see a lot of it. Luckily, another character picks up the slack, but she's only there for half of the game.And the characters. Almost all of them come back in this game, and there's more besides. But many of the new ones feel weird for weird's sake - and they're somewhat one-dimensional. There are some crazy connections, although some of them are badly foreshadowed and feel like they came out of nowhere - but still enjoyable.Of course, the Somnia make a return. In general, I didn't enjoy them as much as in the previous game - but they did have some interesting changes. For one, every interaction gives you a piece of a 'key' - a hint, meaning to explain how the dream world works. I found many of those keys rather useless - but in some cases they were incredibly helpful. So it's a bit of a mixed bag.Perhaps my biggest complaint is that the Somnia didn't feel like dreams, more like escape rooms. In one case you literally have to do math puzzles. Luckily, if you're too stuck, your AI-Ball partner will solve it for you... if you have enough time, that is, because even inspecting objects now costs precious time (and you can't use timies for these). There are also additional mechanics introduced. Halfway through the game, hostile entities show up in Somnia; they move even when you stand still, and if they catch you, you're losing a lot of time. There are also sneaking segments with QTEs. In fact, there are so many QTEs in this game - often in fight scenes which feel like Bollywood rather than anime. And if you fail a QTE once, you have to redo the whole scene; the difficulty can be adjusted, but it's simply not fun at all either way.So that's all good, or not, but we are all here for one main reason: the story. Is it good? In general - yes, although there are some major issues.For the most part, it's what you expect. Seemingly impossible killings which look like they're part of something greater. This part is pretty good; you can actually walk around crime scenes and use X-Ray and Thermal modes on pretty much anything - a welcome change. The game also has you explain everything at the end of each investigation, Danganronpa style - making sure that the investigator and the player are on the same page.However, the story suffers from some pacing issues. Often things just halt completely because you need to talk to some people about something totally unrelated to the investigation... because there might be something related to those relationship plot twists I mentioned earlier. Overall that part is incredibly boring and often doesn't even serve the story in a meaningful way - I can think of several characters which could be cut from the script entirely.And there are two other major issues. One - I feel that the game doesn't follow the rules of fair whodunnit. There is a certain twist which is, I feel, impossible to guess, even if it's somewhat foreshadowed. The first game's twist was foreshadowed in such a masterful way that the player and Date figured it out at the same time, which was fantastic. Nothing like this here. And two - if you're familiar with Kotaro Uchikoshi's work, this game pretty much recycles one of his previous twists/storylines. Except the original did it in a meaningful and interesting way, but here it seems to serve no purpose whatsoever - it's just there to confuse you.On top of all that, the ending is pretty middling. And if you follow the aforementioned twist, you get an even more unsatisfying ending. Some plot threads are left unresolved, and some things make no sense if you think about them a bit more. I enjoyed myself quite a bit when playing this - but I also got frustrated many times, and rolled my eyes rather hard. At the unskippable dances, at the awkward fight scenes, at the long-winded conversations about nothing - and at all-too-common pixel hunts during the point-and-click sections of the investigation. I'd say this is Uchikoshi's weakest work story-wise, and the only one I'm familiar with that I wouldn't recommend.That said, the spirit of the first game is still there. So if you just want to see some Porno Mag hijinks, talk to breasts sitting at the desk, and watch teenage girls talk about occult... I won't stop you. Just a word of advice: lower your expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: What a weird, weird game. And a weird, weird sequel. AI: The Somnium Files from 2019 was some of the tightest, most compelling stuff either Uchikoshi or Spike Chunsoft had ever done. It used its sparing budget to effectively portray a tense, grim story of thrills, gore and sci-fi hijinks interspersed with ridiculous humor using solid 3D visuals, cutscenes and great voice acting. The experience felt complete, near perfection even. It seemed a sequel had a straight path to enlightenment. Nirvana Initiative, though, goes balls to the wall. It really screws up that weirdness knob. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ humor is turned up to 11. Everything from the visuals to the events playing out in the story take on a note of farce until it starts taking center stage. There are times where the story gets completely lost in it - was this supposed to be a murder investigation?I'd say it's a shame, but the characters kept the game enjoyable and compelling and the laughs were very genuine. When we do get to the meat of the murder mystery, the writing is often inconsistent due to the sheer oddity of what it wants to accomplish. When Uchikoshi finally pulled the rug from under me, I had to spend at least 15 minutes staring at the screen, going through the events in my mind to take it in. It's not the most elegant mindf*ck, but boy it it compelling.And that last sentence about sums up my experience with the story. Maybe not the smoothest or most thrilling ride in the park, but man is there nothing quite like it. I wouldn't rate it as high as the previous game, but I definitely don't feel like I've lost anything playing it. There are so many cool concepts, visuals and ideas packed in there.As for the *game* part of the game, I do still feel like the machanics could take better advantage of the setting and story to create better brainteasers like the latter games in Zero Escape did, but there ARE some really neat Somniums and gameplay scenarious that blow the previous game out of the water in that respect.All in all, another great Uchikoshi experience. It's not the direction I would have expected from a sequel to AI: The Somnium Files, but a fantastic thought experiment none-the-less. Except for the ending maybe. That left a bit to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be difficult.  I got this as a gift from a friend after getting the first game for myself for my birthday.  I bought the first game and had a rough time due to having Windows 7 at the time playing it.(Those who know, will know what I'm talking about)Still I absolutely adored it despite the political preaching of THE MESSAGE.I was surprised that they were even doing a sequel, so I was a bit excited.  I start playing knowing about this great twist that is absolutely mind-bending.  What I found instead is probably the most uneven experience I've gotten from Uchikoshi yet.  I've played Ever17, 999, VLR, ZTD, etc.  I'm used to his writing style.  One thing that I've noticed is that he seems to struggle with sequels at times.  I was hoping he wouldn't this time, but sure enough he did.There are aspects here that have better character writing than the first game.  One character is the embodiment of a redemption arc.  One character is probably the most tragic comedian I've ever read about.  One character has a somnium that is flat out a reference to previous works.  These were the absolute highlights.This is where my praise ends.  This game long-winded, even preachier with the politics of THE MESSAGE, has idiotic character moments that are beyond baffling, plot holes larger than caverns that can't be overlooked, and is so painfully...PAINFULLY unfunny that I'm shocked that it released like this.  This game is sequelitis incarnate.There were quirks and funny moments from the first game that people liked, so they tried to reference that, over and over and over and over again.  That's to its detriment.  There's also the optional dialogue that's even worse than before with tons of repeated jokes over the course of the game without any sort differing comments.  Mizuki and Aiba do not bounce off each other in terms of comedy.  It was already established in the first game that personality-wise, they were very similar.  This created so many awkward, nonsensical lines of dialogue between the two.  Ryuki and Tama had better dialogue, but that's because Tama only made sex jokes and Ryuki is kinda weird. It worked alright, but that's half the game if not less than half the game.The endings, oh my god, the endings.  There was ONE ending that I liked.  Maybe Two.  In the first game, I liked ALL of them.  This game had two endings that were the worst endings in his writings history.  Yes, the true ending is one of them.  That twist was unsatisfying.  It was initially confusing, but I got the gist of it.  I think they created this story just for the twist and wrote everything around it rather than the other way around.  The story REALLY suffers for it.I'm being vague on spoilers, because there's no way I can dissuade someone from not giving this a shot anyway.  I'm just saying, I'm going to call this game the second worst game I've played from Uchikoshi.  The first worst was Zero Time Dilemma.  I can't recommend it unless you are SERIOUSLY bored, and even then...I'd rather play other visual novels.

So, they have very flat personalities, and usually have one extremely strong character trait that vastly overshadows everything else.The twists are cool, but also extremely contrived. _childDocuments_.review: By far the stupidest Uchikoshi game I've ever played. And that's saying A LOT.AI1 was silly at times, but it made sense at the end. It wasn't anything revolutionary, but the twists were interesting and possible to figure out.AI2 is actually quite boring until the midway point, where you're assaulted with approximately 37 stupid plot twists in quick succession, all in service of achieving one underlying idea which is, to be fair, quite interesting in concept. However this came at the expense of destroying my suspension of disbelief, and when I reached the ending I could not care less.I'm also quite tired of the gameplay at this point. The somnium sections were a fun new concept in the first AI, but they have not built anything on top of them for this game. If you're lucky, a somnium section might have one interesting puzzle, but more often than not, they just felt like trying a lot of options randomly under a time limit for some reason, which often led to me running out of time and having to replay the entire section with the solutions I already knew just to have 1 more minute at the end to finish it. huge waste of time.There are also QTEs in this game. They're bad as all QTEs are, but they're also very samey and cringy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has fantastic characters which I really enjoyed seeing and learning more about mixed with the characters from the first game who are a little bit different than last time but not so different that it's really noticeable with a handful of exceptions.The wonderful cast of characters are put into a story that makes genuinely no sense what so ever. At the end of the game your understanding of the flow chart changes and that alone made it next to impossible for me to figure out what happened when. Did I meet this person yet? Did I get this plot point in this timeline? Is this character dead? all questions I had and couldn't answer until the very end of the game after they're finished hammering it into your head though to be honest i STILL don't understand the plot completely because this game was not written to be understood. the game was written to make you say WOW I NEVER EXPECTED THAT and it shows in just about every twist reveal this game has.The Zero escape series has always been about branching pathways and differing timelines. things learned in one time line can help in another and eventually you reach multiple endings and solve the whole puzzle. this was brought over to AI The Somnium Files so when buying this game i expected the same. What i got however was a total of 6 endings (being generous) 3 of which are character endings where the two characters are happy now and drive off into the sunset because you solved all their problems by entering their brains and winging it. this also means that the amount of somniums with branching paths are 4 and the first one is only to force you to play the events from 6 years ago as Ryuki.There are assuming i counted right 8 somniums that are 100% straight lines and in all of them you will be dragged through them by a string making them next to impossible to fail. the only puzzle that has any challenge is Lien's because the game doesn't tell you how to do it and in fact pushes you to solve it the wrong way. I had to look up a walkthrough because the game had conditioned me to only do what it showed and that it would not keep secrets from me unless they are plot related like how at the beginning of the game you are asked to type the killers name but having just started you don't know the killers name. Honestly this ended up with me being frustrated more often than not because you would get asked these impossible questions in the same style as questions the game yells at you for not knowing the answer to so it's impossible to know if you have heard the answer before or if the game just expects you to know it.Not to mention these puzzles that the game expects you to know are really difficult at one point i had to google it because i came across the right answer but didn't realize because it was a shortened set of words. there are a couple puzzles in this game i genuinely don't know how a normal person would be able to solve without googling. all and all i think Special Rito's negative review is a good sum of how i feel about this game. it's not nearly as good as the first game and honestly as much as i don't regret buying this and playing it myself i don't recommend anyone else do it

_childDocuments_.review: : This review is a bit long. Scroll to the bottom for a TLDR if you don't want to read through everything.After playing the first Somnium Files game, I was completely enamored with the AI world. Though I was more than satisfied with the ending to the first game, I still had several unanswered questions, such as: . I was also left with the desire to get to know Mizuki more as a character, as I felt like she didn't get her due diligence. Needless to say, all of this and more was answered in . The continuation of story elements first discussed in the original AI game were incorporated flawlessly into this sequel. However, unlike other sequel games, this one opens up by asking you if you're familiar with the events of the previous game. If you are, then appropriate references to the game are made. If not (say, you play these out of order), you can choose to not have the first game's events spoiled for you. This level of consideration to the player-base is unusual, in my experience, and shows a dedication to the quality and integrity of the series. If you have played the original game, the changes to game play are refreshing without being entirely novel. This allows players to enjoy novel aspects expected in a sequel while staying true to the elements that are hallmarks of the series (such as psyncing). I also enjoyed seeing characters that I was familiar with, as well as memorable new characters that were introduced in a very natural way. Tama is a great counter-personality to Aiba, which makes the game more interesting and adds a depth to the AI-assisted storyline that I really appreciate. And, of course, I thoroughly enjoy the twisty-turny mindf**ks that Spike Chunsoft always puts us through. However, they truly outdid themselves with this one, and I loved every second of it. As a mystery, action, and story-rich game fan, this hit *all* of my sweet spots. So, TLDR; If you enjoy mysteries, story-rich world/character building, sexual humor, deep philosophical themes, technology and AI, puzzles, pop-culture references, and kick-ass action scenes, with a little bit of dancing and J-pop thrown in, you will be hooked on , especially .

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect that a game as quirky and unusual as AI: The Somnium Files would get a sequel, much less so soon, but here we are and I can't be any happier. This game has more or less the same idea - investigating a gruesome murder case as a secret unit police officer who can enter the mind of others - but it adds several spins to it and retcons some aspects of the original. Now there are two protagonists who investigate the case at different time periods, QTE sections are less abundant and Somniums (dream sequences) are overall more streamlined. The dialogues, which was in my opinion one of the strong points of the original, remains as funny and ridiculous, but I'd say it's a bit more toned down compared to the first game.The main aspect of the game is definitely the plot though and it is legitimately great. I don't remember a game where the further I was going the less I was understanding what was going on, but here the resolution of the the plot twists was satisfying and didn't feel forced. I sort of enjoyed being in the dark and feeling as clueless as the protagonists. Everything makes sense if you analyze it and the game perfectly uses foreshadowing. Diverging paths return, but this time they felt more like a way to learn new clues, rather than being complete endings. That is basically the only thing that the original does way better. It's not that these endings aren't emotionally heavy, but they didn't destroy me like some of the endings from the first game. That being said the game is still just as tear jerking, but these moments mostly don't come with endings I'd say. I also have to mention the characters. It's nice to see the returning ones, but the new characters are just as great and I hope they all return in the next game that I will be expecting now. I especially liked the new protagonist Ryuki and his companion Tama, I definitely missed them in the second half of the game where the protagonist is Mizuki.I am only scratching the surface with this review, but I don't want to give away too much. This is definitely a must play for any fan of visual novels and for those who enjoy complicated stories with crazy twists with hilarious dialogues and emotional sequences.

_childDocuments_.review: While it's definitely not as good as the first game, I highly recommend this to anyone who played the original, though I suggest waiting at least a few weeks before moving on to this game. This may just be the fact I've played it more recently, but this game leans far more into the ridiculous aspects of the first game and does so sooner, which makes it a bit off putting at first. While the story is alright, in my opinion it was nowhere near as satisfying to watch all the pieces fall together when compared to the first game. However, this game has good characters, including most of them that were not in the original game, so I definitely still would recommend playing this. Hopefully a third game, if it ever occurs, manages to use the best aspects of both games. tl;dr highly recommended for anyone who played the first game; if you haven't played the first game try that first and then see if you want to play this.

_childDocuments_.review: At the end of the day, when it comes to a visual novel or adventure game, it lives and dies by its writing. This is maybe the first time I've seen a game be technically competent, have enjoyable puzzles, fantastic music, compelling atmosphere, and intriguing themes, only to then  die by the writing. This is a cast of compelling characters, interesting mysteries, and an evolution of a fantastic game before it, all culminating in truly no interesting result whatsoever. It's not bereft of great moments, and I've come around on some games with unsatisfying conclusions before, but... this has no idea what it wants to be as a mystery, as a sequel, or as a game, and having played through it a few times to really try to soak in all the little details I missed and 100% completing it to make  sure I wasn't just missing something, I, uh, wasn't.Somnium Files is an easy, easy recommend. This, however, is probably a testament to why you might wanna leave the audience wanting more.

_childDocuments_.review: This game expands significantly on the systems introduced in the first game so much so that it's functionally a direct upgrade in every aspect besides things like the comedy, characterization, and/or themes as that's subjective. I don't feel like the new AI companion gets enough time to shine as I found myself growing more fond of the other new characters introduced in this story but it's not really to a fault, the side characters in this game (much like the previous title) are just that compelling. The story touches on a lot more interesting topics with the narrative presenting some really neat questions to the player without giving them a clear side as to which part of the debate is the "correct" answer which is really cool to see in a modern VN. The Somniums are also just significantly improved over the previous title where they were more so random with hardly any puzzles to speak of. This game's got puzzles all over the place and it actually feels like it's possible to fail on certain Somniums even when playing on Standard. The types of puzzles is also quite varied and doesn't get old at all.Lots of QoL improvements across the board to certain systems and introducing the customization feature isn't a bad thing even if I didn't really engage with it until I started my 100% quest. The optional content in the game is pretty doable for anyone and easy to look for without a guide; though, a few of those achievements were a bit out there but not terribly convoluted. Can't say much more without spoiling the story and optional content but it's a wild wide and I can definitely see why Uchikoshi has been putting so much time into the current duology of this series. I strongly recommend picking it up if you enjoyed the first game or have previously played the Nonary Games series!

_childDocuments_.review: (Forward: The Original  (Hereafter )  is available for game pass at time of writing. While this sequel claims that it's playable without context from there,  (hereafter ) borrows almost the entire cast from the original and a number of it's locations and plot points.)Well, what are the odds, right? If there was any game I'd have bet money against getting a sequel, the weird widget Visual Novel / Soft Puzzler of the original  would have been at the top of the list. Mired in extremely strange controversy and seemingly doomed to obscurity, it appears to have found new life through word of mouth, GamePass, and director/visionary/real life crazy person Kotaro Uchikoshi's single minded passion. But even becoming a sleeper hit should have resulted in little more than an afterlife of getting re-mastered every six years for the next generation of consoles.And for the most part, I was fine with that future.  is my favorite visual novel; complete in it's vision and absolutely the product of one deeply creative mind, it's (many) faults were buoyed by a tremendous performance from it's two leads who shared easy chemistry and writing that gave them as much time as possible to bounce off each-other. The original lived and died by the strength of it's characters performances, less than by it's soft-science nightmare of a story that never could find a use for the titular somnium device. Indeed, the whole framing device of the Psync Machines was almost completely burnt out by the end of  . Had the game gone much longer it's likely that the already exposed wiring of the story would have started to form a fire hazard.Much like Kotaro, I am engaging in some subtle foreshadowing here. So I walked into  with some trepidation. Would this be the sophomore slump that dragged down the whole franchise back into the hole it had just resurrected itself out of? Well, yes and no. But let me say that unequivocally, the cast is fantastic. While the localization suffers everything that the original did, a lot of "This joke was untranslatable, so we didn't bother", for every miss there's a lot of sharp humor that lands. Not everything is going to get the localization that  got, and comparing things to the platinum ideal is unfair. No matter how weird it gets, the voice actors and actresses sell the ever loving hell out it. Special note to Stephen Fu as Ryuki who's given an absolutely thankless task of doing "Anime Boy" but when given rare chances to act hits it out of the park. Which leads to our crime solvers: Sassy Aiba is now paired with powerhouse Mizuki while newcomers Horny-On-Main Tama and Stock Anime Boy Ryuki who are doing their best to catch lightning in a bottle. Neither has the effortless charm or strangely warm chemistry that Aiba and Date had, but both pairings are giving it 100% and that counts for a lot. It also helps that  lacks the narrative dead ends that threatened to constantly to cripple , there are some of us who still wake up screaming about 'The Iris Arc'. However, because the story is split near evenly between Ryuki and Mizuki, neither really get the screen time that Date and Aiba got, and the pairings are just inherently weaker. Ryuki is too much a cold fish to ever catalyze Tama's sweaty heat into a meaningful character relationship. We're told that they care for each-other, but they're doing schtich: Tama does something horny, Ryuki acts flustered or clueless, audience chuckles, next scene. There's never a moment where you feel worried that they'll be separated, hell, you start to wish for it just so that the stakes might get raised a bit.Mizuki and Aiba have a similar issue, where there just doesn't seem to be much going on between them. Mizuki seems more than capable of handling the investigation herself, and Aiba (likely as a result of not being able to discuss the original game) doesn't really seem to have any connection to her metaphorical step-daughter. Date at least had this clueless audience surrogate-ness about him that made Aiba feel like an essential part of his whole. It's what makes the climax of  work at all – Date was such a terrible detective that without his trillion-yen cybernetic implant/girlfriend, he was basically helpless. Mizuki is physically invulnerable, emotionally stable, and mentally razor sharp, so Aiba has this terrible sense of just being around to drop a joke and strut her model – she isn't really necessary, Mizuki could be a perfectly capable cop without the ability to psync at all.And the Psync sessions have their own issues, mostly in that they're all horrible slogs. They were horrible slogs in the original too, but here there seems to be an almost conscious effort to drag every single person in Japan into these machines regardless of whether or not the characters have any reason to (more than once a Psync level is triggered by someone who has every possible reason to just tell you flat information). The investigation is going well, the plot is really moving and then you need to slam to a halt to go and do some benign point-and-click adventure gaming to get information that you could have just gotten with a warrant. If you're unlucky, you end in a Somnium with an incredibly tight timer and a puzzle designed to waste your time and force you to do it twice and walk out knowing less than you knew going in. But I was delighted for the Somnium sections compared to the action sequences - brief moments where you do Resident Evil 4 QTEs. While the action scenes in  were mediocre at best and completely nonsensical at worst, everything has been jacked up to an exponential in . It starts to chafe when the game is asking us to take the murders very seriously only to have the entire cast effortlessly shrug off bullets, lasers, collapsing super structures...and then do it again. And again.  until you've long forgotten how anyone in this universe could possibly die if even supposedly vanilla humans like Ryuki are dodging bullets and kicking power-armoured space marines into unconsciousness. Yeah, it's an anime, sure, but the issue is less that you get the occasional goofy action scene, but that the goofy action scenes keep happening until you're forced to start asking questions. It doesn't help that the action scenes never really escape feeling like a late stage RWBY episode. does not feel complete or cohesive in the way it's predecessor felt. It feels wild and bloated, it swaggers with the invulnerability of the unexpected sequel and promise of more. It knows it has nothing to prove and so just goes absolutely wild with it's worst impulses. It has entirely too much time to dedicate to things it doesn't need and not enough time to dedicate to what would have elevated it. It's a bloated disaster with zero restraint or sense, it is a complete downgrade in everything I loved from the original. I despise it. I wish it hadn't been made. And yet I can't bring myself to give it a thumbs down. Maybe that's residual love for the original, maybe it's the fact that the scenario was so compelling I couldn't put it down despite it's flaws. Maybe it's the incredible performances and the absolute open-heartedness and absolute lack of self-consciousness that I found to be irresistible. Maybe it's the secret ending that hits every checkbox I want out of e mindscrew stories except that it's not the main scenario.  is a messy, bombastic, nonsensical nightmare that wears its fetishes and inspirations on its sleeve and stopped caring a long time ago if you like it, because you don't need to like it for it to survive, you just need to . I love it. I want another one. I too, it seems, am split directly down the middle.

_childDocuments_.review: This sequel get's a lot of things right, but also some things wrong. Overall though, I liked the game, and would recommend it to others, but there's some things players should be aware of first.First, the positives, I have to praise the new somniums in this game. They really changed up the formula and it works extremely well. The new ideas that were implemented led to some of the most memorable somniums this series has to offer. The story presentation was also really well done, the main twist was shocking but also enlightening because the game gives you several hints that if you're paying attention, can probably piece together the twist before it's spelled out for you just before the finale. The virtual reality investigations is also really cool, my only gripe about it is that some of them are really short and feel unfinished, but that can also be attributed to the lack of evidence to really investigate at some scenes. Now for the negatives, the characters are pretty hit or miss. I loved some new additions like Ryuki and Tama, but some people like Lien I just can't bring myself to like. I hate how the game goes out of its way to not spoil anything from the first game, despite being a sequel. Even if you say at the beginning you don't mind spoilers from the first game, it still goes out of the way to not say much about it. My biggest negative however is the overall story, mainly the ending. Don't get me wrong, figuring out the overall mystery behind the murders is really fun and the strongest point of the story, but once you figure out the truth, it feels a little underwhelming, not only that, but the stakes at the end feels extremely over the top and unwarranted. The story up until the finale is some of the best storytelling I've experienced in a while, but the finale itself leaves a lot to be desired. I much preferred the more down to earth story the first game had to offer compared to the over the top stakes this game did for it's finale. Overall though, I enjoyed the game a lot. Gameplay wise, I prefer it over the first game, but I prefer the first game's story over the one that's been told here. You may disagree however. If you like the first game, you'll like this one. If you're new to the series, I recommend playing the first game before this one despite this game not spoiling the first, it still makes more sense to play the first game before playing this one.

_childDocuments_.review: AI: THE SOMNIUM FILES is like Knives Out. Both came out in 2019, and were some of the best pieces of mystery fiction of that year. With well rounded casts of memorable characters, and mysteries that always stayed one step ahead of you to pull rugs from beneath your feet, before tying themselves up in a perfect knot, they were thrilling and unforgettable.nirvanA Initiative is sort of like Glass Onion. Both came out in 2022, and were bigger and bolder than their predecessors, but not necessarily better. They were weaker and more contrived, trying to stay ahead of an audience that was expecting to get rugpulled. But they’re still fun mysteries at the end of the day, even if they don’t quite match the highs that their predecessors set.Before I get into the next part, let me say that I do recommend nirvanA Initiative. It has many of the same strengths TSF does. Great character writing, and a murder mystery that stays engaging throughout. In terms of gameplay, it’s actually even stronger than TSF - there are all sorts of new mechanics and gameplay interactions that expand on those in the first game, and the somniums are less “trial and error” and more intuitive than before.The biggest fault that nirvanA Initiative and Glass Onion suffer from is their smugness. In trying to show the audience how clever they are, they both try to pull an invisible rug. The audience might not even have realized there  a rug in the first place, despite expecting a rug. Plus, it’s an  rug. It doesn’t add anything to the room itself - it’s there solely to trip the audience. Furthermore, in the process of rugpulling, they also spill some of the furniture, and then accidentally get caught on the rug as well.Remember how I said nirvanA Initiative is  like Glass Onion? Glass Onion only knocked over like, a book and a vase, and caught itself before it fell, then set back up what it spilled. You’re a bit upset with it for pulling an invisible rug, a rug that doesn’t actually add to how the room looks, but you admire the boldness of the move, how it cleaned up after itself, and didn’t trip. It was fun as hell to get rugpulled, after all.nirvanA Initiative trashed the entire room pulling this rug, and then tripped on the rug itself. You’re left trying to process what just happened as you look across the trashed living room. You now notice how some of the furniture doesn’t quite fit together. Some furniture isn’t even here at all. Hell, it even managed to mess up some of the furniture in the original TSF room! After a while, nirvanA Initiative wakes up, and slowly begins fixing the room. It takes a while to fix, but it did eventually fix  of the room - but there’s still some knocked over bits here and there, and now you’re fixating on the out of place & missing furniture.In the end, you’re left more confused than anything - getting rugpulled was fun, but were they really decorating this entire room solely for the rugpull? Were they not considering the actual furniture of the room, or how they’d clean up? The rug is still invisible, not actually adding anything to the appearance of the room. You take one more look at the room. Despite everything wrong with it - the spilled furniture, the mismatching furniture, the missing furniture, and the invisible rug that doesn’t add anything to the room, it is ultimately still a nice room.If you loved Knives Out, you probably didn't hate Glass Onion. The same holds true here. If you loved THE SOMNIUM FILES, you probably won’t hate nirvanA Initiative either. Though, that “probably” is a bit more uncertain than the one for Glass Onion.

Which one of it you will like more I think comes down more to a personal preference.All in all, if you liked the first game or you like Uchikoshi's work in general, you should buy AI 2. _childDocuments_.review: If the PC Port was more polished, I'd probably recommend it even though I don't like it because at least it has a soul. Unfortunately, this PC port is worse than the first game. It straight up doesn't have anti-aliasing at all, which leads to all the dialogue text with the AI characters being aliased, you literally see the jagged edges on letters, which is the first I've ever seen in a, uh, VISUAL NOVEL. The controller support is also subpar, it doesn't display the correct buttons for my controller type, and that doesn't matter, but there's weird menu stuff like how it always defaults to being in the middle, before snapping to the top of the list. There's lots of quality of life annoyances like that. If none of that matters to you (fair enough) and you just want a compelling murder mystery thriller, this game is not it. The story frequently writes itself into dead ends, so then characters will just turn up and give you information. There also aren't a whole lot of characters, so everyone has to get roped into the story somehow, which becomes contrived beyond all belief. The characters just do whatever the story needs them to without caring if it makes sense for them, and the payoff doesn't work because it feels like they crowbared in a twist and have to  snap in half trying to make it work instead of thinking of an actually clever way to do it. I liked some of the characters, but others end up coming across as schizophrenic because the cast is so limited they get forced to do actions that don't make sense for them. Weirdly enough, it feels like NI both had less of a budget and more of one than the first game because it has way more somnium puzzle sequences and action scenes, but then reuses numerous characters and locations from the first game. The action sequences are terrible, by the way, as there is virtually no rhyme or reason to how they work. Fight geography, choreography, how many people are fighting, distance, none of it matters. It's jarring, and the total lack of consistency to them makes it impossible to care what's going on. If all you care about is something to kill time and is somewhat entertaining and has a soul, this game is worth playing, but the first game managed to tell a compelling and interesting mystery while still also doing all of that. If they make a third game, I really hope they shore up the writing, which isn't an unreasonable ask for a VISUAL NOVEL like come on the story is the whole point.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply put, a fun mystery game with its own share of big twists. Fans of the previous game might enjoy this one, but it struggles to separate itself from its predecessor. Personally, it felt like they were leaning too much into what people liked from the previous game that it's hard for this entry to stand out. Humor feels similar, plenty of reused environments, and Somniums feel a bit hand-holdy and lose some of the mystique as a result. Not dealbreakers, but it made me feel like there could've been so much more as a sequel.The good parts from the previous game are still here in full force: the humor is still enjoyable, the main mystery of the game is unique, and the relationships between characters are often complex and interconnected. Quite a few things can be inferred, but it's not often that you'll have a blatantly obvious "oh they're the killer" kind of situation at a first glance. It's mostly about the how and why, rather than who, and finding the answers to those questions is the main driving force of AI.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll say this upfront - Nirvana Initiative is not as good a game as the first Somnium Files. The narrative is more rickety, the Somnium puzzles feel significantly more linear and less engaging as a result, and the game's core structural twist is a gimmick that, frankly, doesn't really make a difference to the game's actual narrative. With all that said, though, if you enjoyed the first game, and if you enjoy this specific brand of puzzle/mystery game, you'll still get a lot of enjoyment out of Nirvana Initiative.Story-wise, I was still very engaged with the main mystery throughout, even if it felt like there were a few more holes and necessary plot contrivances in Nirvana Initiative compared to the first game. The first game was the kind of puzzle box where every single piece mattered, every story element, every character, every scene contributed directly to the mystery and the story being told. In Nirvana Initiative, there are several elements that feel like they were written solely to solve an issue with the narrative, without any real merit on their own, and most of the returning characters feel superfluous and inessential to the narrative (especially Ota and Iris). On the other hand, I appreciate that the game allowed us to spend time with these characters without re-opening their character arcs - the returning characters had stories that were "solved" in the first game, and this game leaves them solved, which was a breath of fresh air, considering the game easily could've laid more conflict on top of them and "unsolved" their personal stories for the sake of their reappearances.The new characters, by contrast, all hit hard for me - character design and backstory are things that Uchikoshi's team never miss on, and the work done in that regard in Nirvana Initiative is stellar as always. Even the returning characters that DO get major story time feel like they've earned it, evolving in new and interesting ways where they previously were secondary or tertiary to the narrative. It's a balance that you don't always see struck very well, especially as a series goes on and on and more characters are added that the developers then feel the need to shove back into subsequent games, no matter how little it makes sense. It's still early in the AI series, and there may not even be more games after this, but the early signs seem to me like they'll be able to manage well.Gameplay is still solid, with a slightly cleaner interface, but as I said before, there's something off about the Somnium design compared to the first game. So many of them have a clear flowchart to them, where you don't need to suss out the right answer for progression, you just need to find the object that will advance the story of the Somnium. There are still full puzzle-style Somniums over the course of the game, but it felt like they were few and far between, and I found that disappointing, because the puzzles are the primary gameplay aspect of the game. If even those are linearized, there's even less to actually "play," given the rest of the game is essentially a visual novel. Hopefully, if a third game is made, more emphasis is put on making the Somniums fully interactive puzzles again.On the whole, there's a lot more to nitpick about Nirvana Initiative than the first game, and in some ways, that's disappointing, but I think that perspective is needed on this. The first game is a masterpiece of this genre, telling an incredibly tight, cohesive story with no wasted movement, and that's not easy to do. It sets a standard to live up to that is basically impossible to consistently reach, and it's unfortunate that it makes Nirvana Initiative look worse in comparison, because I do believe this is still a great game overall. I really hope there's more on the horizon.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: It is a funny, albeit reference heavy sequel to an already great choose-your-own adventure anime detective game. It expands on the original game in most ways you would want, but has some really dumb puzzles and messier narrative that the game's greater scope may not be enough to overshadow for some people. I played AI: the Somnium Files on the Nintendo Switch and found it to be one of the most enjoyable semi-linear stories I have interacted with in gaming. This game is very much sequel and, while it does have things to help mitigate spoilers for the first game, I would highly recommend playing it predecessor first. It really is a much better experience if you do. For those new to AI: Somnium Files or Nirvana Initiative, these games are basically somewhere in between Blade Runner meets in Inception, but by the way of a late night Adult Swim cartoon. They are choose your own adventure, detective games where you go inside people's dreams and through genre saviness or trial and error you mess around to find out secrets and sometimes diverge the story down multiple paths. Much like other visual novels/adventure games, you will eventually go through all of these narrative paths and find out the greater context of what is going on and why.  The stories in both are best for those going in blind. Just know the games are equal part camp, edginess, sexual humor, and genuinely good mysteries. These games are full of anime and pop culture references which will tell you if this is up your alley or not. On spectrum of "so-random" type humor, it is closer to Freakazoid than Deadpool. If that sounds appealing, then you are in for a wonderful ride. For those who played the first game, this game is that with most of the quality of life improvements you would want. I did encounter an issue where I couldn't save after completing a route without going back into previous scene; this meant when I left narrative map for the main screen, it didn't save several hours of progress to end that route. Don't be me, always go back into a scene and save. Other than that, the gameplay is mostly* better and the store has way more to it than the first game. You will probably have mixed feelings about this narrative though. Its still recommended and is an absolutely wonderful sequel; but, the story is more convoluted and has a bunch of unresolved setups. Its cool how much this game can add to the world-building of the AI universe, but this game will gladly hint at something more than never touch on it again. The main points of the story do conclude and the game definitely will surprise you like the first one might have. The twists and turns of the second game may not be as well implement in this second game though. Don't go in expecting to be as a cleanly done in the first one (unfortunately). The puzzles in this game are generally better, BUT you will probably be better off knowing the solutions don't always have to be actual words. I won't say more so as to not spoil things, but there are some puzzles without clear solutions, no explanations and don't really make sense if you assume a "real word" as an answer. Just knowing that will improve your play experience; sometimes just go with the obvious solution even if the answer makes absolutely no sense. This game would be like 10/10 if it wasn't for these factors; but it pans to around an 8 or so. It is still very good and there is a lot of cool things they put into the game from the original. The side content and replay-ability of this game is much higher than the first. Over all, very good and I would still recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted this game to be better than the original Somnium Files. It isn't. That doesn't make it bad, in fact I'd argue that on the individual aspects Nirvana Initiative improves on almost every part of the first game. But there's issues here that one didn't have.Praise first. Keep the mood light. Everything works. The new Somniums are all well done - some great ideas and creative expansions from the first game. Ryuki works better than I expected (and Mizuki remains a treat). The sex jokes are much improved: still here, but placed better and don't detract from the mood of more serious scenes. The new VR investigations are cool - they need a little work, but it was nice to have an alternative to Psynching occasionally.Now the one, overwhelming bad point that IMO almost sinks this game.This isn't a detective story.Oh, it'll try to fool you at first. You've got a mysterious serial killer running around, suspects, crime scenes. But even if the specifics elude you, roughly what's going on will become clear pretty quickly. This isn't like the first game, where you're running through a list of suspects, tracking the victim's movements and trying to work out what's going on. The feel's more of a thriller, focused on the action beats, the philosophical motivations of the villains and Ryuki's issues with trauma.This isn't inherently bad, but that is harder material to use for a visual novel's plot, and Nirvana Initiative doesn't quite make that mark. It's got more and better action than the first game, but not enough for it to really carry the whole production. Without the strong through line the previous game had, the slower paced looks into the lives of our side characters come off less like a welcome change of pace and more like a distraction.Plus there's a knock on effect to the gameplay. This lessened focus on the mystery aspect robs weight from both the CSI segments and many of the Somniums. Both feel much less important this time out. A lot of psynchs feel like paper thin excuses to inject gameplay into the plot: characters being called to ABIS to extract one specific piece of information from them that could've been gotten through regular interrogation. Even if the resulting Somnium is fun, I felt like my time was being wasted. One crime scene investigation section boils down to 'Mizuki figures out how a lock works'. (And no. Not a complex puzzle lock. A 'press two buttons' lock.) The interrogation segments are gone, and frankly are missed as another part of the detective story mould this game forsakes.This review is listed on Steam as positive for a reason. There is good content here that I was able to enjoy. But I came into this really hyped - loved Mizuki in the first game, wanted a chance for her to really shine here. And I didn't get that. Both because Ryuki is given a lot more screentime and prominence, (Damn you Uchikoshi and your light Kodaka-ing! It's Kaede all over again!) but also just because the game doesn't come together quite as well. I hope that the Too Kyu/Spike Chunsoft collab continues though - there is progress here, and a third game of some sort could really rock.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been thinking about this game a lot over the past few days, and whether or not I wanted to review it at all. The sheer amount of time I spent thinking about it ultimately lead me to do this self indulgent review and review it favorably despite many misgivings I have about it. Spoilers will be present later!In the very beginning of the game they make it clear that you can play this game without prior knowledge of the first game, but give you the option to prove you've played Ai: Somnium Files 1 to unlock bonus dialogue. I played with this "spoiler mode" on, and I'm not sure how much the game changes if you choose to play in the "spoiler-free" mode. Not really sure the point of this however, as I feel as though this game truly is a sequel: it really benefits from knowledge of the first game and prior attachments to the characters. I highly recommend playing the first game first, as it is well worth it in terms of aiding your experience in this game as well as its standalone merits. In terms of gameplay, I think Nirvana Initiative largely improves on the first game. The formula is pretty much untouched, with the VN elements and Somnium exploration largely being the same but with added bonuses. All of the Somniums have an underlying mechanical theme to them that makes the experience a lot more grounded compared to the super fantastical dreams and actions taken in those of the first game. There was a greater emphasis on solving puzzles in the Somniums of Nirvana Initiative which I felt aided the detective experience compared to the first game's approach of doing somewhat weird, arbitrary things in a dream world to experience a different route. Many of them also had unique mechanics to complement the theme of the dreams which was a great touch. There were some very rough stealth sequences that in my opinion were the big negative gameplay-wise, but they were so few and far between that ultimately I appreciate their presence purely on novelty. Generally I found the cast of characters for this game to be very likable as well. There are a lot of recurring characters from the first game, and (very funny) returning gags to go with them. The relationships and interactions between the cast was definitely the highlight of the game for me, and I feel I can recommend Nirvana Initiative off the back of cast alone. If you liked the characters of the first game, expect this one to mostly be more of the same and better. This praise doesn't extend to  Ryuki, who in my opinion was a victim of the plot which is the source of most of my issues with this game. Shoma is the other character I personally felt lacking, acting more as a plot device than an actual character. Since this review is already very long and ultimately I still feel like the experience is worthwhile I don't want to get too into it, but the plot of this game is insanely clumsy. A major plot point of the game is the Nirvana Initiative, a plan to free humanity from the simulation they live in. This premise of "humanity living in a simulation" is intrinsically tied to every aspect of the game, from the plot to the gameplay itself. The Half Body killings (which are the primary plot device of the game) seem to involve time travel, with events in the present and 6 years in the past. The killings themselves seem impossible to have been pulled off, and many characters say strange things or react abnormally to events. At certain points the player is referenced and spoken to directly. About 85% of the way through the game there is a twist where it is revealed that about half of the events you thought were in the past were in the present, and vice versa. The first game had a really great twist in my opinion, and this one had potential as well, but the execution was so shoddy that it nearly ruined the whole story for me until the very last scene. In order to support this twist the game outright lies to the player in insane ways, going so far as to introduce a character who is a clone of one of the protagonists that is 6 years older, looks exactly the same, has the exact same name, and speaks and fights in the exact same way in order to make you believe you're playing in the present. Pretty much every character doesn't acknowledge the fact at all for the sake of not giving away the trick. The game bends in a lot of ways to try and enable this twist to the point of breaking.My opinion of the plot was somewhat salvaged by the final scene, where the world is in fact revealed to be a simulation. You're given a secret code at the end of the game which you can give to a character at an earlier point, resulting in the simulation breaking down due to information you shouldn't have. It's a really cool scene and I believe it has the potential as set up for a great third game. To me, this final scene was kind of the whole point of Nirvana Initiative, but it succeeded despite the rest of the story, not because of it. The whole timeline shifting twist felt too ambitious and forced, with "the world is a simulation" feel really only being present in the final scene and the other, subtler continuity errors sprinkled throughout.I really liked the first game, and the characters and ideas of Nirvana Initiative were ultimately very entertaining as well. I just can't help but feel a bitter taste in my mouth thinking of the shoddy execution of those ideas, and I hope a potential third game doesn't fall into the same pitfalls.

_childDocuments_.review: MINOR SPOILERS (I feel like they aren't really spoilers but read at your own risk)I loved the first game so much. One of my favorite games ever. But they kind of dropped the ball on this one. Thats not to say I didn't enjoy this game because I did, but the first one is 10 times better. First of all, the Somniums felt a bit more forcefully weird.  I feel like the Somniums and the solutions in the first one made sense despite the weirdness of them, but this one had very weird somniums with very weird solutions to progress them that don't rly make sense. Also, the time given in each somnium (at least for the standard difficulty) is very short imo. It always cuts it close for me. In the first one, u were able to explore and stuff and experiment with certain solutions and if u messed up enough times, then yeah u would run out of time. But for this one, there was barely any leeway for the timelimit. I got lucky and guessed right enough times to pass before the time limit. I was always down to the last 30 seconds for each one, and that's only if I guessed right. I had to reset it sometimes because of the very short time limit.
