_childDocuments_.review: Just finished Metro Exodus earlier today and just thought I'd share my thoughts on it.Overall, I liked the game a lot. Just like the previous games in the series, the best thing about this game is the atmosphere, and the survival elements like scavenging for ammo and resources. There are some seriously suspenseful and creepy sections in the game.I also really liked the more open, semi-open world sections of the game.Visually the game is amazing. When you're fighting in the desert and a sandstorm will just roll in and you've got all this dust blowing around with the sun casting these huge rays of light through it as you try to shoot enemies down. The story is also strong, although I didn't like how Atryom is a silent protagonist. It just feels jarring when characters address you directly and you don't reply. It took me out of the game a bit and it just feels like an odd, outdated choice. It also makes the dialogue less engaging when everything is a one way conversation just spouting exposition. Overall though I did like the story and there were some really good characters that you get to know through the course of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! ONLY BUY ON SPECIAL!!! I would give this a neutral review, but F%$#ing $team doesnt allow that of course, so screw them. I didnt even bother to finish it, I just dont care about the story, and the gameplay in the last level was dull and boring.Really good until the last stage, which ABSOLUTELY SUCKS! They completely abandon the really enjoyabe game play style of all of the stages leading up to the last one, which ends up pretty much being on rails, albeit with a stupid roundabout map. The "story" is basic, dull, predictable, and overly sappy to the point where it lost me. The side missions and world building was more interesting. The last stage also has none of the suspense or excitement of the whole rest of the game, and literally makes no sense. Things started moving around on their own and I thought the game bugged, but turns out you are just hallucinating for some unknown reason (radiation - though it hasnt done that before?). BTW, Im only playing single player. A few minutes later my character starts reacting wierdly to input - lagging (2-3 seconds!), floating, and not responding to keyboard input - something I have never seen before in any other game. I had to reboot to fix it. It happened again a few minutes later - and none of the rest of the game had this issue.The ending has pissed me off so much its soured my impression of the rest of the game.I havent bothered to finish the damn thing, the last stage SUCKED SO BADLY!!!! I might go and finish it, but after the awful gameplay leading up to it, I really dont want to. I wanted more of the open maps where you can explore, gather, and survive in the post apocalypse in any way you like, not this BS that reminds me of the early games and why I never bothered to get into any of them.A random annoyance too with the keys - they block the Win key, and other similar system command keys, so you cannot easily switch back to your browser etc, or when the game crashes. You HAVE TO CTRL+ALT+DEL to be able to then do anything. Also, the only way to exit the game is press ESC, no visible button to exit.I just started to watch the endings on YT, but realised I just dont care enough to even watch the ending.  UNINSTALLED.** SPOILERS **Reading comments/reviews it seems that Metro fans like the linear style of levels like the last one (that I hated and made me quit), and did not like the open maps. I found the open maps more suspenseful and fun, whereas the linear level felt so cliche'd and like a bad horror movie, that all suspense was lost. I just wandered past all the worms etc, and shot the ones I had to, as they really werent a threat. I honestly cant think of anything else that was even vaguely threatening except the mutant polar bear (s?), which was just annoying.The "boss" of the last stage is just dumb too. I was able to very easily beat him with the rail gun on the rooftop. I saw his supposedly dead body, but as soon as I leave that area, he is alive again and stalking me in a very tight area where you have very little chance of getting out of the way of his one shot kill. Also, the game punishes you about half way through by taking away all of the resources you have stored, and your weapons, so you cant even change your loadout or set things up the way you had been playing up until that point. After that, the game just didnt feel the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus feels like a poor clone of Fallout 3 & 4. The environments, mutants and guns all feel similar, but it just feels lacking in so many ways. I suffered through Metro 1 and 2, hoping I would eventually enjoy them... which I didn't much. With Exodus being so highly praised I was hoping that this might be good, but aside from some minor differences like the size of the environments you're in (it's not really "open world", it's just slightly less linear), it's pretty much the same as the first two games but with significantly worse voice acting and writing.- Interesting story, or at least a premise as to why you leave the metro- Same great environments with lots of detail in them- It's the same engine as the Redux versions of 1 and 2, so all the same pitfalls apply. Buggy scripted events, weapons that don't tell you what they do when you find them, and wonky movement- If you play on a widescreen monitor, the game forces you to play on widescreen. There's no way to play at 16:9 - but all the subtitles and loading screens are all squished as it tries to fit a widescreen into a 16:9 box in the middle- Unskippable long cutscenes every time you open the game- Long load times on an SSD- You can’t adjust system volume while the game is open- The combat is just as bad as the first two games- Graphics are good, but feel dated for 2019. I guess that's because it's the same as the 2014 Redux engine- The "moral points" system for good or bad endings based on whether you stab or knock out bad guys is simplistic and annoying- Over the top amount of cutscenes and quick time events. Sometimes it's hard to tell if I'm actually in a fight or watching another quicktime event- The story starts with you getting shot in the face and falling backwards off a cliff... then you get up and carry on as if nothing happened. It's later revealed that your dog tag saved you from the bullet.... right.- In lots of sections where NPCs have story dialogue, they all talk over the top of each other, which makes it difficult to work out what's going on - like they're not quite timed correctly- The voice acting and animation of NPCs is terrible. It really reminded me of an amateur play at the theatre- Although Artyom doesn't talk in either of the two previous games, it feels even weirder in this one because so many people talk to him. There are lots of dialogues where people seem to just pretend that he replied to them and carry on talking to themselves
_childDocuments_.name: Metro Exodus

_childDocuments_.review: What could have been a near perfect game for me turns into a 7/10 because of the absolute garbage quality control.Where to start?Constant glitches, Black screens, Ridiculous buggy achievements.Some areas you need to redo entire areas because of the stupid limited save slots, If you miss a collectable too bad, Start over.Black screen still not patched as of April 2024 on Two colonels DLC, You have to save game then quit entirely, Go into Nvidia control panel and turn off unlimited frame rate, Set it 60 fps, reload game and it will get past the black screen cut scene part, save game quit again and turn back on your unlimited fps.Achievements in this game are a complete nightmare to get 100%, Glitchy with new game + mode sometimes not activating and for some achievements you will need to reload a previous save, Problem is with new game + it will delete all your previous save slots.I hope future Metro games do not have all these problems, Shouldn't be happening in this day and age.Game would have got a 10/10 from me if it were not for the stress of these bugs.I'm yet to finish Two colonels and Sam's Story but already feel compelled to write a review on how bad some of these problems are.If you were to pay full price for this game I can't recommend it, If you pick it up under $20 then go for it, The story is good.Edit. I forgot to mention just how annoying the unskippable cut scenes are especially when doing your 2nd or 3rd play through to get 100% achievements, Not joking it seems like you lose hours just having to sit through it.
_childDocuments_.name: Metro Exodus

_childDocuments_.review: Extraordinary game. Initially I bought the game for the sole purpose of testing my new graphics card's ray tracing feature, but the game absolutely exceeded my expectation and become one of my favorite games in recent years.Pros- Incredible atmosphere. I'm a survival horror fan, this shooter is absolutely top 3 on my list out of all games in terms of atmosphere. Thanks to the beautifully designed environment and possibly the best raytraced global illumination implementation, the survival aspect of the game feels very immersive.- Great gunplay. Weapons feel impactful in combat, and it's visually and auditorily satisfactory to use them. (Those modded weapons looks really cool to me.)- Good writing. The game gives me some of the most memorable gaming moments in the last a few years, some intense and some touchy. Characters are memorable and the writing makes me really wanna give them their best fate. The peaceful sequences on trains should be particularly noted. This is only game besides Red Dead Redemption 2 that makes me feel like I really had a bunch of friends and a family like this. Occasionally the some dialogues can be chessy though.- Survival mechanics are generally fun and they have details. Gas mask, lighter, and gadgets, they all contribute to the immersion. Funny I didn't notice a broken gas mask affects your breathing until end of the game, maybe because I played on normal difficulty. Cons- the game is 9 for me, so many of the cons are just nitpick, but they are noticeable.- While the game has a stunning raytraced lighting, occasionally the in-game model and texture can be a hit-or-miss, to 2022 standards at least. Especially with the good writing, character looks wooden sometimes.- I find the game's music score particularly uninspired and generic.- Some open-world map are big but lacks content and and some are simply not big enough in my opinionMixed opinion- I don't know if it's due to my difficulty and raytraced settings. Some mechanics are underused in my opinion. For example, the night vision goggle looks really cool and there's a particular infrared laser gun attachment made for it, but there's barely any environment in the game to make them shine. And I heard there's a unfixed bug that lasers are supposed to visible to enemies (which is why there is infrared laser), but somehow it's invisible to them and makes everything easier. Weird.I feel bad I let this game fly under my radar for so long, but I'm glad I finally played it and had great experience. Definitely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Metro Exodus

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely fun game.  It with some pretty annoying bugs.  It seems that all AAA are required to become a AAA game.  Overall, I am glad I played it and would recommend it  to anyone that enjoyed the first 2 games.  The only issue is that they did a more map.  It felt like they did that so that this game instead of taking 5 hours would be extended to double that aka this is part walking simulator.  I would still recommend it even with the issues I had.
_childDocuments_.name: Metro Exodus

_childDocuments_.review: It's not fun. This game plays like Far Cry 2 but half of it is Cinematic Experiences™ and the other half is OPEN WORLD COMBAT EXPLORATION™ but you're not allowed to kill people because otherwise that means YOU'RE IMMORAL and YOU GET BAD KARMA!!!The game deincentivizes you from just enjoying the (subpar) combat by waggling its finger at you every time you go through combat sections with combat. The open world aspect of the game sincerely adds nothing to the game because you have to go complete objectives in a linear fashion anyway. The game keeps telling you to reduce collateral damage as much as possible, or to go through combat sections as quietly as possible, but when you avoid entire outposts and only do the obviously moral things (like freeing the slaves in the Caspian Sea), apparently, that isn't good enough to make you a moral man, since you need to go through EVERY outpost, just make sure that you STEALTH it, okay?The story is mind-numbing. I DON'T CARE about what the characters tell me. I'll get their guitar, or their bear, sure, whatever - but their characters are all either one-dimensional as hell (looking at you, Miller, what the hell's your problem?) or just non-existent. You lose all sense of direction past the Evil Bad Guys Government Hell Bunker and just start chugging along because Anna and Artyom wants to have babies in some non-irradiated hellhole. Cool. Great. Really cool goal we're working towards here. All of it just falls flat and makes me feel even less interested in the game as a whole, which wasn't impressing me from a gameplay standpoint to begin with.The breaking point of this game for me was the forest section. Hey, what if we took every frustration I had with the game (being forced to stealth through LITERALLY EVERYTHING or OTHERWISE YOU ARE BAD!) and made an ENTIRE chapter out of it? I can respect the people who enjoy this game or whatever, but god. It's boring as hell. It's sincerely just a bad imitation of Far Cry 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Metro Exodus

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully haunting and soul-stirring game! I was infatuated by the gripping story, the astounding soundtrack, and the brutal combat. The plot revolves around human connection and sacrifice. Without giving too much away, Artyom's great lengths for his wife Anna culminate in a very satisfying ending which will tug at your emotional core.I will say, however, that you will need some patience with the game. It develops slowly at first, and the combat takes some getting used to, but with enough time, the story-line comes together really well, and the characters become memorable.The combat is both brutal and stealthy. Because ammo and work benches are limited, you'll need to be on high alert at all times. I can't tell you how many times I was on the edge of my seat, shouting obscenities and jumping in surprise when a monster emerged out of nowhere. The horror element is exceptionally done and contributes to the game's gripping nature.This is without a doubt the most visually stunning game I've ever played. _childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is an excellent shooter, and one I'm going to remember for a while.  It's far from the most mechanically sophisticated, but the atmosphere and immersion of this game really stood out to me above all else.  It just feels very grounded in a way I'm not used to experiencing in shooters, and I really appreciate that.  I definitely recommend checking it out.Also, I need to give 4A Games some serious props for their excellent enhanced edition.  This version uses just ray-traced lighting, and it is extremely impressive.  I think this is the second-best optimized PC game I have ever played, only behind DOOM Eternal.  On an RTX 3060, AMD Ryzen 5 3600, playing at 1440p high settings and high ray tracing with DLSS set to quality, I managed to get 70-100 FPS.  The only exception was the Taiga level, where framerates varied between 30-60 FPS (and although the framerates were bad, the latency actually felt pretty solid so it was playable during this section.)  I'm very willing to give games crap for bad performance, but on the flip side, I believe I owe it to call out the games that I think have great performance.  The enhanced edition is nothing short of outstanding.  It also helps that thanks to the ray-traced lighting, the enhanced edition is easily one of the best-looking video games I've ever played.  Metro Exodus already looked super impressive, but the enhanced edition looks on par with or better than most 9th-gen titles I've seen.  I hope every 4A Games employee who worked on this game is damn proud of what they managed to accomplish, in both the quality of the game and the exceptional visuals and performance of the enhanced edition.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I do not get the hype.It's like Fallout 3 mixed with a tiny bit of Thief: The Dark Project and 10 hours of Half-Life tram ride.  Standing around listening to unskippable dialogue during in-engine cutscenes while NPCs prattle on an on and on, checking my phone to pass the time because the last 20 years of PC hardware advancements means game developers think terabytes of hard drive storage means they should indulge in 400,000 lines of spoken dialogue.   This is interwoven with skippable in-game dialogue, where "skipping" means you can just walk away from NPCs while they're talking.  Fine when it's just NPCs milling about in a safe area, who cares what they have to say.  Not fine when it's, say, after an objective.  Can I leave?  Will I miss out on something important if I walk away now?  Me, anxiously hopping back from one foot to the other, uncertain whether I can go yet and no player cues whatsoever.Characters non-stop repeating "ARTYOM" like Bran invaded their mind and gave them a seizure.Gameplay that hasn't advanced past Fallout 3.  Mediocre gunplay.  Pistol, SMG, rifle.  Generic AI.  Wandering around the wasteland, scavenging for supplies, picking off ghouls and wererats.  And once you get a scope for the pistol and the suppressor mod, it's over.  Easy Mode: Unlocked.  Tedious additions, like press G to wipe crud off of your gas mask.  Press T to change your air filter every 3 minutes.  Adds nothing to the experience, not immersive, just a nuisance button press.  Like something out of the worst ideas for motion controls in Wii games.  "It'll be fun if the player has to crank their arm to roll down a window.  Rolling down a window is fun, right?"I encountered a bug early in the Moscow area during the level where you play alongside Anna.  She got stuck, wouldn't move or respond, so the game wouldn't advance and I had to restart the level.If you have an RTX card, it's great looking.  Sound is moody and atmospheric.  Performance is great with all settings at max.  That's all the good I have to say about it.  I quit when I got to the Caspian desert area.  I try to finish every game I buy, even if I'm not enjoying them, but this is so boring and the unskippable dialogue felt like such an exhausting time sink that I couldn't bear to finish and just uninstalled.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro: Exodus is the best game in the series for me, and considering how much more I enjoyed the first game than the second that was definitely not a guarantee.  But with this title, 4A Games nailed the delicate balance between the open-world apocalypse of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. or Chernobylite and the focused linear apocalypse of, well, Metro 2033.  It always kept you guessing whether you were about to enter a new area that would take you six hours to explore or would be 30 minutes of intense and terrifying corridors instead.  Funny just how rare this kind of design is, maybe outside of the Deus Ex series at times (well and perhaps there are other games I have not played that do it???  GAMES I HAVE NOT PLAYED WHAT?).  This style allows for hard-hitting emotional narrative to live comfortably alongside free-wheeling do-it-yourself adventure exploration, and lots of games could learn from that combination.This title also likely did the best job incorporating light RPG elements; the bullet-based economy of earlier in the series is gone, but in its place is the most complex and rewarding system of equipment upgrading and modification so far.  It is certainly not as in-depth mechanically as, say, Dead Space or Fallout 4 (to use two very different examples), but it kept things interesting and honestly has me interested in eventually playing through it again purely to test out different weapons as I almost entirely used the same three for the entire game despite there being about ten total.Combat is very viscerally rewarding and fun; depending on your difficulty level, enemies can be anything from sort of confused about how to hurt you to deadly instant-killers if you drop your guard, and in turn you can take out just about anything with one shot if you did your homework and/or have the reflexes for it.  That said, there are definitely times when I wonder if the designers actually played through certain sections, like when one particular enemy that has a habit of sticking its face through walls kept killing me before I could even get close enough to it it, due to my own inability to warp through walls.Also a word of advice for the next game in the series: Please make your water less horrible.  Between not being able to tell I was stepping in water, not being able to tell the water would kill me THIS time when it did not kill me LAST time, and discovering things that looked solid (pipes, fences, cars) that I tried to jump on to reach a nearby place but turned out to be illusory and dropped me into the deadly water, I absolutely died more to "falling in the water" in this game than any of the many human or mutant enemies therein.  While that is hilariously in keeping with Eastern European Game Design where I died more often to falling off a ladder in Day Z in the ArmA ][ mod days than to ever actually getting killed by a zombie, I would really appreciate it if the game itself were not the antagonist so often.Overall, once again we have a game proving my rule that any game featuring geiger counters and gas masks is bound to be worth picking up.  I am genuinely curious if there are going to be more games in the series; certainly the world-building of the games and the novels could support plenty more sequels or spinoffs.  My secret dream is that we get a crossover between a few of the different games of this same vague genre, even if of course logically their timelines are fairly incompatible.  It would still be cool if S.T.A.L.K.E.R. were ultimately a Metro 2033 prequel though, is all I am saying

_childDocuments_.review: Road Trip!Metro Exodus manages to distance itself from 'just another post-apocalypse shooter' by fleshing out six different types of 'wastelands', including diverse characters, hostile and vibrant ecosystems, and the monsters within-and-without that plague all six. Each stage has just enough lore and detail to keep you entertained for the full tourist experience, all while you're busy solving a puzzle on how to safely knock out everyone who wants you dead - or murder them. Between missions, you're stuck on a thin train that somehow manages to pack character and humanity into every square inch.Unfortunately, AAA games have this tendency to add ridiculously grindy achievements, and ME is no exception. Iron Mode risks deleting your progress if you run into one of the game's otherwise acceptable collision glitches, while some achievements can be disabled for a playthrough even if you reload your save.The crafting system is bare-bones. It makes health packs and Tikhar pellets easy to craft, giving you an unfair overload of medkits and ammo, while barely scratching any other possible uses for scrap. While the series did need a better version of exchangeable currency than high-quality bullets, this wasn't it.+++ Diverse Post-Apocalypse++ Solid Stealth / Action hybrid gameplay++ Fleshed characters, interpersonal story-- Crafting is uninspired-- Annoying Achievements are back- That charger

_childDocuments_.review: This is the perfect finale to the Metro trilogy.  The story and character development are superb.  The world is extremely immersive.  The graphics are gorgeous.Many of the annoyances of previous games have been ironed out.  In previous games, various enemies had "plot armor" for no good reason.  The demons were indestructible in 2033 until the plot decided otherwise, at which point they simply died.  The Librarians in Last Light were annoying, in part because they were invulnerable.  In Exodus, neither of those enemies (or their analogues) are invulnerable, although it may be prudent to avoid them instead of fighting.  The only enemy I could find that couldn't be damaged until you progressed to a certain point kind of made sense (due to its size), and wasn't that much of an annoyance.  The karma system is finally sensible!  You get good points for doing good things and bad points for doing bad things.  Listening to boring conversations, strumming guitars, finding ammo caches, and other irrelevant Easter eggs are gone!  The conversations are fun to listen to, and the instruments are fun to play, but the developers didn't tie them to an inane morality system to force the player to feed their egos by finding their favorite Easter eggs.  Instead, if you play a good guy, you get the good ending--period.  Being the "good guy" often means using stealth in order to avoid killing people who sort of don't deserve it (i.e. moral gray area), so if you're the "run and gun" kind of player, you might still be frustrated with this mechanic.  At least it makes sense, which is all I really want from the karma system.Ammo is somewhat scarce, but far less so than in previous games.  Personally, I think this is a vast improvement.  You will still run out, sometimes, especially if you aren't a good shot, but you aren't having to constantly count bullets, anymore. The gunplay is rather good, and the stealth mechanics are very good.The DLC is decent but not spectacular.Two Colonels is best thought of as an immersive and well-written short story that you get to play a little.  In that context, it's quite good.  If you're expecting something with more in-depth gameplay, you'll be disappointed.Sam is basically the opposite: it's more action focused with minimal story.  It's also longer than Two Colonels.  Personally, I liked this one better, just because there was more to do.  I found myself wishing that this were its own game, rather than medium-length DLC.Both DLC campaigns are longer than a typical Call of Duty single-player campaign, for what that's worth.Overall, this is an excellent game, and I strongly recommend it for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the enhanced edition with all the DLCs. So, 28 hours later...Where this game truly shines is in its capacity to immerse the player with top tier world building and atmosphere. While some of the comrades and characters you come across in the English dub have that "drunk Russian" vibe — which I find eternally infuriating — the game boasts many memorable moments both intimate and set piece. Mechanically, this game is a very polished experience, though at least in the main game, I found some AI bugs at times, with a wee smidge of Euro jank thrown in.For the seasoned FPS and survival shooter veteran, I would say the apt phrase would be "very fun," but not "challenging." The easy comparison is to weigh this against western mainstay, Fallout. Where Fallout has a far more deep and charming open world RPG universe, Metro excels in the aforementioned department of truly immersing you within the struggles of the world, oddly making you care about scrounging for everything you can find (despite the aforementioned lack of difficulty), and making you pause to look at the expertly crafted post-nuclear world.Aspects like wiping away condensation from your gas mask visor, recharging your flashlight, crafting items with your real-time rucksack in the field, and so on really do add a lot to making you feel vulnerable. Guns can jam if you don't clean them, and you can suffocate if you don't pack enough gas mask filters. The weapon and gear modification system is very well implemented, allowing you to switch mods on the fly from your real-time rucksack, with more advanced gear and armament alterations available at the game's various work benches and safe houses. I find I much prefer the concept of traveling from hub to hub during your "exodus" across a former Soviet Union forever trapped in, presumably, the late 80s.You will experience several semi-open world environments with optional places to explore — with some exceptions where the game turns more linear. It's a much more curated experience than some open world RPGs where certain areas can feel like filler. In Metro Exodus' case, this is to the game's advantage, and the amount of love thrown into the universe is evident. There are surprises thrown in throughout, so be sure to keep an eye out. The game is not without the occasional flaw in pacing, but it was a pleasure to play throughout.I'd give this a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the most immersive games i've ever played in my life.Lots of little details that let you feel like you're really interacting with the environment and the characters, which feel more like people and true companions. Nearly everything is a step up from the previous game and the graphics in the Enhanced version look unreal at times.PROS-Gunplay is satisfying and the weapons feel great to handle and quite realistic in their behavior.-Weapon customization is WILD, you can modify some weapons so drastically that they change category entirely, and it can all be done on the fly, whenever you need a different approach.-The storytelling is a lot better than previous games, and whereas the story from Last Light felt all over the place to me, this one is a lot more coherent as the Spartan team is always working tightly towards a clear objective.-Almost all characters often have something to say, be it personal experiences or objective-related intel, but you're rarely forced to listen to them, so you can just walk past them or, if you have the patience, you can always spend a couple minutes with a character to learn more about them or about useful mission information, like secondary access points etc.-It's a semi-open world, with three non-interconnected main areas that you're free to roam as you please, and exploration can be very rewarding.-Your playstile and choices matter, and if you choose to kill a lot of people or ignore those who need help, you may end up losing crewmates and changing the ending into something a lot darker.-You're rarely forced to fight head-on, instead you can choose to sneak your way through enemy camps or use deception on some monsters to avoid a firefight, as ammo and medikits are precious resouces and not cheap to craft.-The survival mechanics are nicely intertwined and add a lot of immersion.CONS-(this is more of a personal gripe) The gas mask wipe mechanic, which was once essential because the visor would get so dirty during fights and heavy weather you coudn't see crap, is now useless, as i never found the need to wipe my visor throughout the whole game beacause it would never get dirty. It's such a little thing, but it's what had me in awe the most immersion-wise when i first played Metro Last Light.-The player feels absolutely weightless when sprinting, and everytime i'd try running downhill i would just end up launching forwards and dying of fall damage.-Pretty sure this is an Enhanced Edition exclusive problem, but unless you lower your brightness a lot, the night is going to be as bright as day due to the devs forgetting to dim the raytraced light from the moon (i think?).Overall a solid 9.5/10, i was fully immersed most of the time and i'm glad i put in the extra time to follow the story and explore everything.Play this game people, it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ steal when on sale and it's so much better than most AAA games nowadays while costing half the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is a game masterfully created by 4A Games. I recently bought an RTX 3070 card after the crash in price and remembered that I owned Metro Exodus PC Enhanced Edition, a game that requires RTX."Oh, good, a game to test my 3070. Great." -- I didn't know that this game was one of the best adventures I would ever go on.Something you should always keep in mind with Metro Exodus: It's boring and long. In its efforts to be immersive, Artyom is slow and stamina runs out after a few seconds of sprinting. The first few hours of the game are absolutely harmed by this but as the game goes on, you get used to it.I played (and am playing) this game on Ranger Hardcore, not Full Dive because not having interact prompts is dumb. It MAKES you go stealth, not encourages you, or simply tells you to, but it MAKES you. Artyom dies in a bullet to the head, that simple. Metro Exodus also has an extremely tight-knit stealth system, using light and sound properly, but some surfaces (like containers) not having proper cover implemented needs to be fixed. I once got stuck on a quest because enemies could see me through a container! Other than that, the sound you make is important, but not as important as light. If you have an HDR monitor, unlike me, you will definitely have an easier time with this.And the performance? It's better than Minecraft, even! On my Ryzen 5 1600 and PNY RTX 3070 combo it stays at a static 75 most of the time when v-sync is on, and when it's off, I've even seen it go to the hundreds while everything is at max! This is a beautiful, and beautifully optimized game. If you want to play it, add the -deependark command-line arguments, though. It makes the game  dark. Oh, and lest I forget the PC Enhanced Edition's benefits. Every light has ray-traced global illumination, which as a beginner C++ Vulkan graphics programmer, makes this game seem like magic. Realtime, ray-traced. Two things I thought would never go together. Especially in such an immersive game and genuinely, beautifully art-directed game.This is a post-apocalyptic world. There is one caveat though: the mutants. I get that it's a post-nuclear-war world, but mutants' inclusion in this grounded and realistic game (especially the enhanced edtion), simply makes you snap out of your immersion, and takes you away from the experience.Aside from my one or two caveats (unfinished cover system and mutants), this game is fabulous, and gets an honest 9/10 from me, and I'm only halfway through the game! If you have the money, and want to support this Ukrainian developer, please buy Metro Exodus, especially if you have an RTX card. You won't regret it!

_childDocuments_.review: I've finished whole campaign on Ranger Hardcore mode before reviewing.Try to give this game a chance until the first open-world level. You'll know when you travel on a train, leave said train, and then complete first major quest. This starts the best part of the game, and if that does not gel with you - rest of the game won't either.Unfortunately this will put you well past the 2h refund limit on Steam.About 50% of this game is a legit 10/10 experience. The rest 50% ranges from being ok to being boring to being tedious and unfun.I recommend because the good parts are really good.Metro Exodus is an FPS game with several linear and several open-world-style levels. Gameplay focuses a lot on stealth, but there is an option to shoot every problem you encounter as well if you don't care about getting the best ending.Story continues where the second game in the series left off. Main hero - Artyom - is now a member of an elite special-ops force. He also has a wife, who in turn is a daughter of your commanding officer. Artyom's strive to find survivors outside of Moscow lead him and rest of his team on a run from their former friends at Moscow's metro and they leave to search for a better place to live outside the city.Fundamelntals of a good FPS game are all here. Game plays well.If you explore a lot you will find many minor upgrades to your weapons or equipment. You may find batteries that power your flashlight for longer before needing to recharge, or you can happen upon a perfectly working pair of nightvision goggles.Weapons can be customized with different parts to be better on short or longer range, have more ammo at the cost of higher recoil or have a suppressor at the cost of damage and many more.There are 2 (3, but the last one sucks) open-world levels with sidequests, hidden treasures and a lot of stuff in general to do. These levels are the best this game has to offer as they challenge your ability to fend off mutants while you travel the world and then your stealth skills when you encounter human enemies. Conserving ammunition and using your takedowns or throwing knives is a preferred tactic. Looking for supplies becomes second-nature as you can always use materials to make ammunition, medkits or gas-mask filters.Sometimes I would go to an area and not get a checkpoint for like 10 minutes, die, and on repeat I would get like 3 checkpoints in those 10 minutes. Thy just seem to trigger at random.Ranger offers a very well-balanced experience. You and your enemies will die very quick to a couple of well-placed shots and you get spotted very quick if out in the open and not in shadows.However there are some stealth sections, especially near the end of the game, which are just badly designed with 0 checkpoints and if you get spotted - it's either kill people (which hurts your chances for best ending) or to reload last save. I've wasted around 40 minutes replaying the same section over and over again, listening to the same guard conversations in wait to get them to move and progressing just a little further before getting spotted by a next enemy, which I could not be expected to see coming.If not on Ranger - you can quicksave, alleviating the problem.After the first 2 big levels there is a 3rd, which forgoes freedom and becomes much more linear. You also lose all your stuff and are forced to scavenge, which would be fine if you got your stuff back relatively quick, but unfortunately you'll have to play the whole thing like that.After this things go further downhill, with tedious walking segments with NPC's "leading" you, or scenarios where you are alone, but the encounters you are dealing with are boring. Sewers, for example, are long, uninteresting to look at, filled with tedious rawboat segments and in general bad pacing.And then it gets even worse near the end with hallucination segments.Ugh... what a jarring drop in quality comparing to the first half of the game, which is nothing short of fantastic.If 3rd map had the same quality as the previous 2 and a bunch of tedious things like the sewers were made shorter then this game would have been an easy 9/10, possibly a 10.As it stands I cannot justify giving it anything more thanVery uneven game that can be amazing, but can also be frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr .. Realistic open-world shooter that gives you limited resources pits you against infinitely respawning enemies, and forces you to "play its way" (stealth / pacifist) or get punished with bad ending. Film at 11.The Good:+ Gritty setting+ Focuses on realism (you're slow, hurt easily, better to be stealthy than rambo, etc.)+ Large "open-world" levels allow exploration once you're off your leashThe Bad:- First 2 hours is cut-scene / tutorial spam. 75% of time is cut-scenes while other 25% is you having control, but led around by the nose. (eg: "go here", "follow me", "go through that door", etc.) Feels like a 3D visual novel until you finally get to the first open-world area where they let you off your leash and you can do as you please. I can see this being very off-putting to some folks (I almost gave up). But, if you stick with it, it gets better.- Like previous Metro's, human enemies are weak and a pushover while beasts are bullet sponges that swarm you and absolutely wreck you, all on the same difficulty. Having played other Metro games, I started Exodus on Easy mode expecting this. And, sure enough.. I'm picking humans off easily at camps. Meanwhile, when I see 1 wolf beast, I try to skirt around and avoid it. But, ti spots, me, and calls 5 others to come jump me. Another time, wolves and "rat" things were fighting.. and they all decided to turn on me... while a flying demon was also dive-bombing me. Like I said, had same experience in other Metro games. There's just no balance in a Metro game.- Guns get dirty easy, then fail / jam. So, you're having to find a workbench every 30 mins to clean your guns. Is it realistic? I guess. But, it's annoying baby-sitting gear. I play games for fun, not "daily grind" minutiae. Why not force me to take whiz and dump every hour as well? Or force me to go wash my clothes, or cook or whatever? People play video games to zone out, not be reminded of what a grind daily life can be.- Annoying "karma" system punishes you if you want to shoot / kill / clear areas, b/c then you get a "bad" ending. Instead, they force you to go stealth & knock-out enemies and/or be a pacifist if you want the "good" ending. It's often not clear which enemies will give you bad karma, though, especially since they're all shooting at you and/or show up as red under your cross-hairs. EG: you see a bandit camp. You headshot some. You get negative karma. Turns out they're part of some cult that tried to kidnap you, but you're supposed to suddenly be nice to them? No indication of that before I started shooting.- Pacifying surrendering enemies is also annoying. You have to walk up to them, and either shoot them or knock them out. Why can't I just interact with them and tell them to scram and be thankful I spared them? That would make more sense. A person knocked-out is suddenly supposed to show up later "thankful" I punched their lights out instead of telling them to buzz off? That makes no sense to me.The Ugly:- RESPAWNING ENEMIES in a game world where resources DO NOT respawn!I cleared bandits guarding a train car. This is a gritty, realistic shooter with limited resources. So, I think to myself "cool, got that area done. I can come back later when I'm ready to get the train car."I wander 50m away, then circle back after hitting a dead end.THE BANDITS HAVE RESPAWNED.smhSame with mutants / beasts. Clear an area while passing through. Come back.. they're all there again.This insults the player by making them feel like their actions don't matter. The game wants you to take it seriously, but it doesn't take your actions seriously. It's a slap in the face.Think about it. You come up to an area with enemies. You take it seriously. You spend a good 30 minutes being stealthy, tactical, smart. You have a feeling of accomplishment; cross that area off your list. Then come back 5 mins later to see all of your hard work gone; the area's reset. Wow. Making me feel special. *rolls eyes*This ruins the immersion of the game, and teaches the player to avoid / ignore areas until they absolutely need to go there and one-n-done it.But, you won't know that about an area until you go in. So, you learn to save scum. Save, check area out, if it's just some gear, clear it and move on, never to return. If it's got plot-related junk and respawning enemies, reload and ignore until ready to come back to one-n-done it.So, you have this open-world area to "play your way".. but..- you're punished if you kill people (who are trying to kill you!)- you're punished if you clear areas (b/c they just repopulate while your gear does not)Overall:I still recommend the game. It's interesting to play once it lets you actually play it. It just has baffling design decisions that are aggravating when you realize what's going on. But, if you know about them ahead of time, and are ok with them, then you can adjust your expectations accordingly and not be as p*ssed off about them.

_childDocuments_.review: In short this game, makes it alot harder to wait for S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2Metro Exodus is a very on rails story experience, that has one main goal: Tell & finish Artyom's story. The writing in this is at best very wholesome and at worse, a rough draft take. Exodus has several "open world" segments that each house different enviornments and vista to take in. The GFX are one of the main features in this game as all the other metros were about. This game is best eperienced by taking your time, and slowly taking in the story, vistas, and dialouge. There is combat, and action scenes but the main focus is the story. There is nothing "Out of this world" in reguars to combat, was never metro's stong point. but it does do a great job at telling a compelling story to a point. It lacks a bit of flavor in some sections and some points are overdone in other media, as well the odd bug and hit reg/ collision. But overall a pleasent experice that was surprising to see the departure from the common tunnels to the open air. I wish there were more "tunnel" sections, to give some more older feeling but i understand why there arent. I would love if they went truly more open world with actually have alot of the mechanics that are involed in those game ( I. E. S.TA.L.K.E.R.), but in terms of a metro game it fits really well given their previous works.      In Conclusion : Metro Exodus is a great game, but greater story. 7/10 (8/10 w/ dlc) I would reccomend if your interested in the pure form of atmosphere that is Metro Exodus. In comparrison to the other metro games im torn, as its more of a perfernce of which atmosphere you prefer, I do wish they had more story anomoly's. As it didnt quite feel all metro without it. Would recc just for the atmostphere alone. But just as a reminder its very on rails (quite literally). You don't scavenge as much ammo/meds/filters and are expected to craft said items from the stale crafting system you see in every Ubisoftlike or open-world style game.  At the time I might've been playing something else or was still pissed off about their Epic Games store exclusivity.  I played 2033, Last Light, bought Redux upgrades, and you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ me over by going to Epic.Coming back and playing it in prep for the VR game Metro: Awakening, I am enjoying this style of game again. It could possibly be that AAA games have become so trashy and inundated with MTX or are injected with DEI/woke propaganda that a good old fashioned romp through the nuclear Russian wasteland amongst mutants and your Russian soldier bros is just a plain good time.  There's an FOV slider in the enhanced edition, however I still keep it pretty narrow as the binoculars/gasmask/blood decals are cut-off and made for the base 68 degree fov. The wide fov also greatly distorts your gun/hands stretching them out making them look odd. Playing this in 2024 with graphics maxxed and full Ray-tracing is insanely immersive.  It's a graphical jump that brings you back to how immersed you felt in the initial playthrough of Metro 2033. Looking at DigialFoundry comparisons on YT really shows how far they've come in the Enhanced Edition of Exodus. Essentially, I can forgive having to hold down keys to loot/open/backpack etc. and collect boring crafting materials because of how enjoyable the game is outside of that.  Rebind some of the crappy default keyboard binds to something better on your keyboard or mouse (controls designed primarily for console) and you'll be having a good time.  It's a shame 4A's other game was Quest exclusive VR game. If it was made as well as the Metro series and on PCVR it would probably be a banger too.TLDR; Metro FPS gameplay, with wider exploration. Plagued by console-style controls/fov/crafting.  If you're rocking a 30 or 40 series card you can live the "RTX ON" meme and have a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is a masterpiece in the gaming world. From the opening moments, it's clear that this post-apocalyptic shooter is something special. The immersive gameplay and compelling storyline make you care about your actions and their consequences.One of the things that sets Metro Exodus apart is the multiple ways you can approach each objective. Whether you want to go in guns blazing or use stealth tactics, the game offers a range of options to suit your playstyle. You can even mix it up and try a bit of both, making for a truly unique and customizable experience.But what really sets Metro Exodus apart from other first-person shooters is the way it makes you care about the world and the people in it. The consequences of your actions feel real, and you'll find yourself weighing every decision carefully. I found myself becoming more aggressive in combat just to save a dying character, a testament to how invested I was in the story.The graphics, lighting, and sound design all contribute to the game's immersive atmosphere. From the desolate wastelands to the cramped underground tunnels, each location feels unique and alive.Overall, Metro Exodus is a beautiful game and a great conclusion to an awesome trilogy. I have no doubt that it will stand the test of time as a classic in the gaming world.

_childDocuments_.review: ==Not that anyone reads reviews==Metro Exodus is a rough-cut gem, a treat for fans of Metro 2033 and Last Light, who wondered what 4A Games could accomplish utilizing large level formats for specific chapters. If you are looking for a short story experience with decent replayability, you're getting a 30-60 hour story with two solid ending choices. I'm addressing this as a story experience because while the action is definitely intact, the action is less of a focus compared to the previous games. For those who understand the difficulty and action experience of the Metro series, you're primed for Exodus and there are only a few additional mechanics to master. Metro Exodus is a good look at the short story format in gaming, but this can throw people off balance who are looking for an experience akin to Fallout. This isn't Fallout in Russia, but it's Metro. In fact, if you're reading this and expecting a Fallout-killer, you're in the wrong place. 4A Games envisioned this experience, where it leads players out of the Metro not so you can aimlessly tackle quests, but take on missions which carry tremendous dramatic weight.== Linear large levels over before you know it==That sounds like a bad thing but hear me out. Metro Exodus presents large levels to traverse, but they're actually quite linear if you pay close attention to them. In my experience, I continuously tripped over sequence and found myself compulsively bringing up the map. This sounds like a symptom of disastrous game design, but somehow I made it through and actually wished I toned down the difficulty for my first playthrough. I beat 2033 and Last Light Redux on the higher difficulties (Ranger Hardcore), because the games I'm used to demand it to keep me invested. The majority of games at large have conditioned me to expect a poor experience if I play on Easy or Normal. 4A Games didn't skip out on the new challenges, which means I underestimated the challenge.Metro Exodus almost asks you to lower the difficulty so you could focus on enjoying the story. That doesn't mean the gameplay offerings are unrewarding. On the contrary, you can unlock a dozen or so difficulty enhancements for players who crave punishing modifiers, and encounters are rightfully intense. But as someone who was unfamiliar with this new campaign format, I found myself looking up guides and maps just to find the best way to progress without tripping over side missions and story sequences before I was ready. The difficulty is so well done that I continuously under-estimated very intelligent and very well choreographed humanoid and monstrous enemies. The remedy to all of these problems is to play on Easy or Normal so you can get a look at the land and then return to it on a higher difficulty with experience intact. For all of the janky issues and rough-patches I sometimes went deliberately out of my way to encounter, the game never fell apart on me. I had a day where I did a 10-hour session, saw floating characters, had audio glitches, almost went out of bounds, and went inside environmental entities which didn't have collision, but kept progressing because I was just that invested in the story and the action.== Two Solid Endings ==I read several different guides and looked for a better explanation of how the Moral system worked in Exodus compared to 2033 and especially Last Light, but in Exodus it really boils down to how you carried out your missions. Every level centers around a different supporting character to a certain degree. You learn their motivations very quickly and this introduces a variable which influences their decisions or their ultimate fate within the chapter. Who you spare and who you kill is still a major deciding factor. Instead of collecting good boy points which miraculously affect your outcome, you can almost perceive the changes leading up to your fate and theirs.To boil it down further without spoilers:	- Spare [these people], sometimes without being caught	- Supporting Character survives, or is intactThe story does a better job explaining this from the perspective of an ethical dilemma, as the over-arching theme of Exodus addresses the Explorer Dilemma but with a post-apocalyptic hint of irony. You're the strangers in a brutal land and the influential power in the region doesn't know you and why they should trust you, do business with you, or just remove you with ease. Finally, the ending conditions simplified:To get the good ending, have 2 of the 3 supporting characters still in your team by the final level. If you reach the final level and have 1 or none of the supporting characters who were the focus in their respective levels, you're doomed.==Conclusion==That being said, both endings are solid. They're perfect for how they treat the dramatic themes of the game. Both deserve their respect because they represent a different kind of heavy drama that only can be found in video games. Truly, this is a rough-cut diamond of a game. I almost feel bad mentioning any flaws but at the same time if you're the kind of gamer looking for a game like Metro, you know you're already in the right place. Just know what you're in for.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus comes in two flavors: the base edition, and the 'enhanced' edition, which ray-traces every light source. It also provides DLSS, which downsamples the image, and then upsamples using ai to create an image that is indistinguishable from native resolution. In other words this game is simultaneously gorgeous and less demanding on hardware.	I can't speak to how the base game looks minus ray-tracing, but the enhanced version looks amazing. Obviously this all depends on your hardware and how high you can push the settings, but with DLSS it's a visual treat for the majority. Being outside of the Metro allowed the devs to create lush environments with light sources other than dim candles and light bulbs.	Anyone familiar with the franchise already knows what to expect. First person shooter with a bit more nuance to it than what is typical. You have a flashlight that needs manual recharging, weapons that cam jam and need cleaning, and a lot of little gadgets that you can customize. There's crafting of ammo, weapons, and upgrades now. Otherwise, same quality shooting as before. I miss the 'bullets as ammo' feature from the first game, but given that we're leaving the metro it wouldn't work anyway.	The real selling point here is the 'open world' aspect of the game. The 'semi-open world'. Exodus features several maps. The introduction is as linear as ever. But once you're out in the world proper, you get what I'd call a 'mid-sized' open-world map. The story progresses linearly, but you also have side-objectives that present themselves. Not a lot, but enough of them. When it's time to pack up for a new location, we have a short intermission on the train before entering a new 'semi-open world'.	I like it. It doesn't become GTA or Far Cry, so the narrative remains in-tact and you won't be spending days outside of the main plot. But it gives you more freedom of movement than the basic A to B map structure of most linear shooters. And it hammers home the 'survivalist' aspect of managing air filters and health because you can more realistically be in trouble away from base. 	The only downside is that, narrative-wise we are leaving the Metro. We are searching for life outside of it. Which is fine, but we are also leaving a defining plot-point of the franchise: The Dark Ones. They're creatures that hide in the tunnels of the Russian Metro and have telekinetic abilities. The first two games established them as a misunderstood force for good that hold a connection with the protagonist. A connection that holds promise for rebuilding society in a post-nuclear war world.	Because we are no longer in the metro, we no longer see them. Which is so...odd. THE plot point is just...dropped. The plot is logically moving to the next step, but it's abandoning half of the franchise lore and direction. It's very weird. Not bad, necessarily. Just...odd. 	And while we're on it, I want to mention how long the characters yap on and on. About not much. You don't have to stick around for every character speech or interaction, but if you want the full story you'll feel obligated to. And wow do they babble on and on and on. I don't know if the intent was 'immersive' writing, but the effect was 'wow this guy won't stop talking get to the point'.	I feel like the narrative is a missed opportunity, because it eliminates a lot of the mystique of the world. It goes in an interesting direction a quarter of the way through, before becoming a tale of finding somewhere to settle. Fair enough, but it's very 'basic' as opposed to the fantastical writing you'd expect of a game. There's a 'is the war still on-going?' subplot before being resolved, which is a bit of a shame. It feels like we left the dark ones and a lot of the interesting plot threads for the most sensible and realistic, but also the most basic.	I'd still argue that this is the best game in the franchise. It doesn't do anything new, but it does what it's been doing better than before. Where the franchise goes from here will be interesting, because given how it ends it feels like we're becoming Fallout. Settlements in the wasteland and bandits roaming around, with cults and weirdos making new societies. I'd love to see how they'll tie it back to the Metro and dark ones, because they can't leave those plot threads hanging.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10, 10/10 10/10 9/10 10/10  9/10, 9/10The plot of Metro: Exodus is a very compelling tale of leaving everything you know and trying to survive in the greater world, which can certainly be a comforting tale for someone who is experiencing a big life change. The plot does develop very naturally throughout the story and has its share of emotional climaxes. The dialogue is spectacular and superb, feeling like real people trying to live in a post-apocalyptic world. I was completely convinced by the voice actors and the writers, so great job in that regard.The setting and art design of Metro: Exodus provides us the familiarity of the gray and bleak tones of the Metro, while also combining it with the vibrant settings of the Caspian sea, a beautiful forest valley, and the desert of the Yamantau mountains. The developers put a lot of time in trying to immerse you in this world and they do a spectacular job of this. All the weapons also look extremely well-detailed, the enemies, and the various characters. Really spectacular job.The soundtrack is really great in this game, providing us the classic post-apocalyptic guitar vibes that are accompanied by a great orchestra. The soundtrack really helps the emotional climaxes and the general feeling of despair that comes with being in the post-apocalypse, with some hope for a better future.This game has a completely ray-traced version, and it looks gorgeous. I don't know how they were able to do it, but the game runs incredibly smoothly while looking fantastic. Great job on their part.The gameplay is excellent, providing us three different weapon slots, a much better and refined stealth system, and an inventory management/crafting system. Each of these systems have a good amount of depth to them, but not overly complicated. You only have two different crafting materials that can be applied to everything you craft. It forces you to evaluate what is important and what isn't important for you to craft. The guns feel like guns in this game, with weight behind each round you fire. I appreciate not having a crosshair, as it helps the believability of the world we are immersing ourselves into. Enemies are smarter and will use tactics to defeat you, the animals and creatures you will fight all present their own distinct qualities as well.The sound design is superb in this game, with everything sounding just right.This is the best post-apocalyptic game out there. It really does a fantastic job of immersing you in its universe as the game never takes you out of the eyes of your character, except for when you want to save or quit the game. I highly recommend this game to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: While the gameplay is very different from the previous two titles in the franchise, Exodus can stand on its own as a masterpiece of its time. The plot of the game can take some turns at points that might seem odd if you aren't paying close attention and some of the explanation is hidden away for those who are keen to search the levels for more information. But that is OK. Where the previous two games focused on drawing you in with their world building, this game draws you in with its cast of diverse and interesting characters, each with their own flaws, struggles, and stories that interact with each other in realistic ways. This game really made you feel like one of the Spartans where Last Light didn't. The ending truly got me choked up which says a lot. You truly start to care for the other characters and feel as though they care for you too. Few games focus on storytelling on this level nowadays and I commend the writers for their excellent work.That aside, the gun play and environments are both extremely immersive experiences, especially if you have a decent GPU. Finished the main story with some decent exploration in ~30  hours wish there was more. Diving into the expansions now and loving the attention to the characters once again. Hats off to the devs.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is absolutely phenomenal, in virtually every aspect, and a beautiful, worthwhile send-off to a trilogy of games that, while not always perfect, were genuinely special for a lot of people, with world-building, storytelling, atmosphere, and horror all coming together to make a series of games unlike anything else. Visually stunning, with immersive gameplay and deep, meaningful customisation and exploration, allaying our fears that it would be another Ubisoft-style Open World. I strongly recommend this game to fans and newcomers alike, although I would definitely advise the newcomers to go play the first two games first, to be properly immersed in the incredibly detailed and oppressive world of Metro. I loved the first two games already, like many others. The claustrophobic atmosphere, the tension inherent in the dark tunnels of the Moscow Metro, where the remnants of humanity cling to survival like beasts, factions spreading and vying for control, while horrors evolve and lurk and hunt in the darkness, you could tell it was based off of books, it all felt so real, and dense and detailed. So we were a little worried when we got the news that Metro Exodus would be Open World, fearing that the unique atmosphere and survival-horror gameplay would be dumbed down or just done away with altogether in favour of vapid, bloated open world bulls*it we're so used to. Couldn't have been more wrong. Yes, there are several large zones, in which you can explore at your own pace, but it's all handcrafted. Each location feels unique, with purpose behind it, and exploring is always rewarded, with meaningful upgrades to your arsenal. Add to that fantastic environmental storytelling that further contextualises and deepens the world of Metro Exodus, and we have the opposite of AC Valhalla. The Visuals and overall atmosphere could be talked about all day honestly, but suffice it to say Metro Exodus is one of the finest looking games ever made, especially the Enhanced Edition. Not only in terms of textures and "realism", but colours, shadows, leaves floating in the wind, sandstorms rolling through what used to be the Caspian Sea, the way your lighter illuminates the mutated spiders scurrying through the darkness, the moonlight filtering through the trees in the Taiga, it's all so damn good. There's almost too many things to talk about, like the storytelling, the expertly handcrafted levels, the way you will recoil at the sound of something huge slithering through the water in the metro tunnels deep underneath a dead city, spiders stalking you through their home, and you in turn hunting down bandits by day- or moonlight, loud or quiet, your prerogative, the characters, of whom Anna is the best by far, it all comes together to create a masterful experience. The only genuine complaint I have is Artyom still being a silent protagonist, it kinda worked in the other games, as he was mostly an observer, but here it's just stupid, as there's people literally talking to you and asking questions and you're just mute. It felt jarring and was the only thing, ironically, that kinda took me out of the immersion a little bit. Other than that though, Metro Exodus is marvellous, and even though the story of Artyom has ended, I really hope we get more games set in this grim, seemingly hopeless world where humanity nevertheless never stops clawing for survival, for life, for hope. I strongly recommend Metro Exodus.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game. The mechanics, gorgeous environments and sound design all complement the story to create an engrossing atmosphere of surviving against all odds. Moments of struggle and triumph are well-paced, so that the overall feeling isn't too oppressive. As with other games in the Metro series, it's very linear and the specifics of your actions aren't too consequential. However, there's a greater variety of environments and enemies than before, which makes being on rails an enjoyable experience overall. If you're picking a difficulty, Hardcore is probably the best for relatively experienced survival FPS players. It requires some careful management of resources, but not to the extent that it becomes the whole game. It also forces you to be tactical in your approach to tough encounters, but doesn't feel unfair.

(go into .cfg file and change 2 settings to get it right no big deal but annoying..)-movement feels floaty and wierd sometimes (can be minimized by getting used to the engine)-flashlight bug can be avoided if you know about it and play carefully but playing though dead city without a flashlight on ranger hardcore blindly was definetly more challenge then i signed up for.. i made it, but damn was it annoying at times.-hit registration can feel WAY off sometimes.. which is a shame considering how important it can be to hit your shots sometimes for a stealth approach or to not waste precious ammunition.-this last one i'll reserve for just how frustrating and painful the game can be on higher difficulties. get used to starting section over and over again until you get it right. with bugs and glitches making it even harder sometimes. like getting hit through a wall or something similar.so why am i still recommending the game after listing all this bulls**t that i just went though ? because as i said.. it is great when it works. so if you feel like you have the patience to sit though a few things that feel off and break you out of the immersion sometimes. maybe you are also not planning to play on the hardest difficulty right away either.. well in that case, you will be rewarded with an experience, few games manage to pull off.as for performance i played on a 13th gen intel with an 8 gig 4060ti on ultra (not extreme) with raytracing and dlss in 1080p and had over 100 fps pretty much all the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Very different from Metro 2033 and Last Light, but still manages to keep the same feeling. Side characters are a lot more fleshed out, and the romance plot is done way better here compared to Last Light. The story is gripping, and the game looks phenomenal (also probably one of the best implementations of Ray Tracing). The're a lack of menus in the game as all the animations are done through the main character interacting with his belongings, which adds to the immersion (for example, the main character will drop his bag down rather than show a menu with your items). The areas are beautiful with a lot of attention to detail (especially The Volga). The final level (Dead City) gives you the same tense atmosphere mixed with the supernatural elements of Metro 2033 and Last Light as well. Humanimals (sand zombies) are pretty annoying to deal with, and sometimes hits don't feel like they register, but otherwise this is a great game, especially if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is a stunning single-player FPS. The graphics and lighting look great, whether you're exploring vibrant forests filled with bandits or navigating through abandoned cities teeming with monsters. The game's visuals excel at depicting both hopeful and hopeless scenarios, from the beauty of nature to the haunting scenes of war-torn cities filled with corpses.The gameplay is equally impressive. The guns in Metro Exodus are satisfying to use, with a powerful feel and sound. You have the flexibility to choose between a stealthy approach or going in guns blazing. However, opting for the latter can be particularly challenging on higher difficulties due to limited ammunition and resources, adding a layer of strategy and tension to the game.The story is compelling and kept me interested. I found myself genuinely caring for some of these characters. Their development and interactions throughout the journey added depth to the narrative, making it an engaging experience from start to finish.Overall, Metro Exodus delivered me a good time with its beautiful graphics, immersive gameplay, and a gripping story. A must-play if you're a fan of the single-player FPS genre.

This sort of thing happens a a number of times throughout the game.Most non-human enemies are bullet-sponges that conveniently engage in spastic head-banger mode to avoid headshots.The map, journal, and objectives are often vague and almost completely unhelpful and thus an annoyance.The open-world experience is okay, sometimes fun, usually just serviceable.I rarely quit a game before finishing, but that looks like what will happen here; why play a game that is a miserable experience? _childDocuments_.review: Having enjoyed Metro Last Light and having played a bit of Metro 2033 Redux, I decided to dive into Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition. Graphically, the game is absolutely stunning and runs smoothly on my system, showcasing some of the best visuals I’ve seen in recent games. The story is compelling, and the atmosphere remains deeply immersive, extending beyond the claustrophobic tunnels to explore a variety of beautifully designed outdoor landscapes and diverse enemies.One standout feature is the game’s high level of interactivity with its environment and characters, which adds depth to the experience. The variety of terrains and the different stories told in each location are impressive. However, aiming for 100% completion would require replaying the story, which feels a bit redundant. I completed the game in one go, and that was more than enough for me.Overall, I’d rate Metro Exodus 15/20. While the Metro games have typically been “one-shot” experiences for me, this game is definitely worth playing. If you’ve enjoyed the previous games, you’ll find this one to be a fantastic continuation of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: The devs screwed up and never cleaned up their mess. This game is in SERIOUS need of a patch or two to fix numerous issues and bugs, especially since they insist on keeping such limited save slots. If you have a serious issue, it's easy to not be able to load a save over 5 or 10 minutes prior to your issue.If you have a previous save in the regular version, achievements will be bugged in Enhanced Edition. If you want to go for them, make sure to go into your saved games files and delete your previous saves and user configurations. Otherwise some achievements simply won't track progress.Enhanced Edition also has some issues with visuals. Gamma settings are utterly broken, so the game is just incredibly bright and washed out. This apparently has something to do with HDR being forced on, even on monitors without it. This can be fixed by accessing your launch options via steam and typing in "-deependark -forcenohdr" and it will mostly fix this issue.In spite of these problems, Metro Exodus is simply fantastic. It has unmatched atmosphere, absolutely stunning visuals, engaging storytelling, a plethora of dialogue with decent enough voice acting, and very fun combat. While the stealth system can break at times, the higher difficulty settings feel rewarding. Rather than making combat tedious with bullet sponge enemies, Ranger Hardcore will put you and enemies on relatively equal footing; while you can absolutely die in a single headshot, your enemies will too.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an excellent game. Good balance of Metro series indoor levels and more open larger levels without becoming an open world checklist game like the far cry series or other ubisoft open world crap. I like how you can change the attachments on your weapons on the fly. It means you can play a lot more tactically and use equipment for different situations with your weapons. As usual, the unique weapons such as the Tikhar are a really fun part of the game and a fun concept. I played through Hardcore, then Iron Mode on the easiest difficulty, then Ranger Hardcore. Playing through quickly is fun as is exploring everything slowly.The story is fine, but I found it a lot more generic than the previous games. Also, the "revelation" at the very beginning of the game kind of cheapens the gravity of the previous two games' stories. But AT LEAST it allows for some interesting and fun differentiation between each level in this game since they're set in massively different places around Russia.The Sam's Story DLC is really cool. I had a lot of fun playing through that one, and it was like a whole new excellent level to the game that tied into the rest of it pretty well.So I recommend this game for the gameplay, which is fun and the challenges that affect the story such as playing through levels rather stealthily were quite fun to do rather than a chore. I also enjoyed that even when playing through as a "good guy" run, you can still use your weapons on bandits and other enemies often without consequence. What good is having such excellent weapons if you never get to use them while going around stealth knocking out everyone?I also liked how if you max out your ammo, if you pick up more of that ammo, it'll be converted to scraps to make medkits, gas mask filters, or other ammo. You never feel like exploring is a waste of time if you do it really thoroughly because you will always pick up more scrap rather than be full up and have to leave things behind. No need to worry about the dreaded inventory management and carry weight, you can just explore all you want everywhere without hassle. Excellent design choice!I have a couple of gripes about the game.- Biggest one: It doesn't have borderless windowed mode, aka "actual full screen mode". Yes, I want full screen mode that doesn't crash my computer for 10 seconds when I decide to do something else by alt tabbing. Especially when the game takes forever to boot up. That's the entire point of "borderless windowed mode" and really should just be how you design your full screen mode to begin with. No, I don't want a full screen mode that messes with my screen resolution. I have literally never played a game on PC at a different resolution than I do everything else on my computer. On top of that, windowed mode insists on putting a bar at the bottom of my screen that tends to flicker like crazy.- As I mentioned, the game takes ages to boot up, even on an NVME drive with a 4070 ti. It looks nice but honestly not THE BEST THING EVER...dunno why it is so massive and takes so long to boot up.- THE GAME NEEDS A CUTSCENE SKIP BUTTON. On repeat playthroughs in-engine cutscenes take like 2-3 hours of the game. I had to use cheatengine to speed up the game with speedhack so I could get to the gameplay.
