_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird game to review. It's functionally reviewing an entire TCG while also reviewing a game at the same time but I'll give it a try. Also I really wish there was an inbetween recommending and avoiding a game on Steam but I still play this game close to every day so, I do like it still. The Actual Yu-Gi-Oh part of Master DuelYu-Gi-Oh! is over 20 years old and because of that the game has iterated and evolved since the days of Duel Monsters Era card design and a ton of people who played it as kids might be dissuaded by that but I still do urge people to atleast try to give the TCG a chance when they can even if its casually. The game has shifted away from "Good Stuff" piles of decks to archetypes of related cards and away from hyper powerful spells and traps like Pot of Greed and Mirror Force (Not to say there aren't good S&T, just that there isn't as many must include S&Ts) to equally as strong Monster effects and Extra Deck summons. Every couple of years until of recent with the anime detaching itself from the TCG with VRAINS, they've introduced a new summoning type that pushed the limits of the card design within the game all of which have had their moment in the spotlight. As the speed of the game increased this leads to evolution in the need against dominant strategy, leading to the introduction of Hand Traps (Cards such as Ash Blossom & Joyous Spring, Maxx "C", and Infinite Impermanence) and I do think that handtraps overall has made Yu-Gi-Oh much more interesting and interactive than any other card game I've played, now there's counterplay between both opponents on turn one instead of them just solitairing forever (Not to say that doesn't happen but we'll get to that). Overall, I do very much enjoy how Yu-Gi-Oh! has evolved over it's many years of existence and while it has it's ups and downs, I very much enjoy every era of this game.Master DuelAfter so many years of unofficial sims ranging from YGOPro to Dueling Network/Book and "official" ones such as Legacy of the Duelist which had their own issues. We finally an official simulator that is stated to have continual support and actually plays and looks great. We as players waited excitedly for more news and for the game to come out and when it did it felt like a renaissance for the game as over 200K new players were playing the game on release and for the first week. The game has a honeymoon period, you're given so much as a new player, tens of thousands of gems just given to you to open packs and make decks and it's one of the best things about master duel. You can just build anything you want with the gems given to you and within the first week I was playing full power Pendulum Magicians and Zoodiac like it was 2017-8 all over again. I was climbing the ladder and having the great time seeing all of the different strategies from casual to competitive and it was a blast. Then it kinda just stopped, not to say the game isn't fun anymore but you could feel the game become slower with the gems and people wanting to win so much more. Not to say there's anything wrong with the latter point but the atmosphere was different with Season 2 and beyond.Gems and the Economy of Master DuelLike stated before the overall Gems given to you at the start is staggering honestly, you can build essentially anything you want if you're smart with your Gems but after that, the game becomes a lot more stingy with Gems, now after you complete Solo mode and got all of your beginner gems, it is so slow to get over a thousand gems to buy 10 packs, this is aliverated with monthly events which gets a couple thousand if you do everything and they're fun! and I've built so many decks just being free to play but that's only because I played every event and done most of my dailies every day. Gem prices are also awful, 1 Dollar isn't even enough to buy 1 pack so you can imagine the conversion rate on the rest of price options are bad. So this game is weird where the game gives a lot but only at select times and very much discenstive from spending money on gems.Card Pool and BanlistI think my biggest problem with Master Duel is these two things, the card pool as of the recent update is up to Dawn of Majesty and Synchro Storm but that means the game is behind two core sets in the TCG and almost 4 in the OCG meaning a lot of strategies included in this update like Despia don't even have a good chunk of what makes them good as does Magikey and Suship along with newer decks like HERO and not having Destroyer Phoenix Enforcer. So we have this game in the state of being perpetually behind the modern game which is a major problem especially when the competition in Arena and Pokemon Online both have cards in the game Day 1. Because of this we also have a metagame that is exactly 1 year behind and a banlist that mostly based around the OCG and by God do i think that is the single thing holding Master Duel back. The OCG and TCG functionally most of the Asia territories versus the rest of the world have had separated banlists for a couple of years now and have distinct differences in changes. The Master Duel banlist is full of some of the most toxic and uninteractive cards of the last couple of years, cards like V.F.D. which lock your monster effects, Rhongomyniad which completely locks summons, full power Drytron with seemingly endless Negates because of EVA and Benten, Simorgh summoning either Apex Avian or a Barrier Statue from deck and protecting it, Union Carrier buster locking you and Halq with O-Lion and Jet making ridiclious boards, just the works.And honestly I don't think all of this hurt my enjoyment more than a single card being Maxx "C", theres a lot of debate around this card and whether its better at 3 or 0 as a way to curb combo but by god it is the single most overcentralizing card of them all, it is essentially a three of in any deck and anytime I resolve Maxx "C" I feel like I always win. The ability to draw every time your opponent special summons is so strong that so many decks also want to play cards that hate out Maxx C or just pass and hope you don't kill them. Maxx "C" existence basically kills any handtrap diversity in exchange for essentially only two handtraps either Ash or Maxx C instead of interesting meta calls like D.D. Crow, Ghost Ogre or Veiler. and don't even get me started on trying to break through a board when your opponent Maxx "C"s you, essentially refilling their entire hand as you try to playthrough it all and dying on the crackback. I just cannot wait to see something change about the legal cards so the game becomes more healthy at the higher levels of play.Misc Thoughts.Most of my thoughts were above but heres some thoughts about other parts of the game. Solo mode is serviciable, though like a lot of parts of the game theres just a lot of weirdly formatted and translated parts of the text that just make it seem like a robot was telling the stories it almost laughable at times. A lot of the loaner decks are severely underpowered and bricky and are very frustrating to playthrough though the ones that are competently built are super fun to play and get even inspire to try them out on ladder.Customization could be better but its fine. Summon cut ins are great and add a lot to seeing a lot of old favorites get this cool animation but some feel like missed opportunities to have one like the Egyptian Gods and The Arrival Cyberse @Ignister.Closing ThoughtsOverall I do think Yu-Gi-Oh has the potential to be the best sim on the market it just hurdles to go through and I'll continue playing it until becomes that.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is visually very nice, awesome graphics, cosmetics, pictures, interface and all (pls add cubic boss monster a summon animation monkas :'c ). But it is missing in a lot of other things: 1) Shortcuts and tools for the deck building phase (simulator like keybinds to add, search cards ecc.) and it also misses some decks and cards (floowandereeze, despia ecc.). 2) Surely the thing that i'm missing the most in this game is the bo3 format ( especially using side deck, having a chance to play full matchups changing cards from game 1 to game 2 ecc.) that, in my opinion, is one of the most crucial strategic parts in the game (it's not really fun to play competitive ygo in only 1 game maybe against a counter matchup not going 1st and not having the chance to play at all, thing that is fixed in irl format with bo3 and side decking). 3) The banlist itself does not make any sense to me, there is an official tcg/ocg banlist, why not using that? Instead i find questionable the game's banlist choices by konami (ex. 3x maxx c while that card has been banned in ages in the irl format, or vfd ecc.). 4) I think that it makes no sense from the players to cry about ranked games on stuff like: long turns, game is unfair, "why can't my 6yrs old lightsworn synchro elementary school champion deck win nowdays" ecc. I mean the game evolved in yrs and now it is complicated and long, adapt to it or leave my guy, but it's true that it misses a casual mode for testing stuff and having fun, maybe a 2v2 tag duel mode, choosing old formats themed duels, being able to choose bo1 or bo3, what banlist to use, time limits  ecc. (all this not as events but as something you can always choose to play casual/for fun if you don't wanna rank and play meta). 5) The ranked system is really bad imo, I got plat1 in ~20 hours of game with a simple qliporth deck not even using meta stuff (i've been playing the game since ygogx in competitive format). Maybe add a rank above Plat or a sort of high elo monthly league/tournament with top ranked players to raise the challenge. 6) I can't really complain about gems system and stuff cause you can have about 3/4 decks if you manage gems properly and craft staples early, but still it's pretty boring after a bit and it requires you to shop gems to have 10+ working decks. (or clearing every single solo and play 24/7 to have a fifth if you don't want to spend money). 7) I can understand why there is no in-game talk/chat option in ranked games ( XD ), but they could add a voice chat / texting system at least for friends and friendly matches, otherwise i find the friend add mechanic pretty useless.In conclusion the game is pretty much new but i feel like it is losing hype and player base for these reasons, it has so much potential and with some work it could be a pretty good ygo competitive game. For now i would not recommend to play it an invest so much time and money, when you can have infinite decks and better working mechanics in any other simulator for free (if ur not obsessed with stuff like cool graphics and opening packs).

_childDocuments_.review: As a gamer and a die-hard fan of the anime series, I was super excited to get my hands on this game, and let me tell you, it didn't disappoint.First off, the graphics are fire. The game looks amazing, and the animations are top-notch. Watching my favorite monsters come to life and battle it out on the screen was a sight to behold. The sound effects are on point too - every attack, summon, and effect has its unique sound that adds to the overall immersion of the game.But what about the gameplay, you ask? Well, let me tell you, it's as intense as ever. The game is faithful to the original card game rules, so if you're a seasoned duelist, you'll feel right at home. But even if you're a newbie, the tutorial is super helpful, and you'll be dueling like a pro in no time.The single-player campaign is fun, with various challenges that test your skills and knowledge of the game. But the real meat of the game is the online multiplayer. The matchmaking system works great, and finding a worthy opponent is a breeze. The best part? It's cross-platform, so you can duel against players on different consoles or even PC.Overall, Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel is a must-play for any fan of the series or trading card games in general. With great graphics, intense gameplay, and online multiplayer, it's a game that you won't put down anytime soon.

It can be both great and terrible. I would say that as a CCG, out of the ones I've played (MtG, Yugioh, Hearthstone) it has the greatest potential for moments where a great topdeck allows you to do something really cool, where a duel can be a back and forth that feels like it truly wasn't over until the very last card was played.It also has the greatest potential for moments that can be extremely frustrating, as your opponent sets up what is essentially an unbeatable board before you've even taken a turn. I enjoy it, but I also understand very well the reasons people would hate it.Finally, if you already play Yugioh regularly and simply want to know: Is this, finally, a good online matchmaking client? Is it fun and easy to play Yugioh with other people on this? Yes, it is. But it will likely bust your wallet every bit as bad as paper does.

Hand Traps are still as obnoxious as in real life- I still think Ash Blossom deserves to be banned, even today.What I listed above are simply problems with Yu-Gi-Oh itself though. Many cards have been missing, with only a few being added recently. Along with how zero changes to the banlist have been made to fix degeneracy, the format has remained stale. This wouldn't be a problem, except you have to play Ranked in order to obtain most Gems provided by daily quests, and also Duel Rooms are a nightmare to figure out.Legacy Tickets are useless and give you nothing except crap that clogs up your catalog. Having OCD, this is an actual problem. Unless I can get rid of the cards I don't want, I will not be able to stop thinking about how they're ruining the tidy inventory that I want to have. At least let me get rid of them- I don't even want points for dismantling them. Let me have control over what I keep.Solo Mode is enjoyable, but you have to go through most of them in order, making it a hassle if there's a deck you don't enjoy prior to one you do. Plus you're likely to get sick of it by replaying it to earn daily rewards. Oh, and the music sucks. Not the popular opinion, but I don't want to listen to opera music when playing a card game. Lastly, I found the deck builder a bit hard to use. Unless you add filters, it loads every card in the game on the side instead of just the ones you own. Because there's so many, it is difficult to scroll due to the slightest nudge sending it flying. Not terrible, but it can be obnoxious.On the positive side of things, the events so far have been great. Additional rules that shut down many degenerate combos, and creating a new environment to play different decks with rewards added in as an incentive to join in. No ranks to stress out about either- Everyone is on an even playing field. Unfortunately, there have only been a couple so far, and the time spent in-between has little to offer. I want Master Duel to become better, but right now, it has become a chore.

_childDocuments_.review: Thou art hereby graced with a tale of wondrous mirth and strategic prowess, forsooth, a game known as "Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel" hath taken stage upon the digital realm. In this veritable feast of cards and cunning, a reimagined incarnation of the ancient "Yu-Gi-Oh!" doth unfold, bearing the promise of prodigious duels and tactical exploits.Methinks, as one delves into the pixelated expanse of this game, one is immediately beguiled by the resplendent visual tapestry that adorneth each card, a pantheon of imagery drawn from the annals of the Yu-Gi-Oh! mythos. The cards do spring to life with an animation both vivid and enchanting, the creatures and spells portrayed as though plucked from the very ether.The dueling stage, a digitized amphitheater, doth set the backdrop for these battles of wit and strategy. With reverence to the original card game's mechanics, players dost lay their cards upon the proverbial table, weaving a tapestry of offense and defense, all while maneuvering through a labyrinthine terrain of rules and interactions. The complexity of this dance, while daunting to the uninitiated, doth provide a rich tapestry of possibilities for the seasoned duelist.And lo, the game doth boast a bountiful array of cards, drawn from epochs past and present, from antiquity to modernity. Assembling a deck of such heterogeneous compositions doth challenge one's intellect and foresight, for in the realm of dueling, no stone can remain unturned. The confluence of archetypes and strategies dost yield a symphony of options, rendering each confrontation a unique ballet of tactics and foresight.Furthermore, the game hath embraced the digital age with an online dueling realm, wherein duelists from the four corners of the globe may lock horns and test their mettle. Aye, the connectivity of this realm doth make it feasible for players to commune and compete, transcending the confines of time and space. Yet, 'tis not without its perils, for connectivity issues can mar the experience, leading to a duel's undoing in the most dire of moments.Alas, even this reimagined gem is not without its blemishes. As with any digital creation, bugs and imbalances doth plague the landscape. The fair balance that is the cornerstone of any strategic endeavor doth falter at times, leaving the diligent strategist vexed and confounded. 'Tis a lamentable affliction that doth mar the otherwise splendid tableau painted by this game.In conclusion, "Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel" doth present itself as a modern marvel, a digital tapestry woven with threads of strategy and spectacle. Its resplendent visuals and complex mechanics dost beckon both the neophyte and the sage to partake in its dueling ballet. _childDocuments_.review: If you're coming into Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel to relive your childhood duelling experiences, then this is decidedly not that.Master Duel is the simulator for the game Yu-Gi-Oh! is *today*, not the game you remember it was 20 years ago. The game does a decent job tutorialising a lot of the new mechanics that have come in over the last 25 years of the game's existence (Synchro, XYZ, Pendulum and Link summoning, for instance all have dedicated turorials), but the new player experience is similar to that of paper Yu-Gi-Oh!: Horrible. However, once you spend some time getting bodied on ladder by opponents that seemingly can draw every card in their deck and summon like 9 bodies in a single turn, you start to pick it up. Master Duel does a really good job at signalling what effects of a card have been used this turn already, what effects you can chain, and when you have monsters in the Extra Deck that you meet the summoning requirements for. It takes a lot of the work of remembering game-states and whatnot and does it for you, allowing you to focus on piloting your deck. Misplays still happen (Even with the new effects, I still end up playing into the Imperm Collumn) but the game signals everything in a given duel really really well.MD is also pretty relaxed as far as F2P games go. Right out of the gate, the game will give you a decent amount of gems so you can, if you know what you're doing, build at least one competitive deck. However, with frequent banlists and pack releases, the meta is always shifting, and what once ruled the roost might slip down a few tiers pretty quickly. The Duel Pass, this game's version of a battle pass, also progresses rather quickly. I managed to snag all the Free rewards after a couple of days of dedicated duelling, but each pass lasts for about 3 months, giving you plenty of time to scoop everything up. These award you with new cosmetic items like Profile Icons or Mates (Little buddies that sit on your field during the duel).Speaking of Cosmetics, Master Duel is maybe the best *looking* official TCG simulator on the market. The soundtrack goes as hard as any Triple A game i've played this year, and all the various duel fields look incredible, while still remaining cohesive. The Mates are all wonderfully animated, and even things like drawing a card *feel* really satisfying. The weighty SLAM of your boss monster coming down, following a unique Live2D animation really is something, and just makes everything feel less like you're playing with virtual cardboard.If you're coming to Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel to chase childhood nostalgia, then this isn't the game for you. I'd recommend looking at Legacy of the Duelist's singleplayer campaign instead, or perhaps trying out Duel Links. However, if you want to learn Yu-Gi-Oh as it is today, Master Duel is a fantastic place to start doing that.

_childDocuments_.review: My first personal review:I have only read the comics. I have collected a box of Yu-Gi-Oh cards since elementary school. I spent 50 cents on the pirate-printing card packs every day. The box is still lying in a corner of the attic. When I first came into contact with Yu-Gi-Oh, I was limited to appreciating the card patterns/attack and defense values. Because there was no specific deck and I didn’t understand the rules very well, I only discussed with friends which cards had stronger text descriptions.Later, I didn’t study it until I played DL on my mobile phone. Now the latest MD has been released. As a newbie, I started to catch up on the rules again. This game is indeed not friendly enough for newcomers. The more popular the game is, the more difficult it is to master the board games with simple rules. For example, International chess/Go/Texas Hold'em, you may only need dozens of minutes to get familiar with the rules, but it takes a lifetime to play well. For games like Yu-Gi-Oh/Magic: The Gathering/Hearthstone, it often takes a certain amount of time to get familiar with them. To a certain extent, it is not based on intelligence but on the familiarity with the rules and the understanding of the cards. Imagine that a newbie just entered the game and did not know what decks or cards tricks the opponent had. He would just play blindly. After all, there are more than 10,000 cards in the game. Or if you have a certain understanding of the rules, you can play with a cognitive gap. I don't know the tricks you know/I know the details you don't know. A feather shows the way the wind blows.I haven't played MD released in 2022 many times, but Konami obviously realized that the graphics of DL released in 2017 are obviously behind the times. Look at Magic: The Gathering/Hearthstone/Witcher, etc., which have better graphics/better interactions/better card effects. Konami is really doing well in this regard. After all, Yu-Gi-Oh is one of the three major TCG cards in the world, and this big IP should be taken seriously. No comment on the mechanism environment for the time being.Finally, for those who are not professional/semi-professional card players, enjoying it is the most important thing. Don't take it too seriously. Studying a deck to play, or appreciating cards, collecting cards, and dueling with friends are more important.Take it easy and just enjoy it, friendly greetings from Chinese players~(2024/07/28)

_childDocuments_.review: If you understand what modern yu-gi-oh actually looks like, this game is a very smooth, well put together platform for playing that online.  If you're fine with the rather limiting way they implemented card crafting, it's a solid game.If you haven't played yugioh in about 4 years, this is not the game you remember.  This game is one where one player tries to play solitaire and the other player waits for what they hope is the right moment to interrupt them so they can then take their turn playing solitaire.  The game now comes down to who has more omni-negates or can lock their opponent out of their extra deck first.  To figure out if this game is for you, I recommend using the games excellent spectate feature which allows you to watch replays of high tier games.  The game it showed me was an Eldlich deck vs. a Drytron Fairy deck.  I think that represented the game pretty well, especially knowing that those decks are now considered outdated and not up to the current meta.TL;DR: If you wanted an online version of modern yugioh, this is it.  If you wanted the nostalgia, this game is a kick in the teeth.

_childDocuments_.review: At least here I won't get beat up for playing Yu-Gi-Oh. :)How do you do, fellow Yu-Gi-Oh kids.Yugioh has changed a lot since we played as kids, especially if your experience was a casual one and you never got a taste for what the actual early competitive meta was like.The game is now designed to be overwhelmingly faster and synergy-oriented. Furthermore, due to the freedom of information on the internet, the vast majority of players you’ll find online will be using well-made decks that fully embrace these changes. Due to the fact that every card of the same rarity can be crafted for the same number of materials, price is no longer an object for most decks, meaning that anyone can play the most optimized version of a deck possible.These aren’t bad things. I personally love the Yugioh we have today (mostly) and it’s a good thing that Master Duel is so approachable. However, it’s important that you use this information to temper your expectations. You won’t be able to use most of your old school cards without getting steamrolled, you will have to learn new summoning mechanics, and you’re probably gonna lose a lot when you’re just starting out.Not a day goes by without an old school fan complaining about running into similar  decks or getting frustrated at the pace of the game. Depending on what you’re looking for and what your tolerance is for change, this may happen to you.Like I said, I love Yugioh and Master Duel. There’s really nothing else like it in the TCG space and it’s definitely worth trying out. Just keep what I’ve said in mind when you start. Stay humble, be open to change, take as much time as you need reading new cards, do some research into what kinds of decks might appeal to you (YouTube is great for this, but you can also look at the decklists of your opponents after each match ends in MD), and treat each early loss as an expected learning opportunity and each victory as a big moment.Stay safe. May the heart of the cards guide you out there fellow nerd.

name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS
detailed_description: An otherworldly labyrinth has suddenly appeared on the outskirts of a quiet town. Make clever use of your abilities to chart the depths, overcome obstacles and defeat your foes in thrilling battles! From some of the key development team behind the legendary FINAL FANTASY franchise, DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS is a dungeon exploration RPG where you must strategize to survive. The streamlined interface gives you the freedom to prepare and manage your party as you strive to reach the final floor. With a minimalist design philosophy, the deliberately streamlined visuals and presentation allows you to focus wholly on the challenging and fun gameplay mechanics. A formidable 99 floor dungeon beneath the earth awaits you! During your expeditions, you'll discover rare and powerful items, meet lost adventurers who might just become new allies, and come face-to-face with deadly monsters. You will need to use trial and error to reach the deepest levels of the dungeon, making use of your best strategies and tactics. Do you have what it takes to overcome the numerous trials that await you and discover the dungeon's secrets? KEY FEATURES Events By uncovering and visiting spaces with white numbers, you may obtain items, unlock and change abilities, restore your party to health, find hidden merchants, and much more. Battle encounters, marked with black numbers, are hidden throughout the map. However, they can be revealed with a special ability, allowing you to choose when and where to engage your enemies. Previously discovered events will be recorded in the Event Log, a valuable resource that allows you to reference past experiences to tackle future challenges. Battles Test your strategies in thrilling battles, featuring the Active Time Battle (ATB) system made famous by the FINAL FANTASY series. Under the direction of Ito Hiroyuki, creator of the ATB system, battles play out in real-time, utilizing a polished and refined iteration of this classic design, which promises exciting, challenging combat. Map The blank map awaits you, and by exploring and investigating every tile on each level, you will be awarded ability points. Navigate obstacles, including secret passages and hidden traps, and conquer the dungeon!

short_description: Dungeon Encounters is a unique dungeon exploration RPG in which you lead an expedition to chart the depths of an otherworldly labyrinth. Plan and prepare to overcome numerous obstacles, solve puzzles, and defeat monsters. Strategize to survive!

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, as others have stated, this is not a game for everyone.If you are looking for voice acting, a gripping story, tons of abilities, and flashy graphics, you won't find it here. If, instead, you are looking for a dungeon crawling RPG with nice art that has been stripped down to its most basic form - that is, dungeon crawling, killing creatures, leveling up, and looting - but that doesn't require large amounts of time in one sitting, then this may be a game for you. The animations are minimal and your characters are represented in battle with portrait cards.Combat is quite simple. Creatures and your own characters have physical and magical defenses, and HP.  Upon one of said defenses being lowered to 0, any further damage of that type will directly hit your HP. If that hits 0, you die. Some attacks can also attack HP directly (such as unarmed or poison). There's no mana, no stamina, the only limiting factor for attacking is the ATB gauge.With all that said, there are some challenges to the game, which you may have already seen in other reviews. Did you get poisoned and don't have access the the passive ability that prevents it? Well, you'll need to drag yourself back to the nearest shrine/statue/whatever that you found to clear it. And petrification. I got petrified on floor 9 and had to leave the petrified character behind to haul the rest of my party back up to floor 7's Gorgon Altar to clear it. It wasn't a huge deal to me since it was only 2 floors away, it only took me a few minutes to backtrack. But I could see that being problem later in the game. Also, at this time, if a character dies I have to go back and find the nearest resurrection shrine to get them back in the game. If any of this sounds not-so-fun to you, you might want to skip out on this. Perhaps later there will be abilities or something that allow you to revive your characters aside from the shrine, but I'm not far enough in yet and information on the game seems to be relatively scarce at the moment.In the end, I would recommend this game as long as you don't mind that it has next to no story, the minimalist style and gameplay, and having to backtrack to revive or otherwise heal your characters.Edited 1 day after original review:So I encountered a group of 4 monks on floor 15 that had about 10 times normal defenses and health. I didn't have time to whittle them down before they wiped my party, and was unable to flee despite attempting to use the Withdraw ability (I haven't yet had this succeed). I was forced to either restart from what appears to be an earlier save (around floor 4 or so), restart anew with levels intact, or return to the main menu. Those monks essentially deleted my party. For some reason I thought you would continue with current progress using other surviving characters but apparently not. My recommendation still holds, but, man, that kinda hurts lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Randomly came across this either in discovery queue or related to recommendation about a month ago and thought it looked interesting so i wishlisted it right then. Fast Forward to now i got an email a few hours to my pleasant surprise that it had released today! I don't find myself purchasing more than 10 games a year as I'm getting older and i felt inclined to purchase this one. It is such a wonderful breath of fresh air and new take on old classic JRPG concepts and tropes. I just finished bingeing the first ten floors to 100 percent and am pausing to write this review. This game fills me with nostalgia to an era of gaming far past where single player games could sweep you up in their story or strategy for hours on end now gaming seems to be where can one get the next quick hit of dopamine from x y or z online game. I will be honest this game looks a bit primitive and in some ways it is but that only adds to the charm for me. It has a massive roster of unlockable allies you can find and recruit as you progress. The difficulty thus far has curved out super nice I have had a few close calls where i almost wiped including one narrow getaway with one party member alive and to me that is the perfect balance for a JRPG where you are riding that fine line between dominance and having that creeping fear in the back of your mind that one wrong move could spell disaster for your entire squad. Also it requires a bit of imagination since all of the dungeons are just tile maps you can explore however if you're here looking and reading this you are probably already aware of dungeon crawlers/ fantasy genre titles. I would pay 30 dollars again for this, however if you're on the fence don't fret waiting for a sale down to the 20 range, but for that price its an absolute steal with all the little nuances and breadth of characters available to command!TL;DR This game is a breath of fresh air for any fans of classic JRPG games who enjoy strategy exploration/ completionist things. A bit bare bones in the graphical department but don't let that gate you from experiencing this hidden gem! Overall a very good first step back to the genre that spawned a golden era of gaming and tons of fantastical journeys and memorable companions! Hope to see more games come out that build on this very solid foundation of turn based greatness!

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. But only for those that like old school dungeon crawlers. Remember, those where your party travel on a grid based map and you sit there with a list of paper and a pen trying to draw a map so that you don't get lost and remember where all important locations are? If you looked at store page which describes the game and didn't decide to get it right there most likely it is not the game for you and reviews won't change this decision.Basically the game is played in a 100x100x100 dungeon (most floors are filled with passable tiles only at about 10% so the total density is 88k tiles or just 8% of that cube), still that's a lot to explore. First floors (~40) are quite challenging and you have a lot of ways when something can get wrong - one of your characters get petrified and you have to leave him and go look for a cure then come back for it, suddenly enemies twice normal level appear and if you are not looking at who you are attacking you die before you can flee, the battle which you were supposed to win somehow due to bad RNG goes bad and you lose your party and have to send another party to rescue those guys, ... After floor 40 you get so many useful exploration abilities that exploration becomes very easy, you basically can take your level 1 character to the bottom of the dungeon and if you are careful you will even feel safe with it. And after you collect some more abilities from remaining floors you become so overpowered that you breeze through the enemies.Overall I liked first part (up to level 40) because of interesting combat and right when I was getting tired of it it suddenly switched to interesting exploration. And after exploration was finished it was just few hours of clearing up the remaining combat stuff using overpowered tools that I got by exploring. I didn't finish all the map and math puzzles, and I didn't kill some extra bosses but completed the rest of the game with 100% exploration and killing the final boss in 44 hours (with maybe up to 4-6 hours of idling) so you can estimate the length of the game as 40-50 hours with all things completed.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be perfectly blunt:  you are either going to love this game, or hate it.  Reviews so far have essentially confirmed that.It's a bare bones, stripped down, boiled to the very essence of a dungeon crawling RPG in the vein of Wizardry.  You will die, you will be hit with unfair difficulty spikes, and you will be praying for some sort of aid every floor.  You find yourself subject to petrification, level based one-hit deaths, and party wipe moments.  All the while, there is no grand encompassing story, or character revelations, or cinematic moments and cutscenes.  Dungeon themes are ambient soundscapes, while battle themes are guitar riffing public domain tracks.And yet, there's a strange zen-like feeling to adapting to these mechanics.  You'll find that battles are less about brute strength and stats, and more about the most plausible methods of dispatch, turning them into almost puzzle like solutions.  You'll be seeing encounter numbers and cross referencing them in your battle guide.  You'll be looking out repeatedly for new party members you can rescue as you continue to dive deeper.  You'll search for hidden tiles that could lead you to new passive or battle abilities to make things more manageable.You can tell that all these things are by design.  This was definitely made by a team who had a fondness for the PC dungeon crawlers of old.Still, it really is not a game for everyone, and that $30 price tag as of writing this is a hard pill to swallow.  Still, if you can snag it for $20, and you are one of those who want something in the vein of an old 80s PC dungeon crawling RPG (flaws those titles had and all), this may be your jam.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this game has a nice art style and the combat mechanics feel well done despite the grinding required to sustain multiple party members at the appropriate level of gear, but the game at large doesn't have any really strong hooks.  I've played quite a few other Square Enix products, including most of the Final Fantasy games. When I picked up this game, I really expected it to be a Final Fantasy styled game with Pokemon Mystery Dungeon style mechanics. What I found was really lacking that Final Fantasy heroism that I had expected. The game begins with a brief intro about how a bunch of heroes dove into this massive dungeon that appeared and never came back, so now the common folk have opted to go in after them in a rescue attempt while also finishing the job of charting the dungeon and possibly sealing it. These commoners begin the game at the Academy.You begin with something like 8-10 heroes who begin there journey at or around the Academy. Each hero starts out with a name, a unique sprite, some personal lore (that can be accessed from the menu if you seek it out), and a bit of weaponry/armor. All characters are functionally identical outside of their starting equipment. There isn't a class/job system that enables specialization in certain skills, weapons or armors. As such, you have the flexibility to create any specific combination of weaponry and armor on any four characters who have a high enough level to wield that combination of gear. Consequently, you don't benefit from caring about any more than 8 characters of the 20-30 total (4 in your main party and as many as 4 to rescue them if they get TPK'd).  There is no character dialogue. There is no NPC dialogue.There is no mentor type character who gives tutorials (there is still a starting tutorial and additional tutorials in the menu). Skills are based on your party, not your characters. I'm disappointed that the characters feel so detached from the gameplay. This is a real missed opportunity in my mind, and something I was looking forward to when I started with the game. One of the biggest features of the game is navigating through 100 floors of dungeon and mapping out each floor while dealing with monsters and puzzles. Completing the map for each floor will drop you ability points, and completing a total number of tiles overall will give you an ability point every so often. These points can be spent on abilities for your party, including including a spread of exploration skills, passive combat skills, and active combat skills. This feature of expanding the mapped area is pretty cool and unique, I'm fairly impressed with it. It would be nice if Active combat skills could be used out of combat (like Resurrection), but the system seems pretty robust as it is.Each floor poses a collection of static non-combat encounters and dynamic combat encounters. The non-combat encounters include data on the defenses of different enemies and their droppable loot, puzzles that point to unique items on different floors, healing stations, merchants, skills, etc. The combat encounters of course feature combat (see below) and are randomly distributed across the floor each time you enter the floor, making each pass through a floor somewhat unique in what you might encounter and what paths might be accessible without getting into a fight. I think these mechanics are really cool, but I would prefer that the most common non-combat encounter tiles be swapped out with a modeled icon - 01 and 02 should be swapped for stairs, 04 could be a campfire, etc.Wanderers: The characters who are lost in the dungeon are dubbed "Wanderers" and can be viewed from the Composition menu. Finding these wanderers means you have more backup party members to work with in the event of a TPK or you may simply prefer the level and sprites of your new companions over your old ones, so you can swap them out accordingly. The big issue I have with the Wanderers mechanic is that there are wanderers in the Floor 0 with the Academy that you can reasonably run a tutorial with to demonstrate how to identify a wanderer and bring them back to the academy, but no such tutorial is ran. Given that finding wanderers largely follows the same mechanic of finding previously KO'd parties, this tutorial seems like it should be among the first things shown to new players. Overall, I think the exploration aspect of the game is really cool and facilitates grinding in an interesting completionist way. While I would have liked a bit more on the aesthetics front, functionally the features in place are pretty sound (including a color-blind friendly filter for the tile colors. Thanks Square Enix!)The weapon system: There are 8 different weapons (excluding unique weapons). Each weapon does Physical or Magical damage, targets one or all enemies, does set or random damage, and is ranged or melee. Building parties to meet the needs of any combat situation is a good exercise in preparation and forethought, though you probably won't need to diversify your starting party until you get through the first few floors of the dungeon. Beyond that, enemies scale up faster than you will acquire random drops, and you will likely need to double back to Floor 0 to adjust your loadouts.  The Combat system: Having made it down nearly 30 floors, my biggest mechanical problem with the game lies in the combat itself. Most encounters are fine and normal ATB combat as anyone familiar with the genre might expect (except that all members of the party share all skills, and damage in excess of armor doesn't affect health). BUT there are more specialized encounters that cause some major gameplay problems.  In summary, the combat system is pretty nice. The gimmicks of certain encounters may ruin the whole experience for you, but it's pretty nice.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this game, but it has taken me a while to appreciate it.  I would say that if you haven't reached at least level 10 in the dungeon, you haven't even scratched the surface yet.I don't want to give too much away, because I think the beauty of this game is uncovering what it is about, but here are a few tips so you don't give up too early.- This is a deconstructed RPG.  You will do well to remember the mechanics / tricks / process of RPGs.  There is very little explanation in the game, but things that you thought were basic in the beginning are actually well-crafted analogs of RPG elements.- Do not neglect the extra characters at the beginning.  Level them up - you will need them sooner or later.  You can probably wait until level 9 to work on them though.- There is a portal back to "town" on level 9.  To me, this is the point in a typical RPG where you just finished your first linear quest and now have an opportunity to buy new items, swap out characters, and do a bit of grinding (level 9 has some good enemies for that)- When you find a new character, take them back to the Academy.- There is no true Game Over, even if all your characters die and there are none left in the Academy.  There are options if that happens.For a bit more detail and if you want some spoilers, here's how my experience went:I plowed through without a ton of thought until I ran into a really strong enemy on level 17 that wiped out my party.  Up until that point, I hadn't really run into much trouble and only had a character die once or twice and was easily able to resurrect them.  Because I thought the initial characters didn't really matter and were redundant, I hadn't bothered to level them.  Now my party was dead on level 17 and all I had were level 1 characters.  They couldn't utilize the warp tile to level 9 because they'd get wiped out there, so I had to start from level 1.  Luckily, I had some money and the shops had better stocks so at least I didn't have to grind for weapons again.  I should also note that I left a character on level 2 or 3 when I found a new one, so I was down to just 1 character back in the academy.  I started my descent again, thinking that my weapons would be enough to get me to my dead party without too much effort...Around level 6, one of my characters was petrified and another was killed.  When a character is petrified, you have to remove them from your party and leave them where they stand until you find a Gorgon Altar to un-petrify them, the first of which is on level 7, and I couldn't make it there, so I decided to go back and get my remaining character from the Academy, without bothering to get the character on level 2 or 3 that I had left behind.  I made it all the way back, and then started to descend again...Around level 6, I made a fatal mistake during a fight and all my characters died.  At this point, I didn't have anyone back at the academy, so I had a few options for how to continue (I don't remember them exactly or which I chose, but my current party was reduced to level 1 and I got to keep my inventory).  At this point, despite the setbacks, I started to really appreciate and enjoy the game.  I looked back at the mistakes I made and appreciated them for what they were - common mistakes that I would never had made in a typical RPG because they hold your hand the whole time.  I started to look at the game differently.  Of course I should have leveled my characters.  Of course I should have brought the extra characters back to the Academy so I could access them later.  Of course I should have saved up some extra equipment.  Of course I should avoid the fights with the petrifying enemies.  And I'd certainly watch out for the battle with that overpowered monster so I don't get killed on level 17 when I try to rescue my party.As I worked my way down again, I also started to see things differently.  That random group of shops that are on level 14 or so?  That's a town.  The secret tiles that you walk through to get to an ability?  Probably an old man hidden behind a waterfall who teaches you his long lost skills, or a secret room that only opens if you push against a bookcase, or maybe just a treasure chest obscured by a bush.  The seemingly random paths that make up the dungeon?  Well level X feels like a map with a river where the bridge is out and I have to walk up / down a river bank to find a space where I can cross and then go the opposite direction back to my destination, and level Y feels like a forest, and level Z feels like a mountain pass that occasionally splits and comes complete with a few caves that have secrets in them.  If you told me that every level in the game is really a deconstructed level from an actual map in a game, I wouldn't be the least bit surprised.  At the time of writing this, I've managed to gather all of my characters at the Academy, except for my initial party.  I've spent some time grinding to level them all up a bit.  I bought them the best equipment they can handle, along with some extra for when they level up or if I run into any more enemies who can destroy your equipment.  And now I'm taking a break until tomorrow when I launch my rescue mission to reclaim my initial party.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a hardcore veteran of dungeon crawler games, spanning back to Wizardry, Might and Magic, and other classics. This kind of game is my jam. I am going to give this game a positive review, but do understand that the game is severely flawed in several ways. The first thing I am going to say is that this game conveys the core essence of the dungeon crawler very well. The exploration and gradually increasing complexity of the dungeon fields are interesting. There are a good variety of combat encounters and events. The music is sparse, mostly consisting of guitar arrangements of public domain classical music pieces, all of which are only heard during combat. The graphical style is solid and generally interesting. And now we get to the negatives. There is no story. The only story is literally the tiny blurbs of information on each character profile. That's it. There is no plotline. There /is/ a final boss (and a post-game superboss encounter or three) however. Combat is very simplistic and lends itself to a lot of bouts of rocket tag. Status effects are generally extremely lethal until they suddenly aren't when you pick up the immunity Abilities (and you WILL turn them on ASAP, some of the special effects are absurd). If you don't understand that you need to fight in order to stock the shops, you might make the mistake of beginning to avoid fights, which leads to you being undergeared, which leads to you avoiding more fights... etc. But there is a decided lack of complexity in the combat system which generally means that the battle system can become more or less a solved game, especially once you get the tools to quickly ferret out the rest of the missing Academy members (some of which are exceptionally powerful).And then there's that. Some of the Academy members have restrictions on their gear that is not made apparent. Generally, though, the more restricted a character, the more powerful they actually are. I made a party consisting of the cat, dragon, robot, and a human, and was demolishing most encounters once I pulled up the specialist gear for the three. Honestly, the combat system balancing and simplicity issues are the biggest drawback. Considering you spend half your time in combat, this is a big problem. I spent a good amount of time more or less mindlessly completing the map and grinding encounters. A good romp, but I don't know if it's 30 dollars good. It really feels like a basic shell of something that could be much greater if more content was added into the game. Every minute I played it, I was thinking, 'man, if they only did THIS it would be so much cooler...'This game is worth it if you absolutely love the genre and want something enjoyable but not complex. Otherwise, hope that the developers use this core to make something even better.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had 3 separate people message me while playing this game to ask the same question: Is it good?It's great if you're an extremely weird person like me who enjoys numbers going up and filling in squares but you've also got the patience of a saint. Or at least the patience of a 2000's MMO player.If you want to buy it but see all the negative reviews talking about ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like sudden high level fights or monsters putting you in extreme debt, here's a hot tip from your ol' pal.Very early on you get an ability to see the monster encounters on the game board. These are all represented by hexadecimals. (Base-16, meaning 16 distinct symbols. 0-9, 0 being the smallest, 9 being the largest. And then A-F. A is "Bigger" than 9, essentially representing 10 but with a single digit.. So you'll see early encounters like 14 or 1F (Read as ONE FOUR, not Fourteen). The First Digit gives a general representation of the enemy level. Not exact, but if you're on floor 14 you'll mostly be seeing encounters that begin with 1. The second digit isn't nearly as important, but if you suddenly see encounters with higher numbers in the first digit, or worse, LETTERS in the first digit do not engage.So let's say you're on floor 23. You see two encounters. 2C and FE. 2C starts with a 2, so it's roughly around the 20~ level range. But FE starts with F, which we stated is representing 16. The highest digit. This fight is way too high for a level 20. If you managed to read that, understand it, and didn't instantly think "Yeah ♥♥♥♥ that it's too much work" congrats! You might enjoy this game. If it does sound like too much work that's okay too, I genuinely struggle to think of more than like 2 friends I could recommend this game to.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exactly what they advertise in the trailer. It does not need a demo because it's exactly what's in the trailer. If you were interested by the trailer above and wanted to try the game out, I'd recommend it. If you think the price is too much or are on the fence about it still after watching the trailer, check out some gameplay proper or just wait for a sale and pick it up then, but this game is exactly as marketed.There's no huge sprawling story, no five minute introductory tutorial, no cutscenes when you pick up a new party member, hell the game doesn't even give you proper tutorials, just Play Manuals you can open anytime that explain how to equip items or do battle in a few pages. And that's exactly what I wanted.I'm someone who has fond memories of buying $7-12 3DS eShop-exclusive games that ended up being really interesting/fun experiences with a specific attitude (for instance, RPGs entirely controlled by dice rolling, or a detective novel where you hold the DS like a book, or a JRPG where you play as the blacksmith who makes the weapons for all the generic JRPG protagonists, or a tower-defense where you play as a cowboy armadillo who runs around the map by rolling, or........etc.). This super minimalist take on dungeon crawling instantly appealed to me, someone who loved randomly buying these slightly-strange and less-than-traditional games that had unique takes. I almost never play dungeon crawlers, but this one instantly appealed to me by focusing NOTHING on a traditional big dramatic story, soundtrack or set design. What story that exists is relegated to a single paragraph of text setting the stage, the character backgrounds hidden in the team configuration menu, and the imagination of the player. _childDocuments_.review: I would probably not recommend this game at full price. But at the 50% off I paid for it, yeah, sure.There's no story here beyond party members' character bios, and one note you can read near the end of the game. You just pick your guys, head off into the dungeon, and start mapping the place and fighting. That's all you're gonna be doing for 99 floors. And it's pretty good, actually.The game is supported by fairly strong mechanics from its dungeon exploration to its battle system. Characters have Physical Defence, Magical Defence, and HP, and one of the former two needs to be depleted before HP can be damaged by a given attack. This means you have to think about which attacks to use on which enemies and it's almost puzzle-like in figuring out the most efficient way to kill an enemy with your current equipment. For the most part battles are good, outside of some enemies with particularly obnoxious skills.Every location in the dungeon has distinctly different design in its floor layouts which makes them stand out, and there are some gimmicks that come up too. It's not as in depth as something like Etrian Odyssey but it's enough to feel refreshing when you reach a new region.Unfortunately the game is a bit on the easy side and the focus on simple menus means no real items and skills can only be used in battle, which is a little counterintuitive when you have a KO'd party member that you have to take into battle to use a revival skill on if there's no resurrection altar nearby.Also, the music is terrible. Honestly some of the worst I've ever heard in a video game. You get one really bad song every 10 floors and that's it. I can only recommend disabling music entirely and listening to something else instead.I would recommend this if you appreciate some well designed dungeon crawling and don't care about story propping it up.Also, I'm going to say this for your own benefit: Floors 60-69 are the worst part of the game and an absolute slog to get through. If you do play it, you should warp down to floor 70 and work your way back upwards. You'll thank me later.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly enjoyed this game, but I simply can't recommend it to your "average" rpg gamer, or gamer in general.This is a very simplistic game. There are probably like ten battle animations in the whole game, several enemy sprites are reused all the time, the only map differences are in the color of the background and the music played during fights. Speaking of the music, it's all played in a single instrument.One of the main reasons I cannot recommend this game to most people is that this game is absolutely unfair. Sure, there are ways to combat this, but this is the kind of game that will go out of your way to ruin your experience in any way it possibly can, which can honestly be a positive for you masochists out there (myself included), such as enemies being able to permanently break your equipment, deal direct defense bypassing damage, steal your money in large quantities, EAT YOU, instantly kill you, and in the absolute worst case scenario, banish your party members. Depending on where you are in the game, banishment is a one way ticket to restarting your entire game. Essentially what happens when you get banished is that party member is sent to a random tile on a random floor, and considering there are 99 floors and 88,000 tiles... yeah, you might be looking for a while, if you even have the means to do so.Beyond all its flaws though, if you're looking for a board-gamey quality in your video games, you'll find it here. If you like exponential stat growth you'll get that too, and it is honestly nice seeing new enemies, getting new gear, hearing new music, it's the simple things that make the game work, which fits the theme because this is a very simplistic rpg. I personally do like this game, I enjoyed my experience (floors 91 to 99 less so), but for MOST PEOPLE, and those who actually value their sanity, I feel like I have to give this game the big red thumbs down.If you do decide to get this game, just remember this is essentially dnd but the dm hates you. This game hates you.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm recommending this game because I feel like a lot of people are passing on this because of the visuals. I started it up with that mindset, too until I found myself hooked after I figured our how weirdly intuitive the mechanics were and how strategic the fights felt.I think the problem a lot of people are having with this game is that it has so much untapped potential. That and the price point for such a bare game. Bare but surprisingly deep. There's a lot going for it but at the same time not enough. Some design decisions baffle me like the lack of any graphics besides creature and player avatars. Wizardry games got away with this by being in first person so you really just needed graphics for the walls and creatures. If they really wanted the game to look so simplistic they really shoulda just stuck with 2D sprites or something.That said the mechanics themselves are strangely intuitive and perfect for dungeon crawlers. Having an armor buffer that replenishes after every fight keeps your HP from feeling like it's draining constantly when you just want to explore. Abilities learned in the dungeons are interesting and can change how you play the game. Proficiency points are a good way to keep your characters from being overpowered just because you got lucky and found a crazy good weapon. Decisions like these make me feel like they wanted this game to be so much more than it is and I hope we do eventually get something that looks a bit more pleasing because right now it feels like Q-Bert the RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: First time I've ever written a negative review :(I'm sure other people have complained about the Treasure Hunter already, but here's another. The game was fun for awhile then I came across an enemy that could steal money, by the second time I matched up to it I was hoping some status weapons could give me a chance. Here I am experimenting with the game, trying something new a fun, then it says it's stolen 30,000 gold from me. I had 6000 to my name and thought, "well that's a bummer, I'm broke" but then when I get back to my menu (clearly didn't beat the creature) I'm in debt 24,000 gold.In no RPG have I experienced a game that could put you in debt without that being an important part of the game (Looking at you Dokapon Kingdom). So honestly, I'm pretty pissed. TBH losing all your money wouldn't be the biggest deal, but since your equipment determines how powerful you are, your characters are going to stagnate immediately. You'll pick up drops along the way but not reliably enough to be in a situation where you're not buying anything. At some point soon, if I keep playing, I will hit a moment where I can get through the difficulty level without better equipment. So the only way to fix the issue is to spend hours grinding just to make up for this debt. I'm more frustrated than anything that I've spent hours enjoying the game only to get punished for not knowing what the outcome would have been in that fight. The is a rude design decision and I'm disappointed by their disregard for the player experience.  I won't be continuing this game, not looking forward to grinding, and I have no confidence this game won't do something like it again down the line. It's a let down, pretty damn bummed about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but man....it's just not fun. I like grindy games. I like old school RPGs. But there needs to that "keep ya going" factor--that element that hooks you in and makes the game addicting, or the very least enjoyable. Some kind of challenge/reward pathway. This game doesn't have it. The character development is shallow and not diversified (which I think is the nail in the coffin tbh). The exploration element is tbh, fairly good, especially with the occasional exploration puzzle--and the secret doors are SUPER old school, frustratingly so and I do like that. As in, grab your graph paper and pencil. But the game isn't fun. I don't feel like I'm playing FOR anything. If my grind was leading to cool "abilities" (even if it was just a cool name) or more interesting equipment. Or if there was some class diversity. But they all feel the same. And they also made the character teams similar to mystery dungeon--so if you wipe you have to "rescue" your team.... Except you don't rescue them, you have to then swap out the characters you WANT--thus leaving your rescue team stuck where you wiped.  That part just feels like poor game design--not even old school there, just plain poor design choice. Overall, I think this is a game that at first glance has lots of charm, but after about 30 min the charm wears off and you're left with what feels like a cheap, unfinished RPG--not the streamlined, retro RPG of days gone. If you want to grind for very little reward and just do something monotonous, go ahead. But please realize the game has basically no story. It is grind for grind sake, and unfortunately, it doesn't put enough carrots in front of this horse to make it worth the effort.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the riddles/puzzles. I like that characters get a unique model on the map. I enjoyed the remixes of classical music (though perhaps they should have used a suite instead of thematically unrelated pieces).However, this game seems to be one of those intentionally difficult and frustrating ones with the light at the end of the tunnel being, "Well, we eventually give you skills to stop all of the mean things." As such, the mechanics have little to no explanation and/or justification. For example, how can a certain enemy steal currency you simply don't have? If you fall through the map "endlessly", how do your characters predictably wind up back in the 70-90s floors? Who or what is extracting money from you on toll squares?Finally, most of the time in game (if you leave it on speed 1) will be spent walking between tiles: mapping them out, back-tracking, etc. There is a huge amount of empty space. Previous to having certain abilities (or solving all the puzzles), maybe there's an illusion that some tiles are interesting (re: invisible answers to puzzles). After getting the abilities that reveal everything, it became clear that most of the game is a vast wasteland of nothingness that I charted out if only to acquire the number of charted tiles/cleared maps to get the number of ability points to slot the abilities to make it hurt less.Due to that emptiness, there are some technical concerns. Namely, I started playing it in windowed mode, which I have 2 issues with. First, the game seems to do something window-related on a per-save basis. That feels weird. The window opens, I move the window to where I want it, I load the save... and the window changes. Second, there's no option to turn off the pausing on focus lost. This game has a lot of slow animations (re: not affected by speed 1-4), and I'm supposed to wait them all out in-application? Got it, but that's nonsense.This game/experience could probably be salvaged/make more sense if it was released with the intent of having people make mods for it to flesh out content. This is Square Enix, though, so that's probably off the table. However, this game's content being so basic could allow it to act as a good base for more complicated things, and there's definitely enough empty space to do them in.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually, when Dungeon Crawlers get talked about, its usually in danger of one of two pitfalls: hewing too close to classic series of old, or desperately trying to sell itself as something its not (ie, a soft game genre). Caught between tradition and the need to expand, the question of "how" is almost an afterthought.But now, thanks to Ito scrounging enough loose change to his basement cubicle to craft a game, we have that answer. Similar but via a very different route to his coworker Kawazu, DE strips down to its roots and rebuilds not just the Crawler, but all video game RPGs to a large extent. The presentation is pure theater of the mind. Graphpaper grids, highly abstracted characters more portraits than lavish animations, and two very vital changes: teardown stats and a wildly potent movement system by mid-game.Stats basically boil down to HP + Defense of the type vs. weapon power x random, aerial, and/or all. That's it. Yet there's this depth from such simplicity; enemies with 0 armor, characters bringing but one weapon, the value of a few more PP or Speed. Well, there's a bit more to that like exclusive gear, but you get the drift. And you get teleports. Oh the kind of BAMFing most DC makers wouldnt dare: past an easily visible enemy, up to safety, randomly about the floor, randomly about the dungeon, down to the next available square. Its to the point where it tempts you to find the Wandering/KOed party members once you have the ability, then switch to them then a quick jaunt to end boss. It's nuts.​I guess the music is kinda bleh like my 2015 GOTY Rocket League? Just Uematsu electric guitaring out old Classical standards.​At any rate, this is Square Enix putting one of gaming's greatest minds for use for once; lets hope they do this again soon.

_childDocuments_.review: From a design and development perspective, I think this game is a  minimalistic masterpiece. It really cuts to the heart of what makes traditional RPG mechanics tick.For folks that enjoy this genre of game and are intrigued by the concept, this is an easy recommendation. It won't be for a lot of folks, but I think it won't be too hard to figure out whether it's for you or not. * The system for progression marries the exploration and combat aspects nicely (need to level up to increase your equip capacity, but many powerful pieces of equipment can be found without combat).  * Exploration is open-ended in an interesting sort of way; you're free to shortcut your way around the dungeon to seek out powerful characters and tools, or you can take things slow and methodical.  * The ability-equipping system also lends the game plenty of replayability - you can do plenty to customize your play experience.  * Combat actually utilizes the ATB system really well. Setting the game to "active" pushes you to make quick calculations to stay efficient. Even when not playing in "active" mode, it still adds an additional strategic layer - killing monster with a nearly-full ATB bar can be the difference between a character getting KO'd and escaping the fight with full HP for everyone. * Combat appears very straightforward, in keeping with the minimalist theme. There aren't arcane interactions between character stats to decipher and status effects are limited and number and high-impact. The system that's left behind leverages the game's variance (in enemy team composition / actions, some damage values, and starting ATB values) in a way that keeps combat feeling fresh. It certainly doesn't hurt that every turn can be very impactful, which tends to reduce that "mash A to clear" sort of combat that crops up in the genre from time to time. * There isn't much art in the game, but I think the monster and character portraits look quite nice. Nothing feels half-baked to me, they picked their scope quite well. * This game is very light on story (you only get the tiniest tidbits of lore from various character descriptions).  * Most equipment feels like it was mathematically generated according to the dungeon's difficulty curve, don't expect much flavor there either.  * The choices in music are a bit odd. I kinda suspect that it was all pulled from some royalty-free collection of music - "Electric Guitar Covers of Classical Songs Vol. IV" or whatever. The arrangements are fine, but it's a bit odd when you hear such well-worn songs in the place of your traditional FF or DQ post-battle fanfare. * There's good flexibility and strategy in choosing your team's equipment composition, but many characters are more-or-less interchangable (slight differences in HP or equip capacity aside). Progression is not very strongly tied to individual characters - there's no sprawling Etrian Odyssey-esqe skill point allocation system to dive into if that's what you're looking for.Altogether, it looks to me like some RPG designers were given total freedom but nearly zero budget, so they focused on putting their resources where it really counted. This game really got me thinking about what's essential for an RPG to function. DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS cleanly demonstrates that many of the standard trappings of progression and structure that I've gotten used to aren't really necessary for these games to function. It's very focused in its goal and execution, and it does what it aims to do very well.If you do decide to pick it up, I hope you enjoy it as much as I have!

_childDocuments_.review: An interestingly weird minimalist dungeon crawl style jRPG.Recommended if you are a fan of JRPGs and are interested in seeing a weird, competent deconstruction of jRPG mechanics.The game takes the basic mechanics of JRPG combat and exploration, strips them down to their fundamentals, and makes something as interesting as possible with what's left. I think it is a successful experiment, but it wont be to everyone's tastes.Exploration:You explore a dungeon made out of a large 100 x 100 x 100 3d grid, starting from the top, and fighting increasingly more powerful monsters as you dig deeper down in the cube, each layer a different "level", and every 10 layers make up a stratum of the dungeon with its own set of enemies, visual themes, music and level design gimmicks to keep things fresh.Some grid spaces are marked by white or black hexadecimal numbers (00,01,02... through FC,FD,FE,FF) that mark those grid spaces as special. Black numbers mark the location of random battles, and are scattered at random every time you enter a floor. White numbers are fixed special locations, such as stairs up/down, special abilities to collect and shops.Along the way, you discover new movement and exploration abilities you can use to explore, such as a leap that skips over a few spaces, or the ability to dig straight up or straight down one level.These abilities allow you to find shortcuts by figuring out short 3d paths through the maze that allow you to return to safety in few steps, or sometimes allowing you to find secrets or access special locations on certain levels. However, some of these abilities are dangerous to use: One of the "dig down" abilities, if used carelessly, can result in your party falling through the entire maze and down into the void below, which leads to your whole party getting scattered all over the map.Combat:Battles use a simple but effective, stripped-down active time battle (ATB) system such as found in most Final Fantasy games from FF IV onward.Much of battle strategy comes down to prioritising targets in combat, choosing the right attack ability for the right enemy, and building a party with varied attack options so you can reliably take down any combination of enemies with various strengths and weaknesses. The game manages to do this with shockingly simple components that strip these sorts of combat fundamentals bare, removing nearly all obfuscating layers that would otherwise hide them.Enemies and party members all have very simple characteristics and combat actions which you can see at a glance during combat. You know exactly how much damage your attacks do, and how much damages enemies can soak up before they die, which allows you to pick exactly the right moves in combat to eliminate your foes while taking as little damage as possible.Enemies have three separate life bars: HP, Physical Defence and Magical Defence. You need to deplete either physical defence or magical defence (using physical or magical attacks) before you can attack an enemy's life directly. Your own defense bars replenish between battles, but your characters' life bars do not. A lot of enemy variety comes simply from giving them a different balance between these three numbers. There are some patterns in their designs, such as undead enemies always having exactly 1 hp but high physical and magic defence, making them very vulnerable to the few rare abilities and weapons that pierce defence and attack life directly. There are also flying enemies that cant be targeted with Melee attacks, and Reflecting enemies that bounce Spell attacks back to the caster.The weapons/abilities you can equip to your party members are very straightforward, and can all be described with only 5 characteristics: Damage Amount (from 1 to 999999), Damage Variance (either Fixed or Random), Damage Type(Physical or Magical), Range(Melee or Ranged) and Targeting (Single or Multi). All abilities and weapons are just different combinations of these, with very few exceptions.Conclusion -It is impressive how much depth the game manages to pull out of such stripped-down mechanics, it really squeezes every last drop of blood out of that stone. it feels like playing a JRPG that's been taken apart, all of its pieces labelled and categorised for you to poke at as you play. Never quite played any other game like this. It's not for everybody, but I think if you played a lot of JRPGs before, this could be interesting to you. If you're not sure, get it when its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Just a little too shallow for my tastes.  As far as I can tell, all the characters are exactly the same- only differentiating by what you equip them with.  They can equip a weapon OR spell in each hand, and that's their moves.  There's no rock paper scissors, no buffs or timing- it almost feels like playing Octopath, except your whole team has only sword and spear equipped, and every enemy breaks to sword and spear.  And also you don't learn moves.Three's not enough mechanically to make up for the minimalism elsewhere, and it ends up feeling a bit like playing a cross between a spreadsheet and a wallpaper cycler.It's really a shame because you get the sense that someone built this stylistic prototype of a game, arguing "if we boil the game down to its core components, combat and fighting and strategy and progression, it'll feel refreshing and bracing!"  But then at the end instead of actually making those mechanics they just said "eh, here's some clipart for the rest of the enemies and levels, ship it."

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - it is too minimalist, it feels slightly more polished than homework for a student of game design.  Maybe check it out if you can pick it up for less than $5, but be warned what you experience in the start of the game is the same all the way to the end, there's very little worth liking here.While I'm a fan of traditional RPG games, this just doesn't cut it.  It's like it was reduced to the absolute most basic of components.  I've played a lot of the experimental games from SquareEnix, I very much enjoyed FF-MQ and Ehrgeiz, as they had tidbits where you could see ideas that would be implemented in future games.  DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS doesn't seem to have any of that in my opinion, the characters are all essentially just cookie-cutter copies, only 3 of the ~24 having any real discernible difference.  And the last ~9 levels in the 100 level dungeon were almost undoubtedly designed to purposely be as frustrating to the player as possible.  We are talking "the only way to descend a level is to use a skill dropping you down a floor, but there is the very real possibility that you can be dropped down and miss the flood below and fall out the bottom of the world at which point your characters can be lost to an unreachable tile and the only way to get them back would be to download a third party program to physically edit their location code."  I kept hoping for something more to shine through on this, but it really just ended up being a turd sandwich and I'm glad I didn't pay for this trash.
