_childDocuments_.review: A radical deconstruction of both traditional dungeon crawlers and more modern, 'emergent story' style game-mechanics. There is almost zero actual writing in this game but despite that I found myself building a narrative and forming relationships between the characters based on their gearing. BY eschewing the guard rails of the modern RPG, death really does lurk around any corner; it evokes the feeling of a Bard Tale.One wrong step spells doom. And so it was for me, ultimately, after some 20 hours and around level 60 of the dungeon. Some players fell prey to pit-traps leaving their parties scattered and doomed, but my death was one of over-confidence: seeking to cheese an encounter I felt could yield an OP gear set for my level, a couple of unlucky dice rolls later and my party were toast.Permanently toast. My last 'expedition' (aka the last time my party had a full wipe) was some 10 hours previous but that's OK - the fun is in the tension, the tension is in the risk, and the risk isn't real if you can save scum every time you lose!Honestly all the criticisms of the game are absolutely fair and valid but I absolutely loved my time with it and I look forward in a year or two to revisiting. Maybe the point of the game is that the puzzle is less fun once you've figured it out, and a game can be good without a $200 million budget.

_childDocuments_.review: Through and through this is a distilled take on a Wizardry style dungeon crawling CRPG of old with a lot of moving parts hidden under the surface. The story is brief but little vignettes are told through character profiles that not only tie everyone together but can even indicate clues as to where to find them or even what happened to them in their descent into the Labyrinth. The big thing to note is that the star of the show is, well your in game notes. To best deal with Increasingly more violent foes you should be constantly checking your notes to the composition of certain encounters. Either avoidance for particular troublesome foes with little wanted gear, or through seeking out those gold nuggets of enemies that have precious powerful equipment that will drastically alter your killing power. Not to mention the absolute mountain of riddles to solve for incredibly valuable tools that can change how you engage battles. There is much more to the map than there initially seems to be, and i assure you much more to the -game- than there will be on first glance. The graphics are intentionally minimalist, your focus on the dungeon and the denizens therein. This isn't to say the art style is without substance or even a bit of soul, honestly I quite enjoy the portraits and 3D models for all the party members, and there are various effects that will play our depending on what levels you are on. Dank dripping dungeons, a fast field with a gently babbling creek, the oppressive desert wind battering you with sand. All of these environments even lead to drastically different styles of mazes, it's very deliberate and a nice touch. I feel there's actually a lot of attention and love that went into making this game that touts itself on being gameplay focused first, and I for one quite appreciate that. Old dungeon crawler fans and those willing to be put in the mindset of analyzing every suspicious square will find an absolutely fascinating experience that I feel is worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeon Encounters is an incredibly low-budget dungeon RPG, explored from a third-person perspective instead of the typical first-person perspective. This wouldn't be bad on its own, but the dungeon is both very large (100 floors, with a little over 88000 tiles) and rather boring, with very little in the way of gimmicks and very few puzzles, only some riddles you have to solve to find hidden items.Likewise, the combat mechanics are fairly simplified, with attacks either hitting physical or magical damage (or rarely, applying a status effect or going straight to HP), for either a fixed or random amount, but each character can only equip two attacks. It's not terrible, but there's very little room for interesting encounters, just ones you win quickly or ones you run away from quickly.The graphics and sound are very limited, with the graphics being basically as seen in the screenshots only, and the BGMs being classical music played poorly by angry guitars. It's an interesting choice, but I didn't end up thinking it was a well-executed one.And, while it's a very budget game, it's $30, with very little in the way of redeeming features. So: not recommended, go play a different dungeon RPG instead. The PC is a bit short of great recommendations, since Experience's PC ports tend to be bad and Etrian Odyssey isn't on PC, but there has to be something better, or at least cheaper, than this.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game.  It has some neat concepts.  I knew the graphics were minimal.  That didn't bother me.What bothered me was the grind.  The game forces you to go up and down 10 or more floors with characters not equipped to handle any of the enemies you would encounter, just to do a stone to flesh or to revive a party that fell...and they do fall.  A lot.  As a result of this tedium, it pays to have multiple high level parties...but that, within itself is more tedium.  And when it comes to party members, there is nothing you get to do to create your party or to improve upon it.  Level ups are automatic, you don't get to customize your character or feel any connection with them.  They are just...characters...nothing more.  A game with crappy graphics...I can handle that.  Tedium...I can tolerate more than most...but the emotionless party building and pointless aim...it, by itself is awful but when combined with the tedium and bad graphics.  I truly cannot recommend this game unless you are truly a glutton for punishment.This is one of those games where beating it is an accomplishment within itself.  Maybe bragging rights appeals to you.  You certainly earned it if you do beat it.

_childDocuments_.review: Simplistic design and simplistic fights, make for a boring game. I am currently floor 94~  level 110~Characters arent different from one another, damage is FIXED by the weapon you are using.This means that you will always deal the same amount of damage no matter what, which means get the best weapon/magic and since all characters are the same... well the same equips for all 4 characters. By the way this means all you characters will have maliare1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8... and you will spam that every single fight all the game. physical damage is garbage because they cant hit flying enemies(unless you have a bow, but then you can only hit one enemy), but guess what? magic can!Talking about hitting enemies, there are normal enemies and flying enemies, physical weapons are thrash because they cant hit flying enemies, magic is OP because it can hit everything. Did I mention that all fights are the same? it takes 4 magic AOEs to kill everything in this game when you have the current equips.BUT I READ THAT IN THIS GAME YOU CANT GRIND!?False, you can absolutely grind, you level up more, you get free items, and all leveling up does is get more PP which allows you to equip better stuff, also you can farm items that give you max PP / max HP boosts. Also, completing floors forces you to fight vs everything, and you get more ability points which in turn allow you to get abilities that increase your damage in fights under certain circumstances.I see reviews complaining about poison/petrification... you get abilities to become immune to that in the floors...assuming you explore 100% all the floors all the time. And by the way the game designers decided to make invisible tiles HAVE FUN!... (or just get the ability to see them in floor 69 all though if you are like me you get to that floor and then realize all the time you wasted finding the tiles)Talking about annoying mechanics lets talk about death, when you die your characters stay in the tile where you died, so you use the other characters you left in the academy and rush your way to get to them. And you cant carry more than 4 characters so you either go one by one to pick them up or leave the pickup party there and leave with your party.... WHICH BY THE WAY the game doesnt warn you that if you do it the easy way, next time you die you dont have characters to pick them up so its game over, or restart from the last time a pick up party left.... so yes I wasted 2 hours because of this.Lets talk about end game mechanics, the developers decided to put pits, so if you fall into a pit you descend in the dungeon to the next tile available, ASSUMING there is one... If there isnt one GOOD LUCK your party disappears in the dungeon SCATTERED thru all 99 floors. finding them again will take you about half an hour if you are lucky (this is probably the worst mechanic in the game by far). ASSUMING of course that you have all the abilities on previous floors to find them, otherwise good luck. Also there is a skill later in the game called teleport, which does that teleport you to a specific tile in the game, however if the tile doesnt exists well it works just like pit, and you need to find your party.Now lets talk about end game mechanics, the developers decided to add a new status effect in the last floors in floor 90ish to be specific, well there isnt a way to get rid of this status unless you know that the way to get rid of this status is in floor 97... so good luck going thru the 90-97 floors without one unit.And yes I am salty because my unit got turned into a hamster, I got into a fight, clicked ran 8 times and it failed 8 times in a row (how is this even possible? I was 20 levels above the enemy), and my party got wiped in floor 94, I dont know if I want to spend 30min-1hour going to go get them back.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it - but agree that it isn't for everyone.  It has a bare bones approach that focuses mostly on game-play.  EG: Exploration, a bit of puzzle solving, mapping, JRPG grinding / level-up, and note taking with respect to dungeon positions & encounters.This isn't a game you want to play if you don't like to think about what you're doing.  As others have said there's a risk/reward component and you have to choose if the fight is necessary or worthwhile before choosing to engage with an encounter.There are new mechanics added periodically as you go deeper into the dungeon which can keep things interesting.  I eventually managed to sequence break - lost my whole party - got them all back again and then developed a better system of navigating to keep my group together.In general - there's almost no story to the game and I usually like story driven narratives but in this case I didn't really mind the lack of story.  There's sort of a subtle hint of a story in different areas of the game just in terms of 'flavor' but it really is just a game.  And I thought it was fun. :-D

_childDocuments_.review: Gonna refund the game - not because it's bad, but because I'd prefer to play it on Switch insteadThat being said, if you're looking for a recommendation, it has to depend on how much you like the barebones (but with a lot of mechanics-transparency) approach of the game.Do you like a game that has ultimately interchangable characters that you can mold pretty much as you see fit?Do you like a game that seperates weapons by how they deal their damage? (Swords always deal fixed damage, Axes are stronger but are highly random, Lances deal weaker fixed damage but hit all enemies, you get the idea)Do you like a game where you need to take notes, both mentally and via notepad / screenshots?Do you like a game where you might have to build up & send a rescue party to save your main party if things go sour?Do you like a game that's very transparent about enemy stats and drops?Do you like a game where you're gonna go back to a central town to outfit your party a lot?If all or most of these sound good to you, I highly encourage you to check this game out at least. You might find something you maybe even didn't know you wanted here.On the other hand, if you're looking for a complex plot or deep magical systems (magic falls pretty much in the same sorting categories as the weapons, just that they deal magical damage - there's no Fire / Water / Thunder spell or something) or rich environments without having your brian fill in the blanks, you're probably best to move on from this

_childDocuments_.review: A solid dungeon crawler that gets straight to the action. Combat is satisfying if ultimately simple, the exploration is pleasant in a completionist way, and the variety of locations keeps the visuals fresh as you progress.However, a lack of plot and world-building and some glaring omissions on the QoL side leave this game falling short of what it could have been.7/10 if you enjoy the dungeon crawler genre. Even then I'd probably wait for a sale, since $30 is a bit steep.Hard pass otherwise, as there's nothing else on offer.- The combat mechanics reward paying attention to the damage numbers and allow you to make the most of each attack.- You can choose fixed damage weapons or random damage weapons - I preferred fixed damage for the most part, but random damage can spike much higher and make stronger enemies much more manageable.- Each biome features distinct tile patterns that make them surprisingly recognizable. This ties in well with the "Map Riddles" where you have to identify a specific location based purely on the tile layout.- As you explore, you will find special abilities that you equip to the whole team, varying from in-combat things like healing or resurrection to exploration utility such as revealing hidden tiles or allowing a wider view of the map.- Earning upgrades by defeating enemies is inherently satisfying and provides a good push to move forward and tackle the next set of enemies.- Overall, the lack of random battles works here. It can make some sections of exploration trivial and allows you to dive much, much deeper than your party could otherwise survive, but the punishing nature of party wipes and status effects balances that out with higher risk. - Warp points at the end of every biome mark a significant step forward in progress and really work to limit how painful backtracking can get.- A key ability to show unmapped tiles in each direction salvages what would have been an absolutely tedious nightmare trying to reach 100%.- Characters (with some minor exceptions) can use any equipment and have no special abilities or limitations. This means you can use any character you want without sacrificing strategic or tactical options, for the most part, but also means that the characters all basically feel the same in terms of gameplay. - There are special status effects and instant-kill effects that your characters can use, but the random nature makes them quite unsatisfying to use. I found that fixed damage was just as effective and allowed me to plan my attacks rather than just flailing and hoping for the best.- There are special abilities to protect against things like Petrification, Poison, Instant KO attacks, etc. They are powerful, but the status effects are so brutal that they feel more necessary than nice-to-have.- Knowing which enemy you are about to fight allows you to customize your party loadout in preparation. Unfortunately it's largely unnecessary - the lack of special abilities for characters and enemies limits how deep the combat can really get. It boils down to a damage race, for better and for worse.- The capacity for multiple "parties" exploring the dungeon felt like a mechanic where we've just barely scraped the surface. As implemented, a party wipe isn't the end of the game and recovering your main party is a minor chore.Deeper character customization (classes, party synergies, etc.) and more complex exploration and puzzles (for example, requiring multiple parties in different areas of the dungeon to take actions), or even just different biomes requiring very different tactics to deal with could have added a lot to this game.- There's too little plot or world-building. The rest of the game is so "minimalist" in presentation that the bits of lore that do exist feel disjointed and almost random.- The "Wandering" character mechanic is an interesting concept, but the implementation falls flat and ends up as annoying rather than fun.- Return To Base abilities come late in the game, and are still awkward to use thanks to being one-way.- Lack of shortcuts or full map views make backtracking within a biome very awkward. Not showing the full map upon completion is a huge miss - it would have been a great reward for full exploration, and an in-game grid view where you could flip between levels would have made abilities like ascend/descend much more useful and satisfying.- The final biome (which is largely optional, to be fair) is very annoying to explore, requiring blind ascents/descents, gamble shifting, and so on to fully explore. It didn't feel like it rewarded careful note-taking or methodical exploration... it just felt awkward.- I didn't get hit by this myself, but going into negative funds because an enemy stole your money is ridiculous. There's punishing, and then there's game killing.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeon Encounters is exactly what it sets out to be - a minimalistic (although arguably too minimal) - dungeon RPG with an emphasis on map exploration.  Story is scoped entirely to a single background paragraph for each character, map locations are all denoted with a single two-digit-hex number with corresponding reference lookups in the menus. Gameplay-wise, it reminded me a lot of Etrian Odyssey, but while Etrian Odyssey incorporate map notes and marking as a game mechanic, here that burden is put on this player to do with old-fashioned notepad and pen - which is certainly needed for this game.Many of Dungeon Encounter's game mechanics can be very frustrating - there is an enemy which can steal your gold and put you negative (possibly *very* negative).  With how the game incorporates the need to constantly buy/equip new weapons/armor in order to have a realistic opportunity to defeat increasingly challenging enemies, this put me at a disadvantage until I could get myself out of debt.  That took a while for me to do (2-3 hours or so).  My lesson learned was to never fight that monster again. The game also has a way to scatter your entire party across the dungeon if you fall into a pit sometimes.  I had my main party get scattered in that manner and I had to try to find them all - reassembling my team took me about 4 hours, during which time I had to explore a lot of the dungeon with a massively underleveled backup team avoiding monsters and exploring maps.  It was a wildly different gameplay experience than the more classic RPG method I had been employing up to that point.Overall, I enjoyed this game and think there is a lot of replay value now that I am more familiar with the mechanics. I don't see it being wildly popular because it is not a traditional RPG. I also think the minalistic nature of it takes away more than it adds, but I do appreciate the novelty of such an approach. While it doesn't scratch the exact same itch as Etrian Odyssey it is close enough in a niche genre with relatively few options.EDIT: Also, I forgot to mention that I liked the music.  It had a cool sort of metal/classical feel to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Every single review on this game's page is wrong.Here's the thing: It is **trivially easy** to fully map out every floor in this game without fighting any enemies. They just rest in random places, and the game keeps giving you new teleportation and displacement abilities to move around them, and by a third of the way through you get one called "Greater Descension" which effectively lets you warp to any floor in the entire game without much hassle. You can walk on every tile and collect all the treasure without having to fight a single enemy. If you manage to get your party wiped (most likely by accidentally walking into the always-visible battle tiles), you can just warp down and pick them back up.You can skip down to the final floor and find out that every floor along the way is exactly the same. The dungeon doesn't introduce any meaningful new elements or challenges, aside from some negligible nuisance gimmicks such as a section where you can't see the tiles until you've moved into them (but you can still see where all the battles are, lol), or a section with tiles that steal a tiny amount of gold from you, or a section with random trapdoors everywhere just to waste your time warping back up.So there's no real exploration, even of the minimalist kind, and there's no puzzles aside from some crappy math riddles that encode treasure coordinates. What's left is a purely mindless grind: kill weak-enough enemies and level up, forever. The dungeon might as well not exist once navigating it becomes trivial. Since every battle can be either avoided outright or selectively engaged, and it even tells you what difficulty and composition each encounter will be, there is no meaningful tension or danger. Since you are never far from unlimited replenishment, there is no resource management. This game is not hardcore, it is not even as interesting as the old Wizardry games were, and it is nothing but a waste of your time.If you would like to play an actually hardcore minimalist top-down dungeon crawler that constantly forces you to make meaningful decisions with actual consequences, check out Tactical Nexus. It has a free demo that lasts about 20 hours. It's very ugly, but didn't you say you weren't here for the graphics?

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game. It's a basic dungeon crawler which not everyone will like but it just hits differently. If you enjoy games like etrian odyssey or various other dungeon crawlers you'll like this. The only complaints most people have seem very...weird based on my experiences.The game works off a grid system, you run around filling in untouched tiles and gain abilities, events, new people through finding and solving little puzzles. Each black number is a battle corresponding to a specific monster and each white number is an event. The battle system is very simplified. You have physical defense and magic defense and your attacks do either physical or magical depending on your weapon which 'shreds' the armor. Once the armor is gone you do direct hp damage so you'll come into contact with enemies with no physical armor, but high magic, or vice versa. Any 'overkill' damge to the armor doesn't go to hp as well so you can't just one shot a ton of stuff.The characters only gain hp and 'pp' (equipment point sbasically) everytime they level, but the monsters also have a chance to drop items that give you a max hp or max pp increase on use. I've been to about floor 20 and i've enjoyed the hell out of it. It's very relaxing and a nice dungeon crawler if you like it. It's not for everyone but if you enjoy dungeon grinding with randomized gear then you'll love it. It's not a game you can just 'overlevel' and 'gain skills from leveling' it's purely 'gear based'. It's fun and I enjoy it! Don't let the negative comments dissuade you!

_childDocuments_.review: Kind of sad to see this game get Mixed reviews.It's more appropriate to say this is an old school traditional rpg where the game has been stripped down to it's bare bones ignoring many other nuances like graphics, story telling or a complex/detailed world.However, the underlying core gameplay is still very fun despite it looking like... well... this. This is where the emphasis on the non-traditional design is apparent (Which lead to the negative reviews). Some of them are as follows:The game is technically unforgiving if you stick to common rpg troupes. If you think about how the system works however, you'll come to realize that breaking out of the troupes also exposes the game to obvious cheese.For example, undeads are commonly tough enemies that have huge defenses and damage. However, they usually have 1 hp. Guess what? Unarmed damage does literally 1 direct hp damage irregardless of defense. You can slap an undead for an instant kill as opposed to hitting them with your weapon (Granted you knew what unarmed attacks did via trial and error).Another one would be equipment tying strongly to what attacks/skills you have. The caveat here is equipments come with an equip cost (PP) based on your level. However, if you strip naked, you could technically equip a strong weapon, which allows for a level 1 character to deal massive damage. An easy method of power leveling weaker players in an area level that is way higher than they should be in (Or alternatively just do the original way and bring some high lvls for safety).And finally, getting cheesed on in this game is also a thing. Death/petrification in particular is like the no.1 reason why this game gets poor reviews. Instead of a game over screen, you are sent back to camp and now need to scrounge up another team to extract your dead team.Normally, good planning can avoid this by having a B team of sorts however even if you didn't a viable way to extract your dead team would be to avoid encounters and go straight to recovering them or just power level some heroes to a decent level. Either ways, this is the players fault for not having a contingency plan and blaming their poor planning onto the game.Also LOL to the top rated negative review. There is a skill in the dungeon that will provide you with a compass towards your wandering hero. On the other hand, you could avoid such an issue to begin with by just having pitfall clairvoyance. Again, negative review on a game mechanic which could have been easily mitigated from good planning but the player is either too stubborn or dumb to realize.Overall, play the game with the expectation that this is not your typical current era RPGs with handholding, lovely crafted visual or typical rpg logic. Instead, expect that this is a barebones non-traditional rpg with an emphasis on unique gameplay mechanics that can open itself (And you) to obvious cheeses.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I finished the game, I must say that it is the biggest surprise in 2021 for me.It might not be a fancy looking, beautiful sounding and most complex game out there, but for what it does (being a JRPG Dungeon-Crawler) it delivers it very well.The games focus of preparing your companionship to explore every inch of a dungeon, while fighting monsters, that get stronger and stronger every floor you enter, feels so well made. You are constantly rewarded for exploring the floors and solving the puzzles, starting with 200 Gold to getting a companion with stronger gear up to finding a weapon that almost kills every monster in one hit. And while the monsters are being very weak in the beginning of the floors, if you are over-confident, you get punished pretty fast and you have to backtrack all the way to get your dead allies back to the main camp to heal them up.  (I read that many people used to be frustrated by the fact, that there were much stronger monsters in the early floors, than to the rest of the monsters. If you checked the monsters ID in your combat log, you would see that the monsters are way below the list, than the ones you fought before. Therefore, you don’t even need to know Hexadecimal to know that FC is much higher than a 09 or 11 and you should avoid those. )However, the game is not perfect. Some Floors were a pain to navigate through or complete to 100% and one specific floor was made to guess, where to drop to fill the tiles. The early game also has some very punishing negative effects to your allies (petrified) , that doesn’t allow you to move the companion and you have find a Gorgon Alter to cure the ally, while remembering the coordinates , where the companion was petrified at (luckily you can check the companion log book to see , where his last position was).  Same goes with the fact, that the companion detector for finding a new ally is not really well made in my opinion. Some of the puzzles could have more hints to solve them than for example having a puzzle only saying (cdefab / 2 = abcdef). And while I did enjoy the simplistic and minimalistic take on this game, I do wish, we would have got more story written for this game. Overall, I really enjoyed the game and it really isn’t for everyone, but if you enjoy pure dungeon crawling with JRPG combat, where exploration is mostly very well made, you should get this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeon Encounters feels like an , an attempt to distill only the necessary core elements of a JRPG. I bought it because I love seeing developers take risks, and I'm a huge fan of grids in general.I do think DE gets a little *too* minimalist though. My assumption is that these icons were left out on purpose, to show that players don't  that art to enjoy a JRPG. I guess that is also in my "must have" bucket for an RPG. I do like the core combat mechanics, but the characters lack the depth that makes them feel special. _childDocuments_.review: Played about 10h on the Switch version. This is a very minimal dungeon crawler akin to oldschool RPGs like Nethack or the original Rogue. Except that instead of proceduralizing each new run through, it leans into the player experience of building the knowledge of the dungeon and its content. In-game, this is lore-ified by your heroes "charting the dungeon". So over time, you will learn what enemy combinations you will encounter, where certain shops or secrets are located - you will unlock shortcuts between different levels, etc. Your long-term progression is also facilitated through levelling up your heroes and collecting equipment (equipment being much more important to character strength, as others have said). This is not an easy game, but also not as harsh as some of the comparable oldschool games. Party wipes or partial wipes are part of the game - at which point you essentially send in your "B-team" in a rescue operation to retrieve the bodies of the A-team for resurrection. It is a very minimal experience, without any chrome or fancyness - just a pure dungeon crawling experience focused on the mechanics. The combat system is very pure as well, and feels more like a puzzle game experience rather than the standard power growth focused RPG system. It starts very barebones, but then layers of complexity and interaction are introduced that make battles a rewarding min-maxing experience.If you enjoy games like Into the Breach or oldschool dungeon crawlers, this might be a gem for you. Just be aware that it has some JRPG twists to the experience, and that you need to be willing to look past a very barebones minimal presentation. Graphics are high quality, like the character art - it just has very little of it. The one complaint I would have about the game is the music, in particular the battle music. It is just not good, so I ended up playing on mute the whole time.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeon Encounters is a minimalist dungeon crawler that requires actual tactics to overcome encounters. The game breaks down the RPG formula into the most barebones form it can take: there's no story, no character arcs, and the character customization depends on equipment only. The dungeon is a simple maze of tiles, peppered with encounters and "events" that offer places to heal, revive your characters, purchase equipment, etc. That said, the depth comes from the battle system, which is a case of "easy to learn, hard to master". The game has a satisfying gameplay loop, with exploration that's somewhat reminiscent of the pokemon mystery dungeon series. Hidden secrets makes a completionist playstyle rewarding, and the level carry over between playthroughs gives it a rogue like feel. People complaining about a bland battle design have not gotten deep enough to experience all the combat has to offer. Sometimes, all I want from a game are tight mechanics that I can hop into and enjoy. If you get tired of RPGs and their superfluous cutscenes, trite stories, and flashy but insubstantial combat and dungeon design, Dungeon Encounters is the perfect game to turn to.

_childDocuments_.review: It's wonderfully addictive stuff. _childDocuments_.review: I've played enough, the basics are clear and it's time to review.This game is made by Square Enix. That means it's going to be beautiful with excellent animation (where there is animation). Seeing a heavily muscled humanoid cat with two tails and a cloak walking is fluid and believable. Unfortunately, it also means that it's designed for a controller and any mouse/keyboard usage is tacked on, badly, as an afterthought. Feels awful, looks worse. Heck, they even use the default windows mouse cursor. Every menu is designed for a controller, which means you need to go menu to menu like a controller would. Clunky and awkward. Mildly annoying each and every time. You'd think a big, successful company like Square Enix could afford to hire ONE PERSON capable of setting up a decent PC oriented UI, but nope. There are a lot of games by independent developers, 1-2 person studios, that have better UIs than this. Hey, Square Enix, if you're reading this, contract someone to make your UIs for PC games, every single employee you have is utterly incapable of it and it makes the games feel bad.Ok, moving on, and this time with an example. There is an early sword, I think the first dropped weapon you get, that does 60 damage. A nice upgrade. Then you encounter enemies with 62 points of armor and 62 hp. But your sword does 60, only 60, no more no less. So it takes 4 hits to kill. Those enemies always have that armor and hp, and your sword will always hit for 60. My exact reaction when I saw those enemies was "Really guys. REALLY?" I'm sure you'll feel the same. I have no reason to expect this to be any different later on in the game, it's just more pronounced early.The starting beginner stores. These do not contain enough of the items you'll want to fully outfit your group after you've made a couple trips into the first couple levels of the dungeon and back. Oh, the worst stuff they'll have enough, but then it's like 1 of this item or 2 of that. So your team won't be evenly outfitted anymore, making your 4 person team have weaknesses and combat (after you delve deep enough to have a little risk) will start to feel like "don't hit guy #2, please don't hit guy #2 (or whoever you select for the bad armor or bad magic resist). That ties into the next point. Scroll up, look at the photos of the game again. See how they have different armor/mr/hp? That's not class based, it's due to availability and "PP" or points used to be able to equip things. When they level up, they get PP, and it's not the same for everyone and not the same with each level. This fits right in with the difficulty in getting/keeping everyone equipped roughly the same. In most games that comes with a class system, and maybe something like a tank that taunts or a rogue with agro reduction. This game doesn't have those things, everyone is equally likely to get attacked, so your weak points are always exposed and you can't really do much about that. For this I will say that this is still early, maybe there are taunts later, but the weakness gap with no way of addressing it is present before any way to mitigate it shows up in game, if there is one it comes after you're dealing with issues and crossing your fingers.There are no combat animations, which probably saved a lot of money in game development. There's also no classes, which also probably saved a lot of money on time spent balancing things. It feels like it was a venture into the price range/market that is normally held by indy developers, since there is real money to be made there as long as you don't let development costs get away from you. But the difference is that indy developers put passion into their games, and try hard to make them the best that they can. Indy devs don't have a giant studio backing them up, so they need to produce a good product, and built their reputation from the ground up, and if it doesn't work out they can't quit their day job (or need to go back to one). SqE can just shrug if it doesn't work and not care, and it shows.If this game was to be worthwhile, it would need a significant rework. Classes, maybe, or talent trees perhaps. More control and customization of the leveling up process than just "oh, they leveled, some HP, PP, whatever, I get what I get and I guess I like it". ***Make my party feel like they're MY party.*** I still don't know why I'd pick one character over another outside of appearance and their PP at the level that they're at. See that muscular cat guy? What makes him different or special? His unarmed attack still does 1 damage, same as everyone else. Frankly, could be 4 blobs for all that it matters, and when they level, that doesn't feel satisfying either.If you want to play disappointment: the video game, play this. It could be good, what they have is a great basis for building the game on, but (outside of it being completely bug free as far as I can tell) frankly most games that show up with an Early Access tag have more features and customization than this does...and they're early access so there's even more that will be coming in the future. This isn't early access. I'm pretty sure this is it, it's all you get, nothing more will be coming (unless it's DLC maybe).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not for the feint of heart. This game is not for people who want to play an RPG where you easily overgear/overlevel the enemies and can just coast your way through a narrative. It will not baby you, spoon feed you answers, or hold your hand. What story that is there is mostly a background, given to you through a quick paragragh at the beginning and pieced together through character bios. The deck is stacked against you. You can (and probably will) see your entire party get K.O.'d, Petrified, Banished, or Devoured whole. And you'll probably want some pen and paper to take notes.So why recommend this?What starts off as the appearance of a "barebones RPG" hides a leviathan of depth mechanically few games out there will ever achieve. The deeper into the labyrinth you go the more unique and challenging the game becomes, even while maintaining the appearance of a simplistic and minimalist design. I have almost 30 hours into this title and i'm not even half way done. _childDocuments_.review: From the outset it looks like a simple game. And for the most part it is. But it has boiled down to the fun parts gameplay. The combat is actually fun, which if it wasn't this game wouldn't hold up. The level maps vary in size and are not too big to really get lost in or spend a ton of time trying to find a station to heal a character or restore them from KO status. Sure there is a little looking around, as you cannot fully zoom out to see the map. (Unless there is an ability that can do this?). Each tile has a coordinate y,x. So the game tracks for you where is the last healing station you visited for example.You can speed up the animation speed of movement and also speed of combat animations too.Where the game gets interesting is abilities you can unlock and activate, that allow you do do things like go up or down a floor anywhere there is a tile to go to. Jump across to another path on a floor. Those are the only map abilities i know about so far. There are also abilities you can use in Combat, eg. restore HP for 1 character. These costs ability points, which you earn from exploring the floors. The combat is easy to learn. It uses a blue speed bar that increases in real time, but you have all the time to choose your strategy before choosing who to attack. So quite easily you can see which enemy is going to attack next. There are two types of attacks and defence, magical and physical. If you deplete either defence you can directly attack the enemies HP. Later on some enemies have some abilities to reduce or deflect certain type of attacks. Some weapons you get can have random range of damage and some fixed. Both have its uses. If one of your party is KO you have to find a revive station. This can mean going back up a floor you already explored. There is one ability you get very early to see where the enemy encounters are on the map, so if it is possible you can choose another path around them. Also your party members can be petrified, and will remain on the tile it occurred in combat. But you can find a station that will remove this state on another floor. As too a revive station, so you never have to worry about permanently losing everyone and having to start again. Although, that might be possible if they all get wiped in combat, i suppose. Not sure what happens then.So making notes as to which floors have a lot of stations you can use such as activating a new ability.  There are puzzles in the game too. I have only encountered one so far, but i believe there are some hidden areas associated with them. The puzzles aren't on every floor but some.Of course with any dungeon crawler game there is loot, these are not plentiful. Maybe 1 loot drop every 10-15 combat fights. Its random no doubt, buy what you do get is often useful to equip right away, providing your character has enough Proficiency points to manage it. Making for a simple weight system. One loot drop i got was a resource which i could increase one of my party max HP. There are other party members you can unlock by finding them. I have yet to myself, not sure if they are randomly placed or fixed. In summary, this is a good game that doesn't have a story plot to unravel or conversations or cut scenes. Its purely an explore and fight game, with a layer of strategy on top of it. Do you go back up two floors to heal your party or risk going down a level where there might not be a heal station. One note, this game seems to be geared for controller play, but you can use mouse and keyboard just fine. Just remember to use RMB or backspace to come out of or go back a menu page. Its a good UI system once you get the hang of it. There is information on enemies you unlock along the way and you can equip your party at anytime (not in combat).Another nice addition is you can quit and save at anytime. So no worries about losing progress because you had to close the game late at night or when you have to leave the computer. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is it. This is a real gamer's game. This is the game.I'm sure you've seen those negative reviews crying about the Treasure Hunter and those that cry about the game's presentation, its graphics. Commentary of that kind is, of course, direly misguided and a sign of ignorance in regards to the video game medium on the part of the commenter. In fact, a large part of what elevates Dungeon Encounters from the troughs of _manure_ that constitute the video game industry these days is precisely how tightly, masterfully designed it is, both audio-visually and gameplay-wise. And while the developers made a handful odd decisions with their game design, none of them ruins the experience of playing Dungeon Encounters and especially not in any of the ways as is let on by the negative reviews.So what Dungeon Encounters is is a dungeon crawler that is (un-)surprisingly well designed. Head of the game's design is Hiroyuki Ito, the guy who came up with Final Fantasy's Active Time Battle system introduced in Final Fantasy IV and who designed and co-directed Final Fantasy XII, the best Final Fantasy game in the series with by far the best fighting system out of all JRPGs, ever. This is a fact. Knowing about Dungeon Encounter's pedigree and then looking at its trailer, surely you will realize that there lies purpose behind the presentation.It is true, the game's trailer reveals just about everything you will encounter in the game. Dungeon Encounters truly is that abstract. As mentioned above, however, the abstract presentation is the result of the game being incredibly well designed. The combat system is an iteration on classic JRPG turn based battles and has a couple neat tricks up its sleeve. Exploration is weirdly addicting as the environments change frequently and new events and mechanics are introduced. It is truly remarkable how versatile its means of presentation are while operating within such tight bounds. At first glance, Dungeon Encounters appears to be heavily constricted by compromises. But I claim it actually is uncompromising, experimenting with interesting ideas and able to explore its game design space exhaustively. Playing every card in your deck does not mean running out of options, it rather displays complete mastery of the underlying domain. What an act to behold!Included in this act are some quite unconventional and yet amusing mechanics of punishing nature, pulling out the rug from under you with no regard towards neither the characters' safety nor the player's sense of humour. Trolling the player in the year 2021, how daring! Frustrating in the first moment yet amusing for a while. This pattern resurfaces a lot throughout your playthrough of Dungeon Encounters as you will discover (or remind yourself) that video games can also deliver honest joy by something as pure as an old fashioned jest. I also want to mention that for most types of obstacles you (dungeon) encounter (hehe) you will find an ability to alleviate or even neutralize the burden.But while I've not gone into detail with my praises -- as you're supposed to just play the game already -- the one specific thing I want to point out is the Math Riddles since they are the only aspect of Dungeon Encounters that surprised me in a negative way. The Math Riddles are called Math Riddles on account of few of them are actual riddles and almost none involve actual mathematics. Imagine that! The least interesting ones expect you to recognize a number pattern (like for example a string of digits forming a ubiquitously known constant) while others are unreasonably obscure. In fact, at least one of them references an aspect of Japanese culture that if you aren't Japanese or a weeaboo that _really_ went off the deep end you will have no way of solving this "Math Riddle." You will easily find the solutions online, though, so don't worry if you can't figure one of them out after only a quick moment.Storywise there isn't much to talk about as there isn't much of a story in Dungeon Encounters. There is a bit of a plot unfolding as you reach the deeper levels of the dungeon but it only serves as a definitive ending point to the game rather than providing an overall narrative arc. Lorewise you'll find that each character is provided with an introductory paragraph of flavour text that in some cases references another character's, but this isn't anything to write home about, either. But here's the thing: Dungeon Encounters is a dungeon crawler! Telling a whole story with a proper arc would run counter to the point of it all!Now the soundtrack makes a real point of minimalism, here's the analysis:  - Broke:   It's just guitars playing classical music's greatest hits.  - Woke:    Something something the theme of abstraction that snakes itself throughout the entirety of the game is further explored in the soundtrack, venturing into a direction which expands orthogonally to all others and thus bringing immeasurable value to the metaphorical video game table.  - Bespoke: It shreds!The pieces they've selected are neat and the acoustic experience in general is one more aspect in which Dungeon Encounters shows how little it is concerned with industry standards and how much it is concerned with doing what is right for the game.To bring it back to my opening statments and tie this review up I'll leave something that's more of a comment, really:Dungeon Encounters is a proper video game. It is the result of talented people actually sitting down and deliberating over and experimenting with ideas for a fun game instead of subscribing to the common game design cargo cult. It is an honest video game effort and it shows and it pays off. If you belong to the sort of person who does not actually like video games, go back to playing your Skyrim and your Assassin's Creed and your Call of Duty which give a rat's arse about the medium; if you are someone who takes legitimate interest and is curious about video games go right ahead and enjoy Dungeon Encounters.Dungeon Encounters gets a full recommendation from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeon Encounters is a very barebones dungeon crawler that cuts out everything but the bare minimum to be called one. Maps are giant advant garde crossword puzzles that you traverse to fill out. It will take 40-50 floors before you'll find interesting layouts. The background will change every 10 floors, most of the time featuring really bland colored backgrounds for things like lava, sand, etc. Encounters feature a more detailed background.Throughout the bland maps are numbered tiles that use the hexadecimal numbering system, ie. 10 is 0A. There are two types of numbered tiles: black and white.The black tiles are enemy encounters and white tiles in the game that are used to represent:* treasures* riddles* monster info* new abilities* one/two-way teleporters* shops* healing stationsYou'll find these through each of the stratums. Shops and healing station location vary between which floors of a stratum they appear on. Floor 0 contains all the tiles that will appear throughout aside from the Academy (00). Certain shops only exist on certain floors such as firearms providing an incentive to explore the floor. There is also a special station that exists in order to help fix some specific status effects.Instead of random encounters, players step black numbered tiles (if you equip an ability). As you traverse floors the numbers increase to signify more difficult encounters.Sometimes a floor will feature enemies far above the floor's difficulty. The game features a barebone but usable beastiary that lists possible enemies that will appear foreach numbered tile allowing you to avoid/engage at will.Battles utilize Final Fantasy's ATB system which makes the combat fast. You and enemies have three gauges: Physical defense, Magic defense, and HP. HP is obvious, but in order to damage it the attack must be able to bypass the physical and/or magic defenses. There is no overkill damage so even when inflicting 200% the defense value it will not affect the HP. Physical and magic do not recover during battle unless using an ability but fully recover at the end.A party consists of maximum four characters, each of which can equip 2x weapons, armor, helmet, and accessory. Some weapons can only be equipped on a certain character such as katana which can only be used by a specific wanderer you have to find. There are two types of weapons: Magic and Physical. Each type could be multi or single target with either fixed or random damage. Random damage has higher damage ceiling but also really low damage floor if dice roll is unfavorable. Fixed is average damage but will always do that damage without modifiers. Physical weapons are limited by ranged and melee so attacking flying enemies without a bow will miss. Magic hits at any range. Additionally there are a handful of weapons that can be found as treasures that can cause status effects, bypass defenses, reset ATB, etc. There are no attacks that cripple offense, defense, nor speed.Treasures can be found on some numbered tiles which give equipment or money. The really good treasure are hidden behind riddles. There are two types of riddles: Math and Map.Map riddles are obscured sections of a floor you have to find and interact with to obtain a treasure. The most intersting aspect of the game are the math riddles although some are references and less math. These could involve binary numbers, numbers of pi, primes, repeating series, etc.There are some stat differences per character. To recruit new characters you must find them wandering across the floors. They could be knocked out, petrified, or just sitting about.You could go out of your way to gather them but not only will they not make any notable difference but you'd also end up wasting time re-leveling characters. The main benefit ofgoing after them early is to steal their item or speed run thru dungeons with a high level character in low level party.Abilities are scattered throughout the game which alter map interactions, passive bonuses, and provide active skills. See closeness to wanderer, teleport to nearby tile, see encounter tiles, zoom out (yes, this is a thing), recover defense, etc. Although it sounds interesting since it introduces new ways to approach situations, the variety of viable builds possible is verylimited since you go through the same motions every time.Ambient music are different renditions of classic pieces for each stratum which are pretty good and set the atmosphere for the bland maps. However, the same cannot besaid about battle music which are horrid renditions on a guitar.I do not recommend anyone get this at full price. It's worth it if you can get it for 20USD, and just maybe 25USD. Why? I've managed all the way to floor 9x and it does not get anymore complex. You've already experienced most of the game's mechanics by floors 20-30+. It doesn't take long to get that far and very possible to hit around floor 20 in 2 hours. If you're expecting Etrian Odyssey please just turn around and just get a copy of Etrian Odyssey, any Experience Inc. RPG, or any other worthwhile dungeon crawler available. This game is absolutely nowhere near EO in charm, presentation nor mechanical richness and is only considered to be by the dolts that could barely get through it without stubbing their toe. Any illusion of complexity is the barebone nature of the game where it omits details. There isn't a good reason for this and white knights can justify it as much as they want but obscurity for the sake of it is retarded.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Okay so apparently you can fall through the floor in the upper 90s levels and your party falls infinitely and you perma-lose your save file. Not... great.This is an RPG with zero frills. There's basically no graphics, the sound design is minimalistic, and the game systems are utterly barebones. It's glorious. No faffing around with defense and magic defense and attack and magic stats. No mana or class stats, just skeleton characters waiting to be built the way you want. Offensive stats are purely based on your weapon of choice - you can equip 1 physical weapon and 1 magical weapon. You can equip 1 hat (magic defense) and 1 armor (physical defense). You get a trinket slot for other things (like phys/mag evasion). All your equipment is limited by a single stat, Proficiency, with every item requiring a certain amount of proficiency points, and each character gaining more PP as they level up.Both magic and phys weapons are split between fixed damage and random damage, single target and target-all. I prefer fixed damage most of the time, but random damage weapons of the same tier have extremely high payoffs but also can deal 1 damage. High risk, high reward. There's so much depth in this deceptively simple game that I honestly feel a bit rushed writing this, as I want to get back to it. Strongly recommend this game if you like RPGs that are more transparent with stats/damage/numbers and you like planning/strategy-focused RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Here are the issues that I have with this game so far:They borked the ATB system. One of the things I liked about ATB in other games (such as Final Fantasy 4) is that you can control the order of actions. If someone has a particular action that you want to do first, you can wait for them to charge even if other characters have charged first. If two characters charge at once, you pick who goes first. You don't need to do it in a set order. In Dungeon Encounters, even if you set the ATB to 'Active' instead of 'Wait' you still have to do the actions in a set order, and the only way to change the order of actions is to skip a character's turn entirely (which provides no benefits to Defence, Speed or anything else).There's very little difference between the characters. Aside from the ROM accessory, you can basically equip anything to anyone. There's no Physical or Magic stat to determine who should get what, let alone any character limitations (ie: certain equipment for certain characters). This means that the characters feel like blank slates who are only there to boost your total number of reserve characters, which also means that selecting characters for a party has no depth or strategy behind it and seeking out new characters is just a way of boosting your total reserves rather than unlocking new abilities and options. Also, their backstories aren't very good.No overhead map for fully explored floors. If you're trying to backtrack and looking for the stairs it can be frustrating if you don't remember the way back. Being able to check a map would be nice.The soundtrack is terrible, which I guess might be a good thing if you want to play this with the sound off.If these things were fixed then this could be a great game, because the basic gameplay is actually quite good. Exploring dungeons, backtracking to buy new equipment, battling monsters (the basic combat mechanic re: how damage is dealt is really interesting), having to leave characters behind and go back for them later... all the elements are there for a neat little dungeon crawler that would be PERFECT to play while listening to podcasts, watching something or playing on a Steam Deck when you're out somewhere. Unfortunately the game is just too shallow to be truly compelling, even as a 'second screen game'.There's a game on Steam called Brave Dungeon (by INSIDE SYSTEM) which I actually think is a much better take on the same formula. If that's not to your taste, find any good RPG or SRPG that has a grinding or dungeon crawling component and it will probably do the job better than this one.It's not a terrible game, or even a terrible concept. It's just a missed opportunity from a developer that should be consistently nailing this formula by now.

_childDocuments_.review: A completely unique spin - takes me back to old school classics like Bard's Tale (I, II & III), Wizardry, the Gold Box TSR games and the like.  Also reminiscent of the newer turn based combat games like the original Final Fantasy games and other JRPGs from the 8-bit days.  Enjoyed playing through this game - so much so I found myself wanting to 100% the achievements (which I did...).  Smooth gameplay and always felt like there was "one more thing" to do.  The only negatives to me:- You have to use the pre-generated characters - wish they had a system similar to old school games for generating characters.- Other than hitpoints & equipability points, levels mean little.  Even more so once you start gathering a lot of potions and (spoiler alert) find the potion shop... then you can just pour them into your favorite character to pump up their capacity for high level / high dps gear.  Wish they had more impact on gameplay.- Very lacking in story here - it's basically run through the maze and murder everything in your path.  For me this wasn't a big concern though.- Lack of variety in weaponry / spells / etc.  Basically everyone can use everything with a few very specific exceptions.  Fairly linear progression / feel regardless of who you put in your party for the most part.Overall though would I play this again?  Maybe.  Would I recommend it to RPG enthusiasts?  Absolutely.  Would I play Dungeon Encounters II if they addressed some of the negative points above?  Hell Yes!
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: In short: after having disappeared for nearly two decades, legendary Final Fantasy designer/director Hiroyuki Ito made a surprise comeback with this rather unique and stripped down dungeon crawler. And for the most part, he nailed it.It's definitely an acquired taste with limited appeal due to it's the minimalist approach to visuals and design, but if you're the type of player who really likes to take their time to thoroughly explore everything, pay attention to the information available and even write down notes as you go along, you just might be in the niche for this game. Some of the reviews claim the game to be unfair and cheap and while I don't mean to dismiss anyones experience with the game, I didn't find the Dungeon Encounters unfair at all. The game is definitely punishing and harsh if you aren't careful, but it also gives you all the tools and abilities you need to overcome obstacles, and is even pretty lenient about it.The only somewhat unexpected setback I encountered during my playthrough was finding out that in Dungeon Encounters, money can actually go to negative. A certain little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that you may run into fairly early on in the game can steal a whopping 500k from you in an instant, basically turning the game into an debt paying simulator for the next couple of hours, lol. Still, I'd consider that a fairly minor inconvenience overall in a game of this type.Of course, there are the math riddles which... I have no shame in admitting that I never would been able to figure out some of the later ones without some outside hints. Still, I appreciate the thought process behind them.My only major complaint with the game is the soundtrack. While the songs - mostly consisting of heavy/electric guitar renditions of various classical compositions - aren't bad per se, they do get grating and monotone pretty fast when it's all the game has to offer, and I definitely wish they had gone with a more varied selection of instruments for the arrangements. On the other hand though, this is a perfect podcast game if you turn the music down.Another smaller gripe I have is that... even though this obviously isn't a game you'd play for the story in the first place, I kinda wish there was juuust a bit more of it. I found the world inside the labyrinth oddly compelling and the character descriptions were generally pretty neat, so it would have been nice to have some lore and character specific events unfold within the dungeon.Here's hoping we don't need wait to wait for Ito's next game for quite so long.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: I'm an old millennial who grew up playing Final Fantasy 1 and Dragon Warrior 3 on NES. I used to have so much fun drawing out maps of dungeons and grinding for levels before going somewhere new to make sure I was ready, using my imagination to fill in the blanks of the primitive graphics. A part of me felt a bit sad when RPGs started using less grid-based maps in the SNES era so it was harder to draw them out on paper, and let you just walk from one place to another without preparing at all first. I haven't enjoyed a JRPG since the original FF7, because they've become more about the story cutscenes that go on and on and on than about exploring and figuring out the system and challenging yourself to get ever stronger until those monsters that were so dangerous to you are now pushovers. No more grinding! No more maps that I can draw! Tutorials that last five hours until they just let me play the damn game! But all the "hard mode" RPGs are action-based now, so they're no refuge either if you don't have great reflexes.If you have similar frustrations about modern RPGs, buy this game! It is everything I miss from my childhood. It just dumps you into the world with barely any instruction, letting you figure out the systems on your own as you go, starting out very simple and getting more complex as you get further down. The characters are more or less interchangeable, just a picture and a few paragraphs of backstory and that's it, their stats are slightly different from each other but equipment makes up the difference. Leveling up doesn't make you better in combat except that it increases your PP that lets you equip better stuff, and the shops don't have many better items in stock for you to keep upgrading to, so if you already have enough points to equip everything you have, there's not much point in leveling further.The battles are very puzzle-like, making you think about who is going to use which attack in what order to kill the enemies in the fewest number of turns, rather than just punching auto-attack over and over, and different enemies have different strategies based on how many hits they might take to kill with certain weapons. You don't have enough copies of the best items that everyone can have them. So you might want to avoid having a weaker character attack an enemy whose shield is too big, to let someone with a better weapon do that instead, or alternately have a couple of weaker characters break through a shield first to set up for the heavy hitter to take down the enemy's HP in one blow. The music is metal guitar duet renditions of classical music, which I didn't realize until the second battle theme gave me Fantasia flashbacks.At first, I was leveling them all up together, shuttling my extra party members from stairway to stairway every time I cleared a floor, swapping out the highest-level members and their equipment for lowest-level ones whenever I did so, allowing me to replace anyone who died right away, assuming if I wiped I'd be shunted to my still-alive reserve group on the same floor so I could go rescue the ones who died. This was apparently the wrong choice, because I encountered a ridiculously powerful group of ninjas somewhere in the mid-teens floors and failed to run away four times and died to their AoE attack, and since all of my party members were "in the dungeon", I got a game over screen with three options:  -- Retry With Last Expedition, which I assumed was what I wanted to do (try again with my other party) but ended up wiping ALL of my progress since around floor 2 (supposedly the last time you went to the Academy tile on floor 1 from what I'm reading online, which I hadn't touched since the last time I shuttled my party members out of it since I can swap party members on ANY tile so why go back to that one specifically?) so maybe that's an option to be avoided in the future, because returning to Floor 1 is rare enough that I'm not going to be doing it often enough to swap out characters much. -- The third option on the list is to return to the title screen, which doesn't do anything apparently, since you can't load a save that's been defeated.  -- So I really *should* have picked the second option, "Retain Levels and Begin Anew" which wipes everything except your EXP levels, so I would have at least been able to keep those.I guess my new strategy is to pick six characters and leave the rest at home, bringing a couple of spares along in case of death and swapping them out/grinding them up to par any time I find a teleport back to Floor 1....

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly the game it appears to be. If you look at the screenshots and video and think this game would appeal to you, it probably does, and if you think it wouldn't, it probably won't.That being said...Dungeon Encounters is far more a game about moving your party on a grid than it is about fighting opponents.The more squares you map in the dungeon, the more points you have to equip different abilities. These abilities include different movement options (up and down a dungeon level, jumping over or across tiles, randomly teleport to another square, etc etc) which in turn let you more easily and more completely map out the dungeon. Most play involves diving down as quickly as possible and trying to uncover more abilities, reaching the next two-way teleporter to the town, and then re-exploring older maps with new gear and new abilites until you 100% a floor.There are abilities to see invisible squares and to avoid toll squares, so feel free to come back to any floor that has those later in the game.The battle system is extremely streamlined and mostly reduces to equipping each of your characters with the strongest "attack all enemies" weapons and/or magic you can get. As you get deeper in, you'll probably want to avoid most encounters except those which drops you want (hint: weapons and magic that attack all enemies, and the damage boosting accessories).Some opponents have obnoxious status effects or instant death attacks that you'll need to avoid until you unlock immunity.My two biggest complaints are that bottomless pits which scatter your party are disproportionately punitive, and that the final half-dozen or so floors are obnoxious to chart completely, with isolated areas that can only be reached by teleportation.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a fairly monotonous and mildly grindy turn based rpg with little story then you might enjoy Dungeon Encounters. The combat system is reasonably good, a classic Square ATB system that is really pared down. Exploration can be fun albeit fairly slow/grindy dealing with all the random encounters. The sound when you run over a string of unexplored tiles is very satisfying to me. And the game gives you some very interesting exploration abilities.I don't really understand some balancing decisions in the game. There are *extremely* powerful items locked behind puzzles which are liberally called "math riddles." I think the way these puzzles are constructed is often very lazy and you might as well just look them up online if the solution doesn't become apparent after a couple minutes. The other type of riddles, map riddles, are very grindy but not completely unfun to do because it gives you an excuse to use the game's exploration abilities. The redeeming factor is that the game tells you what every riddle's reward is in the Event Log so you don't have to search for rewards you don't care about. But still, the game would be better if the riddles were just enjoyable to solve.The riddles also give a lot of the more interesting weapons/accessories in the game. They might not be obviously overpowered but if you don't find them I imagine the combat may start to feel very stale late in the game. The stuff you can buy in stores is just kind of boring and all about scaling damage/defense/speed numbers.The game can also lightly troll and force you to lose party members which you need to find/revive/retrieve using other characters which you haven't leveled up. Everything I've experienced and heard about is not devastating but some people will probably just rage quit the game right after that happens.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stripped down, bare-bones game. No fluffy graphics, just resource management, puzzles, and intensity. _childDocuments_.review: Very old school game, no graphics to speak of, expect to grind, be routinely screwed by RNG, and be punished greatly for mistakes. Enemies can permanently destroy your equipment and cause petrification which forces you to leave the petrified member behind until you can find an altar on a different floor that can remotely heal them, then come back for them (you eventually can become immune to equipment breakage and petrification). The RNG is extremely sharp, meaning an attack can deal from 1 to 10000 damage, or your character can gain 1 to 100 HP from a levelup. There is no saving and loading, only suspend and resume. You can quit mid-fight, but you will load into the start of the fight and the random outcomes are fixed for that fight.Not a game for everyone as you can see by the positive/negative ratio, but very rewarding to defeat the brutal game mechanics and RNG.
