_childDocuments_.review: This is a stripped down approach to a traditional JRPG. This game is about strategy and optimizing the math of your defense and attacks. There is no story other than the initial premise and the music is fun but quickly becomes repetitive. It can be ruthlessly punishing and requires the player to know what they are getting themselves into with every new encounter. Information is plentiful and very simply presented, so it is possible to look up encounters before engaging them.This is a game that is balanced with the expectation that the player will be optimizing their builds. It rewards smart tactics with smooth clears of encounters and can heavily punish brute force approaches. Much like a first edition D&D dungeon, it can be downright unfair.Your experience during your playthrough builds the story of this game and it will end up being unique to your own build. Like how I lost my level 15 team to a ninja encounter (that I could have avoided) on level 13 and had to train up a new team from the first level to go and recover them. I considered starting over or just quitting all together. A game that makes that kind of encounter possible so early implies that death and rebuilding is part of the designed loop.This is not for everyone and anyone going into this should do a bit of research first, especially if they are on the fence about this purchase. I find it fascinating and enjoyable to pick away at. Long sessions are stressful, but it saves on quit so I can just dip in and out as I want.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeon Encounters is a very vintage dungeon crawler that reminds me a bit of the very old Bard's Tale 3 (that game was very labyrinthine too). You have to chart the 99 floors of a dungeon, split into thematic segments of 9 floors each. All characters are pregenerated and have a little story attached to them that links them either to the dungeon itself, the Academy (floor 0, where you start) or other characters. The game is very bare bone when it comes to mechanics: you move around the square grid that represents the dungeon and when you meet a monster (black squares) or an event (white squares) you can interact with it by either fighting, collecting what's in the square or accessing a shop. The deeper you go, more mechanics are exposed to you, with various status effects (some of them are REALLY nasty, like Petrified which you will meet very very early and Cavied later on) which can be cured most of the times only by nearby statues. As you explore the dungeon you gain Ability Points which can be used to enable party wide abilities, the most prominent of which are the immunities to the various status effects which can be a real plague: activate these ASAP because they will make traveling through the dungeon a lot less tedious.Combat is very simple, but it has good depth: every character or monster has three values: physical defense, mystical defense and HPs. All attacks deal either physical or mystical damage: if the defense that they hit is zeroed, then the damage is done to the HPs. The intersting aspect is that there is no damage spillover when zeroing a defense: if a character has 1 point of mystical defense and suffers one million mystical damage, its defense will drop to 0, with no damage to HP (but will receive damage from the next mystic attack). Due to the fact that characters have a limited amount of proficiency points that restrains how powerful of an object you can equip, this system allows for a good variety of strategies.There are a few tedious things I do want to mention just because they might affect your intention to buy this: there are a few ruthless mechanics that are not really well explained in the game and that will cost you a LOT of time if you are hit by them.Very early on you will start meeting monsters that petrify. If by any chance one of your characters is petrified, you will soon discover that you have to leave him in the dungeon, exactly in the square where he was petrified, look for a Gorgon Altar (there are a few throughout the dungeon, but I would not say they are common, particularly in the beginning), unpetrify the character from the altar and then trace back to where you left him. To make matter worse, to retrieve a character from a location, you need to have a slot in your party (or an ability which you find VERY late in the game, around floor 75 if i remember correctly) so you have to go back to where you were with only 3 members, which can sometimes prove challenging.Worse than Petrified there is Cavied: the character can be brought with you, but his Miss chance will become exceptionally high, making him useless. There is only one place in the entire game where you can cure Cavied, and it can indeed be accessed near the floor where you encounter the first enemies that inflict Cavied, but it's a long trip and a difficult one too.At a certain point you will start encountering pits, which can be seen exclusively if you have an ability that allows you to see them. If you fall into one, if by any chance there is not a square right below the pit (in which case you just fall to the floor below), your party is entirely lost and scattered, meaning that all of them become Wanderers.Speaking of Wanderers, these are characters which are lost in the dungeon. Some of these are INCREDIBLY strong, but you have no real way of tracking them easily, aside from a lot of guesswork and triangulation with a certain ability (that doesn't give you any information on floor distance, just tiles). Your characters can become Wanderers too if they get lost due to a wrongly calculated teleport or a pit (and maybe a few other ways). Until VERY late in the game, one of your characters becoming a Wanderer will have a crippling effect on your expedition and will potentially take hours to recover them.Finally, please be advised you cannot save scum in this game: everything is saved and permanent, so anything happening will require rescue expeditions or clever strategies. Sometimes it will be fun to mount a desperate rescue and succeed. Sometimes it will be infuriating to cast Gambler's Shift on a huge floor and end up teleporting on top of a pit and lose your entire party to an exceptionally unlucky event. Sometimes it's gonna be hilarious to see Sir Cat use succesfully Consume on enormous mobs. If this relentlessness is something that entices you, then Dungeon Encounters is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if I can accurately sell this game to people, but I'm gonna try. It's a stripped down JRPG experience using the ATB system from earlier Final Fantasies. People who loved Final Fantasy XII for its combat and sometimes RNG difficulty curve will find something comforting and occasionally infuriating here. But every time you run into a new wrinkle in the battle system that feels unfair or too brutal/onerous to deal with, the game gives you the tools to fix it and avoid it, then mitigate it altogether later. The core gameplay loop is therefore extremely satisfying, which it has to be because there's nothing else going on in this game. Clear tiles, fight enemies. Acquire abilities and gear, clear more tiles, fight harder enemies. And it feels GOOD.If you want graphics, voice acting, and a deep story, this ain't for you. If you want a pure old-school JRPG experience in terms of combat, you'll find much to love. I know I did.And a helpful tip: Solve the math riddles as early as you can because they provide IMMENSE rewards.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good - it very much reminds me of playing Bard's Tale on the PC in the late 80s and maybe playing various text based Rogue like in the early 90s.  It is very stripped back and doesn't have lots of the trappings of RPGs (even then) - but there is something good albeit a bit grindy about the game.  I am interested to see what happens next
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not for everyone. If you need story or pretty graphics or amazing cinematics, this game doesn't have 'em.What it DOES have is crisp, minimalist, turn-based dungeon-crawling JRPG goodness. The game takes the core fundamentals of what makes dungeon crawlers fun (things like exploration and puzzles), and paired it with what makes JRPGs fun (things like party management, resource management, decision-making in combat). The result is a game that seems simple but has a surprising amount of depth.The game takes a "less is more" approach. Everything is distilled down and, to my pleasant surprise, is still satisfying and fun. The soundtrack is comprised of classical music rearranged by Uematsu in a metal guitar style, but there are only ever at most two instruments on the same track. There's (basically) no story. The controls and UI are simple and straightforward.DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS doesn't hold your hand much, either. There are some basic tutorials you can access at any time but the rest is up to you to discover for yourself. It can be punishing, at times, if you're not careful. But all in all I have been finding this game super enjoyable and incredibly addicting.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: What you see in the trailer and screenshots is what you get. It delivers a minimalistic styled game where you dive deeper and deeper into the labyrinth with your band of characters with their small snippets of story attached to them. Does it look kinda bare and almost as if you're traversing a crossword puzzle? Yes.Is the combat a little boring after awhile? Sure.Is there barely any plot, story, or significant difference with the characters? None at all.Am I addicted? Sure am.Why do I keep playing? I don't know but I sure do love exploring each and every tile to get 3 ability points.There's something about this game which got me playing every night until 3am when I need to wake up for work in 4 hours that's got me hooked. I found it hard for me to keep interest in labyrinth/dungeon exploring games like Etrian Odyssey or Paper Sorcerer but strangely enough, this game has me hooked. The combat albeit simple, has me desperately praying for a high roll on an attack's random generated damage and each encounter has me on my toes as my characters can die at the drop of a hat. Even with new tools you get with your ability points, combat can still be difficult and require some thinking. I also love how each 10 floors has a specific theme to it, and the tiles reflect it as well.If you're looking for something to kill time or fancy a little labyrinth diving, why not give it a go?
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: The minimalist approach won't be for everybody.  The lack of tutorials for certain matters will either infuriate or excite.  The first 10-20 floors will lull you into a very false sense of security.  The battle system evolves very little over the course of the game but remains tense.I couldn't stop playing until I beat it.  I went through every emotion while playing.  I almost quit at a few points.  I'm glad I finished the game, it felt 'good' to complete it.  That being said, I'll never play it again.  The experience of it all was very memorable.  It isn't an easy game to recommend, but if you fall for it you'll fall hard.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshing, stylish minimalism 'concept game' that lets you concentrate on what matters in this kind of dungeon crawlers: mechanics and exploration. Being able to play just from the keyboard (no mouse required) is a plus.If you dare going beyond the first handful of 'easy' levels (and be aware that this is a massive, deep game), you start having to deal with perhaps unexpected status attacks, or the need to temporarily abandon a party member until a cure is found. You are on your own, precious little hand holding here, and yet the interface and its menus give you the information that you need to proceed. The graphics, though reduced at a minimum, are lovely and just perfect as they don't get in the way of battles conveying the information that matters (did the last attack bypass armor, for example?). Excellent production, and a very encouraging sign from a major player such as Square Enix: they obviously know that not all gamers need simulation-level graphics to be drawn into adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: Simple graphics, simple game play, lots of depth. The entire game is more like a puzzle/strategy game - you need to plan what you are doing, or pay the price for not thinking.  The simple graphics means it doesn't take huge resources to run, but they are fully functional, providing almost all the information you need. One exception: the attack information of the various creatures is not displayed in the logs; you just get to see their defense, HP and drops. Tracking their attacks is via memory (or note pads...).The map is only missing the ability to see the entire level layout at once, but you can always draw it on paper to get this view yourself. (Old school manual mapping...)Combat is turn based, but really is strategic - you need to eliminate defense before you can wound the target (with some exceptions). So plan your actions to clear the defense then kill the target.If high res graphics are a must for you, stay away. If great game play and dungeon crawling are what you want - then give it a try. You'll probably like it.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: Pure mechanics, you will have to superimpose your own story.For some of us, this comes naturally. Not having an existing story getting in the way makes this easier.If you're the kind of person that makes up a narrative in your head while playing a rogue-like, this is for you.If you play a game to unlock new art, there are no rewards here.Not for everyone, but for a select few, this is perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: A fun experience that focuses on game mechanics over everything else. The combat system has some RNG elements but a lot of it can be worked around since the A.I. isn't the brightest most of the time and there are items that can be used to avoid it. The items and such variations are very clear, understandable and easy to use and the ability system is implemented well, encouraging you to explore each and every tile within the depths. I'd say one weak point about the mechanics is the characters as there isn't much variation between them. HP/PP starting level, starting items and a few unique items are the only things that separate one character from the next. So using any character is likely not going to screw you over, though there is the possibility for minor optimisation.Story is very basic, but enough and should you want extra lore, all the character bios offer a little about each one. Exploring is quite fun and I enjoy the prospect of finding the previous adventurers who went on ahead and adding them to your party or returning them to the academy.If you are super into RPGs for the mechanics, then this may be worth it, but if you like in-depth story or unique characters, this may not be the game for you, all-in-all though I enjoy it and will continue to do so for a while.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: This had to grow on me for a bit, but I like it. Extremely minimalist with very little hand-holding. A few things could be better explained because even the in-game help is pretty minimalist... I think the expectation is you go in and figure things out just by experimenting.This is for folks who want to be challenged. Will also probably inspire a lot of projects, like making a full 3D atlas of the labyrinth (if someone hasn't already done it).As a side note, whatever guitar band they have doing the music here needs to be highly applauded. I hope this game releases the OST here on steam because that deserves to be its own product. I've gotten down to about the 40th floor and so far the floor 20-29 battle music is my favorite track.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: I've lost time playing this. The lack of fluff in some areas doesn't take away from the depth in others. I play it easily while watching movies. There are times when I hunt for games with these specific qualities: minimal micromanagement, mouse driven, no voiceovers/soundtrack, has loots, collector, tasks/map clearing. I have to point out that it's a huge pain in the ass when you get petrified. THAT almost destroys the zen of my runs. But I recommend ON SALE 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: Please Square Enix, let Ito direct a retro-style mainline FF game. Why not let Dragon Quest take a turn at evolving into something unfamiliar and bring this series back for a bit?As for this game, it starts out feeling pretty simplistic, but after going through several floors, acquiring new abilities, figuring out how the party system works, etc., I really began to enjoy it. I think it's intended to be exactly what it is, and as long as I accept it for that, I can get lost in it and forget who I am for a couple of hours. But really, having a bandit cat steal $10,000 from me, putting me down to -$7,000? That hurts 😕
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: Petrification sucks.But it solves one of the main problems of large-party RPGs where you can usually just pick your preferred party members and coast through the game with them. But with how the dungeon is laid out, losing even a single party member and having to leave them behind makes the rest of the dungeon scarier, and encourages you to not be too reliant on any one party member. Combat largely boils down to making sure that between ranged, magic, and high-damage options, that you have your bases covered (at least for Wait mode in the ATB system), since healing is a shared resource among the party. Since you get the ability to see enemy tiles very early on, it becomes a strategic guess as to whether you can handle an encounter or need to find another way around. I love the mechanic of recruiting party members by actually finding them on the map. There's a tool later on that helps with this, but it also ties back into the risk/reward of venturing with an open space in your party to snap up a new friend. And once you get your head around how the grid system works, you can start narrowing down places where certain things could be.I will say that the one thing that could make exploration better is a wayfinder for the entrance and exit to each floor, and to log each instance of a heal tile rather than just the last one visited, but both of these problems can be solved by player notes.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: I own Dungeon Encounters on both the PC and PS4.  I've spent the majority of my time on the PS4 and I have to admit that I love this game as a jump in/ jump out kinda thing.  It's simple and doesn't require a lot of brain sweat... the graphics are suitable for something that you just want to forge ahead with and not get overly hung up on whether or not something in the background is important to the story.  I'm still early in the game... I've reached... level 22 I think... it's hard and easy at the same time.  The hard is making sure that the battle you're getting into isn't above your ability and the easy is... if you're armed and armoured right... the battles will be a dawdle unless something goes horribly wrong.  (and this happens in the real life AD&D as well)If you're looking for a regular tactical RPG kinda thing... this isn't it.  This is just to enjoy and relax with... play for a bit and then drop out until you get the hankering again.  It's got enough meaningful choices so that you're not going to feel like it's a cake walk but it's not going to steam roll you... unless you decide to go stupidly deep and get your head handed to you.It's a no brainer... buy the game.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: This game is barebones in almost every detail.  In battle, your attack animations, especially magic have little visual effects, there is no overworld music while you are traveling through dungeon floors and the battle music is the worst in the Square Enix library IMO.  There are no classes, characters only have 2 offensive abilities, and if you get wiped the grind to get back to  where you were is tedious and boring.  A hard skip for me, save your money.  My full video review is below.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. While I don't think it's for everyone, I do think that this game set out to make a gameplay focused rpg and succeeded greatly. The game doesn't mess around with lengthy tutorials or a big story. You make your party, and explore a dungeon almost immediately. I do think the depth of the game increases as it goes on, with more status effects, riddles etc. I'm enjoying this game a lot, and if you know what you're in for, I definitely think it's worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and minimalistic dungeon crawler that takes a bit more thinking.My only complaint is that this game is , but nothing is on the radar.The mechanics aren't that deep, (like creature vulnerabilities, elemental resistances, and such), but if you like dungeon crawling in general, then you might want to give it a try.This game is very nostalgic for me, reminding me of old-school text based games like Adventure, Arthur, etc., where you had to make your own tile-based maps to keep track of where you were.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this for £20 when it was on offer, and personally, it's been worth it. This game is basically what the name says it is, to simply put it. To extend on that, you're exploring a maze of tiles that can affect you in positive, negative, or neutral ways. You traverse through floor after floor of twisting and turning tiles to descend further into the labyrinth, coming across various types of enemies and events, all for the thrill of exploration and dungeon crawling. It's not for everyone, and you can see within the reviews, but if you enjoy just exploring and finding new things, you'd probably enjoy it. I came across the trailer one time on Youtube, and was interested by its simplistic design - a map of tiles that you fill up once you cross the space, a slightly detailed background to show the theme of the floor with simplistic effects to show where you're at, and to top it off, minimalist music or sounds to make the floor sound eerie or soothing. The idea of having a variety of party members that come in all shapes and sizes (even a huge cat when you unlock him like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥???) and using your newly gained knowledge to descend further down to battle stronger foes or just enjoy the thrill of exploration.There's nothing in terms of a major story to indicate you going into the depths, it's as the description says - a labyrinth appears outside of the town, you go and explore it. The characters have a little bit of story behind them, which gives them that bit of individuality, but at the end of the day, they're all here to do the same thing. Throughout the dungeon exploration, you can get Exploration and Battle Abilities that can support you throughout, which can be applied within Tile 03 - the Ability Station, some of which are a bit awkward in terms of their use and some can be limited in how many times you can use them, but it's all about using a strategist plan of where and when to use them, which is where a lot of other reviews mention - Yes, you are going to need a notepad/word document open to help you note down what you find. I did this during my second run of the game after dying to a fateful tile, but making notes has been beneficial to me.During your exploration, you get to battle monsters, indicated on tiles with Black Letters and Numbers, and I really enjoy the battle system. Your party and your enemies have 4 bars - a Speed Bar (indicating their recharge and when their next turn is), a Physical and Magical Defence bar (damaged through using Physical and Magical damage) and their HP bar. During fights, you have to plan what moves to use against your enemies, depending on your weapons or spells. It's all about identifying and using these to effectively win the battle. Some weapons come with debuffs or DOTs which can aid your battles too.Purchasing this game is all up to you though, if you like dungeon crawler games where it's all about the exploration, go for it, it'll be up your alley. It's not for everyone, and it's not making itself out to be.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: The dungeon is the enemy. It is full of hidden treasures, dangers, tricks, and traps. Boils down the dungeon crawl to it's basic elements, and only gives enough information to make meaningful choices. I am very much enjoying my expedition.edit: 14 hours in and the game is still fun. I'm around floor 30-something and I'm having to make sure at least one or two of my characters has low health which gives a high bonus to damage. Paths are all straight, so no jumping around too drastically. Equipment comes in waves. Sometimes you just don't have the gear to deal with what you are facing, so you go a bit deeper than you should to try and unlock items from the shop by fighting monsters you haven't met before. Game moves fast. Mistakes are still made.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS is one of the worst video games I've ever played in my 33 years on this planet. At first glace, it sounds like a cool, little, simplistic concept, but in reality, this "game" hides some of the worst game mechanics I've ever seen. First off, there isn't a story whatsoever. Nothing for the characters, nothing in terms of a goal; when I say nothing, I mean not-a-thing. Then we get into the gameplay mechanics which are boring at best and infuriating at worst. There is, no joke, hidden tiles that will drop you to the very bottom floor of the game and completely scatter your party members on any of the floors you passed on your way down. Whats more is that they'll be completely invisible, which means you have to retread the entirety of the game looking for your party members, but this time, without glowing tiles to mark where you have and haven't been yet, because they're already highlighted from your first time on the floor. The part of this game that really hurts the most though, is that this game came from the guy who gave us Final Fantasy IX, which was amazing! What the hell happened?! The developers should honestly be embarrassed of this abomination. Square Enix is seriously a shell of their former self. Avoid this game at all costs.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

_childDocuments_.review:
A new dungeon exploration RPG where you must strategize to survive. An otherworldly labyrinth has suddenly appeared on the outskirts of a quiet town. Make clever use of your abilities to chart the depths, overcome obstacles and defeat your foes in thrilling battles. From some of the key development team behind the legendary FINAL FANTASY franchise, DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS is a dungeon exploration RPG where you must strategize to survive. The streamlined interface gives you the freedom to prepare and manage your party as you strive to reach the final floor.

During your expeditions, you'll discover rare and powerful items, meet lost adventurers who might just become new allies, and come face-to-face with deadly monsters.

Do you have what it takes to overcome the numerous trials that await you and discover the dungeon's secrets?

■Events
By uncovering and visiting spaces with white numbers, you may obtain items, unlock and change abilities, restore your party to health, find hidden merchants, and much more.

Battle encounters, marked with black numbers, are hidden throughout the map. However, they can be revealed with a special ability, allowing you to choose when and where to engage your enemies.

Previously discovered events will be recorded in the Event Log, a valuable resource that allows you to reference past experiences to tackle future challenges.


■Battles
Test your strategies in thrilling battles, featuring the Active Time Battle (ATB) system made famous by the FINAL FANTASY series.
_childDocuments_.name: DUNGEON ENCOUNTERS

name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn
detailed_description: Digital Premium Edition Contents The Digital Premium Edition includes the following content: -Tactics Ogre: Reborn Standard Edition (the core game) -Tactics Ogre: Reborn Original Soundtrack This soundtrack includes new pieces composed by Hitoshi Sakimoto for Tactics Ogre: Reborn, as well as rerecorded live versions of Tactics Ogre favorites like Fight It Out! and Limitation. *The Tactics Ogre: Reborn Original Soundtrack is planned to be sold separately at a later date. About the Game Tactics Ogre, crown jewel of the tactical role-playing genre, is reborn! Based on the 2010 release, the game features improved graphics and sound, as well as updated game design, bringing to life a new Tactics Ogre that remains true to its roots. Tactics Ogre veterans will experience a game that surpasses their fondest memories, while players new to Tactics Ogre will discover a game unlike any they've ever played. Reborn and deeper than ever, the game enables players to immerse themselves in the world and intrigue of Tactics Ogre like never before. The Valerian Isles, jewels of the Obero Sea. Long a center of naval commerce, the people of the isles struggled throughout history for dominion over her shores. Finally there rose a man to put an end to this conflict: Dorgalua Oberyth. But history would know him as the 'Dynast-King.' King Dorgalua strove to stamp out the hatred among the people of the isles, and for fully half a century, Valeria knew prosperity. Yet upon the king's death, civil war erupted anew as three factions vied for control: the Bakram, who comprised much of Valeria's nobility; the Galgastani, whose people made up the majority of the isles' population; and the Walister, who numbered but few. The isles were soon divided between the Bakram and Galgastani, and an uneasy peace settled across the land. Yet none believed the calm would last... Your choices affect how the story unfolds, and even how it ends, with a game system that allows for multiple paths through the game and multiple endings. The story takes place through the eyes of a young man named Denam. The decisions he makes will alter the fate of those around him, and shift the course of Valeria's history. Fight pitched tactical battles on three-dimensional battlefields. The completely revamped AI enables enemies to adapt their tactics to the situation, providing a battle system that always keeps you thinking and never grows old. The class-wide level management system used in Tactics Ogre (2010) has changed to a unit-by-unit level system. Theorycraft your way through endless combinations of classes, equipment, skills, and magic. Enjoy numerous playability improvements, such as a quicker pace of battle, auto save, and a complete overhaul to the controls and UI to make it easier to get into the game than ever. The unparalleled details of the characters and backgrounds from the original Tactics Ogre (1995) have been recreated in high definition, while the detailed pixel art that gives the game its unique feel has been preserved and enhanced. The cutscenes are fully voiced in English and Japanese, and all of the music has been rerecorded with live performances! The voices bring new life to the complex motivations of the characters that make up the factions and shifting political alliances of this epic story. When you advance far enough in the game you'll unlock the World Tarot, enabling you to travel back in the story with the power of your forces intact; an incredibly useful feature in a game where your choices have such a huge impact on how the story unfolds. If you wonder what a different choice would have led to, now you can find out! Traveling back isn't limited to the story; the Chariot Tarot lets you rewind up to a certain number of moves during battle. In a game of tactical battles where a single mistake can mean the difference between victory and defeat, you can play without worrying that you'll back yourself into a corner. Enjoy a wealth of endgame content such as the 100-level Palace of the Dead. A world of endless stories and intrigue awaits!

_childDocuments_.review: I have 90+ h in the Switch version and double dipped here. I disagree hard with the negative reviews of this game. Every version (from SNES to this one) has its own quirks and that might be what is captivating most fans of this series. If you are looking for a game vaguely like FF Tactics or older Fire Emblem titles with a heavy and complex story campaign, chances are you will love this! The endgame can get pretty challenging and might require some guide-reading, but I am having tons of fun with it! Highly recommended, especially if you like old-school tactics games!

_childDocuments_.review: I have loved this game ever since I played the Knight of Lodis in the GBA. This game is rich, expansive and requires many hours and replays to get the entire story out of it. It is not for the fainthearted, and needs a lot of commitment. But I can say from experience that you will love every second of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Story seems interesting so far.Cons:- The game is missing all the Quality-of-Life (QOL) improvements for turn-based games over the last ~30 years. Managing your inventory is a chore. Managing your skills is a chore. Managing your units is a chore.- Most importantly, fighting the turn-based battles is a chore. There is no default way to tell apart your allies form the enemy as they use the same sprites. Not only that, the damage you do to enemies is nerfed. At the same level, enemy units can kill your units in 2-3 hits while you need to do ~8+ hits on them just to kill one of their units. As such, fights are unnecessarily extended and by the end, you are exhausted and it is just not fun. - The game implements a "buff" card system that is half-baked at best. - The Devs also seem to be too incompetent to properly balance their game and instead, implemented a "Union Level" system. Essentially, your units cannot level past the union level. I really hate when Devs try to halt the players progress to maintain the "difficulty" in a single player game. If I wanted to grind to 5+ levels beyond the recommended level, I should be free to do so.Overall, 3/10. Tried to like it but honestly, it's just not fun and is a chore to play. Wish I refunded it.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: It's the definitive version of Tactics Ogre. Is it perfect? No, there's a couple of odd changes and the character spritework feels pretty primitive for a 2022 release, but it beats grinding your life away in the PSP version, and it's much more refined than the PSX release. If you've never played Tactics Ogre before, and enjoy the genre at all, I highly recommend picking this up. It's leaps and bounds better than squeenix's typical "remasters"

_childDocuments_.review: Writing a revised review after 100% the achievements.Tactics Ogre: Reborn is a game filled with political intrigue, diverse tactical turned based combat, and oceans of optional content.  It is a well focused game that knows what it wants to be.  This is essentially a remaster of a remake of a port so this version has undergone multiple layers of polishing, and improvement that make it a contender of being the definitive version of the game.  I only use the word "contender" because some of Reborn's changes from its previous iteration (Let Us Cling Together on PSP) can justifiably be considered a downgrade.  While the more controversial changes didn't bother me enough to prevent me from spending over a hundred hours of enjoyment within TO: Reborn I can definitely understand why it would hinder the experience for others both newcomers & returning vets alike.  Although on the flip side there have been many quality of life improvements that in my opinion benefit the game far greater than how much the controversial changes weigh it down.[PROS]• Incredible morally nuanced storytelling with multiple branches that can influence which characters live, die, or join you throughout. • Remastered soundtrack is also a 10/10 for me.  Tracks like "Theme of the Dark Knight" or "Clash of Giants" are incredible tracks that goes well with the game play loop.• English voice acting is decent.  At first I was skeptical because the trailer used a bunch of random clips spliced together, but most of the dialogue is spoken normally yet elegantly so the conversations between characters feels natural.• Turned based tactical combat is straightforward, and easy to learn although difficult to master.  The player is given many tools for their team to utilize different build combinations.• Plentiful amounts of content.  It has taken me over 150 hours to clear the three branching pathways, and optional dungeons although there was still a large amount of events, battles, and endgame content that I haven't even touched yet.  However, the game presents this extra content in a way where you do not have to participate if you choose not to.  Reaching the endgame only takes about 30-50 hours, and it can also serve as a good stopping point to still feel fulfilled. • Achievements are not maliciously implemented.  Every single one can be obtained by clearing content you haven't seen before.  Even the extremely difficult CODA chapters at the end of the game are not required to beat for a 100%.  The greatest challenge however is a 100 floor dungeon that can burnout unsuspecting completionists although the auto battle feature helps make this less of a chore.• Crafting, menu navigation, and grinding have all been streamlined in a way where it saves the player time.  All of these have had quality of life improvements that will make it near impossible to revert to an older version of the game.• Mouse compatibility is incredibly implemented.  You can play the game one handed if desired.  Sometimes it can be a bit iffy trying to click around in Isometric view mode, but you can always shift to a top down view by clicking the mouse wheel button to easily work around those.[Cons]• This version implemented a level cap.  Which isn't bad for about half of the game when you are fighting enemies of equal level, but the issue I have is that they use this level cap to grant the enemy a level advantage quite frequently.  My critique is that the level cap should've simply just been an optional feature so it could cater to both the grind loving players, and those that want to challenge themselves.• There was one class removed in this version to "better the AI".  On one hand there is so many other build options where the absence of this class isn't as heavy as it sounds on paper, but on the other hand the AI isn't exactly the best still so it does feel like an "uneven trade" in retrospect.  Player AI will frequently stand near cliff sides, avoid using de/buffs, and burn revive resources before repositioning properly.  Enemy AI will still rush in, spread out attacks, and make questionable targeting decisions.  I don't mind the removal of the class, but "cut content" is never a thing I'm a fan of.• Buff cards are not as bad as most people make them out to be.  I enjoy the element of choosing between the most optimal location for my unit, or the choice to stray off the beaten path for a buff during the battle.  The only thing I don't like is that after a certain point they will give bosses a full stack of buff cards at the beginning of the fight which gives them a massive advantage.  Pair this with them being higher level than you due to the cap, and having more units deployed to be a miserable encounter.  After awhile you get used to it, and the added challenge makes the battle intriguing - although with those elements working against the player there is understandable reason to why the difficulty is considered "artificial" to some.• Some people are mad about the removal of random battles because they "can't grind", but there are still ways to grind XP & goth/gold throughout the game to your hearts content.  So I really don't consider this a con personally, but I will include it because I think I am in the minority with this opinion.[RANDOM TIPS]• Breach status is your best friend.  Use the item, or a blue dragon to inflict this consistently on bosses.• Shields have a high chance of knocking an enemy back without a crit.  Bottomless pits, and cliffs are now your friends.• Don't stress about "making the wrong decision" play the game blind for the first time.  You will eventually be given a tool that makes exploring the content you missed much better than keeping track of multiple saves.• Still keep multiple saves though.  Some areas have "multiple parts" that won't let you return to the world map until cleared.• FF Tactics veterans will be used to high customization for individual units, and may find it unappealing to not have as many options for their individual units in Tactics Ogre.  That is why it is important to look at your "build" of the entire team instead of individual units.  It can be beneficial to have multiple units of the same class if it can counter the enemy formation better.• Use "scout" often to see what enemy team you are up against.  Switch units accordingly to make each battle much easier.  Trying to maintain a static team throughout the game will just lead to frustration.• This game rewards tactics/preparation over grind.  It is likely that the answer to a defeat can be found at the drawing board.• Auto Battle is nice to use during the long optional dungeons.  Although if you use it then always check the Warren Report after winning an auto battle to make sure no units got permakilled while on auto pilot.• Also always check the Warren Report "Talk" section frequently because some optional content is unlocked within those entries.In conclusion. Tactics Ogre: Reborn is an incredibly deep game with an fantastic story to go with it.  I will recommend this game because it caters to my love for RPG's, strategy, Game of Thrones (before the bad ending) levels of political intrigue, and has enough content to justify the price tag even without a discount.  However, I acknowledge that this is a game that doesn't cater to a player that isn't fond of the previously mentioned themes.  There is a good chance you will like this if you loved Final Fantasy Tactics, but some of the differences might also be unappealing to those players as well.  Although this is a game that when it "clicks" it definitely clicks, and it will be a rewarding experience if it turns out to be your cup of tea.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best version of this game and the perfect one for newcomers, even if you're new to the series. I wish they would make a new one in the classical vein and not turn it into some stupid shallow action combat game or something, but alas this will do and do well it does.It's not an easy game or a short one, and there are multiple story paths (though only 3 major ones and the neutral path is short), but the game makes it easy for you to go back and replay through segments, it's literally a click away and you get to keep your levels and stuff kind of like new game +, just with more options. There's also a Disgaea-ish endgame that will eat away too many hours of your life if you really care about min/maxing and grind.Overall, no, this isn't going to be going viral the way more casual-friendly games are, but if you're a JRPG fan, and especially if you're a SRPG/TRPG fan, this is definitely one of the must-play games in the genre.Fantastic story, actually respectful remaster/remake that has had thought go into modernizing the mechanics, tons of QoL features that honestly even new (J)RPGs need, and bonkers voice acting, the kind Square Enix used to be famous for a few years ago before they started cutting corners.Well worth it if you like these kinds of games or want a blast to the past.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a classic with a few new bells and whistles. The story is top-notch and the gameplay loop does hit that tactical roleplay spot. It isn't worth $50 though. _childDocuments_.review: This will mostly try to address some of the common negative opinionsOn the level cap there seems to be two negative camps. The "muh freedom" and "its too hard":It's not so much the level cap but the lack of cross changing classes that causes this. You're trading "complexity" for streamlining. You can still be creative and play different unit comps. It's just not the specific way they the nay sayers want. Many of the negative reviews seem to be people who want to have a character change into a wizard and learn a skill. Then change into cleric and learn a skill. Then change into their preferred class and then use those skills. Now you can make a super unit.Now, the classes are more niche and specialized. Along with the other balance changes, each unit has a more defined role.In the PSP version, you literally only played archers and 1-3 support units. The balance was very poor.For example,A dragoon is specialized at killing beasts/dragons. However if there are no beast/dragon enemies you might bench him for a better dps.A beast master is very strong if you decide on a monster party but probably won't see play if you don't recruit monsters.Because it's easy to level cap, you can level up many different units without issue (or feeling that you need to grind). This can promote subbing in/out 1-2 units that aren't optimal for a map.I think the lack of cross-class change is a perfectly valid complaint but it seems to overshadow dozens of other positive changes that were made.: It's true that with the level cap, in "major" fights the enemy units will be 1-2 levels above you. Many negative reviews are complaining that this is unfair. This is a rather odd claim because it's more likely they did this so the story battles can at least have some challenge. This is rather subjective but on the whole they've made the game easier/less bloatly. Many game systems already favor the player as well.- Many fights you only need to kill the boss to win. You need to full wipe to lose.- When your unit "dies", you get 3 rounds to revive them. The enemy dies instantly and can't rez- Each of your units can carry 4 items (with very powerful healing effects). Typically the enemy carries no items except for their mages- Crafting is 100% success rate (it used to fail in the psp version). this means you're going to have better equipment than the enemy. - You can rewind turnsWithout the level cap in place you literally rollover the AI.The biggest issue with the level cap is that they didn't smooth out the exp curve.The format usually goes like this:Important story battle -> level cap raised4-6 interim battlesImportant story battle -> level cap raisedYou can reach the level cap in like 2 battles. This leads to the remaining battles feeling pointless because you're not getting rewarded. According to people this is simultaneously ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ when the enemy gets it but the game is too easy when you get it.Random buffs spawn on the field. When a unit steps on the tile they receive a permanent buff for the reminder of that battle. I don't have a strong opinion either way.- It gives your units something to do during turns they don't have useful actions- it speeds up the time battle take- you can do broken stuff which is what the "mah creativity" people want- the buffs can promote moving your units more. in these games you can typically turtle the enemy outThey've made substantial additions in - VA- balance- QoL menuing changes for both battle and party management - basic AI for units- pretty good settings options you can enable/disableAt the end of the day this is a very very old game. Some of the systems will still feel archaic even with the changes. The game doesn't have the modern flashiness. All that being said, I feel like SE certainly tried with this re-release. That's something I cannot say with their other ports.

_childDocuments_.review: The first quintessential tactics game with superb quality of life improvements to gameplay, graphics, audio, and UI. It has come a long way from it's original in 1995 on Super Famicom. This is the spiritual progenitor of Final Fantasy Tactics. If you enjoy mastering complex systems and tactics games in general, then this is the game for you. There have been some simplifications from the PSP version for the better that keep you engaged in battles and their objectives. The crafting system from the PSP version has had a huge overhaul and is not as tedious as it used to be. You can mass craft items all at once up to 999 per item instead of the constant button spam one had to do in the PSP version, crafting one item at a time. This is only the cream on the surface.I can only hope SE will do the same level of polish for the rest of the series: Ogre Battle: March of the Black Queen, Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber, and Tactics Ogre: The Knights of Lodis.Bravo and enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good. Got a lot of satisfaction out of the super crispy voice acting and riveting story. It may not be the first time people have seen this kind of story, but it's told pretty well! The World Tarot system is great for people like me who experience a lot of FOMO when playing anything. If you're new to this game and have no biases from the earlier releases, you'll find that the story alone (not considering the hundreds of battles the game offers you) is great value when considering most other Tactical RPG games available on Steam right now.The combat, although a lot of people have mixed feelings about it, has been a blast. There is a level cap and it's not for everyone, but it introduces a different kind of challenge from the 2010 release. You can't grind your way to victory and I understand that this frustrates a lot of people, but I hope potential buyers still give it a shot because tactics turned into strategy really do overcome a lot of the challenges in this game.After 180h into the game, I can say that TOR has definitely scratched that TRPG itch I've been feeling for a while now. Let us cling together!
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: It is soooooo boring. I had a hankering to play Final Fantasy Tactics, and I no longer own a PS1 or PSP version of the game so I bought Tactics Ogre to scratch the itch. It did the opposite. The entire time I was thinking, "I just want to play FFT." Credit given where credit is due -- I do understand this is the predecessor, however, it is so lackluster in every way compared to strategy games that followed. The story and characters are just not interesting to me, which would be alright if I enjoyed the gameplay, but I don't. You've got versatility in choosing job classes for each character but you're limited to equipping 4 abilities and 4 spells (and of course many classes can't use magic) so the actual strategy is... like... IDK, a game of checkers? It's so shallow. Your options are far too limited. For example, in Tactics Ogre, a mage can use 4 spells. In FF Tactics, a mage can use like 20 spells. There are other minute reasons I don't enjoy the game but obviously story and gameplay are dealbreakers. Not having one is rough, not having both is... why play it? Admittedly the remaster is quite beautiful but honestly just wait for a FF Tactics remaster. It's surely on the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: When I started playing I thought of refunding the game. I expected it to play like Final Fantasy Tactics and it doesn't. Once you get over that expectation the game has a lot to offer which it does better than Final Fantasy Tactics and I am really enjoying the game now. One of the biggest problems with this game is that it does a very poor job of explaining the underlying game mechanics to you of how attack and defence works and so you feel that for example Archers are trash because they only do 1 damage and noting in the game explains to you why this happens and how to overcome enemy defences. I had to watch literal hours of YouTube videos by Coffee Potato to explain the mechanics to me, and only once I understood it did I begin to enjoy the game. This game is hard and offers a lot more puzzle solving than games like FFT. A lot of decisions are made before combat even begins as to which units you want to take and how you want to solve the puzzle of the battle presented to you. I had a number of battles where I tried one approach only to fail, but I learnt how the map plays as a result and brought different units and took a different approach and won easily. The game has a beautifal tactical depth when you understand what each unit's role is  (which meant even more long Youtube videos by Coffee Potato) and enemy behavour and the role of the terrain. In Chapter three the game became a little bit grindy, I was constantly short on money and consumables and I had to grind quite a bit for money to get to a good spot. This might be due to an error of me relying too much on consumables, but again the game did not teach me otherwise. I am using clerics a lot more now along with equipment that breaches enemies defences which means I need to rely on items less and that has certainly helped my in game wallet, but this is another example of how the game feels very punishing if you don't play it in a way that takes advantage of your classes correctly. This game is definately worth playing if you are willing to take the time to overcome the obstacles in learning the game's mechanics, and now I think I enjoy it much more than FFT where it was far too easy to build completely overpowered units by the end-game, whereas with this game I need to keep thinking and using my units optimally to succeed.

_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Can't recommend this game, not at this price.It's a very good game, or at least it would be wasn't it for the absurd mechanics forced upon the player that completely prevent an enjoyable TBS experience.It feels like the devs set out to make a true masterpiece and at the same time put in place a bunch of BS quirks in order to prevent people to actually enjoy it.The progressive level cap is utterly ridiculous, the game won't let you progress for several battles only to immediately level you up to the next max as soon as you pass a threshold taking away any sense of achievement and satisfaction coming from training your squad.The games constantly throws a bunch of enemies that outlevel and outgear you, not giving you any possibility to even the play field. That would make the game impossible but thing is the AI is as dumb as they come and all you have to do to win is kill the enemy leader who, although ridiculously offensively overpowered, is also just as easy to take down in a single push with a few finisher moves. That is the extent of the strategic element in the whole game, that's literally all you need to  do in almost every single battle to get through it all.If this wasn't enough there's a crappy hidden loyalty score in place just to make sure you cannot kill enemies, like you would in any other TBS that actually makes sense, lest your army starts deserting.The story is really good though and the characters are interesting, would be an awesome game if not for the inexplicable silliness of the aforementioned absurd limitations. What a terrible waste...
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game from level design to difficulty to the story and new voice acted scenes.  If you love tactical games you will love this one, it did not disappoint in any way.  Some may not like the level cap restriction as you progress but I find it a wonderful edition as it makes the game more challenging to the point you cant just over level and walk threw the entire game.  There has not been one battle where I felt ultimately weak or unable to progress and i'm not a tactical genius by any means.  Personally I am very pleased to have to have a challenge and having to actually strategize in order to win.As for farming consumables or new units lets just say you don't have to worry about this for long,And early game you have a plethora of supplies to get you to that point.The last negative thing I see is the randomness of the cards that can change the way a battle turns out drastically.  Thisis true it can change a battle drastically.  Do I find myself pigeon holed into a certain strategy in order to win or certain parts of the game impossible?  Absolutely not, honestly I ignored the cards a lot of the time and never felt weak or unable to win a battle.  Enemies that grab cards should change your strategy to prioritize them, but even left unchecked they should not pose a huge threat.I find this game a gem and what I wish more tactical rpgs would shoot for, If you love tactical rpgs and never played this before or even if your coming back and wondering should I play it again.  Yes odds are it has something you will love, whether it be story, design, strategy its all so well done.Just look at the hours people have put into it.

Gave up in chapter 3 when I realized I just didn't care about the ending or characters.The games UI is awful. The main reason I never made it past a couple battles in prior Tactics Ogre versions was that I found the graphics to be quite bland, particularly in the colour scheme, but also I found it rather busy, and and just not as aesthetically pleasing in general to the wonderful palette, subtle animations, and engaging sfx of FFT. This game has improved on a lot of that, IMO. The Palette is still a little bland, but the graphics are lovely, and the voice acting is excellent, as is the score. I am thoroughly excited to see this one to the end. Side note, I have played a ridiculous amount of tactics games, in anticipation of finding one that would even begin to scratch the itch that was left in the wake of FFT, and honestly none have been particularly gratifying, although the GBA FFT games were close, and some of the FE older releases like Sacred Stones were quite excellent, albeit a different sort of experience. Tactics Ogre, also the child of Yasumi Matsuno, with this latest Reborn entry, I think is the perfect game continue the magical feeling of Final Fantasy Tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: They butchered it, the game I revered, ruined so many elements of the combat system that it's nearly unrecognizable. Union level is hands down one of the most egregious issues. Limiting your levels creates soooo many issues, a few examples:- Multiple stages in a row where your union level is fixed, your team is level capped = enemies are obnoxiously easy or arbitrarily hard - (Some of the hardest fights are ones where your level "cap" is lower than the lowest level enemies) - while you might believe this encourages more strategic play, it doesn't, it encourages gimicky play where you try to one-shot the enemy leader since it is nearly impossible to actually fight the opposing team given the unequal footingSecond main issue I have is the degree to which they butchered class/skill system, since a character is always the same level no matter what class they choose, they had to get rid of the skill system of old where once a character learned a skill on one class, they could use it with other classes. This added a whole host of customization, progression, and depth. Gone, the only remnant is that you still have to level combat skills which provide finisher skills. This has resulted less "unique" characters that I have felt almost zero investment in since nearly everyone is the exact same if they are on the same class.This game is now at a point where it's either stupidly easy or obnoxiously hard depending on when your union level cap last increased and there is very little you as a player can do about it due to almost all ability to customize your team being removed.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: a great tactical rpg with a solid gritty political war story.It seems like a number of people here who were fans of the PSP version were disappointed in the game, and the reasons they fell in love with that version might not be here, but from a new fan's or potential player's perspective this is what I see when I look at this version.1) Preserving abilities between classes is gone, and you can no longer build units into exactly what you want them to be, but on the flip side, a lot of bloat was cut, the game is much more balanced, and each class feels like it's useful in its own way and is unique. (Don't believe the archer hate btw, they're good just more niche)2) Building team comps is fun, and the game does take both strategic and tactical skill. I like looking at a battlefield and having to consider what units I ought to bring and how to approach the fight.3) Random encounters are gone and grinding is pretty much unnecessary for the main story stuff. I realize some people like grinding, but c'mon, it's 2022 and most players don't want that, especially when it's required. It's just not fun for most people.4) A ton of convenience features were added over previous versions. Crafting items is easy, auto-prompts for selling coins, the fast forward feature is amazing, etc... I don't think I'd want to go back to a version without this stuff5) This is one of the least convoluted and esoteric jRPG stories I've played. It's gritty and mature but in a mostly realistic fashion. The localization is great, and the voice acting is surprisingly decent. 6) The negatives are that the game is pretty slow to start off, and a lot of things just aren't explained to the player. You really have to look up guides or videos to understand parts of the game. Some sidequests require you to just randomly be in random locations at a specific time that isn't well explained. I also didn't like how often I had to update my equipment, but that is a taste thing so YMMV.Overall a pretty great package, and I wasn't expecting to enjoy it this much. A solid pickup.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an updated review after almost 500 hours of playing the game and unlocking all achievements.I really enjoyed my experience with this game and would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of strategy games and the RPG genre. I never played the original 1995 game or the remake of 2010, so I have no frame of reference to compare this game to. With the exception of having played "Tactics Ogre: the Knight of Lodis" and "Final Fantasy Tactics", Reborn was a completely new experience for me in getting back to this genre of games.Tactics Ogre Reborn is a turn-based strategy RPG with a compelling story, stellar voice acting, and creative game design that encourages players to experiment with their units and build to create their most optimal team as they engage in battle. Player choice matters as decisions can make subtle and major changes as the story unfolds.The best asset of Reborn in my opinion would have to be the CHARIOT System, which is a feature in the game that allows the player to go back previous turns during a battle and make changes in hopes of ending up with a more favorable outcome. Having played Tactics Ogre and other old strategy games in the past, this genre can be quite difficult, making one careless move could be extremely punishing to the point of needing to restart and load a previous save which was exhausting. This feature erases all of those problems by allowing players to go back and correct their mistake. The CHARIOT system is such a significant quality of life improvement that I wish more games implemented.Another significant feature that enhances the game is the WORLD System. Upon completing the game for the first time, the player gets access to a feature in the game's menu that allows the player to go back in time by selecting one of the several "Anchor Points" spread out in the game's timeline map. The reason why this is so significant is because it enhances the game's replayability by allowing the player to replay the game from any point of the story without having to start a new game. With the WORLD system, players are able to go to specific points in the timeline and make a different choice than they did previously all while retaining the items and enhancements they acquired over their first playthrough. Like with the CHARIOT system, being able to rewind to previous points of the story while still keeping your progress is a quality of life improvement I wish more games implemented, especially if they're games with branching timelines.Some minor complaints I did have with my experience was the level cap in the game. It didn't really bother me at first, and given the features I mentioned earlier I can understand why it was implemented, otherwise the game might've been too easy. That being said though, The difficulty spike gets higher in the post-game which can be exhausting even if you acquired powerful items and enhanced your units appropriately. Overall, the level cap isn't too much of a hindrance and by no means a deal breaker. Side note, there's a lot of dungeon crawling in certain locations of the game which can take a long time to navigate through if you want to get rare and powerful weapons which you'll need if you plan to survive in any battle in the post-game storyline if you decide to engage with it. The dungeon crawler aspect is probably where the game really shows it's original (1995) age, meant to be a game to be played in parts rather than binged in one sitting. Not many people have the time to pour hours of their day into the game's dungeons for rare items or bits of story, which I understand can be a deterrent for some and an attraction to others. Luckily, the dungeons are optional and aren't required for you to progress.The post-game (CODA) is by far the most difficult portion I've played of any game by far, it can be incredibly frustrating and it's where all of the positive and negative aspects of the game collide honestly. The level cap should've been optional at this point, but luckily all of the enhancements and rare items/weapons I had acquired over the game made it enough to even things out. Completing the post-game storyline was probably the most agonizing yet rewarding experience I've ever felt in a game, it's also the only game I ever 100% completed.Overall, if you like strategy games, dungeon crawlers, or RPGs I'd strongly recommend this gem of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre is one of my favorite games of all time and is still a great experience to play today. I’m glad Square Enix decided to release the game as Tactics Ogre reborn with many positive changes for modern times and to attract newcomers. If you are new to SRPGs or a SRPG fan, it’s a great game with many in depth systems, ways to manage your army, and tools from units, items, equipment and skills to overcome the battles in game. This game plays well on a steamdeck and reminds me of having a PSP back in the day.I’m still very impressed with the number of interactions you can do within the game that can affect how the story unfolds and multiple endings.  Very crazy from a game originally released in 1995 and improved upon again in 2011 and 2022. There is a ton of missables but the game is replay friendly with the WORLD tarot system to replay the other parts of the story or get characters you haven’t recruited yet. In my opinion, this design is user-friendly and encourages a new player to play how they want without using a guide to experience things without spoilers.Pros:+Game is re-balanced to be harder until the end of the main story. No more grinding to steamroll things until POTD, CODA and World Tarot. This creates a feeling of self-accomplishment when beating the final boss in Chapter 4.+There are many ways to play this game and to challenge yourself with the tools this game has to offer. For example, go nuts with fielding mostly dragons or undead to spice things up or limit yourself to using melee units only. The options this game offer is vast and can accommodate many different play styles.+The main game will take 20-60 hours for the main story (depending if you play the other story paths as well) and 100s of hours if you want to grind to beat CODA episode 4 and the 12 heavenly generals which are optional challenges. +Status effects like charm, poison, fear, stun, breach, stop and petrify can make a hard fight controllable and can make the game feel tactical if used properly.+Classes are re-balanced to be more usable and archers are now situational good and not overpowered like the original game.+Voice acting is a nice touch in my opinion and enhances things.+The User interface looks great and was redone from the PSP version. Things are easy to navigate after a few hours of game play.+The remastered music is still iconic and was well done.+Great story that tells the horror of war and how a group of rebels overcome challenges to save the Valerian Isles. Without spoiling things, characters can be killed/saved in battle or from dialog choices affecting the endings in either minor or major ways.  Actions like massacring ethnic groups in battle and lowering your public perception from story choices will affect one of the endings as well.+Things can be steamrolled late and post game and there are many things to grind for like equipment, spells, and charms (stat boosts) by the repeatable content of POTD and San Bronsa. Eventually you can grind out the challenge of the game and make it a cakewalk. AI controlled units can make this process automated after some setup and grinding. Look up a guide for drops and use the tarot system to reroll while farming to be efficient on items to target.+Quirky systems like snapdragon and retissue still exist from the original game but was somewhat rebalanced. Retissue (bodyswap form ogre blade) can break the game with 999 stat Mag/MND units which can inherit tons of skills of other classes making a god unit. Cons:-Union levels puts an artificial cap on grinding which can get annoying at times. I hated this at first but understand it's for game balance.-Bosses can feel cheap with their blue card buffs especially towards the end of the game which can one shot units. You can overcome this with debuffs from items and status effects from units.-Drop rates for some POTD, Shrines, and San Bronsa items are very low and need to be rerolled by using the chariot system which can take a while. This can become a large time sink at times and become annoying.-Some item/spells rebalancing makes the game less fun with the old school bow from palace of the dead no longer petrifying units or the apocrypha spells not hit everything on the screen like the SNES/PlayStation version of the game. For the spells, this makes the in-game lore doesn’t make sense anymore.-Some of the voice acting doesn’t match the characters or make them sound way older than their age in Warren’s report. Thankfully it’s only a few characters and like 90% of the casting sounds great.Overall, I really enjoyed my time with Tactics Ogre Reborn and hope this game does well! I would like a continuation of the Ogre series of games which haven’t had any new games in over 10 years. Good job Yasumi and Square Enix, you guys did well for re-releasing the game with improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: I held off on making this review until I've finished most of the game and gave the devs time to patch the game. I'm at the end (  ) and am ready to do a review. In terms of tactics RPGs it's pretty good but there are still issues and I'm unsure I will finish the game. I am at the point where any external suggestions are that I need to grind a significant amount to stand a chance and I'm not interested in doing so. The mechanics are still extremely clunky. I understand this is an old game but it's still too difficult to understand exactly how things like resistances or other mechanics work. Yes they have explanations but what does it mean statistically when I have improved piercing or what exactly does breach provide in terms of negative impacts against the enemy?The lack of clarification around systems is pretty bad and the tiny in-game explanations are not sufficient, not to mention they waste your time because you can't scroll through the explanation text but have to slowly wait for it do so by itself. The team has also been relatively slow to fix various bugs or confusing functionality (AI wasting my items or not casting spells, etc.) while also doing a very poor job communicating.Let's get in to the card system since a lot of people complain about it. I'm not going to approach this from an old versus new perspective because I didn't play much of the old versions, I'm not replaying this game after having put in 1000 hours in to the original or anything. The cards suck. The impact they have on stats is ridiculous and abusing them by having bosses come stacked with 4 card abilities (which cannot be removed unless the cancellation card is touched) feels cheap and like a lazy way to try and fix balancing issues. It's not a good system and the impact it has is far too large.The story is pretty good but still feels drawn out unnecessarily at points.Overall I can't recommend the game. Square is asking WAY too much money ($50) for a re-release that has too many bugs, flaws, and general lack of modern polish to be worth that much money. You might as well play the PSP version with the One Vision mod for an experience that is significantly more polished.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre Reborn is the PC remake of PSP version of TO: Let us Cling Together.Everything is fully voiced now, there are no new content or characters compared with the PSP version BUT there are plenty of modernization to this version:1. Game is less grindy than before, gone are the days of repeatedly going to the Woods or maps for random encounters, as...2. Battles can be fast forwarded to twice the speed....3. Levels are tied to the characters, so gone are the days with level 1 unique character due to their new class...4. But you'll live with what essentially is a level cap tied with the storyline called 'Union Level', so no more over-levelling your way through difficult battles...5. And the tough boss battles often come outfitted with 4 bonuses making them a one-shot nuker.6. Auto-skills and bonus cards/charms can be polarizing, as it makes the game less grindy but sometimes more annoying due to the luck involved.7. Some game mechanics were made easier, no more farming for materials and see it being wasted away in that god-awful crafting system.8. And everyone can get Deneb comparatively easier now, no more stupidly wasting your life taming dragons and farming pumpkins just to get her.I missed the ability to fully custom your characters with the 10 skill slots, Reborn is more streamlined than the PSP version, but Squeenix should put another mode into the game, a 'classic' mode for the masochist die-hards, or perhaps make it customizable.Do I recommend this? Yes, I'm an adult now with less time compared with my teenage years, but the charm and darker storyline of TO always made it memorable in me.

_childDocuments_.review: The voice-acting is stellar, the aesthetic is entrancing, the portraits for the intro and characters are all great.But the combat is tepid, drawn-out, and doesn't seem to get better, even as your party progresses. And that's the majority of the game as each combat is minimum 30 minutes. Everyone has 1-2 attacks to start, move painfully slow, have limited range even on support abilities, and hit like a wet noodle. Every enemy takes 5-6 hits (essentially everyone in party getting a hit in) to bring down, all while navigating a dicey turn order that is hard to account for, AND hit chances yaaay, everyone's favorite dynamic.It's just a really big, draining slog every fight, where once you start to win, there's no more challenge but often leader units waaay afield you need to move-cycle every unit over to go kill. On the other hand, once you take a few too many losses (with revive items being useless with how turn order and attack priorities go), you've lost, and can suffer through the rest of the combat denying it, cuz you  don't want to have to restart, or suck it up, restart, and lose a good 20min to no benefit, save lessons learned, right?Sorry, not my idea of a good time. Challenging? Fine. Boring? No.I might also note I had no nostalgia for this game, this was my first time playing, so that may be coloring people's opinions too. It does look nice, for what it's worth, as far as pixelart games go, but, well, as I've said.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who played Final Fantasy Tactics and never realized it was based on Tactics Ogre, here are the differences between this game and FFT:- obviously the plot- the music:  FFT is the same style of music, but while Tactics Ogre has really great music, FF's is legendary so it has an advantage there- Tactics Ogre: Reborn (TOB) limits your character level to your party level, which increases based on main story progression.  The purpose of this is so you can't grind out meaningless encounters to overpower the story.  FFT accomplishes this differently by scaling up all main story encounters to your current power level.  I think FFT did it better because you never DONT see character progression after a fight.  However FFT people say is the "only game that gets harder the more you grind it" which is true!  You can grind that satisfying progression all day but continuing the main story will be ever MORE challenging!  - Job unlock system in TOB is by progressively encountering and defeating new jobs.  In FFT it is by meeting pre-requisite combinations of other job levels.  For example to unlock Samurai your character needs to be level 3 knight, level 4 monk, and level 2 lancer and then you can learn Samurai.  The progression in FFT is better- ENDINGS this game has lots of decision-making that determine which characters live and change story trajectory and lots of endings and a convenient way to replay the game from different turning points rather than starting over.  FFT doesn't have that- CRAFTING there is no crafting in FFT and TBO does have crafting.  The crafting system is very limited and tedious but its consistent. - The feel - FFT totally copied the entire game style from Ogre.  I don't know if Ogre copied any of it from previous games - not a historian on these games - but SE had more resources and one-upped it a bit.  But the difference is not huge.  TBO is a fantastic game and anyone who loved FFT will love this game.
