_childDocuments_.review: Originally I gave this game a good review but after playing the game till the end of chapter 3 chaos route I am changing my review due to the constant artificial difficulty that is enforced by the level cap, enemies having better equipment than you and starting the battle with max cards to min-max their attack power.There are some crazy design choices with this remake that just add up in the end to being an annoying game.They allow you to level up quicker but now you have to farm money from the forest in chapter 2 since training only allows you to get class XP. You will have to grind those training missions to level up your weapon XP which is painfully slow and you need to level that up because 1 level can mean the difference between doing 50 damage and 100 damage. Weapon skills are capped to your level so essentially you will have to level twice one going very fast and is based on enemies defeated which is then given out after the battle and one going painfully slow and is based on actual attacks against enemies for each unit in your army.You might hit that level cap nice and quick but enemies will almost always be much higher level than you but good tactics can still win. That is until chapter 3 when you face armies 3 levels higher than you with max stat cards at the start that will run into your line and do 600+ damage with one weapon skill killing almost anyone. This artificial difficulty spike is very noticeable in the forced duel sections on the chaos route against Vyce and Leonar.They can kill you in 1 to 2 rounds and the only way to win those fights is to use hit and run tactics and hope they cannot catch you. Those fights are not in anyway shape or form tactical they are annoying and the limited inventory means you might get max 4 heals and still that might not be enough to win. Those items also cost decent money that adds up and before the midway point of chapter 2 in which you can unlock the forest area by looking in the Warren Report, this might trip up new players since they have no idea in game that a whole new area of the map unlocks at some point by looking in what amounts to a biography area.If you run out of money before the midway of chapter 2 you are basically just stuck with nothing and have to do the main missions and hope they drop coins or the sub objective has a coin reward.The optimal tactics seems to be to spam magic items and then spam weapon skills at the enemy. They thought of this and so you can no longer buy magic restoration items in the shop you have to grind the forest and hope you get one than craft a better version of it.The way around this is to play a class with meditation which can sometimes give you free magic points and just spam weapon skills.I really hope they do some balancing around some of these extreme fights that are so one sided against you and really think about either dropping the level cap or matching it to each fight so you are never artificially weakened in order to make the fight harder.Finally no enemy should start with max cards and be able to walk up to anyone on your team and one shot them and especially so in 1v1 fights.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great remaster all around except for a few troubling spots:-The voice acting is horrible. I have to play with voices off. I don't know what's wrong with SE these days, but the English VO in their sprite games is just terrible. It's nothing like the Shakespearean-esque acting in Final Fantasy XII, and it should be since Tactics Ogre is out of the same vein as FF12. There's really great writing in this localization, but the acting doesn't come anywhere near to doing it justice.-There are level caps between every major story milestone. It's not fun when you can't level up as you please. I like being OP when facing off against particularly challenging bosses. I shouldn't have to be penalized for that, in a sense. You'll keep getting into battles where you can still get EXP awarded, but it won't count towards your level. Instead, you'll get an item that you can later use to quickly level up new units. In theory, this is nice. But I'd rather be able to freely level my main party as I please.-The menus can be quite cumbersome sometimes. There's a lot of information there and a lot of micromanaging that should be easier. For example, I wish it was easier to see which items are new in the shop. There's no indicator for that. I'd also like to be able to purchase raw materials for crafting while in the crafting menu. I'd also like to be able to see which characters in my party can equip new gear and how that affects their stats. It shows you which classes can equip, which isn't the same as showing my active roster. This is just basic stuff that you'd find in most RPGs, so I'm not sure why it's not in this one.-Too many cards all over the map and it's really annoying collecting them. Plus I don't like how I can't see exactly what the modifier on my stats is--like, I can't tell how much more attack power I get per card. It'd be nice to have some kind of percentage indicator or a "x2, x5" multiplier to let me know how much worth my while it is to get more than one of each. As it stands, it's all just guesswork.-Your party, especially archers, can feel really weak unless you pick up cards. I don't like how I have to basically run a fetch quest and leave myself vulnerable before I can do any serious damage.-I don't like how tickets for each class are consumables. It makes me really reluctant to spend any unless I know I can get more somewhere. Some you can't buy early on but have to get lucky with item drops--when you're actually in a battle with item drops. I had my first dragoon ticket stolen by a boss because he picked it up then warped away when I went in for the kill, taking all those spoils with him. It'd be funny if it wasn't frustrating.-This is a minor complaint, but but if you play on a really high resolution, the graphics can get kind of blurry.Aside from these criticisms, I really love this game. I'm glad they did away with random battles. I like being able to pick and choose when and where I fight. The gameplay is really fun and the story is engrossing and thought provocative. I sincerely hope that SE remasters the rest of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: A Very disappointing Tactical RPG. If you want the story, I would recommend watching the game played online before purchasing or seeing if you can play a different version of the game.Another user’s review summarises the issues with this game very well:Damage: Inconsistent and heavily dependent on getting ‘cards’ that buff your damage or enemy damage. It becomes a race to get to the certain locations. There are some ally units that have fly, but there are more enemy units with fly. Whether these are humanoids or flying monsters/creatures.Ranged damage + Magic is a joke. Walking glass cannons that are nuked by enemy ranged units or melee flying units.AI: Ally AI is incredibly stupid. They rush into enemy units. Take up terrible positions, then get nuked down.The combat mechanics associated with elemental strength/weaknesses doesn’t make any sense. You can’t prepare for this – It’s RNG, based on what enemy ‘types’ they have vs what you have. If it’s unfavourable for you, the enemy takes less damage and does more damage to you. The opposite applies if you have an elemental bonus on them. It’s just a standard buff/debuff that’s calculated into your damage rolls.Story: I haven’t progressed very far. Somewhere in Chapter 1 or 2There are hints that some characters are backstabbing individuals. But what really makes no sense is that story pathways make no sense.There character choices and who you end up recruiting in your game down the road makes very, very little sense.Example (Spoiler):  Don’t kill them people. Your allies betray you. Your neutral ally that should be on your side gets killed. And going further into the story and everyone conspires against you. Even those that you originally allied yourself with. Note: The game was originally released in 1995. This is the 4th remake. The story, mechanics, and gameplay are very, very dated. Overall, I can’t recommend this. I would recommend Triangle Strategy instead. A True RPG with fair game mechanics and excellent story telling that makes sense. Your choices matter, and it influences the story very well. A very deep and rewarding title.

_childDocuments_.review: There were numerous changes to Tactics Ogre Reborn (TOR) compared to the PSP version no doubt about it. I honestly have mixed feelings about some of the changes. Some of the changes that I really appreciated was the leveling systems and the training areas.On the PSP version it was the class that leveled not the character. This created problems in 2 ways. An example would be if I had hired a warrior and his level is 17 and wanted to change his class to a samurai which was level 20. He would have to battle a lot to get the necessay SP to acquire skills and in the PSP version skills determined life or death much more than TOR.Training grounds didn't exist the PSP version, you would have to level up new classes as you got them, I would have to find a battle that took 12 players and have 3 of the characters be the new class and basically have them avoid combat since they could get one-shot by any enemy on the field and they would only do about 1 hp of damage and have a less than 50% chance of hitting them. Equipment had level requirements on the PSP version that also contributed to reason why new low leveled classes couldn't do much in combat. The worst part of that was that special classes that are limited to 1 character would be the most annoying to level. You would have to swap every other class in combat so that class could slowly catch up ( I won't say which class(s) they for those who haven't got past chapter 4).TOR added battle specific cards (blue and red cards) in the game. These didn't exist in the PSP version and I feel that the permanent stat cards (green cards in TOR) drop less frequently in TOR than the PSP version.Another change was the removal of the TP gauge/bar. That was used by skill like meditate, double shot etc. In TOR they have been changed to auto skills (except the instill spells, they were spells that you would have to cast yourself). I don't necessarily like or dislike this change since you would have to get the cards on the field to increase the chances of it happening versus having to build the TP by either damaging the enemy or taking damage yourself.Changes to the finishing moves in TOR is that they only take the required MP. In the PSP version finishing moves required 100TP and would consume the remaining TP and in exchange, increases the damage output of that move.The changes I didn't like was the spells and item slots as  well as the boss(s) changes.In the PSP version you start with 4 skill slots and could increase it to 10 by paying in sp. If you wanted to use elemental magic, you would have to equip it in a skills slot however, when you picked the element you wanted to use you would have access to all the spells you acquired that your class can use. The trade off was that you would have to equip an augment type skill to do good damage or have a decent damage resistance to that type for example; augment fire (elemental damage buff) and attenuate fire (fire damage defense). Those skills would cost skill points(SP) and honestly attenuate wasn't worth the 440 sp cost. TOR remade this and is somewhat disadvantageous to you since some weapons only do parry and others counter. Those were skills you would equip in the PSP version and yes, you can have parry III and counter attack III equipped together. You didn't have to equip healing items or support items in the PSP version. you would have access to your entire inventory by equipping the Field Alchemy skill. Not much else to say there.In TOR the bosses getting buff cards at the very beginning of battle was annoying to me at most. PSP version bosses have higher level gear ( like a sword that you can't find until way later in the game but you were still able to steal it) and support abilities like deflect IV when you would have deflect III for example.   Despite these changes would I recommend this game? Absolutely, the game is still fun and a little more challenging than it's predecessor in a few ways. That's it for my rambling. Sorry for the long winded comparison.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are big into turn-based tactics and want to experience the predecessor to FFT, you will enjoy it. The voice acting and UI upgrades provide a modern feel to the elaborate story and familiar play style that the retro enjoyers will be looking for. Some critical feedback: Multi-classing should be a thing not limited to Lord class. The blue buff cards were too powerful and I wasn't really a fan of it. It just made the balance issues more apparent.Speaking of, some balance changes occurred for Reborn. Aside from those, there are combat formula calculation errors new to this version. They make certain items or builds perform unexpectedly. Incoming damage compares the defender's Armor's attributes vs their own weapon type, not the attacker's. Also, spell damage does not take the equipped weapon's INT bonus into account with certain gear equipped. These have been known since release and not fixed still after 6 months.These issues weren't game breaking, but they shouldn't exist in the 2nd? 3rd? re-release of a classic game.I do recommend the game, still... but these devs can do better!

_childDocuments_.review: I played the PSP version years ago and liked it. I think that Reborn is worth buying if you enjoy these types of games. There are far too few of them on the market as of now. The genre is woefully underserved, and, hopefully, it's sales will be sufficient for SE to finally give us a Final Fantasy Tactics remaster.Contrary to several recent reviews, I think the level cap is a good feature. There were around 3 cases during my playthrough where I felt underpowered. For the first two I felt the need to do no more than 3 non-story missions to level my soldiers. The experience charms, earned by fulfilling mission specific objectives, resolves most of the hastle of leveling up. The last case was the final fight which I do think is somewhat unfair and hard to deal with without a dragon with the dragon scale ability in the party. Nonetheless, if a tactical game can be steamrolled just by grinding out a few more levels, it loses any semblance of challenge. Reborn is not a hard game, but it does become a lot more manageable if you know of and use every avenue of power available to you. Crafting gear upgrades, having all manner of consumables, having a balanced roster for your required attack strategy, recognizing which fights are winnable only if you rush down the enemy leader etc.

_childDocuments_.review: The vast majority of positive reviews are due to the disease I once referred to as "Nostalgiticulitis".They played the old version as kids and now they're playing a tweaked version that can do no wrong.Here's the thing.  It's fine to enjoy the battle engine.  But for me to recommend a game, it has to do more than that.The story is basically non-existent.Characters don't matter.It's just fight-to-fight-to-fight.Worse, the battle engine itself isn't really that good.  Simple things like excessive amount of clicking around just to end turns or the number of button presses necessary to load up on items (and no, the answer is not to play with a keyboard.  It originated on consoles, so it should have been improved with that experience in mind).It's a relic of its era.  I'm not down on it because it's throwback.  I'm down on it because despite being a throwback, it's a bare basic experience that isn't worth full price.  It's not my kind of game at all, but if you're into tactics games, it's probably worth about $20-30 maximum if you can get it for that price.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre: Reborn is my favourite version of Let Us Cling Together. I have played the original release, the PSP version, the One Vision mod and the Chronicle Valeria ROM hack yet I still find Reborn to be the best version of the game.I've completed a no-chariot, no-incap, no retreat run with mostly generics and I've played through each route, beat the 12 generals and completed the final CODA battle with just the 3 main characters so I think have a good idea of how Reborn fares compared to previous releases.I'm going to throw a TL;DR here because I don't write many reviews so I'm probably not good at writing them and I may end up rambling:- If you're put off by complexity but aren't concerned with having less content/variety then play the SNES release- If you don't mind a tedious amount of grinding, are put off by randomness or you want a (reasonably) balanced iteration of this game play the One Vision mod- If you care a lot about quality of life features, can't stand reading or want a voice acted experience play RebornI'll mainly be comparing Reborn to the PSP version since they're so similar so if you're unfamiliar with the game already this review isn't really going to help you decide if you should buy the game (although it is a pretty good game and I do recommend it)The Good:- Practically no grinding required. The game throws EXP at you in spades from story battles, EXP charms and if that's not enough training battles exist.- The levelling system is back to the per-unit system as opposed to the PSP version's class level system- The crafting system no longer has a chance to fail and if you don't have the ingredients but they can be purchased from the shop you can just add the cost of the ingredients to the cost of the crafting which saves a lot of time.- The redone music is great. Most of the tracks in Reborn have become my favourite versions of the tunes from the Ogre Battle series. There are a few which I feel are inferior to the PSP's renditions (namely Accretion Disk) but they are by no means bad- The Japanese voice acting is a nice addition. It adds a lot of impact to the more emotional scenes- Recruitment for a couple of unique characters has been made less time consuming- The skill and magic bloat has been reduced from the PSP version, skills that affect movement have been moved onto the +1 variants of armour and some skills that were barely worth a slot on your characters have been made into auto-skills which can turn the tide of battle yet cost no MP or actions. Skills that were all but required in the PSP version have either been moved to equipment or built into characters (the unit element system replaces augment element)The Bad:- Item progression through the story is a bit of a drag, magic classes have to wear linen slops throughout the entirety of the main campaign.- RNG plays a larger role in Reborn. Status spells in the PSP version usually had around a 50% chance to hit in the early game but in Reborn be expected to see chances as low as 20% for even average enemies. Buff cards are a new feature added to reborn which I'm not a fan of, they can spawn almost anywhere on the map and while there seems to be something in place to ensure a variety of different types of cards show up there's nothing stopping a bunch of power up cards appearing on the other side of the battlefield while a bunch of auto-skill activation cards appear on your side when you have a team that has little benefit from these cards. Auto-skills are a nice way to simplify some classes but if you're unlucky and they never activate then you can be left with a dead weight unit who can't do their job, sure buff card skills exist to increase the change to activate these skills but the cards themselves are subject to RNG. Another weird and honestly unwelcome addition is a slight randomisation to the stats gained from levelling up, it's not like Fire Emblem where you can get a garbage level where you only get +1 luck but you have a chance to gain an extra point in some stats. I don't know the full extent of this but I have tested it by feeding EXP charms to a level 1 units all the way to level cap, writing their stats down, reloading and doing it again only to find there is some variance across all of their stats. This isn't a major issue and most players aren't even going to notice it but for idiot min-maxers (such as myself) this is rather booty blasting.- Something that many complained about in the PSP version was how luck based the drop system was for endgame items and they didn't change this in Reborn. When hunting for relics there is no indication of which enemy will drop them and they aren't guaranteed to drop the item. This wouldn't be that bad but in the Palace of the Dead if you don't refer to a guide you may miss a lot of these on your way down. Honestly they should've gone with the system from The Knight of Lodis. In that game some units had rare/unique items and you could see these by checking their inventory and they also had a 100% chance to drop these items/spells. This is a simple but effective way to indicate how to obtain rare items because players will figure out after killing a couple of these units that the rare items will always drop.- Random battles being removed may sound nice to reduce tedium but without them recruiting non-humans has become much harder, they could've just made it so training battles are possible outside of towns with the possibility of recruiting monsters, reptiles etc.- Elemental charms have class restrictions but you can just ignore some of these restrictions. For instance Wizards can't become Dark but you can make them into Terror Knights, make them Dark and them switch back to Wizard. Some classes are also locked into Dark and even force you into Dark upon changing into them.- Rogue being made an AI only class was reportedly done for AI optimisation (I can only guess that the AI didn't know how to use steal or traps) yet mages clearly have unoptimised AI but remain in the gameThe Ugly:- The character sprites. I'm not going to argue whether they are upscaled or redrawn but they just don't look as good as the sprites from the older releases.Mixed:- The English voice acting, Arycelle and Tartaros are notably worse than the other voice actor's delivery in my opninion. I dislike Arycelle's voice and Tartaros' voice doesn't fit with his character.- The AI was advertised as being smarter and while some things about it do improve its chances against the player (like bosses not blindly charging into your army allowing you to beat the map in 5 minutes) some things about it just don't work (AI mages REFUSE to use status spells, you can give them no equipment and only status magic and they'll choose to punch the enemy over trying to use status spells)- While I do like that the bloat from the PSP version is gone only having 4 slots for skills and spells is rather limiting. One skill slot will be used for a weapon skill on 90% of characters, for double attackers and mages another slot is taken to even make them usable.- Class balance is better than in the PSP version and in combination with the return to unit levelling I found myself using a bunch of different classes throughout my playthrough, however some classes were nerfed a bit too much in my opinion: Archers are fine against squishy units but they deal laughable damage to front-line units, not just Knights but even classes like Beast Tamer just shrug arrows off. In addition to having a lot of their flexibility taken away, Mages are reliant on Meditate activating to actually be usable for a decent part of the game. Even then you may need to bring an MP restoration item on them in case your luck is abysmal so you don't have a unit just sitting around twiddling their thumbs. Clerics suffer from the previous problem but their almost non-existent.- The level cap does prevent people from just steamrolling the game but I wish it had a smoother curve.

_childDocuments_.review: So I never played Let Us Cling Together, but i did put literally HUNDREDS of hours in Tactics Ogre The Knight of Lodis. I did in my false reality want THAT game again, that nostalgia. Though after seeing many months of views I knew It wouldn't be and that was ok. Just something at least for myself because I loved Tactics.Story so far is what I imagine to have happened to this war torn continent. With some of the usual twist and turns but you probably are not recruiting people or finding the hidden treasures throughout. Unless you're reading a guide right away. So it'll take a couple play throughs to discover them all.Even though they did say they revamped the AI, god are they dumb as rocks. You can set AI of attacker, defender, mender, etc only after a few missions in of your characters, BUT you can't change the guests (or I'm just dumb and missed that)? Either way the guests go in guns blazing and will burn through any items unknowingly gave them. They then run away, maybe use a spell on themselves and then run back in. Then they wash repeat till they either die (shift out) or you win. The enemy AI also likes to single target/bully, which is a fine play style of a computer to do. I single out the weakest, divide and conquer and win.The lvl capping though sounded interesting but then when you see it in action, it's just kinda, dumb. In Lodis the enemy I found out would be based off of your MC. So after beating the game and redoing the whole thing, I made sure he didn't level. Ever. I wouldn't even put him in the training grounds and just maxed my other characters out. Power overwhelming a bit. However because you are capped you just do training mode a few times with AI controls and boom, you're done. Though if you really want to min max skills, you stay even longer in the training grounds to max abilities. Since you are capped in exp it turns into exp charms for later use. Though it is pointless when you just go and stay in the training areas anyway to max skills. Which they take a lot longer than easily leveling up. So far I have not used a single one. Also with training modes characters sometimes shout out something when they use an ability. There's no way to remove this? So if you want to just auto battle while you read, youtube, ♥♥♥♥ off, you need to always look back every once in a while to click it away so the battle continues. Training mode battles usually also tend to be the same enemy and bonus objectives so nothing random/unique about them sadly.Along with leveling they did take out one of the best features ever I think in an RPG from Lodis. The 99 hidden skill cards. This was amazing, you only could create a Valkyrie if they had the card from using a spear against two units. This did add to grinding at times to get the right cards to create the right class like Angels where you had to have your character die then be rezzed but then it offered also bonuses and negatives depending on the card. Now you just find a card and make a class. Where's the fun in discovering!?With the random encounter taken off, good and bad things occur. Money seems tighter. Sure you can auction monsters (haven't done it) and sell your junk, but what if you use it for something? Good because if you are trying to just go through main story as fast as possible, nothing will slow you down.Combat is really fun, exactly what I wanted in my nostalgia. The top down view is a nice touch, though I think even in Knights of Lodis, there was a 4 point camera swivel. They did also add a feature for casting/bows/range for a path of attack, which is really nice because then you can really know or not if an attack will hit with like 99% accuracy.If you are complaining about the price, idk, just wait till christmas or use gmg? You'll always find deals. Though at 50 I know I will sink many hours into this and sequential play throughs to find the loot, the people to recruit and all the endings.Biggest gripe would be the the buff cards and the green cards. Buff cards make it just as it sounds, buffs you. I find it distracting and not very tactical. You come into the battle with what you are given and learn. This just adds training wheels to characters that can steam roll with 4x attack buffs. Then the green cards which add permanent stats to characters when you pick up are up to the RNG gods to give you something you want. I've only seen two drop and I only snagged one while the enemy got the other. Cool. The one I did get was more MP to a character who didn't really need more mana. They did switch abilities to be just MP based but I would've rather had more of another stat.While it may sound like I'm just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and moaning, I still like this game and needed a nice tactical itch with some nostalgia. Next play through I'll see about characters and loot, but not endings.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic iteration on one of the top 3 tactical RPG's of all time.This is the best version of Tactics Ogre by far.I am a long time fan, played it at least a dozen times on PS1, and played it a couple of times on PSP.I was disappointed by the PSP version, felt like it tried too hard to be FFT when tactics ogre has perfectly stood up on its own against FFT forever.This version dials it back a little, while keeping some of the novelty the PSP remake brought.The only real complaint I have is how they smoothened the sprites, and that is not togglable.9.5/10 remake, will play it again and again.A few complaints I've seen and my answers:-"This is not like FFT, why not make it more like FFT?"TO has always stood on its own and was always more based on characters' raw stats and face to face crossing of swords. Magic, huge skills and such were never part of TO's pedigree. There are some in this remake, but they've been dialed back a fair bit. Overall, the entire package is more reminiscent of the original TO, while bringing some modern sensibilities to it.-"Characters can only equip 4 spells!"Tough luck man, on the ps1, if classes could equip 1 spell, it was pretty pog, mages could equip 2~4 in the very end-game. This feels a lot more in line with TO.-"Enemies are damage sponges!"If you chip away on a 1000HP health pool on an armored knight with piercing weapons, that's on you brother. Moreover, there's plenty of high impact moves designed to drop huge chunks of HP. Try using a warrior with mighty blow and a crushing weapon ? Things like that. In short, there are damage types, and it's advantageous to use the appropriate damage type against the appropriate armor.-"Archers are useless!"They were actually waaay too strong prior to this version. They've toned that back to balanced levels. I run two archers, they take potshots every turn, while they don't do high impact shots, the damage racks up quick. That's not even counting the huge hits they can land on caster classes.-"Rune Fencers/Valkyries are op!"Yeah, they absolutely are, especially compared to original TO. >.>They absolutely still feel balanced, though ? They are reliable fighters on all fronts, but if you overextend with them, it gets dangerous fast for their survival.-"Healers are useless!"They aren't, healers can land pretty big heals when everything works in your favor considering it costs no resources to heal with them. If you want big lifesaving heals, you need items, but that costs resources.-"I can't carry my class skills between class changes!"That has always been a FFT thing, leveling multiple classes to make one OP package. Never was what TO is about, although you could level a character in one class that has better stats, and then class change. I'm fine with this, I'm fine with this game requiring me to think a little rather than grind my way to an easy victory.-"The party level system is too restrictive! I can't grind as much as I want!"I mean, if you always grind to the max level you can, you'll be overleveled for content anyways. Grinding more would remove the necessity to think tactically and would remove all challenge from the game. And with how fast grinding is in this iteration, you'd be level 50 within hours. The original required you to throw stones between your characters for days to get to 50 lol, it was really thankless and boring, yeah, you could grind your way to max level really early, but that sapped your soul and your will to live. I'd much rather have this. :P

_childDocuments_.review: If you like turn-based strategy games with a solid political plot I highly recommend it.The game paints a very gray and blurry line of what is right or wrong. There are almost no characters, among ally and foe, who are 'villains'. You will encounter all sort of people, those driven by selfishness, and those driven by duty, and see how both of these when taken to an extreme can lead to some hard times.The game through dialogues and events will add a flavor of philosophy as to what is the right way to rule over a people, without any answer to the question. Your choices in the game will simply outline one possible outcome of how things can develop.One of my favorites from the PS-X era. Thoroughly enjoyed the story and this newer version has added a several features to  make the game a bit more challenging when navigating the main plot.Several improvements that have been added to this version of the game:* removed a lot of unnecessary grinding that was introduced in the psp version which is a huge bonus. They also added a bit of a speed-up to the auto-skill animations, a small boon.* added some nice end-game features that allow you to replay the plot with different dialogue options without replaying the whole game. * simplified the crafting system with the option to auto-craft any missing components if able. This really reduces the menu toil that had to be dealt with in the PsP version* Added relics that can be pamped for some end-game contentSome not so great feature they have added imo:* new card system that randomly spawn throughout the map and grant various boosts. I personally don't like this system as it makes either your or enemy units fairly strong, for not particular reason other than you were lucky to be within range of the card, or often bosses just start with them already acquired.* spell drop rates are much lower it seems, and the system is changed from the original such that now you need upgraded spells in order for them to deal more damage or increase their area-of-effect. Originally this was driven by a unit's intelligence stat. You will eventually be able to buy almost all spells beside a few that you will need to trawl dungeons for, so it is a minor thing.* they carried over from the psp version 2 new elements lightning and ice, but they are wholly unnecessary and don't add anything new to the game (imo).* removed the water healing spell, which I liked using on my main character, and my lizard folk as they can't use holy magic otherwise :(.Some neutral changes:* removed elemental status effect spells, and effectively just grouped them all in the dark element category. This makes things simpler and doesn't have much bearing on the game other than improving balance a bit and encouraging usage of Beasts if one wants an AoE petri-burst effect.* added new elemental spells geared towards Shaman class, these spells do more damage but imo weren't particularly necessary.* removed access to the rogue class for player owned units - admittedly stealing is not as necessary as it used to be in the PsP version.One of my favorite features of the game is that you can recruit enemy units you encounter, just gotta bash their head in till the brink of death first (naturally). But through this process you can form a Lizard-Race army, an undead army lead by Liches and Necromancers, and a beast army consisting of Dragons and other beasts.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the hell out of Let Us Cling Together as a kid and have never forgotten how much fun I had. I put off buying this because the reviews complained about difficulty and about all of the changes from the original, but eventually I got a strong craving and got it on sale.Let me be clear: this game is not simple. The level cap is a great change which creates a difficulty curve that can't be bypassed through brute force, taking you from Pokemon to an actual game that adults can enjoy without arbitrary restrictions. I've used training only to catch up niche characters that I need for a specific fight (second Cleric before an undead fight, for example) and to level up weapon skill.However, if you have any background in tactical RPGs, the game is not overly difficult. I could definitely see how someone new to the genre would be super overwhelmed because there are tons of mechanics that take time to learn, but otherwise, I think this version of the game does a really great job of providing a real challenge that requires strategy and foresight without forcing you to painstakingly map out every potential path in advance. I've had several battles where the enemy forces my hand and makes me pivot my strategy mid-battle which is such a great feeling - I have to react to what the game is throwing at me, understand my outs and decide which of my characters are key to closing out the end of the battle. And something that I think is perhaps lost on a lot of people is that half of the battle takes place outside of combat. You have to take time to reinforce your small army, make sure that they're all stocked up with the best equipment. You get to cover your weaknesses with varying classes and elements, try out different team compositions, prepare for a variety of different types of fights. If you jump into each combat without making any adjustments and expect the same 10 characters to get you through to the end of the game, you're really going to struggle.The story is so rich, and the Warren Report allows you to explore the world, dive deeper into each character and get a backstory to even the most trivial of one-off bosses. The choices that you make throughout the game are at times gut-wrenching, and I found myself more than once regretting a past decision based on the way that other characters interacting with mine and the subsequent decisions I was forced to make. This is quite possibly my favorite game of all time and undoubtedly my favorite franchise. I'm sure it's not for everyone, but if you like tactical RPGs, in my opinion this is the greatest among them. I'd give a kidney to get another game in the series, and until then, I'll gladly keep playing through this one until I've seen multiple endings.

_childDocuments_.review: The current incarnation of this review is an update to a previously negative review that I personally considered "mixed", which I will occasionally call back to when discussing the game's flaws.Tactics Ogre is an incredible game by any measure. Akihiko Yoshida's artwork is a joy to look at, the soundtrack highlights the experience, the characters are interesting and the gameplay is thoroughly strategic.In many ways, "Reborn" is a great way for old and new players to experience the game for the first time or replay a timeless classic. The addition of fully voiced dialogue elevates this complex narrative to new heights, combined with the option for top-down view, removal of random encounters and a variety of cards littered about the battlefield which provide buff and debuff modifiers to characters that collect them, Tactics Ogre Reborn makes it difficult to name any previous incarnation as a superior version.However, rather oddly as a modern remaster, Tactics Ogre Reborn does not feature any difficulty or Accessibility options for players not keen on new systems or the game's overall difficulty. Further, Reborn goes out of its way to introduce the "Union Level" system, which caps the max level for player units very low until it is raised incrementally at various points in the game. This means that players can no longer simply out level their opponent's unit and are forced to fight on equal ground, or worse. Much of my initially negative review relates to the decision of introducing the Union Level and how that affects the experience as a new player unfamiliar with the game. I found myself genuinely stuck when confronting Oz and his knights at Boed Fortress, unable to progress as his forces simply overwhelmed mine time and time again. I was only able to just barely defeat him due to a lucky combination of his AI making bad decisions and recruiting a dragon to my party as a damage sponge.Depending on who you are, the previous section might sound unbearable to you, or perhaps it'll make you even more intrigued in the way that the game truly asks you to consider all of the options at your disposal in creating a competent party. However, as a newcomer to the genre primarily seeking to experience the game's narrative, I found the added lengths I had to go to just to progress to be an unnecessary chore, largely because of the new level-caps imposed by the Union Level at various points in the game.How did I overcome this? I modded the game of course, and circumvented the Union Level system. Without it, the game feels much easier to pick up and play for beginners while still offering those hard hitting options while building your team for those who want to make the most of everything. removing the Union Level makes this game a lot closer to the PSP version, which this remaster is based on. While not everybody will require mods to enjoy their experience with TO:R, those who would like the ability to level-up more freely in response to challenges may want to consider downloading them.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface by saying that I loved Tactics Ogre: The knight of lodis on GBA, it will go down in history as one of my favorite games ever. There was something magical and brilliant about it. The different story lines, an early game where your choices mattered, and you could develop your characters into something awesome, that you could be proud of.I would sum up my experience with Tactics ogre: Reborn primarily as IRRITATING which is why, even though it is a reasonably good game, I can't recommend it. It lacks the magic and brilliance of it's predecessors. Let me share a few of my irritations and let you decide for yourself. I don't write a lot of reviews and I wanted to wait until I beat the game to write this one, so I have completed the main story successfully and there are some spoilers in here.Irritations:1. The terrain - much of the irritation in battles is created by the terrain, not because it's cool and interesting, but because it's in the way and annoying. Some units can step in water, others can't, some can fly others can't and levels where you have to get around terrain that's in your way don't make for an interesting tactics game, it's just in the way.2. Level caps - part of the fun of tactics games is training your units to become something great, levels caps make this impossible. The last boss is massively overpowered and all you can do is play over and over again until you find the right combination that wins, not level them up so they are better. This is randomness, not tactics/strategy.3. Class system - This is honestly really boring, the classes are what made games like FF Tactics and Tactics ogre stick out, collecting things in battle to change from one boring class to another is not fun. I got to the Lord class with my main character and it was so anti-climactic. 4. Final boss/level - Sooooo long if you don't find the secret door and speaking of the secret door, that's an entirely new mechanic that never existed anywhere else in the game previously. Plus the final boss is overpowered, not in a "that was a great challenge" sort of way, but in a "this game is stacked against me" sort of way. By playing your characters against you and removing key mechanics in the game (inability to raise your units again, characters taking mp damage) after a long road where you have no ability to buy new equipment, prepare or use all of the things that you earned in the long road up. Irritating and disappointing.5. Beasts - I'm sure there are ways to make this exciting and maybe I didn't but I was really underwhelmed with the beasts I recruited and there didn't seem to be a way to make it more exciting. It was such a catch to recruit certain things in previous tactics ogre games and that excitement just wasn't there.There are a lot more irritations but these are the main ones and by the time I got to the end, I just wanted to be done, not because it was so fun, but because the end just dragged out forever.Good things:Plot as always is excellent and so is the voice actingWeapons and creation system is funI disagree with the people that say it's too hard, I think the beginning and the end are overly and unfairly difficult but most of the middle is just normal. I only had to retry a few battles. I love tactics games, it's pretty much all I play and I liked this game, but there were just too many things about it to let me recommend it. Overall, not a good representation of the genre or the brand, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: As some have said before, this release is one step forward and two steps back from previous iterations of this title. This iteration is a very fun, but very flawed gem. It was worth my $50 wholeheartedly, but that endorsement comes with a number of caveats.I think the voice acting they've added to this game is frankly incredible, and really helps to sell the quasi-elizabethan translation. Additionally, I think the randomly spawning field card system adds an interesting risk/reward mechanic for enemy asset denial or powering up your units has to be carefully weighed against your ability to command that part of the field. In other words, I feel like the game's difficulty is appropriate; especially when a risky strategy plays off in your favor. The game encourages creative, off the cuff strategies that can sometimes pay off, sometimes go horribly awry. I think they were attempting to emulate the reported chaos of a battlefield, and IMHO, the attempt worked. There is an "edge of the seat" quality to this game that isn't commonly replicated in other titles in the SRPG genre. The AI has also gotten a lot better when compared to previous releases. The enemy makes sensible decisions in who to prioritize when attacking based on proximity and their defensive position. They also attempt to monopolize strategic positions, such as choke points or high grounds. The new AI adds a great deal of nuance to scenarios which used to be pretty cheesable through gimmicky strategies.However, the attempt to streamline mechanical character development is not to my taste. I have played LUCT PSP all the way through on the chaos route, and partially through the SNES release of this title. Both have a level of depth that I don't think that this one shares, unfortunately. I really miss being able to mix abilities and skills between characters. This title eschews that in favor of having a restrictive 4 skills equippable for each character with nothing transferable between classes. But this is usually only three skills for most classes because a weapon skill, necessary for all physical hitters, has to take up one of the four slots available. While this does force the player to develop and experiment with a diverse host of characters and abilities throughout the game, it feels stifling when one became accustomed to the freedom of character development in previous iterations of this title. At the very least, weapon skills should have been their own thing that doesn't take up a skill slot. Character development and theorycrafting around character development is one of the best things about SRPGs, and this game really dropped the ball in this department. That isn't to say development strategies and theorycrafting are unimportant in this iteration; they're just a lot less fun than they used to be. There has been a lot of criticism levied at the "union level" or intermittently increasing level cap between story events. I can appreciate its implementation, and I feel like it has its place. However, I feel like its imposition should be the "hard mode" option of the game. There have been a number of people in the community saying that there should be an easier method of dealing with this game's myriad challenges, and making the union level optional would be an elegant way of doing so. This is especially true when some of the game's encounters have enemies that are a couple levels higher than you can possibly be during that fight, which is a pretty big deal in this game. Finally, the equipment and level scaling of your team when using the "world tarot" or the ability to go back in time to previous story events is really irritating. Let me opt into the level scaling rather than forcing it upon me. Sometimes I just want to see the story, not get neutered after finally feeling like I've accumulated some measure of power. I don't get the point of end-game grinding if what effectively serves as a new-game plus prevents a general sense of progression.Here are a few tips for those that are struggling:1) Read the Warren Report intermittently to open up optional, repeatable map locations and sidequests.2) Get a winged beast master (preferably with lobbing, wading gear, and poison gauntlets and empower beast) and some gryphons/cockatrices to crowd control/offtank/status effect the back enemy lines.  This will effectively destroy their support system and throw their formation into chaos. 3) Each set of equipment has its own advantages. I found weapons with status effects were far more valuable than other weapons that hit harder. Enemies in this game are pretty tanky, so being able to whittle away their HP over time or stunlock them (or both!) goes a long way. Huge damage dealing through weapons is usually achieved through finishers anyway, so it's better to have diminished damage from an individual hit if it means that doing so effectively cripples the enemy before they can release the same on you. 4) Tanks with rampart aura are better used to divide and restrict enemy movement rather than protect a cleric.5) Clerics are absolutely worthless after the early mid-game. Healing magic does basically nothing and their inclusion in a party creates a huge team-wide liability when the name of the game is to divide and conquer enemy forces. Their only conceivable usecase is as an exorcism bot for undead enemies, but exorcisms can be done with a relatively cheap item that you can equip if you scout a map beforehand. You're better off with some kind of back rank saboteur with crowd control and healing items.

_childDocuments_.review: You sit at the screen, contemplating whether to buy this RPG. Your butt is itchy. You scratch it. There are so many games like this already... why even bother? I have so many games to play already...1. It's priced reasonably, and the sprites are kinda cute. Let's try it.2. Eh, pass. I'll go replay Pillars of Eternity or something (reinstalls League of Legends). If you took the first choice, you're ready to spend 30-50 hours on a storyline with memorable characters, deep quests, meaningful decisions like the one you just took, and an epic soundtrack. It's FFT's edgier cousin. When I played the prequel to this, Knight of Lodis (my first TO title) I thought using a mermaid as bait was messed up. In this remake of Let Us Cling together you're deciding what war crimes you want for breakfast. Want to keep playing post-campaign? There's dozens... maybe even hundreds of post-game material. I'm just now skimming the surface. Don't believe me on the soundtrack? Check out "Chivalry and Savagery" on Youtube. Or even the titular "Tactics Ogre Symphonic Suite". Let's say you took the second choice and regret your decision to jump back into Solo Queue. Or maybe you went (1) but want another chance at recruiting another character. After you beat the game you can go back and replay parts of the game. It's not a re-do, it is in addition to the game you've already experienced. Forget Cloud and Sora... you become a veritable timeline traveler Michael J. Fox would be proud to share a Delorian with, or wear a pair of pants fashioned from a material of your namesake. Some reviews complain about simplification of combat. All you're really missing is the facing of your characters mattering more for accuracy. You'll hit most of the time, and so will your enemies. They also made some of the end-game characters less Herculean to recruit. If that's the worst thing they changed in this reboot of a classic I still would have traded my Gameboy Color, Skip-it, guinea pig, and Razor Scooter for to have played in the 90's (yeah, I didn't own a PSP in 2011- I was in college) and still played it again on the PC. My own personal criticisms are just nit-picking some of the storylines. There are a couple of instances where minor phrasing deeply impacts certain characters in big ways, and without a little research it's nigh impossible to recruit some. The Wheel of Fortune go-back mechanic fixes some of this, but with over 100 levels of Palace of the Dead alone I just can't be bothered to go back at this point. Second, the last actually new Tactics Ogre game released was Knight of Lodis for the Gameboy Advance in the mid 00's. I really hope we get that remake next (the soundtrack is even better and the story even cooler, though I understand playing this game first kind of spoils that one), or Philaha-forbid a new TO game. Less of a critique and more a desperate plea for more. I will be buying the soundtrack, partially to force the continuous loop of Chivalry and Savagery out of my head by playing it 80 more times and partially to show Square Enix I am ready to continue to drop Gil... crap I mean dollars... denarii? Is it really just gold? okay, gold... on this franchise. I give it 9 out of 10 glass pumpkins.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's how to win at Tactics Ogre Reborn:1. Unlock the Ninja class2. Equip them with a 1-handed katana in each hand and the corresponding skill3. Equip the Double Attack skill4. Equip the Back Attack skill5. Cast Leaping Monkey6. Cast Waterstep7. Set your party's AI to Fierce Attacker8. Fall asleep on the keyboard9. Wake up, collect spoilsSeriously, who thought giving Ninjas all of these skills was a good idea? The first 1-handed katana Finishing Move that you learn has a massive range of 5 squares, only costs 40mp, ignores terrain, ignores elevation and pierces walls.Leaping Monkey lets you ignore elevation, meaning that those archers on top of the castle are in for a nasty surprise.Waterstep lets you walk on water. Half of the maps in the game have water in them. Under normal circumstances, water is a challenging obstacle, slowing down your entire army and acting as natural barriers, forcing you to take the scenic route. However, with Waterstep you can waltz over the river or pond like Naruto.To further illustrate how absurdly effective Waterstep is, I went through all 100 floors of the Palace of the Dead. 99 of those floors were either dry or had water in them, and only the 100th floor had lava!In addition to all of this, ninjas can also cast elemental attack magic. As if that weren't enough, they can also directly debuff enemies, directly buff allies, and even go so far as to magically enhance weapons with poison, silence or stunning effects that debuff enemies even more!Why are there other classes in this game?

_childDocuments_.review: Never played the original but played the hell out of Final Fantasy Tactics, so going into this somewhat blind but wanted more of that style of game. At a first glance there are a lot of similarities - fights looks similar, class system, focus on story, similar music but after some more gameplay the faults show more:Leveling system was my biggest gripe. You think the "party level" aka limiting the party based on story battles is there to give some balance and challenge, but the problem is how quickly you level and max your level only to go into a story fight and the enemies all have one or two on you. Then, you go through one or two or three more battles and its the same but you get no experience so you start to just grind the story fights and these fights tend to be just small side stories with side characters. You just want to fly through the filler fights.Due to the leveling system, if you get a new class and a new weapon skill sayyyy katanas, then you have to start with a higher level character and a level 1 skill. Now, you have to grind to get that skill up but you cant just do it through the story battles especially if you're already max. Speaking of katanas... when they become available, you have crafting unlocked so now, the crafting items are just better than regular store items. Every shop has the same items. I don't see the point in having other towns and fields and such when they serve no purpose - you get the same from one town.Recruitment is encouraged but almost pointless due to again, level caps and weapon skills starting from one. Do you want your knight with a couple weapon skills(though not maxed) and crafted gear, or another knight with standard gear, only one weapon skill but slightly better stats? Its really not worth the trouble.I stopped somewhere into chapter 3 and 40hrs into the game - between chapter 1 and 3 you only get a couple new classes, so learn to love em early. Not much variety there. OH you want some new abilities? Well you're level locked. OH maybe a new spell? sorry locked by story progress and when they are available, theyre at all the stores, no unique or creative ways of getting them just... keep slogging on through story fights.Music got very repetitive, I swear fights only have one song, couldn't there have been a slight tonal shift or a different upbeat song idk man something else.The one thing that does stand out to me is the choices that change the story - thats a fun feature that had me wanting to see alternate versions but I was just so drawn down by the fight lengths and the time it takes to drone through the game, I couldn't be bothered to pursue it.***Overall, it just got old and tedious. I enjoyed some fights but it feels very not rewarding when you finish a big fight and its like, no new classes, no new abilities/spells, no new items, just 3-5 more story fights and thats where the road ends so maybe you'll get more. Or maybe after you'll get some actual story and like 10 new items(maybe one or two for half the classes), no new classes, 2 more levels to get but then more slogging on AND the next battle have opponents who are two levels above yours so to pass you have to grind - yet again, you end up capped though and just have to push push push. Now, apparently the level lock was introduced with the remake and to me it just ruins any potential for forward progress. IDK the balance changes that were made but with lack of classes/items and therefore lack of complexity/diversity of the team members, it just feels dull. I hate to compare it back and forth with FFT but it just seems like that game did what this game did and took it further. I know that game too has its faults but you can explore character builds and the game rewards gameplay, and there is more depth of story(an explanation), the music is done better, even the maps are better. I tried to push through and I wanted to like this but I couldn't do it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played most popular strategy rpgs. Does this game have a few minor flaws? Yes. Would I recommend it? Absolutely. All the haters saying the level cap ruins things are completely missing the point. The level cap is genuinely a brilliant mechanic and I would love to see it in every strategy rpg I play (except maybe something like Disgaea--it wouldn't fit there due to that game series' identity being focused on the grind). It stops you from overleveling and trivializing battles. This cap, combined with the lack of needing to level skills--barring weapon skill which are pretty chill and not super important to have maxed asap--means you aren't sitting in a map for hours grinding out any kind of experience for your characters. It's a huge breath of fresh air compared to the norm of many other strategy rpgs where characters don't feel usable until you've grinded out necessary levels and skills on them; whenever you pick up a new story char you can just run with them immediately. For this alone I'd recommend it, but there's much more to love that you can find out for yourself (or read about in other reviews).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great blast from the past.  The changes to "to make the game retain some challenge" per the developers is more of a cheat code for the CPU than anything else.  Apparently you could over-level your characters in previous versions and steam roll the game -- which, I have no problem with.  It has a weird level limiter to try to add "challenge" to the game.  Its a stupid fix to a "problem" that's not really a problem.  Its more frustrating than anything.  Half the fun of games like this is vastly out leveling the enemy and then smashing them to pieces.  This creates some really radical difficulty spikes where the player is forced into a weird harrowing turtling strategy to pick off the enemies rather than a more advanced and aggressive strategy.  Though the story is engrossing, its pointless as there is a nasty battle somewhere in the Chaos route of Chapter three where the game has kept you at level 19 for the past ten battles, decides it'll be a "challenge" to put you up against 15 guys four of them golems with 1000 HP each that can wreck a standard 12-person PC party pretty quickly.  Mind you, the boss of the level is heavily armored and requires some sort of insane strategy to take them down between the golems, wizards, and two clerics making a terrible mess of things.  But the game would be too easy if it let you over-level your characters -- which is kinda the point of these "Tactics games" in the first place -- so here, have a frustrating battle that sucks the fun out of everything and brings the game to a grinding halt.  The level locking is just some artificial non-sense that just makes this a terrible game in the end.  Which is sad, because its fun up until the third chapter.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre is, without a doubt, a classic in the genre of turn-based tactics. The story is of high quality, mature, and full of human characters. It features a lot of opportunity for the player to make moral choices within its narrative, and the story morphs and changes around the player's decisions. Additionally, the tactical combat is top-notch, offering a great deal of challenge and rewarding sound tactics with victory.That being said, Tactics Ogre did always exhibit some flaws. Friendly AI, in particular, has always been atrocious. Guest units will, infamously, charge suicidally into the fray, with zero regard for the way their units ought to behave, or what support they have available to them in the form of allied units. Cistina is infamous for this very early on, as is Arycelle—an Archer—who seems to push forward regardless of where the party is situated. Catiua, herself, will often choose to push forward and melee attack enemies, puzzlingly, considering she is a back-line healer. Reborn, like Let Us Cling Together before it, has done nothing to solve these AI issues.The changes Reborn does make are to systems that, frankly, didn't need changing. Reborn most notably completely neuters something the classic Tactics Ogre did wonderfully: The ability to tactically grow units and shape them as you see fit via the learning and assignment of skills through experience and fruitful grinding and class change planning. Reborn has completely removed the ability of the player to learn specific skills for its units, instead locking everything behind class. The only agency the player now has over these units is to change their class and equipment and assign which 4 skills of the class they wish the unit to equip. Skills, additionally, are now extremely limited to only 4 slots. All of this, presumably, has been done in the name of "streamlining", which caters to players newer to the genre and series at the expense of the extreme and, in my opinion, excellent variability of the original game. The deeper features of creating powerhouse units with the skills the player sees fit has been completely ripped from the game, leaving the player feeling rather helpless and rendering the game's characters far more generic than they were before. All the player really has available, now, is to do training battles and raise the units' levels. The game now manages all skill growth automatically, which is an unfortunate loss of a huge amount of the original game's complexity and the agency it provided its player to sculpt their team of units, and what made the game truly great.Being able to grind and develop a unit's skillset is what makes these games so addictive. There's no longer any fun to training or grinding, as all satisfaction in developing your characters when their abilities are nearly all but set for you from the outset. All passive abilities now trigger automatically and automatically applied to the character by RNG at the start of their turn.In addition to this, Reborn has added a card system, pumping up RNG and adding an unacceptable element of chance to the game. There's already a decent amount of RNG at play with hitrate, why do we need cards? Some of these cards, when gained early on, can make for a snowballing effect on one side or another, effectively removing agency from the player to dictate the outcome of the battle via tactics. I wish there was a way to disable cards entirely. They feel far too gamey for my tastes and the genre of turn-based tactics, in general, already suffers from too much RNG in the first place, in my opinion.The game has also been significantly altered regarding HP levels. There is significant health bloat that begins to appear as you get later into the game, which is an odd design choice.These changes should have been offered as an option, if they were offered at all. I would greatly relish the opportunity to turn features such as streamlined leveling and cards off and play the game in a sort of "classic mode" instead of having everything macromanaged for me and having to drive for card drops. Additionally, I found the "union level cap" to be a dreadful addition, requiring a grind battle here and there for very little tangible reward for the player. They may as well have just removed training altogether if they were going to streamline the grinding experience so much. Grinding has gone from a thoughtful activity and an enjoyable, rewarding part of the game to an experience to one in which the player will just turn AI on for each unit, set the battle speed up, and go AFK for five minutes until the battle is finished and their units to gain a level. It's busywork. There's very little player agency involved in growing units whatsoever. Simply choose a class and let the game do it for you.  — Reborn is effectively an exercise in fixing what isn't broken. The PSP's Let Us Cling Together is still the definitive way to play this game.Why are we adding these cards? What, exactly, do they add to the game? There's enough chance already built-in. And further, unit building was one of the game's strengths, why alter it at all? And why leave if we're making such drastic changes to the core experience, why aren't we altering the infamously poor friendly AI? Why do units now have thousands and thousands of HP? The story is still worthwhile, but the rest of the changes from Let Us Cling Together have been almost entirely for the worse.Seeing such a disservice done to a turn-based tactics classic makes me extremely worried for the same treatment to potentially be visited upon Final Fantasy Tactics. 🧾 Feel free to follow  if you like my reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: An update done right. Well written, well scored, excellent character artwork, and now well acted. Only held back by being a "tactics" game, a genre that never comes close to living up to the name and often stops respecting your time.All the years later this is still one of the best written games I've played with an excellent soundtrack and now with the added bonus of solid voice acting. Not always the most detailed plot or character building with the style of game not allowing as much conversations or cutscenes as something like a JRPG and with the limited time most characters get but so much of what is said is memorable and makes full use of the limited time and scenes that most characters have. With further world and character details available in written reports accessed on the main map that give you more details about events or the characters you have met or heard of, even detailing the pasts or actions of minor boss characters that show up for one fight, making the world feel more alive. The main character, Denam, is frequently given excellent lines and comebacks to the rest of the cast while also being one of the strongest voice actors. The plot deals with Denam, initially joined by his sister, friend, and characters from the previous game Ogre Battle: March of the Black Queen now saying they were banished from their kingdom, all fighting to free the leader of a minor oppressed clan of people in the Kingdom of Valeria. The Kingdom was once united in the past but is now made of different factions of clans fighting to rule over the Kingdom, all with the much more powerful Holy Lodissian Empire possibly looking to claim the territory for itself and with members of their Dark Knights working within Valeria. The Dark Knights being lead by the main character of the game Tactics Ogre: The Knight of Lodis who seems to have his own plans outside of the Lodissian Empire and of the nobles that he ingratiates himself with. Soon after being declared a hero of his faction Denam learns that neither the men he works for or fights against can be trusted to lead while learning more about the history of his nation, his sister's past, and the goals of the Dark Knights and the banished knights from the Kingdom of New Xenobia.There are minor to large plot differences and alternate scenes or potentially different battles and deployed boss characters depending on your path through the game, character deployed in battle, or if certain characters have joined you, died, been refused when they offer to join you, or if they desert or are let go from your army. The time traveling system made available after you complete the game once will allow you to travel back to other points in the game to get characters that you missed or to make different decisions to see how other paths play out. When you do this you will keep your characters, levels, and equipment and will play new battles with your level set to match the stages and your equipment weakened (though your skills, better unique characters, and late game equipment still having unique abilities will still see much easier battles). This allows you to see the game's other story paths much faster than by replaying the game and allows you to bring all the characters together that may have been locked to a particular route.While what is being said tends to always be very well written, there are issues with certain routes. The Chaos route is the best as everything makes sense, the plot fits together well, and everyone sticks to their characterizations. The neutral route is a path you can take after going one chapter in the Chaos route and is just kind of an odd path to choose to take (that almost no one does), you end up with the worst characters, a character important to the end game content dying, and characters rightly calling Denam out on his pathetic decision making. The Law route seems to often be held up as the best as it portrays you as a person more willing to do bad things to accomplish your goals and then struggling to accept and justify those decisions later. I did not at all find this to be true. The Law route had characters acting unlike themselves (sometimes in ways that should be wildly out of character) in Chapter 1, endings, and in other routes, Denam never really addresses or has any issues come up from his decisions and a side character tends to be the one having Denam's arc in conversations in other side content if you deploy him, Vyce is used poorly and then just cast aside, there are multiple plot/character inconsistencies from later dialogues or dialogue options you can choose, characters join you that shouldn't, and you miss some of the game's best conversations.There are a few character classes and monster types most people are unlikely to use but for the most part they do a good job in giving each class a role to fill or at least type of battlefield or a type of enemy unit they excel at being brought out for. They have removed the previously playable Rogue class from being a recruitable unit though. The new skill system is easy to use where all spells, active skills, and weapon finishers require MP to use. You can assign four item types (that will auto refill after battles if you have more of them), four spells (for units that can use them), and four class skills that include passive bonuses that can activate at the start of a turn, active skills you can use when you have enough MP (sometimes outside of your regular movement and attack action), and weapon skills. Your weapon skills level up when you have a weapon skill equipped and actively use that type of weapon or cast offensive spells, you get slightly more damage as it levels up and every ten levels you can use a new finisher special attack with that weapon type. The cap for your weapon skills and many of the passive skills strength increases naturally as your character levels up, higher level spells are eventually just sold from shops or found from completing certain side quests. This works well, though there are a few classes that feel like they really should have had one more skill slot, it probably would have been better if weapon skills were just assigned based on your equipped weapon. It almost seems like four is more of a limit because that's the space they gave it in the UI and not for any kind of balance reason, there will likely be times when you forget to swap in or out for a Clerics exorcism spell to use on regenerating undead or a dragoons two skills to fight dragons or two skills to fight beasts because you forget what is currently equipped.Default accuracy has been raised so high that the agility stat is even less important than it used to be and a few skills have been made pointless or only practical for certain situations, though with the still frequent blocks, deflections, and counters allowed by weapons and shields outside of to hit accuracy it is still possible to miss against certain character types or through inflicting status effects that lower accuracy. I feel like this makes the game play better from what I remember from past versions.There is a large amount of side and end game content, even outside of the differences to the three story paths, though a few of these are tedious grinds through massive dungeons that want you to complete the full things in one go. This is partially helped by being able to let the AI get through a lot of the stages for you. These areas allow you to acquire unique spells and weapons and items that have effects that normal equipment don't have that can do things like change your movement style by allowing characters to fly, float, teleport, or to walk on hazardous ground or allow you to cast spells or use abilities through your weapon.The main issues come from it being a Tactics style strategy game, which is just never a completely well made, balanced --Full Review:

_childDocuments_.review: Will stick with this for a while more, but disappointed in what I've seen so far. First off, I've played many hours of the original Tactics Ogre (not the PSP version) many years ago and I don't care for a number of the cosmetic and gameplay changes.  First thing I noticed was the way too smooth-looking sprites that almost always looks terrible but developers and publishers for the last dozen of years or so seem to love when re-releasing 2d pixel games.  Then there's the all-caps font that looks like it's pulled out of a comic book.  Even worse, the font is slanted for reasons beyond my understanding.  UI elements have a different, but very sterile and boring font.  Speaking of UI elements, they are all over the screen at all times and distracting.Gameplay-wise, why are all these cards just constantly appearing on the battlefield during turns?  This feels like gacha level stuff and very off-putting and out of place.  Yes, there were stat drop cards upon defeating enemies in the original but now cards just randomly show up on the battlefield because things need to be happening at all times or the level of player engagement will fall off or something.  There are also skills/finishing moves in this version that aren't in the original but I haven't played enough to have thoughts on them, but I'm guessing they're reason enemies have substantially more health in this version.  For example, in the opening fights, enemies in the original have around 60-80 HP, here they have 200-300.Also there seems to be name changes for name changes sake because localization felt the need to to show their worth to the project.  Tons of names from the original are taken from the Ars Goetia and now have stupid minor changes just cause.  There's stuff like Barbatos being changed to Balbatos and a ton of other r to l differences just to be different.  Seriously, if you were translating a game from jp to english and came across the characters for Barbatos, would you translate it as Barbatos or Balbatos?  What is this?  Also RIP to former Houston Oiler great Warren Moon.  I can't find the jp characters for his name to know if the new version is correct or not but I want to believe he was named after the quarterback.Thank you for reading my book report.edit: I miss the "Fight It Out" guy
