_childDocuments_.review: That Steam description is no lie: Tactics Ogre is one of the crown jewels of the tactical role-playing genre. And Reborn does introduce changes that improve upon the PSP release and would push the game towards greatness. Unfortunately, so many other changes of the game mechanics in the name of streamlining and game balance make this a  experience than the PSP version.The Good Parts:- Speedup feature is king, as always- New crafting is free of all hassles, fast and efficient (game will straight up buy missing materials for you to avoid having to make a checklist, it’s great. This is one of two changes I wanted for a remaster/rerelease.)- Voice acting is actually pretty good! The main trio of Denam, Vyce and Catiua are really solid imo. Leave it to Square Enix to upload the worst lines from the game (the infamous Lanselot Tartaros clip) in an attempt to sabotage the game pre-release. - Replacing the class-wide level system with a unit-by-unit level system like your average SRPG. The other change I wanted Reborn to have. No more getting a new character only to have to grind him for 20 levels to catch up with the rest of the main party.- Being able to see the trajectory of missile spells and arrows automatically sir yes sir oorah- Scout feature letting you actually see the battlefield and prepare accordingly is a godsend- Mouse and keyboard controls actually work really well what the heckThe Mixed:- The removal of random encounters, which were replaced with training. On one hand, no more random encounters means you don’t have to save and reload when you just wanna head from one place to the next on the map. On the other hand, this means you only have dungeons like the Phorampa Wildwood or the Pirate’s Graveyard to get money (which becomes irrelevant once you get the Baldur’s Blowgun recipe), recruit special races like lizardmen, dragons, etc. or correct your Chaos Frame because of course, which is only unlockable around chapter 2.- The Union Level cap, which is how the game caps your party’s max levels according to where you are in the story. Now, there have been complaints about the Union cap, but I don’t think it’s a bad idea . It serves to control the levels and stat bloat of not only your party members, but that of the enemies as well, which prevents you from growing overpowered, and were this the PSP release, it would reinforce the idea that equipment and skills are the difference makers, not simply being 10 levels above the enemy ranks. In practice is where the Union level falls apart. For one, it’s too restrictive: the cap is tied to the plot, but it increases in increments of 2 or 3 for every 4 or 5 battles. This means you’ll quickly hit your cap, waste potential experience and all the while, the enemies KEEP leveling ahead of you. Two, what I said about the Union level being a prime opportunity for skill mixing and customization? Well…The Bad:- The skill system was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ . For one, skill points are gone; skills are merely obtained through leveling, which, again, is capped. Second, all characters are now limited to 4 skill slots (and since you’ll always want your weapon skill equipped to be able to use finishers, this realistically leaves you with 3 skills). Finally, skills do  carry over from class to class (with one exception that’s unique to one character). I can’t stress enough how awful this is. Skills like Counterattack, Parry, etc. are either straight up removed or tied to equipment. No mixing and matching skills, no customization, nothing! “Theorycraft your way through endless combinations of classes, equipment, skills and magic” my ass! Speaking of;- Magic is ALSO limited to 4 spells per character, probably because Square Enix thought having more spells than you can count on one hand was too confusing for would-be players. Having mages use two elements (like having one guy with Dark spells for ailments and Water for some healing on the side, or giving every member of your team access to Fire spells to blast away at people with the same element) was cool, but there’s no way to do that now since, again, you only have 4 spell slots.- The removal of tactical points (TP) is such a questionable decision. In Let Us Cling Together, TPs were a third resource that could be used for skills and for finishing moves; spellcasters traded it for MP in the form of Meditate, and fighters used it for skills like Berserk, Phalanx, Fearful Impact, etc. In Reborn, TP was removed, and instead finishers consume MP (which means classes like Rune Fencers who get Meditate can spam them with impunity). As for the aforementioned skills like Phalanx (which knights used to get a 90% damage reduction until their next turn), Berserk (an integral part of the Berserker’s moveset that hits enemies in an AoE) and others? Well, it would simply make too much sense for them to require MP to use, so instead, Square went ahead and pulled off a brilliant move: they trigger *randomly*. Berserker never proccing the skill they were named after? In Reborn, it’s possible. Enemy knights triggering Phalanx four turns in a row and being untouchable? Sure enough, it can happen. Your mages not getting Meditate off and enemy mages getting it every turn? Hell yeah brother, cheers. It’s not enough that skills should be removed or neutered; tactical decisions like when to use one are also now stripped from you. Very cool!- The addition of buff cards. These things litter the battlefield and appear randomly to offer buffs like higher crit chance, better odds of triggering your random skills, higher damage, etc. These SUCK. Not only because they’re pure random, but because you have to go out of your way to grab them around the place and it kills the pace and the momentum of battles. No one wants to spend 3 turns going around gathering cards so your character can actually deal more damage. ♥♥♥♥’s bad! And not only that, but they went super lazy with this one by having every boss start with 4 buff cards right at the beginning of the battle, which strongly encourages you to use the same strategy for every fight: have two guys with lobbers throw debuff items at the enemy leader, then rush that ♥♥♥♥ down.- HP bloat is a ♥♥♥♥♥. You can find screenshots that compare the HP totals of enemies at certain stages in the game: we’re talking four to eight times the health compared to the PSP version, without upping the damage to compensate. Clerics also didn’t get a buff to their healing capacity, which means they are even worse than before because healing salves that you can easily buy at the store heal per percentage (50, 75 and 100%). - They removed the Rogue class because?There’s probably a lot more I didn’t mention like archers getting nerfed hard and the devs not fixing the potential issues that can arise from the WORLD system, like going through the whole-ass postgame dungeon only to realize you were on the wrong timeline and you wasted your time because you didn’t take the time to read up on the matter. Reborn is NOT the definitive edition of Tactics Ogre, which is a shame because it comes SO CLOSE but falls just short. A bittersweet experience overall.

_childDocuments_.review: This was one of the worst Strategy RPGs I've played unfortunately. It just has too many issues. There are no positives for me so here is my list of Cons.Level RestrictingYes you only have a maximum level of 25, which is lame, but that is not the issue. At every point in this game your level cap is artificially limited to a very low level and gradually expands as you play. It only ever takes 1-2 battles to reach every level cap, so 90% of the game you are playing at a capped level. You are always playing at exactly the level the devs want you to be, so why have levels at all? There is no overleveling, no grinding, basically a visual novel.Skills/Spells You can only ever equip 4 skills and 4 spells per character. 1-2 of the skill slots are taken up by a weapon so you can attack things, so really you only have 2 skills to try out per character. This is another way they artificially limit your power to keep you from getting too strong. There are tons of spells but you can only equip 4 so I don't see the point. I guess you are supposed to read a walkthrough and find out the resists/weaknesses of the next boss, and equip the right spells ahead of time. I can't be bothered with something like that. ControlsThis is why I ultimately quit this game. The controls just don't work and it's unfortunately very hard to describe. You attack or cast spells by clicking twice on an enemy, sounds simple but just doesn't work a lot of the time. Sometimes it will attack after clicking once, and sometimes it will attack a completely different square than the one you clicked on. Now I know it sounds like I'm just misclicking things but I've seen the cursor jump across the map after I very deliberately clicked on a square right in front of me, most the time it ends up with me attacking an ally or healing an enemy when that happens. And it does happen maybe 4-5 times per map. I should have used a controller to play, but I just don't care anymore. Guest CharactersThe game will dump characters in your party that the CPU controls, and sometimes if they die they will be gone for good. So every map is like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ escort mission. What this means is you have to forget any strategy you want to have for a map. You can spend time getting your archers and mages in position around your frontline units to draw the enemy in, only to have your guest characters beeline for the enemy group and immediately get surrounded by 5 enemies. If you want the guest characters to survive, you have to send everyone out as far as they can go every turn including your squishy healers in order for the guest idiots not to kill themselves.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played the older versions of this one, so I cannot really compare it to previous iterations.So far I've enjoyed the game, I'm probably somewhere around mid-game (Chapter 3 stuff) and while the game does have couple of issues, it's not something that breaks the game enough for me to not recommend it.The story has been interesting political drama with a mix of personal growth, building your roster has been pretty nice as it is fairly easy to catch up with new recruits to the point of them being good enough for the new fights.Setting up the skills and gear is straightforward enough and crafting has so many short cuts that you don't have to deal with most of the hassle that games usually struggle with.Elemental affinities and spell stuff could use a bit more clear tooltips, but its more limited nature makes you tailor it for the fights instead of just learning everything and forgetting it like most games.I still have to experiment and try more mixes of useable items as there's A LOT of them.The voice acting has also been surprisingly good, I actually end up listening through the lines instead of pre-reading and skipping like with some other games with awkward voices.The game does take bit odd stance on leveling and such compared to your typical RPG. Your characters can swap their Jobs with items, which allows for a lot of customization if you haven't built a huge roster and they are instantly decent in their new Jobs aside from weapon skills, unless they use their old weapons as the new Job.Your max level is capped by the story point to keep things challenging and also allowing you to funnel every extra exp gained into newer units that are not capped or into later to use charms to make it easier to catch up, though the rate of exp to charm is pretty bad.Random encounters don't exist, but you can do Training battles at certain locations to catch up if you are falling behind. Downside is that you cannot recruit troops from them nor gain items. This can make money tight if you aren't going for a lot of kills in most of the story maps (yet sometimes enemies have a lot and sometimes basically no gear).None of my fights have been unbeatable due lack of gear so far though, but saving often and optimizing the money a bit seems like a nice way to edge some advantage. A lot of upgraded versions of the items via crafting hold their own to higher tier pieces.Some of the boss fights are pretty rough, but I haven't found them completely unfair so far.The main issues I have with the game are the Recruiting enemies in battle system as it has generally low chances even with preparation and people seem to abuse the time rewind to try different steps to re-roll the recruit until they finally hit the low % gamble. It just doesn't seem worth the effort if you aren't into purposefully manipulating the low rolls over and over. I have yet to start catching monsters because it's so annoying to go gambling while trying to do the objectives. I'll probably try it more later if there's areas that are good for it.Another one is the "Guest" character's AI. They can be absolutely infuriating to deal at times, whether it's charging straight into enemies or not understanding to retreat. I did manage to manipulate them a bit by tweaking their skills and positioning some of my other units to bait enemies.Thankfully early on the AI seems quite merciful and if you are on top of your game they rarely get fully focused down unless they have become vastly underleveled. I just started to consider them as extra fodder for the most part as the key characters seem to just teleport out when they are dealt lethal or near lethal damage. If they manage to stay alive one map later they instantly catch up anyway.There's some exceptions where they can straight up die though which made dealing with them a bit frustrating, usually their gear and levels are decent enough though so they don't evaporate as long as you bee-line to them.I've seen other people gripe about the Job balance, but I've found it good enough. It does feel that some early base Jobs just get outclassed by stuff you unlock, but its not by so much that you can't use them. I decided to try to get at least 2 of every Job (one for each gender) and try a mix of different gearing on some of them and even the seemingly worst ones still have their uses depending on the map.If you want to keep smaller roster though, you can probably just keep 1s of the most critical and just transition out of most early stuff without losing key tools to engagements.Overall I've had a really good time playing so far aside from like one encounter where I had to restart a few times to get more kills and see more dialogue.I really hope more games would use the crafting shortcuts this game does as it cuts down the annoying middle managing and time spent A LOT.If you are interested in this game without previous experience in similar ones, I can recommend it despite some of the issues. The game eases you in, has few sudden difficulty spikes, but in general plays fair and sometimes even eases up a bit when you are struggling (sometimes allowing you extra turn to save weak unit instead of alpha striking it with their last one).Hopefully we get more Remasters with similar effort put into them.

_childDocuments_.review: They aren't kidding when they say the "crown jewel" of tactical role-playing.I played thousands of hours on the PS1 version, probably about 1000 on the PSP version, and this version's looking to be more of the same amount of enjoyment.The revamped systems might not be for everyone, but I think it's a lot more streamlined without dumbing it down like so many other franchises do. The difficulty has definitely gone up since the PSP version, but it's still pretty manageable if you think out your moves carefully ... or "tactically" dare I say?This is definitely not a port, if that's what you're wondering while looking at the reviews.This is a full remake. The graphics aren't changed much, but that was by choice.Edit: Still loving this game, btw, but with regards to other reviews:The skill number complaint is one I really don't understand.Correct, you have 4 skill slots in this game as opposed to the 10 in the PSP version. 4 is indeed a smaller number than 10. I know it. You know it. Pretty much anyone above the age of 5 knows it.The problem is that this is the point when people turn off their brains and make a post in the discussion board about how "dumb" and "gutted" the skill system is.However, when the devs combined skills and shed passive ones that everyone HAD to have to be viable, it comes out where you're actually  customizable than before.For example: Let's take a knight in mid Ch2. I want him to be a tanky boi in the front line with a 1-hand hammer and shield, throwing out the occasional healing spell.In Reborn I would put on:Skill - Concentration (HP up)Skill - Phalanx (chance on turn to a % of all damage taken)Skill - HammersSkill - Rampart AuraEquip - Going with the Ch2 theme, crafting is already available, so +1 version of shop armor all around since none of that requires any rare materials.To have a unit with the same setup in the PSP version, I would need:Skills - Hammers, Anatomy, Divine Magic, Augment Light, Concentration, Phalanx, Rampart Aura, Swiftfoot I, Jump I, Strengthen I, Fortify I, Truestrike (probably), Wade I, Counterattack I.That's 14 skills worth of stuff in Reborn using up 4 skill slots and a few pieces of equipment.Last I checked, 14 is bigger than 10. Then figure that aside from Phalanx and Rampart Aura, all classes get all of these skills (not necessarily hammers, but SOME weapon). Phalanx is knight-specific and can't be carried over to another class, and Rampart Aura can be transferred to dragoons, rune fencers and TKs. In Reborn, dragoons and TKs get Rampart Aura without having to do any kind of transfer.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: As somebody who played through old versions of this game about 6 times total, I can't recommend this enough. I was terrified after seeing the blurry character sprites but everything else that's new or drastically adjusted is genius.This re-make has none of the jank that the PSX version was known for and very little of the endless grinding that the PSP version was known for. The end result is that you can build your units with skills that do what they say and play though the story without gazing into a spreadsheet full of crystal balls for an hour to figure out what any given attack or animation actually does, or beating on a knight with 4 noodle-armed clerics for multiple hours if you ever want to actually see what the cudgel finishers look like.And sure, I guess the voice acting isn't miracle work, but it was a nice surprise that the style is theatrical rather than the cornball scenery chewing common in games and anime dubs. Definitely stuffy but a good fit for the game's heavy themes.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Fun but disappointing. There are some great things about this game: The story and branching paths, lots of characters to recruit, no random encounters while traveling the map (you'll do a lot of this towards the end of the game).The disappointing part is the class system: You pick a class and that determines all the skills you get and what items you can use. You can pick which skills to equip but are limited to four and four spells (if you class can use spells). You also get four finishing moves IF you have the skill equipped for it. Lastly, many skills activate randomly which takes away from the tactical nature of the game.Overall, a good game but the way the class system works is disappointing enough to keep me from playing over and over again.

_childDocuments_.review: This was originally released in 1995 in what many dub to be the "golden era" of JRPGs (With a PSP remake in 2010, which 'Reborn' is based off of).This is actually my first exposure to Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together (Reborn), and it's well worth diving into today. I've been aching to play this title for a long time with it sitting in my mental backlog for years, and now with this official release via a lovingly done remaster I'm finally able to do so. People laud this alongside FFT (Final Fantasy Tactics) as underrated masterpieces and I can see why.   The storytelling is engaging with a high fantasy war drama full of political intrigue and various tragedies via the bloodshed that takes place. This was definitely ahead of its time and the added voice cast is able to bring to life this emotional tale. I can't say much more without spoiling things, but if you like mature storytelling that delves into heavier subject matters you'll enjoy this (Relative to most other JRPGs). It definitely gets crazy at the conclusion of chapter 1 which basically sets up the rest of the wild ride you'll go on. All of this to say that Yasumi Matsuno is a goated Director/Writer especially with projects he was able to see to full completion.Gameplay wise this is a difficult yet rewarding tactical RPG experience. If you've only played more contemporary SRPGs then you may find the difficulty curve a bit overwhelming at first. Since there is no difficulty setting be prepared to learn if you don't want to fight an uphill battle both literally and figuratively speaking. Especially with the Union Level mechanic which prevents you from overleveling your party to preserve the general challenge. However you can still level up weapon skills which can unlock finishers (powerful techniques) or allow certain abilities to proc more often once at a higher rank. I could ramble on about other stuff, but there's just a lot of nuance and depth that you yourself will have to dive into.Aesthetics wise (Visuals and Sound/Music), I'm a little disappointed with how they treated the sprite work in particular since they could have done better than this oddly up-res'd and smoothed out version of the models. However during gameplay it becomes a blur and not that big of a deal. Although the UI elements and character portraits look incredible at least. Akihiko Yoshida's gorgeous artwork comes into full display here. Also it's crazy as mentioned before how the newly added voice over work really brings the story to life. While I don't mind reading dialogue having actors express the script just adds a new dimension to the narrative experience. A few individual performances are somewhat lackluster, but the overall voice direction is good IMO. Also the OST (Which I believe is re-orchestrated in this edition) sounds amazing, and is fitting for the game.  Overall this is an incredible game that I still have much more to go through despite my 15+ hour time investment so far. This is definitely not lacking for content. The freedom and flexibility with your party builds alongside the emotional war drama that Matsuno is presenting is enticing. Plus since battles really take some time and planning to get through with minimal casualties it feels rewarding coming out of the other side of a hard fought encounter. Sometimes it can be a nail biting experience depending on the circumstances of a specific fight. Oh and the PC port is good, it won't blow you away but there's solid mouse and keyboard support with enough in the settings to tailor the experience to your rig (No ultrawide monitor support though unfortunately for those that want/need that). Great though compared to the many questionable Square PC releases. Although this game isn't graphically demanding and could run on a potato fairly easily regardless of the resolution you play on.I'd definitely recommend this to SRPG fans who want a gripping story and challenging gameplay. You really owe it to yourself to give this a try since it has influenced a lot of future games that would be released over the years after it.  Also if you just admire Yasumi Matsuno's catalog of incredible games since he's a one of kind creator alongside the likes of other greats like Kojima, Shinji Mikami, Yuji Horii, and Sakaguchi to name a few.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time fan of the original PSX port (who played way too many times) and its PSP remake, I can say this feels like the best version of the game. _childDocuments_.review: Alright, I am a mid twenty-something that doesn't have much time for video games. That being said, over 200 hours of my life has been spent on this game. The pacing and combat provide perfectly timed sessions that enabled me to play in smaller chunks. HOWEVER - I also took a week of vacation and was able to absolutely lose myself in this game without getting bored. The combat system is easy to learn but even at 100 hours in, I was still learning the more detailed plays/approaches/etc. The leveling and character/party customization is paced PERFECTLY, I had to work for levels but I never got burnt out while trying to grind my party. On top of everything else, the story is amazing and the endgame allows you to play through all of the different paths that your decisions can take you down throughout the game. I would seriously recommend this game, even if you didn't play the original Tactics Ogre or Tactical RPGs aren't traditionally your thing.

It's false when they say improved these game features.Here what i've noted yet:-Game Balance definitly different:+Now there is a character lvl cap fixed (Squad Lvl) by the advancement of the story, lvl cap straight from the begining, and in a few combat you lvl up (a bit too easy).+You begin with damage already powerful and HP to the top (50 to 200 dmg and 300 to 500 HP, stuff like when you're lvl 25 or more in the original game), so lvl up feel empty with this major UP.+With these 2, grinding will be far less useful and getting over leveled to bypass problematic fight is not an option anymore. For the begining, the game is way easier than the original (i don't remember that was this easy)... i'll see for later in the game EDIT: well, it's not that fast after, but main story is enough to fill lvl cap for your main characters without grinding that much.+Lot AND LOTS of boosting cards poping on the map (1 every 2 of character making a turn), it feel weird.-Skills:+No skill points anymore to unlock, it come with lvl up (not see it with also mastery of skills i supose)+Max of 4 skills Slots to equip (Vs 10 in the original game, what a nerf)+No way to know how to unlock some (maybe i missed it yet)-Spells:+No way to learn them (you could do it a lot using Grimoires in the first game and adapt your gameplay with it) +You're limited to 4 Spells to equip (like for skills, again a nerf) -Consumable Items:+Arcana removed (no more grimoire to one used, you equip them in spell, that's all), fair enough, it was barely useful, sometime for Heal, Rez or Exorcism when stucked.+No More direct use for Items from inventory, you need to equip the again, still anothe 4 Slots (well... another nerf) -Game Controls:+Annoying controls -> there is some but Right mouse click doesn't go back *directly* to your action (conter intuitive).+For movement, you need to select move, click on a cell you want to go AND again on this cell, cancel move, you need to do all again... Most other games have movement selected by default, and you just need to click one time to move, cancel, the character go back on click an other cell the character go there... how did they messed that up, it's basic, it's PAINFUL here.+Always need to double click, even when you select back you character+If you click terrain, the back key does nothing, the right click there open system menu while you naturaly try to go back to your current character (need to use next our previous character in line key, most people don't even commonly use)+Finishing a move will leave your pointer in your a cancel movement button at the end+Rotation view not responsive in current action (need to often cancel action to be able to move camera to get back doing your action), it's painful when terrain block view to no manage correctly that.+Impossible to navigate in the game menu with my controler (it work on the world map, but failed to do anything in inventory or the moment you're in city menu, only character switch work) even all keys binded-> A LOT OF REDUNDANCE IN BASIC KEYS, making game tiring to play, you even need to type the Escape key 2 times to get to the system menu (1st time making just the cursor disapear... why?) -No more random encounter...+Replaced by Skirmish to choose to each maps, BUT, there is NO DROPS AT ALL -> No way to grind money? (if you later need to resort to tame beast to put them to auction... it will be painful)Yet to see:-Tame/Recruit in battle (i had the option but always 0% to succes, bugged?)-Craft-Tarrot cardsLet's finish with at least the positive stuff added:+New element affinity stuff, a rock paper scissor mecanic more advance and for all character with a way to change it.+Voices...+Improved graphics (well it's just fine enough Remaster for it)+That's it >< (for what i've seen yet)

_childDocuments_.review: For anyone who played earlier games in the series (Ogre Battle 64, for me), this is an instant nostalgia hit. The music brought me back before I'd even played a level.Beyond that, though, TO:Reborn takes a familiar formula, updates it with some QOL changes for the modern day, and unleashes it. Voice acting is largely better than I expected. Dialog is period-based, but consistently so. Game will begin to punish you if you don't take the time to learn about the world, but like most tactics-style games, it's beatable with patience if nothing else.TL;DR: Like Tactics games + permadeath options for your squadmates (but not punishingly difficult) + JRPG style story? Wholeheartedly endorse.

_childDocuments_.review: For the record, I love the PSP Tactics Ogre despite its flaws. This is a review of this remaster specifically. I got a refund for a couple main reasons:1 - The redrawn sprites are UGLY. Like I *think* they did slightly more than just run them through a filter but it still looks muddy to me and I wish there was an option to restore the original pixel art.2 - The game has been redesigned in a bunch of way, some of them are fine but other feel completely unnecessary. The big one I dislike is the game now CONSTANTLY spawns temporary buffs and debuffs on the map. You can stack up to 4 on a single unit and they're pretty significant stat buffs. It makes the map feel really cluttered. It completely changes the dynamic of how battles go compared to the original. In a vacuum it's not necessarily a bad idea for a tactics game but to me it feels completely out of place in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a pointless grind fest to mediocrity. The game designers import pointless complexity in place of depth. The story missions are generally either soft balls, or cheap nonsense where the game designers make you play against the the system, rather than the event. Fights are either nearly impossible or trivial because you bought a load of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ win buttons.The game makes you grind to level up, then spits in your face by instituting a level cap on you while placing the enemies a few levels above that. They give the computer opponents nonsensical advantages that make conventional approaches pointless. They are winnable, but not without making it less about leading your group of soldiers and more about how to cheese the system in such a way that when you do win, you feel less like a competent commander and more like a basement dwelling, neck beardy rules lawyer.This is a game for "git gud" system focused chess players who make every game they play about exploiting the system, rather than experiencing the game. This game is for people who think they can win D&D. The writing is okay, the story is reasonably interesting, but honestly the amount of d*&#s you have to suck to get to the prize make this game a hard sell to people who want to play a role playing game. This game was made for the new game + feature. Don't expect much from your first run through.If you want to spend a lot of hours learning the systems and exploits behind a 2.5 D turn based single player strategy game that will immediately lose relevance the second you get out of your chair, you are in the right place.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre is a series I heard about way back in 2010 when the first remake wqas coming out on the PSP. Never got a chance to play it almost 15 years later till now, but I did, and I have some things to say.The tale of Tactic Ogre is grandiose  and people who are familiar with A Song of Ice and Fire will be quite at home here.(What’s funny is that it predates it by a year). A man by the name of King Dorgalua brought peace to the warring Valeria Islesi, full of ethnicities that didn’t quite care for one another. But after dying without leaving an heir (hint hint), the different groups such as the Wallister, Bakram, Galgastani, and the Dark Knights (Who are basically just here for the ride....maybe) all went back to their schoolyard brawl.  But the thing about those is the bigger kid tends to be the one with the fewer bruises, and the shrimps by the name of the Wallisters get the brunt.Three childhood friends by the name of Denam, our protagonist, Catiua, and Vyce have started their own Wallister resistance group. After chance meeting with a knight named Lanselot and his cohorts, they have been urged to save Juda Ronwey, one of the leaders of the Wallister Resistance. Don’t really want to go much further, but this is no tale of good vs evil. You may be playing as a bunch of kids fighting from oppression but remember this....anyone can be capable of great goood...and great evil (Epic Foreshadowing).Tactics Ogre Reborn is a strategy RPG game by Quest, with the rights and development furthered on by Square Enix. You and your band knights, wizards, witches, and arhers take turn spilling blood and growing stronger. The director Yasumi Matsuno would go on to make Final Fantasy Tactics after his work, and alot of the trappings and designed are very similar. I would definitely say that Tactics Ogre is far more technical and generally nothing about the game is linear outside of a few areas. There are a wealth of Jobs that your troops can get, and unlike FFT, generally all of them will see some use well into the late game. There are Knight tanky soldiers who can wield a wealth of weapons and shields as well as healing magic but don’t do much damage themselves and are very slow. Warriors who can use heavy armor but can dish out some good damage but don’t have the durability knights have. Archers, that do exactly what you’d expect (And even then they have a few options for bows and crossbows that affect their range and damage), are a bit nimbler but in exchange squishier, and Wizards, who rain down elemental magic like a human carpet bomber, and Clerics that do the same but for your side. There are also plenty of unconventional units to recruit to your side such as the many monsters you can get on your side like Gryphons, Golems, Ogres, Dragons of various element, Skeletons, etc. Since every job has there uses, I would definitely say there isn’t an upgraded besides a select few rare ones and you should consider it them more akin to “specialized classes” or side grades, such as the Dragoons who have thee tankiness of the Knight but lack the healing in exchange for being able to do heavy damage to monsters, or the Fulsier who can use Handguns and in exchange for being far smaller ranged, can deliver a wallop.There are also things you have to worry about beyond your troops equipment, abilities, and the like such as elemental strengths and weakness (Doubt you thought that questionnaire at the start was for show.) which can determine how effective your attacks can be. A lot of it goes over even my head but I did enjoy my playtime with it....until about Chapter 4.The game is broken in 4 Chapters. Each chapters have a slew of battles and cut scenes as well as lore to read up on to get the full context. Although I tend to avoid guides unless absolutely necessary, I highly recommend you use one or else you might find yourself missing out on powerful allies and Jobs that have very strict deadlines. Chapter 4 is the worst of all of them and sheer amount of side quest available there is probably worth all the previous chapter combined and then some. Some of my issues with the game is that the monotony does set in very much so during the mid game and it became much more efficient to just get a bunch of gryphons to act as meat shields and then have Canopus come in like the winged assassin that he is and slaughter the enemy lord rather than having a drawn out fight like a lot of the games really end up being. Once you beat the game, you get access to something known as a World Tarot, and you can go back to previous story events even with your late game Chapter 4 party. In order to really get the most of the game, you’re going to be doing that quite a lot. It is quite common that most people would recommend you beat the game first at least once but in order to truly see everything the game has to offer (and whether it’s worth it to you is obviously your prerogative, but I found quite a number of good things to like) you have to really play it minimum 3 times to get all the endings. And then there is the Palace of the Dead waiting for you...and the Shaman Quest...and Coda....It is quite overwhelming. I’d say avoid trying to play the game all at once and perhaps take place in between playthroughs to not just simply burn out on the game all together. I do recommend it, still, but definitely keep the turbo on and try to focus on the enemy leader when you can. On the changes between the PSP release “let Us Cling Together.” and Reborn, I can’t speak as Reborn ism y first experience with it, but the changes seem generally positive. Apparently Reborn removed a lot of the tedium, and that just shocks me that the game was already FAR more tedious than it could be. The card system some might not favor as it can be cheap, but I think that it could make battles generally snappier.

_childDocuments_.review: After a bit of patching, things have improved a bit.. but there are some really dumb plot holes that sorta ruin the story for me. You spend all this time building characters, getting attached to them and outfitting your team to be effective.. then along come guests, which are usually under-leveled, don't allow you to change their class and some even instantly die in battle and never come back. I don't understand the point of guests. The enemy recruitment mechanic is really weak, combining the buggy or glitchy overlapping cursor placements and poor AI, trying to tame or recruit is almost pointless. The chances are astronomically low and AI decides to spend all their MP and skills to kill one enemy with 20 HP. This game is still just so rough, counter-intuitive and lacks a lot of QoL changes to streamline things.Elevate the camera angle just a tad and all camera problems are basically gone.Give better information regarding effects and buff/debuff tooltips.NEVER make players endure carrying guests around and then let them DIE in battles with no chance to save them.Improve the AI not to just overkill weak enemies or stand in place doing nothing because of pathing.Healers should be more streamlined, movement and strength-wise in combat. Immobile healers makes it seem stupid to have them.Being shown items in a store that I cannot make or haven't come across yet is just plain dumb. Ninja weapons are available via crafting, albeit non-craftable before you ever encounter one or can change class to be one.. Kinda feels like a slap in the face.It's just a lot of dumb issues that seem to be QoL problems where it shows there's no polishing. It just feels low quality all around.BTW; this game repeatedly puts you in gloriously unbalanced one-sided fights where the enemy starts with MP, buffs and mysteriously increased stats regardless of the same possibilities for you. There's difficulty and then there's just "THIS ISN'T AN OPTION!" but all-in-all the poor story points and boring NPCs make you want to throw yourself against the wall anyway. I'm uninstalling this mess before it ruins my outlook on RPGs.

First 20 hours or so went fine. The story is nonsense and the names of places and people have been generated by mashing face to the keyboard. But who cares about such things, you're in it for the strategic battles and cards that you can pick up during fight, oh maybe not because of those, since those feel like super tacked-on addition. But how are the fights ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!? Cool at first but then you start to see the cracks. You either hit, shoot or cast a spell, that's it. Shooting and casting spells is okay against units that shoot or cast spells but are pretty useless against anyone with defense. Healers can't heal enough to be useful in the long run. There are two kinds of fights: You either have to vanquish all foes or a certain foe to win. So either you methodically pick enemies one by one or you rush to kill the boss in order to win. It gets old real fast. Doing the same thing for 30 hours was enough for me. In the last mission I was supposed to take out two targets... so I lied, there's "variety"... Guess it all boils down what the framework of this game is. It's an old game with new paint but it doesn't hide the fact that there should be more. It would be a good game if there was more, if the classes felt more different, if there were different kind of missions and if there were a cohesive plot. What did I like then? I can't remember anymore but it wasn't neither of the two missions I kept playing.This isn't yes or no review, it's a maybe.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best TRPG out there. The mechanical changes from the PSP version address a lot of the issues that version of the game has, especially with regards to catching up new characters and classes to your main group. Some of the side quests have also been simplified a bit, such as the Deneb recruitment questline. I also really like the ability to double the battle speed, which really helps when you're grinding side content.The only negatives I would give this version of the game is that the English voiceovers are hit and miss. Some of the characters feel miscast, but I really think it boils down to poor vocal direction and a tight budget. You can change the voiceover dialogue to Japanese if the English voices bother you. There's also some issues with the ally AI on mission where you have to rescue someone. But that was present in the PSP remake so that's more of a game design problem. Another issue is that the upscaled sprites look a bit smudged, but honestly that was an issue in the PSP version too. I don't think it detracts from the experience too much, but it would have been nice to have some sort of filtering you could enable or disable.Overall, I'd definitely recommend this game if you're a fan of TRPGs or turn based RPG combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Going to preface this with the fact that I am bad at strategy games, I do not make use of the breadth of options available (especially with complex mechanics), I just try to learn what I can and make do with the party I choose to build. I also did not put much time, if any, into the original release, so I can't really compare this to the older versions. So if you're looking at this review for an opinion of someone that knows their stuff about this particular genre, maybe read one of the others!The story is the main reason behind my enjoyment of the game, I really did appreciate that you at least had some agency over the path both the major and minor conflicts would proceed. The UI offering a nice drawn out timeline of events and descriptions of what happened in each instance was really appreciated, especially if I had to take a break from the game for any length of time. I had thought mostly even the character portraits were mostly static, but they did the extra work to give them better representation of the emotions of the current story beats. Characters were fleshed out well and you have tons of voice acting to complement the cutscenes around all the battles. I ended up going the (what I feel was) the most morally right route, but you are eventually free to see the result of the other choices. Obviously won't spoil things, but the plot centered around political power and the backstabbing/deal making that goes on around it is very entertaining, and some people definitely get their deserved comeuppance. If you're a fan of mostly a small set of factions and the main characters within them, you should have a good time.The gameplay I can mostly jive with, aside from some caveats. You will have to (of course) use some strategy, placing your units in specific places to overcome the enemy. You are offered a (limited) mechanic to roll back your turns to previous actions, giving you some freedom in which you are able to make a different decision if things don't go your way. This at least gives you some options if you make moves that give you unfortunate results, but as I said, it is limited. I was able to at least use some specific strategies, which sometimes involved "beeline for the target" or "protect units while whittling down the enemy's forces." That worked for the most part! One important part of this game is that there really is no over leveling, you have a certain level cap based on how far you are in the story, and that is your max of which you can ascend. This particular mechanic does force you to manage your units well, and I did have some battles where it was juggling keeping units alive/not incapacitated too long while trying to bring down the main foe(s). Most battles I did fairly well, with some I scraped by. Until the endgame.The endgame is something to warn about, it is extremely punishing and lengthy, giving you extremely tough battles. I was able to mostly fumble my way through the entirety of the game with may main party with little issue, but the endgame is a difficulty cliff that definitely puts your current setup to the test. For those that may not handle these games the best (like myself), you may have to retry a bit, so that may be a point of frustration. I was able to complete it, but I won't deny that it was a surprisingly difficult challenge.All in all, I did really enjoy the game. I think it's a fun strategy RPG, manageable for those that maybe don't read all the tutorials entirely, and the story is fun for people that enjoy mix of medieval/fantastical settings. If you are interested by that and aren't put off by the challenging gameplay, then it is worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a huge fan of Tactics Ogre when I first played it on Playstation One years ago.  Some of the changes are interesting, for example, they made some of the classes more worthwhile to play and versatility to others.  The old tactics ogre to had more content and battlegrounds, this one railroads you through the story battles.  The random battles are gone, which sucks because it gave me different terrain to do battle in and increased opportunities to recruit different units.  They also added a level cap as their attempt to balance the game.  But the reality is, they could have easily allowed the story battles to scale with you.  Some of us enjoyed going on adventures with Denam and Friends and testing the limits of the game mechanics.  As an old fan who enjoys more freedom in my games, I give this game a D.  I would not recommend it.  You are better off getting an emulator and playing the original.  I would change this rating if they remove these annoying features in future updates, something other developers have done with other games on steam.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish they had a middling recommendation option instead of yes/no.LUCT on the SNES/PSX was and is one of my favorite games of all time.  To the point where I had created a memory map and index tables of all of the classes/items/etc in the game so I could play around with even the AI-only classes and abilities.  I played the PSP remake and enjoyed it, but there were changes I wasn't fond of and still thought the original was better.  This seems to be a re-release of the PSP version with more mechanical changes that I don't like, to the point where I'd probably rather play the PSX version on an emulator unfortunately.  The party level cap, randomly spawning buff cards, and removal of random encounters all seem like such bad ideas I'm amazed that the game shipped with them.I really love the Ogre Battle series though so I'm still a sucker that will throw money at Square/Enix in the hopes that they will put out new chapters of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Bad remake.(Edit summery: Clarified previous points, added one more that kind of irked me)I was fine with it being overpriced; I love Tactics Ogre so I was fine with dealing with square enixs overpricing. Not much good was changed in this remake, the voices and upscaled spritework are good but the gameplay is worse than the 2010 psp version(edit: I'm referring to the fan patch since that's what I played):You can't rename your character.They basically level locked class changes with the class system and took away stat unique stat growths for classes.Stats dynamically change when a character changes classes meaning there is no loss in just switching classes when it suits you, a warrior can change to a wizard and they'd be just a strong as someone who got all their levels as a wizard.  Levels are capped with story progressXP is gained equally by everyone, you gain a lot more and you can pretty much reach the cap without even trying.These are the main things which took away the strategic, classic TRPG feel, there's less choice, it feels like you're being dragged through the game in chains.The choice and strategy required to play this game made the game good in the first place. _childDocuments_.review: I wasn't going to review this, but I'm surprised at just how many negative reviews this game has. I never played the previous versions, so I went in with zero nostalgia, but this is an excellent SRPG. It's long, a little unforgiving, and a ton of its systems are not very well explained... but that doesn't hold it back from being a deep and immersive tactics game with a huge amount of replayability. It also runs perfectly on a Steam Deck (I played this almost exclusively on the Deck). I'm seeing a lot of people complaining about controls, but I'm not sure where that's coming from. _childDocuments_.review: Coming from a guy with thousands of hours in the originals...This is a remake that's incredibly aware of the ins and outs of it's system, and delivers an incredible top to bottom rework of a very deep and confusing system into the stellar depressing chess it always wanted to be. Every feature I ever thought removed turned out to be reworked into something really slick somewhere else. -Thought Augments were gone? The elemental interactions between units, their gear, and their spells goes way deeper than you'd expect. Instead of just building for Aug Stacks, you're looking for openings, breaking defenses, and using good teamwork to take that one elemental finisher you never thought you'd use, and exploiting it on top of a Breach and Elemental Advantage to one shot a boss. - Thought the cards looked random? Spawn your own, or theory craft those tools you never used in earlier versions for building teams that can take advantage of every situation. Vartan can cast spells? Oh well. Vartan can use those spellcasting options to also get better spells off his anti dragon crossbow and Dragonslayer set to become a unit capable of being an effective caster, sniper, or anti tank bird no matter what their situation? Neat.-Thought they nerfed Archers? Oh, no, they just built a little fence to contain the beast. Breach, Fear, Element Advantages, Racial Weapon bonuses, all of these will take your pew pew soldiers and turn them into Rambo. Pair them up with a Terror Knight and watch the numbers fly. -Thought there were less skills? Oh hell no. Everyone just got those boring passives as part of their gear. The better skills, though, all can be combined at the same time now, can be triggered on the same round (Since you can easily guarantee Auto skills), and most have entirely new situations. Ever saw anyone use Threaten back in PSP? Nope. Slowed you down, it never hit, and you might as well whack the wizard than try to remove MP and Silence. Oh, what's that, MP and TP got merged since only like a third of the classes used MP last time? Oh, that means Threaten can cause a unit to lose access that Finisher they were about to launch while also stopping that healer over there in this new situation? Fantastic.I could go on. I also have, got an entire channel dedicated to these games. This is one hell of a remake, and easily my favorite version by miles. I still love the incredible One Vision mod on the road or work, but when I want to sit down and do some very well written war crimes...I go for Reborn.One year and thousands of hours across two platforms combined, this remake still rocks.

_childDocuments_.review: Avoid this, it's way too expensive for what it is. A lot of work has been done on the game but as an originally old game the gameplay is supremely outdated. Every battle boils down to either being so easy you wipe the map or so unbalanced that you have to snipe the leader for the win before all your units die. You have 4 skill slots but you are basically locked into picking certain things since without weapon skills you do very little damage. Also because of this you have to keep using the same weapon or else lose all your accumulated levels just to try something else out. So you end up having to use the same classes and skills repeatedly just to do any damage at all, so there are not really any alternative playstyles. The world building is solid and the voice acting is...passable I guess, so if you have nostalgia goggles you might be able to make it through. But this game is not even remotely as good as Final Fantasy Tactics was back in the day, so if you're looking for that experience you will be disappointed. It is most certainly not worth the $50 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Tactics Ogre.  It is my favorite game of all time.  But in almost all the ways that count, this is a step backwards as compared to the original.  The one positive I will point out is the voice acting is done really well, and it adds to the great story.  But, in my opinion, there are 2 significant negatives that ruin this remaster.  First, random battles have been completely eliminated.  So your only options to level your group up are story missions or a new Training feature that lets you do battles in towns without consequences, but you also get no loot.  These training battles are the exact same every time, and you can't recruit enemies in them.  So all you can really do is level your group up to the current max (each unit's level is capped at the overall group level, determined by your progress through the story), and then continue through the story missions.Second, the skill system has been severely dumbed down.  Each unit only has 4 skill slots, and you don't spend skill points to acquire the skills you want; instead, the skills are automatically learned at certain level increases.  I wish I could recommend this game, but you're way better off playing the psp version.

_childDocuments_.review: New players, go for it this is an amazing classic brought back to life, you will likely love the story and have fun. returning players.... read on....they massacred the overhaul. even removed an entire class!the original game was buggy, had obnoxious character choice limitations and very complicated story pathingpsp version fixed all that and while it had a few flaws, it overall was a huge improvementthen somone made this version and gutted it.  ive never been so disappointed with a relaunch. on a side note the voice active is surprisingly mostly great, well done. but they could have done that without ripping out the mechanicslevel caps? class removal? can only cast 4 spells, only use 4 skills? no cross class except for hero (hero DOES work, but you have to cycle the other classes to get the skills to show up on the hero), skill learning is a little buggy too sometimes you have to swap jobs to get the game to realize you were suppose to learn somethingits like a reddit story where a work place works fine then a manager comes in with new ideas and the company closes from it, thats this mechanics overhaul.story wise everything looks fine, they seam to mostly have rewrote a few confusing lines. no problems thereoverall if they hadnt meddled with the mechanics it would have been perfect.  if you are a return player from the previous version, this version may utterly depress you

_childDocuments_.review: I'm at 100 hours so I feel I can put a review in, even though I'm not finished the game. Note, I never played the original, just this remake.Overall, this is a good tactics style game, where the pros vastly outweigh the cons. The cons they have are pretty large though.You've got plenty of different types of units you can fill your army out with, and they all specialize in different things, so it feels like there's a reason to have them. The classes all seem to be pretty well balanced, which is good. I know a lot people hate the 4 spells/abilities but I actually thought that makes the game good. There are some units with like 6-8 good abilities and if you had them all you'd be unstoppable, the point is to make you make a choice, to customize for certain battles or situations. I found it also meant carrying more than 1 of each class of unit.The soundtrack is good to very good at times, and the visuals are fine. The story feels like a fairly large letdown. It feels like I missed a game or something and it just picked up where the other left off, but I was left way behind. A lot of the game has to deal with clans, but all the clans seem exactly the same. Not enough time was spent on backstory, or plot, imo. I understand this is a remake, but that's the old game showing its age.The game looks like it has TONS of replability. There's 3 'main' paths to the game, and a few endgame dungeons you can repeat. I got it for something like $40 bucks and i'm at 100 hours without replay. I will say its a tad grindy because each time the level cap goes up I have to level my entire army. Keep your army 25-30, mine is like 70, way too big. If you like this type of game, you'll like this. If you don't, there's nothing new here to change your mind.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far my favorite tactics RPG of all time. I played the Knight of Lodis on GBA when it was released and this game (Let Us Cling Together) on the PSP back in the day too, so I am a long time fan and highly recommend it. The HD remaster of the pixel graphics is beautiful and I love the voice-overs they added to Reborn. The 2x battle speed is a nice QoL addition too. The only complaint I have on the changes from the PSP version are to the skill system. Instead of the flexibility of learning a skill and being able to use many of them after switching jobs (particularly the dual wield), it is more restrictive. The level cap can be frustrating to some, but it makes you be more strategic in battle, which is kind of the point of a tactics game. It is a bummer that they got rid of rogue as a playable job, but there are plenty of jobs so it's not missed much. The crafting system got a much needed overhaul, which I was very happy to see. Overall, this game is amazing and I was ecstatic that it got some love from Square-Enix with this remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite negative reviews for this game call it a ripoff of Final Fantasy Tactics, not even realizing that the game that eventually became FFT was initially being developed as a sequel to the original version of this game. There's a very good reason they have so much in common - this one came first and pioneered much of the Tactics RPG genre. While this remake isn't perfect (such as the sprites being stretched on larger monitors and the union level system creating some unintended issues with Palace of the Dead) it feels both faithful, yet fresh. The AI is smarter than it has been in other versions of the game, leading to more challenging battles. The voice acting is more hit than miss, with a few truly excellent performances. And of course the newest iteration of the soundtrack is beautiful and breathes new life into a game I'd already played upwards of a dozen times.
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I'm liking it so far. Played some of the original back in the day but my monkey brain couldn't get pass a certain level so here I am again with the remake.The things I don't like about this remake is the filter. I prefer the pixelated look of the original, now it kinda just looks like someone smeared Vaseline on everything, that being said though, you do get used to it and it stopped bothering me after a bit. The controls take a bit of getting used to, at first I thought I could combine kb+m but it seems like they are independent control schemes. By that I mean when you press something on your keyboard, the UI changes to have keyboard on the menu's (kinda like how when you change from kb+m > controller) and snaps into the nearest object (e.g reading a skill with the cursor then if you hit a key on the keyboard, it snaps to the top left of the menu). That being said though, it's nice being able to play the game completely on just the mouse.Another one I find annoying is that the game doesn't tell you what status effects does (apart from the basic ones/I'm blind and it's harder to find than it should be). I has to Google what some effects do and the tooltip at the top scrolls slow as molasses and I have no idea if there's a way to make it scroll faster after 3-ish hours of play.Everything else I love. I love that they took out the random battles and just made it into training so I can just fight whenever I want, I absolutely hate random battles in games. It's less grindy but there is still some grind it seems. I'm weird but I also like the fact that there is a level cap tied to the story. My dumb ass usually either over levels and make everything trivial or be under leveled and make everything harder than it should be. It let's me know when I should do some training to reach the level cap instead of just moving back and forth in a node back in the day to level myself up.I also love the fact that they added voice acting, makes me more engaged and gives me time to sit back and relax and enjoy the story, there's even an option to auto advance the dialogue so I can just have some english men and women read me a bed time story. Everything else people have already talked about and I honestly don't mind any of the changes. I welcome the quality of life changes and even the changes based on changing classes. Keeps my monkey brain from getting overwhelmed/trying to min/max stats to get a specific class.All in all a great remake! Would I recommend it at full price? Ehhh,,, Not really since $50 for an old game remake like this is a bit steep, grab in on a sale! (Or grab it at full price if you like games like this/played a bit of the original). Despite it being the way it is, I still highly recommend it and it stays 2nd place in my top SRPG's of all time (I'm a FFTactics nerd).
_childDocuments_.name: Tactics Ogre: Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far one of the best classic OG tactics-based games of it's time, featuring three distinct endings and later added equivalent "DLC" called CODA for post-game. Lots of replayability. Game I would say is most comparable to Final Fantasy Tactics, and although FFT had a more robust skill/class system, this VERSION of the game forces more challenge and strategy into you. (To me, still a pretty easy game, though.)The storyline is good, the character development good, music is GREAT, and post-game stuff is a lot of fun. It is a bit more "challenging" to some, depending on you as the person. To 100% all the achievements.. there is parts of tedium, only thing I didn't like about the game is near end game and parts of post game felt.. undeveloped. Not that it makes it a bad game, as a lot of it was extra side content that was optional, but still.As someone that has the OG copy from the 90s, I would HIGHLY recommend this to play it through a "nostalgia" lense, the voiceovers definitely add to the dynamic and fun.For those that have played before on older versions. Some new things:Level caps now, and no random encounters. Added a few new systems, and made recruiting more challenging chars a lot less challenging.To show my true passion, I took the time to 100% it, and going to enjoy replaying through some CODA again soon!

_childDocuments_.review: Played and finished the game, but wasn't a pleasant experience. The cons:1- story was convoluted and hard to follow. Some of the plot twist were so forced and hard to make sense of. The  cast is excessively large  - half the time, i can't even tell who is who in the storyline and just prefer to get on with the actual gameplay.2 - consequence of your choices were really obscure. You have a few branching story depending on your choice, but i ended up with the bad, and abrupt ending despite trying to make noble choices throughout. I later found out that one simple dialogue choice changed the course of the ending but it was too late to go back. Some choice of dialogue wasn't even distinctly different, so it was hard to tell apart the "good" vs "bad" choices. You'll likely need to read a guide to get the "good" ending. 3 - the final chapter was a slog and the final boss wasn't well designed. You can beat it, but it was made to be REALLY grindy rather than challenging your thinking; i.e. spending hours just to make through a few stages. The second last dungeon, was a series of long battles with no story progression or boss. Just levels of fights after fights - it gets tiring. 4 - as others have pointed, the cap level is an issue (which i can live it) and you can remove with mod. But the inventory management and equipment handling is really frustrating. New equipments you picked up are not easily identified, you can;t tell what new items are in the shop for sale, you can't compare new and exising equipment directly, you can't easily tell what items are meant for whom. You have to spend hours going back and forth the shop and inventory, and I often mistakenly bought items that my members can't equip. I like turn based strategy games, and did manage to complete this game. But looking back -it's obvious  this game is a remaster of an old and dated game. It wasn't even really that good originally on SNES, and it shows. It's also sad that the game has much potential but this "reborn" version didn't innovate enough to try to appeal to newer players. It feels old and dated.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is everything I hoped for up until the middle of act 3. That's where the game decides to steamroll you into playing it one specific way. Tactics in fighting no longer becomes prevalent. It's a race to kill the enemy boss before his side wipes you. You can't spend time to level up your party to be on-par skill wise with the enemy, as the Union Level caps you. Up until that point, you can have fun. You can send your team out to battle the entirety of the enemy. But once you get to that point in the game, your enemies will have better spells, better gear, and hit 3-4x harder than you can. Example. Boss at Boed Fortress can one shot you, while I did, with a finishing attack, less than 1/10th its full health. That's all while its team is doing a third of each unit's health per attack minimum. Every fight becomes a race to kill the enemy leader, and you no longer get to enjoy the tactical RPG side of the game.It's a fun 30 hours, but afterwards it became the biggest letdown of any game I've paid for on steam. There is no difficulty setting, or way to improve your odds in these fights. The game has become trying to rush through the battles to get to the story. It's a game I had looked forwards to for so long, but became such a massive disappointment, to the point that I can only hope that they never attempt to make another Tactics Ogre game.

_childDocuments_.review: Whenever you see this review, odds are exceedingly high the recent reviews will be 'mixed' on this game. You may look away and ignore it, but if you came here to find out why the reviews are mixed, I can tell you! I can also tell you you should Tactics Ogre Reborn is a remake of Let Us Cling Together, a PSP remake of the SNES game Tactics Ogre. In this version, they made an extensive list of smallish improvements (I cannot possibly fit them all here, there are literal /hundreds/) from the PSP version that add up to make this easily the best tactical RPG I've ever played. And I'm no stranger to this genre!The main selling point this adds is making the postgame even better, and adding voice acting that by and large is phenomenal and adds a lot of depth of meaning to the script. I'm not going to go into the story beyond telling you it's one of the best in the medium (though I think there's some rockiness in how chapter 1 is handled, it's incredible from chapter 2 on) but I truly, genuinely know it to be so.The following is a brief overview of key features other people cite as negatives, and the counterpoints to them/why those people are wrong:"Battles are too slow" battles actually require thought, oh no. Your team composition matters, movement is deliberate, and the end result is a game you don't sleep through while playing it. How tragic!"Level cap exists" the Union level mechanic replaces random encounters (of which there are /zero/ in the entire game) which means /less/ grinding overall. It's trivial to stay at union level cap (I usually get to it in three fights whenever it raises) and there's nothing in the game that's insurmountable at your current level cap. The fights are challenges that have readily available tools to help overcome. Use debuffs and status effects! They actually matter in this one game!"You can't recruit non-humans out of combat" and??? Recruit them in combat. It's not /that/ hard."Tarot cards exist! they weren't in the game before! I hate change!" any time you see this complaint, auto translate it in your brain to "I hate not being able to do the same rote mechanical actions in every map I play ever, it's BS I have to care about my units' positioning and can't run 12 archers and park at the map start the game is BAD because I am incentivized at all to leave the starting position!"In an era of terrible rushed cash-grab ports that don't work (side eyeing metal gear solid) and "remakes" that offer nothing of value or in many cases miss a lot of the value from the original (yakuza kiwami 2), Tactics Ogre Reborn is proof positive that you can actually improve on perfection... and that in doing so, the dumbest people on the internet /will/ come out to decry your efforts to make a game fun, complex and deep in gameplay.Everyone says they want deep gameplay but what so many mean is "I want the box to tell me the game is hard so I can grind for 40 hours and steamroll it". Step outside the grind and use your brain to play. I believe in you.This game is an 11/10 masterpiece. Out of the over 500 games in my Steam library, this is the one I recommend the most of all. Give it a chance. A lot of people bounce off it early, but if you stick with it - if you use Dynast-King Mead from the shop on priority targets, if you use a balanced team composition instead of trying to find the One Unit That Matters and sticking with it, if you open your mind to the possibility that perhaps actually using your brain could be fun, this game is phenomenal.Don't be scared off by negative reviews; they don't have the stomach for actually putting effort in to achieve victory. You're better than that.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright.  Let's start applying some caveats to this recommendation.  I would divide potential customers into four distinct groups:People Say This Is a Good Game, So I'll Try It - Oh, my sweet summer child.  No.  Unequivocally no.  You need to get away from this.  There are better alternatives that actually ease you into the experience and - most significantly - have difficulty settings that you can use if you're really getting stuck on something.  Starting with this game is going to make you hate the whole genre, and that would be truly unfortunate.  Play Triangle Strategy.  Seriously.  It's the best way into the genre I've ever played.I Am an XCOM God, So This Can't Be So Different - Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha.  Oh.  Okay.  Seriou - ha ha ha ha ha.  Okay.  Got it together.  Some of what you know will transfer over here, but not as much as you think.  In particular, you might have trouble getting around the idea that cover doesn't really work the way you think it does and ranged weapons are silly.  A somewhat forgiving sort of perma-death is enabled, which is something you should be used to, but I wouldn't put this at the top of my list.  It's just not the same experience.  There's no other side to this game, either, and your ability to improve your units is a bit more conservative than what you're used to.  Levels make a difference in some cases, but not all, and there are a number of passive skills that you'll spend a long time never leveling.  The criticality of grabbing cards on the battlefield may also come as a little bit of a shock to the system, and the AI feels a lot crueler than what I remember (i.e. if you expose a unit that's important or vulnerable, this thing will chase it to the ends of the Earth until you can find a way to outdistance any pursuers).  Go in knowing that you are not very good at this game.  Again, I would actually start with Triangle Strategy - a simpler game that eases you into the mechanics.Look, I Play Fire Emblem All the Time - You're in a good spot to play this game and not hate your time, but it's harder than you want to think.  Unit weaknesses are less of an explicit thing and there is no real triangle of super murder that you can use to plan out your forces before the engagement.  The closest this thing has to a tutorial is a block of text that I am firmly convinced no human has ever read from back to front without falling asleep, so you're probably going to have to do a little trial-and-error to work out how things really operate.  There is a high potential for fun, though.  Do try.I've Played Previous Iterations - You're used to the difficulty.  That's good.  You need to pay some really, REALLY close attention to the things that have changed since you last checked in, though, because they're substantial.  You've got to be incredibly stingy with your funds until the one repeatable battleground opens, because there's no such thing as random encounters anymore, and some of your favorite units probably don't work the way that they used to.  For instance, my go-to was grabbing the high ground early and stacking it with three or four archers.  I found out that archers...well, they're not useless and they don't suck, but they're not what they were in the PSP version.  Unless you always played the game as a brawler with magic only acting as a supplement, you're going to be in for some changes.  That said, it is fundamentally the same game you remember.  Feel safe playing it.So, given all that, why the positive review?  It's the game it intends to be, it's the game that it's rebirthing, and it's a deep turn-based strategy experience in the Final Fantasy Tactics vein.  If that sounds appealing, this can be for you - just maybe take an intro course in Triangle Strategy before you try to bite into this.  The complete lack of any sort of difficulty adjustment means that you don't have an option for making a hard thing easier, and if you don't have an army with the right units to win a fight...welp, guess you're going back to an older save home slice, unless you've got the right class marks and a lot of time on your hands to do training battles (which reward ONLY experience - you're not getting any new cash to buy equipment or expendables).  You can't hire non-humans, so some of the race-exclusive classes aren't going to be available until you sweet talk a new lizard over.  There are enough changes to make it a fresh experience while only making it about 20% more irritating until you get all the way into the swing of things.

_childDocuments_.review: The PSP version of the game (back from 2011) was already really good and with this, unfortunately they made one step forward and two steps back.The level cap is too restrictive, and only 4 slots per unit for items, spells and skills respectively is also just not enough. This also completely stunts certain unique classes in this game, effectively decreasing the ways in which you can play the game. Random battles have been replaced with training battles but those don't allow for recruitment of units and they don't give you any drops. _childDocuments_.review: Wow I had no idea this was so good. Probably one of my new favorite RPGs of all time.I've been a huge FFT fan since I was a kid and this game's story is very thematically similar, but honestly way better. It's also much darker... To the point where it almost makes FFT look like a Disney movie.The story also has multiple different paths based on your decisions, and these are not minor deviations. While the overarching plot remains the same, each branching point leads to a completely separate arc where you fight on different sides of the conflict, recruit different characters and kill others, etc.Combat is more or less the same as FFT, but with no cross-class skills. I thought I would dislike that aspect but it actually makes the game much harder because you can't cheese everything with OP combinations. Changing classes is also easy and only requires money, so you can experiment without being locked into a single role. The story is also level-gated at certain points so you can't just overlevel to win, which I actually like. It more or less removes the tedious grind and keeps the game challenging throughout.As far as battles go, there's an interesting mechanic where powerful buffs spawn randomly across the map, which are game-changing and can stack up to 4 times. It sounds gimmicky but it's a great way to make encounters more dynamic and difficult because you can't just turtle... If you let the enemy get all the buffs, things tend to spiral out of control very quickly.My only gripes are that the menu, equipment and item screens leave a bit to be desired in terms of QoL features... And the fact that classes being generic leads to some being fairly terrible while others are overpowered. Valkyrie, for example, is one of the starting classes and probably the most powerful aside from the special ones, but there are other great classes that are better suited towards filling specific roles.
