_childDocuments_.review: Context: I am a big fan of the previous PSP release as well as its One Vision mod, but have not played the other editions (going back to the SNES). I like this version better and highly recommend it to those that like tactics.For players new to the series:This is reasonably well told and reasonably nuanced medieval tale of war and betrayal, with a surprising amount of choice in the story for what was originally a SNES game. The meat in the game is in tactical battles and even more than that the out-of-battles management of your team of misfits (outfitting, class-choices, skills and magic choices, etc.). I like how much depth there is to building your team, and how slow and methodical most battles play out (although as soon as there is a mod to tweak or blatantly turn off ally-AI I will install it immediately -- this game is very much a victim of the 'uncontrollable team-mates do stupid things' trope). For those that played previous versions, here are some things I really appreciate: + Per character levels instead of class levels+ Massively simplified skill system without loosing depth (at least at this point in the game), with more interesting choices to make+ Trajectory predictions for spells! (in the older games you couldn't see them and thus would often end up hitting own units)+ Japanese voice acting is great (was less of a fan of the English voice acting -- but I come with a bit of a weeb bias)-+ Your character levels are bounded by story progress -- personally I like this but for those that like grinding levels this might be less great (you can still grind skill levels).

_childDocuments_.review: On first playthrough it felt pretty great. Never played the original so this was a great callback and new experience compared to the old tactics games I loved like FFTA.Except the more I played, the more the cracks started to show.The gave is very prescriptive and restrictive. Sure you can make a team of anything, equip them with a variety of weapons! But you only get a couple of skill slots, a couple of spells, and you'll need passives which eat up room. Retraining people from one weapontype to another is a bit of a grind and don't forget the level caps!I love tactics games for the ability to approach a sort of puzzle in any way I saw fit... In this your solution is almost predetermined. It's not like "You HAVE to use this or you fail!" but a cleric is a cleric, a mage a mage, your choices on what you equip them with are not broad enough to feel like there are a variety of builds. Heaven forbid you aren't a solid gamer either, as the level caps mean there are a few brutal levels in store and no way to grind past them.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre: Reborn is...a complicated game.Tactics Ogre, the original, is itself a complicated game with a complicated history. Back in 1993, it was seen as an exceptionally inventive game and one of the progenitors of the strategy RPG genre. Problem is, it only initially released in Japan. There was a PS1 port that released internationally later, buuut it had the misfortune of coming out after Final Fantasy Tactics, a later and much more successful game that took many of its foundational blocks from it, and also looked more 3D in an age when everyone was chasing the 3D craze. It's no surprise then that it largely went overlooked.That said, the game, while enjoyable if you overlook several of its quirks, certainly shows its age today. The difficulty is all over the place, there's blatant balance problems with the classes, and the strategy tends to end up overtly favoring ranged damage over everything else, which really affects the depth of the game.The PSP remake, released in 2010, attempted to fix these issues...with limited success. More damning was that the developers of that port attempted to mash together it and FFT, without seemingly understanding what made either game work. The result was a very kludgy game that demanded a lot of obnoxious micromanagement, and, despite being considerably easier than the original, with some genuine quality of life enhancements, ultimately felt more irritating to play in almost every respect.Thankfully, Reborn is not the PSP remake.Instead, it's an attempt to fix many of the complaints of the PSP remake, and deliver an actually enjoyable modernization of the original game. In this at least it's commendable, and should deserve credit - it reverses several of the most egregious flaws of that remake, and adds some genuinely smooth quality of life on top of its already existent quality of life features.Unfortunately, it's still not fully there. There's still a lot of design bloat left from the PSP remake, and further, some of the design decisions taken in response to complaints about that remake feel like massive overcorrections. This is most notable in the HP and defense stats of units, where they have really bloated numbers and end up taking a lot of effort to kill, at least until you chain a bunch of super moves or use some very specific and very overpowered tools.Still, I can't be wholly negative. It's still Tactics Ogre, it retains a fair amount of the original's game's strengths, mainly its storytelling, flavor and engaging mechanics(despite the balance issues), and there are glimpses of a great game throughout. I just wish that it had realized its vision more completely.In short, this is a good SRPG, but one that should be bought cautiously. I mainly recommend it to hardcore SRPG fans and fans of the Ogre series of games. Everyone else should get it on a sale, and perhaps consult a few playthroughs before committing to the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: In my extremely biased opinion, a solid remake of one of the greatest games ever made.I've played through TO tons of times on the PSP remake and I was playing the SNES version until Reborn was announced and released. Tactics Ogre Reborn is a beautiful fusion of the two, along with clever and useful new additions to the gameplay that improve its quality of life and provide new elements to strategize around.Don't have the time to write out everything atm but maybe I can come back and edit it once I do.In the meantime I'll list things I like:-Equipment expanded beyond PSP version while limiting skills, spells, and consumable items like SNESMaybe a divisive one, this allows classes to focus in on their roles and gives a spotlight to some like Beastmaster with lobber. Was there a reason to learn every single spell possible in PSP when you were going to specialize in one element anyway? In my opinion not really. All the same, was there a reason taking an item had to block off one of your 4 equipment slots in SNES? No. I think this is a happy medium.-Augments, Anatomy, Strengthen, Truestrike, Trueflight, etc skills removed. Trimmed a lot of filler. Classes all feel useful and some seem to have received buffs (Berserker) to do better damage and have reasonable accuracy-Mass Crafting is a very welcome addition, especially on equipped items-Auto Restock for loadouts-Level Cap. Also very divisive from what I've seen, but I like that you can't overlevel and then make fights into total slogs when their equipment tiers increase beyond what you can purchase. Had a really nasty run in with that on PSP.Individual leveling is back but it's extremely easy to play catchup with the cap. Lets you try out very diverse team comps without sweating if someone helping them grind up will accidentally overlevel and ruin everything.

_childDocuments_.review: SE has never been good at remasters, remakes, or anything resembling the two. From completely changing storylines (ff7 remake) to not even being able to write a coherent storyline (Kingdom Hearts 1-3), to destroying the balance of a franchise through borderline insane combat systems (Final fantasy 8, and 13).They did all of the above here and its still fine just like the titles I mentioned.The card system, the level cap, the difficulty recruiting, etc are all annoying and the game is still somehow fun.Stop listening to the haters and give it a shot, and if you dont like it, they got emulators for a reason.

_childDocuments_.review: So, a lot of.... well... lazier people have been making commentary about the game, lets get some things straight. This is not the PSP game, it is not the OG. They have streamlined the system to make classes each fill their role and handle things based on itemization, innate passives, and using your skills to that advantage.Pros:-Your classes seem to matter so much more than before. Each class, whether it be unique to a character or generic, seems to matter how you build it. Element, items, skills you choose. You can have a knight that is specifically built to walk past their knights, and one to stop their knights. Every decision regarding class composition makes it so you can't really afford to run 4 of the same class with identical everything.-General enemy balancing. The game doesn't let you over level, and it doesn't let the enemy over level you. That is unless, of course, you don't make full use of the training system. I recall the old game beating the hell out of you if you didn't grind at certain points. I am thrilled I do not have to do that or can train up new units without wasting things. Train when you need to, bring up your weapon skills.-Cross classing isn't required to make efficient characters. You can make a character with a class and element, customize them to the weapon you want and play-style and never swap them. Yes people don't like this because they are used to min-maxxing in tactics games and making monsters. This limits the break point of classes making most (but not all) functional in their own right. Meditate is innate in most mage classes. No need to train for certain passives.-Grinding reduced. Oh my god if you played the PSP because of how LUCT and the classes and not the unit levels. I can't even explain. Just no more of this silliness. I'm 60+ hours in and thrilled at how the game is going without it.-NO CRAFTING FAILURE. Simple enough.Cons:-Clerics feel unfortunate still. I don't know, the healing just isn't there. I have played with testing stats and not a lot helps the healing too much. While the whole "field alchemy" behavior isn't needed and they keep you just out of death, you are sitting at hell's gates some fights because of the damage:healing ratio. AOE healing needs so much more.-Rock-Paper-Scissors. Armor, weapon types, magic, ranged, elements. It really could have been simplified but still feels too complicated. You can change elements if you really want to set things up a certain way, and have backup weapons that specialize the unit from what you see from a scouting session, but.... Archers shouldn't do 1 damage.... Ninjas shouldn't do 1 damage.... Sometimes its just very oppressive how it interacts.-Lack of randomness. I know people like and don't like the random encounters. I feel like they would be fun still. I do enjoy running across the map to do things, but miss the stress of a random fight. -Money. Early game its a hassle but late game not as much. Getting money is obnoxious up till a certain point. This is incredibly minor, but I needed to state the irritation it brings.I have written this with at least 5 glasses of wine in me. I enjoy this game. I love the improvements. I love that I can play it and stream it to friends in discord and share a smile with them. The voice acting.... barring one sister that's a healer.... is superb. Honestly, whoever was directing her should be fired. Its so bad, she sounds so out of place. And this game can now be shared with others who find the new, simpler system, complicated. And those that played the old game can keep their minds closed and stay bitter.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy Tactics fan here, this game is dreadfully boring.It's like someone said let's make a game out of the FFT beginner units and mages can only target one unit... and if there are any targets between the caster and the destination it will detonate on them instead of the intended target. So it's like having a cloth user that basically does the same thing as archers but it has to occasionally wait a turn to get MP where an archer doesn't. That's not to say the game is shallow- there are weapon skills that can be used by any class that use MP and you get one every 10 levels. There is a crafting system where you'll be looking back and forth between the copious menus comparing stats until you outfit everyone with +1 of the current generation of gear. There are branching paths to the story that you can explore, once you beat the game you can pick up the game at any of the many points provided in the 4 chapters. There are monster units that you can invite to your party and unique NPCs with special jobs you can acquire as well.But like I said earlier... boring. People will say this granddaddy of tactical role playing is the quintessential masterpiece of the genre. "The strategy found in this game is unmatched." Yeah nothing like standing around at one side of the map as the enemy army approaches throwing rocks into bushes in hopes of finding one of the 4 buffs that eventually litter the battlefield. Or perhaps it's the number of units you can use in battle, 12 instead of 5. No, in my opinion having more units taking more turns doesn't make this any more engaging. I suppose they just appreciate the bland "fairness" of each battle. Nothing flashy or extreme. Probably similar to how I can't enjoy games like Call of Duty because I've experienced older games with dynamic 3rd/1st person view not balanced around arcade-y respawn unblemished by knifing and game unbalancing kill streaks and level ups. True tactical squad based action as opposed to headless chicken battles with obscenity screaming 12 year olds. But I digress.There is light at the end of the tunnel. I'm 170 hours in and I've just finished the main story for the first time. That's probably quite a generous amount of time to complete it, but I didn't exploit the goth trick so I did a fair bit of money grinding. After you beat the game there is level sync for any new battles and you get to use late game skills and your late game party as you progress back through the other storyline paths. It's wonderful, the mages can not only cast in cross patterns and hit multiple units, but they can cast large area of effect spells 2 spaces away from center now too, completely breaking the game, and in my opinion making the game more enjoyable. I speak too much heresy I can hear the townsfolk picking up their torches and pitchforks. I still think this game is more similar to the game boy advance FFT titles, and for the record I like those games too.I'm looking forward to playing the paths with my now OP group and I hear there is extensive post game content that rivals the length of the main game itself so I'm hyped to play another couple hundred hours in this game. It's just a shame that many of the likable aspects come at the end of the game.I'm not saying fans of Final Fantasy Tactics wont like this game, but they should know what they're getting into before buying. It's long, repetitive, many of the character classes don't feel unique. The game doesn't really evolve into something more interesting until late/post game and I'm afraid that will turn many people away from ever finishing it. But if you're in for the long haul with plenty of time on your hands and you enjoy tactics games I'm sure you can find your way into liking this one.

_childDocuments_.review: a recommended buy BUT there is a caveat as it is essentially an improvement not a remake of the PSP port of Let Us Cling Together.++POSITIVES++-good voice acting-a rather simple but compelling story that does push the player forward-classes feel more powerful, useless classes such as dark knights, berserkers, and Valkyries are now powerful and capable of facing knights whereas in past versions these classes would struggle being in the front lines-removes  the bloat of grinding by letting the player essentially lvl up units through training battles-music has been remixed, very good-crafting is simple, easy, and enables units to play specific roles on the battlefield-faster turns and actions make the game so much more playable, i cannot imagine playing any other version simply because this feature makes battles so much faster-they made skill points grind much faster and only apply to the main weapon whereas in the past you would need to train both a weapon skill AND an element skill which made switching elements or weapons much more accessible -negative status magic such as poison cloud is still op as in past versions but now offensive magic is also no slouch, enabling mages to do more than using status magic and actually deal direct damage -archers are no longer the broken pls nerf class anymore, now they play a specific role rather than a sniper rifle that kills everybody on the map, allowing your other units to be more of an impact-There is a LOT of content that even after finishing the story there is even more endgame content where you can go through 100 floor dungeons, collect unique characters, and experience the main story though a different choices--NEGATIVES---there is only 4 skills per class, with one being the weapon skill it means that each class would most likely play in a certain path since there isn't a lot of skills per class now anyways-the level cap is sometimes... unfair. this might not seem that bad but units 2 or 3 levels above the level cap deals devastating damage to player units enabling one shots of your tanks-buff cards. i don't quite like it as getting 3 or 4 of the damage cards just make that unit a destroyer of worlds capable of one shotting their targets when they have enough mp to cast critical arts. -all bosses have buff cards on them at the start of battle. this means that they have 3 critical art usages that are BUFFED with damage cards and they will spam that critical art every turn meaning during certain stages they will just move around one shotting your units.-since its an old RPG, battles are quite long. Certain stages can last up to 30 minutes per fight even with the fast forward feature. Although its not a negative for certain people, playing this game in a long session can be tedious.-The game is very LONG like 40 hours++ long. The final dungeon itself would take 4 hours to complete due to the amount of battles and for people new to the genre it would feel slow Overall 8.5/10its a very good RPG that improves on the PSP version with every change they made, The only things that I do not like is that they did not add any more new content or new side dungeons or classes for a 60 dollar game so that if you prefer you could just get the PSP version and it would just be a more tedious but is technically the same story and experience.

_childDocuments_.review: If you haven't played the game since the PS1 version I would say this game is worth every penny. Massive amount more content verses the original predecessor. Can't say much in regards to the PSP remaster on that issue though. My one and only gripe with this version was the way the game manages the level cap. When forcing a level cap in this way leveling becomes more or less moot. I get the idea is to balance the encounters, but it's a shoddy way of doing it. The whole point of training and out gearing is to prepare better than your upcoming opponent.  So the forced level caps via "union level" strikes me as a somewhat dumb design. If you're willing to put in the time to grind out the xp and acquire materials to craft better gear you should be allowed its full use. Beyond the aforementioned this game has been an improvement in almost every way over the PS1 version. I give it a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: As I did not have access to the PSP version, I can't really compare to that, so my comments will be related to the PS1 version.In a nutshell, I'd say I found the game to be quite a bit easier than my first playthroughs of the original, but a lot more annoying. And that's considering in my very first playthrough, an enemy stole Aloser's revivify, so I went the whole game without.Pros:- The voice acting is quite good, though very wordy and I was often skipping dialog once I'd read it later on.- The new classes (compared to PS1) were fun, though I found the more free use of heals for example trivialized some early encounters, i.e. too many characters could heal in a pinch.- I played through the C route and the first CODA so far and I appreciate the new story additions.- The soundtrack is phenomenal, but it was that already, just improved in quality.- For those unfamiliar with the original, the depth of class, gear and squad customization are sure to be a big plus, but it was mostly what I expected as a player of the old one.Cons:- The buff cards. A thousand times the buff cards. Atrocious. They clutter the game screen, bosses are unfairly buffed later in the game by just coming with a full set of cards, and get some 2/3 cards on the right character and a whole battle becomes trivialized anyways.- Archers. What have you done to archers? Yes, I understand archers were very powerful in the original, but this goes too far in the other direction. The simple existence of equipment restrictions already makes it so you can't plop a bow on everyone so why nerf arrows so hard?- Level sync/cap. For using the wheel of time and doing the other timelines, I understand level syncing, but the constant level caps per chapter and the syncs toward the end of the game are just frustrating. A solid tactic in most RPGs has always been to go and overlevel if you're facing some difficulties and this just prevents that. It doesn't even prevent you from becoming overpowered anyways since you can farm permanent buffs easily later on, just takes a different kind of grinding than grinding for levels.- The chance of hitting attacks going for a more RNG feel with the activation of passives is kind of annoying and reduces the value of stats. No more AGI/DEX Haborym parrying everything but magic.- The fact that there are multiple levels of spells instead of simply scaling off your stats means you don't really feel like your character is becoming more powerful, you're simply buying better gear. The AoE range being dependent on the equipped spell level rather than your stats, or (what I hoped for) something you can choose before you cast also restricts your options.- Tankiness. Battles take far too long because of the availability of heals and generally bigger HP pools, even sped up, and the buff cards don't help. No one likes bullet sponges.Conclusion: The game is still fantastic. For anyone who hasn't played the original, I can easily recommend getting this for the fantastic story. The graphics are much nicer, and the spells look alright, though I prefer the pixel style of before rather than the current particles based effects.For those who have played the original (and maybe the PSP version) this is a much harder sell. This is basically not the same game, the gameplay changes are too big and, in my opinion, few of them are for the better.If you're new to Tactics Ogre, buy the game. If you aren't, buy it on (a deep) sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic update to a genre classic. The level cap is great because I'm pushed towards learning the mechanics and strategize instead of powering through with mindless grinding. But beware the final area: the Hanging Gardens is a marathon of battles, and the final fights can feel unfair if you are not insanely prepared. I still had fun with most of the battles I fought.The story is very engaging. I played the PSP remake "Let Us Cling Together" years ago, and thankfully Square Enix kept the same script but fully voice acted. A story of civil wars and opposing the rulers who pit clans against one another. It's easy to root for the protagonist fighting for peace, especially when the story choices let me nudge the characters to which decision I felt was right for the moment. It also affects who joins my party and who I fight, so this adds replay value to when I play the post-game. Or at least that's what I did in LUCT, I've yet to beat Reborn as of this review.Overall a great game that I highly recommend any fan of tactical RPGs to try at least once to appreciate.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun.  Until it wasn't.  In an effort to fix a few overpower issues in the psp version (which you didn't have to take advantage of), this version crosses over in the other direction and has the opposite problem. It reminds me of those many games that tout being feature rich with lots of depth, but you're forced to play only one or two ways.  It gets boring fast and inexplicably punishing if you try to go against that.  It's a shame, because all of the other aspects of the game are well done.

_childDocuments_.review: Not nearly worth the price. They took a pretty good game, cut most of the fun bits out, slapped on some pretty decent voice acting, ran it through a filter, added a level cap, and ♥♥♥♥ it on the floor. They then slapped an absurd price on a 4th generation port. Shameful.To be clear, this is the Final Fantasy Advanced 3 PSP version rework, with new gimmicky  mechanics like buff cards raining down, crafting, level cap, skill levels, and item levels. _childDocuments_.review: I hate that I don't love this game.  The class mechanics are shallow and uninteresting, the price is simply too high, and the cards that absolutely litter the maps are an annoyance.If you haven't played Fell Seal, give that a shot instead.  Character builds are much more interesting and the developers deserve the support._______Edit:  Additionally, this PC port doesn't utilize mouse and keyboard properly for menu navigation or in-game controls. _childDocuments_.review: I've played the SNES and PSP versions. This is the best iteration. Less grindy, a little more balanced (though some new classes are overpowered this time), and significantly more accessible due to a plethora of quality of life improvements. The simplified skill, spell, and item systems are intuitive and force impactful choices. Classes are more specialized, meaning you'll want to change your lineup around instead of just fielding archers and ninjas.And then there's the buff cards. Buff cards are a bit hit or miss. I don't really like or dislike them, they're just an extra mechanic thrown on top of the tactical layer. It's left some fights feeling better and some worse. I guess my main issue is that they're potent enough to eschew strategy and planning, which spits in the face of all the improvements we got to those in Reborn. It's a neat idea that needed a little more time in the oven.Overall, would highly recommend to fans of the game and the genre in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Gotta start with the one thing I dislike. The mouse controls for selecting tiles are horrid. Some tiles just can't be selected no matter what angle you set the camera to. Thankfully you can circumvent this using WASD, and it's a non-issue on controller, but I'm currently limited to mouse and keyboard at the time of writing and it's been a constant annoyance.Now onto the rest of what I have to say. This game is great. I never played the original game, but I had been craving some FFT and this is scratching that itch perfectly. Love the high quality spritework, the soundtrack is incredible, and the gameplay is exactly what I hoped it would be. Also quite shocked by how many branching story paths there are. I nabbed it on sale, but honestly I wouldn't have minded paying full price knowing what I know about the game now. It's solid, and is definitely worth playing.On a scale of 1-10, I'd give it a solid 8. Would be an easy 9 if it wasn't for the cursor bug when using mouse control.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I've never played older iterations of this game and can't comment on changes in this version, I have played a ton of FFT in the late 1990s. Since then, no other game has managed to reproduce a similar experience, except for Tactics Ogre. It's all here: great music and artwork, a story that's worth following with interesting characters, captivating fights and a bunch of engaging systems to play around with. Accessibility and configurability are absolutely up to 2022, however this game is probably best enjoyed with a gamepad.I can't say how it will play out in the late-game, but so far it has given me an experience I was searching for for over 20 years. Verdict: I'd recommend this game for most people who read through Steam reviews of it ;)

_childDocuments_.review: The good:  The Japanese voice acting is an all-star cast (I never thought Shirou from Fate/Stay Night would be my rival), this is the best official version of a TRPG/SRPG classic, the gameplay still holds up rather well and the story is more clear than FFT.The bad:  The job system in this one while very forgiving takes a long while to give you enough interesting options, and while the gameplay is solid it's just not as good as its younger brother FFT and there are lots of great, new old school TRPGs out right now that are slightly more engaging like Symphony of War, Brigandine, and Fell Seal.I'm still giving this a positive as revisiting a refurbished classic is totally worth it in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of turn based tactical games, I've definitely heard about this game since forever, having missed it in it's heyday. Almost bought a PSP in the wayback just for the remake, but couldn't bring myself to. Thankfully, there is now 'Reborn'. A handful of battles took nearly six hours, and while it's scratching the TBS itch for me, it just makes me want a Final Fantasy Tactics remake more than ever, as that game has been living rent free in my mind since I first played it. The depth of Tactics Ogre doesn't seem apparent in the first few battles, but the game takes off the training wheels pretty quickly. Difficulty feels about perfect, the story and music are better than I anticipated, and the graphics are about what you'd expect for a remake of a game that's older than most of Steam's userbase. The port feels good, too. No bugs so far, everything functions smoothly, there is definitely a lot of clicking involved, but that was to be expected. I'll probably give the controller a try, but glad that kb/m works just fine Very excited to continue my playthrough, and thrilled to have the grandpappy of one of my all time favorite games on PC.

_childDocuments_.review: 33 hours in and I am very bored and disappointed. All the new limitations they added from what I have read online (This is my first Tactics Ogre experience) lead me to believe that this game was very similar to FFT, which begs the question why the developers thought it was a good idea to take out the most fun aspects of that type of game and add in a level cap, limited skills and inventory space and no longer allow cross classing skills. (From what I have read all those things seem to have been removed)  The RNG buff pick up system and RNG stat cards that the enemy AI pick up half the time before you even get to your next characters turn is just awful, and the person that came up with that idea needs to be demoted as they have zero understanding on what fun game design is. All this to say, don't buy this game unless you love Tactics Ogre regardless of gameplay. As a strategy turn based game, this is one of the more poorly designed combat and class systems that I have seen. I was really looking forward to this game, now I don't know if I will ever bother trying to finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend, but there are things that I took away from my game play so far I think people so know before buying...1. As someone who enjoys SRPGs, I am really enjoying the classic combat. It seems a little TOO basic though. The amount of skills you can have is only 4, and that's for both active and passive abilities. Which is REALLY limiting when it comes to strategies. And the AI is super smart and VERY aggressive.2. The story is great! The fact that I can choose how I want to progress is nice for a game like this. It's usually very linear. 3. Back to combat, specifically the enemies combat tactics. In the beginning of the game it tells you something like 'go after one enemy at a time to make things easier' and it seems the enemy AI does the same too. I'm used to strategy games where combat is happening all over the battlefield. The AI has pin point focus. They will gang up on your characters and try to take them out one by one. And they will do so in the MOST efficient manner. Which drives me crazy when I have to redo a battle i just spent 15 minutes on, over and over, because the AI decided to target my VIP guest ONLY. Screw the fact they have 2 of my guys right in their face. They HAVE TO KILL THE GUEST! Oh and you can't revive the guest. 3. Oh and don't get over leveled! It ruins the fun! Oh wait, you can't! Now this actually pisses me off. They created story oriented level caps. Which means if you are struggling, you can't just grind some more and come back. NOPE! You better figure it out. To me it's just another way they found to artificially inflated the difficulty. Cuz another way is they start almost every battle where you have to climb a hill while ALSO being funneled. WHY? WHY EVERY TIME!? Just give me a flat field for ONCE!!! 4. The lack of weapons is rediculous. How are you gonna let me become a ninja, let me craft upgraded ninja weapons, but not give me access to the neccesary base weapons for the class. And this kept happening. And the fact that you have classes that won't get a new weapon for HOURS! So it makes exploring new classes risky in the early parts of the game. Basically this is how i feel. The game is a classic. And I'll play through it all. And i'm sure I'll enjoy it. But right now, I can only play 2-3 hours at a time because of all these other things. I'm gonna go make something to eat and come back to this...hopefully I won't be so frustrated. lol

_childDocuments_.review: A full and complete remake of the original psp version - better in literally every way shape and form. The best in class tactics style game. Story is complex and deep with intersecting characters, your decisions shape and form the world around you, voice acting (new) is superb, gone are the days of "leveling up classes" (the biggest flaw of the original), and incredibly deep strategy with unrivaled variety of how you accomplish your goals. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favorite games of all time, and that is primarily because the narrative and characters are fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: I never played the original Tactics Ogre but I played and loved FFTA and FFTA2. Compared to FFTA, the only thing I like more about this game is the overall theme and the story, which is quite mature and nuanced. I found may aspects of the gameplay frustrating and poorly balanced/executed. -Level cap/union level: I don't think there is anything fundamentally flawed about the idea, it's just the execution is terrible. It's baffling why I hit the level cap and didn't gain exp for 3-4 battles, and as soon as the level cap was lifted the next story battle had enemy 4-5 levels above me. This was not as bad early game but late game the level gap can be quite significant and the enemies did like 1.5x the damage my units did on average. And grinding for level is just super tedious with how long each battle in this game lasts, and how spongy the enemies feel.-Buff cards and auto skills: again, the idea is ok, but the execution is garbage. The buff is just too strong relative to your units' strength. Auto skills are mostly fine except for meditation, which is poorly balanced. In general both the buff cards and auto skills just add big layers of rng which make the gameplay annoying rather than fun.-Class/skill system: The skills are exclusive to class and not transferable when you switch class. It just kills any excitement of switching classes and building your units. Switching weapon is also not encouraged because each weapon has its exclusive weapon skill that takes quite a bit of effort to level up especially in late game. -Enemy/battle: The battles are not varied enough and often do not feel "fair". The backline enemy magic users always use mp item at the beginning of the battle so they can always cast the strongest spells or heals every turn. Meanwhile I could not do the same because mp items cannot be bought and I had to rely on rng-gated meditation. Enemy has more units, higher level/damage, uphill advantages and the map boss is often busted as well. So all battles just ended up being similar: try to hold the enemies and survive until the boss moves closer, then focus all units on the boss and kill him in 1-2 rounds. It's just boring. I really like tactical rpg and I was excited to try this game out after hearing good things about the original. However I was quite disappointed with the game except for the story. Overall, I would give this 6/10 and not recommend it unless you are a fan of the genre or if you love a good war theme/story.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the PSP version of this game 3 times over, I spent around 400hrs or more back then. I played this game for around 30hrs and realized it has been destroyed by simple but determining decisions. It is now a horrible game.The fact that random buff and debuff cards can randomly appear through the battlefield makes this a game of chance. Strategy has been thrown out of the window now and players are no longer rewarded for thinking out strategies and building a party with an attack plan in mind. A single enemy or enemy boss, that is already buffed, can single-handedly one or two shot your strongest units thanks to these buffs and you have to resort to debuffing enemies as much as possible and racing to the cards before enemies are able to get them. This alone is the absolute *worst decision* that has rendered this game nearly unplayable and a game of chance rather than strategy. This alone is enough reason to stop reading this review and just forget about this game.Want to read more? Okay.In the PSP version of the game, known as The Wheel of Fortune version, archers were OP and having two was enough to carry a player throughout the whole game. I'm not saying I'm happy they got nerfed but it was the only way to make way and justify the existance and usage of other classes. In the WoF (Wheel of Fortune) version grinding and obtaining items was a pain because you had to move from location to location hoping a battle would start and that enemies that drop what you wanted actually spawned and then that the enemy actually dropped what you wanted. Drop rate of items is now 100%, that helps a lot, but acquiring items has been made more difficult because now 'training battles' have taken the place of actually battles where you could earn loot. There is now a Level cap. It is not possible to grow stronger beyond the limits established by the developers. This in combination with enemy bosses who are buffed beyond belief makes grinding pointless and nearly impossible to deal with enemies. Grinding is part of an RPG, no matter which one, and it was taken from this game as if the developers wanted to smooth the experience so much that now removing part of the gameplay was the solution. The soundtrack is nice but it's nor better than the PSP version. The graphics look okay I guess. I prefer pixels but I won't debate the graphics of this game. Those are my biggest gripes with the 'crown jewel' of tactical rpgs. Thank you Square Enix, for ruining an already amazing game. You had the power to make it better and somehow managed to screwed it up, you had a winner here and this is not, by any means the definite version of this game. Play the PSP version instead. If you really want to play this game wait for a sale. If you enjoy it despite my criticism that is amazing. Try the game before you buy it if you can. Cheers.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, after a good amount of playing time, I can critique the game fairly.Positives:Great storyEngaging charactersCombat where positioning actually matters - you are not just fighting on flat ground, but multiple levelsChoices that really do matter - affects the story and who you can recruitMultiple paths - based on aboveAbility to change classes - but, there are negativesAbility to train your troops - meaning you can level you lower level characters or level skillsNegatives:Difficult to know what choice you should pick without a guideEnemies always have mana seeds or proc meditate (which regens mana)Hard to find codexes (you will need a guide to find them) - these are recipes for weapons, armor, etc. that basically +1 your weaponsHard to find class marks - change classesHard to find spellsMap bonuses are static - they never seem to play on subsequent play throughsSome classes are not as useful - I found archers pretty weak - and most map bonuses required one or a class you do not have a mark forScouting - you cannot place units - sometimes you'll forget to look for something and have to back and forthRemoving debuffs - you can only remove one at a time and in the order it was receivedWhen casting spells, you can make an enemy averse to the element type afterwards, but it is overwritten when another spell of another affinity is cast on themEnemies will have access to spells long before you - and they're always AOEDamage types seem inconsistent - Crushing dmg to an armored unit does massive damage with a hammer, but crushing dmg with a sword does not.Neutral:Caster specials are mostly close rangeChanging classes - if the class uses a different weapon and you have not leveled it, it will start at 1 - you should plan early or grind trainingChariot - the ability to go back in time to a past move (up to 10 I think) - makes the game much easierPro tipsDon't stand near ledges - you will insta die if you get knocked off - same for enemies (and you do not get loot) - you can't knock winged units off ledges...You do not have to clear maps of enemies - if enemies are too tough, just focus on the TargetYou do not have to revive your units before completing a mapGrind the forest if you need moneyAny move or action can/will affect the next unit; i.e. if an enemy is parrying you from all positions, you can go back using chariot to the unit before and literally move him somewhere else and your next unit may actually hit that unit.Try a no chariot runWhile it seems there's a lot of negatives, overall, I think the gameplay has aged very well.  It's still fun and engaging while providing a good challenge.  You can see a lot of systems have been used in other games.  Clearly, there are things that could be ironed out, but won't.  Hopefully there's a sequel that can.

_childDocuments_.review: Trying to encapsulate what this game means to me will be hard to do in a review, but I will try to convey my meaning.  Tactics Ogre: Reborn is a beautiful and faithful remake to a game that presents you with a story that does not always make you feel good.  It shows you how ugly war is.  How corrupting power can be.  How easy it could be to have noble intentions slip to awful acts, all in pursuit of your goals or ideals.  The grotesque nature of genocidal blood wars in a bid for power amidst a backdrop of a multitude of political machinations.This story was exceptionally formative to me in my youth when I encountered it on the first Playstation.  A choice you are presented with early on left me stunned that you can actually make and there is no voice of reason pulling you as the player back from what immediately is a gripping choice for branching paths.The mechanics of the game itself are likewise a masterclass of strategy RPG design.  This game truly laid the foundation upon which the genre as we know it today grew from.  Final Fantasy Tactics, a game I love and adore made by the same director no less, often gets the praise but you can see the bones truly being formed here.This remake is rather immaculate with a very faithful adaptation of the core game.  There are arguments for and against the game presenting level caps for your party, and while I did not really love feeling like I was wasting potential XP or feeling hampered in wanting to pursue growth in my character builds, I do recognize it tailors the experience so that you do not either trivialize the game nor hardlock yourself due to over-leveling.  I understand both sides of this coin and do not necessarily have much to put forth to the topic, but just for your consideration I would mention it.If you love strategy RPGs, I encourage you to go forward with this game immediately.  You can appreciate the mechanics the genre was built upon in this game that, to me at least, still do not feel too dated.And if you love rich narratives with twists, turns, and schemes, showcasing the best and worst of people, then I implore you to see this game through.  It may not always be a happy story, but it is one that will easily demand your attention.

Magic system, gear/equipment system, music and sound design, class options, class building and party composition, all not as good as a game that is many years before it. Story was okay, of what I saw. But that's because it is designed to be just like FFT. It's an okay game. But I think compared to other experiences in this genre it is under-baked and disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the PSP version ~10 years ago and didn't love it for strictly gameplay reasons, Tactics Ogre: Reborn fixed  all of my complaints with the PSP version. They did significantly scale back individual unit customization, but they also removed the hours and hours and hours of grinding that were required if you wanted to do anything other than cheese the game with a party full of archers and maybe ninjas. Levels are now tied to characters rather than classes, unique characters join at appropriate levels instead of always joining at level 1, and the lack of cross-class skill transfer means that you don't have to spend hours grinding in a bunch of random useless classes to get the skills you want on each character - they just always have the skills for their class at their level.The classes in general are also far more balanced (at least until postgame) - e.g. archers no longer dominate everything, and terror knights and dragoons are actually really useful in this version! Nearly every gameplay change they made seems to have been in the spirit of either reducing/eliminating grinding or improving balance.My one complaint they didn't address is that the optional dungeons are all still mind-numbingly tedious slogs. Phorampa Wildwood is at least good for recruiting, but Pirate's Graveyard, the 6 elemental temples, and especially the 100-floor Palace of the Dead are all mindless grinds for the AI to auto-battle through. You can completely ignore them if you're only interested in the main story, but the highest-level equipment and 75% of the postgame story are locked behind reaching the bottom of Palace of the Dead, which I think is unfortunate.The level cap seems to be the most controversial aspect of this remake. I'll just say that I felt the difficulty curve was very tight - there were some very tough battles, particularly in Chapter 3, but I was always able to get past them by changing up my team and/or my battle tactics. Most maps let you deploy 10-12 units so you have a lot of flexibility in how you compose your team and approach battles. This is a difficult game for sure but it never felt insurmountable. That said, if you're the type of player who prefers to spend an hour or two grinding levels when you encounter a difficult fight, you might want to stay away from this game because it doesn't let you do that.The aesthetic and QoL changes in Reborn are all great. I was iffy on the sprites at first, but on closer inspection they did touch them up instead of just lazily applying a smoothing filter. I still think they look pretty bad when zoomed in but they look good at the default zoom level. The voice acting is surprisingly good aside from a few characters whose voices don't fit very well, one of those being one of the main villains unfortunately. The streamlined crafting system (no more failure chance!) and the much-needed fast-forward toggle are extremely welcome.Overall, if you're the type of player who enjoys spending hours grinding and customizing individual units then you will probably prefer the PSP version, but in that case I'd actually recommend playing Final Fantasy Tactics instead because I feel it does a much better job at that style of gameplay. Tactics Ogre: Reborn is far more on the strategy & tactics side than the RPG side - your max power is strictly limited, so you have to figure out how best to work with the options that you have. The $50 price tag is a bit steep, but on sale at $40 or less I'd definitely recommend it if you enjoy turn-based strategy/tactics games.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original games, and I really wish I had. Especially the PSP one. I started rambling towards the end here, but TLDR is that I find the combat shallow and it really just makes me want to play Final fantasy Tactics again. This game feels like a slog.Full disclosure, I'm still in chapter 1, I just left my game open in the background by accident one day. I just beat the beastamer's gryphons. And despite owning this game for a week now, it just feels completely lackluster. The story is intriguing, but it's not enough to carry the fantasy-by-numbers combat that seems counter to every other TTRPG game I have ever played and have heavily adored. Reading the other reviews just makes me crave the original experience. I cherish customization and tactical decisions, the ability to build characters up and shape them how I want. To layer systems and classes and characters to create unique combinations that might not be meta or even all that terribly useful, but it was always fun. Screaming to the heavens and gaining enough power to solo the end-game boss as Darknight Ramza was some of the most fun I've had in a video game. Creating an intricate roster of characters who each fill their own niche in terms of gear and status and ability was just great, and I don't fault a game for being simpler than that, but replacing random encounters with training battles is just boring. Placing a level cap is just boring. Removing customization options is just boring. Individual leveling is moot, because everyone gets shared EXP anyways, which is boring.. Unbalanced gameplay is just fun, especially when you get enemy units that are equally unbalanced, because it means you never really know what to expect. 'Fixing' game balance by restricting the player is just boring. Worse than that though is that most the time I feel like combat is just two sides flailing sticks at each other, except sometimes someone randomly pulls out a handgun. Squishy units like archers are virtually useless, because they can only do any actual damage against other archers and squishier units- They do shave damage to mainstay units. Healers are seemingly only important if you're facing undead, because you can only finish off undead with a spell restricted to their class- Otherwise, you're better off with a knight with a generic healing spell, because they have more survivability. Maybe once I start fending off status ailments they will have more of a presence, but unless ailments are just thrown at you willy-nilly in lieu of strategic difficulty, one of the most iconic and mainsty units of any video game ever is delegated to a niche role. Mages are slightly more versatile, since they can actually do consistent damage to the enemy, but that damage thus far is still a quarter of what a good melee attack does (Or a sixth if I do a guaranteed critical hit skill, which is what I have room for most of the time), but really all they are good for is casting debuffs and ailments, which have a pathetic chance to hit even with an auto-skill that boosts hit chances. All you need is a bunch of knights to tank damage and heal, a bunch of warriors to hit with big numbers, whatever specific counter-unit you might want, and maybe a couple of bird people to take out enemy squishies faster than your normal melee units. Any deviation from that (early game) is a waste of a unit slot, because they're not going to be doing anything of value. A mage makes combat more interesting, but they're unreliable and a liability. A healer will take so much damage from enemy ranged attacks that they will spend more time healing themselves and each other than your attack units. I haven't recruited any monsters yet, but I find it difficult to believe they are going to be any different after fighting them- At best, they'll just do more DPS. Since spells are so simple and units can only ever hold four skills (Including their weapon proficiency), I just can't see any layers to this game. Positioning barely matters- Give a tether to your healers and don't abandon your units and you're g olden. Auto-skills are too inconsistent to be tactically relied upon, and these maps are small awkwardly spaced so you're just a mob of units anywaysAlso, the camera is really annoying. Either I'm overlooking the field and see no height differences, or I'm at an angle where units are constantly overlapping.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is about gameplay, not graphics or sound design or the new voicework. Unfortunately, this game is not worth buying as it currently stands. 1. The vaunted AI mentioned in reviews does not exist. The AI will rush into your units from a positional advantage without care or consideration. Once you realize that the AI also seeks to maximize damage with each individual attack, it becomes trivial to bait the AI into stupid moves again and again. Beast units have massive health pools and relatively low defenses, so the AI will singlemindedly pursue beast units with spells and arrows to the exclusion of almost anything else. The AI also seems determined to not focus fire your units to death and I suspect it's because they're coded to either 1)maximize damage, not damage as a percentage of the health left on their target or 2)not focus fire because the large number of units on the field at once naturally results in big chunks of enemies moving at the same time and players would get a bit upset if five enemies in a row ko'd their units without being able to do anything about it. 2. The game is balanced around long battles with large health pools and relatively small damage values. To add to this, battlefields spawn random buff tiles (cards) as the fight progresses which the AI barely pays attention to. This rewards units that can attack at range, because they can pick up cards and fight at the same time. It also encourages the player to charge the enemy since cards spawn around the middle of the field at the start of the fight. I suspect this is why most reviews mention tactical chokepoints and smart AI: almost every map has 1-3 chokepoints that consistently turn into a slog. If the player goes for the cards at the start of the fight, they will naturally end up in the chokepoints with enemy units which all feels very tactical until you realize it's just emergent behavior from a one-trick AI. As the battle progresses, the player picks up enough cards to turn the tide in their favor and kill one enemy at a time. Players can resurrect. Enemies cannot. 3. Units are boring. Each unit can be a single class and gets access to all that class' skills available at the unit's level instantly upon switching. What's worse is that each class has its own stat adjustments. Every class gets the same stat bonuses upon levelling up,  so a level 30 knight turned into a wizard will be exactly as good of a wizard as a level 30 wizard that started levelling at level 1. Special characters just get extra stat padding and a shorter recharge time for moving in combat. This means that there is no real investment in any class or sense of identity that grows with a character. 4. Classes are boring. Of each class' skills, most are either weapon skills (basically required, choose one based on what the unit is holding) or straight upgrades to previous ranks of the skill. There are four ranks to the meditate skill, each of which just provides a larger recharge to a character's MP pool. A character may select up to four skills. Until extreme lategame there is no way to access skills across classes, so every knight in the game will have access to the same skills, every archer will be the same, and every berserker will be the same. The most interesting classes in the game exist on lizardmen. Several classes are rendered obsolete as the game progresses. In the original game, wizards and warlocks had different roles. In this iteration of the game, warlocks are better wizards, necromancers are better warlocks, and liches are better necromancers. The only reason to pack a wizard once you gain access to better classes is if you want to recruit a lizardman (which, if you are still buying this game, you should). 5. Status effect magic has been utterly nerfed. Enemies do not purposefully inflict status effects. Enemies do damage, and if they have a skill or weapon or spell that happens to do damage and inflict status effects, then you might actually suffer from one. There is no AI for inflicting breach on your heavy armor guys. No AI for inflicting silence on your mages. Nothing. This is probably because the default % chance to inflict said status effects with spells is incredibly low, and the AI spamming useless status spells was a problem in the PSP version of this game. 6. The AI never gets better. Seriously. Lategame fights are exactly like early game fights, but now the enemy can make the same tactical decisions at greater range and for bigger numbers and the units you're fighting have higher stats. That's it. That's the progression. The. Fights. Don't. Change. I beat the game and made it to level 25 in the Palace of the Dead. There were no surprises, only occasional speed bumps when the AI was given a particularly nasty advantage (here's looking at you, chapter 3 Oz fight where Oz started with card buffs that allowed him to oneshot most units). 7. Random encounters were removed in favor of running the same dungeon maps over and over. God help you if you wanted a sense of place from Valeria and a reason to visit old maps and listen to thematic music in context while battling. If you want to recruit a lizardman before chapter 4, don't forget to pack a wizard into one of the story battles where lizardmen appear. 8. Clerics. Healing spells do not scale with unit stats. Clerics get a skill that randomly triggers at the start of their turn that allows the cleric to double their healing effectiveness with their next healing spell. They can also randomly charge their own MP by meditating. That's their only advantage over other, more durable classes at healing. Early game clerics are fine, because healing ~100 HP for a 400-600HP unit is fine. Late game clerics can heal 250 HP with late game healing spells for units that can have up to 4000HP. Healing items outclass clerics in every way in late game. Even exorcisms can be performed using a cheap consumable item bought in shops, so clerics function mainly as AI bait. There are more things that are bad or mediocre about gameplay, but these are the major points for me. I played this game with love for the first half hour or so, then skepticism for another few hours, then I finished it because I wanted to see what they did to my boy. Until modding tools exist for this game, I really, really, really don't think it's worth your time. Unless you like lizardmen. Those are still good and feel fun and unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Being a game from 1995, I doubt many people have played the original. So, for the first-timers; it is a fun turn-based strategy game, with a decent story, nice music, lots of classes, secrets, hidden dungeons, abilities, weapons, armors, accessories. If you're into turn-based strategy, this could keep you occupied for a good few hours. Though, is it worth the asking price? Mmm... frankly for a remake, they didn't do much remaking in this one, at least not the good kind. The world map is new and looks very nice, the stages look a bit sharper than before, although the character models could have been made to look much better than the blurry mess that they are. So, errr... unless you're REALLY dyin' for some turn-based strategy, you could certainly wait for the price to come down a bit.If, like me, you have played the original, you might wanna know how it is compared to the classic. So yeah, there certainly is some good, and in the typical Square Enix fashion for remakes, there is quite a bit of bad.I so hate it when game makers try to drag me through the game like I'm their dog on a leash, as if I'm too dumb to know how to have fun and they have to show me exactly how to do it. And why would you go out of your way to make it LESS user friendly? Why would you artificially limit it to reduce player options?My final rating: As just another TBS game, I would rate it 6/10, compared to the original though it is more like a 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: During the first 15-20 hours or so I would recommend this game, but getting deep into chapter 3 and well, some nagging things become pretty big nagging things. I'll bring up some positives too though. - The limited scale of the story is pretty great. The branching paths are alright too. The story is served up a bit thinly though, where a lot happens "between" scenes/chapters in a summary and then you spend an entire chapter chasing pirates and doing 20 random battles. - Maybe some "escort the dumb AI" style battle (or three) to try to recruit a special unit. These battles REALLY SUCK.- Character Artwork is fantastic, but clashes pretty heavily with the super-chibi style of the battle sprites. I would have preferred something closer to Vandal Hearts here.Now to the main nagging parts, the Gameplay.- Gameplay is fun at first, but gradually turns into a slog. There's also a ton of battles which don't advance the story. An entire chapter can be 90% "You bump into random group of enemies, a enemy knight you haven't encountered before calls you a cur. You slay him. The next commander will be angry about this".- The randomized buff cards that spawn can heavily tilt the battle. If the enemy gets a couple of +physical/crit cards and you don't... whelp. Later on the enemy will simply spawn already buffed by cards.- The battles by chapter 3 are very samey, you'll be in some disadvantaged terrain position (usually fighting up hill where the only units that can maneuver are flying units, and ranged units can attack anything you have) and the enemy will outnumber you with something like 2 healers, 2 spellcasters and 3-5 1000HP monsters in addition to fielding your number of normal troops. Later in the game the enemy will be spamming AoE attacks, combined with fighting up hill in cramped terrain.- The level-scaling means you'll always be fighting up hill here too, at best (after some grinding each time the level cap is raised) with even levels, and at worst the enemy will have some units that out level yours.- Enemy commanders will out level you and start the game with 4 buff cards, requiring you to have several of your troops to scratch them (remember those extra healers the enemy gets?). - Basically, the enemy will always out HP you and out-damage you, which in the more unfair battles (well, they're all some degree of unfair) means you'll have to focus fire the enemy commander to win before your force is demolished.- Or I dunno, you find some broken classes and field several of those instead of the "weak" classes. Yay.- Your gear matters in so far that you need specific gears that does things like stun or makes the enemy miss more attacks. Like levelling, "better" gear doesn't matter much.- The AI is heavily tilted to going after squishies in the rear (which they can easily hit with their archers for MASSIVE DAMAGE) + doing as much damage as possible. Better finish the battle before your downed guys die in 3 turns! (If you spend a units turn rezzing, the enemy will out damage you even more heavily). This AI focus can be exploited though.All of these combined means the game is "challenging" and "strategic", but the solution is always trying to find the one "exploit" you can push to your advantage. If you´re the kind of player that loves to endlessly kite a dumb AI, you'll probably love this game.Random nags:- The elemental system seems overly complex for the minimal impact it has. Only Light/Dark Magic has unique spells (well, and one later spell book type you don't have for a long time). The elemental magic like fire/water/stone/wind etc seeminly does no difference at all aside for the color of the spell. They all have the same spells (Single Target, AoE). I gather that this system has been changed from how it previously worked, but not for the better.- RNG dependence on proccing. For a game that has reduced the impact of the RPG aspects with a level cap, level scaling and gear stats, but there's instead a ton of RNG in the game. Aside for the randomly spawned cards that has huge impact on a units damage, all attacks have RNG to them - and the enemy can randomly block/parry attacks. Whelp I guess you lose this 1 hour battle because a couple of vital attacks came up snake eyes! Strategy!This gets even worse when the game has a big focus on "recruiting" enemies, but your chances of doing this is not well explained in the game at all. Basically, get as close as possible to the enremy (right next to them) and wound them down to minimal HP. Now maybe one of your units with the right recruit skill has a... 24% chance of recruiting them per turn. (This also means you can't have any friendly AI on while trying to do this).

_childDocuments_.review: I have been itching for a Tactics style rpg for a while, and there wasn't much that successfully scratched that itch. I enjoyed Triangle Strategy (played on Switch), but it wasn't what I was really looking for. Job system, elevation changes, equipment changes, and more that we loved about FF Tactics.Tactics Ogre: Reborn scratches that itch for me in spades.Tactics Ogre: Reborn is my first true Tactics Ogre game. I had the GBA game, but did not get very far, and was stupid and traded it in for... Something.  The only other Tactics Ogre game I played, wasn't even Tactics Ogre; it was Ogre Battle 64.  That was a game I loved dearly, as it was one of the first RPGs I played, and have great memories of playing with my friends and learning about how to play and where to go.  As a side note, I'd love a game like Ogre Battle 64 created in some capacity, whether it be a remaster or an indie title that is just clearly inspired by it.  Anyway, on to the game we're actually here to discuss...On my difficulty rating scale of "Baby's first X-COM (Mario+Rabbids)" to "X-COM: UFO Defense", I would put Tactics Ogre: Reborn 1 to 2 points shy of X-COM: UFO Defense.  The combat can be difficult at times, ranging from enemy leaders to be being pre-buffed and just nuking your 'weaker' targets, to standing near a ledge and the enemy just "happens" to crit you and knock you off, losing your character to the void (unless they have wings, which is neat).One thing that Tactics Ogre: Reborn has that FF Tactics and X-COM doesn't have, is the Chariot system; a built in system that allows you to rewind up to the start of the turn if something happened that you don't like.  Your wizard moved up to grab a magic buff and blast the enemy archer, only to be crit and killed by the terror knight a few spaces away? Well, you can back the turn up to the wizard's turn, and move him somewhere else instead, or move him up and quaff a potion instead.When I say grab a magic buff, I mean that on the battlefield, buff cards will spawn in. These cards allow you to boost your Physical Attack, Magic Attack, MP Restoration, or trigger your Auto-Skills more frequently.  You can carry up to 4 buffs at a time.  The enemy can also pick up these cards, which can make for a frustrating time, or clearly label who you need to focus fire on first (depending on how you look at it).  As mentioned earlier, some bosses will be pre-buffed at the start of the fight, making it clear that you're in for a rougher time.The job/class system is there, but not as in depth as FF Tactics.  Granted, this game was made before FF Tactics (and from a lot of the same devs who would go on to make FF Tactics from what I'm told), so the idea of keeping skills you learned from the job you were in was not there yet I guess.  You can switch classes at just about any time on the world map, and as long as you have a 'mark' available to do it. Some marks can be purchased at the store, some have to be found from enemy drops, or from particular dungeons. Which is another thing that this game has more of compared to FF Tactics; optional dungeons.My biggest complaint about Tactics Ogre: Reborn is the leveling system.  The game has a 'Union Level' which limits the max level your characters can level up to.  So if your Union Level is 20, you can only level up your party to a maximum of 20 until your Union Level increases, which is done by story progression. On the one hand, I understand why this system was put in.  It's to make sure you don't over-level for content.  However, the power gamers in us enjoy our power leveling, and breezing through content sometimes.  It just makes some fights more difficult when you are only at a particular cap, and the enemies you are up against (granted, this scenario the combat was optional) are at a higher level than you.  This leaves you having to try and make some smarter decisions in combat (which is great in a tactics game), but there is more of a feeling of "git gud" rather than "try and think of the best strategy and protect your weaker characters and send your tanks up" etc.  That particular fight I'm referring to just involved being nuked, even at max level at the time, and was just harder than I felt it needed to be.The last thing I want to mention that Tactics Ogre: Reborn has that FF Tactics didn't have (but Triangle Strategy did) is a branching story system. This is a game where your choices matter to a degree, and dramatically change your progress in the story, what characters you will encounter in combat, and who you will be able to recruit (unique characters). This was a refreshing change, and unexpected for me.  I know I just got done saying Triangle Strategy had this, but I went in to that game after playing the demo, and the game very early on tells you that this will be a game where you make choices.  I had not gotten that impression from Tactics Ogre: Reborn until the end of Chapter 1.At this point, I haven't finished the game yet, but still wanted to put my recommendation out there for others.  If you enjoy Tactics style games, you will LOVE Tactics Ogre: Reborn.  It's a challenging game at times, but it feels fresh and rewarding.  I can't recommend the game enough. Don't sleep on this.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great. I liked it a lot on the PSP. There are some major changes but mostly for the better. I'm not a huge fan of the random cards on the battlefield affecting gameplay so much, it doesn't feel good when they spawn for enemies but not for you. That's only happened to me in 2 out of 70+ battles though. The union level cap is poorly implemented. On one hand it makes sure the encounters stay difficult. On the other hand, you're always going to be underleveled to bosses and it makes some encounters much harder than they should be (won't go into it because of spoilers). Additionally, if you don't train up to your level cap then encounters become almost impossible, especially without card luck on the battlefield. This causes the additional issue of story encounters not feeling particularly rewarding because you don't level up or gain exp because you're already capped. Overall, I enjoy the game a lot. I think the streamlined improvements while annoying at times don't outweigh how good the game is. I'll probably play through a few times as this is one game that has always stuck out in my mind as fantastic. Story is great, gameplay is great, this is one of the rare gems that demonstrate that graphics don't dictate a good game (that being said the art style is also great)

_childDocuments_.review: I have started and stopped this game a few times over the years (I missed the PSP release) but I am an original-release-fan of Final Fantasy Tactics so this has been on the list for a long time. I was excited to see Reborn release on Steam but decided to wait because of the price they were asking for a remaster (Reborn) of a remaster (PSP version).I saw a lot of complaints in the comments about how they've removed grinding, the battle cards are terrible, etc etc. Here are my ~12hr impressions as a complete newcomer to Tactics Ogre, if not tactical RPGs.+ The voice acting and script are top-notch; same folks that did FF12 / War of the Lions from the looks of it. Shakespearean in a way that lends gravitas and drama in ways you'll remember.+ I have played the early game conservatively in that I establish a solid frontline and hold until the enemy units have gotten within reasonable range. That said, when cards start appearing on the map, I tend to wait to pursue them until the melee has started to avoid splitting my forces to get them and exposing my ranged units. Once that happens, it's super easy to pick them up during the flow of combat, rather than chasing them. I think they're a fun layer but you can ignore them entirely 12hrs in and do just fine. I like the cards.+ Chapter 1 is long, full of great foundational storytelling, and a shocking decision point at the end! As an FFT fan I ate this up, the similarities in exploring the grey morality of feudal society between the two games is frankly a lot more nuanced than other, modern games. For a game that hails from the mid-90's, it was  ahead in its storytelling.~ The impulse is to grind between story missions because that's how I've played FFT for ~25 years, but the "party level" system they use here to discourage it is not terrible. Essentially: story missions are level capped so you cannot out-grind them to trivialize the battles. In practice I don't mind it, but I understand the complaint. That said: without grinding, I am unclear on how I am supposed to tame with my beast master? Maybe that opens up in Chapter 2, but I just want to snag a monster pal for the crew.~ This is a personal preference but worth mentioning: the emphasis in character building in Reborn seems to be passive skill mixing and stat growth based on the classes you choose throughout the game. That's totally cool but it lacks (imo) some of the depth that FFT had once they let you mix in primary skills as well. I would prefer more but it's a "meh" thing, don't let it deter you, this came before FFT and likely inspired the evolution.- The full price for this game is far too high. I picked it up on sale and feel very good about the value so far, I'd recommend you do the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal remaster so far. First of all, the biggest plus for me: mouse support in a classic Tactics game is worth its weight in gold, and it is by no means phoned in - they really took every control style into account, to the point where I have not so much as touched the keyboard for anything but text entry, and fights just FLY by with accurate, fast mouse control. (I'm sure controller still works as well as it has in the past, though!)The sheer amount of voice acting is impressive, as well as high-quality with the occasional odd misstep (but never enough to mar it so far,) some of the QoL changes are intensely good (HP bars with element colors over each unit's head, yes please!) The levels are now back to per-unit instead of per-class (phew), the charm system is great and allows for flexibility, and the revamped skill system is SO amazing, with more abilities being set to auto-use or use alongside an attack, allowing for way faster combat than the original.I know the graphics are a contentious point, and while the upscaling is as rocky as most upscaling is, the texturing they apply on top makes the design choice look a little more deliberate. I wouldn't have wanted just upscale sprites from the SNES version, but it would have been wild to see the characters get re-sprited for HD. It's not a nitpick for me though, and for a remaster it's perfectly sensible. It doesn't get in the way of gameplay.I could not put it down despite needing to sleep, with all these changes (*especially* the mouse control, which again, cannot stress how good it is,) making it so easy to get into a "just one more battle" situation. A great remaster on a Quest classic - Final Fantasy Tactics Reborn next, please Square?

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre: Reborn is an amazing SRPG, this game is just as good if not better than FFT, and it is a clear inspiration for Final Fantasy Tactics, down to the setting and overall style.TO:R have three story paths, with different interactions and endings, all classes can have at least two weapon choices, most have more, which allow the player to explore and see how he will set up his army. All these factors make the game very replayable and every walkthrough will be unique, because all the customization and story interactions.Pros:In-depth mechanics and systems allow a very customizable experience for each player;Story is very compelling and make you push through to see the end;Almost all dialogs have voice over, which gives even more flair to the game;Presentation, sprite work, portraits, everything is beautiful and adds to the game themes;The songs are amazing, loved the orchestration, very epic.The few cons I have to point out are very minor: First the quantity of classes available is not that big and sometimes I think that you cannot access some of the classes depending on your story choices. Even with all customization, it would be good to have more unique classes to explore.I don't like the limitation on the number of skills you can choose, maybe a more open approach would benefit the players to try things, it is frustrating that the skill to recruit occupy a precious slot, when most of the time you won't be using it, but as soon as you take it out, you will see a new class or new beast to recruit, but don't have the skill with you. It is very annoying and limits how we build our classes.And the other problem is the difficult, this game can be crazy hard at times, and the card system always benefit the AI making it even harder and unfair. If the RGB is against you, you are ♥♥♥♥♥♥. The auto skill always trigger for the AI enemies, while your barbarian with 2 skill triggers and 2 attack plus will never trigger if you are surrounded by enemies and could inflict crazy damage on the AI. Also the stages were the AI can push your unit from ledges to permadeth are BS!This is a certified classic masterpiece, SRPG fans have to try this ASAP!
