_childDocuments_.review: People in the reviews don't understand this game.1. This is not Final Fantasy Tactics and it has a good reason for it.2. They barely removed any skills compared to the previous version and you will find most of those "lost" skills integrated into new skills or mechanics while certain broken mechanics were removed for a good reason. They also made things more challenging which i see as a welcome change. Things are also generally more viable and that is never a bad thing.3. You don't need to grind in this game, so why do i see people bring up grinding? Sure there's 40 weapon levels but in the endgame you get max level after like a couple battles if you really feel like you need to grind it out. In the previous version you had to level up a ton of different skills and some of them went up very slowly so there's actually a lot less grinding in this one.4. The reason you're struggling with doing damage is not because the game is bad, it's because you're not looking at what your equipment does or you don't understand it. The attack value in weapons is a base value which is used to penetrate your targets armor. It makes sense to do 1 damage against a person wearing heavy armor if you're firing an arrow at them. All the various boosts that you get in this game are applied to the damage you do AFTER you penetrate your targets armor. In order to do real damage to heavily armored targets you need to either use the right kind of weapon to attack them or make use of the new elemental system since now every character has an element that can be used to deal more damage OR you can simply apply a debuff to them since debuffs affect their defensive value directly. So yes this is not a game where you always win by rushing at your enemy and pressing attack. You have to understand how the game works and going through that process has been incredibly fun for me.5. You don't need to worry about those permanent stat gain cards or leveling your unit in a certain class to get the best possible stats. What you get from doing that isn't really going to make a difference if you're not playing well enough BUT if you really want to have a super powerful godlike unit, this game still allows it through those mechanics.6. The buff cards on the field are also not something you're required to make use of to beat the game, they're just there to make the battlefields more interesting and a way to make boss-characters stronger without directly cheating their stats.7. They removed random battles but you don't need random battles for anything because you can recruit units in the various long dungeons or simply go back in time to recruit a specific unit from any level in the postgame.In summary it's a game that requires you to think a little bit but as you understand more you can also make things that seemed underwhelming at first viable because you found a way to make use of them. The story is also integrated into the gameplay so it's easy to keep interested in it especially since you get to make choices that affect both the story and gameplay. As a remake it definitely feels like they remade the game completely as it's so different from all the original versions. It's not for everyone and it doesn't have to be but hopefully the enjoyers of games like FFT or fire emblem will not dismiss this because of the reviews since this might become one of your favorite rpgs if you just bother to look into it without wanting it to be a cheap remake. It's too easy to jump into conclusions when we live in a world filled with terrible "remakes" popping up each year. This is all so ironic too as the spirit of this game when it comes to the story and gameplay alike is that you will never truly win by jumping into conclusions and there will always be something you didn't consider.Update: Replying to comments and addressing things for people who are familiar with the originals: I don't think they took away anything so vital that it would ruin the game. I can't really think of anything important other than the rogue class myself. You can call it removal but I'd rather say that they moved a lot of stuff to a different place from the list of skills and changed a lot of them to better fit the new card system and the new skill/spell limits. Yes in my original review I didn't mention anything about the skill limit being reduced from 8 to 4. I think this change mostly just made the game easier to understand and when it comes to strategy I don't think anything was lost. You were going to use those extra 4 skill slots for things like strengthen or spellcraft either way and with the new scouting system moving around 8 skills before each encounter would probably be a little tedious (as it already feels tedious to setup units with the current system). And when it comes to spells, I simply can't understand why I would want to have access to more or all equipable spells as it would result in casters being a lot stronger than what they are supposed to be. This also makes each caster class more defined instead of them just being some kind of upgrades of each other so that a lategame class like the shaman can be a lot less useful in certain situations than your starting mage class because they don't have access to debuff spells but in return they hit super hard with their damaging spells.What else did they remove? They reworked the weird elemental system  into something that's always in play and I find this change very welcome as it adds another layer of strategy to the game especially through finishers and equipment bonuses even for non-spellcasters (but is still a little weird to get the hang of at first). They removed spell scrolls... yeah i probably dont have to mention why I see that as a good thing as well.And sure you can dislike these changes but we have to remember that steam reviews are black and white. Posting a negative review based on a subjective change is indistinguishable from saying "this game is trash don't even look at it" when it comes to statistics which is what everyone first sees when they open the store page of a game. I'm completely on the same page with you about playing your own favorite version, whatever you prefer and I myself would like to mess around more with things like One Vision in the future. But imo giving this game a negative review is also bad for the reputation of other versions of tactics ogre.And ofc the game is definitely not perfect there's still imbalances and some skills are pretty underwhelming compared to what they used to be (RIP Rampart shadows...). But imo this is better than what I've seen from literally any other game remake ever so I simply can't agree with calling it a bad remake.

_childDocuments_.review: While Final Fantasy Tactics was responsible to popularize SRPG genre in the West, in Japan, the genre was popularized by Fire Emblem and Tactics Ogre. Tactics Ogre has been long considered as one of the best SRPGs ever made, and it prompted Squaresoft to recruit the team behind Tactics Ogre and they released the masterpiece that was called Final Fantasy Tactics. When SRPGs became more popular in the western JRPG market, Atlus USA saw an opportunity to finally release the english version of Tactics Ogre and it filled the gap left by the absence of SRPG games after the release of Final Fantasy Tactics (the gap was not actually bad - 3 years after its original release on SNES). How these two games western release were released in the same year remained a mystery though.Visiting TO after playing FFT was an awkward experience because FFT allowed the players to customize each individual unit and overpower their characters by learning different job skills, however this feature was notably absent from the original TO, each character only allowed to equip three spells and one extra skill they got from the bonus dungeon. Battles were slow and felt less dynamic compared FFT, despite being enjoyable. You need to replay the games three times to get a full experience.In 2010, the game got a remake called Tactics Ogre: Let's Us Cling Together in the western market (TO: LUCT), which incorporated many elements from FFT while keeping the game's unique flavor. Levels are distributed based on class instead of individual units, and there are plenty of options to customize your characters. They also added a lot of anti-frustration features such as Chariot arcana to reverse the flow of battle (which used by Fire Emblem Three Houses), basically allowed you to save scum. Unlike the original release, you could experience the whole branching scenario without restarting a new game. There are a lot of improvement that showed the influence of FFT, for example, in the original SNES release, magic knight class "Valkyrie" was only available for female characters, in the TO LUCT, they allowed both genders to have this class (Rune Fencer for male characters). They also overhauled the english script, and made it closer to the ye olde english style used in FFT War of the Lions. There's some influence of George Martin's A song of ice and fire series and Game of Thrones (TV series) seen in the TO LUCT as the characters talk in flowery and poetic manner compared to the PSX english script.TO Reborn is a faithful remaster of TO LUCT. The main graphic doesn't look so different compared to the PSP release, but there have been additional features such as voice acting (English/Japanese), buff/debuff cards, more inventory items, individual units gain a level instead of class-based level, etc). One of the most interesting design choices is probably the way they overhaul the skill system. While TO LUCT seemed to incorporate FFT skill system, TO R seems to borrow elements from the modern Fire Emblem as it limits each character to pick 4 skills only in the battles. Previously on the PSP version, everyone could access the item bag as well. This seems a shout out to both modern Fire Emblem and the original TO. Whether this is a better design compared to TO LUCT remain to be seen. The game also introduced a level cap, which will prevent you from overeleveling and building god-like characters like you did in FFT or Fire Emblem games. This is not a bad thing as it will push the players to play more strategically. Story wise Tactics Ogre has a solid storytelling. It was inspired by the Yugoslavian war, ethno-religious wars, and some mix of Babylonian culture. The game features three branching scenarios with multiple outcomes and different endings. You will encounter  your ally as an enemy in one story branch and vice versa. It's one of the rare JRPGs where the main character is actually sliding into a morally grey area, because you need to do something morally ambiguous and paid the consequences later for the sake of achieving its goals. There are a lot of missable contents if you don't read Warren report regularly. Don't be hesitate to use a guide to recruit the characters.  In the music department, the songs were composed by Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata who gained a mainstream popularity for the soundtrack they composed for FFT. TO: R featured a remastered version of orchestrated songs featured on TO LUCT, and it's majestic and will get you pumped. The music from TO is one of the best, and actually one of the my favorite OSTs ever. I cannot believe my ears when they could actually make things are even better than the last time.A complaint from me is probably the party management UI. I find the overhaul makes the interface looks more complicated than it supposed to be and may intimidate new gamers to progress further as it looked cluttered. I just hope it's my bias because I already played the PSX and PSP version, and expected them to not change. Also, I also have a similar complaint from the original PSP remake. The game introduced so many status effects to the point it's  kinda... too many. I also didn't bother to use the Craft system since it seems unnecessarily complicated, and by the end game, you will get a lot of end-game equipment that are strong enough without being crafted anyway. Also, I am not sure why they keep sticking the Ogre Battle Episode VII because Tactics Ogre's popularity has surpassed Ogre Battle in the fandom. Tying Tactics Ogre with Ogre Battle is almost a self-parody, because the game's story never completed, and there are not so ,many overarching narratives between each of the game that has been released. Even Tactics Ogre Knight of Lodis which made a direct reference to Tactics Ogre in its ending has a weak tie with this game, and Yasumi Matsuno didn't seem to bother to retcon the events from KoL as the story was written by someone else. Final verdict: Tactics Ogre Reborn is a solid deluxe remaster of one of the best SRPGs ever made. The story is solid, battles can be brutally lengthy, and the gameplay is is easy to learn and addictive despite being too grindy at times. However, this game is definitely worth the full price. You will be lucky to finish this game in 100 hours though because there are three scenarios to finish, a bonus dungeon, multiple hidden characters, and 4 extra post-game scenarios that will keep you engaged for quite a while. While the tag episode VII seems to imply as if there's a prequel of this game and you need to play the other Ogre series, it's not the case because the story of the other games are not referred at all in this game.Additional note:After playing this game for a while (Chapter 3 Law). I could understand the frustration related to the level cap. Some battles in this game is extremely tough because the enemies now have a superior AoE magic before you. Once you hit a level cap, there are not so many things you can do other than grinding to increase your skills or piling up items. This makes the game much harder than the original SNES/PSX and the PSP version as you are forced to be very tactical when managing your battle resources. Some battles can last HOURS because they are hard,  and you don't want to have a perma-death.Update after 40 hours:They really want to rebalance the game huh? Ozma - the most powerful character you can get from the game nerfed down so hard. When she joined, she doesn't come with Rose Whip, and this can only be gotten from Coda 4 - which mean you need to go through the 115 floors of Palace of the dead. Isn't it kinda redundant? I am kinda disappointed with their decision to change the items loots.Update after 122 hours:Finally reached the 100th level of POTD. This is the worst part of my gaming life ever. Update after 228 hours:I think I am done with this game. What a blast!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best tactics game that has ever been made. It pains me deeply to give this version of it a bad review.Mind you that I have been playing the PSP version of this game for years, and that I will continue playing Reborn after this review. That is not the issue. I understand that a lot of people are angry at Reborn because it's not a port of Let us Cling Together - this is not the case, but it's still useful information in case that is the reason you're considering buying this: Again, it's not a port, just as the PSP version is not a port of the SNES one - it's a remake, with all that it entails. Every version of this game has its own strenghts and shortcomings, and I love it about them.In Reborn, specifically, what it entails is a full revamping of the system. Yes, some things have been fixed - like crafting, albeit I personally feel that the crafting system is now oversimplified and doesn't feel as rewarding as the old ones did. Ill luck, this - perhaps the next remake will fare better. It is the revamping of the combat system that makes me give it a negative vote. Leveling feels basic and unrewarding now, and the level cap makes it a much more basic experience that the continuously adjusting progression in LUTC. But the main issue is that the system feels unfair and unbalanced. Yes, I know - Tactics Ogre was never balanced. It felt fair, though. This version seems to expect that you know the game mechanics intimately, and that you'll be able to optimately adapt to specific problems. It artificially inflates difficulty by buffing certain targets in battle and making them way overtuned, to the point that if you do a quick google search about any given major fight you'll find there are a lot of people asking about it as if it is a nigh impossible challenge.Let me be clear: It's certainly not an impossible game, and everything can be overcome. Every class can be useful with the right gear and enough levels, but until you have those, it will feel like some classes are way underpowered and that you've made a mistake by leveling them. It will feel like you have made mistakes that can't be fixed without a lot of work (Training new characters, recruiting some beasts, grinding skill levels). This, in my opinion, is a mistake. The old versions were difficult, but they never made you feel punished for your choices, nor did they make you feel like you've hit a brick wall and you need to reasess your complete party strategy. They forced you to change strategies and find workarounds, which is sort of what a strategy game is about, if you ask me. This one expects you to grind until you outcheese the problems, and to abuse one single tactic - debuffs. Again, I love this game. And other than that, it's a great game: The story is great, the system is fun and engaging (Though, again, massively oversimplified from the other versions). It saddens me to leave a negative review, but it's what it is right now. Only buy this game if you are interested in Old-school games, this game goes directly opposite to the current generations game design, the game really brings out the tactical in TRPGs. The game is slow, repetitive but has an amazing story attached to it.Pros:1.Amazing story, with good decision trees and one can really feel the emotions when listening to character dialogues mid fights2. Good voice acting3. Good tactical game where you really have to think abt what action to take4.Fun animations for finishers and spells5. Some classes are amazingly designed like the dragoon and terror knight, where they really fit their nicheMiddle:1. The level cap: I like it as it provides a challenge as you have to think out of the box to deal with scenarios but at the same time I feel like it really makes you hate the game. Not all players who play the game are skilled at trpgs and making someone use the internet to find a way to win a fight is the worst thing a game can do. I feel like the level cap could have been made into a difficulty setting or an achievement. All in all cool concept but very badly executed2. The infinite money exploit, I know many will say its a cheese way to play the game but for me it streamlined so many of the issues of the game, now I dont need to be stressed abt using consumables and can upgrade items before next area. It really streamlines some of the grinding for items.Cons:1. The game-play is slow in every aspect, movement in restricted and most classes dont provide any advantage in movement(the only one I came across till now was ninja) , the turn meter wants me to kill myself as most fights you just want to get to your damage characters to finish off people. The AI is horrendous and as a result you have to manually control the whole squad which further adds to the boredom2. The UI is not user friendly except for the crafting section. 3. Most weapons/armour don't mean much, as they are just stat sticks( some have slight passives but they are very forgettable)4. You really do need more skills, you can play a beast tamer and most your skill slots are just beast empowerment5. Spell casters and healers are dependent on luck to actually do something on the first turn due to requiring meditate to proc, as a result many turns you are just skipping the turn.6. Training feels so pointless, most of the time I just put every one on auto and left my pc. The worst thing this game adopted from modern game design(AFK farm).7. While some classes have an identity some have none at all.8. Class skills and weapon finishers compete against one another too much , why waste mp on a 200 damage skill when you can spend it on a 300 damage dealing finisher9. The battle map is so hard to navigate, sometimes you just cant select some tiles and you have to change the camera view and then change it backAll in all not a good game for beginners and only fun for fans

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to review my favorite game of all time with an unbiased opinion. This is the first legitimate version of the game on PC which I've been waiting for ever since SE started remastering their old games and porting them to Steam.I can't believe reviews saying the game was not played by many people initially - the game was huge. Ignore bad reviewers.First off, the game is beautifully remastered. It stays true to the original graphics but can be played on ultra high resolutions without getting grainy.Voice acting is good.  It's not how I heard them in my head growing up - which is probably a good thing too.  I always imagined Canopus to a bit cooler though.The Lord class being the only one able to use skills learned from all classes (compared to the PSP version) really dumbs down the game, probably my biggest annoyance.  It was fun making custom builds.  Now you're stuck with cookie cutter builds for each class.I would not say this is the BEST iteration of Tactics Ogre, but I will say it takes nearly all of the best qualities of the old games.  There is very little "new" content added to the game, but there is a decent amount of "extra" removed (titles and skill customization as stated before).The game is the same game that I have loved since playing the SNES rom that had no translation, yet I still played it in Japanese. It's not perfect, and games like Final Fantasy Tactics grew off of it - but the nostalgia keeps it at the top of my list for now.

_childDocuments_.review: I used to have Tactics Ogre: Let us Cling Together on the PSP.  I enjoy Reborn still.  Great story with the characters and different story lines to diverge from, Law, Neutral, Chaos, and those alignments don't necessarily mean it's clear cut good, evil, either.  Characters on opposing factions may not be evil or totally wrong, and you can understand why they do what they do.  Lots of depth with different professions and team makeup to go with.The only negative thing that comes to mind is the terrible UI, at least for me playing on mouse and keyboard.  Clicking on tiles during battle is awful, you click on something but the game selects something else entirely.  This can be a major irritation during battle because I want an attack, item, or ability to be used specifically somewhere, I click, and the marker goes somewhere totally different.  This doesn't happen all the time, but it has arisen enough to make it an issue to raise in this review.  The character equipment and inventory system is a hindrance as it limits what you can see via small popup windows.  Trying to find out what abilities, status effects do is a pain because you have to go back to character information screens.Reborn is a good game, but the horrible UI prevents it from being great.

_childDocuments_.review: After having the extremely bland taste of "Triangle Strategy" left in my mouth, I was hesitant to give this game a go, as 1) I was feeling rather unenthusiastic about giving SquareEnix more money, especially just to play an "updated" older game, and 2) thinking that maybe tactic games weren't as fun as they used to be after everyone shouted from the rooftops that Triangle Strategy is actually a fun game and heavily considered maybe I was just doing the whole getting old thing and just had reached my RPG gamer shelf life and wasn't simply capable of enjoying things anymore.Well, after playing just a small bit of this game I can safely say now this game is incredible, not even a few hours in I'm fully convinced this game is a goldmine of tactical goodness.  I was pulled in right away with the story/characters and the gameplay is actually good.  This is everything a tactics game deserves to be and all the updates make the game absolutely worth your time and money.  My only complaint is that I wish they updated the pixel art, like the sprites and tiles a bit more, but honestly the everything else makes the game look nice and clean, even playing in 4k.  All the other art looks sharp, and the voice acting is actually pretty good.  Not 10/10 fantastic but at least not offensively terrible like some other freshly released tactics game that I refuse to mention again.If the price is truly that unappealing (which I can understand) then just wait for a sale, but I'd highly suggest not missing this game if you're a tactics fan of any kind.  Though if you're a big tactics fan, I can safely say even at full price it'd be hard to not enjoy this one.It's a bit sad that we have to play updated games from the 90s in order to actually enjoy RPGs in the 2020's, but here we are.  If you've felt like modern day RPGs lack a certain oomph to them, then playing this game will help remind you why.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but the game did not want to cooperate.Tactics Ogre: Reborn is a turn based strategy RPG that's a remake of the original Tactic Ogre, which came out all the way back in 1995. It's got similar bones and DNA as Final Fantasy Tactics and other games like it: grid based, direction characters are facing matters, elevation matters, positioning matters, and its got a top down isometric looking view. Before I start complaining and enter "whiny pedantic" mode, I'll go into the parts of the game that are good, and there are parts that are good. I actually really like the art used in the game, I needed to go through a play session or so to get used to the look of the sprites, which if you play on a larger resolution than the original like I did, can look like it's got some sort of smoothing filter on it, but everything else was pretty good, spell effects were serviceable and character dialog portraits looked nice. The music is great, with multiple combat tracks ranging from "Just a regular fight" to "IT'S ALL ON THE LINE". The story has a lot going on, both in terms of what happens, with a lot of political machinations happening out in the open and in the background for you to notice later, and with player reactivity, giving you three different routes through the game, so you know for sure that choices matter.  The voice acting also matches up, it didn't feel like anyone was phoning it in, and you can tell some people got really into their roles. Basic gameplay is easily understood, and you can tell what the game is looking for in terms of really digging into the system to get better at it. Now that the preamble is out of the way it's time to get into how it blows it.Now we get into the problems. One of the bigger ones right out in front is that the game is SLOW, to the point of tedium if you're not using the fast forward option. I tried switching back for the final battle because I wanted the real deal intended by developer experience and regretted it, its like swimming through molasses. The difficulty is all over the place, which is odd given that you're locked to a certain max level determined by how far along in the game you are so they should be able to plan and design encounters around that. There would be fights that would be slogs to get through, whether due to what you were up against or where you were fighting, and then there would be stuff that would be no problem to deal with and that just ended up being a chore to chew through. Training up new units is tedious, and while it's clear that you're intended to recruit a bunch of guys to spread out what classes you have covered so you can deal with different situations, how the game actually plays pushes you into sticking with one good team so you can invest stat increases and gear into one place and get the most benefit from it.There are skills that seem half baked and pointless, a whole recruitment mechanic that never mattered, I tried multiple times to recruit an enemy unit and the percent chance never went above a zero. How the game handles calculating stats means that a couple essentially serve no purpose, agility and avoidance governs accuracy and your ability to dodge attacks, and besides the occasional rare situation, most times no one's dodging anything, so unless you're willing to grind a specific item a LOT to make a tangible difference for one character, you can ignore them entirely. Sometimes the game would go "Hey you got a class mark" in a cut-scene and it would not appear in the inventory. The crafting system is somewhat tedious to work with, you can spend money to buy ingredients you don't have for things you want to make, but if you have the stuff to make those ingredients there's no way for the game to go "Hey you got that stuff, want to use it?" automatically, you have to go and make each batch of ingredients manually if you don't want to waste money. The game holds some stuff too close to its chest, there were whole classes I didn't know about until the end because they only show up in specific places or under specific circumstances, there's a special store that is RNG dependent and a super dungeon that you only find out about in game by checking out an otherwise completely unnecessary events recap page buried in the report tab. Nothing points you to it or tells you it might have cool stuff in there, so if you forget about the tutorial that mentions it once you're out of luck.Then there's what the remake specifically added: the cards. During a battle, floating cards spawn in around the map that have different effects: increasing physical or magical attack power, increasing MP generated per turn, increasing the chance for critical attacks, increasing the chance that passive skills will trigger, and a card that will remove these buffs from anyone who picks it up. On the surface this is fine, it's just supposed to be a little bonus that encourages you to stop at a specific tile to pick them up if you're nearby. The problems here are that the bonuses can become very significant if one character happens to pick up multiple of the same type, to the point where in some cases they can start killing things in one or two shots, and that the spawning of the cards is completely random. The enemy can get a bunch of bonuses for free before they even get to your guys and start at an even bigger advantage at no cost to them. There's no rhyme or reason to what spawns, so you can get a bunch of stuff that provides next to no benefit depending on what team you're running with. There's also no limit to what can spawn, so you can end the fight surrounded by a bunch of cards you don't care about which can look like of silly given the tone the game is going for.Like I said, I wanted to like this: I like RPGs, strategy stuff, and I'm not pushed away by things that are turn based. I did beat the game, but I was really pushing that car over the finish line at the end hoping it would be over so I could cross it off my backlog and jump to something else. In the end I give Tactics Ogre Reborn three old timey words out of five, it's a video game. If you like THIS specific type of video game, you might be better off looking elsewhere, unless you did all those other ones already and are jonesing for some more.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine Final Fantasy Tactics, but with extreme customization, yet incredibly harsh restrictions.  For instance, a mage in a different game is assign a class of magic (e.g. White, Black/ Healing, Offensive), and has access to an exhaustive list based on their level.  Here, you get a maximum of 4 spells, where your largest choice is element (as attacks in this game are element based).  I love that concept, however, you have to have extremely well planned out, restricted, and exact skills for each type of class you MIGHT bring into a fight.  income to cost ratio for items and shopping, at least in the beginning, does not constitute a good platform in which to jump from.AI for party members (ones you cannot control) is perilously dumb.  I had a warrior that just ran around healing itself with items until it just died, barely every causing damage.  Same for an AI controlled healer in the party.  Never healing or Exorcising incapacitated undead, just always running to ensure they are out of range.While I certainly enjoy complex games with versatile options, I do not think the amount of restrictions on each character contribute to a 'tactical' game, and more an engrossed punishment for any single slight mistake.  This game may have been translated (I expect it to be, considering the Developer), and the translations are... Odd at times.  A Basic Quality Assurance program would negate that.I will continue to play this game, as it's something I wanted to play, and I haven't truly given it an opportunity to shine.  However, if you are an individual who wanted the challenge, yet widely open options of Final Fantasy Tactics, I would not recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really do enjoy TRPG games but I think what makes them for me is the RPG side more than the tactical side. Ogre really leans on the T more than it does the RPG. There's so many fights, so many that are just another bunch of guys with a leader you need to kill with no context.This might be okay but because the game has a party XP cap I'm doing these fights and literally getting nothing out of them other than stress.There's no options to turn off character death (I just haven't got the patience for it) or anything like that either, so I'm ending up doing fight after fight after fight where a character falls down and I have to rush the boss to get it finished.The class system also doesn't seem to intermingle at all so I feel like I'm levelling as a Warrior for example but not actually getting anything from it other than changing to to something random and unrelated later in the game.A lot of the cool races/monsters are locked behind the recruit mechanic as well. The characters have a hidden stat called Loyalty. If you knock their health down enough you can use the Recruit ability (you have to have the right one too, one for humans, one for lizards, one for fae, one for monsters etc) to recruit them usually with about a 25% chance. I really don't wanna do this, it's a huge hassle trying to keep someone alive in a fight to do that with them.I also feel like it isn't super well documented. Why can my flying guy equip spells? Why do we only have 4 slots - three really because you need a weapon skill equipped - for our abilities, seriously cutting down what we can do? I dunno, there's no reason behind it. For everyone!If these things don't bother you and if you're in it for the fights then this is an ideal game for you, but for me it just feels like a fight simulator and I'm really not enjoying myself.

_childDocuments_.review: What a treat of a game!  I've been playing it non-stop since it came out.Just to be clear, I never played any earlier games in the series, nor Final Fantasy Tactics, so I am not comparing to anything, other than perhaps Triangle Strategy and Fell Seal.  (This is much better than those.)This is a game for people who enjoy the details, who like having to reflect on the various tools at your disposal.  Definitely not a "just level up and hit them with a big weapon" game.  In fact, although units do need to level up, that's not really what the game is about.  It's the array of skills that the (many) classes pick up along the way.  That, plus the equipment you find and craft.  And the interesting ways that these tools interact, offensively and defensively.  It's worth noting that almost all battles can be "scouted" ahead of time, meaning you can analyze in detail the makeup and specific skills of your upcoming opponents.I'd say I spend two thirds of my time in battle and one third of my time preparing for battle.Unlike Triangle Strategy, here the story does not require undue game time, but it is compelling, and your story decisions matter a lot.  Lots of very difficult choices to make, and sometimes there is no right answer, just degrees of painful.The difficulty level has caused some controversy.  I am not a highly skilled gamer, but I find it quite appropriate.  Early on, the game is very forgiving, and it adds the complexities only gradually.  They have done a great job of making battles look far more threatening than they really are, but as enemies add to their toolbox, you are expected to notice and adapt.  If you just go on trying to bull rush with big weapons and damage spells, well, that's on you.  This is definitely a strategy game, after all.If I have a complaint, it would be that the user interface sometimes gets in the way.  It can be difficult to separate friend from foe unless you turn on the color coded hit point bars, and then those hit point bars can make it difficult to click on individual units.  The camera angles often obscure important information, particularly elevation.  And for some inexplicable reason, the actual range of bows (unlike those of spells and crossbows) generally exceeds the indicated range.  However, you can experiment with your possible moves and see estimates of your attack damage and then revert and try something else -- which mitigates a lot of the incovenience.  And, whether it is the UI or the difficulty level bothering you, early in the game you get the ability to use something called the Chariot Tarot which allows you to back up several moves within the battle.  Thus, misclicks are not final, and, if you are so inclined, you can negate bad luck and blunders.The other possible complaint would be that not everything is documented.  There are details upon details, exceptions and complications galore.  Just to give one example, "fear" is probably the best status effect you can place on a threatening enemy.  So you examine the big bad boss, read his immunities over carefully and see that fear is not a listed immunity, so you do what is necessary to inflict a fear attack... and nothing happens. As far as I know, the game does not tell you this, but it turns out that bosses are immune to fear.  Usually.  A few are, but that is not documented either.  The game is riddled with this kind of stuff.Personally, I do not usually mind all that much.  Tactics Ogre is more like an adventure out in the world than it is like a board game, so it kind of makes sense that every conceivable eventuality isn't spelled out for you ahead of time.  But if this bothers you, that's what the game guides and walkthroughs are for.  :)In any case, this is the most fun I have had with a game in a long time, and I hope others enjoy it as much as I am.

_childDocuments_.review: This is among the greatest games in this genre and I'd dare say the greatest. I have put in thousands of hours collectively between the Playstation, PSP and this version on PC and this iteration is by far the best, having preserved the key features that worked in the previous versions and cut the bloat of the PSP version. Of all the versions of the game, this is by far the least "grindy," at least in the early and mid game. Grinding for levels is completely obviated by the Union Level system. Some mind find it annoying, and there are certain points about its implementation that indeed are (for example, the level cap raises after the completion of certain battles, and it never feels good when you get through a rough battle for which you receive no experience but then the level cap goes up), however it becomes irrelevant as soon as one completes the first run through a story route. Because this game was designed with multiple completions in mind with the WORLD system, players who dedicate themselves to this game will spend most of their playtime at either level 40, 45, or 50, where the element of grinding finally makes itself known through the crafting system requiring more and more obscure materials for better gear, and the post-game dungeons having randomly dropping loot that some players may wish to farm. The addition of stat-up cards is not a lot of players cup of tea but I found it quite interesting and rewarding. Yes many bosses begin with the benefit of 4 stat up cards right at the start of the fight but in the grand scheme of things this is generally manageable. The game has a steep learning curve, and the difficulty a player may experience depends entirely on his understanding of the game's systems to make effective use of the myriad of tools at their disposal. Players who prefer brute force playstyles where they simply overpower their enemy through sheer superior stats by overleveling or maximizing for superior equipment may find themselves frustrated, because for the most part this is not an option. Instead, the game demands you familiarize yourself with all of its status effects, with its classes, with their skills, and with the synergies that can be found between them. Archers lose effectiveness quickly in this version against heavily armored enemies (compared to the PS1 and PSP version where they are absolute beasts throughout the course of the game and only get better), however once one becomes aware of their utility for inflicting and helping inflict status effects, they maintain their value, especially when paired with the skill Eagle Eye and other ranged weapon users such as ninjas (with for example, a stun inflicting short bow and the skill envenom which adds the additional effect of poison to their next attack), suddenly the presence of an archer on the battlefield can turn the tide as enemies lose turns, actions, become silent, or and suffer damage over time all thanks to the archer making all ranged weapons hit and inflict effects with 100% accuracy to their allies. Every class in the game has its use, even if it is not immediately apparent, and the options for finessing every battle to achieve victory conditions without sustaining any losses are vast. All that to say, the game expects the player to put in the work, not through grinding, but through accumulating understanding of how various factors interact, and there are a lot of factors with a lot of interactions. So many, in fact, that even 2 years since release more and more are continuing to be discovered.The amount of "post-game" content is massive even compared to the base game, where completing one of the story routes may run 30 to 50 hours, and completing the two others may take an additional 30 - but going through the Coda chapters, Palace of the Dead, San Bronsa ruins, and so on, can take well past 100 hours. As for the story content, this is perhaps the true reason this game has continued to stick in the minds of many players including myself for the past 30 odd years. Tactics Ogre takes places in a high magic quasi-medieval world that it shares with the rest of the games in the Ogre Battle Saga (Ogre Battle: March of the Black Queen on the SNES, Ogre Battle 64 on Nintendo 64, Tactics Ogre: Knight of Lodis on the GBA), which despite its multitude of gods and magical creatures, is grounded in realistically nuanced political circumstances. The director/writer of Tactics Ogre went on to make a name for himself with Final Fantasy Tactics and Vagrant Story and for those familiar with the mood and plotting of those games, expect to find a story in the same voice. What separates Tactics Ogre from those games, and perhaps even the games in its  own series, is the diverging branching storyline (which while present in both Knight of Lodis, and OB64, is nowhere near as detailed or impactful), where the main character must choose his path at pivotal moments in the plot. The choices are significant, and lead to highly divergent experiences - (though it should be noted that all paths re-converge for a largely similar Chapter 4, there are still route differences and events in that chapter exclusive to different routes). The main character could bloody his hands following the orders of a corrupt regime, taking on the mantle of a lawful (evil? or perhaps lawful neutral) officer of a national liberation orders for whom the means are justified by the ends; alternatively he can assert his moral integrity in disobedience to his superiors, and take on the role of an outlaw hero, though perhaps from there he could reconcile with his former allies and return to the fold as well. The overall plot begins in an almost standard Fire Emblem manner however - you are a member of one of three clans, the Walister, which has been recently defeated and suppressed by its rival, the Galgastani, on a war-torn island, Valeria, which is geographically pivotal to the intercontinental trade of the world and thus under observation by the adjacent empires of Xenobia and Lodis - and you join a resistance to liberate your people and bring the tyrants who oppressed you to justice. But is the war you're fighting really what it seems? Are the heroes really the people they believe themselves to be? Where the game shines is in exploring the themes of human conflict and human motivations, and how such are influenced by the choices people make. While thematically and structurally similar to Final Fantasy Tactics, the story has a less personal, and more broad, approach to how its told (focusing on the Valeria conflict itself, rather than on the personal struggle of the main character as in FFT) and concerns itself less with occultic conspiracies and more with the immediate political conflicts, though the game never forgets the setting it is in, so demons and divine entities do play a not-insignificant role too.I cannot recommend this game enough, but with the caveat that it is for the type of gamer who has patience and an appreciation for complex mechanics and learning how to leverage them toward good results. If you are someone who prefers things to be a bit more simple and straightforward, you might find this game frustrating, and if you won't take the time to learn how things work you might find it rather unfair. You might appreciate the earliest iteration of the game on the SNES/PS1 for its more vanilla tactical gameplay which did go on to set the standard for the genre in its own generation a bit more, but be warned that the translation (though bless the people who made the English patch for the SNES) will unfortunately leave much to be desired, and you will miss out on some of the story content that was added or altered in the PSP version and reproduced in Reborn. TL;DR: Recommend, if you like complicated games with overwhelming number of options and realistic political plots in a high fantasy setting. Do not recommend if you are impatient with somewhat obtuse and not necessarily well explained systems.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is near and dear to my heart being one of the first games I've ever played on PlayStation. Since then, it's gone through a PSP iteration, and now, to my disbelief, a PC release! I never thought the day would come for me to see my favorite game of all time remade a  time for PC of all things.Tactics Ogre: Reborn is, first and foremost, a strategy RPG. You gather a group of units and form your army from scratch while playing through an epic tale of man vs morality. There are plenty of abilities, skills, spells, weapons, armor, and classes to choose from! Due to the chaotic nature of the game, no 2 runs will ever be alike. With the addition of some features, this further randomizes the gameplay and outcomes. In the end, it's the story and gameplay that really shine.If you are a newcomer, I highly recommend this game for it's complex and multi-ended story. There are plenty of options for you to choose from, whether it be classes or weapons. Battles will challenge you, though some can be quite frustrating. It's the kind of game that will take time for you to learn and master. Luckily, the game includes a feature where you can rewind turns and replay them from that specific point. You will no doubt enjoy the twists and turns the story has to offer, along with its musical score.At many points in the story, you will be given choices that will affect the outcome of your game. As you progress, you will find yourself wondering,  or  It does a great job at making you question your judgement, as well as test your ideals, beliefs, and morality. Luckily, when you complete your first playthrough, you will have the option to return to specific points in the story. That way, you are able to experience all the branching routes and learn their outcomes.For those who have played the other 2 versions, this game is worth it if you are looking for another fresh take on the game. To me, it seems to take a lot of the best features of the SNES/PS and PSP versions. They did, however, decide to introduce a few changes that left me scratching my head - most notably, the buff card system. They removed the Rogue class for the players and also reduced skill slots. Spells have been limited to 4 per unit, similar to the original. On top of that, you can no longer mix and match classes like you could in the PSP version or in Final Fantasy Tactics where you could learn a skill from one class and equip it on another.Regardless, Reborn is fresh breath of air with voice acting (a mix of great and not-so-great voices imo), improved quality of life features (looking at you, crafting), and a phenomenal instrumental track. Training has been reintroduced, and characters now level up individually with level caps according to where you are in the story. Classes can be changed on the fly using classmarks with weapon skills carrying over from one to the next if the class supports it. Spells and abilities have also been redone, simplifying and streamlining the gameplay to let you focus on the battle.Overall, it's a very solid tactical strategy RPG that sticks to its roots and focuses on what matters - the score, the gameplay, and the story.

_childDocuments_.review: READ THIS FIRST : I hit the character limit, so the rest of the review will be posted in a comment.TL;DR : It has some problems, and isn't a marked improvement over the PSP version. It's not worth 50€, but definitely worth 20€ on a sale.Tactics Ogre : Reborn is a remake of Tactics Ogre : Let us cling together (TO : LUCT for short) for PSP, which itself was a remake of Tactics Ogre : Let us cling together for SNES. Reborn follows the PSP remake much more closely than the SNES version, and so that is what I will be comparing it to.TO : LUCT is one of the great influential games of the TRPG genre, and was a spiritual predecessor to Final Fantasy Tactics (in fact, it was Square that asked for Matsuno to make a simplified version of TO : LUCT for the Final Fantasy franchise, and FFT was born.)The game offers a great variety of classes, enemies, ways to build your party and your characters, and extreme amounts of content. If you want to see everything the game has to offer, you have 200 hours ahead of you at least.The mechanics of the game are also extremely deep and detailed. You can recruit nearly every enemy unit, projectiles have trajectories and get interrupted by terrain or other units, every unit has a loyalty score which, if low enough, can make them leave your party, each map has an elemental alignment which you can influence, and which in turn influences your elemental damage, you can find buried treasure on certain tiles, you can burn away grass to reveal treasure, you can recruit beasts to auction for stat-boosting items, the list goes on and on and on. I cannot overstate the level of detail and polish that went into the mechanics of TO : LUCT. It is one of a kind.To top it all off, the game also comes with a great story, and an amazing localisation by Alexander O Smith (the localiser of FFT PSP and FF XII).To reiterate, Tactics Ogre : Let us Cling Together for PSP was an absolutely amazing game. It had a few issues, but it was still a masterpiece.Next, let's compare Reborn with the PSP version of LUCT. After all, you can play LUCT PSP for free using an emulator, on a lot of different devices. Should you pay 50€ for Reborn ? These are changes that I find are neither improvements or deteriorations. The player's opinion on these changes is largely going to depend on how they like to play the game, and what level of challenge they enjoy.And here's the list of thing in Reborn I consider degradations from the PSP version. Not all of these are dramatic, and none of them make the game unplayable, but they were all detrimental to my enjoyment in one way or another.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre was one of the first games I ever played as a kid, the first one with a story to tell clearly compared to Sonic.  I remember as a kid I had written down on paper what characters are in which route, what stats I need for the stronger classes and I played and loved the game for years. I played it off and on for over 20 years even after knowing the story by heart and all it's twists and turns. And now we have Reborn and I'm still playing it.Reborn...is an interesting rework. Names changed, mechanics added and removed. For the most part I would say that it's a good game but there had always been a very obnoxious aspect that I can't even remember if it's better or worse.Defender Missions...♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. So the AI isn't all knowing and knows how to most effectively utilize it's enemy units, but the AI Guests you have to save are either in such horrible situations it feels impossible to do, or you need to big brain bullcrap knowledge. Like 1 guy, he was in the middle of the Map and I could easily get to him, problem is with him all alone he decides NOT to use his ranged weapon and go towards my group for heals and support, no. He buries himself as deep into the enemy lines till he got pulverized by the decked out boss, mage, archer, and a fighter.Buff Cards, not a bad idea on paper. Encourages you to mobilize and maybe go out of your way to get the advantage. So why are they so bad? Well the game decided to not only restrict your level cap, but bosses later in the game enter the battle with a full deck of buffs ontop of being higher level! There's 1 boss fight with your leader 1v1 with someone with a full deck. Every turn they can do a powerful finisher that could potentially wipe out half your HP each turn. As if that wasn't bad enough, those Defender Missions? Some bosses have a full deck for that too! What moron decided they needed these many advantages? Especially the final boss!?The Chariot, basically a do over button that you can abuse and cheat to spam until you successfully recruit with that 30% chance, make sure the crit hits, or whatever. I guess it makes sense since we were able to save scum for tarot cards. But yeah, it's just a cheating mechanic. I use it a majority of times to abuse the recruit commands.The Chaos Frame feature: A very pointless feature in the original game that at most dictated a potential bad ending. This is something you cannot review or would know ANYTHING about until it's too late and you already finished the game. (This game has New Game+) It's basically something that says you're a bad person to this race cause you kept killing members of it, while a good person for having them suffer under your leadership. It was never a good mechanic but they kept it for some reason.All the same though, I do genuinely enjoy the game and would recommend it. The changes they made, make the game much more challenging, so I guess that's good.

_childDocuments_.review: Back in the 90s, when I was a kid, a friend lent me a copy of the original Tactics Ogre: Let us Cling Together and I immediately fell in love with it, but I felt so bad for not being able to finish the story (which I wasn’t understanding anyway). The gameplay, though, trapped me for countless hours with its huge party management and difficult tactical battles. Years later I played and finished , one of the best turn-based strategic RPGs in the history of gaming. What do these games have in common? They both come from the brilliant mind of Yasumi Matsuno, who later also created  and wrote the story for , before definitely leaving Square Enix. Undoubtedly, Tactics Ogre is and forever will be his masterpiece and this Reborn version is a chance for old and new players to experience this epic tale in its best form.The game features a political fantasy story, which sees you playing as the young Denam, whose village has been razed by the High Champion Lanselot Tartaros and his Dark Knights. Along with your sister Catiua and your friend Vyce, you will join the Walister resistance and fight against the Galgastani for the independence of your country. The story slowly unfolds through mature themes, deep dialogues and unexpected twists, while you are asked to take important choices that drastically change the events; these choices can be either Neutral, Lawful or Chaotic, which means there are three possible routes to follow that also affect cutscenes, battles, alliances and who can join or leave your party. This time all characters are fully voiced in English and Japanese, though the english voice acting can be underwhelming at times. The most defined characters are of course Denam, Catiua and Vyce, while all the secondary ones have very little screen time to shine, with few exceptions. Anyway, the narrative is completely faithful to the original and the replayability is huge thanks to the countless choices you can make during the campaign.Where Tactics Ogre Reborn changes drastically is in its mechanics. As a turn-based strategy, the gameplay basically consists in managing your own army and fighting through different chessboard maps. Before the battle, you can select your units and make a starting formation. Then, you can move your units during their turn and also make another action, such as attacking, using skills or spells (which both consume MP now) or items. If one of your units is defeated, you only have three turns to revive it or otherwise you will be permanently dead. Equipped weapons and skills are based on a class system, but you can change your characters’ classes anytime by using certain items and they still keep the same level. The character progression is now blocked by the party level cap, so it’s impossible to grind beyond the party level, which only increases by progressing with the story. This is a great improvement, as it makes every single battle difficult, intense and well-balanced. Skills and spells are learned naturally after leveling up, but they must be equipped and can only level up with use, which further encourages the implementation of different units and tactics. Random battles have been removed and now the only way to increase your characters’ levels is by simulating battles in the training camp. Another important change is the addition of Buff cards; these are special cards that appear randomly during battles and offer a variety of bonus effects, such as increased physical attacks, critical chance, MP refill and more.The AI have been seriously improved, providing challenging battles despite being on the same level and forcing you to carefully think where to place your units. Many battles require you to kill the commander of the enemy army, so sometimes it’s better to evaluate the best path to reach him rather than blindly attack everyone. I have seen enemies fully taking advantage of the terrain morphology, like positioning archers on the high ground, healing their allies, using skills, grabbing buff cards and surrounding my units. For those who will find combat too difficult, there is a brand new Chariot Tarot system, which is essentially a rewind function that allows you to move back to previous actions and try different ones with no penalty. Maybe you just made a mistake out of distraction and simply want to undo it or you want to avoid the death of one of your beloved characters, in any case this is a great way to retry the same battle without having to constantly load your save file. Speaking of time-saving options, there is also a fast-forward function, which doubles the speed of battle and proves to be really useful considering the slow character’s animations.Visually the game features a smoothing filter, high-res characters’ arts, modern in-game menus and everything you would expect from a proper remaster. The user interface is now more intuitive; every detail of the battle can be easily checked under few screens, every command can be issued with a few clicks and you can even activate the AI for all your units so you don’t have to touch a thing during battle. A small, but appreciated, addiction is the possibility to zoom in, zoom out and change the camera angle to a top-down view, which is really helpful during the more crowded moments when multiple units overlap on each other. Unfortunately, when the game zooms in during cutscenes, you can still see the blurred 2D sprites of characters, which probably needed more love too.Tactics Ogre: Reborn includes a long list of big and small improvements that bring new life to the original game. If you have already played the 2010 version on PSP, there are not enough reasons to replay this immediately, especially considering the high price. If you never tried Tactics Ogre though, this will be one of the best stories you will ever experience in a tactical RPG, with plenty of difficult choices and challenging battles that will constantly push you to reconsider your strategy. Seriously, don’t miss this masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Herewith a rambling collection of my thoughts:Recommended? Yes, massively!Price: Not overly excited about 40 to 50 dollars for a reboot, but I did note the logic in the Discussions section by folks relating how it's VERY competitively priced if we compare it to the cost of TO in the 90s and early 2000s, so fair enough really.If you LOVED FF: Tactics like I did (playing on the Advance back in the day), and struggling with modern ports, even some of the accomplished ones, this game REALLY scratches the itch, and even exceeds that game in my opinion, being as it is the OG from which the likes of FFT is derived! I will DEFO buy FFT: Reborn once that comes out too.With FF: Tactics there was a LOT of emphasis placed on the story and characters and set-pieces. But I'm more of a person who most of the time just wants to battle with my dudes. But the story is good enough, and even in parts AWESOME for hanging everything together and giving us a narrative hero's arc (sort of).And speaking of battles, my absolute favourite element of these games versus non-Square Enix titles (especially Western stuff), is the recruitment. And TO gets it spot on. I see cool beastie on the field, I WANT cool beastie beating stuff for me. So this is already just AWESOME from that point of view. Nothing turns me off a TBT game quicker than seeing "Can I recruit, can I charm" in the forums and the devs saying "Nope. Not something we wanted". In a fantasy world where money and magic talk, logically, I SHOULD be able to get my hands on something I've fought, or some beast like it, if I have the means. Zombie, Dragon, Ogre? MUCH nicer fighting for me. Something I LOVED in the Age of Wonders series. Nothing is more immersion-breaking for me in a strategy game than being limited to one faction's units to the exclusion of everything else. Booooring (but it's easier to develop games following that rule. I get it, especially for balancing etc. But this is a Single-player game, so, come on! Let me get shiny stuff for my team dagnammit!)The Job/Class thing: I loved the FFT side of things for trying out classes and progressing a build via multiple class stopping off points, so it's kind of a shame that we can't (for the most part), do something similar here. BUT: with the fact that you can have a MUCH larger roster of dudes, and bench certain guys, (including monsters and undead etc, SO COOL) I'm satisfied with this approach. After all, FFT can at times get a bit over the top and its easy to lose all sense in a spaghetti build, especially if you've got an army of dozens.Speaking of FFT and circling back to my first thought, I love the chariot element and replaying. FOMO is a thing, and this makes it easier to discover what might have been. All in all, a superb purchase which I've already managed to get up to 22 hours of fun from, even just in Chapter 2 so far. Now if Santa had just delivered me a Steam Deck for being a good-ish boy this year, I'd have had the perfect vehicle for TO:R but nooooooo, no Steam Deck. I got some frakkin' socks, t-shirts and other nonsense though. Who says Santa doesn't have a sense of cruel humour...

(cheers prick!) and your cleric (or cleric(s) if you're a sadist) are 100 yards back on a hillside playing with their cudgel while they await a meditate proc.At some point you will look for defensive options and realize everyone has, "resist charm" they can socket using 1/4 of their skill allotment (I've never seen charm myself 1/2 way through chapter 4 neutral) and you will think, didn't this game used to have actual customization/skills?I would not recommend this iteration to anyone due to the poor balance.

_childDocuments_.review: When it comes to Tactic RPGs, I had only ever played Disgaea before coming to Tactics Ogre - and even though Disgaea is a fun series, it doesn't hold a candle to this game here, not even close. :DTactics Ogre: Reborn just does everything right, at least in my opinion. Sure, the in-game pixel graphics are a bit dated at this point, but they did a great job making them look really nice on modern monitors. The character portraits and -artworks, the map, the background and the menues are simply beautiful. I'd only wish we had a way to look at the full character arts instead of just close-up portraits.The soundtrack is incredible and, having listened to the OST of older game versions out of curiousity, the new orchestral arrangement of each song just brings the most out it. The voice acting is top-notch and immersive, you can really hear that the voice actors were feeling it when playing their respective characters - and that doesn't only go for the Japanese audio, also the English voices are really well done and convincing.The gameplay is fun but also challenging. There are numerous different character classes and countless ways to equip and build each of them. There are so many things to take into account that can help or hinder you in your battles apart from the classes of characters that you bring: The weight of their equipment, the layout of the battlefield, the type of ground the characters are standing on, even the weather - it really never gets boring!A lot of the criticism with this version of the game that I saw both in reviews and on the forums are about some of the changes they made by implementing an overall level cap that steadily rises with your story progression, as well as there being some items that you cannot purchase in shops anymore.After a lot of research reading and watching comparisons of Reborn with previous versions of the game, it's pretty clear that these changes have been made to avoid being able to breeze through the main story of the game by mindlessly grinding levels and I have to say - even though I haven't played the older versions myself, I find these changes very welcome!Actually having to use every tool you're provided with, having to take into account all the ways that your classes, equipment and use of environmental factors may grant to the edge in battle, and utilising your tactics (e.g. actually using your head) is exactly what makes this game so fun and addictive. Also, from what I've gathered while trying to avoid any spoilers, there will be enough grinding in the extensive post-game content for the ones willing to do so. :DAs for the story, at the time of writing this review I'm only in Chapter 3, but it has already been an exciting and compelling journey up to this point and I can only imagine all the excitement, tragedy and betrayal that's yet to come. What I particularly like is that even the most seemingly unimportant head of a group of bounty hunters or leader of knights you fight on your journey gets their own little backstory ... just in case you didn't feel bad for besting them in battle.^^ The story also features lots of branching paths, which I imagine adds to the replay value quite a bit (not even taking into account the post-game content). I will yet edit this part when I've finished the story myself.But for now, I can wholeheartedly recommend Tactics Ogre: Reborn without a second thought.

_childDocuments_.review: It is understandable that the difficulty changes and the new card system can be frustrating at times. All in all, whether you're a new player or a veteran, this game still has a hundred hours worth of content to enjoy and deserves its title of crown jewel of tactical RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most played game in my Steam library because it offers a great challenge, but at the same time is not based on reflexes or is the kind of game where I have to wait to pause because I'm in the middle of an action-sequence. Having said that, this game is not for everyone. I enjoy it because I like tile based strategy games like FFT and the Tactics Ogre series. Having played the PS1 iteration of this game, I was pleasantly surprised by the difficulty spike. Although I admit that this difficulty is artificially created (bosses having 4 power up cards and level caps), it is also this 'unfair' difficulty that forces you to strategize more. However, I do admit that it would have been good if the developers had given players to turn cards and level caps off for players who prefer a different experience. After finishing the my first playthrough, I just finished Chapter 4 on my no incap, no chariot run and I'm having a blast. coffee potato guides on YouTube helped a lot because I'm finding niche uses and potential for classes that I hadn't used in my first run, like Faeries and undead, and makes gameplay slightly more varied than just 'get as many shamans as possible. Overall, a great game if you are into tile based strategy games. Difficulty is artificial but worth it for players who don't mind the extra challenge and it has tons of replay potential with world tarot or a brand new run.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved Final Fantasy Tactics (well over 2000 hours) and had Reborn recommended to me as comparable title, however I still found Tactics superior to :Reborn in several ways.(Note: I never played the previous tactics ogre, only the reborn version and I am aware the previous version has a lot of the things i disliked about Reborn)The game has some solid benefits and I will list each Pro and Con below: -  CHOICES MATTER! the story will adjust and go down an alternate path based on the choice so there is lots replay-ability - I enjoy the Rock, Paper, Scissors combat system or well PIERCING, CRUSHING, SLASHING and what armour / class counters each, however I found it was not explained overly well to the player and I had to search online for a more in-depth explanation of this, there are also character "Elements" where you have your standard Fire beats ice beats Earth which is explained however if the units are weak to one another I do not know, only found that they were weak/strong to that damage type - They balanced a lot of the classes to where you cant just run 3 archers 4 ninjas and absolutely wreck the game, (this is both a negative and positive to me, sometimes its fun to just absolutely roll through the game with certain builds) and feel the need to take a lot of different classes as each does its own version of damage (Piercing, crushing, slashing) sticking to a single class will get you absolutely rolled if you run into its counter - The addition to Craft and improve your gear is brilliant, it feels more open with equipment and you know your characters are going to get stronger when you see that "New items are now in stock at the shop" text appear - The AI makes the correct choice in almost every situation and will burst your healer or caster if they get too close - The overworld is similar to that of FFT where you move around the map from tile to tile, they removed the "Random battles" and instead added a "Training" option to the citys which allows you to farm up to level cap prior to a story engagement, I do like this change as it was annoying as hell to go from A-> Z and have to do 5 battles in a row, or running out of items and saving after every tile. - Its strange to see that a lot of classes can use magic, its neat because you dont need a healer to heal other units without the use of items, however they are limited to the weaker versions of the spells. - This has to be my favourite part of Tactics Ogre, Once you get level 10 in a weapon skill you unlock a skill that costs between 40-50 mana (based on the weapon) and feel extremely powerful, you unlock more and more as you level up and these skills hit HARD and are your main source of damage when you have the mana to spare. - I know some people enjoy this change as it removes the need to play other classes & potentially breaking the game, however it removes the "Tactics" feel, it is always fun mixing up class skills (ex. taking dual wield on Berserker would have been a blast) - This is an interesting addition however it feels not needed or maybe a select-able option? there have been several missions I found in the story where you are just at an extreme disadvantage (i.e Enemy has a castle and 8 archers and 3 mages, 2 knights and they have like 7 free turns to rain arrows down while you slowly move your warriors up and my archer couldn't shoot over the edge, on top of having a +1 level advantage on you) I also get that this is used to stop people from over-levelling the quest, but it feels limiting. - You are limited to Early / Mid-Late game classes as they are based on a Token system. you cannot farm classes early and are stuck to the basic classes for quite some time until you either kill that enemy in the battlefield or buy it in the shop. Unlike in tactics where you are able to learn Ninja / Samurai fairly early and begin mastering them. I am not a fan of being tied down to a single class for a majority of the game, however there is a sense of reward when you find a battle that has THAT class you want and you kill it and get the token - Some maps are copy and pasted but turned around, some maps have like 3-4 SINGLE PATHS meaning you can send like 4 characters one and are forced to split the party into opposite sides of the map or just skip skip skip until the enemy gets close :(  - Your characters are able to take 4 skills, however I have found that you NEED to take your characters weapon skill otherwise they do 1 damage with everything, so realistically you are limited to 3 skills, which I have not run into any issues with it yet, but I can see myself running into issues later (Currently my Berserker has Sanguine Strike (Mandatory), Fist weapon, Berserk) I found all of these are mandatory for my character to even be useful, So i only have 1 skill slot that is flexible, also they dont have a list of skills or anything ANYWHERE IN THE GAME, you need to either level up your character and just hope you get something new, or just look up an old skill guide from the previous version. surprised in a reborn game from 20+ years ago you couldnt add this in as a list somewhere? If this game ever goes on sale below the over priced AAA title price I would recommend picking it up, however its very very difficult to recommend this game at full price as I do believe it would be better to just emulate the old version as its vastly superior to :Reborn in just about every single way and its a lot cheaperAll in all I think this is still an enjoyable product and I would give it an honest rating of 6.5/10, if they added a CLASSIC & REBORN mode where you can play the old combat, class & Levelling system on the updated engine + story that would honestly make this a 10/10 but the changes to the Cross class skill + Level cap dropped it down a few ratings in my books, and the fact that you feel forced to rush the boss down rather than full clear the battlefield to get new classes & items, and some maps just feel unfair to the player.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactics Ogre Reborn is a classic in every sense of the word, a strategy RPG that some may argue is the best srpg ever made, my opinion this rings true, I had the original version on the PlayStation and wow what a game it was then, this game is revitalized every aspect of the game and made it more intuitive, and they have done an amazing job with the developer that actually made the game supervising the whole production, it really shows and shines in this game, strategy RPG lovers rejoice this is a masterpiece. And the only game that even can get near it is Final Fantasy Tactics, and this is always been my favorite and still is to this day, I'm very excited about this game, everything about it is amazing, it tells an awesome story and now has voice acting which is done magnificent, and the musical score is a thing of genius and the game overall is 100% worth the price tag, this is one game if you're an srpg fan that you must buy, excellent job on this game and I highly recommend it. After 40 hours playing I'm even more impressed, the game has a level cap so you really don't have to grind a whole lot, I found myself just leveling up my weapons and stuff is really the only reason you would want to grind at all, but you can pretty much find items in game you can find charms to up your experience or up your swords and various other things then you got Chariot cards which can rewind, honestly I don't see any reason to rewind because it has a canceled move, so you can move and get an idea where you're at in the game, but if you move and then perform an action then you can't cancel out and that be the only time a chariot card would be needed, I will say the level cap is the one part I wish they would have left alone cause with it it makes the game harder then it should be, I completed chapter 1 relatively easy the game can get hard, but if you can level up your weapons and then you don't have to worry about too much, strategy does play a big part of it, I recommend two archers in your party cuz they seem to be overpowered at the time being and can be very effective long as you protect them and keep them in the back line, I really think they did a great job on this game and I can't recommend it enough.9.5/10
